# Patrologia Latina, volume 14 — English translation

*Patrologia Latina*, Vol. 14

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library … of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III … FIRST SERIES.*

**VOLUME XIV OF PATROLOGY: ST. AMBROSE**

**FIRST PART OF THE FIRST VOLUME**

Published by the editor, in the street called d’Amboise, near the gate called, in French, d’Enfer, in the village of Petit-Montrouge. 1845.

Volume front matter

Series title page

**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, ENTIRE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE DOWN TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION EXTANT THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, ACCORDING TO THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, COMPARED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES, AND MOST DILIGENTLY CORRECTED; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED WITH ALL WORKS DISCOVERED after THE MOST EXTENSIVE EDITIONS COMPLETED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; FURNISHED WITH PARTICULAR ANALYTICAL INDICES FOLLOWING EACH VOLUME OR EACH AUTHOR OF SOME IMPORTANCE; PROVIDED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY ARRANGED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND ALSO WITH HEADINGS DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF THE INDIVIDUAL PAGES AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT MATTER CONTAINED THEREIN; AUGMENTED WITH WORKS BOTH DOUBTFUL AND APOCRYPHAL, PROVIDED THAT THEY POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY IN RELATION TO ECCLESIASTICAL TRADITION; ENRICHED WITH TWO COPIOUS GENERAL INDICES: THE FIRST, NAMELY, AN INDEX OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH WHATEVER EACH Father wrote on any topic may be seen at a glance; THE OTHER, AN INDEX OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY READILY LEARN WHICH FATHERS COMMENTED ON THE SEVERAL SCRIPTURAL TEXTS OF EACH BOOK, AND IN WHAT PLACES IN THEIR WORKS. A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, EASILY TO BE PREFERRED TO ALL OTHERS, IF ONE CONSIDERS: THE CLEARNESS OF THE TYPE, THE QUALITY OF THE PAPER, THE INTEGRITY OF THE TEXT, THE THOROUGHNESS OF THE CORRECTION, BOTH THE VARIETY AND THE NUMBER OF THE REPRINTED WORKS, THE HIGHLY CONVENIENT FORMAT OF THE VOLUMES, CONSTANTLY UNIFORM THROUGHOUT THE COURSE OF THE WHOLE WORK, THE LOW PRICE, AND ABOVE ALL THAT ONE, METHODICAL, AND CHRONOLOGICAL COLLECTION OF SIX HUNDRED FRAGMENTS AND SHORT WORKS HITHERTO SCATTERED HERE AND THERE, BUT NOW FOR THE FIRST TIME GATHERED TOGETHER IN OUR LIBRARY FROM WORKS BELONGING TO EVERY AGE, PLACE, LANGUAGE, AND FORM.**

**FIRST SERIES, IN WHICH APPEAR THE FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND WRITERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH FROM TERTULLIAN TO GREGORY THE GREAT.** Edited by J.-P. Migne, editor of Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

**VOLUME XIV OF PATROLOGY**

**ST. AMBROSE**

**FIRST PART OF THE FIRST VOLUME**

Published by the editor, in the street called d’Amboise, near the gate called, in French, d’Enfer, in the village of Petit-Montrouge. 1845.

**THE COMPLETE WORKS OF ST. AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN**

An edition more complete than all others and capable of serving as their model; revised and corrected from Vatican, French, Belgian, and other manuscript codices, as well as from earlier editions, but especially from the Benedictine edition; continually illustrated with notes and variant readings placed beneath the text; further enriched with various short works which the learned Benedictines either omitted or did not even mention.

[Col. 0009]

**DEDICATORY LETTER**

[Col. 0009A] To the most illustrious prince of the Church, the Lord Francis de Harlay, Archbishop of Paris, Commander of the royal orders, Duke and Peer of France, Provost of the Sorbonne and Navarre, etc.

Having completed, as accurately as we could, what you seemed to expect from us in preparing this edition of Ambrose’s works, most illustrious Prince of the Church, only one thing remained to crown the undertaking: that we should adorn the front of the work with the splendor of some most distinguished name, by whose light the whole work might be illumined, and that we should secure a patron who, by his kindness, would be willing, and by his authority would be able, to ward off the force and attack of detractors. You immediately presented yourself to us as one in whom all things capable of contributing either to security or to ornament shine forth with wondrous brilliance; and in whom no other person could be found more eminent in glory, weightier in authority, or—what especially drew us—more gracious in kindness.

For it would have been easy to trace here the dignity of the Harlay family back to the remotest antiquity: a family long joined by affinity and blood to the greatest princes of Europe, and always fertile in eminent men, whose virtue shone marvelously in the highest offices of Church and State. But you, having gathered into yourself the ornaments of all and being the chief glory of your family, rather shed your own splendor upon others than receive from elsewhere anything of dignity or greatness.

Here lies open a vast and boundless field for expatiating upon the praises of an exalted, subtle, keen intellect: acute in invention, mature in judgment, ready in exposition, strong and enduring in memory—gifts divinely granted to you, that you might be equal to every great undertaking to which the favorable Providence governing the French destined you. Here too is an excellent occasion for proclaiming your distinguished learning and knowledge: nothing in history is unknown to you, nothing in doctrine too difficult, nothing in law doubtful or ambiguous, nothing obscure in facts; nothing escapes or deceives you.

Yet the renowned fame of your deeds, most illustrious prelate, shines far more brightly. Your own Rouen saw you long ago, from the very first years in which you happily and auspiciously entered upon the sacred dignity of bishop and primate, appointed successor to your uncle, a man who deserved immortality of memory by his piety, learning, and pastoral labor. It saw how, in your public sermons and private conversations, with what ready and happily extemporaneous eloquence you instilled all that was holiest into your hearers, brought forth the most hidden things, illuminated the darkest, and unfolded the most intricate no less learnedly than clearly. Your own Paris heard you; the great crowds of visitors converging there heard you; we too heard you and were profoundly astonished when, in the most learned public disputations held in your residence concerning morals, faith, and discipline, you displayed such prudence in avoiding the two rocks upon which nearly everyone else is wrecked—excessive severity and too lax indulgence—and so tempered the weight of the matters and force of your speech with the charm of eloquence that truth, received by attentive ears, won the assent of all, and no one, however obstinate, could or wished to resist it.

To these sources of your glory there is added a new, fuller, and brighter stream of light: in the most august assemblies of the Gallican clergy, when, by the common wish of all, you customarily presided over the gatherings of mitred Fathers and others selected from the entire realm, you showed such zeal in providing for the Church and religion, and arranged matters to be considered with such wise skill, that no one can fail to understand that nowhere have sovereign power and priesthood worked together in happier harmony than under you as president of the priesthood and Louis the Great as ruler of the realm. Indeed, the great Harlay, president of the clergy, was due to the greatest of kings; and to the great Harlay, president of the clergy, Louis was due—let no envy attach to the expression. Both belong to the shared happiness and glory alike of priesthood and empire.

As these qualities are distinctive and rare grounds for praise, so they are supreme ones. Nothing more glorious can happen for the praise and recommendation of a name than to win the approval of Louis, the wisest king within human memory. And how could Louis himself, that abundant fountain of light and sun, more clearly or splendidly make it publicly known that he approved you thoroughly than when he wished you transferred from the metropolitan see of Neustria to the see of the foremost city of France; admitted you to a more intimate association in his more sacred council; and summoned you to the most frequent familiarity of his court and private consultation? In all this we admire not so much rewards for merits as the merits themselves.

These, most illustrious Prince of the Church, are the reasons why we call upon you as protector—indeed, as father—light, and pillar of our labor, which is not slight but, owing to our condition, somewhat obscure. We trust that, if you receive it favorably, it will have great worth and great esteem among all who, illuminated by your approval and by the inscription of your name as by a guiding torch, will rejoice that almost countless passages of Ambrose have been restored and repaired to their former integrity.

Nor indeed had we cause to fear or doubt that we should not be received with sufficient kindness by you, the greatest and busiest of prelates. We know that all come to you when occupied, but none finds you prevented, since you are fully equal to far more tasks. Moreover, the grace and courtesy of your incomparable affability open your doors and invite people to the thresholds of your palace. You receive persons of every rank and condition in such a way that no one has ever departed from you without being filled with a certain delight and consolation; and you inspire even persons of the humblest estate with a confident boldness to approach and obtain their request. That is your singular endowment or virtue—or rather, not one among your endowments and virtues, but by far the sweetest seasoning of them all—which does not first present you to the eyes before it makes you sovereign over minds by a certain most powerful force. It bids us be confident and makes us expect from you the honor and protection which we desire for our work. Besides your most gracious disposition, the supreme dignity of the author, the exceptional authority of this outstanding work, and a marvelous fitness of the times make us dare to hope for this so certainly and confidently, and almost to claim it as our right.

It is Ambrose whom we set before you restored to life, greatest of archprelates. Though he may not yet be visible with the care, painstaking labor, complete form, and full majesty with which he once presented himself to the emperors Valentinian, Gratian, and Theodosius, he is nevertheless Ambrose, restored, so far as our zeal permitted, to his former integrity and splendor. To what residence ought an archbishop most steadfast in ecclesiastical discipline to come first, if not to an archiepiscopal one? Whom was it fitting to approach before all others on behalf of the most celebrated doctor of the Church, if not the most worthy provost of the most wise Sorbonne and most learned Navarre, himself an outstanding doctor in the Church of God? Finally, whom would an orator truly *ambrosios*—“ambrosial”—more gladly deem worthy of his address than you, from whose teaching mouth ambrosia overflows?

But with Ambrose thus leading the way, what favor can we fail to hope to receive from you, especially we who are most devoted to you and who ourselves saw, when scarcity of provisions and the harshness of winter raged equally, the poorest people rushing in crowds into the archiepiscopal residence, led by misery alone: received there with such love and fed with such humanity, yet refreshed less by your gifts themselves than by that manner of giving and winning hearts which is peculiar to you? Believe us: by this alone you would have drawn our Ambrose to yourself. For he, the most devoted father of the poor, did not hesitate even to break up and melt down sacred vessels in order to relieve their want in a time of utmost difficulty; and he cannot fail especially to love one whom he sees following in his footsteps along this royal road of charity and renewing his examples.

And this is most timely for those hastening to you, most illustrious bishop: the very character of Ambrose’s works urges those already running to hasten of their own accord—namely, that divine teaching which, to use the words worthy of so great a master, Augustine, flowed from so holy an oracle, from Ambrose’s breast. As there is no remedy more immediate for healing the wounds of corrupted ethics, so there is none more effective for driving away the poison of heresy and schism; none by which the wounds and scars of those returning to sound faith may be healed, united, and strengthened more readily and certainly; none by which both the old Catholic and the neophyte may grow stronger more fully and perfectly in the innermost feelings of Christian piety.

It was an act of your consummate wisdom and most prudent zeal that you most wisely foresaw that the weapons must be taken from the hands of heretics—that is, all the most pernicious books by which they inflicted death upon themselves. Nor was it enough for you to say with Ambrose himself, “We read them so that they may not be read,” or to take away from sick persons, enamored of their own disease, those poisoned cups that flatter them under an agreeable appearance of sweetness and as though with a dripping of honey. You also extended to them with a friendly hand divine and other devout books, from which they might draw the fullest health as from a most wholesome channel. Behold, then, Ambrose comes running to assist and support your wishes, without whom almost every medicine is feeble and weak. Behold the spotless and most limpid fountain of living water which, flowing from Christ, the saving mountain, leaps up into eternal life, that it may make glad the city of God; and, when drunk, may heal every class of the weak and sick. From its spring the wisest and most powerful Persians once came thirsting from the furthest bounds of the East in order to draw; and with only a few drops it instilled perfect health of faith into the king, queen, and people of the Marcomanni. Behold, finally, the most valiant and invincible leader of the sacred word against the enemies of Religion and the Church, accustomed to victories, who offers a fully equipped panoply, in which that army of evangelical laborers, gathered and trained by you for all France, may find and possess, each and every one, the helmet of eternal salvation, the impregnable shield of faith, the two-edged sword of the divine Word, and

> Whatever missiles heaven’s arsenals contain.

But why speak any longer of equipment for evangelical warfare? The Church now enjoys the success of the conflict. A victory of such a kind has restored peace and tranquility to us: wholly productive of benefit to the defeated, but contributing in very great measure to your glory. It must nevertheless be acknowledged that the other princes of the Church contributed greatly, and that each labored vigorously and earnestly according to his piety and vigilance. Yet what envious man could deny that you took the leading role among them, knowing that, in your friendly solicitude for all the Churches, you most lovingly supplied for so great a work capable men formed by your teaching and cultivated by your studies and labors—as no one else did; knowing that you inflamed more and more, with a truly remarkable ardor and piety, the most Christian King’s otherwise most ready will to aid the salvation of his subjects—as scarcely another did; and observing, finally, that with tireless labor and every art as teacher, you have lent your most frequent hand to the pious work with such happy result that every day you admit very many to abjure their errors, and with unheard-of accessibility and affection devote and pour out your whole self in converting, receiving, instructing, and assisting them?

In saying this, far be it from us to wish anything detracted from the immense glory of the most religious king. All that our Church has conquered belongs to him. But since kings conquer by commanding and princes of the Church by persuading, no one should think or regret that anything has been removed or diminished from the King’s glory in order to commend yours, since each is supreme in its own kind. What belongs to Caesar, to Caesar; but all France congratulates you, most illustrious Prince of the Church, for what is yours in this great undertaking. Yet even in Caesar’s portion, we think that you, who are Duke and Peer of France, have cause for congratulation for what faithful servants can accomplish under the best and greatest of kings. The emperor, most discerning of all men, knows well that just as it is most blessed in a ruler to do what he wishes, so it is most miserable not to wish to be advised concerning what he ought to do. By this most equitable and modest disposition, he admits into his more secret counsels all whom he judges most worthy; and thus a certain share of royal glory rightly passes to them under the name of counsel. Hence those who are amazed that the monster of heresy, not long before a matter of no small fear even to kings themselves, has been utterly extinguished in so great a kingdom, in so brief a span of time, successfully and without any bloodshed, summon you to share in so great praise—not merely as a servant of God, but also as a royal servant, whom they know to have been the king’s foremost adviser and promoter of so vast an undertaking, difficult beyond what posterity would believe.

Therefore Ambrose, leader of our choir, arrives fittingly and opportunely amid the festive voices and repeated public applause of all, so that happier and worthier song may be raised through his mouth:

> “One people has been made out of heretics … the Church has been filled”;

and so that this may be added with the greatest delight:

> “The storm has been calmed; concord sails forth; faith breathes; the sailors, competing with one another, return to the havens of faith which they had abandoned, and press sweet kisses upon their native shores, rejoicing that they have been freed from dangers and released from errors.”

May he also furnish and suggest to you and to all the Gallican clergy these words addressed to Louis the Great, witnesses of ancient discipline against heresy and interpreters of new joy:

> “You have restored to me the peace of the Church; you have closed the mouths—and would that you had closed the hearts—of the faithless; and you have done this with authority no less of faith than of power.”

Happy and fortunate shall we be, most illustrious Prince of the Church, if, just as Ambrose has obtained a place among your books through his works, so you may preserve for a very long time, ever more intimately and abundantly, the place which you have granted in your mind to us, his editors. Happy if the most holy bishop, assenting to our vows and prayers, may pray to God and obtain from him that you be kept safe and sound for a very long time—for Religion, the Church, France, ourselves, and all people. Happy, finally, if the Doctor of the Church, who is the truest witness of our devotion toward you, may also be received by you as a hostage and guarantor of the most bound devotion with which we are

Most devotedly and obediently attached to Your Highness,  
the Benedictine Monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur.

[Col. 0013]

**PREFACE**

[Col. 0013]

[Col. 0013C] Since we are presenting Ambrose’s treatises purified by a new care and by no slight labor, there is no need for us, in order to commend this edition to the Catholic reader, to entice his mind with affected praises of the author or of his works. For who among those who have tasted even the first elements of ecclesiastical history would deny that all things in Ambrose were great and truly singular? It is indeed universally acknowledged that his calling to the episcopate, his vigilance and steadfastness in that office, and his integrity, humanity, religion, and other virtues throughout his life shone with unusual splendor. Theodosius the Great was so struck by Ambrose’s magnanimity alone that he burst forth in these words: “I have seen no bishop except Ambrose” (*Theodoret, History*, book V, ch. 17). As for his doctrine, not only have holy Fathers, supreme pontiffs, and ecumenical councils vied in praising it with elaborate encomia, but heretics themselves have done so as well. Yet nothing more clearly shows how great was the power of Ambrose’s teaching and eloquence than the fact that Augustine was recalled from error to the true faith by the efforts and sermons of our Doctor. By this one victory the holy bishop raised for himself a trophy and monument more enduring than bronze. Would that modern heterodox Christians might also wish to imitate the example of the great Augustine! We may certainly affirm with justice that Ambrose spoke in such explicit terms concerning Christ’s presence in the Sacrament, the authority and keys of the Church, the necessity of good works, the veneration of relics, and the invocation of the blessed inhabitants of heaven, that nothing clearer could be desired by a fair-minded and prudent reader.

Moreover, since among other accusations these obstinate persons most invidiously charge the corruption of printed texts, we hope that our edition, at this time when the king’s piety employs all its authority toward the conversion of heretics, will not prove fruitless. What we have accomplished in preparing it will be explained after we have first set forth a few remarks concerning the older editions issued in different places in Europe.

No edition has come to our notice older than that which Maffellus Venia, an Augustinian monk, dedicated to Ambrosius Coranus, general of the same order. In it one can find no definite indication either of place or time; yet perhaps it may be inferred that it was published in Italy and before 1485, both because the form of the book and its type entirely agree with another edition of which we shall presently speak, and because that Coranus, or Coriolanus, died at Rome in the year mentioned. A second edition, prepared by Cribellius, a priest, appeared at Milan in 1490 under Master Leonard Pachel; together with the former edition it is preserved by the Reverend Fathers, the Regular Canons of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris. Both, however, are very imperfect and contain only very few treatises.

Two years later John Amerbach, a citizen of Basel, won no small praise because, having sought out and assembled from every quarter copies of many of Ambrose’s principal works, he arranged those works in three parts and comprised them in as many volumes. In order to make his edition more useful, he also asked John de Lapide, a Carthusian of Paris, to divide each book into a definite number of chapters and to provide an appropriate summary for each chapter; and this was done. It would, however, have been desirable that, just as he published more treatises for us, he should also have published them in a more corrected form. In this we recognize the industry of a most diligent bookseller: that he found so many works; but we attribute the fact that they were so corrupted to the injuries of time. In 1506 John Petri of Langendorf, likewise a printer of Basel, again put this edition under the press. He added nothing to the former one except a very copious index, which he entitled the *Florilegous Register* (*Registrum florigerum*). Conrad Leontorius of the Cistercian order considered the usefulness of this index so great that he did not hesitate to celebrate it in verse and prose.

Undertaking a new edition, Erasmus added one or two treatises to those already made public. He reduced the whole body of Ambrose’s works to two volumes and divided it into four tomes: the first containing ethical works; the second, polemical works; the third, orations, letters, and sermons; and the fourth, explanations of the New and Old Testaments. He also prefixed to the individual tomes and to some books certain critical notices, but these did not sufficiently answer either to his reputation or to the expectations of learned persons. Although he boasts that much labor was expended upon this work—“While, by comparison of ancient codices,” he says, “corruptions are corrected, omissions restored, insertions cut away, displacements put back in order, and Greek passages replaced which either were wholly absent or had been added in meaningless characters”—nevertheless his words were not so trusted that anyone believed him to defer more to the authority of manuscripts than to his own judgment. This was certainly the character of the preceding age: all learned men attached great importance to conjectures; but no one doubts that Erasmus in particular was somewhat bolder, through confidence in his reputation and learning. Accordingly, his edition seemed so far from having attained proper perfection that, two years later, namely in 1529, when it was printed at Paris by Chevallon, many changes were made in the text and some notes added in the margin, as we have discovered by collating several small works. Nor did this occur at Paris alone, but also at Basel, where Erasmus’s first edition had issued from Froben’s press; the same thing is found in its subsequent editions, in which several treatises lacking from the earlier editions were also gradually added.

[Col. 0016A] Nevertheless, the authority of an edition reprinted so often and in so many different places, and revised with the diligence of Gelenius and other learned men, did not deter John Coster, a regular canon of the monastery of Saint Martin at Louvain, from applying himself to preparing and embellishing another. He explains the occasion that induced him to undertake this labor as follows (*Letter placed at the beginning of his edition*): “When, then,” he says, “two years ago I had obtained from the library of the monastery of St. Lawrence, which adjoins the walls of the city of Liège, letters of St. Ambrose written in ancient and more elegant characters, and began, as was my custom, to compare them with printed books, it is astonishing to say how much disagreement and variation there was. I could not help immediately becoming indignant with those who, in published books, with titles splendid indeed but empty and deceptive, promise that everything is most carefully corrected and reborn, as it were, by a more fortunate *palingenesis* [renewal]; whereas for the most part nothing is more corrupt, and everything remains enveloped in its ancient filth.” Moved by this, he resolved to carry out in the remaining works of the same Doctor what he had begun with Ambrose’s letters. Having borrowed several copies from the libraries of three or four neighboring monasteries, and relying on this assistance, especially on one very elegant codex brought into Belgium from Great Britain, he completed his revision. It was published at Basel in 1555, printed and financed by Episcopius. Coster indeed rendered outstanding service in this edition, and we do not think he misled readers when he stated that he had removed more than two thousand errors from Ambrose, besides twenty or more verses which, being absent from earlier editions, he was the first to restore, each to its proper place. Yet he makes it sufficiently clear that the copies mentioned did not afford him enough assistance, when he admits that he sometimes encountered difficulties in which he was compelled to have recourse to the judgment of learned men—that is, to speak more plainly, to conjectures.

For this reason, when John Gillot observed that Coster, owing to the paucity of manuscript codices, had by no means been able to make his edition perfect in every respect, he praised his labor and industry, but nevertheless thought that something of perfection would be added to Ambrose’s works if they were revised anew with the use of other copies. He therefore assembled no small multitude of manuscripts from the principal libraries of this city: namely, the Royal, the Sorbonne, the German, and the Victorine libraries; to which we may add the Dionysian library, or that of the abbey of Saint-Denis in France, in which alone the same author testifies that twenty or more handwritten codices of Ambrose’s works existed. But when he perceived that scarcely several men, much less one man, could suffice for comparing and reconciling so many codices, he was obliged, as he himself does not conceal in his preface, to select and retain from so great a number a few that he could adequately examine. His edition appeared at Paris in 1568, from William Merlin and his associates. Although it may rightly be proclaimed the most complete of all those previously published, nevertheless, as is often the condition of human things, it remained almost the least known of all: the fame of the Roman edition which followed immediately afterward overwhelmed it.

Felix Cardinal de Monte Alto, later Supreme Pontiff under the name Sixtus V, professes that he was induced to undertake the latter edition by the authority and commands of his predecessors Pius IV and Pius V, while he was at Rome serving as general of his order in the convent of the Friars Minor. Accordingly, to discharge the task entrusted to him, he began to investigate the more famous libraries, compare ancient manuscripts with the more corrected editions, and search out any treatise still lurking unpublished. In addition, he diligently prepared all other things which he considered conducive to the perfection of the work. Yet, hindered by the distractions of various journeys and other concerns, he was compelled, as he confesses, to leave it unfinished. Having later become cardinal, he resumed the interrupted work, but no longer alone; for he addresses Gregory XIII, to whom he wished the edition to be dedicated, as follows (*Dedicatory Letter*):

> “Having afterward obtained such rest as I could, and resuming the work I had begun at Your Holiness’s encouragement and command, I selected distinguished scholars, men eminent in learning and piety, in knowledge of languages and acquaintance with histories, and moreover very practiced in scholastic theology and the reading of the Fathers; and I associated them with myself as partners in the labor. Thus, cheerfully undertaking the burden and strenuously applying themselves together to their task for several years, at length, by many vigils and very great expenditure, with God—the giver of all good things—favorable to us, we completed it,” etc.

Then, having explained how, in order perfectly to correct Ambrose’s works, they had not only compared written codices with printed texts, but had also consulted those ancient authors from whom Ambrose had borrowed something, and examined later writers in whom they found something quoted from the labors of the same Father, he recounts the fruit of such great labor and diligence in these words:

> “With their help and assistance,” he says (*ibid.*), “we explained obscure passages, supplied defective ones, rejected additions, restored displacements, corrected corruptions; in short, we diligently took care that everything should breathe Ambrose’s genuine style and answer to his dignity and gravity. We exerted ourselves, so far as our powers permitted, that the author himself might seem to speak, after every spurious matter had been cut away.”

Finally, in order more clearly to disclose his diligence in preparing this edition, he relates that he added several treatises lacking in other editions, instituted a new and more convenient division of the entire work, and at last supplied the text of Scripture in the first three tomes for the reader’s benefit.

Four of its volumes were published at Rome by Dominicus Basa in the years 1580, 1581, and 1582; the fifth in 1585, when Sixtus V already sat in the chair of Blessed Peter, and John Baptist Bandini dedicated that volume to him. Once this edition had been made public, all authority immediately passed to it, the others being neglected; so that everywhere, at least where the profession of Catholic religion flourished, it alone was reprinted. Certainly from the year 1586, when it first appeared at Paris, it was put under the press there almost every ten years, without any change that might seem of consequence having been introduced.

Nevertheless, it is regrettable that in this same edition there are found not a few things that are disapproved, not without reason, not only by heretics but also by the orthodox. First of all, those long passages of Scripture which are placed not only at the beginning of certain treatises but also inserted in the middle of chapters interrupt the author’s discourse and sequence far too much, burden the volume with bulk and weight, and are scarcely ever read by anyone [Col. 0018B]. Secondly, that fivefold division is not sufficiently well arranged. For, leaving aside the fact that the first two treatises of the second volume have much more affinity with the last treatises of the first than with the explanations that follow in the same second volume, it was inappropriate to remove certain letters and sermons from their proper order and transfer them from the fifth volume to the first under the title of annotations; and still less appropriate to relegate elsewhere detached parts of certain books. This further fault is also reproved there: that they inserted certain highly doubtful treatises among those accepted as genuine and legitimate, as though beyond doubt; whereas, on the contrary, even in those works which the consensus of earlier editions had admitted, discrimination and critical judgment [Col. 0018C] were needed to separate true works from false, certain from ambiguous. But nothing in all this is more offensive than the liberties taken in the text itself by those whom the most eminent Cardinal employed to correct it. We do not think that he himself erred otherwise in this matter, except perhaps by placing more trust than was proper in their diligence and judgment. Indeed, their purpose too ought not to be condemned with such severity, since they proposed nothing else to themselves than to soften certain words which seemed somewhat harsh to them, replace those which were more obscure with clearer ones, or finally bring the author’s explanations back into conformity with the sequence of Scripture.

Meanwhile the heterodox, who leave no stone unturned in order to evade the authority of the Fathers, loudly and tumultuously charge us, as we have said, with corruption of the Ambrosian editions. Yet this accusation of importunate men is not recent. For in the preceding century Francis Junius, wishing to persuade people that Catholic printers were not free to act in good faith when printing the works of the Fathers, but were harassed by certain spies sent out by secret inquisitors, began—or invented—the following story (*Preface to the Index Expurgatorius*). He relates, therefore, that when he visited Lyons in 1555, he was shown by Louis Saurius, a corrector employed in the Freslon printing-house, several sheets of the writings of St. Ambrose, elegant indeed with respect to the brightness of the paper, the beauty of the type, and the accuracy of the orthography, but shamefully interpolated and cancelled in their very meaning and wording by [Col. 0019A] two Franciscans. When we saw that this accusation had been eagerly seized upon and twisted by Rivet (*Critica sacra*, book III, ch. 6) and similar writers of that or an equivalent age in order to stir up hatred against the Church, and had even quite recently been repeated with the greatest indignation by a certain minister, we were prompted to learn something more certain about that edition. Accordingly, we searched the more notable libraries of this city, consulted several published foreign catalogues, and finally took steps to investigate at Lyons whether any copy of it might remain there. Yet we could discover no trace of it anywhere. From this one may infer either that it was immediately suppressed, or perhaps that it was wholly fictitious.

[Col. 0019B] But if they raise such tragedies over a matter so uncertain, who could believe that the same men would spare the blemishes and faults of editions which are now publicly available and handled by every Catholic and non-Catholic alike? The aforesaid Rivet certainly did not spare them when he concluded his story about the Lyons edition thus: “It is easy to divine what has been done, or is done daily, in similar cases at Rome” (*book and chapter cited*). Nor did Dallaeus, formerly minister at Charenton, spare them. In the book which he wrote in French, *On the Use of the Fathers*, he spends the entirety of page 93 of chapter 4 attacking that same Roman edition. Yet the injustice of him and others like him is evident in this: they carefully conceal the errors and the extreme freedom in following conjectures of Erasmus, Gelenius, and the rest who worked on the Basel edition before Coster.

But we are confident that by this edition of ours we have achieved the result that the weapons perpetually hurled by the enemies of the Catholic Church against Ambrose’s authority will henceforward be wrested from their hands. First, we wished this to be an inviolable rule for ourselves: never to admit any conjecture into the text. For, as we see Coster most prudently observed (*letter already cited*): “Those who trust their own ingenuity and judgment beyond what is due, and do not place all their reliance in comparing ancient copies, may indeed sometimes restore certain readings contrary to the rules of grammarians; but they can by no means thus heal words wrongly altered, [Col. 0019D] sentences wholly omitted, or sentences displaced to another location.” And lest anyone think that we are deceiving them by these promises, we have not only supplied at the end of the volume a catalogue of the manuscripts used in revising each treatise, but have also indicated in the lower margin of every page what has been changed and on what authority. There we have likewise arranged for variant readings from each manuscript and printed codex to be added; with this distinction, however, that those judged to be of slighter importance were relegated to the end of the volume, while those of no value at all were omitted.

> **Note [Col. 0019D].** We have made a single body of annotations out of both kinds, so that, while reading, nothing may be wanted which is not before the eyes. —EDS.

Thus [Col. 0020A] we have provided both that the reader may be free to choose the reading which he considers best, and that the page not be filled with trivial or useless notes. In biblical passages cited here and there by Ambrose, moreover, we have employed still greater diligence and scruple. For we thought it proper to note variants in those passages—even ones not especially serious—not only from Ambrose’s manuscripts but also from the various languages of the Bible.

We have removed those longer contexts by which, as stated, in the Roman edition both books were separated from one another and even the middle of chapters was not infrequently divided. This division tears and dismembers, as it were limb by limb, the body of Ambrose’s works, which ought, insofar as possible, [Col. 0020B] to be one. There was, however, some debate about dividing the books into chapters and about their arguments, or summaries, as they are called. Some maintained that everything not found in manuscripts ought to be removed from the editions; others, by contrast, thought these things should be retained, but corrected, because the old summaries represented the author’s meaning and purpose either less clearly or in less idiomatic Latin. The latter opinion prevailed. For it is certain that a reader’s mind becomes wearied unless it rests from time to time, as it were, at various stopping places. Yet the chief usefulness of this arrangement seems to be that it prepares the reader before he proceeds to a new subject, so that he may understand more easily what he is about to read. And surely [Col. 0020C] no one will deny that this is especially necessary in the case of a writer for whose reading and understanding, as Antony Godellus—an outstanding glory and ornament of the Gallican Church—observed (*Ecclesiastical History*, year 397), more than ordinary learning is required.

Therefore, in order that in this matter we might, according to our measure, provide especially for younger theologians, we retained the long-established division of the treatises into chapters; distributed the chapters themselves into numbered sections; explained obscure or infrequent words; and, where the matter seemed to require it, added a brief explanation even of matters concerning history, discipline, and doctrine. We have also indicated passages from those ancient writers whom our Ambrose had set before himself for imitation. In all this our purpose was not to hunt for a reputation for learning, [Col. 0020D] but to have regard solely to the usefulness of readers—especially, as we have said, those newly come from theological schools who are preparing themselves to study the writings of our Doctor. Learned men, with whom this learned age of ours abounds, may therefore omit our notes without loss; yet let them not begrudge them to beginners and candidates in this sort of study. Their necessity for such readers is all the more shown by the fact that, in many places, changes introduced into the text reveal that the Roman editors, though otherwise learned men, did not attain the author’s meaning. But while these readers are aided by this modest labor of ours, let them not complain that we have explained too little. We have neglected nothing that was very necessary, and the size of the volume would scarcely have allowed fuller annotations.

As for the division of the entire work, neither the Roman nor the Erasmian arrangement seemed satisfactory to us. In each, many things are not in their proper place, and there is no distinction between legitimate and spurious offspring. We therefore thought nothing more suitable than to divide all works inscribed with Ambrose’s name into only three volumes: the first two containing genuine works, the third spurious ones. In this we departed as little as possible from the Roman arrangement, to which everyone has now become accustomed through long use. Thus in this first volume [Col. 0021A] we have included everything pertaining to the exposition of Scripture [Col. 0021B]. There is no reason to say more here concerning its treatises, since the prefatory notices to each sufficiently set forth and discuss their date, the author’s purpose, and other matters we judged necessary. As for the revised testimonies of Augustine and Gratian, and also of the Scripture cited, with added verses from it, and the various indexes placed at the end—without speaking further of these—the reader himself will sufficiently recognize by use how useful they are.

Nor do those resources and aids which we employed in this revision of Ambrose seem to be passed over here. Certainly it is clear that, for restoring the works of any author, it is not sufficient to compare one or two handwritten codices with some edition; many are needed, so that [Col. 0021C] what is corrupt in one may be corrected by the help of another. Indeed, it is not enough even to have many unless they were written in different regions. For it very often happens that precisely the same errors are found in all manuscripts from one province, because they derive, as from one spring, from one and the same exemplar. Accordingly, we took pains to gather manuscripts wherever possible. First, we arranged for several minor works, for which fewer copies were available in France, to be collated against some codices of the Vatican Library, and for the variant readings used by Cardinal de Monte-Alto himself to be copied. Among these were some observations not altogether useless to us; there were also very many conjectures which we later found published by Latino Latini [Col. 0021D]. Then we arranged for manuscripts in the libraries of our Congregation either to be collated in the provinces where they were kept or brought to this monastery of Saint-Germain. The same was done with several Flemish codices from libraries of our Order, and with many French codices of the Cistercian Order, which the superiors of many monasteries of that Order lent us with the greatest kindness. Here it would be wrong not to mention how much we owe to the labor of the Reverend Father Jean-Baptiste de Noyville, Prior of the abbey of Clairvaux near Laon. He most obligingly collated several treatises with the codices of his monastery, and did not think it burdensome to copy with his own hand certain sermons [Col. 0022A] not yet published. Finally, we carefully searched the more notable libraries of this city—the Royal, Sorbonne, Victorine, Colbertine, and others—from which those charged with the care and custody of these manuscripts most generously supplied us with the codices we required. Above all, we must praise Monsieur Tonnelier, canon of Saint-Victor, who most willingly gave us several gatherings in which he had begun collecting variant readings for an edition of Ambrose he himself intended to prepare. Likewise, the most learned Baluze not only supplied us abundantly with codices from the very rich library of Monsieur Colbert, but also voluntarily brought us, in his kindness toward us, variant readings of Ambrosian sermons and letters which he had gathered from manuscripts of the best quality for a work that he himself had planned. That we were not content merely to consult these codices occasionally, as is customary, but carefully compared the lines of the manuscripts and editions line by line, words with words, syllables with syllables, anyone may understand from the variant readings [Col. 0022B].

Accordingly, nothing more would seem necessary to add here, were there not some who, offended by a kind of prejudice against a few passages of our Ambrose which they consider either obscure or excessively allegorical, show themselves less than fair toward his works. To remedy their distaste, we shall not hesitate to weigh somewhat more carefully the manner of writing and interpretation in which the holy Bishop is found to have delighted. First, it is agreed that Ambrose’s style [Col. 0022C] is lofty, noble, and copious, as befitted a man of patrician rank, carefully trained in civic and forensic eloquence. Yet there is nothing swollen in its elevation, nothing disordered in its abundance; both qualities are tempered by a certain charm and restraint. Nor should you think him devoid of force and vehemence. He has his passions and his stings, but seasoned with such wit that they show no trace of a sourer or more rustic temperament. Observers also note in his expression such remarkable density of thought that it would not easily be possible to find greater in any other writer. Add to this the compact and well-modulated brevity of his periods, distinguished above all by so felicitous a variety that it leaves no room for tedium. Hence the great Augustine testifies in more than one place that he was captivated by our Doctor’s discourse (*St. Augustine, Confessions*, book V, chapters 12, 13, 14, and elsewhere); and when he proposes examples of the three styles of expression, he chooses Cyprian and Ambrose alone (*the same author, On Christian Doctrine*, book IV, ch. 21), drawing and extracting from their writings those various examples of eloquence. Cassiodorus, too, describes no less aptly than briefly the style in which we observe the holy Bishop to have written: “Holy Ambrose likewise, a source of milky speech, keen in gravity, most sweet in his overpowering persuasion” (*Cassiodorus, On Divine Readings*, ch. 20). From this one may sufficiently understand that Ambrose’s style in itself recoils from every obscurity [Col. 0023A]. Whether, however, the method of interpretation which he followed can rightly be charged with this fault must be considered.

He commonly recognizes a threefold meaning in the sacred pages: natural, moral, and spiritual; or, what is the same, historical, ethical, and mystical. Yet in unfolding the last he displays as much fullness as he does brevity in the first. Indeed, at times one might think that, in establishing the spiritual sense, he utterly denies the truth of the history. Yet you will find that the matter is otherwise, provided you weigh each point within the sequence and context of the discourse, as we shall observe in the proper places. Moreover, he is nowhere more accustomed to press the mystical sense than in expounding the Old Testament, especially where the history of events presents something [Col. 0023B] that appears contrary to moral decency and propriety. Then, fearing that believers might thereby seize an occasion for sinning, or pagans and Manichaeans an occasion for insulting the Church, he fittingly has recourse to allegory. This is made clear by his discussions of Noah’s drunkenness, Abraham’s intercourse with the maidservant, Lot’s drunkenness and incest, and David’s adultery. No one could explain the usefulness of this method better than the great Augustine, who experienced it to such great benefit for the Church. Thus he says: “I rejoiced also that the ancient writings of the Law and the Prophets were now proposed for reading not with that eye by which they had formerly seemed absurd to me . . . I gladly heard Ambrose often say in popular sermons: ‘The letter kills, but the spirit gives life,’ when, by removing the mystical veil, he opened spiritually things which, taken literally, seemed to teach perversity” (*St. Augustine, Confessions*, book VI, ch. 4). But he turns to the beauty of the mystical sense not only when something occurs that conflicts with upright morals. Mindful of the apostolic saying, “All these things happened to them in figures” (1 Cor. 10:11), he demonstrates that the most beautiful mysteries of religion lie hidden beneath the covering of the letter where there seemed to be nothing but a simple narrative of deed or event. Consider what meanings, and how noble, he draws from the construction of Noah’s ark, from the blessings of Noah’s sons, from Isaac’s marriage, from the different events in Joseph’s life, and finally from the blessings of Joseph’s brothers and sons. You will certainly confess that those interpreters do nothing but grow cold and creep along the ground, who, having resolved to bring a kind of Jewish servitude into the Church, devote themselves wholly to examining accents and syllables [Col. 0023D], and who, if through the aid of some Hebrew etymology they think they have uncovered the grammatical sense of even a single statement, then exult and triumph in earnest. Nevertheless, we do not say this as though we despised the natural sense, on which the other two are founded. We readily acknowledge that its use is wholly praiseworthy, provided we do not cling to it slavishly and Judaically. The holy Doctor chiefly followed it in the books *Hexaemeron*, *On Paradise*, *On Noah and the Ark*, and in the *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*. As to the moral sense: since it is acknowledged that nothing belongs more properly to pastoral care than concern for forming the morals of one’s flock [Col. 0024A], it would certainly be surprising if so great a bishop had not fulfilled so weighty a part of the episcopal office. But although almost every page attests how much account he made of it—for this sense is, as it were, diffused through nearly all Ambrosian works—yet it is found expounded more deliberately in certain works. Such are the books *On the Sacrifice of Cain and Abel*, *On Abraham*, *On the Good of Death*, *On Flight from the World*, *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, *On Elijah and Fasting*, *On Naboth the Israelite*, *On Tobit*, *On Interpellations*, and in the *Expositions of the Psalms*.

But he did not approach the investigation of the knowledge hidden in the divine books under his own guidance. Although he had acquired no ordinary knowledge of both Latin and [Col. 0024B] Greek, and was extremely well read in every kind of book—poets, historians, philosophers, and especially Platonists—and although he had carefully cultivated in pleading cases the considerable eloquence nature itself had bestowed upon him, he nevertheless did not think that he should pass from the law courts to the sacred pulpit without the support of experienced guides. He preferred to offer himself as a disciple of the ancients rather than to profess himself a teacher of others. Therefore, since Origen was regarded as the guide and standard-bearer of all others in interpreting Scripture, and since earlier Fathers had drawn most of their expositions from him as from a public storehouse, Ambrose also judged that he would be using a common right if he borrowed from Origen’s books what he thought suited his own purpose. In this, however, he exercised the greatest caution and judgment. Since many things were read in that author’s works which were not approved by the Church, he carefully avoided them and took care not to offer his sheep any nourishment that was less sound or pure. We have also found some things in his writings taken from Basil; but we suppose that Ambrose yielded to the friendship formed between them by their mutual esteem for virtue, so that, when occasion required, he willingly followed Basil’s lead. Besides the two Fathers mentioned, Jerome adds two others: Didymus, concerning whom see the preface to the books *On the Holy Spirit*, and the martyr Hippolytus. But since Hippolytus’s works have perished through the adversity of time, we have nothing to add to Jerome’s testimony. (See our preface to the *Hexaemeron*.)

After the Fathers of the Church, we think Philo the Jew should be named, a man of great learning, whom the holy Doctor quite frequently imitated in his fondness for allegorical interpretations. Thus certain passages in Ambrosian works seem obscure to those who do not sufficiently know Philo’s method, from which they are drawn. This occurs especially where either some distinctive word or numbers that arise in the text are transferred to a more subtle allegory. Thus Erasmus himself branded one passage with this censorious note: “Here, it seems,” he says, “someone has been present with [Col. 0025A] his trifles” (*On Abraham*, book II, marginal note to ch. 11), although the same thought may be found in Philo in almost the same words. Yet the holy Doctor should not be singled out for accusation on this account, since other Fathers also commonly sought allegorical and tropological meanings, and believed that great mysteries were contained and concealed in numbers which ought to be candidly disclosed to their people. From this it may indeed be inferred that many things which cast a certain mist of obscurity before us were plain even to the people in those ancient times, accustomed as they were to hearing such things. But if some things were encountered which never failed to surpass the comprehension of the common folk, this should not in the least be attributed to obscurity in the orator. Even today many who speak in the vernacular are praised for clarity, though the populace does not grasp many features of the art in their sermons.

There is besides a somewhat unusual kind of interpretation which Ambrose set before himself for imitation in that same Philo: namely, thematic interpretation. Sixtus of Siena defines it as follows (*Bibliotheca Sancta*, book III, method 22): “The thematic method of exposition is that which applies particular parts of divine Scripture together with their expositions to the treatment of some particular subject, showing that the entire body of the subject undertaken, its members, and each individual part are found, as though depicted in a picture, in the passages of sacred Scripture set forth.” No one will judge this definition difficult to understand who considers [Col. 0025C] how the holy Doctor refers the things Scripture relates concerning the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to show openly that, in the first, the obedience owed to divine commands; in the second, the sincere purity of mind; and in the third, endurance of labors, are expressed as in three living images and set forth for everyone’s imitation. But anyone wishing to know more on this matter should consult the same Sienese writer in the place cited.

Here perhaps some reader may be troubled by the fact that, though Ambrose borrowed not a little from Greek writers, as has been said, he nevertheless almost entirely refrains from citing or naming them. But besides the fact that he quite often clearly testifies, without naming the authors, that he is putting forward another’s opinion, Erasmus gives a twofold reason for this: namely, that Ambrose wished to imitate them [Col. 0025D], not translate them, and that Greek writers were in bad repute among the Latins at that time. “No one,” Erasmus says (*prefatory letter to his edition*), “blames Cicero for following Greeks in philosophical arguments not as a translator but as an imitator. Nor was it theft by a little crow that he suppressed the names of the Greeks, most of whom were then severely burdened among the Latins by the odium attached to condemned doctrines; it was the act of a cautious shepherd, excluding every source of stumbling and discord.” This is certainly not implausible. For no one is unaware what disturbances and disputes Origen’s teaching then raised between his supporters and opponents. Indeed [Col. 0026A], someone might perhaps suspect that Ambrose displeased Jerome somewhere for no other reason than that he was a student of Origenist works. Rufinus certainly states (*Apology*, II) that Jerome spoke more insolently of Ambrosian books in two or three passages of his own writings than the holiness and dignity of so great a man allowed. This charge gains some force not only from the fact that Jerome passes it over silently in his *Apology* and does not charge Rufinus with calumny, but especially because in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he declined to compose a catalogue of Ambrosian treatises and state his opinion concerning them: “lest,” he says, “flattery on one side or truth on the other be reproached in me.” It may therefore not unreasonably be inferred that he encountered certain things in those works which he did not approve, but feared to pronounce his judgment because of the man’s eminent authority [Col. 0026B].

Yet we do not think that his own hostility toward the Origenists was the sole cause of this. For in the same work Jerome treats others far more honorably whom he knew well to be no less devoted than Ambrose to the imitation of Origen. Indeed, he himself had praised our Doctor in his earlier books, and later, in his own *Apology against Rufinus*, praises him more than once; in that very place he does not hesitate to profess his own name among the imitators of Origen. Accordingly, if Rufinus’s accusation is true, perhaps Jerome did not wish to state his opinion because, if he spoke with praise about books he had earlier criticized for an uncertain reason, he would be charged with inconsistency; whereas, if he persisted in holding them in contempt, he would offend the feelings of all by whom the holy Bishop was held in the highest honor and reverence. But if Rufinus falsely attributed this to his opponent in order to make him odious, it would not be easy to guess why that holy Doctor should have wished to pass over, not without a certain disdain, the works of so great a Doctor. “It is not permitted to know everything,” he says; nor do we think this greatly relevant to the matter. However it may be, it cannot but be honorable to our Ambrose that, although opinions on every subject vary so widely, Jerome alone was found to disapprove somewhat of one or two of his books. Certainly all Greek and Latin codices are full of praises of St. Ambrose [Col. 0026D]; but even if other writers were silent about him, Augustine alone would be worth them all. For Augustine allows no occasion to escape him without honoring Ambrose as a parent and following him as a doctor and teacher. Compare the teaching of both, and you will admit that certain most learned men did not speak rashly when they said that the seeds of nearly everything taught by St. Augustine are found in Ambrose (Antony Godellus, *place already cited*), whose more concise and compressed sayings Augustine commonly expands and amplifies at length.

[Col. 0027]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, WRITTEN BY PAULINUS, HIS NOTARY, FOR BLESSED AUGUSTINE. (C, S)

[Col. 0027]

[Col. 0027A] **1.** You urge me, venerable Father Augustine, that just as the blessed bishop Athanasius and the presbyter Jerome committed to writing the lives of the holy men Paul and Antony, who dwelt in the desert, and just as Severus, servant of God, set forth in eloquent speech the life of Martin, the venerable bishop of the Church of Tours, so I too should set down in my own writing the life of the most blessed Ambrose, bishop of the Church of Milan. But I know myself to be unequal, both in merit to such great men, who are the walls of the Churches and fountains of eloquence, and in speech. Yet because I think it wrong to evade your command, I shall briefly and succinctly describe—assisted by your prayers and the merits of so great a man, though in uncultivated language—what I learned from men of the highest credibility who attended him before me, and especially from his venerable sister Marcellina; what I myself saw while I attended him; what I learned from persons who reported that after his death they saw him in various provinces; and what was written to him when it was not yet known that he had died [Col. 0027B]. Thus, even if the style displeases the reader, brevity may nevertheless invite reading; and I shall not obscure truth with verbal ornament, lest, while the writer seeks the splendid display of elegance, the reader lose knowledge of such great virtues. For the reader ought to regard not so much the trappings and pomp of words as the virtue of the deeds and the grace of the Holy Spirit. We know, indeed, that travelers, when thirsty, find water more welcome when it drips from a small vein than streams from a gushing fountain, whose abundance they cannot find in time of thirst. Barley bread also tends to be sweet even to those accustomed every day to belch forth the plentiful dishes of a banquet with a hundred courses. Likewise, people who marvel at the delights of gardens are accustomed to find wild herbs pleasing.

**2.** Therefore I beseech all of you into whose hands this book may come to believe that what I have written is true. Let no one suppose that, out of affection, I have included anything lacking in trustworthiness. It is better to say nothing at all than to utter any falsehood, since we know that we shall render an account of all our words (Matt. 12:16). Nor do I doubt that, even if not everyone knows everything, different persons know different things; and that some know matters which I myself was less able either to hear or see. Therefore I shall begin my narrative with the day of his birth [Col. 0028A], so that the grace bestowed on the man may be recognized from his cradle.

**3.** Thus, while his father Ambrose was serving in the administration of the prefecture of Gaul, Ambrose himself was born.

> **Note [Col. 0027D].** The Mich. codex: “while the father of blessed Ambrose, named Ambrose, was serving in the administration of the prefecture of Gaul, blessed Ambrose himself was born.”

When, as an infant, he lay sleeping in a cradle with his mouth open in the courtyard of the praetorium, suddenly a swarm of bees arrived and covered his face and mouth, repeatedly going into and coming out of his mouth. His father, who was walking nearby with the mother or daughter, prevented the nursemaid, who had charge of feeding the infant, from driving them away—for she was anxious that they might harm the child—and waited with a father’s affection to see how the marvel would end.

> **Note [Col. 0027D].** The same codex: “he awaited the outcome of the event, namely the manner in which that miracle would conclude.”

After a while the bees flew away and rose to such a height in the air that they could no longer be seen by human eyes. Frightened by this, the father said: “If this little child lives, he will become something great.” For even then the Lord was at work in the infancy of His little servant, so that what was said might be fulfilled: “Good words are honeycombs” (Prov. 16:24). That swarm of bees produced for us honeycombs in his writings, proclaiming heavenly gifts and raising human minds from earthly things to heaven.

**4.** Later, when he had grown up and was living in the city of Rome with his widowed mother and his sister, who had already professed virginity, accompanied by another virgin—whose sister Candida, herself also of the same profession, now lives at Carthage in old age—he saw priests’ hands kissed by a household servant, sister, or mother.

> **Note [Col. 0027D].** All editions and certain manuscripts read: “that a priest’s hand was kissed by a household servant [Col. 0028D], sister, or mother . . . that this ought to be done by them”; several other and better manuscripts read as in our text.

Playfully, he himself offered his right hand [Col. 0028C], saying that she ought to do the same for him, since he declared that he would become a bishop. For the Spirit of the Lord was speaking in him, nurturing him for the priesthood; but she, treating him as a boy who did not know what he was saying, rejected the gesture.

**5.** But after he had been educated in the liberal disciplines, he left Rome and entered the service of the praetorian prefecture; he pleaded cases so brilliantly that Probus, an illustrious man and then praetorian prefect, chose him to serve as his adviser. After this he received the insignia of the consular office, to govern the provinces of Liguria and Aemilia, and came to Milan.

### 6

At the same time Auxentius, bishop of Arian perfidy, died. He had pressed upon the Church after Dionysius, the confessor of blessed memory, had been sent into exile. [Note: Col. 28D: Some manuscripts read “was attacking the Church”; the others, and the edition, “was pressing upon the Church.”]

When the people rose in sedition while seeking a bishop, and Ambrose was concerned to calm the disturbance lest the city’s people bring danger upon themselves, he went to the church. While he was addressing the people, the voice of a child is reported to have rung out among them: “Ambrose for bishop!” [Note: Col. 29D: The Fisc and Becc manuscripts read, “the voice of a child rang out three times among the people.” Shortly afterward Fisc alone reads, “of one crying out three times”; in Becc and a few others several words are omitted here.]

At the sound of that voice, the faces of the entire people turned, crying, “Ambrose for bishop!” Thus those who had previously been most violently divided—for the Arians wanted a bishop for themselves and the Catholics likewise—suddenly, their rival claims overcome, agreed upon this one man in a marvellous and incredible unanimity. [Note: Col. 29D: The Fisc manuscript has a vast gap here: after “agreed,” it immediately adds, “Therefore Ambrose, recognizing the people’s assent in his election, when he saw that the matter was proceeding contrary to his wish, prepared flight.”]

### 7

When he learned this, he left the church and had a tribunal prepared for himself; for, soon to become a bishop, he ascended to a higher place. Then, contrary to his custom, he ordered tortures to be applied to persons. While he was doing this, the people nevertheless cried out: “Your sin be upon us.”

But that people did not then cry out in the same manner as the Jewish people. For they poured out the Lord’s blood with their words, saying, “His blood be upon us” (Matt. 27:25); whereas these, knowing him to be a catechumen, faithfully promised him the remission of all sins through the grace of baptism.

Then, troubled, he returned home and wished to profess philosophy—though he was to become a true philosopher of Christ, one who, despising worldly pomp, would follow the footsteps of fishermen. These fishermen gathered peoples to Christ not by verbal embellishments but by plain speech and the reasoning of true faith; sent without bag or staff, they converted even philosophers themselves.

When he was recalled so that he might not do this, he had public women enter publicly to him, solely so that, seeing them, the people’s purpose might be diverted. But the people cried yet more loudly: “Your sin be upon us.”

### 8

When he saw that none of his purpose could succeed, he prepared to flee. Leaving the city in the middle of the night, he supposed that he was making for Ticinum; but in the morning he was found at the gate of the city of Milan called the Roman Gate.

For God, who was preparing a wall for his Catholic Church against its enemies and raising up David’s tower against the face of Damascus—that is, against the perfidy of heretics—prevented his flight. [Note: Col. 30D: Again, the same Fisc manuscript has a gap here, ending with “against the face of Damascus.” The passage was then reported to the most gracious emperor Valentinian, who received with the greatest joy the fact that judges sent by him were being sought for the priesthood.]

When he had been found and was being guarded by the people, a report was sent to the most gracious emperor Valentinian, who received with the greatest joy the news that the judge whom he had sent was being sought for the priesthood.

The prefect Probus also rejoiced that his word was being fulfilled in Ambrose. For when Ambrose was setting out and receiving instructions from him, as was customary, he had said: “Go; act not as a judge, but as a bishop.”

### 9

While the reply to the report was pending, he again prepared to flee and hid for some time on the estate of Leontius, a most distinguished man. But when the report received its answer, he was betrayed by Leontius himself. For the vicar had been ordered to press forward with completing the matter. Wishing to fulfil the charge laid upon him, he issued an edict and summoned everyone, declaring that, if they wished to look after themselves and their property, they should reveal the man.

Accordingly, he was betrayed and brought to Milan. Understanding that God’s will concerned him, and that he could resist no longer, he requested that he be baptized only by a Catholic bishop, for he carefully guarded against Arian perfidy. [Note: Col. 30D: Several manuscripts read, “for he had an anxious concern regarding Arian perfidy.”]

Having been baptized, he is said to have fulfilled all the ecclesiastical offices, and on the eighth day he was ordained bishop amid the highest favour and joy of all.

After some years of his episcopate he went to the city of Rome—that is, to his native soil. There he found the holy maiden mentioned above, to whom he had been accustomed to offer his hand, in her own house with her sister, just as he had left her; her mother had now died. When she kissed his right hand, he smiled and said to her: “See: as I used to tell you, you are kissing a priest’s hand.”

### 10

At the same time, while he was staying across the Tiber as the guest of a certain most distinguished woman and offering the sacrifice in her house, a bath-attendant who lay paralyzed in bed, learning that the Lord’s priest was there, had herself carried in a chair to the same house to which he had been invited. She touched the priest’s garments while he was praying and laying on hands. When she kissed them, she immediately recovered her health and began to walk, so that the Lord’s saying to the apostles might be fulfilled: “You will do even greater things than these, believing in my name” (John 14:12).

This miracle of healing was as remarkable as it was public. For many years later, while I was in Rome, I learned of it in that same district from holy men who recounted it. [Note: Col. 30D: “In that same district” is absent from the edition and some manuscripts, but occurs in other, better manuscripts.]

### 11

When he had gone to Sirmium to ordain Anemius bishop, he was driven from the church by the power of the empress Justina and the crowd she had assembled, so that an Arian bishop might be ordained in that same church, not by him but by heretics.

He was seated upon the tribunal, paying no attention to the things stirred up by the woman. One of the Arian virgins, more shameless than the others, mounted the tribunal, seized the priest’s garment, and attempted to drag him toward the women, so that he might be beaten by them and driven from the church. As he himself used to relate, he said to her:

“Although I am unworthy of so great a priesthood, nevertheless it is not fitting for you, whatever your profession, to lay hands upon any priest. You ought therefore to fear God’s judgment, lest some evil happen to you.”

The outcome confirmed his words. For on the following day he escorted her dead body as far as the grave, repaying insult with kindness. This event struck no slight fear into his opponents and brought great peace to the Catholic Church in the ordination of the bishop.

### 12

After the Catholic priest had been ordained, he returned to Milan. There he endured innumerable plots of the aforesaid woman Justina, who stirred up the people against the holy man by offering gifts and honours. Weak minds were deceived by such promises: she promised military tribuneships and various other dignities to those who would seize him from the church and lead him into exile.

Although many attempted this, they could not accomplish it, God being their protector. One man, more unhappy than the rest, named Euthymius, was stirred to such madness that he prepared a house for himself near the church and placed a cart in it, so that, when Ambrose had been seized and placed upon the carriage, he might more easily be taken into exile. [Note: Col. 31D: The reading “placed upon the carriage” is restored from nearly all the manuscripts.]

But “his iniquity descended upon his own head” (Ps. 7:17). For after a year, on the very day on which he supposed that he would seize Ambrose, he himself was placed in the same carriage and sent into exile from that same house. He recognized, by God’s just judgment, that the thing had been turned back upon himself: he was sent into exile in the carriage which he had prepared for the priest. The priest gave him no small consolation, providing expenses and whatever other necessities there were.

### 13

But this confession of the man restrained neither the woman’s fury nor the madness of the frenzied Arians. Inflamed with still greater insanity, they attempted to occupy the Portian Basilica. An armed force was even sent to guard the doors of the church, so that no one might dare enter the Catholic church.

But the Lord, who is accustomed to grant his Church triumphs over its adversaries, turned the soldiers’ hearts to the defence of his Church, so that, with their shields turned away, they guarded the church doors; they did not permit anyone to leave, but did not at all prevent the Catholic people from entering the church. [Note: Col. 31D: Some manuscripts read: “with their shields turned away … nor did they leave permission to enter, but to depart.”]

Nor was it enough that soldiers had been sent unless they also cried out together with the people for the Catholic faith. At this time antiphons, hymns, and vigils first began to be celebrated in the church of Milan. The devotion of this observance remains to the present day not only in that church, but throughout almost all the provinces of the West.

### 14

At the same time, the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius revealed themselves to the priest. They had been placed in the basilica where the bodies of the martyrs Nabor and Felix are now kept. But the holy martyrs Nabor and Felix were most frequently venerated, whereas the names and graves alike of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius were unknown—so much so that all who wished to reach the railings walked over their graves; those railings protected the graves of the holy martyrs Nabor and Felix from violation.

But when the bodies of the holy martyrs were raised and placed upon biers, the ailments of many possessed by Satan were reported there at length. A blind man named Severus, who still serves devoutly in that same basilica called the Ambrosian Basilica, to which the martyrs’ bodies were transferred, immediately received sight when he touched the martyrs’ garment. Bodies possessed by unclean spirits were also healed and returned home with the greatest joy. In proportion as faith in the Catholic Church grew through these benefits of the martyrs, Arian perfidy diminished.

### 15

Finally, from this time the persecution kindled by Justina’s fury, by which the priest was to be driven from the Church, began to subside. Yet within the palace the multitude of Arians gathered with Justina mocked the great grace which the Lord Jesus had deigned, through the merits of his martyrs, to confer upon the Catholic Church.

They claimed that the venerable Ambrose had purchased with money persons who falsely pretended to be tormented by unclean spirits, and who said that they were tortured by him as by the martyrs.

But the Arians spoke with a Jewish mouth, being plainly their equals. For the Jews said of the Lord that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons (Luke 11:15); these men said of the martyrs and of the Lord’s priest that unclean spirits were expelled not by God’s grace working through them, but that the possessed falsely claimed for money that they were being tortured.

For the demons cried: “We know you are martyrs”; while the Arians said: “We do not know that they are martyrs.”

We read the same thing in the Gospel, where the demons said to the Lord Jesus: “We know you, that you are the Son of God” (Mark 1:24); and the Jews said: “We do not know where this man comes from” (John 9:29). Yet here the testimony of demons is not received, but their confession. The Arians and Jews are therefore more pitiable, since they deny what demons confess.

### 16

Yet God, who is accustomed to increase the grace of his Church, did not permit his saints to be insulted by the faithless for long. One man from that very crowd was suddenly seized by an unclean spirit and began to cry out that those who denied the martyrs, or who did not believe in the unity of the Trinity taught by Ambrose, ought to be tortured as he himself was tortured. [Note: Col. 32D: All editions, with one or two manuscripts, read “that he wished them to be tortured”; the other manuscripts unanimously reject “he wished.”]

Confounded by this utterance, they ought to have been converted and performed repentance worthy of such a confession. Instead, they drowned the man in a pool and killed him, adding murder to perfidy; for a fitting necessity led them to this end.

But the holy bishop Ambrose, becoming a man of still greater humility, kept in reserve the grace granted him by the Lord, and daily grew in faith and love before God and human beings.

### 17

At the same time there was a certain man of the Arian heresy, an exceedingly keen disputant, hard and unyielding toward the Catholic faith.
