While he was in church and the bishop was preaching, he saw—as he later reported—an angel speaking into the ears of the bishop as he preached, so that the bishop seemed to proclaim to the people the angel’s words. Having seen this, he was converted and began himself to defend the faith which he had been attacking.

### 18

There were also two chamberlains of the emperor Gratian at that time, adherents of the Arian heresy, who proposed a question to the bishop while he was preaching and promised that they would be present at the Portian Basilica on the following day to hear its discussion; for the question concerned the incarnation of the Lord. [Note: Col. 33D: The manuscripts and edition read in the opposite order: “who were to put the question to the bishop,” and so forth.]

But on the next day those pitiable men, swollen with pride, forgot their promises. Despising God in his priest, disregarding the insult to the people waiting, and forgetting also the Lord’s saying that whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble ought to have a millstone fastened around his neck and be drowned in the depths of the sea (Matt. 18:6), they mounted a carriage, as if merely for the pleasure of riding, and left the city, while the priest and the people remained assembled in the church.

I shudder to relate the end of this contempt. Suddenly thrown from their carriage, they gave up their lives, and their bodies were committed to burial.

The holy Ambrose, ignorant of what had happened and unable to detain the people any longer, mounted the tribunal and began to speak on the question that had been proposed, saying: “Brothers, I desire to pay my debt, but I do not find my creditors of yesterday,” and the remainder found in the book entitled *On the Incarnation of the Lord* (vol. II, p. 703).

### 19

After the emperor Gratian had been killed, Ambrose undertook a second embassy to Maximus for the recovery of Gratian’s body. Anyone who wishes to know how steadfastly he acted before Maximus will approve it upon reading the letter of that embassy addressed to the younger Valentinian (Epistle 24). We judged it alien to our purpose to insert it here, lest the length of the appended letter weary the reader.

He excluded Maximus himself from communion, admonishing him to repent of the blood he had shed of his lord—and, what was more serious, of an innocent man—if he wished to secure God’s favour.

But when, in his proud spirit, Maximus rejected repentance, he lost not only his future salvation but also his present safety; and he laid aside in a cowardly fashion the kingdom which he had wickedly seized, confessing that he had been the administrator, not the emperor, of the commonwealth. [Note: Col. 33D–34D: All editions read “that he had presided over the commonwealth in the name of the state”; all manuscripts read as in the text.]

### 20

After Justina’s death, a certain soothsayer named Innocentius—innocent in name, though not in deed—was being tortured by a judge in a case of sorcery. He began to confess matters other than those about which he was being questioned. [Note: Col. 34D: Several manuscripts read, “but most cruel in deed.”]

He cried out that an angel was applying still greater torments to him than to the person who guarded Ambrose, because, in Justina’s time, he had climbed to the top of the church roof and performed sacrifices at midnight in order to stir up popular hatred against the bishop.

But the more urgently and carefully he practised evil works, the more the people’s love for the Catholic faith and for the Lord’s priest grew strong. He also confessed that he had sent demons to kill Ambrose; but the demons had reported that they could not merely approach him, but could not even come near the doors of the house in which the bishop lived, because an unconquerable fire encircled the entire building, so that those standing even at a distance were burned. Thus he had ceased the arts by which he thought himself able to do anything against the Lord’s priest.

Another man, carrying a sword, reached the bishop’s chamber in order to kill him; but when he raised his hand with the drawn sword, his outstretched right hand stiffened in the air and remained there. Once he confessed that Justina had sent him, the arm, which had stiffened as it was wickedly extended, was healed through confession.

### 21

At the same time, when the illustrious Probus sent his young secretary, who was grievously afflicted by an unclean spirit, to the bishop, the devil left the boy when he departed from the city, fearing that he would be brought to the holy man.

Thus, as long as the boy remained at Milan with the bishop, no domination of the devil appeared in him. But when he left Milan and came near Rome, the same spirit that had formerly possessed him began again to torment him.

When the exorcists asked why it had not appeared in the boy during his stay in Milan, the devil confessed that he had feared Ambrose. Therefore he had withdrawn for a time and waited in the place where he had left the boy until he returned; then, upon his return, he reclaimed the vessel which he had abandoned.

### 22

After Maximus had been destroyed and the emperor Theodosius had been established at Milan, while Ambrose the bishop was at Aquileia, a synagogue of the Jews and a grove of the Valentinians were burned by Christian men in a certain town in the eastern provinces, because the Jews or Valentinians had insulted Christian monks. The Valentinian heresy worships thirty gods.

The Count of the East sent an embassy to the emperor concerning this deed. [Note: Col. 36D: All editions read “a report was sent”; all manuscripts read “an embassy was sent,” namely one which would present the report to Caesar.]

Upon receiving it, the emperor ordered that the synagogue be rebuilt by the bishop of the place and that punishment be inflicted upon the monks. When the tenor of this command reached the ears of the venerable bishop Ambrose, he sent the emperor a letter (Epistle 40), since he himself could not travel there in time. In it he urged the emperor to revoke what he had decreed and to preserve for him a hearing.

For, if Ambrose were not worthy to be heard by the emperor, he would not be worthy either to be heard by the Lord on the emperor’s behalf, or to receive the emperor’s prayers or vows. He also declared himself ready to undergo death for such a cause, lest by his silence he make the emperor, who had commanded such unjust measures against the Church, into a transgressor.

### 23

After he returned to Milan, with the emperor present in the church, he preached to the people about the same matter. In this sermon he introduced the person of the Lord speaking to the emperor:

> “I made you emperor from the lowest estate; I delivered into your hands the army of your enemy; I gave you the resources which he had prepared for his army against you; I reduced your enemy to your power; I established one of your seed upon the throne of the kingdom; I made you triumph without labour—and you grant triumphs over me to my enemies!”

As he descended from the tribunal, the emperor said: “Bishop, today you have spoken against us.” He replied that he had spoken not against the emperor, but for him.

Then the emperor said: “Indeed, I had harshly commanded that the bishop rebuild the synagogue; but that punishment should be inflicted upon the monks.” The officials present said the same. To them the bishop replied: “I am now dealing with the emperor; with you, however, I must deal differently.”

Thus he obtained the revocation of what had been decreed. Nor would he approach the altar until the emperor declared that he ought to proceed upon the emperor’s faith.

The bishop said: “Then I proceed upon your faith.”

The emperor answered: “Proceed upon my faith.”

When this assurance had been repeated, the priest, now secure, performed the divine mysteries.

These things are written in the letter which he composed to his sister (Epistle 41), in which he included the sermon he delivered that same day concerning the hazel rod seen by the prophet Jeremiah.

### 24

At the same time, the affair of the city of Thessalonica brought no slight distress upon the priest, when he learned that the city had been almost destroyed. The emperor had promised him pardon for the citizens of that city; but, after the officials had secretly dealt with the emperor without the priest’s knowledge, the city was given to the sword until the third hour, and very many innocent persons were killed. [Note: Col. 35D: Several manuscripts read, “the city was given to them until the third hour,” and so forth.]

When the priest learned what had been done, he refused the emperor permission to enter the church. Nor did he judge him worthy of the congregation of the Church or communion in the sacraments before he had performed public repentance.

The emperor replied that David had committed adultery and murder together. The immediate answer was: “You who have followed him in sin, follow him in amendment.”

When the most gracious emperor heard this, he received it with such a disposition that he did not shrink from public repentance. The benefit of this correction prepared for him a second victory.

### 25

At the same time, two most powerful and wise Persians came to Milan on account of the priest’s reputation, bringing with them many questions in order to test the man’s wisdom. Through an interpreter they debated with him from the first hour of the day until the third hour of the night, and departed from him in admiration.

To demonstrate that they had come for no other reason than to know beyond all doubt the man of whose reputation they had heard, on the following day they took leave of the emperor and set out for the city of Rome, wishing there to learn the influence of the illustrious Probus. Having learned it, they returned to their own country.

### 26

But after Theodosius had left Italy and been established at Constantinople, and the emperor Valentinian had been stationed in Gaul, an embassy was sent in the name of the senate by Symmachus, then prefect of the City, to request the restoration of the Altar of Victory and the funding of ceremonial rites. [Note: Col. 36D: All editions read “a report was sent”; all manuscripts read “an embassy was sent,” namely one which would present the report to Caesar.]

When the priest learned of it, he sent a memorial to the emperor (Epistles 17 and 18), requesting that copies of the report be sent to him, so that he might reply on his own side. Having received the report, he composed a most distinguished memorial, to which Symmachus, though a most eloquent man, never dared make any response.

But after Valentinian of august memory ended his life in the city of Vienne, a city of Gaul, Eugenius assumed imperial power. Not long after he began to rule, at the request of Flavian, then prefect, and Count Arbogast, he granted the Altar of Victory and the ceremonial revenues. Valentinian of august memory, though still in his younger years, had refused these requests; but Eugenius, forgetful of his faith, granted them.

### 27

When the priest learned this, he left the city of Milan, to which Eugenius was hastening, moved to the city of Bologna, and went from there as far as Faenza. After staying there for some days, he was invited by the Florentines and went down into Tuscany, avoiding rather the sight of the sacrilegious man than fearing the wrong of the ruler.

He also gave Eugenius a letter (Epistle 57), in which he confronted his conscience. I have judged it suitable to set down a few passages from many:

> “And though imperial power is great, nevertheless consider, Emperor, how great God is. He sees human hearts, examines the inward conscience, knows all things before they happen, knows the secrets of your breast. You do not allow yourselves to be deceived, and do you wish to conceal yourselves from God? Did nothing occur to your mind? If they acted so persistently, was it not your duty, Emperor, to resist more steadfastly out of reverence for God most high, true, and living, and to refuse what was an injury to the sacred law?” (Num. 7)

And again:

> “Since therefore I am bound by my words both before God and before all people, I have understood that I may not do otherwise, nor ought I to do otherwise, except to take counsel for myself, since I could not do so for you.”

### 28

In the aforesaid city of the Florentines, he stayed in the house of Decens, formerly a most distinguished man and, what is more, a Christian. Decens’s very small son, named Pansophius, suffered from an unclean spirit and was healed through the priest’s frequent prayer and laying on of hands. But after a few days the child was seized by a sudden illness and breathed his last.

His mother, a woman most devout and full of faith and fear of God, took him from the upper part of the house downstairs and, in the priest’s absence, laid him on the priest’s bed. When the priest returned and found him on the little bed—for at that time he had been outside the house—he pitied the mother and regarded her faith. Like Elisha, he stretched himself upon the child’s body; and by prayer he deserved to restore alive to his mother the child whom he had found dead.

He also composed a little book for the child, so that he might learn through reading what he could not know because of his infancy. Nevertheless, he did not mention this deed in his writings; but it is not ours to judge the motive by which he declined to mention it.

### 29

In the same city he also established a basilica, in which he deposited the relics of the martyrs Vitalis and Agricola, whose bodies he had raised at Bologna (*Exhortation on Virginity*, p. 227). The martyrs’ bodies had been placed among Jewish bodies, and the Christian people would not have known of them unless the holy martyrs had revealed themselves to the priest of his church. [Note: Col. 37D: The editions, with one German manuscript, read “had revealed themselves to the priest himself”; the other manuscripts read as in the text.]

When they were deposited beneath the altar established in that basilica, there was great joy and exultation among the whole holy people; the punishment of demons confessing the merits of the martyrs.

### 30

At the same time Count Arbogast prepared war against his own people, the Franks. In fighting, he destroyed no small multitude by the sword, but made peace with the survivors.

While at a banquet he was asked by the kings of his people whether he knew Ambrose. He answered that he knew the man, was loved by him, and had often dined with him. He heard this reply: “Count, you conquer because you are loved by that man who says to the sun, ‘Stand still,’ and it stands still.”

I have included this so that readers may recognize how great the holy man’s reputation was even among barbarian peoples. For we too learned it from a very devout young attendant of Arbogast, who was present at the time; he was then serving the wine when these things were said. [Note: Col. 37D: The manuscripts read as in the text, with one exception; the edition reads “when he was saying these things.”]

### 31

The priest therefore departed from Tuscany and returned to Milan. Eugenius had already left there to march against Theodosius. At Milan Ambrose awaited the coming of the Christian emperor, confident in God’s power: that he would not hand over one who trusted in him to unjust people, nor leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity (Ps. 124:3).

For Count Arbogast and Prefect Flavian had promised, when leaving Milan, that if they returned victorious, they would make a stable in the basilica of the church of Milan and test the clergy under arms. But those pitiable men, wickedly credulous along with their demons, opened their mouth in blasphemy before God and deprived themselves of hope of victory. [Note: Col. 37D–38D: All editions read “against God”; all manuscripts read “before God.”]

The cause of the disturbance was this: the Church rejected the gifts of the emperor who had involved himself in sacrilege, and he was not granted fellowship in prayer with the Church. But the Lord, who is accustomed to protect his Church, hurled judgment from heaven and transferred the whole victory to the devout emperor Theodosius.

After Eugenius and his followers had been destroyed, when Ambrose received letters from the emperor, no concern was greater to him than to intercede for those whom he found guilty. He first entreated the emperor by letters sent through a deacon (Epistles 61 and 62). Then, after John—at that time a tribune and secretary, now prefect—had been sent to protect those who had taken refuge in the Church, Ambrose himself went to Aquileia to pray for them. Pardon was readily obtained, because the Christian emperor himself, falling at the priest’s feet, testified that he had been saved through Ambrose’s merits and prayers.

### 32

Returning from the city of Aquileia, Ambrose arrived one day before the emperor. Not long afterward, the emperor Theodosius of most gracious memory, having received his sons in the church and entrusted them to the priest, departed this life. Ambrose survived him by almost three years.

During this time he raised the body of the holy martyr Nazarius, which lay in a garden outside the city, and transferred it to the Basilica of the Apostles, which is in the Roman district. [Note: Col. 38D: All editions read “which is Roman”; the manuscripts, conversely, read “which is in the Roman district,” that is, near the Roman Gate of the city of Milan.]

In the tomb where the martyr’s body lay—we cannot know to this day when he suffered—we saw the martyr’s blood as fresh as if it had been poured out that very day. His head also, though cut off by impious persons, was so whole and incorrupt, with the hair of his head and beard, that it seemed to us that, at the moment it was raised, it had been washed and laid out in the tomb.

And what wonder is this, since the Lord promised beforehand in the Gospel that not a hair of their head would perish (Luke 21:18)? We were also filled with so great a fragrance that it surpassed the sweetness of every perfume.

### 33

Once the martyr’s body had been raised and placed upon a bier, we immediately went with the holy priest to pray at the holy martyr Celsus, who lay in the same garden. We had never known him to pray there before; but it was the sign of the martyr’s body having been revealed that the holy priest went to pray at a place where he had never previously been.

Yet we learned from the guardians of the place that their parents had handed down to them the obligation never to depart from that place throughout every generation and line of their descendants, because great treasures lay there. And truly they were great treasures, which neither rust nor moth destroys, and which thieves neither dig up nor steal (Matt. 6:19), because Christ is their guardian and the heavenly court their dwelling-place; for them, “to live was Christ and to die gain” (Phil. 1:21).

After the martyr’s body was transferred to the Basilica of the Apostles, where the relics of the holy apostles had long before been deposited with the highest devotion of all, the bishop was preaching when a man among the people, filled with an unclean spirit, began to cry that he was being tortured by Ambrose. [Note: Col. 38D: Some manuscripts read, “where, on the preceding day, [the relics] of the holy apostles [were deposited].”]

Turning to him, Ambrose said: “Be silent, devil. Ambrose does not torture you; the faith of the saints and your own envy torture you. For you see human beings ascending to the place from which you were cast down. Ambrose does not know how to be puffed up.”

At these words the man who had been crying fell silent, was thrown to the ground, and uttered no further sound with which he could make a disturbance.

### 34

At the same time, when the emperor Honorius, during his consulship, gave a spectacle of Libyan beasts in the city of Milan and the people flocked there, soldiers sent by Count Stilicho at the urging of the prefect Eusebius were given leave to seize a certain Cresconius from the church. [Note: Col. 39D: Thus the Gill edition and most manuscripts; some others read “permission was given to the unjust soldiers,” while the Roman edition reads “permission was given to the soldiers.”]

When he fled to the Lord’s altar, the holy bishop, with the clergy then present, surrounded him in defence. But the multitude of soldiers, which had two leaders adhering to Arian perfidy, prevailed over the few. [Note: Col. 39D: Some manuscripts read “which had two leaders.”]

Having taken Cresconius away, they returned exultantly to the amphitheatre, leaving the Church in no small grief; for the priest lay prostrate before the Lord’s altar and wept long over what had been done.

But when they later returned and reported to those who had sent them, leopards were released. With swift leaps they mounted to the very place where those who had triumphed over the Church were sitting and left them grievously torn.

When Count Stilicho saw this, he was moved to repentance, so that for many days he made satisfaction to the priest. He released unharmed the man who had been taken; but because he was guilty of very grave crimes and could not otherwise be corrected, Stilicho sent him into exile, though not long afterward clemency followed.

### 35

At the same time, when he was going to the palace and we were following him by reason of our office, Theodulus then being secretary—he afterward governed the church of Modena with the highest favour—a certain man happened to slip and fall to the ground. [Note: Col. 39D: Some manuscripts read “Theodore, then secretary”; one reads “Theodore was then secretary,” less well.]

The priest turned to the person laughing at the occurrence and said: “You also who stand, see that you do not fall” (1 Cor. 10:12). At these words, the man who had laughed at another’s fall immediately came to regret his own.

36. At the same time, a certain Frigitil, queen of the Marcomanni, having heard from a Christian man who had happened to arrive in her country from Italy a report concerning the bishop, believed in Christ, whose servant she recognized him to be. She sent gifts to Milan and, through envoys, asked the Church that she might be instructed in writing how she ought to believe. He wrote her an excellent letter in the form of a catechism, in which he also urged her to persuade her husband to keep peace with the Romans. Upon receiving the letter, the woman persuaded her husband to surrender himself and his people to the Romans. When she came to Milan, she was greatly grieved that she did not find the holy bishop, whom she had hastened to meet; for he had already departed from this life.

[Col. 0040A] 37. In the time of Gratian, to return to an earlier point: when he had gone to the residence of Macedonius, then master of offices, to intercede for someone, and, by order of the aforesaid man, found the doors shut and was not allowed to enter, he said: “You too will come to the church and, though its doors are not shut, will find no way to enter.”  
[Note: [Col. 0039D] All editions, with one Colbert manuscript: “nor will you enter”; [Col. 0040D] although the doors are not shut. One German manuscript: “and, with the doors open, you will find no way by which I may enter.” The remaining manuscripts read as in the text.]  
And so it happened. For after Gratian’s death, Macedonius fled to the church, but, though its doors stood open, was unable to find admission.

38. This venerable bishop was a man of great abstinence, many vigils, and many labours. He wore down his body by daily fasting, being never accustomed to take a meal except on Saturday, Sunday, or the anniversaries of the most celebrated martyrs. His constancy in prayer, by day and by night, was likewise great. Nor did he shrink from the labour of writing books with his own hand, unless some illness afflicted his body.  
[Note: [Col. 0040D] Thus seven manuscripts; one German manuscript and the editions read: “unless his body was weakened.”]  
He also bore concern for all the churches, and showed great constancy and perseverance in interceding. In performing divine rites he was exceedingly vigorous: what he had customarily performed alone for those to be baptized could scarcely be accomplished by five bishops at the time of his death. He was also exceedingly solicitous for the poor and for captives. When he was ordained bishop, he gave all the gold and silver he possessed to the Church or to the poor. He also gave his estates to the Church, reserving their usufruct for his sister, and left himself nothing that he could call his own in this world, so that, naked and unencumbered as a soldier, he might follow Christ the Lord: “Though he was rich, for our sakes he became poor, that we through his poverty might become rich” (2 Cor. 8:9).

39. He also rejoiced with those who rejoiced and wept with those who wept (Rom. 12:15). Whenever anyone confessed his falls to him in order to receive penance, he wept so greatly that he compelled that person also to weep; for he seemed to himself to lie fallen together with the fallen person. Yet he spoke to no one but the Lord alone, before whom he interceded, of the causes of sins confessed to him. Thus he left a good example for later priests: that they should be intercessors before God rather than accusers before human beings. For, according to the Apostle (2 Cor. 2:8), love ought to be confirmed toward such a person, because that person is his own accuser: he does not wait for an accuser, but anticipates one, so that by confessing he himself may lighten his sin,  
[Note: [Col. 0040D] Four manuscripts: “may absolve”; one: “may wash away”; another: “may bind”; the remaining two and the editions: “may lighten.”]  
lest the adversary have anything of which to accuse him. Therefore Scripture says: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself in his speech” (Prov. 18:17). He takes away the adversary’s voice and, as it were, breaks by the confession of his sins the teeth prepared for the prey of hostile accusation, giving honour to God, before whom all things are naked (Heb. 4:13), and who wills the sinner’s life rather than death (Ezek. 18:32). For confession alone does not suffice for the penitent unless amendment of the deed follows, so that the penitent may not do things needing repentance. Let him also humble his soul, as holy David did: after he heard from the prophet, “Your sin is forgiven” (2 Sam. 12:14), he became more humble in correcting his sin, so that he ate ashes like bread and mingled his drink with weeping (Ps. 101:10).

40. He also wept most bitterly whenever news happened to be brought to him of the death of any holy priest, so much so that we tried to console him,  
[Note: [Col. 0041D] All editions: “we tried to console him”; all manuscripts: “we seemed to console him.”]  
not understanding the pious affection of the man or why he wept in this way. He would give us an answer of this kind: he did not weep because the man reported dead had departed, but because he had gone before; or because it was difficult to find a man who could be judged worthy of the highest priesthood. He also foretold concerning his own death that he would remain with us until Easter; and this he obtained by entreating the Lord, that he might be released from this life sooner.

41. He groaned deeply when he saw the root of all evils, avarice, sprouting forth. It can be diminished neither by abundance nor by want, and he saw it growing more and more among people, especially among those established in positions of power. Thus it was an exceedingly heavy labour for him to intercede with them, because everything was sold for a price. This was what first brought every evil into Italy, and from this all things are turning for the worse. And what shall I say, when avarice exercises its fury so fiercely in persons of this kind, who are accustomed to plead the causes either of children or relatives, “to devise excuses for sins” (Ps. 140:4)? For frivolity has seized even many celibate priests, whose portion is God, so that they too may desire it (Deut. 18:2). Alas for us wretches, because not even the end of the world urges us to desire release from so heavy a yoke of slavery, which plunges us into the depths of hell, so that we might make friends for ourselves from unrighteous mammon, who may receive us into eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9). Yet blessed is the person who, at last converted, having burst the bonds and cast off the yoke of such dominion, will take and dash its little ones against the rock (Ps. 136:9): that is, will dash all its impulses against Christ, who, according to the Apostle, is the rock. He destroys all who dash themselves against him, while himself remaining inviolable; and he does not make guilty the one who dashes against him the worse offspring of a most wicked womb, but makes that person innocent, so that he may safely say: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. 118:57). For to the one who has nothing in the world Christ is truly a portion; and “whoever despises small things shall receive great things, and besides shall possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29).

42. A few days before he was confined to his bed, while he was dictating Psalm 43, with me both taking it down and watching, a short flame in the shape of a shield suddenly covered his head, and gradually entered through his mouth as though entering the house of its inhabitant. After this his face became like snow, and afterwards his countenance returned to its usual appearance. As this happened, I was struck dumb with astonishment and could not write what he said until the vision itself had passed. For at that time he was speaking a testimony from divine Scripture, which I retained very well. That very day he ceased writing and dictating; indeed, he could not complete the psalm. What I had seen I immediately reported to the honourable man Castus, the deacon under whose care I lived. Filled with God’s grace, he taught me, from the reading of the Acts of the Apostles, that I had seen in him the coming of the Holy Spirit.

43. In earlier days, a slave of Count Stilicho, who had suffered from a demon and now remained healed in the Ambrosian basilica, commended there by his master—for it was said that Stilicho held him in affection—was discovered to have forged letters of military appointment, so that men were arrested when they went to present themselves for service. But when the matter came to concern his own servant, Count Stilicho was unwilling to punish him. At the bishop’s intervention he released the men who had been deceived, though he complained to the bishop concerning the servant himself. As the holy man was leaving the Ambrosian basilica, he ordered the servant to be sought and brought before him. After questioning him and discovering him to be the author of so grave an outrage, he said: “He must be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that no one may dare commit such things hereafter” (1 Cor. 5:5). At that very moment, while the words were still in the bishop’s mouth, an unclean spirit began to seize and tear the man. At this sight we were filled with no small fear and amazement. In those days we also saw many people cleansed from unclean spirits when he laid hands upon them and commanded them to depart.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] Thus the manuscripts. The edition reads: “it was discovered that he forged letters of military appointment.”]

44. At the same time, a certain Nicentius, formerly a tribune and notary, was so afflicted with pain in his feet that he was seldom seen in public. When he approached the altar to receive the sacraments and was accidentally stepped on by the bishop, he cried out; and he heard: “Go, and from now on you shall be well.” He testified with tears that his feet did not pain him thereafter until the holy bishop departed this life.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] Erasmus and Gillius, with some manuscripts, spell this name thus; the Roman edition, with other manuscripts, reads “a certain Nicetius.” Immediately afterwards, instead of “formerly a tribune and notary,” the Beccensis manuscript has “an ex-tribune and notary.” One German manuscript: “from a tribune, a notary.”]

45. But after these days, when a bishop had been ordained for the Church of Ticinum, he fell ill and was confined to his bed for many days. Count Stilicho is said to have declared that, if so great a man departed the body, Italy’s ruin was imminent. He therefore summoned distinguished men of that city whom he knew to be loved by the holy bishop, and partly threatened them and partly persuaded them with gentle speech to go to the holy bishop and urge him to ask the Lord for permission to continue living. When he heard this from them, he replied: “I have not lived among you in such a way that I should be ashamed to live; nor do I fear to die, because we have a good Lord.”

46. At the same time, at the far end of the portico in which he lay, Castus, Polemius, Venerius, and Felix, then deacons, were discussing among themselves in tones so low that they could scarcely hear one another who should be ordained bishop after his death. When they mentioned the holy Simplicianus by name, Ambrose, though he lay far from them, as though he had been present at their discussion, cried out approvingly three times: “An old man, but good.” Simplicianus was indeed advanced in age. Terrified at hearing this voice, they fled. Yet after Ambrose’s death no one else succeeded him in the priesthood except the one whom he had designated three times as “the good old man.” Venerius, mentioned above, succeeded Simplicianus. Felix still governs the Church of Bologna; Castus and Polemius, nourished by Ambrose, the good fruits of a good tree, serve as deacons in the Church of Milan.

47. In that same place where he lay, as we learned on the report of the holy Bassianus, bishop of the Church of Lodi, who had heard it from Ambrose himself, while he was praying with the aforesaid bishop, Ambrose saw the Lord Jesus come to him and smile upon him. Not many days afterward he was taken from us. On the day he departed to the Lord, from about the eleventh hour until the hour in which he gave up his spirit, he prayed with his hands outstretched in the form of a cross. We saw his lips moving but heard no voice.

Honoratus, a priest of the Church of Vercelli, had retired to rest in an upper part of the house when, three times, he heard a voice calling him and saying: “Rise, make haste, for he is about to depart now.” Going down, he offered the holy man the body of the Lord. When Ambrose received and swallowed it, he gave up his spirit, carrying with him good provision for the journey, so that his soul, refreshed by the strength of that food, might now rejoice in the company of angels—whose life he had lived on earth—and in the fellowship of Elijah. For as Elijah never feared to speak before kings or any powers, neither did Ambrose fear, for the fear of God, to speak.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] All editions: “When he received it, he gave up his spirit”; all manuscripts read as in the text.]

48. From there, at the pre-dawn hour in which he died, his body was carried to the greater church. There, on the same night on which we kept vigil for Easter, very many infants newly baptized, as they came from the font, saw him. Some said that he sat in a chair in the apse; others pointed him out to their parents as walking. But those parents, though they looked, could not see, because they did not possess purified eyes. Very many also related that they saw a star above his body. But at daybreak on Sunday, when the divine sacraments had been completed and his body was carried from the church to be borne to the Ambrosian basilica, in which he was laid, such a multitude of demons cried out there that they were tortured by him that their howlings could not be endured. This grace of the bishop remains not only in that place but also in very many provinces to the present day. Crowds of men and women also threw their scarves or girdles so that they might somehow touch the saint’s body. The funeral crowd was innumerable, comprising every rank, both sexes, and almost every age—not only Christians, but Jews and pagans too. Yet the order of those who had been baptized went before with greater favour.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] All editions: “his body before dawn”; most manuscripts: “before the pre-dawn hour”; all restore: “at the hour at which he died.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0043D] Some manuscripts: “others pointed out that he was ascending . . . But none except the newly baptized could see him, because they had such purified eyes,” etc.]

49. On the very day on which he died—as the text of a letter declares, sent from the East to his successor, the venerable Simplicianus, as though addressed to Ambrose while he was still alive among us, and still preserved at Milan in a monastery—he appeared to certain holy men, praying with them and laying hands upon them. The letter bears the date on which it was sent; when it was read, we found that the date was the day on which he died.

[Note: [Col. 0044D] Thus the editions and not a few manuscripts; others read: “he appeared in the monastery of a certain holy man.”]

50. Within Tuscany also, in the city of Florence, where the holy man Zenobius is now bishop, we learned on the testimony of Zenobius himself that, because Ambrose had promised those who asked him that he would visit them often, he was frequently seen praying at the altar in the Ambrosian basilica established there by him. In the same house in which he lodged while turning aside to avoid Eugenius, during the time when Radagaisus was besieging the aforesaid city and the citizens had completely despaired for themselves, he appeared in a vision to someone and promised that help would come to them on the following day. When this was reported, the citizens’ spirits were raised; for on the next day Count Stilicho came with an army and victory over the enemy was won. We learned this from the report of the devout woman Pansophia, mother of the boy Pansophius.

[Note: [Col. 0044D] All editions: “because he had promised that he would visit them often . . . he was seen praying, as the holy priest Zenobius himself,” etc.; all manuscripts read as in the text.]

51. To Mascezel also, when he despaired for his own safety and for that of the army he was leading against Gildo, Ambrose appeared in a nocturnal vision holding a staff in his hand. As Mascezel rolled himself at the holy man’s feet, the old man struck the ground with the staff on which he leaned and said three times—for this was the form in which he appeared to him—“Here, here, here,” marking the place. He gave understanding to the man whom he judged worthy of such a visitation, so that he might know that on the third day he would win victory in the place where he had seen the holy bishop of the Lord; and thus, confident, he began and completed the battle. We learned this while we were staying in Milan, from Mascezel himself. For in this province, where we now are and write these things, he related the same account to very many priests; and, reassured by their reports as well, we thought it proper to append this knowledge to this book.

[Note: [Col. 0044D] One German manuscript: “on that day at Milan.”]

52. When we received with the greatest devotion at Milan the relics of the martyrs Sisinnius and Alexander, who in our own times—that is, after the death of holy Ambrose—received the crown of martyrdom in the region of Anaunia while pagan men persecuted them, we learned from a certain blind man who came and reported that on the very day he had touched the bier in which the relics of the saints were carried and received his sight. In a nocturnal vision, he had seen a ship approaching the shore, in which was a multitude of men clothed in white. When they came ashore, he asked one of the crowd who those men were and heard: “Ambrose and his companions.” On hearing the name, he begged to receive sight and heard from him: “Go to Milan and meet my brothers who will come there, on the appointed day, and you will receive sight.” For, as he himself asserted, he was a man from the Dalmatian shore. He said that he had not come into the city before he met the saints’ relics by a direct route, while still unable to see; but when he touched the bier, he began to see.

[Note: [Col. 0045C] The edition reads, “while pagan men persecuted them, [they received] the crown of martyrdom”; certain Paris manuscripts, with one manuscript, read “the crown of true martyrdom”; the remaining manuscripts support our reading.]

53. Having recounted these matters, I do not think it burdensome if we go a little beyond the bounds of our promise, in order to show fulfilled the saying of the Lord spoken through the holy prophets: “Him who secretly slanders his neighbour, I pursued” (Ps. 100:5); and elsewhere: “Do not love slander, lest you be uprooted” (Prov. 20:13). Thus anyone perhaps held captive by such a habit, when he reads how punishment was inflicted upon those who dared slander the holy man, may also amend himself in relation to others.

54. A certain Donatus, an African by birth and a priest of the Church of Milan, while dining in company with certain devout military men, slandered the memory of the bishop. They rejected and abandoned his wicked speech; suddenly he was struck by a severe blow, lifted from the very place where he lay by other people’s hands, placed upon a bed, and carried from there to the grave.

[Note: [Col. 0045C] The same editions read: “certain devout men”; the manuscripts: “certain military men,” etc.]  
[Note: [Col. 0045C] Most and the better manuscripts read thus; the edition with some others: “lifted by hands.”]

In the city of Carthage likewise, I had gathered for a meal at the house of Fortunatus, deacon and brother of the venerable bishop Aurelius, with Vincentius, bishop of Colossae, Muranus, bishop of Bolita, and other bishops and deacons. When Bishop Muranus slandered the holy man, I related to him the end of the priest mentioned above. What had been said of another he proved to be an oracle concerning himself by his own speedy death. For, suddenly struck by a grievous blow in the very place where he lay, he was carried by other people’s hands as far as a bed, taken from there to the house in which he was lodging, and ended his last day. Such was the end of those men who slandered him; those then present, seeing it, were astonished.

[Note: [Col. 0045C] Some manuscripts: “Vincentius, bishop of Culusium”; one: “of Colita.”]

55. Therefore I exhort and entreat every person who reads this book to imitate the holy man’s life, praise God’s grace, and avoid the tongues of slanderers, if he wishes rather to share with Ambrose in the resurrection of life than to undergo with those slanderers the punishment which no wise person fails to avoid.

56. I also beseech your blessedness, Father Augustine, to deign to pray for me, Paulinus, a most humble sinner, together with all the saints who invoke the name of our Lord Jesus Christ with you in truth, so that, since I am unworthy to share with so great a man in the attainment of grace, having obtained pardon for my sins, I may have as my reward the escape from punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0045C] There have not been lacking persons who, deceived by the name Paulinus, failed to distinguish this writer from Paulinus, bishop of Nola, and did not hesitate to preface this Life of Ambrose in some manuscripts thus: “Here begins the Prologue of Bishop Paulinus.” The same title was inscribed at the beginning of the Erasmian edition. Yet, apart from the fact that in very many more manuscripts the author’s name is either not placed at the head of the Life, or is accompanied not by the title “bishop” but only by that of “notary of Ambrose,” it is beyond dispute that this Paulinus is altogether different from the Nolan. From what he himself says above in §42, we understand that a few days before Ambrose’s blessed death he was still a cleric of inferior rank, whereas Paulinus of Nola testifies in his letter to Alypius that he had already become a bishop before Ambrose’s death. It is commonly inferred from Isidore, On Illustrious Men, ch. 4, that this Paulinus later attained the rank of presbyter. Had Erasmus and those who followed him, certain heterodox persons, considered these matters more carefully, they would have rendered a less unjust judgment on this author. But the former disliked the inclusion of several miracle accounts, while the latter could not avoid being offended by certain passages plainly contrary to their errors.]

[Col. 0045]

# The Life and Conduct of Our Holy Father Ambrose, Bishop of Milan

[Note: [Col. 0045D] This Life of Ambrose survives in several elegantly written parchment manuscripts in the Colbert Library, from which we present it here. It is not a careful work, since it recalls only those deeds of Ambrose reported by Theodoret, from whom the anonymous author—perhaps none other than Metaphrastes—compiled it in almost the same words. Nevertheless, since this same Life has not, to our knowledge, previously been published, we have not hesitated to make it public, so that after the Latin historical Life of Ambrose written by Paulinus, the reader may see at a single glance what opinion the ancient Greeks held concerning our bishop.]

[Note: [Col. 0045] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## Greek version

[Col. 0045D] 1. After the death of Jovian, Valentinian succeeded to the imperial sceptres. Bringing his own brother Valens from Pannonia, he made him partner in the empire, entrusting to him the sceptres of Asia and Egypt as well; he assigned Europe to himself. Having come to Rome, he led all the western peoples toward the true knowledge of God, beginning his rule above all with proclamations of piety.

2. For when Auxentius, who had accepted the corruption of Arius and had been entrusted with the church of Milan, had been condemned in very many synods and died, Valentinian summoned the bishops and addressed them in these terms:

“You know clearly, since you are versed in the divine words, what manner of man he ought to be who is judged worthy of the high priesthood; and that he must regulate those under his rule not merely by speech but also by life, setting himself forth as an exemplar of every virtue and having his conduct as a testimony to his teaching. Establish, then, such a man now upon the high-priestly throne, so that we too, who direct the empire, may sincerely bow our heads to him and welcome his rebukes as medical treatment. For, being human beings, it is altogether necessary that we should stumble.”

3. When the pious emperor Valentinian had said these things, the synod asked him to make the choice, since he was wise and adorned with piety. But he said: “The undertaking is greater than we can manage. You, who have been judged worthy of divine grace and have received that radiance, will make the better choice.”

So they went out and deliberated by themselves. But the inhabitants of that city were in factional conflict, some contending that this man and others that that man should be appointed. Those infected with the disease of Auxentius voted for men of their own mind; those of the sound party, by contrast, sought to have a high priest of like belief.

The divine Ambrose, illustrious in the Roman senate, had, after holding many other offices, been entrusted at that time by the pious emperors Constantine and Constans with the governorship of Italy. He was a man pure in life, a lover of virtue, distinguished in word and deed; nourished by the wisdom of the divine Scriptures, though not yet initiated [in baptism], and trained both in Greek eloquence and in poetry. He judged justly and soundly, and was a strict reprover of every wicked action.

[Col. 0048D] 4. When he learned of this disturbance and feared that some revolutionary act might occur, he hastened to the church and calmed the turmoil in both parties. They then ceased their contention and raised a common cry, asking that blessed Ambrose himself be appointed their shepherd. When the emperor heard this, he immediately ordered that this praiseworthy man be baptized and ordained. He knew that Ambrose’s judgment was straighter than any balance and his decisions more exact than any rule. He also inferred that the choice was divine from the agreement of those who had formerly held opposing views.

[Col. 0049A] 5. When Ambrose had received the gift of the all-holy baptism and accepted episcopal grace, the excellent emperor, who was present at these events, is said to have offered this hymn to the Saviour and Lord:

“Thanks be to you, almighty Master and our Saviour, because I entrusted bodies to this man, but you have entrusted souls; and you have declared my decision to be just.”

6. A few days later, when this divine Ambrose addressed the emperor with greater freedom and reproached him because certain matters had not been rightly conducted by his officials, the emperor said: “Indeed, I had long known this freedom of speech of yours; and, knowing it clearly, not only did I not oppose your ordination, but I also gave my vote with it. Therefore heal, as the divine law commands, the offences of our souls.”

7. This is what Valentinian, the great and pious emperor, said and did at Milan. Having governed the empire well and shone in orthodoxy, he ended his life in the sixteenth year of his reign. He left as successors his sons Gratian and the younger Valentinian. His brother Valens was already ruling in the East, and he adhered to the Arian heresy. When Valens fought the Goths and was defeated, he took refuge in a barn and was consumed there by fire. The whole Roman dominion passed to Gratian, son of Valentinian and nephew of Valens: first he had received from his father the sceptres of Europe and of the entire West, and then, when childless Valens had been killed, he also received Asia and the remaining regions of Libya. Since he was pious like his father, Gratian recalled from exile all the bishops whom Valens had made exiles and driven from their homeland because of the Arian heresy. When Gratian learned that Thrace was being ravaged by barbarians who had overcome Valens, he left Italy and came to Pannonia.

8. At the same time Theodosius was highly renowned both for the distinction of his ancestors and for his own courage. Attacked by the envy of men of equal rank, he was living in Spain, where he had been born and raised. Gratian, uncertain what should be done—for the barbarians, inflated by victory, were formidable and were thought invincible—considered Theodosius’ generalship the remedy for these evils. Immediately summoning him from Iberia, also called Spain, appointing him general, and sending him out with the gathered army, he dispatched him against the enemy. Armed with the invincible weapon of orthodoxy, Theodosius advanced confidently against them. Entering Thrace, he won the battle decisively. The barbarians did not even endure the first onset, but all fled together. A great slaughter of them ensued, inflicted not only by the Romans but also by themselves; for the more numerous they were, the more they appeared to harm themselves rather than their enemies.

9. Thus, when almost all had been destroyed, a few who managed to escape notice crossed the Danube. Gratian, delighted that he had made so excellent a choice of Theodosius as general, immediately proclaimed him emperor and entrusted to him the sceptres of Valens’ former dominion. Gratian himself crossed into Italy, while he sent Theodosius to the authority granted him. Having assumed imperial rule, Theodosius took the utmost care for concord among the churches and commanded the bishops of his own jurisdiction to assemble at Constantinople. For that city alone was full of the Arian corruption. The western regions were free from the disease, because Constantine and Constans, sons of Constantine the Great, had preserved their father’s faith uncorrupted, and Valentinian likewise had not betrayed his own piety. But the eastern portion had received this corruption in many places, beginning first in Alexandria and spreading onward.

10. These things occurred while Gratian was still alive. Afterwards, when he had already shown his character in military affairs and governed cities with moderation and justice, he died through treachery. He left no sons to succeed to the empire, but made his very young brother, who bore his father’s name, successor to the imperial power. Then a certain Maximus, despising Valentinian’s youth, seized the throne of the western empire.

[Col. 0052C] 11. At that time Justina, wife of the great Valentinian and mother of the younger Valentinian, who had long received the seeds of Arian teaching, disclosed them to her son. Knowing her husband’s zeal for orthodox faith, she had tried to remain hidden while he lived. But knowing that her son’s mind was tender and susceptible to influence, she dared to produce her deception openly. The young man, thinking his mother’s suggestions beneficial and looking toward nature’s alluring bait, suddenly fell into the trap. Great Ambrose, who had long before driven every Arian deception out of Italy, learned that the young Valentinian also had fallen into it, and did his utmost to free the young man’s soul from it. Yet Valentinian regarded the man with suspicion and hostility, as though preparing for war against an acknowledged enemy.

12. Ambrose reminded him of his father’s piety and urged him to preserve inviolate the inheritance he had received. He taught him the difference between the doctrines, showing how one accorded entirely with the Lord’s teaching and the preaching of the apostles, while the other openly opposed the spiritual law. But the youth, being young and charmed by his deceived mother, not only refused to receive the bishop’s words, but was filled with anger, armed himself with threats, and surrounded the church precincts with shield-bearers.

[Col. 0053A] 13. Since none of these actions frightened that greatest champion, divine Ambrose—for he regarded them as children’s bogeys—Valentinian, enraged without restraint, ordered the man to leave the sacred doors. But Ambrose replied: “I shall not willingly do this or betray the sheepfold to wolves, even at the cost of blood. But if you think fit to kill me, bring sword or spear against me within; I shall receive such slaughter most gladly.” Such were the words of divine Ambrose.

14. After considerable time had passed, Maximus learned what was being dared against the great-voiced herald of truth. He wrote to Valentinian, instructing him to end his war against piety and advising him not to abandon his paternal piety. If he did not obey, Maximus threatened him with a most grievous war. He also raised an army and advanced against Milan, where Valentinian was said to be staying. Learning of Maximus’ expedition, Valentinian fled into Illyricum, discovering by actual experience what profit he had gained from his mother’s counsel.

15. Emperor Theodosius learned what had happened to the young Valentinian and what Maximus had written to him. He wrote to the fugitive youth that he ought not to be surprised that fear attended the emperor and power the tyrant: “For the emperor has made war against piety, while the tyrant has come to its aid. The one who abandons it flees naked, while the one armed with it overcomes the unarmed; for the lawgiver of piety stands with piety.”

16. He wrote these things while still far away. But when he came to give assistance and saw Valentinian, having left his own empire, arrive in his, he first applied healing to his soul, removed the disease of impiety that had come upon him, and restored him to his father’s piety. Then, encouraging him to take heart, he marched against the tyrant, restored the empire to Valentinian without bloodshed, and killed the tyrant. He judged that he would be acting unjustly toward the compacts made with Gratian unless he exacted some penalty from those responsible for the slaughter. This most faithful emperor also exerted every effort against Greek error [paganism] and promulgated laws ordering the destruction of idol temples.

17. Constantine the Great, worthy of every praise, had first adorned the empire with piety. Seeing the inhabited world still mad, he utterly forbade sacrifice to demons, but left their temples standing, ordering them to be inaccessible to all. His sons followed in their father’s footsteps. Julian revived impiety and more fiercely kindled the flame of the old deception. When Jovian assumed imperial rule, he again prevented the worship of idols. Valentinian the Great, using the same laws, governed Europe. Valens allowed all others to worship as they wished and to observe their chosen religious rites; only those defending apostolic doctrines did he continually persecute. Throughout his reign, fire was kindled upon the altar, libations and sacrifices were offered to idols, public feasts were held in marketplaces, and initiates into Dionysus’ mysteries ran about in goat-skins, dragging dogs along, raving and celebrating Bacchic rites, and doing other things that displayed their teacher’s wickedness.

18. Theodosius, the most faithful emperor, abolished all these practices as though they had never existed and introduced many other benefits for Christians. Yet it is not easy wholly to escape all the nets of the common enemy of humankind. Often someone who has escaped the passion of sexual license may be caught in the snare of greed; if superior to this as well, the abyss of envy springs up from another quarter; and if one surmounts this too, one finds the net of anger set before him. The evil one lays countless other snares for human beings, hunting them toward destruction. He makes the body’s passions serve the schemes which he devises against the soul. Only a wakeful mind, by turning to divine things, prevails against the schemes and exposes their malice. Therefore this admirable emperor too, sharing human nature, did not remain untouched by its passions. An excess of righteous anger conceived something harsh and unlawful, as will immediately be told. Yet this account contains not only an accusation against the admirable emperor, but also praise most worthy of remembrance, especially the freedom of speech then displayed by noble Ambrose and his great zeal for piety.

19. Thessalonica is a great and populous city in Macedonia, presiding also over Thessaly, Achaia, and many other peoples subject to the prefect of Illyricum. When a riot occurred there, certain officials were stoned and dragged about, and ended their lives in this disgraceful manner. The emperor, inflamed by reports of what had happened, did not bear it gently. Instead, unleashing all his anger against all alike and drawing unjust swords, he killed the innocent together with the guilty—seven thousand, it is said—without even one judicial inquiry preceding the act.

20. Learning of this disaster full of tears, great Ambrose met the emperor at a distance when he came to Milan and wanted, as usual, to enter the divine church. He would not allow him even to set foot within the sacred gates, saying:

“Emperor, it appears that you do not know the magnitude of the blood-guilt you have committed. Even after anger has ceased, reason has not recognized what was dared. Perhaps the power of sovereignty does not permit you to recognize your sin; authority overmasters reason. Yet you must know your nature: its mortality and transience, the original dust from which we came and to which we return. Do not, deceived by the splendour of purple, ignore the weakness of the body it covers. You rule over those of the same nature, emperor—indeed, over fellow slaves—for the maker of all things is the one Lord and King of all. With what eyes, then, will you look upon the temple of the common Master? With what feet will you tread that holy ground? How will you stretch out hands still dripping warm blood? How with such hands will you receive the all-holy body of the Master? How will you bring the precious blood to your mouth after unlawfully shedding the blood of so many in anger? Depart, then. Do not try by a second transgression to increase the first; accept the bond with which God, Lord of all, agrees from above to bind you. It is medicinal and brings you health, unless you choose to suffer incurably.”

21. Yielding to these words—for, having been brought up in divine laws, he clearly knew what belonged to priests and what to emperors—the emperor returned to the palace groaning and weeping. When eight months had passed from that time, the birthday feast of our Saviour came. Theodosius sat in the palace grieving most bitterly. A certain Rufinus, then master of offices, saw this and approached him; being kindly disposed and familiar with him, he asked the reason. The emperor groaned bitterly and shed hotter tears:

“You, Rufinus, are at ease, for you do not perceive my evils. But I groan and mourn as I consider my own misfortune: the divine church is open to servants and beggars, and they enter without fear and approach their own Master; but to me it is inaccessible, and heaven too is closed against me. For I remember the Master’s saying: ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.’”

22. Rufinus wished to help the emperor’s healing and to obtain pardon at the proper time. “If you wish,” he said, “I will run and persuade the high priest by much entreaty to release you from your bonds.” But the emperor replied: “He will not be persuaded. I know Ambrose’s just judgment: he will never violate the divine law out of deference to imperial power.”

But Rufinus used many more words and promised to persuade great Ambrose. The emperor ordered him to go quickly; himself enticed by hope, he followed shortly afterward, trusting Rufinus’ promises. Divine Ambrose immediately said to Rufinus: “Rufinus, you imitate the shamelessness of dogs. Are you neither ashamed nor afraid after raging so fiercely against the divine image?” When Rufinus implored him and said that the emperor would shortly come, divine Ambrose, inflamed with divine zeal, said: “Rufinus, I tell you: I will prevent him from crossing the sacred threshold. But if he turns imperial rule into tyranny, I too shall gladly receive slaughter.”

23. Hearing this, Rufinus immediately conveyed the bishop’s judgment to the emperor through someone and urged him to remain in the palace. But the emperor, already in the middle of the marketplace when he learned this, said: “I shall go and receive the just insults.” When he reached the sacred enclosure, he did not enter the divine temple but sat in the reception hall, earnestly begging to be released from his bonds.

24. Ambrose called his arrival tyrannical, saying that Theodosius had raged against God and trampled his laws. But the emperor, in contrition of heart and humility of spirit, said: “I do not presume against the established laws, nor do I seek unlawfully to cross the sacred threshold. But I ask you to loose my bond, to consider the loving-kindness of the common Master, and not to shut against me the door which the Master has opened to all who repent.”

The high priest replied: “What repentance have you shown after such lawlessness? By what remedies have you healed wounds so hard to cure?” The emperor again answered in a contrite spirit: “It is certainly your task to show and prepare the remedies.”

Then divine Ambrose said: “Since you permit anger to judge and reason does not issue the decision but anger pronounces it, enact a law making the judgments of anger ineffective and superfluous. Let capital and confiscatory decisions remain in writing for thirty days, awaiting the judgment of reason. After the thirty days have passed, let those who have written the decisions show them to you. Then, when anger has ceased, let reason judge the decisions by itself and examine whether they are just or not. If it finds them unjust, let it tear up the written orders and invalidate the judgment. But if they are just, let them stand; the number of thirty days will not harm decisions made rightly.”

25. The emperor accepted this proposal, judged it excellent, immediately ordered the law to be written, and confirmed it with letters in his own hand. When this had been done, divine Ambrose released the bond. The emperor confidently entered the divine church. He did not entreat the Master standing or bending his knees, but fell face-down upon the bare ground and uttered David’s words: “My soul cleaves to the dust; give me life according to your word.” Tearing his hair with his hands, striking his forehead, and sprinkling the ground with drops of tears, he pleaded to obtain forgiveness. When the time came to bring the gifts to the holy table, he rose with the same tears and entered the sanctuary. Having offered the gifts, he remained within the rails, as was his custom. But holy Ambrose would not keep silence even about this. He taught the distinction of places and first asked whether the emperor needed anything. The emperor said that he was waiting to partake of the divine mysteries. Ambrose then instructed him through the chief deacon: “The inner space, emperor, may be entered only by priests. To all others it is inaccessible and untouchable. Go out and stand with the others, for purple makes emperors, not priests.”

26. Most faithful Theodosius gladly accepted this instruction, declaring that he had not remained within the rails out of boldness but because he had learned that practice at Constantinople. The emperor and the high priest alike shone with such great and remarkable virtue. I admire both: the bishop’s freedom of speech and the emperor’s obedience; the bishop’s fervour of zeal and the emperor’s purity of faith. Whatever the emperor had learned from admirable Ambrose at Milan, he observed upon returning to Constantinople and departed from none of it.

27. For when a divine feast again led him to the divine church, after offering the gifts at the holy table he immediately came out. The president of the church—Nectarius held that office at the time—asked him why he had not remained inside. The emperor, distressed, said: “Only with difficulty have I learned the distinction between emperor and priest; only with difficulty have I found a teacher of truth. Ambrose alone is worthy to be called a bishop.” So great is the benefit of rebuke from a man shining in virtue.

28. The emperor had another source of benefit as well. His wife continually reminded him of divine laws, having diligently trained herself in them with exactness. The power of the empire did not exalt her; rather, it kindled in her a greater love for God. The greatness of the benefit bestowed produced in her a greater affection for the benefactor. Accordingly, she took every kind of care for persons maimed in body and afflicted in all their limbs. She did not use servants or armed attendants as ministers, but did the work herself. She went to their dwellings and supplied each person’s need. Going herself through the hospices of churches, she served, cared for, and treated the sick: she handled the pots, tasted the broth, brought the dish, gave bread, cleaned the cup, and performed every other task considered the work of male or female servants. She continually said to her husband:

“You must always consider, my husband, what you once were and what you have now become. If you keep this constantly in mind, you will not be ungrateful toward your benefactor. You will govern the empire you have received lawfully, and by it you will serve the one who gave it.”

29. By continually using such words, she brought, as it were, beautiful and appropriate irrigation to the seeds of her husband’s virtue. Yet she died before her husband. Some time after her death, an event occurred which demonstrated the emperor’s great disposition and affection toward her. Compelled by frequent wars and lacking money, the emperor imposed taxes on the cities. Antioch, seeing other cities taxed and the money exacted forcibly and inexorably, could not bear this public impost. It performed other acts such as a crowd, taking a pretext for disorder, is accustomed to perform; it threw down and dragged about through much of the city the bronze statue of the most illustrious Placilla—for that was the empress’s name.

30. Learning these things, the emperor was angry, as was natural. He deprived the city of its privileges and gave precedence to the neighbouring coastal city of Laodicea, thinking that this would especially grieve Antioch, for Laodicea had long envied Antioch. Afterwards he also threatened to burn and destroy it and turn the city into a village. The officials arrested some men caught in the very act and put them to death before the emperor learned of the tragedy. The emperor threatened all these things but did not immediately carry them out, being prevented by the law which great Ambrose had advised should be enacted. When the bearers of these threats—Hellenichus, then a general, and Caesarius, head of the imperial offices, whom the Romans call *magister*—came near Antioch, everyone was afraid and horrified by the threats. But the athletes of virtue dwelling on the mountain slopes—for there were many at that time—gathered around those subject to the threat, ran everywhere, and interceded, as far as they could, for those about to be punished.

31. One among them was a holy man adorned with every virtue, offering pure prayers day and night to the Saviour of all. Neither frightened by the emperor’s anger nor mindful of the authority of those sent, he entered the middle of the city and, grasping the cloak of one of the two dispatched officials, ordered both to dismount from their horses. At first, seeing a small old man clothed in shabby rags, they took it badly. But then some of their attendants made known the man’s virtue. They immediately dismounted, seized his knees, and asked forgiveness. Filled with divine wisdom, the holy man addressed them thus:

“Tell the emperor, my friends: you are not merely emperor, but also a human being. Therefore look not only to sovereignty, but consider your nature. Since you are human, you rule over those of the same nature. Human nature has certainly been created in the image and likeness of God. Therefore do not order God’s image to be slaughtered so cruelly and inhumanely. In punishing his image, you provoke its maker. Consider that you do these things because you are angry over a bronze image. Yet how far a living, animate, rational image surpasses one without life is plain to all who possess both mind and sense. Consider this also: we can easily make many bronze images in place of this one, but it is plainly impossible for him to create even one hair of those who have been killed.”

32. Hearing this, those admirable men conveyed these words to the emperor and extinguished the flame of his anger. Instead of the threats, he immediately wrote an apology and explained the cause of his anger: “It was not right that, because I had done wrong, a woman most worthy of every praise should after her death receive so great an insult. Those who were indignant ought to have armed their anger against me.” He added that he was grieved and pained to learn that some persons had been killed by the officials. Thus the Christ-loving emperor had been instructed in these matters by admirable Ambrose and received from him so great a grace and spiritual benefit.

[Col. 0065C] 33. This divine Ambrose, having shone, in the manner described, in the Church of Christ through orthodox doctrines, having become a zealot and champion of truth, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, set forth teachings of orthodoxy and instruction, expelled every heresy innovated by Arius and Apollinaris, ordered all the affairs of his church well, attained deep old age, and, full of days, rested in peace. He was laid in the Church of Milan, leaving his life and achievements as a true memorial. May we be judged worthy to become imitators of these things and to attain with him the same rewards and crowns, through the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power unto ages of ages. Amen.

## Latin parallel version

[Col. 0046D] 1. When Valentinian, after the death of Jovian, had assumed the sceptre of empire, he summoned his brother Valens from Pannonia and made him partner in supreme authority. Transferring to him the sceptre of Asia and also Egypt, he retained Europe for himself. Coming to Rome, he led all the peoples of the West to the true knowledge of God, inaugurating his reign above all by the preaching of piety.

2. For after Auxentius, who had embraced Arius’ schism, had died—having been entrusted with the Church of Milan but rejected in many synods—Emperor Valentinian summoned the bishops and used these words among them:

“You know plainly, as men nourished by divine words ought to know, what manner of person is fitting for one promoted to the honour of the episcopate; and how he should govern those subject to him not by word alone, but by life as well, set himself forth as an example of every virtue, and finally have the conduct of his life as witness to his teaching. Place such a man, then, on the episcopal throne now also, so that we, by whom the empire is governed, may sincerely bow our heads before him and receive his reproofs as medicinal treatment. Since we are human beings, it is altogether necessary that we should also offend.”

3. The assembly asked the devout emperor Valentinian, after he had said this, to cast the deciding vote himself, since he was adorned with wisdom and piety. But he said: “Such an undertaking far exceeds my strength. You, adorned by divine grace and endowed with this very radiance, will cast the more fitting vote.”

They therefore left and deliberated among themselves. But the citizens of that city stirred up a riot among themselves, some contending that one man and others that another should be preferred. Those infected with Auxentius’ plague voted for persons who agreed with them, while those who stood on the sounder side sought a bishop sharing their faith.

Thus divine Ambrose, illustrious in the Roman senate, had at that time, after many other stages of public office, obtained the prefecture of Italy from the pious emperors Constantine and Constans. He was a man pure in life, a lover of virtue, approved in word and deed, nourished by the wisdom drawn from sacred writings although he had not yet been initiated. He was also trained in Greek eloquence and poetic ability, an equitable and sound judge of affairs, and a strict investigator of every wicked action.

4. When he learned of these disturbances and feared that some revolution might occur, he hastened with great speed to the church and calmed the agitation of both parties. They then laid aside their contention and uttered one common cry, jointly asking that blessed Ambrose himself be ordained as their shepherd. When the emperor learned this, he immediately ordered that this praiseworthy man be baptized and consecrated. For he knew that Ambrose’s mind was straighter than any balance and his judgment more exact than any rule. He also suspected that this had occurred with God’s approval, inferring it from the agreement of those who had previously disagreed in opinion.

[Col. 0050A] 5. After Ambrose had received the gift of most sacred baptism and episcopal grace, the excellent emperor—who was himself present at these events—is said to have offered this hymn to the Saviour and Lord:

“Thanks be to you, almighty Lord and our Saviour, because I entrusted bodies to this man, but you have entrusted souls; and you have shown my judgment to have been just.”

6. A few days later, when this divine Ambrose addressed the emperor with greater freedom, he reproved him concerning certain affairs improperly conducted by his officials. The emperor said: “I had indeed long known this freedom of yours and, knowingly and deliberately, not only did not oppose it, but also added my vote to your ordination. Therefore heal, as the divine law commands, the wounds of our souls.”

7. After Valentinian, the great and pious emperor, had said and done these things at Milan, governed the empire well, and shone in the profession of right faith, he died in the sixteenth year of his reign. He left as successors his sons Gratian and the younger Valentinian. His brother Valens was ruling in the East, the very man who had allied himself with the Arians in faithlessness. When Valens fought the Goths and was defeated, he took refuge in a straw-thatched hut and perished there by fire. The whole power of Roman dominion passed to Gratian, son of Valentinian and nephew of Valens through his brother. First, he received from his father not only the sceptre of Europe but that of the whole West; then, when Valens was removed from the world without children, he obtained Asia as well and whatever remained in Africa. Since he cultivated piety in imitation of his father, he recalled from exile all bishops whom Valens, for the sake of the Arian heresy, had made exiles and driven from their homeland. When Gratian learned that Thrace had been devastated by barbarian victors during Valens’ reign, he left Italy and came to Pannonia.

8. At the same time Theodosius too was most renowned both for the nobility of his ancestors and for his own courage. Driven away by the envy of his equals, he lived in Spain, where he had been born and educated. Gratian did not know what ought to be done, for the barbarians, puffed up by their victory, were nearly invincible and were thought to be so. He considered Theodosius’ military skill the remedy for these evils. Immediately summoning the man from Iberia, also called Spain, appointing him commander in war, and sending him with a gathered army, he dispatched him. Theodosius, fortified with invincible arms—that is, orthodox faith—advanced with great confidence against the hostile line. Entering Thrace, he won the battle by force; the barbarians, unable even to withstand the first assault, all immediately turned their backs. A great slaughter of them was made not only by the Romans but now also by themselves, for the greater their numbers were, the more they harmed themselves rather than their enemies.

9. Thus, when almost all had been destroyed, very few who could hide themselves crossed the Danube. Gratian, delighted that he had entrusted the conduct of the war to Theodosius, immediately declared him emperor and committed to him the sceptre of the dominion formerly held by Valens. Gratian himself crossed to the administration of Italy and dismissed Theodosius to the empire granted him. Taking up imperial dignity, Theodosius took as much care as he could for concord among the churches and urged the bishops of his own dominion to assemble at Constantinople. For that city alone had been filled with the Arian plague, while those regions situated toward the West were free from that disease. For Constantine and Constans, sons of Constantine the Great, had preserved their father’s faith uncorrupted; and Valentinian likewise had in no way betrayed his ancestral piety. The eastern region, however, had admitted this pest in various places: having first begun in Alexandria, it was advancing into more distant regions.

10. These events took place while Gratian was still alive.
