Later, when he had already displayed his character in military affairs and governed the cities with moderation and justice, he was deprived of life by treachery, leaving no sons to succeed to the throne, but making his very young brother, who bore his father’s name, heir to the empire. Then a certain Maximus, despising Valentinian’s youth, usurped the throne of the Western Empire.

11. At about the same time Justina, wife of the great Valentinian and mother of the younger one, who had long since received the seed of Arian teaching, revealed it to her son. For, knowing her husband’s zeal for the orthodox faith, she had tried to conceal it as long as he lived; but, aware that her son’s mind was tender and easily moved, she did not hesitate to bring her deception into the open. He, regarding his mother’s suggestions as beneficial, and, because of his age, beholding the seductive bait of nature, suddenly fell into the snare. Therefore the great Ambrose, who had long before expelled every Arian deception from Italy, on learning that the boy Valentinian too had fallen into it, strove, so far as lay in his power, to free the young man’s soul from it. But Valentinian regarded that man with suspicion, as an adversary, and was prepared against him as against a declared enemy.

12. Ambrose in turn recalled to his mind his father’s piety, and earnestly entreated him to preserve unimpaired the inheritance he had received. He taught what the distinction between the doctrines was, and how the one set was wholly consonant with Christ’s teaching and the preaching of the apostles, while the other, on the contrary, attacked the spiritual law. But the boy, being indeed a boy and allured by the blandishments of his deceived mother, armed himself with words and surrounded the precincts of the church with armed soldiers.

[Col. 0054A] 13. But when that great champion, the divine Ambrose, was in no way intimidated by what was being done by them—for he regarded these things as children’s bogeymen—Valentinian, bearing it with intense annoyance, ordered him to leave even the thresholds of the churches. Ambrose replied: “I will never willingly do that, nor betray the sheepfolds to wolves, even if my blood must be shed. But if it is your will to kill me within, bring sword or axe against me; I shall embrace such a death most gladly.” Such was the divine Ambrose.

14. After no small interval of time had elapsed, Maximus learned of the attempts which they had made against that most illustrious herald of truth. [Col. 0054B] He therefore sent to Valentinian, warning him to desist from the war he had undertaken against piety itself and exhorting him not to cast aside his father’s religion. If he did not comply, he threatened him with a most grievous war; and, having actually gathered an army, he advanced toward Milan, for Valentinian had chosen that city as his residence. When Valentinian learned of his invasion, he fled into Illyricum, having learned by this very experience how much profit his mother’s counsels brought him.

15. When the Emperor Theodosius learned both what Maximus was plotting against the younger Valentinian and what he had written to him, he informed the fugitive youth by letter that no one ought to wonder if fear had been joined to the king and strength to the tyrant: [Col. 0054C] “For,” he said, “the king has made war upon piety, while the tyrant has aided it. The one, abandoning piety itself, fled naked; the other, armed with it, wins victory over the one stripped bare. For the Lawgiver of piety himself was his helper.”

16. Thus he reported these things by letter while he was far away. But after he came to the rescue and found Valentinian present in his own realm, though he had abandoned his own, he first applied a remedy to his soul; and, driving out the disease of impiety from which he suffered, restored him to his ancestral piety. Then, bidding him take courage and advancing his standards against the tyrant, he restored the empire to him without bloodshed, while he punished the tyrant. For he believed that he would violate the agreements made with Gratian unless he exacted punishment from those who had murdered that prince. This most faithful emperor also devoted every effort to opposing the errors of the pagans, and promulgated laws commanding the destruction of the temples of idols. [Col. 0054D]

17. Constantine the Great, most worthy of every praise and proclamation, adorned the Empire with piety. Seeing that the whole world was still then mad, he wholly forbade sacrifice to demons, but allowed their shrines to remain, ordering that everyone should be kept away from them. His sons likewise followed in their father’s footsteps. Julian, however, renewed impiety and kindled a fiercer flame of an error already grown old. Jovian, upon obtaining the Empire, again proscribed the worship of idols. [Col. 0055A] The great Valentinian also governed Europe under precisely the same laws. As for Valens, he allowed all others to worship however they wished and openly to cultivate whatever they worshipped; but against these alone—those who defended the apostolic doctrines—he never ceased to wage war. Therefore, throughout the time during which he reigned, fire was kindled upon the altar, libations and sacrifices were offered to idols, public banquets were celebrated in the streets, and those who performed the rites of Bacchus ran about in goatskins, dragging dogs with them, raving, reveling in Bacchic frenzy, and committing other such acts as openly displayed the wickedness of their master.

18. But the most faithful Emperor Theodosius [Col. 0055B] removed all these things as completely as though they had never existed, and established many other things in their place for Christians. Yet all the nets of him who from the earliest times has been the enemy of humankind are escaped only with difficulty. For often, when someone has escaped the sickness of luxury, he is perhaps caught in the snare of avarice; and but if that proves stronger, another abyss of envy springs up. Even if he has again leapt over that, he encounters traps of anger set before him. That malignant one, who hunts for the ruin of human beings, lays six hundred other snares for them. Bodily impulses cooperate with the engines constructed by him against the soul; but the mind that remains watchful alone overcomes them, checking the malice of his schemes by its inclination toward divine things. Therefore, [Col. 0055C] although that admirable emperor shared human nature, he was not always free from its passions. Yet some excessive outbreak of anger, joined to lawful indignation, produced something cruel and unjust, concerning which the following account will immediately speak. For it contains not only a rebuke of the admirable emperor, but also praise most worthy of remembrance—above all, the freedom of that noble Ambrose and the great fervour of spirit which he displayed in matters concerning piety. Whatever the matter may be, the narrative will make it clear.

19. Thessalonica is a great and populous city, assigned to Macedonia but the capital of Thessaly and Achaia, as also of many other territories, all those subject to the prefect of Illyricum. [Col. 0055D] When a sedition arose there, certain magistrates were stoned, dragged through the streets, and ended their lives by a most shameful death. The emperor, inflamed by the reports of what had occurred, did not bear the matter with moderation; instead, pouring out all his wrath against everyone and drawing unjust swords, he put innocent persons to death with the guilty—seven thousand, it is said—without having conducted any judicial inquiry whatsoever beforehand.

20. When the great Ambrose learned of this most lamentable calamity, he went out to meet the emperor from afar as he was coming to Milan and wished, according to custom, to enter the temple of God; he did not even permit him to enter the doors of the church. [Col. 0058A] “You do not know, Emperor, it seems, the magnitude of the impious slaughter that has been committed; nor, after your anger ceased, have you recognized by reason what kind of deed you dared to commit. Perhaps imperial power does not allow you to recognize the crime, but authority set in opposition to reason deprives you of light. Yet nature itself must necessarily be known by itself: it must recognize both what in it is mortal and perishable and that mother-earth from which we were made and into which we are dissolved. One ought not, bewitched by the splendor of purple, to be ignorant of the frailty of the body it covers. You rule over subjects who share the same nature as yourself, O king—indeed, over your fellow servants; for one Lord and King of all exists, namely the Creator of all. With what eyes, then, will you look upon the temple of the common Lord? With what feet will you tread this holy pavement? [Col. 0058B] How will you stretch out hands still dripping with warm blood? Or how will you receive with such hands the most holy body of the Lord, and bring the precious blood also to your mouth, when through the unrestrained force of anger you have shed so much blood contrary to every law and right? Depart, therefore; do not attempt to heap a second offense upon the first. Accept that bond which God, Lord of all, confirms by his judgment from heaven. It will be medicinal for you and will bring healing—unless, perhaps, you choose to endure an incurable wound.”

21. The emperor obeyed these words—for, having been brought up from childhood in the divine laws, he knew clearly what belonged to priests and what to kings—and, pouring out groans and tears together, withdrew into the palace. But after eight months had passed, [Col. 0058C] the feast of the Nativity of our Saviour came; Theodosius sat in the imperial residence and wept most bitterly. When Rufinus, at that time master of the palace, saw this, he approached him—as a man useful and familiar to his master—and asked the reason. Then Theodosius, groaning bitterly and shedding still warmer tears, said: “You amuse yourself, Rufinus; you do not feel my evils. But I groan and lament my own misery when I consider that the divine temple is open even to servants and beggars, and that entrance there is safe and freely available to them, so that they may meet their own Lord; but I am forbidden it, and heaven also is shut against me. For I remember the Lord’s saying, by which it is declared: ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven.’”

[Col. 0058D] 22. Rufinus, wishing to administer a remedy to the emperor and render him a timely service, said: “If it pleases you, I shall run to the bishop and, with many entreaties, persuade him to absolve you from these bonds.” But the emperor said: “He will not be persuaded; for I know how just Ambrose’s judgment is. Nor will he ever permit regard for imperial power to make him transgress the divine law.” But after Rufinus had advanced many further arguments and promised that he would undoubtedly obtain the request from the great Ambrose, the emperor ordered him to depart with all speed. The emperor himself, enticed by hope and trusting Rufinus’s promises, followed not long afterward. Immediately the divine Ambrose addressed Rufinus: [Col. 0059A] “Rufinus, you imitate the shamelessness of dogs; you are neither ashamed nor afraid, after raging with such fury against the image of God.” When Rufinus replied that the emperor would arrive after a short interval, the divine Ambrose, kindled with divine zeal, said: “Rufinus, I declare that I will prevent him even from setting foot in the church porch; and if he turns royal authority into tyranny, I shall accept death with pleasure.”

23. On hearing this, Rufinus immediately reported Ambrose’s intention to the emperor through someone and urged him to remain in the palace. But the emperor, who had already reached the middle of the forum, said when he heard it: “I shall go and pay the penalty for my madness.” When he had arrived at the sacred enclosure, [Col. 0059B] he did not enter the house of God but sat in the reception hall, asking that he be released from his bonds.

24. Ambrose called the emperor’s arrival tyrannical, declaring that Theodosius raged against God and trampled even his own laws. But the emperor, in contrition of heart and humility of spirit, said: “I do not arrogantly set myself against the laws, nor do I attempt unlawfully and impiously to tread the sacred threshold. But I entreat you: release me from the chain of my bonds; and, keeping before your eyes the mercy of the common Lord, do not shut against me that gate which the Lord himself opened to all penitents.” The bishop answered: “What repentance have you shown after so great a crime? By what remedies have you brought together for healing these wounds, so exceedingly difficult to cure? [Col. 0059C]

The emperor again replied in a contrite spirit: “It is wholly yours both to prescribe and to compound the medicines.” Then the divine Ambrose said: “Since you permit your own anger to pronounce judgment, and not reason but the heat of passion gives sentence, I wish you to enact such a law that every decree issued in an impulse of anger shall be rendered inoperative and void. Let a written sentence of death or exile remain for thirty days, awaiting the judgment of reason. When the thirty days have elapsed, let those who drew up the decrees present them again; then reason, judging while anger has rested, shall weigh its former decision and examine whether it is just or otherwise. If it finds it unjust, let it tear up the documents and make the sentence void; but if it is just, let it remain. The passage of thirty days will not invalidate what has been rightly judged.”

[Col. 0059D] 25. The emperor willingly accepted this admonition, persuaded that he was being treated very well, and immediately ordered the law to be drawn up, confirming and establishing it by the writing of his own hand. When this had been done, the divine Ambrose released the emperor from his bond. The emperor, now confident that he might enter the church, prayed to the Lord not standing or kneeling, but cast down and prostrate upon the bare ground, uttering that saying of David: “My soul cleaves to the pavement; give me life according to your word” (Psalm 118 [119]:25). Tearing his hair with his hands, striking his face, and watering the pavement with abundant tears, he hastened to obtain pardon. When the time came [Col. 0062A] for presenting the offerings of the sacred table, he rose with no less abundant weeping and ascended the steps of the altar. Having presented the offering, he remained within the rails, as was his custom. But the holy Ambrose could by no means be induced to overlook this; he instructed him concerning the distinction of places. First he asked whether he required anything. When the emperor replied that he awaited participation in the divine mysteries, Ambrose, employing the archdeacon as minister, clearly declared: “The inner parts, O Emperor, may be entered by priests alone. Go out, therefore, and keep the same station as the other laypeople; for purple makes kings, not priests.”

26. The most faithful Theodosius likewise took this address in good part. He explained that he had not remained within the rails through presumption, but because he had learned this custom at Constantinople. [Col. 0062B] Emperor and bishop shone with the light of such great virtue. I admire both: the one for his noble freedom, the other for his ready obedience; the former for fervent zeal, the latter for sincere faith. Indeed, after returning to Constantinople, the emperor observed the practices which he had learned under that admirable Ambrose at Milan and omitted none of them.

27. One festival day, when he was again summoned to the church of God and had offered the gifts at the sacred table, he immediately withdrew. The president of the church—Nectarius at that time—asked him: “Why did you not remain within?” [Col. 0062C] The emperor replied with regret: “I have only at last learned what difference there is between an emperor and a bishop. For I found a teacher of truth with difficulty: Ambrose, namely, who alone is rightly called a bishop.” So beneficial is a rebuke that proceeds from a man distinguished for virtue.

28. The emperor had another source of benefit as well. His wife continually reminded him of the divine law, in which she herself had diligently and carefully trained. Imperial power did not exalt her; rather, it kindled in her a greater love for God, since the greatness of a benefit awakens a greater incentive of love toward its author. Therefore, from the very beginning, she took every kind of care of those afflicted by bodily blindness or by the weakness of all their limbs. [Col. 0062D] She did not employ the service of household staff or attendants, but personally put her hand to the work; she did not disdain to enter their huts and supply each with necessities. She herself also went around and inspected the hospices of the churches, ministering to the sick and providing them with service and care: heating the pots, tasting the broth, bringing the dish, handing out bread, rinsing cups, and doing all the other things thought to be the work of male and female servants. She regularly addressed her husband as follows: “You should always reflect, O husband, both on what you once were and on the rank to which you have now attained. If you continually keep these things in mind, you will never be ungrateful to your benefactor; [Col. 0063A] but you will govern the empire entrusted to you by just laws, and by that means render the due service to its giver.”

29. While she continually used words of this kind, able to provide a beautiful watering and increase to the seeds of virtue in her husband, she died before him. Some time after her death, an event occurred which made it plainly known what feelings and how great an affection the emperor bore toward her. For, compelled by the frequency of wars and suffering a shortage of money, the emperor imposed taxes upon the cities. When the city of Antioch saw other cities subjected to those taxes, with money exacted by force and no excuse admitted, [Col. 0063B] it would not endure this common levy; seizing this as an occasion for disturbance, it committed the kind of act the mob is accustomed to commit. It threw to the ground a bronze statue of the most noble Placilla—for that was the empress’s name—and dragged the statue itself through several quarters of the city.

30. When the matter was reported to the emperor, he felt, as was fitting, great distress. He punished the city by taking away its own laws and placed it under the neighboring city of Laodicea, situated on the seacoast, believing that this was above all the way to make it feel his displeasure; for Laodicea had long been Antioch’s rival. Moreover, he threatened to burn and destroy it and to reduce it to a village. Some leading men, seized in the very act of the offense, had been put to death before the emperor learned of the outrage. [Col. 0063C] Theodosius threatened all these things, but did not immediately carry them out, being restrained, of course, by the law which, at Ambrose’s urging, he had caused to be enacted. But when those ordered to convey the threats arrived in Antioch—the commander at that time was Hellenichus and Caesarius was prefect of the praetorian guard; the holder of this dignity is called *magister* by the Romans—everyone was in fear, dreading the outcome of the threats. But those athletes of virtue who lived at the foot of the mountains, of whom there was then a great multitude, pitied those overwhelmed by the threat; running about everywhere, they comforted, as far as they could, others concerning the men who had been executed.

[Col. 0063D] 31. One of them was a holy man, adorned with every virtue, who day and night offered pure prayers to the Saviour of all. Fearing neither the emperor’s anger nor reckoning in his mind the authority of those who had been sent, he came into the midst of the city, seized the cloak of one of the envoys, and ordered both men to dismount from their horses. At first, seeing a little old man dressed in cheap cloth, they were indignant. But when one of those following them afterward disclosed the man’s virtue, they immediately leapt from their horses, embraced his knees, and begged pardon. The holy man, full of divine wisdom, addressed them thus: “Tell the emperor, O dear heads: you are not only emperor, [Col. 0066A] but also a human being. Consider, therefore, not only the empire but nature itself; for, being human, you rule persons who share the same nature. Human nature was entirely fashioned in the image and likeness of God. Do not, then, command the image of God to be slaughtered so cruelly and inhumanely; for in punishing his likeness, you stir the Maker to anger. Consider, therefore, how deeply you yourself were moved on account of a bronze image when you devised these measures. But how much more excellent a breathing, living, rational image is than an inanimate one is evident to all who possess mind and sense. Moreover, reflect also on this: it is easy for us to cast many other bronze statues in place of this one; but for him it is utterly impossible [Col. 0066B] to forge even one hair of those who have been killed.”

32. On hearing this, those admirable men reported what had been said to the emperor and extinguished the flame of his anger, so that he wrote as soon as possible an apology in place of the threats and explained the reason for his anger: “It was not fitting,” he said, “that, because I had sinned, my wife—far more worthy of every praise—should endure so great an insult after death; rather, those who yielded to their own inclination ought to have armed their anger against me.” He further added that he was distressed and grieved to learn that some persons had been put to death by the prefects. In this way the emperor, a friend of Christ, had been formed by such precepts from the admirable Ambrose and received from him such great grace and spiritual [Col. 0066C] benefit.

33. This divine Ambrose, as has been said, shone in the Church with orthodox doctrines and became an emulator and defender of truth. Having built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, expounded the words of right doctrine and discipline, driven away every heresy recently introduced by Arius and Apollinarius, and established his church excellently in all things, he advanced into a deep old age and, full of days, rested in peace. He was buried in the Church of Milan, leaving behind a true memorial of himself: namely, his own life and righteous deeds. May he himself deem us worthy, by the grace and kindness [Col. 0066D] of our Lord Jesus Christ—to whom belong honour and power unto ages of ages. Amen—that we too may become imitators of these deeds and obtain the same rewards and crowns with him.

[Col. 0065D]

# LIFE OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, COLLECTED CHIEFLY FROM HIS OWN WRITINGS AND ARRANGED ACCORDING TO CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER

[Col. 0065]

[Col. 0065D] 1. Saint Ambrose shone with such greatness of deeds, renown for learning and for the books he published, and finally praise for sanctity and [Col. 0066D] episcopal virtues, that it would be something like a miracle if learned men had been lacking to entrust his history to literary records. Accordingly, not a few Greeks and Latins arose who undertook to adorn this Sparta; foremost among them stands Paulinus, notary and deacon of the holy bishop, whose reliability and diligence cannot be called into question. Yet this deficiency is found in him: in narrating events he scarcely observed any chronological order, nor did he take care to compile a catalogue of our Doctor’s writings—something Possidius did not omit in the Life of Augustine. The most learned Cardinal Baronius had resolved to remedy this defect when he composed the Life of Ambrose which was prefixed to the Roman edition of Ambrose’s works and afterward reprinted so often with them. But this work of so great a man failed so completely to gain universal approval that it did not satisfy its own author; for some years later, while laboring over his immense work, the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, he declared concerning that same Life (under the year 397): “As for what I wrote concerning him—namely Ambrose—in the *Annals*, when you find something different in it, understand that it is to be conformed to the later account, since later thoughts are usually better.” Therefore, apart from the fact that the same Life is rather long, we could not submit it to the press without corrections and alterations—which we did not wish to presume to do in another’s work.

2. After Baronius, Hermannus Sorbonicus, doctor of the Sorbonne, published a new Life of Ambrose. Everyone received it with the esteem deserved by its author’s diligence and learning. But even if it had not been written in the vernacular language in which it was published, since it embraces matters done in Ambrose’s age both in the Empire and in the Church, its bulk is certainly greater than the limits of these volumes could contain.

3. Therefore, it seemed best to us, after first presenting two Lives—the one published by Paulinus, the other compiled by a Greek author—to add a third, more exact in chronological method, to supply the deficiency of both. We shall endeavor to draw it, as far as possible, from Ambrose’s own books, and strive, to the extent of our ability, to bring each part of it into such coherence and proportion that, through its assistance, the reader may not only readily grasp the order of Ambrose’s deeds and writings, but may also become better prepared to devote himself fruitfully to reading those same works.

4. (A.D. 340.) It is beyond dispute that our Ambrose was born in Gaul; that his father, also named Ambrose, held the rank of prefect in those provinces; and that, before Saint Ambrose himself was born, his father had already been blessed with two children, namely Marcellina and Satyrus, so that this saint of ours was third in order of birth (*On the Death of Satyrus*, I.54). But the writers do not agree so fully regarding the time and place where he first saw the light. As to the time: those who assign Ambrose sixty-four years of life maintain that 333 was the year of his birth; those who assert that he lived no more than fifty-seven years contend categorically that his birth occurred only in 340. Both opinions agree in holding that the holy bishop died in 397 or 398. The whole difficulty turns upon the number of years he lived, because the holy man states in Letter 59, addressed to Severus, that he was in his fifty-third year, and there writes these words also (Epistle 59, §3): “But we, exposed to barbarian disturbances and storms of war, are amidst every kind of trouble.” Those who, with Baronius, interpret this passage of the war waged against the tyrant Maximus infer from it that Ambrose reached his fifty-fourth year, since in 387 that same war filled all Italy with alarm and terror, whereas the holy bishop did not die before 397. But those who maintain that the quoted words must be understood of the war of Eugenius, carried out in 393 or 394, do not at all doubt that Ambrose died at fifty-seven years of age. We acknowledge that the second opinion seems to have a greater appearance of truth; but we do not think there is much value in laboring over this question. For it is agreed that these seven disputed years belong to the life Ambrose spent before baptism and in secular occupations; while the authorities nearly agree among themselves about the years during which he lived as bishop and to which his principal deeds belong.

5. As for the place where he was born, Paulinus’s words sufficiently establish that it was the city in which the prefect of Gaul customarily had his seat (Basil, Letter to Ambrose; Paulinus, *Life of Ambrose*, etc.). But there is no small dispute as to which city this should be considered. Some assign this honour to Arles, others to Trier or even Lyons, each relying upon the ancient nobility and prerogatives of those cities; but in truth they produce no argument by which one can plainly be demonstrated to be preferable to the others in this respect. There are also those who call Rome itself Ambrose’s homeland; but in these passages *patria* means nothing else for them than the native soil of his family and ancestry, as well as the customary residence, for no small period, of the holy man’s parents and of Ambrose himself.

6. Therefore our Ambrose was brought into the light in whichever of these cities contained the praetorium of the prefect of Gaul. It was there too that Paulinus (*Life of Ambrose*, §3) records the portent in which little bees, entering and leaving the infant’s mouth in turn, seemed to foretell his surpassing sweetness in speaking and in drawing people into Christ’s service.

7. (A.D. 353.) After his father’s death, Ambrose returned with his mother to Rome. There he found Marcellina—who, as Paulinus attests (*Life of Ambrose*, §4), had already professed virginity—living with another consecrated virgin. Since we learn from Ambrose himself that Marcellina was consecrated by the hands of Pope Liberius, on the birthday of Christ the Lord, with the bridal veil of virginity (*On Virgins*, III.1.1), and since there is no doubt that that bishop was installed in the see of his predecessor Julius only on 22 May 352, it follows that Marcellina’s consecration could not have taken place before 25 December in 353 at the earliest, or more probably in 354. Further, Paulinus—whom we shall frequently cite below—places after Ambrose’s return to the city the incident in which Ambrose extended his hands to the aforesaid girl to be kissed, as though he were a future bishop. From that plainly childish game it may reasonably be inferred that Paulinus’s words, “when he had grown up,” are better understood of our saint’s twelfth or thirteenth year than of his nineteenth or twentieth. This may provide no slight confirmation for assigning Ambrose’s birth to 340.

8. Brought up in the companionship of these virgins, our Ambrose was thereby filled with so great a love for virginity and celibacy that he not only cultivated that manner of life with the greatest zeal throughout his own life, but also propagated it far and wide with all his strength. This is plainly shown by his published writings, by the virgins solemnly consecrated to Christ by his hands, and by the monasteries finally established by him in various places. Among the virgins trained by the holy bishop toward the perfection of their profession, none shone with more outstanding evidence of every virtue than Marcellina, as the portrait of her drawn in literary style by her pious brother clearly demonstrates (*On Virgins*, III.4.15 ff.). This virgin lived at Rome, but remained always united to her brother by an intimate bond of souls. Thus, whenever necessity drew him to the City, she was not satisfied merely to enjoy the sight of him, but repeatedly traveled to Milan to visit him. Whenever distance separated them, they consoled their mutual longing by frequent letters, chiefly written about virtue and religion. Moreover, if anything made Ambrose anxious or troubled, his most loving sister never ceased to share his brotherly concern as long as he lived; for there is no doubt that she survived him.

9. While Ambrose lived at Rome, he devoted himself to the liberal disciplines (Paulinus, *Life of Ambrose*, §5) and, as may be learned from his writings, made great progress both in reading good authors and in knowledge of Greek literature. Thereafter, when he turned his attention to pleading cases in the forum, he displayed such talent, eloquence, and dignity that Probus, prefect of the praetorium, selected him to give counsel. Satyrus likewise, having completed the course of his studies, followed the profession of the forum and, to use Ambrose’s own words, “shone forth in the lofty court of the prefecture with incredible admiration” (*On the Death of Satyrus*, §29). In fact, both brothers attained the most distinguished offices through the testimony of their virtues. Ambrose clearly indicated the spirit in which they entered those offices when he said: “The honours of this world . . . we obtained them not because their acquisition was to be sought, but lest concealment should seem contemptible” (ibid., §25). How Satyrus administered the province entrusted to his care can be learned nowhere better than from this fraternal testimony: “What manner of man he was toward all the provincials over whom he presided is shown by their affection: they spoke of him as more their own parent than a judge, as a welcome arbiter of a loving relationship, a steadfast adjudicator of equitable law” (ibid., §58)., so exceedingly difficult to cure?” The emperor again replied in a contrite spirit: “It is wholly yours both to prescribe and to compound the medicines.” Then the divine Ambrose said: “Since you permit your own anger to pronounce judgment, and not reason but the heat of passion gives sentence, I wish you to enact such a law that every decree issued in an impulse of anger shall be rendered inoperative and void. Let a written sentence of death or exile remain for thirty days, awaiting the judgment of reason. When the thirty days have elapsed, let those who drew up the decrees present them again; then reason, judging while anger has rested, shall weigh its former decision and examine whether it is just or otherwise. If it finds it unjust, let it tear up the documents and make the sentence void; but if it is just, let it remain. The passage of thirty days will not invalidate what has been rightly judged.”

[Col. 0059D] 25. The emperor willingly accepted this admonition, persuaded that he was being treated very well, and immediately ordered the law to be drawn up, confirming and establishing it by the writing of his own hand. When this had been done, the divine Ambrose released the emperor from his bond. The emperor, now confident that he might enter the church, prayed to the Lord not standing or kneeling, but cast down and prostrate upon the bare ground, uttering that saying of David: “My soul cleaves to the pavement; give me life according to your word” (Psalm 118 [119]:25). Go out, therefore, and keep the same station as the other laypeople; for purple makes kings, not priests.”

# LIFE OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, COLLECTED CHIEFLY FROM HIS OWN WRITINGS AND ARRANGED ACCORDING TO CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER

[Col. 0065]

But the writers do not agree so fully regarding the time and place where he first saw the light. As to the time: those who assign Ambrose sixty-four years of life maintain that 333 was the year of his birth; those who assert that he lived no more than fifty-seven years contend categorically that his birth occurred only in 340. Both opinions agree in holding that the holy bishop died in 397 or 398. The whole difficulty turns upon the number of years he lived, because the holy man states in Letter 59, addressed to Severus, that he was in his fifty-third year, and there writes these words also (Epistle 59, §3): “But we, exposed to barbarian disturbances and storms of war, are amidst every kind of trouble.” Those who, with Baronius, interpret this passage of the war waged against the tyrant Maximus infer from it that Ambrose reached his fifty-fourth year, since in 387 that same war filled all Italy with alarm and terror, whereas the holy bishop did not die before 397. But those who maintain that the quoted words must be understood of the Eugeni(an) war, carried out in 393 or 394, do not at all doubt that Ambrose died at fifty-seven years of age. We acknowledge that the second opinion seems to have a greater appearance of truth; but we do not think there is much value in laboring over this question. For it is agreed that these seven disputed years belong to the life Ambrose spent before baptism and in secular occupations; while the authorities nearly agree among themselves about the years during which he lived as bishop and to which his principal deeds belong.

5. As for the place where he was born, Paulinus’s words sufficiently establish that it was the city in which the prefect of Gaul customarily had his seat (Basil, Letter to Ambrose; Paulinus, *Life of Ambrose*, etc.). But there is no small dispute as to which city this should be considered. Some assign this honour to Arles, others to Trier or even Lyons, each relying upon the ancient nobility and prerogatives of those cities; but in truth they produce no argument by which one can plainly be demonstrated to be preferable to the others in this respect. There are also those who call Rome itself Ambrose’s homeland; but in these passages *patria* means nothing else for them than the native soil of his family and ancestry, as well as the customary residence, for no small period, of the holy man’s parents and of Ambrose himself.

6. Therefore our Ambrose was brought into the light in whichever of these cities contained the praetorium of the prefect of Gaul. It was there too that Paulinus (*Life of Ambrose*, §3) records the portent in which little bees, entering and leaving the infant’s mouth in turn, seemed to foretell his surpassing sweetness in speaking and in drawing people into Christ’s service.

7. (A.D. 353.) After his father’s death, Ambrose returned with his mother to Rome. There he found Marcellina—who, as Paulinus attests (*Life of Ambrose*, §4), had already professed virginity—living with another consecrated virgin. Since we learn from Ambrose himself that Marcellina was consecrated by the hands of Pope Liberius, on the birthday of Christ the Lord, with the bridal veil of virginity (*On Virgins*, III.1.1), and since there is no doubt that that bishop was installed in the see of his predecessor Julius only on 22 May 352, it follows that Marcellina’s consecration could not have taken place before 25 December in 353 at the earliest, or more probably in 354. Further, Paulinus—whom we shall frequently cite below—places after Ambrose’s return to the city the incident in which Ambrose extended his hands to the aforesaid girl to be kissed, as though he were a future bishop. From that plainly childish game it may reasonably be inferred that Paulinus’s words, “when he had grown up,” are better understood of our saint’s twelfth or thirteenth year than of his nineteenth or twentieth. This may provide no slight confirmation for assigning Ambrose’s birth to 340.

8. Brought up in the companionship of these virgins, our Ambrose was thereby filled with so great a love for virginity and celibacy that he not only cultivated that manner of life with the greatest zeal throughout his own life, but also propagated it far and wide with all his strength. This is plainly shown by his published writings, by the virgins solemnly consecrated to Christ by his hands, and by the monasteries finally established by him in various places. Among the virgins trained by the holy bishop toward the perfection of their profession, none shone with more outstanding evidence of every virtue than Marcellina, as the portrait of her drawn in literary style by her pious brother clearly demonstrates (*On Virgins*, III.4.15 ff.). This virgin lived at Rome, but remained always united to her brother by an intimate bond of souls. Thus, whenever necessity drew him to the City, she was not satisfied merely to enjoy the sight of him, but repeatedly traveled to Milan to visit him. Whenever distance separated them, they consoled their mutual longing by frequent letters, chiefly written about virtue and religion. Moreover, if anything made Ambrose anxious or troubled, his most loving sister never ceased to share his brotherly concern as long as he lived; for there is no doubt that she survived him.

9. While Ambrose lived at Rome, he devoted himself to the liberal disciplines (Paulinus, *Life of Ambrose*, §5) and, as may be learned from his writings, made great progress both in reading good authors and in knowledge of Greek literature. Thereafter, when he turned his attention to pleading cases in the forum, he displayed such talent, eloquence, and dignity that Probus, prefect of the praetorium, selected him to give counsel. Satyrus likewise, having completed the course of his studies, followed the profession of the forum and, to use Ambrose’s own words, “shone forth in the lofty court of the prefecture with incredible admiration” (*On the Death of Satyrus*, §29). In fact, both brothers attained the most distinguished offices through the testimony of their virtues. Ambrose clearly indicated the spirit in which they entered those offices when he said: “The honours of this world . . . we obtained them not because their acquisition was to be sought, but lest concealment should seem contemptible” (ibid., §25). How Satyrus administered the province entrusted to his care can be learned nowhere better than from this fraternal testimony: “What manner of man he was toward all the provincials over whom he presided is shown by their affection: they spoke of him as more their own parent than a judge, as a welcome arbiter of a loving relationship, a steadfast adjudicator of equitable law” (ibid., §58).

10. (A.D. 374.) It is by no means certain what province Satyrus received to govern. As for Ambrose, however, Probus, already mentioned, appointed him governor of Liguria and Aemilia—provinces generally thought to have comprised the archbishoprics of Milan, Liguria, Turin, Genoa, and Bologna. When Probus dispatched Ambrose thither from his own presence, he is said to have addressed him in these words: “Go,” he said, “act not as a judge, but as a bishop” (Paulinus, *Life of Ambrose*, no. 8)—admirably warning him to show the provincials episcopal clemency rather than a judge’s severity.

11. Ambrose proved by no means forgetful of this injunction. By his affability and gentleness he bound the people’s hearts so closely to himself that, after the death of Auxentius—that treacherous Arian who had occupied the see of Milan, from which Saint Dionysius had been expelled and sent into exile—Ambrose himself was appointed in his place, in the manner elegantly described by Paulinus. Ambrose frequently complained that force had been used against him in this election (*Ibid.*, no. 6 ff.). In the first book of *On the Duties* (nos. 2 and 4), he sometimes laments that the obligation of the priesthood was laid upon him while he fled from it, and sometimes that he was snatched from the tribunals and the insignia of administration to the priesthood. In another work he says:

> It will be said: “Behold, he was not reared in the bosom of the Church, nor trained from childhood; but he was snatched from the tribunals, drawn away from the vanities of this world, and accustomed, instead of the herald’s voice, to the Psalmist’s song.”  
> (*On Penance*, II.8, no. 67)

And shortly afterwards:

> Preserve the gift which you bestowed even upon one fleeing from it. For I knew that I was not worthy to be called a bishop, because I had given myself to this world; but by your grace I am what I am. Indeed, I am the least of all bishops, and deservedly the lowliest.

Likewise, in his letter to the people of Vercelli, he speaks thus: “How I resisted being ordained! … But prescription did not prevail; pressure prevailed” (*Epistle* 63, no. 65). Certainly, from what Paulinus relates on this subject (*Life of Ambrose*, no. 7 ff.), it is perfectly clear that this saint of ours tried every possible means to avoid submitting his shoulders to this burden. Nevertheless, when Emperor Valentinian’s letter was brought, he was compelled to obey the divine will, which, after so many indications, he could no longer call into doubt. For this reason, in later times, when he was most violently attacked by the Arians, he addressed Valentinian II in these terms:

> I pass over the fact that the people themselves have already judged; I pass over the fact that they requested from the father of Your Clemency the man whom they now possess; I am silent about the fact that the father of Your Piety promised that there would be peace if the elected man accepted the priesthood. I relied upon this assurance of his promises.  
> (*Epistle* 21, no. 7)

12. Therefore, after obeying the divine commands, he wished to be cleansed by the laver of regeneration at the hands of a Catholic bishop. Having been baptized, he is said to have fulfilled all ecclesiastical offices, and on the eighth day he was ordained bishop (Paulinus, *Life of Ambrose*, no. 9). Nevertheless, in order that the laws of the Church, which forbid the consecration of a neophyte, might in some degree be observed, he strove with all his strength at least to postpone his ordination (*Epistle* 63, no. 6). But since such inauguration is forbidden for no other reason than lest one, puffed up with pride, fall into the judgment of the devil (1 Tim. 3:7), and since Ambrose’s humility did not appear liable to that danger, the urgent needs of the Church were judged to require that it should not be delayed longer.

Indeed, Western bishops approved that ordination by their judgment, and Eastern bishops even by their example, as Ambrose himself testifies. He adds: “If ordination lacked delay, it was due to the force of compulsion; if the humility appropriate to the priesthood is not lacking, where the cause is not defective, the fault is not imputed.”

13. It is probable that this consecration took place on the seventh day before the Ides of December, that is, 7 December, since it is commemorated on that very day among both Greeks and Latins. Ambrose himself also seems to indicate this when, speaking of the ordination of Felix, bishop of Como, which recurred at the very beginning of the Kalends of November, he addresses him thus: “We shall commemorate your birthday with our prayers; and do not forget ours in your petitions” (*Epistle* 4, no. 2). For if the word *ours* qualifies *birthday*, it is highly probable that the holy man was moved to write this only because he was then thinking of the approaching anniversary of his own episcopal inauguration.

Yet the agreement of chronologists concerning the year of this saint’s consecration is much greater: the most learned of them place it in 374. Some, however, have wished to defer it to the following year, evidently not sufficiently considering that Valentinian—who, it is certain, was still alive when Ambrose was chosen for the episcopate—died in November 375. As soon as the holy bishop had announced his election, according to custom, to the bishops of both the Eastern and Western Church, the excellent letter of the great Basil, replying to Ambrose’s letter, still survives (Basil, *Epistle* 55). Some think that remnants of the letter of Dionysius, whom Ambrose succeeded in the episcopate, were attached to it. Saint Dionysius died in exile on 25 March of that same year, 374.

14. Moreover, as soon as our Ambrose was elevated to so great a dignity, he put aside every concern except that of fulfilling his office. He relinquished all the temporal goods with which his family was wealthy—since the holy man denies that his brother Satyrus had been poor in resources (*On the Death of Satyrus*, no. 56)—and, distributing gold and silver to the needy, he gave his estates to the Church, reserving for his sister only the usufruct of the land (Paulinus, *Life of Ambrose*, no. 58). Hence, during the Arian persecution, he could answer with such confidence:

> If the emperor asked of me what was mine—that is, my estate, my silver, or anything else of that kind that was mine—I would not resist; although all that is mine belongs to the poor.  
> (*Epistle* 20, no. 8)

He did not wish to divide his inheritance with his brother, but entrusted its care to Satyrus, as he did that of other secular affairs, including the management of servants and household. That beloved brother had come to Milan to him; for neither could live separated from the other, so that Ambrose says on the matter: “The honors of this world did not delight even us, because they separated us from one another” (*On the Death of Satyrus*, no. 25). Satyrus discharged this administration with such prudence and gentleness that, after his death, his holy brother bore him this testimony: “Without giving offense to anyone, you governed your brother’s house and commended his priesthood” (*Ibid.*, no. 20).

15. Thus freed and released from earthly affairs, the new bishop devoted himself wholly to acquiring heavenly things. Although, before receiving holy baptism, he had ordered his life so honorably and so Christianly that episcopal perfection seemed scarcely to require anything further, he nevertheless applied himself to every virtue with as great an exertion of spirit as if he had been convinced that none was present in him. By this means, himself becoming such as he most earnestly desired each of his subjects to be, he never ceased to hold before them the torch of good works.

Above all, he so devoted himself to the worship of the holy altars that no business could prevent him from offering the divine sacrifice daily (*Epistle* 20, no. 15). But since Paulinus has described with sufficient care Ambrose’s daily exercises (*Life of Ambrose*, no. 38 ff.), there is no need to set them out here in detail. The holy bishop, however, carefully considering the charge of that Church committed to him—a Church which Auxentius, having occupied it for a full twenty years, had endeavored with all his power to infect with the poison of Arian doctrines—judged, conversely, that he ought to strain every nerve in order to uproot from the people’s minds not only the evil shoots of that Arian madness, but those of every other heresy as well.

Saint Jerome declared the result of this pastoral concern in these words: “After the late death of Auxentius, when Ambrose had been established at Milan, all Italy was converted to the right faith” (Jerome, *Chronicle*). This success is all the more worthy of admiration because the holy man required only a short time to attain it. During the Arian crisis—namely, in 385 or 386—he himself wrote:

> No one among the Arians dared appear publicly, because there was none among the citizens, few among the imperial household, and some Goths.  
> (*Epistle* 20, no. 12)

At about this same time the holy bishop delivered Augustine from the snares of the Manichaeans. Nor need we doubt that many others, less obstinate than Augustine, had already owed Ambrose the removal of their first error.

16. Yet those abundant fruits cost the new bishop great zeal and many labors. Although we have observed that he had been trained from youth in liberal letters and disciplines, no one will deny that ecclesiastical learning was lacking to him when he was advanced to the episcopate. Therefore, in order to acquire this knowledge, he devoted, with incredible diligence, every moment not occupied by the duties of his office or by the necessary care of his body wholly to meditation on Sacred Scripture.

We have the great Augustine as witness to this, in the following words:

> When crowds of busy people, whose infirmities he served, excluded me from access to his ear and speech, then, whenever he was not with them—which was only for a brief time—he either refreshed his body with the necessary sustenance or his mind with reading.  
> (*Confessions*, VI.3, no. 3)

Nor did that most faithful disciple judge it right to neglect or pass over in silence his master’s manner of reading. In the same place he adds:

> When he read, his eyes ran over the pages and his heart searched out their meaning, but his voice and tongue were silent.  
> (*Ibid.*)

Nor was the course of daylight sufficient for his eagerness. Rather, making night almost continuous with day in this work, after returning from the sacred vigils he resumed reading at once, as he frankly acknowledges to his dearest Irenaeus in these words: “While reading, after I had given my mind a little rest, because I had ceased from my night-work, I began to turn over in my mind that verse which we had used in the vigils of the evening” (*Epistle* 29, no. 1).

Even after he had become advanced in years, he relaxed nothing of this strenuous effort, as may be learned from one of his letters written to Sabinus, his friend and intimate. There we read: “For we do not dictate everything, especially at night, when we do not wish to burden and inconvenience others” (*Epistle* 47, no. 1). Thus he who never spared his own labor spared that of others.

Therefore, since he was endowed with a most acute intellect and excellently educated in humane letters, especially Greek—in which, among the Latin Fathers, he yielded first place only to Jerome—it will not seem strange that, constantly turning over the works of both Greek and Latin Fathers and comparing with one another the sacred texts of both languages, he made such great progress in so short a time. The claim of the great cardinal (*Life of Ambrose* and *Annals* for 375 and 385), that Pope Damasus, on hearing of the election of Ambrose while still a catechumen, sent Simplicianus to Milan to instruct him in ecclesiastical learning during the first years of his episcopate, rests on an insufficient foundation. For Ambrose’s closing a letter to Simplicianus with the words, “Love us with a parent’s affection” (*Epistle* 65), and Augustine’s calling him “the father of Bishop Ambrose in receiving grace, and one whom he truly loved as a father” (*Confessions*, VIII.2), arose, as we have already shown, from no other cause than that this priest had perhaps instructed Ambrose, while still young, in the first elements of religion at Rome; or that, after his election, he had endeavored to prepare him to receive the sacraments of regeneration and ordination.

17. (A.D. 375.) Ambrose labored to acquire knowledge of ecclesiastical matters, and especially of the Scriptures, for no other purpose than that he might fulfill the office of teacher, as these words plainly signify:

> I desire only to attain earnestness and diligence concerning the divine Scriptures … and to learn precisely this by the zeal of teaching.  
> (*On the Duties*, I.1, no. 3)

For this reason, from the first years of his priesthood he hastened to undertake that work. He makes this clear enough when, with such modesty and self-abasement, he confesses that it happened “that I began to teach before I had learned. Therefore I had to learn and teach at the same time, because I had had no opportunity to learn beforehand” (*Ibid.*, no. 4).

The clergy whom he addresses here were not the only persons to whom these earliest concerns extended. He also labored greatly in preparing and instructing catechumens for the sacraments of rebirth. The many books composed from sermons delivered to them abundantly show that scarcely anything was more important to him than to render these tender plants fit so that, striking the roots of piety more deeply, they might someday bear abundant fruit. He was tireless in this office and, as Paulinus says, “most vigorous in fulfilling divine duties” (*Life of Ambrose*, no. 38), so much so that what he customarily performed in relation to those to be baptized could scarcely afterwards be accomplished by five bishops in the period when he died.

18. These two preceding classes of persons did not lead the holy bishop to forget the people. He devoted diligent care not only to cultivating and adorning their morals with every ornament of virtue, but also to fortifying their minds against the artifices and perfidy of heretics. This was evidently his purpose when he published his book *On Paradise*, which we think was issued in this very year: “lest the disciples of Apelles, or rather the Manichaeans, lead simple minds astray by malicious interpretation” (*On Paradise*, V, no. 28).

To this book he added two others entitled *On Cain and Abel*, in which one may discern still more easily those sermons which display the talent of a Christian orator not yet fully mature, although these very sermons are everywhere interspersed with precepts most suitable for good conduct.

19. Augustine testifies that Ambrose customarily addressed the people every Sunday, when he declares: “I heard him every Lord’s Day rightly handling the word of truth among the people” (*Confessions*, VI.3). Yet these words are to be understood only of the sermons customarily delivered during the course of the year. On more solemn feasts, and also on extraordinary days, he ascended the pulpit daily—indeed, sometimes once or twice on the same day—as we have observed in the appropriate places (*Preface to On the Mysteries* and *to the Hexaemeron*).

20. In the first years of Ambrose’s episcopate, Valentinian the Great also experienced that noble freedom which this priest of Christ had resolved to exercise toward the rulers and great men of the world. To reproduce in its own words the account of Theodoret, to whom we owe it:

> A few days after his ordination, when the divine Ambrose addressed the emperor with great freedom and reproved certain matters which appeared not to have been rightly done by the magistrates, the emperor replied: “I had long known of this freedom of yours; yet, although I knew it well, not only did I not oppose your ordination, but I even gave it my assent. Therefore apply the remedy to the sins of our souls, as the divine law commands.”  
> (*Ecclesiastical History*, IV.7)

21. This emperor died on 17 November, leaving two sons, Gratian and Valentinian. The former had already completed his seventeenth year and had been proclaimed Augustus on 24 August 367. Valentinian, however, still only four years old, was declared emperor on the sixth day after his father’s death. Ambrose always embraced both princes with a tender and truly paternal love, and they in return never failed to honor him in the place of their own father. The most grievous persecution endured by the holy bishop under the younger emperor must therefore be attributed to the rage of the heretical woman who exploited her son’s childish age (*Oration on the Death of Valentinian*).

22. (A.D. 376.) However much every form of life concerned the blessed bishop, no institution ever seemed more worthy of the labors of his care than virginity. From the beginning of his episcopate he judged that his night studies ought to be devoted to the brides of his Lord. For not later than the beginning of this year, those most elegant sermons appear to have been delivered to them from which the books *On Virgins* were compiled.

The great fruit produced by them when they were delivered may sufficiently be inferred from the fact that a man otherwise most modest could not suppress it: “Virgins come from the district of Piacenza to be consecrated; they come from the district of Bologna; they come from Mauretania, to receive the veil here” (*On Virgins*, I.10, no. 57). These words also sufficiently indicate the time at which those sermons were delivered. Since Ambrose, in the third year of his priesthood (*Ibid.*, IV.6, no. 39), put them into the form of books, one understands that at least a year was required for the fame of those discourses to spread to places so distant, and especially as far as Mauretania, and to draw thence to Milan virgins to receive the veil.

Accordingly, if the feast of blessed Agnes was celebrated on 21 January, as it is now customary, we may reasonably believe that the first of these sermons was delivered in this very year on the birthday of that martyr, and the others on different days at intervals. Ambrose accomplished this with such eloquence and ornament, and at the same time with such force and persuasive effectiveness, that he himself excused the excessive luxuriance of his speech; and mothers, lest their daughters, persuaded by the eloquence of so great a teacher, should consecrate their virginity to Christ, carefully shut them up in their rooms and did not permit them to come to church to hear him.

23. When the Arians saw that the new bishop had declared war upon their heresy and omitted no opportunity from the first day of his ordination to attack them, they began seriously to deliberate among themselves by what devices they might oppose an adversary threatening imminent ruin to their cause. With this purpose, as some reasonably think, they selected Valens as a suitable instrument of their fury. He had been disgracefully expelled from Poetovio, whose episcopal throne he had violently seized after expelling Marcus, and had made his way into Italy to disturb its churches. But his madness was checked by Gratian’s authority; for from the opening words of Book IV *On Heresies* we may learn that this emperor enacted a law against him.

24. (A.D. 377.) We have already recounted how widely the fame of Ambrose’s sermons on virginity had spread. Hence sacred virgins who, because of the distance of their homes, could not drink in those exhortations with their ears, earnestly desired at least to read them in written form. Nor indeed is it credible that Marcellina, Ambrose’s sister, who had publicly professed that mode of life many years earlier, could have endured being forestalled by another in making this request. The holy bishop most willingly complied with their wishes, as he himself plainly testifies in these words: “At the request of virgins, I did not think that even this should be refused” (*On Virgins*, I.1).

For that reason he transformed those same sermons into three books *On Virgins*, while still not three years a priest, as has already been said. He wished the same work to be inscribed to his sister Marcellina, and in it he included the discourse which Liberius delivered while placing the veil upon that nun (*Preface to On Virgins*).

25. Not long afterward he published for general circulation the book *On Widows* (*Preface to On Widows*), likewise composed of sermons. In it he praises the advantages and merits of Christian widows and suitably proves that their condition comes close to that of virginity. The occasion for the little work was a widow who had some daughters already married and others of marriageable age, and who had consulted him as to whether it was advisable for her to enter a second marriage.

26. We assign the book *On Tobit* to this same period, though not on necessary arguments, but on probable conjectures (*Preface to On Tobit*). Taking his occasion from the story of Tobit and the money lent by him to Gabael, Ambrose attacks usury, then raging with savage violence. He assails and overthrows it with arguments of such weight that one might wish the people of our own time would order their lives by them.

27. (A.D. 378.) Whoever examines the tract *On Virginity* somewhat attentively will find it to be nothing other than a continuation of the book *On Widows* (*Preface to On Virginity*). It was similarly composed from sermons which Ambrose wrote in order to calm the troubled mind of the aforementioned widow. Before addressing that widow, however, he discusses at length the practice of virginity and proves by arguments that it is neither wrong, nor novel, nor useless (*On Virginity*, VI, no. 27 ff.). Thus both virgins and widows are treated there, but especially the latter. Since the book *On Widows* could not have been completed before the closing of the preceding year, it is evident that the book now under discussion could not have been written before this year.

28. Meanwhile, while Ambrose was working so successfully to defeat heresy, uproot vices, and implant virtues, Emperor Valens, who persecuted Catholics so cruelly, suffered the greatest defeats at the hands of the Goths. Gratian, on the other hand, the nephew of Valens through his brother, triumphed everywhere through the benefit of the right faith. Learning of his uncle’s peril, he resolved to cross into the East to bring him assistance. Accordingly, in order to strengthen himself with a more powerful safeguard against the dangers he was about to encounter, either at the end of the preceding year or at the beginning of this one, he asked Ambrose to prepare a treatise (*Preface to On the Faith*) establishing the divinity of the Son of God, so that, on entering regions infected by the Arian contagion, he might not lack an antidote.

Although Ambrose would have preferred to undertake the office of exhorting to the faith rather than of disputing about the faith (*On the Faith*, I.6, no. 4), he nevertheless obeyed the prince’s request and sent him the first two books *On the Faith*. Having done this, he directed all his concern to obtaining for the emperor a successful expedition by continuous and fervent prayers to the Lord. He himself attests this in the letter sent to Gratian upon his return:

> I followed your daily journey; night and day I was present in thought and concern in your camp; I kept watch in the outposts of prayer—weak indeed by merit, but diligent in affection.  
> (*Epistle* 1, no. 1)

29. When Valens learned that Gratian was hastening toward him along the banks of the Danube, he hurried to engage in that most disastrous battle, lest the young emperor, whose courage he greatly envied, should share in the victory. In it he was routed together with all the forces of the Eastern Empire; he himself was burned alive in a rustic hut on 29 July.

30. The barbarians, among whom were the Taifali—a people more devoted than all others to the shamefulness of unchastity—used their victory to invade many provinces of the Empire, especially Thrace and Illyricum. They devastated everything as far as the foot of the Julian Alps. It cannot be described how many crimes they committed, how they confused all things with slaughter and fire, or how great a number of captives they carried off, displaying them everywhere for sale like cattle. “These things,” says Ambrose, “are all too well known from the devastation of Illyricum and Thrace: how many captives everywhere were for sale throughout the whole world” (*On the Duties*, II.15, no. 70).

The same writer indicates that many of these were redeemed by the churches. But he surpassed everyone in charity in this service, for he not only gladly spent money on their redemption but also broke up and melted down the vessels of the Church itself. In this matter, observing the rules of prudence at first, he broke up vessels not yet consecrated; afterwards, however, if those could not suffice, he considered that even consecrated vessels should not be spared. Saint Augustine and other most eminent bishops later approved this splendid example both with praise and imitation. The Arians, however, on the contrary, tried to create the gravest prejudice against the holy man from it:

> We at one time incurred odium because we broke up the sacred vessels in order to ransom captives. This could displease the Arians; and the deed itself displeased them less than the fact that it afforded them something with which to reproach us.  
> (*Ibid.*, no. 136)

Therefore, to repel their accusation, “having mounted the pulpit of the Church, we addressed the people,” he says, “so as to confess it and establish much more fittingly that we should preserve souls for the Lord rather than gold” (*Ibid.*, no. 137).

31. Toward the end of this year Satyrus (*Preface to On the Death of Satyrus*), to whom his blessed brother had entrusted the management of all Ambrose’s household affairs, neglected the winter cold and sailed to Africa (*On the Death of Satyrus*, no. 50), in order to compel a certain Prosper to make payment. Of this man Ambrose says: “He congratulated himself that, because of my priesthood, he would not be required to restore what he had taken” (*Ibid.*, no. 24). Ambrose omitted nothing to recall his brother from that voyage and have the business entrusted to another (*Ibid.*, no. 26). Yet Satyrus did not abandon his purpose; rather, in order to cross the intervening sea more quickly, he did not fear to use an old and leaky vessel (*Ibid.*).

32. Meanwhile the holy bishop fell ill:

> Recently, at last, when I was pressed by some grave, and would that it had been final, illness, I grieved only that you yourself were not standing beside my bed and, sharing that desired service with your holy sister, closing the eyes of the dying man with your fingers.  
> (*Ibid.*, no. 36)

From these words one may also infer that, during this journey of Satyrus, Marcellina came to Milan to visit her dearly beloved brother and ministered to him diligently in that dangerous sickness.

33. Not long after embarking in so defective a ship, Satyrus was shipwrecked. When the vessel struck a shoal, its structure immediately came apart. In so great and immediate a danger, he asked from those who had been washed in the water of rebirth—for he had not yet received that grace—the divine sacrament of the faithful. “He had it bound in a cloth, and wrapped the cloth around his neck; then he cast himself into the sea … believing himself sufficiently safe and protected by these things, he sought no other aid” (*Ibid.*, no. 43). His hope did not fail him in the least, for, as Ambrose testifies, he was the first to be saved from the waves.

As soon as he reached land and rescued his own servants from danger, he hastened to turn all his care to giving thanks to God and receiving holy baptism. When he heard that the bishop of the place where he had landed adhered to the Luciferian schism, he sought out a Catholic by whom he might be washed. He obtained such abundant grace in that sacrament that, according to Ambrose’s testimony, he never afterwards lost it (*Ibid.*, no. 52).

34. Besides this shipwreck, Satyrus was also afflicted by illness on that journey. When news of it reached Ambrose and Marcellina, it caused them immense sorrow. It seems uncertain to us whether it was in the aforementioned shipwreck or in this illness itself that he made the vows to Saint Lawrence of which Ambrose speaks as follows:

> We now learn that, through your vows to Saint Lawrence the martyr, you obtained the provision for life; and would that you had asked not only for provision, but also for a long span of life! You could have obtained many years of living, since you could obtain provision for coming.  
> (*Ibid.*, no. 17)

35. Having prudently and effectively completed the business for which Satyrus had sailed to Africa, on his return he passed through Rome. Although he was detained by his relative Symmachus (*Ibid.*, no. 32)—whom Ambrose calls so either as a term of honor or perhaps also of patronage—lest he fall into the hands of the barbarians, since Italy was said to be ablaze with war, nevertheless no danger could delay his desire to see his dearest brother again.

But scarcely had he returned to Milan when, overwhelmed by a deadly illness, he departed this life after a few days. “For,” says his holy brother, “he was taken away promptly after he came, as though his delay had been only for this: that he might return to his brother and sister” (*Ibid.*, no. 17). Ambrose and Marcellina had the most sorrowful consolation that they were able to show their tenderly beloved brother every office of service and care, both in his sickness and after his death. Satyrus’s body was carried with great ceremony into the church and placed opposite the apse, with his face uncovered. The holy bishop, overcoming his grief, praised his brother before a great multitude in that oration than which nothing more tender can be imagined, as may still be recognized today from its reading.

36. Satyrus made no will, although Ambrose and Marcellina urgently pressed him to do so; rather, he left his property to the discretion of them both. This was indeed a more noble manner of leaving and bequeathing it to the poor, one wholly free from vanity. For the holy bishop and his sister interpreted his will not otherwise than as if they had been appointed stewards, not heirs; thus all the reward of that act returned to Satyrus.

37. On the seventh day they returned to Satyrus’s tomb, in order to propitiate the divine power for his soul by the customary prayers and ceremonies. Then our saint, delivering another address, showed that consolation should be admitted and that the death of relatives or friends should not be mourned excessively, since death is common to all human beings, and without it no one can be delivered from the miseries of this life or attain the blessed resurrection and possession of the infinite good.

The same bishop, if Dungal deserves credence, composed his brother’s epitaph and had it engraved on his tomb. Moreover, between no two brothers has there ever been found not only so great a harmony of spirit, but also such similarity of bodily constitution and even of countenance. It often happened (*Ibid.*, no. 36) that when one was ill the other was ill, and again, when one recovered, the other recovered; and many people thought they were speaking to one when in fact they were addressing the other.

38. (A.D. 379.) From Satyrus’s winter departure one may draw the highly probable inference that he did not depart to heaven until this year, and that his funeral orations were delivered then. The Church enrolled him among the saints and announces his feast on 18 September.

39. In this same year Emperor Gratian, deeply concerned to repair the provinces of the Roman Empire devastated by the disasters arising from Valens’s fatal death, made Theodosius his colleague in the Empire. By this appointment—than which nothing could have been more salutary for the welfare of the Empire—the provinces of the East, to which Macedonia and Greece were additionally joined, were assigned to Theodosius. Augustine (*City of God*, V.25) and other writers greatly praise Gratian’s judgment; but none rejoiced in it more than Ambrose, since he loved Gratian exceedingly and held Theodosius in the highest esteem on account of his outstanding virtues.

40. After Theodosius was declared emperor of the East—an act performed at Sirmium on 19 January of this year—Gratian went into Gaul to defend it from Germanic ravages. On the journey itself he wrote a most respectful letter to our bishop, earnestly requesting him to visit him and again deliver to him the first two books *On the Faith* (*Letter to Ambrose*, vol. II, p. 751), while also adding to them a faithful discussion *On the Holy Spirit* demonstrating that Spirit’s divinity. Ambrose replied that he could not meet him so soon, but excused himself in such a way as to promise that he would satisfy Gratian’s wish at the first opportunity. Meanwhile he sent him the requested books *On the Faith*; but with regard to a treatise *On the Holy Spirit*, he asked for time.

41. This holy Doctor was not unaware that certain heretics—perhaps Palladius and Secundianus—had raised some objections against his books *On the Faith*, and that they charged him with having deliberately aimed at brevity, so as not to be obliged to answer their arguments. Therefore, before writing [Col. 0081A] *On the Holy Spirit*, he resolved to add other books to the two already mentioned *On the Faith*, composed so aptly that all together might grow into a single work. His plan succeeded so well (*Admonition to the book On the Faith*) that those who had not become wholly hardened in unbelief were recalled, the minds of Catholics were reassured, and Gratian ordered that the one Church be restored to them—the Church whose sequestration the shameless petitions of the Arians had extorted from him.

42. At the beginning of Lent in the present year, Ambrose sent a letter to Constantius, recently invested with episcopal consecration, in which he discusses at length the duties of bishops and their teaching. Among other things he writes to him:

> I commend to you the Church at Forum Cornelii, so that you may visit it more frequently, since it is nearby. Occupied with the approaching days of Lent, I cannot travel so far. You have there Illyrians holding the wicked doctrine of the Arians: beware of their tares. . . . Let them consider what has befallen them because of their unbelief—understand, the death of Valens—let them be quiet, and follow the true faith.

(Epistle 2.)

43. The holy bishop also laments in the book *On Noah and the Ark* (ch. 1, no. 3, and the *Admonition* to that book) those same disasters which came upon the Church and the Empire through the death of that unhappy emperor. From this work and the foregoing writings we learn that this book too must be assigned to this very year, and that the diligent Doctor devoted himself with untiring labours both to comforting the miseries of the orthodox and to repelling the errors of the heterodox. Indeed, he testifies sorrowfully that he also laboured to draw even the Jews [Col. 0081C] into the Church, but that his effort among them proved fruitless because of their obstinacy.

44. (A.D. 380.) Felix, the first bishop of Como, had received the laying on of hands from our Ambrose; it is therefore no wonder that so close a friendship existed between them. The letter in which our saint gracefully and courteously praises truffles of remarkable size received from him (Epistle 3) may be said to have been written in this very year, if any credit is to be given to Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. 2). In the same letter Ambrose inserted very affectionate complaints that Felix had not yet come to see him; Felix accordingly excused himself in a letter to him. When this reply was delivered to Ambrose, he was confined by illness and was speaking about Felix with Bassianus, bishop of Lodi, who was then visiting him. Thus, in his second letter to Felix (Epistle 4), he informed him of these matters and added that Felix had promised to attend the dedication of the basilica built by Bassianus; therefore, he no longer had any excuse for delay.

45. About the same time Ambrose became involved in a rather serious affair with Syagrius, bishop of Verona. It preserves an outstanding example, scarcely to be found elsewhere, of the ancient practice customarily observed by the Church in criminal trials. Indicia, a consecrated virgin, had been accused before Syagrius of violated virginity and of destroying a fetus. She had been denounced by a certain Marcellus, [Col. 0082A] who had married her sister; and, with no regard for the relationship by marriage, he had by evil arts and contrivances secured her submission to examination by midwives. Indicia appealed to the tribunal of Ambrose. Syagrius also considered that he ought to write to Ambrose in defence of his judgment. Ambrose examined the case with several other bishops; having recognized Indicia’s innocence, he invalidated the decision of the bishop of Verona and moreover imposed on the virgin’s slanderers the penalties demanded by the atrocity of their crime. He informed Syagrius by letter (Epistle 5) of what he had determined in the case, setting forth the defects and faults in Syagrius’s judgment. Yet, fearing that he might have alienated that bishop, a few days later he sent him another letter (Epistle 6), in which, while giving an exceptional assurance of goodwill, he set before him [Col. 0082B] the grave injury he had intended to inflict upon the entire order of consecrated virgins by condemning Indicia to the penalty of so disgraceful an examination.

46. Another controversy, by no means lighter than the preceding, arose between Ambrose and Justina concerning Anemius. At that time the episcopal see of Sirmium, the capital of all Illyricum, was vacant. It had for a long time been occupied by the Arian bishops Photinus and Germinius. The Empress, apparently then residing there, left no stone unturned to ensure that the future bishop should be chosen from the Arians.
