Holy Ambrose hastened there; and although Justina, surrounded by the forces of a heretical conspiracy, struggled against him, he nevertheless prevailed by steadfastness that a Catholic bishop should be appointed. Paulinus relates the manner of this [Col. 0082C] election, as well as the miracle performed at it (*Life of Ambrose*, no. 11), and testifies that the new bishop was named Anemius. Since this same Anemius was present at the Council of Aquileia in the following year, his election cannot more plausibly be assigned than to the present year.

47. Justus of Lyons was also present with Anemius at the Council of Aquileia. The friendship between this bishop and Ambrose was one of the closest attachment. After the assembly of the Fathers was dissolved, Justus withdrew into the Egyptian deserts. It follows that, before he set out from Lyons for this Synod, our Ambrose had written to him the letter (Epistle 7) in which he explains a passage of Exodus concerning which Justus had consulted him. Not very long afterwards, in another letter sent to [Col. 0082D] him (Epistle 8), Ambrose again answered his question whether the sacred authors had taken care to write according to the rules of rhetorical art.

48. (A.D. 381.) We have said that Ambrose had promised Gratian that he would prove the divinity of the Holy Spirit in a published treatise. At the beginning of this year he fulfilled his promise in this matter (*Admonition to the book On the Holy Spirit*), and sent the Emperor his three books *On the Holy Spirit*, which he made public when Athanaric, king of the Goths, died at Constantinople on the eighth day before the Kalends of February [25 January]. In composing them he made fortunate use of the writings of Didymus and Basil, not in order, like Aesop’s crow, to display himself in borrowed feathers, but in order, with the industry of a bee, to make honeycombs from diverse flowers.

[Col. 0083A] 49. Although it appears that Gratian, while still staying at Sirmium and being most importunately pressed by Palladius and Secundianus, bishops of the Arian faction, reluctantly consented to the convening of a synod at Aquileia, it cannot be admitted that it was held before September of that year. They wished this council to be ecumenical, and that all bishops should leave their flocks and assemble there. But Ambrose persuaded the Emperor that so great a labour would be superfluous; on his advice Gratian exempted the senior or weaker bishops from undergoing this exertion. Accordingly, only a small number of bishops assembled there, but they were distinguished for the merit of their lives and the excellence of their doctrine. We have dealt sufficiently with this assembly in its proper place (*Admonition to the Epistles*); here we add only that [Col. 0083B] Ambrose there performed the roles of nearly all the other Fathers, both in disputing against the said heretics and in proclaiming their condemnation by synodical letters to absent bishops or rulers.

50. (A.D. 382.) Some suppose that Epistle 13, which bears this superscription, “Ambrose and the other bishops of Italy,” belongs to the same Council of Aquileia. Others maintain that it should be assigned to another council held in one of the cities of Italy at the beginning of this year. The Fathers of the Synod laid their complaints before Theodosius because, after Meletius’s death, a successor had been put in his place, whereas by an agreement already made the see of Antioch was due to Paulinus alone. They also complained about the election of Nectarius to the episcopate of Constantinople. For Maximus had brought them letters from Peter of Alexandria, and they believed that Maximus had been truly and canonically elected. The Emperor replied most graciously to the council and disclosed to it the frauds of Maximus the Cynic. Therefore the synod sent another letter to the same ruler (Epistle 14). It first explained why it had acted as it had regarding Maximus and Nectarius; then it gave thanks that, through his beneficence, the eastern and western Churches enjoyed peace; and finally it reported that it had restrained by just condemnation a certain supporter of the Apollinarians.

51. This year is also assigned the incident mentioned by Paulinus: when the holy bishop approached the palace in order to seek from Gratian a pardon for a certain person, Macedonius, Master of the Offices, refused him [Col. 0083D] entry. Ambrose thereupon foretold divine vengeance against him: “You indeed will come to the Church, but, when its doors are shut, you will not find a way by which you may enter” (*Paulinus, Life of Ambrose*, no. 37). Macedonius actually experienced this after Gratian’s death. If this threat of Ambrose is placed in this year because Gratian was at Milan when it was uttered, then it may with equal right be referred to either of the two preceding years, since he also stayed there in both of them. Thus nothing is certain concerning its date. Yet it seems more likely that this defendant was the same man who, according to Sozomen, while he was a pagan, had reviled Gratian with insults and called him unworthy of his father (*Sozomen*, book 7, ch. 25). Since no one was willing to intercede with the Emperor for him, Ambrose, as Sozomen relates, entered Gratian’s presence by a private door and obtained pardon for the wretched pagan’s offence.

52. In this same year two imperial chamberlains (*Paulinus, Life of Ambrose*, no. 18; and *Admonition to the book On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*) who supported the Arian party challenged the holy Doctor to a public discussion on the mystery of the Incarnation. He had undertaken to do this in the Portian basilica, and he did not fail to keep his promise at the appointed time. But, having fallen from their horses and broken their necks, these men breathed their last. Ambrose, not yet informed of that terrible event, delivered to the people the discourse from which the little book *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation* was composed. To the same subject, however, were added [Col. 0084B] solutions to two difficulties which the Arians had proposed to the holy man through Gratian himself. The first difficulty concerned the terms “begotten” and “unbegotten”; the second concerned Christ’s omnipotence. In this Ambrose’s modesty shines forth remarkably: although he could not have failed to learn of the event mentioned before he gave his discourse the form of a book, he made absolutely no mention of the death of these unfortunate young men.

53. Toward the end of this year Ambrose went to Rome to attend the great council held there. While he was staying there, he fell ill. Saint Acholius, summoned to the City for the same purpose, did not fail to visit him; [Col. 0084C] our bishop regarded this meeting as a very great benefit. Some are of the opinion that this was Ambrose’s first journey to Rome since his election to the episcopate. If that is true, the events which, as Paulinus relates (*Life of Ambrose*, nos. 9 and 10), happened to him some years after his ordination should be assigned to this journey. He did not find his mother alive, but there he saw the girl to whom he had formerly been accustomed to offer his hand for kissing; and finally he restored the use of her limbs to a paralysed woman. Baronius adds that the holy bishop foretold a dreadful vengeance against a certain innkeeper’s wife, who had become insolent because of her prosperity; but no ancient writer’s authority supports this tradition. Since Paulinus considered it useless to explain how great Marcellina’s delight was at seeing and conversing with her [Col. 0084D] most beloved brother, and how solicitously she ministered to him in his illness, we too leave it to the reader’s reflection.

54. Moreover, this year saw the pious edict of Gratian ordering the removal from the Senate of the Altar of Victory, which Constantius had already removed but Julian the Apostate had restored. It further abolished the privileges of the Vestals, the benefits of the priests of sacrifice, and the monies assigned to defray the expenses of sacrifices. The idolaters omitted nothing in attempting to have this decree revoked; for that purpose, through Symmachus, a man of highest rank and most eloquent orator, they submitted a petition to the Emperor. But our holy bishop—on whose advice it is probable that the Emperor had decreed these measures—when he received from Damasus, bishop of Rome, the petition of the Christian senators (Epistle 17, no. 10), acted so effectively with the Emperor that the force of the rescript was preserved unimpaired, and Symmachus’s petition was not even read by Gratian, as may not rashly be inferred.

55. (A.D. 383.) In this year Saint Acholius exchanged temporal life for eternal life. The bishops of Macedonia and the clergy of Thessalonica announced his death by letter to blessed Ambrose, who by some more wonderful means had already learned of it. The holy bishop sent them a reply in which, after revealing his deep grief at the death of so great a bishop (Epistle 15) and honouring his outstanding virtues with due praises, he testifies that he rejoiced [Col. 0085B] that Anysius, the worthy disciple of the same saint, had been appointed in his place. He also wrote another letter to Anysius (Epistle 16), in which, after the customary office of congratulation, he exhorts him to imitate the virtues of his teacher and predecessor.

56. This year also suffered a famine, which in the following year Symmachus attributed to the Christian religion (*Report to Valentinian*, p. 831, no. 14), on the ground that the privileges of the virgins of Vesta and the priests of idols had been removed. But Ambrose admirably demonstrated the frivolity of his arguments: the shortage of grain had not been universal, since most provinces had overflowed with grain, and in the immediately following year there had followed a harvest repaying, as it were, with interest and the benefits of a more generous vintage [Col. 0085C] (Epistle 18, no. 17 and following).

57. Maximus’s rebellion inflicted a calamity far more grievous upon the Empire than the grain shortage. That tyrant was proclaimed Emperor in Britain through wicked devices; yet he pretended that he had not usurped the purple, but that it had been forced upon him against his refusal and will. With a great army he crossed into Gaul. When Gratian saw that he had been betrayed and abandoned by his own men, he attempted flight toward the Alps. But when he had hurried to Lyons, he was killed by a monstrous crime on the eighth day before the Kalends of September [25 August], in the twenty-fourth year of his life, the seventh year and ninth month of his reign. Held in the power of his enemies, the unhappy prince had nothing more often in thought and on his lips than the name of Ambrose, his father: [Col. 0085D]

> In your dangers you sought me; in your final extremity you called upon me; you grieved more over my sorrow for you.

(*On the Death of Valentinian*, no. 79.)

Certainly anyone can readily judge how great this saint’s grief was. He himself expresses it in various places, for example in his exposition of Psalm 61, where he affectionately praises the virtues of the murdered prince and sharply condemns the treachery of his murderer. But after Valentinian too was later killed, he could scarcely contain his grief. For, joining both brothers together in his lamentations, he mourned that his eyes had, as it were, been torn out, and complained in David’s manner:

> Would that, my sons, I had been permitted to pour out this life for you! I should have found a shortening of my grief, and it would have been more glorious for me to die for such great pledges.

(*Ibid.*, no. 39.)

Yet [Col. 0086A] he did not grieve so greatly on his own account as on account of the Church, which was wounded by a terrible blow through the cruel murder of this prince, from whose character and virtue he had hoped that he would become its greatest defender (*Ibid.*, no. 6).

58. Moreover, the holy bishop showed not merely in words how much grief Gratian’s death had caused him, but wished by deeds also to declare how dear the latter’s memory was to him. For when Gratian’s brother Valentinian had not yet passed beyond boyhood, Ambrose displayed toward him fully a father’s disposition and protection, as he himself testifies in these words:

> I received you when you were a little child, when I was going as envoy to your enemy; I embraced you when you had been entrusted to the motherly hands of Justina.

(*On the Death of Valentinian*, no. 28.)

For Justina, when all was thrown into confusion and disorder by Gratian’s sudden death and she saw herself and [Col. 0086B] her son in the utmost danger, was compelled to have recourse to Ambrose, however hostile she had been to him. Therefore, in those most difficult times, Ambrose did not decline the dangerous embassy to Maximus. While awaiting with him the return of Count Victor, whom the same tyrant had sent to Valentinian, he remained there through the whole winter (Epistle 24, no. 7). Although everything was then full of danger, he did not think that his dignity should be lowered. Rather, employing both courage and prudence, he dealt with the tyrant in such a way as to obtain the requests he had made. Indeed, there was no one who did not approve this embassy, except Maximus. For in the following year he complained that Ambrose had deceived him. The bishop, though he considered these complaints honourable to himself, made it altogether clear that they were nevertheless unjustly made [Col. 0086C] (ibid., no. 5).

59. This we learn from Ambrose himself. Moreover, Paulinus states that Ambrose thought Maximus should be excluded from communion, warning him to do penance for the blood he had shed of his lord—and, what was more serious, of an innocent man (*Paulinus, Life of Ambrose*, no. 19). But since the holy bishop went as envoy to Maximus once and then again, while this same author does not distinguish the two embassies here, the sequence of the narrative makes it more likely that the cited passage fits the latter one. Nevertheless, if Ambrose had communicated with Maximus during the first embassy, he would not seem to have been able justly to exclude him from communion during the second. It is therefore more probable that the holy bishop neither ever became Maximus’s participant in sacred rites nor [Col. 0086D] wished to employ any compromise toward him.

60. On returning to Milan, Ambrose resumed his episcopal duties. We think that he then delivered those excellent sermons from which the books *On the Interpellation of Job and David* were composed. The subject suited those times: there (*Admonition to the same books*) are treated the complaints in which each of those saints lamented the bodily and spiritual calamities of human life. There too are examined the complaints commonly elicited both by the prosperity of the wicked and the adversity of the good. In treating and embellishing this subject, Ambrose elegantly expounds the finest passages of the Book of Job; nor less skilfully does he interpret and elucidate Psalms 41, 42, and 72.

[Col. 0087A] 61. (A.D. 384.) Likewise, the holy bishop seems to have revealed his grief over Gratian’s murder in the sermons of which the *Apology of the Prophet David* consists (*Admonition to this book*), though he nowhere [Col. 0087B] there names Gratian himself. He was led to speak on this subject because David’s twofold crime—adultery and murder—very gravely offended certain persons. He therefore proves that it is not surprising that a frail human being should fall into such sins; rather, what deserves admiration is that so great a prince was able to make so prompt and humble a confession of the crime he had committed, and both to wash it away by a longer and harsher penitence and to cover it by the continuous exercise of good works. If we trust the title in some very ancient manuscripts, our bishop later sent this book to Theodosius in order to urge him to expiate, after David’s example, the slaughter of the city of Thessalonica which he had ordered.

62. Symmachus was administering the prefecture of the City in this year. Thinking the confused state of affairs and the alarm of the boy Valentinian and his mother Justina opportune, he resolved again to seek the restoration of the pagan religions, the Altar of Victory, and the privileges. Accordingly he presented to the Emperor a petition adorned and polished with every artifice of eloquence (vol. II, p. 828). This orator had indeed attempted the matter secretly, but he could not prevent it from coming to Ambrose’s knowledge. Once informed of the plan, Ambrose at once sent Valentinian a petition (Epistle 17), or rather a letter full of episcopal vigour, asking that a copy of Symmachus’s petition be supplied to him, so that he might answer it more carefully. Accordingly, as soon as he received this document from the Emperor, he so lucidly and forcefully dissolved and refuted each of its heads (Epistle 18) that he imposed upon Symmachus a necessary silence concerning the affair. Our Ambrose arranged that this second petition be delivered to the Emperor after the vintage holidays. From the holy bishop’s letter to Eugenius we may learn that this petition, like the earlier one, was read in a full consistory and obtained what it requested.

63. During his prefecture, this same Symmachus rendered Christianity a better service than he had intended. Since the people of Milan had asked him for a teacher of rhetoric, he arranged for Augustine to go there for that purpose. Augustine himself elegantly describes the friendly reception he received from Ambrose on arriving there; we shall therefore not hesitate to borrow his words:

> And I came to Milan to Ambrose the bishop, known throughout the whole world as among the best, a devout worshipper of you. His eloquence at that time vigorously dispensed to your people the fatness of your wheat, the gladness of oil, and the sober intoxication of wine. I was led to him by you without knowing it, so that by him I might knowingly be led to you. That man of God received me fatherly, and loved my pilgrimage with sufficient episcopal kindness. And I began to love him, at first not as a teacher of the truth—for in your Church I had wholly despaired of finding it—but as a man kindly disposed toward me. I listened attentively when he disputed before the people, though not with the intention I ought to have had, but as though testing his eloquence: whether it matched his reputation, or flowed more copiously or less than was reported. I hung upon his words with attention, but stood by indifferent to and contemptuous of the things said. I delighted in the sweetness of his speech, although it was more learned, yet less cheerful and soothing in manner than that of Faustus. But as for the matters themselves, there was no comparison: Faustus wandered through Manichaean deceits, whereas Ambrose taught salvation most healthfully.

(*Confessions*, book 5, ch. 23.)

Thus far Augustine. By this account he makes known to us not only with what lofty purpose he was, as it were, led by the hand to Ambrose, that he might be recalled from errors, but also how great was our bishop’s reputation among people and what method he followed both in receiving strangers and in instructing the people. Augustine then explains by what stages Ambrose’s words first brought the light of truth into his mind and finally changed his will. He speaks of it as follows: “And while I opened my heart to receive how eloquently he spoke, there entered at the same time also how truthfully he spoke—gradually, indeed” (*ibid.*, ch. 24).

64. We also judge the two books *On Penance* (*Admonition to the same books*), written by Ambrose against the Novatians, to belong to this year. In them he utterly overthrows both the senseless and cruel opinions of these heretics and irresistibly proves the authority, given by Christ to the Church, to forgive sins. Moreover, since these words occur there, “I have undertaken some labour for [Col. 0088C] the holy Church” (book 2, ch. 8, no. 73), if that labour indicates the work undertaken by Ambrose against Symmachus and the pagans, no one will think that these books should be placed far from this very year.

65. (A.D. 385.) Monica, who had followed her son by land and sea and through every danger, came to him at Milan not long afterwards. Holy Ambrose honoured her with the same kindness and goodwill which he had already shown Augustine (*Confessions*, book 6, ch. 1). But the mother found Augustine alienated from the inventions and disgraceful teachings of the Manichaeans, although he was not yet sufficiently inclined toward the truth of Catholic doctrine. His inward agitation filled her with the greatest joy, for from it she drew a sure hope that his conversion was near. Therefore, in order to obtain it from divine mercy, she redoubled her prayers and began both to run more eagerly to the Church and to hang upon Ambrose’s lips, “at the fountain of water springing up into eternal life.” She loved him “as an angel of God,” because through him she had learned “that I had meanwhile been brought to that doubtful wavering” (*ibid.*).

66. One may further understand with what reverence that devout widow regarded the holy bishop from the following. When, Augustine says, she had brought “porridge, bread, and unmixed wine” to the memorial shrines of the saints, as she had been accustomed to do in Africa (*ibid.*, ch. 2), she heard from the doorkeeper that the bishop had forbidden this practice because of certain abuses. She accepted it so devoutly and obediently, Augustine continues, “that I wondered how readily she became an accuser of her own custom rather than a disputant against that prohibition” (*ibid.*).

67. Meanwhile Augustine was constantly advancing farther on the way of truth. Yet he thought of Ambrose in this way:

> I considered Ambrose a certain happy man according to this world, because such great powers honoured him; only his celibacy seemed burdensome to me.

(*Ibid.*, ch. 3.)

He greatly desired to have a longer conversation with him, in order to disclose the movements and agitations of his mind. He frequently went to him for that purpose; and since the episcopal residence was open to everyone, he readily gained access to him. But because the holy bishop was either serving the weaknesses of different people or occupied in meditation upon the Scriptures, Augustine had no opportunity [Col. 0089B] to ask what he wished. Still, Ambrose sometimes spoke with him and congratulated him because of his mother’s devotion.

68. But Augustine was by no means satisfied with so casual an interview. To satisfy his desire as far as possible, he heard Ambrose every Sunday preaching the word of truth rightly to the people (*ibid.*). Through these sermons the clouds which had darkened his inward sight were dispersed; and he began to recognize the truth of the Catholic faith and especially to despise the errors of the Manichaeans concerning the testament of the ancient covenant. “I often heard Ambrose,” he says, “in his sermons to the people, teaching repeatedly: ‘The letter kills, but the spirit gives life,’ when, removing the mystical veil, he opened spiritually those things which, taken according to the letter, seemed to teach perversity” (*ibid.*, ch. 4). There is therefore no reason why anyone should be surprised that Ambrose so strongly pressed the mystical sense in the sermons delivered from the pulpit in this and the following year, many of which were reduced to books. Certain fastidious people would certainly value these books more highly if they gave some consideration to the necessities of those times and to their manifest efficacy in the conversion of the great Augustine.

69. Ambrose, whose concern extended beyond the boundaries of the Church of Milan, at the request of Vigilius, recently raised to the see of Trent, set forth for him by letter the principal duties of episcopal dignity (Epistle 19). Above all, he warned him not to allow marriages to be contracted between persons differing in religious worship—that is, between Christians and unbelievers. The necessity of this warning arose from the multitude of idolaters within the territory of Trent, so great at that time that Vigilius himself, when he sought to bring them to the knowledge of Christ, is said to have suffered martyrdom at their hands.

70. As soon as Justina saw that Maximus had granted her peace, she resolved to use that opportunity to declare war upon Ambrose. For, thinking her son’s authority now sufficiently established, she cast into oblivion all the services rendered by the holy man to herself and to the Empire. The approaching feast of the Lord’s resurrection gave her an occasion to send persons to Ambrose (Epistle 20) demanding the Portian basilica—that is, the basilica outside the walls—for the Arians. When the holy bishop refused with great courage, the empress, enraged by this, attempted to extort the matter in her son’s name and by threatening him. Therefore, on the Friday before the Sunday called Palm Sunday, certain court officials came by her order to demand from Ambrose the New Basilica—that is, the basilica inside the walls, larger than the former one (*ibid.*). Ambrose again replied, with modesty as well as courage, that a priest could not surrender the temple of God (*ibid.*, no. 2). On the following day the prefect himself visited the holy man, asking that at least the Portian basilica be yielded. The people protested with the greatest devotion and constancy; seeing this, the prefect returned to the palace to report to the Emperor what had occurred.

The holy bishop, undeterred by such disturbances, duly performed the customary rites on Palm Sunday. Nevertheless, while he was delivering the Creed to the candidates for baptism, he heard from some persons that the *decumani* had been sent from the palace to the Portian basilica and were hanging curtains there (*ibid.*, no. 4), to signify that Valentinian was taking possession and asserting his claim to that church. Ambrose did not cease from offering the sacrifice when it was reported that a certain Arian presbyter, named Castulus, had been seized by the people. The bishop was deeply grieved and immediately sent presbyters and deacons there (*ibid.*, nos. 5 ff.) to free the priest of sacrifice. Justina, however, treating this as sedition, cast many citizens into prison, declared a suspension of business at the palace, and directed great threats against the leading men. Nevertheless tribunes and officials were again sent to Ambrose [Col. 0090C] to compel him to surrender one of the basilicas (*ibid.*, no. 8 ff.). Meanwhile soldiers were ordered to go and occupy it. But after the blessed bishop had addressed them, they immediately returned to their post.

Ambrose spent the entire Tuesday in the Church; but as night approached he returned to the episcopal residence, so that, if they wished to drive him into exile, they would find him prepared (*ibid.*, no. 10). Before dawn on the following day, he left his house and found the Church surrounded by soldiers, although the customary readings were nevertheless being recited there. The bishop ordered that the soldiers be excluded from the right of holy communion; terrified by this, they came over to the Catholic side. Then, mounting the basilica’s ambo, he preached to the people from the Book of Job, which happened to be read at that time (*ibid.*, no. 14 ff.). While he skilfully adapted his sermon to present circumstances, people interrupted him to report that the curtains were being removed from the basilica—a sign that the Emperor was abandoning his undertaking. Our bishop continued his sermon when, behold, a notary came to him from the Emperor, called him a tyrant (*ibid.*, no. 22), and addressed him in most insulting terms. Ambrose replied with restraint, indeed, but yielded nothing of his steadfastness. He was not allowed to return home that day; instead, with the brethren they all spent the night in the smaller basilica, singing psalms.

On the following day—that is, Thursday of Holy Week—the prophecy of Jonah was read as usual. Ambrose began to expound it in a sermon [Col. 0091A] (*ibid.*, no. 25). He had not progressed very far in his intended discourse when some persons reported to him that Valentinian had ordered the soldiers to withdraw and the citizens held in prison to be released. This news produced incredible joy among the Catholics. But although that persecution ended here (*ibid.*, nos. 27–28), certain words of the Emperor were nevertheless reported which did not permit these Catholics to feel secure. Caligonus, Valentinian’s chamberlain-prefect, sent someone to Ambrose to say in his own words: “While I live, do you despise Valentinian? I will take off your head” (*ibid.*, no. 28). Ambrose gave him this courageous and wholly episcopal reply: “May God permit you to accomplish what you threaten; for I shall suffer what bishops suffer, and you shall do what eunuchs do.”

Ambrose refers to the same eunuch, though suppressing [Col. 0091B] his name, in the treatise *On Joseph the Patriarch*, where these words also occur, truly indicating the holy bishop’s restraint:

> I do not even take pleasure in recalling his words—words which at that time he either poured out or extorted by insult to the Church.

(*On Joseph*, book 6, no. 33 ff.)

He adds, however, that the man paid the penalty not long afterwards, though he was condemned for another crime. Augustine explains it thus: “We know that Calligonus, eunuch of the younger Valentinian, was punished by the avenging sword, convicted by the confession of a prostitute” (*Against Julian*, book 6, ch. 14).

71. It cannot be said how dismayed Marcellina was when she received the first reports of this disturbance. She therefore immediately begged her brother in frequent letters to keep her informed of everything. But Ambrose, not allowing his dearest sister, anxious as she was for him, to remain in suspense, wrote her an orderly account of all that had occurred; from his letter (Epistle 20) we have borrowed what we have narrated concerning this persecution. Some, moreover, suppose that this persecution was stirred up in the following year; but we have shown in its proper place that it must not be deferred beyond this very year (Preface to Epistles 20 and 21).

72. (A.D. 386.) Although Justina’s assaults appeared to have subsided, Ambrose nevertheless clearly foresaw that this Arian woman would not remain quiet. And indeed she did not long restrain her hatred. In order more effectively to carry out her designs, from as early as January of this year she persuaded her son to promulgate a law granting Arians the right to assemble in church [Col. 0091D], and imposing the penalty of death upon those who should dare to oppose it, not merely openly, but even by private petition (last book *On the Faith*). The empress ordered Benevolus, prefect of the archives of the *memoria*, to draft and seal this law (ibid.). But he, preferring conscience to favour, refused this task and therefore gladly submitted to exile.

Auxentius supplied his services in his place, a man who, as Ambrose testifies, boasted that he was bishop of the Arians. Yet the holy bishop speaks thus of him to the emperor: “For my part, I know no bishop, nor do I know where he comes from” (Epistle 21, no. 9). Nevertheless, we learn from our bishop that he was a native of Scythia and, when he came thence to Milan [Col. 0092A], he laid aside the name Mercurinus—under which he had become notorious for crimes—and took the name Auxentius. “For,” Ambrose says, “he was so ashamed that he changed his name” (*Sermon against Auxentius*, no. 22). He wished to be called thus because he believed that, through the memory of the former Auxentius, he would be more acceptable to the small number of Arians—and especially to the foreigners—who followed the empress. Such was Justina’s chief agent, through whom this dreadful edict was written: it indeed drew tears from Catholics, but could not in the least break Ambrose’s resolve.

73. After the promulgation of this law, the emperor, leaving Milan with his mother, came to Ticinum; and there he issued the law on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March [15 February]. It is likely that at that time this same sovereign, ever hostile to all orthodox Christians [Col. 0092B], attempted to extort a widow’s deposit entrusted to the faith of the bishop of Ticinum (*On Embassies and Decrees*). But the bishop, after consulting Ambrose, adopted a course by which the inviolability of deposits might be kept safe and whole (*On the Duties of Ministers*, Book II, ch. 29).

74. Thereupon Justina, doubtless more inflamed against Ambrose, devised harsher and more grievous measures against him. For when she returned to Milan, Dalmatius, tribune and notary, approached the holy man in the emperor’s name, requiring him, like Auxentius, to choose judges (Epistle 21, no. 1), before whom, sitting in the palace, he should dispute concerning the doctrines of his faith; otherwise, he was to leave the city and yield his see to Auxentius.

Ambrose summoned the bishops and presbyters then present at Milan [Col. 0092C] and reported to them the imperial command. Since all judged that a petition ought to be presented to the emperor, Ambrose himself undertook to write it. In it he set before the emperor the reasons why he could not dispute concerning the faith in the palace before secular judges (ibid., no. 2 ff.), but why the controversy ought to be dealt with in a council. He added also that, whenever he expounded the faith in church, access to hear him was open to everyone; that he would have come to the palace to say these things in person (ibid., no. 17), but that the bishops and Catholic people would not permit it. They likewise earnestly forbade him to leave Milan, being convinced that, in the existing circumstances, to abandon the Church was one and the same thing as to betray it to heretics.

Afterwards he withdrew into the church, where for some time the people surrounded him day and night in vast numbers, lest he be carried off by force. Indeed, detachments of soldiers sent by the emperor encircled the church. Yet he displayed not the slightest sign of fear; rather, he desired with all his heart the grace of martyrdom. He even implored the people not to hinder him from it, setting before them how vain their watch was: a blind man had found a gate open which they believed they had carefully shut, and which the soldiers themselves had been unable to find open. While he was guarded in the church, he consoled his people both by readings from Scripture and by expounding them.

[Col. 0093A] There still survives one of the principal sermons delivered by him at this time (*Sermon on the Basilicas*, vol. II, p. 863). It records no small part of the efforts by which Arian fury harassed the shepherd and Catholic flock during the holy days of the Resurrection in this same year. In this common sorrow Ambrose added, beyond the consolations already mentioned, another remedy: the sacred singing of hymns which he himself had composed in honour of the most divine Trinity. The whole people sang these hymns with such an inward movement of devotion and feeling that very many shed floods of tears. Augustine, certainly an eyewitness of all this, after speaking of his mother in these words—“There my mother, your handmaid, foremost in anxiety and vigils, lived by prayers” (*Confessions*, Book IX, chs. 6–7)—adds concerning himself: “How I wept amid your hymns and songs, deeply moved by the sweetly sounding voices of your Church!”

That this manner observed in these songs had not previously been customary in the Western Church, but was afterwards spread throughout it, is attested by Augustine’s words: “Then it was instituted that hymns and psalms should be sung according to the custom of the Eastern regions; and from that time it has been retained to the present day, with many—indeed almost all—of your flocks throughout the rest of the world imitating it” (ibid.). Paulinus also reports the same concerning this practice (*Life of Ambrose*, no. 13). Yet what kind of psalmody and hymnody is to be understood here is not sufficiently agreed among authors; nor is this the place to investigate the matter more laboriously.

[Col. 0093C] 75. Something clearer and more remarkable, as the two writers just mentioned relate, happened by divine intervention, “to restrain,” as Augustine says, “the feminine, yet royal, fury” (in the cited passages). For at this time the bodies of the brother martyrs Protasius and Gervasius were revealed to our Ambrose by divine direction. In recounting their solemn exhumation and translation, Ambrose does not pass over in silence either the sermons delivered by him during that celebration or the numerous miracles then wrought by the martyrs (Epistle 22); nor does he omit the calumnies of the heretics, who, more faithless than the devil himself, dared stubbornly and shamelessly to deny those whom he here acknowledged as Christ’s martyrs. Augustine, who was present, also mentions these events more than once (*Confessions*, Book IX, ch. 7; *City of God*, Book II).

[Col. 0093D] Paulinus likewise does not omit these matters, and records certain details connected with this persecution which Ambrose and Augustine passed over. Such is his account of Euthymius (*Life of Ambrose*, no. 14 ff.). Having, by order of the empress, prepared a carriage in which to carry the holy bishop away into exile, he himself was ordered in the following year to leave his country, and was compelled to depart in that same carriage. But Paulinus does not explain to which persecution this should be assigned. He also asserts that about this time an Arian returned to the bosom of the Church (ibid., no. 17), claiming that he had seen an angel standing beside the holy man and suggesting to him what he was to expound to the people.

[Col. 0094A] 76. In fact, it is by no means obscure that at this very time those sermons were delivered from which the most outstanding works of the holy Doctor were composed. The *Exposition of Psalm CXVIII* (Preface to this Psalm), rightly counted among his finest monuments, contains many sermons of this year, but also many of the following year, as has been shown in its proper place (Preface to the *Exposition of Psalm CXVIII*). The purpose of this work is that Christians might both be instructed in the knowledge of their duties and urged to fulfil them by upright conduct and devotion. The blessed Father judged that this could in no way be done better than by explaining the noblest of psalms, so full of moral precepts; and he further chose to append [Col. 0094B] explanations of a considerable number of passages from the Song of Songs, which he judged more fitting to his subject.

77. Although Baronius held that Ambrose’s commentaries on the Gospel according to St Luke had been written from the year 376 onward, it is beyond doubt that the sermons of which this work is composed mention the harassment by Arians as a very recent event. Since, moreover, it is apparent from elsewhere that these same sermons were completed only over two years, some may conjecture that our Doctor preached on alternate Sundays, now on Psalm CXVIII and now on Luke’s Gospel. But those who maintain that each subject was treated on successive Sundays continuously to its conclusion (Preface to the same works) will have nothing to prevent them from assigning the sermons on Luke to the following year [Col. 0094C].

78. The bishops of the province of Aemilia, now included within the archbishopric of Bologna, consulted Ambrose by letter in this year concerning the day on which the feast of Easter should be celebrated in the following year. For, seeing that it would fall on the seventh day before the Kalends of May [25 April], they were uncertain whether that day belonged to the first lunar month after the equinox. The holy bishop answered their inquiry (Epistle 23) and, resolving every difficulty, made it clear that the aforesaid feast ought to be celebrated on that day.

79. At the vintage season Augustine, upon whose conversion God had set the finishing touch, came to Cassiciacum, the country estate of Verecundus (*Confessions*, Book IX [Col. 0094D], ch. 5). From there he immediately sent a letter to Ambrose, whom in this work he regarded as the chief minister of divine grace (ibid., ch. 6): “And I made known by letter to your true and holy bishop Ambrose my former errors and my present purpose, that he might advise me what books of yours I should read above all, so that I might become more ready and fit to receive so great a grace. But he directed me to the prophet Isaiah, I believe because he is more explicit than the others in foretelling the Gospel and the calling of the Gentiles.” Yet, since Augustine could not sufficiently grasp the meaning of this prophet, he decided to postpone reading him until another time.

80. (A.D. 387.) As soon as the time came when catechumens customarily enrolled themselves for baptism, namely toward the end of Lent, Augustine returned to Milan with his Alypius and his son Adeodatus, so that they might together be admitted among the *competentes*, those preparing for baptism: “When,” he says, “the time came for me to give in my name, we left the country and returned to Milan.” It happened that Ambrose was then giving daily instruction on moral matters (*On the Mysteries*, ch. 1, no. 1). Elsewhere it has been shown that this moral instruction, to which the same bishop refers here (Preface to *On Abraham*), can most fittingly be understood as the sermons from which the books *On the Patriarchs* were composed. First among them are placed the books *On Abraham*, in which Ambrose displays the vigorous devotion of that holy man’s faith (*On Joseph*, Book I, ch. 1, no. 7), and shows fulfilled in his deeds what philosophers had scarcely understood even as a bare notion [Col. 0095B].

81. The book *On Isaac and the Soul* follows those two. Its purpose is, by placing before the eyes the purity of sincere mind found in that holy patriarch (ibid.), to show that he was a type of Christ the Lord and that Rebecca, his wife, was a type of the Church; and likewise to adapt that married pair to the nuptials of the faithful soul with its heavenly bridegroom.

82. What Ambrose had said about the soul in the preceding little book led him, in publishing the treatise *On the Good of Death*, to make clear that there is nothing terrible in death. At the same time he maintained that, renouncing bodily pleasures, every desire, and the enticements of the world (*On the Good of Death*, ch. 3, no. 9), we must die permanently to the world [Col. 0095C].

83. Augustine and the others, imbued with these sermons most suitable for preparing catechumens, were washed in the living water during the Easter vigil, at the feast which, as we have said, was celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of May [25 April] of the present year. Immediately after their initiation by holy baptism, the holy bishop duly instructed them by an exposition of the sacraments they had received, as well as of those rites which had formerly been customarily concealed. From this catechesis, we believe, the book *On the Mysteries* was produced (Preface to *On the Mysteries*).

84. Saint Ambrose returned to moral precepts. In order to deter more strongly that bright throng of neophytes from returning to the world which they had renounced in baptism, he delivered the sermons which, now reduced to book form, have come down to us under the title *On Flight from the World* [Col. 0095D] (Preface to that work).

85. This treatise is followed by the two books *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, in which Ambrose, proposing for imitation the remarkable endurance of mind and hardships displayed by the same saint (*On Joseph the Patriarch*, Book I, ch. 1, no. 1), clearly teaches that blessedness lies amid calamities, afflictions, and sufferings.

86. Our bishop did not pass over the history of Joseph, but preached upon it more than once, above all splendidly praising the chastity of that patriarch (*On Joseph*, ch. 6, nos. 30 and 38). There he testifies that he had already preached on the same subject in the preceding year; but those sermons have either been lost or perhaps were never committed to writing [Col. 0096A].

87. The book *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs* determines the sequence of these treatises (Preface to that book). It is probable that this work followed after a brief interval the treatise of which we were speaking immediately before, and was publicly delivered before Ambrose’s second embassy to Maximus.

88. Let us now come to that second embassy. All this tyrant’s movements sufficiently showed that he was threatening the provinces of Italy and had resolved to despoil Valentinian. Greatly alarmed by so grave a danger, Justina judged that no one’s assistance was more immediately available than that of Saint Ambrose. Therefore, since he retained no memory of injuries, he again undertook, at the empress’s request [Col. 0096B], the burden of an embassy to that tyrant. “I, your ambassador, again went to Gaul; and it was sweet to me—first, for your safety; then, for peace and for the filial devotion with which you sought your brother’s remains—to be still anxious for you, and already concerned for the honour of your brother” (*On the Death of Valentinian*, no. 28).

These words disclose the cause of the embassy. The holy bishop himself informed Valentinian by letter of the outcome he had obtained from it (Epistle 24), setting out in full the whole course of his dealings with the tyrant. On his return, he sent this letter to the emperor from the journey itself, lest anyone arriving beforehand maliciously preoccupy the emperor’s mind, and also so that the sovereign, being informed of everything, might be prepared against so formidable an enemy, who had resolved to crush him. Ambrose found with Maximus two kinds of bishops from whose communion he wholly abstained. The first were those who communicated with Maximus himself (ibid., no. 12); hence Paulinus asserts that the blessed bishop excluded him from participation in communion (*Life of Ambrose*, no. 19), as has already been said. The second were those who sought the death of certain persons, however far astray from the faith they might be (Epistle 24, no. 12): namely, the Ithacians, by whom Priscillian was accused before Maximus and through whose proceedings both he and his followers were put to the sword. The tyrant could not bear this constancy and greatness of spirit in Saint Ambrose; deeply angered, he ordered him to return at once (ibid.).

89. Maximus quickly followed Ambrose as he returned and, meeting no resistance [Col. 0096D], invaded Italy. Valentinian, fearing that he might fall into his hands and be treated with the same cruelty which Gratian had suffered from him, embarked on a ship, came to Thessalonica, and wholly entrusted himself to the loyalty and protection of Theodosius. Theodosius received the fugitive with great humanity; yet he piously admonished him not to doubt that these great disasters had been divinely inflicted because he had defended the Arian heresy and harassed the Catholic Church.

90. Although Maximus had made the bitterest threats against Ambrose, he apparently did him no harm. Virtue found such reverence even among the wicked. Besides the works already enumerated, we believe that several letters also belong to this period, in which the holy man gave answers to many questions eagerly submitted to him by letter. Among these may be placed the two letters to Studius (Epistles 25 and 26). He was a judge in the secular court. Seeing that, after Priscillian had been condemned to death through the urgings of the Ithacians, many were withdrawing from the communion of all who had pronounced a capital sentence upon anyone, he asked Ambrose whether he himself ought to abstain from the sacraments whenever he had condemned someone to the ultimate penalty. Ambrose answered his question thus: “Many abstain voluntarily, and they are indeed praised; nor can we fail to praise those who observe the Apostle’s authority so far that we do not dare deny them communion.” Then, speaking as a bishop, he rather exhorts Studius to show clemency than severity toward accused persons [Col. 0097B].

91. At this time Ambrose also wrote often to Irenaeus, his dearest son and a presbyter or deacon of the Church of Milan. The first letter explains a verse from Deuteronomy (Epistle 27) and advises avoiding association with wicked men. The second, which followed not long after (Epistle 28), teaches that Irenaeus’s life, as that of one distinguished by a more divine character, ought to be more perfect and far holier than the conduct of secular persons. On the same day, after returning home from the vigils, the holy bishop resumed his usual studies and began to ponder the verse of Scripture which he had just heard sung in the assembly. At once he put pen to paper and, having written a third letter [Col. 0097C], exhorted Irenaeus through an interpretation of the same verse (Epistle 29) to cleave solely to the supreme good through contempt and renunciation of the world. He had scarcely handed this letter over for delivery when a passage from Haggai occurred to him, wholly suited to that very theme; it supplied material for composing a fourth letter (Epistle 30).

92. Drawn by such proofs of Ambrose’s kindness and accessibility, Irenaeus did not hesitate to consult the holy bishop concerning various questions. The first of his questions was whether the love of those who had devoted themselves to God’s service from childhood should be judged greater, or that of those who did so only at a more advanced age. Ambrose had initially included an explanation of this not unpleasing difficulty in one letter [Col. 0097D] (Epistle 31), but soon added another on the same subject (Epistle 32). When Irenaeus received the first letter, however, he encountered some difficulty over a passage from Deuteronomy cited in it, and presented the matter again to Ambrose; he immediately received the desired solution of the same question (Epistle 33).

93. Horontianus, likewise a disciple of the holy Doctor, had been educated from childhood among the clergy and had been consecrated deacon or presbyter by Ambrose’s hands. He asked his teacher whether the human soul was of heavenly substance. In two letters (Epistles 34 and 35), the latter following the former after a very short interval, the holy bishop taught him that the nature of our soul is spiritual [Col. 0098A], and strongly urged him to read through the Fourth Book of Ezra. The same Horontianus wished to know Ambrose’s view of certain words of the Apostle, whose preceding context Ambrose had quoted. Our bishop satisfied his wish (Epistle 36), but on the occasion of those words he could not refrain from lamenting to him, in most weighty language, the opportunities for martyrdom taken away from him: “What opportunities I had,” he says, “and I was recalled almost from the very end!” (ibid., no. 4).

94. Simplicianus informed Ambrose how delighted he had been to read the things which Ambrose had expounded to the people on the Pauline epistles, and how welcome it would be if he sent him something more of the same sort. Ambrose’s respect for this man was too great for him to refuse his wishes. He therefore sent him a letter in which he included what he had preached to the people on another passage of the Apostle, and in which he further demonstrated that our freedom is in Christ’s wisdom (Epistle 37). Repeating this latter point, he then clearly shows in another letter that true riches also consist in that same wisdom (Epistle 38).

95. Finally, about this time, Ambrose consoled by letter a certain Faustinus, who was mourning with altogether excessive tears his lost sister, a woman of singular virtue and merit (Epistle 39).

96. (A.D. 388.) It is commonly believed that Justina, that Arian empress, did not return to Italy but died in her flight; so that, not without divine judgment, she who had so often attempted to drive Ambrose into exile herself died an exile and a homeless wanderer. If any inference may also be drawn from Paulinus’s words (*Life of Ambrose*, no. 20), we may say that about this year a certain magician named Innocentius, while being tortured for various crimes, confessed that, while Justina held power, he had been hired by Arians to stir up popular hatred against the bishop; that he had performed abominable sacrifices, but without success. Paulinus adds (ibid.) that the hand of an assassin sent against Ambrose withered, and was soon restored to him by the holy man. He relates further (ibid., no. 21) that Probus arranged for a boy notary to be brought to Ambrose, so that through his help the boy might be freed from a demon.

97. Theodosius entered Italy with Valentinian and, having rapidly won two victories over the tyrant Maximus, besieged Aquileia, to which that tyrant had withdrawn. After taking it, he executed him by the sword. Historians have vied in heaping praise upon Theodosius’s extraordinary restraint in these victories; if we undertook to add anything, we should exceed the bounds of our purpose. Yet we cannot refrain from recording here, in Ambrose’s own words, what the emperor granted at his prayers: “I owe it to your benefits that, at my request, you freed very many from exile, from prison, and from the punishments of final death” (Epistle 40, no. 25).

98. After Maximus’s party had been crushed, Theodosius came to Milan, from which Ambrose had departed for Aquileia [Col. 0099A]. The reason for Ambrose’s journey is unknown. Cardinal Baronius supposed (*Annals*, under the year 388) that it was undertaken to appoint a new bishop in place of Valerian, who had governed that Church. Yet no testimony can be found to establish this opinion. However the matter may stand, Ambrose was there when news reached him of an edict of Theodosius directed against the bishop of Callinicum, where a Jewish synagogue had been burned by some Christians, and against monks who had burned a temple of the Valentinians. The holy bishop immediately wrote to the emperor on behalf of the bishop and the monks. But because Theodosius, giving more attention than was right to the counsels of courtiers, had not revoked his edict, Ambrose, at the first opportunity for preaching before the emperor, demonstrated with such freedom the injustice of the rescript that the good emperor could not refuse to revoke it.

Although scarcely an example nobler than this can be found of episcopal courage, since it is described exactly both by Paulinus (*Life of Ambrose*, no. 22) and by two Ambrosian letters (Epistles 40 and 41), we refrain from saying more of it here [Col. 0099B].

99. In this year the pagans did not hesitate again to test whether they could wrest from Theodosius the restoration of the profane religions, a restoration they had already requested repeatedly. We may readily believe that Symmachus again acted as standard-bearer in this petition; but, when on this occasion too he encountered Ambrose as champion of the Christian religion, he suffered a most disgraceful refusal from the emperor. Ambrose himself relates it as follows: “Afterwards I also addressed the most clement Emperor Theodosius in person, and did not hesitate to speak to his face. I told him that, although not the whole senate had requested it, he had nevertheless at last given his assent to a representation of this kind made by an embassy of the senate; and so for some days thereafter I did not approach him. He did not take it ill, because I was not acting for my own advantage, but because I was unashamed to speak in the king’s presence what was beneficial both to him and to my own soul” (Epistle 57, no. 4).

100. (A.D. 389.) It is probable, as we have shown (Preface to this book), that the sermons contained in the books of the *Hexaemeron* were delivered during the latter part of Lent in this year. He frequently delivered two of them on the same day [Col. 0099D]. But amid such great labours he found no small consolation in seeing the flock of believers increased day by day by the conversion of pagans and heretics (*Hexaemeron*, Book III, ch. 1, no. 3).

101. As soon as the work *Hexaemeron* was completed and had come into the hands of the holy bishop’s friends and disciples, they studied it carefully. Horontianus, one of their number, after reading it with attentive mind, wondered that neither Moses nor Ambrose had attempted to explain why the human being, though the last of creatures, had been created. Therefore, by the right of familiarity granted him by Ambrose himself, he questioned him concerning this. The holy bishop answered him (Epistle 43), and after observing that the Lawgiver had written nothing which he had not himself received by divine revelation [Col. 0100A], he offered several reasons highly suitable for resolving this problem.

102. Horontianus also asked why the whole universe had been created in six days. Ambrose resolved his question in another letter (Epistle 44).

103. Sabinus likewise, having read the *Hexaemeron*, asked the holy man by letter whether he had discussed anywhere the location of the earthly paradise, or what his opinion of it was. Ambrose replied (Epistle 45) that he had not treated in those books the question which he had discussed before; but in his answer he nevertheless examines the difficulty according both to the spiritual and to the moral sense.

[Col. 0100B] 104. Sabinus wrote Ambrose again and reported that a follower of Apollinaris had come to Piacenza and spread his errors in that city; when he had been refuted there, he had set out for Milan. In replying to this bishop, our Ambrose said (Epistle 46) that this erring man had tried secretly at Milan to infect minds with his opinions and had loudly attacked certain passages in his books, doubtless *On the Faith*. When Ambrose learned this, he sent persons to tell him in his own words that he was not acting from charity; for Ambrose, being human, was likewise liable to error and did not refuse willingly to acknowledge his mistakes if they were pointed out to him privately. But when at last he understood that this obstinate heretic was spreading his errors more widely [Col. 0100C], after publicly refuting him he had left himself no alternative but flight.

105. Along with his letter, Ambrose had sent Sabinus the treatise which the Apollinarian had criticized, so that Sabinus might freely tell him what judgment he made concerning it. But Sabinus could not read the books because they had been written with insufficiently distinct lettering, and he returned them to Ambrose. Ambrose then had them sent again to that bishop in a more elegantly written copy, adding another letter (Epistle 47), in which a passage of Scripture was discussed, as Sabinus himself had desired.

106. Ambrose received word that Sabinus had read and approved this work, but immediately sent him another, asking him earnestly to examine it strictly. “Everyone,” he says (Epistle 48), “is deceived by his own writings, and they escape his ear; and just as even deformed children delight their parents, so unpolished discourses flatter their writer.” This was said well and prudently, but another reason also moved him: in that book one of the principal questions of the faith was under discussion. Hence we think it may be inferred that no other book is indicated here than *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*, a work in which not only the errors of Arians and Sabellians, but especially those of the Apollinarians, are refuted [Col. 0100D].

107. To these letters of Ambrose to Sabinus is added another (Epistle 49), in which he elegantly argues that he is never less alone than when he is alone. But we know that other letters of his to Sabinus have perished, because in this letter he promises that he will write to him more frequently.

108. Ambrose learned by a letter from Chromatius of Aquileia that it would give Chromatius great pleasure if Ambrose treated something concerning the old covenant in letters. He immediately wrote to him and interpreted the history of Balaam the false prophet (Epistle 50). Although in this letter he promises Chromatius that he will add others, we find no letter to him except this one.

109. When Jovinian’s errors had publicly broken out at Rome, Siricius, the supreme pontiff, summoned his presbyters and other clergy together in council and condemned that heresiarch and his doctrines [Col. 0101B]. Since those same errors had infected some monks of his monastery, founded near the walls of Milan, he sent envoys to that city, by whom a synodical letter (vol. II, p. 963) might safely be conveyed to that Church. Upon receiving the letter, Ambrose, to whom the care of the said monastery especially belonged, quickly assembled the clergy of his Church and, in the presence of the papal envoys, likewise struck down that heresy on its own native soil, so to speak. In a letter written in the name of the whole assembly, the holy man not only made known the council’s decision to the supreme pontiff, but also set forth there most powerful arguments by which the madness of this heresy was overthrown.

[Col. 0101C] 110. After the year 385 but before 390 (Preface to the same *Expositions*), Ambrose wrote his *Exposition of Psalm I*, to which he prefixed a most beautiful introduction to all the psalms. Both were compiled from sermons publicly delivered, since he himself indicates that catechumens, apparently including those enrolled among the *competentes*, were among his hearers; this certainly points to the latter part of Lent. The *Expositions of Psalms XLV, XLVII, XLVIII,* and *LXI*, which we also judge to have been made from sermons (ibid.), were published at about the same time.

111. (A.D. 390.) We have shown (Preface to that book) that the book *On Elijah and Fasting* consists of three sermons. The first exhorts Christians to undertake the works of Lent [Col. 0101D]; the second and third prepare the *competentes* to receive baptismal grace at the end of that same Lent. Ambrose combined these sermons into a book after Basil’s example.

112. When the city of Thessalonica, having risen in revolt, had killed certain officials, Theodosius judged that it must pay the penalty for so great a crime. But Ambrose, who was especially prompt in imploring the emperor’s clemency on behalf of that unhappy city, pressed Theodosius so warmly and persistently that he promised to forgive the offence (*Life of Ambrose*, no. 24). Overconfident in this imperial promise, as also in the emperor’s innate goodness, Ambrose was calmly holding a council at Milan, attended by bishops from Gaul [Col. 0102A]. That synod was held because of the Ithacians and their ordination of Felix of Trier, by which all Gaul was disturbed.

What was decreed in that synod concerning this affair—which some wrongly place in the preceding year—is indicated by Canon 6 of the Council of Turin in these words: “If any persons wish to separate themselves from his communion, that is, from Felix’s, they are received into the fellowship of our peace, in accordance with letters formerly issued by Bishop Ambrose, of venerable memory, or by the bishop of the Roman Church” (Council of Turin, canon 6). But the letters in question have not come down to our time.

Meanwhile, as those bishops continued the council they had begun, Theodosius, overcome by the persuasion of court attendants, who kept urging that it would be an example of the most dangerous and harmful kind if a revolt of this sort remained unpunished, ordered the citizens of Thessalonica to be punished with extreme severity. As a result of this decree, countless killings were carried out, of guilty and innocent alike [Col. 0102B].

113. When the Fathers of the council learned of so great a barbarity, they were profoundly distressed by it. As Ambrose testifies, not one of them failed to groan, nor did any receive it with indifference: “There was no absolution for your deed within Ambrose’s communion; indeed, the odium of the offence committed would have been aggravated in my case if no one had said that reconciliation with our God was necessary” (Ep. 51, no. 6). Thus spoke the holy bishop. For, hearing that Theodosius was returning to Milan, he judged that the fresh wound ought still to be handled with a gentle hand [Col. 0102C], yet that there must be no departure from discipline by even a hair’s breadth; he therefore resolved to leave the city. He himself gives the reason for this: “I do not dare,” he says, “to offer the sacrifice if you wish to be present” (ibid., no. 13). By these words, although he declared Theodosius excluded from the right of communion, he nevertheless left him no occasion for offence, since he entrusted these matters to a private letter: “I write in my own hand,” he says, “that you alone may read it” (ibid., no. 14). Indeed, he further indicated that on the very night on which he was preparing to depart he had been divinely forbidden to perform the sacred rites at the altars while Theodosius was present.

Finally, from this letter all bishops may learn with how much prudence and caution they ought to conduct themselves toward rulers who have fallen into serious crimes, and how they ought to employ less severity than gentleness toward them. For what more fully displays this prudent moderation than these words? “I put forward,” he says, “a bodily illness—truly severe, and scarcely to be relieved except by milder men; yet I would rather have died than not await your arrival for two or three days” (ibid., no. 15).

114. Theodoret relates (Ecclesiastical History, V.18) that, after the emperor had abstained from the ecclesiastical assembly for a full eight months, he wished to enter the church on the feast of the Lord’s Nativity. Ambrose sharply rebuked him and did not permit him to enter until he had both submitted himself to public penance and promised that he would enact a law [Col. 0103A] forbidding any convicted person to be subjected to capital punishment before the thirtieth day after condemnation.

The emperor fulfilled both promises. As regards public penance, he embraced it with such self-abasement that we cannot refrain from inserting Ambrose’s own passage concerning it:

> “He laid aside every emblem of royalty in which he took pride; in the church he wept for his sin, which had crept upon him through the deception of others; with groans and tears he prayed for pardon. What private persons are ashamed of, the emperor was not ashamed publicly to do in penance; nor thereafter was there a day on which he did not grieve over that error.”  
> (On the Death of Theodosius, no. 34)

Theodoret, already cited (V.18), and Sozomen with him (VII.25), add that not long afterward Theodosius, while taking part in the sacrifice and having offered his oblation at the altar, remained within the railings of the presbytery. Ambrose sent someone to remind him that only clerics were permitted to stand in that place; the emperor immediately obeyed the admonition. Theodoret further adds (loc. cit.) that, not long afterward, when Nectarius invited the same ruler to enter the enclosure of the altar in the basilica at Constantinople, he uttered this saying, so glorious for our bishop: “I know no bishop except Ambrose.”

115. About this same time, two Persians of very great power and wisdom, stirred by Ambrose’s fame, as Paulinus relates (Life of Ambrose, no. 25), came to Milan with the sole purpose of learning for themselves whether the man’s presence corresponded to his reputation. According to the testimony of the same Paulinus, they departed from him in admiration.

116. (A.D. 391.) At this time Ambrose enjoyed the greatest peace through the favor of both emperors, by whom he was intensely loved and honored. Lest he allow this tranquillity to pass unused, during this leisure he appears to have composed for his clergy his books *On the Duties of Ministers*. Into these books he inserted several discourses delivered at various times, even at the beginning of his priesthood. For he knew that the life of clerics, who must shine as an example before other Christians, ought to have nothing holier; and accordingly he always took the greatest care in forming them and the greatest caution in selecting them.

Nor perhaps will it be unpleasant to the reader if we offer here, in his own words, a twofold example of this concern. Thus he says:

> “You remember, my sons, that a certain friend, although he seemed to recommend himself by assiduous services, was nevertheless not admitted by me into the clergy for this reason alone: his manner of movement was exceedingly unbecoming. When I found another already in the clergy, I ordered that he should never walk before me, because he struck my eyes, as it were, with the lash of an insolent gait. . . . Nor did my judgment deceive me: both departed from the Church, so that, as each had betrayed himself by his gait, so each displayed the treachery of his mind. For one, in the time of the Arian persecution, abandoned the faith; the other, through love of money, denied that he belonged to us in order to avoid ecclesiastical judgment.”  
> (On the Duties of Ministers, I.18, no. 72)

From this anyone may readily understand that the work in question was intended above all for clerics. Yet since their duty is, as it were, to season the lives of others by their character and speech, so many precepts useful to every human condition are interwoven there that all may draw from it no small benefit.

117. Ambrose’s care, which embraced all without exception, did not neglect the monastic profession. Augustine mentions a monastery situated in the suburbs of Milan: “There was,” he says, “a monastery at Milan, full of good brethren outside the walls, under Ambrose’s fostering care; and we did not know it” (Confessions, VIII.15). Nor only here, but elsewhere also, he mentions those monks with honor (On the Morals of the Catholic Church, I.33).

Yet among those good imitators of apostolic life there were found two who emulated the treachery of the traitor. [Col. 0104B] Their names were Sarmatio and Barbazianus. Ambrose touches upon them more obscurely in his Exposition of Psalm 36 (no. 49), but portrays them in their proper colors in the letter to the Vercellians (Ep. 63, no. 7 ff.). Those who desire further information concerning their vices and errors may consult those passages.

118. (A.D. 392.) As the preceding year turned, Theodosius had returned to the East and had left Valentinian undisturbed in the empire of which Maximus had deprived him. But when this youthful ruler went into Gaul to protect it from barbarian incursions, he did not long enjoy the peace that he had resolved should obey his rule. For, as reports of an impending barbarian invasion of Italy grew frequent, the prefect and magistrates asked Saint Ambrose to go to the emperor [Col. 0104C] and persuade him to bring aid to that region by returning. Ambrose did not undertake this journey, because meanwhile Valentinian was reported to have crossed the Alps.

At this point letters from Valentinian himself were brought to the holy bishop (On the Death of Valentinian, no. 25), urgently summoning him, both because Valentinian wished to be baptized by him and because he desired to give him as a pledge of his good faith Count Arbogast. Troubled by these tidings, Ambrose immediately set out and had already crossed the Alpine heights (ibid.) when he received news of the unfortunate emperor’s death. He was slain by the said count on the Ides of May, the day before Pentecost, being only twenty years old. Ambrose immediately retraced his journey, watering it with many tears. Nothing could be imagined more tender than his grief, as he reflected how ardently Valentinian had wished to be baptized by him, though surrounded by so many and such great bishops; how much hope he had placed in Ambrose’s arrival; but above all, Ambrose mourned the loss suffered by the Church: “You were struck,” he said, “on the cheek, O Church, when you lost Gratian; you offered the other also when Valentinian was taken from you” (ibid., no. 6).

119. His body was not long afterward brought back to Milan. While Ambrose waited for Theodosius’s instructions concerning his burial, a letter from that emperor anticipated him, expressing sympathy with his grief. In answering it, Ambrose explains his silence and testifies to the emperor that nothing stirred in him a greater longing for his Valentinian than this: “By your instruction,” said the holy bishop (Ep. 53), “he had assumed so great a devotion toward our God and had devoted himself to me with such affection, that he loved the man whom previously he had persecuted, and regarded as a father the man whom previously he had repelled as an adversary.”

After first saying the following concerning the burial of that ruler—“There are most precious porphyry tablets with which the covering is clad, by which the royal remains are enclosed”—he immediately urges that the remains be buried promptly, lest they decay in the heat, and also that provision be made for the excessive grief of Justa and Grata, the dead ruler’s sisters.

120. When Theodosius’s orders had been brought to Milan, the funeral rites for Valentinian were performed about the middle of July. The holy bishop had already come into the church and had spoken upon the Gospel publicly read (On the Death of Valentinian, no. 30); whence we infer that these funeral observances were celebrated on a Sunday or on some more solemn feast-day. Finally, when the emperor’s body had been magnificently placed in the basilica, as befitted so great a ruler, Ambrose delivered his funeral oration over him. Nothing is fuller of piety and charity; nothing more effective in drawing tears from the hearers.

121. Most importantly, he promises that by prayers night and day he will commend both brothers to God and will remember them in every offering (ibid., no. 78), just as he would Theodosius and Valentinian’s sisters who were present at the ceremony. Finally, after praying God to join in heaven the souls of brothers whose bodies were now to be joined in the tomb [Col. 0105C] (ibid., no. 79), he descended from the pulpit.

122. At this time Ambrose wrote to Titianus, who was in litigation with his niece (Ep. 52), and urged him, out of piety, to come to an agreement with her. Some maintain that this Titianus had held the office of praetorian prefect, though others think this may be doubted.

123. At Bologna there was then one Eusebius, head of a noble and wealthy family, who corresponded with Ambrose. He used to send his sons and grandsons to Milan (Epp. 54 and 55) to be educated under the eyes of so great a teacher. Among others he sent the girl Ambrosia, to be consecrated by Ambrose’s hands under the sacred veil of virginity. Nothing could have happened more pleasingly to the holy bishop. Therefore, at this consecration, arranged, as it seems to us, for the Paschal feast [Col. 0105D], he delivered a public discourse in which he argued at length against the followers of Bonosus, by whom Mary’s perpetual virginity was assailed. After prefacing this sermon with two chapters, he made it into a single treatise, entitled *On the Formation of a Virgin*, and dedicated it to Eusebius (Admonition on the same book).

124. There are besides two Ambrosian letters to Eusebius. One (Ep. 54) reports that an offence against an attendant has been forgiven and announces to him the arrival of the boy Faustinus, who is suffering from a cough, to his sister. The other (Ep. 55) states that the same Faustinus is returning to Bologna with his father Faustinus, while two Ambrosii remain meanwhile at Milan.

[Col. 0106A] 125. Two matters had been discussed in the synod of Capua. The first concerned the controversy between Flavian and Evagrius over the see of Antioch; the second concerned the case of Bonosus, summoned to judgment because he denied the perpetual virginity of the Mother of God. Consideration of the first matter had been assigned by the said council to Theophilus of Alexandria and the Egyptian bishops. But when Flavian refused to obey the council’s decree, he approached the emperor and requested a larger synod. Theophilus informed Ambrose of this matter by letter. Ambrose answered him that, if possible, he should settle the dispute without prejudice to the decrees of the Council of Nicaea and also of the Synod of Capua (Ep. 56), and should report this to the bishop of Rome; for peace could best be secured in this way, and Ambrose would most willingly subscribe to what the Roman Church approved.

As to Bonosus, Ambrose judged that his examination should be referred to Anysius of Thessalonica and other bishops of Macedonia. Those bishops, however, wrote on the matter to another bishop, whose name is unknown. He replied that this judgment belonged to them (vol. II, p. 1008), for it had been assigned to them by the Synod of Capua. Nevertheless, in his letter he affirmed that Bonosus had rightly been reproved concerning the children of Mary.

126. (A.D. 393.) After Valentinian had been killed, Arbogast, as we have already said, did not dare to assume the purple himself; he therefore ordered Eugenius, formerly a grammarian and rhetorician, to put it on. As soon as Eugenius was proclaimed emperor, he sent a letter to Ambrose. [Col. 0106C] But the holy bishop did not even deem him worthy of an answer, because he foresaw that this tyrant would not reject the petitions of the pagans. “At the beginning of your reign,” he says, “I did not answer when you wrote, because I foresaw that this would come to pass” (Ep. 57). He immediately adds: “Yet when a matter arose involving my duty toward those whose care I bore, I both wrote and pleaded, in order to show that in matters concerning God I possess a righteous fear.”

The envy of antiquity did not permit those letters, which evidently were sent in the preceding year, to reach later ages.

127. At the beginning of this year Eugenius crossed the Alps. When Saint Ambrose heard that he was also coming to Milan, he immediately withdrew from there, since he could not endure the presence of a tyrant who, when Flavian, then prefect, and Count Arbogast requested it, “forgetful of his faith, granted them the altar of Victory and the expenses for ceremonies . . .” (Paulinus, Life of Ambrose, no. 26). Yet, although Eugenius had twice rejected the pagans’ prayers, we understand that at the third entreaty concerning the same matter he yielded, from the letter in which the holy bishop explained to Eugenius the reason for his withdrawal (Ep. 57, no. 6).

Ambrose, moreover, as Paulinus teaches, went from Milan to Bologna and from there as far as Faenza (Life of Ambrose, no. 27). The writer adds that, while Ambrose was at Florence, he restored life to the boy Pansophius: “For this little child,” he says, “he composed a booklet, so that what he could not know through the infancy of his age, he might learn by reading” (ibid., no. 28).

[Col. 0107A] 128. The holy bishop did not return to Milan until the Kalends of August in the following year, after the aforesaid tyrant had departed (Ep. 61). In what city he chiefly resided during this interval is unknown to us. But we know that, when he was at Bologna, the bodies of the martyrs of Christ Vitalis and Agricola were raised by him from their tomb.
