They had previously lain unknown amid the very burial grounds of the Jews, unless, as Paulinus says, the holy martyrs revealed themselves to the bishop himself (Life of Ambrose, no. 29), or, as several manuscripts read, “revealed themselves to the bishop of his Church”—that is, presumably, to the bishop of Bologna.

129. At about the same time Saint Ambrose, invited by the Florentines to come to Florence for the dedication of a new basilica, could not refuse their most urgent entreaties, though he himself had resolved to go elsewhere (Admonition on the book *Exhortation to Virginity*). Coming to that city during the fasts of Lent, he brought with him portions—or, as he calls them (*Exhortation to Virginity*), *apophoreta*, “gifts to be carried away”—of the relics of the holy martyrs exhumed at Bologna, to be deposited in the basilica to be dedicated.

During the sacred ceremonies of this consecration he delivered a sermon in which he highly praises the widow Juliana, who had built that church at her own expense. After relating her exhortation to her children, all of whom, moved by it, had dedicated themselves to God, he at last addresses them in his own words and urges and encourages them to virtues suited to their vocation. We still possess this sermon in the treatise entitled *Exhortation to Virginity*.

130. In the most difficult times of Eugenius’s domination—that is, in this year or the next—Ambrose wrote to Severus, bishop of the see of Naples, commending to him a certain Jacob, a presbyter who had withdrawn from the farthest recess of Persia (Ep. 59) into the solitudes of Campania. Yet some consider this letter to belong to the time of the war with Maximus. This is sufficiently examined in its proper place (Admonition on the same letter).

131. The holy man also wrote to Paternus (Ep. 60), who had attained very high rank. Paternus had resolved to unite in marriage with his son his granddaughter by a daughter and had consulted his own bishop’s judgment in this matter; the bishop referred him to Ambrose. Paternus therefore sent Ambrose a letter setting out all the reasons that moved him to unite the uncle with his niece in marriage. Saint Ambrose answered it in such a way as both to pay due respect to Paternus’s bishop and to demonstrate that the reasons by which Paternus had persuaded himself that the marriage was lawful were no reasons at all.

132. Ambrose’s letter was not without effect. For we have another of his letters (Ep. 84), to Cynegius, in which we read: “I refused the granddaughter to her grandfather, as I think; by some wholly unknown notion he desired her to become his daughter-in-law, so as to turn her grandfather into his father-in-law.” We do not doubt that this Cynegius was the son of Paternus, about whom Paternus had consulted Ambrose and who, as this letter shows, had himself written to the holy bishop concerning the same matter.

133. (A.D. 394.) Ambrose also spent some part of this year at Florence, since common opinion has it that, while he was staying in that city, Saint Paulinus passed through it with his wife Therasia on his way to withdraw to Nola, to the shrine of the martyr Felix. The holy bishop had already heard with what contempt for transient things Paulinus and Therasia had distributed among the poor the proceeds from their possessions, which had been very extensive. Ambrose himself had defended the generosity of both against the clamors of worldly people in a letter written to Sabinus (Ep. 58). From this one may infer with what joy and delight he received Paulinus.

Certainly Paulinus himself openly declares that his association with Ambrose was neither sudden nor recent, saying:

> “I have always been nurtured in the faith by Ambrose’s love, and now am cherished in the order of the priesthood. Finally, he wished to claim me for his own clergy, so that, although we live in different places, I might be reckoned his presbyter.”  
> (Paulinus, Ep. 4, to Alypius)

Nor does he mention Ambrose only in this place. Elsewhere, and especially when numbering him among those great and holy men who illuminated various provinces by the sacred deposit of their ashes, he sings of him thus:

> No lesser grace shone forth in the western lands:  
> Ambrose in Latium, Vincent in Iberia;  
> Gaul received Martin, Aquitaine Delphinus.  
> (St. Paulinus, Poem 27, *On the Birthday of St. Felix*, 11)

[Col. 0108C] 134. As was said above, Ambrose had withdrawn from Milan so as not to endure the sight of the wicked man Eugenius. It is very plausible that he strictly forbade his clergy to defile themselves by communion with that tyrant. “The gifts of the emperor, who had involved himself in sacrilege,” says Paulinus, “were rejected by the Church, nor was he granted fellowship with the Church in prayer” (Life of Ambrose, no. 31).

But Arbogast and Flavian, knowing that Eugenius was disgraced in this way because he had granted their petition for the restoration of profane worship, were inflamed with such fury that, on leaving Milan, they threatened that when they returned victorious they would make a stable of the basilica of the Church of Milan and would test the clergy under arms (ibid.). Paulinus adds that this impiety of madmen did not go unpunished; Ambrose too bears the same witness (Exposition of Psalm 36, no. 25), though he passes over the names of both counts in silence.

135. As soon as Eugenius had left Milan to lead his forces against Theodosius, Ambrose returned to the city about the Kalends of August (Ep. 61), not doubting that heavenly protection would aid that same Theodosius as he defended the cause of justice and piety. And indeed that great ruler won so remarkable a victory that the miracles by which it was made illustrious were celebrated not only by our bishop (Exposition of Psalm 36, no. 22), [Col. 0109A] but also by Augustine (City of God, V.26), Orosius (VII.35), Claudian (Panegyric on the Third Consulship of Honorius), and countless others.

136. After that great victory and the removal of the tyrant on the eighth day before the Ides of September, Theodosius instructed Ambrose by letter to render public thanks to God for so auspicious a success. The holy bishop fulfilled Caesar’s commands with incredible eagerness and informed Theodosius of this in a letter, in which he says:

> “I placed the letter of Your Piety upon the altar; I held it in my hand as I offered the sacrifice, so that your faith might speak in my voice, and the written characters of Augustus might perform their office through the ministry of the priestly offering.”  
> (Ep. 61)

He then earnestly implores him to pardon those who had followed Eugenius’s cause, especially if they were not guilty of any other offence. A second letter (Ep. 62) was appended to this one, and soon a third; but the iniquity of the times intercepted the latter. The former, requesting pardon for those who had fled to the sanctuary of the churches, has been preserved to our age.

Moreover, not content with this, the pious bishop himself went to the emperor at Aquileia, as Paulinus asserts (Life of Ambrose, no. 31), and obtained whatever he requested. Paulinus, Augustine, Orosius, Claudian, and others vie in praising this ruler’s clemency toward conquered enemies. But Ambrose records an additional fact, by no means unworthy of mention: “What of this: although he had won a splendid victory, nevertheless, because enemies had been overthrown, he abstained from communion in the sacraments until he should experience the Lord’s grace toward him in the arrival of his children” (On the Death of Theodosius, no. 34). One can readily persuade us that the same Ambrose who had so ardently urged Theodosius toward clemency was also the author of this abstention from the heavenly sacrament because of the blood that had been shed.

137. After returning to Milan, the holy bishop delivered from the pulpit his Expositions (Admonition on the Expositions on the Psalms) on Psalms 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, and 40. Since these make mention of Theodosius’s victory over Eugenius, we do not doubt that they were delivered either toward the end of the present year or at the beginning of the following one.

138. (A.D. 395.) At the beginning of this year our Ambrose was overwhelmed by the bitterest grief when Theodosius died—a man whom he had always regarded not only as a pillar of Church and empire, but whom he had never failed to find most affectionate toward himself. Paulinus speaks thus of his death: “Nor was he long in this light,” he says, “after receiving his sons in the Church and entrusting them to the bishop” (Life of Ambrose, no. 32). Ambrose plainly indicates in these few words that the ruler gave him proofs of affection up to death: “I loved the man,” he says, “who, in his last moments, sought me with his final breath” (On the Death of Theodosius, no. 35).

He died, according to the common opinion, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February. Forty days after that death, the Caesar Honorius, who had come from the East to his father in his final illness, arranged, before transferring the body to Constantinople and the tombs of the deceased emperors, for it to be honored with a funeral procession in the church at Milan. The same ruler was present at these ceremonies (On the Death of Theodosius, no. 3); and, while he listened and the royal body lay before the altar, Ambrose praised Theodosius’s virtues in an oration both noble and Christian. In this funeral discourse, while celebrating the victories won by that ruler through the benefit of the saving cross, he digressed at length upon the discovery of that cross (ibid., no. 43 ff.). At the end of the peroration, he attempted to soothe Honorius’s mind, cast down by no slight grief because the needs of the empire did not permit him to accompany his father’s funeral all the way to Constantinople (ibid., nos. 55–56).

[Col. 0110B] 139. In Paulinus’s account, the death of Theodosius is immediately followed by the revelation, divinely inspired to the blessed bishop, of the sacred relics of the martyrs Nazarius and Celsus (Paulinus, Life of Ambrose, no. 32 ff.), and by their translation, celebrated by Ambrose, into the basilica of the Apostles. The same writer relates that, while Ambrose was preaching, a demoniac was freed by him from a demon. He then adds the sign by which it was understood that the holy relics had been revealed to the pious bishop, speaking as follows: “But this was the sign also of the relieved demoniac: if the holy priest went to pray at a place to which he had never previously gone” (ibid., no. 33).

We learn from Paulinus’s own poem that Ambrose sent a substantial part of the bodies of these saints as a gift to Saint Paulinus, then a presbyter at Nola, where he says:

> Here too is the martyr Nazarius, whom, by the faithful gift  
> of noble Ambrose, I received with a heart laid low, etc.  
> (St. Paulinus, Poem 24, *On the Birthday of St. Felix*, 9)

The same Paulinus further indicates, writing to Severus (Ep. 32), that relics of Saints Protasius and Gervasius were added to these; the passage may be consulted there.

140. To this time, or at least to a date not remote from it, should be assigned those sermons which may still be read, arranged in book form under the title *On Naboth the Israelite* (Admonition on this book). He deliberately undertook to deliver these sermons both to rebuke the cruel avarice of the rich of his time and to support and console the poor in enduring their miseries. How deeply he was affected by the hardships and calamities of the needy is abundantly clear from Paulinus (Life of Ambrose, no. 40). Nor is there any room for doubt that the inhumanity of wealthy persons, which increased immensely after Theodosius’s death, compelled from his lips those complaints which he could no longer contain in his breast.

141. (A.D. 396.) In this year, under the consulship of the new emperors Arcadius and Honorius, Paulinus relates (Life of Ambrose, no. 34) that an example was given through which God himself showed how inviolable the asylum of churches ought to be. For when a certain Cresconius had been forcibly dragged out of a church by soldiers, and Ambrose lay prostrate at the altar lamenting the violation of the holy places, those soldiers, upon returning to the Circus, were torn to pieces by leopards.

In the same place Paulinus (Life of Ambrose, no. 35), after recounting the affectionate correction by which this holy man reminded Theodulus—later bishop of the Church of Modena—of a neighbor’s fall, appends an embassy from the queen of the Marcomanni to Ambrose. That queen, according to the cited author, was named Fritigil. When she heard of Ambrose’s fame, she sent gifts to the church at Milan and, through envoys, asked him to instruct her in writing how she ought to believe. He wrote her an admirable letter in the form of a catechism (ibid., no. 37).

We regret that this letter has perished. After reading it, Fritigil was inflamed with so great a desire to see Ambrose that for this reason she herself came to Milan; but because she did not arrive there until after the holy bishop’s death, so much labor came to nothing.

142. Limenius, bishop of Vercelli and successor of Saint Eusebius, died about this time. In selecting his successor, the clergy and people of that city divided into factions and interests and could not agree with one another for a very long time. When Ambrose learned this, he was troubled. Since the correction of this discord belonged to him as metropolitan, he wrote the same church a letter at once extensive and elegant (Ep. 63). In it he strongly urges the Vercellians to peace and unity of mind; then, turning his pen to set forth the gifts and virtues which ought to exist in a candidate for that bishopric, he says: “Two things alike seem required: the continence of the monastery and the discipline of the Church” (ibid., no. 66), because both institutions had been joined together in that church by the blessed Eusebius.

Finally, he inveighs against Sarmatio and Barbazianus (ibid., no. 7), the apostate monks already mentioned, who had come to Vercelli not only to disseminate heresy but also to foster dissension.

143. We do not know what that letter accomplished. But, if credit is to be given to the Acts of Gaudentius of Novara, Ambrose himself had to go to that city in order to call the divided minds back to concord.

144. (A.D. 397.) This year placed a blessed crown upon Ambrose’s life, since during its course the holy bishop obtained from God, best and greatest, an abundant reward for the outstanding virtues by which he had always shone in the Church and for the many labors and most grievous dangers he had endured for the Church. Paulinus, who witnessed the final actions of the saint, recounts them with sufficient detail.

Among them, the following remarkable event was shown: while Ambrose was dictating to Paulinus an exposition of Psalm 43, Paulinus saw a fiery globe, which had first appeared above the bishop’s head, gradually pass through his mouth into his breast. This signified that he burned with a more intense fire of divine charity. Indeed, in that final period of life certain greater proofs of his virtues broke forth. A notable proof of his humility was that he professed himself unequal to the interpretation of Holy Scripture. No less an indication of divine zeal was that he never ceased, until his last breath, to fight against heretics and especially Arians. Finally, his charity toward his flock shone in this: he died while preparing spiritual nourishment for its use.

145. Ambrose’s life had been a continual meditation upon death. It is certain that, before the translation of the bodies of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, he had already thought of his own tomb and designated a place for it (Ep. 22, no. 13). No one, therefore, will wonder that, as his final hour drew near, he candidly said to his own people: “I have not so lived among you that I am ashamed to live; nor do I fear to die, because we have a good Lord” (Paulinus, Life of Ambrose, no. 45).

This saying has always stirred the admiration of great men, especially Augustine. Possidius testified concerning this: “And in these words,” he says, “our Augustine, now an old man, admired and praised their polished and balanced expression” (Possidius, Life of Augustine, ch. 27). The grounds of this admiration may be seen in the same Possidius. Yet other things reported by Paulinus concerning this final struggle of Ambrose are no less admirable, though we omit them for brevity’s sake.

To come, then, to the blessed death of the holy bishop: at the very moment, Saint Honoratus, bishop of Vercelli and successor of Limenius, warned three times by a divine voice, administered the divine Eucharist to him. As soon as he had devoutly received it, his soul, freed from the bonds of the body, flew away to the heavenly homeland.

[Col. 0112C] 146. The same Paulinus continues as follows: “Then, at the hour before dawn at which he died, his body was carried to the greater church; and it remained there through that same night in which we kept vigil at Easter” (Life of Ambrose, no. 48). These words plainly show that his death occurred at the very end of Friday night, and that the holy body remained in that greater basilica throughout Saturday and until the morning hours of Easter. Therefore, since in that year the said feast fell on the Nones of April, the holy bishop died on the day before the Nones; this is also confirmed by the consensus of all the martyrologies.

147. We are not unaware that Marcellinus’s Chronicle reports Ambrose’s death only in the following year. But that chronicle is not so exact that it does not often assign to the same year many things belonging to different years, and conversely to different years many things belonging to the same one. Those who follow this chronology are compelled to maintain that his death should be placed on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May; but since they rely on no adequate reasons for doing so, we judge that greater deference should be paid to the authority of the martyrologies and of the churches of Milan and Rome.

148. We therefore firmly assign the precious death of the holy man to the day and year already given; and this agrees most aptly with the testimony of Paulinus, who expressly states that the blessed bishop survived Theodosius by almost three years (Paulinus, *Life of Ambrose*, no. 32). [Col. 0113A] That is, not by a full three years. For if he died only in the year 398, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, he must be said to have outlived Theodosius beyond that interval, since, as we have shown, that emperor departed this life in January 395. Further, the Council of Carthage held in this very year, in September (Council of Carthage, 397), consulted Simplicianus, Ambrose’s successor, by letter, as though he were already installed upon Ambrose’s throne. Those who think that Simplicianus was consulted, while Ambrose still lived, merely as a man very learned in the question under discussion, think too little honorably of Ambrose and show themselves insufficiently acquainted with the discipline of those times.

149. Here we shall omit those miracles which followed the holy man’s death, [Col. 0113B] since they may be read in Paulinus (*Life of Ambrose*, no. 48 and following). [Col. 0114A] Although our chief purpose has been briefly to set forth the order and sequence of Ambrose’s writings, thereby assisting readers in their study of them, his deeds and virtues are nevertheless so bound up with his writings that we have had to present them everywhere together. For at every turn one encounters either that loftiness of spirit which knew not how to yield, through terror or danger, in the cause of Christ and the Church; or, again, the modesty of a man who attributed nothing whatsoever to himself. At one point appears his tireless care in feeding the flock; at another, his vigilant watch and labors against the snares of heretics; elsewhere, his supreme kindness toward the poor and captives; and everywhere, finally, an altogether singular piety toward God and divine things. These virtues ought to be objects of imitation for all Christians, but especially [Col. 0114B] for priests; and this is our wish.

[Col. 0113B]

## SELECT TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING SAINT AMBROSE

[Col. 0113]

### From Basil’s Letter 55, written to Ambrose himself

Because we have come to know the beauty of your inner man as if from a variegated picture of your discourses . . . we glorify our God, who in every generation chooses those who are pleasing to him. In former times he raised up from shepherds of sheep a leader for his people, and endowed Amos, taken from a herd of goats, with his Spirit; now he has drawn to the pasture of Christ’s flocks [Col. 0113C] a man from the imperial city, to whom the government of an entire people had been entrusted, eminent in wisdom, nobility of birth, splendor of life, power of speech, and secular affairs. Casting aside all the riches of this life and regarding them as loss in order to gain Christ, he has undertaken in the faith of Christ the helm entrusted to him of a great and illustrious ship, namely, the Church of God. Go on, then, O man of God: since you neither received nor were taught the Gospel of Christ by men, but the Lord himself transferred you from among the judges of the earth to the apostolic chair, etc.

### From a discourse of Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, delivered on the day of his ordination

I beseech our common father Ambrose that, after the brief dew of my discourse, he himself may water your hearts with the mysteries of the divine Scriptures. For he will speak by the Holy Spirit with whom he is filled; rivers of living water shall flow from his belly; and, as successor of the Apostle Peter, he himself shall be the mouth of all the priests standing around. See also the following discourse, where he mentions the discovery of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius.

### From Jerome’s Letter 22 to Eustochium, chapter 10

Read the little works which our Ambrose recently wrote to his sister, [Col. 0113D] in which he has poured himself forth with such eloquence that he has sought out, expressed, and arranged everything bearing upon the praise of virgins.

### From the same author’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Ambrose, bishop of Milan, writes to this present day. Since he is still alive, I shall withhold my judgment concerning him, lest either flattery or truth be reproached in me, according to whichever side I incline.

### From the same author’s *Apology against Jovinian*

If anyone thinks it harsh and deserving of reproach that we have made as great a distinction between virginity and marriage as exists between wheat and barley, let him read Saint Ambrose’s book *On Widows*. Among the other things he disputed concerning virginity and marriage, he will find that Ambrose also said this.

Whoever asserts these three, that is, three hypostases—that is, [Col. 0114B] *ousiai* [essences] . . . let Ursicinus be joined to Your Blessedness, and Auxentius be associated with Ambrose. Far be this from the Roman faith, etc.

### From the same author’s Letter 65 to Pammachius

Recently Ambrose compiled Origen’s *Hexaemeron* in such a way that he followed rather the views of Hippolytus and Basil.

### From the same author’s Letter 90 to Augustine

Our Ambrose followed the former of these—Origen, namely—in certain matters.

### From the same author’s Letter 151 to Algasia, Question 6

You may read in Ambrose’s commentaries what the bishop of Milan thought concerning this [Col. 0114C] passage.

### From the same author’s First Apology against Rufinus, chapter 1

If he was constructing authority for his work and wished to show whom he followed, Hilary . . . Ambrose . . . and the martyr Victorinus were ready at hand. He says nothing of all these; passing over, as it were, the pillars of the Church, he pursues me alone—a flea and a man of no account—into corners.

### Likewise, from the Third Apology, chapter 3

I did not accuse you of translating Origen as you pleased; for I too have done this, and before me Victorinus, Hilary, and Ambrose did so. He had also said the same in the Second Apology, chapter 4.

### From the same author’s *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Gratian III and Equitius

After the late death of Auxentius, Ambrose having been installed at Milan, all Italy was converted to the right faith.

### From Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia, *Second Invective against Jerome*

He attacks Ambrose, [Col. 0114D] the bishop—a man worthy of every admiration, who was not only a kind of pillar and impregnable tower of the Church of Milan, but also of all the Churches . . . who was chosen by God for the glory of the Churches of God; who spoke in the sight of the Lord, in the sight of persecuting kings, and was not confounded. Saint Ambrose wrote concerning the Holy Spirit not only in words but also in his own blood; for he offered his own blood to persecutors, which he shed upon himself. But he was still reserved by God for other labors . . . Saint Ambrose, the holy man, whose memory of a life still illustrious remains vigorous in the minds of all.

### From Augustine, *Confessions*, Book V, chapter 13

I came to Milan, to Ambrose the bishop, known throughout the world as one of the best, a devout worshipper of you. His words then diligently ministered to your people the richness of your wheat, the gladness of oil, and the sober intoxication of wine. I was led to him by you without knowing it, so that through him I might knowingly be led to you. That man of God received me as a father, and loved my coming as a bishop should . . . I delighted in the sweetness of his discourse; although it was more learned, it was less cheerful and caressing than that of Faustus, so far as manner of speaking was concerned. But in the matters themselves there was no comparison: Faustus wandered amid Manichaean deceptions, whereas Ambrose taught salvation in the most health-giving way.

### From Book VI, chapter 1, where he writes thus concerning his mother Monica

She hastened more eagerly to the Church and hung upon Ambrose’s lips, at the fountain of water springing up into eternal life. She loved the man as an angel of God, because through him she had learned that I had now been brought to that perilous wavering . . . Therefore, when she had brought porridge, bread, and unmixed wine to the memorial shrines of the saints, as she was accustomed to do in Africa, and was forbidden by the doorkeeper . . . once she learned that this had been ordered not to be done by that illustrious preacher and bishop of piety . . . she most willingly abstained.

### From the same book, chapter 3

[Col. 0115B]

I considered Ambrose a certain happy man according to this world, because such great powers honored him. His celibacy, however, seemed laborious to me. Yet what hope he bore within him, what struggle he waged against the temptations of his high position, what consolation he had in adversity, and what savory joys his hidden mouth—that is, his heart—chewed over from your bread, I neither knew how to conjecture nor had experienced. And later in the same chapter: Yet I was certainly given no opportunity to ask that most holy oracle of yours, his breast, what I desired . . . I heard him every Lord’s Day rightly dispensing to the people the word of truth; and I was ever more firmly convinced that all the knots of crafty calumnies which those deceivers of ours tied against the divine books could be untied.

There was at Milan, outside the city walls, a monastery full of good brothers, [Col. 0115C] under Ambrose as their fosterer.

Then it was instituted that hymns and psalms should be sung according to the custom of the eastern regions, lest the people waste away through the weariness of sorrow. From that time it has been retained down to the present day, many—indeed almost all—of your flocks throughout other parts of the world imitating it.

Ambrose followed up and said to me: “When I go to Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am here, I do not fast.” [Col. 0115D] You likewise, when you come to whatever Church it may be, observe its custom, if you do not wish to be a scandal to anyone, nor anyone to you. When I reported this to my mother, she gladly embraced it. For my part, considering this judgment again and again, I have always regarded it as though I had received it by a heavenly oracle. Augustine recalls the same response of Ambrose also in Letter 38, formerly 163.

### From Letter 44, formerly 163

I asked him—Fortunius the Donatist—whether he thought Ambrose, bishop of the Church of Milan, a just and religious man. When, therefore, he was compelled to say things by which Ambrose could not be considered Christian and just, I recalled how great a persecution Ambrose had endured, the Church even being surrounded by armed soldiers.

[Col. 0116A]

If you approve these things, hold with me the judgment of Saint Ambrose, now confirmed not by his authority but by truth itself. Hear how Pelagius himself praises Saint Ambrose in that very recent work of his whose mention he invokes in his own defense, namely in the third book *On Free Will*: “Blessed Ambrose the bishop, in whose books especially the Roman faith shines forth, who stood out among Latin writers as a certain beautiful flower, whose faith and most pure understanding of the Scriptures not even an enemy has dared to reproach.” . . . [Col. 0116B] Let him therefore hear that venerable bishop speaking and teaching . . . At Milan, among the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius, demons confessed by name that Ambrose was bishop, although he was still alive, just as they named the dead whom they commemorated in the same manner; and they begged him to spare them. ### From Paulinus’s Letter to Alypius, found in Augustine’s Letter 24, formerly 25

[Col. 0116D] I confess that, since you indicated that you had already learned my name, though unworthy, at Milan when you were initiated there, I desire rather curiously to learn more, so that I may know you in every respect and rejoice the more if you were either invited to the faith by our father Ambrose, whom I revere, or consecrated to the priesthood by him, so that we may both seem to have the same author. ### From Pope Nicholas I, Letter to Photius, vol. VIII of Labbe’s edition of the Councils, p. 1304

[Col. 0118D] While he was still an infant lying in the cradle, a swarm of bees suddenly flew up and settled on his face; with some entering and others leaving, they filled his mouth. When his father saw this, he said prophetically: “If this child lives, he will be great.” Later, as an adult, he went to Milan, then deprived of a bishop. When the people had assembled to elect a pastor, behold, a certain child cried out, “Ambrose for bishop!” The people took up the voice as one sent not without divine power, and together rushed to seize the man. He withdrew and sought hiding places by every means; yet he could not remain hidden, since the entire people, together with the clergy, chose him. Thus, proceeding from catechumen through each ecclesiastical grade, on the eighth day at last—now designated by a divine oracle, and with the entire Catholic Church consenting—he was consecrated bishop.

Quite similar things are read in Letter V of the same pontiff, to Emperor Michael, p. 280, where he adds: “Throughout the whole course of his life he observed the norm of ecclesiastical rules, battling every heresy, girded with zeal for the Word of God.” See also Letter VI to Photius, p. 284, where Nicholas treats these same points even more fully and calls our Ambrose a most illustrious and splendid lamp of the Church.

Remember the memorable deed of Theodosius and the memorable man Ambrose. Happy was that emperor who in his time had such a priest . . . And happy was Ambrose, priest of God, who lived in the time of such an emperor. For it is written: “Blessed is he who declares justice to a willing hearer” (Ecclus. 25). Both priest and emperor were likewise happy, because, lest God’s wrath descend upon the emperor for his offense, he had in his own time a priest of whom the Lord did not complain as he now complains concerning us, saying: “I sought one who would set a hedge and stand opposed before me, that I might not destroy it, and I found none” (Ezek. 22).

### From the same author’s Book II *On Predestination*, chapter 25

Saint Ambrose, whose judgments are most firm pillars of faith, of the Church, and of every virtue; who through the grace of God illumined Saint Augustine with faith, consecrated him by baptism, and instructed him in the teaching of piety, thus says in his book, etc.

### From Photius’s own *Bibliotheca*, chapter 231, p. 890

That spirit immovable in divinely inspired freedom and piety—Ambrose of Milan, surely.

### From Odilo, abbot, *Chronicle of Cluny*, p. 402

Blessed Ambrose, a man praiseworthy in every respect, a true defender of the Catholic faith . . . a most learned teacher.

### From Guitmund, bishop of Aversa, Book III *On the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of the Lord*

[Col. 0119C]

But you, excellent teacher, most blessed Ambrose, spiritual father of blessed Augustine—whom that most holy man himself calls holy and blessed in his books; whose authority, Augustine testifying, Paul the Apostle, revealer of the martyrs, commends; whom blessed Gregory, a man truly apostolic, sets before himself; whose teaching most blessed Benedict, as Saint Gregory testifies, judged ought to be received, being filled with the Spirit of the holy prophets; to whom the glory of the entire Church of Milan gives particular testimony; whom the whole world, because of the merit of his faith, reverently embraces—for if so many and so great witnesses had known that you erred in the Catholic faith, they would not have proclaimed you with such praise—explain, I ask, what you think concerning the sacraments of the altar.

### From Durand, abbot, *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, Part IV

[Col. 0119D]

I should like to cull certain things from Saint Ambrose, whose authority [Col. 0120A] in the Catholic Church after the Apostles is held to be foremost; the abundant eloquence of whose flowing speech is an ornament and model of the Latin language.

### From Pope Gregory VII, Letter 2, Book IV, vol. X of Labbe’s edition of the Councils, p. 149

Nor should they overlook that blessed Ambrose not only excommunicated King—indeed truly Emperor—Theodosius for his conduct and exercise of power, but also forbade him to presume to remain in the place of the priests in the Church.

### From Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, Letter 77

Believe me, I am hard to tear away from these two pillars—I mean Augustine and Ambrose. With them, I confess, I either err or am wise.

### From Petrarch, Book I, Letter 1

Among some authors I find Ambrose alone without rival or detractor, alone adorned with full and unplucked praise, whose reputation not even in youth biting envy touched. This may perhaps be attributed to his pure and simple teaching, free from all ambiguity. Consult also his Book II *On the Solitary Life*, section III, chapters 2 and 4, where he relates very noteworthy matters concerning Ambrose, which for brevity’s sake we omit here, as we also omit many other things that readily occur in historians, library catalogues, and legendary collections.

### From Andrew of Petra, archbishop of Colossae, an oration delivered at the Council of Basel, vol. XII of Labbe’s edition of the Councils, p. 877

That the teaching of the holy Fathers has driven away every error is attested by . . . Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, the brightest lights of the Christian religion, who wrote most invincibly against every kind of heresy.

### From Cardinal Bessarion, Dogmatic Oration, Council, vol. XIII, p. 403

We have likewise those who extinguished from the West [Col. 0120C] the flames of errors by sound and most illustrious doctrine: Hilary, Ambrose . . . who by their roar frightened away all heretics.

### From an unknown author, Colbert manuscripts, about the year 600

I dare to append these verses in a humble style;

My reader, do not deem them worthless.

Love compels me to say what I say concerning Ambrose,

Whom my mind, tongue, and hand desire to serve.

Whoever you are that seek the true joys of paradise,

Hasten to submit yourself to Ambrose’s counsels.

Ambrose shows you the rule of law and justice;

Happy are you if you can learn, know, and follow it.

By Ambrose’s writings one is led to better things—

He who reads his writings and performs them without delay.

Read Ambrose, if you seek pastures of life;

Do what you read, and thus you shall be blessed.

The end is at hand: may he who is Three and One grant the gift

[Col. 0120D]

Of himself to me; and may pious Ambrose so intercede.

# HEXAEMERON

[Col. 0119D]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE SIX BOOKS OF THE *HEXAEMERON*

[Col. 0119]

Many have already observed—and the thing itself plainly declares it—that this Ambrosian offspring consists of sermons in which the holy Doctor expounded the creation of things to the people of Milan. Some suppose that a notary took these down from the speaker’s lips, inferring this from the opening words of the eighth sermon. Yet Ambrose certainly committed them to writing after they had been delivered and arranged them in the form of the treatise in which they circulate. For, writing to the deacon Orontianus (*Letter to Orontianus*), to whom, as also to Bishop Sabinus, he sent this same work, he indicates that he himself wrote out his *Hexaemeron*. He did the same also in other books. Nor is there any doubt that this practice arose because he wished both to comply with the requests of friends and to provide for the benefit of other Christians, and because he did not wish to be imposed upon by notaries.

The author himself gave his work the title *Hexaemeron* (*Letter to Sabinus* and *Letter to Orontianus*), and, if the manuscripts are to be trusted—for in all of them one reads, “The first day ends; the second day begins,” and likewise for the rest—he divided it into six days. [Col. 0121] This division agrees with its title and with the entire work. But since it appears that it had already been divided into six books from the time of Cassiodorus Senator, nothing seemed fit to be altered in so ancient a division, perhaps deriving from Ambrose himself.

Jerome teaches that Origen, Hippolytus, and Basil preceded our Doctor in this subject (*Letter to Pammachius*, cited above). What Ambrose borrowed from the first two we cannot know, since their mentioned books have by no means reached our own age, as was said in the Preface. Yet, while we by no means deny that he took very many things from Basil, we utterly deny that he servilely imitated Basil’s works or performed the office, as it were, of a translator. For although he frequently follows Basil’s footsteps, he very often departs from them; he adds, removes, and rearranges. Indeed, he does not scruple to disagree with Basil (*Book III*, chapter 4; *Book IV*, chapter 7; *Book V*, chapter 18), whom he sometimes sharply criticizes, though without naming him. He also inserted into his work many things borrowed from pagan authors, Pliny and others, which anyone can readily observe. Yet this should not be passed over: in imitating Virgil, he so played with his language, when treating of bees (*Book V*, chapter 21), that, after freeing the words from verse metre, he often retained the poet’s actual words.

Moreover, wherever he imitated Basil, this occurred especially in the arrangement and economy of the whole subject. Hence we shall not hesitate to assign nine sermons here, precisely the number extant in blessed Basil. Certainly it will not be difficult to establish that number. For in the third book two sermons are most plainly distinguished: the first, contained in the first five chapters, was delivered in the morning; the other, extending through the remaining chapters of that book, in the evening. Nor is it less clear that Book V likewise contains two, since the one we judge to be confined within the first eleven chapters differs greatly from that which runs thence to the book’s end. The former was delivered in the morning, as is most clearly shown by the final words of chapter 11, where the whole discourse concludes from the heat of the sun, now too far advanced. The latter was delivered in the evening, as is evidently proved by what it says of nocturnal birds; moreover, the conclusion of the homily confirms it, for there the devout bishop, as the day of stricter fasting drew toward its close, dismisses his hearers to their late meal.

Although it is not so easy to prove that Book I too was divided into two sermons, we are nevertheless led to that view because the end of chapter 6 seems to present nothing but the conclusion of a discourse, which agrees beautifully with Basil’s first homily. The remaining chapters of this book, which also correspond most fittingly to Basil’s second homily, sufficiently clearly exhibit another discourse, complete in its own proper proportions. Finally, the other books, as in Basil, each contain one sermon.

You may perhaps ask to what year they should chiefly be assigned. Although we do not venture to determine this with certainty, nevertheless, if some latitude may be given to conjecture, we should judge that they are not much earlier than the year 389. For, since ecclesiastical chant is mentioned more than once there (*Book III*, chapters 1 and 5; *Book V*, chapter 4)—chant which the holy man had instituted at Milan in 385 or 386—he cannot be said to have composed his *Hexaemeron* before that time. Further, he does not conceal that he was then of more advanced age: “What,” he says, “which we laughed at as boys, can we, as old men, recall?” (*Book IV*, chapter 5). According to the more common chronology, however, Ambrose was not so old when he died in 397; therefore one would judge that he scarcely proclaimed himself an old man before the year 389.

To this may be added that, describing what was then occurring in his Church, he teaches that there were no longer many congregations to which pagans and heretics were separately compelled to go: “But,” he says (*Book III*, chapter 9), “there has become one people; the Church has been filled from heretics and Gentiles.” How well these statements accord with the dates assigned can readily be understood by anyone. They plainly signify those happy days when, Justina the empress—so obstinately devoted to the Arian party—having died, and Symmachus, the stout defender of pagan rites, having been refuted and repelled, Theodosius the Great at last triumphed over the tyrant Maximus and in that year enacted so many laws (*Theodosian Code*, title concerning pagans and heretics), with such prudence against pagans and heretics, that writers of that age observed that very many of them had fled into the bosom of the Catholic Church (Jerome, Letter 7; Prudentius, Book I, *Against Symmachus*).

As for the season of the year, it is indeed clear that a fast was observed on those days; but it is probable that it was none other than that of the closing Lent. For that those very days possessed an exceptional religious character may be inferred from the fact that, very early in the morning, a great crowd of people flocked to the church, from which they did not depart until after sunset. Thus one may rightly say that they were such as Ambrose describes during the very persecution of the raging Justina, when throughout the holy week all the people assembled to celebrate the morning and evening synaxis. Let us add further that the same things were performed in both gatherings. For concerning these gatherings the holy bishop writes (Letter to Marc.) that they were days on which penance was relaxed; concerning the others (Book V, ch. 25), that they were a time when forgiveness of sins was celebrated. In the former he affirms that the prophecy of Jonah was read (Letter to Marc.); in the latter he plainly indicates that the same was done (Book V, chs. 11 and 25). Therefore, in these assemblies, when he sometimes spoke twice on the same day, in the manner of Basil, he completed the subject undertaken in altogether six days—that is, within the limits of a single week. This is indeed proved by the division of the sermons which we have established; but Ambrose himself demonstrates the same thing in these words (Book VI, ch. 1): “Although our discourse has now proceeded through five days with no slight labor; nevertheless, on the present day,” etc.

[Col. 0123A]

# SIX BOOKS OF THE *HEXAMERON* OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN

[Note: Written about the year 389.] (C)

[Col. 0123]

## BOOK ONE. ON THE WORK OF THE FIRST DAY

[Col. 0123]

### CHAPTER I. (Sermon I)

On the beginning, duration, and unity of the world. The errors of the philosophers are reported and briefly refuted.

[Col. 0123A]

1. Have human beings assumed so much presumption that some of them should establish three principles of all things—God, exemplar, and matter—as Plato and his disciples did, and should maintain that these are incorruptible, uncreated, and without beginning? They held that God made the world from matter, which they call *hyle*, not as the creator of matter but as an artisan directing his attention to an exemplar, that is, an Idea; matter, they assert, supplied the causes of generation to all things. They also judged that the world itself was incorruptible, neither created nor made. Others likewise, such as Aristotle with his followers, thought it necessary to posit two principles, matter and form, and along with them a third, called the efficient principle, which might be adequately able to bring about whatever it had undertaken.

[Note: One Corbie manuscript and the Colbert manuscript: “thought it necessary to debate, [whether] to posit two principles.” Better in other manuscripts and editions: “thought … [that they] should posit.” For this final verb depends upon the opening of the chapter itself: “Have human beings assumed so much presumption that some …,” etc.]

2. What, then, is so unfitting as to join the eternity of a work to the eternity of almighty God, or to call the work itself God, so as to pursue heaven, earth, and sea with divine honors? Hence it came about that they believed the parts of the world to be gods, although there is no slight dispute among them concerning the world itself.

3. For Pythagoras maintains that there is one world; others say that there are innumerable worlds, as Democritus wrote—a man to whom antiquity assigned very great authority in natural philosophy. Aristotle habitually says that the world always was and always will be; Plato, on the other hand, ventures to maintain that it did not always exist but will always exist; while very many testify in their writings that it neither always was nor always will be.

4. Amid these disagreements of theirs, what assessment of truth can there be? Some say that the world itself is God, because a divine mind, as they think, appears to be present within it; others, that its parts are gods; others, both. In this matter neither what shape the gods have, nor what number, nor what place, nor what life or providential care they possess can be comprehended. For, according to their estimation of the world, one must understand God to be revolving, round, fiery, driven by certain movements, and without sensation—a god carried by another’s motion, not by his own.

[Note: Royal, Corbie, and Colbert manuscripts: “according to the estimation of the world.” Chartres manuscript: “the estimation of the world [is] revolving, round, driven.” Others and the editions: “according to the world’s estimation.” This is sound, if interpreted as equivalent to “as the world is judged to be.”]

### CHAPTER II

Moses’ teaching concerning the beginning of things, the author of the world, and the creation of matter. Moses is commended on many grounds; it is shown that he alone should be believed, atoms and Ideas having been rejected.

[Col. 0124B]

5. Therefore holy Moses, foreseeing by the divine Spirit that these human errors would arise, and perhaps had already begun, said at the beginning of his discourse: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), comprehending the beginning of things, the author of the world, and the creation of matter. Thus you might know that God existed before the beginning of the world, or rather that he himself is the beginning of all things; just as in the Gospel the Son of God, when they said to him, “Who are you?” replied: “The Beginning, what I also say to you” (John 8:25). He himself gave created things their beginning, and he himself is the creator of the world—not an imitator of matter led by some Idea, so as to form his works from matter, not according to his own will, but according to a proposed pattern. He also fittingly said, “In the beginning he made,” in order to express the incomprehensible swiftness of the work: the result of the completed operation was displayed before any indication of its commencement had been explained.

[Note: Gemeticensis, Coenomanensis, and the Vulgate: “The Beginning, who also speak to you.” Royal, Germanensis, and the editions of Amerbach and Petit: “The Beginning who.” Dionysianus below, ch. 4, §15: “The Beginning which.” Ten manuscripts: “The Beginning, what.” So also below in the cited section, and in *On Faith to Gratian*, Book III, ch. 4; Book V, ch. 4. But in Greek: *tēn archēn, ho ti kai lalō hymin*—“the beginning, that which I also say to you.” Tremellius translates: “that which I say to you from the beginning.”]

[Note: Five manuscripts and the editions of Erasmus and Rome: “affection.”]

6. We must notice who says this. It is Moses, surely—that Moses instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, whom Pharaoh’s daughter, having taken him from the river, loved as a son and, supporting him with royal resources, desired to have educated and trained in every discipline of worldly wisdom. Yet although he received his name from water, he nevertheless did not think it should be said that all things consist of water, as Thales said. And though he had been brought up in a royal court, he nevertheless preferred, for love of justice, to undergo voluntary exile rather than to gain the pleasures of sinful indulgence at the summit of tyranny. Finally, before he was summoned to the task of liberating the people, stirred by a natural zeal for equity, he avenged one of his countrymen when he was receiving an injury; he exposed himself to hostility and withdrew from pleasure. Avoiding all the turmoil of the royal household, he withdrew into the solitude of Ethiopia. There, removed from other affairs, he directed his whole mind to the knowledge of God, so that he might see the glory of God face to face. Scripture testifies concerning him that “there arose no prophet in Israel thereafter like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face” (Deut. 34:10). He spoke with the supreme God mouth to mouth—not in a vision or in dreams, nor in a form nor through riddles, but endowed with the clear and manifest condescension of the divine presence.

[Note: Eight manuscripts of older and better quality, and the old editions: “whom the Lord knew.” Royal and Rheims: “whom God knew.” Dionysianus: “whom God knew face to face.” Germanensis: “who saw the Lord.” Septuagint: “whom the Lord knew, him, face to face.” Vulgate: “whom the Lord might know.”]

[Note: Several manuscripts: “nor in sleep.”]

[Note: The Roman edition with one manuscript: “the knowledge [or recognition] of the divine presence.”]

7. Therefore Moses opened his mouth and poured forth what the Lord spoke in him, according to what he had said to him when sending him to King Pharaoh: “Go, therefore, and I will open your mouth and instruct you what you ought to say” (Exod. 4:12). For if he received from God what he should say concerning the dismissal of the people, how much more what he should say concerning heaven! Accordingly, not in the persuasion of human wisdom nor in the pretended disputations of philosophy, but in the demonstration of Spirit and power, as a witness of the divine work, he dared to say: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” He did not await a long and idle process by which the world might cohere through the collision of atoms; nor some discipline of matter, by contemplating which he might fashion the world. Rather, he judged that God should be set forth as its author. For this man, full of wisdom, perceived that the divine mind alone contains the invisible substances, origins, and causes of things—not, as philosophers argue, that a stronger combination of atoms supplies the cause of enduring permanence. Instead, he judged that those weave a spider’s web who assign such minute and unsubstantial principles to heaven and earth—principles which, as they were joined by chance, would also by chance and rashly be dissolved, unless they were upheld by the divine power of their governor. Nor without reason are they ignorant of the governor, who do not know God, through whom all things are ruled and governed. Let us therefore follow him who knows both the author and the governor, and let us not be led away by empty opinions.

[Note: Ten manuscripts of better quality: “nor some disciple.”]

[Note: Four manuscripts and Coster’s edition: “the origins of invisible substances and the causes of things.” Amerbach, Erasmus, and Gillot omit “origins.” Four manuscripts: “the substance of invisible [Col. 0126D] things and the causes of things.”]

### CHAPTER III

The world has its beginning from God and therefore, although it has a spherical shape, is not eternal.

[Col. 0126A]

8. “In the beginning,” he says. How good the order: first he affirmed what they are accustomed to deny, so that they might acknowledge that the world has a beginning and human beings might not suppose that the world exists without a beginning. Hence David also, speaking of heaven, earth, and sea, says: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:25). Therefore he gave the world a beginning; he also gave the creature frailty, lest we believe it to be *anarchon*—without beginning—uncreated, and a participant in the divine substance. And he fittingly added, “He made,” lest it be thought that there had been delay in making; so that even thus human beings might understand how incomparable was the maker who completed so great a work by the brief and slight moment of his operation, so that the effect of his will anticipated the perception of time. No one saw him at work, but everyone recognized the completed work. Where, then, was delay, when you read: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5)? Therefore he expended neither the use of art nor force, he who by the moment of his will fulfilled the majesty of so great an operation, making what did not exist exist so swiftly that neither will preceded operation nor operation will.

[Note: Some manuscripts and Gillot’s edition in the margin, and the Roman edition in the text: “formless matter.” Nine other manuscripts of the best quality and the old editions: “frailty,” that is, as Latinius says, “corruption.”]

[Note: All editions unanimously read: “He added concerning the swiftness of creation, ‘He made.’” But the words “concerning the swiftness of creation” are absent from all manuscripts.]

[Note: Thus thirteen manuscripts and the old editions. But the Roman edition: “he might complete [it] by a moment of his will, and by the effect of the operation, perception,” etc.]

[Note: Chartres manuscript: “anticipated the perception of the body.”]

9. Do you marvel at the work? Do you seek the maker—who gave a beginning to so great a work, who made it so quickly? He immediately added, saying that God made heaven and earth. You have heard the author; you ought not to doubt. This is he in whom Melchizedek blessed Abraham, father of many nations, saying: “Blessed is Abraham by God Most High, who made heaven and earth” (Gen. 14:19, 22). And Abraham believed God and said: “I will stretch out my hand to God Most High, who made heaven and earth.” You see that this was not discovered by a human being but proclaimed by God. For Melchizedek is God, who is king of peace and righteousness, having neither beginning of days nor end. It is therefore no wonder that God, who is without beginning, gave a beginning to all things, so that things which did not exist might begin to exist. It is no wonder if God, who holds all things together by his power and embraces the universe in incomprehensible majesty, made these visible things, since he also made the things that are not visible. Who can deny that invisible things are superior to visible ones, when visible things are temporal but invisible things eternal? Who can doubt that God made these things, he who spoke through the Prophet: “Who has measured the water in his hand, and heaven with his palm, and the whole earth in his closed hand? Who has set the mountains in a balance and the rocks in scales and the woods in a yoke? Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor, or who has instructed him?” (Isa. 40:12). Elsewhere we also read of him: “For he holds the circuit of the earth and has made the earth as nothing.” And Jeremiah says: “The gods who did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the earth and from beneath this heaven. The Lord made the earth in his power and established the world in his wisdom; in his prudence he stretched out heaven and the multitude of water in heaven” (Jer. 10:11). And he added: “Man has become foolish through his knowledge” (ibid., 14). For one who follows the corruptible things of the world and thinks that from them he can comprehend the truth of the divine nature—how does he not become foolish through the cleverness of subtle disputation?

10. Therefore, when you hear so many oracles by which God testifies that he made the world, do not believe it to be without beginning merely because the world is said to be like a sphere, so that no beginning of it appears; or because, when it thunders, all things seem to be stirred in a circuit, so that you cannot easily comprehend where they begin or where they end, since it is considered impossible to grasp the beginning of a circle by perception. You cannot find the beginning of a sphere, or where the globe of the moon began, or where the monthly waning of the moon ends. Yet if you yourself do not comprehend it, it does not on that account lack a beginning or fail to have an end. If you draw a circle yourself with ink, a stylus, or a compass (*kentron*, “point” or “spike”), you do not easily discern with your eyes, or retrace in your mind, where you began or where you ended, when an interval has been interposed; and yet you are yourself a witness that it began and ended. For even if it eludes perception, it does not overthrow truth. Things which have a beginning also have an end; and it is evident that those to which an end is given have been given a beginning. The Savior himself teaches in his Gospel that the world will have an end, saying: “Heaven and earth shall pass away” (Matt. 24:35). And below: “Behold, I am with you unto the consummation of the world” (Matt. 28:20). And the Apostle: “For the form of this world passes away” (1 Cor. 7:31).

[Note: “Compass,” Greek *kentron*, that is, “a point” or “spike.” See below, Book V, ch. 10.]

11. How, then, do they maintain that the world is coeternal with God, associate it with the Creator of all things, and argue that the creature is equal to him? How do they think that the material body of the world should be joined to that invisible and inaccessible divine nature, especially when, according to their own view, they cannot deny that, if its parts are subject to corruption and change, the whole must necessarily be subject to the same affections to which its individual portions are liable?

### CHAPTER IV

The various kinds of “beginning”; and in what sense God is to be understood to have made heaven and earth “in the beginning.”

12. Therefore, he who says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” teaches that there is a beginning. “Beginning” refers either to time, to number, or to foundation—as, in building a house, the foundation is its beginning. We learn on Scriptural authority that “beginning” can also be said of conversion and corruption. Art itself, from which thereafter the activity of various craftsmen begins, is also a beginning. The best end is likewise the beginning of good works: for the beginning of mercy is that what you do should please God. For this chiefly moves us to provide help for human beings. Divine power also exists, which is expressed by this designation. It refers to time if you wish to say at what time God made heaven and earth, that is, at the beginning of the world, when it began to be made, as Wisdom says: “When he prepared heaven, I was with him” (Prov. 8:27). If you refer it to number, it suitably means: “First of all God made heaven and earth; then hills, regions, and uninhabitable boundaries.” Or thus: before the other visible creatures—day, night, fruit-bearing trees, and the various kinds of living creatures—he made heaven and earth. If, however, you refer it to foundation, you have read that the foundations are the beginning of the earth, Wisdom saying: “When he made strong the foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging all things” (Wis. 8:29). There is also a beginning of good instruction, as in: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. 1:7), because the person who fears the Lord turns away from error and directs his paths toward the way of virtue. Unless one fears God, one cannot renounce sin.

[Note: Four manuscripts and the editions of Amerbach and Petit: “with him, composing.” Six manuscripts and the Septuagint: “with him, arranging.”]

13. We may understand in the same way the saying: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months” (Exod. 12:2), although this may also be understood of time, because he was speaking of the Lord’s Passover, which is celebrated at the beginning of spring. In this beginning of months, therefore, he made heaven and earth, because the beginning of the world ought to be taken from the point at which the spring’s temperateness was suitable for all things. Thus the year set forth an image of the world being born, so that after winter’s ice and wintry gloom the brightness of springtime shines forth more serene than usual. Therefore the first rising of the world gave a pattern for the future courses of years, so that, by this law, the cycles of years should arise, and that at the beginning of each year the earth should bring forth new shoots of seed—just as the Lord God first said: “Let the earth bring forth the grass of hay, sowing seed according to its kind and according to its likeness, and the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit” (Gen. 1:11). And immediately the earth brought forth grass of hay and the fruit-bearing tree. In this, both the divine providence of perpetual order and the speed with which the earth germinates support our estimate of a spring season. For although at any time God was ready to command and earthly nature to obey, so that the earth, germinating under the warmth of the heavenly command amid winter ice and wintry frosts, might produce offspring, it was nevertheless not in accord with the eternal arrangement suddenly to open fields stiffened by rigid frost into green fruits and mingle blossoming things with bristling rime. Therefore, in order to show that springtime was present at the constitution of the world, Scripture says: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be for you the first among the months of the year” (Exod. 12:2), calling the first month the spring season. For it was fitting that the beginning of the year should be the beginning of generation, and that generation itself should be fostered by milder breezes. The tender beginnings of things could not bear either the hardship of harsher cold or the injury of torrential heat.

14. At the same time, one may observe that it is fittingly concurrent that entrance into this generation and these uses should seem to have been granted at the time when a lawful passage from this generation into regeneration takes place. For in the springtime the children of Israel left Egypt and passed through the sea, baptized in the cloud and in the sea, as the Apostle said (1 Cor. 10:1 ff.). At that time the Passover of the Lord Jesus Christ is yearly celebrated: that is, the passage of souls from vices to virtues, from passions of the flesh to the grace and sobriety of the mind, from the leaven of malice and wickedness to truth and sincerity. Therefore to those who have been regenerated it is said: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be for you the first among the months of the year” (Exod. 12:2). For one who is washed abandons and forsakes that intelligible Pharaoh, ruler of this world, saying: “I renounce you, devil, and your angels, and your works, and your dominions.” Nor will the one who, with all malice sunk like lead, armed on right and left with good works, strives to cross unimpeded over the seas of this world’s age, any longer serve him, whether through the earthly passions of this body or through the errors of a depraved mind. Scripture also says in the book entitled *Numbers*: “Amalek is the beginning of nations, and his seed shall perish” (Num. 24:20). Certainly Amalek is not the first of all nations; but because Amalek is interpreted as “king of the wicked,” and the wicked are the nations, see whether we ought to understand the ruler of this world, who governs nations that do his will, and whose seed shall perish. His seed, moreover, consists of the impious and unbelieving, to whom the Lord says: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:24).

[Note: Four most excellent manuscripts omit: “and your angels.”]

[Note: It is not easy to say from where Ambrose derived this interpretation; it must nevertheless be acknowledged that it is rightly rejected. For it has no affinity with the word. Blessed Jerome reports another meaning of this name from Philo in *On Hebrew Names*: “Amalek,” he says, “a people lapping or licking.” A third explanation may also be found at the end of R. Stephani’s Bible, where Amalek is explained from Hebrew and Syriac as “a people striking.”]

[Note: All editions with several manuscripts: “But the nations are wicked.” Others, better: “the wicked [are] nations,” etc.]

15. There is also a mystical beginning, as in: “I am the first and the last, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1:8). Especially in the Gospel there is that saying in which the Lord, asked who he was, replied: “The Beginning, what I also say to you” (John 8:25). He is truly, according to his divinity, the beginning of all things, because no one is before him; and the end, because no one is beyond him. And according to Solomon (Prov. 8:22), he is the beginning of the Lord’s ways for his works, so that through him the human race might learn to follow the ways of the Lord and work the works of God. Therefore, in this beginning—that is, in Christ—God made heaven and earth, because through him all things were made, and without him nothing was made. What was made was life in him, because all things subsist in him. He is also the firstborn of every creature, either because he is before every creature, or because he is holy—for firstborn persons are holy, as Israel is firstborn not because it is before all others, but because it is holier than the rest. The Lord is holy above every creature, even according to the assumption of a body, because he alone is without sin, he alone without vanity. But every creature is subjected to vanity.

16. We may also understand: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” that is, before time; just as the beginning of a road is not yet a road, and the beginning of a house is not yet a house. Accordingly, some have said *en kephalaiō*, “in summary,” as though “at the head,” by which is signified that the totality of the work was completed in a brief and slight moment. Thus there are those who take “beginning” not for time but for “before time,” and *kephalaion*, or “head”; so that we may say in Latin, as it were, “the sum of the work,” because heaven and earth are the sum of visible things. They seem to pertain not only to the adornment of this world, but also to the manifestation of invisible things and to a kind of proof of things not seen, as in the prophetic saying: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18:1). The Apostle followed this and expressed the same conclusion in other words: “For his invisible things are understood through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20). For we readily understand that he who by a moment of his command made from nothing this great beauty of the world—which did not exist—to exist, and granted it substance not from pre-existent things or causes, is the author of Angels, Dominions, and Powers.

### CHAPTER V

The world is a specimen of divine operation. The Gentiles wrongly call it a shadow of God; for to the Son alone belongs being the image of God.

17. This world, then, is a specimen of divine operation; for when the work is seen, its maker is presented. Among the arts, some are active, consisting in bodily movement or vocal sound; once movement or sound ceases, nothing remains or is left for spectators or hearers. Others are theoretical, exercising the vigor of the mind. Others are such that even after the activity of operation has ceased, the service of the work appears—such as building and weaving—which, even when the craftsman is silent, display his skill, so that the work bears witness on behalf of its maker. Similarly, this world is an emblem of divine majesty, through which the wisdom of God is manifested. Seeing it, and at the same time lifting the eyes of his mind to invisible things, the Prophet says: “How magnified are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24).

[Note: An old Corbie manuscript and Germanensis: “which are exercised by the vigor of the mind.”]

18. Nor do we read “made” without purpose. For many Gentiles who wish the world to be coeternal with God maintain that it subsists of itself, as though it were a shadowing forth of divine power. Although they acknowledge that God is its cause, they nevertheless maintain that he, though a cause, produced it not by his own will and disposition, but in the manner in which a body is the cause of a shadow. For a shadow adheres to a body, and radiance to light, by a natural association rather than by voluntary choice. Moses therefore fittingly said that God made heaven and earth. He did not say that he caused them to subsist; he did not say that he supplied the world with a cause for its existence. Rather, he made, as one good, that which would be useful; as one wise, that which he judged best; as one almighty, that which he foresaw would be most extensive. But how could it be as a shadow where there was no body, since there cannot be a bodily shadowing of the incorporeal God? And how can the splendor of incorporeal light be bodily?

[Note: All editions and two manuscripts: “yet [they say] the cause made.” Two others: “yet [they say] the cause as made.” Two more: “yet [they say] cause made.” More numerous and better manuscripts: “yet [they say] the cause [is] made,” where “made” is to be referred to God.]

19. But if you seek the splendor of God, the Son is the image of the invisible God. Such as God is, such is the image. God is invisible; the image also is invisible. For he is the splendor of the Father’s glory and the image of his substance. “In the beginning,” he says, “God made heaven and earth.” Therefore the world was made and began to be, though it had not existed; but the Word of God was in the beginning and always was. Even Angels, Dominions, and Powers, although they began at some time, nevertheless already existed when this world was made. For all things, visible and invisible, whether Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, or Powers, were created and established: “All things,” he says, “were made through him and created unto him” (Col. 1:16). What does “created unto him” mean? Because he is heir of the Father, since the inheritance has passed from the Father to him, as the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance” (Ps. 2:8). Yet this inheritance passes from the Father to the Son and returns from the Son to the Father. Thus the Apostle excellently calls the Son in this passage the author of all things and the one who holds all things together by his majesty. And in Romans he says of the Father: “For from him, and through him, and unto him are all things” (Rom. 11:36). From him is the beginning and origin of the substance of all things—that is, from his will and power. For all things began from his will, because there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things. For he made as from his own, because he made from whatever he willed. Through him is continuation; unto him, the end. From him, therefore, is matter. Through him is the operation which bound and held together all things. Unto him: because, so long as he wills, all things remain and subsist by his power, and their end returns to God’s will; by his decision they are dissolved.

[Note: Thus five manuscripts of better quality and the editions of Amerbach, Petit, and Erasmus; Greek: *eis auton*, “unto him.” The remaining manuscripts and the editions of Gillot and Rome: “in him.” What does “in him” mean?]

[Note: Thus the Corbie manuscript and the Thuaneus edition; Coster’s edition and some Paris editions read similarly below. The remaining manuscripts and editions: “in him.”]

### CHAPTER VI

In heaven and earth the four elements from which all things are composed were created. What the substance of heaven is, what the position of earth, and how diversely philosophers have judged the nature of the heavens; these are to be set aside, and divine authority heeded.

20. Therefore God made heaven and earth at the beginning of time. For time is from this world, not before the world; and day is a portion of time, not its beginning. Although from the sequence of the reading we may establish that the Lord first made day and night, which are the alternations of times, and on the second day made the firmament, by which he separated the water under heaven from the water above heaven, nevertheless it is sufficient for the present argument that in the beginning he made heaven, from which comes the precedence and cause of generation, and that he made earth, in which was the substance of generation. For in these the four elements were created, from which all the things belonging to the world are generated. The four elements are air, fire, water, and earth, and in all things they are mingled with one another. Indeed, you will find fire in earth, which is frequently struck from stones and iron; and in heaven, although the pole is fiery and gleaming with shining stars, water may be understood to exist—either water above heaven or water frequently sent down upon the earth in abundant rain from that higher place. We might gather more arguments for this, if we saw that these things contributed anything to the edification of the Church. But because it is an unprofitable occupation to be engaged with such matters, let us direct our minds rather to those things in which there is advancement toward eternal life.

[Note: Three manuscripts: “from which [comes] the priority and cause of generation.”]

21. Concerning the quality and substance of heaven, therefore, it is enough to bring forth what we find in the writings of Isaiah. In ordinary and familiar language, he expressed the quality of the heavenly nature, saying that God “established heaven like smoke” (Isa. 51:6), wishing to declare its subtle, non-solid nature. As to its appearance, it is also sufficient that he himself said concerning the firmament of heaven that God made heaven “like a vault,” because within heaven’s compass all things are enclosed—whatever takes place either in sea or on land (Isa. 40:22). The same is indicated when we read: “The Lord stretches out heaven” (Isa. 34:4). For it is stretched out either like a skin for the tents and dwellings of the saints, or like a book, so that the names of the many who have deserved Christ’s grace by faith and devotion may be written there—those to whom it is said: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

[Note: Old Corbie and Benignianus: “for the tents of habitation.” Gemeticensis, corrected by a second hand, like Coster’s edition: “for the tents of protection and habitation,” etc.]

22. It is of no benefit for the hope of the future to discuss either the character or the position of the earth, since for knowledge it is enough [Col. 0133A] that we grasp what the sequence of the divine Scriptures contains: that He “hangs the earth upon nothing” (Job 26:7). Why should we debate whether it hangs in the air or upon water, and thereby raise the question how the thin and softer nature of air can support the mass of the earth? Or how, if it rests upon the waters, the heavy collapse of the lands is not submerged in the water? Or how the sea’s wave does not yield to it and, displaced from its place, spread itself over its sides? Many have also said that the earth is in the middle of the air and remains motionless by its own mass,

> [Note: Col. 0133D: Two manuscripts: “because it hangs evenly.” Roman edition: “because it hangs by an equal balance.”]

because it inclines equally this way and that. On this matter we consider that the Lord said enough to Job His servant when, speaking from the cloud, He declared: “Where were you when I founded the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding. Who set its measures, if [Col. 0133B] you know? Or who stretched a measuring-line over it? Or upon what were its circles fixed?” (Job 38:4). And below: “I shut up the sea with gates, and said: ‘Thus far shall you come and no farther; here your waves shall be broken’” (ibid., 10). Does not God plainly show that all things subsist by His majesty in number, weight, and measure? For the creature does not give a law, but receives it and keeps what it has received.

Therefore the earth is not held in the middle as though suspended upon an even balance; rather, the majesty of God binds it by the law of His will, so that it remains firm above what is unstable and void, as David the prophet also testifies when he says: “He founded the earth upon its foundation; it shall not be moved for ever and ever” (Ps. 103:5).

> [Note: Col. 0133D: Thus six manuscripts and the editions of Amiens, Petavius, and Erasmus; likewise a little later. But the other manuscripts and the Roman edition read, “its firmness.”]

Here God is proclaimed not merely as an artisan, but [Col. 0133C] as Almighty: He has suspended the earth not upon some center, but upon the firm support of His command, and does not permit it to incline. We should therefore understand not a measurement of a center, but that of divine judgment: it is not a measure of art, but of power; a measure of justice, a measure of knowledge. For all things do not escape His knowledge as though immeasurable; rather, they lie beneath His knowledge as though measured out.
