Nor, when we read, “I have established its pillars” (Ps. 74:4), may we suppose that the earth is literally supported upon pillars, but upon that power which props up and sustains the substance of the earth. Finally, infer also from this that the earth’s establishment lies in God’s power, since it is written: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” (Ps. 103:32). And elsewhere: “Yet once more I shake [Col. 0133D] the earth” (Hag. 2:8). Thus it does not remain immovable through its own balances; rather, it is often moved by God’s nod and decision, as Job also says: “For the Lord moves it from its foundations, and its pillars are shaken” (Job 9:6). And elsewhere: “The underworld lies naked before Him, and death has no covering. He stretches out the north over nothing, hanging the earth upon nothing; binding water in His clouds . . . The pillars of heaven fled and were terrified at His rebuke; by His power He calmed [Col. 0134A] the sea, by His discipline He subdued heaven; but the bars of heaven fear Him” (Job 26:6).

Therefore by God’s will the earth remains unmoved and stands for ever, according to the saying of Ecclesiastes (Eccles. 1:4); and by God’s will it is moved and shaken. It does not subsist supported by its own foundations, nor remain firm by its own props; but the Lord has established it and holds it fast by the firm support of His will, because all the ends of the earth are in His hand. This simplicity of faith surpasses every argument.

Let others praise the fact that the earth nowhere falls because, according to nature, it occupies its own region in the middle; because it must remain in its own place and cannot incline toward another direction when it moves not contrary to nature, but according to nature. Let them proclaim the excellence of the divine craftsman and eternal worker—what artisan has not received from Him? Or who gave women wisdom in weaving or skill in variation? Yet I, unable to comprehend the depth of His majesty and the excellence of His art, do not entrust myself to the balances and measurements of disputation. Rather, I judge that all things are placed in His

> [Note: Col. 0134D: The edition and quite a few manuscripts read “power.” Nine other, better manuscripts read “will.”]

will: His will is the foundation of all things, and because of Him this world still endures. This may also be established by the example of apostolic authority. For it is written: “Creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of Him who subjected it in hope” (Rom. 8:20). Creation itself will be freed from the bondage of corruption

> [Note: Col. 0134D: Thus eleven manuscripts of the best quality and old editions. But the Roman edition and a few manuscripts read, “with . . . glory,” etc.]

when the grace of divine recompense has shone forth.

23. But concerning the nature and character of the substance of heaven, [Col. 0134C] why should I enumerate the things philosophers have woven into their arguments? Some assert that heaven is composed of the four elements; others introduce a fifth nature, a body of a new kind, for its constitution, and maintain that it is an ethereal body, mixed with neither fire, air, water, nor earth. Such elements, they say, have each its own course, function, and natural motion: heavier things sink and are borne downward, while empty and light things rise upward. Each has its proper motion; but in the revolution of a sphere these motions are confused and lose the force of their own course, since the sphere rolls about in its orbit and higher things exchange places with lower, and lower with higher. But where natural motions are altered, there [Col. 0134D] necessarily the qualities of their substances are usually altered as well.

Why, then, do we maintain that heaven is an ethereal body, lest it appear liable to corruption? Whatever is composed of corruptible elements must necessarily be dissolved. Indeed, because elements of the same nature are nevertheless different, they cannot have a single and inviolable motion, since the differing movements of the elements conflict with one another. One motion cannot suit all things or agree with elements [Col. 0135A] that are unlike. A motion suitable for light elements becomes unsuitable for heavier ones. Thus, whenever the upward motion of heaven is necessary, it is weighed down by earthly matter; whenever a downward course is sought, that fiery force is violently drawn down—for it is compelled downward contrary to its natural function. But everything compelled in a contrary direction, serving necessity rather than nature, is quickly dissolved and divided into the things of which it seems to be composed, each returning to its own region. Accordingly, some, judging that these things could not be stable, supposed that heaven and the stars are ethereal bodies, introducing a certain fifth bodily nature so that they might think the substance of heaven would endure for a long time.

24. Yet this opinion could not withstand the [Col. 0135B] prophetic declaration, which the divine majesty of the Lord Jesus Christ also confirmed in the Gospel. David said: “In the beginning You founded the earth, O Lord, and the heavens are the works of Your hands. They themselves shall perish, but You remain; all of them shall grow old like a garment, and like a cloak You shall change them and they shall be changed; but You are the same, and Your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:26 ff.). The Lord so confirmed this in the Gospel that He said: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but My words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24:35).

> [Note: Col. 0135D: Manuscripts Colbert, one Corbie manuscript, and one Victorine manuscript read “shall perish.” The Roman edition reads “shall pass away.”]

Therefore those accomplish nothing who, to maintain the perpetuity of heaven, thought a fifth, ethereal body must be introduced, when they can equally see that a portion unlike the rest, joined to a single body, has generally brought defect rather than stability to that body. Observe also that when the prophet David [Col. 0135C] named the earth first (Ps. 148:5) and heaven afterwards, he intended to declare the Lord’s work. For when he said, “and they were made,” it makes no difference which you mention first, since both were made together. Thus even this prerogative should not seem allotted to the substance of heaven, as though it were judged superior by the privilege of being the first-born creature.

Let us therefore leave such persons to their controversies, by which they refute one another. For us, the truth of the commandments, not the conflict of debates, is enough for salvation; the faith of the mind, not the cleverness of argument—so that we may serve the Creator rather than the creature, who is God blessed for ever.

## CHAPTER VII. (Discourse II.)

A reply to those who try to establish the eternity of matter from words of Scripture. The earth is called invisible because it was covered by waters. Why it is indicated as made before it was adorned.

25. “But the earth was invisible and unformed” (Gen. 1:2). A good craftsman first lays the foundation; then, once the foundation is laid, he distinguishes the parts of the building and adds ornament. Therefore, after laying the foundation of the earth and establishing the substance of heaven—for these two are, as it were, the hinges of all things—he added: “But the earth was invisible and unformed.” What does “was” mean, except to prevent them perhaps from extending their opinion [Col. 0136A] indefinitely and without a beginning and saying: “See: matter—that is, *hyle*, as the philosophers say—had no beginning even according to divine Scripture”?

But you will answer those who say this: “Cain was a worker of the earth” (Gen. 4:2). And Scripture says of the man called Jubal: “He was the father who showed the psaltery and the lyre” (ibid., 21). And: “There was a man in the land of Ausitis, whose name was Job” (Job 1:1). Therefore let them cease to raise a question from the word, especially since Moses first stated that God made the earth. It “was,” then, from the time it was made.

For if they say that it exists without beginning, then, while saying that not only God but also *hyle* is without beginning, let them determine where it was. If it was in a place, then they assert that the place too, in which the matter of things existed, was without beginning. But if it seems absurd to believe this about place, take care lest we must perhaps consider the earth to have been flying, suspended, though it had no foundation, by the rowing of wings. From where, then, shall we provide it with wings—unless perhaps we force into this sense the prophetic saying: “We have heard wonders from the wings of the earth” (Isa. 24:16)? And this: “Woe to the land of the wing of ships” (Isa. 18:1)?

> [Note: Col. 0136D: Gembloux and Cîteaux manuscripts: “Woe to the land of the wing of birds.”]

But if we accept this, in what air did the earth fly? It could not fly without air; but air could not yet exist, because the distinction of the elements had not yet been made from the matter of things, since the elements themselves had not yet been made. Where, then, was this matter, supported by the rowing of wings? It was not in the air, because air is a body of the world. The reading teaches that air is a body (Wis. 5:12): “a discharged arrow [Col. 0136C] passed into the place at which the archer aimed, and the divided air immediately closed again upon itself.” Where, then, was *hyle*, unless it is said with some mad intention that it was in God? Then God—who is of invisible and inviolable nature, who inhabits inaccessible light, incomprehensible and most pure Spirit—was the place of worldly matter; and a portion of the world was in God, although not even the minds of His servants are of this world, as we have it written: “They are not of this world, just as I am not of the world” (John 17:14).

26. How, then, could invisible things be joined with visible ones, and unformed things with Him who bestowed order and beauty upon all things? Unless perhaps, because it says, “But the earth was invisible,” they understand it to have been invisible in its substance; and because it was covered by waters, it could not be visible [Col. 0136D] to bodily eyes—just as many things lying in the depth of waters escape the sight and gaze of the eyes. Nothing, however, is invisible to God; it is called invisible according to the estimation of a creature of the world.

The earth was also invisible because the light which illumined the world did not yet exist, nor the sun; for the heavenly luminaries were made later. If the sun’s ray frequently illumines even what is covered by water and reveals, by the brightness of its light, things submerged in the depths, who can doubt that things in the deep cannot be invisible to God? Unless perhaps we understand the earth as invisible because it was not yet visited by God’s word and protection—[Col. 0137A] because it had no human being, on whose account the Lord might look upon the earth, as it is written: “The Lord looked down upon the children of men to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God” (Ps. 13:2).

> [Note: Col. 0137D: Ten manuscripts and the editions of Amiens, Petavius, and Erasmus omit the words “to see.” The Roman edition reads “to say.”]

And elsewhere He says: “He shot judgment from heaven; the earth trembled and was still” (Ps. 75:9). It was rightly invisible because it was unformed: it had not yet received from its own Creator a fitting shape and appearance.

27. Perhaps they will say: Why, when God said and things were made, did He not immediately give appropriate ornaments to the elements as they arose—as though He could not have caused heaven, adorned with stars, to shine as soon as it was created, and earth to be clothed with flowers and fruits? He certainly could. But things are declared first to have been made and afterwards to have been formed, lest they truly be believed uncreated and without beginning [Col. 0137B] if the appearances of things were seen as though innate from the beginning rather than added later.

The earth is described as unformed, and is accorded by philosophers the same privileges of eternity as God. What would they say if its beauty had flowered from the beginning? It is described as submerged in waters, as though devoted to a shipwreck of its first principles, and still some do not believe it was made. What if it claimed the beauty of a first-born? Moreover, God wished us to be imitators of Himself: first to make certain things, then to adorn them, lest, while we attempt both at once, we be unable to complete either.

Our faith grows by a certain progression. Therefore God first made and afterwards adorned, so that we may believe that the One who made also adorned, and the One who adorned also made; lest we suppose that one adorned and another created, but [Col. 0137C] that the same One performed both works—first making, afterwards arranging—

> [Note: Col. 0137D: The Gembloux manuscript, though in another hand, one Victorine manuscript, and the Gillot and Roman editions read “lest one be lacking to the other.” The editions of Amiens, Petavius, and Erasmus read “lest one be without the other,” etc.]

so that the one might be believed through the other. You have a clear testimony of this in the Gospel (John 11:44). For when the Lord was about to raise Lazarus, He ordered the Jews to remove the stone from the tomb, so that, seeing the dead man, they might afterwards believe when he was raised. Then He called Lazarus; he rose and came forth, his hands and feet bound. Could not He who could raise the dead remove the stone? Could not He who could restore life to the deceased loose the bonds? Could not He who gave a man movement with bound feet restore walking to him with the bonds broken? But clearly we see that He wished first to show the man dead, so that they might believe with their own eyes; then to raise him; thirdly, to command them themselves to loose the burial wrappings, [Col. 0137D] so that amid these things faith might be poured into unbelievers and belief might arise by certain stages.

## CHAPTER VIII.

The earth was unformed: first because nothing in it was distinct, then because it was veiled in darkness. The Holy Spirit, who was borne over the waters, and other considerations show that evil is not to be understood by the darkness; above all, because evil arises only from us.

28. Therefore God first made heaven and earth, yet He willed them [Col. 0138A] to be subject to the consummation not as everlasting but as corruptible creatures.

> [Note: Col. 0138D: Thus twelve manuscripts and old editions. The Le Mans manuscripts, one Corbie manuscript, and the Roman edition read, “everlasting,” but “a corruptible creature.” The Vatican codex reads, “an everlasting . . . corruptible creature.”]

Thus in the book of Isaiah He says: “Lift up your eyes to heaven and look down upon the earth; for heaven has been established like smoke, but earth shall grow old like a garment” (Isa. 51:6). This is the earth which was formerly unformed. For the seas had not yet been defined by their proper boundary, and therefore the earth was flooded by wandering waves and the deep abyss. Consider that even now the earth commonly bristles with marshy damp and cannot endure the plough where moisture poured over the land overflows.

It was therefore unformed, as the ground of an industrious farmer, untilled by cultivation because a cultivator was still lacking. It was unformed because it was bare of living growth: neither grassy with beds of herbage along the banks, nor shaded by woods, nor cheerful with crops, nor dark beneath the brows [Col. 0138B] of mountains, nor fragrant with flowers, nor pleasant with vineyards. Rightly was it unformed, since it needed adornments and lacked garlands of sparkling vines. God wished to show that even the world itself would have no grace unless its Maker had adorned it with varied cultivation.

Heaven itself, woven with clouds, usually produces horror in the eyes and sadness in the mind. The earth, soaked with rain, is wearisome. The seas, troubled by storms—whom do they not strike with fear? The appearance of things is most beautiful; but what would it be without light? What without moderation? What without the gathering of waters, beneath which the beginnings of this world, formerly submerged, were held? Take the sun from the earth, take the globes of stars from heaven: all things become grim in darkness. So they were before the Lord poured light into this world. Therefore Scripture says: “Darkness [Col. 0138C] was over the abyss” (Gen. 1:2). There was darkness because the brightness of light was absent. There was darkness because air itself is dark. Water itself beneath a cloud is dark, because water in the clouds of the air is dark. Therefore darkness was over the abysses of waters.

I do not think that evil powers should be understood here, as though the Lord created their wickedness. For wickedness is not a substance but an accident; it has turned aside from the goodness of nature.

29. Accordingly, in the constitution of the world, let the notion of evil be set aside for the moment, lest we seem to mix what is disfiguring into the divine work and most beautiful creation—especially since there follows: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (ibid.). Although some understand this as the air and others as the breath we breathe and draw from this life-giving breeze, we agree with the judgment of the saints and faithful in understanding it as the Holy Spirit, so that the operation of the Trinity may shine forth in the constitution of the world.

For after the statement that “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”—that is, God made in Christ, or the Son of God made as God, or God made through the Son, since all things were made through Him and without Him nothing was made—the fullness of the operation in the Spirit remained, as it is written: “By the Word of the Lord [Col. 0139A] the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of His mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6). Accordingly, just as in the Psalm we are taught the operation of the Word, which is the Word of God, and the power supplied by the Holy Spirit, so here the prophetic oracle resounded: God said, and God made; the Spirit of God too was borne over the waters.

For as the vault of heaven was being adorned and the earth was to bring forth vegetation, the Spirit was fittingly borne over it, because through Him the seeds of new offspring had to germinate, according to the prophet’s words: “Send forth Your Spirit, and they shall be created, and You shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103:30). Indeed, the Syriac, which is close to Hebrew and in many respects harmonizes and agrees with it in language, has: “And the Spirit of God brooded over the waters”—that is, gave them life, that He might draw them forth into new creatures and animate them into life by His fostering warmth. For we also read that the Holy Spirit is Creator, Job saying: “The divine Spirit made me” (Job 33:4).

Therefore, whether the Holy Spirit was borne over the waters, the darkness of opposing powers could not be over them where such great grace claimed its place; or, if, as some wish, they understand it as air, let them explain why he called it the Spirit of God, when it would have been enough simply to call it spirit.

30. These persons, then, hold that our Lord God first produced four elements—heaven, earth, sea, and air—because the causes of things are fire and air, earth and water, from which the world’s appearance and form consist. Where, then, could the darkness of spiritual wickedness have had a place, when the world put on the beauty of this august form? Did God create wickedness at the same time? Rather, it arose from us; it was not created by God the Creator, but is produced by moral frivolity. It has no prerogative of creation and no authority belonging to a natural substance; it is a defect of mutability and the error of a fall.

God wishes to root it out from the souls of individuals; how could He Himself generate it? The prophet cries: “Cease from your wickednesses” (Isa. 1:17). And especially holy David: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33:15). How then do we assign its beginning to the Lord? This deadly opinion belongs to those who thought the Church ought to be disturbed. From this came the Marcionites, from this the Valentinians, from this those plagues of the Manichaeans attempted to bring deadly contagions upon the minds of the saints.

Why do we seek the darkness of death within the very light of life? Divine Scripture offers salvation and breathes the fragrance [Col. 0139D] of life, so that by reading you may receive sweetness, not incur the danger of a precipice. Read simply, O human being; do not, as a perverse interpreter, dig a pit for yourself. The statement is simple: God made heaven and earth. He made what did not exist, not what did exist. The earth was, from the time it was made; and it was invisible because water overflowed and covered it, and darkness was poured over it because the light of day did not yet exist, nor the ray of the sun, which usually reveals even what lies hidden beneath the waters.

What, then, do they mean by saying that God created evil, when opposites and contraries do not generate what is contrary to themselves? Life does not generate [Col. 0140A] death, nor light darkness. The progressions of generation are not like the changes of dispositions. Dispositions turn from contraries into contrary things through a change of purpose; generations do not turn from contraries into opposites, but, created from causes or authors of the same kind, are referred back in likeness to their author.

31. What, then,

> [Note: Col. 0139D: Paris edition: “What, then, is worse?”]

shall we say? If evil is neither without beginning, as though uncreated, nor made by God, whence does wickedness have its nature? No wise person has denied that there are evils in this world, since falling into death is so frequent in this age. Yet from what we have already said we may infer that it is not a living substance, but a corruption of mind and soul, straying from the path of virtue, which very frequently steals into the souls of the careless.

Thus no danger from without is greater to us than the danger from ourselves. The adversary is within; within is the author of error; within, I say, enclosed in ourselves. Examine your intention; explore the disposition of your mind; set a watch against the thoughts of your mind and the desires of your soul. You yourself are the cause of your own wrongdoing; you yourself are the leader of your crimes and instigator of your sins. Why do you summon an alien nature to excuse your falls? Would that you did not yourself drive yourself onward, hurl yourself down, entangle yourself in excessive zeal, anger, or desires, which hold us caught as though in nets.

Certainly it lies within us to moderate our zeal, restrain anger, and curb desires; it lies within us also [Col. 0140C] to indulge luxury,

> [Note: Col. 0139D: Roman edition: “abolish.” All the others, most consistently, read “kindle,” that is, “increase.”]

kindle lusts, inflame anger, lend an ear to one who inflames it, rise higher in pride, pour ourselves out into cruelty rather than restrain ourselves through humility, and love gentleness. Why do you accuse nature, O human being? It has certain hindrances, as it were: old age and infirmity. Yet old age itself is sweeter in good morals, more useful in counsel, readier for constancy in facing death, and stronger to restrain desires. Bodily infirmity too is sobriety of mind. Hence the Apostle says: “When I am weak, then I am powerful” (2 Cor. 12:10). Therefore he gloried not in strengths but in weaknesses. The divine response also shone forth in the saving oracle: “Power is perfected in weakness.”

Those things must be avoided (15, question 1, chapter *Illa cavenda*) which proceed from our own will: the sins of youth and the irrational passions of the body. Let us not seek outside ourselves the origins of things of which we are masters, nor attribute them to others, but recognize what is properly our own. For what we can refrain from doing, if we do not wish to do it, we ought to ascribe the choice of evil in it to ourselves rather than to others. Thus even in the courts of this world guilt binds and punishment condemns defendants who act voluntarily, not those compelled by necessity. For if someone kills an innocent person in madness, he is not liable to death. Indeed, by the oracle of the divine law itself (Exod. 21:13), one who has caused death through inadvertence receives hope of impunity and the opportunity of refuge, so that he may escape.

Let this suffice concerning what appears properly to be evil. For evils are only those which involve the mind in guilt and bind the conscience. But no wise person would call poverty, obscurity of birth, illness, or death evils, or count them among evils, since their opposites are not considered the greatest goods either. Some of these things seem to happen to us by nature, others by circumstance.

32. This digression has not been idle; it has shown that darkness and abyss must be understood simply. Darkness existed because of the shadowing [Col. 0141A] of heaven. Every body produces a shadow, by which it casts shade upon or confines what is near or below it—especially that which appears to cover and enclose. The vault of heaven encloses, because heaven is stretched out like a vault, as we demonstrated above. Therefore darkness was not a primary substance; rather, the gloom of darkness followed the body of the world as a shadow.

Thus, when the world arose at the instant of the divine command, it enclosed its shadow within itself. If someone in the middle of a field illuminated by the noonday sun should suddenly fence off a spot and cover it with thick leafy branches, would not the more brightly the appearance of that place shines outside, the more darkly its little shelter within becomes shadowed from above by a grim

> [Note: Col. 0141D: A *scena* is a place covered by branches of trees. Vergil, *Aeneid* I: “. . . then a stage of gleaming woods / hangs above, a dark grove with its grim shadow.”]

canopy? Or why did they call such a place, enclosed on every side, a cave, except because it is made grim by its dark situation and the spreading of darkness? Such darkness, then, was over the abysses of waters. For that *abyss* means the multitude and depth of waters is taught by the Gospel reading (Luke 8:31), where the demons begged the Savior not to command them to go into the abyss. But He who taught that the wishes of demons were not to be granted ordered them to go into the pigs. The pigs hurled themselves into the lake of waters, so that the demons would not escape what they refused, but would be submerged by a fitting plunge. Such, then, was the unformed appearance and shape of the world.

## CHAPTER IX.

Light is created; it is distinguished from darkness and approved. Why light was called day, and darkness night.

33. “And the Spirit of God,” he says, “was borne over the waters; and God said: ‘Let there be light’” (Gen. 1:3). Rightly the Spirit of God was mentioned first where a divine operation was about to begin. “Let there be light,” He says. With what should God’s voice in divine Scripture begin, if not with light? From what should the world’s adornment take its beginning, if not from light? For it would be pointless if it could not be seen.

God Himself was indeed in light, because He inhabits inaccessible light; and He was the true light that enlightens every [Col. 0142A] human being coming into this world. Yet He wished that light to be made which could be perceived by bodily eyes. One who desires to construct a building worthy of the master of a household’s dwelling investigates, before laying its foundations, how to admit light into it; and this is the first grace, which, if lacking, makes the whole house grim with ugly neglect. Light commends the remaining ornaments of a house. “Let there be light,” He says. The full utterance of light does not indicate the preparation of a plan but shines forth with the result of action. The Maker of nature spoke light and created it. God’s word is His will; God’s work is nature. He created light and illuminated darkness.

“And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” He did not speak so that action might follow; by speaking He completed the work. Thus the Davidic saying is apt: “He spoke and they were made” (Ps. 148:5), because the result fulfilled the word. God, then, is the author of light; the world is the place and cause of darkness. But the good Author so spoke light

> [Note: Col. 0141D: The Le Mans and Gembloux manuscripts, corrected, read “spoke”; so also several times below. Other manuscripts and editions read “loved.”]

as to open the world itself with infused light and beautify its appearance. The air suddenly shone, and darkness recoiled in terror at the brightness of the new light. The brilliance of light, poured in throughout the whole world, restrained it and, as it were, suddenly submerged it in the abysses. Therefore it was beautifully and properly said: “There was light.” For just as light swiftly illuminates heaven, earth, and sea, and in an instant of time, beyond all grasp, reveals regions with the splendor of rising day and pours itself around our sight, so its rising had to be described as swift.

Why should we wonder that God spoke light and light flashed upon the darkened world, when, if someone submerged among waters emits oil from his mouth, he makes clearer [Col. 0142C] things hidden beneath the secret depths? God spoke—not so that some sound of speech should emerge through vocal organs, nor that the movement of a tongue should form a heavenly utterance and some clamor of words strike this air—but so that the judgment of His will might be disclosed by the effect of His operation.

> [Note: Col. 0141D: Thus the old editions and the more numerous and better manuscripts. Four read “thought”; the Roman edition, “arrangement.” But “judgment” should, I think, be retained, here having the sense of an opinion and decision, just as a *cognitor* is a judge and *cognoscere* means “to judge.” In the same place, some manuscripts read “might disclose the effect of His will”; some, “its effect”; many others and all editions, “by its effect.”]

34. “And He separated light from darkness; and God saw the light, that it was good” (Gen. 1:4). He spoke, and no one heard a sound of His voice; He separated, and no one perceived the exertion of His action; He saw, and no one beheld the direction of His eyes. “And God,” it says, “saw the light, that it was good.” He did not see what He had not known, nor approve something which He had not previously known or seen; rather, it is characteristic of good works that they require no external commendation, but, when seen, themselves testify to their own grace. What is approved by sight is greater than what is praised in speech, for it uses its own testimony, not another’s approval.

If we render judgment through our eyes, by which we grasp at once both the grace of beauty and the measure of things, how much more does God see all that He approves and approve all that He sees, according to what is written: “The eyes [Col. 0143A] of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. 33:16)? The nature of light is such that its grace lies not in number, measure, or weight, as with other things, but wholly in appearance. Therefore He expressed the nature of light in fitting words: it pleases by being seen, since it itself supplies the function of seeing. Nor without reason could it find so great a herald, by whom it is rightly praised first, since it made even the remaining members of the world worthy of praise. Therefore God saw the light, illuminated it with His countenance, and saw that it was good. The judgment is not partial on God’s part, but universal. Thus the grace of light is approved not only in splendor but in every usefulness. Hence too the separation between light and darkness took place,

> [Note: Col. 0143D: One Dionysian and one Colbert manuscript: “so that the nature of things, separated . . .”]

so that, once the nature of light and darkness was separated, nothing might appear confused within itself.

[Col. 0143B] 35. “And God called the light day, and called the darkness night” (Gen. 1:5), so that He distinguished day and night by their very names. We observe, therefore, that the rising of light appears to open day before the sun does; for the beginnings of day close the end of night, and the boundary of time and condition appears to have been prescribed for night and day. The sun brightens the day; light makes it. The sky is often covered with clouds so that the sun is hidden and none of its ray appears; yet light still shows the day and conceals the darkness.

## CHAPTER X.

Here day is placed before night, contrary to what seems right to some. Why it is called one day rather than first, and why it is concluded with the end of morning.

[Col. 0143C] 36. “And there was evening, and there was morning, one day” (Gen. 1:5). Some ask why Scripture mentioned evening first and morning afterward, lest it seem perhaps to signify night before day. They fail to notice, first, that it had already introduced day, saying: “And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night”; then, that evening is the end of day, and morning the end of night. Therefore, in order to give day the prerogative and primacy of birth, it first indicated the end of the day, after which the ensuing night would come, and afterward added the end of the night. Yet Scripture could not prefer night to day so far as to encompass the times both of day and of night under the name of day, as though it claimed them by the authority of the principal name. We prove by many [Col. 0143D] examples that this is Scripture’s custom: to assign the designation to what is more important. Thus Jacob said: “The days of my life are few and evil” (Gen. 47:9); and again: “All the days of my life.” David too wrote: “The days of our years” (Ps. 89:10); he did not say “and nights.” Hence we perceive that the matters now set forth in the form of history [Col. 0144A] established for the future the force of a law. The beginning of day, therefore, is the voice of God: “Let there be light”; and light was made. The end of day is evening. The next day now succeeds from the end of night. God’s judgment, moreover, is clear: first he called the light day, and second he called the darkness night.

37. He also aptly said “one day,” not “the first day.” For, with a second and third day to follow, and then the remaining days, he could have said “the first”; and this would have seemed to follow the order. But he established the rule that the twenty-four hours of day and night should be defined by the name of day alone, as though he had said: “The measure of twenty-four hours is the period of one day.” For just as the succession of men is counted, while that of women is also understood, because the latter are joined to [Note: [Col. 0144D] Several manuscripts and the Roman edition: “the second to the former.”] what is prior and more important, so days too are numbered, while the nights are reckoned as attached to them. As there is one circuit, so there is one day. For many also call a single week one day, because it returns, as it were, into one day and, as it were, recurs seven times into itself. A circuit has this form: to begin from itself and return into itself. Hence Scripture also sometimes calls an age one. For although elsewhere it calls them ages, it seems rather to signify differences of public conditions or affairs than to define any succession of ages: “For the day of the Lord is great and very glorious” (Joel 2:11). And elsewhere: “Why do you seek the day of the Lord?” (Amos 5:16). “It is darkness and not light.” For it is clear that this day is dark to those of evil conscience and the unworthy—a day in which innocence shall shine forth and the guilty mind shall be tormented. But Scripture teaches us that that everlasting day of eternal recompense will be without interruption by nights or succession of darkness (Isa. 60:19).

38. Beautifully, then, when he was about to call the twofold succession one day, he concluded it with the end of morning, so as to teach both that the day begins from light and ends in light. For the period of day is not complete unless that of night too has been fulfilled. Therefore let us always walk honorably, as in the day, and cast off the works of darkness. For we know that night was given for bodily rest, not for the performance of some duty or work, which passes away in sleep and forgetfulness. Let there not be among us revelry, drunkenness, sexual indulgence, or indecency. Let us not say: “Darkness and walls cover us; and who knows whether the Most High will see?” But let there be in us love of light [Col. 0144D] and concern for uprightness, so that, walking as in the day, we may desire that our works should shine before God—to whom belong honor, praise, glory, and power, with our Lord Jesus Christ and with the Holy Spirit, from ages past, now and always, and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK TWO. ON THE WORK OF THE SECOND DAY

[Col. 0143]

## 21 CHAPTER I. (Sermon III.)

After briefly reviewing the works of the first day and rejecting those who ascribed eternal matter to the world, he proceeds to the second day; and he teaches that, in the creation of things, one must consider not nature’s [Col. 0144D] capacity, but God’s power.

[Col. 0143D]

1. We have completed, as best we could, the first day—or rather, the one day; for let it retain [Col. 0145A] the prerogative of the prophetic expression. In it we have recognized, through the operation of God Almighty, of the Lord Jesus Christ, and likewise of the Holy Spirit, heaven founded, earth created, [Note: [Col. 0145D] Roman edition: “the overflowing of the waters restrained.” The word “restrained” is absent from the other manuscripts and editions, and rightly so; for the waters had not yet been gathered.] the overflowing of waters, the air spread around, and the separation of light from darkness. Who, then, would not marvel that the world, with its unlike and unequal parts, should rise into one body, and that things so far apart should come together into partnership and mutual connection by the indissoluble law of concord and charity, so that things distinct in nature might be bound into the bond of unity and peace by a kind of indivisible joining? Or who, seeing these things, would probe with feeble intellect the possibility of their rationale? The divine power, incomprehensible to human minds and inexpressible by our words, has joined all these things together by the authority of its will.

[Col. 0145B] 2. Therefore God made heaven and earth and commanded them as their author, not as an inventor of shapes but as the maker of nature. For how can the operative power of the impassible God and the nature of passible matter agree with one another, as though each borrowed from the other what it needed? For if matter is uncreated, then God seems to have lacked the power to create matter and to have borrowed from it what lay subject to his operation. But if it was unformed, it is exceedingly strange that matter, coeternal with God, could not confer beauty upon itself, though it received its substance not from a creator but possessed it itself without time. Thus the maker of all things found more than he bestowed. He found matter upon which he could work; but he bestowed form, which brought beauty to the things found [Col. 0145C] already there. Hence this day ought to be set apart from the others as one day, not compared with them as the first day: it is the day on which the foundations of all things were laid and the causes began by which the substance of this world and of the whole visible creation is sustained. Therefore let our discourse proceed to the wonderful works of the second day, whose excellence must be referred to the Creator’s praise, not according to the capacity of our exposition, but according to the truth of the writer.

3. I ask you, therefore, to weigh naturally what we say plausibly, and to consider it with simple mind and diligent intelligence—not collecting the persuasive probabilities of philosophical tradition and vain deceit [Note: [Col. 0145D] Thus the old edition and many manuscripts, including Bigotian, Colbertine, and Dionysian, read “things like the true.” The Vatican codex does not contain the word “probabilities” (*verisimilia*). The Roman edition and three manuscripts read “persuasively”; Theodorian and Reginensis, “persuading probabilities”; Benedictine and first hand of Corbie, “of persuasion . . .”; Carolinian, “persuasive,” etc.—not badly. For “the teaching” may be understood.]—but according to the rule of truth expressed in the oracles of the divine word and poured into faithful hearts by contemplation of so great a majesty. For it is written: “Confirm me in your words. The unjust have told me their exercises, but not according to your law, O Lord; all your commandments are truth” (Ps. 128:28, 85–86). Let us therefore consider what has been made not according to the natures of the elements, but according to Christ, who did all that he willed, abounding in the fullness of his divinity; and let us not inquire into nature’s capacity. For when, in the Gospel, he healed lepers and restored sight to the blind, the people present who saw these things did not investigate the method of medicine; rather, marveling at the Lord’s power, they gave praise to God, as is written (Luke 18:43). Nor did Moses stretch out his hand according to Egyptian calculations and the conjunctions of the stars, or according to measures of the elements, in order that the Red Sea might be divided; rather, he obeyed the command of divine power. Hence he himself says: “Your right hand, O Lord, has been glorified in power; your right hand, O Lord, has shattered the enemies” (Exod. 15:6). Holy people, therefore, raise your mind to him and direct your whole soul toward him. God does not see as man sees: God sees in the heart; man, in the face. Nor, then, does man see as God sees. You hear that God saw and praised. Do not therefore judge what has been made by your own eyes or draw conclusions from opinions; [Col. 0146B] rather, do not suppose that those things which God saw and approved are to be called into question by you.

## 24 CHAPTER II.

The firmament is created in order to divide waters from waters. The existence of several heavens is proved, and the harmony of the heavenly spheres is refuted.

4. “And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between water and water; and it was so” (Gen. 1:6). Hear the words of God: he says, “Let there be.” This is the language of one commanding, not of one estimating. He commands nature; he does not submit to possibility; he does not calculate measures or weigh quantities. His will is the measure of things. His word is the completion of the work: “Let there be,” he says, “a firmament in the midst of the water.” Everything that God establishes is firm. And he quite fittingly prefaced it: “Let there be a firmament,” before adding “in the midst of the water,” so that you might first believe that the firmament was made at God’s command before you doubted because of the flowing character of the waters. If you consider the nature of the elements, how could a firmament be solidified amid waters? They flow; it is held fast. They run; it remains. “And let it,” he says, “divide between water.” But water is accustomed to mingle, not to divide. How does he command what he knows to be contrary to the rationale of the elements? Yet since his word is the origin of nature, he rightly claims the power to give a law to nature, he who gave it its origin.

5. But first let us consider what the firmament is: whether it is the same thing that he called heaven above, or something else; whether there are two heavens, or more. For there are those who say that there is one heaven, and that there could have been no substance available for making another heaven, since there was one *hyle*, as they call it; for when all had been expended upon the higher heaven, nothing remained that could serve for the construction of a second or third heaven. Others, however, assert that there are innumerable heavens and worlds, and their own people ridicule them. Indeed, their conflict is no greater with us than with their own adherents, who strive to prove by geometrical numbers and necessities [Col. 0147A] that another heaven cannot exist, that nature cannot permit there to be a second or third, and that the maker’s power is not sufficient to create many heavens. Who would not ridicule their ingenious eloquence, when they do not deny that human beings can make many things of the same kind from one and the same material, yet doubt whether the Creator of all could make many heavens—of whom it is written: “But the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95:5), and elsewhere: “He did all whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 113:3)? For what is difficult for him whose willing is making? Their argument from impossibility, therefore, wavers when they dispute about God, to whom it is truly said: “For nothing is impossible to you.”

6. Accordingly, we cannot deny that there is not only a second but also a third heaven, since the Apostle confirms by the testimony of his writings that he was caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor. 2). David too places “the heavens of heavens” in the choir that praises the Lord (Ps. 148). Imitating him, philosophers introduced the harmonious motion of the spheres of the five stars, the sun, and the moon. They say that all things are connected with their orbits—or rather, their globes—which they suppose are mutually interwoven and, as it were, inserted into one another, revolving backward and carried in motion contrary to the rest. They say that from this impulse and motion of the spheres there is produced a certain sweet sound, full of charm, art, and most pleasing modulation, because the cleft air, under such artful motion and blending high notes with low, produces varied harmonies so evenly as to surpass all sweetness of musical song.

[Col. 0147C] 7. If you seek and expect proof of this matter to be supplied to us by sense and hearing, they hesitate. For if it were true, how would it not be heard by us amid the resounding motion of so great spheres? That heavenly sphere to which they attach the courses of the stars, ever revolving without interruption, has, they say, a more rapid revolution and produces a sharper sound; the lunar sphere, by contrast, a very low one. Yet we are accustomed to hear lighter sounds. If, therefore, we demand that the credibility of this argument be demonstrated by our testimony and the faculty of hearing, they reply that our ears have been deafened and our sense of hearing dulled by the habitual sound conceived from the beginning of our birth. They offer as an example the Nile, the greatest of rivers: at the point where it hurls itself from the highest [Col. 0147D] mountains into those *catadupa* [cataracts], the magnitude of its roar, they say, stops the ears of the inhabitants, so that they are said to lack the faculty of hearing. [Note: [Col. 0147D] The more numerous and better manuscripts read *catadyta*, from which the other, though corrupt, readings are not far removed. The old Corbie manuscript, Gembloux, and Cîteaux have “the hidden places of the stream for the purpose of explanation.” Others and the editions read *catadupa*, the cataracts of the Nile, mentioned by Cicero in the *Dream of Scipio*.] But truth itself readily answers them. We hear thunder generated by the collision of clouds: would we not hear the revolutions of such great spheres, which are thought to move with greater motion and therefore to produce more violent sounds? They add further that this sound does not reach the earth lest human beings, captivated by its sweetness and delight—the effect of the heavens’ most rapid motion from east [Col. 0148A] to west—should abandon their own businesses and occupations, leaving everything here idle through a kind of rapture of the human mind toward heavenly sounds. But let us leave matters foreign to our inquiry and to the sequence of divine reading to those who are outside; let us hold fast to the instruction of the heavenly Scriptures.

## CHAPTER III.

The firmament is not the same as heaven. The denial that real waters rest above it is shown to be mistaken by Scripture, examples, and manifold reasoning; in this connection those who refuse to admit that the sun has a hot nature are refuted.

8. Our subject, then, is this: God said, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between water and water.” From this arises the question whether he calls this firmament that which he had already made before, concerning which it is written: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Nor are we unaware that some before us have understood it in this way, on the ground that Scripture above stated that heaven was created and founded by God, while here it set out more fully the exposition of the work and creation: there, as it were, the sum of the work was briefly comprehended; here, the character of the operation was arranged through the individual kinds of concurrent things. But we are moved by the fact that [Col. 0148B] another name is used, a more solid form is indicated, a cause is distinguished, and the person of the co-worker is added. For thus it is written: “And God divided between the water which was under the firmament and the water which was above the firmament” (Gen. 1:7).

9. First, they wish to destroy what has become habitual and impressed upon our minds by frequent reading of the Scriptures: that waters cannot be above the heavens. They say that the sphere of heaven is round, with the earth in its middle, and that water cannot remain within that circuit but must necessarily flow down and slip away, since its course is from higher to lower places. For how, they ask, can water stand above a sphere when the sphere itself revolves? This is that subtlety of dialectic: “Grant me the premise from which I may answer you. If it is not granted, no answer can be given.” They ask us to concede that the axis of heaven is twisted in rapid motion while the globe of the earth remains motionless, in order to establish that waters cannot be above the heavens because the revolving axis would pour all of them out. Yet, even if I grant what they ask and answer them according to their opinions, can they deny [Col. 0148D] that at that height and depth there are length and breadth, which no one can comprehend except the one who, as the Apostle says, is filled unto all the fullness of God (Eph. 3:18–19)? For who can easily assess a divine work? There is, then, breadth in the very height of heaven. Moreover, to speak of things that we can know, many buildings are round outside and square inside, or square outside and round inside; their upper surfaces are flat, and water commonly adheres there. We say these things, however, so that they may perceive that their opinions can be refuted by opinions more plausible, and may cease to measure so great a work of God by contemplating human workmanship and our own capacities.

10. We, however, follow the sequence and order of the Scriptures; we assess the work by contemplation of its author; and we ask what was said, who said it, and to whom he said it. “Let there be,” he says, “a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between the waters.” I hear that, by command, a firmament is made to divide water, so that the upper water might be distinguished from the lower. What could be clearer? He who ordered the water to be divided by the firmament inserted between and in the middle provided the means by which it could remain divided and distinct. God’s word is the power of nature [Note: [Col. 0149D] The old Corbie manuscript reads “the enduringness of substance.” The remaining manuscripts and editions read “the substance of enduringness.”] and the substance of endurance, for as long as he who established it wills it to remain; as it is written: “He established them for age upon age; he set a commandment, and it shall not pass away” (Ps. 148:6). And so that you may know that he said this of these waters which you deny can be in the higher regions of heaven, hear what comes before: “Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (ibid. 4–5). Does he not speak as if in opposition to you: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. He established them for age upon age; he set a commandment, and it shall not pass away” (ibid. 5)? Or does he not seem to you a sufficient author to give a law to his own work? It is God who speaks: venerable in nature, inestimable in greatness, boundless in rewards, incomprehensible [Col. 0149C] in works. Who could easily search out the height of his wisdom? He speaks to the Son—that is, he speaks to his arm, to his power, to his wisdom, to his justice. And the Son acts as mighty; he acts as the power of God, as the wisdom of God, as divine justice. When you hear these things, why do you wonder that a mass of water could be suspended above the firmament of heaven by the operation of such majesty?

11. Infer this from other things, from what human eyes have seen: consider how, at the crossing of the Jews, the water divided itself, if you seek an explanation. It is not nature’s custom for water to be separated from water and for mingled waters in the deep to be separated by earth set between them. [Note: [Col. 0149D] Three manuscripts: “amid the water”; the Roman edition: “without water in between.”] For the waves froze and, taking the appearance of a firmament, held back their course at an unfamiliar boundary. Could he not have liberated the Hebrew people in another way? But he wished to show you that, through that spectacle, you might judge that those things also which you have not seen are to be believed. The Jordan too, its stream turned back, returns to its source. [Col. 0149D] It is unusual for water to stand fast while flowing; to return upward without any barrier is considered impossible. [Note: [Col. 0149D] Roman edition: “for water to stand while it flows and return upward”; editions of Paris, Erasmus, and Gillius: “for water to stand and thus return upward”; the manuscripts as in our text, except that the better copies in the first hand have “usual,” and in the second hand “unusual.”] But what is impossible for him who gave power to the weak, [Note: [Col. 0149D] Thus the old Corbie, Benedictine, Theodorian, and Carolinian manuscripts. Others and all editions—except Paris 1614, which has “to the weak”—read, “who gave power to whom he willed,” or “gave power to weaknesses.” If the latter word is retained, the sense is not changed. For *weakness* can be used for *a weak person*, as, by metonymy, *old age* for *an old man*, or *sacrilege* for *a sacrilegious person*.] so that the weak person may say: “I can do all things [Note: [Col. 0150D] Corbie and Carolinian: “in God who strengthens me.”] in him who strengthens [Col. 0150A] me” (Phil. 4:13)? Let them at least say how air is compressed into a cloud: whether rain is produced from clouds or gathered in the bosom of clouds. We often see clouds issue from mountains. I ask whether water rises from the earth, or whether the water above the heavens descends in abundant rain. If it rises, it is surely contrary to nature for what is heavier to rise upward and be carried by air, since air is subtler. Or if water is carried away by the rapid motion of the whole sphere, then just as it is carried away by the lowest sphere, so it is poured out by the highest. If, as they wish, it does not cease to be poured out, it certainly does not cease to be carried away, [Note: [Col. 0150D] Thus twelve manuscripts; but the Bigotian, one Victorine, and Gembloux read: “as the axis of heaven is always moving, so the water is always drawn up”; the editions read: “it is always moving, and the water moves, and the water is always drawn up.”] because the axis of heaven is always moving and the water is always drawn up. If it descends, then there remains continually above the heavens that from which it can descend. Further, what prevents them from admitting that water is suspended above the heavens? For by the same argument by which they say that the earth is suspended in the middle and remains motionless, although it is certainly heavier than water, they can say that the water above the heavens is not hurled down by the revolution of that heavenly sphere. For just as the earth is suspended in emptiness, or remains motionless because its weight is balanced on every side, so water too is balanced by weights either heavier than, or equal to, the earth. And therefore the sea does not readily overflow the lands unless it is commanded to go forth.

12. Again, since they themselves say that the sphere of heaven, shining with blazing stars, revolves, did not divine providence necessarily provide that water should abound within and above the sphere of heaven, to temper those fires of the burning axis? Because fire overflows and burns fiercely, water likewise overflowed upon the earth, lest the heat of the rising [Col. 0150C] sun and glittering stars should burn it up, and unfamiliar vapor should harm the tender beginnings of things. How many springs, rivers, and lakes irrigate the earth because a certain inward fire causes it to steam! For whence would trees shoot forth, grain or crops break out, or what has sprung up be ripened, unless an inner fire also gave them life? That fire is often struck from stones and frequently leaps from wood itself as it is cut. Therefore, just as the creation of fire is necessary for ordered and arranged things to endure, and the mildness of heaven tempers the harshness of the waters, so the abundance of waters is not superfluous, lest one should consume the other. For unless there is a fitting measure of each, just as fire dries up water, so water extinguishes fire. Therefore he weighed all things by weight and measure; for even the drops of rain are numbered by him, as we read in the book of Job (Job 28:25). Knowing how easily things might fail or the universe be dissolved if one prevailed over the other, he so tempered the loss of both that [Col. 0151A] fire should not burn up too much, nor water overflow; rather, there should be a moderate diminution of each, which would remove the excess and preserve what was necessary.

Thus, although immense streams of the greatest rivers burst forth from the earth—the Nile flooding Egypt in its outpoured river; the Danube, running from western regions and dividing barbarian and Roman peoples until it is itself swallowed by the Black Sea; the Rhine, directing its course from the Alpine ridge to the depths of Ocean, a wall of the Roman empire memorable against savage nations; the Po, a reliable carrier of seaborne supplies for Italian resources; the Rhône, driven by swift course and cutting through the straits of the Tyrrhenian Sea, where navigators are said to face no small danger while sea-waves and river currents contend with one another; likewise, from [Col. 0151B] the northern region, the Phasis, flowing from the Caucasian mountains and plunging with many others into the Euxine Sea [Note: [Col. 0151D] Two Vatican manuscripts: *Tanais*; Bigotian: *Eusis*; one Victorine, Gembloux, Cîteaux, and one Corbie: *Euxis* . . .; seven manuscripts: “plunges”; the remainder and all editions: “plunging.”]—it would take too long to pursue the names of individual rivers that either flow into our sea or empty into Ocean. Yet, despite such abundance of waters, the earth in southern regions is often scorched by heat and, dissolved by the burning temperature, crumbles into dust, after consuming the labor of the pitiable farmer; so that, with wells dried up and riverbeds dry, even the life-giving aid of drinking water frequently fails. There will indeed be a time when he says to the deep, “Be desolate, and I will dry up all your rivers” (Isa. 44:27), as he announced through Isaiah would happen. But even before that day comes, [Note: [Col. 0152D] Old edition and several manuscripts: “governed by divine decision.”] governed by divine decision, the very nature of the elements contends with itself not a little. Thus this world is often shaken by floods [Col. 0151C] or afflicted by excessive heat and dryness.

13. Therefore do not suppose the multitude of waters incredible; look instead to the force of heat, and you will not be unbelieving. Fire absorbs much. This ought to be evident to us from the fact that physicians attach to the body certain vessels narrow at the mouth, broader above and hollow within, with the slight light of a lamp enclosed in them: how that heat draws all moisture into itself. Who, then, could doubt that the fiery aether, boiling with great heat, would set fire to and consume everything unless it were restrained by some law of its Creator, so that neither rivers, lakes, nor the seas themselves could extinguish its force? And therefore water descending from above with a certain force often breaks forth into such great rains [Col. 0151D] that rivers and lakes are suddenly filled and even the seas overflow. Thus we frequently see the sun moist and dripping with dew. In this it gives clear evidence that it has taken water as nourishment to moderate itself.

14. So great is their zeal for attacking truth that they deny the sun itself to have a hot nature because it is white, not reddish or fiery-looking. Thus they say it is not fiery by nature; whatever heat it has, they maintain, results from the excessive movement of its revolution. They think this must be said [Col. 0152A] in order that it may seem to consume no moisture, since it does not possess a natural heat by which moisture is diminished or often drained away. But they achieve nothing by composing such arguments, because it makes no difference whether someone has heat from nature, from an affection, or from some cause: all fire consumes moisture or material of this kind, which flame is accustomed to burn. For whether fire is struck from pieces of wood not at all half-burned but rubbed against one another, and caught in leaves, it nevertheless kindles a flame just as if you lit a torch from fire; or whether you light one light from the flame of another, the appearance and nature of the light are the same, even if a non-natural fire kindled it or an incidental cause generated it. At least let them consider the heat of the sun from this: God appointed for its course different places and times, lest, if it remained always in the same places, it should burn them up by daily heat. They themselves say that the sea has salt and bitter water because that which flows into its straits from rivers is consumed by heat, and that as much is consumed by daily vapor as is brought in each day from the various courses of rivers. This, they declare, happens through a certain sorting action of the sun, which draws to itself what is pure and light but leaves what is heavy and earthy. Consequently, that salt and dry residue remains, devoid of usefulness and the pleasantness of drinking.

## CHAPTER IV.

“Heaven” is a common name, but “firmament” a particular one; and the derivation of each term. From this, several senses of “heavens”; finally, a moral interpretation of the heavens and firmament, and of the waters.

[Col. 0152C]

15. But let us return to the subject: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water.” As I have already said, do not be troubled because above he said “heaven,” while here he says “firmament.” David too says: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18:1); that is, when the work of the world is seen, it praises its own author. For his invisible majesty is recognized through the things that are seen. It seems to me that “heavens” is a common name, since Scripture testifies that there are many heavens, but “firmament” is a particular name. For here too it is written: “And God called the firmament heaven” (Gen. 1:8), so that above he seems to have said generally that heaven was made in the beginning, comprehending the whole fabric of the heavenly creation; while here he denotes the particular solidity of this outward firmament, called the firmament of heaven, as we read in the prophetic hymn: “Blessed are you in the firmament of heaven” (Dan. 3:36). For heaven, called *ouranos* (οὐρανός) in Greek, is called *caelatum* in Latin because it bears the impressed lights of the stars like engraved marks; just as we call silver embossed with raised figures *caelatum*. But *ouranos* [Note: [Col. 0152D] The Erasmus edition and those following: ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁρᾷν ἄνω, “from seeing above” (the Roman edition adds, or ὁρᾶσθαι, “because it is seen,” τὴν ὅλην ὁρᾷν ἄνωθεν γῆν, “to see the whole earth from above”). The manuscripts read ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁρᾷσθαι, “it is called because it is seen.” Five excellent manuscripts: “because it is divided.” But the Greek words which follow are written so confusedly that none of those consulted could read them. We suspect, however, that they indicate something about the division of heaven marked by the horizon-circle.] is called from *horasthai* (ὁρᾷσθαι), “to be seen” . . . . . . Therefore [Col. 0153A] it is called *ouranos* in relation to the earth, which is darker, because it is bright, as though visible. Hence I think the following is also said: [Note: [Col. 0153D] Some Paris editions: “The birds of heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven,” and “birds flying over the earth by the firmament of heaven.” The Septuagint: ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς κατὰ τὸ στερέωμα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, “upon the earth according to the firmament of heaven.” Here, however, that angels are meant is clearly shown from Ambrose, *On the Interpellation*, book I, chapter 9. Blessed Job also uses the same metaphor at Job 28:2; see the interlinear gloss on this passage.] “The birds of heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Gen. 1:20). And: “birds around the firmament of heaven,” because the powers which are in that visible place behold all these things and hold them subject to their sight.

16. Finally, heaven was said to be shut in the time of Elijah, when faithlessness reigned in Ahab and Jezebel and the people served royal sacrilege, because no one raised his eyes to heaven, no one revered its author, but they worshiped wood and stones. From what do we infer this? Because God also said among the curses of the people Israel: “The heaven above your head shall be bronze, and your earth iron” (Lev. 26:19), when [Col. 0153B] the Jewish people, paying the price of faithlessness, are punished by the intemperance of heaven and the barrenness of earth; for from heaven comes the cause of fertility. Thus Moses bestowed blessings on the tribe of Joseph from the bounds of heaven and the dew of the deep springs beneath, [Note: [Col. 0154D] Thus the more numerous and better manuscripts; but some later manuscripts and editions: “from the bounds of heaven, and from dew, and from deeps of springs coming from below.” Vulgate: “from the fruits of heaven and from dew and from the deep lying below.” Septuagint: ἀπὸ ὡρῶν οὐρανοῦ, καὶ δρόσου, καὶ ἀπὸ ἀβύσσων πηγῶν κάτωθεν, “from the seasons of heaven, and dew, and from deeps of springs beneath.”] and from the season determined by the sun’s course, and from the suitable months, and from the summit of mountains and everlasting hills, because the earth’s fertility is nourished by heavenly moderation. Heaven is therefore iron when it sweats out no moisture, when [Note: [Col. 0154D] Roman edition: “no rain bursts forth from clouds.”] rain breaks from no clouds. Heaven is also iron when the air is dim, dense, and clouded with an iron-gray color; when the earth is gripped by bitter cold, moisture seems then to hang suspended over our heads and threaten from moment to moment. Often too the waters, frozen by icy blasts of wind, are solidified into snow, and, when the air breaks, snow is poured forth. For this firmament cannot exist without some [Note: [Col. 0154D] After the words “break with a crash,” the editions add “or be pierced.” And in section 17, after “the glory of God,” they add “and the works of his hands.” Both additions are absent from the manuscripts.] breaking crash. Therefore it is called a firmament, because it is not weak or slack. Hence Scripture says of thunder, when a spirit enclosed within the bosom of clouds violently strikes in its effort to burst forth and resounds with a great noise: “Establishing the thunders” (Amos 4:13). Thus *firmament* is named from firmness, or because it has been made firm by divine power, as Scripture teaches us when it says: “Praise him in the firmament of his power” (Ps. 150:1).

17. Nor should it escape notice that some have referred the “heavens of heavens” to the intelligible powers, and the firmament to the operative powers. Thus the heavens praise, or declare the glory of God, while the firmament announces it; yet they do so not as spiritual beings, [Col. 0153D] but as works of the world, as we said above. Others likewise have interpreted the waters above the heavens as purifying powers. We receive these interpretations as ornaments of discourse; nevertheless, it does not seem foreign or absurd to us to understand real waters, for the reason we have stated. For dew, frost, cold, and heat, according to the prophetic hymn, bless the Lord; the earth also blesses him (Dan. III, 64 ff.). We refer these not to intelligible natures, but to reality. Dragons also praise the Lord (Ps. CXLVIII, 7), because their nature and appearance, when seen, display no small degree either of beauty or of rational design.

## CHAPTER V

The complete union of Father and Son in their works. In God, seeing is identical with approving. To praise a work before its parts are complete belongs properly to God.

[Col. 0154B] 18. “And God saw that it was good” (Gen. I, 3). The Son does what the Father wills; the Father praises what the Son does. Nothing of a degenerate nature is found in him whose work does not depart from the Father’s will. Certainly, he saw not by directing bodily eyes, but determined that it accorded with the fullness of grace, so that his judgment might become known to me; for we are accustomed even to dispute about matters that are divine. And what wonder if those who raise questions about the generation of the very Worker himself can criticize the work? They summon him himself to judgment; they endeavor to assert that he is unequal and degenerate. Therefore you read: “And God said,” and “God made.” Father and Son are honored by the same name of majesty. “And God saw that it was good.” He spoke as one knowing all that the Father willed; and he saw as one holding in knowledge all that the Son did, and as a partner in the operation that accomplished it.

19. “He saw that it was good.” Certainly, he did not learn what he had not known, but approved what pleased him. The work did not please him as something unknown; for neither was the Father unknown who was well pleased in the Son, as it is written: “This is my beloved Son, 32 in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17). Now the Son always knows the will of the Father, and the Father knows that of the Son; the Son always hears the Father, and the Father the Son, through unity of nature, will, and substance. Finally, in his Gospel the Son testifies to this, saying to the Father: “I knew that you always hear me” (John XI, 42). For the Son is the image of the invisible God. As image, he expresses all things of the Father; as the radiance of glory, he illumines and makes all things manifest to us. The Son sees the Father’s work, just as the Father sees the Son’s; as the Lord himself declared: “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing” (John V, [Col. 0155A] 19). Therefore he sees the Father acting, and sees through the mystery of the invisible nature; and likewise he hears. Finally, he says: “As I hear, I judge; and my judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me” (John VIII, 16).

20. This is mystical; that is moral. “He saw,” that is, “he approved.” What God has approved, do not call blameworthy; for you remember that it is written to you: “What God has cleansed, do not call common” (Acts X, 15). Therefore let no one blaspheme the good of God.

> [Note: Codex Bigotianus and Gemblacensis: “Let no one blaspheme the good name of God.” Four other witnesses: “… do not blaspheme.”]

If the firmament is good, how much more good is its Creator—even though the Arians refuse and the Eunomians protest that the fruit is inferior to its degenerate root.

21. “God saw,” he says, “that it was good.” Craftsmen ordinarily make individual things first and afterwards join them together by skillful fitting. Thus those who carve human faces or bodies from marble, fashion them in bronze, or model them in wax do not yet know how the separate limbs may fit together, or what grace the future joining will bring; and therefore they either do not dare to praise, or praise only in part. But God, as the appraiser of the whole, foreseeing what is to come, praises as already complete what is still at the beginning of the first work, anticipating the end of the work by knowledge. Nor is it surprising that he, with whom the perfection of things lies not in the completion of the work but in the predestination of his will, praises each thing as suited to what is to follow; he praises the fullness composed from the beauty of the individual parts. For this is true beauty: that each individual member should possess what is fitting, and likewise the whole; so that grace in each part, and the fullness of harmonious form in all, may be praised.

22. But let the second day now also be brought to a close for us, lest, while we establish the work of the firmament, we weary weaker hearers by the length of our speaking; while the discourse is prolonged into the night—which, still lacking the light of moon and stars, since the lights of heaven have not yet been created, [Col. 0156B] can bring the darkness of heaven upon those returning home.

> [Note: Four manuscripts: “which may remove the darkness of heaven for those returning home.”]

At the same time, let bodies be cared for with food and drink, lest, while souls feast, the frailty of the flesh complain also of its nightly fast.

# BOOK THREE: ON THE WORK OF THE THIRD DAY

[Col. 0155]

## CHAPTER I (Discourse IV)

Since the waters obey the divine command, it is shameful for human beings not to obey the same command. In the gathering of the waters, the figure of the Church is expressed. What splendid spectacle this same Church displays, and how it is founded upon rivers.

[Col. 0155C]

1. Let the third day be born for us today in discourse, as it rose in the reading. A splendid day, which freed the earth from shipwreck, when God said: “Let the water which is under heaven be gathered into one gathering” (Gen. I, 9). It is fitting to begin with this preface. “Let the water be gathered” was said, and it was gathered; yet people are often told, “Let the people be gathered,” and they are not gathered. It is no small shame that insensible elements obey the command of God, while human beings do not obey, though they have received sense from their very Author. And perhaps this shame has caused more of you to assemble today, lest on the day when water was gathered into one gathering, the people should appear not to have assembled in the Church of the Lord.

2. Nor do we have only this example of obedient water; for elsewhere it is written: “The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you and were afraid” (Ps. LXXVI, 17). Nor is it implausible that this is said of waters, when elsewhere the same prophet says: “The sea saw and fled; Jordan turned back” (Ps. CXIII, 3). Who does not know that this truly happened—that, for the passage of the Hebrews, the sea fled when its wave divided? The people crossed with dusty footprints, believing that the sea had vanished and the waves had fled. Finally, [Col. 0156B] the Egyptian believed this and entered; but the wave that had fled returned upon him. Water therefore knows how to gather, [Col. 0156C] to fear, and to flee, when God commands. Let us imitate this water, and let us acknowledge one gathering of the Lord, one Church.

3. Water was once gathered here from every valley, every marsh, and every lake. A valley is heresy; a valley is paganism, because God is the God of mountains, not of valleys. Thus, in the Church there is rejoicing; in heresy and paganism, weeping and sorrow. Hence he says: “He appointed [a place] in the valley of weeping” (Ps. LXXXIII, 6–7). From every valley, therefore, the catholic people has been gathered. There are now no many gatherings, but one gathering, one Church. Here too it was said: “Let water be gathered from every valley”; and a spiritual gathering came into being, and one people was made. The Church has been filled from heretics and pagans. The theater is a valley; the circus is a valley, [Col. 0156D] where the deceitful horse runs to victory, where contest is cheap and degrading, where there is the ugly deformity of disputes. From those, therefore, who had been accustomed to cling to the circus, the faith of the Church has grown and the daily assembly increases.

4. A marsh is luxury; a marsh is intemperance; a marsh is lack of self-control. In it are the wallowings of lusts, the noises of beasts, the lurking places of passions; there those who fall in are submerged and do not emerge; there the footprints of feet slip, and each person’s steps drift. There coots, while washing themselves, defile themselves; above are the mournful cries of doves; there the sluggish tortoise clings in the muddy pool; finally, the boar is in the marsh, the deer at the springs. From every marsh, therefore, where they sang their old complaint like frogs, [Col. 0157A] faith has been gathered, purity of mind has been gathered, and simplicity of soul.

5. Water has been gathered from every lake and every pit, so that no one may dig a pit for his brother into which he himself may fall; but let all love one another, let all cherish one another, and let diverse members support one another as one body. Let not deadly songs and theatrical entertainments soften the mind for loves, but let the harmony of the Church, the people’s consonant voice in praise of God, and a devout life delight them.

> [Note: Several manuscripts: “the deadly songs of theatrical *cromatum*.” Not badly. For *chroma*, or rather *cruma*, is the sound of musical instruments, from Greek κρούειν, “to strike.” A large number of other witnesses: “… and of theatrical *acromata*.” Better: “… and theatrical *acroamata*.” The term is from Greek ἀκροᾶσθαι, “to hear,” and is sometimes used for recitation and song. Yet it may be that the word *acromata* was in popular use in Ambrose’s time.]
