Let it not be a pleasure for them to look upon purple tapestries or costly curtains, but upon this most beautiful structure of the world: this union of elements distinct from one another; heaven spread out like a vault to cover those dwelling in this world; earth given for cultivation; the extended air; the enclosed seas; this people, the instrument of divine operation, in whom the melody of the divine oracle resounds and the Spirit of God works within; this temple, the sanctuary of the Trinity, the dwelling place of holiness—the holy Church, in which the heavenly curtains shine, of which it is said: “Enlarge the place of your tents and of your curtains; stretch them out, spare not; make your cords longer and strengthen your stakes. Extend still to the right and left, and your seed shall possess the nations as an inheritance and shall inhabit deserted cities” (Isa. LIV, 2–3). The Church therefore has curtains by which it raises up a good life, covers sins, and overshadows guilt.

> [Note: Thus all manuscripts except Reginensis, which, like all editions, reads: “and may a devout life delight them.”]

6. This is the Church which is founded upon the seas and prepared upon the rivers. For it has been established [Col. 0157C] and prepared upon you, who, like rivers, flow into it from the pure fountain of the world, concerning whom it was said: “The rivers lifted up, O Lord, the rivers lifted up their voice, above the sound of many waters” (Ps. XCII, 3).

> [Note: The Roman edition and a few manuscripts of little authority read, “you flow into it from a fountain on every side”; other manuscripts and the older editions, “from the pure fountain,” that is, purified from the errors of heresy and paganism.]

And he added: “Wonderful are the surges of the sea; wonderful on high is the Lord” (ibid. 4). Good rivers indeed: for you have drawn from that perennial and full fountain from which you flowed, he who says to you: “He who believes in me, as Scripture says, from his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John VII, 38).

> [Note: Thus not a few manuscripts. Some others: “from whom you flow, who …”; or, with the Roman edition: “from whom flows he who …” Several also, and the older editions: “from whom you flow, which you flow, who …”]

Now he said this concerning the Spirit, whom those who were to believe in him were beginning to receive. But now, like the streams of the good Jordan, return with me to the source.

## CHAPTER II

The earth, formerly invisible because it was covered with waters, appeared when those waters flowed together into one place. By divine power waters were endowed first with stability and afterwards with fluidity, as is shown by various examples. How marvelous that all waters are contained in one place, and that God was able to set their bounds.

[Col. 0157D]

[Col. 0158A] 7. “Let the water,” he says, “which is under heaven be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear.” And it was so. Perhaps someone has given too little credence to our earlier discourses, in which we argued that the earth was invisible because, being covered over by waters, it could not be seen by bodily eyes. For the prophet referred this to himself—that is, to our condition—not to the nature of divine majesty, which surely sees all things. But so that you may recognize that we undertook this labor of exposition not to prove our own ingenuity, but for your instruction, we cite the sequence of the reading as supporting us; it plainly proves that, after the gathering of the water which was upon the earth and after its channeling into the seas, the dry land appeared.

> [Note: Some Paris editions: “the sequence of the reading supports us, which …” All others and many manuscripts: “we testify, with the sequence of the reading supporting us, which …” The Roman edition: “… testifies the things which …” The remaining manuscripts, superior in authority and no fewer in number, support the reading printed in the text.]

Let those, then, who use dialectical disputations to stir up controversies cease saying to us: “How could the earth be invisible, when every body naturally possesses both form and color, and every color is subject to sight?” The voice of God cries: “Let the water be gathered, and let the dry land appear.” And again Scripture says: “The water was gathered into one gathering, and the dry land appeared.” What need was there to repeat this unless the prophet judged that objections must be met? Does he not seem to say: “I did not call it invisible according to its nature, but according to the flooding of the waters”? Finally, he added that, once its covering was removed, the dry land appeared, which had not been seen before.

> [Note: All editions with a few manuscripts read: “Let those, therefore, who use dialectical … say.”]

[Col. 0158C] 8. Again they raise other questions, saying: “If water was in different gatherings, how, if those gatherings were in higher places, did the water not flow down into the place [Col. 0158D] to which it was channelled after the Lord’s command? For the nature of water is spontaneously to flow downwards. But if those gatherings were in lower places, how did the water rise to higher places against its nature? Therefore, either its natural course had no need of a command, or it could not proceed against nature by command.”

> [Note: Amerbach and Erasmus, with some manuscripts: “they raise other questions.”]

> [Note: All editions and several manuscripts: “to which it was channelled by the Lord’s command afterwards.”]

> [Note: All editions and certain manuscripts: “or according to natural courses.”]

I shall readily answer this question if they first answer me whether, before the Lord’s command, the nature of this water was to slide and flow. It does not possess this as a habit shared with the other elements, but as something special and proper—not from some fixed order, but rather from the will and operation of the supreme God. They heed what God has commanded. [Col. 0159A] The voice of God is productive of nature.

> [Note: All older editions, and some Paris editions with two or three manuscripts: “the voice of God is the efficient nature.” Several manuscripts of excellent quality: “the voice of God is the image of nature.” Yet others and some editions are preferable: the saint meant to express Basil’s phrase, φύσεώς ἐστι ποιητική, “it is productive of nature.”]

The effect of the operation fulfilled that voice. Water began to flow and to converge into one gathering; previously it had been spread over the lands and adhered in very many receptacles. I have not read of its former course; I have not learned of its former movement; neither my eye saw it nor my ear heard it. Water stood in various places; at God’s voice it was moved. Does it not seem that God’s voice made this its nature? Creation followed the command and adopted its practice from the law. For the law of the first constitution left a pattern for the future. Thus he made day and night once; from that time their lasting succession and continual renewal remain. Water also was commanded to run into one gathering; from that time it runs: springs flow into rivers, rivers run into straits, lakes are channelled into seas; [Col. 0159B] water itself goes before, presses on, and follows itself. There is one course, one body. And although its depth varies, the uniform level of its surface is undivided. Hence, I think, it is called *aequor* (“level water”), because its surface is level.

9. I have answered according to their supposition; now let them answer me whether they have never seen springs well up from lower places, or water rise from pavement. Who compels it? From where does it burst forth? How does it not fail? How is it that the lowest margins of the ground pour forth water?

> [Note: Some manuscripts: “that the lowest and more solid [places] …”; others and all editions: “that the lowest solid [places] …” Corbeiensis, Carnotensis, Benedictinus, and Theodorianus: “that the lowest margins of the ground …” Germaniensis: “that the lowest [parts] of the ground …”]

These things occur according to the hidden mysteries of nature. Besides, who does not know that water, often descending with rapid force into low places, rises again to higher places and is lifted to a mountain ridge? Often too, when channelled by the hand of an artisan, it rises again as far as it has descended. Therefore, if it is carried by its own force, or by an artisan’s skill is led and raised contrary to its nature, do you wonder that through the operation of a divine command something was added to the use of its nature which had not been in its use before? Let them now tell me how God “gathered the waters of the sea as in a skin-bottle” (Ps. XXXII, 7), as it is written; how he brought water out of the rock. He who could bring water from a rock where there was none could not bring forth water that already existed? “He struck the rock, and waters flowed,” David cries (Ps. LXXVII, 20), “and torrents overflowed.” And elsewhere: “Waters shall stand above the mountains” (Ps. CIII, 6). You have in the Gospel (Matt. VIII, 24 ff.) that, when there was a violent storm and great disturbance at sea, so that the apostles feared the danger of shipwreck, they awakened the Lord Jesus, sleeping in the stern; [Col. 0159D] rising, he commanded the wind and sea, the storm was calmed, and tranquility restored. He who could calm the whole sea by command could not move the waters by command? Yet in the flood we read that the fountains of the abyss burst forth (Gen. VII, 11), and that afterward he sent a spirit and dried the water (Gen. VIII, 1). [Col. 0160A] If they refuse to admit that nature obeyed and that the use of the element was altered by God’s command, let them at least concede that, when a wind was sent, waters could run—as we see every day at sea, where waters run in the direction from which the wind has blown. If, in Moses’ time, the sea was dried by the rising of a strong south wind, could not the gathering of waters likewise be dried and the water flow into the sea—the water which later was divided from the bottom upward?

> [Note: Editions with a few manuscripts: “divided in the depths”; better, the remaining manuscripts: “from the depths,” that is, from bottom to top.]

But let them learn that nature can be changed, when the rock poured out waters and iron floated upon water—a result which Elisha deserved to obtain by prayer, not by command. If, therefore, Elisha raised iron contrary to nature, could Christ not move the waters? But he did move them, he who could say, “Lazarus, come forth” (John XI, 23), and raised the dead; for God does what he commands. [Col. 0160B] Therefore receive the saying in the same sense: “Let the water be gathered,” and it was gathered. By saying “Let it be gathered,” however, he not only moved it from its place, but also set it in a place, so that it would not flow past but remain.

10. This, therefore, is the greater miracle: how all gatherings flowed into one gathering, and the one gathering was not filled. For Scripture itself counts this among marvels, saying: “All rivers run into the sea, and the sea is not filled” (Eccl. I, 7). Both things, therefore, are by God’s command: that water should flow, and that it should not overflow. The seas are enclosed within boundaries imposed upon them, lest, flooding the lands, they inundate everything and, leaving the cultivation of fields abandoned, hinder the gift of earthly fertility. Let them therefore recognize that this is from a divine command and a heavenly operation. For the Lord says through the cloud to Job, among other things concerning the enclosure of the sea: “I set bounds for it, placing bars and doors. And I said to it: ‘Thus far shall you come, and no farther; within yourself your waves shall be broken’” (Job XXXVIII, 10). Do we not ourselves see the sea often so wave-tossed that its waves rise on high like a steep mountain of water, yet, when it has dashed its force against the shore, it is dissolved into foam, driven back by barriers, as it were, of lowly sand, according to what is written: “Will you not fear me, says the Lord, who set sand as a boundary for the sea?” (Jer. V, 22). Thus the untimely force of the sea is held back by the dust of the feeblest and cheapest sand, and, as if by reins, is recalled to the limit prescribed for it by the decree of heaven; the motion of the violent sea breaks upon itself [Col. 0160D] and divides into its returning inlets.

> [Note: All editions: “the force of the sea in a storm is held back by the dust of cheap sand.” All manuscripts: “of cheap *sablon* or *sabulon* …” Carnotensis, Corbeiensis, Benedictinus, Theodorianus, Germaniensis, and Reginensis: “untimely”; others as in the editions, “in a storm.”]

> [Note: Dionysian manuscript: “and, returning into its own inlets, is divided.”]

11. Besides, unless the power of the heavenly ordinance restrained it, what would prevent the Red Sea from being mingled with the Egyptian sea across the plains of Egypt, which are said especially to lie low in flatter valleys? Finally, those who wished to connect and pour these two seas into one another teach this. The Egyptian Sesostris, who lived earlier, and Darius the Mede, who in view of his greater power wished to bring to completion what had previously been attempted by a native, undertook it. This indicates that the Indian Sea, into which the Red Sea enters, is higher than the Egyptian waters that wash the lower region. And perhaps each king abandoned his undertaking because the sea, rushing from higher to lower levels, would spread itself too widely.

## CHAPTER III

The gathering of waters is one and continuous, though its names differ according to the diversity of regions. How God prepared a place for waters spread over the whole world. Likewise, lakes and pools are included under the one gathering.

[Col. 0161B] 12. I now ask: when he said, “Let water be gathered into one gathering,” how could one gathering receive water scattered through lakes, marshes, pools, and waters spread over valleys, plains, and every flatter place, flowing through springs and rivers? Or how can there be one gathering, when even today there are different seas? For we call the Ocean a sea, and also the Tyrrhenian, Adriatic, Indian, Egyptian, Pontic, Propontis, Hellespont, Euxine, Aegean, Ionian, and Atlantic seas. Most people also call the Cretan, Northern, and Caspian waters seas. Let us therefore consider the words of Scripture, weighed on a balanced scale.

> [Note: Thus the older editions and nearly all manuscripts, and likewise below in §13. The Roman edition, with one or two manuscripts: “Let the water be gathered,” as at the beginning of Chapter II and below in Chapter IV; in those passages all manuscripts and editions agree.]

> [Note: Roman edition: “Most also call the Baltic, Northern, and Caspian [waters] seas.”]

13. “Let water be gathered,” he says, “into one gathering.” There is one unbroken and continuous gathering of waters, but different bays of the sea, as one of the secular writers says (Plato, *Timaeus*). For the Pontus is a very broad gulf of our sea; and rightly there are different names in different places, because names have attached themselves to waters from the names of the regions. But there is one gathering of waters because the continuous wave extends from the Indian Sea to the coast of Gades, and, surrounding the world at its outermost edge, encloses the inhabited world in Ocean; inwardly too, the Tyrrhenian mingles with the Adriatic, and the other seas with the Adriatic—distinguished by names, not by waves.

> [Note: All editions and most manuscripts read: “the harbor of our sea …” Corbeiensis and five other excellent witnesses read “the expanse.” Perhaps likewise one may say “the expanse of the sea,” as “soil of the earth” and similar expressions are used.]

> [Note: Roman edition: “continuous from the Pontic Sea …”]

> [Note: Some manuscripts and the Amerbach and Erasmus editions: “surrounding the world at its outermost limit”; some: “the world”; several and the Roman edition: “surrounding the world at the outermost limit”; others and the Gillot edition as printed in the text. At the same point Vict., Colb., and Big. read: “Ocean encloses [it].”]

Hence you fittingly read that “God called the gatherings of waters seas” (Gen. I, 10). Thus there is one general gathering, called “sea,” and many gatherings called “seas” according to regions. [Col. 0161D] For just as there are many lands, called Africa, Spain, Thrace, Macedonia, Syria, Egypt, Gaul, [Col. 0162A] and Italy after the names of their regions, while the earth is one; so many waters are called seas after the names of places, while the sea is one, as the prophet says: “Yours are the heavens, and yours is the earth; you founded the world and its fullness. You created the north and the sea” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 12). And to Job the Lord himself says: “I shut up the sea with doors” (Job XXXVIII, 8).

14. Now that we have spoken of the one gathering, this question arises: when waters had been spread almost over and throughout the whole earth—through the low places of fields, the hollows of mountains, and the flatness of plains—how could a single expanse of sea receive all those waters and empty the lands which had previously stood as pools beneath a flood spread throughout the universe? [Col. 0162B] For if everything was covered in this way—for he would not have said, “the earth appeared,” unless he wished to show it uncovered in every place—then, if the flood in Noah’s time hid even the mountains, when a separation of waters above the heavens and below the firmament had already occurred, how much less can it be doubted that the peaks of mountains also lay hidden beneath that flooding? Where then was all that excess of water channelled? What receptacles could absorb it, so continuous and connected? On this subject much could be said.

> [Note: Thus the older editions and most manuscripts. Some read: “with one gathering spread out.” Reginensis: “the scattered [waters], one gathering.” This is not a reading to be despised. But the Roman edition patches the whole passage as follows: “when low-lying regions had been spread almost throughout the whole earth …”]

15. First, because the Creator of all things could also spread out the spaces of the lands themselves—a position which some before us, affirming it, advanced as their own opinion. I do not pass over what he could have done; what he did, which I have not openly learned on the authority of Scripture, I pass over as a secret, lest perhaps they seek further questions for themselves from this also. Yet according to the Scriptures I affirm that he could spread out low places and open plains, as he himself says: “I will go before you and make mountains level” (Isa. XLV, 2). He could also have made deeper the very places in which the force of the waters had settled, by so great a movement of waves and so powerful a surge of the agitated element, which daily is accustomed to churn the depths of the sea and turn up sands from the deep. Who, moreover, does not know how far that great sea extends—untried by navigators and unattempted by sailors—which encloses Britain in its roaring waters and stretches into regions farther still, inaccessible even to fables? Who, moreover, would not infer how much sea has been added and poured into Lake Lucrinus and Lake Avernus in Italy, also into Tiberias in Palestine, [Col. 0162D] and into the lake beside which the Arabian deserts extend between Palestine and Egypt, into the various harbors of Augustus [Col. 0163A] and Trajan, and into other places throughout the world?

> [Note: All editions read, “Who, moreover, would infer.” But in all manuscripts the negation is present.]

> [Note: Codices Benedictinus and Coenobii: “they advanced their own opinions.” Vaticanus and one Colbertinus: “his own [opinion],” etc. Dionysianus adds: “I do not know what he could have done; I do not pass over …”]

16. But there are also lakes and pools not joined together and not mingled by waves, such as Lake Larius, Lake Benacus, Lake Albanus, and many others. How, then, is there one gathering of waters? But just as it is said that God made two lights—that is, the sun and moon—although there are surely also lights of the stars, so one gathering is spoken of although there are very many. For things which are not compared are not counted together.

## CHAPTER IV

The principal quality of earth is signified when it is called dry land. What are the properties of the elements by which they are mutually joined; this is examined especially in relation to earth.

[Col. 0163B] 17. But, it seems, because we were speaking about the sea, we have overflowed a little. Let us return to the subject and consider what the Lord means when he says: “Let water be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear,” and does not say “earth.” Who would fail to notice how excellently this is put? For earth can be mixed with mud and soaked with water, so that its appearance cannot be seen beneath waters poured over it. But “dry land” refers not only to the genus but also to the specific condition of lands, [Col. 0163D] so that it may be useful, dry, fit, and suitable for cultivation. At the same time, provision was made lest it appear to have been dried more by the sun than by God’s command, since it became dry land before the sun was created. Hence David, distinguishing sea and land, says of the Lord God: “For the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands formed the dry land” (Ps. XCIV, 5). “Dry land” is an expression of nature; “earth” is a simple designation of the thing, which contains its own property. For just as “animal” signifies a genus, in which there is something proper and excellent, while “rational” is proper to a human being, so earth may be spoken of generally whether it is overflowing with waters, or desert, trackless, and waterless. Therefore even that earth which overflows with water possesses the capacity to be dry. For when water is removed, it begins to be dry, as you have written: “He turned rivers into a desert, and springs of water into thirst” (Ps. CVI, 33); that is, he made dry land out of watery land.

18. Earth therefore has its own proper quality, just as each of the elements has its own: air a moist quality, water a cold one, fire a hot one. [Col. 0163D] And this is the principal property of the individual elements, which we ascertain by reason. But if we wish to apprehend them sensibly and bodily, we find them joined and compounded: earth dry and cold; water cold and moist; air hot and moist; fire hot and dry. Thus the elements are blended with one another through these paired qualities. For since earth is dry and cold in quality, it is joined to water through the kinship of coldness, and through water [Col. 0164A] to air, because air is moist. Water, then, seems by two arms, as it were—coldness and moisture—to embrace earth with one and air with the other: earth through coldness, air through moisture. Air also, standing between two elements naturally opposed to each other, namely water and fire, reconciles both to itself, because it is joined to water by moisture and to fire by heat. Fire too, naturally hot and dry, is attached to air by heat, but by dryness is brought into communion and association with earth. Thus by this circuit and a kind of choir the elements come together into one framework of harmony and fellowship. Hence they are called in Greek στοιχεῖα, which in Latin we call *elementa*, because they fit together and sound together.

> [Note: Some better manuscripts: “as if joined and compounded.”]

> [Note: All editions and some manuscripts: “and water to air.” More numerous and better manuscripts, with Basil: “and through water to air.”]

> [Note: Thus all editions and most manuscripts. Some: “through this circuit the elements …” Bigotianus and Gemblacensis: “of the elements … come together into one framework of harmony and fellowship.”]

19. We have gone this far because Scripture [Col. 0164B] says that God called the dry land “earth”; that is, he named by the property of its nature what is its principal characteristic. For dryness is earth’s natural property; this prerogative has been preserved for it. Dryness, therefore, is primary. It is also cold, but secondary things are not set before primary ones. Its moisture, however, it derives through kinship with waters. Thus the former is its own, the latter alien: its own, that it is dry; alien, that it is moist. Therefore the Author of nature retained what he first bestowed, because the one belongs to nature, the other to circumstance. Hence earth’s property had to be defined from its principal characteristics, not from accidental ones, so that our understanding might be instructed according to the prerogative of its quality.

## CHAPTER V

Some think that certain words have been added at this point in Scripture. Praise of the sea from its beauty and manifold usefulness, but especially because it embraces island-dwelling anchorites with its waves and represents the figure of ecclesiastical assemblies; this chapter concludes with the author’s devout little prayer.

[Col. 0164C]

20. And God saw that it was good (Gen. 1:10). We do not pass over the fact that some think these words are found neither in the Hebrew nor in the other translations: “the water was gathered into its collections, the dry land appeared, God called the dry land earth, and he called the collections of waters seas.” Since God had said that it was done thus, they consider the utterance of the Creator sufficient indication of the accomplished work. But since in the case of the other creatures Scripture also contains both the determination of the command and a repeated indication or effect of the work [Col. 0164D], we do not think it absurd that the addition reported here should stand, even if truth or authority is thought to support the other interpreters. For we find that the Seventy have added and joined many things to the Hebrew reading not without purpose.

21. God therefore saw that the sea was good. Although the appearance of this element is beautiful—whether it whitens with rising heaps and whirling crests of waves, while the rocks are wetted with snowy spray [Col. 0165A], or whether, when the surface is rippling beneath gentler breezes and calm serenity, it displays a purplish colour, often cast before the eyes of those looking from afar; and although, when it does not batter the neighbouring shores with violent waves but, as it were, enfolds and greets them in peaceful embraces, its sound is sweet, its roar delightful, its echo pleasing and harmonious—nevertheless, I judge that the beauty of the creature is not to be assessed by the eyes, but that it has been declared fitting and consonant, according to the reason of its operation, by the judgment of its Creator.

22. The sea, then, is good: first, because it necessarily supports the lands with moisture, secretly supplying them through certain veins with no useless sap. The sea is good as the lodging-place of rivers [Col. 0165B], the source of rains, the channel of inundations, the conveyance of goods; through it peoples distant from one another are joined, through it the dangers of wars are removed, through it barbarian fury is shut out. It is aid in necessities, refuge in dangers, charm in pleasures, healthfulness for the body, the joining of those separated, a shortening of travel, an escape for the weary, support for revenues, nourishment against barrenness. From it rain is poured out upon the lands; for water is drawn up from the sea by the rays of the sun, and its subtler part is carried away. Then, the higher it rises, the more it is cooled by the shade of the clouds, and becomes rain, which not only moderates the earth’s dryness but also makes the hungry fields fruitful.

23. Why should I enumerate the islands, which it commonly bedecks like necklaces [Col. 0165C], where those who renounce the enticements of worldly intemperance choose, in the sure purpose of continence, to lie hidden from the world and to avoid the uncertain windings of this life? The sea, then, is the retreat of temperance, the exercise-ground of self-restraint, the seclusion of seriousness, the harbour of safety, the tranquillity of the age, the sobriety of this world; and it is an incentive to devotion for faithful and devout persons, so that chants of psalm-singers may vie with the sound of gently washing waves, and the islands may applaud with the tranquil chorus of waves, may resound with hymns of the saints.  
[Note: Some manuscripts read, “with the tranquil chorus of waves, with hymns”; others, “hymns of saints,” etc. The Roman edition reads: “with the tranquil movement of waves, let the choirs of saints resound with hymns.”]

How can I encompass all the beauty of the sea which the Creator saw? And what more need be said? What else is that harmony of waves but a kind of harmony of the people? Hence the Church is aptly often compared to the sea: at the first throng of people entering, she pours forth waves through all her entrances [Col. 0165D]; then, in the prayer of the whole people, she resounds as though with returning waves, when, with the responsories of the psalms, the singing of men, women, virgins, and little children echoes back like the harmonious roar of waters. And what shall I say of this: that water washes away sin, and the life-giving breath of the Holy Spirit blows upon us?

24. May the Lord grant us that the rivers of our fortunes may run beneath a favourable tree; that we may come to rest in a safe harbour; that we may not know trials of spiritual wickedness heavier than we can bear; that we may be ignorant of shipwrecks of faith; that we may possess deep peace. And if anything should arise to stir for us the heavy waves of this world, may we have the Lord Jesus as our wakeful helmsman, to command with a word, calm the storm, and restore the sea’s tranquillity. To him be honour and glory, praise and everlastingness, from ages past, now and always, unto all ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER VI. (Sermon V)

That the earth was fittingly endowed with its own appearance, consisting in germination and greenness; that God’s word provides the cause of fertility; and that some wrongly attribute this to the sun’s heat.

[Col. 0166B]

25. Once the water had departed, it was fitting that the earth should be given form and grace, so that it might cease to be invisible and unformed. For many say that whatever has no form is also invisible; and therefore they understand the earth to have been invisible, not because it could not be seen by the supreme God or his angels—for human beings had not yet been created, nor even cattle—but because it lacked its own form. The earth’s form is the germination and greenness of the field. Therefore, in order to make it both visible and ordered, God said: “Let the earth bring forth the grass of hay, sowing seed according to its kind, and the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit according to its kind, whose seed is in itself” (Gen. 1:11).  
[Note: The Roman edition and the Septuagint add: “according to its kind and according to its likeness, and the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit according to its kind, whose seed may be in itself.” “According to its likeness” is absent from the Vulgate and the old editions of Ambrose, as also from the manuscripts followed here.]

26. Let us hear words of truth, whose sequence is salvation to those who hear them. That first utterance of God, bestowed upon each creature to bring it forth [Col. 0166C], is a law of nature, remaining with the earth for all time and giving a rule for future succession: how the practice of generation and fruit-bearing should thereafter develop. Thus germination comes first, when things being born are seen to break forth; then, when the shoot has emerged and advanced, it becomes grass; and the grass itself, when it has grown somewhat, becomes hay. How useful, how powerful is this utterance: “Let the earth bring forth the grass of hay.” That is, let the earth itself bring it forth of itself; let it seek no other’s aid and need no one’s service.

27. Many commonly say: “Unless the gentler warmth of the sun has warmed the lands and in some way cherished them with its rays, the earth cannot germinate.” For that reason the nations assign divine honour to the sun: because [Col. 0166D] by the power of its heat it penetrates the earth’s recesses, cherishes scattered seeds, and loosens the veins of trees stiffened by frost. Hear, then, God as though uttering this declaration: “Let the foolish speech of men that is yet to come fall silent; let vain opinion depart. Before the sun’s luminary is made, let the grass be born; let its prerogative be older than the sun’s. Lest human error grow strong, let the earth germinate before it receives the sun’s fostering warmth.” Let all know that the sun is not the author of things that grow. God’s mercy loosens the earth; God’s graciousness causes its fruits to burst forth [Col. 0167A]. How can the sun provide the means of life to things springing up, when they were brought forth by the life-giving power of divine operation before the sun had come for these uses of life? It is younger than the grasses, younger than the hay.

## CHAPTER VII

Why fodder for cattle was created before food for humankind. Green grass is an image of the human condition, whose frailty is expounded in an elegant description. We ought to imitate this grass in bearing fruit; here the Manicheans and Eunomians are reproved.

28. And perhaps someone may wonder that fodder for cattle was created before food for humankind. Here we must first observe the profound counsel of God [Note: The edition, with a few manuscripts, reads “the profound counsel of God.” Most and better manuscripts do not contain *counsel*], namely, that he does not neglect even the smallest things, as Divine Wisdom says in the Gospel: “Look at the birds of heaven: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth more than they?” (Matt. 6:26). Since they are fed by God’s grace, no one should flatter himself on account of his own industry and strength.

Then, because simple nourishment and natural food ought to have been preferred to other foods. This is food of sobriety; the others belong to delight and luxury. This food is common to all living creatures; that other food belongs to few. It is therefore an example of frugality and an instruction in moderation that all should be content with the diet of simple grass, cheap vegetables, or fruit which nature has offered and God’s generosity first bestowed [Col. 0167C]. That is wholesome and useful food: it repels illnesses, removes indigestion, is poured out by the divine gift without the labour of human production—crops without sowing, fruit without seed—so sweet and agreeable that it is a delight and a benefit even to those already full. Indeed, it was given for the first tables and remained for the second.

29. What miracle of this creature should I add, and how should I express the proof of the wisdom that works? For in the appearance of these shoots and the gift of green grass there is an image of human life; an emblem of our nature and condition is beheld, and a mirror shines forth. That grass and the flower of hay are a figure of human flesh, as the good interpreter of divinity expressed through the instrument of his voice when he said: “Cry.” “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is hay, and all human glory is as the flower of hay. The hay has dried up and the flower has fallen; but the word of the Lord remains for ever” (Isa. 40:6 ff.). The human voice is God’s pronouncement. God says, “Cry,” but speaks in Isaiah himself. Isaiah replied, “What shall I cry?” And, as though he had heard what he was to say, he added: “All flesh is hay.”

And truly so: the glory of humankind flourishes in the flesh like hay. What is considered lofty is slight like grass, premature like a flower, perishable like hay. It produces the greenness of life in appearance, not solidity in fruit; it displays the delight of a more cheerful life like a flower, yet is destined to fall in a shorter time, like hay-grass that withers before it is pulled up [Col. 0168A]. For what firmness is there in flesh? What healthfulness can be lasting?

30. Today you see a young man strong, coming into manhood, flourishing in the greenness of his age, with pleasing appearance and lovely complexion; the next day he meets you altered in face and expression. He who the day before seemed to you most splendid in the grace of handsome form appears on another day pitiable, broken down by the weakness of some illness.  
[Note: The old edition and some manuscripts read, “the day before, most elegant in your sight”; Regius, “most praised.” Both are absent from the best manuscripts, some of which read, “the day before, pleasing to you in beauty.” Corbie, corrected by a second hand, reads, “was seen as handsome in the grace of form”; others, “the day before, was seen as more pleasing to you in the beauty of form.”]

Many are broken by toil, worn away by poverty, tormented by indigestion, ruined by wine, weakened by old age; luxury makes some effeminate and sensuality drains their colour. Is it not true that the hay has dried up and the flower fallen?

Another is noble in forefathers and ancestors, honoured with the fillets of his forebears, illustrious in the emblems of ancient lineage, abundant in friends, surrounded by clients and protected on both sides, leading out and bringing home a great household. Suddenly, shaken by the weight of some misfortune that has occurred, he is abandoned by all, deserted by companions, attacked by neighbours. Behold: it is true that human life, like hay, withers before it is pulled up.

There is also one who recently overflowed with abundant resources, whose reputation for generosity flew through everyone’s mouths, distinguished in honours, pre-eminent in offices, exalted on tribunals, raised upon a throne, deemed blessed by the peoples. While he is escorted amid the cries of heralds, a sudden reversal of circumstances drags him into the prison into which he himself had thrown others [Col. 0168C], and among his own accused persons he weeps over the misery of a punishment about to come. How many, the day before, were escorted home by a crowd applauding them and by the enviable pageantry of a numerous and favourable people; yet one night blotted out the splendid glory of that procession, and a sudden pain in the side, pouring out their joys, mingled in the mournful succession of grievous sorrow!  
[Note: All editions read, “the frequent house of a favourable people,” etc.]

Such, then, is human glory, like the flower of hay: even when it is bestowed, it adds nothing to one’s works [Note: Some Paris editions read, “adds no help.” The Dionysian and German manuscripts: “adds nothing to riches …”; Coenobite: “adds nothing to work,” etc.], and no fruit is gained in it; when it is lost, it vanishes, suddenly stripping away the whole stage-setting of the human being, both what overshadowed him from without and what animated him within.

31. Yet would that we imitated this grass of which the Lord said: “Let the earth bring forth the grass of hay, sowing seed according to its kind and according to its likeness” [Col. 0168D]. Let us therefore sow seed according to our kind. What that kind is, hear the speaker who says that we ought to seek the divine, if perhaps we may touch or find it: “Though it is not far from any one of us. For in him we live and are and move; as some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his kindred’” (Acts 17:28). According to this kind, let us sow seed not in the flesh but in the Spirit. For we who wish to attain eternal life must sow not fleshly things but spiritual things [Col. 0169A].

And you know what the likeness is, since you were made in the image and likeness of God. Grass corresponds to its own kind; you do not correspond to yours. A grain of wheat scattered on the earth renders the grace of its own kind, while you degenerate. Crops do not adulterate the purity of their seed; you adulterate purity of soul, vigour of mind, and chastity of body.

32. Do you not acknowledge that you are Christ’s work? He himself formed you with his hands, as we read; yet you, Manichean, claim for yourself another creator.  
[Note: Seven manuscripts read: “and you, Manichean, [claim] an adulterous [creator].” Other manuscripts of better quality, and the editions, read: “and you, Manichean, another,” etc.]

God the Father says to the Son: “Let us make humankind in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26); and you, Photinian, say that Christ did not yet exist at the founding of the world. And you, Eunomian, say that the Son is unlike the Father. But if he is the image, he is surely not unlike: rather, wholly expressing the whole Father, whom the Father marked by the unity of his substance.  
[Note: “Wholly expressing the whole [Father]” is absent from five excellent manuscripts; “the whole” is absent.]

The Father says, “Let us make”; and do you deny that he is a co-worker? What the Father said, the Son did; and do you deny his equality, he in whom the Father was well pleased?

## CHAPTER VIII

On seminal power; on the plainly marvellous manner of germination and fruit-bearing; likewise on the earth’s fertility, the beauty of a field in full growth, and the health-giving properties and remedies of herbs.

33. “Let the earth bring forth the grass of hay according to its kind,” he says. In all things called the earth’s growths, there is first a shoot; when it has raised itself a little, it becomes grass; afterward, hay; then fruit. Some growing things germinate from a root, as trees that are not planted arise from the roots of other trees. In the reed we see how, at its extremity, a sort of node forms on one side, and another reed germinates from it. There is, then, in the root a certain seminal power. Grafts also germinate in their upper parts.  
[Note: The Gill and Roman editions read: “Therefore, some [derive] from seed.”]

Thus, in some cases the succession of propagation is obtained from seed, in others from a root, by a different dispensation. For in every growing thing there is either seed or some seminal power, and this is according to kind, so that what springs from it may germinate like the things sown or those from whose root it arises. From wheat comes wheat; from millet, millet; from the pear-tree comes the pear-tree, bursting forth with a white flower; likewise a chestnut-tree arises from the root of a chestnut-tree [Col. 0169D].

34. “Let the earth bring forth the grass of hay according to its kind,” he says. At once the earth, in labour, poured itself forth into new births, clothed itself in a garment of greenness, assumed the grace of fertility, and, adorned with diverse shoots, received its proper ornaments. We marvel that it germinated so quickly. Yet how much greater are the miracles if you consider each case: how seeds cast into the earth dissolve and, unless they die, bring forth no fruit; but if dissolved through a kind of death of themselves, rise again into richer fruit.

The wheat grain is received by the yielding clod [Note: Five manuscripts of no poor quality read, “the nursing clod.” Better manuscripts and editions read, “the yielding clod,” that is, a dissolvable clod, as Virgil, *Georgics* I: “And the yielding clod loosens itself beneath the west wind.”], and the harrowing keeps it where it was scattered [Note: That is, the breaking up of clods], while the earth cherishes and presses it as in a motherly womb. Then, when that grain has dissolved itself, it puts forth grass: already a pleasing appearance of budding greenness, which immediately reveals its cultivated kind by its likeness, so that at the very beginning of its growth you may recognize what kind of plant it is, and fruit may be apparent in the grass. Gradually it grows into hay; it becomes downy in its stalk and stands erect.

But once the jointed ear has raised itself, certain sheaths are prepared for the future crop, within which the grain is formed, lest its tender beginnings be harmed by cold, scorched by the heat of the sun [Col. 0170B], beaten down by the harshness of winds, or struck by the fierce force of rains. There follow rows of the ear, fashioned with marvellous skill, pleasing in appearance and, for protection, bound tightly among themselves in a kind of natural interlacing, which divine providence has formed. And lest, under the weight of the numerous crop, the stalks’ support should give way, the stalk itself is enclosed in certain sheaths, so that, strengthened twofold, it can bear the abundant crop and not bend to the ground unequal to its burden. Then above the ear itself there is built a rampart of awns, as though it stood in a citadel, lest the ear be harmed by the bites of small birds, stripped of its fruits, or trampled by footsteps.

35. What shall I say of the way in which God’s mercy has provided for human usefulness? The earth returns with increase what it has received [Col. 0170C], multiplied by the accumulation of interest. People often deceive, and even defraud their lender of the principal itself; the earth remains faithful. And if it has not paid on some occasion—perhaps because the severity of cold, excessive drought, or an immense force of rain has opposed it—it compensates in another year for the losses of the preceding year. Thus, even when the yield disappoints the farmer’s hope, the earth commits no fault; and when it smiles upon him, the abundance of a fertile mother pours itself out into births, so that it never inflicts any loss upon its creditor.

36. What a sight is a field in full growth! What fragrance! What sweetness! What delight for farmers! What can we adequately explain if we use our own speech? But we have the testimonies of Scripture, by which we observe that the sweetness of a field is compared to the blessing and grace of the saints. Holy Isaac says: “The smell of my son is like the smell of a full field” (Gen. 27:27). Why then should I describe purple violets, white lilies, glowing roses, fields painted now with golden, now varied, now yellow flowers, in which one does not know whether the flowers’ appearance or their fragrant power gives greater delight? The eyes feed upon the pleasing sight; the fragrance spreads far and wide, and we are filled with its sweetness.

Hence the Lord divinely says: “And the beauty of the field is with me” (Ps. 49:11); for what he himself has formed is with him [Col. 0171A]. For what other craftsman could express so great a loveliness in every individual thing? “Consider the lilies of the field” (Matt. 6:28): how great is the whiteness of their leaves; how the leaves themselves, packed closely together, seem to rise from bottom to top, forming the shape of a cup; how within shines a kind of appearance of gold, yet enclosed by a surrounding rampart of the flower and exposed to no injury. If someone plucks this flower and separates it into its leaves, what hand of so great an artist could restore the lily’s appearance? Who is so great an imitator of nature as to venture to make this flower whole again? The Lord bore such testimony to it that he said: “Not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these” (ibid., 29). The king most abundant in feasting and most wise is judged inferior to the beauty of this flower [Col. 0171B].

37. Why should I enumerate the health-giving juices of herbs, the remedies in shrubs and leaves? A sick stag chews branches of olive and becomes well. Leaves of olive, gnawed by locusts, also free them from sickness.  
[Note: The Bigotian, Colbert, and Corbie manuscripts read, “olive and rose”; the Gembloux and Reims manuscripts, “olive and rose.”]

Blackberry leaves laid upon a serpent kill it. Gnats will not touch you if you boil wormwood herb with oil and anoint yourself with it.

## CHAPTER IX

That harmful things are not produced alongside useful things without reason, since what is harmful to one is useful to another; and that God has implanted in brute animals instinct, but in human beings reason, for avoiding harmful things. How fitting an order is preserved in the earth’s fruitfulness.

[Col. 0171C]

38. But perhaps some may say: “Why are deadly and harmful things produced together with useful things?” With wheat there is hemlock (*conium*), which is found harmful among the foods of life and, unless it is foreseen, habitually harms health. Among other means of sustenance, hellebore is also found. Aconites, too, often mislead and deceive the gatherer. But that would be as if you reproached the earth because not all human beings are good. Yet take something greater: not all angels in heaven are good. The sun itself, by excessive heat, scorches the ears of grain and burns the first beginnings of growing things. The moon also shows travellers their route and reveals the ambushes of robbers. Is it therefore right that, while neglecting to acknowledge the Creator’s grace in things that are useful, we should disparage the Creator’s providence because of certain harmful foods [Col. 0171D], as though everything ought to have been created for the sake of gluttony, or as though the things divine generosity has supplied for our stomach were scanty? We have foods assigned and known to all, which both produce pleasure and preserve bodily health.

[Note: Four manuscripts read *lolium* (“darnel”); others, better, *conium* (“hemlock”). For Basil reads: *μετὰ τοῦ σίτου τὸ κώνειον*, “hemlock with wheat.”]

39. Each thing produced from the earth has a particular rationale, by which it contributes according to its capacity to the fullness of the whole creation. Thus some things are born for food, others for another use [Col. 0172A].  
[Note: Five manuscripts and the Roman edition add, “others for drink”; this is absent from the better manuscripts. Regius: “Thus some things are born for use, others for food.”]

Nothing is idle; the earth produces nothing empty. What you consider useless is useful to others—indeed, it is often useful even to you in another respect. What does not aid food supplies medicine; and often the very things harmful to you furnish harmless fodder to birds or wild animals. Starlings eat hemlock, and it does them no harm, because, by the constitution of their bodies, they escape the poison of its deadly juice. For its juice has a cold power; drawing it through subtle pores into the region of their heart, they forestall it by rapid digestion before it can reach the vital organs. Those experienced in these matters say that hellebore is food and nourishment for quails, because by a certain natural balance of their bodies they avoid the power of this harmful fodder. For if, by medicinal preparation, something apparently contrary to health is often adjusted to promote the health of the human body, how much more does what a physician’s hand turns to health profit as food by its natural property?

Sleep is also often induced by mandrake when sufferers are distressed by the inconvenience of sleeplessness. What should I say of opium [Note: The Gill edition and many manuscripts read, “of celery”; Basil, however, with the remaining manuscripts and editions, reads “of opium.”], which has become known to us almost by daily use, since by it the most severe pains of the internal organs are often soothed? Nor should it be overlooked that hemlock has often subdued frenzied lusts, and hellebore has relieved long-standing afflictions of the sick body.

40. Therefore, there is not only no ground here for reproaching the Creator; there is even an increase of reasons for gratitude [Col. 0172C]. For what you thought created for danger works for you as a remedy for health. What is dangerous is avoided by providence, and what is healthful is not lost through diligence. Have not sheep and goats learned to avoid what is harmful to them? Although devoid of reason, by smell alone and through a certain mystery of nature [Note: Thus the manuscripts in an older hand, and the editions of Amerbach, Petri, Erasmus, and Gill in the margin. Other manuscripts and the Gill and Roman editions read “service.”], they nevertheless recognize the means of escaping danger and preserving health, distinguishing harmful things from beneficial; so that, when they perceive arrows armed with poison, they are said often to seek out familiar herbs and apply these as a remedy to the wound? Thus food is medicine to them, so that you may see arrows spring back from the wound and poisons flee rather than spread.

Indeed, poison is food for stags. The serpent flees the stag; it kills the lion. The dragon entangles the elephant, whose fall is the death of its victor [Col. 0172D]. Therefore they contend with all their strength on both sides: the dragon, to bind the foot in such a way that the fall of the bound animal cannot harm him; the elephant, to avoid being caught by its hindmost foot or in a narrow track, where it cannot twist itself around and crush the dragon under its heavy tread, nor receive the aid of an elephant following behind.

41. Therefore, if irrational animals know by which herbs they may heal themselves or bring aid through remedies, does the human being, in whom rational understanding is inborn, not know? Or is he so estranged from truth that he fails entirely to discern what is suited to each use? Or is he so ungrateful for nature’s benefits that, because drinking bull’s blood is deadly to a human being, he therefore thinks that the laborious animal either ought not to have been born or ought to have been produced without blood? Yet its strength supports farmers by diverse services: useful for tilling fields, suitable for drawing wagons, pleasant for food. God has given them all these things, if they know his gifts, saying: “Let the earth bring forth the grass of hay, breathing forth seed according to its kind” [Col. 0173A]. For this embraces not only spontaneous nourishment, which is found in herbs and roots and in the fruits of trees and other fruits [Note: Thus the old edition and several excellent manuscripts. The Roman edition and some manuscripts delete *and*. One Victorine manuscript, the Dionysian, Gembloux, Colbert, Bigotian, and one Corbie manuscript read: “and in the shoots of trees and other fruits.” Another Victorine manuscript reads: “and in trees and other …”], but also that nourishment which is procured by labour and gained through the cultivation of rural work.

42. How fitting, moreover, that he did not command the earth immediately to pour forth seed and fruits, but first decreed that it should germinate, then that the fields should grow green, and afterward that seed should develop according to the property of its kind. Thus the grace of the fields would never be lacking: first they would blossom with pleasing beauty, then provide the usefulness of fruits.

## CHAPTER X

Seeds never properly degenerate, since their kind is not changed but only their perfection; darnel and tares do not arise from wheat-seed. Before humankind sinned, God’s word bestowed marvellous fertility on the earth; yet even now the earth is not wholly deprived of it.

[Col. 0173C]

43. But perhaps someone will say: “How does the earth produce seeds according to their kind, when seeds sown often degenerate, and good wheat, once sown, produces a discoloured appearance and an inferior form?” Yet whenever this happens, it seems to be attributed not to a change of kind but to some disease and deficiency in the seed. Wheat does not cease to be wheat if it is scorched by cold or soaked by rain [Note: The Amerbach and Petri editions with the Benedictine manuscript read, “if by a south wind”; the Carnotensis manuscript, inserted between the lines in the same hand, “if by scorching,” that is, blight. All other editions and manuscripts read, “if by cold.” Perhaps there is an allusion to Virgil, *Georgics* I: “And the piercing cold of the north wind burns.”]; rather, it is changed in appearance more than in kind, by colour and corruption.

Indeed, grain that has been made wet often returns to the appearance of its kind if it is scorched by sun or fire, or if, entrusted to diligent cultivators, it is fostered by the mildness of the air and the richness of fertile lands [Col. 0173D]. Thus what had degenerated in the parent is restored in the offspring. We therefore need not fear that God’s command, whose practice has become established in nature, has been deprived in later generations by the defect of succession, since even today the purity of its kind is preserved in seeds.

44. For darnel and other spurious seeds, which are often mixed among crops, we have learned from the Gospel reading to be called tares (*zizania*) (Matt. 13:24). But they possess a kind proper to themselves; they have not acquired a degenerate nature through wheat-seed being changed by discolouring alteration into another kind of seed. The Lord teaches this when he says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while people slept, his enemy came and sowed tares over the wheat” (ibid.). Surely we observe that tares and wheat appear distinct both in name and in kind. For the servants also said to the householder: “Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field? Whence then does it have tares?” And he said to them: “An enemy has done this” (ibid., 27).

For the devil’s seed is one thing, and Christ’s seed [Col. 0174B], sown unto righteousness, another. The Son of Man sowed one thing, the devil another. So different is the nature of each seed that their sowers are opposed. What Christ sows is God’s kingdom; what the devil sows is sin. How, then, can kingdom and sin be of one kind? “The kingdom of God,” he says, “is like this: a man casts seed upon the earth.”

45. There is also the man who sows the word, of whom it is written: “The sower sows the word” (Mark 4:14). This man sowed the word upon the earth when he said, “Let the earth bring forth grass”; and suddenly shoots sprang up from the earth and diverse kinds of things shone forth. Here the green grace of meadows supplied an abundance of fodder; there the yellowing ear in the fields, stirred by the richer crop, portrayed the image of a surging sea [Col. 0174C]. The earth freely supplied all fruits. Though it could not be ploughed without a cultivator, for the farmer had not yet been formed, still it overflowed unploughed with rich harvests—and, I do not doubt, with a greater yield. For the cultivator’s negligence could not deprive the earth of its abundance.

Now fertility is gained by each person according to the merit of labour, where cultivation of the fields is considered; and the richness of fertile soil is penalized with barrenness through negligence or offence, floods of rain, drought of land, hailstorms, or any other cause [Note: The Dionysian manuscript, one Victorine manuscript, one Corbie manuscript, and Colbert read: “the richness of the soil [is penalized] with barrenness.” The other Victorine manuscript and Coenobite read: “with the barrenness of corrupt air.”]. But then the earth brought fruits everywhere by spontaneous yield, because he commanded it who is the fullness of all things. For God’s word bore fruit in the earth, and the earth had not yet been condemned under any curse [Col. 0174D]. The beginnings of the world’s birth are earlier than our sins; later came the fault for which we were condemned to eat bread in the sweat of our face and, without sweat, not to know food.  
[Note: Thus ten manuscripts of excellent quality. Others and the editions read, “without pain.”]

46. Even today, indeed, the earth’s fertility preserves the ancient abundance of spontaneous fruitfulness in practice. How many things still arise of themselves! And even in those things obtained by human hands, divine benefits largely remain with us, so that grain is supplied to us while we rest. The example of the reading set before us teaches this, as the Lord says: “The kingdom of God is like a man who casts seed upon the earth; and he sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed germinates and grows, while he does not know it” (Mark 4:26). For the earth bears fruit of itself: first the grass, then the ear, then full wheat in the ear. And when it has brought forth the fruit, immediately he puts in the sickle, because the harvest is present. Thus, while you sleep, O human being, and do not know it, the earth produces its fruits of itself. You sleep and rise, and marvel at the growth of grain during the night [Col. 0175A].

## CHAPTER XI

On the origin of trees; and, in this connection, on the rose, which was first born without thorns but afterward bristled with them and became a mirror of our life.

[Col. 0175B]

47. We have spoken of the grass of hay; now let us speak of the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit according to its kind, whose seed is in itself. He spoke, and they came to be; and suddenly, just as the earth above was clothed with flowers and the greenness of herbs, so here it was clothed with groves. Trees gathered together, forests rose up, and mountain summits suddenly put forth leaves. Here pines, here cypresses lifted themselves to lofty heights; cedars and firs came together. The silver fir also, not content with earthly roots and an airy top, advanced, destined to undergo safely even the hazards of the sea by means of oars [Col. 0175C], and to contend not only with winds but with waves.

Likewise the rising laurel gave forth its fragrance, never to be stripped of its own covering. Shady holm-oaks also put forth their tops, to preserve their bristling foliage even in winter. For nature assigned to each of them permanently this privilege which it received at the world's rising; and from that time the holm-oaks retain their prerogative, as the cypresses do: no winds strip them of the honour of their foliage.

48. Before then the rose had sprung up, mingled with the tender flowers of the earth, without thorns; [Note: All editions read “mingled with tender flowers.”] and the most beautiful flower bloomed without any deceit. Later the thorn enclosed the charm of the flower, presenting, as it were, a mirror of human life, which often pierces the sweetness of its course with the neighbouring stings of cares. For the elegance of our life is surrounded and hedged in by certain anxieties, so that sorrow is joined to grace. Therefore, whenever anyone rejoices either in the pleasure of reason or in the successes of a more prosperous course, it is fitting that he remember the fault through which, while we flourished amid the delightfulness of Paradise, thorns of the mind and briars of the soul were assigned to us by the justice of condemnation.

Therefore, though you shine, O human being, whether by the splendour of nobility, the height of power, or the brilliance of virtue, a thorn is always near you; there is always a briar. [Note: All editions and several manuscripts omit “a thorn is always near you; there is always a briar”; the latter words have been restored from ten highly reliable manuscripts.] Always look to what is below you: you grow above thorns, and grace does not endure long. [Note: The Coenobian manuscript and one Victorine manuscript read: “you always bring forth thorns.”] When the flower of life’s course has swiftly passed, each person withers. [Note: Three older manuscripts read, “when the flower of sweet beauty …”; five read, “when the flower of the course of age …”; the rest, with the editions, read as in the text.]

## Chapter XII

The vine is praised and compared with the Church; its example is also proposed for our imitation.

49. Certainly, just as you should know that you share with flowers things that fall away, so also you share joyful things with vines, from which wine is produced to gladden the human heart. Would that you, O human being, might imitate the example of this kind, so that you yourself might bear for yourself joy and delight! The sweetness of your grace is in yourself; from yourself it springs, in yourself it remains, within you it is present. [Note: All editions read: “the grace of your sweetness is [in yourself].”] That is, the delight of your conscience must be sought in yourself. Therefore Scripture says: “Drink water from your own vessels, and from the fountains of your own wells” (Prov. 5:15).

First of all, nothing has a more pleasing fragrance than a flowering vine. For juice pressed from its blossoms produces a kind of drink that serves both pleasure and health. Then who would not marvel to see the vine break forth from its wine-bearing berry all the way to the highest summit of a tree, which it cherishes, as it were, in an embrace, binds with certain arms, encircles with tendrils, clothes with leaves, and crowns with garlands of grapes? In imitation of our life, it first fixes a living root; then, because its nature is pliant and perishable, it clasps whatever it can seize with certain arms—namely, with its tendrils—and by them raises and lifts itself. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “with tendrils, as though with certain hands.” The editors evidently referred to a passage in Cicero’s *On Old Age*. Ambrose may have borrowed both this remark about the vine and his preceding remarks about wheat from that orator; nevertheless, contrary to the authority of the editions and manuscripts, no change is made.]

50. The people of the Church are like this vine. They are planted, as it were, by a certain root of faith and restrained by the shoot of humility. Of this the Prophet beautifully says: “You transplanted a vine from Egypt and planted its roots, and filled the earth. Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God. You extended its shoots as far as the sea, and its offshoots as far as the river” (Ps. 79:9). [Note: Thus the old edition and nine manuscripts. The Carnotensis, Corbeiensis, and Theodulfian manuscripts, with the Septuagint and Roman Psalter, read “the earth was filled”; other manuscripts and the Roman edition read “it filled the earth.” At the same place the Roman edition reads “he extended his shoots”; most manuscripts, “its shoots”; others and the old edition, “you extended,” etc.]

And through Isaiah the Lord himself spoke, saying: “A vineyard was made for the beloved upon a horn, in a fertile place; and I built a wall around it, dug about the vineyard of Sorech, and built a tower in its midst” (Isa. 5:1 ff.). For he surrounded it as with a rampart of heavenly precepts and with the guardianship of angels. “For the angel of the Lord shall encamp around those who fear him.” In the Church he set, as it were, a tower of apostles, prophets, and teachers, who are accustomed to stand forth for the peace of the Church. He dug around it when he relieved it of the burden of earthly cares. For nothing weighs the mind down more than the anxiety of this world and the desire either for money or for power.

This is shown to you in the Gospel (Luke 13:11), when you read that the woman who had a spirit of infirmity was bent over so that she could not look upward. Her soul was bowed down because it inclined toward earthly advantages and did not see heavenly grace. Jesus looked upon her and called her, and immediately the woman laid aside her earthly burdens. He also shows that those to whom he says, “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28), were weighed down by those desires. Thus that woman’s soul, as though dug around, breathed freely and was raised upright.

51. But once this vine has been dug around, it is bound up and raised, lest it bend down to the ground. Some branches are cut back; others are propagated. Those are cut back which luxuriate in vain profusion; those are propagated which the good husbandman judges fruitful. Why should I describe the rows of supports and the beauty of the yoking, which truly and plainly teach that equality must be preserved in the Church, so that no rich or honoured person may exalt himself, and no poor person be cast down or person of low birth despair?

Let there be for all in the Church equal and one liberty; let common justice and grace be imparted to all. Therefore there is a tower in the midst, which sets before us the example of those rustic men, those wandering fishermen, who deserved to hold the citadel of virtues. By their examples may our disposition be lifted up, and may it not lie low, worthless and contemptible upon the ground; [Note: All editions and many manuscripts read “nor [may it lie] low”; some add “let the rich … lie.” The Benedictine, Carnotensis, and Germanensis manuscripts read: “nor worthless and contemptible upon the ground,” etc.] rather, let the mind of each raise itself toward what is above, so that it may dare to say: “But our citizenship is in heaven.”

And lest it be bent down by any storms of the age or driven down by a tempest, it embraces each of its neighbours with those tendrils and coils, as though with embraces of love, and rests in union with them. Love, then, binds us to things above and grafts us into heaven. “For whoever remains in love, God remains in him.” Thus the Lord also says: “Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me. I am the vine; you are the branches” (John 15:4).

52. Clearly, then, he indicated that the example of the vine should be summoned for the formation of our life. The vine is said first to bud when warmed by the mildness of spring; then to send forth fruit from the joints of its branches, from which the emerging grape is formed. As it gradually grows, its unripe offspring retains its sharpness and cannot become sweet until it is ripe and fully matured.

Meanwhile the vine is clothed with green leaves, which provide no small protection against cold and every injury, and defend it from the heat of the sun. What sight is more pleasant, or what fruit sweeter, than to see hanging clusters like necklaces of a beautiful countryside, or to gather grapes gleaming with golden or purple colour? You might think hyacinths and other gems were shining—Indian stones flashing and white jewels gleaming. [Note: The Roman edition and some manuscripts read “Indian”; the old edition with eleven manuscripts, “Indian [stones].” In the margin, the Coenobian codex explains: “He calls Indian stones those brought from India; the white ones are what blessed Gregory calls *albulæ*, commonly called pearls. We also read of a white emerald and a white sardonyx.”]

Do you not perceive, O human being, that by these you are warned lest the final day find your fruits unripe, or lest deeds unprepared disgrace the time of full maturity? [Note: Five manuscripts read, “lest small deeds disgrace [it]”; three, “lest evil deeds disgrace [it]”; one, “disgrace”; and another, “delight.”] An unripe fruit is customarily more bitter; nor can anything be sweet unless it has grown to the maturity of perfection. Neither the cold of dreadful death nor the sun of iniquity is accustomed to harm the perfect person, because spiritual grace shades that person and quenches every blaze of worldly desire and bodily lust, and wards off its burning heat.

May all who behold you praise you, and may they marvel at the companies of the Church as at garlands of branches. Let each of the faithful observe the beautiful necklaces of souls; let them delight in the maturity of prudence, the splendour of faith, the beauty of confession, the loveliness of justice, and the abundance of mercy, so that it may be said to you: “Your wife is like an abundant vine on the sides of your house” (Ps. 127:3), because you imitate the overflowing fruitfulness of the vine, rich in the gift of generosity.

## Chapter XIII

On the usefulness and variety of trees; the method of yoking and treating them; finally, the properties of tree saps, with a moral exposition of each.

53. But why do I linger over the vine alone, when every kind of tree is useful—some born for fruit, others given for use? For even those whose fruit is less abundant nevertheless have a more valuable use. Cedar is suitable for supporting the summits of roofs, because such timber is tall enough for wide spans and does not burden walls. Cypress too is suitable for panelled ceilings and adorned gables. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “suitable also for decorating gables.”] Therefore the Church says in the Song of Songs: “The beams of our houses are cedar; our ceilings are cypress” (Song 1:16), declaring that therein are the beautiful ornaments of her height: those who, like beams, support the summit of the Church by their virtue and adorn its lofty structure. [Note: The Roman edition, with a few later manuscripts, reads “ornaments of the summit which, as though …”; the other witnesses more correctly read “who, as though …,” etc. There is a syllepsis in “ornaments,” by which the Apostles are signified.]

Laurel and palm belong to the insignia of victory. The heads of victors are crowned with laurel, and the palm is the adornment of the victorious hand. Hence the Church says: “I said, I will climb the palm tree; I will hold its heights” (Song 7:8). Seeing the eminence of the Word and hoping to ascend to his height and the summit of knowledge, she says: “I will climb the palm tree,” so as to leave behind all things below and strive toward those above, toward the prize of Christ, [Note: See note (c) appended to column 182.] that she may pluck and taste his sweet fruits. For the fruit of virtue is sweet.

The poplar also, a shady tree for victorious crowns, and the pliant willow, suitable for binding vines, what else do they mystically declare except that Christ’s bonds are good bonds—bonds that do not harm: bonds of grace, bonds of love—so that each may glory in his own bonds, as Paul too gloried when he said: “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ” (Philem. 1:1)? Bound with these bonds, he said: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Rom. 8:35): bonds of self-restraint, bonds of love. Bound with these bonds David also said: “Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments” (Ps. 136:2).

Boxwood too is useful for forming the letters of an alphabet; its light material trains the use of a child’s hand. Hence Scripture says: “Write upon boxwood” (Isa. 30:8). At the same time, by its material—which is always green and never sheds its leaves—it warns you never to be stripped bare through dissembling your hope, but always to let the hope of salvation sprout in you through faith.

54. Why should I enumerate how great is the variety of trees, how diverse and beautiful the adornment of each: how spreading the beeches, how tall the firs, how leafy the pines, how shady the holm-oaks, how two-coloured the poplars, how woodland-like and reviving the chestnut, which, as soon as it has been cut down, is accustomed to sprout from itself like a forest? Or how in the trees themselves an old or youthful age may be perceived? For younger trees have more slender branches; older trees have stronger and knotted limbs. The former have leaves smooth and spread out; the latter, more contracted and rough.

There are also trees which, if cut down, do not know how to restore their own succession from an aged and dead root. Others, either youthful in green vigour or more fruitful by nature, find cutting a benefit rather than a loss, so that by their renewed succession they are passed on to many heirs.

55. There is also something to marvel at: even in fruits there are sexes, and in trees a distinction of sex. For you may see the palm which produces dates often bending and lowering its branches, presenting the appearance of desire and embrace toward the tree which country boys call the male palm. [Note: That is, country people. This idiom is borrowed from the Greeks, among whom παῖδες φιλοσόφων (“children of philosophers”) has the same meaning as φιλόσοφοι (“philosophers”). Among the Hebrews too, “son of man” is frequently used in the Old Testament for “man,” and there are many similar usages.] That palm, then, is the female palm and acknowledges its sex by the appearance of submission. Therefore cultivators of the ground cast upon its branches the male seed of dates or palm shoots, [Note: The Roman edition reads: “the seeds, as it were, of male palms”; other editions and several manuscripts, “the seeds of male palms.” But ten manuscripts of the best quality read “of vine-shoots,” etc.] by which a kind of sensation of intercourse is infused into that female tree and the pleasure of the desired union is represented.

When endowed with this gift, it rises again, lifts its branches, and raises its foliage once more to its former condition. There is a similar opinion concerning the fig tree. Accordingly, many are said to graft the wild fig after the domestic and fruitful fig, because the fruits of that fertile domestic fig are said soon to fall to the ground when disturbed by some breeze or by heat. Those who know this remedy tie wild figs to that fruitful tree and treat its weakness, so that it can preserve its own fruits, which, if remedies failed, would presently fall.

By this, as by a certain riddle of nature, we are warned not to shun those who have been separated from our faith and fellowship. For a Gentile who is won over may, the more forcefully he had defended error, become the more vigorous defender of faith; and if someone is converted from heresy, that person may, as it were, strengthen the party to which he has transferred himself after changing his opinion—especially if there is in him something upright by nature, so that his judgment may be lively, provided that the attention of sobriety and the observance of chastity support it. Therefore devote deep care to such a person, so that, in likeness to that fruitful fig tree, you may strengthen your own virtue through the presence and conjunction of that wild tree. Thus your purpose will not be dissolved, and the fruit of diligence and grace will be preserved.

56. How many things teach that natural hardness can be softened by the diligent application of care, as agriculture provides examples! Pomegranates often bloom quickly but cannot bear fruit unless they are cultivated with suitable remedies by skilled persons. Often the inner juice fades away, while a strong and beautiful appearance is outwardly displayed. Not without reason is the pomegranate compared with the Church, as you have in the Song of Songs, spoken to the Church: “Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate” (Song 4:3). And below: “If the vine has flowered, the pomegranates have flowered” (Song 7:12).

For the Church displays the good brilliance of faith and confession, beautiful with the blood of so many martyrs and, what is more, endowed with Christ’s blood. At the same time, under one protective enclosure, she preserves within herself many fruits according to the use of this fruit and embraces many exercises of virtue. “For one wise in spirit conceals matters.”

Farmers are also said to treat almond trees in this way, so that bitter fruits become sweet: they bore through the root of the tree and insert in the middle a shoot of the tree which the Greeks call *peukē* (πεύκη), and we call *picea*, “pine.” When this is done, the bitterness of the sap is removed. If agriculture changes the qualities of stocks, then can not the studies of learning and diligent discipline soften whatever diseased passions there may be?
