[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “whatever passions of souls.”] Let no one, then, placed upon the slippery ground either of youth or of intemperance, despair of his own conversion. Timber is often turned to better uses; and can human hearts not be changed?

57. We have shown not only that there are diversities of fruits among trees of different kinds, but that fruits often contend with one another even in the same species of trees. For one kind is of male fruit, another of female fruit, as we said above concerning dates. But who could comprehend the variety, appearance, and charm of fruits, the usefulness of each fruit, and the properties of their juices—what seems suited to each purpose; how more bitter fruits treat diseased human organs and moderate internal swelling and harshness; or, again, how harsh bodily humours are tempered with sweet fruits?

Indeed, medicine is older when it is accustomed to heal with herbs and juices; and no health is firmer than that which is restored by wholesome foods. Thus nature teaches us that food alone is medicine for us. Certainly, open ulcers are closed by herbs, and internal ailments are treated by herbs. Therefore it is the task of physicians to know the powers of herbs. From this the practice of healing arose.

## Chapter XIV

On the differences among simple fruits and the diversity of leaves; especially on the vine leaf and the fig leaf, and on the various shapes of other leaves.

58. But, to return our discourse to simple fruits: some are ripened by the sun, while others are completed when enclosed in shells or rinds. Apples and pears, and every kind of grape, are exposed naked to the sun; but nuts, nut-kernels, and the fruit of stones, although covered with shell and rind, are nevertheless nourished and fed by the sun’s heat. [Note: Older editions read: “but the fruit of the nut, of the knot, and of the kernel, covered both by shell and rind, is nevertheless born and nourished by the sun’s heat.” The Vatican codex lacks “of the knot and of the kernel.” The Roman edition reads: “but the fruit of the pine nut and of the little nut, covered both by shell and rind, is nevertheless equally nourished by the sun’s heat.” Some manuscripts read “nuts,” others “of the nut”; the remainder agrees with the text.] And in proportion as the kernel is hidden by the density of the pine cone, it is nourished by the sun’s heat.

59. How great, moreover, is the Lord’s providence: where the fruit is softer, there the thickness of the leaf provides a stronger covering to protect the fruit—as we see in the fruit of the fig tree. Accordingly, more delicate things must be guarded by stronger things, as the Lord himself teaches through Jeremiah, saying: “As these good figs, so will I regard those of Judah who have been carried away, whom I sent from this place into the land of the Chaldeans for good; and I will set my eyes upon them for good” (Jer. 24:5). [Note: The Roman edition reads: “As these good figs, so will I acknowledge …”] For, as delicate fruits, he enclosed them, as it were, with the stronger covering of his mercy, lest their tender fruits perish prematurely.

Indeed, later he also says concerning them: “My delicate ones walked harsh paths” (Bar. 4:26). And below he says to them: “Be steadfast, children, and cry out to God” (Bar. 4:27). For this alone is an inviolable covering and an impenetrable defence against every storm and injury. Therefore, where there are tender fruits, there are thicker coverings and protections of leaves. Conversely, where fruits are stronger, there are more delicate leaves, as the apple tree teaches. A stronger fruit does not need much assistance of protection; indeed, the shade of too thick a protection might harm the fruit more.

60. Finally, let the vine leaf teach us the grace of nature and the inward mysteries of divine wisdom. We see it so cut and divided that it seems to display the form of three leaves. Its middle part is marked off in such a way that, unless it remained attached to the lower parts, it would appear separate to those looking at it. Nature seems to have observed this arrangement so that it may admit the sun more easily and provide covering shade.

Accordingly, its middle part stretches out more prominently and becomes thin at its very summit, so that it displays more beauty than covering. For it seems to form the appearance of a prize (*bravium*, Greek βραβεῖον), [Note: Greek βραβεῖον: a crown or prize of victory. It was bestowed from branches of various trees, some of which are discussed in the preceding chapter, §55. See Lucian, *Anacharsis, or Concerning Gymnasia*, and others.] signifying that among all fruits that hang, the grape holds pre-eminence: by a certain silent judgment of nature, yet by evident indication, there is born into it the appearance and prerogative of victory. Thus it carries its prize with itself: it is afforded protection against injuries of the air and the violence of rains, while no impediment is made to receiving the sun’s heat, by which it is warmed, nourished, coloured, and enlarged.

The leaf of the fig tree likewise, almost as much as the vine leaf, is cut apart by a fourfold division. This appears more clearly because the leaf is larger, though certainly not as with the vine leaf, which is crisped around all its edges and at its summit. For as the thickness is stronger in the fig leaf, so the appearance is more elegant in the vine leaf. The thickness of the leaf is useful for repelling the injury of storms; its division, for allowing the fruit the benefit of warmth. Thus this kind of fruit does not quickly feel hail, but quickly feels ripening, because it seems both to lie hidden against injuries and to lie open to grace.

61. Why should I describe the differences of leaves—how some are round, others longer; some flexible, others stiffer; some scarcely falling in any winds, others shaken off by the light movement of breezes?

## Chapter XV

The astonishing diversity of water. From it also arises a difference among the fruits nourished by it and among the tears that drip from trees; an excuse is added for not examining these matters too minutely.

62. It is impossible to seek out the properties of individual things, to distinguish their differences by manifest testimony, or to disclose their hidden and secret causes with unfailing proofs. For water is one and the same, yet it often changes itself into diverse appearances: yellow among sands, foamy among rocks, greener among groves, variegated among flowers, brighter among lilies, redder among roses, clearer in grass, muddier in a marsh, more transparent in a spring, darker in the sea. Taking on the colour of the places into which it flows, it runs onward.

By the same principle it also changes its temperature: it boils among steaming places, grows cold among shady places, is heated when the sun strikes it back, and turns whitish with icy moisture when watered by snow. How too is its taste itself transformed, so that it is now sharper, now more bitter, now stronger, now more astringent, now sweeter, varied according to the quality of the substances into which it is poured? It is made sharp by unripe juices, by bruised walnut rind and crushed leaves; it becomes more bitter through wormwood, stronger through wine, more astringent through garlic; it becomes heavy through poison and sweet through honey. But if mastic, the fruit of the terebinth, or the inner part of a nut is mixed with it, it is easily transformed into the soft nature of oil.

Although it nourishes all shrubs, it supplies different uses to each. If it washes the roots or descends poured out from clouds, it gives distinct powers to all: [Note: Many manuscripts and the old edition read: “If it nourishes the roots.”] it fattens the root, advances the trunk, spreads out the branches, causes the leaves to grow green, nourishes the seeds of fruits, and is accustomed to enlarge the fruit. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “nourishes the fruit and causes the seeds of fruits to grow,” etc.] Therefore, although it is the same nurse of all, some kinds of trees produce more bitter juices, others sweeter; some late, others early. They also differ among themselves in pleasantness: there is one sweetness in the vine, another in the olive, another in cherries, another in *fleu* [reading uncertain], distinct in the apple, different in the date.

63. The touch of water itself is gentle in one place, rougher in another, and often richer in another. It also frequently differs in weight as in appearance: in most places it is judged heavier, in most lighter. It is therefore no wonder that, since water itself differs within itself, the tears of trees also differ among themselves, though they are produced by the washing of the same water. And though the cause of all is one, the use of each is diverse and its nature diverse.

The tear of the cherry tree has one power, that of mastic another. The fragrant trees of the East are also said to sweat a balsam drop unlike the others. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “and the tear hardens into the solidity of a stony nature.”] By some more secret power of nature, the shrubs of ferula in Egypt and Libya also shed a different kind of tears. Why should I tell you, though the statement may seem humble, that amber is the tear of a shrub, and that a tear hardens into the solidity of so great a material? Nor is this established by slight evidence, since leaves, the tiniest portions of shoots, or certain small kinds of living creatures are often found in amber. It seems to have received them while it was still a softer drop and, once hardened, to have retained them.

64. But why should I determine by a lowly discourse matters of nature so lofty and precious, when this discourse is nourished by human ingenuity, whereas divine providence has formed the nature of all things? Therefore the flow of words must be restrained as though by reins, lest we seem presumptuously to expound what appears to have been divinely bestowed specifically upon Solomon as a gift of wisdom: the differences of trees, the powers of roots, and whatever things are hidden and unforeseen, as it is written (3 Kings 4:33). Yet these matters are not reported as having been disclosed even by Solomon himself. Thus it seems to me that he could discuss the kinds of shrubs, but could not fully explain all the principles of creation. [Note: This is the reading of the more numerous and better manuscripts. Some, with the editions, read “fully explain every secret of creation by reasoning”; others, “fully explain every secret of reasoning.”]

## Chapter XVI

How, at the Lord’s word, every kind of shrub suddenly blossomed and supplied food, pleasures, and medicines. In what way all plants have in themselves either seed or something that supplies the function of seed. On God’s great power in individual things, especially the pine and the tamarisk.

65. If crops are generally more luxuriant where waters irrigate them, beans greener, and the manifold beauty of gardens raised up and revived; if the bank of a river overflowing over green beds is adorned— [Note: Some Paris editions read: “is adorned; how is it not …?” The Gemblacensis, Bigotianus, Dionysianus, and Colbertinus manuscripts read: “is adorned; do you marvel how at …?” The remaining manuscripts and editions agree with the text.]how is it that, at the word of the Lord, which is more overflowing than every course of waters, the whole creation of shrubs suddenly blossomed? The fields hastened to yield crops not entrusted to them; gardens hastened to produce unknown kinds of vegetables and miracles of flowers; riverbanks to clothe themselves with myrtles. Trees hastened quickly to rise, quickly to put themselves into flower, to provide food for human beings and fodder for cattle. [Note: The old edition and four manuscripts read “to clothe themselves with flower”; the Roman edition, more correctly with the remaining manuscripts, “to clothe themselves in flower.” This appears to have been taken from Virgil, *Georgics* 1: “When the abundant walnut clothes itself in flower in the woods.”]

The fruit is common to all, and use also was given to all. Trees produced both at once: one thing by which we might eat, another by whose refreshing shade we might be protected from the sun. Food is in the fruit; the pleasant use is in the leaf. [Note: Several excellent early manuscripts read “food unfruitful of pleasantness in the leaves.” This is a scribal error; those who tried to emend it supplied “food in the fruit” or “in fruits, pleasantness in leaves.” The editions followed them. But the Benedictine, Carnotensis, and Germanensis manuscripts restored the true reading.] Yet because the providence of the Creator foresaw that human greed would claim the fruit especially for itself, he provided for the other living creatures by granting them a special nourishment. Thus there is no insignificant food for them in leaves and wild bark. Things useful for healing were likewise supplied: juices, tears, and shoots.

Thus those things which we afterward learned to be useful by experiment, practice, and example, the Creator commanded to come forth from the bosom of the earth from the beginning, assigning each to its proper use by the majesty of his foreknowledge. [Note: The old edition reads: “the divine foreknowledge of majesty gave [them], from the beginning of creation, fitted for use.” Some later witnesses and two manuscripts add “and by the majesty of his foreknowledge”; some read “by the majesty of his providence.” The remaining manuscripts and editions agree with the text.]

66. Since the Lord commanded that “the earth should bring forth green grass and a fruit-bearing tree making fruit according to its kind, whose seed is in it,” lest anyone perhaps say that in many trees neither fruit nor seed is visible, and think that the divine command falters in any respect and deviates from truth, let such a person observe that it cannot possibly be that all things which generate do not either use seeds or possess something that appears to agree with the power of seeds. Whoever attends carefully may grasp this by evident testimony.

Willows seem to have no seed; yet they have in their leaves a certain grain possessing the power of seed. When this is committed to the earth, a tree rises up as though placed from a shoot, and revives itself as though from seed. By that grain, therefore, the root first takes hold; from the root springs up a grove not only of willow but also of the remaining trees similar to this kind. The propagation of a root also has the power of seed; hence many have propagated their growth by that planting. [Note: Eleven manuscripts read thus. Others and the editions read: “But roots also have the power of seed.” The sole Colbertinus manuscript and two Victorine manuscripts read: “by that means they propagated the increase of their own stock,” etc.]

67. Great is God’s power in each thing. Nor should anyone marvel that I have said God’s power is great in shrubs. For he said that his great power was in locusts and the *bruchus* [a devouring insect], because the offence against divine majesty was to be discharged by the great restraint of Jewish barrenness and scarcity. For patience is a great power; providence is a great power. [Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read: “wisdom … providence”; the Remensis and Coenobian manuscripts, “of wisdom … of providence.” Nine highly reliable manuscripts read “patience,” etc.] They were indeed unworthy to enjoy the fruitfulness of the earth, since they had injured the Creator of the earth. And truly great is he who avenges the crime of such great impiety through a pitiable famine. Therefore, if the earth produced the barren *bruchus* by God’s great power, how much more does it produce fruitful things by great power!

68. Who, seeing the pine cone, would not marvel at so great an art implanted by the divine command and impressed upon nature: how, though its measures recede from the very centre, it rises with equal joining, by which it cherishes its own fruits? Thus the same appearance and arrangement are preserved around its circumference, and in each section there is a certain abundance of kernel-bearing offspring; the fruit and its beauty return in a circle. Thus, in this pine cone, nature seems to express an image of itself: it preserves the privileges received from that first divine and heavenly command, and brings forth its offspring by a certain annual cycle and order until the completion of time is fulfilled.

69. But as in this fruit nature marks an attractive image of itself, so in tamarisks—that is, low shrubs—it has expressed the figure of wicked cunning. For just as people of double heart are everywhere at hand, presenting grace and simplicity among the good while attaching themselves to the most vicious, so these shrubs too grow, by a kind of contrary habit, both in watery places and in deserts. Thus Jeremiah compared doubtful and insincere character to tamarisks (Jer. 17:6). [Note: Four manuscripts read: “a doubtful and insincere mind of these persons.”]

## Chapter XVII

After rebuking the deafness of the human heart, the wonderful providence of God is shown in the smallest things; especially in evergreen trees and their differences, and then in the first cultivator of the vine and the use of wine.

70. “Let the earth bring forth green grass,” he says; and immediately, as every shoot sprang up, the earth was filled. Yet the human being is told: “Love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:5), and the love of God is not poured into every heart. Human hearts are deafer than hard rocks. The earth supplies us with fruits not owed to us, because it obeys its Creator; we deny the gift owed by us because we do not worship the Creator.

71. See, in small things, what God’s providence is; and since you cannot comprehend it, marvel that he has kept some things ever green, while he has willed others to undergo the changes of stripping and clothing. Amid the whiteness of snows and the frosts of cold, the fields preserve their greenness; and though they themselves are covered with ice, yet they clothe the offspring they bear with no slight appearance of verdure. Even among the kinds of trees that are arrayed in long-lasting foliage, there is no small difference. The olive and the pine always retain their covering, yet they often change their leaves; they display them not as enduring, but as succeeding one another in their tree’s beauty, and by replacement make up for the completeness of a perpetual garment. But the palm remains always green through preservation and endurance, not through a change of leaves. For it retains the leaves which it first put forth, without any succession of replacement.

Imitate it, therefore, O human being, so that it may be said of you also: “Your stature has become like a palm tree” (Song 7:7). Preserve the greenness of your youth and that natural innocence which you received from the beginning, so that, planted beside streams of water, you may have your fruit prepared in its season and your leaf may not fall. Following this greenness of grace, ever flourishing in Christ, the Church says: “I desired and sat in his shadow” (Song 2:3). The Apostles also received this prerogative of unfading gift: their leaf could never fail, so that even their shadow healed the sick.

> [Note: Col. 0186D] All editions and several later manuscripts: “For it gave shade to infirmity.”

For faith of mind and the flourishing merits of virtues give shade to bodily infirmities. Remain, therefore, planted in the house of the Lord, that in his courts you may flourish like a palm; that the grace of the Church may rise in you; and that “the fragrance of your nostrils” may be “like apples, and your throat like the best wine” (Song 7:9), so that you may be made drunk in Christ.

72. This little verse aptly reminds us to return to what was almost passed over, since we said that the vine also sprouted forth at the Lord’s command, although afterward we learned that it was planted by Noah after the flood (Gen. 9:20). For thus you have it: Noah was a tiller of the earth; he planted a vine, drank of its wine, and fell asleep. Noah, then, was not the originator of the vine, but of its planting. For unless he had found it already produced, he could not have planted it. He was therefore the cultivator, not the originator, of the vine.

But God, knowing that wine drunk soberly confers health and increases prudence, while drunk immoderately it gives occasions for vices, gave the creature but left its abundance to human judgment; so that moderation might be nature’s instruction in sobriety, while the human condition might ascribe to itself the harmful excess and lapse of drunkenness. Thus Noah himself became drunk and fell asleep, overcome by wine. Accordingly, through wine he lay open to disgrace who through the flood had emerged into glory. Yet even in this God preserved the grace of his creature, so that he might turn its fruit to our salvation and through it forgiveness of sins might come to us.

Hence Isaac piously said: “The fragrance of Jacob is the fragrance of a full field,” that is, a natural fragrance (Gen. 27:27). For what is sweeter than a full countryside? What more delightful than the fragrance of the vine? What more pleasing than the flower of the bean? Therefore, although someone before us has ingeniously said, “The Patriarch did not smell the vine, the fig tree, or the crop, but breathed forth the grace of virtues,” I nevertheless take the very simple and sincere fragrance of the earth as a grace of blessing: no deceit compounded it, but the truth of heavenly favor infused it. Indeed, among the most sacred blessings is reckoned the gift that the Lord may grant us, from the dew of heaven, the abundance of wine, oil, and grain—to whom belong honor, praise, glory, everlastingness from ages past, now and always, and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

# Book Four: On the Work of the Fourth Day

[Col. 0187]

## Chapter I (Sermon VI)

He prepares the reader rightly to understand the creation of the sun and to avoid idolatry concerning it. To this end he compares it with its Creator, considers the order in which it was created among other things, and adds an elegant personification of the earth.

[Col. 0187B]

1. One who gathers the vintage customarily cleans beforehand the vessels into which the wine is poured, lest some chance (*sors*) spoil the wine’s flavor.

> [Note: Col. 0187D] All editions, and several manuscripts in part: “lest some dirt … discolor”; in part: “lest some dirt … discolors.” Ten manuscripts of approved authority: “lest some *sors*, etc.” A good reading, whose rationale may be understood from Francisco Sánchez’s *Minerva*, on homonymous words, p. 408.

For what good is it to set the vine in order, dig about it yearly, draw furrows with ploughs, prune it, prop it up, join it to elms and unite it in a kind of marriage, if wines obtained by so much labor turn sour in the vessel? Likewise, whoever wishes to watch the morning risings of the sun cleans his eyes, lest any dust or impurities settle upon them and dull the sight of the beholder, or lest some misty haze cover the bodily eyes of one looking on.

> [Note: Col. 0187D] Editions and a few manuscripts: “settle upon his eyes.” The others have *insidat*, “may settle upon,” not improperly; unless one prefers to write *incidat*, “may fall upon.”

For us, in this reading, a sun is about to rise which was not there before. We have now passed the first day without a sun, spent the second without a sun, completed the third without a sun; on the fourth day God commands the lights—the sun, moon, and stars—to be made. The sun begins: cleanse the eyes of your mind, O human being, and the inner sight of your soul, lest some splinter of sin blunt the edge of your understanding and disturb the vision of a pure heart. Cleanse also your ear, that you may receive in a pure vessel the clear streams of divine Scripture, lest any contamination enter.

The sun comes forth, advancing the day with great radiance, filling the world with great light, and steaming with heat. Beware, O human being, of considering its magnitude alone, lest its excessive brightness blind the vision of your mind. One who fixes his gaze directly upon its ray loses all sight at once through the reflected light; unless he turns his face and eyes toward other directions, he thinks that he sees nothing and has been deprived of the faculty of sight. But if he turns his gaze aside, its proper function remains unimpaired. Take care, then, lest its rising ray also confuse your sight.

Therefore first look upon the firmament of heaven, which was made before the sun. Look upon the earth, which began to be visible and ordered before the sun came forth. Look upon its shoots, earlier than the sun’s light. The *bruchus* was before the sun; the herb was older than the moon.

> [Note: Col. 0188D] Where all editions and many manuscripts read “the bush was before,” six most ancient manuscripts read “the *bruchus* was before,” that is perhaps “a branch,” whence the Italian *broncho* and French *branche*. See Aldrovandi, *Dendrologia*, book I, p. 22. But Ambrose, in the preceding chapter, no. 67, appears by this word to indicate some barren shrub.

Do not, therefore, believe the sun to be God when you see God’s gifts placed before it. Three days passed, and no one sought the sun, while the brightness of light abounded. For the day also has its own light, which is the sun’s forerunner. Do not then rashly entrust yourself to the sun’s great splendor. It is the eye of the world, the delight of the day, the beauty of heaven, nature’s grace, the excellence of creation.

2. But when you see it, consider its maker; when you admire it, first praise its Creator. If the sun, a fellow servant and participant in creation, is so pleasing, how good is that Sun of righteousness! If this one is so swift that in rapid courses it traverses all things by day and night, how great is he who is always everywhere and fills all things with his majesty! If the one commanded to go forth is admirable, how beyond admiration is he who “speaks to the sun, and it does not rise,” as we read (Job 9:7)! If great is the one which by the alternation of hours daily approaches places or departs from them, what kind is he who, even when he emptied himself so that we might be able to see him, was “the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world”? If most excellent is the one which often suffers eclipse through the obstruction of the earth, of how great a majesty is he who says: “Yet once more I will shake the earth” (Hag. 1:7)! The earth hides the former; it cannot endure the motion of the latter unless it is supported by the substance of his will. If it is a loss to the blind not to see the grace of this sun, how much greater a loss is it to the sinner, deprived of the gift of the true light, to endure the darkness of perpetual night?

3. Therefore, when you see the sun, attend to the earth, which was founded before it; attend to the grass of the field, which has precedence by the privilege of order; attend to the trees, which applaud because they began to exist before the lights of heaven. Are the merits of grass greater than those of the sun? Or is the prerogative of a tree superior? Far be it from us to prefer things perceptible to the minister of so great a gift. What then did the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God foresee in causing trees to begin to exist before those two lights of the world and, as it were, heavenly eyes of the firmament? It was so that all might learn, by the testimony of the divine account, that the earth can be fertile without the sun. For the earth which could sprout the first seeds of things without the sun can surely nourish the seeds it has received and bring forth its offspring by its own fostering, without the sun’s heat.

4. Therefore nature cries out, as it were, with this voice concerning its gifts: “The sun is indeed good, but as a servant, not as a ruler; it is a good helper of my fertility, but not its creator; a good nourisher of my fruits, but not their author. At times it even scorches my offspring; often it is harmful to me, and in many places it leaves me without dowry. I am not ungrateful to my fellow servant: it has been given to me for use; it has been made subject to labor with me; with me it has been subjected to futility, with me subjected to the bondage of corruption. With me it groans together and labors in birth, until the adoption of children and the redemption of the human race may come, so that we too may be freed from slavery. Standing with me, it praises the Creator; with me it sings a hymn to the Lord our God. Where its grace is greatest, there it shares fellowship with me. Where the sun blesses, there the earth blesses. Fruitful trees bless, cattle bless, birds bless with me (Ps. 148:3 ff.). Set at sea, the sailor blames the sun and longs for me; in the mountains, the shepherd avoids it and hastens to my shoots, to my trees, beneath which he may be shaded when overheated, and thirsty and weary runs to my springs.”

## Chapter II

The sun serves the Son of God, by whom it was created along with the other lights as an ornament of heaven. Fertility was bestowed upon the earth by God, not by the sun; for the sun was made to rule the day, just as the moon was made to rule the night. This is also applied to Christ and the Church.

[Col. 0189D]

5. But lest the testimony of your eyes seem slight to you, cleanse your ear and apply it to the heavenly oracles. For every word stands by two or three witnesses. Hear the one who says: “Let lights be made in the firmament of heaven for the illumination of the earth” (Gen. 1:14). Who says this? God says it. And to whom does he speak, if not to the Son? Therefore God the Father says, “Let the sun be made,” and the Son made the sun. For it was fitting that the Sun of righteousness should make the sun of the world. He himself brought it into the light, he himself illuminated it, he himself gave it the power to pour forth light.

The sun, therefore, was made; and for that reason it too serves, since it is said: “You founded the earth, and it remains; by your ordinance the day remains, because all things serve you” (Ps. 118:90–91). For if the day serves, how does the sun not serve, which was made to rule the day? How do the moon and stars not serve, which were made to rule the night? Indeed, the greater the grace which the Creator gave them—so that the air shines more brightly than usual with the sun’s radiance, the day gleams more serenely, the darkness of night is illuminated by the brilliance of moon and stars, and heaven, crowned as it were with flowers, sparkles with fiery lights, so that you might suppose it shines like a paradise in spring, painted with living necklaces of breathing roses—the more beauty appears to have been bestowed on them, the more they owe. For “to whom more is entrusted, more is owed.” Hence it has rightly been called by many the ornament of heaven, because it is a precious necklace of stars.

6. And so that we may know that the fertility of lands is not ascribed to the sun’s heat but credited to divine bounty, the Prophet says: “All things wait upon you, that you may give them food in due season; when you give to them, they gather it; when you open your hand, all shall be filled with goodness” (Ps. 103).

> [Note: Col. 0189D] All editions and many manuscripts: “shall be filled with abundance.” Seven manuscripts of the best quality, and the Septuagint: “… with goodness.”

And below: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth” (ibid., 30). And in the Gospel: “Consider the birds of heaven, for they neither sow nor reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matt. 6:16). The sun and moon, therefore, are not the authors of fertility; rather, God the Father through the Lord Jesus grants to all the bounty of fertility.

> [Note: Col. 0190D] Certain Paris editions: “but God through the Lord,” etc.

[Col. 0190C]

7. The Prophet has also finely explained to us what he means in saying, “God made the sun to rule the day and the moon to rule the night” (Ps. 135:8–9). For in that one hundred and third psalm mentioned above he wrote: “He made the moon for seasons; the sun knew its setting” (Ps. 103:19). When the day begins to complete its hours, the sun recognizes the setting owed to it. Thus the sun is under the rule of the day, and the moon under that of the night; it is compelled to obey the alternations of seasons and is now filled with light, now emptied.

Although many appear to understand this passage mystically of Christ and the Church: Christ recognized the passion of his own body, he who said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son” (John 17:1), so that by that setting of his he might give eternal life to all who were pressed down by the setting of perpetual death. And the Church has its seasons, namely, of persecution and peace. For it seems to wane like the moon, but does not fail. It can be overshadowed, but cannot fail, because it is diminished by the departure of some in persecutions, in order that it may be filled by the confessions of martyrs and, made glorious by the victories of blood poured out for Christ, may pour forth over the whole world a greater light of its devotion and faith.

For the moon has a diminution of light, not of body, when it appears in the monthly cycle to lay aside its light in order to borrow it from the sun. This can readily be perceived when the air is clear and transparent and no cloud drawn over it makes it dim. For the moon’s disk remains whole, although not all of it shines equally. It is as large as it usually appears when full of light, but, deprived of its light through a kind of shadow, it appears otherwise. Hence its horns shine, because its body is spread out in a circle and, as the light of a portion fails, is gradually revealed.

> [Note: Col. 0191D] All editions: “is curved by the light.” By contrast, almost all manuscripts: “is gradually revealed by the light,” a compound in place of a simple verb.

## Chapter III

The light of day is one thing, that of the heavenly bodies another. The distinction of day and night is marked by two signs; fire has a double operation, to illuminate and to burn, which will be separated in the recompense of merits. God is called a consuming fire, and the reason why. Finally, every body has its own shadow attached to it.

[Col. 0191B]

8. It may cause difficulty that he says: “Let lights be made for illumination over the earth, to distinguish between day and night” (Gen. 1:13). For above, when he made the light, he had already said: “God separated light from darkness, and there was evening and there was morning, one day.” But let us consider that the light of day is one thing, and the light of sun and moon and the light of stars another, since the sun itself seems by its rays to add brilliance to daylight; this can be shown both by the rising and by the setting of the day. For before the sun, the day is indeed light, but does not shine brightly; for with the midday sun it shines more brightly still. The Prophet shows this in saying: “He will bring forth your righteousness as light, and your judgment as the noonday” (Ps. 36:6). For he compared the righteousness of the saints not only to light, but even to noonday light.

> [Note: Col. 0191D] The Roman edition alone: “for illumination of the earth.” And certainly in the preceding chapter it is quoted thus in all manuscripts and editions. But either reading may be approved. For although the Septuagint commonly has *eis phausin epi tēs gēs* (“for illumination upon the earth”), one ancient codex, as Nobilius attests, has *eis phausin tēs gēs* (“for illumination of the earth”).

[Col. 0191C]

9. Then he willed there to be not merely one sign but two of the distinction between day and night: both light and the rising of the sun distinguish the day; and again, the waning of light and the rising of the stars distinguish the day’s setting and the beginning of night. For when the sun has set, some remnants of day nevertheless remain until darkness covers the earth; then the moon and stars rise. Concerning the night, certainly, it is plainly clear that the illumination of moon and stars marks out the spaces of night, since by day the rising sun conceals that lunar brilliance and the light of all the stars.

But concerning the day, even the blazing heat of the sun can teach us that daylight and the sun have different natures, and that their appearance itself differs in color. The appearance of light is simple: it provides illumination. The sun, however, possesses not only the power of illuminating but also that of warming; for it is fiery. Fire both illuminates and burns. Hence, when the Lord wished to show Moses the miracle of his operation, by which he might summon Moses to obedience and kindle his disposition to faith, he appeared in fire in the bush; and the bush was not burned, but the fire was seen merely to shine in appearance. One function of fire, therefore, was inactive; the other was at work. The power to burn was inactive; the power to illuminate was at work. Moses therefore was amazed because fire, contrary to its nature, did not burn the bush, though it is accustomed to burn even stronger material. But the Lord’s fire is accustomed to illuminate, not to burn.

10. But perhaps you say: “How then is it written, ‘I am a consuming fire’?” (Deut. 4:24). You have rightly reminded me. It is not accustomed to consume anything except sins alone. In the recompense of merits, too, we infer that the nature of fire is divided: it illuminates some and burns others; it illuminates the righteous and burns the impious. It does not burn those whom it illuminates, nor illuminate those whom it burns; rather, its illumination is unquenchable for the enjoyment of the good, and its burning vehement for the punishment of sins.

> [Note: Col. 0192D] Manuscripts of Reims, Corbie, and the Royal collection: “the nature of divine fire.”

> [Note: Col. 0192D] Four manuscripts: “for the perfection of the good.” Better are the others and the editions: “for their enjoyment,” that is, for fruition. Basil has *eis apolausin tois dikaiois*, “for enjoyment by the righteous.” Ambrose uses this word more than once.

[Col. 0192B]

11. But let us return to the distinction between day and night. When the light of day rises, night is put to flight; when day departs, night is poured forth. For light has no fellowship whatever with darkness; indeed, by natural law the Lord established this in his first operation. For when he made the light, he also made a distinction between light and darkness. Thus, in the day itself, when the sun has already been spread over the earth, we see the shadow of a person or some little shrub separated from the light: in the morning it extends westward, in the evening it turns back eastward, and at midday it inclines northward. Yet it is not confused or mingled with the light, but yields and flees from it.

Likewise night appears to yield to the day and withdraw from its light. For, as those more learned men who preceded us either in age or office have proved, it is the shadow of the earth. For a shadow naturally adheres and is joined to a body, so much so that painters too endeavor to portray the shadows of the bodies they paint, and assert that it belongs to art not to omit the force of nature; one whose painting does not also depict its own shadow is regarded as a violator, as it were, of natural law. Therefore, just as in the day, when some body comes directly opposite the sun, the shadow lies on the side from which the light is reflected, so, when day declines and the earth’s obstruction comes directly opposite its light or the sun, the air is overshadowed. Hence it is clear that the earth’s shadow makes night.

> [Note: Col. 0192D] The Amerbach edition and some Paris editions, with four manuscripts: “on the side on which it is struck by the light,” less suitably.

## Chapter IV

The lights were made for signs, but not for birth-nativities. The science of astrologers is useless and impossible. How absurdly it transfers the characteristics of terrestrial animals to heavenly things, and those of heavenly things to human beings. How ridiculously it asserts that a fixed condition of life depends upon wandering signs. How impiously it attributes to them qualities that injure the innocent. Finally, how foolishly it proposes manifest falsehoods and supplies an excuse for wickedness and idleness.

[Col. 0192D]

12. He therefore made the sun, moon, and stars, and assigned them measures of time: measures of the day to the sun, measures of the night to moon and stars, so that the former might increase the grace of day and the latter illuminate shadow and darkness. “And let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years” (Gen. 1:14). The sun and moon with the stars have divided seasons and equal measures according to the cycles of the months, and they are for signs.

We cannot deny that some signs are gathered from sun and moon, for the Lord also said: “There shall be signs in sun, moon, and stars” (Luke 21:25). And when the Apostles asked for the sign of his coming, he answered: “The sun shall be darkened, the moon shall not give its light, and the stars shall fall from heaven” (Matt. 24:29). He said that these would be signs of the coming consummation; but a fitting measure must be kept by our care.

13. For some have attempted to set forth the qualities of nativities—what sort of person each one born will be. This is not only vain but also useless for those who inquire, and impossible for those who promise it. For what is so useless as for each person to persuade himself that he is what he was born? No one, then, ought to change his life, condition, or character and strive to become better, but ought to remain in that persuasion. Nor can you praise the virtuous or condemn the wicked person, if each appears to be answering to the necessity of his birth. And how could the Lord have set rewards before the good and punishments before the wicked, if necessity produces discipline and the course of the stars shapes one’s way of life? What else is this but to strip a human being of humanity, if nothing is left to character, instruction, or endeavor?

> [Note: Col. 0193D] Thus eleven manuscripts. Others and the editions: “and strive to become better.” But in that persuasion neither the virtuous, etc.

How many do we see rescued from crimes and sins and turned to a better state! The Apostles were redeemed and gathered from among sinners. Certainly it was not the hour of their birth, but Christ’s coming that sanctified them; and the hour of the Lord’s Passion redeemed them from death. The condemned thief, he who was crucified with the Lord, passed to the eternity of paradise not by the benefit of his birth but by the confession of faith.

> [Note: Col. 0193D] Editions and a few manuscripts: “that thief condemned to capital punishment, he with the Lord,” etc. Ten others of better date, as in our text.

Jonah was cast into the sea not by the force of his birth but by the offense of having disregarded the divine command; the sea monster received him and, as a sign of the future mystery, vomited him out after three days, preserving him through the merit of prophetic grace. The angel of Christ, not the ordering of the stars, delivered Peter from prison and imminent execution. Blindness converted Paul to grace; when bitten by a viper and shaken by shipwreck, he was preserved not by remedies supplied by his birth but by the merits of devotion. What shall we say of those who, having died, rose again through their prayers? Did their own birth or apostolic grace restore them to life? What need was there for them to give themselves over to fasts and dangers if they could arrive wherever they wished by the benefit of their birth? If they had believed this, while waiting for the necessity of fate they would never have attained so great a grace.

> [Note: Col. 0193D] Eight manuscripts of not poor quality: “But if they had not believed.”

This persuasion, then, is useless.

14. Moreover, it is impossible. For, to take something from their own argument for the sake of refuting it, not approving it: they say that birth has great force, and that it must be determined by certain minute instants; unless it is determined with complete accuracy, the difference is immense. For, in a brief atom and tiny moment, they say, the birth of poor and powerful, needy and rich, innocent and guilty persons differs; and often one destined for long life and one who will die at the first age of childhood are born in the same hour, provided the remaining circumstances differ and are distinguished by some point. Let them explain how they can determine this.

Suppose a woman gives birth. The midwife surely first knows it, examines the cry by which the life of the newborn is inferred, and observes whether it is male or female. How many moments, if you please, may pass during these delays? Suppose the astrologer is ready. Can a man be present at childbirth? While the midwife sends word, the Chaldean hears it and sets the horoscope: the fate of the one already born has passed into another’s lot; inquiry is made about one person, and another’s nativity is proposed.

> [Note: Col. 0193D] An instrument for marking the hour of birth.

Suppose their view concerning the necessities of births to be true: the calculation cannot be true. Points pass; irrecoverable time flees. There is no doubt that time exists in an atom and in the moment of an eye. I am led to believe it, since we all shall be raised in an atom, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, as the Apostle testifies, saying: “Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall indeed all rise, but we shall not all be changed, in an atom, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet shall sound, the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Cor. 15:52). Between the bringing forth, receiving, and laying down of the little pledge, between its cry and the announcement, how many atoms have passed! And this is if I have treated these matters simply.

For they themselves divide that life-governing circuit of the twelve signs into twelve parts. And because in thirty days the sun traverses the twelfth part of the sphere, said to be immeasurable, in order that the sun’s revolution may complete the circuit of the year, they divide each of those twelve parts into thirty small portions, which the Greeks call *moirai* (“degrees”); they further divide each small portion into sixty turns. Again, each of those sixty they cut into sixty parts. How incomprehensible it is that the moments of birth should be determined by the sixtieth part of a sixtieth portion, and that anyone should know the motion or character of each sign at the birth of the person born! Since it is impossible to comprehend temporal minutiae so subtle, while a slight variation introduces error into the whole calculation, the entire business is full of vanity.

> [Note: Col. 0194D] All editions: “in what sixtieth so many sixtieths … the moments are situated.”

Those who debate matters belonging to themselves do not know them; how can they know things belonging to others? They do not know what threatens them; how can they announce to others what will happen to them? It is ridiculous to believe that, if they could do so, they would not rather provide for themselves.

15. Further, how absurd it is that, if someone says he was born under the sign of Aries, he should be judged outstanding in counsel from the habit of a sheep because such an animal stands out in its flock; or richer because the ram has a natural covering and gains annually from its garment, and that financial profits should therefore seem familiar to that man! Similarly, they argue from the signs of Taurus and Pisces, judging that the motions of heaven and the powers of the signs are to be interpreted from the nature of cheap animals. Thus our food establishes for us the decrees of life, and our provisions—that is, ram, bull, and fish—imprint upon us a discipline of character.

How, then, do they derive from heaven the causes of things and the substance of this life, when they assign to the heavenly signs themselves the causes of their motion from the qualities of lowly food? They call one born under the sign of the ram generous because the ram does not unwillingly lay aside its wool; and they prefer to ascribe such a virtue to the nature of a lowly animal rather than to heaven, from which fair weather shines upon us and rain often falls. They call those whom Taurus has seen at their birth industrious and patient in service, because it is a hard-working animal, accustomed to the yoke and submitting its neck to voluntary servitude.

> [Note: Col. 0195D] The most ancient manuscripts of Chartres and Corbie: “and submits its neck to the yoke in voluntary servitude.” An old edition: “submitting its neck.” Five manuscripts: “placing it beneath.”

They likewise call one whose birth Scorpio has encompassed in its own portion a striker and one vomiting forth the poisons of wickedness, because it is a venomous animal. What authority for life, then, do you pretend will be given by the dignity of heavenly signs, while you derive the support of your assertion from such trifles? For if characteristics of conduct derived from animals are impressed upon the motions of heaven, heaven itself appears subject to the power of animal nature, from which it received the causes of the vital substance that it was to bestow on human beings. But if this is abhorrent to truth, far more ridiculous is their drawing from this source the credibility of their argument, destitute as they are of the support of truth.

16. Next let us consider this: they call those signs “planets,” from whose movements they assert that the necessities of our lives are formed. Whether, then, as the name indicates, they always wander, or—as they themselves say—they are borne with swift motion and ten thousand times in a day, or, if that seems incredible, change their appearance in many ways through their innumerable revolutions, it lacks credibility that by so wandering an irregularity and such swift motion they should determine for us a fixed and immovable substance and lot of life. Yet they say that the motions of all are not equal, but the circuits of some are swifter, others slower, so that in the same hour they often see one another and often hide one another, while one passes beyond another.

17. They say, moreover, that it matters greatly whether beneficent signs or maleficent and harmful ones behold the birth of the person born; and that the difference in a nativity lies in this: the aspect of a beneficent sign contributes greatly, while that of a maleficent and harmful sign harms greatly. For this is how they habitually call the very signs that they worship. I must necessarily use the names of those whose assertions I use, lest they complain that their arguments have been mentioned as unknown rather than emptied and demolished.

And so, since they cannot comprehend that wandering and swift motion, it often happens that, through the imperceptible subtlety of a point and moment, they posit the aspect of a beneficent sign where a grave and harmful influence intervenes. What wonder if people are deceived there, where harmless signs are blasphemed? If they are believed harmful by nature, then the supreme God is accused, if he made what is evil and was the maker of wickedness. But if they are thought, by their own will, to have undertaken to harm innocent persons who as yet know themselves guilty of no evil deed—persons to whom punishment is assigned before guilt—what is so irrational, surpassing even the savagery of irrational beasts, as that the experience of fraud or favor should be attributed not to human merits but to the motions of signs?

“He committed no offense,” they say, “but a harmful star looked upon him. Saturn’s star came in his way. It turned aside a little, removed misery from him, and acquitted him of crime.”

18. But their wisdom is comparable to a spider’s web: if a gnat or fly falls into it, it cannot free itself; but if any kind of stronger creature is seen to encounter it, it passes through, breaks the weak meshes, and scatters the empty snares. Such are the nets of the Chaldeans: the weak stick in them, but those stronger in understanding cannot be caught by their trap. Therefore you who are stronger, when you see astrologers, say: “They have woven a spider’s web, which can have neither any use nor any binding force unless you, like a gnat or fly, fall into it through the stumbling of your weakness; but, like a sparrow or dove, you should scatter the feeble meshes with the swift speed of your flying.”

For what sensible person would believe that the movements of signs, which often change within a day and return upon themselves in many ways, bear the marks of powers? If this were so, how many figures of royal nativities would be formed each day! Kings, then, would be born every day, and royal succession would not be transmitted to sons; rather, from every different condition persons would arise who acquired the right of imperial power. What king, then, calculates his son’s nativity to discover whether rule is owed to him, instead of transferring the succession of his own kingdom to his descendants by his own decision?

Certainly we read that Abijah begot Asa, Asa begot Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat begot Joram, and Joram begot Uzziah (Matt. 1:7–8); and all the remaining succession down to the captivity was carried through kings alike in lineage and in rank. Could they, because they were kings, command the heavenly signs to shape their movements? For what human being can have dominion over them?

19. Next, if our actions and deeds are to be attributed to the necessity of birth rather than to moral choices, why have laws been proposed and legal enactments promulgated, by which punishment is assigned to the wicked or security granted to the innocent? Why is pardon not given to the accused, when, as they themselves say, they have sinned not by their own will but from necessity? Why does the farmer labor [Col. 0197B], instead of waiting for the unworked fruits, by the privilege of his birth, to be carried into the storehouses? [Note: [Col. 0197D] Thus the manuscripts of better quality. Yet most manuscripts and all editions read: “If he was so born that riches and wealth flow to him, so that the earth may bear for him spontaneous revenues without any seed or labor.”] If he was so born that wealth flows to him without labor, let him certainly wait for the earth to bear him spontaneous revenues without any seed; let him not drive the ploughshare into the fields, lay his hand to the curved sickle, or undertake the expense of gathering the vintage. Rather, let flowing wines pour of their own accord into all his *seriae* [wine jars]; let the berry of the wild olive, without any trunks having been grafted, sweat forth oil for him of itself. Nor, if a treasure of riches can fall upon him while he is idle by some, as they say, natal lot, should the merchant, anxious for his own safety, dread the risk of crossing the wide sea. But this is not the judgment of all men. [Col. 0197C] Accordingly, the tireless farmer cleaves the earth with the lowered plough: naked he ploughs, naked he sows, naked beneath the burning sun he threshes on the floor the grain parched by heat. [Note: [Col. 0197D] Manuscript Car.: “he threshes on the threshing-floor grain scorched in summer.” Editions: “he gathers grain scorched in summer.”] And the merchant, impatient when the east winds blow, often furrows the sea in an unsafe vessel.

Therefore the prophet, condemning their recklessness and rashness, says: “Be ashamed, Sidon,” says the sea (Isa. 23:4). That is: if dangers do not move you, at least let shame restrain you; let modesty confound you. Be ashamed, Sidon, in which there is no place for courage, no concern for safety, no young men devoted to guarding their country in war and trained in arms, but every concern is for gain and every pursuit for trade. “The seed,” he says, “of merchants is like a harvest” (ibid., v. 3). But what reward is there for the Christian, if he arranges his cares and labors not by will [Col. 0197D] but by necessity? For where necessity is decreed, there industry is without honor. [Note: [Col. 0198D] Five manuscripts and all editions: “direct necessity.”]

## CHAPTER V

The yearly seasons are determined by the proximity or remoteness of the luminaries; this is applied to Christ, the Synagogue, and the Church. Why shadows are greater in winter and smaller in summer, and certain other matters of this sort. Finally, how the same luminaries are “for days.”

[Col. 0198A]

20. We have said much; we do not wish to say more, lest anyone think that what we have taken up from their assertions in order to refute them has been adopted for approval. For what we laughed at as boys, can we, now old men, be able to recount? Let us now direct our pen to the matters remaining according to the reading.

21. “Let there be,” he says, “lights for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years.” We have spoken of signs. But what are seasons except the alternating changes—winter, spring, summer, and autumn? In these seasons the sun’s passage is either swifter or slower. Some things it lightly touches with its rays; others it inflames with its heat. Thus, when the sun lingers in the southern [Col. 0198B] regions, it is winter for us. [Note: [Col. 0198D] Carnotensis, Benedictine, and some others: “the day is far from us.”] For when the sun is farther away, the earth stiffens with frost, is bound by cold, and the abundant shadow of night covers the lands, so that the intervals of night are much longer than those of day. Hence arises the reason why, in winter winds, an excessive force of snow and rain is poured forth.

But when, withdrawing from the southern regions, it returns over the earth, it makes the times of night and day equal. And the more delays it adds to its courses, the more gradually it restores the mildness of this air and recalls the gentleness of the breezes, which, cherishing all things, compels them to renewed offspring: the earth sprouts, seeds loosened in furrows revive, trees grow green, and the succession of annual progeny is propagated for the perpetual preservation of the kind, both of those things which are on land and of those that delight in the waters. But when it raises itself toward the summer turning-point in the north, it lengthens the daylight hours and contracts and shortens the nights. Therefore, the more continuously it is joined and mingled with this air, the more it heats the air itself, dries the moisture of the earth, causes seeds to grow, and ripens the fruits of the woods, as it were, into vigorous juices. Then, because it burns more fiercely, it makes smaller shadows at noon, since from on high it illuminates this region.

22. Hence the Synagogue says in the Song of Songs: “Tell me, you whom my soul loved, where you feed, where you rest at noon, lest perhaps I become veiled among the flocks of your companions” (Song 1:6). That is: Tell me, Christ, whom [Col. 0198D] my soul loved. Why not rather, “whom it loves”? But the Synagogue loved; the Church loves; and it never changes its affection toward its Christ. “Where,” she says, “do you feed, where do you rest at noon?” I desire to follow you like one brought up by you, [Note: [Col. 0198D] Old edition with a few manuscripts: “who, as though joined to you, was formerly held back.” Roman edition: “whom . . . I held back.” Eight better manuscripts: “whom . . . I held back.” One: “whom . . . was holding back.”] whom, as though joined to you, I formerly held back, and to seek your flocks, because I lost my own.

“You feed at noon”: that is, in the place of the Church, where righteousness shines, where judgment gleams [Col. 0199A] like noon, where no shadow is seen, where days are longer because the Sun of righteousness lingers over them longer, as in summer months. Thus the day of the Lord is not short but great, because it is written: “Until the great day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2:31). Hence Jacob also says: “All the days of my life which I have lived are few and evil” (Gen. 47:9). For doubtful light is evil. Therefore, days of doubtful light are short and shadowy; great days are without shadow, as many have learned by practice and example in certain hotter regions.

The Synagogue, therefore, in short and evil days—of which Jacob often bears the type in his own person, or the shadow of its people—had very much shadow, because it did not see the Sun of righteousness, and saw him not from on high [Col. 0199B] over its head, but shining from the south, when it was winter for it. But to the Church it is said: “Winter has passed; it has gone away; flowers have appeared on the earth; the time of harvest has come” (Song 2:11). Before Christ’s coming it was winter; after Christ’s coming there are the flowers of spring and the harvest of summer. Therefore, seeing him shining from the south and from the conversion of the Gentiles, it is overshadowed.

But the Gentile people—those who were in confusion, the Gentiles who sat in darkness—“saw a great light; for those sitting in the region of the shadow of death, light has arisen” (cf. Isa. 9:2). [Note: [Col. 0199D] Thus almost all manuscripts. The Benedictine edition, however, has: “who was in Gentile confusion, and who sat in darkness.” The editions have: “who was of confusion and Gentile” (some Paris manuscripts omit “and Gentile”), “who sat,” etc.] It is the great light of divinity, which no shadow of death obscures. Therefore it shines from on high, because this too is written, Zacharias saying: “By which the Dayspring from on high has visited us, to give light to those [Col. 0199C] who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1:78–79).

There is also a certain shadow of salvation, not of death, as in this: “Protect me beneath the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16:8). It is a shadow indeed, because it is of the body; a shadow, because it is of the cross; but a shadow of salvation, [Note: [Col. 0199D] Many good manuscripts: “because forgiveness of sins was present.” Others and the editions: as in the text.] because in it were forgiveness of sins and the resurrection of the dead.

23. We may therefore take an example: winter days are short but have larger shadows; summer days are longer but have smaller shadows. At midday too the shadow is smaller than it is either at the beginning or at the end of the day; and this is so among us in the western region. [Note: [Col. 0199D] Edition with certain inferior manuscripts: “Moreover [Col. 0200D] there are those who say that for two …”] Moreover, there are persons who, for two days of the whole year, are without shadow in the southern regions, because, having the sun above their head, they are illuminated all around in every direction; whence they are called in Greek *askioi* (ἄσκιοι), “shadowless.” Many also report that the sun so stands directly above them that, through the narrow openings of wells, they see the water in their depths shining.

Those who are called *amphiskioi* (ἀμφίσκιοι), “double-shadowed,” are said to be in the south, because they cast their shadow on either side. For, when one walks opposite the sun, the shadow lies behind one’s back: for example, if you go toward the east in the morning; if [Col. 0200A] you proceed toward the southern quarter at midday; or if you go toward the west at sunset. Thus from three directions the sun meets you: from the east, south, and west. Morning and evening it is behind your back; at noon it is also at your side. But the sun is never in the north; consequently, if you travel toward the north—whether morning, evening, or noon—the sun cannot be behind your back. [Note: [Col. 0200D] Thus the Roman edition with the Vatican, Benedictine, and German manuscripts, which Basil also supports. Other editions and manuscripts: “shadow. If you go toward the north . . . the sun cannot be behind your back. For there are …” Yet the words “sun” and “to the sun” are lacking in some codices.]

Only those in this inhabited world of ours situated toward [Note: [Col. 0200D] Vatican manuscript and Basil: “situated beyond Arabia.”] the south are seen to cast their shadow toward the southern quarter. This, however, is said to happen in the height of summer, when the sun turns toward the north. Then autumn receives us and indeed breaks the intensity of the heat; but, after the heat has been somewhat relaxed and laid aside, it hands us over through the moderation of a middle tempering, without harm [Col. 0200B] or injury, to the winter winds.

24. “Let them be also for days,” he says: not in order that they may make the days, but that they may have authority in them—so that the sun may illuminate the day’s rising with richer grace and, by the service of its course, may have the power to mark out the whole day. Some understand in this way the prophet’s statement: “The sun for dominion over the day; the moon and stars for dominion over the night” (Ps. 136:8). For they carry light around. They are also appointed for years, the sun and moon. The moon, completing its course twelve times in three hundred days, completes the year according to the Hebrews, with certain days added; according to the Romans, by the insertion of one day once in five years, with the bissextile day observed. The solar year also occurs when the sun, having completed its circuit through all the signs, returns to that point from which it took the beginning [Col. 0200C] of its course. For it is said to complete the whole interval in a year.

## CHAPTER VI

The greatness of the sun and moon is proved from the fact that they appear the same to everyone. An objection concerning the view of remote things is resolved and elegantly discussed; then, after the sun’s greatness has been established, something is added concerning its tempering.

25. God therefore made these two great lights. We may understand them as great not so much by comparison with other things as by their own office, just as heaven is great and the sea is great. For the sun is great, filling the world with its heat, and the moon with its light; and not only the lands, but also this air, the sea, [Col. 0200D] and the face of heaven. Wherever they may be in heaven, they illuminate all things and are viewed equally by all, so that individual peoples believe that they linger only over their own regions and are present and shine only for themselves. Yet they shine equally for all, so that no one thinks anyone else is nearer to them than he himself is.

A clear example of their greatness is that the same lunar disk is seen by all the people of the world. For although its light sometimes increases and decreases, nevertheless on the same night it appears to all as it appears to me. For if it appeared smaller to those far away, it would shine larger to those nearer, and thereby reveal a sign of narrowness and smallness. Indeed, we judge all other things smaller when they are far away and believe them greater when we behold them more closely; the nearer you are, the more the size of the thing you see increases for you. The sun’s [Note: [Col. 0201D] The Roman edition alone: “The disk of the sun is nearer to no one.”] ray is nearer to no one and farther from no one; likewise the moon’s globe is equal for all. The sun appears alike to Indians and Britons at the same moment when it rises. Nor, when it inclines toward its setting, does it appear smaller to eastern peoples than to western; nor is it judged lower to western peoples at its rising than to eastern peoples. “How far,” he says, “is east from west?” (Ps. 103:12). These are distant from one another; but the sun is distant from no one, more present to no one, more remote from no one.

26. Nor should it trouble you that, when it rises, the sun’s disk appears about a cubit across to you. Rather consider how great is the space between the sun and the earth, which the weakness of our sight cannot traverse without great loss to itself. Our sight grows dim; does the sun or moon grow dim? Our vision is narrow; does it therefore make the things seen narrower? The appearance is reduced; the magnitude is not diminished. We should not ascribe the afflictions of our weakness to an affliction of the lights. Our sight deceives us: therefore do not judge its verdict trustworthy. The visible form of heavenly things becomes smaller, not their actual form.

If from the summit of high mountains [Col. 0201C] you wish to look upon a plain lying beneath your eyes, and upon herds grazing there, do you not judge their bodies to be like ants? If you view the sea from some coastal lookout, do not the largest ships among the blue waves, and their shining white sails, seem to you from your distant position to present the appearance of flying doves? And the islands themselves, which divide the sea and split apart the fields of land—within how narrow a boundary do they seem to be enclosed! How do rough things appear rounded, dense things sparse! Weigh, therefore, these weaknesses of your sight, and summon yourself as a just judge of the truth of what we have established.

27. If you wish to estimate the magnitude of the sun not only with the eye of the mind but also with that of the body, consider how great the globes of the stars appear to weave the axis of heaven [Col. 0201D] and mark it with innumerable lights. Yet they cannot wipe away the darkness of night and the clouds of heaven. As soon as the sun has sent forth the signs of its rising, all the fires of the stars vanish beneath the brilliance of one luminary; the air is opened and the face of heaven is suffused with a purpling glow. Though it is only breathing its beginning, the splendor of full light already flashes with instantaneous speed, and the sweet preceding breeze of the rising sun breathes forth. [Note: [Col. 0201D] Six manuscripts: “the sweet dawn breathes forth.”] Tell me, I pray: unless its disk were great, how could it illuminate the great circle of the earth?

28. What, moreover, should I say of the Creator’s great tempering and [Col. 0202A] moderation, who assigned such a measure to the sun’s function that its fiery vapor, as it appears, might neither burn up, when poured in, the veins of the earth, its juices, and the forms of things; nor, on the other hand, might it be cooled through so great an expanse of the world and impart no seed of heat to the lands, leaving them barren and poor in fruits, and warming them toward no grace of fertility?

## CHAPTER VII

Many things said of the sun also apply to the moon; yet it has effects of its own, some of which are here enumerated.

29. The same considerations concerning the moon apply as those we have mentioned regarding its companion and brother. For it has undertaken the same ministry as its brother: to illuminate [Col. 0202B] darkness, nourish seeds, and increase fruits. Yet it has many characteristics distinct from its brother. The heat that has dried the earth’s moisture throughout the day is restored by dew during the brief time of night; for the moon too is said to be generous with dew. Thus, when the night is clearer and the moon shines all night, dew is said to soak the fields more abundantly. Many who rest in the open air have felt that, the more they were under the moon’s light, the more moisture gathered upon their heads. Hence Christ says to the Church in the Song of Songs: “For my head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of the night” (Song 5:2).

Then it decreases and increases, so that it is smaller when it rises anew, and, when diminished, is filled out. In this there is a great mystery. For the elements also suffer with its waning; and with its increase, things which have been depleted [Col. 0202C] are replenished, such as the brains of animals and moist creatures of the sea. Indeed, oysters are said to be found fuller, along with many other things, when the lunar globe is growing. Those who have learned it by their own observation assert the same concerning the insides of trees. Thus we see that its rising and waning are due to design, not weakness. It would never cause so great a change in things unless it possessed outstanding power and grace bestowed by the Creator.

30. Some learned and Christian men have also maintained that the air is accustomed to change at the moon’s rising. But if this change were produced by some force of the moon’s alteration, the heaven would be covered with clouds at every rising of it, and rains would be poured out. Thus, when there had been discussion some days earlier about rain said to be going to be useful, someone said: [Col. 0202D] “Look, the new moon will bring it.” And although we desired rain, I did not want assertions of that kind to be true. Accordingly, I was pleased that no rain was poured out, until it was given through the Church’s prayers, demonstrating that rain must be hoped for not from the moon’s beginnings but from the Creator’s providence and mercy.

Certainly, although the Euripi swell on every side according to the other phases of the moon and pour back the waves they have received—or themselves are carried with great force—yet at its rising they stand calm so long as the moon is without light. But when the advance of days [Note: [Col. 0202D] Old edition and certain Paris editions with four manuscripts: “has increased its advance.”] has uncovered it, then [Col. 0203A] they return to their ebbing courses. [Note: [Col. 0203D] *Ampotis*, Greek ἄμπωτις: “the return-flow of waves,” i.e. ebb-tide.] The *ampotis* also, which is said to occur in the Ocean, although on other days it is said to maintain its regular order, is reported at the moon’s rising to give clear evidence of its change: the western sea itself, in which the *ampotis* is observed, advances and withdraws more than usual and is carried in a greater surge, as though drawn backward by certain breathings of the moon, and then, driven and drawn back again by the same influences, is poured back into its proper measure.

## CHAPTER VIII

The moon’s change teaches the instability of things; but this is shamefully reproduced in our moral life. It also represents the mystery of Christ and the Church; those who believe that it can be drawn down from heaven by magical chants are to be ridiculed.

[Col. 0203B]

31. Therefore, if you wonder how the moon can suffer waning, although it possesses so great a power of change, consider that in this too there is a great mystery: by its example you learn, O human being, that nothing among human affairs or the whole creation of the world can exist without at some time being dissolved. For if even the moon, to which the Lord entrusted so great a ministry—to illuminate the world—and which both grows and wanes, [Note: [Col. 0203D] Thus the better manuscripts. The others read in part: “all things which,” or “and all things which have arisen from nothing and come to perfection, again”; in part: “because all things which . . . again,” etc. The Vatican manuscript alone: “and all things which have arisen from nothing, as soon as they have come [Col. 0204D] to perfection, again,” etc. The editions: “because all things from nothing,” etc., as in the text.] for all things which have arisen from nothing and reached perfection diminish again once perfected—for heaven and earth shall pass away—why do we not adopt such moderation, so as neither to cast down our spirit in adversity? For he who made all things from nothing can easily raise you also to the highest and perfect things. And conversely, let us not be lifted up in prosperity, nor boast in any power or riches, nor glory in [Col. 0203C] bodily strength or beauty, where corruption is easy and change frequent; but let us pursue the grace of the soul that abides into the future.

For if the moon’s setting grieves you, though it always repairs and renews itself, much more ought it to grieve you if the soul, once filled by the progress of virtue, afterward, turned aside from its purpose by inconstancy of mind and neglect, often changes its pursuits. That belongs to folly and ignorance. Hence Scripture says: “The fool changes like the moon” (Sir. 27:12). Therefore the wise person does not change with the moon, but will remain with the sun. Hence the moon is not a participant in folly: the moon does not change like the fool; rather, the fool changes like the moon. Thus the seed of the righteous remains like the moon, perfected forever, and the faithful witness in heaven. For it is one thing to perform a ministry, another to be carried about in one’s disposition and, through weakness of understanding, to have no settled judgment.

The moon labors for you and is subject for God’s will. “For creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope.” Therefore it does not change willingly; you change willingly. It groans and labors together in its change; you do not understand and often rejoice. [Col. 0204A] It frequently awaits your redemption, that it may be freed from the common service of all creation; you bring impediment both to your own redemption and to its freedom. Thus it is due to your folly, not its own, that, while you are awaited and do not turn even late, it still changes.

32. Therefore do not assess the moon with the eye of your body, but with the keenness of your mind. The moon is diminished in order to fill the elements. This is truly a great mystery. He who gave grace to all things gave this to it. He emptied it, in order that he who also emptied himself might fill all. For he emptied himself in order to descend to us; he descended to us in order to ascend above all. “He ascended,” it says, “above all heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph. 4:10). Therefore he who had come emptied [Col. 0204B] filled the apostles from his fullness. Hence one of them says: “For from his fullness we all received” (John 1:16).

Thus the moon proclaimed the mystery of Christ. It is no insignificant thing in which he placed his sign; no insignificant thing that bears the type of the beloved Church, as the Prophet signifies in saying: “In his days righteousness shall arise and abundance of peace, until the moon be taken away” (Ps. 72:7). And in the Song of Songs the Lord says of his bride: “Who is she that looks forth like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?” (Song 6:9). The Church is rightly beautiful as the moon: it has shone throughout the whole world and, illuminating the darkness of this age, says: “The night has passed; but the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13:12).

He beautifully says, “looking forth,” as though looking down upon her own from above, as you have: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men” (Ps. 14:2). Therefore, looking forth, the Church, like the moon, has frequent wanings and risings; but it grew through its wanings and deserved to be enlarged through them, being diminished by persecutions and crowned by the martyrdoms of confessors. This is the true moon, which borrows from the perpetual light of its brother the light of immortality and grace. For the Church shines not with its own light but with Christ’s; it draws its splendor from the Sun of righteousness, so that it may say: “Now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).
