Blessed indeed are you, for you have merited so great a distinction! Hence I call you blessed not because of your new moons, but because of the type of the Church. In those you serve; in this you are loved.

33. How ridiculous, moreover, that people often believe you can be drawn down by magical spells! These are old women’s tales and popular opinions. For who would think that a work of God, appointed to so great a ministry, could be assailed by Chaldean superstitions? Let that one fall who transforms himself into an angel of light, and who is brought down by his own will, not by the power of spells. Certainly in this also you are thought, like the Church, capable of being brought down from your place and station. Many attack the Church, but the spells of witchcraft [Note: [Col. 0204D] Some manuscripts: “of sagacity”; others: “of sacrilegious art”; most: “of witchcraft.” Editions: “of magical art,” which comes to the same thing.] cannot harm it. Enchanters [Col. 0205A] have no power where Christ’s song is sung daily. The Church has as its enchanter the Lord Jesus, through whom he rendered void the spells of magicians and enchanters and the poisons of serpents. And it itself, like the serpent lifted up, devours the serpents of Egypt: though a deadly charm may mutter, it is blunted in Christ’s name.

Thus Paul blinded Elymas the magician not only with the weakness of magical art but also with loss of sight. [Note: [Col. 0205B] Manuscript Car.: *Hymum*; Benedictine: *Etymum*; Bigotian and Gemblacensis: *Jeu*; Caen manuscript, first hand, and Gemblacensis, second hand: *Hymeneum*; one Corbie manuscript: *Barjeu*. Elymas in Acts 13 is elsewhere called Barjesus, or, according to some manuscripts, Barjeu. But nowhere do we read that he was called Hymnus [Col. 0206B] or Hymenaeus. One Hymenaeus is indeed mentioned in 1 Timothy 1 and 2 Timothy 2, upon whom the Apostle marks the charge of heresy; but no one has said that he was the same as Elymas.] Thus Peter cast down and overthrew Simon, who sought the heights of heaven by magical flight, when the power of his spells was broken.

## CHAPTER IX

Conclusion of the fourth day. How vain it is to avoid it, and whence the hostility of demons and Gentiles toward it has arisen.

[Col. 0205B]

34. The fourth day, I think, has ended beautifully. Why then are most people accustomed to avoid the fourth day and think it useless to begin something on that number, by which the entire world shone forth in new light? Did the sun begin under sinister omens? And how can it signify good things to others, if it did not know how to choose for itself the day of its rising? Or how do they approve its signs whose rising they do not approve? What, too, shall we say about the moon, which began on the fourth day and marks the day of salvation on the fourteenth? [Note: [Col. 0206B] Some manuscripts: “and on the fifteenth day [it marks] the signs of salvation.”] Does the number by which the mystery of redemption is celebrated displease them? Therefore demons persuade men that this number should be avoided: it is the number by which their wickedness was destroyed. Therefore the Gentiles assert that nothing should be undertaken then, because they know that their arts first began to lose their power at that time and that Gentile peoples migrated to the Church.

They certainly think that the fourth-day moon, if it is clear and its horns are not blunt, gives an indication of fair weather for the remaining days until the month is complete. Thus they do not wish to begin with the same beginnings with which fair weather begins. [Col. 0206B] But now we must beware lest the fourth day set upon us in our discourse: for greater shadows fall from the mountains, the light diminishes, and the shadow increases.

# BOOK V: ON THE WORK OF THE FIFTH DAY

[Col. 0205]

## CHAPTER I (Sermon VII)

After the two higher elements have been adorned, the sea is granted its own prerogative. The obedience of the waters and their wonderful fertility are described—an abundance which humanity abuses by tasting what was forbidden. Finally, it is shown that “creeping things” denotes not only serpents but fishes as well.

[Col. 0205C]

1. The whole earth, clothed in various green growths, was verdant; heaven also shone, adorned by the sun and moon—the twin lights of its countenance—and by the beauty of the stars. The third element remained, namely the sea, so that the grace of vivification might also come to it by divine gift. For all offspring of the earth are nourished by the heavenly spirit. The earth too, releasing its seeds, gives life to all things; and especially when it was first commanded by God’s word to grow green, it put forth shoots by the gift of its life-giving power. Water was idle and seemed to have been granted a holiday from the benefit of divine operation. The Creator still had something to give it, by which it might equal the functions of the earth; he reserved for it the right also to claim something proper and special to itself as a prerogative of the gift bestowed upon it. The earth had first given life, but to things that had no breathing soul. Water is commanded to bring forth things bearing the strength and dignity of a living soul, receiving a sense for preserving life and fleeing death.

2. God therefore said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls according to their kind, and birds flying [Col. 0206B] over the earth according to the firmament of heaven” (Gen. 1:20). [Note: [Col. 0205D] Seven manuscripts omit the words “over the earth”; but below, chapter 22, Ambrose shows why they occur in Sacred Scripture.] The command came, and at once water poured itself out in the births commanded. Rivers began to generate, lakes to give life, and the sea itself to bring forth diverse kinds of creeping things and to pour out according to its kind whatever it had formed. No small pools, no muddy marshes were idle: all assumed the power of creating bestowed upon them. Fish leapt from the river, dolphins played in the waves, shells adhered to rocks, oysters to the depths, and sea-urchins grew.

Alas for me! Allurement—the abundance of resources, [Note: [Col. 0205D] These words are lacking in certain manuscripts: “the abundance of resources, [Col. 0206D] mother of our luxury.”] the mother of our luxury—began before humankind. Delicacies existed before humankind. Human temptation, therefore, came before nature; [Note: [Col. 0206D] Certain manuscripts: “but creation committed no fault.”] but nature committed no fault. It gave food; it did not prescribe vices. It gave these things in common, lest you claim any of them as though they were your own. The earth produces its fruits for you; the waters produce for you parrotfish, sturgeon, and all their offspring. Yet not content with these, you tasted foods forbidden to you. Everything is assembled to your disgrace, so that the transgression of your greed may be made burdensome.

3. But we cannot describe how many kinds and names there are, all of which were animated in the instant of the divine command. At once bodily form came together and the soul was at work, together with the life-giving [Note: [Col. 0206D] Many manuscripts: “some vigor of power.”] vigor of the remaining faculties. The earth was filled with plants; the sea [Col. 0207A] filled with living creatures. There insensible things sprouted; here sentient beings move about. Water even on land claims its own portions for itself. The fishes of the waters lap at the earth and seek their prey from it. Gnats also and little frogs make noise around their breeding marshes; they too heard the Lord’s command saying: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls.”

4. We know that kinds of serpents are called “creeping things” because they creep upon the ground; but far more, everything that swims has either the appearance or the nature of creeping. For even if those that plunge into the deep seem to cleave the water, [Note: [Col. 0207D] Certain manuscripts: “seem to enter.”] nevertheless, when they swim on the surface, they creep with their whole body, which they draw along over certain backs of the water. Hence David also says: “This sea is great and wide; there are creeping things without number” (Ps. 104:25).

Indeed, although many have feet and the use of walking, because they are amphibious and live either in waters or on land—such as seals, crocodiles, river-horses, which they call hippopotamuses because these are produced in the river Nile—nevertheless, when they are in deep water, they do not walk but swim, and do not use the track of the foot for moving, but use it like an oar for creeping. For a ship driven by oars glides and furrows the waters with its keel.

## CHAPTER II

By the power of the words, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things,” far more things were produced in the sea than on land; and the waters received the further grace that creatures harmful on land should be harmless when produced in the sea.

5. “Let the waters bring forth creeping things,” said the Lord. A brief word, but forceful and far-reaching: it infused a common nature into the least and greatest alike. At the same instant the whale is produced and the frog is born by the same power of operation. God does not labor over the greatest things, nor disdain the smallest. Nature did not suffer in bringing forth dolphins, just as it did not suffer when producing tiny purple-shells and snails. Observe, O human being, how many more things there are in the sea than on land. Count, if you can, all kinds of fish, both the smallest and the greatest: cuttlefish, [Note: [Col. 0207D] Four manuscripts have: “*litos*, *ostriotas*, trout, crabs.” Carnotensis: *clitostriata*. German manuscript: *lithostrata*. Caen and Corbie, second but ancient hand: “octopuses, *lithos*, trout, crabs”; perhaps λειόστρακους, “covered with a smooth shell.” Besides, Basil places crabs and crayfish among what are called μαλακόστρακα, that is, creatures covered with soft shells; whereas he places octopuses and cuttlefish among μαλάκια, whose flesh is soft and tender.] octopuses, *lithostraci*, crabs, crayfish, and within these innumerable kinds of their own. What should I say of the kinds of serpents—sea-dragons, morays, eels? Nor shall I pass over scorpions, frogs, tortoises, weasels and sea-dogs, sea-calves, huge whales, dolphins, seals, and sea-lions. What shall I add also about blackbirds, thrushes, and peacocks, whose colors too we see reproduced in birds: black blackbirds, peacocks with backs and necks painted in varied color, thrushes mottled on the belly, and the rest, whose kinds and names the land has claimed for itself? For these first began in the sea [Col. 0208A] and in diverse rivers. Indeed, water was the first, at the command of the divine will, to produce creeping things of living souls.

6. Add this further benefit: what we fear on land, we love in the water. For creatures harmful on land are harmless in water; even snakes themselves are without venom. The lion is terrible on land, gentle amid the waves. The moray, which they say possesses something harmful, is a more valuable food. The frog, repulsive in marshes, is attractive in the water and excels almost every kind of food. If anyone wishes to know more, let him ask fishermen from different regions; for no one can comprehend everything. Yet beware of dogs even in the sea—dogs which the Apostle teaches are troublesome and to be avoided even in the Church, saying: “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers” (Phil. 3:2). The weasel’s smell is offensive on land, pleasant in water. The land creature knows how to avenge itself by the stench of its foulness; this creature has no less charm when caught than when free. Nor shall I dismiss you, thymallus [grayling], without the honour of my account—you whose name has become associated with a flower: whether the water of the river Ticino or that of lovely Athesis [the Adige] has nourished you, you are a flower. Indeed, the common saying bears witness that of one who gives off a pleasing fragrance it is wittily said: “He smells either of fish or of a flower.” Thus the same scent is attributed to fish as to flowers.

> [Note: At [Col. 0207D], many manuscripts read *dictu* or *dictum facessi*, that is, “he goes away” or “wanders about.”]

What is more pleasing than your appearance? What more delightful than your sweetness? What more fragrant than your scent? What honey gives off in fragrance, you breathe forth from your own body. Why should I speak of the gentleness of ravens, or even of wolves? The lamb does not know how to fear these wolves. So great is the grace of the waters that even lions flee their calves, that the prophetic saying concerning the holiness of the Church rightly applies to them: “Then wolves and lambs shall feed together, and the lion and the ox shall eat straw together” (Isa. 65:25). Nor is this surprising, since in the Church too the waters accomplish this: once the wickedness of robbers has been washed away, they are joined with the innocent. Why should I also mention purple dyes, which adorn royal banquets and colour garments? What is worshipped in kings, therefore, belongs to the waters; that splendour which gleams belongs to the waters. Add also sea-pigs, agreeable even to the Jews; for nothing is common that water does not wash, and therefore they cannot regard them as common, as though they had been born on land.

> [Note: [Col. 0208D] Some manuscripts read: “Why should I speak of pigs,” etc.]

> [Note: [Col. 0208D] Thus fifteen manuscripts and the Costantinian edition. Other, inferior manuscripts and the editions of Amerbach, Petri, Erasmus, and Gillius read: “whose calves and lions are represented.” The Roman edition: “… are joined, and lions.”]

## CHAPTER III

That fish have many modes of reproduction and a singular affection for their offspring; how great is their purity, by which they surpass not only other animals but human beings themselves.

[Col. 0208D]

7. Innumerable, then, are the uses and kinds of fish. Some lay eggs, such as the larger spotted fish called *troctae*, and entrust them to the water to be warmed. Water, therefore, gives life and creates, and still fulfils the office of that first command as though it were an everlasting law—a gentle mother of living creatures.

> [Note: [Col. 0208D] All editions, with a few manuscripts: “such as those which they call *tructae*.” Many manuscripts, of considerable number and authority: “such as the larger spotted fish which they call *troctae*.” The distinction between *tructae* or *truttae* and *troctae* is that the latter live in the sea and the former in rivers.]

Others bring forth living offspring from their own bodies, such as weasels, dogfish, huge whales, dolphins, seals, and other creatures of this kind. After they have given birth, if they happen to sense some scheme of ambush or terror being devised against their young, then, in order to protect them or to soothe the fearfulness of their tender age with maternal affection, they are said to open their mouths, suspend their offspring harmlessly by their teeth, receive them within their bodies, and hide them in their generative wombs. What human affection could imitate this devotion of fish? Kisses are enough for us to satisfy affection; for them, it is not enough to open their inward parts and receive and recall their young whole, and again restore them to life by a certain cherishing warmth of their own heat—

> [Note: [Col. 0209D] Some manuscripts: “and nourish them with breath.”]

—and nourish them with breath, so that two live in one body, until either they convey them to safety or defend their young from dangers by exposing their own bodies. Who, seeing this, even if able to prevail, would not yield to such devotion in fish? Who would not wonder and be astonished that nature preserves in fish what it does not preserve in human beings? Very many women, prompted by suspicion and stepmothers’ hatred, have killed their own children; others, in famine, as we read, have eaten their own offspring. A mother has become a tomb for her human pledges; but for the offspring of fish the parent’s womb is like a wall, preserving its pledges unharmed behind a rampart of inward organs.

8. Thus different kinds of fish have different functions: some lay eggs, while others give birth to living and fully formed young. Those which lay eggs do not weave nests as birds do; they do not undertake the labour of prolonged brooding; they do not feed their young with trouble to themselves. The egg falls, and water, like a gentle nurse, receives it in a kind of womb of its own nature and quickly restores it as a living creature. For an egg, quickened by the parent’s touch, falls at once, and a fish emerges.

9. Then again, how pure and inviolate is their succession! No one mates with another species, but each with its own kind: grayling with grayling, sea-wolf with sea-wolf. The scorpion-fish likewise preserves, for its own kind, the chastity of an unstained union. It therefore possesses the modesty of its kind, but not its kind’s venom: for the scorpion-fish does not strike, but refreshes.

> [Note: [Col. 0209D] Some manuscripts in an ancient hand: “a partner of another species … when the kinds of asses … come together … great,” etc.]

Fish do not know the adulterous contamination of alien species, such as occurs when the breeds of asses and mares are crossed—something accomplished through great human effort—or again when a horse mates with a she-ass: these are truly adulteries against nature. For surely what is committed as a pollution of nature is greater than what is committed as an injury to a person. Yet you, human being, arrange these things as the broker of beastly adultery; and do you consider the adulterine animal more valuable than the genuine one? You yourself confuse foreign breeds and mingle diverse seed; you often compel unwilling creatures to forbidden unions, and call this industry! Because you cannot do this among human beings, so that the mixture of different kinds may produce offspring, you take from a human being what he was born with, strip a man of his manhood, and, by cutting off a part of the body—

> [Note: [Col. 0210D] Five manuscripts: “you kill the sex.”]

—you deny his sex and make him a eunuch, so that audacity may accomplish among human beings what nature has refused.

## CHAPTER IV

That water and fish teach what the mutual bond of parents and children ought to be; and how water supplies fish with the function of respiration.

10. Consider from this also how good a mother water is. You, O human being, have taught repudiations of fathers toward children, separations, hatreds, and offences. Learn what the bond between parents and children ought to be. Fish cannot live without water, nor be separated from the fellowship of their parent or distinguished from the service of their nurse; and this occurs by a certain law of nature, so that when separated they immediately die. For they do not, like all other creatures, live by the breath of this air, since the capacity for drawing breath and respiration is not available to them. Otherwise, they could not always live beneath the waters while receiving no influx of breath. What breath is to us, water is to them. As breath supplies us with the substance of life, so water supplies it to them. When access to breath is cut off, since we cannot even for a brief interval be without vital breath, we immediately perish; fish likewise, when removed from water, cannot remain alive without the substance proper to their life.

11. And the reason is plain: in us the lung receives breath through the spacious recesses of the chest; and, because it is itself permeable through many pores, it cools the inward heat by the influx of breath. For the chest, while receiving food, also separates the superfluities of food, wholesome juices, and blood. The lung becomes permeable, so that the inhalation of breath may more easily reach it. Fish, however, have gills—

> [Note: [Col. 0210D] Gills, in Greek *branchiai* (βραγχίαι), are parts in fish which gape on both sides of the head in the manner of bellows.]

—which they now fold and draw together, now unfold and open. Thus, while water is received, passed through, and penetrates during this contraction and opening, it appears to perform the office of respiration. Fish therefore possess a nature proper to themselves and not shared with other creatures: a special function, and a particular, separate, and hidden means of life unlike that of others. Therefore they are not reared, nor, like land animals, delighted by the touch of a human hand or by any caress, even though they remain alive when kept in their fish-ponds.

## CHAPTER V

Why fish are so well provided with teeth. They become food for one another; this is imitated by the greedy, who are severely rebuked.

[Col. 0210D]

12. What shall I say of the closeness of their teeth? They do not have teeth on one side only, as an ox or sheep does; rather, both sides are armed with teeth. Since they live in water, if they chewed their food for too long and did not swallow it quickly, the food might be swept away and washed from their teeth by the influx of water. Therefore they have close-set and sharp teeth, so that they may cut quickly, consume food quickly, and swallow it readily, without delay or hesitation. Thus they do not chew the cud; only the *scarus* is said to chew the cud among them, according to those who have had the opportunity, practice, or interest to learn such things.

13. Indeed, fish themselves have not escaped the violence of those of their own kind who are more powerful; everywhere the weaker are subject to the greed of the stronger. The weaker any fish is, the more exposed it is to prey. Very many feed on plants and tiny worms. Yet some devour one another and feed upon their own flesh. Among them, the smaller is food for the larger; then that larger one is attacked by a stronger fish and becomes the food of another predator, itself the predator of another. Thus it happens that, after it has devoured another, it is devoured by another, and both come together in one stomach, the first having been swallowed along with its own devourer; and thus in one set of entrails there is at once a partnership of prey and retribution.

Perhaps this wrong accrued to them spontaneously; among us, however, it did not begin from nature but from greed. Or perhaps, because they were given for human use, they have also been made a sign, that in them we might see the vices of our own conduct and avoid their examples, lest someone stronger attack an inferior and thereby offer a stronger person an example of wrongdoing against himself. Therefore, one who harms another prepares a snare for himself, into which he himself may fall.

14. You too are a fish—you who attack another’s possessions, who submerge the weak, who pursue one retreating even into the depths.

> [Note: [Col. 0211D] Carnotensis: “who pursue one retreating, you yourself will fall even into the depths.”]

Beware lest, while pursuing him, you yourself fall into the hands of a stronger person, and he whom you pursue, avoiding your snares, lead you into another’s traps; he who feared his own suffering while you pursued him may first behold yours. What difference is there between the rich man, whose greedy gluttony swallows up the estates of the weak, and the sheatfish whose belly is filled with the entrails of smaller fish? The rich man has died, and his spoils have profited him nothing; indeed, the disgrace of his plunder has made him more detestable. The sheatfish has been caught, and its useless prey has been exposed. How many are found in it who had devoured others! And you, rich man, have in your own bosom another man’s predator. He possessed the resources of the poor man which he had seized; you, by crushing him, added two estates to your own wealth, and are still not satisfied with so great an increase. Yet you say that you have vindicated others, although you commit the same things that you punish—more unjust than the unjust, more iniquitous than the iniquitous, greedier than the greedy. See that the same end does not overtake you as overtook that fish. Beware of the hook; beware of the nets. But you rely upon your power, believing that no one can resist you. The sheatfish too relied upon this: that no one would cast a hook for it or spread nets, and that, if it fell into them, it would tear everything apart. Yet it did not escape the trident, or avoid the bonds of a stronger net from which it could not free itself. Without doubt, the more serious the crimes human injustice commits, the less able it will be to remain secure through its own wrongdoing; rather, at some point it will pay what cannot easily be avoided as the price of its crimes.

## CHAPTER VI

That the human being is a fish; but that one fish is good and another bad; and that the good fish should not fear Peter’s hook or bosom.

[Col. 0212A]

15. Therefore, O human being, you are a fish. Hear that you are a fish: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, which gathered fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it to shore; and, sitting down, selected the good into their vessels, but threw the bad out. So it will be at the consummation of the age. The angels will go out, separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire” (Matt. 13:47–50). There are, then, good fish and bad fish: the good are kept for a price; the bad immediately burn. Nets do not entangle the good fish, but raise it up; nor does the hook wound and kill it, but bathes it in the blood of a precious wound. In the confession of its mouth is found a good price, by which the apostolic tribute and Christ’s tax may be paid. For it is written thus, as the Lord says: “From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax—from their own sons or from strangers?” And when Peter replied, “From strangers,” the Lord said: “Go to the sea and cast a hook; take the first fish that comes up, and when you open its mouth you will find a stater there. Take it and give it to them for me and for yourself” (Matt. 17:24–27).

16. Therefore, O good fish, do not fear Peter’s hook: it does not kill, but consecrates. Do not despise yourself as worthless because you see that your body is weak: in your mouth you have that which you may offer both for Peter and for Christ. Do not fear Peter’s nets, to whom Jesus says: “Put out into the deep, and let down the nets.” For he does not cast on the left side, but on the right, as Christ commanded him. Do not fear his bosom, for it was said to him: “From now on you will catch people alive.”

> [Note: [Col. 0211D] Four manuscripts of very low authority: “you will catch people.”]

Therefore he cast the nets and enclosed Stephen, who first rose from the Gospel, having in his mouth the stater of righteousness. Hence, in steadfast confession, he cried out: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” For this fish the Lord Jesus stood; for he knew that the price of his tax was in Stephen’s mouth. Finally, by his glorious martyrdom Stephen abundantly fulfilled and vindicated Peter’s judgment and teaching, and Christ’s grace.

## CHAPTER VII

That the sea signifies the Gospel and the Church, and what the human fish ought to do in this sea. Husbands and wives are urged, by the example of the viper, to mutual tolerance of character, love, and fidelity; and why the same example is used in both directions.

[Col. 0212D]

17. Nor should you be disturbed because I have set the Gospel in place of the sea. The Gospel is that in which Christ walked. The Gospel is that in which Peter, though he faltered when he denied, nevertheless found through Christ’s right hand the bulwark of faith and the grace of a firm standing.

> [Note: [Col. 0211D] Thus the manuscripts and the Amerbach and Petri editions; Erasmus, with subsequent editions: “The Gospel is that in which Peter, although he faltered, nevertheless did not deny, when,” etc. In the same place, some manuscripts read: “found the firm supports of faith”; some, “of faith”; the old edition, “of faith”; the Roman edition, “found the firm support of a faithful station”: “The Gospel,” etc.]

The Gospel is that from which the martyr ascended. The Gospel is the sea in which the Apostles fish, in which the net is cast that is like the kingdom of heaven. The Gospel is the sea in which Christ’s mysteries are figured. The Gospel is the sea in which the Hebrew escaped and the Egyptian was slain. The Gospel is the sea because the Church, Christ’s bride and the fullness of divine grace, is founded upon the seas, as the Prophet said: “He founded it upon the seas” (Ps. 23:2).

Leap over the waves, O human being, for you are a fish. Let not the waves of this age overwhelm you. If there is a storm, seek the deep and profound waters; if there is calm, play among the waves; if there is a tempest, beware of the rocky shore, lest the raging surge dash you against a rock. For it is written: “Be prudent as serpents” (Matt. 10:16).

18. And since the example of prudent serpents has been introduced, let us be prudent in seeking and preserving marriages; let us love the unions allotted to us. If those who had been separated into far-distant regions at the time of their birth should come together, and if the husband should journey to foreign lands, no distance and no absence should diminish the love that has pleased them. The same law binds those present and absent; the same bond of nature has constrained the rights of marital love among those distant and those together. The necks of both are joined beneath the same yoke of blessing, even if one passes through the long separations of divided lands; for they have received the yoke of grace not upon the neck of the body but of the mind.

The viper is a most wicked kind of beast and, above all creatures of the serpent race, more cunning. When it is seized by the desire for intercourse, it seeks the familiar union of the sea-moray, or prepares a new one. Going out to the shore, it signals its presence by hissing and calls the moray to marital embrace. The invited moray does not fail to come and grants the poisonous serpent the desired use of union. What does such an account mean, except that the dispositions of spouses must be endured, and that, if one is absent, the other’s arrival must be awaited, even if he is harsh, deceitful, uncultivated, slippery, or drunken? What is worse than poison, which the moray does not flee in a spouse? Called, it does not fail to come, but embraces the serpent’s slippery form with diligent affection. He bears your faults and the fickle instability of womanhood; and can you, O woman, not endure your husband? Adam was deceived through Eve, not Eve through Adam (33, question 5, chapter *Adam per Evam*). The man whom woman called to fault, she ought rightly to accept as her governor, lest she fall again through feminine inconstancy. But he is harsh and uncouth. He pleased you once. Is a husband to be chosen repeatedly? Even the ox seeks its mate, and the horse loves its companion; if another is substituted, the mate of another does not know how to pull the yoke and does not consider itself whole. Yet you repudiate your own yokefellow and think he must be changed often; and, if he is absent one day—

> [Note: [Col. 0213D] Certain manuscripts read, “you suspect a rival”; or, with some editions, “you suspect a rival woman.” Others: “and immediately, with an unknown cause as though known”; or, with other editions, “and immediately, an unknown matter as though known,” etc. But twelve excellent manuscripts, together with the Petri and Gillius editions, read as in the text.]

—you bring in a rival, and immediately, treating an unknown charge as known, you avenge an affront to chastity. The viper seeks its absent mate, calls to it when absent, and cries aloud with a gentle hiss; when it senses that its partner is approaching, it vomits out its venom, rendering respect to its husband and reverencing the grace of marriage. But you, woman, drive away with insults the husband who returns from afar. The viper looks out over the sea and watches for the path of its mate; you bar your husband’s way with injuries. You stir up the venom of quarrels rather than cast it out. At the time of marital embrace you boil with dreadful poison; you neither blush for your marriage nor reverence your husband.

19. Yet you also, husband—for we may understand the matter in this way as well—put aside the swelling of your heart and harshness of character when your diligent wife comes to meet you. Drive away indignation when a gentle wife calls you to love. You are not a master, but a husband; you have not received a slave-woman, but a wife. God willed you to be the guide of the weaker sex, not its tyrant. Return zeal for zeal; return gratitude for love. The viper pours out its venom: can you not lay aside hardness of mind? But you possess a natural severity; you ought to moderate it by reflection upon marriage and lay aside the savagery of your spirit out of reverence for the union.

> [Note: [Col. 0213D] All editions, with some manuscripts, read: “and out of reverence for the union.” This is also possible. Nine manuscripts agree with our reading at [Col. 0214D], except that most have *deponat* or *deponet*; Dionysius has *depone*; Caenensis more correctly has *deponere*. The words “This may also be understood thus” are omitted in some copies; yet the transition is necessary.]

This may also be understood thus: Husbands, do not seek another’s bed; do not lie in wait for another’s union. Adultery is grievous and an injury to nature. God first made two, Adam and Eve—that is, man and wife—and made the wife from the man, that is, from Adam’s rib; and he commanded both to be one body and to live in one spirit. Why do you divide one body, why do you separate one spirit? It is an adultery against nature. This is taught by the embrace desired between moray and viper, not by right of species but by the heat of lust. Learn, O men—whoever seeks to seduce another man’s wife—

> [Note: [Col. 0214D] Some manuscripts read *permovere*, one *praemollire*. Others, better, together with the edition, read *permolere*. It is a metaphorical word used of obscenities; Horace, Book I, Satire 2.]

—what serpent’s companionship he wishes to adopt, and to what serpent he himself is comparable. He hastens to the viper that pours herself into a man’s bosom not by the straight path of truth, but by the slippery way of errant desire. He hastens to her who takes back her venom, like the viper which, it is said, after completing the act of union, drinks again the venom it had vomited out; for the viper is adulterous (Prov. 23:32). Therefore Solomon also says that one who is drunken—since lust commonly grows hot through wine—is stretched out as though by a serpent’s bite, and venom is poured into him as though by a horned snake. And, that you may know he spoke of the adulteress, he adds: “When your eyes have looked upon a strange woman, your mouth speaks perversities” (ibid., 33).

20. Let no one suppose that we have advanced contradictory points because we have employed the example of this viper both for good and for evil. Both serve instruction, if we blush either not to show fidelity to one beloved, to whom even a serpent shows it, or if, abandoning holy marriages, we prefer slippery and harmful unions to what is wholesome—as does one who mingles with a serpent.

## CHAPTER VIII

On the cunning of the octopus and the crab, by which deceitful people are portrayed; with an exhortation to flee greed.

21. And since we have begun to weave into our discourse the subject of cunning, by which each person strives to cheat and deceive his brother and to devise new frauds—so that one whom he cannot overcome by force, he may ensnare by deception and cloak with a certain artificial disguise—I shall not pass over the deceitful ingenuity of the octopus. Finding a rock on a shallow shore, it fastens itself to it and assumes its colour by its misty cunning. Covering its back with a similar appearance, it catches in the nets of its furtive art many fish that glide toward it without any suspicion of fraud, because they do not guard against what is familiar and suppose it to be a rock; it intercepts them in a fold of its flesh. Thus prey comes of its own accord and is captured by such contrivances as belong to people who frequently alter their disposition and employ diverse arts of harm, testing the minds and feelings of individuals: when placed among the self-controlled, they preach self-control; when among the intemperate, they behave as though estranged from the pursuit of chastity and immersed in the mire of excess. Those who hear or see them trust themselves with unwary readiness, and so fall more quickly because they do not know how to turn aside or to avoid what harms them; for wickedness is more grave and harmful when shadowed beneath a veil of kindness. Therefore we must beware of those who spread far and wide the tendrils and arms of their deceit, or put on a many-formed appearance. For these too are octopuses: they have many bonds and the devices of crafty minds, by which they can ensnare whatever falls upon the rocks of their deception.

22. The crab also devises what tricks for the sake of food! It too delights in the oyster and seeks a feast from its flesh. But while it desires food, it also looks ahead to danger, since the hunt is difficult and dangerous: difficult because the inner food is enclosed by stronger shells. Nature, the interpreter of the imperial command, has fortified the softness of the flesh as if with walls, nourishing and warming it in a hollow fold between the shells and spreading it out as if in a valley. Therefore all the crab’s attempts are in vain, because it cannot open a closed oyster by any force; and it is dangerous if the oyster closes upon its claw.

> [Note: [Col. 0215D] The *chelae* are, in crabs, like pincers or certain fingers with which they seize what comes in their way.]

It resorts to contrivances and devises traps through a new deception. Since every species is soothed by pleasure, it watches to see whether the oyster, in some place remote from every wind, opens its double shell toward the sun’s rays and unbars the enclosure of its shells, in order to enjoy a certain pleasure in the free air within its body.

> [Note: [Col. 0215D] He calls the two sides of oyster shells a *diptych*, because they close and open in the manner of a book; from the particle *dis* [twice] and the verb *ptyssein* (πτύσσειν), “to fold.”]

Then it secretly inserts a small pebble, preventing the oyster from closing; and thus, finding its enclosure open, it safely thrusts in its claws and feeds upon its inner organs.

23. There are, therefore, people who, in the manner of the crab, creep into the use of another’s loss by deceit, prop up the weakness of their own ability by a kind of cunning, weave treachery against a brother, and feed upon another’s misery. But be content with what is your own, and do not let another’s losses feed you. The good food is the simplicity of innocence. One who possesses his own goods does not know how to lie in wait for those of another, nor is he set ablaze by the fires of greed; for to one such as this every gain is a loss to virtue and fuel for covetousness. Therefore poverty with truth is blessed, if it knows its own goods, and is to be preferred to all treasures; for “better is a little given with the fear of God than great treasures without fear.” How much, indeed, is needed to sustain a human being? Or, if you seek enough also to abound for the benefit of others, even that is not much. For hospitality with vegetables and goodwill is better than the preparation of fattened calves with discord. Let us therefore employ ingenuity to seek grace and preserve salvation, not to undermine another’s innocence. We may use examples from the sea for the advancement of our own salvation, not for another’s peril.

## CHAPTER IX

On the foreknowledge of the sea-urchin, which announces a coming storm; that it has received this gift from God, whose providence is proclaimed in all created things.

24. The sea-urchin—an insignificant, lowly, and contemptible marine animal—is often accustomed to be an indicator of coming storms or a herald of calm for sailors. When it has foreseen a storm of winds, it takes hold of a heavy stone and carries it as ballast, dragging it like an anchor lest it be tossed about by the waves. Thus it is not balanced by its own strength—

> [Note: [Col. 0216D] Thus the old Corbie manuscript, Theodoric, and Reginensis. Some others: “it is steadied and governed by another’s weight.” Carnotensis: “it is governed by another’s stability and weight.” The remaining manuscripts and editions: “it steadies and governs by another’s weight.”]

—but is governed by the weight of another’s stability. By this sign sailors take warning of the coming disturbance and protect themselves, lest an unforeseen storm find them unprepared. What mathematician, astrologer, or Chaldean can so comprehend the courses of the stars, these motions and signs of heaven? By what intelligence did it collect this knowledge? From what teacher did it receive it? Who was the interpreter for it of so great an omen? People often see disturbance in the air and are often deceived, because it is frequently dispersed without a storm. The sea-urchin is not deceived; its signs never fail it.

25. Whence does so small an animal have such knowledge that it can foretell what is to come? The more clearly it has nothing in itself by which it could possess so great a prudence, the more you should believe that it has received even this gift of foreknowledge through the Lord’s gracious providence over all things. For if God so clothes the grass that we marvel; if he feeds the birds; if he has prepared food for the raven—for its young cry to the Lord; if he gave women wisdom in weaving; if he did not leave the spider, which hangs its loose nets in doorways so subtly and skilfully, devoid of wisdom; if he himself gave strength to the horse and freed its neck from fear, so that it leaps in the field, mocks kings as it charges to meet them, scents battle from afar, and is roused by the sound of the trumpet; if he has filled many irrational creatures and even insensible things, such as grass and lilies, with the wisdom of his ordering, why do we doubt that he has bestowed upon the sea-urchin too this grace of foreknowledge? For he has left nothing unexamined, nothing neglected. He sees all things, who feeds all things; he fills all things with wisdom, who made all things in wisdom, as it is written (Ps. 103:24). Therefore, if he did not pass over the sea-urchin as excluded from his care, if he considers it and instructs it with signs of future things, does he not consider you? Indeed he does consider you, as his divine Wisdom testifies when it says: “If he looks after the birds, if he feeds them, are you not of greater value than they?” (Matt. 6:26). “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which exists today and tomorrow is thrown into the fire, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith?”

## CHAPTER X

That each kind of fish has its prescribed dwelling places, by which human fickleness and luxury are condemned; yet some fish change locations for the sake of offspring. The reason for this is examined, and human incontinence rebuked. Also concerning the particular qualities of certain fish.

26. Or do we suppose that fish remain without some endowment of nature even in this gift: that every kind of fish has prescribed dwelling places, which no individual of its kind exceeds and into which no foreign fish intrudes? What geometer divided for them dwellings that must never be violated? We have heard of a geometer, but never of a “sea-measurer”; yet fish know their own measure—not one prescribed by city walls and gates, buildings of houses, or boundaries of fields, but the measure of what is fitting: that each may have as much as suffices and abounds for use, not as much as some unrestrained greed claims for itself. It is a law of nature to seek only as much as is sufficient for sustenance and to reckon one’s patrimony according to the measure of nourishment.

> [Note: [Col. 0217D] Vatican and Caenensis manuscripts: “as much as accomplishes sustenance.” Dionysius: “as much as suffices for sustenance and nourishment, and to assess one’s patrimony only by this allotment.”]

One kind of fish is fed and born in one gulf of the sea, another in another. Indeed, you will not find the kinds of fish confused: what is abundant here is lacking elsewhere. One gulf feeds mullets, another sea-wolves; one feeds rock-fish, another lobsters. They have no unrestricted power of wandering; yet their passage is impeded neither by a barrier of mountains nor by intervening rivers. Rather, the use of nature implanted in them, as if by the boundaries of a homeland, keeps each within its own domain and makes it hazardous to venture beyond its inhabitants.

> [Note: [Col. 0217D] Some manuscripts and the Roman edition have *facit* (“makes”). Others, greater in number and antiquity, with the old edition, omit *facit*. Not wrongly: after “implanted … and suspect,” the substantive verb “is” may be understood at [Col. 0218D].]

27. But our disposition is altogether different: we change homes by exile, are held by contempt for our inhabitants, seek the favour of strangers, move the everlasting boundaries established by our fathers, join field to field and house to house. The land fails for human beings; even the seas are paved over. Again, according to the whim of individuals, land is cut away and sea poured in, in order to make islands and possess straits. They claim expanses of sea as private property, and declare that the rights of fish, like the condition of household-born slaves, are subject to their servitude. “This gulf of the sea,” one says, “is mine; that belongs to another.” The powerful divide the elements among themselves. For these people oysters are nourished in the waves; for these, fish are confined in a pond. The sea is insufficient for luxury unless they have storehouses of oysters. Thus they count the ages of oysters and furnish holding-places for fish, lest the sea should be unable to supply the rich man’s banquets. With what ears do they hear the word “neighbour”? With what eyes do they behold their neighbours’ possessions? How they devise, day and night, some means of taking something from the one next to them! “Will you dwell alone upon the earth?” cries the prophet (Isa. 5:9). The Lord recognizes these things and reserves them for vengeance.

28. How far removed from fish is the rapacity of greed! They seek nature’s hidden places, and beyond the limits of the inhabited world they know a sea interrupted by no islands, where no land lies between or farther beyond. There, it is said, the whales hide themselves—those immense kinds of fish, bodies equal to mountains, according to those who have been able to see them. There they pass a quiet lifetime, keeping their regions and distributed dwellings apart from islands and separate from all contact with maritime cities.

> [Note: [Col. 0218D] Dionysius manuscript: “they keep their regions distinct from islands and separate from the contact of all maritime cities.” Caenensis: “there they keep their regions remote,” etc.]

They remain there without offending the boundaries of their neighbours and do not seek changes of place by restless wandering. Rather, they love them as their native soil and judge it pleasant to remain there. They chose them, I think, in order to be able to live a solitary life far from the intrusion of observers.

29. There are, however, certain kinds of fish which change their place not through cleverness of mind, but from the necessity of nurturing their offspring. At the fitting and lawful season for attending to this, countless multitudes gather from many places and from different expanses of sea, as though by common counsel, in a united shoal; they seek the north wind and, by a certain law of nature, make for that sea in the northern regions. If you saw them ascending, you would call it a kind of *rheuma*—that is, a tide or torrent—for they rush on in such a way, cutting through the waves and flowing with violent force through the Propontis into the Euxine Sea.

> [Note: Basil, *rheuma* (ῥεῦμα), that is, a tide and torrent.]

Who announces these places to the fish, or appoints their seasons? Who grants them an arrangement for travelling, an order for moving in company, the bounds and seasons of their return? Men have their own commander, whose order is awaited; the watchword is issued, edicts are set forth for provincials to assemble, letters are sent to the military tribunes, and a day is fixed—yet many cannot appear on the appointed day. What commander gave this command to the fish? What teacher bestowed this instruction? Who lays out the routes as surveyors do? Who directs the way as leaders do, so that none is absent from the rendezvous?

But I recognize who that commander is: he who, by divine ordering, instils his command into the perceptions of all creatures; who silently grants to dumb animals the order of a natural discipline; who penetrates not only great things, but diffuses himself even through every least thing. The fish obeys the divine law, while men resist it! The fish solemnly obeys the heavenly commands, while men make God’s precepts void!

Does the fish seem contemptible to you because it is dumb and lacks reason? Take care lest you begin to be more contemptible to yourself, if you are found more irrational than an irrational creature. For what could be more rational than this migration of the fish? They do not indeed explain its reason in words, but they speak by their deeds. In summer they make for the strait of Pontus, because this inlet is fresher than the remaining expanse of the sea. For the sun does not remain over that strait for as long as it does over the rest; consequently it does not draw off all the water, which is sweet and drinkable. Who does not know, moreover, that even creatures of the sea generally delight in fresh waters? Thus, as they follow rivers and ascend upstream, fish of foreign species are often caught in rivers.

Therefore, since this cause makes Pontus more agreeable to them—

> [Note: Gemetensis manuscript: “or because, at the season of the tide, the customary north wind blows there.”]

—or because the customary north wind there moderates the tide, they judge it more suitable than other places for breeding and for rearing their own offspring. Their tender young could scarcely bear the hardship of an alien region; there the gentle mildness of the air cherishes them. Thus, once their task is completed, all together return in the same shoal in which they came.

30. Let us consider what the reason for this is. The inlet of Pontus lies exposed to the most violent blasts of Boreas and of the other winds; hence a severe storm rages there and tempests are stirred up, so that sand is turned from the depths. The sandy wave bears witness to this: rising high through the movement of the winds and then becoming heavier by its weight, it is undoubtedly considered unbearable not only to sailors but even to the sea-creatures themselves.

Moreover, very many and very great rivers flow into Pontus; and in winter the gulf itself is made colder by the incoming streams. Therefore the fish, as judges of the currents, are accustomed to seek there in summer the mildness of the breeze that breathes upon it. Having enjoyed its pleasantness, they strive again to avoid the harshness of winter; fleeing the savagery of the northern quarter, they betake themselves to the other inlets, where either the winds are more gently calm, or the warmth of the sun is accustomed to bring spring.

The fish, then, knows the season for breeding—a matter Solomon declared to be a great mystery in Wisdom:

> “It knows the time for going and returning; it knows the time of fulfilment and of casting forth, and knows how not to be deceived” (Eccles. III.2 ff.).

For it does not employ rational calculation or argumentative reasoning, but the inspiration of nature, which is the true teacher of dutifulness. Indeed, every living creature has prescribed seasons for breeding; man alone has seasons indiscriminate and confused. Other kinds seek the mildness of the season; women alone bring forth their offspring unseasonably. For wandering and intemperate desire for generation produces an unfixed age for childbearing.

Fish cross such great seas to secure some benefit for their kind. We too cross broad seas; but how much more honourable is a voyage undertaken from love of succession than one undertaken from greed for money! For them the crossing is credited to filial devotion; for us, to gain. They bring back offspring dearer than all merchandise; we, from miserable desire for profit, bring back merchandise far unequal to the risk. Thus they return to their native land; we abandon ours. By swimming, they acquire an increase of their kind; by sailing, ours is diminished.

31. Who, then, can deny that such intelligence and power have been infused into them by God? One sees these creatures make, with lively instinct, so solemn a pilgrimage toward the North for the fulfilment of fertility; others, in their tiny bodies, assume such strength that they stop in mid-wave great ships running under full sail. Thus the small fish called the remora (*echeneis*) is said with such ease to stop an enormous ship that you may see it cling to the sea as though rooted there and remain unmoved. For a time, it keeps the vessel motionless. Do you suppose that even this creature could possess so great a power without the Creator’s gift?

Why should I speak of swordfish, sawfish, sea-dogs, whales, or hammerhead sharks? Why also of the *turturis centrum*—the “sting of the turtur”—even when it is dead?

> [Note: Ben., Carn., and Germ. manuscripts: “For if anyone should tread only upon the loins of vipers, this is reported to injure more grievously than poison.”]

For just as, if anyone treads upon the mouth of a viper while it is still fresh, it is said to do harm more severely than poison, and an incurable wound spreads; so too the *turtur*, by its sting, is said to bring more danger when dead than alive. The little hare also—timid on land, but formidable at sea—brings a swift corruption which cannot easily be removed. For the Creator willed that you should not be safe enough even at sea from those who lie in wait; so that, because of the few things that cause harm, you may stand, as it were, on guard, always girded with the arms of faith and the shield of devotion, and may hope for the protection of salvation from your Lord.

## CHAPTER XI

**On the fish of the Atlantic Sea; likewise on salt, coral, and certain other things. Because of these, but especially because of navigation, the sea is superior to the land. After a brief mention of Jonah and Peter, the discourse closes.**

32. Let us come to the Atlantic Sea. How huge are the whales there, and of what boundless size! Whenever they float upon the waves, you might think islands were moving, or lofty mountains rising with their highest summits toward heaven.

> [Note: *Acta*, Greek ἀκτή: a secluded and pleasant shore.]

They are said to be seen not near the shore nor along the coasts, but in the depths of the Atlantic Sea, so that their sight recalls sailors from the presumption of navigating in those places and prevents them from invading the secrets of the elements except with the utmost terror of death.

33. But now let us ourselves rise from the depth of the sea; let our discourse emerge a little and lift itself toward higher things. Let us observe matters familiar to many and full of grace: how water is transformed into the hardness of salt, so that it is often cut with iron. There is nothing surprising in this with British salts, which shine with the snowy brightness of the same substance in the appearance of solid marble, wholesome for bodily food and exceedingly pleasant to drink.

> [Note: Ben. and Germ. manuscripts: “wholesome for the body.” Carnotensis: “wholesome for bodies,” etc.]

How too the not unbeautiful coral, which is a plant in the sea, becomes hardened into the solidity of stone when transferred into the air. From where has nature fastened the most precious pearl into oysters, and how has sea-water hardened it within such soft flesh? Things hard to find among kings lie cheaply, as it were, in abundance on shores; they are gathered from rough rocks and crags.

The water also nourishes a golden fleece, and the shores produce wool in the likeness of the aforesaid metal, whose colour none of those who dye fleeces with diverse pigments has yet been able to imitate. So greatly does human skill fail to equal the grace of maritime nature! We know with what care fleeces of sheep, even less precious ones, are tended. Though they be excellent, nevertheless that dye does not grow naturally upon them. Here is a natural colour which no dye has yet equalled:

> [Note: All manuscripts and old editions read thus. The Roman edition has, “the fleece is from the pinnae.” This derives, evidently, from Basil: “Whence do the *pinnae* nourish the golden fleece?” (πόθεν τὸ χρυσοῦν ἔριον αἱ πίνναι τρέφουσι).]

this too is the fleece of a fish. The purple-shellfish themselves, which furnish the royal distinction, are creatures of the sea.

34. What charm of meadows or delightfulness of gardens can equal the picture of the deep-blue sea? Though flowers shine like gold in meadows, wool shines in the sea with the splendour of gold as well. Those soon wither; this is preserved to endure long. Lilies gleam in gardens from afar; sails gleam upon ships. Here fragrance breathes; there the wind. What usefulness is there in a leaf? What commerce is carried by ships! Lilies carry delight to the nostrils; sails convey the safety of human beings.

Add leaping fish and playing dolphins; add waves sounding with a hoarse murmur; add ships running toward the shores or setting out from them. When four-horse chariots are released from the starting-gates, with what enthusiasm and passion do spectators compete! Yet the horse runs in vain; ships do not run in vain. The former in vain, because empty; the latter for utility, as though laden with grain. What is more pleasing than things moved not by the lash but by the breath of the winds? There no one opposes them, but all are supporters; no one who reaches the goal is defeated, but all ships that have completed their passage are crowned. There the palm is the reward of safety, and victory the prize of return.

How great is the difference between outward and return voyages! The former are prolonged; the latter are brought to an end. Join to these the shores lined with oars, for which the breeze from heaven is the signal for departure. Thus charioteers receive empty applause; these pay vows as those who have been saved.

35. What worthy thing shall I say of Jonah, whom the whale received for life and restored to the grace of prophecy? Water corrected the man whom earthly things had led astray. He sang psalms in the whale’s belly, though he had grieved upon land. And, lest the redemption of either element be passed over, the salvation of the land preceded in the sea, because the sign of the Son of Man is the sign of Jonah. As that man was in the whale’s belly, so Jesus was in the heart of the earth. In each there is a remedy; yet in the sea there is the greater example of divine mercy, because fish received him whom men rejected, and fish saved him whom men crucified.

Peter also staggers on the sea, but does not fall; he confessed amid the waves, yet denied on land. Therefore there, as one devoted, he is grasped by the hand; here, as one forgetful, he is confronted by a reproving gaze.

But now let us pray to the Lord that our discourse, like Jonah, may be cast out upon land, lest it long continue to toss upon the salt sea. And fittingly, now the gourd has sprung up to shade us from our evils; but when it is dried up by the advancing sun, it also warns us that we should rest, lest our minds begin to burn on land and words too fail us. Certainly, in the waters a remission of sins greater than that given to the Ninevites has been granted to us.

## CHAPTER XII  
*(Discourse VIII.)*

**He imagines that birds have flown away from his memory, and elegantly returns his discourse to them. He says that his hearers will give him their attention, while he will give them brevity. Finally, he desires the sweetness of various birds.**

36. And when he had been silent for a little while, he began his discourse again and said:

> [Note: All editions read, “And when I had been silent for a little while … I say.” All manuscripts read, “when he had been silent … he says.” Either reading may be approved: the first because Ambrose testifies in his letter to Orontianus that he wrote this work; the second because some maintain that these are not Ambrose’s words but those of a notary, an opinion supported by the agreement of the manuscripts.]

“Beloved brethren, the necessary discussion of the nature of birds had escaped us, and our discourse upon them had flown away with the birds themselves. For it happens by a sort of natural principle that those who are observing something, or wish to express it in speech, take on the quality of the things which they observe or discuss. Thus, when we linger among sluggish things, and when we are swept along by the swift sight of swift things, we use in writing either a slower or a more rapid manner.

“Therefore, while I took care that things submerged in the sea should not pass unnoticed and be hidden from me beneath the waters, every flying creature escaped me. For while, bent over, I searched the lowest whirlpools of the water, I did not look back to aerial flights; not even the shadow of a swift wing turned me aside, though it might have been reflected in the water. But when I thought every matter settled, believed myself finished, and considered the fifth day complete, the nature of birds came to mind. When they go to rest, they are accustomed, as though joyfully completing their task, to soothe the sky with song. They are accustomed to renew this solemnly at the rising and setting of day, rendering praises to their Creator alike for the night and day which have run their course or are about to begin.

“I had therefore missed a great incentive for arousing devotion in ourselves. For who possesses human understanding and does not blush to end the day without the celebration of psalms, when even the tiniest birds attend with solemn devotion and sweet song the beginnings of days and nights?”

37. Let our winged discourse then return to us—having almost escaped our sight and, seeking its flights aloft like an eagle, having drawn them behind clouds. But, because after washing our eyes in water we raise them from the deep to heaven and observe the empty air borne along by flights, we judged that it must be recalled to the necessity of writing.

You shall be the judges—you who are fowlers of the word—whether it would have been wiser for it to fly away, or whether it has usefully fallen back into your nets. Nor do I fear that weariness may steal over us in searching out flights, when it did not steal over us in investigating whirlpools; or that anyone may fall asleep during our discussion when he can be aroused by the songs of birds. Surely, one who has kept awake among dumb fish cannot, I do not doubt, feel sleep among singing birds when he is invited to wakefulness by such grace.

Nor should that which could have been passed over be deemed insignificant, since it is the third division among created living beings. For there is no doubt that living creatures are of three kinds: terrestrial, flying, and aquatic. Thus it is written:

> [Note: Eleven manuscripts of better quality read “let the waters bring forth” (*educant*). Yet above, chapters 1 and 2, as also below in the following chapter, one constantly reads “let the waters produce” (*producant*).]

> “Let the waters produce creeping things of living souls according to their kind, and flying birds flying above the earth beside the firmament of heaven according to their kind.”

38. We are recalled to higher matters like forgetful travellers who, having passed by without thought, return upon their own tracks and pay the penalty of their carelessness in the labour of repeating their journey.

> [Note: Five manuscripts: “the great labour of a repeated journey” (two, “of a journey repeated”). Three: “the great labour of a journey repeated.” One: “the many losses of a repeated journey.”]

Yet there is also a good traveller, who compensates for the loss of returning by the swift brevity of the remaining journey. This, I think, is what I must do, especially since the subject is birds, which are accustomed to strike human eyes with their rapid flight. What suits it to linger over things in which swiftness is customarily pleasing? Let our discourse, then—unfrequented and unusual in such a kind of writing—resound and echo with singing birds.

39. But from where shall I obtain swan-songs, which delight even under the heavy terror of approaching death? From where shall I obtain those natural measures of song by which even sounding marshes yield the sweetness of most delightful music? From where shall I obtain the voice of the parrot and the sweetness of blackbirds? Would that at least the nightingale might sing, which awakens one sleeping from sleep! For that bird is accustomed to mark the rising of the coming day and bring a more abundant joy at dawn.

Yet if the sweetness of those birds is lacking, there are mourning turtle-doves and hoarse doves; then, too, the crow calls for rain with a full voice. Let us therefore pursue this rustic aviary in such speech as we can command, and with such knowledge as country people have taught us.

## CHAPTER XIII

**Beginning with water-birds, he first discusses the halcyon; setting forth how great is the divine kindness toward that bird, he exhorts us to await help from God. On birds which foretell rain or wind, and on the faithful vigilance of geese.**

40. Since we have spoken of aquatic creeping creatures, it is difficult for our discourse suddenly to ascend to the birds of heaven. Therefore let us first speak of those birds which live about the waters of sea and rivers, with which we may rise up. Let us begin, then, with the halcyon.

It is a sea-bird that is accustomed to bring forth its young upon the shore, laying its eggs in the sand about the middle of winter. For that season has been allotted to it for brooding its offspring, when the sea rises most fiercely and the stronger wave beats against the shores. Thus the grace of this bird may shine forth more brightly through the marvel of sudden calm. For whenever the sea has been rough, once the eggs are laid it suddenly grows mild; all storms of wind fall, the blasts of breezes cease, and the sea remains calm against the winds until the halcyon broods its eggs.

The period of incubation is seven days. When these are ended, it hatches the chicks and completes the birth of its young; immediately it adds another seven days in which it nourishes them until they begin to grow. Do not wonder that the time for feeding is so short, since the hatching of the young takes so few days. Such grace has been divinely granted to this tiny bird that sailors observe these fourteen days as a time of assured calm—

> [Note: The fourteen days are called “halcyon days.”]

—and during them they do not dread any disturbances of stormy weather.

41. “Are you not of more value than sparrows?” says the Lord (Luke XII.7). If, therefore, at consideration of so tiny a bird, the sea rises and is suddenly restrained; if amid the severe storms and tempests of winter the clouded heavens are cleared of harsh winds and tranquillity is suddenly poured into all the elements, calming the waves—then you recognize, O human being made in the image of God, how much you ought to hope, provided only that you imitate this bird’s faith by zeal for devotion.

She sees tempests rise and winds rage; amid the terrors of winter she is neither recalled nor turned back, but is urged onward. She lays her eggs upon the shore, where the sand, still wet as the wave recedes, receives them. Nor does she fear the rising waves which she sees murmuring and rolling toward her.

42. And do not suppose that she seems to despise her eggs. As soon as she has laid them, she makes her nest and broods her young with her own body; nor is she terrified for her own safety by the washing of the shore. Secure in God’s grace, she entrusts herself to winds and waves.

Nor is this all. She adds an equal number of days to feed them; nor does she fear that the tranquillity of the treacherous sea will be interrupted during so many days, but tests her claim, now founded in nature’s established ordinance. She does not hide her tender young in some shelter or under a roof, nor shut them into caves; but commits them to naked, frozen ground. She does not protect them from the cold; rather, by divine warmth, through which she thinks they will be safer, she scorns other precautions.

Which of us does not cover little children with clothes and hide them under roofs? Who does not shut them within the enclosure of rooms? Who does not carefully block every window on all sides, lest any breath of air penetrate even slightly? Rightly, while we dress and cherish our children with such anxiety, we strip them of the covering of heavenly mercy; but those whom the halcyon casts forth naked, it clothes in a divine garment.

43. Nor will I pass you by, divers (*mergi*), to whom this name has attached itself from your continual diving. How often, as you dive, do you gather signs from the breezes; foreseeing a coming storm, you swiftly turn back from the midst of the sea and hasten with cries to the safety of the shore. Likewise you coots—

> [Note: Thus the edition of Erasmus and subsequent editions, with a few manuscripts. The edition of Amerbach and many good manuscripts read, “which delight in the depth of the sea.” If this reading is accepted, it should be written parenthetically: “(as also you coots, which delight in the depth of the sea),” and what follows should be referred to the divers. Two manuscripts read, “delighted in the depth of the sea.”]

—you who delight in the deep sea: fleeing a disturbance of the sea which you have foreseen, you play in the shallows. The heron itself, accustomed to remain about marshes, leaves its familiar haunts and, fearing rain, flies above the clouds, so that it cannot feel the storms of the clouds. Let us consider the various birds of the sea and see how, when the winds’ movement is imminent, they betake themselves to safer and at that time more agreeable pools, and seek their familiar food in hidden recesses of the land.

44. Who would not marvel at the nightly watches of geese, which attest their vigilance even by the constancy of their cries? They even saved the Roman Capitol from the Gallic enemy. Rightly, Rome, are you indebted to them for your dominion. Your gods were asleep, but the geese were awake. Therefore on those days you sacrifice to a goose, not to Jupiter. For your gods yield to the geese, by whom they know that they themselves were defended, lest they too should be captured by the enemy.

## CHAPTER XIV

**Birds are joined to fish by a manifold kinship; nevertheless no bird lacks the service of feet. On the various kinds and differences of different birds.**

45. Fittingly, after the description of fish, the discourse proceeded to those birds accustomed to the waters, because they likewise delight in the practice and function of swimming. Hence the first kinship of these birds with fish seems to lie in the fact that both kinds have certain common endowments of swimming.

There is also a second kinship between all birds and fish: the activity of flying is a likeness of swimming. As a fish cleaves the water by swimming, so a bird cuts the air by swift flight. Both kinds alike possess the ruddering aid of tail and wings: fish raise themselves forward by their fins and move toward what lies ahead; by the rudder of the tail they readily turn themselves wherever they wish, or direct their course straight onward with a certain impetus. Birds likewise swim through the air in their flights as though through water, stretching out, as it were, certain arms; with their tails they raise themselves upward or plunge downward.

Since, therefore, in certain respects their function and form are the same, the birth of both kinds from the waters proceeded at the divine command. For God said:

> “Let the waters produce creeping things of living souls according to their kind, and birds above the earth beside the firmament of heaven according to their kind.”

It is not without reason, then, that, because both kinds are produced from the waters, the property of swimming belongs to each.

46. Certainly, while the slippery snake and all serpents—for the name *serpent* was given because they cannot walk but creep—and likewise dragons, like most fish, have no feet, no kind of bird lacks the use of feet. For all their food comes from the earth; hence they are supported by the service of feet, since they need this assistance in seeking food.

Thus some birds are armed with talons for seizure, such as hawks and eagles, which pursue prey by hunting; others use a service and function suited either to walking or to preparing food for themselves.

47. The name “bird” is one, but the kinds are diverse. Who could comprehend them by memory or knowledge? There are birds that feed on flesh. Therefore they have rough talons, a curved and sharp beak, and swift flight, because they live by plunder; thus they can readily seize the prey they pursue and swiftly disembowel it with beak or talons. There are also birds that feed upon seed they find, and others upon various chance food.

There is also a difference in their pairings. Those intent upon prey lack the pleasure of such unions.

> [Note: Thus eleven manuscripts and certain Paris editions. Some other manuscripts and the remaining editions read, “beasts lack [such unions], which …” Coenobium manuscript: “they almost lack”; Remensis: “they easily lack,” etc.]

For, because of their greed for plunder or their plotting of ambushes, they do not even agree among themselves and so avoid pairing with their own kind. Avarice shuns the company of many. Moreover, a union of many would easily betray itself. Thus these birds have no union except the companionship of a yoked pair. Such is the manner of life among eagles and hawks.

Doves, cranes, starlings, ravens and crows, and also thrushes, by contrast, delight in association with many.

48. There are also kinds of birds that are native (*enchoria*) and remain always in the same places; others are migratory, visiting other regions and returning when winter is over; others return in winter and migrate from us in summer—either because some withdraw to warmer places during winter, or because many in turn spend summer in places which they have found more pleasant. Thrushes, for example, return at the end of autumn, on the threshold of winter, as though summer had ended.

We, with inhuman harshness, prepare snares for them, striving by different means now to deceive them with a treacherous perch, now to trick them with birdlime, now to capture them in nooses. The return of storks raises the banner of spring. Cranes, because they seek lofty places, are fond of frequent migration.

49. Some birds submit themselves to the hand, become accustomed to their master’s table, and are soothed by touch; others are fearful. Some delight in the same dwellings as human beings; others love a solitary life in wastelands and compensate for the difficulty of finding food by their love of freedom. Some merely make noise with their voices; others delight with tuneful and sweet melody. Some naturally, others by training, imitate the distinctions of different voices, so that you might suppose a person had spoken when a bird has spoken. How sweet is the song of blackbirds, how distinct the voice of the parrot!

Some are also simple, as doves; others crafty, as partridges. The cock is more boastful; the peacock more beautiful. There are also differences among birds in their manner of life and work: some love to provide for the common good and, by combined strength, to administer, as it were, a commonwealth and live as though under a king; others provide each for themselves, reject rule, and, if captured, wish to leave an unworthy servitude.

## CHAPTER XV

**On cranes, their watchfulness on guard, and the order they observe in flight. On this occasion, the condition of the ancient commonwealth and the causes of human negligence.**

50. Let us begin, then, with those birds that have offered themselves to us for imitation in our own use. For among them civic order and military service are natural; among us they are compulsory and slavish. With what uncommanded and voluntary practice do cranes keep anxious watch by night! You may see sentries posted; while their other companions rest, some go around and keep watch lest ambushes be laid from any quarter, and with tireless exertion provide every protection.

Then, when the time of their watch has been fulfilled, one that has completed its task settles itself to sleep after uttering a cry, in order to awaken the sleeper to whom it will hand over its turn of duty. The other willingly receives the lot; unlike our practice, it does not reluctantly and sluggishly renounce sleep, but briskly shakes itself from its resting-place, performs its turn, and renders back the favour it has received with equal care and service. Thus there is no desertion, because devotion is natural; thus the guard is secure, because the will is free.

51. They preserve this order also in flight and lessen all their labour by this arrangement: they perform in turn the function of leading. For one goes before the others for the time assigned to it and runs ahead, as it were, before the standards.

> [Note: Gronovius says that one should write, “runs ahead before the standards … This is an imitation of the ancient commonwealth and an image of a free state.” But this is supported by the authority of no manuscript. One manuscript of Victor and the Corbeiensis, by correction, have *antesignatus* (“standard-bearer”); Gemeticensis likewise, by correction, has *antesignana*.]

Then it turns aside and yields the lot of leading the flock to the next. What could be more beautiful than that both labour and honour should be common to all, that power should not be arrogated by a few but transferred among all by a kind of voluntary lot?

52. This is a function of the ancient commonwealth and the likeness of a free state. Thus from the beginning men began to practise civic order, received from nature by the example of birds:

> [Note: Some manuscripts in an ancient hand read: “having received civic order from nature, by the example of birds, they began …”]

labour was to be common, dignity common; each person in turn was to learn to share responsibilities, divide obedience and command; no one was to be excluded from honour, none exempt from labour.
