This was the most beautiful condition of affairs. No one became arrogant through perpetual power, and no one was crushed by prolonged servitude. Promotion, bestowed by an order of office and a moderation of time, came without envy; and a guard-duty imposed by common lot seemed more tolerable.

> [Note: Three manuscripts of respectable quality: “the guard-duty which shared the lot.”]

No one dared oppress another by servitude when he would have to undergo the reciprocal burdens and succeed to that person’s honour. No labour seemed heavy when a following dignity relieved it. But once the desire of ruling began to claim powers not due to it, and to refuse to lay aside powers once gained; once military service ceased to be a common right and became servitude; once the method of receiving authority became not an orderly process but the ambition of seizing it—then the very discharge of labour began to be endured more harshly. Whatever is not voluntary soon yields place to neglect.

How reluctantly men undertake the duties of watch, how unwillingly each person assigned danger in camp keeps watch, when the defence is entrusted to him by royal command! The punishment for negligence is set before him; and yet carelessness commonly steals in, and the watches are not kept. For necessity, which imposes obedience upon the unwilling, generally brings disgust. Nothing is so easy that it does not become difficult when done unwillingly. Thus unbroken labour turns away affection, and continuous, long-lasting power breeds arrogance.

What person can you find who willingly lays down authority, yields the insignia of command, and from being first willingly becomes last in rank? Yet we contend not merely for first place but often even for the middle, and claim the first couches at a banquet; if precedence has been granted once, we wish it to be perpetual. Thus among cranes there is equality of spirit in labours and humility in authority. They need to be reminded to perform their turns of guard; they do not need to be reminded to resign power. For there the natural rest of sleep must be interrupted; here the benefit of voluntary diligence must be rendered.

## CHAPTER XVI

**How storks set out, and how they are escorted and defended by crows. The hospitality of these crows is praised, and human negligence reproved. Finally, our impiety toward parents is contrasted with the filial devotion of storks.**

53. Storks, it is said, set out in a gathered flock whenever they judge that they must go somewhere. In many regions of the East they are carried along together, and all move at once as though by a military watchword. You would think an army was advancing with its standards: so carefully do they all observe the order of travelling, moving in company, and going before.

Crows escort and guide them, following like squadrons of guards. Indeed, they are believed to bring a kind of assistance to combatants against hostile birds, and to undertake another’s wars at the risk of their own lives. The evidence is that no crows are found resting in those places for a certain interval of time; and that when they return wounded, they declare by the evident testimony of their blood and by other signs that they have endured the clash of severe battles.

Who imposed upon them the punishment for desertion? Who prescribed terrifying penalties for abandonment of military duty, such that none attempts to withdraw from escorting friendly flocks, but all eagerly perform the task and service of escort?

54. Let people learn to keep the laws of hospitality and discover from birds what reverence ought to be shown to guests, what services should be rendered—when crows are not accustomed even to spare their own lives in such matters. Yet we shut our doors against those for whom birds even risk their lives; those whom they accompany in fellowship of danger, we bar from the hospitality of a roof; those whose wars they undertake, we frequently make war upon.

I am lying if this was not the cause of punishment for the Sodomites; or if Egyptian fury, when it sought to wage war upon a guest people, did not pay the penalty of faithless inhospitality by the shipwreck of its people.

55. We must consider how far the mercifulness of this bird surpasses the filial devotion and prudence of rational creatures, when none of us has been able to imitate it even after the example of irrational creatures. For—

> [Note: *Depositi*, that is, “given up for lost,” as in *Aeneid* XI:]

“that he might recount the fate of his abandoned father.” The offspring, standing round their father’s limbs, stripped bare by the long passage of old age of their covering of feathers and the rowing of their wings, warm them with their own feathers. And why should I say that they feed him with their pooled food, when they even repair nature’s losses, so that, supporting the old bird now on this side, now on that, with the prop of their wings, they exercise him for flight and recall the limbs of their dutiful father, now unaccustomed to it, to their former uses? Which of us does not shrink from lifting a sick father? Who puts a weary old man upon his own shoulders—something scarcely considered believable even in history? Who, if he is to be dutiful, does not assign this service to slaves? But for birds, that which is full of filial devotion is not burdensome; what is rendered in payment of nature’s debt is not heavy. Birds do not refuse to feed their father—something that very many people have refused even when necessity prescribed it under threat of penalties. Birds are bound, not by a written law, but by one with which they are born.

Birds are summoned to this duty by no commands, but by the offices of natural gratitude. [Note: Some editions and manuscripts: “are summoned by no command, but by the office of natural gratitude.” Several and better manuscripts: “no commands … offices.”] Birds are not ashamed to carry the limbs of a venerable old bird; for it is a conveyance of filial devotion. This has become so widely known through frequent testimony that it has received the reward of an appropriate recompense. For in Roman usage this bird is called “dutiful” (*pia*). And what is said scarcely to have been conferred deliberately by the senate upon a single emperor, these birds have deserved in common. Thus these birds possess decrees of the Fathers as an emblem of their distinctive compassion. For dutiful children ought first to have been proclaimed such by the judgment of their fathers. They also possess the votes of all; for the repayment of benefits is called *antipelargēsis* (ἀντιπελάργησις), “requital like that of a stork”; for *pelargos* (πέλαργος) means “stork.” Thus a virtue has taken its name from them, since gratitude is designated by the term for a stork.

## Chapter XVII

On the swallow’s diligence, industry, and devotion toward its young. On its poverty, by which the impatience, wickedness, and despair of a human being reduced to want are reproved.

56. We have an example of filial devotion in a brood of birds toward the care due to their fathers; let us now take a great lesson in a mother’s diligence toward her children. The swallow is tiny in body, yet exalted by an outstandingly dutiful affection. Though lacking all things, it builds nests more precious than gold, because it nests wisely. For the nest of wisdom is better than gold. What could be wiser than for it both to enjoy the roaming freedom of flight and to entrust its little ones to human dwellings and shelter, where no one may attack its brood? For this also is admirable: from their first birth it accustoms its young to life among human beings and makes them safer from the snares of hostile birds.

Then there is the splendid skill with which, without any helper and as though expert in an art, it constructs a home for itself. It picks up straws in its beak and coats them with mud so that it can glue them together. But, because it cannot carry mud with its feet, it dips the tips of its wings in water, so that dust may readily cling to them and become mud; with this it gradually collects and fastens together straws or small twigs, and by this method builds the entire structure of its nest. Thus, as though upon the level ground of a paved floor, its young may move about within their home without injury, and no one may thrust a foot through the openings of the weaving, nor may cold creep in upon the tender chicks.

57. Yet this work of industry is nearly shared by many birds. But the following is unique, in which there is a striking care of filial devotion, a mark of prudent understanding and knowledge, and even a certain skill in medicine: if any of its young have their eyes impaired by blindness or punctured, it has a kind of remedy by which it can restore the use of their sight, once obstructed. Therefore let no one complain of poverty because he has left his own house empty of money. Poorer is the swallow, which, empty of money, abounds in industry. It builds without expenditure; it raises roofs and takes nothing from its neighbor; nor is it driven by need and poverty to harm others; nor, in the severe weakness of its children, does it despair.

But we are distressed by poverty, tormented by the necessity of want, and many are forced by need into shameful conduct and driven into crime. For the sake of gain we turn our ingenuity to fraud and adapt our inclination to it; and in our gravest sufferings we lay aside hope. Broken in spirit, we collapse; without foresight and inactive, we lie helpless—although then we ought to hope all the more in divine mercy, when human resources have failed.

## Chapter XVIII

That people should learn love for their children from ravens, and that their impiety is condemned. That hawks and eagles are by no means to be accused of cruelty; but that the coot, which nourishes an eagle’s rejected chick, should be commended.

58. Let human beings learn to love their children from the practice and devotion of ravens. Even when their children are flying, ravens diligently accompany them; anxiously fearing that the tender young may perhaps fail, they offer them food and do not abandon their duties of feeding them for a very long time. But women of our race quickly wean even those whom they love; or, if they are wealthier, they disdain to nurse them.

[Note: Four manuscripts: “The poor man complains because he has left his own dwelling empty of money. But the poorer …”]

But poorer women cast off their little ones, expose them, and deny them when they are found. Even wealthy women themselves, lest their inheritance be divided among too many, kill their own offspring in the womb and extinguish the pledges of their own womb by parricidal juices within the very generative belly; life is taken away before it is bestowed. Who except man taught that children should be disowned? Who devised such savage rights for fathers? Who made brothers unequal within nature’s fraternal fellowship? The children of one rich man are cut down by differing lots. One is flooded with grants of the entire paternal estate; another laments his drained and impoverished share of a rich ancestral inheritance. Did nature divide the deserts of children? She bestowed equally upon all what they might have as the means of being born and living. Let nature herself teach you not to distinguish by inheritance those whom you have made equal by the title of brotherhood. For those to whom you have jointly given what they are by birth, you ought not to begrudge their jointly possessing that for which nature has established them.

59. Hawks are said to display harsh cruelty toward their own young: when they observe them trying the first beginnings of flight, they drive them from their nests and immediately expel them. If they hesitate, the parents push and hurl them down with their wings, beat them with their pinions, and compel them to dare what they fear; afterward they bring them no further provision of food. Yet what wonder if those accustomed to seize prey disdain to feed? Let us consider that they were born for this purpose: that fear of them may train even birds to be watchful, lest they relax their vigilance everywhere, but may foresee dangers to be avoided from predators.

Moreover, since a certain office of predation has become natural to them, they seem rather to train their young from tenderness for prey than to deny them food for reasons of economy. They take care lest the young become sluggish at a tender age, be weakened by indulgence, languish in idleness, learn rather to await food than to seek it, or lay aside the vigor proper to their nature. They suspend their efforts at feeding so as to compel them boldly into the practices of taking prey.

60. The eagle too is much spoken of as rejecting its own young; yet it does not reject both, but one of two chicks. Some have thought that it does this because it is unwilling to provide doubled food. But I do not think this is easily credible, especially since Moses gave this bird so great a testimony of devotion toward its young that he said: “As an eagle protects its nest and trusts in its young and spreads out its wings, so it took them up and bore them upon its shoulders. The Lord alone led them” (Deut. 32:11).

[Note: Roman edition: “and desired [or cherished] its young.” Vatican manuscript: “… settled [upon them].”]

How, then, did it spread out its wings, if it killed one chick? Therefore I think that it becomes unmerciful, not from greed in feeding, but through an examination in judgment. For it is always said to test those it has produced, lest the deformity of degenerate offspring tarnish a certain royal eminence of its race among all birds. Thus it is asserted that it exposes its chicks to the sun’s rays and suspends the little ones in mid-air by its talon. If any chick, with the sunlight reflected upon it, preserves an undaunted sharpness of vision and an unimpaired power of sight, it is approved, because the constancy of its clear gaze has shown the truth of its nature. But if, dazzled by the sunbeam, it has turned away its eyes, it is rejected as degenerate and unworthy of so great a parent; nor is one thought worthy of rearing who was unworthy of being received. Therefore the eagle condemns it, not through nature’s harshness, but through the soundness of judgment; and it does not reject it as its own, but refuses it as alien.

61. Yet, as some think, the compassion of a common bird excuses this supposed cruelty of the royal bird. For the bird called the coot, which in Greek is called *phēnē* (φηνή), takes in the eagle’s chick—whether rejected, disowned, or unrecognized—and joins it to her own brood. Mingling it among her own, she feeds and nourishes it with the same maternal diligence and equal provision of food with which she feeds her own young. Thus the *phēnē* nourishes strangers, while we cast out our own with savage cruelty. The eagle, if it casts one out, does not cast it out as its own, but does not recognize it as degenerate. We, what is worse, disown those whom we recognize as our own.

## Chapter XIX

The turtledove is praised for widowhood, and on this account is preferred even to Christian women.

62. But let us come to the turtledove, which the law of God chose as an offering of a chaste sacrifice (Lev. 12:8). Accordingly, when the Lord was circumcised, it was offered, because it is written in the law of the Lord that they should offer as a sacrifice “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Luke 2:24).

[Note: German manuscript: “when the Lord was offered in the Temple,” etc.]

This is the true sacrifice of Christ: bodily chastity and spiritual grace. Chastity is referred to the turtledove, grace to the dove. For the turtledove is said, when bereaved by the loss of its proper mate, to loathe the marriage-bed and even the name of marriage, because its first love has deceived it through the death of the beloved; since the beloved was unfaithful as regards permanence, and bitter as regards gratitude, producing more grief by death than sweetness by affection. Therefore it refuses to repeat the union; it neither dissolves the obligations of modesty nor the covenant with its pleasing husband, but reserves its love for him alone and keeps for him the name of wife.

[Note: Some Paris editions: “having grown weary of marriage-beds and the name of marriage”; the last: “… which bears the name of marriage.” All older editions: “and to bear the name of marriage.” One Victorine and one Colbert manuscript: “having grown weary of marriage-beds,” etc.; the Coenobial manuscript and another Victorine: “having grown weary of the use of the marriage-bed,” etc. Better are the others which agree with the old edition. For there is an ellipsis here, which may be supplied thus: “They report that the turtledove has grown to hate the business of marriage-beds,” etc.]

Learn, women, how great is the grace of widowhood, which is praised even in birds.

63. Who, then, gave these laws to the turtledove? If I seek a human being, I find none. For no human being has dared to do so, since not even Paul dared to prescribe laws requiring widowhood to be maintained. Indeed, he himself says: “I desire, therefore, that younger women marry, bear children, manage households, and give the adversary no opportunity” (1 Tim. 5:14). And elsewhere: “It is good for them if they remain as they are; but if they do not have self-control, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:8). Paul wishes in women what persists in turtledoves. Elsewhere he urges younger women to marry, because our women can scarcely fulfill the chastity of turtledoves. Therefore God infused this disposition into turtledoves and gave them this virtue of continence—he alone being able to prescribe what all should follow.

The turtledove is not inflamed by the bloom of youth, nor tempted by the allurements of opportunity; it does not know how to make void the first pledge, because it knows how to preserve the chastity promised in its first marriage-lot.

[Note: Some manuscripts: “The turtledove does not make use of its bloom,” etc. Some manuscripts and the old edition: “the first lot of marriage having been passed over.”]

## Chapter XX

Vultures, said to breed without union with a male, establish the possibility of virginal childbirth.

64. We have spoken of the widowhood of birds and of this virtue as first arising among them. Let us now speak of integrity, which is indeed affirmed to exist among many birds, so that it may even be found in vultures. For vultures are said not to indulge in sexual intercourse, nor to mingle through a certain marital practice and the lot of nuptial union; rather, without any male seed, they conceive, and without union, they give birth. Their offspring also advance to a great age in long-lived existence, so that the course of their lives is extended even to one hundred years, and they are not easily overtaken by the end of a brief lifetime.

65. What do those say who are accustomed to mock our mysteries when they hear that a virgin gave birth and judge impossible the childbirth of an unmarried woman whose modesty no intercourse with a man had violated? Is that thought impossible in the Mother of God which is not denied possible in vultures? A bird gives birth without a male, and no one refutes it; yet because Mary, though betrothed to a man, gave birth while a virgin, they raise a question against her chastity.

[Note: All editions: “her chastity.” Latinius: “chastity for her.” Better manuscripts: “for her chastity.”]

Do we not observe that the Lord beforehand sent forth from nature itself many examples by which he might demonstrate the fittingness of the incarnation he undertook and establish its truth?

## Chapter XXI

On birds organized under a kind of political constitution; especially concerning bees, their wonderful nature in producing offspring, choosing a king, loyalty toward him, constructing honeycombs, gathering honey, and its usefulness, and so forth.

66. Come now, let me explain which birds seem to administer something like a commonwealth and to pass the course of this life under laws. For this is the practice of a commonwealth: that laws are common to all and observed with common devotion; that all are held by one bond; that one person does not claim a right which another understands is forbidden to himself; rather, what is permitted is permitted to all, and what is forbidden is forbidden to all. There is also common reverence for the fathers, by whose counsel the commonwealth is governed; a common dwelling-place in the city for all; a common function of association; one rule for all; one deliberation.

[Note: Some manuscripts: “reverence for offspring.” Better several others and the old edition: “for senators.” Nevertheless, most manuscripts and the Roman edition read as in the text.]

67. These things are great, but how much more excellent are they in bees. Alone among every kind of living creature, they have offspring common to all; they all inhabit one dwelling, are enclosed within the boundary of one native land; their labor is common to all, their food common, their work common, their use and profit common, their flight common. What more need be said? Their generation is common to all, and virgin bodily integrity and childbirth are likewise common to all. For they neither mingle with one another through any intercourse nor are dissolved by lust, nor are they shaken by the pains of childbirth; but suddenly they send forth a great swarm of offspring, gathering their brood with their mouths from leaves and herbs.

68. They appoint a king for themselves; they create peoples for themselves; and though placed under a king, they are nevertheless free. For they retain both the prerogative of judgment and the disposition of faithful devotion: they love him as one appointed by themselves and honor him with so great a host. Their king is not chosen by lot, for in a lot there is chance, not judgment, and often, by the irrational accident of a lot, the last is preferred over the better. Nor is he marked out by the popular shout of an unskilled multitude, which neither weighs the merits of virtue nor investigates the advantages of public usefulness, but wavers in the uncertainty of fickleness. Nor does he sit upon royal thrones by the privilege of succession and lineage; for one ignorant of public life cannot be prudent and instructed.

Add the flatteries and indulgences which, ingrained in tender years, are accustomed to enervate even a keen intelligence; then the training of eunuchs, most of whom incline the king’s mind more toward their own profit than toward public welfare. But among bees the king is formed with conspicuous marks of nature, excelling in size of body and appearance; and then, what is foremost in a king, in gentleness of character. For although he has a sting, he does not use it for vengeance. For there are laws of nature written not in letters but impressed upon dispositions: those who possess the greatest power ought to be gentler in punishment. Indeed, those bees which have not obeyed the king’s laws punish themselves by a penitent condemnation, so as to die from the wound of their own sting. The Persian peoples too are said to observe this even today: according to the price of the offense committed, they themselves execute upon themselves the sentence of their own death.

[Note: Old edition: “Thus none, like the kings of the Persians, [observe] so very grave … so great [a reverence] as bees.” Some manuscripts: “thus no one so follows, or pursues, a king … so great [a reverence] as [bees].” But this is a scribal error, restored by others and by the Roman edition. Moreover, the holy author intended to imitate *Georgics* IV:

> Moreover, neither Egypt, nor vast  
> Lydia, nor the peoples of Parthia, nor Median Hydaspes,  
> observe their king in this manner.]

Therefore no one observes a king with such reverent devotion as bees do—not the Persians, who have very severe laws against subjects; not the Indians; not the peoples of the Sarmatians. No bee dares leave its home or go forth to any feeding-ground unless the king has first gone out and claimed for himself the leadership of the flight.

[Note: Many manuscripts: “nor go to any [feeding-ground].”]

69. Their departure is through fragrant fields, where gardens breathe in flowers, where a running stream passes through the grass, where the riverbanks are pleasant. There is the play of lively youth; there the exercise of the open field; there the release from cares. The work itself is pleasant: from flowers and sweet herbs the first foundations of their camp are laid. For what else is a honeycomb but a kind of camp? Indeed, the drone is excluded from these bees’ stalls. What square-built camp can possess as much art and elegance as the lattices of honeycombs, in which tiny round cells mutually support one another by their interconnection? What architect taught them to construct those hexagonal cells with the indistinguishable equality of their sides, to suspend thin wax between the partitions of their homes, to pack in honey, and to extend storehouses, interwoven with flowers, with a kind of nectar?

You may see all competing in their task: some watch over the search for food; others provide anxious guard for the camp; others investigate coming rains and observe the gathering of clouds; others shape wax from flowers; others gather in their mouths dew poured upon flowers. Yet none plots against another’s labor or seeks life by plunder—though I wish they did not have to fear the plots of robbers. Still, they have their little weapons; when provoked, they pour poison amid their honey and lay down their lives in the wound, in the ardor of vengeance. Thus that moisture of dew is poured into the hollow spaces amid the camp and, through the gradual passage of time, is condensed into honey. Although liquid at first, when it has united with wax and begun to be fragrant with the scent of flowers, it takes on the sweetness of honey.

[Note: Some manuscripts: “and, when the wax has been nourished and joined together,” etc.]

70. With good reason Scripture praises the bee as a good worker, saying: “Go to the bee, and see how industrious it is.” It also says, “What a venerable work it carries on, whose labor kings and ordinary people employ for health. For it is desirable to all and renowned” (Prov. 6:8).

[Note: Roman edition: “performs a venerable [work],” following the Septuagint according to the Vatican and Florentine codices, where *poieitai* (ποιεῖται, “it performs”) is read. Other editions and all manuscripts: “… carries on [or trades in],” according to the Venetian codex, where *emporeuetai* (ἐμπορεύεται, “it carries on business”) is read.]

[Note: Four manuscripts: “dear.” Others and the editions: “renowned.” Septuagint: *epidoxos* (ἐπίδοξος, “illustrious, esteemed”). The entire passage in the Coenobial manuscript reads: “Go … and imitate its work. For the bee carries on a work how venerable, whose …”]

Do you hear what the prophet says? He sends you, certainly, to follow the example of that little bee and imitate its work. You see how laborious and how pleasing it is. Its product is desired and sought by all; it is not distinguished according to differences of persons, but with its impartial grace it sweetens alike kings and ordinary people with equal pleasantness. It serves not only pleasure but also health: it sweetens the throat, heals wounds, and pours medicine even into internal ulcers. Thus, though the bee is weak in physical strength, it is powerful in the vigor of wisdom and the love of virtue.

71. Finally, they defend their king with the utmost protection and think it honorable to die for him. While the king is safe, they do not know how to change their judgment or alter their purpose. When he is lost, they abandon their faithful performance of duty and themselves plunder their own honey, because he who held the office of leadership has been slain.

72. Thus, while other birds scarcely produce a single brood in a year, bees produce two and outweigh the rest by a twofold fertility.

## Chapter XXII

Why flying creatures are called those “flying above the earth beside the firmament of heaven.” Also concerning the bodily diversity observable among birds. Finally, some remarks are added concerning the swan and cicada.

73. Let us now consider what it means when he says: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls according to their kind, and winged creatures flying above the earth according to their kind beside the firmament of heaven.” Why he said “above the earth” is clear: because they seek their food from the earth. But how “beside the firmament of heaven,” when eagles fly higher than other birds, and yet even they are not beside the firmament of heaven? But because in Greek what we call heaven in Latin is called *ouranos* (οὐρανός), and *ouranos* comes *apo tou horasthai* (ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁρᾶσθαι), that is, “from being seen,” because the air is transparent and clearer for seeing, he referred to kinds of animals flying in the air. And lest his saying “beside the firmament of heaven” trouble anyone: he has not used “firmament” here properly but figuratively, because in comparison with that ethereal body, even this air which we can comprehend with our eyes performs the function of a firmament as something thicker and denser.

74. Now that we have said what winged creatures are, what nature and grace they possess—only a few things out of many, for there is no leisure to describe everything, since they are alike and of the same kind—let us nevertheless consider how much diversity the birds themselves have among one another. We find that the feet of ravens are separated and divided as though by certain toes; and we see that the feet of crows and chickens too have been shaped differently by nature. The feet of birds which feed on flesh appear bent and curved, as though prepared for prey. But those which have the use and habit of swimming possess broad feet, with the toes joined and connected by a sort of membrane. In this the admirable design of nature is evident: that the former may be suitably fashioned for seizing or snatching food, while the latter have suitable aids for swimming, by which they may better float upon the waters and, as with oars, drive back the streams by means of the broad extension of that membrane on their feet.

75. It is also evident why the swan uses a longer neck. Because its body is somewhat slower and it cannot easily penetrate the lower depths of waters, it stretches out its neck toward prey; this neck, as though preceding the rest of the body, seizes the food it finds and draws it up from the depths. Add also that its sweeter and more melodious tone is formed through its long neck, and by longer exercise resounds much more clearly.

76. How sweet also is the song in the tiny throat of cicadas. In the heat of noon, groves resound with their singing; for, being more melodious in the midday heat, and drawing in at that time purer air with their breath, they send forth clearer songs.

[Note: Some manuscripts: “and because at that time they draw in purer air by breathing.”]

Nor do bees themselves sing anything unpleasant; for in that rough murmur of their voice they have an agreeable sweetness, which we seem at first to imitate more slowly by the broken sound of trumpets—a noise judged especially suitable for stirring minds into vigor. This grace remains to them, although they are reported to possess neither lungs nor the function and use of breathing, but to feed upon aerial breath. Accordingly, if anyone pours oil over them, they quickly die because, their pores having been blocked, they cannot draw in that aerial breath; and immediately, if someone pours vinegar over them, they revive at once, because the force of vinegar is said quickly to open with its moisture those pores that are blocked by the thickened fluid of oil.

[Note: Some manuscripts: “if anyone pours [oil] over them or the drones.”]

[Note: Several better manuscripts: “which are said to be opened by the moisture [of vinegar], though blocked by the more congealed fluid of oil.”]

## Chapter XXIII

On the Indian worm, the chameleon, the hare, and the phoenix, by which we are instructed concerning faith in the resurrection and preparation for death. On the foreknowledge of vultures; and the locust’s service in carrying out divine vengeance, though it is devoured by the bird *seleucis*.

77. Since we are speaking of winged creatures, we do not think it irrelevant to include what history, or the report of those who were able to see, relates about the Indian worm.

[Note: Some manuscripts: “This black, horned worm is said …”]

This horned worm is said first to change into the form of a cabbage stalk and to be transformed into that nature; then, by a certain progression, it becomes a *bombylius* [silkworm or moth]. Yet it does not retain even that appearance and shape, but, with loose and broader leaves, appears to assume wings.

[Note: All manuscripts and editions except the Roman read “into the form of a stalk.” The Roman edition reads “into the form of a caterpillar.” Latinius conjectures “into the form of a larva (*campa*).” Undoubtedly because of Basil: “having first changed into a caterpillar” (*hos eis kampēn ta prōta metaballōn*, ὃς εἰς κάμπην τὰ πρῶτα μεταβαλών).]

From these leaves the Seres comb out those soft fleeces which the rich have appropriated for their own use.

[Note: Roman edition: “From its threads.” All other editions and manuscripts: “From these leaves.” Virgil, *Georgics* II: “and the Seres comb their fine fleeces from leaves.”]

Hence the Lord also says: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A man dressed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 11:8). The chameleon too is said to counterfeit different appearances through changing color. Hares, certainly—as we have readily learned from nearby observation—undoubtedly grow white in winter and return to their own color in summer.

78. I have sampled these matters for this reason: that these examples too may prompt us to believe in the transformation which is to occur in the resurrection. But let us understand that transformation in the way the Apostle clearly expressed it, saying: “We shall indeed all rise again, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51). And below he says: “The dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (ibid., 52). For many people, interpreting a kind and forms of transformation which they had not received, have not been free from the inappropriate usurpation of unwarranted presumption.

[Note: Some manuscripts: “they interpret, who by no means …”; Coenobial manuscript: “by a certain interpretation of unwarranted presumption, they have overthrown [the sense] by an incongruous usurpation.”]

79. The phoenix too is said to live in regions of Arabia and to reach an age of five hundred years. When it perceives that the end of its life is at hand, it makes for itself a casket of frankincense, myrrh, and other spices. When the span of its life has been fulfilled, it enters this and dies. From the moisture of its flesh a worm rises, gradually grows, and, in the course of the appointed time, puts on the rowing feathers of wings and is restored to the appearance and form of the former bird. Let this bird, therefore, teach us by its own example to believe in the resurrection—a bird which itself renews for itself the marks of resurrection without precedent and without rational understanding. And certainly birds exist for the sake of human beings, not human beings for the sake of birds. Therefore let it be an example to us that the Author and Creator of birds does not permit his saints to perish forever—he who did not allow one single bird to perish, but willed it, rising again, to be renewed from its own seed.

[Note: Some manuscripts: “willed it to be propagated.”]

Who then announces to it the day of its death, so that it may make itself a casket, fill it with pleasant spices, enter it, and die there, where the stench of its funeral may be abolished by sweet fragrances?

80. Do you, O human being, make a casket for yourself: stripping off the old person with his deeds, put on the new. Your casket, your sheath, is Christ, who protects and hides you in the evil day. Do you wish to know that a casket is protection? “I protected him,” he says, “in my quiver” (Isa. 49:2). Therefore your casket is faith. Fill it with the pleasant fragrances of your virtues—that is, chastity, mercy, and justice—and enter wholly into the innermost chambers of faith, fragrant with the sweet scent of excellent deeds. May the end of this life find you clothed in that faith, so that your bones may grow fat and be like a well-watered garden, whose seeds quickly spring up.

Recognize, therefore, the day of your death, as Paul too recognized it, who says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; for the rest, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Tim. 4:7–8). He therefore entered into his casket like a good phoenix, which he filled with the good fragrance of martyrdom.

81. I shall ask you, and you answer me: whence have vultures customarily announced human death by certain signs? By what indication have they been taught and instructed, so that, when opposing battle-lines prepare a lamentable war against one another, the birds follow in a great flock beforehand, signifying thereby that a multitude of people will fall in battle and become prey for the vultures? They seem, certainly, to infer this by some reasoning from the appearance of human planning and preparation.

82. Divine grace has reached even the locust. When it has occupied the expanse of a region in a dense swarm, it is first directed against a harmless dwelling and does not consume its crops by its inhospitable invasion unless it has received the sign of a divine command.

[Note: Edition: *fertur*, “is borne” or “is directed.” Manuscripts: *feriatur*, “is struck.”]

For, as we read in Exodus (Exod. 10:12), it too carries out the heavenly vengeance for an offense, as a dutiful minister of vengeance.

83. The bird *seleucis* (σελευκίς)—for this bird is so called by the Greek name—also devours it. This bird was given as a remedy for the evils which the locust is accustomed to inflict; its Creator gave it an insatiable nature for devouring, so that by its unappeasable feeding it might extinguish the plague of which we have spoken above.

## Chapter XXIV

On nocturnal birds; first, on the song of the brooding nightingale; on the owl, bat, and cock; and how certain matters are adapted from them to our conduct.

84. But what is this? While we prolong our discourse, behold, nocturnal birds now fly around us; and in the very act by which they remind us that the discourse must end, they also occasion the addition of their own commemoration. The various birds return to their bird-homes, compelled by evening to withdraw into the night, and hide themselves in their retreats, accompanying the day’s setting with melodious song, lest they depart without thanksgiving—those creatures by which all creation praises its Creator.

85. Night too has its songs, with which it is accustomed to soothe human vigils; and the owl has its songs. But what shall I say of the nightingale, that ever-watchful guardian which, while it warms its eggs in the hollow and lap of its body, comforts the sleepless labor of the long night with the sweetness of song? Its highest purpose seems to me to be that it may animate the eggs it broods not less by sweet melodies than by the warmth of its body.

This slight-bodied but modest woman, imitating it, draws the millstone with her arm in the service of the mill, so that bread may not be lacking as food for her little children; with her night-song she soothes the sorrowful feeling of poverty. Although she cannot imitate the sweetness of the nightingale, she nevertheless imitates it in the diligence of filial devotion.

[Note: Five manuscripts: “with an inner [or beaten-in] stone.” Five likewise, together with the Costantinian edition and some Paris editions: “struck [or driven] in.”]

86. How the owl itself, with its large blue-gray pupils, does not feel the dreadful gloom of nocturnal darkness; and the darker the night is, the more it carries on unimpeded flights, contrary to the habit of other birds. But when day has risen and the splendor of the sun is spread around, its sight grows dull, as though it wandered in darkness. By this sign it declares that there are some who, though they have eyes for seeing, are not accustomed to see, and employ the function of their sight in darkness. I speak of the eyes of the heart, which the wise people of the world possess but do not see; in light they perceive nothing, and they walk in darkness while they investigate the dark things of demons and believe that they see the heights of heaven, mapping the world by a ray and calculating the measure of the air itself.

But those who have strayed from faith are entangled in the darkness of perpetual blindness. Though the day of Christ and the light of the Church are near them, they see nothing; they open their mouths as though knowing everything, acute for vain things, dull for eternal things, and, through the winding course of lengthy disputation, reveal the blindness of their own ignorance.

[Note: Amerbach and Erasmus: “wise in their intricate course, unaware of their own ignorance.”]

Thus, while they desire to fly aloft in subtle arguments, like owls they have vanished in the light.

87. The bat, an insignificant creature, takes its name from the evening (*vesper*). It is a flying animal and yet a quadruped; it has teeth, which you would not ordinarily find in other birds. Like quadrupeds it gives birth, not to eggs, but to living young. It flies through the air in the manner of birds; but at evening twilight it is accustomed to be obscured. [Note: Some manuscripts read *consuevit offendi* (“it is accustomed to be impeded”).] It flies, moreover, supported not by any oarage of feathers but by that of its membrane; suspended by this, it is carried about as though in a flight of wings and is sustained. [Note: The Roman edition reads “wanders,” following the Basel edition, which has Greek ἐπιπολάζει, “moves about on the surface.”] This lowly creature also has the characteristic that they cling to one another and hang from some place as if in a cluster of grapes; and if the last of them loosens itself, all are released. This happens through a certain service of charity which is difficult to find among the people of this world.

88. The cock’s crow is also pleasant in the night; and not only pleasant, but useful. Like a good fellow-dweller, it wakes the sleeper, warns the anxious, and comforts the traveller, announcing the progress of the night by its melodious signal. [Note: Compare this passage with the Sunday hymn for Lauds.] At its crow the thief abandons his ambushes; at its crow the day-star itself, awakened, rises and illumines heaven. At its crow the frightened sailor lays aside his sadness, and every storm and tempest, stirred up by the frequent evening winds, grows calm. At its crow devout feeling springs up to pray and renews also the task of reading. Finally, at its crow the very rock of the Church washes away the fault which it had contracted by denial before the cock crowed. By its crow hope returns to all; the suffering of the sick is relieved, the pain of wounds is diminished, the burning of fevers is tempered; faith returns to those who have fallen, Jesus looks upon those who stagger, and corrects those who stray. In short, he looked upon Peter, and immediately error departed: denial was driven out and confession followed. The reading teaches that this did not happen by chance, but according to the Lord’s purpose. For it is written thus: Jesus said to Simon, “The cock will not crow before you deny me three times” (Matt. 26:34). Peter was rightly strong by day, but troubled at night; and before the cock’s crow he fell—and fell a third time—so that you may know that his fall was not merely an unconsidered outpouring of speech, but that he was troubled by a change of mind as well. [Note: Some manuscripts and the editions of Amerbach and Petri read *nutatione turbatum*, “troubled by wavering.”] Yet after the cock’s crow he became stronger, and was now worthy for Christ to look upon him, for “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.” He recognized that the remedy had come, after which he could no longer go astray; and, changed from error into strength, he wept most bitterly, that by his tears he might blot out his error.

## CHAPTER XXV

The author’s devout prayer. Commendation of tears. Dismissal of the hearers for refreshment. Finally, an invitation to the mysteries of the Lord’s body.

89. Look upon us also, Lord Jesus, so that we too may recognize our own errors, may loose our guilt with devout tears, and may deserve forgiveness of sins. For this reason we deliberately prolonged the discourse: that the cock might crow for us also and assist us as we speak, so that, if any offence had crept into our words, you, Christ, might pardon the fault. Grant, I pray, Peter’s tears; I do not want the sinner’s joy. The Hebrews wept, and through the sea, when its waves parted, they were delivered. Pharaoh rejoiced that he held the Hebrews shut in, and he perished, drowned in the sea with his people. Judas too exulted in the payment for his betrayal, but strangled himself with the noose made from that very payment. Peter wept for his error, and deserved to blot out the errors of others.

90. But now it is time that we should end and close our discourse; it is time when it is better either to be silent or to weep; it is the time when forgiveness of sins is celebrated. Let this mystical cock crow for us also in the sacred rites, since Peter’s cock has now crowed in our discourse. Let Peter weep for us—he who wept well for himself—and let the merciful countenance of Christ turn toward us. Let the passion of the Lord Jesus hasten on, which daily forgives our offences and effects the gift of remission.

91. The good Lord does not wish to send people away fasting, lest anyone fail on the way. If he says, “I have compassion on this crowd, because they have remained with me for three days and have no food; and I do not wish to send them away fasting, lest they fail on the way” (Matt. 15:32)—he for whose discourse Mary, intent upon it, declined preparations for a feast—how much more ought we to take thought, since there are not many who live upon the word of God, and therefore bodily refreshment is desired! Certainly, this day after that three-day period is more laborious for us.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “the day after”; Carnotensis, Corbiensis, Theodorianus, and Regius read “after the day before”; Bigotianus and Gemblacensis, “after the following day”; Germanensis and Colbertinus, together with Victorius, “two days after.” Amid this variation and obscurity, it seemed best not to depart from the editions.]

92. And therefore, having played with the birds and sung with the cock, let us now sing the mysteries of the Lord; and let eagles, renewed by the washing away of sins, gather to the body of Jesus. For that great whale has given us back the true Jonah; and let us rejoice that for us the fifth day has come to be evening: let the sixth day become morning for us.

# BOOK SIX: ON THE WORK OF THE SIXTH DAY

## CHAPTER I  
*(Discourse IX)*

The difficulty of this final discourse is explained by the example of competitors in public games; attention is also won through the pleasure and usefulness of the matters under discussion.

1. This is the sixth day, on which the origin of the world’s creatures is concluded; and therefore an end is prepared also for our discourse, which we undertook concerning the beginnings of things. [Note: Three manuscripts read “concerning the beginnings of the days.”] Although during the five days already elapsed it has proceeded with no small labour for us, yet on this present day it increases with a greater burden of cares, because in it lie both the risk of the preceding days and the issue of the whole contest. For in contests of lyre-playing or singing and in the repeated—and even the greatest—competitions of athletes, the earlier days pass without any loss of the crown; but the final day bears the lot of the crown, in which there is both the danger of decision, the disgrace of yielding, and the reward of victory. How much more, then, in this great contest of wisdom, before the judgment not of a few but of all, when today a kind of crown of the contest lies before us, is greater anxiety pressing upon us, lest we squander the labour of the former days and incur the shame of the present one. For the condition of speaking is not the same as that of singing or wrestling: in those, failure is a matter of sport; in this, stumbling is death. There, if you make a mistake, it is the spectators’ disgust; here, it is the hearers’ loss.

2. Stand by me, therefore, as judges of the crown, and enter with me into this great and admirable theatre of the whole visible creation. If a person who receives newly arrived guests conducts them around the whole circuit of a city, showing them its more distinguished works, he earns no small gratitude. How much more ought you to receive without distaste what I set before you when, as it were by the hand of discourse, I lead you through this common homeland and display the forms and kinds of individual things, [Note: The Carnotensis, Corbiensis, Theodorianus, and Regius manuscripts read: “through this communion I lead you about into the homeland.”] wishing from them all to gather how much more abundant a favour the Creator of all has bestowed upon you than he has given to all other things. This crown, then, is set before you; today I wish to be crowned by your judgment. For we do not seek, in the manner of athletes, withering garlands, but the ever-green verdict of your holiness: by it may you judge that divine providence pervades all creatures, but that, although you share with the rest a fellowship in bodily frailty, you nevertheless excel the rest by the strength of mind, which alone has nothing in common with the others.

## CHAPTER II

Ambrose approaches the discussion of the nature of beasts: he teaches that Scripture must be taken simply; compares himself to a poor host; warns against curious questions, confirming this point by the example of Moses.

3. Come now, let us speak of the natures of beasts and of the creation of humankind. For I have long heard some whispering and saying: “How long are we to learn about things foreign to us while remaining ignorant of ourselves? How long are we to be taught knowledge about other living creatures while we do not know ourselves? Let him speak of what benefits me, so that I may know myself.” The complaint is just; but we must preserve the order that Scripture has woven together, and also because we cannot know ourselves more fully unless we first know the nature of all living creatures.

[Note: All editions read “question.” The manuscripts more rightly read *conquestio*, “complaint.”]

4. “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kind: quadrupeds, creeping things, beasts of the earth, cattle according to their kind, and every reptile. And God made the beasts of the earth, and all cattle according to their kind, and every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind. And God saw that they were good; and God said: ‘Let us make humankind’” (Gen. 1:24–26). At this point, I know that some have referred the kinds of beasts, cattle, and creeping things of the earth to something else, so as to apply them to the enormity of crimes, the folly of sins, and the wickedness of thoughts. But I take them as the simple natures of each kind.

[Note: Most and better manuscripts read: “beasts of the earth, cattle according to their kind, and creeping things of the earth according to their kind.” The Roman edition reads: “according to their kind”; it alone also adds: “and it was so.”]

5. Nor do I fear that anyone will think I should be compared to the presumption of a poor host, who, from a desire to show hospitality, invites many guests but sets before them nothing except cheap and ordinary foods, and by the meagre provision of his poor table incurs more blame from the guests’ distaste than gratitude for his hospitable intention. For Elisha’s friends did not reject him as a bad host for setting before them rustic vegetables (4 Kings [2 Kings] 4:39). A banquet sought out with empty refinements is like this: a pheasant or turtle-dove is served in appearance, but a chicken is eaten inside; or a chicken is brought in stuffed with oysters or *spondyli* [shellfish]; or a cup is drunk whose differing colour and scent change into unfamiliar flavours. Sea-food is stuffed with land-food, and land-food with sea-food. This is to criticize the providence of the Creator, who gave us everything for nourishment, because he did not mix those things together. But such things seem sweet at first and afterwards become bitter. For the more abundant luxury is, the more harmful is excess. Elisha, however, set before them bitter things, but they afterwards became sweet. Indeed, those who first thought there was death in that food afterwards found in it the grace of sweetness and life.

[Note: The Roman edition reads “with various reports”; the old edition and most manuscripts, “with empty refinements”; Ben. and Germ., “with empty rejections.” Ben. adds between the lines, “that is, refinements.” Yet there *refutatio* seems to mean distaste, for *refutare* sometimes means the same as to disdain or reject.]

6. Nor again need I fear that I may seem to have invited more people than I can feed, and that the loaves of my words may fail you. For Elisha, though inimitable for us in merit, is to be imitated in faith: he did not consider how many loaves he had, but wished to divide what he had among all and judged them sufficient for all (ibid., v. 42). Thus he ordered his servant to distribute ten barley loaves among the people. And the servant said: “What? Shall I set this before a hundred men?” And he answered: “Give them and let them eat, for the Lord says this: ‘They shall eat and leave some over’” (ibid., v. 43). Your faith, then, will make the feast from a poor tongue abundant. Nor do I fear that fasting may make you so voracious that, though filled, you will return hungry and empty; for it is written: “The Lord strengthens the righteous, and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied” (Ps. 36 [37]:17, 79). It is much more beautiful not to be ashamed of barley loaves and to set forth what one has than to refuse. Elisha, who kept nothing for himself, had abundance for the peoples. Therefore Elisha was not ashamed to set out barley loaves; are we ashamed to understand creatures simply, which are declared by simple and proper names? We read “heaven”: let us understand heaven. We read “earth”: let us understand fruitful earth.

[Note: All manuscripts and the old editions consistently read “ten loaves”; the Roman edition, following the Septuagint and Vulgate, reads “twenty loaves.”]

7. Why should I inquire what the extent of its circumference is, which geometers have estimated at one hundred and eighty thousand stadia? I gladly confess that I do not know what I do not know—indeed, what it would profit nothing to know. It is better to know the kinds of lands than their extent: surrounded by the sea, with regions of barbarians lying between, and land flooded and made impassable by marshes, how can we comprehend it? Scripture shows that this is impossible for humans, when God says: “Who has measured the water in his hand, and the heaven by the span, and the whole earth in his closed hand? Who has weighed the mountains in a balance, the rocks in scales, and the woods in a yoke?” (Isa. 40:12). And below: “He who holds the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like locusts; who establishes heaven as a vault” (ibid., v. 22). Who, therefore, would dare to claim for himself power and knowledge equal to God’s, so as to presume that what God has marked by his own oracle as belonging to his majesty can be available to human knowledge?

8. Moses, certainly, had been instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. But because he received the Spirit of God, as God’s minister he placed that empty and presumptuous teaching of philosophy beneath the rule of truth. He described for me those things which he judged suitable to our hope: that God made the earth; that at the command of almighty God and through the working of the Lord Jesus the earth brought forth plants from the ground and every living creature according to its kind. But he did not think that he should tell how much space the earth’s shadow occupies in the air when the sun withdraws from us, removes the day, and illumines the lower regions of the heavens; or how the globe of the moon, entering into the region of this world’s shadow, produces an eclipse. For he passed over matters that are nothing to us, as bringing no benefit. In the Holy Spirit he saw that we should not pursue those vanities of a wisdom already withering away, which occupy our minds with inexplicable matters and make sport of our labour; but rather that he should describe those things which concern progress in virtue.

[Note: Some manuscripts and the Roman edition read: “entering into the region of this shadow.” Others and the old editions read: “entering into the region of this world,” or “advancing into” it. Car. and Ben. read: “entering into the region of the shadow of this world”; the first reads “entering,” the second “advancing.”]

## CHAPTER III

The law of generation implanted in living creatures by God’s word persists in the succession of species. The truth of the nature of created things must not be denied; but for a human being to imitate the life of beasts is disgraceful. Finally follows an account of certain vices characteristic of particular animals and therefore to be avoided.

9. Let us therefore hold fast to the prophetic sayings, and not hold the addresses of the Holy Spirit in contempt as though they were cheap. “Let the earth bring forth living creatures: cattle, beasts, and creeping things.” Why do we reason about other matters, where the nature of earthly creatures is plainly formed? In the establishment of the world, God’s Word runs through every creature, so that immediately all the kinds of living things which God ordained may be produced from the earth and may thereafter, under the prescribed law, succeed according to their own kind and likeness: the lion producing a lion, the tiger a tiger, the ox an ox, the swan a swan, the eagle an eagle. What was commanded once took root in nature forever. And therefore the earth does not cease to render the service required of it, so that the ancient forms of living creatures may be restored for new ages through the renewing succession of their kind.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kind: cattle, beasts, and creeping things of the earth,” etc.]

10. But do you wish to turn created things to human use? Do not deny to each kind the truth of its own nature, and you will adapt them all the more to human benefit. First, nature has cast all kinds of cattle, beasts, and fish down toward the belly: some creep on their bellies; others, though supported by feet, are sunk more deeply by the four-footed motion of their bodies, and you may see them as though fixed to the earth rather than free. Since they do not have the power to raise themselves up, they seek food from the earth and follow only the pleasures of the belly toward which they bend.

Take care, O human being, not to bend like cattle. Take care not to bend down toward the belly, not so much in body as in desire. Look at the form of your body and assume the bearing suited to lofty strength. Let the animals alone feed bent down. Why do you cast yourself down in eating, when nature has not cast you down? Why do you delight in what is an injury to nature? Why, intent upon food night and day, do you graze upon earthly things in the manner of cattle? Why, devoted to bodily enticements, do you dishonour yourself by serving the belly and its passions? Why do you take away from yourself the understanding that the Creator gave you? Why do you compare yourself with beasts of burden, from which God wished you to be separated, saying: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31 [32]:9). Or if the gluttony and intemperance of the horse delight you, and it pleases you to neigh after women, let it please you too for your jaws to be bound with bit and bridle. If cruelty feeds you, this is the madness of wild beasts, which are slaughtered for their savagery. See to it that the fierceness of your cruelty is not turned against you as well.

[Note: The editions and a few manuscripts read: “If animals alone feed bent down.” More and better manuscripts read: “Let animals alone … feed”; some, “feed themselves.” Ben. and Germ. read best: as in the text.]

11. What else does the sluggish ass, exposed to plunder and duller in perception, teach except that we ought to be more alert, not to grow sluggish through bodily and mental idleness, and to flee to faith, which is accustomed to lighten heavy burdens?

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “and exposed to burdens”; the Roman edition reads: “and exposed to a burden.”]

12. Does not the deceitful fox, plunging into dens and hiding places, indicate that it is an unprofitable creature, worthy of hatred because of its plundering and contempt because of its weakness, and therefore careless of its own safety while it lies in wait for another’s?

13. The cunning partridge, which steals another partridge’s eggs and broods over them with its own body, cannot possess the fruit of its deceit. For when it has hatched the chicks, it loses them: when they hear the voice of the one that laid the eggs, they leave her and, by a certain natural gift and affection, go to the one whom they recognize as their true mother through the generation of the eggs. Thus they show that the one performs the office of a nurse, the other that of a parent. So she pours out her own labour in vain and is punished by the cost of her deceit. Hence Jeremiah says: “The partridge cried out and gathered together what it had not borne” (Jer. 17:11); that is, it gathered eggs and cried as though rejoicing in the success of its deceit. But it wastes its labour, because with costly toil it raises for another those whom it itself has given life by long and diligent brooding. The devil imitates this partridge, striving to seize the offspring of the eternal Creator. If he can gather up any who are foolish and lack the vigour of their own judgment, he broods over them with bodily enticements; but as soon as Christ’s voice has been instilled into the little ones, they depart and betake themselves to that mother who embraces her young as a bird in maternal love. For the devil gathered the Gentiles, whom he had not created; but when Christ uttered his voice in his Gospel, they especially came over to him, who received them beneath the shadow of his wings and gave them to Mother Church to be nourished.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “We know the partridge to be cunning, which …” There is evidently an ellipsis here, which may be supplied by such words as “we know,” “they report,” or the like. We give the author’s text as it occurs in ancient manuscripts and editions.]

14. The lion, proud in the fierceness of its nature, does not know how to mingle with the kinds of other wild beasts; but, as a kind of king of many, disdains their company. It also disdains food from the day before and turns away from even the remnants of its own meal. What beast would dare to join itself to it, when such terror naturally belongs to its voice that many creatures which could escape its attack by speed fail, as though stunned and struck by some force, at the sound of its roar?

[Note: Nearly all manuscripts read thus. Others and the editions read: “The lion, proud through the force of its nature, does not mingle its own fierceness with other kinds of wild beasts.”]

15. Nor did Scripture pass over the leopard’s appearance, namely, that through its diversity of colour it reveals the varied motions of its soul. Jeremiah says: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard its spots?” (Jer. 13:23). This must be understood not only of outward form but also of the instability of rage: because the Jewish people, discoloured by the dark, restless, shifting changes of an unfaithful mind and spirit, can no longer retain the grace of a good purpose or return to any amendment and correction after once putting on bestial savagery.

## CHAPTER IV

On the remarkable instinct of certain animals in avoiding what harms them and pursuing what benefits them; and on the natural virtues in them which we ought to imitate.

Yet there is also in the nature of quadrupeds something which prophetic discourse urges us to imitate, so that by their example we may beware of idleness and not be turned aside from the pursuit of virtue by the smallness or weakness of our body, nor be recalled from the greatness of any undertaking. The ant is small, yet it ventures on tasks beyond its strength; it is not forced into labour by servitude, but through the intention of voluntary foresight stores up for itself future provisions of food. Scripture urges you to imitate its industry, saying: “Go to the ant, O sluggard; imitate its ways, and become wiser than it” (Prov. 6:6). It possesses no cultivation, has no one to compel it, acts under no master; yet how it prepares food, storing up a harvest for itself from your labours! While you often lack, it does not lack. No granaries are closed to it, no guards impenetrable, no heaps inviolable. The guard watches and does not dare stop the thefts; the owner sees his losses and does not punish. The booty is carried across the fields in a black procession; the paths seethe with the company of travellers; grains too large to be grasped in narrow mouths are pushed along upon their shoulders. The owner of the harvest sees this and is ashamed to deny such modest gains to devout industry.

17. What should I say of dogs, in whom a certain natural disposition to repay kindness has been implanted, and to keep watch anxiously for their masters’ safety? Therefore Scripture cries out against those who forget benefits and are sluggish and cowardly: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56:10). There are, then, dogs that know how to bark for their masters and know how to defend their own homes. Therefore learn also to exercise your voice for Christ when grievous wolves attack the fold of the Church. Learn to hold the word in your mouth, lest, like a dumb dog, you seem by a kind of treacherous silence to have deserted the guardianship of faith entrusted to you. Such a dog is the traveller and companion of the angel, whom Raphael, in the prophetic book, thought it worthwhile to join to himself and to Tobit’s son when he went to drive away Asmodeus and strengthen the marriage bond (Tob. 6:1; 11:9). For by the grace of a grateful disposition the demon is driven away and marriage is made firm. Thus, by the image of a dumb animal, the holy angel Raphael taught the young Tobit, whose protection he had undertaken, an inclination to return kindness. Who would not be ashamed not to repay kindness to those who deserve well of him, when he sees even beasts shun the crime of ingratitude? They preserve the memory of food given them; do you not preserve the memory of salvation received?

[Note: Five manuscripts of better age read “and to Tobit”; four others read “and to Tobi,” as in what follows. The Septuagint has Τωβίτ, “Tobit.”]

18. Though the bear lies in wait, as Scripture says (Lam. 3:10)—for it is a beast full of deceit—it is nevertheless reported to give birth to shapeless offspring, then to shape them with its tongue into its own form and likeness. Do you not marvel at such offices of a loving mouth in a wild beast, whose nature is expressed in maternal affection? The bear, then, forms its young after its own likeness; can you not train your children to resemble you?

19. What of its knowledge of healing, which it has not neglected? For when severely wounded and afflicted with injuries, it knows how to heal itself by applying to its wounds the herb which the Greeks call *phlomos* (φλόμος), Latin *verbascum* [mullein], so that they are cured by touch alone. The serpent also repels acquired blindness by eating fennel. Thus, when it feels its eyes becoming covered, it seeks its familiar remedies and is not cheated of their effect. When the tortoise, having fed on the entrails of a serpent, perceives poison creeping through it, it employs oregano as a remedy for its safety. Though immersed in muddy marshes, it nevertheless knows how to cure itself by its own antidote and proves that it too knows the powers of herbs through a sure means of health. You may see even the fox healing itself with a little resin of pine and, by such a remedy, prolonging the span before impending death.

20. The Lord himself cries out in the book of Jeremiah: “The turtledove and the swallow, the sparrows of the field, have kept the times of their coming; but my people have not known the judgments of the Lord” (Jer. 18:7). The swallow knows when to come and when to return. The pious bird also knows how, by the evidence of its arrival, to announce the sign of spring. The ant too knows how to observe the seasons of fair weather. When it notices that its fruits have become wet and damp with rain, carefully observing the weather to see when it may remain continuously temperate, it opens its stores and carries its grain from its caves on its shoulders, so that its own provisions may dry in uninterrupted sun. Indeed, you will not see rainstorms burst from the clouds on any of those days unless the ant has first recalled its grain to its own storehouses. Oxen know, when rain is impending, to keep near their stalls. When, by natural perception, they have detected a change in the sky, they look out and all together stretch their necks beyond their stalls in one posture, testifying that they wish to go out. At the approach of winter the sheep greedily and insatiably snatches at grass, because it foresees that, as winter’s harshness comes, grass will fail; it stuffs itself beforehand with the fodder of grass before all grass fails under the burning frost. That land hedgehog, commonly called the *ericius*, if it senses any ambush, closes itself within its spines and gathers itself into its own weapons, so that whoever thinks to touch it is wounded. The same hedgehog, foreseeing the future, fortifies for itself two avenues of breathing: when it has detected that the north wind will blow, it blocks the northern side; when it has learned that the clouds of the air are being cleared by the south wind, it moves toward the northern side, so as to avoid winds blowing against it and likely to harm it.

[Note: Six manuscripts read “the times of its nest.”]

[Note: That is, the stork, which was discussed above in Book V, chapter 16.]

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “the future harshness of winter”; some read “the approaching harshness.” The oldest manuscripts read as in the text.]

21. Hence the Prophet offered worthy praise to the Lord, saying: “How magnified are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103 [104]:24). Divine wisdom penetrates all things and fills all things; and this is gathered more abundantly from the instincts of irrational creatures than from the argument of rational beings. Nature’s testimony is stronger than doctrinal argument. What living creature does not know how to protect its own safety: if it has strength, by resisting; if speed, by fleeing; if cunning, by taking precautions? Who taught them the use of remedies and knowledge of herbs? We are human beings, and often are deceived by the appearance of herbs; we frequently find harmful those which we thought healthful. How often has deadly food crept among sweet banquets, and fatal fare penetrated the vital parts of kings even amid the guards of courtly attendants! Wild animals know by smell alone how to distinguish harmful from beneficial things: they pluck no herb with a scout or taster beforehand, and are not harmed. For nature is the better teacher of truth. Without anyone’s instruction, it instils into our senses the sweetness of health; it likewise teaches that the bitterness of pain must be avoided. From this comes a sweeter life; from this, a more bitter death. Nature entrusts her cubs to the lioness and softens the savage beast with maternal affection. It checks the tiger’s fierceness and turns it back when it is about to seize prey. For when it finds the lair empty of its stolen offspring, it immediately follows the robber’s tracks. But the robber, though riding a swift horse, sees that he may be overtaken by the beast’s speed and has no resource by which he can escape; he therefore contrives this trick by deceit. When he sees the tiger close upon him, he throws down a glass sphere. The tiger is deceived by its own image, thinks it is her offspring, stops her charge, and desires to gather up her young. Delayed again by the empty appearance, she throws all her strength into catching the horseman and, made swifter by the goad of anger, presses upon the fugitive. Again he retards his pursuer by throwing down a sphere. Yet recollection of the trick does not exclude the mother’s care: she turns the empty image about and crouches down as though to suckle the young. Thus deceived by devotion to her maternal affection, she loses both vengeance and offspring.

22. This is what Scripture sets before us when it says: “Children, love your fathers; parents, do not provoke your children to anger” (Col. 3:20). Nature instils this in beasts, that they love their own young and cherish their offspring. They do not know the hatreds of stepmothers; nor, after a change of mate, are parents estranged from their offspring. They do not know how to prefer the children of a later union and neglect those of an earlier one. They know their own pledges; they do not know distinctions in affection, incentives to hatred, or the discriminations of offence. The nature of wild beasts is simple; it knows no slanders against truth. Thus God ordered all things: to those to whom he gave less reason, he granted more affection. What wild beast does not offer itself especially to death for its young? What wild beast, though surrounded by innumerable ranks of armed men, does not cover its offspring with its own body? Though a shower of weapons falls, it nevertheless keeps its little ones safe from danger, enclosed behind the wall of its body. What does the human being say, who neglects the command and erases nature? A son despises his father; a father disinherits his son. They think this is a right when fruitfulness is condemned. Rather, the father condemns himself when he makes void what he has begotten. And this is thought to be authority when the nature of fertility is punished.

23. No one would doubt that a dog lacks reason; yet if you consider the keenness of its senses, you would think that by its perceptive sagacity it acquires for itself the power of reason. For when it finds the track of a hare or deer and comes to a fork in the path, to a crossroad where the ways divide into several directions, it goes over the beginnings of the individual paths and silently considers within itself, as though uttering a syllogistic argument through the keenness with which it gathers scent: “It turned either in this direction or in that, or surely entered this winding path. But it entered neither this road nor that. It remains, therefore, that without doubt it turned in this direction.” What human beings can scarcely establish after long meditation upon a complex art is naturally available to dogs: they first detect falsehood, then, after rejecting what is false, discover truth. Do not philosophers spend whole days in the dust, dividing propositions before themselves, drawing each separately with a rod? Since, of three propositions, one must be true, they first eliminate two as agreeing with falsehood, and thus decide that the force of truth adheres in the one remaining.

[Note: Nine manuscripts read: “they draw out for themselves each separate fancy, and of three …”]

Who can be so steadfast in kindness and mindful of gratitude? Dogs know how to spring even upon robbers for their master; to prevent the nocturnal approach of strangers; to die for their masters, and are ready to die with them. Often too, by clear evidence of a killing that has been committed, dogs have supplied indications for convicting the guilty, so that their mute testimony has often been believed.

24. At Antioch, they relate that at twilight, in a more remote part of the city, a man who had a dog attached to him was murdered. A certain soldier, eager for plunder, had been the instrument of the killing. Concealed by the still-dark beginning of the day, he had withdrawn to another quarter. The corpse lay unburied; a crowd of onlookers stood about; the dog, with lamentable cries, mourned its master’s misfortune. By chance, the man who had inflicted the murder, such being the cunning of human ingenuity, approached the ring of watching people and, in order to acquire the credit of innocence by moving about among them with assumed confidence, drew near the funeral as though pitying the dead man. Then the dog, setting aside for a little while its cries of grief, took up the weapons of vengeance, seized him, and held him fast; and, murmuring some mournful song, as though in a certain epilogue—

> [Note: “Epilogue,” that is, a lamentation; because orators especially employ lamentations in the epilogue and conclusion of a speech, in order to move judges to compassion.]

—it turned all to tears and entrusted belief to the proof, because, out of so many, it held that man alone and did not let him go.

> [Note: Several manuscripts of no small authority read: “it turned [Col. 0252D] them to belief; it brought forward proof.”]

At last that man, disturbed because he could not invalidate so manifest an indicator of the deed by alleging hatred, enmity, envy, or any injury, was unable any longer to refute the charge. Thus he pursued what was more difficult—vengeance—because he could not offer a defence. What worthy return do we make to our Creator, whose food we consume, while we overlook injuries and often set before God’s enemies the feasts that we have received from God?

25. What is simpler than lambs, to whose innocence we compare that of little children? Often, in a great flock, a lamb that has wandered through the whole sheepfold strays from its mother; and, when it cannot find her, it repeatedly calls for the absent mother by bleating, in order to awaken her answering voice, so that at its sound it may retrace its wandering steps. [Col. 0251D] Though it may move among many thousands of sheep, it recognizes its parent’s voice, hastens to its mother, and seeks the familiar fountains of its mother’s milk.
