Though it is held by desire for food and drink, it nevertheless passes by the swollen udders of strangers, even though they overflow with milky moisture. It seeks its mother alone and declares that the scanty juices of its mother’s breast alone abound for it. Likewise, amid many thousands of lambs, the mother knows her son alone. The bleating of many is one and the same; their appearance is the same; yet she distinguishes her own offspring from the rest and recognizes her son alone by the silent testimony of affection. The shepherd errs in distinguishing the sheep; the lamb does not know how to err in recognizing its mother. The shepherd is deceived by appearance; but the sheep is not deceived in its affection. There is one scent for all; yet nature possesses its own domestic scent, which beloved offspring seem to breathe forth with a certain special distinctiveness.

26. Nature has its own uses and familiar instincts. Hardly have an infant’s teeth begun to emerge, and already it knows how to try its weapons. The puppy has not yet teeth, yet, as though it had them, it seeks revenge with its own mouth. The stag has not yet antlers, yet it practises with its forehead and threatens weapons that it has not yet tested. If a wolf sees a human being first, it takes away his voice and despises him [Col. 0252B] as a victor who has deprived him of speech. But if it perceives that it has itself been seen beforehand, it lays aside its fierceness and cannot run. A lion fears a cock, especially a white one. A wounded roe-deer seeks dittany and expels arrows from its wound.

> [Note: In Greek, δίκταμνον (*diktamnon*), an herb that grows especially in Crete; it is otherwise called pennyroyal and garden ginger.]

Even beasts know their remedies. A sick lion seeks out an ape in order to devour it, so that it may be healed. A leopard drinks the blood of the wild roe-deer and escapes the force of sickness. Every sick wild animal is cured by drinking a dog’s blood. A sick bear devours ants. A stag chews branches of the olive.

27. Thus wild animals know how to seek what benefits them; but you, O human being, do not know your remedies! You do not know how to take strength from an adversary, so that, like a wolf anticipated beforehand, he cannot escape you: how, with the eye of your mind, to detect his treachery; how to impede beforehand [Col. 0252C] the course of his words; how to blunt his shamelessness and the sharpness of his argument.

> [Note: Not a few manuscripts read: “like a wolf that has been seen beforehand.”]

But if he anticipates you, he takes away your voice. And if you have become mute, loosen your garment, so that you may loosen your speech. If a wolf rises against you, take up the rock, and it flees. Your rock is Christ. If you flee to Christ, the wolf flees and cannot terrify you. Peter sought this rock when he wavered amid the waves, and found it, because he clasped Christ’s right hand.

28. Why should I say that people take pleasure in garlic and use as food what even the leopard flees? Indeed, wherever anyone thinks that garlic should be crushed, the leopard leaps away from there and does not resist. What that venomous beast cannot endure the smell of, do you take as food and pour into your inner organs? Yet it sometimes treats pains. [Col. 0252D] Let it be taken as medicine, not as food; by the sick, not by banqueters. You seek medicine and flee fasting—as though you could find any greater remedy. If a serpent tastes the spittle of a fasting person, it dies. You see how great is the power of fasting: by his spittle a human being kills an earthly serpent, and deservedly also the spiritual one.

29. How much wisdom the Lord has poured even into the smallest creatures! The turtledove lays leaves of squill upon its nest so that a wolf may not attack its young. For it knows that wolves are accustomed to flee leaves of that kind.

> [Note: The editions of Costerius and Rome read, “The little bird knows.” This is suitable, if some ancient manuscript supported them.]

The little fox knows how to cherish its offspring; and do you not know—do you neglect—how to make the offspring of this life safer against the wolves of spiritual wickedness?

## CHAPTER V

Why the Lord created shorter necks in some beasts and longer ones in others. Here especially the elephant’s limbs, characteristics, and military uses are described.

30. But let us return to the order of creation and consider why the Lord formed narrower necks for some beasts—for lions, tigers, and bears as well—and longer ones for others, such as elephants and camels.

> [Note: The Roman edition reads, “such as camels and horses.” Against this, other editions and all manuscripts read, “such as elephants,” etc. But when God is said to have given elephants longer necks, their trunk must be understood, which supplies for them the function of a longer neck; whence Basil: “It has a trunk which fulfils the need of a neck.”]

Is not the reason plain? Those wild beasts that eat flesh had no need of a long neck. They do not lower their necks and mouths to the ground for grazing; rather, they attack a stag or tear apart an ox or sheep. But since the camel is taller, how would it feed on the smallest grasses unless it extended its longer neck to the ground for feeding? Thus the camel received a longer neck in proportion to its height; so too the horse in proportion, and the ox likewise, for these feed on grass.

31. The elephant also has its projecting trunk, because, being higher than all others, it cannot bend itself down in order to graze. Therefore it uses this as an instrument for gathering food. It pours abundant draughts of water into that huge beast; and for that reason it is hollow, so that, to quench the thirst of so great a creature, it may draw up full pools or, having gathered a stream, may pour it over the drinking animal. Its neck, indeed, is smaller than the bulk of so great a body might require, lest it too be more a burden than a use. For this reason it does not bend its knees: it needed stiffer legs, so that so great a mechanism of limbs might be supported as by columns. It bends its heel slightly; the rest of the feet are rigid from top to bottom. Nor can so great a beast bend itself down as we often do upon our elbows or knees.

> [Note: *Ancylae*: the joints or bendings of the elbow or leg. Basil: “It is articulated neither at an elbow-bend nor at a knee.”]

It is propped on either side by very large beams, so that in sleep it may bend back a little without danger, since its foot is not differentiated by any joint of limbs. Accordingly, supports like props are devised by human ingenuity for tame elephants, which have this use; but for wild and untamed ones, because no one places beneath them such supports on which they may rest, this results in danger.

32. For, leaning against a tree, they either rub their sides or relax themselves in sleep. The tree, sometimes overcome and bent by so great a body, breaks; and the elephant that had thrown itself back upon it falls and cannot raise or lift itself. Lying there, it dies, or, betrayed by its groaning, is brought down [Col. 0254A] while its belly and the other softer parts nearby lie exposed to a wound. For no missiles ordinarily penetrate its back and other outer parts easily. Some, however, lay these traps for them on account of the ivory: they cut partway through, on the side to which the elephant less frequently turns, those trees against which it is accustomed to lean, so that when the elephant leans back, the tree cannot bear the weight of its limbs and brings about its fall.

33. But if anyone criticizes these things, let that person also criticize the heights of buildings, because they more quickly threaten a grave collapse and, once fallen, are restored with greater difficulty. Yet if we often raise such buildings either for beauty or for a lookout, we ought likewise to approve these things in elephants, because they provide great usefulness in warfare. Hence the Persian people, fierce in war, [Col. 0254B] strong in archery and every casting of missiles, advance their battle line enclosed as though by moving towers, because weapons are hurled with greater force from above to below. In the midst of open fields they fight as though from a wall; placed as though in a citadel and watchtower, they look upon wars rather than undergo them. Thus they appear removed from danger, safe behind the bulk of the beasts. For who would dare approach them, when he may easily be struck by missiles from above and trampled beneath by an elephant’s charge? Indeed, battle lines and wedges of armed men give way before them, and those square camps are broken apart. For they rush upon enemies with intolerable force, so that no line of warriors, no close-packed mass of soldiers, no opposing barrier of shields can delay them. Like moving mountains they range about in battle, and, like hills, they tower with lofty heads; with their bellowing [Col. 0254C] they shatter everyone’s confidence. What can an infantryman do, however strong in arm and ready of hand, when a walking wall, enclosed by crowds of armed men, meets him? What can a horseman do, when his horse, terrified by the monstrous size of such a beast, flees? What can an archer do, when the iron-clad bodies of the men above cannot feel the blow of the missile, while the beast itself is not easily pierced even by bare steel and, protected with armour, cuts through opposing battle lines without danger to itself and crushes squadrons?

34. Therefore, just as immense buildings are supported by stronger foundations, so are elephants; otherwise, supported on unequal feet, they would collapse within a short span of life. But now they are said to prolong their lives to three hundred years and more, because all their limbs correspond to their size. For this reason their limbs are not distinct, as ours are, but compact, so that they may be stronger. How quickly human knees and soles are troubled if people stand long, run too swiftly, or walk continually! For joints and articulated limbs more readily admit either the sensation of pain or the shock of a fall than limbs that are fused and solidified.

35. And why are you surprised that they are feared when clothed in armour, since they are always armed with their teeth as with natural darts? Whatever they wrap in their trunk, they break; whatever they crush with their foot, they kill as by the fall of some immense ruin. With their trunks they enfold groves for their food; and, like very great dragons, they lash with serpent-like coils whatever they seize. They often gather these coils into a circle, especially when food is picked up from the ground or drink is drawn. They are therefore a lesson to us that nothing has been created superfluously; and yet this beast of such huge mass is subject to us and serves human commands.

## CHAPTER VI

The strongest and fiercest beasts are subjected by the Creator to humankind; and the smallest animals are terror and destruction to them. Then, after a brief discussion of the usefulness of serpents, the human being is urged toward knowledge of self and of one’s own soul.

[Col. 0255B]

36. Since we are about to speak of the creation of the human being, we ought first to prepare and set forth its excellence. Nothing in creation seemed stronger than the elephant; nothing so terrible or tall; nothing so fierce as lions and tigers. Yet these serve the human being and lay aside their own nature under human training. They forget what they were born to be and put on what they are commanded to be. Why say more? They are taught like little children; they serve like the weak; they are beaten like the fearful; they are corrected like subjects; they adopt our habits, because they have lost their own impulses.

37. Nature, then, is marvellous in the greatest things; for the Lord is marvellous [Col. 0255C] in the heights, and marvellous also in the least things. For just as we admire the level plains no less than the heights of mountains, and marvel no more at the height of the cedar than at the fruitfulness of the lowly vine or olive, so I marvel no more at the elephant because it is tall than at the mouse because it is frightening to the elephant. Such, then, is nature’s power: things terrifying to some are fearful to others. For a certain prerogative has been granted to each creature, so that each is supported by its own particular privileges. The elephant, formidable to bulls, fears a mouse. The lion, indeed the king of beasts, is tormented by the tiny sting of the scorpion and killed by serpent venom. The lion’s exceptional beauty shakes out the mane upon its neck, or, with breast raised, lifts up its face. But who would not marvel that death should issue from the brief sting of a scorpion—so small that one might think it incorporeal—for bodies of such enormous size?

38. Let no one criticize this: that the Creator has mingled serpents among his creatures, and other poisonous kinds either of animals or of plants.

> [Note: Nine fairly reliable manuscripts read, “that the creator of the serpent [has done] such things for his creatures, or …”; others, however, and the editions are to be preferred.]

For these were born for our correction, not for our disfigurement. Things which are commonly an occasion of stumbling and terror to the lazy, weak, or impious are useful to others, just as tutors are to little children. They seem bitter, harsh, troublesome, and frightening with the rod; they deny freedom for self-indulgence; they require the necessity of discipline; by fear they restrain childish minds lest they dissolve into luxury. Thus, through their severity, children become upright, sober, self-controlled, and more devoted to praise than play. You see what those dreadful whips accomplish. So also serpents are whips for those whose maturity of soul is weak and whose strength of mind is somewhat childish; but they cannot harm the stronger. Hence it was said to one confident in the Lord: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and you shall trample down the lion and the dragon” (Ps. 90:13). A viper bit Paul, and they thought that he, having scarcely been saved from shipwreck, must be a sinner and would die from the venom. But after he remained unharmed and shook the viper into the fire, he gained greater reverence among those looking on. The Lord himself also says to all: “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved; but whoever does not believe shall be condemned” [Col. 0256B] (Mark 16:6). He said that these signs would accompany believers: they would handle serpents with their hands, and poisons and every deadly thing, even if they drank them, would be unable to harm them. Therefore, O human being, your unbelief is more to be feared than serpents’ venom. Fear these things, then, so that at least, while they are feared, they may be able to summon you to faith.

> [Note: The manuscripts of Carnoët, the old Corbie manuscript, Th. and Reg. read: “that you may gain salvation, while those things are feared.”]

But if you do not fear God, at least fear the avenging poisons of unbelief.

39. Now, since you see elephants and lions subject to you, know yourself, O human being. This saying belongs not, as they report, to Pythian Apollo, but to holy Solomon, who says: “Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women” (Song 1:7); although Moses had written much earlier in Deuteronomy: “Take heed to yourself, O human being. Take heed to yourself,” says the Law (Deut. 4:9). And the Prophet [Col. 0256C] says, “Unless you know yourself.” To whom does he say this? “O fairest,” he says, “among women.” Who is beautiful among women except the soul, which possesses the excellence of beauty in either sex? And rightly is it beautiful, since it desires not earthly but heavenly things, not corruptible but incorruptible things, among which beauty does not ordinarily perish. For all bodily things wither through the course of age or the unevenness of illness. “Take heed,” Moses says, “to this in which you are wholly present, in which the better part of you resides.” Finally, the Lord explained who you are, saying: “Beware of false prophets” (Matt. 7:15); for these weaken the soul and undermine the mind. Therefore you are not flesh. For what is flesh without the soul’s governance and the mind’s strength? Today flesh is put on; tomorrow it is laid aside. Flesh is temporary; the soul enduring. Flesh is the garment [Col. 0256D] of the soul, which clothes itself in a kind of bodily covering. Therefore you are not the garment, but the one who uses the garment. Thus you are told to strip off the old human being with its deeds and put on the new, which is renewed not in bodily quality but in the spirit of the mind and in knowledge (Col. 3:10). You are not flesh, I say; for it is not to flesh that it is said: “For the temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). And elsewhere: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (ibid., 5). Rather, this is said to the renewed and faithful, in whom the Spirit of God remains. But in the fleshly it does not remain, because it is written: “My Spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3).

## CHAPTER VII

The author begins the creation of the human being from consideration of the Creator. He demonstrates that the Son is the image of the Father, and that unity as well as distinction is found between them. Finally, he admonishes the human being to recognize whence he arises, whose image he bears, and in what part he bears it.

40. But let us consider the sequence of our very creation. “Let us make,” he says, “the human being according to our image and according to our likeness” (Gen. 1:26). Who says this? Is it not God, who made you? What is God? Flesh or spirit? Certainly not flesh, but spirit, to which flesh cannot be like; for God is incorporeal and invisible, whereas flesh is grasped and seen. To whom does he speak? Certainly not to himself, since he does not say, “Let me make,” but, “Let us make.” Not to angels, for they are ministers; and servants cannot share in the act of creation with their master, nor works with their maker. Rather, he speaks to the Son—even if the Jews do not wish it, even if the Arians oppose it. Let both Jews be silent and Arians be mute with their parents,

> [Note: The old edition and five manuscripts read, “with their equals.” The Roman edition and the Benedictine manuscript read, “with their parties.” Several others read, “with their fathers.” The manuscripts of Carnoët, old Corbie, and Th. have the text as printed.]

for while they exclude the One from participation in the divine operation, they insert many; and the prerogative which they deny to the Son they grant to little servants.

41. But grant, if you will, that God seemed to you to need the assistance of little servants in order to create. If the operation is shared by God and angels, is the image shared by God and angels too? Would he say to angels: “Let us make the human being according to our image and according to our likeness”? But hear what the image of God is, as the Apostle says: “He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom [Col. 0257C] of the Son of his brightness, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins, who is the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of all creation” (Col. 1:13 ff.).

> [Note: Thus the majority and better manuscripts, with the older editions. The Benedictine and others, with the editions of Gill and Rome, read: “the Son of his love.”]

He is the image of God the Father, who always is and was in the beginning. For the image is he who says: “Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14:8–9). And how, when you see the living image of the living Father, do you say, “Show us the Father”? “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” The image of God is power, not weakness; the image of God is wisdom; the image of God is justice—but divine wisdom and everlasting justice. The image of God is he alone who said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), having such likeness to the Father that he possesses unity of divinity and fullness. Where he says, “Let us make,” how can there be inequality? When again he says, “according to our likeness,” where is dissimilarity? So also in the Gospel, where he says, “I and the Father,” there is certainly not one person; but where he says, “we are one,” there is no difference of divinity or work. Thus there is not one person in the two, but one substance. And he appropriately added, “we are,” [Col. 0258A] because to be always is divine, so that you may believe coeternal the one whom you thought unlike. For he is eternal of whom Moses says: “He who is sent me” (Exod. 3:14). He also fittingly placed first the words, “I and the Father.” For if he had placed the Father first, you would judge the Son lesser; but he placed the Son first, whom it is not fitting to believe superior to the Father. He joined the Father, so that you may recognize that God the Father and the Son are not bound by the prejudice of rank.

42. “Take heed to yourself alone,” he says (Deut. 4:9). For we are one thing, ours are another, and the things around us another. We are—that is, soul and mind. Ours are the limbs of the body and its senses. Around us are money, servants, and the equipment of this life. Therefore take heed to yourself and know yourself: that is, not what sort of arms you have, nor how great your bodily strength, nor how great your possessions or power, but what kind of soul and mind you possess, from which all counsels proceed and to which the fruit of your deeds is referred. For that soul is full of wisdom, full of piety and justice, because every virtue is from God. God says of it: “Behold, Jerusalem, I have painted your walls” (Isa. 49:16). That soul—

> [Note: *De Poenitentia*, distinction 2, chapter “That Soul.”]

—is painted by God when it has within itself the shining grace of virtues and the brightness of piety. That soul is well painted in which the likeness of divine operation shines forth. That soul is well painted in which are the brightness of glory and the image of the Father’s substance. According to this image which shines forth, the painting is precious. According to this image was Adam before sin; [Col. 0258C] but when he fell, he put aside the image of the heavenly one and took up an earthly likeness. Let us flee this image, which cannot enter the city of God, because it is written: “Lord, in your city you shall bring their image to nothing” (Ps. 72:20). The unworthy image does not enter; and an image that would enter is excluded, because, he says, “Nothing unclean, and no one doing abomination and falsehood, shall enter into it” (Rev. 21:27). But the one shall enter whose forehead bears the Lamb’s name written upon it.

43. Our soul, therefore, is according to God’s image. In it, O human being, you are wholly present; for without it you are nothing, but are earth and shall be resolved into earth. Finally, that you may know that flesh is nothing without the soul: “Do not fear,” he says, “those who can kill the body but cannot [Col. 0258D] kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28). Why then do you put confidence in flesh, when you lose nothing if you lose flesh? Fear rather lest you be deprived of your soul’s aid. For what exchange shall a human being give for his soul, in which lies not a small part of himself but the substance of the whole human being? It is through this that you rule the other living creatures, wild beasts and birds alike. It is according to the image of God; the body, however, is according to the appearance of beasts. In the soul is the pious mark of divine imitation; in the body is a lowly fellowship with wild beasts and animals.

## CHAPTER VIII

To understand more precisely where the divine likeness resides, the qualities of body and soul are examined. It is shown that the whole human being is designated by the term “soul.” Those who blot out God’s image by cosmetics, cruelty, and treachery are rebuked. There follows an exhortation to vigilance against vices, and the chapter concludes with a comparison of poor and rich.

[Col. 0259A]

44. But let us examine more closely what it is that was made according to God’s image.

> [Note: The Roman edition reads: “But let us examine more closely what was made according to God’s image. Was flesh made according to God’s image? No. Therefore in God, etc.”]

Was flesh made according to God’s image? Then there is earth in God, since flesh is earth. Therefore God is bodily. Therefore he is weak like flesh and subject to passions. Perhaps the head seems to you to be according to God’s likeness, because it rises above the rest; or the eyes, because they see; or the ears, [Col. 0259B] because they hear. If you consider height, do we seem tall because our heads rise a little above the earth? Are we not ashamed to be called like God because we are taller than serpents and other crawling things, or than deer, sheep, and wolves? Yet how much taller than we are camels and elephants in that respect! Sight is indeed an excellent thing: to behold the elements of the world and know what no one announces, but your own gaze discovers. Yet how much is it that we see, that we should say on this account that we are like God, who sees all things, observes all things, detects hidden dispositions, and searches the secrets of the heart? Are we not ashamed to say this, when I cannot even see all of myself? I see what is before my feet; I cannot see what is behind me. I do not know my neck; I do not know the back of my head; I cannot see my loins. Likewise, how much is it that we hear, when I cannot see or hear what is a little distance away? If walls intervene, sight is hindered and hearing is hindered. Moreover, our body remains fixed in one place and is confined in a narrow space. All wild animals are broader than the human being, and all are swifter as well.

45. Therefore flesh cannot be according to God’s image, but our soul can, which is free and ranges here and there with far-reaching thoughts and counsels, which beholds all things by reflection. Look: now we are in Italy, yet we think of matters that seem to concern the eastern or western regions. We seem to associate with those situated in Persia, and we see those dwelling [Col. 0259D] in Africa, if that land has received any persons known to us. We follow those departing, remain attached to travellers, join ourselves to those absent, converse with those separated from us, and even raise the dead again for conversation; we embrace and hold them as though living, and render to them the services and offices of life. This, then, is according to God’s image: that which is not measured by bodily capacity but by the mind’s strength; which sees the absent, travels in vision across the sea, runs through all things by sight, searches hidden places, and in a single moment carries its senses hither and thither across the boundaries of the whole world and the secrets of the universe; which is joined to God, clings to Christ, descends into hell, and ascends; [Col. 0260A] which moves freely in heaven. Therefore hear the Apostle saying: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Is that in which God always is not according to God’s image? But hear that it is according to God’s image. For the Apostle says: “We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of God, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18).

46. Since, then, we have learned that the soul is according to God’s image, let us now consider whether it could be said of the soul: “Let us make the human being according to our image.” But hear this as well: the soul is designated by the name “human being.” For it is written in Genesis: “The sons of Joseph who were born to him in Egypt were nine souls. All the souls, therefore, that entered Egypt with Jacob were seventy-five” [Col. 0260B] (Gen. 46:27). And much more fittingly, the soul is called either *homo* in Latin or ἄνθρωπος (*anthrōpos*) in Greek: the one term deriving from humanity, the other from the liveliness of seeing—qualities which unquestionably belong more to the soul than to the body. In support of this is also the saying in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: “The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul that seeks him” (Lam. 3:25). He spoke of human beings and thought fit to add “soul.” For the soul seeks better when it is alone, withdrawing itself from the mire of the body and from carnal desire. It is itself conformed to the image of God, of the Lord Jesus. Those who are conformed to the Son of God are saints. For thus we read Paul saying: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to his purpose; whom he foreknew, he also [Col. 0260C] predestined to become conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, these he also glorified” (Rom. 8:28 ff.). Please answer whether justification seems to be conferred upon you according to the body or according to the soul. But you cannot doubt, since justice, from which “justification” is derived, belongs surely to the mind, not the body.

47. You have therefore been painted, O human being, and painted by the Lord your God. You have a good craftsman and painter. Do not erase the good painting, shining not with cosmetic pigment but with truth, not stamped in wax but by grace. You erase the painting, woman, if you cover your face with material whiteness or stain it with artificial rouge. That painting is of vice, not beauty; that painting is of deceit, not simplicity [Col. 0260D]; that painting is temporary, wiped away either by rain or sweat. That painting lies and deceives, so that you please neither the one whom you wish to please—for that person understands that what pleases is not yours but another’s—nor your Creator, who sees that his work has been erased. Tell me: if you introduced a second painter over some artist, who covered the first artist’s work with new work, would not the first be angered when he discovered that his work had been falsified? Do not remove God’s painting and take on the painting of a prostitute, because it is written: “Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? By no means” (1 Cor. 6:15). But whoever falsifies [Col. 0261A] God’s work commits a grave crime. It is indeed a grave crime to suppose that a human being paints you better than God. It is grave for God to say of you: “I do not recognize my colours; I do not recognize my image; I do not recognize the face which I myself formed. I reject what is not mine.” Seek the one who painted you; have fellowship with him; receive grace from him, to whom you have paid a wage. What will you answer?

48. But if it is grave to falsify God’s work, what shall we say of those who kill God’s work, who shed human blood, who take away the life God has given, who say: “Let us remove the Just One, because he is useless to us”? Hence today we rightly read: “Foxes have dens, and birds of heaven nests in which to rest; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” [Col. 0261B] (Matt. 8:20). The fox hides in its den; the bird protects itself in its nest; the human being is not hidden in a den but deceived. The den, moreover, is a human mouth; the human breast is a deep den, where harmful and deceitful plans and evil thoughts dwell. You walk, and another prepares a pit for you. You walk amid snares which your enemies have hidden for you on the way. Look around in every direction, therefore, so that you may escape like a deer from nets and like a bird from a snare. The deer avoids nets by the quickness of its sight; the bird escapes snares if it rises to higher things and flies above earthly things. For no one spreads nets in the heights, and no one hides a snare there. Therefore the capture of one whose citizenship is in things above does not ordinarily become prey. But why are you surprised if a human being is deceived by a human being, when the Son of Man [Col. 0261C] had nowhere to rest? He indeed made such a human being in whom he might lay his head. But after our breast began to be not a resting place for a neighbour but a den; after one person began to lay snares for another whom he ought to help, Christ turned his head away from us. Yet afterward he preferred to offer that head to death for us.

> [Note: The words “yet afterward he preferred to offer that head to death for us” are absent from the Paris editions of 1614 and 1632.]

Therefore do not be deceitful, cruel, or harsh, so that Christ may lay his head in you.

49. Finally, when He had made the monsters of the fishes, when He had made the kinds of wild animals and beasts, He did not rest; but He rested after He had made man in His own image. Hear Him say in whom He rests: “Upon whom shall I rest, unless upon the humble and quiet man, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). Therefore be humble and quiet, that God may rest in your disposition. He who did not [Col. 0261D] rest in beasts will much more not rest in a beastly breast. For there are beastly souls; there are savage creatures clothed in human form, concerning whom the Lord says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7:15). Therefore God did not rest in these; but He rested in human character, which God made in His image and likeness, when He made the man who ought not to veil his head, because he is the image and glory of God. To this man’s soul He says: “Behold, Jerusalem, I have painted your walls” (Isa. 49:16). [Col. 0262A] He did not say, “I have painted your belly”; He did not say, “I have painted your lower parts” [Note: [Col. 0261D] Five manuscripts: “your inner parts.”]; but He said, “I have painted your walls,” asserting that He had given man the strong defenses of walls, so that, if a watchful sentinel stands at the gates, he may repel the danger of siege. Therefore He says: “I did not give you pleasures, nor the enticements of desires, nor incentives to lust, nor longing for another’s beauty; but I gave you foundations of walls, I gave you lofty battlements of towers, in which, once stationed, you need not fear to be stormed by the enemy, nor dread—even though terrifying—the assaults of advancing legions.” Finally, in Isaiah you have that the soul of the righteous man, or the Church, says: “I am a fortified city; I am a besieged city” (Isa. 27:3): fortified through Christ, besieged by the devil. But one whose helper is Christ ought not to fear a siege. For it is fortified by spiritual grace and besieged by worldly dangers. Hence also in the Song of Songs you have the saying: “I am a wall, and my breasts are towers” (Cant. 8:10). The wall is the Church; its towers are the priests, who abound both in discourse concerning natural things and in instruction concerning morals.

50. Know yourself, beautiful soul, because you are the image of God. Know yourself, O man, because you are the glory of God. Hear [Note: [Col. 0261D] The manuscripts of Carpentras, Th., Reg., Colbert, and the old Corbie manuscript: “Hear how the Prophet, glorying, says.”] how you are glory. The Prophet says: “Your knowledge has become wonderful from me” (Ps. 138:6); that is, in my work your majesty has been made more wonderful; in the design of man your wisdom is proclaimed. While I contemplate myself—whom you apprehend even in hidden thoughts and inward dispositions—I recognize the mysteries of your knowledge. Therefore know yourself, O man, how great you are, and [Col. 0262C] attend to yourself, lest, entangled in the snares of the devil, you become prey for the hunter; lest perhaps you run into the jaws of that dreadful lion who roars and prowls about seeking someone to devour. Attend to yourself, that you may consider what enters into you and what goes out from you. I do not speak of food, which is swallowed and expelled; I speak of thought, I mean speech. Let not desire for another’s marriage-bed enter into you; let it not creep into your mind; let not your eye seize upon the beauty of a passing woman; let not your mind enclose it; let not your speech weave devices of temptation, betray through deceit, or bespatter your neighbor with the reproach of slander.

God made you a hunter, not an assailant; He said: “Behold, I send many hunters” (Jer. 16:16): hunters not of accusation but of acquittal; hunters not indeed of guilt but of grace. [Col. 0262D] He is Christ’s fisherman to whom it is said: “From now on you will make men live” [Note: [Col. 0262D] Four manuscripts: “catching men”; likewise above, book V, ch. 6, no. 16.] (Luke 5:10). Thus cast your nets; thus cast your eyes; thus send forth your words: so that you may oppress no one but raise up those tossed by the waves. “Attend,” he says, “to yourself” (Ecclus. 28:30). Thus stand, lest you fall; thus run, that you may reach the prize; thus contend, that you may often win the contest, because the crown is due to lawful striving. You are a soldier: carefully scout out the enemy, lest he creep upon you by night. You are an athlete: be nearer your opponent with your hands than with your face, lest he strike [Col. 0263A] your eye. Let your gaze be unconstrained, your step alert, so that you may throw down one who rushes at you, seize one who gives way, avoid a wound by watchful sight, and repel it by a strong encounter. But if you have been wounded, attend to yourself: run to the physician; seek the remedy of repentance. Attend to yourself, because you have flesh that quickly slips: let the good physician of souls, the divine word, come to you; let the Lord’s oracles sprinkle you like health-giving medicines. Attend to yourself, lest an evil word become hidden in your heart; for it creeps like poison and brings deadly infection. Attend to yourself, lest you forget God who made you, lest you take His name in vain.

51. “Attend to yourself,” the Law says, lest, when you have eaten and are satisfied, have built houses and begun to dwell in them, have been filled with cattle, have abounded in gold and [Col. 0263B] silver, and in everything that is yours, you exalt yourself in your heart amid abundance and forget the Lord your God (Deut. 8:12 ff.). For what have you, O man, that you have not received? Do not all these things pass away like a shadow? Is not this your house dust and ruin? Are not all these things [Note: [Col. 0263D] Thus the manuscripts of Carpentras, old Corbie, Th., and five others. But the Benedictine edition, with the remaining manuscripts and editions: “a fable.”] false? Is not the treasure of this age vanity? Are you not yourself ashes? Look into the graves of men and see what will remain of you except ashes and bones—that is, of your body. Look, I say, and tell me: who there is rich, and who poor? Distinguish the destitute from the powerful. We are all born naked; naked we die. There is no distinction among the corpses of the dead, except perhaps that the bodies of the rich, swollen with luxury, stink more grievously. Whom have you heard of—a poor man—who died of indigestion? His poverty benefits him: it exercises his body; it does not crush it. Yet we have not heard of the righteous man forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread, since he who works well in his own land abounds in provisions. Attend, therefore, to yourself, rich man, because you too bear flesh just as the poor man does.

52. Attend to yourself, poor man, because your soul is precious. Though the flesh is mortal, the soul endures; though money is lacking to you, grace is not lacking; though you have no spacious house or extensive estate, heaven lies open and the earth is free. The elements were given to all in common; the adornments of the world lie equally open to rich and poor. Are gilded ceilings in the most costly houses more beautiful than the face of heaven, marked out with gleaming stars? Are the estates of the rich [Col. 0263D] broader than the expanses of the earth? Therefore to those who join house to house and farm to farm it was said: “Will you dwell alone upon the earth?” (Isa. 5:8). You have a greater house, poor man, in which you cry out and are heard: “O Israel,” says the prophet, “how great is the house of God, and how vast the place of His possession! Great, and it has no end; high and immeasurable” (Bar. 3:24 ff.). God’s house is shared by rich and poor; nevertheless it is difficult for the rich to enter [Col. 0264A] the kingdom of heaven.

But perhaps you grieve because no light from gilded lamps shines upon you. Yet the moon, surrounded by light, shines for you with a much more splendid radiance. Perhaps you complain of winter because no hypocausts steam for you with breathing fires; yet you have the warmth of the sun, which moderates the world for you and defends you against winter cold. Or do you think happy those who are crowded about by troops of attendants? Yet those who require others’ feet do not know how to use their own. Finally, they are preceded by a few and carried by many. Unless perhaps you admire the fact that they abound in gold, silver, and money: you see the things in which they abound; you do not see the things they lack. But you think it precious to recline on ivory beds, and do not consider that the earth is more precious, spreading beds of grass for the poor, upon which [Col. 0264B] rest is sweet and sleep pleasant—sleep which the man lying on a golden bedstead seeks through an entirely sleepless night and does not obtain. O how much happier than himself he judges you, while he keeps watch and you rest! I pass over [Note: [Col. 0263D] Ten manuscripts of the best quality: “Moreover, I pass over this.”] what is much more excellent: that the righteous person who has lacked here will abound there; and he who has endured labor here will have consolation there; but he who has received good things here will not be able to hope there for their reward. For poverty preserves its reward; wealth consumes it.

53. Attend therefore to yourself, poor man; attend, rich man: because there are temptations both in poverty and in riches. Therefore the Wise Man says: “Give me neither riches nor poverty” (Prov. 30:8). And he explains why he asked this: it is enough for a man to have what suffices him. For riches, as banquets expand the stomach, so expand the mind with cares and anxieties. Therefore he asks that what is needful and sufficient be allotted to him: “Lest,” he says, “being filled, I become false and say, ‘Who sees me?’ Or, becoming poor, I commit theft, [Note: [Col. 0263D] Roman edition and manuscripts of Carpentras: “and swear the name [Col. 0264D] of the Lord.” Coenobium manuscript: “and forswear the name of the Lord.” The old edition and very many manuscripts: “and swear in the name,” etc. The most ancient manuscripts do not recognize the preposition.] and swear by the name of the Lord” (ibid.). Therefore the temptations of the world must be fled and guarded against: lest the poor man despair, lest the wealthy man become insolent. For it is written: “When you have driven out nations and begun to use their lands, do not say: ‘My strength and my hand have provided this possession for me’” (Deut. 8:17). Such is the person who ascribes his wealth to his own merit. And therefore, as though approved, he does not recognize his own error, but draws out [the cord of] sin by a long rope. For if he believed that the increase of money came either from chance events or from shameful cunning, insolence would have no place in matters where either there is no praise and only fruitless [Col. 0264D] labor, or there is shameless desire unable to set a limit to pleasure.

## CHAPTER IX

### On the excellence of the human body, and the formation, arrangement, and functions of its individual members

54. But now something must also be said concerning the very body of man. Who would deny that it surpasses all others in beauty and grace? For although the substance of all earthly bodies seems one and the same, and in some beasts strength and stature are greater, yet the form of the human body is more beautiful, its posture upright and lofty: so that there is neither monstrous tallness nor mean and abject [Note: [Col. 0265D] Thus twelve manuscripts with the old edition. But the Coenobium manuscript and one Vatican manuscript: “smallness.” Others and the more recent editions: “pusillanimity.”] smallness; then the body’s very proportion is pleasing and graceful, so that neither beast-like bulk is horrifying nor slender thinness a weakness.

55. First of all, let us recognize that the structure of the human body is fashioned after the likeness of the world. For just as heaven rises above [Note: [Col. 0265D] All editions: “just as heaven rises above the air, and the seas above the lands, which,” etc. Some manuscripts: “… the lands and the sea.” Others, greater in number and authority: as above in the text.] air, land, and sea—which are, as it were, certain members of the world—so too we see the head rising above the remaining limbs of our body, supreme among all, like heaven among the elements, like a citadel among the other walls [Col. 0265B] of a city. In this citadel a kind of royal wisdom dwells, according to the prophetic saying: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Eccl. 2:14). This is safer than the other parts, and from it vigor and providential care are conveyed to all the members. For what benefit are the strength and power of the arms, what the swiftness of the feet, unless the commanding power of the head, as of their ruler, gives support? From it all things are either deprived or sustained. What can courage do unless it uses the eye as guide in battle? [Note: [Col. 0266D] Carpentras manuscripts: “What can you do? If sight is lacking, it is a prison,” etc.] What can flight do if sight is absent? The whole body is a prison, grim in its dark condition, unless it is illuminated by the sight of the eyes. What the sun and moon are in heaven, the eyes are in man. The sun and moon are the two lights of the world; but the eyes are certain stars shining above in the flesh, [Col. 0265C] illuminating the lower parts with clear light and not allowing us to be entangled in a kind of night-darkness. They are, as it were, our watchers, keeping guard by day and night. For they are awakened from sleep sooner than the other limbs and, while awake, survey everything; they are nearer to the brain, from which all power of sight flows.

Nor should anyone suppose that I have descended here too hastily, praising the eyes while leaving the crown of the head, since it is not foreign to the subject to praise the principal thing in one of its parts. For the eyes are certainly a portion of the head. Thus the head explores all things through the eyes, investigates hidden things through the ears, recognizes what is concealed, and hears what is done by others in distant lands.

56. How pleasing and graceful is the crown of the head itself; how beautiful the hair; how reverend in the old, how venerable in priests, how [Col. 0265D] terrible in warriors, how becoming in young men; how adorned in women, how sweet in children! Long hair does not suit one sex; shorn hair does not suit the other. From trees one may judge what grace belongs to the human head. All the fruit of a tree is at its head; there is all its beauty; its foliage either covers us from rain or shields us from the sun. Take the foliage from a tree, and the whole tree is unattractive. How much greater, then, is the adornment of the human head, which protects and clothes our brain—that is, [Col. 0266A] the seat and origin of our senses—with the hair of the head, lest it be afflicted either by cold or heat? For there is the source of all things; and therefore where injury is harmful, there grace is pre-eminent.

57. What is man without his head, when he is wholly in his head? When you see a head, you recognize a man; if the head is absent, there can be no recognition: an ignoble trunk lies there, without honor, without a name. The heads of princes alone, cast in bronze, and faces fashioned in bronze or marble, [Note: [Col. 0266D] One Corbie manuscript and one Vatican manuscript: “are adorned by men.”] are worshipped by men. Not without reason, therefore, do the other members serve this head as though it were their counselor, carry it with servile bearing as though a divinity, and bear it aloft. Hence, with censorial authority, it directs wherever it wishes the services of certain slave-like attendants, and assigns to each the commands it must perform. [Col. 0266B] You may see each member serving its commander with unpaid military service. Some carry, some feed, some defend, or render their particular service: they obey as a ruler; they serve [Note: [Col. 0266D] Bigotian, Gembloux, one Corbie, and one Vatican manuscript: “as a mistress.”] as a lord. From it goes forth, as it were, a password: what region the feet ought to traverse; what duties of service the hands ought to perform in completing works; what rule of abstaining or eating the belly ought to observe under its imposed discipline.

58. To this belongs the open forehead, exposed in its bare temples, which by its appearance reveals the disposition of the mind: now cheerful, now sadder; now raised in severity, now more relaxed in gentleness; which expresses the inward will by outward signs. A kind of image of the soul speaks in the face; it is the foundation of faith, upon which the Lord’s name is daily inscribed and held fast. It is followed by the twin hedges of the eyebrows, [Col. 0266C] which provide defenses for the eyes and lend grace to them: so that both the beauty of comeliness may smile and the care of protection stand by. For if any dirt falls from the head, or dust of sand, or misty dew, or sweat from the moistened crown, it is caught by the eyebrow, lest its impact disturb the delicate sight of the tender eyes.

59. The eyes cling, as it were, to certain mountain-like brows, so that they may be safer beneath the protection of the mountain’s summit and, placed as though on a height, may survey all things from a higher stage. For they ought not to be lowly like the ears or mouth, or the inward cavities of the nostrils themselves. A lookout-post is always on high, so that the approach of hostile incoming bands may be observed, lest they unexpectedly seize either the unguarded [Col. 0266D] people of a city or an emperor’s army. Thus attacks by robbers are also guarded against if scouts are stationed on walls, towers, or the lofty brow of a mountain, so that they may look down upon the plains of the regions where robbers’ ambushes cannot lie hidden. Likewise, at sea, if someone supposes that he is approaching land, the watchman for the desired land climbs to the very top of the mast and the high horns of the yardarms, and from afar greets the land still invisible to the other sailors.

[Col. 0267A] 60. But perhaps you will say: “If a higher lookout was necessary, why were the eyes not placed above the very crown of the head, as they are at the top in crabs and beetles, which, though they may have no visible head, nevertheless have necks and backs higher than the rest of their body?” But those creatures have a hard shell, not such a thin membrane as ours, which can easily be injured and cut by brambles and other thorns. Other living creatures also have this sort of form, so that they can draw their eyes either back toward the neck, as horses, oxen, and almost all wild beasts do, or toward their wings, as birds do, so that they may enjoy secure rest. But in us the eyes had to be placed almost at the highest part of the body, as in a citadel, and yet defended from every—even the slightest—injury: two requirements that seemed opposed to one another. For if they were low, for the sake of protection, their function would be impeded; if upon the crown, [Col. 0267B] they would be exposed to injury. Therefore, lest either anything be taken away from the usefulness of their office or anything be lacking for repelling injury [Note: [Col. 0267D] Six manuscripts: “the usefulness of their office.” And shortly afterward the Carpentras, Benedictine, Corbie, and almost all other manuscripts omit the negation before “might be provided for.”], He placed the eyes in a location where the eyebrows above furnish them with no small protection, the somewhat raised cheeks below add considerable fortification, the nostrils fence in the inner part, and the projections of the forehead and cheeks rise outwardly. Although the adjoining parts seem to be enclosed round about by a structure of closely joined and level bones, between them are the globes of the eyes, secure for caution, free for sight, and beautiful for grace, shining like crystal. In their middle are the pupils, which perform the function of sight. To prevent their being hurt by the impact of any incoming injury, they are fortified on every side by closely set hairs, like a kind of rampart. Hence the Prophet, asking secure help for himself, says: “Guard me, Lord, as the pupil of the eye” (Ps. 16:8), that divine protection might be for him as watchful and secure a safeguard as nature deigned to fortify the pupil of the eye with a most secure rampart.

At the same time, because innocence and integrity, sprinkled with even slight filth, are violated and lose the gift of their grace, care must be taken lest the dust of error cloud them or any straw of sin trouble them. For it is written: “First cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see to cast the straw out of your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7:5).

61. Therefore, for the sake of the eyes, those skilled in healing say that the human brain is situated in the head; and that the other senses of our body are located near it for the sake of the brain. For the brain is the origin of the nerves and of all voluntary movements of sensation; from it flows every cause of the things we have mentioned. Most people think, however, that the heart is the origin of the arteries and of the inborn heat by which the vital parts are animated and warmed. The nerves are, as it were, the organs of each individual sense, [Col. 0267D] like strings and cords arising from the brain and distributed through the body’s parts for each respective function. Therefore the brain is softer than the other parts, because it receives all sensations [Note: [Col. 0267D] Some manuscripts and the old edition: “whence all the nerves seek all things.” Roman edition: “for the nerves refer all things to it.” Quite a few other manuscripts: “whence also the nerves, and the things which [Col. 0268D] they refer,” etc. The Benedictine reading in the text is best.]: all the nerves refer to it whatever the eye has seen, the ear heard, the nostril inhaled, the tongue rebuked, or the mouth received in taste. What is soft is more suited to fellow-feeling; but what is hard, through a certain firmness of the nerves, is more effective for action.

62. The function of hearing is also most excellent, and in grace surpasses sight. Therefore the ears project outward, both to display the beauty of their ornament and to receive whatever dirt or moisture may flow down from the crown; and also so that the voice, reflected within their cavities, may enter the inward passages without injury. For unless this were so, who would not be stunned by every stronger sound of voice, when even amid these protections we often feel ourselves suddenly deafened by an unexpected shout? Then you may see them extending, as it were, certain bulwarks against the harshness of cold and the burning of heat, so that neither cold may penetrate the open passages nor excessive heat scorch them. The winding of the inner ears also provides a certain measure and order for modulation. For through the winding passages of the ears [Note: [Col. 0268D] Gembloux and Bigotian manuscripts: “a certain στόμος [stomos], that is, talkativeness.” Other manuscripts and editions: “a certain rhythm, that is, musical measure,” or, as the Benedictine edition has between the lines, “a sweet sound.”] a certain rhythm is produced, and the sound of the entering voice is shaped by certain modulations. Experience itself further teaches us that the winding passages of the ears retain received speech. For as in hollow mountains, rocky recesses, or bends of rivers, a voice is heard more sweetly, and echo resounds in return with pleasant answers. The earwax itself is not useless, since it holds the sound fast, so that its [Col. 0268C] memory and pleasantness may remain more tenacious within us.

63. What shall I say about the nostrils, which, by their double and lofty opening, provide a kind of cavern for receiving odors, so that an odor does not pass by casually but clings longer in the nostrils and, by their passage, nourishes the brain and senses? Therefore a received smell endures longer than speech resounds or a sight appears. Often something smelled for a brief moment breathes in your nostrils all day long. Through them also the purgations of the head flow out and are discharged without harm or injury to the body.

64. There is also no slight faculty in touch, and in it most pleasing delight and unerring judgment. For we often test by touch what we cannot test by the eyes.

[Col. 0268D] 65. Finally comes the function of the mouth or tongue, which nevertheless supplies strength to all. For neither the eyes would have the power of seeing, unless they received the strength of bodily substance conveyed by food and drink; nor the ears the power of hearing, the nostrils of smelling, or the hands of touching, unless the whole body were strengthened by nourishment. For we fail in strength unless we restore it through the regular use of appropriate food. Thus those exhausted by hunger [Col. 0269A] are delighted by none of the pleasures of the senses, but, as though deprived of them, do not feel their charms.

66. Why should I describe the rampart of the teeth, by which food is ground and the full expression of speech is made? What nourishment would be pleasant without teeth? Indeed, we commonly see people advanced in age grow old more quickly for this very reason: because, through their lost teeth, they cannot take in the strength of more solid food. Therefore infancy is mute, because it does not yet possess the instrument of speech.

67. The tongue also has a most precious function not only in speaking but in eating. For it is like the plectrum of one speaking and a kind of hand of one eating, supplying and serving the food that flows down to the teeth. The voice too is borne by a kind of rowing through the air and carried through the void; and the same force which strikes the air [Col. 0269B] now moves, now soothes, the feeling of the hearer: it calms the angry, raises up the broken, consoles the grieving. Let our common possession with birds, then, be song. But the capacity to know with whom and in what tone of voice one should speak—which is rational—cannot be shared with all the irrational animals. For the senses themselves are shared by us with the other animals, yet the other animals do not use them with the same skill. A heifer raises her eyes to heaven but does not know what she sees. Wild animals raise them, birds raise them; all have free vision, but in man alone is there an interpreter of what he sees. With his eyes he watches the risings and settings of the constellations, sees the adornment of heaven, marvels at the circles of the stars, and understands the diverse brightnesses [Note: [Col. 0269D] Thus thirteen manuscripts. Others and the old edition: “understands the constellations.” Roman edition: “… of the stars.” Again, where the Roman edition reads “what risings Orion [has],” other editions and manuscripts read “what motions,” etc.] of each: when Hesperus rises and when Lucifer; why the former shines in the evening, the latter in the morning; what motions Orion has, what eclipses the moon; how the sun knows its settings and observes the revolutions of its course in regular order. Other animals also hear; but who except man knows by hearing? Man alone, of all the kinds upon earth, gathers the secrets of wisdom through hearing, meditation, and understanding; he can say: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me.” This is most precious: that man is the instrument of the divine voice and gives expression through bodily lips to the heavenly oracle, as in this passage: “Cry.” “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40:6). He received what he should say, and cried out. Let those keep their own wisdom who map the expanses of heaven and earth with a ray. Let them keep [Col. 0269D] their understanding, concerning which the Lord says: “I will reject the understanding of the prudent” (1 Cor. 1:19). I will not assign to the place of wisdom the numbers of rhetoric, its modes, and the measures of music [Note: [Col. 0269D] Old edition with certain manuscripts: “numbers, principles, modes, and measures,” etc. Gillot and Roman editions, with more numerous and better manuscripts: as in our text, except that [Col. 0270D] the Roman edition omits “and measures.”]; but I define as wisdom that of which the Prophet says: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Ps. 50:8).

68. What, moreover, shall I say of the kiss of the mouth, which is the pledge of devotion and charity? Doves kiss one another too, [Col. 0270A] but what is that compared with the grace of a human kiss, in which the mark of friendship and humanity shines forth, in which the affection of faithful and complete charity is expressed? Hence the Lord, condemning in the betrayer what was as though a monstrous thing, says: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48). That is: do you turn the sign of charity into a token of betrayal and evidence of unfaithfulness? Do you use this pledge of peace [Note: [Col. 0270D] Three manuscripts: “for the workshop of cruelty.”] for the work of cruelty? Therefore by the oracle of the divine voice He reproves the beast-like service of a mouth bringing death rather than conveying the bonds of charity. This too is pre-eminent: that we human beings alone express through the mouth what we feel in the heart. Thus the silent thoughts of the mind are marked by the speech of the mouth. What, then, is the mouth of man but a kind of entrance for speech, a fountain of discourse, a hall of words, a storehouse [Col. 0270B] of the will? We have completed, as it were, a royal palace of the human body: although one portion may have a certain size, it is nevertheless the form of the whole.

69. The throat follows, through which the life-giving intercourse of the entire body and the passage of this breath are poured in. Next come the arms, the powerful muscles of the upper arms, hands strong for work, and fingers, longer and suited for holding. Hence comes a more fitting use for work, hence the elegance of writing, and that “pen of a scribe writing swiftly,” by which the oracles of the divine voice are expressed. The hand supplies food to the mouth; the hand shines in noble deeds; it is the reconciler of divine grace, brought to the sacred altars; through it we offer and receive the heavenly sacraments. The hand both performs and dispenses the divine mysteries, [Col. 0270C] and the Son of God did not disdain to be described by its name, David saying: “The right hand of the Lord has wrought power; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (Ps. 117:16). The hand made all things, as God Almighty said: [Note: [Col. 0270D] Thus twelve manuscripts and the old edition, except that in some the word “all” is omitted. Others and the Roman edition: “For my hand made all these things.”] “Has not my hand made all these things?” (Isa. 66:2). The hand is the bulwark of the whole body, the defender of the head. Although located lower down, it attends the whole crown and adorns it with honorable beauty.

70. Who can worthily explain the lattice of the chest and the softness of the belly? Otherwise the softer internal organs could not be kept warm, and the hollows of the intestines would undoubtedly be injured by hard bones. What is more healthful than that the lung should be joined in nearest proximity to the heart, so that when the heart burns with anger and indignation, it may more quickly be tempered by the blood and moisture of the lung? Therefore the lung is softer, because it is always moist, and at the same time softens the rigidity of indignation. We have run briefly through these matters in order that we may seem, as [Note: [Col. 0270D] Roman edition: “not unlearned.”] unlearned persons, to touch upon obvious matters in passing, not, as physicians, to investigate and pursue more fully things hidden in nature’s recesses.

71. The spleen also has a profitable proximity to the liver: while it takes in what nourishes itself, it wipes away whatever impurities it finds, so that through the [Col. 0271A] finer fibers of the liver [Note: [Col. 0271D] Almost all manuscripts with the Roman edition: “more fortified.” Vatican and Dionysian manuscripts with the old edition: “smaller.”] the thin and subtle remains of foods may pass, be turned into blood, and contribute to strength, rather than be discharged with dung and filth. And what do the winding circles of the intestines, entwined and yet mutually connected without any knot, show except the divine providence of the Creator? They ensure that food does not pass through too quickly and run down immediately from the stomach. If this happened, unceasing hunger and a continual craving for devouring would arise in human beings. For when the internal organs had been emptied and drained through momentary evacuation, an insatiable and inexhaustible desire for food and drink would necessarily be generated, followed without doubt by [Note: [Col. 0271D] Thus the manuscripts and the old edition. The Roman edition, however: “premature death,” which is by no means without sense.] mature death. Therefore food is providently first digested in the upper stomach; then it is cooked in the liver, and, once digested by its vapor, its juice is conveyed into the other parts of the body. By this substance the human limbs are nourished: young people receive it for growth, old people for continuance; what remains, as superfluous matter, is carried through the intestines and discharged through that transverse outlet.

72. Finally, even in Genesis Noah’s ark is understood as a figure of the construction of the human body. God said concerning it: “Make yourself an ark of squared timbers; you shall make chambers in it, and you shall cover it within and without with pitch; and thus you shall make the ark” (Gen. 6:14). And below: “You shall make a door at the side; and you shall make the lower parts of the ark two-storied and three-storied” (ibid., v. 16). Therefore the Lord signifies by this that the outlet is on the posterior side, through which food’s superfluities are discharged. For our Creator fittingly turned the passage of waste away from the human face, lest, while we empty the belly, we pollute the sight. Consider also that the things full of shame are located where, covered by garments, they cannot be disgraceful.

73. The beating of the veins is either a messenger of illness or of health. Yet although they are spread through the whole body, they are neither bare nor uncovered, but are covered with such light [Note: [Col. 0271D] *Viscera* sometimes means flesh, as it does in Virgil, *Aeneid* I, in this verse: “They strip the hides from the ribs and lay bare the viscera”; but in this passage the word seems to mean skin.] skin that there is opportunity for examination and swiftness of perception, since no thickness of flesh can cover the pulse. All the bones too are covered with thin skin and bound together by sinews; but especially the head is covered with light skin. Hence, that it may have some protection against rain and cold, it is clothed with thicker hair. What shall I say of the genitals, which, by veins drawn from the region of the neck through the kidneys and loins, receive the generative seed for the office and grace of procreation?

74. What shall I say of the function of the feet, which support the whole body without any injury from its weight? Or of the flexible knee, by which, above all else, the Lord’s offense is softened, wrath is calmed, and favor is invoked? For this is the gift of the supreme Father toward the Son: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:10–11). For there are two things which above all others appease God: humility and faith. Thus the foot expresses the disposition of humility and the obedience of diligent service; faith makes the Son equal to the Father and confesses the same glory of both.

Rightly, moreover, a human being has not more than two feet: beasts and wild animals have four feet, birds two. And therefore the person who seeks the heights by lofty vision and, by a kind of rowing, flies among sublime things through the keenness of the senses, is as it were of the birds.

[Note: Vatican manuscript: “may attain lofty things by power”; perhaps from a homoeoteleuton. [Col. 0272D] Formerly in Basil’s tenth homily, but now denied to him, where one reads: συμπαρίπταται δὲ τοῖς πτηνοῖς τῇ τοῦ νόμου δυνάμει, “and by the power of the law he is associated with the birds.” In the same place, after four words, several manuscripts and all editions read “of sublime thoughts.” Dionysius: “of sublime thoughts and the acuteness of the senses.” In the remaining manuscripts, including the most reliable, the word “thoughts” is omitted.]

Therefore it is said of him: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102:5), because he is nearer to heavenly things and loftier than eagles, he who can say: “But our citizenship is in heaven.”

## CHAPTER X

He explains how God is said to have rested when He was about to bring the sixth day, and indeed the whole work, to an end; and he crowns the discourse with praises of the Creator.

75. But let our discourse now come to its end, since the sixth day has been completed and the whole sum of the work of the world has reached its conclusion: namely, when the human being was perfected, in whom lies the dominion over all living creatures, a kind of summation of the universe, and the beauty of the whole creation of the world.

Certainly let us keep silence, because God rested from all the works of the world. Yet He rested in the inward part of the human being; He rested in his mind and purpose. For He had made the human being capable of reason, an imitator of Himself, an emulator of virtues, desirous of heavenly graces.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Roman edition: “of heavenly joys.”]

God rests in those of whom He says: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet person, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

76. [Note: Several manuscripts: “I give thanks to the Lord,” etc.]

Therefore let us give thanks to the Lord our God, who made such a work in which He might rest. He made heaven: I do not read that He rested. He made earth: I do not read that He rested. He made sun, moon, and stars: nor do I read that He rested there. But I read that He made the human being, and then He rested, having one whose sins He might forgive.

Or perhaps even then there came beforehand the mystery of the Lord’s future Passion, by which it was revealed that Christ would rest in the human being, He who predestined for Himself rest in the body for the redemption of the human being, according to what He Himself said: “I slept and rested, and rose again, because the Lord sustained me” (Ps. 3:6). For He rested who made all things: to Him be honor, glory, and perpetuity from ages past, now, always, and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

[ON PARADISE.]

[Col. 0273C]

## NOTICE ON THE BOOK *ON PARADISE*

We do not venture to assert that the book *On Paradise* was Ambrose’s first work; yet we do not at all doubt that it should be numbered among his earliest. There is indeed reason why we should not judge otherwise. For since that treatise is filled with varied and manifold learning, scarcely anyone would suppose that he composed it immediately in the first year when, as he himself said (*On the Duties of the Clergy*, I.1), he was snatched away from tribunals and the insignia of civil administration to the priesthood.

Yet we should not readily agree that it ought to be assigned later than the following year, since the holy man, in a letter to Sabinus, mentions that this very work had long before been elaborated by him when he was not yet an old priest (*Epistle* 42). One may infer that this occurred about the year 375 of the restored salvation, from the fact that, since Ambrose was appointed to the episcopate in 374, nothing seems to prevent us from supposing that he put the finishing hand to this work before he set his hand to the beginning of the books *On Virgins*, which he wrote when not yet three years a priest (*On Virgins*, II, near the end).

In this book he discusses Paradise, and by a very brief exposition of the sacred text shows what it was, of what kind, and where it was situated (Chapter 1); what the first parents did in it; and by what deceit, in what order, and by what artifice (ibid.) they were tempted by the devil and finally fell into sin. But he devotes his chief effort there to refuting the disciples of Apelles (Chapters 2, 5, 6, and following), who attacked the authority of the Old Covenant. Yet, as it seems, through their side he directs his weapon against the Manichaeans, who at that time were harassing the Church of Milan, since perhaps he had not yet dared to attack them openly and in pitched battle.

He dissolves the empty subtleties of the Apellists and rises against them with all the greater vehemence because he anxiously feared that the people recently entrusted to his vigilance might be deceived by the snares of heretics. Nevertheless, the work and diligence of the holy bishop are not confined merely to refuting heretics. They extend also to the Jews, whom, when occasion offered, he attacks and defeats with no slight force. Moreover, he regularly reports various opinions of Catholic people, but assents only to those which he judges truer. Indeed, it happens very often that, rejecting every one of them, he does not hesitate to advance his own view.

Perhaps it was considerations such as these that led some to attach the title *Disputation* to this work. For at the end of the most ancient manuscripts of the Church of Reims and of the College of Clermont there is appended, in the former, “The disputation on Paradise ends,” and in the latter, “The disputation on Paradise concerning the preservation of purity of soul ends.” Yet in both it is inscribed, “The *On Paradise* of Lord Ambrose begins,” where one may conjecture that the word *disputatio* has been omitted from the words with which they conclude. But since Augustine (*Against Julian*, II.5 and elsewhere) more than once cites this very treatise under the name of a book, it seems more probable to us that Ambrose himself gave it that title; and that in the manuscripts mentioned the word *disputatio* should be understood in the sense of “a book” or any kind of writing.

Moreover, it is not easy to determine whether Ambrose first delivered to the people the matters contained in this work, and afterward, according to his custom, arranged them in the form of a book. One might perhaps reasonably prove this to have been so, both because it contains a great many things pertaining to the formation of Christian morals, and especially because the whole discussion seems directed to preventing heretics from misleading simple minds through malicious interpretation (Chapter 5). Yet, since we find none of the character of our Doctor’s other works which were turned from sermons into books, we must conclude either that this treatise is in no way made up of sermons, or at least that they were reduced to such an order that it bears not even the slightest indication of Ambrose preaching.

Here it should not be passed over that he drew certain matters not only from Philo the Jew’s books *Allegories of the Law*, as some have thought, but also from the latter’s work *On the Creation of the World*. But apart from the fact that these matters are few and concern the allegorical sense of Scripture, even in those he follows Philo’s thought rather than his words; and what in that author had been imbued with a Jewish spirit, Ambrose transforms very fittingly into a meaning consonant with evangelical Christian doctrine.

[Col. 0275]

## THE ONE BOOK ON PARADISE OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN

[Note: [Col. 0275C] Written about the year 375.] (C)

[Col. 0275]

145 ## CHAPTER I

How difficult it is to discuss Paradise. Its author, nature, location, and inhabitant are nevertheless indicated; and the subject is carried over to a mystical sense.

[Col. 0275A]

1. “And God planted Paradise in Eden toward the East, and placed there the human being whom He had formed” (Gen. 2:8).

[Note: [Col. 0275C] This text is lacking in the ancient editions and in several manuscripts. Nevertheless, it is found in others of the best quality.]

A discourse undertaken on Paradise seems to cause us no slight anxiety, since we wish to investigate and explain what Paradise is, where it is, and of what sort it is—especially since the Apostle, whether in the body or outside the body he does not know, nevertheless says that he was caught up even to the third heaven. And again he says: “I know such a man—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know, God knows—that he was caught up into Paradise and heard ineffable words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak … On behalf of such a one I will boast; but on my own behalf I will not boast, except in my weaknesses. For if I should wish to boast, I would not be foolish, for I speak the truth” (2 Cor. 12:5–6).

If, then, Paradise is of such a kind that Paul alone, or some man like Paul, could see it while still living this life; and if he himself, whether he saw it in the body or outside the body, could not remember it, while having heard words which he was forbidden to make public—

[Note: [Col. 0275C] Thus most manuscripts and the old editions. Other manuscripts: “which he heard.” Roman edition: “which he was seeing.”]

—how in the end shall we be able to set forth the location of Paradise, which we could not see, and which, even if we could see it, we should nonetheless be forbidden to disclose to others? And since Paul feared to exalt himself because of the sublimity of his revelations, how much more must we fear to investigate too anxiously that whose revelation itself is exposed to danger?

[Note: [Col. 0275C] Several manuscripts: “we must fear to indicate this too anxiously.”]

[Note: [Col. 0275C] Many manuscripts, not to be despised: “we ought not therefore to regard this Paradise as a vile material thing.” Perhaps “visible.” Or, if you prefer *hyle* with other manuscripts and editions, understand “matter.” See *Hexaemeron*, Book I, chapter 1, §1.]

Therefore we ought not to regard this Paradise as *hyle*, that is, matter; and so let it remain Paul’s secret.
