2. Yet because here in Genesis we read that Paradise was planted by God toward the East, and that the human being whom God fashioned was placed there, we can now discover the author of this Paradise.

[Note: [Col. 0275C] Roman edition: “planted toward the East … and every tree beautiful to behold and good for food was brought forth.”]

For who could fashion Paradise except the omnipotent God, who spoke and things were made,

[Note: [Col. 0276C] Old edition with three manuscripts: “perhaps being in need.”]

never needing those things which He wished to bring into being? Therefore He Himself planted the Paradise of which Wisdom says: “Every plant which my Father has not planted shall be rooted up” (Matt. 5:13). Good is the planting of angels; good is that of saints. For saints are said to be beneath fig tree and vine in that future time of peace, in which they are a type of angels (Mic. 4:4).

[Note: [Col. 0276C] The same edition: “are said to rest in that future peace.” But “to rest” is absent from all other editions and manuscripts. Some of these, with the old edition, read “of future peace”; others, more numerous and older, read “… of the future,” namely, saints.]

3. Therefore Paradise has many trees, but fruitful trees, trees full of sap and vigor, of which it is said: “All the trees of the forests shall rejoice” (Ps. 95:13); trees ever flourishing with the verdure of merits, like that tree planted beside flowing waters, whose leaf shall not fall, because all its fruit abounds. Such, then, is Paradise.

4. The place in which it is planted is called delight.

[Note: [Col. 0276C] The Roman edition alone: “The place in which it is said to be planted is Eden, that is, delight.”]

Hence holy David also says: “You will give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35:9). For you have read: “A fountain goes forth from Eden, which waters Paradise” (Gen. 2:10).

[Note: [Col. 0276C] Seven manuscripts and the American edition: “the lights of the saints”; Erasmus: “the rivers of the saints”; Gillot, with other manuscripts: “the trees of the saints.” The Roman edition omits the word “saints.”]

Therefore these trees of the saints, planted in Paradise, are watered as by an overflowing torrent of the Spirit. Of this he says elsewhere as well: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:5). That city is the free Jerusalem above, in which the diverse merits of the saints have sprung up.

5. Therefore God placed in this Paradise the human being whom He formed. Understand also that He did not place there the human being who is according to the image of God, but the human being according to the body. For what is incorporeal is not in a place. Yet He placed him in Paradise as the sun in heaven, awaiting the kingdom of heaven, just as creation awaits the revelation of the children of God.

6. Therefore, if Paradise is a place in which shoots had sprung forth, Paradise seems to be the soul which multiplies the seed it has received, in which every virtue is planted, and in which was also the tree of life—that is, Wisdom—as Solomon said (Wis. 7:25):

[Note: [Col. 0277D] Ambrose, here below in chapter 13 and elsewhere, attributes this book to Solomon in accordance with the opinion of his time. But Jerome later taught that it is pseudepigraphical, and that some ancient writers ascribed it to Philo the Jew, probably the elder. Hence Cassiodorus, *Introduction to Divine Literature*, chapter 5: “Jerome says that the Book of Wisdom was written not by Solomon, as is customary, but by a certain most learned Jew, Philo, and he called it pseudographical because it bears the usurped name of another.” Augustine at one time thought that the same book had been written by Jesus son of Sirach, but later, better informed, declared it to be by an uncertain author. See *Retractations*, II.4; *On Christian Doctrine*, II.8; and the *Speculum* and the notes appended there in the last edition. The more common view of writers in our age is that the work arose from a compilation of many sayings of Solomon by a certain devout and learned man; accordingly this man should be called the compiler of this divine book, while Solomon should be called its genuine author.]

For Wisdom did not spring from the earth, but from the Father. “For she is the brightness of eternal light and an emanation of almighty glory.”

## CHAPTER II

That the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was in Paradise, and that the serpent was there also, is not to be criticized. And what some persons understood by the serpent, Adam, and Eve.

7. Now the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was in Paradise. For thus you have it: “God brought forth a tree beautiful to behold and good for food, and the tree of life in Paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. 2:9). Later we shall see whether this tree also was beautiful to behold and good for food like the others. For it will be more opportune to discuss this at the place where we find the human being deceived by tasting from this tree.

Meanwhile, we have nothing which we should now criticize, even if we cannot know the reason. For in this creation of the world, if some things seem difficult for us to understand and incomprehensible to our intelligence, we ought not, with a certain rash judgment, to condemn the creation of serpents or of some venomous living creature, since we human beings cannot yet understand and know for what reason each particular thing has been made. Thus also in the divine Scriptures we should not readily criticize anything that we cannot understand. For there are many things which are not to be measured by our intelligence but estimated from the height of the divine ordering and word.

8. Suppose, then—without prejudice, however, to the argument to be made later—that this tree of the knowledge of good and evil displeases you because, after human beings had tasted from it, they understood that they were naked. Still, for the completion of the divine work I shall tell you that this tree too sprang up in Paradise and was therefore permitted by God, so that we might know the superiority of the good. For if there were no knowledge of good and evil, how could we learn any distinction between good and evil? For we would not judge that what was evil was evil unless there were knowledge of good; but knowledge of good could not exist unless there were also good; nor, again, would we know that what was good was good unless there were knowledge of evil.

[Note: [Col. 0278D] Thus most manuscripts. Others, and the old edition: “unless there were also evil.” The Roman edition adds: “for evil cannot be discerned except through knowledge of good.” But these words are found nowhere else.]

Take an example from the very constitution of the human body. Surely it has a certain bitterness of bile, which, if you consider its general effect, is found useful for human health. Thus even what we regard as evil is often not evil in every respect, but is useful in general. For just as bile is one part of the body and yet benefits the usefulness of the whole body, so God, knowing that the knowledge of good and evil would benefit all, placed it in one part, that it might benefit the whole.

9. Finally, you find the serpent in Paradise, certainly created not without God’s will. In the figure of the serpent is the devil. For the prophet Ezekiel teaches that the devil was in Paradise too, when he says concerning the prince of Tyre: “You were made in the delight of Paradise” (Ezek. 28:13). We understand the prince of Tyre figuratively as the devil.

Shall we accuse God on this ground also, because we cannot comprehend the treasures of His depth and knowledge, hidden and concealed in Christ, except those which He Himself has deigned to reveal? Yet He has revealed them, so that we may know that even the devil’s malice benefits human beings unto salvation—not because the devil wishes to benefit them, but because the Lord turns even the malice of his resistance to our salvation.

Indeed, that malice made the virtue and patience of the holy man Job more renowned. It exercised his righteousness, so that he might contend and conquer, and a crown might follow his victory. For no one is crowned except one who has competed lawfully. Joseph’s chastity too would never have come into our remembrance unless the wife of his master and fellow-servant, stirred by the fiery darts of the devil, had tempted his affection; unless finally she had sought his death, so that the chastity of the man might be more illustrious—the man who despised death for chastity’s sake.

Do you wish to know the counsel of God? Surely, with the devil as author, murders seem to be prepared for righteous people and the parricidal acts of sons to be set in motion; yet the Lord also tested Abraham by this device, demanding from him that he offer his son in sacrifice. By this temptation Abraham was proved faithful to the Lord, because he was not turned aside from the obedience of devotion even by pity for his beloved son.

Thus the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was in Paradise. It seemed beautiful to behold and good for food in appearance; for it was not in fact good for food, since its food seems to have harmed human beings. Therefore something may harm individuals and benefit the whole: the devil harmed Judas, but, apart from him, crowned all the apostles who overcame the trials of his malice.

149 10. Therefore we should neither doubt nor criticize that the devil was in Paradise, since he could not bar the way to the saints so that no one might ascend. For he did not take away from the righteous their dwelling-place of sojourn as though he were its owner. Even if he has turned aside certain idle and vicious persons from inhabiting the heavenly possession, this is much more august and much more beautiful: that he will be excluded by the prayers of the saints, when this has been fulfilled: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 9:18).

Therefore let us not fear one who is so weak that he himself will fall to earth. He did indeed receive permission to tempt, but he did not receive power to overthrow, unless a weak disposition falls of its own accord because it does not know how to call for help. Therefore we must learn by what deceit he tempted the first human being, what he thought should be tempted in the human being, and in what order and by what artifice, so that we may be able to guard against him.

11. Yet many who wish the devil not to have been in Paradise—although we read that he stood in heaven with the angels—lest they seem offended by our discourse, may accept the interpretation of this passage according to their own will.

[Note: [Col. 0279D] Augustine, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, VIII.1 and following, attests that this was the opinion of certain Catholics: that Paradise and the things read in Genesis concerning the conversation between the serpent and Eve should be interpreted in an exclusively allegorical sense. It is therefore no wonder that Ambrose grants this option. Yet understand it in such a way that he intends to preserve inviolate the truth of the transgression of the first parents and of original sin. This he himself teaches plainly both in the last words of this chapter and in other passages of the same book, especially those which Augustine employs to establish original sin.]

For there was before us Philo, in his book *On the Creation of the World*, who stated that transgression was committed by the human being through pleasure and sense, taking in the form of the serpent a figure of delight, and in the figure of the woman establishing the sense of soul and mind, which the Greeks call αἴσθησις (*aisthēsis*, “sensation” or “perception”).

[Note: [Col. 0280D] Thus ten manuscripts. The Dijon manuscript, and the American and Petavian editions: “but he maintained that the deceived perception,” etc. Erasmus, Gillot, and the Roman edition, with other manuscripts: “but he maintained that the mind, deceived through perception, was transgressive,” etc.]

But he maintained that the mind, deceived through perception, was transgressive according to the history; the Greeks call this mind νοῦς (*nous*, “intellect”). Rightly, therefore, in Greek *nous* receives the figure of the man and *aisthēsis* that of the woman. Hence some have interpreted Adam as the earthly *nous*. The Lord likewise, in the Gospel, set those virgins awaiting the bridegroom’s coming with lamps lit or extinguished (Matt. 25:1 and following) as figures of either the sound perceptions of the wise or the corrupted perceptions of the foolish. For if Eve—that is, the perception of the first woman—had kept her lamps lit, she would never have entangled us in the locks of her transgression or fallen from that immortality of virtue.

## CHAPTER III

By the fountain of Paradise Christ is signified; by the four rivers rising from it, the cardinal virtues and the four ages of the world.

12. Therefore Paradise is a fertile land, that is, a fruitful soul, planted in Eden, that is, in a certain delight, or cultivated land, in which is the soul’s delight. There is also *nous*, as Adam; and perception, as Eve. And lest you should have anything to refer to the weakness of nature or to a condition liable to danger, consider what aids this soul possesses.

13. “There was a fountain which watered Paradise.” What fountain is this, except the Lord Jesus Christ? He is the fountain of eternal life, as is also the Father, for it is written: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35:10). And again: “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38). He is read of as both fountain and river, watering the fruitful tree of Paradise, which bears fruit unto eternal life.

Therefore this fountain, as you have read—“for,” he says, “a fountain goes forth from Eden”—is in your soul. Hence Solomon says: “Drink water from your own vessels and from the fountains of your own wells” (Prov. 5:15). This is the fountain which goes forth from that cultivated soul full of delight; this is the fountain which waters Paradise, that is, the various groves of virtues which spring up in the soul by most eminent merit.

14. “And,” he says, “this fountain is divided into four heads. The name of one is Phison: this is the one that encircles the whole land of Evilath, where there is gold. And the gold of that land is good, where there is carbuncle and green stone. And the name of the second is Geon: this is the one that encircles all Ethiopia. And the third river is Tigris: this is the one that goes against the Assyrians. And the fourth river is Euphrates” (Gen. 2:10 and following).

These, then, are the four rivers—that is, according to the Hebrews. But according to the Greeks, Phison is the Ganges, which flows toward India. Geon, however, is the Nile, which encircles the land of Egypt or Ethiopia. Mesopotamia is so called because the Tigris and Euphrates enclose it, since it is situated between these two rivers; its very name and common opinion have expressed this even among people far away.

But just as Wisdom of God is called a fountain—for according to the Gospel it is a fountain, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37), and according to the prophet it is a fountain, saying: “Come, eat of my breads, and drink the wine which I have mixed for you” (Prov. 9:5)—so, as Wisdom is a fountain of life and a fountain of spiritual grace, it is also the fountain of the other virtues which direct us toward the course of eternal life.

Therefore this fountain proceeds from the cultivated soul, not from the uncultivated one, to water Paradise—that is, certain groves of diverse virtues—of which there are four heads into which this Wisdom is divided. What are these four heads of virtues except one of prudence, another of temperance, a third of fortitude, and a fourth of justice (Plato, *Republic*, IV)? The wise persons of this world also took these from us and transferred them into the writings of their books. Therefore, just as Wisdom is a fountain, so these four rivers are certain streams of virtues flowing from that fountain.

15. Phison, then, is prudence, and therefore it has good gold, a shining carbuncle, and a green stone. For we frequently understand gold to signify prudent discoveries. Hence the Lord also says through the Prophet: “I gave her gold and silver” (Hos. 2:8). And David says concerning prudent persons: “If you sleep among the lots, the wings of the dove are silvered, and the back of her body is in the appearance of gold” (Ps. 67:14), because one who clings to the Old and New Testament may proceed, in the very secrets of God’s Wisdom, with the abundance of exposition.

Therefore he calls this good gold—

[Note: [Col. 0281D] Thus the Erasmus edition with the following reading and a few manuscripts. But the American edition and eight manuscripts: “gold, he says, not coined gold”; the Reims manuscript: “… not coined”; Dijon: “beautiful, coined gold.”]

—not that coined gold which is corruptible and earthly. It also has, he says, a shining carbuncle, in which a certain little fire of our soul lives. It has also a green stone, which by the appearance of its color seems to display something verdant and vital. For living shrubs are green, whereas whatever dies withers; the earth is green while it flowers, and seeds are green while they shoot forth.

And this river Phison is rightly placed first. According to the Hebrews it is called Phison—

[Note: [Col. 0281D] Several manuscripts: “Phison is placed first, which … is called Pheouson.” A little later the Roman edition: “it encircles, however, almost the whole of India.” All the old editions read as in the text. The manuscripts also agree, except two, which read “it flows through Lycia.”]

—that is, “change of mouth,” because it does not encircle one nation only, but also flows through Lydia. For prudence, which benefits many, is not narrow but rich in usefulness. Thus it is first, so that if anyone has gone out from Paradise, a river of prudence, as it were, may receive him, lest he quickly wither; but through it he may easily return to Paradise.

This river is frequented by many people and is reported to possess very great beauty and fertility. Therefore prudence is understood in the figure of this river, since it has brought forth very many fruits in the Lord’s advent. And it flows at the ends of the earth because through Wisdom all human beings have been redeemed. Hence it is said: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5).

16. The second river is Geon, beside which the law was given to the Israelites when they were living in Egypt, that they might depart from Egypt and, with loins girded, eat the lamb—an emblem of temperance. For the Lord’s Passover ought to be celebrated by those who are chaste and sanctified. Therefore the observance of the law was first established beside this river, because its name signifies a certain opening of the earth.

Just as an opening swallows up the earth and whatever refuse or leaves are in it, so chastity customarily abolishes all passions of the body.

[Note: [Col. 0281D] Thus the manuscripts of better quality. In the others, as also in the editions, there is great variation which does not affect the sense, since “earth” is used for “the earth,” “filth” for “leaves,” “by an opening” for “an opening,” and certain other such forms occur.]

The establishment of observance is rightly first there, because carnal sin is swallowed up through the law. Geon, in which is the figure of chastity, is therefore aptly said to encircle Ethiopian land, so that it may wash the abject body and quench the burning of most vile flesh. For “Ethiopia” in Latin interpretation signifies what is abject and vile. And what is more abject than our body? What is so like Ethiopia, since it too is blackened by certain darknesses of sins?

17. The third river is Tigris, which goes toward the Assyrians, to whom transgressing Israel was led captive. This river is said to be swifter than all others. The Assyrians inhabit it—that is, “those directing,” for this is what the interpretation signifies. Therefore, whoever by strength of soul has taken captive the transgressing vices of the body, directing himself to things above, is judged similar to this river. Thus fortitude too flows from the fountain that is in Paradise. Fortitude, in a kind of rapid course, pierces through every opposing thing and is not held fast by the obstacles of any impediments in its course.

18. The fourth river is Euphrates, which in Latin is called fruitfulness and abundance of fruits, bearing a certain mark of justice, which feeds every soul. For no virtue seems to have more abundant fruits than equity and justice, which benefits others more than itself and, neglecting its own advantages, sets common benefits before them.

Many think that Euphrates is named ἀπὸ τοῦ εὐφραίνεσθαι, that is, from rejoicing, because humankind rejoices in nothing more than justice and equity. We have received the reason why the regions through which the other rivers pass are described, whereas those through which Euphrates passes are not described, as follows: its water is said to be life-giving, nurturing and increasing. Hence learned Hebrews and Assyrians called it Auxen, “Increase.”

[Note: [Col. 0282D] Thus all manuscripts and the old editions, with strong agreement. But the Roman edition reads: “Hence Perath … they called it … which is αὕξειν in Greek,” attempting to restore the Hebrew word, which seems to have been omitted here through scribal carelessness.]

The water of the other rivers, on the other hand, is said to be contrary in character. Then, because where prudence is, there is also malice; where fortitude is, there is also anger; where temperance is, there is often intemperance or other vices; but where justice is, there is harmony of the other virtues—therefore justice is not known from the places through which it flows, that is, not from a part. For justice is not a part, but is, as it were, the mother of all.

Therefore in these four rivers are expressed the four principal virtues, which, as it were, encompassed the ages of this world.

19. The first age, then, from the beginning of the world to the flood, was that of prudence. In this age are numbered the righteous Abel, whom God called righteous (Matt. 23:35); and Enos—that is, the human being made in the image of God—who hoped to invoke the name of the Lord God; and Enoch, whose name in Latin means “God’s grace,” who was caught up to heaven; and Noah, who likewise was righteous and a certain directing toward rest.

20. The second age is that of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the remaining number of patriarchs, in whom a certain chaste and pure temperance of religion shone forth. For Isaac, the spotless son of Abraham, was given by promise, displaying not so much a bodily birth as the gift of divine favor; in him the figure of the truly spotless one came beforehand, as the Apostle teaches when he says: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as though of many, but as of one: ‘and to your seed,’ who is Christ” (Gal. 3:16).

[Col. 0283A]

21. The third age is in the law of Moses and the other prophets. For time would fail me in recounting Gideon, Barak, Samson, David, Solomon, and Samuel, and the other prophets—Hananiah, Azariah, Mishael, and Daniel, Elijah and Elisha—who through faith conquered kingdoms, wrought righteousness, received promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped

[Note: [Col. 0283D] Several manuscripts and some Parisian copies: “escaped.”]

the edge of the sword, were made strong from weakness, became mighty in battle, and captured the camps of foreigners (Heb. 11:32 and following). Therefore it is not without reason that in these there is a figure of fortitude. For they were sawn asunder, as you have below; they were tempted; they died by slaughter of the sword. They wandered about in goatskins, needy, afflicted, and tormented—persons of whose merits the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and holes of the earth (ibid. 11:37–38). Therefore we rightly place in these the figure of fortitude.

22. But according to the Gospel it is rightly an image of righteousness, because it is the power for salvation to everyone who believes. Finally, the Lord himself says: “Allow it for the present; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15). [Note: Eight manuscripts read, “Allow us to fulfill,” etc.; others, as does the edition, “Allow it for the present; for thus,” etc.] Righteousness is indeed the fruitful mother of the other virtues. Wherever any one of the virtues we have mentioned is the principal virtue, the rest too are present, because the virtues are interconnected and joined together. Thus Abel was righteous; Abraham most strong and patient; and the prophets most prudent. Moses, moreover, “instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians,” judged the reproach of Christ to be greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt. And who was wiser than Daniel? Solomon too asked for wisdom and obtained it.

Therefore it has been said concerning the four rivers of virtues, whose draught is beneficial. And because Pishon is said to possess the good gold of the land, carbuncle, and the green stone, let us consider what this too may mean.

23. Enos seems to us like good gold, since he wisely desired to know the name of God. Enoch, however, who was translated and did not see death, is a kind of carbuncle, a fragrant stone, which holy Enoch offered to God by his works, breathing forth a certain grace through his deeds and character. Noah, moreover, displayed the life-giving color of a green stone (*prasinus*). For in the time of the flood he alone was preserved in that ark, as a life-giving seed for the future restoration. Therefore paradise, irrigated by many rivers, is rightly “toward the East,” not “opposite the East”: that is, according to that East whose name is “the Rising” (*Oriens*), namely according to Christ, who poured forth a radiance of eternal light, and who is in Eden, that is, in delight.

## CHAPTER IV

A man was not made in paradise but placed there; whereas woman was made in it, and through her he was deceived. Then, what does it mean to “work” and “guard”?

24. “And God took the man whom he had made and placed him in paradise, to work it and to guard it.” You see that he who already existed is taken. Now he was in the land of his formation. Therefore the power of God took him up, inspiring advances and increases in virtue; finally, it placed him in paradise, so that you may know that he who was taken up was, as it were, breathed upon by divine power.

At this point observe this: the man was made outside paradise, and the woman within paradise, so that you may recognize that each person acquires grace for himself not by nobility of place or lineage, but by virtue. Thus the man made outside paradise—that is, in the lower place—is found the better; while she who was made in the better place, that is, in paradise, is found inferior. For the woman was deceived first, and she herself deceived the man. Hence the apostle Peter recalls that holy women, subject to the stronger vessel, obeyed their husbands as lords (1 Pet. 3:1). And Paul says: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, fell into transgression” (1 Tim. 2:14).

From this we must observe that no one ought readily to presume upon himself. For behold: she who was made as a help for the man needs the protection of man, because the man is the head of the woman; while he who thought that he would have the help of his wife fell through his wife. Therefore no one ought readily to entrust himself to another unless he has tested that person’s virtue; nor should one who thinks himself appointed as a help arrogate anything to himself. Rather, if he finds stronger the one to whom he thought himself a protection, let him borrow grace from that person. So too the apostle Peter commands men to render honor to women, saying: “Husbands likewise, dwelling with them according to knowledge, rendering honor to the woman as to the weaker vessel, as also to a co-heir of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered” (1 Pet. 3:7).

25. Therefore the man was placed in paradise, and the woman was made in paradise. Yet even then, before the woman was deceived by the serpent, she possessed the man’s grace, since she was taken from the man—although this is a great mystery, as the Apostle said (Eph. 5:32). For this reason she derived from him the cause of life.

Accordingly, Scripture said only of the man that he was placed in paradise “to work and to guard.” To work and to guard are not the same thing. In work there is a certain progress of virtue; in guarding there is discerned a certain completion of work, because it guards what has, as it were, been completed. These two things are required of a human being: both to seek new things by works and to guard what has been acquired. This is the general sense.

Philo, however, because he did not apprehend spiritual things with a Jewish disposition, confined himself to moral matters [Note: The manuscripts of Clairvaux read: “confined himself within mortal things”], saying that these two things are sought: work in the field and guarding of the house. And although paradise, he says, had no need of agricultural labors, nevertheless, because the first man was to be the law for posterity, he therefore undertook even in paradise a lawful image of labor [Note: The Roman edition reads: “undertook a specimen of labor”], in order to bind us to work and to the guarding of our due duty and the office of hereditary succession.

These two things, therefore, are demanded of you, whether morally or spiritually. The prophetic psalm also teaches you this, for it is written: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it have watched in vain” (Ps. 126:1). You see that those labor who are engaged in the progress of work and building; but the others watch, who have already undertaken the guardianship of completed work. Hence the Lord also says to the Apostles, as though already more perfected: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41). [Note: The manuscripts of Reims and Clairvaux read, “to certain Apostles already more perfected,” a reading that appears genuine.] He teaches that the gift of perfected nature and the grace of full virtue must be preserved, and that no one, however more perfect, ought to be secure concerning himself unless he watches. [Note: Five manuscripts read: “teaching through the gift of upright nature,” etc.]

## CHAPTER V

The command not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is examined, and the difficulties arising concerning it are resolved.

[Col. 0285B]

26. “And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying: ‘From every tree that is in paradise for food, you shall eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat. But on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death’” (Gen. 2:16–17).

Why, where he commanded that one should eat from every tree, he said in the singular, “You shall eat,” but where he spoke of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, he said in the plural, “You shall not eat,” is not an idle question. Yet, if you attend carefully, it can be resolved by the authority of Scripture. For what is good is what must be done; and what is good and must be done is harmonious and coherent. But what is disgraceful is discordant, disordered, and divided. Therefore the Lord, always directing toward unity, commanded according to unity. Indeed, he effects unity, he who “made both one.” And not only both, but all also one. For he commanded us all to be one body and one spirit. In all things he is the firstborn; and, being in unity with the Father, he is always most closely joined to the Father, because “the Word was with God.” Thus he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), in order to show that he possesses unity of majesty and divinity with the Father. But he also commanded us to be one, and through the grace of adoption poured into us a likeness of his own nature and unity, saying: “Father, as I and you are one, so may these also be one in us” (John 17:22).

Therefore, where he commands what is good, he commands as though addressing one person, saying, “You shall eat.” For unity cannot transgress. But where he says that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is not to be tasted, he speaks as though to many persons: “You shall not eat.” For what is prohibitory is commanded, as it were, to a plurality.

I, however, think otherwise, and find in God’s very utterance already what was to happen. He commanded Adam alone to taste of every tree, knowing that he would observe the command; but he says, not in the singular but in the plural, that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is not to be tasted. For he knew that the woman would transgress, and therefore through the plurality showed that they would not observe it, because a divided decision belongs to several persons.

27. So far as the rendering of the Seventy men is concerned, the difficulty that disturbed us has been resolved. But because Symmachus rendered both expressions in the singular, we understand this to follow from the fact that in the Law also, when God addresses the people, he speaks in the singular, as you have: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4); and, “You shall love the Lord your God” (ibid., 6).

Nor does Symmachus’s translation prejudice me, he who could not perceive the unity of the Father and the Son, though both Aquila and he himself have at times confessed it in their wording. Nor should anyone think that the fact that God addresses in the singular a people that would transgress his commands is contrary to our preceding argument, because the Jewish people violated even precepts given in the singular. For the Law is spiritual; and therefore, in one way in speech and in another in predestination, God addressed the people by his divine oracle. Thus he says: “You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk” (Exod. 34:26). [Note: So the older manuscripts read from the Septuagint, in which occurs οὐκ ἑψήσεις ἄρνα, “you shall not boil a lamb.” Others, and the old edition, have “you shall not boil a sheep.” The Vulgate has “… a kid.”]

28. The sequence of heavenly commands from here would seem easy, were it not that very many raise questions which must be answered by us, lest they lead astray simple minds by malicious interpretation. [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read, “The sequence from here would more easily,” etc.] For many, whose authority is Apelles—as you have in the thirty-eighth volume of his work—propose these questions:

How does the tree of life appear to accomplish more toward life than the breathing of God? Next, if God did not make man perfect, while each person acquires the perfection of virtue for himself through his own effort, does it not seem that a human being gains more for himself than God bestowed upon him? Thirdly, they object: if man had not tasted death, he certainly could not know what he had not tasted. Therefore, if he had not tasted it, he did not know it; and if he did not know it, he could not fear it. In vain, then, did God set before men death as a terror which they did not fear.

29. Let us therefore learn that God brought forth the tree of life in the same place where he also brought forth the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For you have that he brought forth the tree of life “in the midst of paradise,” ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ παραδείσου. [Note: All manuscripts exhibit Greek characters so corrupt that they cannot be read. Some write in Latin, from which *amaenos* seems to be understood in place of *Apaenos*. The Amiens edition has ἐν μεσόυ ρόενυς. In so great a corruption, it seems preferable not to depart from the printed editions.] Among us, ἐν μέσῳ means that he brought it forth “in the midst.” Therefore, in the midst of paradise there was both life and the cause of death. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “and understand what the cause of death is,” etc.]

Understand that man did not make life, but could find it either by working or by guarding God’s commands. Now life, as the Apostle says, “was hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3). Therefore man was either in the shadow of life because of the life to come—for this life which is now ours on earth is a shadow—or he was in a certain pledge of life because he possessed the breathing of God. [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read: “because of the future image.”] He therefore possessed a pledge of immortality; but, being placed in the shadow of life, he could not see or apprehend, by some ordinary touch and sight, the life hidden with Christ in God.

And though he was not yet a sinner, neither was he of incorrupt and inviolable nature, as one who afterward fell through sin, though not yet a sinner. Thus he was in the shadow of life; but those who are sinners are in the shadow of death. For the people of sinners, as Isaiah teaches (Isa. 9:2), sat in the shadow of death; for them a light arose through God’s grace, not through the merit of their own virtue.

Therefore there is no difference between the breathing of God and the food of the tree of life. Nor can anyone say that man can acquire more for himself than was bestowed upon him by divine generosity. Would that we could retain what we have received. Our labor, indeed, advances only so far as to recover what has been granted. The third point proposed—that one who had not tasted death could not fear death—readily finds its resolution from the common practice of nature. For it is implanted in the nature of all living creatures that they fear as harmful even things which they have not yet experienced as harmful to themselves. Whence comes the terror of a hawk to doves at their very birth? [Note: The Vatican and St. Michael manuscripts, in their first hand, read: “they are frightened on seeing a hawk.” Some others read: “they receive terror by the sight,” or, “on seeing.” In almost all the rest there is nothing sound.] Whence are wolves terrible to sheep, and kites to chicks? If, then, among irrational animals there is a natural fear of animals of an opposing kind, so that even irrational creatures receive an awareness of fleeing death, how much more ought there to have been in the first man, who was surely most full of reason, a natural apprehension that death must be avoided.

## CHAPTER VI

He resolves several further doubts raised concerning the command given to Adam and Eve’s transgression.

30. Again they raise other questions in this manner: It is not always evil not to obey a command (XI, question 1, chapter *Non semper*). For if the command is good, obedience is honorable; but if the command is wicked, disobedience is useful. Therefore it is not always evil not to obey a command; rather, it is wicked not to obey a good command.

But the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is good in its operation, since God knows both good and evil. Thus he says: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” (Gen. 3:22). [Note: The Roman edition reads: “as one of us, to know good and evil.”] [Note: The Roman edition reads: “But the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is good.”] Therefore, if it is good to possess knowledge of good and evil, and if this knowledge is good because God also has it, then he who forbids it to human beings seems not to forbid it rightly. This is what they propose.

But if they understood what it is “to know,” what force this word has—if they understood it as they ought: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19)—he certainly knows those who, out of many, have become one, in whom he dwells and among whom he walks. To know, certainly, does not consist merely in superficial knowledge, but in performing the things that ought to be done. Now man ought to have obeyed the command; but by not obeying, he transgressed. Therefore he who did not obey erred, because transgression is sin.

But even if they wish to diminish the force of “knowledge,” so as to suppose that a superficial knowledge of good and evil was forbidden, even in that case the fault of transgression lies in failure to obey the command; for the Lord God judged even a cursory knowledge of good and evil to be restrained.

31. Another question: He who does not know good and evil differs in no respect from a child. But children bear no guilt before a just judge. And the just maker of the world would never have called a child to account for not knowing good and evil, because a child is without any crime of transgression or fault.

But since we have said above that there is a twofold understanding of the knowledge of good and evil, if we take it as superficial knowledge, then it is surely false that one who has not known good and evil differs in no respect from a child. But if it is false that he differs in no respect from a child, then Adam was not a child. If he was not a child, sin is certainly imputed to him as to one who was not a child. If sin is imputed to him, punishment follows sin, because the person who did not take care to avoid sin is found worthy of punishment. [Note: The manuscripts and old edition read: “who could not avoid sin.”]

It may also be that even one who does not possess knowledge of good and evil (Isa. 7:16) is not a child, because before the child knew good and evil, he did not believe evil. And again you have: “Before the child knows how to call father and mother, he shall receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria” (Isa. 8:4). Therefore one who does good is perfect, even if he has not acquired knowledge of good and evil, just as many, before they know the Law, are a law to themselves.

The Apostle, before the Law said, “You shall not covet” (Rom. 2:14), did not know that coveting was evil. Thus he himself says: “I did not know sin except through the Law; for I did not know coveting unless the Law said: ‘You shall not covet’” (Rom. 7:7). In this respect even a child may be perfect by the law of nature before he knows that coveting is a crime or commits the crime of coveting.

Therefore, according to superficial knowledge, God did not will that man should know what evil is, lest, as though imperfect, he might be unable to avoid it. [Note: The Michaelinus, Bigotianus, Gemmeticensis, Theodoricus, and Volutianus manuscripts read, “God willed.” The Laon manuscript and old edition read, “God knows.” Other manuscripts and the Roman edition read more fittingly, “God did not will.”] But by not obeying the command, we incur guilt; therefore we acknowledge guilt. Yet if we mean the deep and profound knowledge of good and evil, which indeed makes one perfect, one who could not attain to deep and profound knowledge is not immediately, and rightly, condemned as though not a child.

32. Again they sow questions: “He who does not know good and evil,” they say, “does not even know that failing to keep the command is evil, nor does he know that obedience to the command is good. And therefore, because he did not know, he who failed to obey was worthy of pardon, they say, not condemnation.”

This question has its resolution in the points we mentioned before. For man could consider, from the things God had previously bestowed upon him—that he had received the breathing of God, that he had been placed in the paradise of delight—that the highest obedience was due to his maker. Therefore, even if he did not know the force of good and evil, nevertheless, because the author of such great gifts had said that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was not to be tasted, he ought to have kept faith with the one who gave the command. For skill was not required from him, but faith. He understood, certainly, that God excelled all things; and for that reason he ought to have considered the person who commanded. Even if he did not understand the force and character of what was commanded, he nevertheless knew that reverence was due to the commander. He had this apprehension by nature, even if he did not have discernment of good and evil.

Thus the woman too said to the serpent: “We shall eat from every tree of paradise; but concerning the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of paradise, God said: ‘You shall not eat from it’” (Gen. 3:3). She therefore knew so well that the command must be obeyed that she said, “We shall eat from every fruit,” as the Lord had commanded; but concerning the tree in the midst of paradise, she says that God commanded that it not be tasted, lest they die by death. Therefore, because she knew that obedience was due to the command, she surely knew that it was evil to transgress, and consequently she is justly condemned for having transgressed. [Note: Thus the manuscripts of St. Remigius and St. Theodoric read. But the old edition reads: “Therefore she knew that the command must be respected.” The Gemmeticensis, Theodoricus, Divionensis, and Laon manuscripts read: “Therefore she knew that respect must be given to the command.” The Michaelinus reads: “that the command must not be abandoned.” Finally, the Roman edition reads: “Therefore, he who knew that deference was not to be given to the command.”]

33. Consider another point. If taking from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was so operative that good and evil were recognized—which Scripture appears to show when it says, “When both had eaten, their eyes were opened, and they knew that they were naked” (Gen. 3:6–7)—that is, the eyes of their heart were opened, and they knew that it was shameful to live naked; then without doubt, when the woman tasted from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, she sinned and knew that she had sinned.

Therefore, having known that she had sinned, she ought not to have invited the man into partnership in sin. But by enticing the man and giving him what she herself had tasted, she did not avoid sin but repeated it. For, if you truly consider the matter rationally, she ought not to have drawn the man whom she loved into partnership in punishment, but rather ought to have recalled him, though ignorant, from what she herself had recognized to be sin. Yet this woman seems to have feared, knowing that after her fault she could not remain in paradise, lest she alone be cast out of paradise. Thus after the fault they both hid themselves. Therefore, recognizing that she was to be excluded, she did not wish to be deprived of the companionship of the husband whom she loved.

34. Consider this again: knowledge of evil is not itself evil; rather, evil arises when an act carries out wickedness. For one who knows evil does not immediately do what is evil; but one does it who performs what he knows to be evil. The incentive to doing what is evil is usually either anger or desire. Nor is it immediately necessary that someone possessing knowledge of evil should do what he knows to be wicked, unless he is overcome by either anger or desire. Hence, as we have said, the incentives to sinning are anger, desire, or often fear, though desire arises from fear when each person wishes to avoid what he fears. Therefore we rightly set anger and desire as the incentives to the two remaining vices. [Note: We would gladly read “the two remaining ones,” unless the manuscripts and editions objected.]

Let us consider, then, whether Eve was incited to vice by these impulses. But she was neither angry with her husband nor overcome by desire; she errs only in the second instance, in giving her husband to eat what she herself had already tasted. At first, desire had been the author of her error, when she herself ate, and it was the cause of the subsequent sin. For she could not desire what she had already tasted; and by tasting she had acquired knowledge of evil. Therefore she ought not to have transferred to the man the evil which she had recognized, nor made her own husband a transgressor of the divine command. Thus she sinned knowingly and deliberately, and knowingly drew the man into her own error.

Otherwise the statement concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil will be found false, if, even after she ate from that tree, she could not possess knowledge of evil. [Note: Two manuscripts read: “could not possess knowledge of good and evil.”] But if the statement is true, she could certainly not have had desire as her motive—although many think she should be excused in this way: that, loving her husband, she feared to be separated from him, and they allege this as a motive of desire, namely that she wished to be with her husband.

## CHAPTER VII

It is asked whether death came upon man from God, from the tree, or from some other source; and the objection is resolved by a manifold answer.

35. Again another question arises: whence did death come to Adam—from the nature of that tree, or rather from God? If we ascribe it to the nature of the tree, the fruit of this tree appears to surpass the breathing of God in power to give life, since the fruit of this tree drew to death the person whom God’s breathing had made alive. Or, if we declare God to be the maker of death, they say that we accuse him on a double count: either that he was so harsh that he did not wish to forgive when he could, or, if he could not forgive, that he appears weak.

Let us see, then, how this is to be resolved. Unless I am mistaken, disobedience was the cause of death; and therefore man himself was the cause of his own death, not having God as the author of his death. For if a physician prescribes to a sick person what he ought to avoid, and that person thinks that he need not abstain from what has been forbidden, the physician is not the cause of his death; rather, the sick person himself is responsible for his own death. Thus God, like a good physician, forbade Adam to taste what would harm him.

36. Consider again: it is better to know what is good than not to know it; and for one who knows what is good, it is fitting to know what is evil, so that he may know how to avoid what is evil and, being prudent, undertake the precaution of guarding himself. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “so that he may know to avoid what is wrong and, being prudent, may command protection.”] Yet it is not enough merely to know what is evil, lest, when you know evil, you begin to be deprived of knowledge of good. It is more excellent, therefore, that we know both, so that, because we know good, we flee what is evil, and, from our recognition of evil, prefer the grace of good.

But you ought to know both in such a way that you know deeply and carry out what you know, and that the act corresponds to the knowledge. Otherwise Scripture indicates as more tolerable the person who knows neither, than the person who has superficially known both (Luke 12:47). For it is burdensome to know what you either cannot carry out or cannot avoid; [Note: Thus the manuscripts and old editions read with great agreement; but the Roman edition has: “what you do not wish, and cannot, either to carry out or avoid.”] it is burdensome to know without the use and work of profound knowledge. Thus it damages a physician’s reputation to know what benefits and what harms a sick person unless he uses that knowledge as he ought. Consequently, knowledge is not good unless you use it as you ought.

37. Likewise consider: the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was not brought forth in the midst of paradise without purpose. And if it had been brought forth for just any human being, the prohibition would have been superfluous. But it was neither made without purpose nor made for anyone other than the human being who received the command, so that he might use it, not by itself, but together with the other things.

For if you examine many matters, you will find very many—indeed plainly innumerable—which can harm the person who does not know how to use them. You will not find even riches profitable if a rich person, possessing means for generosity, refuses food to the poor, excludes from assistance the needy person deprived of support, and extorts what belongs to others because he prevails by power. Beauty itself and a more pleasing bodily form more often draw a person into vice than does ugliness. [Note: The Roman codex reads: “draws into the vice of ugliness.”] Does anyone, then, desire to have uglier rather than more beautiful children, or wish his children to be poor rather than rich? There are many such things which must not be attributed to the imprudence of the giver, but to the error of the person who uses them badly. Therefore the user, rather than the giver, must be accused.

## CHAPTER VIII

Questions concerning God’s foreknowledge of Adam’s transgression, and concerning the divinely impressed awareness of good and evil in human minds, are resolved.

38. Again the question arises: Did God know that Adam would transgress his commands, or did he not know? If he did not know, this is no assertion of divine power. But if he knew, and nevertheless knowingly gave commands that were to be disregarded, it is not for God to command anything superfluously. Yet he gave to that first-formed Adam a superfluous command which he knew he would not observe; but God does nothing superfluously. Therefore Scripture is not from God.

This is the objection made by those who do not accept the Old Testament and who introduce these questions. But they must be defeated by their own judgment and opinion. Since they do not reject faith in the New Testament, they must be refuted by its example so that they may believe the Old, because, since the divine commands and deeds agree with one another, it is clear that both Testaments must be believed to have one author. Let them therefore learn that a command prescribed even to someone who would transgress is neither superfluous nor unjust.

For the Lord Jesus himself chose Judas, whom he knew would be a traitor. If they suppose that he was chosen through imprudence, they detract from divine power. But they cannot suppose this, since Scripture says: “Jesus knew who would betray him” (John 6:65). Therefore let these opponents of the Old Testament be silent.

39. But because, should even pagans raise this objection, a response seems necessary for those who do not accept the example and demand a rational explanation, let them too receive the reason why the Son of God either gave a command to one who would transgress or chose one who would betray him. The Lord Jesus had come to save all sinners; he had to demonstrate his will even toward the ungodly. Therefore he ought not to have passed over even the future traitor, so that all might observe that, even in the choice of his betrayer, he displayed the mark of his purpose to save all.

Neither Adam, because he received a command, nor Judas, because he was chosen, was injured in this. For God imposed on neither the necessity either of transgression in the former or of betrayal in the latter, since each could have abstained from sin had he kept what he received. Thus he did not know that all Jews would believe, and nevertheless said: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). Therefore the fault does not lie in the one commanding, but the sin lies in the transgressor. And God showed to all, as far as lay with him, that he willed to deliver all.

Nor do I say that he did not know the transgression would occur; on the contrary, I affirm that he knew it. But for that reason he ought not to have drawn upon himself the odium of the perishing traitor, so that the fall of each might be attributed to God. Now, however, each is reproved and convicted, because the one received a command lest he fall, while the other was even admitted to the office of apostleship, so that by God’s benefit he might be recalled from the inclination toward betrayal; and, at the same time, so that, while others are refuted, it might benefit all.

For sin would not exist if there had been no prohibition. But if sin did not exist, perhaps not only wickedness but virtue also would not exist; for unless there had been some seeds of wickedness, virtue could neither subsist nor stand out. For what is sin except transgression of the divine law and disobedience to heavenly commands? We do not judge heavenly commands by the ears of the body; but because the Word of God existed, certain notions of good and evil sprang up in us, while we naturally understand that what is evil must be avoided and naturally understand that what is good is commanded for us.

In this, therefore, we seem to hear the Lord’s voice: that it forbids some things and commands others. Accordingly, if anyone does not obey those things which we believe were once commanded by God, that person is judged liable to punishment. Yet we do not read God’s command as though it were written in ink on tablets of stone, but we hold it impressed on our hearts by the Spirit of the living God. Therefore our very moral awareness makes a law for itself. For if the Gentiles, who do not have the Law, naturally do the things of the Law, such persons, not having the Law, are a law to themselves, showing the work of the Law written in their hearts. Human moral awareness, therefore, is to itself as a law of God.

40. Again from this they raise another question: in order to accuse, in turn, the command which we have said consists in human moral awareness, they accuse this moral awareness itself, impressed upon us by God, as though it were a prescription of divine law. “Did he who created man know,” they say, “that man would sin and impress these notions of good and evil upon him, or did he not know? If you say that he did not know, you hold a view unworthy of God’s majesty. But if you say that God, knowing that man would sin, nevertheless impressed upon him common notions of good and evil, so that, because evil was intermixed, he could not preserve perpetual life, then, just as in the former case you would represent him as not foreknowing what was to come, so in this you would represent him as not good.”

From this they argue that the creature, man, was not made by God. For as we showed above that they say there is no command of God, so here too they say: “Therefore the creature, man, is not from God, because God did not make evil. Yet man received an awareness of evil when he was commanded to abstain from evils.” By this argument they endeavor to establish one God as good and another as the maker of man.

They must immediately be answered according to their own opinion. For if they do not wish man to have been made by God because man is a sinner—and they recoil from this lest a good God appear to have made a sinner, because they do not consider good one who made a sinner—let them say whether they believe that the maker of man was made by God. For if that maker of man, as they say, was made by God, how did a good God make a maker of evil? Surely he is not good, since one who makes a sinner is not good. They must beware lest it be more serious to have made the maker of a sinner. For the good God ought to have prevented the birth of one who would introduce the substance of sin.

But if they say that the maker of evil was not born, we must ask whether the good God could in some way restrain evil as it began, or could not. If he could not, he is weak; if he could and did not do so, he is not good. Therefore, if these things do not accord with them, nor do the opinions of the heretics accord with themselves, let us inquire whether perhaps there was a rational cause why God permitted the wickedness of that maker—whether begotten or unbegotten—to enter this world, though he could restrain it.

41. Therefore, while maintaining that God is one and the same—both good and maker—we must establish, if we can, what accords with the grace of both;[Note: Rom. edition: “what indeed accords with grace.” Other editions, better with the manuscripts: “what accords with both,” that is, with the grace of the good God and of the Maker.] nor should we shrink from the odium of the accusation [Col. 0294A] made by those who say: “How can God be good, who not only suffered evil to enter into this world, but even allowed it to reach such great disorder?”

Yet this accusation would have force if evil infected the power of the soul and the inmost secrets of the mind in such a way that it could by no means be removed, and if the poison of incurable wounds settled in our mind and soul. There would indeed be stronger ground for this complaint: that, though God can do all things, He nevertheless allowed man to perish. But since God, in His mercy toward our error, has kept remedies for its rejection and has not removed the possibility of abolishing every contagion, how is it unreasonable or unjust if He allowed our material nature to be tested by a certain trembling born of human frailty, so that afterward grace might return with greater increase through [Col. 0294B] repentance for sins into the human disposition; and so that, conscious of his own weakness—because he had so easily trembled by departing from the course of the divine commands—man might fear to lose the heavenly commandments as the anchor of a storm-tossed soul, attributing more to the divine mercy because he has recovered what he lost, and claiming for himself some share of grace because he returns?

## CHAPTER IX

Whether it was fitting that God should give man a command concerning food; and why, in announcing the penalty, He did not say, “You shall die,” but, “You shall die by death.”

42. Let us now consider what that reason is: why, when God gave man a command, laying down rules for that wonderful and blessed life lest, by acting contrary to them, [Col. 0294C] he should die by death, He thought fit to command him concerning eating and not eating. There are those who think that this command in no way befits the Creator of heaven, earth, and all things; and is in no way worthy of the inhabitants of Paradise, because that life is like the life of angels. Accordingly, we may judge that this earthly and perishable food was not intended for eating, because those who neither drink nor eat will be like the angels in heaven.

Therefore, since in food there is neither reward—for food does not commend us to God—nor great danger, since it is not what enters the mouth that defiles a human being, [Note: Manuscripts Th., Div., Big., and Gem.: “makes common” (*communicat*), not badly; for in sacred writings “common” has the same sense as polluted or defiled. Three or four words later, manuscripts Big., Gem., Mich.: “it appears”; Rem. and Th.: “the command undoubtedly appears [to have been given] by so great an author”; S. Theod.: “unworthy of so great an author.” Gill. and Roman editions: “a command by so great an author”; Div. and Laud., with editions Am. and Era.: “undoubtedly not to have been a command by so great an author.”] but what comes out of the mouth—there appears, without doubt, not to have been a command given by so great an Author, unless you refer this food to that prophetic saying in which the Lord promises His saints, as a great reward: “Behold, those who [Col. 0294D] serve me shall eat, but you shall hunger” (Isa. 65:13).

For this is the food in which eternal life is defined; whoever is deprived of it shall die by death. Since the living and heavenly bread is the Lord Himself, who gives life to this world, He Himself says: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have eternal life” (John 6:54). Therefore there was some bread of which He had prescribed that the inhabitants of Paradise should eat. What bread was it? Hear whom He calls it: “Man ate,” he says, [Col. 0295A] “the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25). For bread is good if you do the will of God. Do you wish to know how good this bread is? The Son Himself eats this bread, concerning which He says: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John 4:34).

43. Let us again consider why the Lord God said to Adam, “You shall die by death”; and what difference there is between saying, “You shall die,” and adding, “You shall die by death.” For we must show that nothing is superfluous in God’s command. This, then, is my judgment.

Since death and life are contrary to one another, in ordinary speech we say that one lives from life and dies from death. But if you wish to double either expression, since life produces life, one says, “life lives,” as you find in the Law. And since death produces death, one says, “he shall die by death.” This doubling is not superfluous. For there is life unto death, and death unto life, because one may die while living, and live while dying. Thus there are four distinctions: to live by life, to die by death, [Note: All manuscripts: “to live by death, to die by life.” By contrast, the editions read: “to live unto death, to die unto life.”] to live by death, and to die by life.

Since these things stand thus, we must set aside the prejudice arising from ordinary usage. For usage has it that one is commonly said to live, whether one [Note: Manuscripts S. Th.: “whether he who dies to death, or he who…” Thus, from those four, etc. Rem.: “whether he who dies by death, or he who lives by life.” Thus, etc. Neither contains “whether he who lives by life” and “whether he who lives by death.”] lives by life or lives by death; and one is commonly said to die, whether one dies by death or dies by life. Thus it signifies two of those four: it says that one who is living lives, without distinguishing better from worse; and it says that one who is dying dies, without seeming to distinguish between a bad and a good death. For it denotes an undiscriminating kind of life, such as that of irrational creatures [Col. 0295C] or even of little children; and likewise an undiscriminating death.

44. Setting aside, then, common usage, let us consider what it is to live by life, to die by death, to live unto death, and to die unto life. For I think, according to the Scriptures, that to live by life signifies that wonderful and blessed life, and seems to indicate this practice of living and the gift of breathing as joined, as it were, with the grace of blessed life and mingled with it by a certain participation. This is to live by life: to live by virtue, to exercise the acts of blessed life in the life of this body.

Conversely, what else is it to die by death than, together with the death of the body, to signify the disfigurement of one who is dying—one whose flesh is deprived of the common gift of life, and whose soul cannot enjoy [Col. 0295D] eternal life? There is also one who dies unto life: one who lives in body but dies in his conduct. Such are those of whom the Prophet says: “They go down alive into hell” (Ps. 54:16). And such is she of whom the Apostle says: “Though living, she is dead” (1 Tim. 5:6).

There remains the fourth case: there are those who even live by death, such as the holy martyrs, [Col. 0296A] who certainly die in order that they may live. The flesh dies, [Note: Manuscript Rem.: “They die in the flesh, but live by the grace of the dead.”] but by the grace of the dead they live. Therefore, far be it from us to live as participants in death; rather, let us die as participants in life. For the holy person does not wish to be a participant even in this life, saying: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ, for that is far better” (Phil. 1:23). And another says: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:5). He grieves, certainly, because, while he hopes for fellowship in eternal life, he is held fast by the frailty of this life.

And therefore, conversely, I can say that, although to live by life is good, to live by life may nevertheless be ambiguous. For someone may be said to live by life—that is, to serve eternal life by the life of this body. Someone may also be said to live by life—that is, whether any person whatsoever or even a saint has a desire for this bodily life; for example, if someone thinks that one ought to live honorably in order to attain a long life by good deeds. Such are many of the weaker persons whom this life delights.

45. Therefore, just as we have understood what it is to live by life, let us understand what it is to die unto death, or to live unto death. [Note: The manuscripts and old edition, with strong agreement: “or to die by death.”] For there can be those who die unto death and those who live unto life. For [Note: Manuscripts S. Rem. and S. Th.: “For he who does not live by life lives according to the death of his soul. He dies to death who is not subject,” etc.] one who does not live in such a way as to live according to the death of his soul dies to death, [Col. 0296B] because he is not subject to death: that is, the bond of wretched death has left him, and he is not bound by the chains of eternal death. He is dead to death—that is, dead to sin and dead to punishment. The contrary of this is to live to punishment: that is, when someone lives for punishment, he lives for death. But one who dies to punishment dies [Col. 0296C] to death.

There is also one who, while placed in this life, dies to life, as he who says: “Yet I live—no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). For he is dead to sin and lives to God; that is, death is dead in him, but life lives—the life that is the Lord Jesus. Therefore, good is the life of those who live to God; evil is the life of those who live to sin. There is also an intermediate life, that of other living creatures, as you have it written: “Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its kind” (Gen. 1:24).

There is also the life of the dead: “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”; for God is not the God of the dead but of the living. There are also those for whom death and life have a certain common fellowship. Of them the Apostle says: “If you have died with [Christ], you shall also live with [him]. For if,” he says, “we have been planted together in the likeness [Col. 0296D] of his death, we shall likewise be [in the likeness] of his resurrection; knowing that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin may be destroyed, so that we may no longer serve sin. For [Note: “For he who has died has been justified from sin.” These words are absent from five manuscripts.] he who has died has been justified from sin” (Rom. 6:5).

But just as we have spoken of many forms of life, so we shall find many forms of death. [Col. 0297A] For death is called evil, according to the saying: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:20). Death is also spoken of in the ordinary sense, as you have, for example: [Note: Thus the manuscripts and old Roman edition: “Adam lived so many years … and was gathered to his people.” Perhaps one might not badly read, “Because someone,” etc., so that it would be an indeterminate example. But we introduce nothing into the text without authority.] “Adam lived so many years, and died, and was gathered to his fathers.” Death is also spoken of through the sacrament of baptism, as you have: “We were buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. 6:4). And elsewhere: “If we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live together with him” (ibid., 6:8). You see that death is indeed [Note: Thus manuscripts Vat., Th., Div., S. Th., Laud., and editions Am. and Era. But manuscripts Big., Gem., and Mich.: “you see that death is indeed judged by the name, but this…” Gill.: “you see … it is called, but this life may be our life.” Finally, Roman: “you see that this death … may be called, but may be our life.”] called by that name, but this is our life.

## CHAPTER X

Why God did not approve man until after woman had been made—especially since through her he was deceived into sin; and likewise why she was created not from earth, as Adam was, but from his rib.

[Col. 0297B]

46. There is another question, because the Lord said: “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Gen. 2:18). First of all, observe that in the earlier passage, where God formed man from the mud of the earth, He did not add, “And God saw that it was good” (Gen. 1:11 ff.), as He did in each of His individual works. For if He had there said that it was good because man had been made, this would be found contrary to His saying here that it was not good, when earlier He had said that it was good.

But understand this there, where He made Adam alone. On the other hand, where He comprehensively includes both man and woman as made, even though He did not say it there specifically, nevertheless, because afterward you have: “God saw all the things that He had made, and behold, they were [Col. 0297C] very good” (Gen. 1:31), it is clearly declared that it was good both that man was made and that woman was made.

47. But from this question another question again arises. For how is it that, when Adam alone was made, it was not said that Adam’s creation was good; but when woman was made from him, then all things were comprehensively declared good? Although there He praised all creation, and the creation of the universe was approved because in man there is the aforementioned community of nature, [Note: Thus six manuscripts and the old edition. Manuscript Div. and Roman edition: “the common nature of creatures is extolled,” etc. But Rem. and Th.: “because in the good thing extolled there is a common nature.”] nevertheless it does not seem idle to ask why, when Adam alone was made, not only was no commendation of goodness added to the work that pleased God, but it was even said that it was not good for man to be alone.

For we know that before woman was made Adam did not err; but after woman was made, she first transgressed [Col. 0297D] the divine command and also drew her husband into error, becoming his incentive. Therefore, if woman truly is the author of fault, how does she seem to have been added as a good thing? Yet if you consider that God has care for the universe, you will find that what contained the cause of the universe ought to have pleased the Lord more than that in which was the cause of sin ought to have been condemned.

And therefore, because the propagation of the human race could not arise from man alone, the Lord pronounced that it was not good for man to be alone. For God preferred that there should be many whom He could save and to whom He could grant forgiveness for sin, rather than one Adam alone, free from fault. Indeed, because He is the author of both works, He came into this world to save sinners. Finally, He did not allow Cain, guilty of fratricide, to perish before he had begotten children. Therefore woman had to be added to man for the generation of the human succession (see St Augustine, *Against Julian*, II.7.20).

Indeed, God’s own words, saying that it was not good for man to be alone, make this clear. For even if woman was to sin first, she—who was to procure redemption for herself—ought not to have been excluded from the exercise of the divine work. For although Adam was not deceived, [Col. 0298B] while the woman was deceived and became involved in transgression, nevertheless, he says, “she shall be saved through the bearing of children,” among whom she bore Christ (1 Tim. 2:14–15).

48. Nor is it without significance (33, question 5, chapter *Nec illud*) that woman was made not from the same earth from which Adam was fashioned, but from Adam’s own rib: so that we might know that man and woman have one bodily nature, one source of the human race. Therefore man and woman were not made as two from the beginning, nor two men, nor two women; but first man, then woman from him. For God, wishing to establish one nature for human beings, began this creation from one origin and removed the possibility of many and divergent natures.

“Let us make,” He says, “for him a helper like himself” (Gen. 2:18). We understand this helper with reference to the generation of the human constitution. [Col. 0298C] And truly it is a good helper. For if you understand “helper” in the sense of the more effective contributor, a greater activity of woman is found in the work of generation—like this earth, which, receiving seeds first, holds them and gradually makes them grow through its own warmth, bringing them forth into a crop. In this respect, then, woman’s help is good, although a helper is also called inferior; as we find in human practice, because those of greater rank commonly enlist a helper of lower merit.

## CHAPTER XI

How the animals were brought to Adam; what Adam’s sleep and the construction of the rib teach us; what the animals brought into Paradise also signify; and in what manner the righteous are caught up into Paradise.

49. Observe now why God also formed from the earth [Col. 0298D] all the beasts of the field and all the birds of heaven, and brought them to Adam to see what he would call them. For what reason was this done, when God brought only the beasts of the field and birds of heaven to Adam? For there were cattle according to their kind. Indeed, below you have: “Adam gave names to all cattle and all beasts of the field. But for Adam no helper [Col. 0299A] like him was found” (Gen. 2:20).

What explanation is there, then, unless that untamed beasts and the birds of heaven are brought to man by divine power? But man also had power to gather domesticated cattle. Thus the former belongs to divine operation, the latter to human diligence. At the same time, understand why all were brought to Adam: so that in all of them he might see that the substance of nature consists of both sexes, that is, male and female, and himself recognize from use and example that the fellowship of woman added to him was necessary.

50. “And God,” he says, “cast a sleep upon Adam, and he slept” (ibid., 2:21). What is this sleep except that, when we apply our mind for a little while to joining in marriage, we seem, as it were, to bend and turn our eyes, fixed upon the kingdom of God, toward a certain sleep of this world; and for a while to sleep with respect to divine things, while we rest in secular and worldly matters?

Accordingly, after He cast a sleep upon Adam and he slept, then the Lord God built the rib that He had taken from Adam into a woman. He fittingly said “built” when speaking of the creation of woman, because in man and woman there seems to be a certain complete perfection of a household. One who has no wife is, so to speak, without a house. Thus it is held. For as a man is considered more suited to public duties, so a woman is considered more suited to domestic services.

Consider that He took a rib from the body, not a portion from the soul. This [Note: All manuscripts with the ancient edition. But the Roman edition: “that is, not soul from soul, but bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh; she shall be called woman.”] is: not soul from soul, but “bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh; she shall be called woman.”

51. Therefore we have recognized the reason for human generation. [Col. 0299C] But many careful observers are troubled by this: if either it was first a great gift of God concerning human beings that they were placed in Paradise, or afterward the catching-up of each righteous person into Paradise appeared to be a reward for great merits, why are the beasts and cattle of the field and birds of heaven also said to have been in Paradise?
