Hence many have wished Paradise to be the human soul, in which certain shoots of virtues spring up; while man is placed to cultivate and guard Paradise—that is, the human mind, whose virtue seems to cultivate the soul, and not merely cultivate it but, once it has cultivated it, also guard it. The beasts of the field and birds of heaven brought to Adam are our irrational impulses, because beasts or cattle are certain [Col. 0299D] bodily passions, whether more turbulent or more languid. What else, moreover, should we regard the birds of heaven as except vain thoughts, which, in the manner of birds, fly about our soul and often carry it hither and thither in varied motion?

Therefore no helper like our mind was found, except sense, that is, *aisthēsis* (αἴσθησις, sensation/perception). Our *nous* (νοῦς, mind) alone could find one like itself.

52. But perhaps you object that God also placed these things in [Col. 0300A] such a Paradise—namely, bodily passions and a certain vanity of fluctuating or empty thoughts—and that He Himself was the author of our error. Consider what He says: “Have dominion,” He says, “over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth” (Gen. 1:28). You see that He has granted you authority: you ought to judge concerning all things and distinguish the kinds of each by the sober determination of your judgment. God called all things to you so that you might know your mind to be above all things. Why did you wish to adopt and join to yourself things that you found in no way like yourself?

He certainly gave you perception, by which you might know all things and [Note: Manuscripts Rem. and Div.: “judge concerning thoughts.”] judge what you know. And deservedly you were cast out from that fruitful field of Paradise because you could not keep the command. For God knew that you were frail; [Col. 0300B] He knew that you could not judge. Therefore He said, as to those who were weaker: “Do not judge, lest you be judged” (Matt. 7:1). Thus, because He knew that you were weak for judging, He wished you to be obedient to the command; therefore He set a precept. But if you had not transgressed, you could not have fallen into the danger of uncertain judgment.

Accordingly, because you wished to judge, He therefore added: “Behold, Adam [Note: Manuscripts Gem., S. Th., and S. Mich.: “you have become one [Col. 0300D] of us, so that you know good and evil.”] has become like one of us, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:22). You wished to arrogate judgment to yourself; therefore you ought not to reject the penalty of wrong judgment. Yet He placed you opposite Paradise, lest you should be able to erase its memory.

53. Accordingly, the righteous are often caught up into Paradise, as Paul too was caught up into Paradise and heard ineffable words. If you too are caught up by the strength of your mind from the first heaven to the second, [Col. 0300C] and from the second to the third—that is, because every human being is first bodily, second psychical, third spiritual—if you are thus caught up to the third heaven, so that you see the radiance of spiritual grace (for “the animate man does not know the things of the Spirit of God”), then ascent to the third heaven is [Note: Manuscripts Gem., Big., S. Th., and S. Mich.: “necessary. You will be caught up into Paradise; you will be caught up,” etc.] necessary for you, so that you may be caught up into Paradise.

You will then be caught up without danger, so that you may judge all things, because the spiritual person judges all things but is himself judged by no one. And perhaps, still frail as you are, you will hear ineffable words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter; and then preserve what you have received and guard what you have heard. The Apostle Paul guarded himself lest he should fall, or at least cause others to err. Or perhaps Paul says, “which it is not permitted for a human being to utter” (2 Cor. 12:6–7), because he was still established in the body—[Col. 0300D] that is, he saw the passions of this body; he saw the law of his flesh resisting the law of his mind (see St Augustine, *Against Julian*, II.5.13). I prefer this interpretation, lest we seem to assert some terror [Note: Thus eight manuscripts. Others and all editions: “to assert error.”] of a danger still to come.

For if there is security even with respect to this life, so that we need not fear any snares of transgression after this: then whoever has been in Paradise through the ascent of virtue will hear the hidden and secret mysteries of God; he will hear the Lord [Col. 0301A] saying to that thief who returned from crime to confession, and from robbery to faith: [Note: Ten manuscripts of the best quality, and the old edition: “from robbery to faith.” Four manuscripts with the Roman edition: “to faith from robbery.”] “Today you shall be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43).

## CHAPTER XII

What sort of wisdom the serpent possessed; how it approached the woman; and what her response was—followed by a lengthy discussion of a certain doubt concerning this matter.

54. “Now the serpent was more prudent than all the beasts [Note: Several ancient manuscripts: “that creep upon the earth.”] that were upon the earth, which the Lord God had made; and the serpent said to the woman: ‘What did God indeed say? You shall not eat from every tree that is in Paradise?’” (Gen. 3:1).

When it calls the serpent more prudent, you understand of whom it speaks: namely, our adversary, who possesses only [Col. 0301B] this wisdom of the world (see St Augustine, *Against Julian*, II.5.13). Yet pleasure and delight are also aptly called wise, because the wisdom of the flesh [Note: Manuscript Div.: “is called wisdom, which is contrary to the divine command.”] is called wisdom, as you have: “For the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God” (Rom. 8:7). Those seeking kinds of delights are crafty because they desire pleasures. Thus, whether you understand pleasure—which is in some respect contrary to the divine command and hostile to our faculties—or refer it to the devil, it is truly the enemy of the human race.

What is the cause of enmity except envy? As Solomon says: “Through the envy of the devil death entered into the world” (Wis. 2:24). [Col. 0301C] The cause of envy, moreover, was the blessedness of man placed in Paradise. And therefore, because the devil himself could not retain the grace he had received, he envied man, who, though formed from mud, was chosen to be an inhabitant of Paradise.

For the devil considered that he, who had been of a higher nature, had fallen into these secular and worldly things, whereas man, of a lower nature, hoped for eternal things. This is what he envies, saying: “Will this inferior being attain what I could not keep? Will he migrate from earth to heaven, while I have fallen from heaven to earth? I have many ways by which I can deceive man. He has been made from mud; earth is his mother; he is clothed in perishable things. Even if the soul is of a higher nature, it too can be liable to falling, being confined in the prison of the body, when I could not avoid falling.

“The first way, then, for him to be deceived is that he desires things greater than his condition. For in this there is a certain striving of ambition. Next, it belongs to the flesh to desire what it does not possess. Finally, in what do I seem wiser than all others, unless I ensnare man and contend by cunning and deceit?” Therefore he devised not to attack Adam first, but to attempt to ensnare Adam through woman. He did not attack the one who had received the heavenly command directly; rather, he attacked the woman, who had learned from her husband, not from [Col. 0302A] God, what she was to observe. For you do not have that God spoke to the woman; rather, that He spoke to Adam. Therefore the woman must be thought to have learned it through Adam.

55. Having recognized this sort of temptation in this passage, you will also find many kinds of temptation elsewhere. Some come through the ruler of this world, who has vomited certain poisons of wisdom into this world, so that people might think false things true and human affections might be captured by a certain appearance. For he does not always enter as an open enemy. There are certain powers that feign affection and display favor, so that they may gradually pour the poison of their iniquity into our thoughts. From them arise those sins born either from pleasure or from a certain pliancy of mind.

There are also other powers which, as it were, wrestle with us. Thus the Apostle says: “For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, and the rulers of this world, of this darkness, against the spiritual wickednesses that are in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). For they wish by this kind of struggle to break us and, as it were, to crush a certain body of our soul. Thus Paul, like a good athlete, had learned not only to avoid the blows of opposing powers but also to strike his opponents. Hence he says: “I strike with my fists, not as one beating the air” (1 Cor. 9:26). And therefore, like a good athlete, he deserved to reach the crown.

Thus the devil’s temptations are manifold. Therefore the serpent is regarded as two-tongued and deadly, because the devil’s minister speaks one thing with the tongue and meditates another in the heart. [Col. 0302C] There are also other ministers who cast, as it were, arrows infected by poison from both heart and voice—from their own words. To them the Lord says: “Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil?” (Matt. 12:34).

56. And the serpent said to the woman: “What indeed did God say? ‘Do not eat from every tree that is in Paradise’?” And the woman said to the serpent: “We shall eat from every tree of Paradise; but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the midst of Paradise, God said: ‘You shall not eat from it, nor shall you touch it, lest we die’” (Gen. 3:2–3).

When you hear that the serpent was more prudent than all beasts, seek its cunning here. It pretends to repeat the words of God and [Note: Rem.: “and more closely weaves its deceits.”] weaves in its own deceits. For when God had said: “From every tree that is in Paradise you shall eat for food; but from the tree [Col. 0302D] of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat; for on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (ibid., 2:16–17), the serpent, as though questioning the woman, altered God’s statement, “From every tree that is in Paradise you shall eat; but from one tree you shall not eat,” by inserting a falsehood: “You shall not eat from any tree.” Yet God had commanded only that the single tree of knowledge of good and evil should not be tasted.

It is no wonder how it deceived, since those who attempt to ensnare someone are accustomed to deceive. Thus the serpent’s question is not idle. But, so that you may know that there could be no defect in the command, the woman replied, as you have: “We shall eat from every tree of Paradise; but concerning the fruit of the tree in the midst of Paradise, God said: ‘You shall not eat from it, nor touch it, lest you die by death.’”

There is indeed no defect in the command, but there is one in the reporting of the command. For, so far as the present reading teaches, we learn that we ought not, even for the sake of caution, add anything to a command. For if you either add or subtract anything, it seems to be a kind of transgression of the command. The form of the command or sequence of testimony must be preserved pure [the canon *Pura*, 3, question IX] and simple. Often, when a witness adds something of his own to the sequence of events, he discolors the entire credibility of his testimony through the partial falsehood.

Therefore nothing, even what seems good, should be added. For what offense does the woman’s addition, “Nor shall you touch anything from it,” have at first appearance? God had not said, “You shall touch”; rather, “You shall not eat.” Yet the fall begins to have its origin here. For what she added was superfluous; or, by adding something of her own, she understood God’s command to be incomplete. The sequence of the present reading therefore teaches us neither to subtract anything from nor add anything to the divine commands.

For if John judged this concerning his own writings: “If anyone adds to this,” he says, “God shall add to him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of this prophecy, God shall take away his part from the book of life” (Rev. 22:18–19), how much more must nothing be subtracted from the divine commands! Thus the first transgression of the command began here.

And many think that this fault was not the woman’s but Adam’s: that Adam, wishing to make the woman more cautious, told her that God had added the command, “Nor shall you touch anything from it.” For we have that Adam, not Eve, received the command from God. The woman had not yet been formed. The reading itself does not disclose Adam’s exact words by which he gave the woman the form and sequence of the command; but we understand that the sequence of the command passed through the man to the woman.

Let others see what they think. To me, however, the fault seems to have begun with the woman, and the falsehood to have originated with her. For even if the point is uncertain between the two, her sex reveals who could have erred first. Add that she is bound by the prejudice arising from the fact that her error was later found to have come first. For woman, not man, is the author of error for man, not man for woman. Hence Paul also says: “Adam was not deceived; but the woman, being deceived, was in transgression” (1 Tim. 2:14).

57. Let us now consider whether, apart from the addition attached to the command, what was added appears to have done harm. For truly, if “Nor shall you touch it” is good and contributed to caution, why did God not forbid this? Indeed, by not forbidding it, He appears to have permitted it. Therefore both points must be examined: why He neither permitted it nor forbade it.

For there are some who say: “Why did He make visible what He did not command also to be touched? [Note: Manuscripts Big., S. Th., Torn., Colb.: “what He made, [He commanded] not to be eaten,” etc.; Gem.: “what He made to be eaten”; Mich.: “what He made, He commanded not to be eaten and did not forbid to be touched.”]” Yet when you hear that the tree possessed the nature [Col. 0304A] of the knowledge of good and evil, it may be judged that He did not wish you to touch evil.

For it is enough for us, according to the Lord’s saying, to see Satan falling like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18), and [Note: S. Th. and edition Era.: “given for food,” not badly.] giving food not to the children of light but of night and darkness; for it is written: “He gave him as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians” (Ps. 73:14). This, therefore, was said concerning the fact that He did not command it to be touched.

But as to why He did not forbid it, hear what I understand. Many things harm us if we wish to take them in before first learning what they are. This often happens with foods and drink. If you first know that something is bitter, you assume patience; and if you understand that bitter things are beneficial, you assume endurance, lest their sudden bitterness offend you and you begin to reject what would profit you. Thus it is beneficial to know beforehand, so that, because you know it will benefit you, you do not disdain bitter things. But these can do less harm. Consider that which can do greater harm unless precaution is taken.

58. A certain pagan is moving toward the faith; he is a catechumen and wishes to receive a fuller measure of teaching and faith. Let him beware lest, while wishing to learn, he learn wrongly—learn from Photinus, from Arius, from Sabellius. Let him entrust himself to teachers of this kind, whose authority may hold some sway over him; and, led by a certain presumption concerning his teachers, he may be unable to judge matters impressed upon his immature mind. Therefore, let him first discern with the eyes of his mind whom he is following [Note: MSS. St. Theodorus and Remigius: “whom he should follow”]. Let him see where life is; finally, let him touch the vital parts of the divine readings, so that he may not be led astray by any perverse interpreter.

Sabellius reads to him: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10), and says that there is one person. Photinus reads: “For the mediator between God and human beings is the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5); and elsewhere: “Why do you seek to kill me, a man?” (John 8:40). Arius too reads that he said: “For the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). The wording, indeed, is plain; but he must first examine with himself on what ground it was said, so that he may perceive the rationale of the sayings. He is led by a certain authority of his teachers; and it would have benefited him not to inquire rather than to have found such a teacher.

Even if some pagan takes up the Scriptures, he reads: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Lev. 24:20). He also reads: “If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off” (Matt. 5:30). He does not understand the meaning; he does not perceive the mysteries of the divine utterance; he goes astray more grievously than if he had not read it. Therefore John taught how they ought to investigate the Word of God: not casually, not rashly, but carefully and attentively. “That which was from the beginning,” he says, “which we heard, which we saw, which we beheld with our eyes, and which our hands examined concerning the Word of life—and we saw and bear witness and proclaim to you” (1 John 1:1–2). You see that he first examined the Word of God as though with certain hands, and afterward proclaimed it. Thus perhaps the word would have done Adam and Eve no harm if, while considering it carefully, they had first touched it with certain hands of the mind.

For the weak, by considering and more diligently investigating each matter which they do not understand, can discover its nature. Certainly those weak persons, before touching that tree in which they had learned that knowledge of evil existed, ought to have examined it. For knowledge even of evil can often benefit us. Thus we read the devil’s deceits both in this passage and in prophecy (Ezek. 28:18), in order that we may learn how we can avoid his arts. For his temptations must be known, not so that we may follow them, but so that, taught and instructed, we may avoid them.

173 59. There are some here who raise the question [Note: Thus seven manuscripts, together with the old edition. In as many manuscripts, however, the words are absent: “whether, concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil alone, he said that it was not to be tasted.” But the Roman edition presented the whole passage thus: “They raise the question, since the Lord said to Adam concerning every tree, ‘You shall eat from it,’ whether, along with every tree, he said that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil also was to be eaten; or whether he said that every tree was to be eaten, but that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil alone was not to be tasted.”]: whether God said that one should taste from every tree in such a way that, as one tasted from every tree, one should also taste from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; or whether one should taste from every tree, but should not taste from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil alone.

They do not even consider this line of reasoning useless: although the food of this tree was harmful, nevertheless, if it were eaten together with the others, it might not be harmful. For it is said that the antidote *theriac* is customarily made from a serpent’s body; and certainly the venom and body of the serpent, when taken by themselves, harm, but when mixed with other things they bring health and healing. So too, knowledge of good and evil, if it possesses any wisdom, if someone always directs it toward life, if someone pursues the other kinds of virtues, is by no means thought useless.

For this reason, then, many thought that this too could be understood: that God appeared to have forbidden the tasting of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil alone, apart from the others, but had not forbidden it together with the others. They suppose this was said because God said to Adam: “Who told you that you were naked, unless you ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat—from this tree alone?” (Gen. 3:11). This might seem to allow some room for such interpretation, if the woman had not previously answered the serpent, when he said, “Why indeed did God say, ‘Do not eat from every tree that is in paradise’?”: [Note: Roman edition: “We shall eat from every tree of paradise, but concerning the fruit of the tree …” But these words are lacking in the manuscripts, as in the old edition. MSS. St. Theodorus and Laudianus: “From the tree which is in the midst,” etc.] “From that which is in the midst of paradise, God said: ‘You shall not eat from it.’”

Although by this the woman’s faith, destined to transgress, appears weaker, I shall nevertheless not strip Adam of all virtues, so as to make it appear that he attained no virtue in paradise, tasted nothing from the other trees, [Note: Thus MSS. Divionensis, Claromontanus, Tornacensis, St. Theodorus, and the Erasmus edition. Other manuscripts and the editions of Amerbach, Gillot, and Rome: “before he fell into guilt.”] and fell into guilt before receiving any fruits. Therefore I shall not strip Adam, lest I strip the whole human race, which is innocent before it receives the awareness of the knowledge of good and evil. For it was not said idly: “Unless you turn and become like this child, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). For when a child is cursed, he does not curse in return; when struck, he does not strike back; he does not know the temptations of ambition and plunder.

60. Therefore I think it more true that he commanded that the tree was not to be eaten even together with the other fruits. For although knowledge is good for the perfect, it is useless for the imperfect. I would venture to call every human being imperfect, since Paul himself, as though imperfect, says: “Not that I have received it, or am now already perfect; but I pursue it, if I may lay hold of it” (Phil. 1:12). Therefore the Lord says to the imperfect: “Do not judge, that you may not be judged” (Matt. 7:1). Knowledge, then, is useless to the imperfect.

Finally: “I did not know sin, unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Rom. 7:7). And below: “For without the law sin is dead” (ibid., 8). For what benefit was it to me to know what I could not avoid? What benefit was it to me to know what the law of my flesh would oppose? Paul is opposed, and sees the law of his flesh resisting the law of his mind and himself taken captive under the law of sin (Rom. 7:23); nor does he presume upon his own conscience (see St. Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book II, ch. 5, no. 13), but through Christ’s grace trusts that he will be delivered from the body of death. And do you suppose that anyone who knows cannot sin? Paul says: “For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish—this I do” (Rom. 7:19); and do you think knowledge benefits a human being when it increases the odium of transgression?

Yet grant that the perfect person cannot sin. In Adam God foresaw all human beings; and therefore it was not fitting for the human race indiscriminately to possess knowledge of good and evil, which it could not, as was necessary, exercise through the vices of the flesh.

## CHAPTER XIII

How the devil’s temptations are full of falsehood; concerning the deception of the woman and Adam’s fall; and how they came to know that they were naked, made loin-coverings for themselves, and what those signify.

61. Let us therefore learn that the devil’s temptations are full of falsehood. For scarcely one thing among those he promised appears true; he fabricated the rest falsely. For thus you have it: “And the serpent said to the woman: ‘You shall not die by death’” (Gen. 3:4). Behold one falsehood: for the human being who followed the serpent’s promises died by death. Then he added: “God knows,” he said, “that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened” (ibid., 5). This alone was true, because below you have: “Because both ate, their eyes were opened” (ibid., 7). But this was a truth that harmed them. Indeed, opening the eyes is not beneficial to everyone, because it is written: “They shall see and shall not see” (Isa. 6:9).

But a falsehood was immediately attached, because he added: “And you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5). In this one may observe that the serpent is the author of idolatry, since a certain serpent’s cunning seems to have introduced many gods into human error. And he deceived [Note: Thus eight manuscripts of better quality, and the old edition. MSS. St. Theodorus and Michael: “because a human being is not like gods.” St. Remigius: “because human beings are not like gods.” But in the Roman edition read: “and he deceived, saying, ‘You shall be like gods.’”] by saying that the human being would be like gods. For human beings not only ceased to be like gods, but even those who were, as it were, gods—those to whom it was said, “I said, ‘You are gods’” (Ps. 81:6)—lost their grace.

62. “And the woman saw that the tree was good for food, pleasing to the eyes for seeing, and beautiful to behold” (Gen. 3:6). Weak was the author of judgment who judged concerning that which she had not tasted. Therefore nothing should readily be taken up for any undertaking unless we have considered it more carefully and tested it by an inward affection. “Taking,” he says, “of its fruit, she ate; and she gave to her husband with her, and both ate.” It is well that the point at which Adam was deceived is passed over, because he fell not by his own fault but through the failing of his wife.

63. “And their eyes,” he says, “were opened, and they knew that they were naked” (ibid., 7). They had indeed previously been naked, but not without the coverings of virtues (*On Penance*, distinction 2, ch. *Ut cognoverunt*). They were naked because of the simplicity of their character and because their nature did not know the garment of deceit. But now the human mind is veiled in many wrappings of pretence. Therefore, after they saw themselves stripped of that sincerity and simplicity of whole and uncorrupted nature, they began to seek worldly and man-made things with which to cover the nakedness of their minds—stitching pleasures to pleasures, and the shadowy delights of this world, as it were leaves to leaves, in order to shade their generative secret.

For how did Adam have the bodily eyes closed, when he saw all living creatures so as to give them names? How did they know—that is, by an inward and higher knowledge—not that they lacked a tunic, but that they lacked the coverings of virtues?

64. “And they stitched together fig leaves,” he says, “and made loin-coverings for themselves” (ibid., 7). The sequence of the divine readings teaches us under what kind the fig ought here to be understood. For Scripture records that the holy are those who rest beneath vine and fig tree (Mic. 4:4); Solomon says: “Who plants a fig tree and does not eat of its fruit?” (Prov. 27:18); and the Lord came to a fig tree, yet was offended because he found not fruit but leaves only.

Adam, then, teaches me what leaves are: after he sinned, he made himself a loin-covering of fig leaves, though he ought rather to have tasted its fruits. The righteous person chooses fruit; the sinner, leaves. What is the fruit? “The fruit of the Spirit,” he says, “is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, modesty, [Note: Roman edition: “self-control, chastity.”] self-control, love” (Gal. 5:22). He had no fruit who had no joy. He had no faith who had transgressed God’s command. He had no self-control who had tasted the tree forbidden to him.

65. Therefore, whoever transgresses God’s command is stripped and made naked, and becomes ugly to himself. He wishes to cover himself with certain fig leaves, perhaps with certain empty or shadowy speeches, which, stitching together fabricated falsehoods and piling word upon word, the sinner weaves into a covering for his conscience and his deed, in order to hide his shameful parts.

For he casts leaves over himself who, desiring to conceal his fault, either names the devil as author of the offense, or puts forward the enticements of the flesh, or discloses some other persuader of his error. He frequently draws examples from the divine Scriptures, by which he alleges that righteous persons fell into guilt. For example, if he has been caught in sexual immorality, he says: “Abraham too lay with a maidservant” (Gen. 16:4), and “David loved and took to himself another man’s wife” (2 Kings 11:4, 27). He stitches certain leaves upon himself—certain examples from the succession of prophetic Scriptures—and does not think that their fruit should be sought.

66. Do not the Jews also seem to you to stitch together leaves when they interpret the words of the spiritual law in a bodily manner? Their interpretation loses every fruit of freshness, condemned by the curse of everlasting barrenness. Good interpretation, therefore—that is, spiritual interpretation—is a fruitful fig tree, beneath which the righteous and holy rest. Whoever plants it in the souls of individuals, as Paul says, “I planted, Apollos watered” (1 Cor. 3:6), shall eat its fruit. But bad interpretation will be unable to bear fruit or retain freshness.

67. What is more serious, therefore (see St. Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, II, ch. 6, no. 16), is that Adam girded himself with this interpretation at that place where he ought rather to have girded himself with the fruit of chastity. For in the loins with which we are girded are said to be certain seeds of generation. Thus Adam was badly girded there with useless leaves, where he signified not the fruit of a future generation but certain sins which remained until the coming of the Lord the Savior.

But after the Lord came, he found the fig tree uncultivated. Asked not to command that it be cut down, he permitted it to be cultivated. Therefore we are now girded, not with leaves, but with the divine word; for the Lord himself says: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35). Hence he also forbids us to carry money in our belts (Matt. 10:9); for our belt ought to preserve not worldly but eternal things.

## CHAPTER XIV

On the voice of the Lord walking in the evening, and the rebuke of Adam: “Where are you?” Why, moreover, Adam is rebuked first although the woman tasted first; and concerning the woman’s excuse and the mysteries signified through these things.

68. “And they heard,” he says, “the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise in the evening” (Gen. 3:8). What is the walking of God, who is always everywhere? But I think that there is a certain walking of God through the sequence of the divine Scriptures, in which a certain presence of God is active: when we hear that he himself beholds all things, and that the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous; when we read that Jesus knew their thoughts (Luke 6:8); when we read: “Why do you think evil things in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4). Therefore, while we rehearse these things, we recognize God as though walking.

The sinner had fled, not because he could hide from God’s sight, but because he wished to hide within his own conscience and did not wish his works to shine. For it belongs to the righteous to see face to face, because the mind of the righteous is not only present before God, but also reasons with God, as it is written: “Judge for the orphan, justify the widow, and come, let us reason together, says the Lord” (Isa. 1:17–18). Therefore, when the sinner reads these divine Scriptures, he hears the voice of God as though walking in the evening.

What is “in the evening,” except that he recognizes his guilt late, and that a certain shame for past error comes late—shame which ought to have forestalled the error? For while guilt is hot in the body and the soul is agitated by bodily passions, the mind that strays does not think of God; that is, it does not hear God walking in the divine Scriptures, walking in each individual mind. For God says: “Because I shall dwell in them and walk among them, and I shall be their God” (Lev. 26:12).

Therefore, when the fear of divine power returns to the soul’s awareness, then we blush; then we long to hide ourselves; then, set amid thoughts of our sins, we are caught in the midst of the tree of paradise where we sinned, wishing to hide and thinking that God does not search out secrets. But he who searches hearts and thoughts, penetrating even to the division of soul, says: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9).

69. How does God speak? Surely not with a bodily voice, but by a power more excellent than a bodily voice can be, he pours forth oracles. The prophets heard this voice of his; the faithful hear this voice; the impious do not understand it. Thus in the Gospel you have that the Evangelist heard the Father saying: “I have glorified, and I shall glorify again” (John 12:28); but the Jews did not hear it. For they said: “There was thunder” (ibid., 29). There, therefore, just as above you have that God who did not walk was perceived as walking, so God who did not speak was heard as speaking.

70. But let us consider what he says: “Adam, where are you?” Even now there is a remedy of healing in those who hear God’s word. Thus the Jews, who shut their ears lest they hear, do not deserve to hear even today. Next, those who have hidden themselves have a remedy. For one who hides blushes; one who blushes turns back, as it is written: “Let them be put to shame and turn back, all of them, very swiftly” (Ps. 6:11). Moreover, the very fact that he calls is evidence that he intends to heal, because the Lord both pities and calls those whom he pities.

By saying, “Where are you?” he does not seek a place, he who knows the secret; for God did not have his eyes shut, so that he could not see the one hiding. Thus he said: “Adam has become as one of us” (Gen. 3:22), because he opened his eyes. [Note: In some manuscripts and the Roman edition, the words are absent: “And he indeed opened his eyes.”] And he indeed opened his eyes in order to see his fault, which he could not avoid. For after we have sinned, somehow or other, we know our offenses; and then we understand to be sin what, before we sinned, we did not think to be sin. Certainly we did not think it a sin to be condemned; for if we had condemned it, we would not have committed it.

But God sees the faults of all and knows the offenses of all: he has eyes upon every soul and every secret. [Note: MSS. Gemblacensis, St. Theodorus, and Remigius: “What then? ‘Adam, where are you?’ That is, ‘Now, among what things are you?’” MSS. Theodorus, Bigotianus, and Michael: “not ‘among what things are you?’” The other manuscripts and all editions read as in the text.] What, then, is “Adam, where are you?” That is, not “in what place?” but “among what things are you?” It is not, therefore, a question but a rebuke. “From what good things, from what blessedness, from what grace, into what misery have you fallen back? You abandoned eternal life and were buried in death, entombed in error. [Note: MSS. St. Theodorus and Michael: “‘Where are you?’ That self-confident assurance of yours … fear in you.” St. Michael: “your fault confesses.”] Where is that assurance of yours, conscious of its own goodness?” This fear confesses guilt; concealment confesses transgression. “Where, then, are you?” That is, I ask not in what place, but in what condition. To what have your sins brought you, that you flee your God, whom before you sought?

Perhaps someone may wonder why Adam is rebuked first, since the woman tasted first. But transgression began with the weaker sex; shame and excuse, with the stronger—so that the woman was the cause of error, the man of shame.

71. “And the woman said: ‘The serpent deceived me, and I ate’” (Gen. 3:13; *On Penance*, distinction I, ch. *Serpens*). A pardonable fault, followed by confession of offenses. Therefore the woman was not without hope, because she did not keep silence before God but confessed her sin; consequently, a healing sentence followed [Note: The same edition: “a medicinal sentence followed,” etc.]. It is good to be condemned in sin and scourged for offense, so that we may be scourged with human beings.

Cain, on the other hand, because he wished to deny his crime, was judged unworthy to be punished in his sin; but he was dismissed without a prescribed penalty—perhaps not so much because of the greater crime of fratricide (for he committed that against his brother), as because of sacrilege, in that he believed God could be lied to, saying: “I do not know; am I my brother’s keeper?” (Gen. 4:9). Therefore his accusation was reserved for the accusing devil, so that he may be scourged with the devil’s angels, since he was unwilling to be scourged with human beings. Thus it is said of such persons: “There is no release from their death … and they shall not be scourged with human beings” (Ps. 72:4–5).

Different, then, was the woman’s case. Although she had fallen into the fault of transgression, she still had food of virtue from the trees of paradise. Therefore she declared her sin, and it was reckoned to her for pardon. “For the righteous person is the accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech.” Nor can anyone be justified from sin (*On Penance*, distinction 1, ch. *Non potest*) unless he has first confessed the sin. Hence the Lord says: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26).

72. Therefore, because Eve herself confessed her offense, a beneficial sentence followed, which condemned the error yet did not deny pardon: that, turned toward her husband, she should serve him. First, so that she might not take pleasure in erring easily; then, so that, placed beneath the stronger vessel, she might not lead her husband astray, but might herself be governed rather by her husband’s counsel.

In this I plainly recognize the mystery of Christ and the Church. For it signifies the Church’s future conversion toward Christ and her religious service in subjection to the Word of God, which is far better than the liberty of this world. Thus it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6:13). This service of God, therefore, is a gift. Indeed, obedience in this service is counted among blessings; for Isaac, in the context of blessing, gave it to his son Esau, that he should serve his brother. Esau, indeed, was seeking a blessing; though he had learned that one blessing had been taken from him, he nevertheless asked for another, saying: “Do you have only one blessing, father?” (Gen. 27:38).

By this service, therefore, he who had previously sold his birthright through gluttony and had lost the favor of blessing through his pursuit of rustic hunting believed that he himself would become better if he revered in his brother the type of Christ. For the Christian people possesses strength through this service, as the Lord also says to his disciples: “Whoever wishes to be first among you shall be servant of all” (Matt. 20:27). Indeed, love produces this service, and love is greater both than hope and than faith. Hence it is written: “Through love serve one another” (Gal. 5:13). This, then, is the mystery which the Apostle says exists in Christ and in the Church (Eph. 5:32). For the Church was indeed first in transgression, but she shall be saved through the generation of children in faith, love, sanctification, and chastity. The human race, which transgressed in the fathers, is saved through the children, so that what had offended in the Jews might be corrected in Christian posterity.

## CHAPTER XV

Why the woman’s sin deserved pardon; what is signified by the serpent, woman, and man; the nature of the serpent’s condemnation; and in what respects it differs from Adam’s condemnation.

73. “The serpent,” she says, [Note: The Roman edition alone: “persuaded me; and this woman’s sin was pardonable before God,” etc.] “persuaded me”; and this appeared pardonable to God, because he knew that the serpent had many ways of deceiving (for it transforms itself into an angel of light, and its ministers are as ministers of righteousness [Note: Four manuscripts and the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus: “ministers of righteousness. It is falsehood that imposes …” The editions of Gillot and Rome: “its ministers are ministers of righteousness, imposing falsehoods …” But since all manuscripts read *imponentis … dicant … imponant*, not, as in the edition, *dicant … imponant*, we judged the passage should be restored as in the text.])—imposing false names upon particular things, so that it calls rashness virtue and gives avarice the name of industry.

For the serpent deceived the woman; the woman led the man away from truth into transgression. Bodily pleasure assumed the type of the serpent; the woman is the symbol of our sense-perception; the man, [Note: Thus MSS. Claromontanus, Gemblacensis, Colbertinus, Bigotianus, St. Remigius, and St. Theodorus. But the other manuscripts and all editions read: “the man, the pleasure of the mind.” Thus, “sense-perception,” etc.] the symbol of the mind. Pleasure, therefore, moves sense-perception; sense-perception conveys to the mind the passion it has received. Pleasure, then, is the first origin of sin. Therefore do not wonder why the serpent is first condemned by God’s judgment, the woman second, and the man third. The order of condemnation follows the order of error. For pleasure customarily makes sense-perception captive, and sense-perception the mind.

But, that you may know that the serpent is a type of pleasure, consider its condemnation.

74. “Upon your breast,” he says, “and upon your belly you shall go” (Gen. 3:14). Who are those who went upon their bellies, except those who live for belly and throat, whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shameful parts, who set their minds on earthly things and, burdened with food, bend toward the earth? Thus he aptly says to pleasure, which is intent upon foods and seems to eat earth: “Upon your breast and upon your belly you shall go, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life.”

[Note: Nearly all manuscripts: “Every excuse of the devil must be removed.”] Every excuse of the devil must be removed, lest perhaps he may be able to allege something for his malice and say that his wickedness resulted from his condemnation, and that he stubbornly strives to harm human beings because he was condemned in order to harm them. This seems close to the point if we take this sentence as a condemnation. For God did not condemn the serpent in order that it should harm; rather, he showed what it would become. And indeed, we showed above that this temptation benefits human beings all the more (ch. 2, no. 9). Yet, when we read what is written, with God speaking: “Those who honor me I shall honor, and the one who despises me shall be deprived of honor” (1 Kings 2:30), we may infer something from these words.

For God works what is good, not what is evil. Therefore the divine words teach you that he works glory and leaves punishment. “Those who honor me,” he says, “I shall honor,” declaring that honor is the work of his goodness. And concerning those who despise me, he did not say, “I shall deprive them of honor,” but, “They shall be deprived of honor,” not assigning their injury to his own action but showing what would happen. Thus here he did not say: “I make you go upon your breast and upon your belly and eat earth all the days of your life”; but: “You shall go,” he says, “and you shall eat,” so that he appears rather to have foretold concerning the serpent what would happen than to have prescribed what it should do.

“For earth,” he says, “shall be your food, not the soul”; for this too benefits sinners. Hence the Apostle delivered such persons over to the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit might be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. He says that the serpent creeps upon breast and belly, not so much because of its bodily form as because it fell from that [Note: Some manuscripts of good age: “heavenly blessing.”] heavenly blessedness through earthly thoughts. For “breast” is often understood as a certain recess of wisdom. Therefore the Apostle rests his head upon Christ’s breast, not casts it down to earth.

Therefore, if the wisdom of the devil is compared to the most savage beasts, whose breast is between their feet, and if even human beings who set their minds on earthly things and are not lifted toward heaven by inward affection seem to creep on their bellies over the earth, then surely we must not fill the belly of our soul with the corruptible things of this age, but rather satisfy it with God’s word. Thus David, assuming Adam’s person, aptly says: “My soul has been humbled into dust; my belly has clung to the earth” (Ps. 43:25). For it clung when it was conformed to the serpent that feeds upon earthly iniquity. Therefore the Apostle says that we ought to be conformed to Christ (Rom. 6:5), so that Christ’s power may be displayed in us. This sentence is not thought severe against the serpent, when Adam, who sinned more lightly, is condemned by such a sentence.

75. For it is written: “Cursed is the earth in your works; in sorrow you shall eat it all the days of your life” (Gen. 3:17). Certainly there appears to be some likeness in the sentence; nevertheless, within that likeness there is a great difference. For it matters whether someone eats earth, as was said to the serpent, “You shall eat earth,” or whether, as was said to the human being, “In sorrow you shall eat.” For the addition, “in sorrow,” makes the distinction.

Consider the force of this distinction. It is better for me to eat earth in sorrow than in pleasure—that is, to seem saddened in a certain bodily action and experience rather than delighted in sin. For many, because of excessive iniquities, do not admit the consciousness of sin. But the one who says, “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery” (1 Cor. 9:27), grieves in repentance for our sins, because he himself had not such great offenses that he ought to grieve over them. Indeed, he also urges upon us that this sorrow is beneficial—the sorrow which is according to God, not according to the world. “You ought,” he says, “to grieve in repentance according to God” (2 Cor. 7:9–10); for sorrow according to God produces salvation, but worldly sorrow produces death.

But learn also from the Old Testament that those who were grieved in bodily works came to grace, whereas those who delighted in the works of this world remained in punishment. Thus the Hebrews, who groaned under the labors of Egypt, obtained the grace of the righteous (Exod. 2:24). And because they ate bread in sorrow, they were given spiritual food (Exod. 16:13 ff.); but the Egyptians, who performed such works with exultation while serving an abominable king, obtained no pardon.

76. There is also this distinction: that the serpent is told it will eat earth; but Adam: [Note: MSS. Bigotianus, Gemblacensis, Tornacensis, St. Theodorus, and Michael: “‘In sorrow,’ he says, ‘you shall eat the grass of the field,’ so that we may understand a certain …”] “In sorrow,” he says, “you shall eat, and with sweat you shall eat, and you shall eat the grass of the field” (Gen. 3:18–19). Thus we should understand that there is a certain progress in these things: when we eat earth, we seem to be in a certain wickedness; when grass, in a certain progress; but when bread, strength has been brought to completion.

Therefore let us too have progress in this life, as Paul had when he says: “But now I live, no longer I” (Gal. 2:20)—that is, no longer I who formerly ate earth; no longer I who ate grass, because all flesh is grass. “But Christ lives in me”: that is, that living bread which came down from heaven lives; wisdom lives; grace lives; righteousness lives; resurrection lives.

77. Next, consider that the human being is not cursed, but the serpent is cursed; nor is the earth cursed in itself, but, “Cursed,” he says, “in your works,” [Note: Claromontanus, Remigius, and St. Theodorus: “it was said concerning the soul.”] which was said to Adam. Then the earth is cursed if you have earthly works, that is, worldly works. Nor is it cursed absolutely, but so as to produce thorns and thistles unless it has been cultivated by the diligent labor of human action. But if [Note: Roman edition: “But if we cultivate it … we shall be in sweat; yet nevertheless,” etc.] we cultivate it, we shall indeed eat bread in labor and sweat.

For the law of the flesh resists the law of the mind. We must labor and sweat in order to chastise the body, reduce it to slavery, and sow spiritual things. For if we sow fleshly things, we shall reap fleshly things; but if we sow spiritual things, we shall reap spiritual things. (St. Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book II, ch. 5.)

[ON CAIN AND ABEL.]

## PREFACE TO THE BOOKS ON CAIN AND ABEL
Ambrose, at the very beginning of his book *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, speaking of two chamberlains of Gratian—men of the Arian sect—who had deceitfully promised to attend his sermon but did not fulfill their pledged word, declares that he will turn his discourse to the proposed history of Cain and Abel. “Therefore,” he says, “while they perhaps are coming, let us turn aside to those husbandmen who have been set before us, of whom one—that is, Cain—etc.” From this, certainly, no slight suspicion may be raised that the treatise on Cain and Abel was not published until after those words had been spoken by Ambrose. Some confirmation may perhaps seem to accrue to this conjecture from the fact that the same faith which the holy man expounds against the Arians in the book *On the Incarnation* is also strongly commended in the work now under discussion, and that in both works the same words of Genesis are interpreted in a not dissimilar manner. But since the aforementioned disputation *On the Incarnation of the Lord* can scarcely have been delivered before the year 382, as will be said in its proper place, someone might perhaps infer that the treatise *On Cain and Abel* should likewise be assigned to the same period.

Nevertheless, the very first words of this work lead us to judge it earlier, as being contemporary with the work *On Paradise*. For there the holy Doctor says: “In the preceding work, on Paradise, we have arranged, according to our capacity and as we were able, the understanding which the Lord poured in.... Now let us undertake the following history and continue our work upon those things which are joined to it according to the divine Scriptures.” These words certainly leave no room for doubt that this little work—which in two manuscripts, written after the book *On Paradise*, bears the title *The Second Book on Cain and Abel*—was appended by him to that book. We may therefore believe it to have been written about the year 375. Besides the conjectures set out by us in the preceding notice, the character of both works points to the same conclusion: it undoubtedly displays not so much maturity as Ambrose’s other works, but, to use Ambrose’s own expression, is in some sense “youthful.” Therefore, when he indicates in the passage from the treatise *On the Incarnation of the Lord* cited above that he is turning aside to Cain and Abel, we think this was said because perhaps the history of the two brothers, whose reading recurred yearly in the Church at a fixed time, had then been read aloud to the people.

What is treated in this work is sufficiently shown both by its title and by what has been said above. As for its method of treatment, it almost everywhere expounds and illustrates its subject through mystical interpretations. It dwells especially on explaining the sacrifices of Cain and Abel, a matter upon which it spends by far the greater part of the entire treatise. Although here Ambrose is not so copious in attacking and refuting heretics as in the book *On Paradise*, but indulges more freely in an oratorical style, he nevertheless sometimes subtly introduces certain doctrines of the Catholic faith which he judged especially useful for forming the minds of the faithful. The matters conducive to the shaping of character he treats more fully and carefully.

Accordingly, one will not seem to have acted rashly in judging that this work was first publicly delivered and afterward reduced to the form in which it is now found. Yet it must not be concealed that this is more easily noticed in other Ambrosian works in which the modes of oratorical speech still remain.

Furthermore, we must acknowledge that this saint of ours transferred very much from Philo into his composition. Compare, if you wish, what he says on the words of Genesis, “I have acquired a man through God,” with the Jewish writer’s book *On the Cherubim*, and you will readily perceive that these things were drawn from there. Likewise, from the middle of the first chapter of the former book through the eighth chapter of the latter, it is manifest that no small portion is owed to that same author’s book *On the Sacrifices of Abel and Cain*. Yet in the last three chapters of the second book, where Ambrose briefly deals with the remaining matters pertaining to that same history, he has imitated exactly three passages from the book entitled *On the Worse Being Accustomed to Plot against the Better*, in which Philo treats the same matters more fully. But there, as everywhere that he borrows something from this author, he always uses the greatest freedom: whenever he wishes, he adds to or subtracts from Philonic opinions, and sometimes even puts contrary views before them.

Moreover, we cannot persuade ourselves that the division of this work originated with Ambrose. We prefer to attribute it to some schoolman, who, observing that nearly everything treated by Philo in two books is contained in this treatise also, judged that it too should be divided in two. But he did this so perversely that he placed the beginning of the second book where not even a chapter ought to begin. The second book would certainly have begun much more conveniently from the point at which the holy man starts to discuss the second fault in Cain’s sacrifice. Yet, although this division is absurd, it has passed down from manuscripts of the most ancient age to the time of printed editions; we too have judged it should be retained, lest any confusion arise in citations.

[Col. 0315C]

**TWO BOOKS OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON CAIN AND ABEL**  
[Note: [Col. 0315A] Written about the year 375.] (C)

## BOOK ONE

### 183 CHAPTER I

After a brief transition from the preceding book to this one, the birth of Cain and Abel is treated; and it is shown that through them, as also through Esau and Jacob, two mutually opposing classes of human beings are foreshadowed.

[Col. 0315A]

1. In the preceding work, concerning Paradise, according to our capacity and as we were able, we arranged the understanding which the Lord poured in, including Adam’s and Eve’s fall. Now, since that fault did not remain with its authors, but—what is worse—found a worse heir, let us undertake the following history and continue our work upon those things which are joined to it according to the divine Scriptures.

2. “Now Adam knew Eve his wife; she conceived and bore Cain, and said: ‘I have acquired a man through God’” (Gen. 4:1). When we acquire something, one normally considers from what, by whom, and through what we acquire it: “from what,” as from material; “by whom,” as from an author; “through what,” as through some instrument. Does she here say, “I have acquired a man through God,” so that you should understand God as an instrument? Certainly not; rather, so that you should understand God as author and worker. Hence she gave greater credit to God when she said, “I have acquired a man through God,” so that we too, whenever we acquire anything, ought to ascribe every favorable outcome more to God than to arrogate it to ourselves.

3. “And she added to bear Abel” (Gen. 4:2). When something is added, what was previously there is removed. This is inferred from arithmetical proportions [Note: [Col. 0317D] One Vatican manuscript and the old edition: “proportions.”], or from the thoughts of the soul: when a number is added, another number results and the former is abolished; and a new thought arriving excludes the preceding one. Therefore, when Abel is added, Cain is taken away.

This is more fully perceived from the interpretation of their names. For Cain means “acquisition,” because he acquired all things for himself; Abel means one who referred all things to God with the devout attention of a pious mind, [Note: [Col. 0317D] Thus three manuscripts and the old edition. But one Vatican manuscript, like the marginal note of Gill: “by the intention of the mind.”] arrogating nothing to himself as his elder brother did, but attributing wholly to the Creator whatever he had received from Him.

4. Therefore, under the names of the two brothers there are two classes, mutually contending and opposed to one another. One attributes everything to its own mind as the ruling principle, and as though it were a certain author of every thought, perception, and movement; that is, it ascribes all discoveries to human ingenuity. The other gives credit to God as worker and Creator of all, and subjects everything to His governance as that of a father and ruler. The former is signified by Cain; the latter is called Abel. [Note: [Col. 0317D] Thus three manuscripts and the old edition. In one Vatican manuscript, in the margin: “The former ... the latter,” etc.; another Vatican manuscript and the Roman edition: “The former is signified by Cain; the latter by Abel.”]

One soul brings forth these two classes; and therefore they are held to be siblings, because they are founded in one womb. Yet they are opposed, because, once they have been brought forth with a kind of birth-pang of the soul, they must be divided and separated. For those who contend cannot permanently share one dwelling. Thus Rebecca, when she bore two dispositions of human character, one evil and the other good, and felt them leap within her womb—for Esau was a type of wickedness, while Jacob bore the figure of goodness—wondered what this was, seeing a kind of discord in the offspring she had conceived. She consulted God, that He might disclose the affliction and give the remedy. Thus this answer was returned to her prayer: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall come forth from your belly” (Gen. 25:23).

If you refer this to the soul, you will understand it as the begetter [Note: [Col. 0317D] All editions: “mother”; one Vatican manuscript: “generation”; three others: “begetting.”] of both good and evil, because each flows from the same fountain of the soul. But the mark of sober and true judgment is to reject evil, nourish what is good, and strengthen it. Therefore, before it gives birth to good—that is, to the reverence due to God—[Note: [Col. 0317D] Thus the manuscripts. The editions: “But before it gives birth, it is good to offer the reverence due to God, that it may ascribe everything to Him and not prefer its own things.”] it ought to ascribe everything to Him and not set its own things before His. [Note: [Col. 0318D] All editions: “not prefer its own things, that is, not call them its own.” The manuscripts, however, omit the negation; and not wrongly, if “its own” is used in place of “His,” referring to God.] But when it has brought forth the confession that gives credit to God, it lays aside the swelling of its heart. Therefore, when God added the good doctrine Abel to the soul, He removed the wicked doctrine Cain.

### CHAPTER II

Cain is a figure of the Jews, Abel of Christians. On this occasion certain matters concerning the fathers are appended, especially concerning Isaac’s burial—through whom Christ’s incarnation is expressed—and Moses’ burial—through whom Christ’s teaching office is expressed. Finally, the burials of Moses and Christ are compared.

[Col. 0318A]

5. Yet in this passage, according to Scripture, I understand rather the mystery of two peoples: by adding to His Church the faith of the pious people, God took away the faithlessness of the transgressing people. For the words themselves appear to signify this, when God says: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall come forth from your belly” (Gen. 25:23). In these two brothers, Cain and Abel, the figure of Synagogue and Church came first. Through Cain is understood the parricidal people of the Jews, who persecuted the blood of their Lord and Creator and—by virtue of His birth from the Virgin Mary—of their brother, so to speak. Through Abel, however, is understood the Christian who cleaves to God, as David also says: “But for me, it is good to cleave to God” (Ps. 72:28), so that he may attach himself to heavenly things and separate himself from earthly ones. Elsewhere he says: “My soul has failed for Your word” (Ps. 118:81), because he had placed the order and practice of life not in earthly pleasures, but in the knowledge of the Word.

From this it is recognized that what we read in the books of Kings was not written idly but deliberately and with careful consideration: “And he was added to his fathers” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 2:11, 21). It is thereby made clear that he was like the fathers in faith. Hence it is evident that the phrase refers not to bodily burial but to fellowship of life.

6. Thus it is not thought casually written of Isaac (Gen. 35:29) that, putting aside the form of this body which was joined to his soul, he was added to his kindred, because he clung to his father’s character. He says beautifully “to his kindred,” not “to his people,” as elsewhere. For we read in other places that men were added to their people, but those men were not so eminent. The one who is like a few rather than many is more eminent; for there are more in one’s people than in one’s kindred, and it is judged more excellent to resemble few than many.

Therefore, he who had been begotten by God’s promise, chosen for sacrifice to prove piety, content with the fellowship of one wife—that is, of Wisdom alone—was to be established by the testimony of divine Scripture as an imitator of that heavenly kindred which is one and always consistent with itself, not an imitator of common vulgarity. For where there are labor, instruction, and meditation, there is a common fellowship with many and a kind of popular association. For many make progress through hearing; these He called “the people.” But where instruction is received not by human tradition but by ingenious inference, without the practice of labor, there is the incorrupt, unalloyed purity of an exalted kindred. Therefore Isaac, as God’s gift, is read as having been added rather to his kindred than to his people, so that you may recognize him as a diligent imitator of divine rather than human things.

7. Blessed also is that mind which, rising above form and even kindred, deserves to hear what was said to Moses when he was separated from the people: “But you, stand here with Me” (Deut. 5:31). For as in Isaac the type of the Lord’s incarnation, transcending the customary course of human generation, surpassed those before him—so that in him there shone forth not an ordinary, popular favor but a special prerogative, as the reading teaches: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as of many, but as of one: ‘and to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16)—so too in Moses was the figure of the coming Teacher, who would teach the Law, preach the Gospel, fulfill the Old Testament, establish the New, and give heavenly food to the peoples. He surpassed the dignity of the human condition so greatly that he was granted the name of God, as we have written: “I have made you a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1).

For he was victor over every passion, captured by no enticements of the world; he had covered this whole bodily habitation with the heavenly purity of his manner of life, governing the mind, subjecting the flesh, and chastising it with a kind of royal authority. He was called by the name of God, to whose likeness he had fashioned himself through the abundance of perfect virtue.

8. Therefore we do not read concerning him, as concerning the rest, that “failing, he died”; [Note: [Col. 0319D] From these words some later writers seem to infer that Ambrose’s opinion was that Moses did not die. Yet, if his somewhat obscure words are weighed more attentively, you will observe that he intended to express Philo’s opinion, who is known to have discussed Moses’ death in a spiritual sense, without being so concerned with the literal sense.] rather, “he died through the word of God” (Deut. 34:5). For God suffers neither failure nor diminution, nor does He admit addition. Hence Scripture also adds: “No one knows his burial place to this day” (ibid., v. 6), so that you may understand rather his translation than his destruction. For death is a kind of separation of soul and body.

Thus he died through the word of God, as Scripture says, not “according to the word,” so that you may observe that it expresses not a message of death but a gift of grace. He was translated rather than abandoned, and no one knows his burial place. For who could discover his remains among earthly things when the Son of God showed in the Gospel that he was with Him (Matt. 17:3)? Indeed Elijah too was seen with Him; he was translated in a chariot and is not read to have been buried or to have died (4 Kings [2 Kings] 2:11). [Note: [Col. 0320D] The Fleury manuscript: “but through the word of God, when he is with the Son of God.”] For he lives who is with the Son of God.

Moses, however, is indeed read to have died, but to have died through the Word of God, through whom all things were made. By the Word of God the heavens were established. Therefore, through the Word of God there is not a collapse of the work, but a firm establishment. Thus he is not discovered as one fallen back to earth through the dissolution of his body, but as one endowed through the operation and gift of the heavenly Word, so that his flesh received rest rather than a tomb.

9. The distinction between lord and servant is rightly maintained. That you may understand the prerogative of the Lord and the grace granted to the servant, it is written of Moses that no one knows his burial place; but of Christ: “His burial was taken away from the earth” (Isa. 53:8). For Moses, according to the mystery of the Law, awaited redemption in order that he might rise; Christ, according to the gift of the Gospel, did not await redemption but bestowed it. Therefore His burial was not unknown but raised up, since creation could no longer hold it, because through Him all creation hastened to be lifted from slavery to corruption.

No one, then, knows Moses’ burial because all know his life; but we saw Christ’s burial, yet now we no longer know it, since we have acknowledged His resurrection. For His tomb had to be known so that the resurrection might be made manifest. Therefore in the Gospel the tomb is described with the utmost precision (Matt. 27:60 ff.); in the Law it is not sought, because although the Law announced His resurrection (Isa. 11:10), the sequence of the Gospel has demonstrated it to us most fully.

### CHAPTER III

By Abel and Cain are signified the successive stages of human wisdom, a process not found in Christ alone; through the order in which the brothers are named, and through their respective occupations, Abel is shown, though younger, to be superior to his brother.

[Col. 0320C]

10. Therefore, to complete what we proposed: “She added,” it says, “to bear Abel”; that is, Eve, who had earlier sinned grievously, produced from herself a better judgment, in order that it might abolish the error of the earlier judgment. I am mistaken if this is not proved in all human beings. For we are born so that first there is in us the weak understanding of infancy, then that of childhood, which knows concern only for the body and has no reverence, no observance of divine things.

Hence, in order to prove the birth of Jesus Christ from a Virgin by the manifest newness of nature, the prophet says: “Behold, the Virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and His name shall be called Emmanuel. He shall eat butter and honey, because before He knows evil or good, He will not believe wickedness, in order to choose what is good” (Isa. 7:14 ff.). [Note: [Col. 0320D] The old edition with the Laudian manuscript: “He shall eat, before He knows evil or good, He will not believe,” etc. The Roman edition: “He shall eat, and therefore before He knows evil or good, He will not believe,” etc. We have restored the passage from two Vatican and two French manuscripts.] And below: “Before the child knows how to call father and mother, he shall receive the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of Assyria” (Isa. 8:4).

For He alone was not captured by the vanity of this world and bodily pride, since He humbled Himself, becoming obedient even unto death. He is altogether unlike each of us, because we vainly exalt ourselves, puffed up by the mind of the flesh. Hence no one is without sin, not even an infant of one day; but He committed no sin. Therefore Cain, preferring himself, is born first in us; afterward Abel is generated, in whom there is reverence for the Godhead. Thus what is evil first creeps in, and afterward what is good is recognized. But where good is, there is justice; where justice is, there is holiness—that is, Abel, who cleaves to God.

11. “And Abel became a shepherd of sheep, but Cain cultivated the ground” (Gen. 4:2). It is not without purpose that, although Cain was born first, as the reading teaches, Abel is put first here; nor is the order of the names the same as the order of nature. What does this change of order mean, that the younger is mentioned first where the condition of life and exercise of occupation are described? Let us inquire into the difference of their offices, so that we may discover the reason for the preference.

To cultivate the ground is prior in practice but inferior in grace to feeding sheep. For the latter is the role of a teacher and ruler. Thus the elder fittingly began with more ancient things; the younger preferred more recent things, which would produce neither thorns nor thistles and would be subject to no sentence. Indeed, Adam, guilty of sin, was sent out of the Paradise of delight to cultivate the ground. Therefore, where these brothers are born, the order of nature is also retained in the narrative; but where the discipline of life is expressed, the younger is preferred to the elder, because, though younger in time, he is superior in virtue.

For innocence is later in time than wickedness and roughly of equal age, but more ancient in the nobility of its merits. For old age is venerable not because it is gray with years but because of character. “The age of old age,” it says, “is an immaculate life” (Wis. 4:8). Therefore, where generation is expressed, let Cain come first; where instruction in disciplines is proclaimed, let Abel run ahead. Who would deny that adolescence, even youth itself at its beginning, boils with the enticements of various passions? But when a more mature age succeeds, does not calm return—as though the storm of youthful wantonness had been dispersed—and does not the vessel of the weary soul withdraw into certain quiet harbors? Thus the violent motions of our youth are calmed by the secure haven of faithful old age.

### CHAPTER IV

Wickedness is earlier in time, virtue in dignity. The same is signified by Esau and Jacob, and by the two women in Scripture, one of whom is an image of virtue, the other of pleasure. Finally, the arts of the latter are described.

[Col. 0321D]

12. Therefore, instructed by such examples of nature, do not doubt that wickedness precedes in time but is youthful in weakness. It has the privilege of age; virtue, however, has the prerogative of glory, to which the unjust commonly yields before the just. Divine Scripture, a faithful witness, teaches this when it tells how Esau—the man whose additional name denotes foolishness—patiently yielded his birthright to his brother Jacob, so that he said: “What is the birthright to me?” (Gen. 25:32). But the man whose name denotes exercise sought to earn the very things Esau despised.

Does not Esau seem to you like one defeated in the contest, who, considering himself unequal through the weakness of his own mind, yielded the victor’s crown to one whom he saw could not be bent by the enticements of passions—whose dust he himself could not endure? “What is the birthright to me?” he says. For among the cowardly there are no badges of virtue; among the wise they hold first place, for pursuits of virtue are certain instruments. Thus, just as a warrior cannot exist without weapons, neither can virtue without exercise. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven is pressed upon, and those who press upon it seize it” (Matt. 11:12). And elsewhere: “Seek the kingdom of God, and behold, all things are ready for you” (Matt. 6:33). Rewards are promised not to sleepers or idlers, but to the watchful and laboring; and a reward is prepared for labor, which, though not agreeable, is fruitful for its reward.

13. The discourse of the Law teaches this, as we find written: “If,” it says, “a man has two wives, one beloved and the other hated, and both the beloved and the hated bear him sons, and the firstborn son belongs to the hated woman, then on the day when he leaves his sons heirs of his property, he may not give the birthright to the son of the beloved woman while passing over the son of the hated woman; but he shall acknowledge the firstborn son of the hated woman, to give him a portion from all that is found in his possession, because he is the beginning of his sons and the firstfruits are owed to him” (Deut. 21:15 ff.). [Note: [Col. 0321D] The old edition: “acknowledging, he shall give him a dowry.” The Roman edition: “he shall acknowledge, so as to give him a double portion.” Evidently from the Septuagint, where one reads: *epignōsetai dounai autō dipla*, etc.]

How profound are the hidden secrets of mysteries in the letter! Soul, recognize your offspring and seek the mystery of this hated woman. You will find her within yourself, if you seek. Recall your thoughts, reread your perceptions, and you will recognize to whom the firstfruits are due. For two women dwell with each one of us, differing through enmities and discords, filling the house of our soul as with rival contests of jealousy. One of them is pleasing and dear to us, a flattering conciliator of favor, called Pleasure. We think her our companion and member of our household. The other we regard as harsh, rough, and wild; her name is Virtue.

14. Pleasure, then, brazen in a harlot’s movement, with an unrestrained gait softened by delights, casts nets with wavering eyes and playful, darting eyelids, by which she captures the precious souls of young men—for “the eye of a harlot is a snare for the sinner” (Prov. 7:10 ff.). Whoever she sees passing by the corner of the street before her house with uncertain judgment, [Note: [Col. 0322D] Roman edition: “a youth lacking judgment”; the Septuagint also follows this reading: *neanian endeē phrenōn*.] she approaches with seductive words, making young men’s hearts fly: restless at home, wandering in the streets, lavish with kisses, cheap in modesty, rich in dress, painted on the cheeks.

For, since she cannot possess the true beauty of nature, she embellishes not reality but an appearance of affected beauty with adulterous cosmetics. Surrounded by the retinue of vices and enclosed by a kind of chorus of wickedness, the leader of crimes attacks the wall of the human mind with these engines of speech:

> “I have a peace-offering; today I am paying my vows.  
> For this reason I came out to meet you, desiring to find your face. [Note: [Col. 0323D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the Laudian manuscript: “I have found you.” The Septuagint agrees: *pothousa to son prosōpon heurēka se*. And shortly afterward the same manuscripts: “let us rejoice together in desire.”]  
> I have woven my bed with cords and covered it with tapestries from Egypt.  
> I have sprinkled my bed with saffron, and my house with cinnamon.  
> Come, let us enjoy love until daybreak; come, and let us wrestle in desire.”  
> (Prov. 7:14 ff.)

For through Solomon’s mouth we see this picture of the adulteress portrayed. What is so harlot-like as worldly pleasure, which enters from the window of its house, first playing out its temptations through the eyes? It quickly penetrates if you look out upon the street—that is, upon the public paths of passersby—instead of directing your mind’s gaze toward the inner mysteries of the Law.

This indeed is she who has woven for us, by stronger bonds, as it were a bed of shared union, so that whoever reclines there may be bound. She covers the bed of her body with the veil of shameful deceit, concealing, to stir young men’s minds, the absence of her husband—that is, the neglect of the Law. For the Law is absent from those who sin; if it were present, sin would not be committed. Hence she says: “My husband is not at home; he has gone on a very long journey, carrying in his hand a bag of money” (ibid., vv. 19–20).

What should I say this means, except perhaps that the rich think that nothing does not yield to their money, and wish the Law to be purchasable for their favor? Pleasure scatters her fragrances because she does not possess Christ’s fragrance; she displays treasures, promises kingdoms, pledges unceasing loves, offers untried intercourse, instruction without a teacher, speech without a monitor, a life without anxiety, soft sleep, and insatiable desire.

“By the abundance of her flattering words,” it says, “and binding him with the snares of her lips, she drew him all the way to her house. But he who followed her is ensnared” (ibid., v. 21).

The palace shone with royal luxury, splendid with carved walls, and its wet floors swam in wine. The ground burned with perfume, covered with fishbones and slippery from flowers already withering. There were the tumult of revelers, the shouting of contestants, the slaughter of quarrelers, the music of diners, [Note: [Col. 0323D] Thus the old edition with one Vatican manuscript and the Dijon manuscript; the Roman edition with others: “the music of singers.”] the noise of dancers, the laughter of those who laughed loudly, the applause of those given to wantonness—everything confused, nothing in nature’s order. Shorn dancing women, boys curling their hair, the surfeit of feasters, the belching of eaters, the thirst of drunkards, yesterday’s excess, today’s drunkenness, drinking cups filled with vomit, more strongly scented with drunkenness than if fresh wine alone gave off its fragrance.
