She herself stands in the midst and says: “Drink and be drunk, so that each may fall and not rise again. He is first with me who is the most utterly ruined of all. He is mine who is not his own. He is more pleasing to me who is more wicked to himself. Babylon’s golden cup is in my hand, making the whole earth drunk; all nations have drunk from my wine. Whoever, therefore, is foolish, let him turn aside to me; and to those lacking wisdom I command, saying: ‘Use hidden bread pleasantly, and drink sweeter water secretly’” (Prov. 9:17). “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. Our life will pass like the traces of a cloud and be scattered like mist” (Wis. 2:8 ff.). “Come, then, let us enjoy the good things that exist and make swift use of creation as in youth. Let us fill ourselves with precious wine and ointments, and let no flower of the season pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither. Let there be no meadow through which our luxury does not pass; everywhere let us leave marks of rejoicing” (Wis. 2:8 ff.).

“All these things are left behind; no one will carry away with himself anything except what he has obtained through bodily pleasure. Indeed, I established this philosophy, and there is no other truer philosophy than that which asserts that the good is what is pleasant and agreeable. Therefore believe either philosophy or Solomon’s wisdom.”

### CHAPTER V

When pleasure has made its assault, virtue gives sounder counsel. It teaches how demonic temptations must be resisted, from whom temporal goods too ought to be sought, and how harmful they are to the wicked. It invites us to Wisdom’s banquet, explains how its intoxication differs from drunkenness, and finally sets forth the evils of avarice.

[Col. 0324B]

15. Hearing these things, he hangs wounded, like a stag struck in the liver by an arrow. Virtue, taking pity on him and seeing that he will quickly fall, unexpectedly comes to meet him, [Note: [Col. 0324D] One Vatican manuscript, the Dijon and Fleury manuscripts, and the old edition: “comes to meet him with truth.” The Laudian manuscript: “truth comes to meet him.” Better: the other Vatican manuscript and the Roman edition: “comes to meet him, fearing lest,” etc.] fearing lest, amid delay and soothing enticements, the human mind be captured.

“I appeared openly to you when you were not seeking me.” Let not the uncontrolled and luxurious woman, who knows no modesty, deceive the unwary and ensnare you: she “sits at the doors of her house on a chair, openly calling to those who pass by in the streets” (Prov. 9:14–15). “Now therefore, son, hear me; attend to the words of my mouth. Let not your heart turn aside into her ways. For she has cast down many by wounding them, and those whom she has slain are innumerable. The ways of her house are the ways of hell, leading into the recess of death” (Prov. 7:24 ff.).

Therefore remove from yourself a perverse mouth and drive unjust lips far away. “Let your eyes look straight ahead” (Prov. 4:24–25); do not attend to a deceitful woman (Prov. 5:2). For honey drips from the lips of a harlot woman; she fattens your throat for a time, but afterward you will find her more bitter than gall. A day would fail me sooner than I could expound her vices, though they have been described and portrayed in Proverbs by the mouth of Wisdom (Prov. 6:24 ff.).

Do not be overcome by desire for beauty. It is adulterous, smeared with cosmetics, and does not shine with true and sincere loveliness. Do not be captured by her eyes, for nets are spread around her (Song 2:8–9). Rather, be like and follow Him who “leaps over mountains and skips over hills, looking through the windows, appearing above the nets.” The bonds of pleasure are evil. It delights the eyes, soothes the ears, but stains the mind; it tells many lies, joins falsehood to them, removes truth, promises money, offers gold, but takes away instruction (Prov. 8:10).

But receive instruction rather than money, and knowledge above tested gold. For it is better than precious stones (Prov. 3:10 ff.). I shall not hide from you the things that are said to be its highest attractions, [Note: [Col. 0325D] All editions and two Vatican manuscripts: “lest I seem to cover up,” etc. Better: the Dijon, Fleury, and Laudian manuscripts: “lest I seem to uncover.”] lest I seem to uncover what displeases in pleasure and cast a shadow over what pleases. For with persuasive words it lifts up and exalts the mind, showing all the kingdoms of the earth and saying: “All these I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me.” There beware lest you be carried away by things that pass by and do not remain, in which there is great temptation.

16. The Lord Jesus certainly taught you how to withstand temptations of this kind. The devil first spread the snare of gluttony, saying: “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread” (Matt. IV.3–4). The Lord answered: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.” By this saying he loosed the snare.

Again the devil set [Col. 0325B] a second snare, that of vainglory, which is accustomed to choke even a good mind as it runs along prosperous paths: “And he led him,” it says, “to Jerusalem, and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down from here. For it is written that he commanded his angels concerning you, that they should preserve you, because they shall bear you up in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone” (ibid., 5–6).

Therefore, although the Lord Jesus—whose spiritual flights were available to him—could have cast himself down without any danger, nevertheless, lest it should be an instance of vainglory, he answered the devil: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (ibid., 7). At the same time he taught us to beware of doing the devil’s will. If, then, vainglory truly must be avoided, how much more ought no one to put forward false things as true? There remains a third snare: that of avarice and ambition. He showed him, from a mountain, all the kingdoms of the world in [Col. 0325C] a moment of time (ibid., 8 ff.). Aptly, in a moment, because they cannot endure for long. Wait a little, and they quickly pass away.

Accordingly, those who follow such things seem to themselves to be on a mountain; but they are not lasting, as you have it written: “I saw the ungodly exceedingly exalted and 192 raised above the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Ps. XXXVI.35). But one who makes much of these things appears to worship the devil, whose god is his belly and whose glory is in shameful things. But seek glory in God, who says to you: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. IV.10), from whom you may receive eternal things, not temporal ones.

17. Yet, if anyone is delighted even by such things, let him ask for them more moderately from him who is the true source of all things.

> [Note: Col. 0325D] Thus all editions. But one Vatican manuscript and the Laud manuscript read: “For money itself, and those things,” etc. The other Vatican manuscript, the Divionensis, and the Florentine read: “For even those moneyed things which,” etc.

For even the private possessions which the devil seems to possess, [Col. 0325D] are another’s, as he himself said: “I will give you all this power and their glory, because they have been delivered to me” (ibid., 9). Therefore hope in him. Although a long provision for a short life need not be sought, nevertheless hope in him who created the whole creation, who delivered these things to the devil for a time—not that he might possess them, but that he might tempt by them. For there could not be a crown without a contest. Those whose standing was uncertain had to be tested, so that the righteous might be crowned.

18. He therefore gave these things to the devil because, in these very things, there is punishment for the recipient if he does not know how to use them. For what is treasure to the luxurious person but expenditure upon luxury? Hence it is not the luxurious but the frugal person who is approved. Therefore use temperately the things set before you, lest, when you eat much, you become odious. “For wakefulness and torments are for a gluttonous man” (Ecclus. XXXI.23). And below: “If you have been compelled while eating, rise and vomit, and it will relieve you, and you will not bring weakness upon your body” (ibid., 25).

Thus gluttony has killed very many; frugality, no one. Wines have harmed countless persons; moderation, none. Many have poured out their lives amid feasts and filled their tables with their own blood. To some, indigestion has at once taken away both voice and sense; and, if indigestion was not harmful to some, drunkenness brought them ruin. For drunkenness has driven some into crime—although it [Note: Col. 0326D] All editions read, “although it is not a crime,” contrary to the manuscripts.—is itself a crime—and has reduced others to poverty.

Finally, hear whom [Col. 0326B] Christ excludes: “When the master of the house has entered and shut the door, you will begin to stand outside and knock at the door, saying, ‘Open to us.’ And he will answer and say: ‘I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all workers of iniquity.’ Then you will begin to say: ‘We ate and drank before you, and you taught in our streets.’ And he will say to you: ‘I do not know where you are from’” (Luke XIII.25 ff.). You have heard what he said concerning those who eat. Now hear what he says concerning those who fast: “Blessed are those who now hunger and thirst, because they shall be filled” (Luke VI.21). And below: “Woe to you who are full, because you shall hunger” (ibid., 25).

19. But do you wish to eat? Do you wish to drink? Come to the banquet of Wisdom, who invites all with great proclamation, saying: “Come and eat my breads, and drink the wine which I have mixed for you” (Prov. IX.5). Do songs delight you, songs that might charm the banqueter? Hear the Church exhorting; hear her singing, not only in songs but also in the Song of Songs: “Eat, my neighbours, and drink, and be intoxicated, [Note: Col. 0326D] Thus the ancient edition, with one Vatican manuscript, the Divionensis, and the Laud manuscript. The Roman edition, with others, reads “my brothers,” as also the LXX; the Vulgate, however, “my dearest ones.”] my fathers” (Cant. V.1).

But this intoxication makes people sober; it is intoxication of grace, not of drunkenness. It produces joy, not staggering. Nor should you fear that, at the Church’s banquet, pleasant scents, sweet foods, diverse drinks, noble fellow-guests, or fitting attendants will be lacking to you. What is nobler than Christ, who at the Church’s banquet both serves and is served? Attach yourself to the side of this reclining fellow-guest, and join yourself to God. Do not disdain the table which Christ chose, saying: “I entered my garden, my sister, my bride; I gathered my myrrh [Col. 0326D] with my spices; I ate my bread with my honey, and drank my wine with my milk” (ibid.).

The Church’s banquet is in the garden—that is, in paradise—where Adam was before he committed sin. There Eve reclined before she created and bore guilt. There you will gather myrrh, that is, Christ’s burial; so that, buried with him through baptism into death, as he rose from the dead, you too may rise. There you will eat the bread which strengthens [Col. 0327A] the human heart. You will taste honey, by which the passages of your throat may be made sweet. You will drink wine with milk—that is, with brightness and sincerity: whether because it is pure simplicity; or because it is unstained grace, received for the remission of sins; or because it nurses little ones at the breasts of its consolation, so that, weaned amid delights, they may grow into the fullness of perfect age.

Enter, then, into this banquet. Or do you fear that a too-narrow house and a small dining-place may confine you? “O Israel, how great is the house of the Lord, and how immense the place of his possession! Great, and it has no end; high, and immeasurable” (Baruch III.24). “There were those giants who were from the beginning, of great stature, skilled in war.” The Lord did not choose them. And rightly he did not choose them, because they knew war, not peace. Therefore learn peace, that you may be chosen by God.

But lest [Col. 0327B] you perhaps think the house’s greatness unadorned, and find pleasure in columned lodging-places: “Wisdom built herself a house, [Note: Col. 0327D] The editions read, “and carved.” The manuscripts read, “and made shine.” Evidently from the LXX translation, where it reads, καὶ ὑπήρεισε στύλους ἑπτά, “and she set up seven pillars.” [Col. 0328D] The Vulgate: “and hewed out,” etc.] and made seven pillars shine.” The Lord Jesus himself also declares that there are many dwelling-places with his Father (John XIV.2). In this house, therefore, you will feast upon food for the soul and drink for the mind, so that afterward you may neither hunger nor thirst ever again. For one who eats eats unto fullness, and one who drinks drinks unto intoxication.

20. But this intoxication is the guardian of chastity; that intoxication of wine is tinder for lust, by which the inner organs steam through the flesh, the mind is set ablaze, and the soul is scorched. Lust is a cruel spur to crimes; it never permits the affections to remain at rest. It burns by night, pants by day, wakes one from sleep, draws one away from business, [Col. 0327C] recalls one from reason, takes away counsel, disturbs lovers, inclines those who have fallen, plots against the chaste, inflames by possession, and is kindled by use. It has no limit in sinning and an unquenchable thirst for crimes, which cannot be extinguished except by the death of its lover. Therefore the Apostle says: “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. VI.18), so that by swift flight we may escape the cruelty of a frenzied mistress and emerge from foul slavery.

21. For what shall I say of avarice: the insatiable desire for money and a certain lust for bronze, which believes itself the poorer the more it has taken away? Envious toward all, worthless toward itself, poor amid the greatest riches, it diminishes in desire what it abounds in by wealth. There is no limit to plundering where there is no measure in desiring. Thus it inflames [Col. 0327D] the mind; thus it feeds it with its fire, so that the difference here is that the former is an adulteress of bodily forms, the latter of lands. It shakes the elements, ploughs the sea, digs up the earth, wearies heaven with prayers, is pleased neither with clear weather nor with clouds, condemns annual yields and complains against the earth’s fruits.

But this is a sickness of the soul, not health. Thus Ecclesiastes says: “There is a grievous sickness which I have seen under the sun: riches kept to the harm of their possessor” (Eccl. V.12). And above: “He who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver” (ibid., 9). And: “There is no end of their acquisition” (Baruch III.18). If you seek treasures, receive invisible and hidden ones, which you may seek in the heights of heaven, not those in [Col. 0328A] the veins of the earth. Be poor in spirit, and you will be rich whatever your wealth; for human life does not consist in an abundance of riches but in virtue and faith. These riches will make you truly rich, if you are rich toward God.

## CHAPTER VI

Virtue is acquired by diligence and labour. This is shown by the example of Jacob, who obtained precedence over his brother; and mystical meanings concerning Abraham, Moses, and those same two brothers are expounded.

22. You have heard the mysteries of pleasure; you have also heard the gifts of our resources. I thought these should be displayed, not clothed with rhetorical ornament, but in the bare words of Scripture, so that they might shine with their own light and utter their own voice to one another. For the sun [Col. 0328B] and moon do not need an interpreter. They have as interpreter the radiance of their own light, with which the whole world is filled. For them faith is illumination without a guide, a kind of self-authenticating witness, so to speak, which does not need another’s testimony, since it immediately pours itself out before the eyes of all.

Therefore our works are not announced; they cry out and announce themselves. Yet, lest I pass over what is considered laborious in our case, faith is required, zeal is desired, deeds are sought. For in these three the Lord Jesus defined the duties of human devotion, saying: “Ask, and it shall be given to you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. VII.7). And below: “Everyone, therefore, who hears these my words and does them is like a wise man” (ibid., 24).

23. Whoever has pursued these things diligently will receive the precedence [Col. 0328C] of blessing, like the patriarch Jacob, who by continence and faith supplanted the traces of human passions. He said: “God has had mercy on me, and I have all things” (Gen. XXXIII.11). Let us therefore merit this mercy by faith, diligence, and works—the disciplines through which Israel found God’s grace and, through it, all things. For he rejoiced not that the resources of this world were available to him, but the disciplines of virtues.

Let us appoint these as our heirs, as holy Abraham appointed them as heirs to himself in his son Isaac, assigning the entire inheritance of all his works to a wise and righteous man and leaving no right of inheritance to maidservants or to the sons of maidservants, but only gifts by donation. For perfect virtues receive the whole inheritance of glory; to common and middling things something cheap is sprinkled. Therefore Hagar, whose Latin name means “stranger” and “sojourner,” and Keturah, which means “fragrant,” are not heirs. For one who employs middling disciplines is a sojourner, not an inhabitant, of wisdom. One is sprinkled with scent, not filled with fruit. Food, not scent, brings health, because scent is the herald of fruits. Thus we recognize that those who follow the chief disciplines, and natives, are to be preferred to sojourners.

24. This is according to the natural sense.

> [Note: Col. 0328D] The Divionensis manuscript reads: “But according to the ministry.”

But according to the mystery, Abraham, father of nations, transferred the whole inheritance of his faith [Col. 0329A] to his lawful seed, which is Christ, who was in this land as a sojourner, in order that he might bear away rather the fragrance than the fruit of this life.

When the mind hears these things, it turns away from pleasure and joins itself to virtue, admiring the grace of true beauty: a pure affection, a simple judgment, a moderate garment—that is, “not in persuasive words, but in demonstration of the Spirit” (1 Cor. II.4)—such as is the form of apostolic doctrine: a garment of wisdom and piety, shining more precious than all gold. Then, welcoming the chorus of prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice, which breathed forth the fragrance of disciplines, instilled reverence, and poured in grace, the mind, moved by such things, chose the pursuits of virtue to which Jacob, a man full of exercise, directed his mind.

Therefore he is introduced as a shepherd of sheep (Gen. XXX.31 [Col. 0329B] ff.), because it is judged more excellent to rule one’s body, senses, and pleasures, and to keep measure in one’s desire, lest it wander uncertainly like a sheep, than to govern peoples or preside over cities. For it is more difficult for someone to rule himself than another. To conquer the mind, restrain anger, and bring the opposing laws of flesh and mind into unity is the work of a certain immortal man, whom the gate of hell has not seized.

Accordingly, the Lawgiver himself claimed this duty for himself: he tended Jethro’s sheep (Exod. III.1)—Jethro means “superfluous”—and led them into the wilderness, because he gathered into certain undiscriminating mysteries of sober teaching the irrational, superfluous chatter of common speech. Therefore shepherds of sheep were an abomination to the Egyptians. For all who are given over to bodily passions of this sort and indulge [Col. 0329C] their pleasures shun, with a kind of abhorrence, the disputant of the word and teacher of virtue.

And therefore Moses taught through these enigmas (Gen. IV.4) that sacrifices acceptable to God are those which every foolish person rejects: namely, the works and commands of virtue. Accordingly Abel is read to have been a shepherd, but Cain a worker of the earth; for Cain, as a foolish man, could not bear the form and image of virtue expressed in his brother.

## CHAPTER VII

Having indicated Cain’s twofold defect in sacrifice, he shows that three vices can creep into our offerings; he also adduces divine testimonies by which these same vices are condemned.

25. “And it came to pass, after days, that Cain offered a gift to the Lord from the fruits [Col. 0329D] of the earth” (Gen. IV.3). There are two faults: one, that he offered after days; the other, that he offered from the fruits, not from the first fruits. A sacrifice is commended both by promptness and by grace. Hence it is commanded: “If you vow a vow, do not delay to pay it. For it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay” (Eccl. V.3–4). For when you delay, you do not pay.

A vow is a request for good things from God together with a promise to render an offering. Therefore, once you have obtained what you asked, it is ungrateful to delay what was promised. But sometimes forgetfulness of benefits received creeps upon the negligent, or upon the proud and self-exalted. To claim events for oneself is the mark of a dull heart: to attribute to one’s own powers the good one does or receives from God, to assign it not to the grace of its author, but to consider oneself the author of one’s own good things.

There is a third kind of sin, indeed a lesser one, but of equal arrogance: that of those who do not deny that God is the giver of good things, but consider that what has befallen them has rightfully come to them on account of their own prudence and the merits of their other virtues. They consider themselves worthy also of divine grace because they did not appear unworthy for such things to come to them through divine benefits.

26. Therefore, lest anything of this kind happen, whereby your vow may become sin to you, the law has instructed and trained you. The Lord who gave the law says: “Take heed to yourself, lest you forget the benefits of the Lord your God and do not keep his commandments, judgments, and statutes which I command you today; lest, when you have eaten and have been filled, [Col. 0330B] and when you have built good houses and begun to dwell in them, and when your sheep and oxen have been filled, and when you are filled with bronze, silver, and gold, and have begun to possess all things, and your barns have become full, your heart be exalted and you forget the Lord your God” (Deut. VIII.11 ff.).

You then forget the Lord when you have forgotten yourself. But if you recognize that you are weak, you will recognize that God is above all things, and you will be unable to be forgetful, so as to render him the reverence due to him.

27. Learn now how every person is warned not to consider himself the author of his own good things. “Do not say,” he says, “in your heart: ‘My strength and my power have made for me this great wealth’; but you shall keep the Lord your God in your mind, because he gives [Col. 0330C] strength to make wealth” (ibid., 17–18). Therefore the Apostle, as an interpreter of the law, rightly did not glory in his own power. Rather, he said that he was the least of the Apostles and that whatever he was came from divine grace, not from his own merit; and that we have nothing which we have not received. “For what,” he says, “do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. IV.7).

You have learned, therefore, to follow humility rather than arrogance; to seek diligence rather than power. You have received salutary precepts: do not neglect the useful instruments of medicine, by which every fibre of the deadly wound is cut away.

28. He also who considers himself righteous, lest he be puffed up by the swelling of his heart, received this salutary command, as the oracle declares in these words: “Do not say [Col. 0330D] in your heart, when the Lord your God begins to destroy those nations from before you: ‘The Lord brought me in to possess this land because of my righteousness’; but the Lord exterminated them from before you because of the iniquities of these nations” (Deut. IX.4–5). “Not because of your righteousness, not because of your goodness, nor because of the uprightness of your heart do you enter to possess this land; but because of the iniquity of the nations the Lord will destroy them from before you and will restore your Testament, which he swore to your fathers.”

The Testament is the perfect grace of God; for God gives nothing imperfect. Virtue is perfect, and so are works of virtue. It is called a Testament because by it an inheritance of good things is conveyed. Rightly it is called both [Col. 0331A] a Testament and divine, since those things which are truly good are bestowed under the attestation of heavenly commandments. And it is called a Testament because it was dedicated with blood: the old in a type, the new in truth. By this Testament we hold the pledge of divine grace, because God so loved this world that he gave his only-begotten Son for us all. Hence the Apostle, proclaiming the perfection of grace, says: “How did he not also give us all things with him?” (Rom. VIII.32).

## CHAPTER VIII

By the example of Abraham’s sacrifice are set forth the qualities by which an offering becomes pleasing to God: namely promptness, continuance, and faith. God commands promptness in both Testaments, and he himself displays it, since he not only gives quickly but also goes before us.

[Col. 0331B]

29. The first grace of a vow, therefore, is promptness in fulfilling it. Accordingly, Abraham, commanded to offer his son as a burnt offering, did not act after days, as Cain did; rather, rising early, he saddled his ass, took with him two servants and his son Isaac, split wood for the burnt offering, rose, went, and came on the third day to the place which God had told him (Gen. XXII.3).

First observe the mature and eager zeal of one about to sacrifice: there was to be no delay of waiting except until the oracle was heard. Then observe that he saddled his own ass, undertook every service himself, and prepared what was necessary for the sacrifice, [Note: Col. 0331D] Thus all editions. The manuscripts, by contrast, with great agreement: “with the two virtues of faith as companions,” etc. This is not bad, provided that the two companion virtues of faith are understood to be hope and charity.] accompanied also by the two virtues of faith and hope, leading his victim, certain of God’s power and secure concerning his goodness.

30. And the phrase, “on the third day,” means either that devotion ought to be continuous and perpetual. For time is threefold: past, present, and future. By this we are warned that no forgetfulness should creep in regarding God’s past, present, or future benefits, but that a tenacious remembrance of grace should endure and obedience should not be lacking.

Or it means that one who sacrifices ought to believe in the one radiance, the one light, of the Trinity. For [Note: Col. 0331D] Absent from the Florentine manuscript: “For to one who sacrifices faithfully, day shines and there is no night.”] day shines for one who sacrifices faithfully, and there is no night. Thus in Exodus Moses says: “We shall go a three-day journey and sacrifice to the Lord our God” (Exod. III.18).

But elsewhere also, when God appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre: “Abraham,” it says, “lifting up his eyes, saw, and behold, three men stood above him. And seeing them, he ran to meet them [Col. 0331D] at the door of his tent, worshipped upon the ground, and said: ‘Lord, if I have found grace before you’” (Gen. XVIII.2–3). He sees three; he worships one. He offers three measures of fine flour (ibid., 6). For though God is immeasurable, he nevertheless holds the measure of all things, as it is written: “Who has measured the water with his hand, heaven with his palm, and the whole earth with his closed hand?” (Isa. XL.12).

Thus the holy Patriarch offered to the perfect Trinity in the individual persons a sacrifice in the inward sanctuary of the mind—that is, of spiritual fine flour. This is the fine flour which that woman in the Gospel, who shall be taken, grinds: “One,” it says, “shall be taken and the other left” (Matt. XXIV.41). The Church shall be taken; the Synagogue shall be left. Or a good mind is taken, while a wicked one is left.

And, that you may know Abraham also believed in Christ: “Abraham,” he says, “saw my day and rejoiced” (John VIII.56). And one who believes in Christ also believes in the Father. One who believes perfectly in the Father believes in the Son and the Holy Spirit. Thus three measures, one fine flour: that is, there was one sacrifice, offered to the venerable Trinity with an equal measure, as it were, of devotion and a fitting fullness of piety [Col. 0332B].

31. Learn further the ardour of prompt devotion: “He ran,” it says, “and took one tender and good calf, and gave it to the servant, and he hastened to prepare it” (Gen. XVIII.7). Everywhere devotion is tireless; therefore his gift was acceptable to God. Elsewhere also you have the command to anticipate sunrise with prayer: “Meet the rising of the sun” (Wis. XVI.28). In the Gospel you have the Lord Jesus saying: “Zacchaeus, make haste and come down” (Luke XIX.5).

And he, because he had obtained what he desired—to see Christ—and had obtained even more, to be seen and called by Christ, hastened down and received him joyfully. Therefore the Lord approved his affection and granted him swift recompense, saying: “Because today salvation has come to this house” (ibid., 9). [Col. 0332C] For the Lord too hastened to do good; therefore he did not wait to promise and afterwards fulfill, but acted beforehand and afterwards declared it. For he said: “Salvation has come,” which [Note: Col. 0331D] The old edition and certain Paris editions read, “which certainly belongs to one going before [Col. 0332D], not to one promising.”] certainly belongs to one who goes before, not to one who promises.

The righteous person therefore commends his vow by promptness. And our fathers ate the Passover in haste, with their loins girded, their feet shod with the bonds of footwear, and, as though laying aside a bodily burden, ready for departure. [Note: Col. 0332D] The Roman edition alone: “with their loins girded, as though laying aside a bodily burden, their feet shod with the bonds of footwear, and staffs held in their hands, in order that,” etc.] For the Lord’s Passover is passage from passions to the exercises of virtue. Therefore it is called the Lord’s Passover, because then, in that type of the lamb, the truth of the Lord’s Passion was announced, and now its grace is celebrated.

32. Seek this swiftly, therefore, O soul, so that you too may swiftly hear, as Jacob heard: “What is this, that you found it so quickly, my son?” (Gen. XXVII.20). And he replied according to the doctrine: “Because the Lord your God delivered it into my hands.” God gives quickly, because “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.” For the Word of God [Note: Col. 0332D] Thus all manuscripts and the old edition; the Roman edition, however: “is not, as someone says, a work, but is working.”] is not a work, as someone says, but working, as you have it written: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John V.17).

He goes before all things; [Col. 0333A] for he is before all things as the Father is, and in all things as the same Father is, penetrating all things. For he is mighty and sharp, sharper than every sword, penetrating even to the division of soul and spirit, joints and marrow. He goes before the thoughts of all, concerning whom God the Father says: “Now you shall see whether my Word will overtake you or not” (Num. XI.23). For where God is, the Word also is, as he said: “We shall come and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV.23).

And as elsewhere you read concerning God: “I stood here before you” (Exod. XVII.6), so also the Word says: “Before you stood under the fig tree, I saw you” (John I.48). And it was said concerning the Word himself, that is, the Son of God: “One stands in your midst whom you do not know” (ibid., 26). For wherever the saints are, [Note: Col. 0333D] The Divionensis and Florentine manuscripts: “therefore the Word of God is in their midst.”] there, in their midst, is the Word of God, [Col. 0333B] filling seas and lands in the hearts of each one. And when he is here, he is also elsewhere—not by a change of place, but surely by the fullness of his presence. For he is everywhere: through all things and in all things, leaving no place free from himself. And where he is present, he was; and where he was, he is present. Therefore one who knows that the Word of God is swift asks swiftly and obtains swiftly.

## CHAPTER IX

Pharaoh is reproved for delay in obedience. Humility, secrecy, and brevity in prayer are commended, along with a censure of wordiness. How the Lord taught the manner of prayer; and finally, for whom one ought especially to pray.

33. But Pharaoh, who bestowed his zeal upon opinions and empty vanities [Col. 0333C]—Egypt being filled with frogs that produced the empty sound and vain clamour of things—when Moses said to him, “Appoint for me when I should pray for you, your servants, and your people, that the Lord may destroy the frogs” (Exod. VIII.9), although, placed in such great necessity, he ought to have begged that Moses should pray at once and not delay, replied: “Tomorrow”—idle and negligent, destined to pay Egypt the penalty of delay by destruction. Thus this man, when he obtained what he sought, became forgetful of grace; and, exalted in the mind of his flesh, forgot God.

34. Humility, however, commends prayer. Thus that Pharisee was rebuked who enumerated his fasts as though they were benefits conferred, cast them up, as it were, to God, and recalled that he was free from crimes. But the publican was praised: standing afar off, he would not lift his eyes to heaven, but struck his breast, saying: “Lord God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII.13). Therefore the divine judgment preferred him, saying: “This publican went down justified rather than the Pharisee” (ibid., 14).

For the one who confesses his own sin is justified, as the Lord himself said: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII.26). And David says: “A sacrifice [Col. 0334A] to God is a troubled spirit” (Ps. L.19). And again: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (ibid.).

> [Note: Col. 0333D] Let it not trouble anyone that this passage, cited under Jeremiah’s name, is found only in the prophecy of Baruch. For it is well established that many have praised this latter writer as Jeremiah’s companion and secretary.

Jeremiah also says: “A soul in distress and an anxious spirit cry to you” (Baruch III.1). Thus Pharaoh also (Exod. V.2), [Note: Col. 0334D] “The king” is lacking in four manuscripts; in its place one Vatican manuscript reads “and Rabshakeh the Assyrian.”] and the king of Assyria, who said, “Which of the gods of these nations shall deliver his land from my hand, that the Lord your God should deliver Jerusalem from my hand?” (4 Kings XVIII.35), were cast down by their self-exaltation.

But the righteous person, like Jacob, refers to God the author whatever good he has attained, saying concerning all the prosperity he recognizes as his: “Because the Lord God delivered them into my hands” (Gen. XXVII.20). This, therefore, is the better fulfillment of one’s vows, as David also says: “Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay [Col. 0334B] your vows to the Most High” (Ps. XLIX.14). To praise God is to commend and fulfill a vow.

Hence that Samaritan is preferred to the others: having, together with nine other lepers and in accordance with the Lord’s command, been cleansed of leprosy, he alone returned to Christ, magnified God, and gave thanks. Of him Jesus says: “Was there none among them who returned and gave thanks to God except this foreigner? … And he said to him: Rise and go; because your faith has made you well” (Luke XVII.18).

35. There is also this discipline for commending prayer and a vow: that we should not make prayer public but should keep its mysteries hidden, as Abraham did, who made cakes baked under ashes (*subcinericia*) (Gen. XVIII.6). The fathers also kept them hidden: they baked the dough which they had brought out of Egypt, making unleavened cakes baked under ashes, which in Greek are called ἐγκρύφια (*enkryphia*, “hidden cakes”), [Col. 0334C] because they are concealed in ashes. They signified also that leaven which the woman in the Gospel hid in three measures of flour (Luke XIII.21), until the whole was leavened, likewise intimating that the doctrine of mysteries must be kept down or concealed.

The Lord taught this more plainly in the Gospel, saying: “But when you pray, enter into your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you. And when praying, do not use many words” (Matt. VI.5). And below: “For your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (ibid., 8). Your chamber is the hidden place of the mind and the secret of the soul. Enter into this chamber of yours [Note: Col. 0334D] The Roman edition, contrary to the manuscripts and ancient editions, had patched the passage thus: “that is, depart from the outer vestibule of your body and enter wholly into the deep recesses of your heart.”], that is, enter into the deep recesses of your heart, withdraw wholly from the outer vestibule of your body, and shut [Col. 0334D] your door.

36. Learn what your door is: “Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth and a door of enclosure upon my lips” (Ps. CXL.3). And Paul asks that prayer be made for him: “That,” he says, “a door of the word may be opened to me, to speak the mystery of Christ” (Col. IV.3). But he, being chosen for the preaching of the Gospel, rightly desired that the door of the word be opened for him, because salvation of the nations went out from his mouth, [Col. 0335A] and the life of peoples proceeded from his mouth.

But let us shut the door, lest fault enter and some lapse of speech go out. Fault enters if a lapse goes out. Hear how fault enters: “In much speaking,” it says, “you shall not escape sin” (Prov. X.19). Much speaking went out; sin entered, because in much speaking no utterance is weighed. It slips out heedlessly, although to speak something beyond measure is itself a great sin.

37. Therefore beware lest you speak heedlessly, for the lips of the imprudent lead him into evils. Beware lest you exalt yourself in prayer, for the prayer of one who humbles himself will pierce the clouds. Beware lest you carelessly disclose the mysteries of the Creed or of the Lord’s Prayer. Do you not know how serious it is to contract sin in prayer, where you hope for [Col. 0335B] a remedy? Certainly the Lord, through the Prophet, taught that this is a grave curse, saying: “And let his prayer become sin” (Ps. CVIII.7)—unless perhaps you think this a slight matter.

For it is to distrust God’s power: to suppose that you will not be heard unless you cry aloud. Let your works cry out; let faith cry out; let affection cry out; let your sufferings cry out; let your blood cry out, as did that of holy Abel, concerning whom God said to Cain: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me” (Gen. IV.10). For he hears you in secret who cleanses in secret. Unless someone speaks, we cannot hear; with God, not words but thoughts speak.

And so that you may know this is true, the Lord Jesus said to the Jews: “Why do you think evil things in your hearts?” (Matt. IX.4). This is not the voice of one asking, but of one knowing, as the Evangelist makes clear to you when he says: “But Jesus knew their thoughts” (Luke VI.8). As the Son knows, so the Father knows. You have learned that the Son knows; hear that the Father knows, from the Father’s counsellor and witness saying: “For your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matt. VI.5).

Bake, then, your cake under ashes with the warmth of the Holy Spirit; bake also the passions of your soul with the heat of the Word. And if your passions are too raw, perhaps having recently come out of Egypt, cover them and cook them through with gentle heat, lest they be unable to bear a stronger fire and be half-scorched rather than cooked.

> [Note: Col. 0335D] Thus the Roman edition, with two manuscripts. The old edition and the other manuscripts read: “For there are many things which, by premature speech,” etc., omitting the material inserted in our edition and in the Roman edition.

For there are many things which, raw, displease but, cooked, delight. Therefore cherish deep mysteries in your breast, lest you entrust them, as though uncooked, to premature speech and to unfaithful or weak ears, [Col. 0335D] and the hearer turn away and reject them with horror; whereas, if he tasted them more fully cooked, he would perceive the sweetness of spiritual food.

38. The Lord Jesus also taught you the goodness of the Father, who knows how to give good things (Luke 11:13), so that you may ask good things from the Good One. He urged prayer earnestly and often—not so that prayer may be prolonged tediously [Col. 0336A], [Note: [Col. 0335D] Four manuscripts: “but assiduously. For vain things are often poured forth in a long prayer,” etc.] but so that it may be poured forth frequently and persistently (ibid., 9). For vain glory commonly steals into lengthy prayer, while negligence entirely creeps into interrupted prayer. Then he warns (Matt. 18:15) that, when you yourself ask forgiveness, you should especially know how to grant it to others, so that you may commend your prayer by the voice of your deed. The Apostle likewise teaches (1 Tim. 2:8) that one must pray without anger and disputation, so that your prayer may not be disturbed or interrupted. He also teaches that prayer must be made in every place, although the Savior says: “Enter into your chamber” (Matt. 6:6). But understand this not as a chamber enclosed by walls, in which your body may be shut up, but as the chamber within you, in which your thoughts are enclosed and your perceptions move about. This chamber of your prayer is everywhere with you, and everywhere is secret [Col. 0336B]; its only judge is God alone.

39. You are also taught to pray especially for the people (1 Tim. 2:1), that is, for the whole body, for all the members of your mother; herein lies the distinguishing mark of mutual love. For if you pray only for yourself, [Note: [Col. 0335D] The old edition and four manuscripts: “if you pray for yourself, you will pray only for yourself” [Col. 0336D]. Below likewise: “if you pray only for yourself, as we have said, you will pray only for yourself.”] you alone will pray for yourself. And if each person prays only for himself, the grace of the sinner is less than that of the intercessor. [Note: [Col. 0336D] Thus the old edition and the manuscripts, except the Florentine manuscript, which reads *precatoris* (“one who prays”) instead of *peccatoris* (“sinner”). The Roman edition also has this word, but deleted it, perhaps because *precator* seemed identical with *intercedens* (“intercessor”); although *intercedens* should be understood as one who interposes—that is, as people commonly say, one who puts himself forward.] But now, because individuals pray for all, all also pray for individuals. Therefore, to conclude: if you pray only for yourself, you alone, as we have said, will pray for yourself. But if you pray for all, all will pray for you, since you too are among all. Thus the reward is great: through the prayers of individuals, the support of the whole people is gained for individuals. In this there is no arrogance, but greater humility and a more abundant fruit [Col. 0336C].

202  
## CHAPTER X

Having explained Cain’s first defect in sacrifice, the author passes to the second: namely, that Cain did not offer from the first fruits. The first fruits of the soul are especially to be offered, and what they are. Abel offered them, and the Law commanded that they be offered. Also: who are called Canaanites; why God is said to have sworn; and why movements of the mind cannot be calmed without his help. Finally, these offspring ought to be offered, to which the distinction of sex contributes nothing.

40. But now it is time to proceed to another point, since we have spoken fully concerning Cain’s offering “after days.” It became the mark of one who is negligent, whereas the very request of a vow ought to be timely; lest we seem to have hoped more for a remedy from human arts—that is, medical skill and the juices of herbs [Col. 0336D]—than to have sought help from God. For we must first flee to him who can heal the passions of our soul. Yet some people, in an inverted order, first summon help for themselves from human beings; but when human assistance has failed, then they suppose that the grace of divine favor must be sought.

[Col. 0337A] 41. Therefore, with that crime of Cain concluded and proved, let us examine another fault in his offering. “He offered,” it says, “from the fruits of the earth,” but not first fruits to God from the first fruits. This means claiming the first fruits for himself first, and bringing what follows to God. Therefore, since the soul, as mistress, must truly be preferred to the body, as to a servant, we certainly ought to offer its first fruits—that is, those of the soul—before those of the body. The first fruits of the soul are the preeminence of good disciplines. Although they come later in time than the first fruits of the body—food, growth, sight, hearing, touch, smell, and voice (while mind and perception are a part of the soul, they are nevertheless part of the body)—they are prior in dignity among the disciplines. Their first offering is thanksgiving offered to God with a pure heart and simple speech.

[Col. 0337B] 42. Abel offered these gifts, and therefore God looked upon his gifts, because he offered from the first fruits. Further, he offered from the firstlings of the sheep and from their fat. Consider that he offered not from inanimate things, but from living creatures. For the animate is greater than the earthly, since the animate is close to the spiritual. “For the spiritual is not first, but the animate; afterward the spiritual.” What is animate breathes and has a living spirit; this is not so with what comes from the fruits of the earth. Next, he offered not what was second but what was first; not what was meager but what was fat. For such offerings the Law approved and commanded, as it is written: “And it shall be, when God brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to your fathers, and gives it to you, you shall set apart for the Lord every male that opens the womb. Every male that opens the womb among your cattle and flocks, whatever males are born to you, sanctify to the Lord. Every one that opens the womb of an ass you shall exchange for a sheep; but if you do not exchange it, you shall redeem it” (Exod. 13:11 ff.). What mystery is so profound, what wisdom so high and hidden, [Note: [Col. 0337D] All manuscripts and the old edition: “as you find in certain veins of simple words? You may discover and draw forth,” etc.] as to discover and draw from certain veins of simple words an abundance of spiritual grace? For the Canaanites are changeable and restless. Therefore, when you have entered their land—those whom you see cast out of their possession because of the fickleness, restlessness, and instability of their conduct—do you maintain steadfastness. Let no trivial argument and no frivolous speech disturb you. For this is the Canaanite: changeable speech, unstable feeling, and restless contention. Rather, calmly preserve tranquility of heart and serenity of mind [Col. 0337D], so that, as on the salt sea, you may provide a safe anchorage for ships in a certain harbor of your mind.

43. The Lord promises you this possession and confirms it by a kind of sacramental bond, in order to establish your constancy. For God does not swear because he needs the faith of one who believes, or because, lacking the support of confirming testimonies, he requires the guarantee of an oath—as human beings do, who secure confidence in ourselves by an oath and therefore swear so that we may be believed to have spoken truth. But God is faithful even when he speaks; his word is a sacrament [Col. 0338A]. Almighty God is not faithful because of an oath; rather, the oath itself is trustworthy because of God. Why then does Moses portray God as swearing? Because we are confined by a certain mortal habit and envelop ourselves, like sea urchins in a shell, in the crust of common opinion; or like snails, which cannot breathe, draw in, or endure the free air unless they remain within the covering of their shell. So we too move about on earth only within certain hiding places of human custom. Therefore, because we are accustomed to believe more truly what is confirmed by an oath, lest our faith falter, God is described as swearing—though he himself does not swear, but is the judge of those who swear and the avenger of those who swear falsely. Thus it is written: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever” (Ps. 109:4).

[Col. 0338B] He surely kept what he swore: he gave us the eternal chief of priests. Thus you too should know that what you have sworn must be kept; so that, because you swear by him who does not lie, you may know that, if you lie, he will be your avenger.

44. Therefore, once restless and changeable thoughts have been driven out, God will give you the vacant possession of heart and mind, so that you may cultivate it with a kind of tranquility and draw fruit from it. Do not permit Canaanites—that is, turbulent perceptions—to return into it. Uproot every conception of Gentile vices; tear down their groves, by which truth is overshadowed and a certain heavenly, unfettered vision of thought is hidden by the horror of dark disputation.

45. But you cannot accomplish this unless endowed with a divine gift [Col. 0338C]; therefore he says: “God will give you” (Exod. 13:11), that is, the best thoughts, calm counsels, peaceful insights. When he has given these, “you shall set apart every male that opens the womb, and sanctify it to the Lord.” God, who has given all, does not demand all from you. For he bestows much for the use of human subsistence, and that cannot be a divine sacrifice where there is merely the use of nature. Eating, drinking, sleeping, and the other services of the body have been granted to you as gifts; they are not gifts brought back by you to God. But whatever holy thought you conceive is God’s gift, God’s inspiration, God’s grace. Conversely, those things which belong to the use of human nature do not defile a person; but what proceeds from the mouth—acts of theft, false testimonies, sacrileges—these are what defile a person.

[Col. 0338D] 46. Let us therefore cleanse our inward parts, so that the offering may not be displeasing. There let us seek everything male that opens the womb—that is, what is righteous and principal, which we ought to sanctify to the Lord. For it is not bodily [Note: [Col. 0338D] Thus the manuscripts and Roman edition. The old edition: “bodily offspring.”] intercourse, conception, and childbirth, by which the womb of a woman is opened through the loss of virginal chastity, that sanctify us. For although a woman sanctifies a man and a man a woman, it nevertheless often happens that a virgin’s womb is opened even without the sanctity of marriage. Nor again does grace belong to the male alone, while woman is excluded from sanctification; nor is the nature of the two sexes so confused [Col. 0339A] that both produce bodily offspring. Men have their own functions; women have the distinct offices of their sex. This generation for the succession of humankind befits a woman; it is impossible for a man.

47. Therefore, if this sense does not apply to the use of the flesh, let us examine the functions of the soul. I find this soul indeed distinguished by no sex; and, though it has no sex, it displays the functions of both sexes: it marries, conceives, and gives birth. And just as nature has given women a womb, in which the generation of every living creature is formed through the monthly periods, so there is a certain power of the soul which, as though in the secret place of a generative womb, is accustomed to receive the seeds of our thoughts, cherish conceptions, and bring forth offspring. For Isaiah would not otherwise have said: “We have conceived in the womb and have brought forth the spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26:18), unless he had known the womb of the soul. Some of these generations are female: malice, wantonness, luxury, intemperance, shamelessness, and other vices of this kind, by which a certain manliness of our soul is weakened. Male offspring are chastity, patience, prudence, temperance, courage, and justice, by which our mind—and even the flesh itself—is strengthened and raised up eagerly to undertake the duties of virtue. That prophetic womb brought forth these offspring. Therefore it says: “We have conceived in the womb and have brought forth the spirit of salvation.” Thus the one who poured out the spirit of salvation both brought forth and gave birth to a male.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0339]

205  
## CHAPTER I

The soul’s offspring must be brought forth at maturity; what form they have; that the common perceptions can be subdued by the mind’s rule; that our perceptions are of two kinds; in what the first fruits to be offered to God consist; and finally, an examination of the composite constitution of which we consist and of its first fruits.

[Col. 0339B]

1. Let our soul bring forth these offspring, and not merely bring them forth in labor, [Note: [Col. 0339D] The editions added “according to what is written”; the manuscripts have the reading in the text: “but also,” etc.] but actually give birth to them, and give birth when the days are fulfilled, lest the day of judgment find the offspring immature. For the Lord Jesus spoke of these offspring when he said: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” (Luke 21:23). Let this birth, then, be completed here more promptly, and let our thoughts be unfolded through the progress of good works, so that our end may find nothing incomplete [Col. 0339C], the limit of life encounter nothing undeveloped, and our practical activity leave nothing as though still laid upon the anvil. Therefore, soul, hasten to form your offspring; complete them more quickly, and nourish more swiftly those whom you have brought forth.

2. The Apostle shows what form so great an offspring should have, saying: “My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). Let all the inward parts of our mind grow together into this form, and let Christ shine in that generative womb of our soul. Let our offspring be faith; let our nourishment be the precepts of doctrine. By these, let a certain infancy of our heart be imbued, childhood trained, adolescence made vigorous, and old age made gray. For the age of old age is an undefiled life. Thus that alone is a good old age of the soul which no stains of unbelief have defiled [Col. 0339D]. And therefore Paul defended his offspring from this stain: “I,” he says, “begot you in the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4:15), lest anyone’s savage whispering should test the infancy of their unformed faith. Thus he begot male offspring, who eagerly desired that the peoples whom he taught should come together into the unity of faith, unto a perfect man, and hold the perfect measure of the fullness of Christ in the knowledge of the Son of God [Col. 0340B] (Eph. 4:13). For he knew this to be the sacrifice acceptable to God, of which it is written: [Note: [Col. 0339D] In the Divionensis and Laudunensis manuscripts the word “you shall set apart” is absent; [Col. 0340D] and shortly afterward, in the same manuscript and in the Vatican manuscript, the second occurrence of “sanctify” is absent.] “You shall set apart for the Lord every male that opens the womb” (Exod. 13:11). And he added: “Every male that opens the womb among the cattle and flocks that are yours, sanctify to the Lord” (ibid., 12). Let us consider this, so that nothing may remain obscure.

3. He had spoken of the principal generations, that is, those full and capable of reason; he added also those of the herd—that is, the remaining, as it were common, perceptions, which are compared to irrational beasts of burden. Yet, when they are governed by some ruler, they are easily tamed. They are accustomed to carry out commands, bear the yoke, hasten their pace at their master’s voice, stop [Col. 0340C], turn aside, or perform, in a kind of human service, whatever duties of their work are commanded. Training has such power that it overcomes nature. Thus creatures that do not share in our substance nevertheless recognize the authority of our voice; although they possess no reason of their own nature, they take up ours and acquire it as though transferred to them. We see horses stirred by the enthusiasm of crowds, rejoicing in applause, delighted by their trainer’s caresses. We see fierce lions change their natural savagery into commanded gentleness, lay aside their own rage, and adopt our ways; though they themselves are terrible, they learn to fear. A dog is beaten so that a lion may be afraid; one made fierce by his own injury is restrained by another’s, and broken by another’s example. How often do they prefer to endure hunger, though prey is ready and food lies before them, while they fear their master’s displeasure? How often, stirred by a sudden impulse, do they open their jaws for biting, then at command relax them? Thus, while they obey our will, they forget their own. It is not so with those wild beasts, or herds of horses, or every kind of cattle that wander without any keeper and grow savage because they lack every guiding rein of a tamer [Col. 0340D–0341A]. Therefore herdsmen, shepherds, and other keepers have been appointed: as it were, teachers of flocks, shaping their duties according to the condition of each living creature entrusted to them.

4. There appears, then, to be one kind of our perceptions that is tamed and gentle, and another untamed, which, with a certain herd-like motion of the mind, sluggish and unrestrained, rushes into the irrational pleasures of the body. The gentle kind submits and yields itself to the restraint of the mind, as to a leader. Whatever is governed by this nature is male and perfect; but whatever, without any guide, domineers with a sort of vulgar presumption—like a city deprived of the counsel of king and nobles—thus weakens all the condition and manly vigor of its body through a kind of feminine dissolution [Col. 0341B]. From these comes that law of the flesh which, warring against the law of the apostolic mind, drew it captive under a certain law of sin. Therefore, in order to be freed from that body of death, Paul placed all his hope not in his own strength but in Christ’s grace (Rom. 7:25). Hence it is clear that those motions which accord with the law of the mind proceed from divine favor, while the other perceptions arise from bodily pleasure.

5. Therefore, those perceptions which are holy are the first fruits of our perceptions; the others belong, as it were, to a certain herd and to common baseness. [Note: [Col. 0341D] Thus the Divionensis manuscript. The others: “which Moses seems to have signified in various ways by different names.” One Vatican manuscript: “…to have signified to the Jews.” The old edition: “which he seems variously…to have signified to different persons.” The Roman edition: “which he seems…to have signified to different Jews.”] Moses seems to have signified these by different names. This is also declared by that mystical threshing floor of the Law, of which he says: “You shall not make the first fruits of your threshing floor and winepress the last. You shall give me the firstborn of your sons” (Exod. 22:29). The holy movements of our perceptions, those according to the virtues, are themselves the first fruits of the spiritual threshing floor; and for this reason they are compared with a rural threshing floor, on which grain is winnowed. For just as wheat and barley are beaten out upon a rural threshing floor, and, when repeatedly winnowed, are separated from chaff—because the chaff and the other refuse of the harvest are scattered in different directions by the light breath of the wind, while the more solid grains, once the dust has been shaken out, fall back into the same place—so the fruits of our thoughts which are firm and best provide the pure and sincere nourishment of virtue. As it is written: “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Luke 4:4). But those which are useless and empty are scattered like smoke and clouds [Col. 0341D], because “as smoke to the eyes, so is iniquity to those who use it.” Iniquity is rightly compared with smoke, because it covers the mind’s sight with a kind of worldly darkness.

6. Therefore the Lord says: “When you enter the land into which I bring you, and when you begin to eat from the bread of that land, you shall offer a separated offering to the Lord: the first fruits of your dough, a loaf [Col. 0342A] as an offering from the threshing floor. Thus you shall offer the first fruits of your mixtures, [Note: [Col. 0341D] The Roman edition: “of your doughs … [Col. 0342D] we are the mixture.” But in sense there is no difference here between *conspersio* (“mixture”) and *confusio* (“compound”), as is clear from Ambrose’s own words.] and give them to the Lord” (Num. 15:2 ff.). We are a compound (*confusio*), composed from a certain mixture of diverse elements. For cold is mixed with heat in us, and moisture with dryness. This mixture has many enticements and pleasures of the flesh, but these are not the first and principal perceptions of this body, because we consist of soul, body, and spirit. This is the principal compound, in which the Apostle desires us to be sanctified, as he says: [Note: [Col. 0342D] All editions: “But may God the Father himself.”] “May the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly; and may your spirit, soul, and body be preserved entire and without reproach on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thess. 5:23). The first fruits of this compound are spiritual: namely, the insights and generations of perceptions which proceed from the vigor of the soul [Col. 0342B]. But not all first and principal perceptions qualify, only those free from malice, wickedness, and every error. Bodily pleasures are necessary, such as sleeping, eating, drinking, walking, and other perceptions of this sort; but the first fruits do not lie in them. Therefore the Lord’s mystery is not in them but in those things in which there are chastity, piety, faith, and devotion. A clear and evident example is the offering of the patriarch Isaac, whom his father offered as a sacrifice without being bent by any movement of human passion: offering to God a pure victim, free from fear and immune from bodily desire, even as a father’s natural affection yielded to the devotion of one making sacrifice.

## CHAPTER II

First fruits are assessed not by time but by holiness. To form a true sacrifice, good works must be joined with faith, which is necessary above all. Labor must be exchanged for fruit, and the soul must be freed from useless things.

[Col. 0342C]

7. Let us now consider the force of first fruits, and whether first fruits are assessed by time or by holiness—that is, whether all firstborn things possess the sanctification of first fruits. For the first fruits of produce are holy according to the Law (Num. 18:8), because in them lies the best sacrifice of prompt faith. But they become holy by devotion, not by time, because it is not growth that sanctifies but devotion. Indeed, where growth is swift, if devotion delays, offense is incurred. Therefore not all firstborn things are holy; but all things which are holy are also firstborn. Cain, indeed, was firstborn, but not holy. Israel too is the holy people of God, though not first in age; nevertheless it is called firstborn, as it is written in the prophets: “Israel is my firstborn” (Exod. 4:22). Levi too was holy but not firstborn, for he is recorded as Leah’s third son (Gen. 29:34); yet Levites are called firstborn, deriving their name from him. For it is written in Numbers:

[Col. 0343A] “Behold, I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel in place of every firstborn that opens the womb among the children of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine; for every firstborn is mine. On the day when I struck every firstborn of Egypt, I sanctified every firstborn of Israel” (Num. 3:12–13).

Therefore the Levites are called firstborn because they have surely been preferred to the other children of Israel by sanctification. Hear the Apostle explaining in what respect they are firstborn: “But you have approached Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and tens of thousands of rejoicing angels, [Note: [Col. 0343D] The older editions: “and the Churches of the firstborn [Gill., ‘of the first fruits’], which are written in heaven … angels, and Churches of the first fruits.” Three manuscripts agree with the Gillot edition. One Vatican manuscript: “and the Church of the first fruits”; the Laudunensis: “and the Church of the firstborn.” Here, with the Divionensis manuscript: “which are written,” etc. The Roman edition gives the whole passage thus: “and the Church of the firstborn, who are written … angels, and the Church of the firstborn.”] and Churches of the firstborn, which are written in heaven” (Heb. 12:22). He made four orders: Mount Zion, the city Jerusalem, the assembly of angels, and the Churches of the firstborn. Thus the Lord God took the Levites from among the people of Israel, because he did not wish them to share in human cares [Col. 0343B], but to be ministers of divine religion. And he made them firstborn who open the spiritual womb; therefore they were not from the womb of nature, like sinners guilty of diverse crimes, but were chosen after worldly worshippers had been destroyed. [Note: [Col. 0343D] Thus the Florentine manuscript. But the old edition, the Divionensis manuscript, and one Vatican manuscript read “chosen after the worshippers have been destroyed”; another Vatican manuscript and the Laudunensis read “chosen after worldly worshippers have been destroyed.” The Roman edition: “chosen after worldly worshippers have been abandoned.”] Hence they have no share in a common possession and are not counted among the people, because they possess the Word of God in their midst, as it is written in the Gospel: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst” (Matt. 18:20). And elsewhere: “One stands in your midst whom you do not know” (John 1:26).

8. From this, therefore, we know that faith ought above all things to commend us to God. When we have faith, let us labor so that our works may be perfect. For this is the full and perfect sacrifice [Col. 0343C], as the Lord himself teaches us, saying: “You shall take care to offer me from your gifts and offerings on my feast days, taking nothing away and dividing nothing, but offering them full, whole, and perfect.” [Note: [Col. 0344D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the Laudunensis: “and from his gifts”; the Divionensis and the old edition: “and from your gifts”; the Roman edition: “and from my gifts.” This exact wording occurs nowhere in Scripture; we believe it to have been composed from various prescriptions in Leviticus.] Now the Lord’s feast day is where the grace of perfected virtues exists. These virtues are perfect when the soul, victorious over worldly anxieties and bodily enticement, excludes the allurements of pleasure; when it is free from the world, devoted to God, diminishing nothing from the path of its direct intention, and not dividing the time of its disposition now for luxury, now for labor. Thus only the wise person celebrates this festival; no one else does. For it is difficult to find a soul free from passions of this kind. Divide, therefore, according to reason, the ruling and obedient parts of the soul; then you will discern what is male and what [Col. 0343D] is female. For there is no virtue without labor, because labor is the progress of virtue. The words of the Law itself signify this, when it says: “Every one that opens the womb of an ass you shall exchange for a sheep” (Exod. 13:13).

[Col. 0344A] For the Law excluded unclean animals from sacrifice and commanded clean animals to be offered in their place. It therefore commands the offspring of an ass—that is, what is unclean—to be exchanged for a sheep, which is clean and fit for sacrifice (Lev. 27:27). This is according to the letter. But if anyone pursues more deeply [Note: [Col. 0344D] All editions: “the sense of the spiritual understanding,” etc.] the meaning of the spiritual Law, it is pleasing to consider that the ass is a laborious animal, while the sheep is fruitful. Therefore it says that labor must be exchanged for fruit, so that the fruit may be the end of one’s work. Or certainly in this way: you shall commend all your labor and all your industry with a pure and simple disposition.

9. “But if you do not exchange it,” it says, “you shall redeem it” (Exod. 13:13). Therefore, according to the letter, another animal or a price is commanded to be offered in place of the unclean animal, lest something inferior or unclean appear to be offered among the tithes of produce. But the deeper sense teaches that your soul must be set free, so that it may cease from things that have no fruit. For one who redeems oneself sets oneself free and in some manner removes a debt. Works that cannot have true fruit and good progress must be abandoned, such as these worldly pursuits, whose use cannot endure. In them the result itself is naked and empty of truth, and, however great the labor expended to obtain it, it offers the soul no benefit. All things that bring the soul into slavery are useless, even if there is no lack of an outcome. Great seems the victory of those who fight, the glory of those who triumph; yet we often see those who have conquered again subjected to the uncertainties of war and, by the fortune of battle, handed over to the enemy; and, by the very fact that they were once victors, made more miserable [Col. 0344C]. Therefore your works must be directed to God, and his favor must breathe upon you. Even the athlete who competes by his own strength, not another’s, believes whenever he enters a contest that he is exposed to uncertain outcomes. And when he has attained the crown, he realizes that this glory of the world withers more quickly than the leaves of the crown itself. When the helmsman has brought his ship into harbor, he scarcely regards his labor as ended, and immediately seeks the beginning of another labor. The soul is released from the body; yet, after the end of this life, it still hangs in suspense over the uncertainty of the judgment to come. Thus there is no end where an end is thought to be. Therefore, through vows, a pure conscience, and a spirit of love, let us cling to our God and win divine favor for ourselves, praying that we may be released and stripped free from worldly cares, as from cruel and savage masters; that we may leave worldly servitude and be called into the freedom of heavenly knowledge [Col. 0344D], which alone is true freedom.

210  
## CHAPTER III

The statement that labor must be exchanged for fruit is confirmed by the example of the Jews serving in Egypt and by the testimony of the Gospel. The author explains from what place and in what manner the soul must be freed, and that Christ is the true Levite, that is, our liberator. Finally, he offers a fine discussion of the benefit brought by the fellowship of the righteous.

[Col. 0345A]

10. To establish the command of the Law by an example: when the Egyptians oppressed the people of the Jews with diverse labors, with mud and brick, the children of Israel groaned and called forth the Lord’s mercy toward them. And he said to Moses: “I have heard the groaning of the children of Israel, how the Egyptians oppress them in slavery, and I have remembered my covenant. Go and say to the children of Israel: I am the Lord; I will lead you out from the power of the Egyptians [Col. 0345B], deliver you from their slavery, free you with an uplifted arm and great judgment, take you to myself as a people, and be your God. And you shall know that I am the Lord your God, who leads you out from the power of the Egyptians and brings you into the land toward which I stretched out my hand” (Exod. 3:7 ff.). See how the Hebrew people exchanged labor for fruit: those who worked in mud now worked in hope of an eternal kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0345D] Laudunensis manuscript: “worked in hope of an eternal kingdom.”] And therefore the Lord, in the Gospel, pitying the empty labor of the peoples of the Gentiles—who built bricks for a muddy superstition and, devoted to bodily pleasure, could not build the solid wall of faith—spoke as though to certain offspring of the ass: “Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28 ff.).

[Col. 0345C] In this calling I seem to recognize more fully the words and mysteries of the Law, because it taught that the ass must either be exchanged for a sheep or redeemed with money: so that we not only exchange an ass’s offspring for a sheep—that is, the unclean for clean things—but also redeem it. This seems to be expressed if we first wash away the defilements of our sins through the sacrifice of purification and the mystery of baptism, and also redeem our crimes through good works, the price of faith, and mercy.

11. The price paid for us is Christ’s blood. Thus the Apostle Peter says: “You were redeemed not with gold or silver, but with precious blood” (1 Pet. 1:18). And Paul says: “You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings” (1 Cor. 7:23). Hence we do not wonder without reason at the Gospel’s statement that the Lord Jesus sat upon an ass’s colt (Mark 11:7), because the Gentile people began to be Christ’s sacrificial victim, having been considered unclean under the Law. Thus it is also written of the Levites (Exod. 12:13) that they are their redemptions, because by both the holiness of their life and prayer they washed away the sins of the people [Col. 0345D]. [Note: [Col. 0345D] Thus the manuscripts. The edition reads “might lighten.” In them the figurative mystery of the lamb preceded, etc.] In these mysteries, the figure of the lamb preceded the true Levite who was to come, who by the suffering of his own body would take away the sin of the world. “Levite” is interpreted as “taken up for me,” or “he himself is light for me”; for he bears the mark of perfect virtue, to impart healing to the people. Thus he who came as the awaited one for the salvation of all [Col. 0346A] was brought forth from a virginal womb for me, offered for me, tasted death for me, and rose again for me. In him the redemption of all human beings has been undertaken, and resurrection assumed. He is the true Levite, so that he might make us Levites: to cling to God, pour forth continual prayers to him, hope for salvation from him, flee earthly occupations, and be numbered among God’s possession, as it is written: “Lord, possess us” (Exod. 34:9). For this alone is the possession which, subject to no storms, bears the fruits of perpetual grace.

The Redeemer is a Levite because a wise person is the redemption of a foolish person. Like a physician, he tends the sick mind of the foolish and sprinkles the mind with stronger remedies of prudence, imitating that physician who came from heaven [Col. 0346B] to show human beings the paths of prudence and reveal to little ones the ways of wisdom. For he saw that those who labor could not be saved without a remedy, and therefore provided medicine for the sick. Therefore he brought the aid of healing to all, so that whoever perishes may ascribe the causes of his death to himself, because he refused treatment when he possessed the remedy by which he could escape; while Christ’s mercy toward all may be openly proclaimed, because those who perish perish through their own negligence, whereas those who are saved are freed according to Christ’s judgment—he who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth. Indeed, if Sodom had had fifty righteous people, it would not have been overthrown; and if it had had ten, it would have been redeemed. For the word of remission of sins frees the soul from slavery, and the fullness of perfect instruction does not allow the mind to be consumed by the devouring heat of desires [Col. 0346C].

12. Yet it matters greatly, and builds up moral disposition, if we also understand simply that the number of righteous persons benefits the safety of peoples. It restrains and cuts off envy, confounds wickedness, encourages virtue, and increases grace. For no one ought to envy another a praise that benefits himself; and every wicked person, when he receives his redeemer, often imitates him; certainly he reveres him, and for the most part even loves him. Even if he knows that it will benefit others, he is increased in zeal; and this grace binds peoples together, accumulates the charity of citizens, and enhances the glory of cities. How blessed is the city that has very many righteous persons; how renowned in everyone’s speech! How the whole is blessed by a part, and its condition is judged blessed and enduring!

How I rejoice when I see some gentle and wise persons living long, when I behold chaste virgins and venerable widows advanced in years, like a certain grey-haired senate of the Church, who, by their very countenance and appearance of gravity, hold before others something that they may reverence, imitate, and by which they may be coloured with every grace of character! For I do not rejoice for their own sake, since in living they undergo many wearinesses of this age, but because they benefit many. Likewise, when someone of this kind dies, though removed after a long old age, I am distressed, because the flock of the young is deprived of its wall of old age. Finally, the first indication of a city about to perish, of impending evils, or of coming disaster is, if prudent men—or even more venerable women—pass away. [Note: [Col. 0347D] The old edition and two manuscripts: “if they fall”; one manuscript: “if they are cut down.” All editions: “men of counsel”; manuscripts: “more prudent men.”] Here first the gate is opened to approaching evils.
