Therefore, just as an entire city is strengthened and pressed together by an assembly of wise persons, but shaken by their death, so grave speech—especially speech of old age, full of prudence—usually stabilizes each person’s soul and strengthens the mind. And if there is added the practice of much reading, a kind of senate of very many precepts and counsels, it produces an enduring state, as it were, for that city which lies in the heart of each individual.

## CHAPTER IV

Why Moses called the firstborn and the redeemers Levites, and designated their cities as cities of redemption; why it is not absurd that criminal persons live together with the pious; concerning the two principal virtues in God, mercy and justice, and their ministers; and concerning the fact that the departure of wickedness always brings about the entrance of virtue, and conversely—as is demonstrated by Gospel examples.

[Col. 0347B]

13. Therefore Moses called the firstborn and the redeemers of the rest Levites (Num. 3:12), because men of more mature and useful judgment, on the one hand, set before others a kind of old age of the soul, and, on the other, confer redemption. Thus Moses also indicated that the cities of the Levites in the Old Testament were cities of redemption (Num. 35:6), because one who takes refuge in that soul in which the Word of God dwells, which is fortified and walled about in the manner of a city, acquires perpetual freedom for himself.

[Col. 0347C] For just as in the cities of the Levites there was remission of penalties—so that if someone who had committed an involuntary homicide took refuge in them, no one was permitted to kill him while he remained within the cities of the Levites—so the person who repents of his own sin, committed either through ignorance or unwillingly, is freed by the law itself from every penalty and punishment for the crime committed, if he adheres to the community of the Levites and thinks that he ought not depart from those teachers who dispense God’s commands.

14. Nor should you think it absurd that criminal persons live with the pious, and defiled persons with those consecrated to God. Those who have been polluted by some contagion of sins need purification. In a certain manner, moreover, the cause converges from opposite directions. For just as the Levite, renouncing worldly pleasures, is an exile from guilt, so a person guilty of bloodshed is a fugitive from his native land. [Col. 0347D] But there is this difference: the latter leaves his own by necessity, through fear of the law; whereas the minister of God renounces fellowship with human passions and withdraws himself from the binding tie of fleshly allurements for the pursuit of virtue.

Nor is it alien from the truth that this man too, as it were, lays certain hands upon himself, in order [Col. 0348A] to kill the pleasures of his body and bring about a kind of death of his flesh. Moses, indeed, killed the Egyptian and became a fugitive from the land of Egypt, in order to escape the tyrant of that land. Yet he would not have killed the Egyptian man unless he had first killed within himself the Egyptian of spiritual wickedness, and had renounced the luxury of royal honours, judging the reproach of Christ to be a greater possession than the treasures of Egypt. This appears to fools as reproach; but to us that reproach of the Lord’s cross is the power and wisdom of God.

15. Add to this that there are two principal kinds of powers in God: one by which he forgives, the other by which he punishes. Sins are forgiven [Note: [Col. 0347D] Gratian, *On Penance*, distinction, chapter “The Word of God,” and the Master of the Sentences, book IV, distinction 18, when citing this passage, give neither Ambrose’s words nor his meaning.] through the Word of God, of which the Levite is interpreter and indeed executor (23, question 5, chapter *Remittuntur*; and *On Penance*, distinction 1, chapter *Verbum Dei*); they are forgiven also through the office of the priest and sacred ministry. They are also punished through men, as through judges who exercise authority for a time, as the Apostle teaches when he says: “Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it; [Note: [Col. 0347D] One Vatican manuscript: “for he is God’s minister, an avenger unto wrath, to you for good.” Editions of Erasmus and Gill: “for she is God’s minister to you for good.”] for he is God’s minister to you for good. But if you do evil, be afraid. For he does not bear the sword without cause; for he is God’s minister, an avenger unto wrath against the one who does evil” (Rom. 13:4).

Sins are punished also through peoples, as we read (Isa. 13:17), because the Jewish people was often subjected to foreign nations raised up by God’s command because of the offence against divine majesty. Nor is even the one who commits some homicide unwillingly outside ministry [Col. 0348C]. For the law says concerning him: “Because God delivered him into his hands” (Exod. 21:13). His hands, then, in the manner of an instrument rendered service to divine vengeance. Therefore the Levite is a minister of forgiveness; but the striker who has committed homicide not by design but against his will is a minister of divine vengeance.

16. Observe also this: when the wicked person is put to death, Christ is poured in; and when abomination is abolished, sanctification is gathered together. [Note: [Col. 0348D] Two manuscripts: “is consecrated.” Roman edition: “is increased.” Old edition with three other manuscripts: “is gathered together.” And, after the three words *ubi* (“when”), the Roman edition with two manuscripts has: “on the day on which I killed,” etc.; the old edition with three other codices: “on the day on which I shall kill . . . I shall sanctify for myself,” etc.; Gratian likewise in the passage cited. But this reading agrees less well with the sacred text, for it reads: ἐν ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ ἐπάταξα πᾶν πρωτότοκον . . . ἡγίασα ἐμοί, etc. — “on the day on which I struck every firstborn . . . I sanctified [them] for myself.”] For the Lord said: “On the day on which I killed every firstborn of Egypt, I sanctified for myself every firstborn of Israel” (Num. 3:13).

You should not refer this to one day of Egypt’s affliction, but to all time. For when wickedness is renounced (32, question 1, chapter *Cum renuntiatur*), virtue is immediately adopted. [Col. 0348D] For the departure of wickedness brings about the entrance of virtue; and by the same zeal by which crime is excluded, innocence is joined to us. You have this in the Gospel (John 13:2): when Satan cast himself into Judas’s heart, Christ withdrew from him; and at the very moment at which Judas received the former, he lost the latter. Thus it is written: “And after [Col. 0349A] the morsel, Satan entered into him” (ibid., 27). Jesus therefore said to him: “What you are doing, do more quickly.” What was that? That, because Satan had entered into him, Judas himself should depart from Christ.

Thus he is cast out and excluded, because he can no longer be with the Lord Jesus, having begun to be with the devil; for there is no fellowship of Christ with Belial. Therefore, driven out at once by the command, he departed, as we read in the Evangelist’s words: “When he had received the morsel, he went out immediately” (ibid., 30); and it was night. He not only went out, but went out immediately, and went out into the night. Nor is it surprising that he possessed the darkness of night, when he was abandoning Christ.

But just as Judas, received by the devil, was excluded from Christ, so Zacchaeus, renouncing avarice, received Christ. Rightly, therefore, seeing his zeal in having climbed a tree [Col. 0349B] in order to see Jesus as he passed by, the Lord says: “Zacchaeus, come down quickly, for today I must remain in your house.” And he came down quickly and received him joyfully (Luke 19:5–6). But in receiving Christ he excluded avarice, banished unbelief, and renounced fraud. For Christ does not enter otherwise than in order to exclude vices, because he does not dwell with errors. Thus he drove the money-changers from the temple because he wished to dwell there himself.

Zacchaeus, understanding this—that he could not receive Christ with his former disposition—commanded his former vices to depart from his lodging, so that Christ might enter. Rightly, therefore, when the Pharisees murmured because the Lord Jesus had turned aside to lodge with a sinful man, he said to the Lord: “Behold, Lord, I give half my goods to the poor; and if I have taken anything from anyone by fraud, [Col. 0349C] I restore it fourfold” (ibid., 8). By this he answered those who said that a sinner ought not have offered lodging to Christ: “That is, I am no longer a tax collector; I am no longer that Zacchaeus, no robber, no deceiver. I restore what I took; I who used to take away now restore. [Note: [Col. 0349D] Roman edition: “what I used to take away.”] I now give to the poor, whom formerly I stripped bare; I now bestow what is mine, whereas I used to seize what belonged to others.” Crimes fled once Christ entered. All blindness of fleshly passions was dispelled where the light of eternal life was poured in.

## CHAPTER V

What the fat and richness of sacrifices and offerings signify.

17. We have spoken of the firstborn; let us speak also of the fats, concerning which David teaches sufficiently when he says: “As with fat and richness my soul shall be filled” (Ps. 62:6). And above he says: “And let your burnt offering become fat” (Ps. 19:4). By this he teaches that the sacrifice is acceptable when it is rich, bright, and fattened with a certain nourishment of faith and devotion, and with the more abundant food of the heavenly Word.

We frequently call a work “fat” when we mean it to be dense and laborious; and an offering is praised as rich when it is not thin or meagre. [Col. 0350A] Hence we rightly call a sacrifice “fat” when we wish to declare it abundant. [Note: [Col. 0349D] Old editions and certain Paris editions: “when we wish to declare it excellent.”] Further evidence for this is that fat cows, in prophetic interpretation, were compared with fruitful years (Gen. 41:26).

## CHAPTER VI

What the Lord means when he says: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be still”; and concerning the four kinds by which sacrifices were commended, if any of which is lacking the sacrifice is not approved, with their very beautiful moral interpretation.

18. Let us now consider what the Lord means when he says: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be still.” This indicates that God is not pleased by gifts offered, but by the disposition of the offerer. Thus Cain, the offerer of a gift, was condemned because, from awareness of his insincere offering, he understood that his sacrifice was not approved by God, and he became sad. For when the mind is conscious of what is right in itself, it rejoices, and the soul is filled with spiritual joy, as by a certain infusion, when anyone’s zeal or works are approved by God. Cain’s sadness, then, is the testimony of his conscience and the sign of rejection. And though he offered a gift, he nevertheless incurred guilt because he did not divide it rightly and lawfully.

19. For there are four kinds by which sacrifices were commended: if they were either new of new things, or roasted, or divided, [Note: [Col. 0349D] In Philo, from whom Ambrose took these matters, it reads καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἐρεικτά, that is, “and finally crushed.” But these do not differ in the allegorical interpretation.] or continuous. “New of new things” were those which, at the first time of the year, were regarded by their appearance among the first fruits; [Note: [Col. 0350D] Thus three manuscripts and the ancient edition. The Laud manuscript: “which are ears of grain.” A reading perhaps not to be despised. Roman edition: “which are kinds.”] but it has now been revealed that they signify [Col. 0350C] those who are renewed through the sacraments of baptism. For this is truly a primary sacrifice: when each person offers himself as an offering and begins with himself, so that afterward he may be able to offer his gift (Rom. 12:1).

Therefore the new faith of those renewed—strong, growing to maturity, acquiring increase of virtue, neither slack nor weary, neither withered by a certain old age nor sluggish in vigour—is fit for sacrifice: a faith that sprouts with a certain green shoot of wisdom and comes to maturity with the ardour of divine knowledge, but nevertheless possesses the sap of ancient teaching. For the teaching of both the New and the Old Testament ought to concur, because it is written: “Eat the old things of old things, and remove the old things before the new” (Lev. 26:10). Let knowledge of the patriarchs be our food; let the soul feast upon the oracles of the prophets; with such rich nourishment [Col. 0350D] let the inner mind be fed. Yet now let there be no mere appearance of a lamb, but the reality of Christ’s body. Let not the shadow of the law merely touch the eyes; rather, let the grace of the Lord’s passion openly illumine the mind’s vision, together with the brightness of the resurrection.

20. “But if you offer a sacrifice from the firstlings of sheep, roasted in fire, roasted fat, you shall offer a sacrifice of firstlings,” as it is written (Lev. 7:2). This signifies that your faith ought to be proven as if by fire [Col. 0351A] and to burn with the Holy Spirit. Thus Jacob cooked lentils and took from his brother the birthright blessing, which a steadfast faith would surely follow. [Note: [Col. 0351D] The Divine and Laud manuscripts: “Here, therefore, [is] a bramble [perhaps *rubeus*, ‘red’] and undivided.”] Therefore this robust and lively man increased; but the other, who did not know how to cook his food, became exhausted, failed, and melted away.

Let the virtue of your soul therefore be burned by the Word of the Lord as by fire. See Joseph burned, as it is written: “The word of the Lord burned him” (Ps. 104:19). Let your faith be roasted like ears of harvest grain. For then they display the ripeness of their fruit, when the summer season has first scorched them by the course of the sun. Thus the abundant discourse of the Scriptures strengthens the soul and colours it with a certain heat of spiritual grace; it also strengthens rational insights and dissolves every force of irrational passions.

For this reason Esau was undone when the bonds of his virtue were loosened. But those who, with loins girded, were commanded to eat not raw nor boiled in water, but the lamb’s head roasted in fire, as you have in Exodus, crossed the seas on foot with a strong and faithful mind (Exod. 12:9). In the Gospel too, the Lord Jesus ate roasted fish, as it is written (Luke 24:43), in whom the fullness of the Holy Spirit overflowed. And perhaps Esau failed for this reason: he desired food boiled in water, which Jacob, as unfit for himself, gave to his weak brother.

21. But offering and prayer ought not to be confused, but distinguished by fitting division. [Note: [Col. 0351D] Two Vatican manuscripts, the Divine and Laud manuscripts, together with the ancient edition: “For in every matter distinction is better than confusion.”] For in every matter distinction is better than confusion, and much more so in prayer and offering, which become more obscure unless they possess definite divisions. Therefore the law often commands the members of victims to be divided and burnt offerings to be offered (Lev. 1:6), so that the sacrifice may be naked, without admixture and [Note: [Col. 0351D] Old edition with four manuscripts: “with a covering of water”; one Vatican manuscript among them: “that it may be a clean sacrifice.”] without any covering; because our faith ought to burn naked and stripped of all coverings, [Note: [Col. 0352D] Old edition and the Florentine codex: “lest it be clothed with empty and deceptive [opinions].” The Roman edition alone: “lest it be [clothed] with various,” etc.] not clothed in wandering and deceptive opinions, but so that the pure and sincere simplicity of the mind may appear.

Then it must be divided into appropriate parts. For virtue is a genus divided into many species, but there are four principal ones: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. Let your prayer breathe prudence with respect to the knowledge of God and the truth of faith; let it breathe temperance, which the Apostle judged must be required even of married persons, saying: “Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by consent for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7:5). [Note: [Col. 0352D] All editions: “And the law [commands] those who have been chastened,” etc.] And the law commands those who have been purified on the preceding and third preceding day to approach the sacrifice (Exod. 19:10).

Let prayer possess fortitude, so that it is interrupted by no fear and fails through no weariness. For then the intentness of prayer ought to be stronger, when adversities press upon us. Let prayer preserve justice; if Judas had held it, his prayer would not have become sin. For when ought we more to abstain from unjust deeds and perverse pursuits than when we entreat God’s justice? Therefore, so that justice might be dear to our heart, the Lord says: [Col. 0352A] “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice’s sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10). This was lacking in Judas; for if it had been present, he would not have handed over the Lord, nor betrayed the teacher. It was also lacking in this sacrifice of Cain; if he had maintained justice, he ought to have brought the first gifts to the Lord, not the later ones.

Thus division was lacking to him, and therefore he received the response: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be still.” You see how great the fault is: where division is lacking, the entire sacrifice is rejected.

22. It remains for us to speak of continuous and unceasing prayer: we ought to persist and devote ourselves to prayer. The Lord spent the night in prayer, not in order to benefit himself, but in order to teach us. For frequent prayer produces a certain discipline of praying, because practice itself makes us teachable by God, whereas neglect makes us unteachable. Therefore exercise is good. Bodily strength, indeed, is increased by frequent exercise; but without exercise it diminishes and declines. For many, through disuse of exercise, destroy even their natural strength.

Similarly, the strength of the soul is made firm by the constancy of exercise, so that the very labour of discipline may become not a burden but a benefit. Let us bring to our mind this food, worn down and polished by much meditation, so that it may strengthen the human heart like that heavenly manna. We do not receive it idly, worn down and polished; for we must long dwell upon and polish the utterances of the heavenly Scriptures, turning them over with all our soul and heart, so that the sap of that spiritual food may diffuse itself through all the veins of the soul.

Therefore, if faith grows up as though coming to maturity, banishing the failure of ageing devotion; if it burns in the Spirit, is held in the proper distinction of lawful division, and is commended by constancy; then there comes about that rich and, as it were, fatty kind of prayer of which the Prophet says: “You have made my head rich with oil” (Ps. 22:5). For just as lambs grow fat on abundant milk, and well-fed sheep shine with fat, so the prayer of the faithful, fed with apostolic sap, grows rich.

23. If anything of those things mentioned above is lacking, the sacrifice is not approved. Therefore it was said to Cain: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” For the world itself is read to have been made with distinction, whereas its part was previously unformed; for “the earth was invisible and unformed” (Gen. 1:2). Surely light was first made; and God called the light, and God separated between light and darkness, and the darkness was called night. And we read in order that each thing was made: heaven, earth, fruit-bearing trees, diverse animals.

The lighter things were distributed to the upper regions—air and fire; the heavier to the lower, namely earth and water. God could certainly have commanded all things to be made at once; but he preferred to preserve distinction, which we should imitate in all our affairs, and especially in the reciprocal exchange [Col. 0353A] of favours. In these it is not enough to return what one has received; one must make what one returns acceptable. For if someone pays a debt but, in paying it, insults his creditor, this is surely more intolerable than not returning what he owed. Thus it is not the quantity of repayment, but the mind of the payer, the quality, and the disposition that are considered.

Cain therefore offered rightly, because an offering is a mark of devotion and an indication of gratitude; but he did not divide rightly, because above all he ought to have brought the first fruits to God, so that he might begin from the grace of the Creator. For this is the order of division: first things should precede second things, not second things first; and heavenly things should be preferred to earthly things, not earthly things to heavenly.

## CHAPTER VII

God, who taught in Adam that one must not sin, taught in Cain that sin must not be defended; and, in this connection, how readily one is precipitated from impiety into other crimes.

[Col. 0353B]

24. But because Cain confused this order, it is said to him: “You have sinned; be still” (Gen. 4:7). God teaches all things. First, that you should not sin, as he warned in Adam; second, that if you have sinned, you should be still, as you are taught in Cain. For we ought to blush and condemn sin, not defend it; because guilt is diminished by shame but increased by defence. By silence we are corrected; by contention we fall headlong. Let there at least be modesty where there is no acquittal.

Hence that saying: “The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18:17). And again we read elsewhere that the Lord himself said: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26). How great is the grace of shame, that modesty may preserve justice which the liability of guilt had taken away! But he says, “Be still,” because [Col. 0353C] you have nothing to excuse. The turning of the guilt toward you belongs to the fault itself. For it is not your brother who is assigned to you, but the error is imputed to you, of which you yourself are the author. [Note: [Col. 0353D] Ancient edition: “is added.” Roman edition and manuscripts: “is assigned.”] “Upon you,” he says (Gen. 4:7), “returns the crime which began from you.” You have no one in whom to accuse necessity rather than your own mind. Your wickedness is turned back upon you; you are its ruler (ibid.).

25. He rightly says: “You are its ruler.” For impiety is a kind of mother of sins; and one who has committed graver sins easily slips into the rest. How can someone refrain from offences against human beings who has violated divine things, or be good to human beings who has injured God? Therefore the remaining vices follow a more atrocious liability of crimes; for wherever the more shameful sins incline, the rest also bend that way. You, therefore, are the ruler of your own deed; you are the leader of the crime. Error did not draw you in unwillingly [Col. 0353D] or unknowingly; but as a voluntary guilty person you committed the deceit by deliberate judgment, not by a fall, through which you convict yourself as guilty of an injury against God.

## CHAPTER VIII

Cain, rejecting the admonition, increases his insolence and crime. His words, “Let us go into the field,” are shown to signify that deserted and barren places suit depraved actions.

26. Thus, though warned to be still, he increases his insolence [Col. 0354A] and aggravates his crime. What then does he mean by saying, “Let us go into the field” (ibid., 8), except that a place bare of growth is chosen for fratricide? For where was his brother to be killed, except where fruit was lacking? As if foreknowing so great a crime, nature had withheld shoots from that place, because it was unfitting that the same soil should receive, contrary to nature, the contagion of fratricidal blood, and yet produce fruit according to nature.

Rightly he himself says: “Let us go into the field.” He does not say: “Let us go into paradise, where fruits flower,” nor “into some cultivated and fruitful place.” Parricides themselves show that they cannot possess the fruit of crime, nor can fruit remain with those who have rendered service to such great impiety. For they flee even the kindness of the elements, as this Cain seems to have feared lest the more generous [Col. 0354B] bounty of the earth should hinder his sad deed and, by the native habit of its generosity—which causes diverse offspring and fruits to spring forth—should, even in this preparation for the crime, recall brotherly affection by its mute appearance.

The thief flees the day as a witness to his crime; the adulterer blushes before the light as though it knew his adultery; the parricide flees the fertility of the lands. For how could he look upon the shared fellowship of offspring who was slaughtering one who shared his own blood? Joseph is put into a dry pit; Amnon is killed inside a house. Nature therefore rendered a just judgment, depriving the places in which fratricide was to occur of the bounty of its gift, so that, by a kind of condemnation of the innocent soil, it might show [Note: [Col. 0353D] Old edition: “might show the future punishments of the guilty to be more harmful.” Roman edition: “might show how much more harmful the future punishments would be.” Four manuscripts: “might show how great the future punishments of the guilty would be, more harmful.” Perhaps it should be read: “how much more . . .” We have followed the reading of the Laud manuscript as the best of all.] how great the future punishments of the guilty would be.

Therefore, because of human crime, the elements themselves are condemned. Thus David pronounced upon the mountains on which Jonathan was killed with his father the penalty of perpetual barrenness, saying: “Mountains that are in Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain fall upon you, mountains of death” (2 Sam. 1:21). [Note: [Col. 0354D] The words “mountains of death” are lacking only in the Roman edition.]

## CHAPTER IX

God questioned Cain not in order to learn, but in order to induce him to confess. Cain’s response is impious toward God and nature; God’s opposing response is shown to teach excellently the piety of brotherhood. God hears the righteous even when dead, because they live to him; sinners, however, are dead. Such persons are tormented by present and future evils, though they are troubled more by present ones.

[Col. 0354D] 27. Let us now consider why God asked Cain where his brother was, as though he did not know that he had been killed. With respect to God’s knowledge, he convicted the denial and replied to the one who denied it as one who knew: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me” (Gen. 4:10). But with respect to the deeper purpose, he admonishes sinners toward repentance. For confession is an abridgment of punishments. Hence, in secular courts, those who deny are tortured on the rack, and the confession of the accused touches the judge with a certain compassion.

There is a certain shame in sins, and it is a portion of repentance to confess the crime, [Note: [Col. 0355D] Laud manuscript: “and not swear away the fault.” Better: the other manuscripts and editions, “shift it away.” To shift away guilt is to transfer it from oneself to another.] not shift the guilt elsewhere, but acknowledge it. The shame of the guilty softens the judge, but the obstinacy of those who deny provokes him. [Note: [Col. 0355D] Three manuscripts: “God wishes to urge you toward pardon.”] God wishes to urge you toward repentance; he wishes you to hope for pardon from him; he wishes to demonstrate by your confession that he is not the author of wickedness.

For those who refer their sin to some necessity of decree or action, as the Gentiles maintain, seem to accuse God, as though his force were the cause of their sin. For one compelled by some necessity to kill has killed, as it were, unwillingly. But actions that arise from ourselves have no excuse, whereas those beyond our control are excusable. Yet how much more serious than the sin itself is it to refer what you have done to God, and to transfer the odium of your guilt to the author not of crime but of innocence.

28. Consider, moreover, the response of the parricide: “I do not know,” he says; “am I my brother’s keeper?” (Gen. 4:9). Although this speech betrays defiance, it nevertheless implies that, if he had regarded his brother as good, he ought to have been the guardian of brotherly devotion. Whom ought he to have protected more than his brother? But how could he preserve the duty of brotherhood when he had not acknowledged the affection of kinship? [Note: [Col. 0355D] Divine manuscript: “had not acknowledged its effect.”] Or how could it happen that he rendered obedience to nature when he offered no reverence to God?

First he denies, as though before one who is ignorant; he refuses the duty of brotherly guardianship, as though he had no share in nature; he evades the judge, as though free in his choice. Why are you surprised that he did not acknowledge piety, when he did not acknowledge the Creator? Thus you are taught by this sequence of Scripture [Col. 0355C] that faith is the root of all virtues. Hence the Apostle says: “Our foundation is Christ” (1 Cor. 3:11); and whatever you build upon this foundation, that alone contributes to the fruit of your work and the reward of virtue.

29. Accordingly the Lord aptly answered his so foolishly denying words: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me” (Gen. 4:10). That is: Why do you not know where your brother is? You were alone with your two parents; among so few persons your brother ought not have been hidden from you. Is it because your parents cannot be accusers? For I do not wish that the kinship which is the source of safety should become the source of danger. Nature has lost its laws in you alone. Therefore, do you think the crime is hidden because your parents ought not accuse? But your condemnation is all the greater for that reason. [Col. 0355D] For if the dear names of kinship ought not accuse, still less ought they to kill.

But if you reject me as witness and flee from me as judge, the voice of your brother’s blood is a witness crying to me. It accuses you with greater authority than if your brother were alive. You were alone: who else could have killed him? If you accuse your parents, you prove yourself a parricide. One who does not spare his parents could kill his brother. He could be a parricide who desires to prove that he sprang from parricides.

30. And he rightly says: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries,” not “your brother cries.” [Note: [Col. 0355D] Thus both the older and more recent editions. All manuscripts, however: “that is, he preserves innocence and the grace of brotherhood even in death itself.” It is difficult to pronounce which reading is better.] This preserves innocence and the grace of brotherhood even in death itself. Brother Abel does not accuse, lest he seem a parricide. Neither his own voice nor his soul accuses, but the voice of the blood that you yourself shed accuses. Thus your own deed, not your brother, accuses you.

At the same time, a guilty person is deprived of the complaint [Note: [Col. 0356D] All editions and the Florentine manuscript and one Vatican manuscript: “a guilty complaint”; the other Vatican manuscript, the Divine and Laud manuscripts: “a complaint [by] the guilty person.”] against the accusation. One cannot complain of another’s testimony who confesses the crime by his own act. The word is less than the deed. Yet the earth also is a witness, which received the blood. And he rightly says: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries from the earth.” He did not say, “It cries from your brother’s body,” but [Col. 0356B] “from the earth.” Even if your brother spares you, the earth does not spare you; if your brother is silent, the earth condemns you. It is both witness and judge against you: a more severe witness, since it is still wet with the blood of your fratricide; a harsher judge, because it has been polluted by so great a crime that it opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand.

The earth indeed opened its mouth as though about to receive words of devotion from brothers, fearing nothing when it saw brothers, because it knew that the law of brotherhood was an incentive to love, not hatred. For how could it suspect fratricide when it had not yet seen homicide? But you shed the blood; grieving at the contagion of it, the earth herself says: [Note: [Col. 0356D] One Vatican manuscript, the Divine and Florentine codices: “he did not dare, he says, [to give] strength,” etc. Yet in the Septuagint it is consistently read: οὐ προσθήσει τὴν ἰσχὺν αὐτῆς δοῦναί σοι—“It shall no longer continue to give you its strength.” The Vulgate has instead: “It shall not give you its fruits.”] “It shall no longer increase its strength to give it to you.” How innocent the vengeance: having been so grievously violated, it is content not to benefit you and does not seek [Col. 0356C] to harm you.

31. This too is no slight doctrine in the statement: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me,” because God hears his righteous persons even when dead, since they live to God. They are rightly reckoned among the living, because even if they have tasted bodily death, they nevertheless receive incorporeal life, are illumined by the splendour of their merits, and enjoy eternal light. Therefore he hears the blood of the righteous; but he turns away from the prayers of the wicked, because, even if they seem to live, they are nevertheless more wretched than all the dead, carrying their flesh around like a tomb in which they have buried their unhappy soul.

For what else is a soul but buried when it rolls about within the earth and is enclosed by desires of earthly avarice and other vices, so that [Col. 0356D] it cannot breathe the air of heavenly grace? A sinner of this kind is cursed by the earth, which is the lowest and last part of the world. Higher, certainly, are heaven and the things in heaven: the sun, moon, and stars; Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, and Powers; Cherubim and Seraphim. There is therefore no doubt that the higher things too have condemned the person whom the lower things condemned. [Col. 0357A] For how is he acquitted by that pure and heavenly judgment [Note: [Col. 0357D] Editions and a few manuscripts: “is acquitted by that pure and heavenly judgment.”] whom not even the things of earth could acquit? And therefore he is commanded to be groaning and trembling upon the earth.

32. The reason is plain and universal: evils are present to every wicked person, and are yet to come. Those which are present produce sorrow; those which are future, fear. But the wicked are more troubled by present things than by future ones. Hence Cain said to God: “My guilt is too great for me to be forgiven. If you cast me away today, I shall hide myself from your face.” For nothing is more grievous than for one who has gone astray to be abandoned by God, so that he cannot call himself back. The death of a sinner brings an end to sinning; but a life deprived of the divine helm rushes headlong onward and slips into graver evils. As, if a shepherd abandons his flock, beasts attack it, so when God abandons a human being, the devil presses in. It is especially grievous for the foolish to lack a guide. Wickedness creeps onward; a wound grows when medicine is absent. Moreover, one hides oneself who wishes to veil guilt and cover sin. For one who acts wickedly hates the light, and seeks darkness and hiding-places for one’s offenses. But the righteous person is accustomed not to hide from the Lord his God, but rather to offer himself, saying: “Behold, here I am: I have no guilty conscience which I fear may be discovered.”

33. Rightly, therefore, the person conscious of evil hides himself and says: “Everyone who finds me will kill me.” A person of lofty spirit fears present death, disregards eternal death, and does not dread divine judgment; he deprecates only the destruction of the body. But by whom did he fear that he would be killed, when he had only his parents on earth? He might indeed have feared attacks by wild beasts, since he had violated the laws of God; nor could he presume upon the subjection of the other animals, having taught that a human being could be killed. He might also have feared his parents as slayers of kin, since he had taught that parricide could be committed. For the parents could learn from their son what later descendants learned from their parent.

## CHAPTER X

God’s threat, “Whoever kills Cain,” etc., is morally interpreted; the divine mercy is declared in the mark placed upon him, as also Cain’s madness in fearing temporal death more than eternal death. From this occasion there is a fine discussion of the incorruptibility of the soul and the life to come. Finally, it is shown that judgment should not be given too hastily, nor yet should crime be allowed to go unpunished.

34. Let us now consider why God said: “Whoever kills Cain shall pay vengeance sevenfold” (Gen. 4:15), and why a mark was placed upon him, lest the parricide be killed, when no provision had been made lest an innocent person be killed. A human being is the eighth; he has the rational faculty by which he surpasses the rest; he has also the five bodily senses, he has a voice, and he has the gift of generation. Unless these seven are governed by that rational faculty, they are subject to death; and therefore in these things the fool possesses every danger to himself. Whoever, then, has lost that rational faculty vainly flatters himself concerning the use of those seven carnal gifts. All these things fall apart unless they are bound fast by, as it were, the reins of reason. Thus the death of reason produces the death of irrational passions.

But a better explanation is that the seventh number is one of rest and remission. Therefore, one who has not spared another sinner, and has begrudged him the gift of remission of sins, will himself take away from himself the hope of remission; and there shall be in him vengeance for grace, according to an equal measure.

35. But in placing a mark upon Cain lest anyone kill him, God wished to turn the erring man back and, by his kindness, invite him to amendment. For we are more readily inclined to entrust ourselves to those whose favor we possess. [Col. 0358B] Yet he grants no great favor; rather, in this very matter he punishes the folly of the foolish man, who, though liable to everlasting punishments, did not ask that his punishment be remitted, but thought he ought to beg for the preservation of this bodily life. [Note: Thus all the manuscripts. The old edition reads, “thought he ought to ask that it be observed”; the Roman edition alone, “thought he ought to ask that it be preserved.”] In it there is more misery than pleasure.

For death is one thing: the separation of soul and body, and the end of this life; and, as soon as it comes, it is accustomed to remove, not increase, every bodily pain. But the fears which frequently press upon those living this life, sorrows, pains, groans, diverse torments, and the wounds of infirmities and diseases bring very many deaths upon humankind, so that this death appears to be a remedy rather than a punishment. For it is not a death-dealing death, by which life is not taken away but transferred to better things. If the guilty die, those unwilling to turn their step back from sins attain, even against their will, an end not of nature but of guilt, lest they commit more offenses—for them life is interest upon their sins. But if they possess a good hope, they should be thought to migrate rather than to perish.

36. At this point is introduced the doctrine of the soul’s incorruptibility: that it is itself the true and blessed life, which every person of good conscience lives far more purely and blessedly when our soul has laid aside the covering of this flesh and has been released from this bodily prison, flying back to that higher place from which, poured into our inward parts out of compassion for this body, it groaned until it fulfilled the office of the charge entrusted to it: namely, to govern and restrain the irrational motions of this flesh by rational guidance.

This is why later the prophets went into captivity with the people of the Jews: lest the remaining populace, deprived of the protection of the saints and bereft of counsel, should undergo a heavier misery; but rather, warned by the more frequent oracles of the prophets, might return with devout affection to the Lord their God, lest, worn down by the adversities of captivity, it should collapse into the sin of unbelief and despair of the remedy of everlasting salvation.

37. Therefore, those who think that this is the only life—the life in this world, where all things are full of ruin and full of grief—are refuted in this passage, and refuted by the straightforward course of events. [Col. 0359A] For behold: a righteous, innocent, devout man, incurring his brother’s hatred because of the grace of his devotion, was carried off by parricide while still untimely in age; while an unjust, criminal, impious man, stained even by his brother’s murder, lived to old age, took a wife, left descendants, founded cities, and received this by divine permission. Does not God’s voice openly cry out in these things? “You are mistaken, who think that all the gift of living is here. You do not understand; you do not observe that old age is an old campaigner in miseries, and the advance of age the wages of affliction; that by a certain Scyllaean condition we are daily surrounded by shipwrecks, battered by waves, dwell among rocky places, and delight in these things, like that creature which is not so much an eternal animal as an immortal evil.”

Therefore, even the length of life granted to this Cain was a punishment, because he lived in fear and traversed a long span in much and fruitless toil. [Col. 0359B] No punishment is more grievous than that a person should himself be the cause of greater punishments to himself. See, then, how the life of the righteous is everlasting, and that of the wicked is nonexistent! The blood of the righteous man cries out even when he is dead, but the life of the sinner is hidden.

38. A third point is this: since parricide had been committed—that is, the chief of crimes—when sin had crept in, the law of divine gentleness also had at once to be extended; lest, if vengeance had immediately been exacted upon the guilty person, people too should observe no patience or moderation in exacting vengeance, but at once hand the accused over to punishment. [Note: One Vatican manuscript with the old edition reads “in judging”; the others and the Roman edition, “in exacting vengeance.”]

But the providence of the divine judgment is such as to teach judges magnanimity and patience, lest anyone be hurried away too rashly by zeal for vengeance and, through the very immaturity of his deliberation, punish an innocent person or, in anger, make the punishment harsher; [Note: All editions agree on “make harsher in anger.” But two manuscripts read “make harsher [the punishment] of the ungrateful”; three read “heap up [punishment] when angry.” What if, with Latinius, one reads “of the erring”? Again at this point the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, with the Florence, Dijon, and Laudian manuscripts, read “and yet that it should not be altogether pardoned”; Gillot and the Roman edition, with the Vatican manuscript, “that it should not be unpunished.”] yet neither would he allow it to remain altogether unpunished in one who had assumed no repentance for his crime.

For God drove him away from his presence and, disowned by his parents, relegated him to a kind of exile in a separate habitation, because he had passed from human gentleness to the savagery of beasts. Nevertheless, he did not will that a murderer be avenged by murder; for he prefers the correction of the sinner to his death. Hence Lamech is avenged seventy-sevenfold, because the guilt of one who did not correct himself even after another’s condemnation is more grievous. Cain had sinned first through a kind of unreflecting impulse; Lamech, surely, ought to have taken care to avoid what he saw reproved in another. The sentence was indeed due to his own judge, lest anyone should think that an accused person ought everywhere to be struck down. And, to come to the mystery: he ought not to have killed the man who had until the natural end of his death a period in which to practice repentance. He could have pleaded in excuse that he had redeemed himself even by a late act of repentance, had an untimely punishment not snatched him away.

# ON NOAH AND THE ARK

[Col. 0359C]

## NOTICE ON THE BOOK *ON NOAH AND THE ARK*

[Col. 0359]

Although there can be no doubt that the book *On Noah and the Ark*—or rather, as Augustine cites it (*Against Julian the Pelagian*, bk. II, ch. 2; and bk. IV, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, ch. 11), and as it is entitled in the Corbie manuscript, *On Noah’s Ark*—should be ascribed to Ambrose, it nevertheless cannot at all be affirmed that it has reached our time whole and entirely uncorrupted. For it is interrupted by gaps more numerous and more conspicuous than would permit us either not to complain of time’s injury to it or not to accuse the incredible carelessness of copyists.

Indeed, not to adduce here every example of omissions of this sort—which will each be indicated in their proper places—one may detect a plainly evident and enormous *anacoluthon* in the words of chapter 25: “But if anyone cannot provide himself with stronger banquets, let him nevertheless have passions of such a kind as do not harm but delight. Therefore, in the beginning Saint Moses informed and instructed us concerning the breathing-in of the soul, lest we fall into the diverse opinions of philosophers,” etc. What coherence and sequence of meaning, pray, is there here? But it will become clear to one who reads the chapter from the beginning that not only has that verse from Genesis, “Nevertheless, you shall not eat flesh with the blood of the soul” (Gen. 9:5), been omitted, but also that all the material is missing by which the holy Doctor explained those same words and from which he drew the conclusion: “Therefore, in the beginning,” etc.

It is established, then, that this work of Ambrose is mutilated; nor is it consequently surprising if passages which Augustine more than once cited from it (*loc. cit.*) can no longer be found there. It is indeed regrettable that the best manuscripts have perished and that we have encountered only defective and shamefully corrupt ones. Nonetheless, by the benefit of those which we have been able to obtain—especially the Corbie, Longpont, and Vatican manuscripts—we present this work in a much more corrected form, having removed no few and no slight blemishes which had crept into the editions.

In this work, Ambrose’s general purpose was to describe the life, character, deeds, and loftiness of mind of holy Noah (ch. I, §1). Yet his principal concern is devoted to explaining the construction of the ark and the universal flood. He carefully weighs every part of this sacred history and endeavors with all diligence to bring out both its literal and its spiritual—or, as he himself calls it, higher—sense. You will scarcely find another of his treatises in which he applied greater effort to examining and eliciting each of these two senses. There too he repeatedly introduces the opinions of others, not without much learning; yet if something occurs to him which seems preferable, he proposes it candidly and without any arrogance.

[Col. 0361] As for the writings of Philo, although it does not seem improbable that he wrote concerning Noah’s ark and the flood, since he published treatises on other parts of that patriarch’s history, we cannot guess whether the holy bishop really had a book of this author on this very subject which he imitated. We may only affirm that certain materials drawn from Philonic books *On Agriculture* and those following are discernible in this treatise.

Likewise, certain traces, as it were, of sermons appear in it (ch. I, §§13, 19); but they are not sufficiently clear for us to assert as an established fact that the work was composed from addresses delivered to the people. Yet there is not the slightest doubt that the devout teacher, while devoting himself to this composition, very often spoke before an assembly of the faithful. For he would never have allowed his consolations to be lacking to the Church entrusted to him by Christ precisely when they seemed most necessary.

Those were, evidently, most sorrowful times, since they compelled him, at the very beginning of this work, to break out in these words: “I am ashamed to outlive my children; when I hear of so many calamities of my dearest ones, I am weary of enjoying this light. Who is so strong as patiently to endure the varied waves and storms of the Churches themselves, whether undergoing them in the present or receiving them in the mind?”

Moreover, that mention of exceptionally difficult times furnishes us, in some measure, with a light by which we may discover the date of this writing. Perhaps there will be those who think that the times meant here are none other than those in which, after Gratian had been killed and Valentinian and Justina—an Arian woman, most hostile to all the orthodox and especially to Ambrose himself, who not long before had raged with a woman’s unrestrained violence against the Church of Milan—had been put to flight, the tyrant Maximus invaded the whole of Italy. Support for this opinion may also be found in the fact that, since those disasters occurred only in the year 387, nothing would prevent this treatise from having immediately preceded the other books *On the Patriarchs*. For Ambrose seems to intimate in the first book *On Abraham* that he appended those books to it, when he begins: “Since the desire has arisen in us to consider in sequence the deeds of this patriarch also.”

But since he laments those calamities in such a way as to indicate that he knew them more by report than by sight, we judge it more fitting to refer the passage to the time when, after the emperor Valens—who had persecuted every Church and the orthodox with savage cruelty—had been consumed by fire, a vast multitude of barbarians devastated all Thrace and Illyricum as far as the Julian Alps with fire and sword. Their invasion was followed by a most dreadful plague and famine, which consumed almost everything of people and beasts that had escaped the barbarian swords. Add to this that these events have no slight affinity with those amid which we find that our Ambrose mourned the death of his most beloved brother Satyrus, who died at nearly the same time.

Nor do we think this book so connected with the other treatises *On the Patriarchs* that it could not have preceded them by an interval of several years. This view is favored both because those other works appear to have been published in peaceful, not troubled, times, and because, at the beginning of the book *On Joseph*, when he lists the other patriarchs, he makes no mention of having written about Noah, as though he had forgotten him. For these reasons nothing appears more probable than to assign this work to the year 379. The chroniclers (Prosper, Cassiodorus, and others) testify that at about this same time Ambrose wrote many works of lofty character. As for Baronius and those who followed his authority, who deny that the books *On Duties* (bk. I, ch. 19), in which it is agreed that the work under discussion is cited, can be earlier than the year 377: we cannot readily agree with them on this matter. But another occasion will arise for examining that difficulty. Meanwhile, we do not judge it should be omitted that Ambrose records in this book *On Noah and the Ark* (ch. 17) that the use of indictions had recently been adopted in Italy.

[Col. 0361D]

# ONE BOOK OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, *ON NOAH AND THE ARK*  
[Note: [Col. 0361A] Written about the year 379.] (C)

[Col. 0361]

227 ## CHAPTER I

Noah, the righteous man left to renew the seed of humankind, should be set before all for imitation, so that we too may rest from every anxiety of this world and from works of iniquity.

[Col. 0361A]

1. We undertake, if we can, to explain the life, character, deeds, and also the loftiness of mind of holy Noah. For since prophecy itself has said, “Nothing is more difficult than to comprehend the inward parts of a human being” (Jer. 17:9), [Note: Vatican, Corbie, and Longpont manuscripts read “Philosophy has said.” Nor perhaps badly; for it is not Ambrose’s custom to cite Scripture under the name of prophecy. Yet he may have imitated this from 2 Pet. 1:21.] how much more difficult is it to know the mind of a righteous man?

For the Lord God reserved him for the renewal of the seed of humankind, that he might be a nursery-ground of righteousness. It is fitting, therefore, that we too should describe him for the imitation of all and rest in him from every anxiety of this world, which we daily endure amid diverse agitations. I am ashamed to outlive my children; when I hear of so many adversities of my dearest ones, I am weary of enjoying this light. [Note: The Roman edition reads “most illustrious persons.”] Who is so strong as patiently to endure the varied waves and storms of the Churches themselves, whether undergoing them at present or receiving them in the mind? Therefore, this rest too ought to be sought by us, so that, while we consider holy Noah with greater attention, we too may be refreshed, just as every kind rested in him from its works and sorrow.

2. Noah is so called because in Latin it means “righteous” or “rest.” Accordingly, his parents also said: “This man shall make us rest from our works and from sorrow, and from the earth which the Lord God has cursed” (Gen. 5:29). If you think this should be referred to the events which occurred, since the flood came under him, it would seem that not rest but destruction was brought upon human beings, and not relief from evils but an accumulation of miseries.

But if you consider the mind of the righteous man, you will perceive that righteousness alone is born more for others than for itself. It seeks not what is useful to itself, but what is useful to all. This makes us rest from works of wickedness; this recalls us from sorrow. For when we perform what is just, in the security of a pure conscience we fear nothing and do not suffer grievous pain. For nothing causes greater pain than the charge of guilt. Let us rest also from every care of earthly life, which vexes our body and soul with frequent pains and wears life away.

## CHAPTER II

What the names of Noah’s sons signify, and what is meant by the order in which they are listed. This is explained by the example of a battle-line drawn up for war and by the ordinance of nature itself. Finally, why the order is reversed when their descendants are set forth is discussed at length.

3. Three sons were born to him: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. These names signify good, evil, and the indifferent. Thus he appears to have possessed goodness by nature’s gift; to have lacked no trials of evils; and to have abounded in indifferent things—that is, as it were, in the equipment of virtues. The reason why he placed evil in the middle is clear: because the good of nature is in everyone. Nature does not cast us out into the light as shipwrecked persons; rather, it supports us with powers, so that we may not be overwhelmed by the assaults of wickedness or succumb as feeble persons. But it arms and clothes us with certain coverings, as it were, of indifferent things: safety, sound health, beauty, energy, wealth, glory, and nobility of birth. Fortified by this endowment, people protect nature’s goodness and shut in that evil, so that it cannot harm them, and, as though enclosed, they strangle it.

4. Do we not see, as it were, a battle-line of virtues arranged for war, so that the weaker forces are in the middle, while the stronger are on the right and left, as though in the wings, through whom the whole battle-line receives strength? Hence a certain Greek poet also says: “He placed the bad men in the middle” (*Iliad* 4): κακοὺς δ’ ἐς μέσσον ἔλασσεν.

So too nature, like a good commander under God’s command, which has known how to bring us forth for the battles of this world, places what goods it has in the first rank, what hinders in the second, and what helps in the third. Thus the enemy, enclosed as it were in the middle, is crushed by doubled forces wherever it turns itself, lest each of these things, as though wearied by equal combats, should have the capacity to escape from its natural confines and spread more widely. [Note: The Roman edition reads “each of them”; the older edition and manuscripts better read “of these,” for the reference is to “what goods it has … what helps.” In the same place, where the edition has “be wearied,” Corbie and Longpont prefer “to weary.” This reading is not to be rejected if, in place of “each,” which appears everywhere, one reads “individual.”]

5. But because this is the order when they are born, whereas when they beget children Japheth is written first and Ham third, the explanation of that passage must also be given, lest anyone think we have contradicted ourselves later. The good which exists, as it were, in a certain nobility of nature comes first; evil follows, for these are contrary thoughts of the mind which arise afterward. So long as they are shut up within, as it were, and do not sprout like plants, they are cherished in the bosom of a good mind lest they emerge.

For so long as evil is in the will and not in *entelecheia* (ἐντελεχείᾳ), that is, in act and effect, the goodness of the governing mind, in the manner of a charioteer, restrains or checks the wickedness that attempts to break forth. But when it has boiled over and broken out into an ulcer, lest it spread more widely and infect what is neighboring, then a just providence takes its place: the indifferent thing which people commonly call the secondary good yields ground, as it were, since it can no longer withstand evil now inflamed.

Accordingly, lest it pour out its harmful poison more broadly and by propagating corruptions infect very many, that first good, which is good by nature, changes its order when it changes its place. It comes to aid the wing which is, as it were, hard pressed and takes up that part of the battle-line which suffers more. For a warrior’s courage is necessary in the more difficult positions, just as the presence of a good guard is more frequent where the walls are weaker.

And lest any part be without a defender, while that good supports the more vulnerable positions, then the indifferent thing occupies the higher position, as though the more perfect good assigned that part to it; for nothing is more perfect than virtue. Indifferent things do not possess the strength of vigorous virtue, but increase and extend its grace. Hence Japheth is so called because the name signifies “breadth” in Latin.

## CHAPTER III

Why, before the coming flood, the whole generation abounded in the begetting of children: so that we may attribute the good things granted to divine kindness, and their withdrawal and the punishments imposed to our own wickedness.

6. Not only holy Noah abounded in children; the whole generation likewise poured itself out most abundantly at that time. This does not seem without purpose. For, since the flood was to follow, it should not be thought that the generation swallowed up by the waters lacked the grace of fruitfulness. Thus the abundance of humankind is to be attributed to divine grace; the flood which followed is to be ascribed to our wickedness, since by our sins we turn away the Lord’s mercy.

So too, in later events, you find that an equal number of years of fruitfulness preceded the Egyptian barrenness which was to follow (Gen. 41:26–27). For it is the chief characteristic of virtue to begin with benefits and to sow grace beforehand. Hence David also says: “I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100:1). The grace of a benefit comes first; the discerning discipline of sober correction follows. Thus, that good things are first offered is divine; that they are changed is ours.

7. God himself makes this clear, saying: “My Spirit shall not remain in human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3). The Holy Spirit is the spirit of wisdom and the spirit of knowledge. Therefore, it possesses wisdom and also discipline, as Scripture says of Bezalel, who was commanded by divine oracle to make the sacred tabernacle: “Because he was filled with the spirit of prudence and discipline” (Exod. 31:3).

This Spirit, then, is given to human beings, but does not remain. The reason why it does not remain is given: because they are flesh. For the nature of flesh resists discipline, because it obeys pleasure. Accordingly, it is written of the Lord Jesus alone: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon him—this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33). For it remained in him whom no obstacles of fleshly corruption drew back from maintaining the order of uncorrupted and unmixed discipline, whose flesh did not see corruption.

## CHAPTER IV

Those who devote themselves to the cultivation of their flesh are like the giants who lived in Noah’s age. Who are called sons of God; in what way God is said to be angry or moved; why irrational creatures too were destroyed because of human sin; and why Noah found grace with God.

8. “Giants were on the earth in those days” (Gen. 6:4). The author of the divine Scriptures does not wish those giants to be understood, in the manner of poets, as sons of the earth; rather, he declares them born from angels and women, calling them by this name in order to express their bodily magnitude.

Let us consider whether people who are devoted to the cultivation of their flesh and take no care for the soul are perhaps like the giants—like those who, according to poetic fable, were born from the earth and, trusting in the bulk of their bodies, are said to have despised the beings above. [Note: Thus the editions; but the Corbie, Vatican, and Longpont manuscripts read “contempt of superiors.” A little later all editions read “they turn away from the vigor of the mind”; the older editions, “they turn away”; the more recent editions, “they oppose.” We restore the passage from the manuscripts.]

Should those be judged unlike them who, though consisting of soul and body, reject the vigor of the mind—than which the soul possesses nothing more precious—and show themselves imitators of this flesh, as heirs, so to speak, of their mother’s folly? Therefore they labor in vain, claiming heaven with proud prayers while devoting themselves to earthly works. By choosing the lower fellowship and despising the higher, they are condemned to a more grievous severity, as persons liable to voluntary sins. [Note: The old edition reads “security.” This reading is by no means absurd, since no punishment is more grievous than security in voluntary sins; nevertheless, the manuscripts read “severity,” which agrees better with Philo, *That the Divine Is Immutable*, from which Ambrose seems here to have imitated the passage.]

9. Scripture often calls angels “sons of God,” because souls are not generated from any human being. [Note: The Roman edition removed the word “souls,” perhaps as superfluous. Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca*, bk. V, anno 77, cited this passage of Ambrose somewhat differently: “Scripture often calls angels sons of God, or faithful men,” etc. But who could guess whence he took this? Undoubtedly the most learned man wished thereby to show that Ambrose did not hold the view that giants were generated from angels—that is, spiritual natures, or, in Philo’s language, souls (ψυχαῖς)—but from the sons of Seth, namely righteous men, as Augustine interprets in *The City of God*, bk. XV, ch. 23. Yet it is more probable that Ambrose here borrowed Philo’s opinion and words concerning evil angels, whom he teaches to dwell in the air, as he explained more clearly in his exposition of Psalm 118, Sermon 2, at the final verse. Even Augustine himself, in *Questions on Genesis*, question 3, did not altogether venture to reject this. Although we frankly acknowledge that our Doctor may here, and at the end of book I *On Virgins*, have subscribed to the ancient Fathers who attribute these things to good angels. If you wish, you may see a long list of them in the same Sixtus, *loc. cit.*, Pamelius, *Paradise* I, Tertullian, and Coquaeus on ch. 23 of bk. XV of *The City of God*. Moreover, Ambrose himself clearly professes in many places that angels and souls are incorporeal by nature.]

Therefore God did not disdain to call faithful men his sons. As, then, men of approved life are called sons of God (Job 1:6), so by the authority of Scripture we call those whose works are fleshly “sons of the flesh” (Ps. 81:6). For John the Evangelist says: “As many as received the Lord Jesus, he gave them power to become sons of God, even to those who believe in his name, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God” (John 1:12–13).

Therefore afterward you read that the Lord was angry, because, although he thought—that is, knew—that a human being placed in the region of earth and bearing flesh could not be without sin (for earth is a kind of place of temptations, and flesh an enticement to corruption), nevertheless, though they had a mind capable of reason and the soul’s power infused into the body, they fell into ruin without any consideration and were unwilling to call themselves back from it.

For God does not think as human beings do, as though some new decision came upon him; nor does he grow angry as one subject to change. Rather, these things are read in order that the bitterness of our sins may be expressed—the bitterness which deserved divine displeasure—as though guilt had increased to such a point that even God, who by nature is not moved by anger, hatred, or any passion, might appear provoked to wrath.

10. He further threatened that he would destroy humankind: “From human being,” he says, “even to cattle, and from creeping things even to birds of heaven, I will destroy” (Gen. 6:7). What harm had irrational creatures done? But since they were made for human beings, once the one for whose sake they were made had been destroyed, it followed that they too should be destroyed, since there was no one to use them.

But in a higher sense this is made clear: the human being is the mind, capable of reason; for a human being is defined as a living, mortal, rational animal. When the ruling faculty is extinguished, every sense too is extinguished, because nothing remains for salvation when virtue, the foundation of salvation, has failed.

But for the condemnation of the rest, and to express divine mercy, Noah is said to have found grace with God. At the same time it is shown that the offense of others does not overshadow a righteous person, since he alone is preserved as the seedbed of the whole race, praised not for nobility of birth but for the merit of righteousness and perfection. For the lineage of a man of proved worth is a progeny of virtue: just as human beings are the race of human beings, so virtues are the race of souls. Human families are ennobled by the splendor of birth; but the grace of souls is made glorious by the splendor of virtue.

## CHAPTER V

The earth was corrupted by human wickedness. Likewise, “the time of every human being is before the Lord” may be understood in two ways. Finally, flesh is taken for the whole human being, and our soul is corrupted by its enticements.

11. “The earth was corrupted before God and was filled,” he says, “with iniquity” (Gen. 6:11). The cause of the earth’s corruption is evident, because human wickedness corrupted the earth. Hence the Lord God also says: “The time of every human being has come before me, because the earth has been filled with their iniquities” (ibid., 13). [Note: The Roman editions read, “The time of all human beings has come before me, because the earth has been filled by them with iniquity.” They also read this below; but in both places they stand against the authority of the manuscripts and the old edition.]

Certainly the time of all human beings is in God’s sight and in his will. For no fated decree is imposed, as people commonly say. Yet I think this is said here in a particular sense, because in the Gospel the Lord, about to redeem humankind by the suffering of his body and cleanse it by his blood and by the sacrament of baptism, says: “Father, the hour has come: glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you” (John 17:1).

Therefore, because in the flood the remnants of humankind were preserved in Noah’s ark as the seedbed of future restoration and renewal, he here prefaced it by saying: “The time of every human being has come, because the earth has been filled with their iniquities.” This is in figure; but in truth he says: “A remnant has been saved through the love of grace” (Rom. 11:5). Thus the Apostle cries: “Sin abounded, so that grace might abound more exceedingly” (Rom. 5:20).

12. “All flesh,” he says, “corrupted its way” (Gen. 6:12). Here he uses “flesh” for the earthly human being, whose way was corrupted by the enticement of the flesh. Had that person understood what gift he had received from God, he would certainly not have allowed flesh to hinder the virtues of the soul.

Thus flesh was the cause of the soul’s corruption too, since it is, as it were, the source and a certain place of pleasure, from which, like streams from a fountain, the rivers of evil desires and passions burst forth and overflow widely. By them the soul’s rowing, with its helmsman cast out, is submerged when the mind itself, overcome as if by storms and tempests, yields its place. [Note: Thus the editions. But the manuscripts read, “as it were a certain region, and a place of pleasure.”]

He aptly says that the human being corrupted the way of his own nature. For his way was in paradise—in that path of blessedness, that flowering of virtues, and that incorruptible grace—a way which he defiled with earthly footprints. Others read: “His way,” that is, God’s way. Scripture customarily declares the Lord’s way by this expression. [Note: All editions read, “to be declared of the Lord.” The manuscripts better read, “to declare the Lord’s [way],” with “Scripture” understood. The sense of this passage depends on the Septuagint reading, τὴν ὁδὸν αὐτοῦ, “his way.” See Nobilius’s notes on that verse and Philo, *That the Divine Is Immutable*.]

## CHAPTER VI
On the construction of the ark, in which the form of the human body is described; and on how its several “nests” signify the individual parts of that same human body, and how these must be coated with pitch so as to adhere firmly to one another.

13. But now we must speak of Noah’s ark itself. Anyone who wishes to consider it more closely will discover, in its construction, a description of the form of the human body. For what does God mean when He says: “Make yourself an ark of squared timbers” (Gen. 6:14)? Certainly, we call that “square” which stands firmly on every side and is harmonious with itself. Thus both God, the author of our body and maker of nature, is affirmed, and the work itself is shown by these words to be perfect. [Col. 0368C] That the limbs of a human being are square is evident, if you consider the human chest and belly, equal in the measure of their length and breadth—unless the natural measure is exceeded when the belly is distended by pleasures and banquets. Again, who does not perceive by sight itself that the feet and hands, arms, thighs, and legs are fourfold in form? [Note: Thus Corbie and Long. The printed editions read: “by use itself.”] Many of these parts, even if they are not of equal length or breadth, nonetheless preserve such proportion that a fitting measure and rationale concur in them too: their length is greater than their breadth, and their breadth than their height. And just as the timbers of the ark have a threefold extent—for He prescribed that its length should be three hundred cubits, its breadth fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits—so in our body too there is a greatest, a middle, and a least dimension: greatest in length, middle in breadth, least in height. Yet the whole body, woven together out of its individual members, appears square. Indeed, in common speech we call “square-built” those whom we judge neither excessive in height nor robust through a powerful bodily constitution.

[Col. 0369A] 14. Nor does what He says, “You shall make nests in the ark” (ibid.), seem at all to be passed over in silence. For I believe it was said in a natural sense, because our entire body is woven together like a nest, so that the vital breath may penetrate all the parts of the internal organs and diffuse itself from our governing part through each limb. Our eyes are certain nests, into which sight inserts itself. The hollows of our ears are nests, through which hearing pours itself in and, as it were, casts itself into a deep cavity. The nostrils are a nest that draws scent to itself. The fourth nest, larger than the others, is the opening of the mouth, in which taste is nourished until it matures, and from which the voice flies forth. There the tongue lies hidden; like an instrument of speech, it modulates its sounds with artistic sweetness, and, though itself irrational, gives expression to rational speech. The half-skull is a nest. [Col. 0369B] That membrane which cherishes and encloses the brain is a nest. The inward parts of the lungs and heart are nests. The lung is the nest of our breath—that is, of the breath which we draw and by which we are sustained in this life; the heart, however, is the nest of blood and spirit. For it has two chambers: one receives the blood, as into a kind of hollow, and transfers it into the veins; the other, moistened from the upper one, conveys it into the arteries in an unceasing flow. The stronger bones also have nests. For they are hollow within, and in those cavities is marrow. In the softer internal organs themselves are nests of desire or pain. Whoever considers further will find still more nests in this fabric of the human body. Hence I think that the Psalmist too spoke not only mystically but naturally when he said: “Indeed, the sparrow finds itself a house, and [Col. 0369C] the turtledove a nest in which to place her young” (Ps. 83:4). For there is now in this body a nest of chastity where once there was a nest of irrational desire. But where lust formerly nourished deformed offspring, there now matures the fair inheritance of chastity.

15. “You shall coat it,” He says, “with pitch” (Gen. 6:14). The human body consists of many bones, sinews, and other parts. Thus, joined together by a fitting arrangement both outside and within, it adheres to itself and is held together by its proper cohesion, which the Greeks call *aphē* (ἀφή), so that the enclosed breath infused within it, or the spiritual substance working inwardly, may not wander abroad as though restrained by twin bonds, but may be held in a fitting and containing unity and a strong connection. [Note: The editions read “fitting and containing”; the manuscripts, “fitting and harmonious.”] Therefore the ark is commanded to be bound with pitch, for pitch has a very powerful binding nature. Hence in Greek it is called *naphtha* (νάφθα), from *synaptein* (συνάπτειν), “to join together,” because it connects what has been separated and binds it with an indissoluble bond, so that you would believe the parts joined together by a natural unity. For this reason the ark is bound with pitch inside and out, lest that connection be easily broken.

## CHAPTER VII

Noah’s ark is compared with the ark of the covenant; its dimensions are shown to indicate that each part of the human body has been fashioned for some use and for beauty.

[Col. 0370A]

16. Elsewhere, that is, in Exodus, the other ark is also overlaid with gold inside and out (Exod. 25:11): it is an imitative image, among holy things, of the intelligible world. For as gold is more precious than pitch, so that ark which is among holy things is superior to this one. Accordingly, here He simply specified timber; there, however, He included timber indeed, but incorruptible timber, declaring the merits of the saints. There too He added that its carrying poles were immovable, because the station of the saints is stable and firm: they have followed the path of an approved life under virtue’s guidance, avoiding fellowship with corruption. This ark, however, being in the flood, was driven here and there by uncertain motion, because the condition of sinners is unstable and, [Col. 0370B] exposed to corruption through a kind of flood of overflowing passions, they wander in the inconstancy of error.

17. Nor should we pass over the fact that, after saying, “You shall make the ark three hundred cubits in length, fifty cubits in breadth, and thirty cubits in height,” He added: “You shall make the ark tapering, and you shall finish it above to a cubit” (Gen. 6:15–16). Thus the human head, in a measure suitable to the rest of the body, might correspond in graceful beauty and be joined to the ark as its royal part. From it all the senses are diffused into the other parts of the body; above all, the eyes, set in place by providence as scouts and guardians of nature, survey from above nearly the whole condition of our world. And the mind itself, placed there according to the opinion of many—and especially of Solomon, [Col. 0370C] who says, “The eyes of a wise man are in his head” (Eccles. 2:14)—as though in an imperial palace gathers about itself a council of virtues, so that, surrounded by their company, it may itself be more secure and, as though from some elevated place, administer the governance of the whole body and give forth answers. [Note: The old edition reads, “bestow the kingdom, to give answers”; manuscripts, “bestow governance, to give answers.” Finally, the Roman edition reads, “bestow governance, give forth answers.” We have followed this reading, since no better emendation presented itself. Unless one prefers to take *responsa proferre*, “to give answers,” as a Greek-style expression for *responsa*, that is, “commands,” by issuing commands. Compare this passage with *Hexaemeron*, book VI, chapter 9, no. 55 ff.] Through it we are able not merely to look behind ourselves, nor only to see what lies at our feet, but also to behold the very secrets of heaven with the deep gaze of wisdom. There, then, is the summit of our salvation; there is grace. From there come protection and beauty for the whole body—a beauty which first blooms in the face.
