For it is fitting that the royal palace should have a more excellent splendor, in which, just as sight is pre-eminent, so too is radiance.

18. Indeed, if you observe each feature which seems fashioned in the human form for some use—eyes for seeing, [Col. 0370D] ears for hearing, nostrils for smelling, a mouth for speaking—they serve their functions in such a way as also to confer beauty. How disfigured are the faces of the blind! And what wonder if a human face without eyes is disfigured, when heaven itself has no beauty without the sun? Days without the sun are melancholy to us; nights without the moon give no pleasure: for these are, as it were, the eyes of the world. Take away the lights of the stars, and there is in heaven itself a certain disfigurement of blindness. The hairs that fringe [Col. 0371A] the circle of the eyes and project, as it were, a kind of defensive line, [Note: Corbie and Long.: “and project, as it were, a kind of defensive line.”] prevent the pupil from being harmed by any dirt or dusty haze; they themselves intercept anything brought against the eye which might harm it. If they fall out through inflammation of the eyes, how unsightly it is; if the eyelid is too contracted; if the eyebrows are shaved away, which shine like precious ornaments woven with gems!

19. The ears likewise have a necessary use and an attractive appearance; if anyone cut them off, he would bring deformity upon the entire face. Nature has worked upon them with such care that the winding curves of their cavities, bent inward by wondrous providence, bring great usefulness, lest a sound suddenly strike the hidden parts of the head. Thus we often see many people startled by an unexpected blast, terrified and stunned by the sound of some voice or commotion. [Col. 0371B] Even the wax which grows among these very windings binds hearing as though with a kind of glue. At the same time, if some sound strikes too violently, it is broken and retarded, so that, being announced beforehand, it may soothe rather than, coming unexpectedly, shake the inner parts. If little worms attempt to enter the ear, they too are caught by a kind of sticky wax.

20. Snub noses appear contrary to nature; but if they should be cut off, how could life continue once the passage for breathing had been removed? The appearance would be judged more that of a beast than of a human face.

21. With what pleasing covering the hair of the head clothes the head, like attendants of a royal palace, lest the brain be injured by the breeze, struck by rain, or scorched by the sun. Yet nature has given it so that, according to sex, it is pleasing either [Col. 0371C] longer or cut short; and according to age, or usually according to the character of the season and year. Gray hair is becoming in old people, prodigious in children; it is pleasant to have one’s hair cut more closely in summer and more freely in winter. A woman’s hair is an ornament; for men it is a disgrace. Accordingly, the Apostle expressed this more plainly when he said: “Does not nature itself teach you that, if a man grows his hair long, it is a dishonor to him; but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory?” (1 Cor. 11:14–15). [Note: The word “to be cut” is lacking in the old edition and the Vatican manuscript; we have restored it from the Corbie and Long. codices. The Roman edition has “cut more closely,” which is not bad if supported by a manuscript.]

22. What should I say of the royal palace itself, through which courtly utterances emerge, certain indicators of our mind and messengers of the soul? What of the very arrangement of the teeth, which by their work supply strength to the entire body and also modulate the voice itself? If any of them fall out, the voice falters.

[Col. 0371D] 23. We have spoken at greater length about the head, because all the senses had to be placed at the summit, from which their functions might be distributed throughout the remaining parts. Behind our head the neck lies nearest; on the right and left are the arms, which guard the imperial citadel as a faithful watch. Accordingly, the parts in us which lie nearer the head are stronger and more excellent. The breast too is like a sanctuary of wisdom; and the stomach, as physicians say, is a kind of witness and confidant of the head’s secrets, [Col. 0372A] sharing its sufferings, into which it transfers all that is beneficial or adverse to it. The sides, buttocks, thighs, and legs signify the dimension of breadth by their very appearance; and the steps of the feet, although they seem slender, become broader when we walk.

## CHAPTER VIII

By the door placed on the side of the ark is suitably denoted the less honorable part of the body, to which, in the Apostle’s words, we give more abundant honor. This is applied both to the members of the Church and to the Church itself and the Synagogue.

24. He aptly added: “You shall make the door on the side” (Gen. 6:16), indicating that part of the body through which we customarily expel food, so that we might bestow more abundant honor upon those parts which we think [Col. 0372B] less honorable. Scripture expressed this much more pleasingly than Socrates is reported to have said in a book of Plato. For Socrates himself—or Plato, who was in Egypt—could have read this in the writings of Moses or learned it from others who had read it. Moved by the elegance of the discovery, he considered a door opened to him through which to proclaim the design of our Creator. He praised the fact that it was especially suited to beauty that certain channels or exits of our passages should be turned toward the rear, lest our sight be offended when the belly is emptied. But the Apostle says: “Those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary,” surpassing the philosophical descriptions in one simple phrase; and “those members of the body which we think less honorable, upon these we bestow more abundant honor; and our unseemly parts have more abundant comeliness” (1 Cor. 12:22–23). For there above all is recognized the proof of our sobriety and self-control. Gluttons are either distended with indigestion to the point of danger or, more often, suffer looseness when their bowels have been emptied.

25. The Apostle also aptly applied this to the members of the Church (ibid., 27 ff.). For what are our unseemly and superfluous things, if not luxury and wantonness? If someone, entangled in these during youth, comes in more mature age to baptism, renounces his former ways, puts off his former habits, lays aside sins, is buried with [Col. 0372D] the Lord Jesus Christ, and is crucified to the world and the world to him—does he not, when granted the remission of sins, seem to possess a more abundant honor than the catechumen whose life was more innocent? [Note: Corbie and Long. manuscripts: “has a more abundant honor than … was judged more innocent.”] And, to use the Apostle’s own example: he was a Jew, he was a persecutor; called to the grace of Christ, he began to be an Apostle. And because more was forgiven him, he began to love more, to labor more abundantly than the other apostles, becoming a chosen vessel and sent as teacher of the Gentiles. Did he not obtain a more abundant [Col. 0373A] and honorable glory than very many of the apostles themselves—he who had previously been both unseemly and inglorious when he persecuted the Church of God? This poor and weak man in the Church has redeemed you by his prayers.

26. And, to open greater mysteries: what is as ignoble as the people of the Gentiles? Poor, because they possessed no oracles of God; weak and lame in both feet, because they had believed neither in the Law nor in the Gospel—yet, when called, they believed in Him, and when baptized received grace. Thus, because more was forgiven them, they love more. The people of the Jews remained, though lame in one foot; although they limp even in the Law itself. Therefore, the one who had been considered most glorious lost everything: the wonderful counselor, the wise architect, and the wise hearer. The one who [Note: Old edition: “immovable.” Roman edition and manuscripts: “ignoble.”] was ignoble obtained everything: through the title of faith, the trophy of the martyrs, and fellowship with angels [Col. 0373B] he glories. Plato, then, employed such elegance of expression as he could; but the Apostle, who possessed the Spirit of God, revealed the mystery. Enough has been said concerning the door, since those who were behind became first.

## CHAPTER IX

By the lower parts of the ark we are taught that the receptacles of food should be made least; and this provides occasion for a discussion of the formation and use of the intestines. It is shown that a flood arises from intemperance, and what remedy must be applied to it.

27. Now let us inquire what the Lord means when He says: “You shall make the lower parts of the ark with two and three chambers” (Gen. 6:16). By speaking of the lower parts, we perceive [Col. 0373C] that He wished us rightly to judge that the receptacles of food—that is, the organs which digest received food—must be assigned a lower place. Food is corruptible; and what is corruptible must be compared not with higher but with lower things. At the same time, food is carried downward: a small portion of it benefits the body’s strength and nourishment, while the remainder is conveyed to be purged by the belly, because the intestines are the means through which the superfluities of food descend.

28. Thus our Creator arranged that the intestines should not run straight from the stomach to the bottom, but should be curved and folded, in order that the usefulness of our life might be prolonged. For if the human intestines which receive and convey food were extended in a straight line, food would immediately pass through without any delay; we would have to be hungry continually and feast continually, or perish at once when the supply of food failed. But now, in that twofold and threefold folding and winding of the intestines, food remains and, as it gradually descends, supplies strength, imparts nourishment to the body, maintains satiety, and postpones the desire to eat. There is no sudden discharge, no abrupt emptying, no insatiable appetite, no unfillable craving for feasting. First, then, there would be need and hunger; next, from these would follow the unceasing continuation of eating. And what is more unattractive than always being devoted to the belly, which, when filled, must be emptied, and, when emptied, must be filled? What third alternative remains except death, mingled among foods [Col. 0374A] and feasts? For how could people live longer if, while eating, they were also hungry; while drinking, thirsty; if, before they were filled, they emptied everything they had taken in and were immediately hungry again? But now, while food descends gradually, natural providence moderates hunger and indigestion. First, food is digested in the stomach, which most call the upper belly; then it is cooked in the liver and digested by its heat. Its juice is distributed among particular portions of the internal organs, and from it the whole body gains strength. The growth of the young and the endurance of the old sufficiently attest this. The remainder of the food flows into the belly which everyone calls simply “the belly,” though most call it the lower belly; from there the dung, now full of corruption, must be expelled through that lateral door.

[Col. 0374B] 29. Although these things seem so artfully arranged by natural constitution according to God’s command, nevertheless, unless we preserve moderation in eating and acting, a flood is produced, as it were, by overflowing passions, and a kind of ruin of the whole body. For intemperance kindles lust, produces indigestion, creates corruption. Thus either the internal parts are stretched by hardness and shaken with pains, or the inner covering of the intestines is scraped by the undigested moisture of food and the harshness of indigestion. For their covering is said to be double, like a sheet of paper: one outer layer, which experts call continuous, or which those who have investigated more carefully say runs straight from top to bottom; the other inner layer, woven, as it were, to the sides. Hence they say it is not wholly dissolved when it is scraped away. [Col. 0374C] For if the inner layer were continuous, its rupture would be incurable; there, through the delay caused by the folds, remnants of food adhere. If these junctions are loosened, half-digested foods pass through and liquids flow out: this is a human flood.

30. Therefore it seems to me that through the figure of this ark God wished to teach us how we might be safe from this special flood. [Note: Thus Corbie, Long., and Vatican manuscripts and the old edition. The Roman edition and another Vatican manuscript read “spiritual.”] For corruption is the cause of the flood. When it has crept in, the waters are opened and all the springs of desires boil up, so that the whole body is submerged in a stream of vices so great and so deep. Nothing subjects a human being to such wretched slavery as lust and desires of this kind, which weigh down the miserable conscience with the heavy yoke of crimes, [Col. 0374D] so that it cannot raise itself, having lost the freedom of innocence. The greatest remedy in this flood, then, is that you set the righteous man before you and choose him as an executor of the heavenly command. Who is the righteous one within us except the vigor of the mind, which encloses within this ark every kind of living creature that is upon the earth? Restrain, therefore, all your irrational passions, and subject all your senses to the mind; accustom them to obey the commands of the soul. Do not permit your desires to fly outside or lust to go forth into public; and through the rational mind you will be able to free even your irrational elements and your unclean sins from every danger of the flood.

## CHAPTER X

On the three reasons why dumb animals were subjected to punishment by the flood, how our senses die through sin, and how God establishes His covenant with the righteous.

[Col. 0375A]

31. “Everything,” He says, “that is on earth shall die” (Gen. 6:17). What sin, after all, had dumb animals committed? For what reason were they subjected to punishment, since they possess no awareness of sinning? Yet just as in war, when the commander is killed by the enemy, his army dies with him and all military strength is crushed, so it was not judged inconsistent with justice that, when the human being perished—to whom the Lord God had given a kind of royal power over every class of animal, so that he might preside over every bird, wild animal, and beast with imperial authority—domestic animals too, and every irrational creature, should die with him. Accordingly, whenever there is a plague and the region of the sky is corrupted, a dreadful pestilence first contaminates irrational creatures, especially dogs, horses, and cattle, infecting those which seem to live in association with human beings; then the force of disease entangles the human race also. This, in my judgment, is the first ground of a just explanation.

32. The second is this: no one blames nature because the remaining members of our body die when the head alone has been removed, although we see many survive after hands and feet have been amputated. But the preeminence of the other limbs is not the same as that of the head. Therefore, when that from which our senses proceed into the rest of the body has been cut off, all the members die with it; nor is the Creator’s providence thereby deficient, nor is the frailty of human substance disproved. Likewise, then, let no one now object that, since the human being is the head and a kind of governing principle of the other animals, it should not seem strange if the other animals die with him.

33. The third reason is that animals lacking reason were created not for themselves but for humankind. They were commanded to exist for the sake of humankind, that the human condition might be distinguished by their subjection. Thus the prophet attributes this as a favor to humankind, saying: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea” (Ps. 8:8), because all those things exist for that person’s sake: some for utility, some for delight, and some for pleasure. [Col. 0375D] Consequently, when the human being for whose sake they were made was blotted out from the face of the earth, it followed that they too should be blotted out by an equal destruction. This is according to the plain exposition of the text.

34. But a loftier and deeper interpretation adds this: when the soul is bent beneath the heavy mass of passions and, as it were, submerged in the tide of diverse desires, all earthly thoughts and desires rush headlong downward. For every sinner becomes more insolent in proportion as he has committed more grievous crimes. Wickedness grows through practice and exercise, and boldness is nourished by impunity. Thus the sinner withdraws from every regard for honor, and in him all earthly things die through the bitterness of deadly sin, which destroys the sinner by a true and everlasting death. No one dies more grievously than one who lives in sin. [Col. 0376A] Individual passions die in such a person. The sight dies which announces sin, which fixes itself upon a deceitful woman, which is captivated by the beauty of another’s face, which the eyes of a prostitute have bound, which the look of a harlot has ensnared. Does not the person seem to die who has driven the weapon of lust into himself, who has of his own accord rushed into the pit of death? Hearing too dies when it reports crimes, when it conveys the words of an adulterer making solicitation, when it introduces into souls the words of the prostitute who seduces a young man with much persuasive speech and binds him with the snares of her lips. [Col. 0376B] [Note: Old edition: “The voice dies through silence”; better, Roman edition and Corbie and Long. codices: “The voice dies in silence.”] The voice dies in silence if it does not confess to God. It dies through excessive speaking, because it is written: “In much speaking you shall not escape sin” (Prov. 10:19). It dies through anger when the mind exceeds the measure of punishment. Finally, every sense dies if it becomes a servant of iniquity.

35. And therefore, because all earthly things die in the flood, while the righteous person alone remains forever, it is said to him: “I will establish my covenant with you” (Gen. 6:18), because he is heir to divine grace, possessor of the heavenly inheritance, and participant in most blessed goods. When human beings die, they customarily transfer their estate by testament; nor does the inheritance pass until the testator dies. But God, being eternal, transfers to the righteous the inheritance of His divine substance; Himself lacking nothing, He gives what is His without any loss through the gift. He is not burdened by companions in His goods; rather, He enjoys that which we enjoy. Thus the Lord Jesus, though rich, became poor, that we might be enriched by His poverty. He fulfilled both Testaments by His blood, in order to make us co-heirs of His life and heirs of His death, so that we might have fellowship in His life and the benefit of His death. He grants much to the righteous when He says: “I will establish my covenant with you,” because the rational and faithful person is God’s covenant. He himself is the inheritance; he himself is the possession in whom lies the power of the divine testament, the fruit of judgment, and the inheritance of promise. Of him David says: “Behold, children are the inheritance of the Lord; the fruit of the womb is a reward” (Ps. 126:3). But now, while preserving the exposition of the deeper mystery, let us proceed to what remains.

## CHAPTER XI

A righteous man is a source of salvation to himself and his household, although error may sometimes creep in when his vigilance relaxes. One who is righteous before human beings is not always righteous before God. Finally, the mind performs among the passions the office of a householder.

36. “Enter,” He says, “you and all your household into the ark, because I have seen you righteous before Me in this generation” (Gen. [Col. 0377A] 6:18). Even in this passage the truth of the prophetic saying is plainly established: “The fool is foolish for himself alone, but the wise person is wise for himself and for many” (Prov. 9:12). Thus, by the merit of righteous Noah, his household too is preserved in the flood. So, those sailing on the sea and armies in war are safe from danger through another’s aid if the former do not lack a pilot’s skill and the latter a commander’s prudence. But because a good commander has a good army, we understand that the praise of the righteous man is not omitted in this matter either: he formed his household in such a way that it shone with fellowship in virtue, and thus his kindred deservedly found salvation. Nor is it objectionable that afterward either his son or his wife sinned. The righteous man was asleep when his son erred (Gen. 9:22 ff.). The woman also, being of the weaker sex and disturbed by the weight of danger (ibid. 19:26), believing that the entire world was perishing in divine fire—why do you wonder that she could not follow her husband, when the righteous man himself barely escaped after being warned by angels? Why wonder if error creeps upon a human being or diligence relaxes? You may object, therefore, that even the righteous man became drunk. But I think this should be reserved for its proper place (below, ch. 29).

37. Let us now consider what remains. He aptly said: “Because I have seen you righteous before Me in this generation.” Many appear righteous to human beings, few to God: one way to human beings, another to God. Human beings judge by the appearance of life; God by purity of soul and the truth of virtue. Human beings approve what is outward; God examines what is inward. He added thoughtfully, “in this generation,” so as neither to condemn those before nor exclude those after, and so as rightly to establish that the flood occurred for the destruction of that generation which had no fellowship with righteousness. This is according to the letter.

38. But a higher meaning invites us to understand that the vigor of the mind is in the soul, and the soul in the body, as the householder is in his house. For what the mind is in the soul, the soul is in the body. If the mind is safe, the house is safe, and the soul is safe; if the soul is unharmed, the flesh is unharmed. For the sober mind restrains all passions, guides the senses, and governs speech. Therefore the Lord rightly says to the righteous: “Enter”—that is, enter into yourself, into your mind, into the governing part of your soul. There is salvation; there is the helm. Outside is the flood; outside is danger. But if you are within, you are safe outside also; because where the mind governs itself, [Col. 0377D] thoughts are good and actions are good. For if no vice casts a shadow over the mind, thoughts are pure. If chastity is pursued and temperance is dear to the heart, no flame of lust burns fiercely and no ulcers of sickness break forth. For sobriety of mind is medicine for the body.

## CHAPTER XII

Seven clean animals of each sex and two unclean animals are brought into the ark, because the number seven is sacred and complete, whereas two is not. There is within us a certain feminine sevenfold element, but through the learned man it is advanced to a masculine condition. Finally, human nature is shown to be capable of opposites.

[Col. 0378A]

39. Let us now consider for what reason He commands that seven and seven, male and female, of the clean beasts be brought into the ark (Gen. 7:2), but two and two of the unclean, so that seed may be nourished over all the earth. In my judgment, He declares that the week is clean, because the seventh number is pure and sacred. It is combined with none other, nor is it generated from another. Therefore it is called virgin, because it produces nothing from itself; and, rightly, although the number seven is designated by a feminine noun, as one without and exempt from maternal offspring and marital union, it possesses the grace of masculine sanctification: “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exod. 34:19). And in the prophet you have: “She poured forth and bore a male” (Isa. 66:7), that is, a holy one. The second number, however, is not complete because it is divided. What is not complete is regarded as empty. But the seventh number is complete, because the week is like the decade and like that first principle, [Note: Corbie and Vatican manuscripts: “because alpha is according to the likeness,” etc. Hence it seems to us not far from the truth that something was previously said concerning the first number; when it was afterward removed, no small obscurity arose throughout this whole passage.] because it was made in the likeness of Him who always is, from whom flow and are moved the virtues existing in every kind. These matters belong to nature.

40. To speak, however, of moral matters: there is no doubt [Col. 0378C] that the irrational element of our soul is divided into the five senses, speech, and the generative faculty—things which by nature appear feminine, because our senses swiftly creep toward material and worldly things. Hence it is clear that they possess a substance of softer nature. But to the learned and industrious man all things are clean, because the wisdom and virtue of a man trained by exercise impart to these things firmness through masculine judgment. Thus, through the purpose of the prudent governor, they are transferred from the quality of the weaker sex into a stronger substance. [Note: Thus Corbie and Long. manuscripts. Vatican manuscript with the Gillot and Roman editions: “there is no doubt that [it is] rational.” Amerbach and Erasmus: “there is no doubt.” For “that which is rational …”] [Note: Amerbach and Erasmus: “the purpose of the governor transfers [them] from the quality of the weaker sex into a stronger substance.” Gillot and Roman editions: “the purpose of the governor is to transfer the quality of the weaker sex ….” Corbie and Long. manuscripts better support the text, in which the word “senses” must be understood.] For the wise person’s judgment is strong and settled, not changeable like that of the foolish and ignorant person, whose counsel wavers in uncertainty, like that of the wicked person, who chooses not what is true and just but what he wants to be advantageous to himself; he separates from truth and divides from justice. Justice is a singular good, esteemed in itself at its own great worth. Injustice, however, gives birth as though divided: now bent by hatred, now by gain, and confuses the things that ought to be distinguished. For the fool changes like the moon and is variegated; or, distorted by a diversity of humors, he stains his soul with shameful contagion into the likeness of a leprous body, often mixing wholesome thoughts with harmful ones.

[Col. 0379A] 41. But perhaps, since you see that both clean and unclean living creatures are commanded to be brought into the ark, you may reasonably be troubled because I said that unbecoming things ought not to be mixed with honorable discussions. Nor do I deny that there are in our soul certain seeds and, as it were, beginnings of irrational yet clean impulses, and also of impulses that are not clean. For human nature is capable of opposites, so that it possesses both the power of wickedness and an entrance for virtue. Accordingly, at the beginning of this book, Genesis, you read that in the form of the tree in the middle of Paradise there was the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2:9). Concerning this tree of the knowledge of good and evil, there was a command that it must not be tasted, because our mind, in which knowledge and instruction reside, receives an awareness of good and evil. Therefore, just as the Maker of nature preserved living creatures for propagating, or even restoring, [Col. 0379B] the race, so that the whole earth might be filled with the seed of living creatures, so too he did not judge that the earthly substance of our body should be left empty of passions of this kind, like unclean animals. When it is submerged, as if by a flood, in pleasures and luxury, it tosses amid the passions mentioned above. But when, through sobriety and self-control, each person has drained away the flood of overflowing passions and restored a certain dryness to the soul, he begins to give life to his body and to the purity of the soul, whose governance is wisdom.

> [Note: [Col. 0379D] All editions read: “he commands the living creatures of the flesh.” The manuscripts read: “you see that living creatures are commanded,” etc.]

> [Note: [Col. 0379D] Thus the manuscripts. The editions, however: “whose kingdom is wisdom.”]

## Chapter XIII

Why, after Noah entered the ark, the flood occurred after seven days; likewise, why Moses said that it lasted forty days and forty nights, and on what principle it continued for forty days. How divine mercy shines forth in the very threat of punishment. Then Noah’s generous obedience is considered.

[Col. 0379C]

42. It is also worth inquiring why, after Noah entered the ark and brought in the living creatures, the flood occurred after seven days. For it does not seem purposeless that neither more nor fewer days were interposed, but precisely as many as there had been in the creation of the world. For the world was made in six days (Gen. 2:2), and on the seventh day God rested from his works. By this sign he declared himself to be the author both of the world and of the flood. He created the world because of his goodness; he made the flood because of the deservingness of our sins. Men were therefore warned, even by the number of days in which the world was created, that they ought to reconcile their Creator not only by tears and prayer, but by reforming their conduct. Thus the Lord gave time for repentance, preferring to forgive rather than to punish; so that, held in suspense by terror of the imminent flood, they might be compelled to seek pardon, and, while dreading the peril of future death, renounce impiety and injustice.

[Col. 0380A] Secondly, from this also let us infer the clemency of the Lord, who is merciful beyond measure: though the offense of many years had accumulated from the creation of the world even to its end, he was willing, if they repented, to remit it in a few days. For God forgets sin and rewards virtue, as he himself says through the prophet: “I am, I am he who blots out iniquities, and I will not remember them. But do you remember, and let us be judged together; declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:25). For when he sees that true virtue has been poured into the soul, he grants it such honor that he not only pardons former sins, but also bestows grace and justification. Therefore he waited also until the seventh day, the very day on which he rested from his work, so that, if pardon were sought, [Col. 0380B] reform might follow and he might rest from indignation.

43. It was also important not to pass over the fact that he said the flood occurred for forty days, and added, forty nights (Gen. 7:12). For we know that “day” denotes that which the sun marks by illuminating the earth, and “night” that which surrounding darkness separates from brightness. Often we signify a day in such a way as not to include the night, and often so as to include it. For when we speak of a month of thirty days, we also signify the nights. Hence, since it would have been sufficient for Moses to say that the flood lasted forty days, it is asked why he added, “and forty nights.” Some before us have understood this to show that both men and women perished in the flood: referring the day to the man, who [Col. 0380C] is purer and like light, and the night to the woman, who is described as created while the man slept (Gen. 2:21). They add that the man came first as the originator, to arouse a woman’s virtue and stir her to childbearing; his activity is more conspicuous in public, while hers is more hidden, as though enclosed by household walls and nearer to night. She arose in second place and, having been formed, now owes the debt of gratitude to the man’s rib; she is also subject to the privilege of the superior and stronger sex, and is comparable to material things by the function of bearing children. Yet the corresponding number of punishment applies to each, because their sins too corresponded; and rightly the spans of time do not differ, because the deserts of their offenses do not differ.

> [Note: [Col. 0379D] Thus the editions of Gill and Rome. But the edition of Amerbach, with the Corbie, Longpont, and Vatican manuscripts, has “formed into the man’s rib.” Erasmus finally has “formed from the rib for the man,” etc.]

44. Many also inquire, not without reason, why the flood lasted forty days. We may say that the material number was assigned to sadder matters, [Col. 0380D] that is, to the destruction of creation; whereas the week was assigned to the constitution of the whole world, that is, to happier matters. But perhaps someone may ask: why was the Law also given in forty days (Exod. 24:18)? Moses observed that many days and remained on Mount Sinai when he received the ordinances of the Law. Rightly, therefore, the commands for turning away from sins are given by the same number through which the punishment for guilt was discharged, so that we may know [Col. 0381A] that from the same period of life in which punishable guilt can be committed, praise ought through reform to be gained. Hence now forty days have been prescribed not for punishment but for life, so that by this number, through fasts and more frequent prayers, we may lighten the penalties of our sins and, attending to the precepts of the Law, correct our error by devotion and faith. Thus through the Lord’s resurrection the fortieth day is no longer counted as the last but as the first; and life is counted from that point from which previously the number of death was reckoned toward the consummation of the world and the destruction of the human race.

> [Note: [Col. 0380D] The Tournai, Vallicellian, Colbert, and Mazarine manuscripts begin the treatise only from these words. Bartolomeo Urbinas, in the Milan Ambrosian manuscript of *On Noah and the Ark*, asserts that the opening words in the manuscripts are “not without reason.”]

45. “And I will blot out,” says the Lord, “every resurrection of flesh from the face of the earth.” O beauty of heavenly words, if anyone examines them with the seemly understanding of a devout mind! God is angered by our sins, but does not forget mercy. He threatens punishment, but does not allow extermination. He tempers vengeance; he recalls severity. He says that he will blot out all flesh, not from the earth, but from the face of the earth. He shakes off the flower, preserves the root; he permits the power of human nature to remain in the depth of its substance, though it labors upon the surface, remaining inwardly impassible and immune from harm, reserved for the replacement of those who are not subject to guilt.

[Col. 0381B] Beautifully, moreover, he says, “I will blot out,” as letters are erased without damage to books and without diminution of tablets. Ink is erased, but the wood remains. Letters are erased so that better ones may often be written. The ink is removed; the substance is not destroyed. “I will blot out,” he says, “the corruption of flesh, that I may write incorruption. I will blot out the resurrection of flesh from the face of the earth, that I may write those who rise in heaven. I will blot out from the book of earth, that I may write in the book of life. Let the letters of iron be blotted out, my Lord, Lord; let them quickly be blotted out, that the letters of Christ may be written. Let earthly resurrection be abolished, that heavenly grace may overflow. Come, Moses: prepare your breast; receive the Law; receive letters which divine mercy will no longer erase. Receive tablets which the Lord may establish forever. Would that you yourself did not break them! Indeed, my own fault had taken them away from me, unless the Lord had restored them.

“Moses was rightly angered, lest those who did not render obedience should possess divine privileges. Yet I think you broke them not for me, but for the Jews. You broke them for the Jews; you received them for me. The first tablets were broken so that the latter might remain. [Col. 0381D] You broke them in the breasts of the Jews. For what good was it that they should hold tablets whose precepts they could not keep? Behold, they say that they hold the second tablets, but they do not hold them. They say that they read the divine letters, but they do not read them (Deut. 9:10). Moses says that the tablets were written by God’s finger; they do not read God’s finger, but read iron. They see ink, but do not see the Spirit of God. But the Church does not know ink; it knows the Spirit. Therefore Paul knows how to write not with ink, [Col. 0382A] but with the Spirit of the living God (2 Cor. 3:2–3). O sacrilegious, foolish people of the Jews! A human being writes by God’s Spirit; and a human being brought up under the Law—and they wish God to have written with ink, not with the Spirit.”

> [Note: [Col. 0381D] Thus the Corbie, Longpont, Valc., and Colbert manuscripts, with the old edition. The Roman edition has: “O sacrilegious, foolish people of the Jews.” Vatican manuscript: “O foolish sacrilege of the Jews.” The Mazarine manuscript finally: “O foolish sacrilege of the Jewish people.”]

46. Therefore, to return to what precedes: God blots out the resurrection of flesh as the writing of letters. This declares that, because of its impiety, he erased the excessive propagation of human beings under the figure of writing; but he chose to preserve the substance and continuance of the human race as though by the permanence of tablets, so that from it a remaining seed might spring up. What he says also seems to agree with this interpretation: “I will blot out every resurrection of flesh.” Yet in ordinary natural usage cleansing appears contrary to reproduction, because through cleansing the luxuriance of reproduction is cut back and restrained. Nevertheless, everything that is cleansed loses its outward appearance, retains its substance, and is improved. Therefore the Lord, who now by the cleansing of the flood restrained bodily indulgence and the continuance of that generation which had degenerated from the beauty of nature and its bestowed gift, restores its beauty. [Col. 0382B] This is according to the letter. But in its higher sense, the image of the flood is a type of the cleansing of our soul. Thus, when our mind has washed itself free from the bodily allurements of this world in which it formerly delighted, it will also wipe away the old filth of desire through good thoughts, as though purer waters absorb the bitterness of formerly muddy streams.

> [Note: [Col. 0382D] All editions read: “he wished to preserve the human race.” The Colbert, Corbie, Longpont, and Mazarine manuscripts have the text as given.]

> [Note: [Col. 0382D] Thus the four manuscripts of better quality. Others and the editions: “the Lord, by the cleansing of the flood … restores beauty by the attractiveness of the gift.”]

47. “And Noah did,” it says, “all that the Lord God commanded him” (Gen. 7:5). The righteous person receives commands; [Col. 0382C] the servant, orders. The one who does whatever he has undertaken to carry out is accounted in the place of a friend; the one who wavers in obedience is assigned to the burden of servitude. Accordingly, the Lord Jesus also says in the Gospel: “You are my friends, if you do what I command you. I will no longer call you servants” (John 15:14–15). A command, therefore, is given as to a friend, to one who with strong love and sober judgment carries out what has been commanded. Nor did the Lord’s judgment deceive him: the righteous man fulfilled everything—not a part, but everything—that had been commanded him; and therefore he received the testimony of divine Scripture. Nor should you think it superfluous that it names both Lord and God together. For God is in the Lord and the Lord in God; but this is so that you may understand the command to be common to Father and Son. Some before us, however, have interpreted it in this way: by saying “Lord” and “God” here, he expressed a twofold authority, one to punish and the other to forgive. Since he who here first punishes sinners exacts vengeance, he named the Lord first; but since afterward he grants pardon so that the seed-bed of the righteous may propagate, he named God afterward. Thus God is named when he is about to make the world: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth. And God said, ‘Let there be light.’”

## Chapter XIV

That the flood occurred in spring, so that people might suffer more severely; and in Noah’s six-hundredth year, so that the destruction of humankind might correspond with its creation. Likewise, that the bursting of the fountains of the deep and the floodgates of heaven signifies a flood of mind and body.

[Col. 0383A]

48. There is also this consideration, which is not superficial: that in the six-hundredth year of Noah, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh of the month, the flood occurred. There is no doubt that the second month belongs to springtime, when growing things increase, the field bears fruit, and the offspring alike of earth and animals pours forth. Therefore he sent the flood then, when the grief of those punished amid their abundance would be greater; then the vengeance was more terrible, as though God were saying: “Behold, rich nature has brought forth everything according to the [Col. 0383B] grace of divine providence and generosity; the more fruitful earth has caused everything to sprout for human use. Crops appear; fields are filled with wheat and barley; the leafy crowns of trees are clothed with blossoms promising fruit. The earth does not fail in its services; the beasts do not fail in their gifts, which are regularly paid in offspring, so that nothing may be lacking to humanity. Humanity alone fails in its proper role: it does not know its Author, from whom all things are provided; it neglects its Creator. Humanity despises its rewarder, though God has not despised his work. Let all things perish with the human being, for whose sake all things were born. Let humanity be consumed amid its own riches; let it die with its own dowry. Before humanity, the earth had committed no offense; it had erred in no fruits. In humanity alone it recognizes that it has degenerated, bearing thorns and thistles [Col. 0383C] instead of fruits. The one admirable gift—the governing faculty of the mind—has perished. Why, then, should all those things be preserved?”

Therefore water was not poured out after the fruits had been gathered, lest the earth should feel it as a benefit rather than a flood. Indeed, among the Egyptians, at the spring season—but in another month—the Nile overflows, so that the ground may be softened for sowing and may receive the seeds cast upon it in a gentler bosom and more kindly womb. That the flood occurred in Noah’s six-hundredth year seems to show that Adam was created on the sixth day. The same number—that is, the even number—is preserved both in the originator and in the restorer, because the sixth number is the source of sixty and six hundred. The same month is also called both the first and the seventh. But we ought rather to observe the first: that after the flood, in springtime, the care of cultivating [Col. 0383D] fields is restored, and the fruitfulness of calm and fertile soil begins to come forth. This signifies that God would never have brought about the destruction of humankind in the number or season in which he made its beginning, unless he had been offended by monstrous sins. At the same time, the reckoning of season and number promises pardon: even when angered, he is reminded by these preceding occasions of [Col. 0384A] his own benefits not utterly to destroy the substance of those whom he himself bestowed.

> [Note: [Col. 0383D] The words “in the second month” are absent from all manuscripts and old editions. Except, however, the Mazarine manuscript, where they were restored by a second hand; likewise “according to the second month,” where the first hand reads, with the Corbie, Valc., Longpont, and Colbert manuscripts, “the seventh.”]

49. “And all the fountains of the deep burst forth, and the floodgates of heaven were opened” (Gen. 7:11). Scripture fittingly expressed the force of the flood by saying that heaven and earth were shaken together, the elements of which constitute the whole foundation of this world. Thus, as masses of water streamed in from every side, the human race was overwhelmed. This is according to the letter. But in its higher sense, heaven symbolizes the human mind, while earth denotes the body and the senses. Great shipwrecks occur, therefore, when the storm and tempest of the mind, body, and all the senses are mingled together.

Let us weigh the language carefully. Often deceit and guile of mind exercise their poison, [Col. 0384B] while bodily sobriety and self-control nevertheless cover over the mind’s wickedness. Frequently the slippery mind is uncertain in its faith and opinion; yet the flesh is free from pleasures and luxury, so that frugality excuses the mind’s error. Thus many heretics wish to display bodily continence in order to win credence for their assertion through the testimony of a sober flesh: though slippery in understanding, they are nevertheless regarded as somewhat more excusable, because they are less shameful. But when the poisons of the mind and the contagions of bodily obscenity confound all perception and vigor; when the soul, slippery in its uncertain motion, foul with the ink of malice and inflamed with the rage of cruelty, is also driven to bodily crimes; when a greedy disposition, unable to endure moderate means, is driven by desire for luxury [Col. 0384C] and a passion for lavish spending into the crime of seeking another’s means of livelihood—then there is a great flood, as all passions rush upon one together. Then folly, injustice, recklessness, wickedness, and faithlessness seem to pour out from above, like floodgates of the mind. From the fountain of the earthly body there burst forth lust, drunkenness, luxury, and, finally, the downfalls of various crimes, which utterly emasculate both bodily strength and vigor of mind.

> [Note: [Col. 0383D] The editions of Amerbach and Gill, with the Mazarine manuscript, read “may be cleansed”; Erasmus and Rome, with the other manuscripts, “may be overwhelmed.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0384D] All editions, with the Tournai and Vatican manuscripts, read “is free from luxury, so that frugality …” But the Corbie, Colbert, and Mazarine manuscripts, with Latinius’s conjecture, read “is free from luxury”; and the Corbie manuscript, with Latinius, “as frugality.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0384D] All editions read “freshness”; the manuscripts, with Latinius, read “vigor.”]

## Chapter XV

By the ark shut from without and floating on the waters, the human body, covered with skin and agitated by varied motions, is signified; by the fifteen cubits of water by which the mountains were surpassed, the human senses; finally, by the death of all flesh, the destruction of a soul corrupted by passions is foreshadowed. But the proud in particular must be destroyed, while the righteous person, with his perverse movements extinguished, meanwhile remains in the body as though incorporeal.

[Col. 0384D]

50. “And the Lord shut the ark from without” (Gen. 7:16). According to the letter, the meaning is clear. The ark had to be shut and secured by safe protection, lest the wandering currents of the flood [Col. 0385A] should penetrate it. Nor is it unfitting, in a higher interpretation, if we judge the human body—of which this described ark is a figure—to be enclosed by skin and protected from cold and heat. God the Craftsman clothed it for the protection of all the limbs with natural coverings and wrapped it in a surrounding covering, so that it might neither freeze in cold nor melt in summer heat.

51. The water therefore overflowed, lifted up the ark, and it was borne upon the surface of the waters. Not without reason did the water overflow, when the floodgates of heaven were opened and the fountains and rivers of water burst forth from the earth. This was said with great emphasis. For where there is a bursting forth, there must be an irreversible outpouring; nor is the fall of vast streams easily held back. Thus the written statement is clear. But if you think it must be viewed more deeply, our flesh is agitated by various passions and tosses like the sea; now by hunger, now by thirst, now by desire, now by joy, now by grief, it is cast here and there as upon the waves of its troubles.

52. I also think it should not be passed over that Scripture did not omit to state by how many [Col. 0385B] cubits the water stood above the earth. It says that the water stood fifteen cubits above the lofty mountains. Thus the simple meaning is plain. But the allegory includes the five senses, which are in our body like lofty mountains overhanging this flesh of passions; they are often assailed by beasts and agitated by their dense and dark thickets. Hence the Lord, coming to his Church through the faith of the believing nations, comes from Lebanon, [Col. 0385C] as the prophet Habakkuk says: “The Lord will come from Lebanon, from the shadowy and dark mountain” (Hab. 3:3). The Church too comes from Lebanon, as the Song of Songs has it. For thus we read: “Come here from Lebanon, bride; come here from Lebanon. You shall pass and go beyond from the beginning of faith, from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards” (Song 4:8). Thus the Gentile peoples, who once endured grave attacks from beastlike passions, now advance through the height of faith and the sublimity of devotion. Through these mountains, therefore, Christ comes, restraining by Gospel arguments the fierce movements of this body and destroying, by his obedience and humility, that height of heart and self-exalting pride. Rightly they began to bear the fruits of gentleness, [Col. 0385D] whereas formerly floods of grievous passions overwhelmed them.

Concerning the number of cubits, some before us have judged that the five senses have a threefold grouping: because sight sees what is visible, hearing hears what is audible, smell smells what is odorous, taste tastes what is tasteable, and touch touches what is subject to tangible substance. Therefore the five senses have been reckoned threefold, perhaps according to the saying: “Write for yourself threefold” (Prov. 22:20). But I think it more fitting [Col. 0386A] to understand the senses of the earthly person, the animal person, and the spiritual person, which those streams of the flood surpassed.

> [Note: [Col. 0385D] These words—from “as Habakkuk says” through “as the Song of Songs has it”—have been restored on the authority of all the Gallican manuscripts, since they were previously absent from all editions.]

> [Note: [Col. 0385D] The Roman edition reads: “which is subject to tangible matter.”]

53. Rightly, every flesh that moved died. This is clear according to the letter, and it properly and naturally expressed the corruption of the flesh by the indication of tempestuous movement. For defective movement exists only through the corruption of affection. Flesh both stirs up pleasures and is itself stirred by pleasures. Such movement produces corruption. Therefore the cause of corruption is the movement of this world, through which each person’s soul degenerates. When vicious passions move the mind, corruption is produced; when the pursuits of virtues stir it, there is progress in instruction. Therefore everyone who was on dry land died; for those whom [Col. 0386B] the wave of so great a flood had submerged could not but die. This follows the written text and sequence of words.

But if you seek the allegory, there is no doubt that, after the example of drier wood, which fire burns as soon as it begins to lick it, a soul will burn in the fire of desires or fall struck by the flood of the flesh, unless it is moistened by the dew of diverse virtues, irrigated by a kind of draught of wisdom, a fountain of justice, and the watering of chastity—as though its vital root had dried up. Therefore the mind should always feast upon thoughts of good works, so that, intoxicated with the juice of prudence, it may grow rich and not easily yield to the violence of the bodily flood, and die emasculated by the dry neglectful decay of barrenness. Therefore the Lord warns us not to withdraw from the fountain of wisdom, but to drink the draughts of virtue, lest anyone dry up under the sun of iniquity and be unable to endure the storm of persecution [Col. 0386C] (Bar. 3:20 ff.). For it is written: “If they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” (Luke 23:31).

> [Note: [Col. 0386D] Old editions read: “emasculated by the thirsty dryness of neglect.” The Roman edition and Vatican manuscript: “emasculated by the decay of neglect.” Other manuscripts: “emasculated by the dry decay of neglect”; the Mazarine: “disemboweled.”]

54. “God blotted out,” it says, “everything that was upon the face of the earth” (Gen. 7:23). The explanation of the text is evident. But the allegory explains to us the pride that exalts itself in this earthly and frail substance, forgetful of divine things and despising human things; it deforms the very bearing and gait of the arrogant person. Such are the daughters of Judah described by Isaiah, flashing with motions of their eyes and tossing themselves with uplifted necks (Isa. 3:16). Such people raise their eyebrows, with swollen heart, lifted breast, and thrown-back neck. They merely brush the ground with the soles of their feet, but poise their entire bodies and suspend themselves in empty balance; they move their steps forward, throwing the head backward. They gaze at heaven and disdain the earth, as though their neck were fixed by pain so that they could not bend it. God therefore blotted these out of the book of life, saying: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14:11); nor does he permit them to adhere among the heavenly records of the merits of the saints.

> [Note: [Col. 0386D] That is, the heavenly registers, or, as he said shortly before, the book of life.]

55. Therefore, after all those outside the ark had been killed, [Col. 0387A] Noah alone was left in the ark with those who were with him (Gen. 7:23). The simpler statement needs no interpretation; its meaning agrees with the letter. But the higher and inward signification shows that the righteous man and lover of wisdom, like a fruitful tree, remains alone with his own people after the destruction of the things that used to gnaw at his food, overshadow his foliage, and constrict the growth of his branches—namely, stripped of irrational passions. His own people are the pure deliberations of the mind that adhere to virtue. It is well added that he remained in the ark, since, after bodily passions had been cut off, it might seem scarcely believable that he still lived in the body. Though he was now free from earthly contagions, he nevertheless retained the incorrupt substance of the body. Thus, as though incorporeal within a body, [Col. 0387B] he was borne above the flood and not swallowed up: he bore a body, as though placed inside an ark, but he governed that very body amid so many movements, unconquerable by passions, as though incorporeal.

> [Note: [Col. 0387D] The Roman edition has: “But his own are of his jurisdiction.” Incorrectly; for here “his own” means the same as Noah’s household, as is clear from the preceding passage.]

## Chapter XVI

Why it is said, “The Lord remembered Noah,” with no mention of his wife and sons; why beasts are named before cattle; and what kind of spirit was brought over the earth so that the waters might cease.

56. “The Lord remembered Noah, and the beasts, and the cattle” (Gen. 8:1). Many ask why the writer did not say that the Lord also remembered Noah’s wife and sons, when he remembered the beasts and cattle. But when he said that he remembered Noah, he included in the head and ruler of the household all his remaining relations. At the same time, a certain harmony among the remaining relations seems to be expressed. For when all are dear to one another, there is one household; but when they disagree, they are separated and divided into several households. Where love exists, therefore, the whole household is signified by the name of the elder upon whom the others depend. Thus, if someone speaks of a tree, he surely includes its branches; if someone names a branch, he likewise comprehends in one and the same expression the fruits upon it.

57. Nor is it purposeless that he first said that the Lord remembered Noah, then the beasts, and afterward the cattle [Col. 0387D]: that is, why he named after the human being not the gentler animals but the fiercer ones. The apparent reason is that the fiercer animals might be tamed by being placed near both sides. This seems also to be indicated in that poetic verse:

> κακοὺς δ᾽ ἐς μέσσον ἔλασσεν  
> “He drove the cowardly men into the middle.”  
> (Homer, *Iliad* 4)

The poet likewise employed this arrangement in ordering an army about to fight: he placed the weaker troops in the middle so that they might receive greater aid from the stronger forces on either side and take up the fighting of both parties. In these words the literal sequence is clear. In a higher [Col. 0388A] sense, however, it is certain that the righteous person holds the thoughts of his heart in the middle, not at one side; and so long as he lives this life, he must have in his body, as in that ark, heavy beasts. For there is no mind, no soul, that does not receive even the savage movements of evil thoughts. Thus the soul of the foolish sharpens beastlike impulses and feeds the poisons of serpents; but the strength of the wise person softens and restrains them.

58. “And the Lord brought a spirit over the earth, and the water ceased” (Gen. 8:1). I do not think this was said so that we should understand “spirit” to mean wind. For wind could not dry up the flood. Otherwise, since the sea is stirred daily by winds, it would surely be emptied. For how would the sea not be drained by the force of winds if the flood, spread over the entire world as far as the [Col. 0388B] Pillars of Hercules, as they say, and surging over the sea called the Great with the peaks of the highest mountains covered, had yielded to it? Therefore there is no doubt that this flood was restrained by the invisible power of the divine Spirit, through heavenly operation and not through a blast of wind. Hence it is written: “All things wait upon you, that you may give them food in due season. When you open your hand, all shall be filled with goodness. You will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust. You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103:27 ff.). Therefore there is a Spirit to whose operation all things seem to yield, in whom is the power even of heaven itself, as it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6). This Spirit is the creator of all things, as Job also says: [Col. 0388C] “The divine Spirit made me” (Job 33:4).

> [Note: [Col. 0388D] All editions read: “therefore by the power of the Spirit.” All manuscripts: “… by the power of the divine Spirit.”]

## Chapter XVII

The closed fountains of water and floodgates indicate that the causes of error must be cut off for the soul’s healing. The reckoning of the time when the ark came to rest indicates that the flood began and ended at the beginning of the year, that is, in the spring season; and that it increased and decreased by the same numbers. The opening of the ark’s window signifies that the mind, through the senses and by contemplating nature, comes to knowledge of God. Finally, the sending out of the raven signifies the expulsion of sin from the soul, to which it does not return after the passions have been extinguished.

59. Let us now consider what divine Scripture means when it says: “The fountains of the waters and the floodgates of heaven were closed” (Gen. 8:2). I do not think it obscure. For the flood decreases through the causes [Col. 0388D] by which it increased. The fountains of waters had burst forth, the floodgates of heaven had been opened, so that the earth might be inundated by waters flowing in from every side. The sources from which the flood had arisen had to be closed, so that it might begin to subside. This is what the letter says.

But a more subtle interpretation shows that the flood of the soul had come through the vice of the mind and bodily luxury, so that malice was mingled with passion and passion with malice. When the physician, God’s Word, enters to visit the soul that had long suffered from the wickedness of its deliberations and the bitterness of its passions, [Col. 0389A] the causes of the sickness first had to be cut away. For the beginning of healing is to cut off the causes of disease, lest the things that harm continue longer to feed the growth of the sickness. The Law also teaches us this (Lev. 13:5–6). When leprosy has become stationary and no longer spreads, it calls that station and settled condition of leprosy clean. For whatever moves contrary to nature is unclean. This, therefore, is the health of the soul; this is the soundness of mind: that the inflow of error should cease and fault should be stopped, lest it spread. When the incentive to fault and sin has ceased, health is secure, and the uninjured strength of the soul flows back into itself.

60. “And the ark,” he says, “came to rest in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month” (Gen. 8:4). Unless you attend carefully, the meaning of this passage is difficult even according to the literal sense. First of all, one must take care that the frequent repetition of “the seventh month” does not confuse anyone. For it is thus written: in the six hundredth year, according to the Hebrew truth, in the first month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the flood began; for one hundred and fifty days there was an inundation of waters; the ark rested upon the mountain in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month; afterwards the waters began to diminish through the mercy of God; the waters decreased for one hundred and fifty days; afterwards the tops of the mountains appeared; then, after forty days, holy Noah opened the door of the ark; he sent out the raven, which did not return; he sent out the dove, which returned empty; again, after seven days, he sent it out, and it returned with an olive branch; a third time, after seven days, he sent it out, and it did not return; then Noah perceived that all the water had receded. Thus the year is shown to have been completed in the six hundred and first year of Noah, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month.

[Note: Mazarinus manuscript, in a gloss and in a later hand, reads “the second” four times and once “of the second,” whereas in the text, together with the other manuscripts and editions, it has “the seventh” and “of the seventh.”]

[Note: Corbie, Longpont, Colbert, and Mazarinus manuscripts: “in the six hundredth year, in the seventh month.” The editions and other manuscripts read as in the text, except that the Roman edition substitutes “second” for “seventh.” Valc. has both: “in the second month, in the seventh month,” etc. Hence we strongly suspect that the words “according to the Hebrew truth” entered other manuscripts, and thence the editions, by conjecture. We admit, however, that those who restored “but in the second month” do not appear to have acted absurdly; see chapter 14, §48, and the following column of this same chapter. Otherwise Ambrose’s calculation would be less consistent. But everyone knows how easily copyists slip in writing numbers.]

[Note: Five of the better manuscripts restore “after seven days”; these words are absent from the others and from the editions.]

[Note: Roman edition and Tornacensis manuscript, in the margin: “in the second month.”]

So far as the plain explanation is concerned, the earth’s equilibrium after the flood was restored in the same month and on the same day on which it was destroyed when the inundation of the flood began. For in the season of spring every field grows green and the earth brings forth its fruits. Then trees begin to bud and fruits to sprout. Therefore the Lord restored and renewed its abundant condition. Thus, in the second month—that is, April (for the first month is March, in which the righteous man has his birth, when the equality of nights and days is reckoned, that is, on the eighth, as the Romans think, or, according to others, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April)—in the second month, I say, that is, April, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the flood began.

[Note: Roman edition: “the trees to sprout, the fruits to germinate.”]

Spring, therefore, is reckoned the beginning of the year, not according to current convention, but according to nature’s pre-eminence: because then the hope of the year begins, and the fruit begins to show itself, that time appears to be the beginning of the year. But the seventh month is counted, according to number, as the one called September. For although the year may seem to begin with September, as the practice of present indictions shows—for then seed is cast—yet its origin is derived from the spring, when fuller grace begins to reveal itself. Therefore the month which is judged first by one reckoning is held seventh by another.

[Note: See what will be said in volume II, in the letter to the bishops of Aemilia.]

Then, therefore, the ark rested—that is, in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month—upon the mountain of the square. From that point the flood began to diminish.

[Note: Roman edition: “upon Mount Ararat.”]

Consider at the same time that by the same numbers by which certain things begin, they are brought to an end. The flood began in the second month of the year, on the twenty-seventh day of the month; for one hundred and fifty days the flood poured in, and for another one hundred and fifty days it receded. For forty days its excessive force boiled over through rain from heaven and the bursting forth of the springs; after another forty days had elapsed, after the tops of the mountains had appeared, in the eleventh month, on the first day of the month, holy Noah sent out the raven. Thus it is established that the flood diminished by the same number by which it had been increased. Hence Scripture teaches us that order must be preserved.

[Note: Thus five manuscripts and the Ambrosian edition; Vatican manuscript and other editions: “when these had elapsed, the tops of the mountains were seen; in the eleventh …”]

61. What the door of the ark is which the righteous man opened has been stated above according to the bodily interpretation. According to the loftier interpretation, however, it seems necessary to say that the bodily senses are regarded as resembling doors. For through them, as through doors, a certain apprehension of sensible things enters our mind. Thus our mind seems to look out through these senses, especially through sight, which is judged superior to all the bodily senses, because it is akin to light. Through it, as we behold heaven, earth, seas, sun, moon, and the stars by which the firmament is adorned, we understand that God is the maker and ruler of the world; and we believe that these things could neither have come into being nor remain in being without God as their author and the creator of such great works.

62. Through this window, therefore, the righteous man first sent out the raven. The reason must be sought, though it is not hidden as regards the literal sense: for many regard the raven as a herald of future events, observing its cries and scrutinizing its flights. But the higher sense signifies that, when the mind of the righteous man begins to cleanse itself, it first repels from itself whatever is dark, unclean, and rash.

[Note: All editions and two manuscripts read, “that every righteous man”; others read as in the text.]

For all shamelessness and sin are dark, and feed upon the dead, like the raven; but virtue, which shines with purity and simplicity of mind, is near to the light. Therefore sin is, as it were, sent out and driven away, and separated from innocence, so that nothing dark may remain in the mind of the righteous man. Accordingly, once the raven has gone out, it does not return to the righteous man; for every sin flees equity, and seems incompatible with uprightness and justice. Indeed, the unjust person thinks that he has escaped as though from chains when the righteous man separates himself from fellowship with him—a fellowship like some flood and familiar corruption. Thus the raven, finding nowhere the dryness of the earth, did not return, but remained.

[Note: After “remained,” the Roman edition adds, “until the water dried up”; but no other edition or manuscript supports this addition.]

63. We should also consider why he says that the raven did not return “until the water dried up from the earth” (Gen. 8:7), as though it returned afterwards. But this manner of speaking is familiar to divine Scripture. For in the Gospel you find it written concerning holy Mary that Joseph “did not know her until she bore a son,” although certainly he did not know her afterwards either (Matt. 1:25). Further, what kind of expression is this, that he says, “until the water dried up from the earth,” rather than “until the earth dried up from the water”? Although ordinary speech too is accustomed to admit such usage, some before us have judged that this wording expresses a certain excessive force of the passions: because the soul is consumed by turbulent and stormy passions, but when they fail and, as it were, dry up, it regains its strength. Therefore the form of sin does not return to the soul of the righteous man, leaving it, as it were, dry and dead, and one to which it can no longer do harm.

[Note: Roman edition: “until the water dried up from the face of the earth,” as also below. The other editions and manuscripts, with strong agreement: “until the water dried up from the earth,” where “itself” is understood, by an ellipsis common among Latin writers.]

## Chapter XVIII

As the raven represents wickedness, so the dove represents virtue. Noah shows that the righteous person is always ready to receive it; by keeping the dove another seven days, he also teaches the patience necessary in correcting others.

64. Nor is it without significance that the dove is sent out afterwards. For simplicity dissolves wickedness, and virtue dissolves sin. Wickedness, therefore, loves the flood, shuns the fellowship of the righteous mind, and remains as though desolate and without any resting-place, having no communion with virtue. But virtue returns, loving the fellowship of the righteous and more disposed to confer benefit: it offers what is salutary and warns against what will be harmful. Thus, when the dove had been sent out and saw that the water had ceased, it returned as though full of justice, so that it might report to him who had sent it what he still ought to avoid and might thereafter obtain a better fruit by waiting.

That the dove, finding no resting-place for itself, returned to him gave a clear indication, through birds of this kind, of how great the difference between wickedness and virtue is. The raven, sent out before, when the flood appeared to be overflowing still more abundantly, seemed to find a place to rest. Yet the raven is not a bird like others that are accustomed to live upon the waters. Therefore, since the raven seems to have found a place in which to remain, while the dove did not find one, the higher interpretation plainly signifies that wickedness is accustomed to mingle itself with the restless passions and desires by which the soul is corrupted; it delights in them as though they were kin and household companions, and there establishes its dwelling. Virtue, however, offended at the first sight, hurried back to the mind and soul of the righteous man, because there it had established for itself the safest lodging; for elsewhere virtue of this kind can no more find a safer station than a dove can. For simplicity is slow to find a harbor amid the wiles of this world and the waves of worldly desires.

65. Therefore, just as justice, having gone out for a little while, as it were for the sake of seeing, hastens to return to the excellent mind and does not withdraw far from the righteous man, so too the righteous person and lover of virtue, when he recognizes that virtue is approaching, opens wide the bosom of his mind. For what does it mean that Noah, a man devoted to virtue, stretched out his hand, received it, and brought it in to himself? Although this seems plain according to the letter, you will not easily grasp it unless you know the custom of the wise man, who makes use of virtue as a kind of scout and seems to entrust to it a certain precedence in exploring and carrying out affairs. That virtue, therefore, weighs natures, so that if it judges any of them capable of advancement, it may join them to itself.

For wisdom possesses a goodness that is common, generous, and liberal in imparting benefit, so that it associates with itself those whom it sees to be compliant. But when it sees the nature of some resisting its purpose, it flies back and returns, as it were, to its familiar lodging; and the wise and diligent man hastens to receive it as though with a hand of the mind, opening all his heart, in which he held it even when it was absent. For the wise man can never be deprived of his own virtue.

66. Furthermore, what does it mean that he kept the dove for another seven days and sent it out again, unless it is so that you may perceive that the good and excellent purpose of the wise man always strives to associate others with itself, to amend those who wander, and to correct those who stray? If he sees someone recoil at the beginning, nevertheless he does not despair of that person’s progress toward change and correction. For just as a good physician, even when it is not the time for treatment, nevertheless first sends forward the watch of visitation, then does not neglect the vigil of fitting expectation, and, yielding for a little while to the passions, waits for an opportunity to heal; when it is offered, he does not abandon his duty. So too the wise man, by words and discussions, as a physician by medicines, desires to heal contrary passions. And because in all things the remedy of divine favor must be employed, he therefore waited seven days, in which the whole world is described as completed (Gen. 2:2) and rest provided for its Maker, so that from that Author of all things the pattern of human action might be received.

## Chapter XIX

Why the dove is said to have returned in the evening with an olive branch in its beak; how Noah knew that the waters had failed; and finally why the same dove, sent out a third time after seven days, did not return.

67. The dove therefore returned in the evening, carrying an olive leaf and a branch in its beak (Gen. 8:11). He did not idly mention both the evening and its return and its carrying an olive leaf and a little branch in its beak. He did so in order that you might not suppose virtue to be fleeing from future progress, if it could gain any; nor, again, might you suppose it to have been without light and concealed in certain darkness. Rather, gleaming with the brightness of day, it waited until the day’s setting and then returned to him with whom it could not possess even the darkness of evening.

The leaf which it carried with it, although it seems to have brought only a small leaf, nevertheless signified some hope, though not great, for those who would repent of their error. A leaf could not exist without a twig. Therefore it bore the token of a correction beginning to germinate—however slight—namely an olive leaf. On the olive tree the olive is produced, from which oil is made; with oil this material light is nourished and the obscurity of darkness driven away. And what is more akin to virtue than light? The leaf and the branch, therefore, are a token of correction; and correction has repentance as, so to speak, its root. That repentance cannot germinate amid turbulence, but only in those who have already received spiritual discourse.

[Note: All editions and the Vatican manuscript read “corruption”; six manuscripts of better standing read “correction” or “rebuke.”]

Nor is it without reason that the olive branch appears to have been carried in its beak, because virtue and wisdom possess the brightness of their own light in speech, and its light shines forth immediately in its very appearance, especially when it speaks peaceably; for those seeking peace are accustomed to carry this branch as well. It brought the branch because simplicity, by purity and sincerity, pours into our ears certain seeds of usefulness: it either rouses us to zeal through the good teaching of virtue, and invites us to the reward belonging to good discipline of which it is conscious, or it instills in the sinner the desire to practice repentance and follow a converted manner of life.

[Note: Thus Corbie, Longpont, Tornacensis, Colbert, and Mazarinus manuscripts, with the Ambrosian and Erasmus editions; Vatican manuscript with the Gillot and Roman editions: “the teaching of virtue.” Likewise shortly afterwards, where editions and two manuscripts read “entrusted to discipline,” Corbie, one Vatican manuscript, and Longpont read “conscious of discipline.”]

[Note: Roman edition: “to follow conversion”—a suitable sense indeed, but this reading is confirmed by neither manuscripts nor editions.]

68. We should further consider how holy Noah knew that the water had subsided from the earth, as is written (ibid.). First, according to the letter, because he could ascertain whether the leaf brought back was dry or moist. Next, because the dove is not a bird of such a kind that it could draw out fruits hidden beneath water. But you must consider whether that leaf had sprung forth before the flood or during the flood. If before the flood, the righteous man rejoiced that some fruit from the old seed had been preserved; from it he inferred a token of divine mercy, namely, that the flood had already withdrawn, since it displayed a fruit which the floods had been unable to harm. If the leaf was born during the flood, then the righteous man perceived that new seeds of heavenly mercy had borne fruit: the roots of the trees lived, and, as though their life had been renewed, they produced their ancient fruits and returned to their accustomed offspring, the prior leaves showing the indication of this.

69.
