But he inferred this rather in the lofty interpretation: that our Lord God, although offended by the bitter errors of our wickedness, had nevertheless preserved for us some seed, however small, of our ancient lineage and our native virtue, lest every mark of His work and creation in the human race should be utterly cut away. Hence Isaiah says: “Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us a seed, we should have become like Sodom, and been made similar to Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:9). In the name of one city he expresses a token of blindness, and in that of the other sterility. For in their native language the Chaldeans named Sodom and Gomorrah as signifying blindness and sterility. Rightly, therefore, in the figure of cities of this kind the Lord cut off human vices rather than judged human beings to be punished.

[Note: Vatican manuscript and editions: “indicated.” Corbie, Longpont, Valc., Tornacensis, and Mazarinus: “judged.” Whether Colbert has “indicated” or “judged” cannot easily be determined.]

70. The dove is sent out for the third time after seven days, and it does not return. Let us therefore consider lest this prove contrary to what we said above. If the dove in word, but virtue in fact, does not return to the righteous man, then has the righteous man been deserted and deprived of his gift? By no means. For such a man is never separated from virtue. Nor, when he sends justice forth from his mouth and introduces a discourse of another virtue, does he strip himself of virtue or deprive others of an equity fit for imitation. Rather, like the sun, he illumines others when he sends out the rays of his own light. Fire indeed warms those who approach it, while it itself retains the heat of its own nature. Does daylight fail when it illumines the whole world with its brightness? It retains its unhindered course and uninjured nature.

So too this virtue under the figure of the dove: while the flood was still raging, it returns to the righteous man—according to the bird, upon the earth; according to virtue, amid human passions—because it could not find a place to cling in the hearts of the wicked. Therefore, returning to that second lodging of its own, it clings there and rests. But when the floods of the passions have subsided, and many have sought to share in the word they have heard and the doctrine they have learned, the discipline of virtue begins to be no longer the possession of one person but a common good. It is drunk, as it were, like a cup of wisdom by many who previously, though thirsty, refused to drink.

Thus now floods rage in the hearts of the Jews; and when the water of heavenly teaching overflows and the drink is abundant, they do not think it should be drunk. The Gospel is read; virtue goes forth from heavenly discourse; the priest expounds in the Church. But lest perhaps, being placed alone within the ark, he cannot be heard, the priest sometimes goes out of the Church; when he encounters a Jew, he admonishes him and brings forward the example of the heavenly Scriptures. They shut their ears lest the fountain wash them even against their will and the moisture of the Lord’s word sprinkle them. But if any believe, they run to the fountain, seek teaching, desire that the Gospel be made known to them, and are not satisfied by continual drinking. Thus they long to be filled in eager rivalry from the fountain of wisdom which formerly they wished to flee. What fountain? Hear Him saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:37–38).

## Chapter XX

That the water is said to have diminished on one day and the earth to have dried on another signifies that righteous Noah was first in two generations. By the uncovering of the ark is expressed the renunciation of bodily pleasure. Why the first or second month is called a day of spring. Finally, the difficulty concerning the discovered leaf is resolved.

71. In the six hundred and first year of Noah’s life, he says that on the first day of the month the water diminished from the face of the earth; but in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, he records that the earth was dry. What is meant by this addition concerning the diminishing of the water, when the foregoing calculation, once reckoned, seems to show that the year was completed—a year which begins in the second month and extends to the second month of the following year?

[Note: The Roman edition, contrary to the authority of the manuscripts and other editions, altered this entire passage as follows: “In the six hundred and first year of Noah, in the first month, the water diminished … on the seventeenth day … he records that on the twenty-seventh day of the month Noah opened the ark.” What is meant by the addition “of the first month” concerning the water, etc.?]

Unless perhaps we should understand that the figure of the righteous man is here set forth: so that the first year was that in which the flood began, namely the first year after the six hundredth; then again the first year and first month after the six hundredth year, when the water diminished from the face of the earth. This is because the righteous man was first in virtue among the generation of sinners destroyed for its offenses; and in the second generation, which began after the flood, he was first also in order, because he was the first of the second generation and had worthily escaped first. Rightly indeed is honor paid to one who was both first in the first generation and the beginning of the later one; who deserved both to escape from that generation and to be propagated as seed for this one. When others had perished, he alone, through the merit of an excellent life and the prerogative of virtue, rich before God, did not experience the corruption of wickedness. Through him it came about that the whole body of humankind was not seen either to have been annihilated on earth or left cut off from God’s grace.

[Note: For the correction of this passage, the manuscripts and early editions agree except in one word. Where the editions read “in that order,” all manuscripts read “and in order.” Some Paris editions printed: “the six hundredth year, namely; the first year again and the first month after the six hundredth of all”; the remainder as in the text. Others, besides the cited words, after “flood,” continue: “in that order he was first. Rightly, therefore, honor is paid to him, because he was first in the first generation that escaped and the beginning of the later one, who deserved to be propagated for this as seed,” etc.]

72. “And Noah,” he says, “uncovered the roof of the ark” (Gen. 8:13). Since, as we interpreted above, we have understood the ark to represent the body, let us understand in the higher sense what it means for the body to be uncovered. Otherwise, it is clear how the ark could be opened according to the letter. What, therefore, is the roof of the human body, which was shut up during the flood, unless perhaps we understand it as pleasure, which covered our body and, through Adam’s error, served as a kind of covering? It is especially considered like a roof because every sense is in the head, and from there pleasure held the whole body subject to itself.

But when the mind of the righteous man, sober and uninjured by the corruption of the flood, inflamed with desire for divine knowledge, desired to spring forth and fly upward to higher things, it uncovered all that impeded it and laid open and removed the appearance of pleasure, which by a certain covering concealed the other parts of the body. Thus it set the body free not only from service to an ignoble mistress, but also apprehended incorporeal things; for “the things which are not seen are eternal.” Therefore the righteous man, free from corruption and desirous of eternity, sought the Lord whom he did not see.

73. As to his saying “the first month” or “the second,” and that it is a day of the spring season, you find elsewhere: “This month shall be the first for you among the days of the year” (Exod. 12:2). For the month that is first in grace after danger rightly received the prerogative of the first month.

74. Nor should it trouble you that we said above that the leaf found upon the branch could have been produced after the flood. Although herbs often grow beneath water, nevertheless, to remove every scruple, what would be remarkable if, at God’s command, on the very day when the water diminished, the earth immediately sprouted? For He is both restorer and creator of fruits, and had not forgotten the operation of His own work. Indeed, in Genesis you have that He immediately commanded the earth to bring forth fodder-bearing grass and fruit-bearing trees with their fruit; and immediately the earth brought forth fodder-bearing grass, having seed according to its kind, and fruit-bearing trees. And that was the one day on which God commanded or made these things (Gen. 1:11). Therefore God, not forgetful of His kindness but forgetful of our wickedness, restored His work within the same span of time in which He had begun it.

[Note: Thus Vatican, Corbie, and Longpont manuscripts. Others and the editions: “but mindful of our wickedness, [He restored] His work of the same …” Mazarinus: “by the same [time] by which He began,” etc.]

## Chapter XXI

Why Noah awaited God’s command to leave the ark. How, by the order in which he and his household are described as entering and leaving, abstinence from generation and then its use are indicated. Finally, what that order teaches us in its spiritual meaning.

75. And the Lord God said to Noah: “Go forth from the ark, you and your wife and your sons” (Gen. 8:16). Thus, when the water had withdrawn and the earth was dry, Noah could have left the ark. But the righteous man claims nothing for himself; rather, he entrusts himself wholly to the divine command. Especially since he had entered at a heavenly oracle, he ought to await a heavenly answer before leaving. For justice is reverent, whereas injustice is irreverent: it arrogates what is not due and does not reverence its author.

76. Let us now ask why, while they entered the ark, the order of those entering was this: first Noah and his sons entered; then his wife and his sons’ wives. But when they left, the order was changed. For it is written: “He went out, and his wife, and his sons, and his sons’ wives” (ibid., 18). The literal sense signifies abstinence from generation at their entrance and the use of generation at their exit. For then the father entered first with his sons, and the sons with their father; afterwards came his wife and his sons’ wives. That is, the sexes are not mingled at the entrance, but are mingled at the exit.

Clearly, therefore, by the very order of entering the righteous man uttered, as it were, a certain declaration: that was not a time for intercourse or pleasures, when destruction threatened all. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says (Luke 17:26–27), reproving those who in Noah’s time ate and drank, married wives and gave daughters in marriage; and therefore, because of their intemperance, the flood came upon them. That time was therefore one of mourning, not joy. Hence the righteous man did not delight in intercourse with his wife, nor did the sons of the righteous man seek marital union. For how unsuitable that, at the time when living people were dying, those destined to perish should then be begotten? Afterwards, however, when the flood had withdrawn, the practice and concern of marriage rightly followed for the propagation of the rest.

[Note: The word “followed,” absent from all editions, has been restored from Corbie, Longpont, Colbert, and Mazarinus manuscripts.]

Thus women leave with men, not men with men; so that an intercourse of males among themselves might appear forbidden, while the union of male and female, permitted by the lawful lot of marriage, might appear allowed.

77. The higher sense is this: when there is danger, certain manly and stronger reasonings should adhere to the mind, and by these the mind should defend itself as though by a kind of offspring of sons, because a certain manly battle-line confronts storms and more grievous passions. But when the danger has passed, there is no harm if gentler thoughts are joined to stronger ones—not so that the stronger are made effeminate by the gentler, but so that the gentler dispositions may be strengthened, as it were, by manly ones, when all our deliberations are directed toward virtue, justice, integrity, and courage, and stronger counsels may arise and grow through a kind of practice and seedbed of virtues.

Therefore, when some confusion of vices occupies the mind, it is not useful to sow thoughts or for the mind to generate and give birth. But when desires have been suppressed and the mind has rested, then, having received a kind of seedbed of deliberation, virtues and good works can germinate.

## Chapter XXII

Why Noah, without being commanded, built an altar to God; why it is said “to God” and not “to the Lord”; why he also offered whole burnt offerings from clean beasts and birds; and what is meant by the Lord’s saying, “Reflecting, I will not again curse the earth,” etc.

78. “And Noah,” he says, “built an altar to God” (Gen. 8:20). It may perhaps be asked why, although above the Lord instructed Noah what he should do and Noah did everything, here he did what he had not been instructed to do. Surely the Lord ought not, like a miser, to demand a reward for grace; and the righteous man understood that the true rendering of thanks was that which was not commanded but freely offered. Therefore he tolerated no delay. For the virtue of a grateful mind excludes the passion of hesitation; whoever waits for the debt of gratitude to be exacted from him is ungrateful.

But that he “built,” he says, “to God,” and did not say “to the Lord,” but “to God,” indicates, according to the interpretation of the name, that this act of thanksgiving was not compelled, as though rendered to a lord; rather, it was the obedient and grateful virtue of the righteous man, as rendered to God. He reserved the imperial title; he named the benefaction.

79. “And he took,” he says, “from the clean beasts and birds, and offered whole burnt offerings” (ibid.). The literal sense is clear: we ought to offer things unstained, in which the disposition of the offerer shines forth. But the higher interpretation is that clean beasts appear to be the perceptions of the wise person, while birds are the intellects, which are far more subtle and light.

80. But now let us consider more carefully what is meant by the statement: “And the Lord God said: Reflecting, I will not again curse the earth because of the works of human beings, because the heart of man persistently attends to evils from youth” (ibid., 21). Therefore He would no longer strike the whole earth, as He had done, for all the days of the earth.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “from his youth. Therefore I will not again strike all flesh as I have done, for all the days of the earth.” Nobilius agrees with the manuscripts on this passage, except that a little above he considers the punctuation should be restored thus: “And the Lord said, reflecting: I will not again …,” which, he asserts, corresponds better to the Hebrew.]

Although He had exacted vengeance upon humankind, nevertheless He had learned that the vengeance of the law is more effective for fear and the knowledge of instruction than for changing nature. Nature can be corrected in some, but cannot be changed in all. Therefore the Lord punished so that we might fear; He spared so that we might be preserved. He punished once as an example of fear; thereafter He spared, lest the bitterness of sin should always reign. At the same time, one who wishes to punish sins too frequently is considered harsh rather than censorious.

Therefore the Lord says: “I will no longer curse the earth because of the works of human beings,” that is, because He wished to display His mercy toward the whole human race; yet He ought not to bring a kind of security and negligence to human minds. He punishes a few; He preserves the greater number. Then, when He says, “I will not again,” He shows that He lightens human afflictions rather than increases them, knowing that human sins cannot be entirely removed. It is as in a proverb: if someone wished to draw water with a fine net, so too is one who tries to remove wickedness from human hearts.

[Note: Roman edition: “I will not again strike all flesh.”]

81. “I will not again,” he says, “curse the earth because of human sins, because the human disposition persistently attends to evils from youth.” See how God indicates that we sin deliberately by saying that the human disposition persistently attends to evils: by this statement He seems to signify that the human heart deliberately inclines toward sins, that there is in our ruling faculty a slippery tendency to sin, and—what is worse—that zeal for it is not absent. For He says “persistently,” as though we were anxious lest immunity from fault should steal upon us. Then He did not say “toward one evil,” but “toward evils.” And He added “from youth”: for wickedness grows from that age, although elsewhere we have read that even an infant of one day is not without sin (Job 14:5).

[Note: Thus the manuscripts and early editions agree strongly. Roman edition: “I will not again, he says, curse the earth because of the works of human beings, because the human heart persistently attends to evils from youth.”]

But infancy is not without sin because of bodily weakness; whereas deliberation and zeal for sinning begin from youth. Thus the child sins as weak, the youth as wicked—deliberately desiring to commit sins and glorying in crimes. For with many, innocence is held to be cowardice and fault to be praise. Thus young people are accustomed to boast of luxury, pleasures, and adulterous passions. Sin therefore grows with the ages. Accordingly, He declares that the whole human race is no longer to be destroyed when He says, “I will not again strike all flesh”; but vengeance is reserved in part.

## Chapter XXIII

The Lord’s saying, “Seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, shall not cease,” is explained according to the letter and morally.

82. What, again, is the meaning of the saying: “Seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, winter and summer, [Note: [Col. 0399D] Only the Roman edition reads, “day and night.”] day and night shall not cease” [Col. 0399D] (Gen. 8:22)? According to the literal sense, it signifies that, so long as they endure according to the Lord’s ordinance, living creatures—or all the woodland things—will remain uncorrupted in their proper state through the seasons. For when the seasons are corrupted, those things also are corrupted which each season produces. But if there is a confusion of seasons, how, once that confusion has occurred, can the things that produce remain? Thus it is the seasons that either corrupt or preserve things, according to the quality they themselves possess. And so the year is composed of contraries—spring, autumn, summer, winter—just as the harmony of a song seems to consist in a mingling of low and high notes. Thus this world too is held together by contraries: air and earth, fire and water. Our bodies likewise preserve a certain order of nature through cold and heat, moisture and dryness. For if natural order and measure are confused, destruction must necessarily follow. Therefore, with the confusion of the flood removed, the Lord promises that a fixed order of seasons will endure for the continuance [Col. 0400B] of the world.

83. The deeper meaning, however, is this: by seed we understand the beginning; by harvest, the end. In both lies the cause of salvation. One is incomplete without the other, because where there is a beginning, an end is sought; nor can there be a beginning if the end is removed; and the end returns into the beginning. Thus he indicates that, while it is in this world, the human race will always return into the same cycle: when the year begins, it comes to an end; when it ends, it begins; the world is not dissolved in mid-course.

So too, when the mind seems to begin something, it should strive onward to the end and seek the completion of its work. When it finishes some work, it should not be struck down as though its work had been completed [Note: [Col. 0399D] All editions and most manuscripts read, “be finished with its work.” Corbie and Longpont read more elegantly, “be struck down with its work.”]; rather, it should return to other works and always exercise advances in virtue. For it sees [Col. 0400C] that the earth is always recalled to its fruits [Note: [Col. 0399D] Thus six manuscripts and the American and Erasmian editions. Others read, “the earth is renewed.” Again, at this same place the Vatican manuscript [Col. 0400D] has, “which are born variously in spring and summer, and in autumn,” etc.]—which are produced variously either in spring and summer, as in the regions of the East, or in summer and autumn, as in the regions of the West.

84. At one time the seedbeds of the earth yield their offspring; at another time we gather the fruits of trees. Thus fruits are divided into necessary and pleasurable: necessary fruits come from the seeds of the earth; pleasurable fruits, however, from the fruits of trees. Accordingly, our body is nourished, as it were in spring—that is, by *aēr*—with natural food. [Note: [Col. 0400D] Since earlier editions presented the word Ἀὲρ as Latin, while the manuscripts gave it partly in Latin and partly in confused characters, the editors of the latest Paris editions, failing to grasp the sense, substituted: “But *aer* is called by a Greek or Latin name.” Incorrectly. For here ἀέρ is used by metathesis for ἔαρ, “spring.” Unless one prefers to write, by contraction, ἧρ, which occurs frequently among authors.] *Aēr* is the Greek name; *ver* is the Latin, for spring. Therefore Scripture took its example from the regions of the East, especially Egypt, through which the Hebrew passed, or from the regions of Phoenicia.

The soul, however, is nourished by pleasurable things—that is, by the fruits of wisdom. Again, corresponding to the contrary cold and heat in our body, fear and anger appear to be opposed in it. But because it is in the body, [Note: [Col. 0400D] We have corrected this with the aid of the manuscripts. Here the editions, with great agreement, give: “it is in the body and has anger [Col. 0401D] and fear, nor can it be without this necessity in the body by nature.”] it must also have anger and fear, nor can it exist without this bodily necessity of [Col. 0401A] nature. Therefore the mind of the wise person dispenses just restraints, lest it mingle anger and fear and produce a kind of confusion and flood in that person’s soul.

85. And in the phrase “day and night,” understand by day the virtue that illumines, and recognize by night dark foolishness. Thus even in fear, as in cold, there can be illuminating virtue. Likewise, temperance can restrain anger, so that some people may not utterly collapse in fear, but direct their fear rather toward works of virtue. For example, if a persecutor presses you, fear God more, and judge eternal punishments rather than present ones to be avoided; while you fear these, be kindled toward glory, angry at faithlessness and wickedness. Conversely, when inflamed by anger, moderate your agitation by divine fear.

## Chapter XXIV

On the prerogative of power over other animals, divinely granted to human beings by the blessing bestowed on Noah and his household; and how the Lord can be understood to have given them all creeping things for food, when some of them are poisonous.

[Col. 0401B]

86. “And the Lord blessed Noah and his sons, saying: Increase and multiply, fill the earth and rule it; and [Note: [Col. 0401D] Here the old editions differ from the manuscripts only in omitting: “the beasts of the earth, and all birds of heaven, and in all.” The Roman edition, however, arranged the entire passage thus: “Your fear and trembling shall be upon all the beasts of the earth, all the birds of heaven, everything that moves upon the earth, and all the fish of the sea,” etc.] your fear and trembling shall be upon all the beasts of the earth, all the birds of heaven, all that moves upon the earth, and all the fish of the sea” (Gen. 9:1–2).

This prerogative of power over the other animals seems to have been granted to human beings also in the preceding passages. But in the place where it says that God made humankind, it is written: “Male and female he made them, and blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, fill the earth and rule it; have power over the fish of the sea, the birds, the beasts of the earth, and the creeping things” (Gen. 1:28). I have noted this so that you may understand that a twofold generation of humankind is expressed: one according to the image of God, the other according to the formation from the clay of the earth.

Indeed, that creation of the human being from the clay of earth appears to have occurred after the world, after God rested from his works. The formation of the earthly statue is produced, as it were, late. [Note: [Col. 0402D] Longpont manuscript: “the formation of earthly substance.”] “There was no rain upon the earth, and no human being cultivated the earth. Then God formed the human being from the clay of the earth, breathed into his face the spirit of life, and the human being became a living soul” (Gen. 2:5, 7). But the former human being was established on the sixth day, as it were by the perfect number in which all God’s works were completed, by a perfect operation according to the image of God; and this one, who was found righteous in the flood, is compared with him. Therefore God placed him above all earthly things, just as he placed the one made in God’s image, [Col. 0402A] [Note: [Col. 0402D] All editions and not a few manuscripts read, “because he restrained both from earthly vices.” The Corbie and Colbert manuscripts read, “because each of them,” etc.] because each restrained himself from earthly vices. The one was so generated as to owe nothing to earthly contamination; this one had been approved amid dangers, tested amid passions, and found not to have been liable to the passion of confusion. [Note: [Col. 0402D] The Corbie, Longpont, and Vatican manuscripts read, “liable to confusion.”]

87. The deeper meaning, however, is that the righteous person is increased by the greatness and multitude of virtue and by teaching; and fills the earth, as it were a heart in which there is a receptacle for intelligible things. Thus he allows nothing to be empty of wisdom, so that foolishness may invade it. Having subdued, therefore, not only all earthly passions but also bodily senses, he subjects even the beasts to himself by a certain terror and fear; in them there seems to be a form of malice and savagery. For all malice is cruel and uncultivated, and is puffed up [Col. 0402B] by a kind of airy swelling. Nor is it obscure that certain creeping things possess a likeness to deadly passions, from which a kind of poison seems to be infused into the mind.

The righteous person, therefore, rules all these things with which he does not mingle; rather, he restrains them, if his mind is not led by pleasure or desire, is not broken by sorrow and fear, and does not run the course of this life as something slippery and falling through luxury and indulgence. Rather, by self-control and temperance, the wise person drives such passions away from himself.

88. But because he immediately adds: “All creeping things that are alive shall be food for you” (Gen. 9:3), lest you perhaps be disturbed because we previously spoke of poisonous creeping things, recognize that some creeping things are poisonous and others gentle. Understand this of the gentle creeping things, which, although not all crawl on belly and breast like serpents, nevertheless have feet so small that they seem to creep rather than walk. Therefore, understand by poisonous creeping things unclean passions in the body like them; [Note: [Col. 0402D] Thus the Vatican and Mazarin manuscripts with the editions. The Corbie and Colbert manuscripts read, “passions like those in the worldly body.” Longpont reads better, “passions like those in the unclean body.”] but by gentle ones, beautiful passions. For every affection that is apart from the allure of shameful pleasure is indeed a passion, but a good passion. Soft desire, anger, and fear are harmful passions of the soul; harmless affections, however, are good passions. A certain use and means of life is provided for us through these; we use them as food for the grace of life, and delight in their banquets.

## Chapter XXV

Whether the Lord commanded that vegetables rather than meat should be eaten; how Moses fortified us against philosophers’ opinions concerning the soul, whose diverse views are reported; likewise, how the rational and sensitive parts of the soul are to be distinguished; and in what sense the soul is called blood.

[Col. 0402D]

89. What also is meant by the saying: “As the green herbs I have given you all things” (Gen. 9:3)? Those who understand this simply, without weighing the force of the expression, do not seem to us to be opposed to us. For some think that vegetables appear to have been assigned to us for food by God’s will, so that we should use them rather than fleshly meals. I would gladly agree with them, that the use of vegetables might become habitual in humankind for the sake of greater frugality and temperance, were I not to see that those who do not gladly accept this could reply that not all vegetables are found suitable for human food. Further, not every kind of human being is led by love of wisdom and self-control, so as to be able to follow self-control. And therefore we cannot restrict to the small portion of a few persons what is a general command: for this command is given to all human beings.

[Col. 0403B]

90. Therefore let us consider what he said: “As green herbs,” he says, “I have given you all things”; he did not say, “I have given you all vegetables for food.” Let those who eat flesh use it as vegetables: not for distension, nor [Note: [Col. 0403D] The Corbie, Vallicellian, Colbert, and Mazarin manuscripts, along with certain Paris editions, read, “for the ruin of the body.”] for fattening the body, which fleshly feasts usually bring about. But just as not all vegetables are fit for use as food, so not every living creeping thing is suitable for use in feasting. Indeed, we must abstain from everything poisonous, although luxury has gone so far even here as to provide more for pleasure than for danger; in many cases, after cutting away what is said to contain poison naturally, it claims the remaining part for food. Though it is not wholly dangerous, it is nevertheless close to danger; and some corruption must necessarily have infused itself into the juice of the whole flesh. Many people also pierce deer and similar swift animals with poisoned arrows and afterwards, having cut away a certain portion of the limbs, use the rest of the body for food.

91. As regards the deeper meaning, this is the point: irrational passions ought to be subject to the mind of the wise person as vegetables are to a farmer; and we should use these reptile-like thoughts as a farmer uses vegetables, which, although they cannot harm, do not possess the value of stronger food. For the command, being general and common to all, does not prescribe the higher kinds of virtues, which belong in any case to few persons. But even if someone cannot provide himself with stronger banquets of virtues, let him at least have such passions as do no harm but give delight. [Note: [Col. 0403D] That something has been omitted here is evident even to a blind person. See what we have said on this in the warning.]

[Col. 0403D]

92. Therefore holy Moses, at the beginning, formed and instructed us concerning the breathing-in of the soul, [266] so that we might not slip into the diverse opinions of philosophers, who cannot agree even with themselves. For many have held differing views. Critias and his disciples, for instance, said that the soul is blood—certainly the soul by which we live, which is sensitive, not that soul which is judged to be rational and intelligible, belonging to the inner [Col. 0404A] human being. Hippocrates, though he did not disapprove of Critias’ ability or refute his argument, nevertheless did not assent to his opinion. Aristotle called it *entelecheia* (ἐντελεχεία, “actuality” or “fulfilment”) (On the Soul, book 1, sections 29–30). Others wished it to be fire.

Let us therefore maintain this division: let us separate that which is rational in the soul, whose substance is the divine spirit, as Scripture says: “For he breathed into his face the spirit of life” (Gen. 2:7). [Note: [Col. 0403D] Editions following the Roman edition substituted, in part, “There is, however . . . there is also”; in part, “But there is . . . there is also.” Yet all old editions with the manuscripts read “there to be” in both places, where one must mentally supply one of the verbs set above—namely, “they wished” or “let us maintain.”] There is also in it a certain vital nourishment by which this body is animated, and there is also what is pleasurable. The substance of these parts of the soul—the vital and the pleasurable—is called blood by some. Scripture also says: “The soul of all flesh is its blood” (Lev. 17:11 ff.). Thus it properly called blood the soul of the flesh. For pleasure and passion are in the flesh, not mind and [Col. 0404B] reasoning.

Yet, if you attend carefully, this passage explains the other one. For when in this place it called the soul blood, it surely indicated that soul is one thing and blood another; so that the substance of the soul is vital spirit. But that vital spirit does not by itself and apart from blood confer the function of living; rather, it is mingled with the blood. For there are vessels called arteries, as it were receptacles of spirit, which contain not only pure air but also blood—though a much smaller portion of blood. For since there are two kinds of vessels, the vein is one thing, called in Greek *phleps* (φλέψ), and the artery another. The vein—that is, the *phleps*—has more blood than spirit; the artery has less blood and far more spirit. The mixture varies according to the differing nature [Col. 0404C] of each individual human being.

93. But the deeper meaning should delight you: it signifies that blood is called soul because blood is hot and fiery, as virtue is. Whoever, therefore, has been kindled by zeal for virtue and has taken on the warmth of praise excludes all indulgences of the belly. “You,” he says, “who are set in the ardor of virtue, shall reject those thoughts that are fleshly and earthly, as unfit for spiritual food.” For he was not eating flesh—that is, he was not entertaining any earthly thought—who said: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John 4:34), inspiring in people the pursuits of virtue and instilling desire for divine contemplation.

Therefore earthly and weak thoughts are regarded as though emasculated and without the use of blood. And one is called emasculated who has lost a great deal of blood; for through the shedding of blood one grows cold. Whoever is diligent in virtue banishes and rejects bodily foods, except insofar as he knows them to be sufficient for nature. But whoever more negligently follows the slippery and watery course of this life falls, as though losing his footing, into womb and belly. Thus he desires earthly things, alien from heavenly food, and cannot say: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” [Col. 0405A] (Phil. 3:20). Therefore, to summon people to hidden things, the same apostle says: “Do not touch, do not handle, do not taste, things which perish through use, according to the commandments and teachings of men, which indeed have an appearance of wisdom in a cult of religion and humility of heart, not in indulgence of the body, nor in any honor directed to the filling and care of the flesh” (Col. 2:21 ff.).

## Chapter XXVI

That one who kills a brother—that is, a participant in the same nature—is worse than beasts; yet that the greater danger is to be feared from one’s own blood-brothers; that they are not deprived of the name of brother, in order that their impiety may be more heavily charged; hence the moral teaching that each person must guard against his own thoughts and words. What threat is made against the shedder of blood; who said, “In the image of God he made him”; and what the added reason for vengeance teaches us.

[Col. 0405B]

94. The passages that follow confirm that this is the sense. For he says: “Indeed, I will demand your blood, the blood of your souls, from every beast and from the hand of a human being” (Gen. 9:5). He compared human wrongdoing to bestial malice—indeed, he intensified human iniquity beyond the savagery of beasts—when he said: “From the hand of a human brother.” [Note: [Col. 0405D] All editions read “embittered.” The manuscripts read better, “heaped up,” that is, “intensified.” This must be noted once for all: where the editions have a word derived from *acerbus*, the manuscripts almost always read one derived from *acervus*.] For beasts have nothing in common with us by nature; they are bound by no sort of fraternal bond. If they harm human beings, they harm strangers. They do not violate the laws of nature or forget the affection of kinship. Therefore a human being sins more gravely who lies in wait for a brother, and the Lord promised that he would exact harsher vengeance, saying: “I will demand the blood of a human being from the hand of his brother.”

Is not a brother one whom a certain womb of rational nature has brought forth, and whom descent from the same mother has joined to us? For one and the same nature is mother of all human beings; therefore we are all brothers, generated by one and the same mother and bound by the same right of kinship.

95. Therefore the Lord called both the one a brother and the one from whom the brother’s blood is required a brother, signifying that danger must be especially feared from those united with us by a fraternal bond. For from them come more frequent plots and dangers against human beings. To mention particular cases: among brothers, hatreds often arise especially in the division of an inheritance. Then, if parents have bestowed more upon one brother, the other brothers become more indignant and attempt to take away by parricide the favor granted by their parents. These are wars more to be suspected: wars not merely of fellow citizens, but of individual [Col. 0406A] households. [Note: [Col. 0405D] Here there is great corruption both in the manuscripts and editions. The Corbie, Colbert, and Vallicellian manuscripts, and the American, Gillot, and certain Paris editions, read, “not only of food, but of individual houses.” The Vatican and Longpont manuscripts and the Erasmian edition read, “but of individual houses.” Other Paris editions read, “not only of themselves, but of individual gifts.” Yet we have restored the passage fairly well from the Mazarin manuscript.] Therefore the Lord brings to the judgment of vengeance those whom he knew would be more likely to plot against their own.

96. A third point is that he called him a brother not because a parricide is worthy of the name of piety, but so that he may be weighed down all the more by the designation of piety, and so that the crime may be increased in proportion as the vengeance upon the criminal is more just. Therefore the Lord our God promises vengeance, so that even in this way the one who has forgotten piety may be broken by fear and may know that, even if a murderer escapes human beings, he cannot escape God’s judgment, but is reserved for a greater and eternal punishment.

97. In a deeper sense, [Note: [Col. 0405D] The Roman edition reads: “By this we understand that we must guard ourselves not only from the plots of strangers, but also from those of our own—that is, domestic—thoughts.” But the manuscripts and old editions overwhelmingly prefer our reading, except that in those editions the word “plots” is absent.] we understand that we must guard ourselves not only against the plots of strangers but also against our own, that is, domestic thoughts. [Col. 0406B] Further, we must be on guard not only against malice of mind but also against our very words. Therefore he says: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Prov. 10:19). Thus this appears to signify that we must render an account to the Lord not only for our deed but also for our speech, which is more intimate. Accordingly, we must consider more carefully lest we incur offense either in speech or deed; for just as confession is made with the mouth for salvation, so a fall into death is made with the mouth.

98. “Whoever sheds human blood,” he says, “in return for his blood shall be shed” (Gen. 9:6). The expression has not erred; it is emphasis—that is, an intensification of the words—because the one who sheds human blood will himself, as it were, be shed as blood: he is deprived of the hope of posterity. For just as blood shed upon the earth is scattered here and there, so the soul of the wicked is dissolved after the manner of bodily frailty [Col. 0406C] (Job 33:28). [Note: [Col. 0406D] Thus the manuscripts and the Roman edition. The old editions read, “is released from the body according to the manner of frailty.”] For it has also been said concerning the soul that its death is corruption, because it is deprived of the gift of heavenly grace and, as though dashed against the rocks of malice, diminishes its body’s soundness.

99. Many are also troubled because he said: “In the image of God he made the human being” (Gen. 9:6), and did not say, “In my image,” though he himself is God. But understand that there is both Father and Son. Although all things were made through the Son, we nevertheless read that the Father made all things and made them through the Son, as it is written: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24). Therefore, whether the Father speaks, he made the human being in the image of the Word; or whether the Son speaks, he made the human being in the image of God the Father. Thus he shows that the nature of the human being—namely, of the rational human being, insofar as we have been created in God’s image—is in a certain familiar and domestic relationship to God. [Col. 0406D] Hence, in God’s sight, an offense committed cruelly and impiously against a creature of his own household [Col. 0407A] cannot go unavenged.

100. The reason added for vengeance teaches us, first, to reject the opinions of certain philosophers who deny that God has care for human beings; secondly, knowing that the prerogative of our vengeance remains with God, not to commit against others what must be avenged by divine judgment; and not to fear death itself too violently, since we know that the killing of an innocent human being is not held in contempt before God.

## Chapter XXVII

It is promised that there will never again be a flood of such a kind as to destroy the whole earth; this is applied to passions of the soul. By the bow said to be set in the clouds is not meant the rainbow, but the stretching and relaxing of divine power.

[Col. 0407B]

101. [Note: [Col. 0407D] The manuscripts and old editions agree here, except that some later manuscripts with the old editions read “every human being” instead of “the whole earth.” But the Roman edition reads: [Col. 0408D] “There shall no longer be,” he says, “a flood of water.” The rest as in our text.] “There shall not be,” he says, “a flood to destroy the whole earth” (Gen. 9:11). The statement seems ambiguous: should “there shall not be a flood” be understood to mean that no flood will destroy the earth—something floods usually do? Or rather, that there will not be such a flood as destroys the whole earth? The subsequent words clarify this, when he says that the whole earth is not to be destroyed. For he shows that floods will indeed occur, but not such as can destroy the whole earth.

102. The deeper sense is that the Lord’s providence will now ensure that there is not so great a flood [Col. 0407C] of bodily passions that every soul perishes. Indeed, I do not dare say that the Lord seems to establish that no soul can perish utterly. For what are we to say of a parricide? What of a murderer? What of an adulterer? What of a traitor? What portions of the soul do we reserve to him for pardon?

Hence I think rather that the Lord God urges us that, even if someone has other, lighter passions, he should not utterly despair of divine grace or wholly lose confidence that he can conquer. Even if he is lustful and cannot avoid the pursuit of lust, nevertheless let him endeavor to refrain from adultery. Let there be pleasure in feasting, not in fornication. Even if some avaricious person has plundered others’ goods, cast out orphans, and driven away widows, let him nevertheless afterward return to repentance [Col. 0407D] and restore what he took. Thus Zacchaeus deserved pardon because he promised not only to restore, but to restore fourfold to those from whom he had taken anything, and also to give half his estate to the poor.

103. Let us consider more carefully, too, what is meant by his saying: “I will set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the eternal covenant between me and the earth. And when I have covered the earth with clouds, my bow shall appear in the cloud, and I shall remember my covenant” (Gen. 9:13 ff.). For he does not mean, as many suppose, the bow [Col. 0408A] which people say exists and by which certain signs of rain are shown, in which diverse colors are formed, like the sun’s rays now glowing red, now shining with brighter light. Hence coming rain is indicated, because a certain instability of fair weather is displayed in a variegated appearance. [Note: [Col. 0408D] Mazarin manuscript: “diverse colors are displayed in that appearance.”] Some call this bow the *iris*, or rainbow; but far be it from us to say that this is the bow of God. For this bow, called the rainbow, is usually seen by day and does not appear by night. Even during the day, if the air is covered by dark clouds, it is not seen unless, perhaps, the heavier clouds begin to open.

104. Therefore let us see whether, because the bow from which arrows are shot is now drawn taut and now relaxed, Scripture may signify a certain stretching and relaxing, [Col. 0408B] through which all things are neither wholly broken by excessive stretching nor dissolved by excessive relaxation; but there is a certain measure and testing of divine power. There is, then, an invisible power of God which, in the appearance of this bow’s being stretched and relaxed, governs according to the divine will, mercy, and power. It permits neither all things to be confused by excessive loosening nor to be broken apart by excessive force.

It says that this power is placed in the clouds because the assistance of divine providence is most needed when masses of clouds are gathered into storms and tempests. Therefore he says, “I will set my bow in the cloud,” not, “I will set my arrow.” For a bow is the instrument for shooting an arrow. Thus the bow itself does not wound, but the arrow. Therefore the Lord places in the cloud the bow rather than the arrow: that is, not what wounds, [Col. 0408C] but what bears a token of terror without ordinarily producing the effect of a wound.

## Chapter XXVIII

Having enumerated Noah’s three sons, Scripture mentions Ham’s offspring first in order to magnify his sin and show the impious race descending from him; morally, this is to be understood of an evil passion, mother of a wicked passion.

105. Why, then, when above it has listed Noah’s three sons—Shem, Ham, and Japheth (Gen. 9:18)—does it here include the offspring of only the middle son? This is what it says: “Ham was the father of Canaan; these three were the sons of Noah” (ibid., 19). Especially since the two others were righteous, while this middle one was unrighteous. Thus the generation of the unrighteous is included before that of the righteous. We cannot deny what is written; but his offspring was added in order to heap up his offense, because although he had a son and was himself a father, he alone did not acknowledge his father—he who ought especially to have acknowledged him. Therefore he deserved to have a wicked son because he had been wicked toward his father.

At the same time, it indicates that the Canaanites descended from this Canaan; after many generations they were overcome by the righteous people and yielded into their possession. Thus it is evident that Canaan was the progenitor of the Canaanites; he was [Col. 0409A] the son of that Ham who proved impious toward his father.

106. The deeper meaning, however, is indicated by the interpretation of the names. Ham means “heat”; Canaan, “their disturbance.” For one who grows hot is immediately moved and disturbed. Thus it is most clearly shown that it was not so much a human being who was the father of human beings, but an evil passion that was the parent of a wicked passion—a passion alien from its father’s character, that is, from the practice of virtue.

## Chapter XXIX

How Noah became a farmer; the difference between a farmer and a worker of the earth; how one cultivates his own flesh while the other works it; why Noah first planted a vineyard—that is, something not necessary, since springs suffice for drink; why it is also written of him, “He drank of the wine,” where a twofold drunkenness is discussed; and, finally, a twofold nakedness of the soul.

107. “And Noah, a man, began to be a farmer of the earth” (Gen. 9:20). At first sight, the righteous man Noah seems to be compared with Adam, who was made from the earth. For it is written also of Adam that, after he was cast out of paradise, he began to work the earth (Gen. 3:23); and of Noah likewise, that after leaving the ark he became a farmer. In each case, moreover, a kind of pattern of flood had preceded: for [Note: [Col. 0409D] Thus the manuscripts and old editions. But the Roman edition reads, “Noah lived after the flood, and Adam . . . was formed according to the body.”] Noah lived after the flood, and Adam after the establishment of the world according to the formation of the body. For in order that the world might be made, water was gathered into one collection so that the earth, which before could not [Col. 0409C] be seen because of the confusion of waters, might be seen.

Therefore, just as that first-created master appears to have worked the earth, so Noah too, leaving the ark, became the originator of sowing and cultivation. These things are considered similar; but if you consider the words, which now express the force of a deeper meaning, it is one thing to be a worker of the earth and another to be a farmer. One serves, as it were, in the role of a hired laborer; the other, in that of a householder. Thus Cain, who killed his brother, was a worker of the earth. And so that you may know that working the earth is more servile than free, his parricidal labor is included in the curse. For it is written: “Because you shall work the earth, it shall not continue to give you its strength; you shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth” (Gen. 4:12).

108. The earth is our flesh, which the wicked person works but the good person cultivates. [Note: [Col. 0409D] All editions and some manuscripts read, “the former seeks from the earth, the latter receives as fruit the good grace of discipline.” The Corbie, Longpont, Colbert, and Mazarin manuscripts read as in our text.] The former seeks from the earth, as it were, a wage; the latter receives, as it were, the fruits and good grace of discipline. He makes his field more fruitful, makes it able to respond to the Lord’s cultivation, and manifests the generosity of its cultivator. But what else does the worker seek except food for his body alone, attending chiefly to the use of the belly and being content to procure only what can profit him for subsistence? The other, however, is nourished by the usefulness of other fruits.

You recognize what fruits the righteous person has: “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, goodness.” Therefore the good farmer has self-control and chastity, so that if any trees bend quickly to the earth and put forth shoots too luxuriantly, he may cut them back with a kind of pruning-hook of his temperance, so that they cast off what is weak and put forth what is beautiful.

109. Why does the righteous person first plant a vineyard rather than wheat or barley? And how could there be a vineyard after the flood and the corruption of the earth? But we spoke of this above (chapters 19 and 20): in the springtime, even the roots of corrupted vines could have sprouted. Hence I think it must be considered with greater care why the righteous person seeks things that are pleasurable [Col. 0410B] before those that are necessary. The necessary fruits are wheat and barley, without which we cannot live; wine, however, is pleasurable and was given as a means of delight. Because he is righteous, therefore, he claimed for himself rather what was second than what was first. For he rendered to God the necessary means of life, [Note: [Col. 0409D] There is plainly a gap here, but neither the manuscripts [Col. 0410D] nor the editions can remedy it. We think, however, that it could be supplied fairly well by adding the word “first,” though we have not dared to introduce it into the text.] namely what was first. Wine, however, was superfluous and nonessential for human beings.

110. But perhaps you will say that people cannot live without drink, any more than without food. Drink, then, is necessary, just as food is: I do not deny it. It was certainly established by the Lord as necessary for thirst: I do not dispute this. And therefore it is fitting to draw for necessary drinking from springs and rivers, which certainly flowed not through human workmanship but by the command and operation of the Lord our God. Yet, lest because we have spoken of the Lord’s operation you refer this back to the fact that Cain’s operation seems to have incurred curses, consider that the term “operation” does not receive the name of what is cursed, but rather what is written: “to work the ground.” For one who works the ground is a hired labourer. But He is not a hired labourer, but the Lord, who says: “My Father is working still, and I too am working” (John 5:17). What does such a worker work? Hear: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John 4:34).

111. “And he drank,” it says, “of the wine, and became drunk” (Gen. 9:21). It did not say, “He drank wine”; nor did the righteous man drink up the wine; rather, “of the wine”—that is, he tasted a portion of it. It belongs to the drunken person to swallow all the wine, and to the intemperate person to drain what he has taken; [Note: [Col. 0410D] Thus the Corbie, Colbert, and Mazarin manuscripts. All editions, however, read: “but self-control is the lawful measure in its use.”] but for the self-controlled, the lawful measure is to be observed in its use.

There are therefore two kinds of drunkenness: one which brings staggering upon the body, trips its steps, and disturbs the mind; the other which warms the mind with the grace of virtue and seems to remove every weakness. Hence the Apostle says: “Use a little wine because of your frequent infirmities” (1 Tim. 5:23). For just as, through this moderation in drinking, wine is not a source of weakness but of health, and relieves every bodily infirmity, so too that splendid drunkenness excludes every infirmity of the flesh, concerning which it is written: “How splendid is the cup that makes drunk!” (Ps. 22[23]:5). What is this drunkenness? “Be filled,” he says, “not with wine, in which is excess, but with the Holy Spirit” (Eph. 5:18), as the Apostle said. Thus, according to the letter, there is a warning; according to a higher understanding of the wise, there is praise. Prudent is the person who, even if he is uncovered, is uncovered nevertheless in his own house, where coverings and certain veils for drunkenness are not lacking, so that he knows how to conceal his faults.

112. Bodily coverings, then, cover the naked body, such as walls and roofs. Let us see what coverings belong to the soul. But we shall find these coverings when we have examined its nakedness.

The wise man’s nakedness is twofold. Thus our mind is clothed with a twofold garment if either it has committed sin unknowingly—for this is nakedness, as it were, of an intoxicated mind, so that it does not know that it is doing wrong, but slips into vice as though led astray by a kind of drunkenness of ignorance—or, again, if, buried in the sleep of negligence and ignorance, it [Note: [Col. 0411D] All editions: “does not know its error.” The manuscripts: “does not not know.”] does not not know its error. When we fall into these things—or rather, when we fall into many sins even knowingly (for there is also a natural drunkenness of our weakness, so that the impulse of pleasure carries us into vice, as very many are inflamed by youthful heat, or are kindled by luxury and pleasure, or are swept away by the desire for avarice)—surely a remedy must be sought for all these things, so that someone may cover such weakness of his, first by a certain sense of shame and modesty. Thus, even if he is still placed upon the slippery ground of sinning, he may nevertheless give a sign of amendment. For it matters greatly whether he wishes to boast of his sins. In the one case there is shameful shamelessness; in the other, tolerable modesty displays hope of future correction.

113. There is another nakedness of the soul: when it casts off and strips away, as it were, a certain burden of the body, escaping from the flesh as from a tomb. For the throat of such people is an open grave, in which the soul, burdened by pleasures and by the various passions of desires, is as it were buried. Therefore it strips itself of its earthly accumulation, and escapes and evades, as it were, certain nets cast around it, whenever it has stripped itself of every snare of the passions and has put away all that deformed appearance of earthly defilement, so as to behold the light of eternal beauty.

## CHAPTER XXX

Why Ham is already called the father of Canaan when the latter had not yet been born; and why, in the person of Ham, all wicked persons are to be understood as rejoicing when good men happen to fall into fault, as though mocking their father.

114. I now ask why it did not simply say: “Ham saw his father’s nakedness,” but: “Ham, the father of Canaan, saw” (Gen. 9:22). Canaan certainly had not yet been born. Why, then, did it add the son’s name, unless so that the inheritance might be disfigured by the founder’s vice, and the progenitor might be burdened by the son’s wickedness? Thus both father in son and son in father are reproved, sharing a common fellowship in folly, wickedness, and impiety. Nor could he produce a good son who had himself proved wicked toward a good father, degenerate both as son and in nature and training. This is according to the letter.

115. But in the higher sense, all evil dispositions take pleasure in the errors of others—and not only in errors, but even in things which seem evil to them, though they are not. Noah did not know himself to be naked, since he was clothed in the garment of wisdom. Indeed Adam too, while placed in paradise, did not think himself naked until after he had committed the error of transgression. [Note: [Col. 0411D] The Tours and Valcena manuscripts, with all editions, read: “And guilty, with a garment”; the Corbie, Longpont, and Colbert manuscripts: “And covered over”; the Mazarin: “And found with a garment.” The remaining manuscripts and editions agree with one another almost entirely.] And, covered with the garment of wisdom and righteousness, when he was stripped by transgression of the heavenly commandments, he saw himself naked and thought that he should be covered with leaves.

Ham therefore laughs when he sees his father naked. For every wicked person, because he himself has strayed from discipline, receives the falls of others not merely as consolation for his own error, because he has found companions in guilt; he also rejoices with a wicked disposition, as though he himself had corrected his own offences. Thus an evil mind rejoices when something happens to a wise person contrary to his purpose, although a bodily fall ought not to be a fault, even if it is thought to be a fall, unless the mind too inclines toward guilt. Finally, errors of this kind should be judged pardonable: they should not be pursued with hatred or made into a mockery. But, as I said, when the wicked mind thinks that the wise person has erred, it judges that he should be insulted, because it thinks his manner of life opposed to its own, and because its own sin is reproved, as it were, by the silent testimony of the wise person. It therefore thinks it ought to rejoice because neither his learning has profited the righteous man, nor his righteousness assisted him, nor those things that belong to the body have run a prosperous course. For among wicked people these are counted the highest goods—wealth or honour—though they contribute no fruit toward the praise of virtue. Therefore those appear to be defenders of folly who think that a lover of virtue has been deprived of the reward of prosperity, and who suppose that every good is to be valued more by temporal than by eternal things.

## CHAPTER XXXI

The piety of Shem and Japheth is commended; and the meaning of their being said to have walked backward is explained. Then, how Noah became sober. Finally, why Scripture, after previously placing Ham in the middle, now calls him the younger.

116. What does it mean that Shem and Japheth placed a garment upon their shoulders, went backward, covered their father’s nakedness, and [Note: [Col. 0412D] The Roman edition: “and their faces did not see,” etc.] did not see his nakedness (Gen. 9:23)? The letter has plainly expressed their feeling of piety: good sons took care not to see their father stripped of his garment, lest filial reverence for their father should be diminished even by the act of looking. For piety is often offended even by a silent expression. Hence it is said that at Rome there was an ancient practice that sons should not enter the bath with their parents, especially when they had reached puberty.

117. The higher sense, however, is this: the foolish person sees only present things, those which are before the eyes; he does not look to the future or think of the past. But the wise person both remembers the past and considers the future. Every wise mind therefore walks backward, that is, it looks upon the past; nor is it hindered by some habit of nature. It allows none of its actions to be void or naked. It covers what has been done otherwise with a sort of garment and grace, whether of a present act or of a future one, so that it passes over nothing unbecoming and leaves nothing unadorned. Hence the Apostle forgot the things behind and sought those before; but he forgot them so as to conceal the errors of persecution, to cover former offences, [Note: [Col. 0413D] Thus all Gallican manuscripts and the Roman edition. The old edition, with the Vatican manuscript: “and might abound in good works.”] and to overshadow them with good works. For blessed also are those whose sins are covered (Ps. 31[32]:1), that is, if they are concealed by good deeds and covered by the subsequent disciplines of virtues.

118. “And Noah,” it says, “became sober from wine” (Gen. 9:24). It is clear that people become sober after drunkenness when sleep intervenes. But the mind is sober when it knows both past and future. Therefore the mind of the righteous man was sober even when he was thought to be drunk. For there is a splendid cup that intoxicates the righteous.

But he was truly drunk who laughed at his father. For one who considered neither the past grace of his begetting, nor the present reverence due to his father, nor the future punishment for injury to his father, was truly drunk; and what he thought he saw, he did not see. Deep blindness was in him, who could not see his father. For if he had seen his father, he certainly would not have laughed. A father is not to be laughed at, but revered. Much more could the foolish person not see the mind of the righteous man. How indeed did he see it when he supposed that there was in it the error [Note: [Col. 0413D] We restore the word “drunkenness” on the authority of the Corbie and Longpont manuscripts; in the others and in all editions “doubtfulness” was read.] of drunkenness, where there was the perfect radiance of wisdom and the other virtues? As it is written: “For she is a vapour of the power of God” (Wis. 7:25). For when is the mind more sober than when it so contemplates the nature of all things and the affairs of present and future times that no temporal wavering of drunkenness appears in it?

119. I also ask why, when it previously called Ham the middle one among the sons, it now makes him the younger. For it is written: “Noah knew all that his younger son had done to him” (Gen. 9:24). Did Scripture previously err in the order of birth? Certainly not. What then? Are contrary things now written? I do not think so. How then is this resolved, unless you take “younger” not in age or time, but as unformed in understanding and set in a kind of infancy of intellect—one who has not imbibed the teaching of more advanced age nor received the counsel of old age? For there are certain gray hairs of human understanding. Hence it says: “When you come into the council of elders, keep your mouth closed” (Ecclus. 32:13). And elsewhere the saying is found: “You must learn before you speak” (ibid. 18–19). Therefore have your ears ready, that you may obtain something from the counsels of the wise. The tongue must be restrained; hearing must be prepared.

## CHAPTER XXXII

Why, in Shem’s blessing, it was said, “Blessed be the Lord God of Shem”; and why not Ham, who sinned, but his son is assigned to servitude. Finally, Japheth’s blessing is explained.

120. In blessing his son Shem, Noah said: “Blessed be the Lord God of Shem, and Canaan shall be his servant” (Gen. 9:26). He called Him both Lord and God, and specifically the God of his son whose name is Shem, because He is the God of the righteous—that is, the God of mountains, not valleys—of those who possess the grace of lofty virtue. Then why, when his son Ham had sinned, did he assign not Ham himself but his son to servitude? Perhaps because a father is more deeply affected by injuries done to his son, especially those of which he himself proves guilty and the cause; and he is more violently grieved when the sentence for his own sin is paid by his son, who is punished not so much for his own desert as for his father’s.

Then, because a son who is a disciple of his father’s teaching and an imitator of his very evil thoughts shares with him one body and mind and the same wickedness. Indifferently, therefore, the son pays the price either of his father’s wickedness or of his own, since he is liable for his guilt; or at least the punishment is prolonged when it extends even to the son, and the affliction of the successor is carried forward through many ages. This is according to the letter.

121. But here it is not so much persons as dispositions that are comprehended, for both have one nature. Ham means “heat”; Canaan, “movement and unrest.” One who is hot is certainly more restless and agitated. Thus in the two there was one passion and one disposition. Accordingly, when [Note: [Col. 0414D] The American edition, with several Parisian editions, has “is added” here, where the others with the manuscripts have “is assigned.” The latter is better, for the subject here is servitude.] one is assigned to servitude, both are condemned.

122. Therefore, when holy Noah, blessing his son Japheth, says: “May the Lord enlarge Japheth; may he dwell in the tents of Shem; and may Canaan be his servant” (ibid. 27), we said above that Japheth signifies, as it were, an indifferent good (above, ch. 2). Things indifferent have breadth: health, strength, beauty, courage, riches, favour, nobility, friends, powers, and the rest. But although these indifferent things are good, they have harmed many who did not possess them with wisdom and righteousness. For riches have made many drunk, nobility and power proud, beauty licentious, [Note: [Col. 0415D] All editions: “whose support corrupted the chastity of another mind.” The manuscripts have the reading adopted in the text.] by whose influence they have corrupted the chastity of another mind. Thus, according to the disposition of the user, these things which we have named are indifferent: their use is either governed by virtues, or, without the government of virtues, they begin to cause harm, though they can be useful.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

On the three hundred and fifty years which Noah is said to have lived after the flood; then, on Japheth’s descendants according to the letter and morally.

123. Now, since Noah is said to have lived three hundred and fifty years after the flood (Gen. 9:28), we think this should by no means be passed over. For the number three hundred certainly signifies Christ’s cross, by whose type the righteous man was delivered from the flood. In fifty is the Jubilee number of remission, in which the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven, pouring grace into human hearts. Thus the righteous man completed the course of this life in the perfect number of remission and grace.

124. “From the offspring of Japheth,” it says, “are Rhodes and the other islands of the nations” (Gen. 10:5). Not without reason is he called breadth, since his progeny extended even into the other part of nature, that is, the maritime. For truly, as though he were breadth, he was not content with what nature had prescribed for human use—that is, possession of land—but entered even the sea and advanced as far as the islands. This is according to the letter.

125. In the higher sense, however, those external things called goods—riches, powers, honours—are spread more widely. Nor are the rich content only with those things which are in their hands and before their eyes; rather, they spread their desires far and wide, whether profit in money is sought from distant places, honour from more persons, a more extensive power, or desire.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

What Ham’s eldest son, the son of that wicked man, was like; and concerning Cush’s son Nimrod, the giant and hunter: the meaning of his name, and the statement that Babylon’s kingdom began with him.

126. I now ask why Scripture records that Ham, that wicked man, had an elder son. There are two kinds of earth: one is like sand and dust—indeed, to state it more precisely, dust; the other kind is fruitful and fertile earth, that is, firmer and deeper soil. What then does the wicked man produce except dust, from which no generation can arise? Hence the Prophet compared the wicked with dust, saying: “Not so the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4). This is because, in the higher sense also, the soul of the wicked is unfruitful and unable to produce useful fruits.

127. Why also did Cush beget Nimrod, a giant who was a hunter before God? [Note: [Col. 0415D] The following words were absent from all editions: “Hence it was said: ‘Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before God’”; yet they are found in all manuscripts.] Hence it was said: “Like Nimrod, a giant, a hunter before God” (Gen. 10:9). What else, then, could dust and sand produce except an earthly person, since the wicked person prefers earthly things to heavenly? For fables represent the giants as wishing to fight against the powers above, and thinking that heaven must be scaled by an earthly ascent.

128. But in the higher sense this signifies that one who loves earthly pleasures, pursues them, and thinks that by them he can attain God’s grace and that the kingdom of heaven is to be bestowed through such errors, fights with a rebellious disposition against heavenly things. Hence there is also a proverb concerning one who has sinned: “Like Nimrod, a giant, a hunter before God.” Now Nimrod is interpreted as “Ethiopian.” The colour of the Ethiopian signifies the darkness and squalor of the soul, which [Note: [Col. 0416D] All editions, and the Vatican and Tours manuscripts: “against the light.” Better are the Corbie, Colbert, Longpont, and Mazarin manuscripts: “opposed to the light,” that is, contrary.] is opposed to the light, devoid of brightness, wrapped in darkness, more like night than day.

The hunter’s practice, moreover, is in woods, and his life is among wild creatures and beasts. Thus the irrational person joins himself to irrational passions; such a hunter is accustomed to track out things of savage and very harsh wickedness, to gain possession of them, and to delight in them. Finally, the beginning of Nimrod’s kingdom was Babylon, that is, “confusion,” because wickedness and power exist not in simplicity and purity, nor in the distinction of virtue, but in the confusion of vices.

[Col. 0415D]

## FRAGMENT OF THE BOOK *ON NOAH’S ARK*

[Col. 0415]

[Col. 0415D] As, for example, there is this passage in the book which blessed Ambrose wrote *On Noah’s Ark*: “Through the one Lord Jesus, salvation to come to the nations is declared; he alone could be righteous when the whole generation had gone astray, provided that, being born of a Virgin, he was in no way held subject to the privilege [i.e. condition] of a generation liable to sin. ‘Behold,’ he says, ‘I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me’—says the man who was thought more righteous than the rest. Whom, then, shall I now call righteous, except one free from these bonds, whom the bonds of common nature do not hold? All were under sin from Adam; death reigned over all. Let the one righteous man come before God, concerning whom it may no longer be said with an exception: ‘He did not sin with his lips,’ but: ‘He did not commit sin.’ Say this to him, if you dare,” etc.

Augustine cites this fragment in two places, namely, Book II *Against Julian*, chapter 2, and Book IV *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 11. We judge that these words belong to the end of the third chapter, as anyone may infer by comparing the two passages.

## [ON ABRAHAM]

[Col. 0417]

## PREFACE TO THE BOOKS *ON ABRAHAM*

[Col. 0417]

Although the very first words of this work seem sufficiently clearly to embrace its whole argument, nevertheless, since they are not altogether without difficulties, we believed that readers would not find it unwelcome if we attempted here to unravel and explain them for greater ease of reading.

As to the title, one reads: “Abraham is the title of this book” (Book I, ch. 1). From these words a twofold doubt may arise. First, why did Ambrose say “of this book,” not “of these books”? This treatise is certainly divided into two books; and that some division was necessary is clearly indicated both by the great difference between the two and by the holy author himself, who, in the opening chapters of these books, sufficiently declares that he is dividing his work and indeed had planned this from the beginning of the first book. We might therefore be persuaded, not unwillingly, that Ambrose comprised this work in one book with two parts, but that in later times they were given the designation “books” by those who observed that the two differ greatly from one another.

For the first book is named more than once by Jonas, bishop of Orléans, who flourished under Emperor Charles the Bald, in Book II of *On the Instruction of Laymen* (chs. 2, 4, 5, 29); and the second book is found cited by Hugh of Saint Victor (*On the Cloister of the Soul*, Book II, ch. 8). A second difficulty about the title is raised by the fact that Gratian (23, question 5, chapter *Dicat*; and 32, questions 2 and 4, etc.), Blessed Thomas (2–2, question 66, article 8, ad 1; ibid., question 154, article 6, and elsewhere), and several others say that the testimonies which they draw from this treatise occur in a book *On the Patriarchs*. Yet it is wholly credible that those authors customarily cited the works of the holy Fathers in their extracts and books under the title then more commonly used. It may therefore rightly be said that this title was given to the work long before. Perhaps no one other than Cassiodorus gave occasion for it. For when he says: “Likewise, Saint Ambrose published seven books *On the Patriarchs*, in which he sweetly unravelled many passages of the Old Testament by raising questions” (*On the Institutes of Divine Reading*, ch. 1), there can be no doubt that among the other books *On the Patriarchs* he included also the treatise *On Abraham*.

Nor should this seem absurd to anyone, since the holy Doctor in fact composed treatises on the principal patriarchs, which he himself enumerates and compares at the beginning of the book *On Joseph*. However this may be, no one can doubt that this very work of which we speak was given the title *On Abraham* by Ambrose, who himself gives the reason: “Because,” he says, “I was moved to consider in order the deeds of this patriarch also.” In these words the outline of the work is, as it were, set before our eyes. Hence one finds it inscribed in the manuscripts under no title other than *On Abraham*.

The holy bishop also professes that he was induced by divine authority to set his hand to this treatise (Book I, ch. 1): “Since the Lord our God,” he says, “has endowed him with the rich gift of His blessing, so that his grace might draw others on and his example correct them; and Moses also described him to us for imitation,” etc. Thus the devout Doctor placed the holy patriarch before the eyes of his hearers or readers in order that, following his example as a mirror, they might cleanse away the mire of vices and strive toward the fullest perfection of Christian life and wisdom.

But what he adds sufficiently indicates that he laboured not only to nourish and advance Christians’ piety, but also to refute the vanity of philosophers. They displayed only an imaginary outline of the wise man, whether in Plato’s republic or in Xenophon’s sage, whereas Ambrose showed that a living and substantial image of that wise man shone forth in Abraham. Therefore, by the particular deeds of this patriarch, he repeatedly establishes that whatever they so grandly proclaimed had been accomplished by Abraham, and had been recorded by Moses in the sacred books long before their age. Nor should you wonder that the holy bishop chose this manner of writing, since he was disputing against people (Augustine, Epistle 31) who, with supreme blindness and rashness, asserted that Christ the Lord had learned from Plato’s writings those divine laws which they themselves could not fail to admire.

Before Ambrose, the Jewish Philo had published a book entitled: *The Life of the Wise Man Perfected by Instruction, or On the Unwritten Laws, or On Abraham*; to this book he had added several others on certain more notable actions of this patriarch.
