Yet if Ambrose followed that writer in the subject of his work, he seems nevertheless to have abstained almost entirely in this work from Philo’s words and opinions, although in several of his earlier treatises he is seen to have borrowed them more freely.

The method he adopted here is very different from that found in his other writings. In the first book, whatever Scripture relates about Abraham’s life—from the divinely received command to depart from Haran until his death—he adapts to a moral interpretation. Taking Abraham’s devotion, that is, obedience in carrying out God’s commands, as his theme, he proceeds through his remaining virtues. In the second, interpreting the first deeds of the patriarch in a spiritual—or, as he calls it, higher—sense, he discloses the soul’s various stages and advances in virtue. He teaches that the soul which had fallen in Adam rises again in Abraham and strives toward perfection.

We said his first actions, not all of them, because he closes that treatise shortly after the patriarch’s circumcision and the promised birth of Isaac, touching only briefly upon his hospitality. Thus the second book contains almost only those matters which had been explained in the first four chapters of the first book, although you will find in it some things treated that are omitted in the former. We suppose that he had no other reason for not continuing the second book further than that he had already resolved to compose also in Isaac a new treatise on the soul’s perfection, or, as he says, on its various advances.

Since Christians can draw a much richer profit for moral formation from the first book than from the second, it seems not without divine providence that the former has been transmitted to us far less corrupted and more complete than the latter, in which many passages occur miserably disfigured by gaps and other defects. We have indeed restored to their former integrity not a few passages, and passages not to be despised; yet it must be frankly admitted that at the end of the same book something confused still remains, for which the handwritten manuscripts have been unable to provide a remedy. It is credible that certain things there were either transposed, torn away, or perhaps even inserted by some heretic in order to procure support for his errors.

It is established that the first book was composed from sermons which the holy bishop had delivered to catechumens who had already enrolled their names for baptism and had become candidates (Book I, chs. 4, 7, and final chapter). He was accustomed especially to teach them personally, and afterward to reduce into books what he had delivered orally. He undertook this either to comply with their requests or because he himself voluntarily provided for them, lest what they had heard and promised during those precious times of their baptism should ever slip from their memory; and also so that other Christians might be admitted to share in the benefit. It is not equally evident that the second book consists of similar sermons; yet, since we see nothing to oppose this, we may not without reason make the same judgment about this book as about the first.

There is somewhat more difficulty in determining the date of these books. Nevertheless, both from their connection and order in relation to the following treatises on the patriarchs, and from Ambrose himself, who at the beginning of the books *On Joseph* and *On the Mysteries* indicates clearly enough that he composed them all at not widely different times, it is quite plainly inferred that they should be assigned to approximately the year 387, in which, as we shall prove in its proper place, the book *On Joseph* was published.

[Col. 0419B]

## TWO BOOKS OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, *ON ABRAHAM* [Note: [Col. 0419B] Written about the year 387.] (C)

[Col. 0419]

## BOOK ONE

281. **CHAPTER I**

The title of the book and its method are explained; then the benefit to be drawn from Abraham’s examples is demonstrated by divine authority and comparison with philosophers.

[Col. 0419A]

1. *Abraham* is the title of this book, because I have been moved to consider in order the deeds of this patriarch also. My first treatment of him will be moral and straightforward. For although, in a higher discussion, a certain progress and pattern of virtue and a certain form may be expressed, yet to look also at the public traces of his actions [Note: [Col. 0419B] The American edition, with four manuscripts, reads “all public things.” Here “public traces” are understood as the outward marks of moral conduct.] is an advance in virtue. For if the things which nature has produced for human sustenance are for a grace not single but twofold, or even more abundant, how much more fitting is it to judge that those things upon which souls feast are of not narrow but more abundant use, and of manifold nourishment.

2. Nor is this a slight or idle undertaking. For since the Lord our God has endowed this man with the rich gift of His blessing, so that his grace might incite others and his instruction correct them, and since Moses has described him to us for imitation, in order that, by contemplating this man, he might raise human hearts falling into vice as from a kind of earthly grave, it should not seem a perfunctory matter if we too examine more carefully the footsteps of the same man.

For if the wise men of this world—Plato himself, the prince of philosophers—proposed that imaginary and shadowy *politeia* (πολιτεία, “commonwealth” or “constitution”) which we read [Note: [Col. 0420B] Thus five manuscripts of better age. The others and the editions read: “proposed a city [πόλιν] to be built.”] for pursuit (Plato, *Republic*, Book IV), so as to teach what sort of state a commonwealth ought to be; and if he thought that one which he had neither heard of nor seen in any city should nevertheless be described, so that those charged with this duty might be instructed how they ought to govern the commonwealth [Note: [Col. 0420B] Nearly all manuscripts read: “might govern the commonwealth.”]; and if Xenophon the Socratic, Plato’s fellow-disciple, likewise wished by fictional events to portray the person of the wise man in that book which he entitles *Cyropaedia* (Κύρου Παιδεία, “The Education of Cyrus”), so that instruction in the just and wise king might proceed from Philosophy’s inmost sanctuary: how much more ought we earnestly to recount, and to follow the paths of, not an invented image of a wise man but virtue itself made manifest and established by divine instruction—of the man whom Moses described in such a way that he himself, in a manner, looked backward?

## CHAPTER II

How Abraham’s devotion is proved by the words of the divine command; what it means to leave one’s kindred; and how God’s promise followed this patriarch’s obedience. Invoking the Lord, Abraham fears for himself because of his wife’s beauty and takes precautions. Pharaoh, punished for taking her, shows how great the crime of adultery is; hence Abraham’s example summons us to the pursuit of devotion.

[Col. 0421B]

3. Truly a great man, illustrious with the marks of many virtues, whom Philosophy could not equal in its aspirations. For what she imagined is less than what he performed, and the simple trustworthiness of truth is greater than the ambitious falsehood of eloquence. Let us therefore consider what manner of devotion there was in this man. For that virtue stands first in order, being the foundation of all the rest; and rightly God first required it of him, saying: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. 12:1).

It would have been enough to say, “from your land.” For therein was departure from kindred and departure from the paternal house. But He added each point in order to test his disposition, lest perhaps He might seem either to have deceived one who was unaware [Note: [Col. 0421D] All editions and a few manuscripts read “to have begun imprudently.” Others, more numerous and authoritative, read “to have deceived one who was unaware,” i.e. “to have deceived.”] or that some deceit was being prepared against the heavenly commands. But just as the commands had to be accumulated so that nothing might be concealed, so also rewards had to be set forth lest perhaps he should despair. He is tested as brave, encouraged as faithful, [Note: [Col. 0421D] Erasmus in the text, and Gillot in the margin, read: “proved as righteous.”] summoned as righteous; and rightly he went out as the Lord had spoken to him.

4. “And Lot went out with him” (ibid., 4). What is celebrated as a great saying among the maxims of the Seven Sages, ἔπου Θεῷ—that is, “Follow God”—Abraham fulfilled. [Note [Col. 0421D–0422D]: Thus the Roman edition, from the Vatican manuscript; the Royal manuscript differs from it only minimally, reading: “fulfilled: for Abraham by his deeds [anticipated] the Sages,” etc. The remaining manuscripts and the edition, omitting *fulfilled*, read: “and Abraham anticipated the sayings of the Sages by his deed,” etc.] Indeed, by his deed he anticipated the sayings of the Sages and, following God, departed from his land.

But since he had previously had another land—that is, the region of the Chaldeans, from which Terah, Abraham’s father, departed and migrated to Haran—and since he took with him his nephew, to whom it had been said, “Depart from your kindred,” let us consider whether perhaps this “departure from his own land” means departure from this earthly land: that is, leaving a certain sojourn of our body, from which Paul departed when he said, “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 10); and leaving bodily allurements and pleasures, which he called, as it were, kindred to our soul, since the soul must suffer with the body so long as it clings to it, bound by its tie.

Therefore we ought to depart from earthly manner of life and worldly delights, and [adopt] the conduct and acts of the higher life, so that we may change not only our places but also ourselves. If we desire to cling to Christ, let us abandon corruptible things. Now corruptible things in us are flesh, pleasure, and the voice subject to bodily passions. [Note [Col. 0422D]: The Roman edition reads: “subject to corruptible passions.”] By “voice,” however, we understand passions. Hence, since our soul is διμερής, that is, twofold, having both a rational and an irrational part—and is divided through the flesh, the allurements of bodily pleasure, and the other passions of the body—the righteous person ought to separate and sever the rational element of the soul from the irrational.

For this is to depart from Haran: to emerge, as it were, from certain caves, tunnels, and hiding places. For to hide belongs to a guilty conscience. Let us therefore, following Abraham, leave our hiding places. For if we are Abraham’s children, let us do Abraham’s works, so that our works may shine before God and before human beings. The righteous person declares his works to the king; the sinner hides himself, as Adam wished to hide himself, though he could not remain hidden. Abraham therefore obeyed the command, and no delay is recorded as having intervened.

5. Having departed, he travelled through the land as far as Shechem (Gen. XII, 6), which in Latin interpretation means “shoulder” or “neck,” by which we understand the execution of the prescribed work. For we also have written below: “He set his shoulder to labor” (Gen. XLIX, 15). Thus, through the figure of places, we perceive that holy Abraham proved his devotion not merely by zeal but also by fruitful effectiveness, by which he reached as far as the oak. 284 There the Lord appeared to him and said: “To your seed I will give this land” (Gen. XII, 7). See how, by frequent promise, He forms and instructs him as still weak; and how Abraham himself, mindful of his own condition and weakness, attributes everything to God and claims nothing for himself. [Note [Col. 0422D]: The Vatican and Royal manuscripts and the Roman edition read, “And he himself, mindful of himself.” This is not bad. Other manuscripts and the edition read better: “… mindful of himself,” that is, of his own condition and weakness.]

Therefore he built an altar to God, who had appeared to him; and he departed thence to the mountain eastward of Bethel (ibid.), desiring to see the sun of righteousness still rising for him. Therefore he placed his tent not in the valleys but on the mountain, because God is God of the mountains and not of the valleys.

6. “And he invoked the name of the Lord” (ibid., 8). Where Bethel is—that is, the house of God—there also is an altar; where the altar is, there is also invocation of our God. Nor without reason did he make such great progress, because he hoped that God would be his help. The athlete of God is exercised and tested by adversities. [Note [Col. 0422D]: Thus six manuscripts of better authority. Others and the edition read, “and is hardened by adversities … famine arose.”] He went into the wilderness, famine arose, and he descended into Egypt.

He had learned that in Egypt there was the wanton luxury of young men, insolent desire, and intemperance in pleasures. He saw that among men of this kind his wife’s chastity would be unsafe, and that his wife’s beauty would endanger him. He warned his wife to call herself his sister.

This teaches that one should not seek too greatly for a wife’s beauty, which commonly brings death to a husband. For it is not so much a woman’s beauty as her virtue and seriousness that delights a husband. Whoever seeks the sweetness of marriage should not court a wife superior in wealth, one whom marital obligations do not restrain; [he should seek] one adorned not with necklaces but with good character. [Note [Col. 0423D]: All editions read: “should not court one superior in wealth, one whom marital obligations do not terrify; [but] one adorned not with necklaces,” etc. The word *so* is absent from the Ambrosian edition and all the manuscripts. Yet these almost unanimously support our reading. Their reading, “one whom marital obligations do not hold,” should be understood as though it said: one who, growing insolent because of wealth, refuses to observe the laws of the marital bond or union.] A husband is often offended if his wife knows herself to be of nobler birth. Such things are close to pride.

Sarah was neither richer in possessions nor more distinguished in birth; therefore she did not think her husband her inferior, therefore she loved him as an equal in affection, therefore she was not held back by wealth, parents, or relatives, but followed her own husband wherever he went. She went abroad; she asserted that she was his sister, content, if necessary, to risk her chastity rather than her husband’s safety. To protect her husband, she falsely claimed kinship, lest those plotting against her chastity should kill him as the rival and defender of his wife. Thus, as soon as the Egyptians saw her and admired her because she was very beautiful, they brought her to their king; and they treated Abraham well, honoring him as the brother of her who had pleased the king.

7. “But the Lord afflicted Pharaoh with great and very severe afflictions, and his house, because of Sarah, Abraham’s wife” (Gen. XII, 17). A great testimony and lesson for preserving chastity. [Note [Col. 0423D]: Thus five manuscripts of better authority. Others and the edition read “of chastity.” The passage should be considered: “… should violate another’s wife.”] The passage is so exhortatory that each person should present himself as chaste, should not desire another’s bed, and should not assault another’s wife in hope of concealment or impunity, nor be provoked by the husband’s negligence or foolishness, or by his prolonged absence. [Note [Col. 0423D]: The edition reads, “should violate another’s wife.” Some manuscripts read “should attack”; the better ones read as in the text.]

God, the guardian of marriage, is present: nothing escapes Him, no one evades Him, no one mocks Him. He protects the absent husband’s place; He keeps watch—indeed, without sentries He catches the guilty person before he does what he has planned. 285 [Note [Col. 0423D]: Some manuscripts read, “foreign and barbarous errors.”] In the souls of individuals and the minds of all, He recognizes the crime. Even if you deceive the husband as an adulterer, you do not deceive God; even if you escape the husband and make a mockery of the court’s judge, you do not escape the Judge of the whole world. He punishes more severely the injury done to the helpless and the insult offered to an unsuspecting husband. For it is a greater wrong that the author of the marriage than its guardian should be disregarded and ignored.

8. Pharaoh himself also, though king of the Egyptians—whom both the arrogance of royal power might have made heedless and Egyptian wantonness and luxury might have drawn away from the pursuit of chastity—called Abraham and rebuked him, saying: “What have you done to me? Why did you not tell me that she is your wife, but told me that she is your sister, so that I would have taken her as my wife? And now, behold, your wife is before you” (ibid., 18–19).

Though savage and barbarous by nature, he nevertheless indicates that even among foreign and barbarous customs there is concern for chastity, and that one must guard against the crime of adultery. [Note [Col. 0423D]: Some manuscripts read, “foreign and barbarous errors.”] He who pleads ignorance condemns intemperance. Nor is it surprising that a barbarian knows the law of nature: dumb animals, though bound by no laws, nevertheless include some that not only keep faith in mating with their equals but also preserve the chastity of a single union. [Note [Col. 0423D–0424D]: All editions read, “although bound by no laws, nevertheless there are some,” etc. Two manuscripts read, “which are of none, nevertheless,” etc. Others read as in the text.] Thus the law of nature is greater than the prescription of laws.

It is therefore no wonder that this Egyptian king also feared God, though he feared no human being, and paid the penalty for adultery though he was liable under no laws. As soon as he learned that she was another man’s wife, he not only restored her to her husband but even provided escorts to conduct him away, lest any person among the barbarian people inflict violence either on the man’s property or on his wife’s chastity.

9. This is a most excellent passage for encouraging the pursuit of devotion: one who follows God is always safe. Therefore we ought to prefer God to all things; neither concern for our country, nor affection for parents and children, nor consideration of a wife should call us back from fulfilling the heavenly commands. For God grants us all these things and is able to preserve what He gives.

Thus Abraham’s descent into Egypt with a beautiful wife is a great example of devotion. The righteous man did indeed have concern for his wife’s chastity; but greater was his desire to hasten devotion, lest he seem to have preferred guarding his marriage-bed to the heavenly commands. Therefore, because for God’s sake he despised all things, he received all things multiplied from God. Yet God first assigned him the reward of chastity, which He knew was dear to his wife. For because, in his zeal to fulfill the heavenly oracle, he had brought even his wife’s chastity into danger, God also defended the chastity of their marriage. [Note [Col. 0424D]: The Royal manuscript reads, “in zeal to perform and discharge the vow of the heavenly oracle.” A little later, where numerous manuscripts and all editions read *castimoniam* (“chastity”), the Corbie manuscript and several others have *castimonium*. Perhaps not wrongly: Augustine, on Psalm XXIX, §13, uses *sanctimonium* for *sanctimonia*, or for the profession of religious women. Nor were there lacking those who accused Abraham of betraying the chastity of his wife Sarah; yet the holy Fathers rightly defend him: Ambrose in this book; Augustine, *Against Faustus*, XXII.33, and *Questions on Genesis* 26 and elsewhere; Jerome, *Hebrew Traditions on Genesis*; Theodoret, *Questions on Genesis* 62; and many others.]

286

## CHAPTER III

On Abraham’s other virtues: namely, his prudence in removing the causes of quarrels; his justice in dividing; Lot’s imprudence in preferring pleasant things to useful ones, and its punishment; then Abraham’s affection toward his nephew, devotion toward God, self-restraint in victory, and choice of the reward offered by God; and finally, the promise received concerning his future offspring and the Christ to be born.

10. Devotion therefore rightly claimed the first place for itself. Let us examine the excellence of his other virtues also. Holy Abraham was comforted by the presence of his nephew, toward whom he showed a father’s affection. A quarrel arose between the servants of nephew and uncle. Being wiser, he observed that the concord of masters is commonly dissolved by the dissensions of servants; he cut off the thread of discord, lest the contagion spread. [Note [Col. 0425D]: Not a few manuscripts read, “he cut off the fringe of discord.”] For he thought it more tolerable that their union should be separated than that their affection should be broken.

This is what you ought to do, if perhaps something of this kind should arise: remove the seedbed of dissension. For you are not stronger than Abraham. He judged that servants’ quarrels ought to be avoided, not despised. And even if you are stronger, beware lest another, weaker person lend an ear to servants’ whisperings. Undivided households among relatives frequently sow discord. Divide instead, so that friendship may remain. One undivided house does not support two persons. Is it not better to move away with goodwill than to live together in discord?

11. The Patriarch also teaches what sort of division there ought to be. Let the stronger divide; let the weaker choose, so that he may have nothing of which to complain. For he cannot criticize the portion of his own choosing. No opportunity remains for withdrawing from one who is given the option of choosing, and the divider is not burdened. For the wiser a person is, the more cautious he is, so that he is neither cheated in the division nor deceived in the choice.

12. Abraham divided, “because,” it says, “the land could not contain them dwelling together” (Gen. XIII, 6), because they were exceedingly rich. It is a worldly vice that the land cannot contain the rich. For nothing is enough for the rich person’s greed. The richer anyone is, the more eager he is to possess. He desires to extend the boundaries of his fields and exclude his neighbor.

Was Abraham such a person? By no means, although at the beginning even he was less perfect. For whence could perfection come before Christ’s advent? He had not yet come who said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21). Yet, as one least avaricious, he offers the choice; as a just man, he cuts off dissension. “Let there be no quarrel,” he says, “between me and you, and between my shepherds and your shepherds, because we are brothers. Is not the whole land before you? Depart from me: if you go to the left, I will go to the right; or if you go to the right, I will go to the left” (Gen. XIII, 8 ff.).

13. “And Lot lifted up his eyes and chose the well-watered region of the Jordan.” 287 It says, “because it was all watered and was like the paradise of God” (Gen. XIII, 10). [Note [Col. 0425D]: Here alone the manuscripts and old editions differ in the word *irriguam* (“well-watered”), for which the Corbie manuscript alone, with the old edition, has *irrigua*. The Roman edition had restored the text thus: “And Lot lifted up his eyes and chose the well-watered [region, namely of the Jordan], because, it says, it was all watered, before God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, like the paradise of God.” But the Septuagint differs somewhat from them all: “And Lot, lifting up his eyes, saw all the surrounding country of the Jordan, that it was all watered before God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, like the paradise of God.” The Vulgate agrees fairly well with it here; consult it.]

Inheritances commonly include properties of differing kinds: some more useful, others more pleasant. In such a division they are not sufficiently advantageous, for the value of the more useful is diminished by their being less pleasant, and that of the more pleasant by their being less useful. [Note [Col. 0425D–0426D]: The expression is somewhat obscure, but we think it has the same force as “fortunate” or “advantageous,” so that the sense is: such properties are not sufficiently advantageous in a division, because the value of the more useful is diminished by their being less pleasant, and that of the more pleasant by their being less useful.] But if the parties cannot agree about the more useful properties, the pleasant ones should be set against the useful ones.

Human dispositions differ: useful things delight some, pleasant things others. The weaker person chooses the more pleasant things and disdains the useful ones. A steward is sometimes useful, or a farm manager may be set against an urban servant. [Note [Col. 0426D]: An *actor agri* is the same as a rustic steward.] If the chooser is foolish, he chooses either a cook or a singer—whom he regards as more charming—and rejects the more useful person. [Note [Col. 0426D]: A *vocalis* here means either one who sings skillfully or a teacher of vocal control and delivery, also called a *phonascus*.] Often, even where the yields are not unequal, the wiser person declines the more pleasant things. [Note [Col. 0426D]: We restore the passage from the Corbie, Colbert, and Mazarin manuscripts; in the others, as in all editions, one reads “where the yields are unequal.”] They quickly stir up envy; they quickly awaken the greedy mind.

Yet Scripture here says nothing about one portion being more useful and the other more pleasant, lest Abraham seem deliberately to have caught the young man’s eye. [Note [Col. 0426D]: *Studio*: that is, deliberately or intentionally.] It described one portion as pleasant, but did not add that the other was more useful. It was necessary to make two portions out of the whole region; moreover, he was dividing things present, not absent. One region could not contain them both. In what he could do with the highest justice, he offered the choice.

14. Lot chose the pleasant portion, which quickly attracted the eyes of raiders. Hence came war among kings, the victory of opponents, and the captivity of inhabitants. Thus Lot too paid the price of weaker judgment: deceived not by the barrenness of the land but by envy aroused by its pleasantness, he himself was carried away captive. For, through the fault of slavish perversity, he had turned aside from one stronger and chosen the portion of the most wicked. [Note [Col. 0426D]: Two manuscripts read, “he had turned aside from one more prudent”; one reads, “he had turned aside [from one] not more prudent.”] For Sodom is luxury and wantonness. Therefore Lot is called, in Latin interpretation, “declining,” because one who chooses vices turns aside from virtue and deviates from equity.

15. When Abram learned this, he counted his home-born servants (Gen. XIV, 14); and with three hundred and eighteen men, having gained the victory, he freed his nephew. The character of his division is proved by the fact that he loved his nephew so greatly that for his sake he did not shrink even from the danger of war.

What does “he counted” mean? It means: he chose. Thus the saying in the Gospel, “Even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Luke XII, 7), refers not only to God’s knowledge but also to the favor shown to the righteous. The Lord knows those who are His; but those who are not His, He does not deign to know. He counted three hundred and eighteen, so that you may understand that it is not the quantity of the number but the merit of the choice that is expressed. For he enlisted those whom he judged worthy of the number of the faithful: those who would believe in the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. For three hundred is signified by the Greek letter τ, while eighteen expresses the sum ιη. [Note [Col. 0427D–0428D]: Thus the Erasmus and Roman editions. The Ambrosian and Gillot editions, with the Tornacensis, Theodorianus, and Royal manuscripts, read, “the sum ιη expresses the name of faith.” The Corbie, Longpont, Colbert, and Mazarin manuscripts read, “the sum [of the letters of] Jesus expresses the name.”] Thus Abraham conquered by the merit of faith, not by a populous army. Accordingly, he set out with a few home-born servants and triumphed over those before whose arms the five kings had yielded.

16. But one who conquers ought not arrogate victory to himself, but attribute it to God. Abraham teaches this, for after his triumph he became more humble, not more proud. 288 He therefore offered sacrifice and gave tithes; and Melchizedek, who in Latin interpretation is called king of righteousness and king of peace, blessed him: “for he was priest of the Most High God” (Gen. I, 18). Who is the king of righteousness and priest of God, except He to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4)—that is, the Son of God, priest of the Father, who by the sacrifice of His own body made the Father propitious for our sins?

17. How great also is the fact that he wished nothing from the spoils of victory to come to him, nor would take even what was offered? For accepting a reward diminishes the fruit of triumph and gnaws away the grace of a benefit. It makes a great difference whether you have fought for money or for glory: the one is regarded as a mercenary; the other is considered worthy of the glory of a savior.

Rightly the holy man refuses to appropriate anything from the spoils, even when offered, lest the donor should say, “I made him rich.” He declares that this alone suffices for him: that he had advanced the sustenance of the young men who fought. Someone may say (23, q. 5, c. *Dicat aliquis*): Since he himself conquered, how does he say to the king of the Sodomites, “I will take nothing from you,” when the spoil was surely in the victor’s power? He teaches military discipline: everything must be reserved for the king. Certainly, he maintains that a share of the gain should perhaps be given, as payment for their labor, to those who had joined him as allies for assistance.

18. Therefore, because he did not seek his reward from a human being, he received it from God, as we read written: “After these words the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision, saying: Do not fear, Abram; I will protect you; your reward shall be exceedingly great” (Gen. XV, 1). The Lord is not slow to reward: He promises quickly and gives abundantly, lest remorse for having despised present things enter weak minds through some delay. And He repays with a kind of usurious abundance, restoring more richly to one who has not been captivated by the offer of present things.

19. Let us consider also what reward he asks from the Lord Himself. He does not demand riches like a miser, nor a long life in this world like one afraid of death, nor power; but he seeks an heir worthy of his labor. “What,” he says, “will you give me? Yet I am dismissed without children” (ibid., 2). And below: “Because you have not given me seed, my home-born servant shall be my heir” (ibid., 3).

Let people therefore learn not to despise marriage or join themselves to unsuitable partners, lest they bear children whom they cannot have as heirs. Thus, if no regard for chastity moves them, let them seek a worthy marriage at least out of consideration for the inheritance that must be passed on.

20. But if Abraham’s judgment is not sufficiently effective for correction, receive God’s oracle condemning an inheritance of this kind: “This man,” He says, “shall not be your heir; but another who shall come forth from you, he shall be your heir” (ibid., 4). Whom does He call “another”? Hagar also bore Ishmael a son, yet He does not mean him; He means holy Isaac. Therefore He added: “who shall come forth from you.” For he truly came forth from Abraham who was begotten in lawful marriage.

But through Isaac, the legitimate son, we may understand that true legitimate Son, 289 the Lord Jesus Christ, whom at the beginning of the Gospel according to Matthew we read to be Abraham’s son (Matt. I, 1). He showed Himself Abraham’s true heir, illuminating the succession of His progenitor; through Him Abraham looked to heaven and recognized the splendor of his offspring, no less illustrious than the brightness with which the heavenly stars shine. “For star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV, 41), says the Apostle, because, granting them a share in His resurrection, Christ made human beings—whom death was accustomed to hide in the earth—participants in the heavenly kingdom.

21. How else was Abraham’s offspring spread abroad than through the inheritance of faith, through which we are compared to heaven, associated with angels, and made equal to the stars? Therefore He says: “So shall your seed be.” “And Abraham believed God” (Gen. XV, 6). What did he believe? That Christ would become his heir by assumption of a body. That you may know he believed this, the Lord says: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” (John VII, 56). Therefore it was reckoned to him as righteousness, because he did not seek a reason but believed with most ready faith.

It is good for faith to precede reasoning, lest we seem to demand an account from the Lord our God as though He were a human being. For how unworthy it is that we should believe human testimony about another person, yet not believe God’s oracles about Himself! Let us therefore imitate Abraham, so that we may be heirs of the earth through the righteousness of faith, through which he became heir of the world.

## CHAPTER IV

Abraham is defended from the charge of adultery on account of the son received from a slave woman: namely, because he was not free from human frailty and had only lately abandoned the superstitions of the Chaldeans; then because he did not sin against a law not yet promulgated; afterward, because he was induced not by lust but by love of offspring. Here much is argued against adultery. Finally, he is defended on the ground that the act itself was a mystery, not a sin. At the end, it is asked whether it was fitting for circumcision to be instituted and later revoked, when it contained in itself only the smallest degree of perfection.

22. But perhaps someone will say: “How do you put Abraham before us for imitation? 290 When he received a son from a slave woman, Or what does it mean that so great a man was subject to such error, when we admire such great works of his?” Therefore, lest we seem, like sailors, to have avoided a passage that many regard as shallow, I desire to explain its rationale.

I do not deny that Abraham received a son from a slave woman, so that you may know that Abraham was not of some higher nature and substance, but one among the number and frailty of all human beings. Indeed, he was called from the land of the Chaldeans, whom we understand to have been more devoted than others to vain superstition. Therefore he found greater favor with God, because he renounced the former things and stretched himself toward the things before him, in order to follow God. [Note [Col. 0429C]: All editions read “because of later things”; all manuscripts, on the contrary, read “because of former things.” The latter is better, as anyone can readily understand for himself.] He is set before you for imitation, so that you too may observe that, if you renounce sins, you can deserve the Lord’s mercy.

23. Yet some may be troubled that he was already speaking with God and went in to the slave woman, as it is written: “Sarah said to Abram: ‘Behold, the Lord has shut me up so that I may not bear; go in therefore to my slave woman, that you may have children by her’” (Gen. XVI, 2; 32, q. 4, c. *Dixit Sara*). [Note [Col. 0429C]: Thus all manuscripts. The editions read, “that you may make a son by her.” The Septuagint has ἵνα τεκνοποιήσωμαι ἐξ αὐτῆς, “that I may have children by her.” This is found in many manuscripts; in some, however, one finds τεκνοποιήσῃς, “that you may have children.”] And so it came to pass.

But let us consider, first, that Abraham lived before the Law of Moses and before the Gospel: adultery did not yet appear to be forbidden. The punishment of the offense belongs to the time of the Law, which prohibited the offense; before the Law there is no condemnation of the accused, but only under the Law. Abraham therefore did not transgress a law, but preceded the Law. Although God praised marriage in paradise (Gen. I, 28), He had not condemned adultery. For He does not desire the death of the sinner, and therefore promises what is a reward, but does not exact what is punishment. He prefers to draw people by gentler means rather than frighten them by harsher ones.

And you sinned when you were a Gentile: you have an excuse. You came to the Church and heard the law, “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX, 14): now you have no excuse for sin. Yet, because I am speaking with those who have enrolled their names for the grace of baptism, if anyone has committed so great a crime, let him know that pardon is granted him; but, as one who has committed the offense, let him nevertheless know that he must abstain from it thereafter.

Thus the Lord indeed forgave the earlier sins of the adulteress whom the scribes of the Pharisees brought before Him in the Gospel, 291 but said: “Go, and from now on see that you do not sin” (John VIII, 11). What He says to her, He says to you. Did you commit adultery as a Gentile? Did you commit it as a catechumen? You are forgiven; it is remitted to you through baptism. Go, and after this see that you do not sin. You have one defense from Abraham.

[Note [Col. 0429C–0430D]: Some seized upon these words as an occasion falsely to accuse Ambrose of holding erroneous views about adultery. Yet it is certain that the holy Doctor consistently taught that adultery was forbidden by natural law and that this law could never be unknown to anyone—namely, with invincible ignorance. This may be learned both from his other works and plainly from this very book. For when he recounts how Pharaoh, after learning that Sarah, whom he had brought into his palace intending to marry, was married, restored her to Abraham, he says: “Though savage and barbarous by nature, he nevertheless indicates … that one must guard against the crime of adultery. He who pleads ignorance condemns intemperance. Nor is it surprising that a barbarian knows the law of nature … Thus the law of nature is greater than the prescription of laws.”

Nor should one suppose that these statements concern only the adultery by which another man’s wife is violated. Apart from the fact that the words are general and thus cannot be restricted to one kind of adultery, the holy man asserts in this very chapter that what is forbidden to a woman is forbidden to a man; and in chapter 7 that all intercourse of man and woman celebrated without the status of lawful marriage has its own guilt.

We therefore think that he wrote that adultery did not seem forbidden before the Mosaic Law was promulgated in order to indicate that in those times there existed an ignorance concerning adultery which, although it did not remove guilt altogether, nevertheless diminished it considerably—that is, vincible ignorance. For no one will deny that this may be found in natural law and may excuse, as the more eminent theologians say, if not from the whole penalty, at least from so great a penalty. This is the ignorance of which it is written in Luke XII, 48: “But he who did not know and did things worthy of stripes shall be beaten with few stripes.”

This was sufficient both to excuse Abraham before those whom Ambrose addressed, who had committed the same acts before their conversion to the faith, and to call those same persons back from such crime in the future, when they no longer possessed any excuse based on ignorance. We think this answer all the more admissible because Ambrose below, §27, testifies that the Patriarch’s act was less approved by God; and in *On Paradise*, ch. 13, §65, and elsewhere he speaks of it as a true sin.

It may, however, also be said that the holy Doctor understood by the term “adultery” nothing other than polygamy and employed this harsh expression in order more effectively to deter catechumens from concubinage. Nor is it surprising if Ambrose was somewhat more vehement on this matter, when Basil, concerning third marriages—which it is certain have never been unlawful under divine and natural law—said in Epistle 1 to Amphilochius, ch. 4, that they are called polygamy, or rather “chastened fornication.” Tertullian himself, in defending Abraham’s polygamy (*On Monogamy*, ch. 6), nevertheless calls it concubinage with a slave woman. In the same sense Leo the Great, *Letter to Rusticus*, ch. 4, calls Hagar Abraham’s concubine—that is, his secondary wife. Indeed, the Jews Josephus (*Antiquities*, I.14 and 18) and Philo (*That God Is Immutable*)—though everywhere most reverent toward their patriarchs—nevertheless call their secondary wives only concubines, and the sons begotten from them illegitimate or spurious; and this should not be considered much milder than calling such a union adultery that did not yet appear forbidden.]

24. The second defense is that Abraham did not, inflamed by any heat of wandering lust or captured by the beauty of a wanton form, prefer companionship with the slave woman to the marriage-bed; rather, he was motivated by zeal to seek descendants and propagate offspring. There was still, after the Flood, scarcity of the human race, and likewise of religious devotion, lest anyone appear not to have rendered the debt owed to nature. Thus the daughters of holy Lot also had this reason for seeking offspring, lest the human race fail; and therefore, for the sake of a public duty, they put forward a private fault as a pretext. [Note [Col. 0430D–0431D]: Latinius conjectures that one should read *culpam praetexunt* (“they put forward a fault as a pretext”). But nothing should be changed here, since the verb *praetexuit* refers to the noun *gratia* (“for the sake of”).]

Nor is it insignificant that the wife is introduced as the author of the act, so that the husband may be excused, lest he be thought carried away by wandering error. At the same time, women should learn to love their husbands, not to be disturbed by groundless suspicion of concubinage, nor to envy stepchildren if they themselves have borne no children. A good wife was concerned to excuse her own barrenness before her husband; and, lest she herself should be the reason why her husband had no children, she urged him to go in to the slave woman. Leah did this, and Rachel did it afterward. Learn, woman, to lay aside jealousy, which often drives women into frenzy.

25. But I also warn you, men—especially those who are advancing toward the grace of the Lord—not to join yourselves to an adulterous body: “for he who joins himself to a prostitute is one body”; nor give women this occasion for divorce. Let no one deceive himself by human laws (33, q. 4, ch. *Nemo*). Every sexual immorality is adultery; what is not permitted to a woman is not permitted to a man. The same chastity is due from a husband as from a wife. Whatever is committed with a woman who is not a lawful wife is condemned by the charge of adultery. You have therefore perceived what you ought to avoid, lest anyone render himself unworthy of the sacraments.

26. Take also this further point: such intemperance dissolves marital affection; it makes maidservants proud, matrons irascible, spouses contentious, concubines insolent, husbands shameless. As soon as the maidservant has conceived by her master, she despises her mistress as though enriched by childbearing; the mistress grieves that she is slighted and accuses her husband as the author of her injuries. Thus Sarah herself had given her husband authority over her maidservant, and afterwards says to him: “I suffer wrong from you. I gave my maidservant into your bosom; but when she sees that she has conceived, I am despised by her” [Col. 0431C]; “may God judge between me and you” (Gen. 16:5). How great her pain was, how weighty the complaint of women, is set forth in the reading.

Give a husband who is thoughtless and frivolous, who does not know how to comply with his wife, and he provides grounds for divorce. But Abraham, a restrained and prudent man, said: “Behold, your maidservant is in your hands; use her as you please” (ibid., 6). For he preferred to keep his wife rather than the servant. Yet even this was not a complete remedy. The angry wife received authority [Note: Vat., Reg., Valc., Theod., and Maz. manuscripts, corrected by a second hand: “a remarkable wife.”] and used the permitted revenge with excessive severity. If Sarah did not preserve moderation, who will? Therefore it is written: “Sarah afflicted her, and she fled from before her face” (ibid.).

Scripture comprises two points: it both expresses the mistress’s grave indignation and the maidservant’s arrogance and pride. That “Sarah afflicted her” [Col. 0431D] refers to the anger of the one afflicting her; that Hagar fled means that she could not bear the insult with a servant’s patience, since she claimed for herself the eminence of sharing her mistress’s husband. She was indignant at an injury, though she had assumed insolence. Accordingly, when the angel asked her where she was going, she answered: “I flee from the face of Sarah, my mistress” (ibid., 8). This too showed excessive pride: she first uttered Sarah’s name and only afterwards indicated that she was her mistress. The former was placed first as an insult; [Col. 0432A] the latter was added to identify the person.

The angel did not approve the maidservant’s insolence, and therefore said to her: “Return to your mistress” (ibid., 9). Certainly it would not have escaped the angel had she fled, overcome by violent punishments; and he would have reproved the cruelty of the woman beating her more than the departure of the fugitive. But, to show that she fled as a proud woman, he added: “And humble yourself under her hands” (ibid.). [Note: Thus Corb., Valc., Colb., and Maz. The editions and other manuscripts read: “lest she should be subject to her mistress.” Except for Torn., which has both readings: “lest she should not, as a proud woman, be subject to her mistress.”] I therefore wish that no one may fall into this fault; but if anyone does fall into it, let him learn to humble his maidservant before his wife, lest, while he wishes to vindicate the maidservant, he exclude the wife.

27. Thus Abraham was both one of the Gentile people and had gone in to the maidservant for the sake of offspring, because his wife, wishing to conceal her barrenness, had been the instigator of that act for her husband. Yet it is not without significance [Col. 0432B] that afterwards God at once, in order to approve his other deeds, [Note: Thus all manuscripts with the Am. edition; Era. and the others read: “as repentance for this deed.”] or as repentance for this deed, said to him: “I am your God; merit approval in my sight, and be without complaint” (Gen. 17:1), as though he had not yet fully merited it, since he despaired of his barren wife’s childbirth and sought posterity from a maidservant.

“Be without complaint,” he says—that is, irreproachable—so that your wife may not complain of you and no one may rebuke your actions. For he changes his name by adding a letter, so that Abram is called Abraham: that is, from “vain father,” as the Latin translation has it, he is called “exalted father,” “chosen father”; or, from being a father, he becomes also the father of a son. He was vain when he did not know God; he became chosen after he knew God. He was a father when he had offspring by the maidservant; but he was not the father of a son, because he did not have a son received in lawful marriage. Sarah gave birth, [Col. 0432C] and he became the father of a son.

He is commanded to be circumcised, being about to receive the inheritance of the true seed. Is not the circumcision of the flesh plainly commanded as a precept of chastity, so that one may cut away the lust of the flesh and restrain desires unruly through luxury and wantonness? Indeed, under the term “circumcision” this is prescribed: that every stench of impurity be wiped away and the incentive to lust removed. We have employed two defenses.

28. There is also a third, supplied us by the authority of the Apostle Paul, who says that the things Abraham did in taking offspring from the maidservant were done as a figure and spoken allegorically. Allegory is when one thing is done and another is signified; as the Apostle himself teaches when he says: “You who wish to be under the law, have you not read the law? For it is written that Abraham [Col. 0432D] had two sons, one by the maidservant and one by the free woman. But he who was by the maidservant was born according to the flesh; whereas he who was by the free woman [293] was born through promise. These things are spoken allegorically. For these are the two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery, which is Hagar” (Gal. 4:21 ff.).

He shows that two peoples issue from Abraham’s progeny: one, the Jewish people, which serves the syllables of the law, because [Col. 0433A] it seems to have been begotten from the maidservant into slavery; the other, the Christian people, which has received through remission of sins the freedom of heavenly grace. What, therefore, you suppose to be sin, you perceive to be a mystery by which things that were to come in later times were disclosed.

Accordingly, he added: “But you, brethren, are children of promise according to Isaac” (Gal. 4:28). Therefore, he says, do not seek the works of the law, “because a person is not justified by works of the law, except through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. 2:16). And, so that you may know that he spoke to Christians: “We also,” he says, “have believed in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law” (ibid.).

Let us therefore recognize that those things which happened as figures were not a charge against them; but they will be against us if we refuse to beware of what was written [Col. 0433B] for our correction. Rather, since we are children of the free woman, who is Sarah, let us not serve the snares of the law, since Abraham kept the free woman and cast out the maidservant. [Note: The Roman edition reads, “that we may be delivered from the snares of the law”—a convenient reading, but one supported neither by any manuscript nor by any edition. Corb., Colb., and Maz. restore the text given here; in the others, as also in the early editions, the particle *ne* was omitted.]

29. I know that this passage (Gen. 17:10) troubles many people. For if circumcision is good, it ought to be observed today as well; if it is useless, it ought not to have been commanded, especially by a divine oracle. But since the Apostle Paul said: “Abraham received the sign of circumcision” (Rom. 4:11), a sign is surely not the thing itself, but the sign of another thing: that is, not the truth, but an indication of the truth. He himself then explained and stated it: “He received the sign of circumcision, a seal of righteousness and faith” (ibid.). Hence we rightly understand that bodily circumcision is the sign of spiritual circumcision. [Col. 0433C]

The sign therefore remained until the truth should come. The Lord Jesus came, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). [Note: All editions read: “He who did not [circumcise] a small part . . . destroyed the sign.” All manuscripts read as in the text.] Because he circumcised not a small part of the body in a sign, but the whole human being in truth, he removed the sign and introduced the truth. For after that which is perfect has come, that which was partial has been abolished; and therefore the circumcision of a part ceased where the circumcision of the whole shone forth. For now the human being is saved not partially but wholly: saved in body and saved in soul.

For it is written: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:24). This is the perfection of circumcision, because [Note: Two manuscripts: “through the removal of the body.”] through the offering of the body the soul is redeemed, of which the Lord himself says: “Whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it” (Luke 9:24).

[Col. 0433D] 30. There remains now this part of the question: whether a part ought to have been set beforehand when perfection was to come. This point is easy to resolve, [Note: The editions add, “or to distinguish,” which is not found in the manuscripts.] if we consider to whom the part was commanded and for whom perfection was reserved. For the part was commanded under the law to the Jewish people: that stiff-necked people, that weak people, that people which [Col. 0434A] did not know its God. Since it was unable to endure even the part, how could it have kept perfection?

If you are teaching a little child letters, you must begin with the individual elements of letters, so that from individual strokes you may lead him to syllables, and from syllables, in due order, to words and speech. Nor can anyone sail the sea fearlessly unless he has first sailed on rivers. Again, if you wish to assign to a child and to an adult some task of completing a journey or lifting a burden, are their loads and labors to be equal?

Thus you should know that the perfection of circumcision was reserved for those who, instructed by Christ, seemed fit for stronger ordinances; [Note: The Roman edition alone: “who, from Christ’s stronger institutions,” etc.] so that believers might be tested—an innumerable multitude of whom would take up the cross, devote their own lives for Christ, and leave unbelievers [Col. 0434B] unable to resist, because they thought salvation was to be sought in the immolation of the entire body, though they considered the scant blood of their circumcision to be saving.

31. We must also consider that God called him while he was uncircumcised, and that while he still remained uncircumcised the inheritance of a lawful son was promised to him; so that you may believe him to be the father not only of the Jews, as they themselves assert, but of all believers through faith. [Note: The Vulgate teaches that Abraham’s wife’s name was changed from Sarai to Sarah; but the Septuagint states that she was named Sarram from Sara, the name by which she had previously been called. Our manuscripts, agreeing with the latter, almost always give this name in no other spelling.]

Sarah too, before her husband’s circumcision, is blessed by the addition of a single letter with no slight recompense, so that she might possess preeminence in virtue and grace. From her nations and kings of peoples are promised to come, so that in her there might be established a type not of the Synagogue but of the Church.

But when Abraham laughed at the promise of a son by her, it was a sign not of unbelief but of exultation. For [Col. 0434C] he fell upon his face—he who worshipped and believed—and added: “Shall a son be born to me when I am a hundred years old? And shall Sarah, ninety years old, give birth?” And he said: “May Ishmael live in your sight” (Gen. 17:17–18). He is neither unbelieving in promises nor covetous in prayers. That is: I do not doubt that you can do this, so that you may give a son even to an old man of a hundred years and, as the author of nature, relax nature’s limits. Blessed is he to whom such things are granted; yet, if this Ishmael whom I have by a household servant should live in your sight, your grace is abundant enough for me. Accordingly, the Lord both approved his disposition, did not deny his request, and confirmed his own promises.

## CHAPTER V

Concerning Abraham’s hospitality: his watching for the arrival of guests and hastening to meet them. The same virtue is commended, and the vain excuse of some people is refuted. How diligently this saint displayed it, and how he associated his wife in the merit. What the offerings made by each mystically signify. Finally, the promise of a son made to Abraham while he ministered, together with an explanation of Sarah’s laughter.

[Col. 0434D]

[Col. 0435A] 32. We have spoken of Abraham’s devotion and faith, prudence, justice, charity, and frugality; now let us speak also of hospitality. For it is no small virtue. Accordingly, the Apostle, by the authority of a twofold writing, teaches that it ought especially to be present in a bishop: that he may be ready for arrivals, go out to meet them, watch for travelers, assist those who do not ask, and seize those who are passing by.

Abraham sat before the door; he sat at midday. When others were resting, he was watching for the arrival of guests. Rightly did God appear to him by the oak of Mamre, because he sought with the greatest eagerness the fruit of hospitality.

33. “And, lifting up his eyes, he saw, and behold, three [Col. 0435B] men were standing near him. And when he saw them, he ran to meet them” (Gen. 18:2). First observe the mystery of faith. God appeared to him, and he beheld three. [Note: The old edition and certain Paris editions with a few manuscripts read, “he to whom God shone forth in the Trinity,” etc. The other and more numerous, better manuscripts read: “he to whom God shines forth sees the Trinity.”] He to whom God shines forth sees the Trinity: he receives not the Father without the Son, nor confesses the Son without the Holy Spirit. This has been discussed more fully elsewhere (*On the Resurrection of the Flesh*). Our present purpose is to pursue the moral sense of the passage.

He does not sit idle who looks out afar; nor, content merely to have seen, did he fail to run to meet them. He hurried to meet them, because it is not enough to act rightly unless you also hasten to do what you do. [Note: The Gill. and Roman editions read, “unless you also hasten.” The Am., Era., and all manuscripts read, “unless you also hasten to”; this requires an ellipsis of “endeavor” or something similar, or perhaps reflects a scribal error.] For the law commands the Passover to be eaten hurriedly (Exod. 12:11). Devotion made swift bears richer fruits. Learn, therefore, how energetic you ought to be, so that you may anticipate the guest, lest someone else get ahead of you and an abundance of good service deprive you of your reward.

[Col. 0435C] 34. Hospitality is good and has its reward: first, human gratitude; then, what is greater, divine recompense. We are all guests in this earthly sojourn; for we have lodging only for a time of dwelling, and we depart quickly. Let us beware that, if we are harsh or negligent in receiving guests, the dwellings of the saints may also be denied us after the course of this life.

Hence the Savior says in the Gospel: “Make friends for yourselves from unrighteous mammon, that they may receive you into their eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). Moreover, even while in this body, the need to travel often arises. What you deny to others, therefore, you decree against yourself; and what you grant others makes you appear worthy of the same. If everyone adopted this policy of not receiving guests, where would travelers find rest? Having abandoned human dwellings, we should seek out the retreats of wild beasts and their lairs.

35. But you plead poverty. The guest does not demand wealth from you, but kindness; not an elaborate banquet, but food readily offered. “Hospitality with vegetables,” it says, “for friendship and kindness, is better than if you slaughter calves at the stalls amid hostilities” (Prov. 15:17). This is pleasing to people and acceptable to God. Hence the Lord [Col. 0436A] Jesus says in the Gospel (Matt. 10:42) that whoever gives a guest a drink of cold water will not be deprived of heavenly rewards.

Thus Jacob watered Rachel’s sheep, found favor, and gained a wife. Again, how do you know whether, when you think you are receiving a guest, you are receiving God? Abraham, while offering lodging to travelers, received God and his angels in hospitality. Indeed, when you receive a guest, you receive God, as you read in the Gospel, the Lord Jesus saying: “I was a stranger, and you gathered me in . . . For what you did to one of these least ones, you did to me” (Matt. 25:35, 40).

By one hour’s hospitality, the widow who received Elijah [296] and fed him with scant food found a perpetual supply of nourishment throughout the famine and received a marvelous recompense: the flour never failed from her jar. Elisha likewise repaid the cost of hospitality by restoring to life the dead pledge [i.e., child].

36. Yet not only readiness to receive, but also the diligence and disposition of the host are required. Abraham teaches you both. He ran to meet them and made the first request, saying: “Lord, if I have found favor before you, do not pass by your servant. Let water be brought, and let your feet be washed; refresh yourselves under the tree; and I will bring bread—eat, and afterwards you shall pass on, because you have turned aside to your servant” (Gen. 18:3 ff.).

He saw three and addressed one as Lord; he confesses himself the servant of that one alone. Then, turning to the other two, whom he thought to be attendants, he eagerly seeks to render service also to them—not now bound by the rightful obligation of slavery, [Col. 0436C] but by the gracious title and practice of attentive service.

37. “And Abraham hastened into the tent to Sarah and said to her: ‘Hasten, and mix three measures of fine flour, and make cakes baked under the ashes’” (ibid., 6). A good husband does not permit his wife to have no share in a religious service, nor does he greedily appropriate the entire service to himself. Rightly, therefore, she is preserved for the sake both of piety and modesty. What belongs to piety he wishes to be shared; what belongs to modesty remains inviolate for Sarah.

Before the tent the husband watches for the arrival of guests; within the tent Sarah safeguards a woman’s modesty and, under the protection of chastity, carries out women’s work. Outside, the husband invites; inside, Sarah prepares the banquet. Abraham himself does not merely hasten: he also tells his wife to hasten, showing her to be his partner in devotion [Col. 0436D] and not unequal in faith.

38. “Mix,” he says, “three measures of fine flour, and make cakes baked under ashes.” In Greek they are called *ἐγκρύφια* (*enkryphia*), that is, “hidden things,” because every mystery ought to be concealed and, as it were, covered in faithful silence, [Note: Thus seven manuscripts. One manuscript and the editions read, “in the silence of faith.” Perhaps “in faithful silence,” as Horace says of the rites of Ceres at Eleusis, Book III, Ode 2.] lest it be rashly divulged to profane ears. Divine majesty is nourished by this; it feasts upon this disposition, which is sparing in speech and does not bring sacred things into public view.

Sarah briefly teaches the mystery of faith by making three measures from one flour. She bears the type of the Church, to which it is said: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail” (Isa. 54:1). She [Col. 0437A] is the one who cherishes faith in the inmost spirit, asserting the Trinity’s identical divinity, worshipping the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit with equal measure and reverence, celebrating them together in the unity of majesty, and distinguishing them by the property of their persons. With this confession of faith, mix your devotion. [Note: All editions and two manuscripts read: “For she who fosters faith in her inmost spirit, asserting the Trinity’s identical divinity, with a certain equal . . . this”; Am.: “she mixes devotion . . . .” Better manuscripts read as in the text, except two: one reads “distinguishing the unity of majesty . . . property”; the other, “mixes” instead of “mix.”]

39. Let the woman offer fine flour: that is, the inward substance of spiritual wheat, or of that grain of which it was said that unless it falls into the earth, it bears no fruit. Therefore Mary was also the first to see the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, and hastened to disclose the message of holy salvation not indiscriminately to everyone but [Col. 0437B] only to Peter and John.

Let the man run [297] to the cattle, take a calf, and with eager, industrious zeal—not slackened by idle delay—receive the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion. Let him entrust it to a boy who preserves the innocence of tender age, does not know deceit, does not know how to strike back, and maintains the chastity of an uncorrupted body. Of this boy the Lord Jesus says: “Unless you are converted and become like this child, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). To this boy and those like him, holy David also assigns the office of divine praise, saying: “Praise the Lord, you children” (Ps. 112:1).

40. Nor is it without significance that he ran to the cattle, took a tender and good calf, and set it before them with milk. Thus in Exodus, when he declared the Lord’s Passover, [Col. 0437C] Moses says: “A lamb without blemish, pure, complete, one year old, male, shall be for you, [Note: Corb., Colb., and Maz. manuscripts: “from the sheep of the house.”] from sheep and goats. You shall take it and slaughter it,” he says, “the whole multitude of the synagogue at evening” (Exod. 12:5).

Hence here also it is described as midday, when Abraham offers hospitality to the Lord. But at supper the calf is sacrificed and eaten with milk: that is, not in blood but with the purity of faith. The calf is good, since it washes away sins; tender, because, not stiff-necked, it accepted the yoke of the law with gentleness and did not refuse the gibbet of the cross. And it is rightly tender: nothing of its head, feet, or inward parts was left, nor was a bone broken in it; rather, it wholly became food for those feasting. Such a one the shadow of the Law prefigured for us; such a one the truth of the Gospel displayed (John 19:36).

[Col. 0437D] 41. “They ate,” it says, “but Abraham stood under the tree” (Gen. 18:8). We perceive that the service of hospitality is commended by humility. [Note: All editions read this, but erroneously. It is remarkable that no manuscript corrects the fault. Some offer, “humility is commended by the service of humility”; others, “the service of humility is commended by humility”; none offers what the sense plainly demands: “the service of hospitality is commended by humility.”] Abraham stood, and do you seize the first place at table? Accordingly, that humility found favor, so that a son was promised to him.

42. “And he said to him: ‘Where is Sarah your wife?’ He answered and said: ‘Behold, she is in the tent’” (ibid., 9). [Col. 0438A] Did the Lord, who subsequently foretells the coming destruction of the Sodomites, not know where Sarah was? He did know; but he wished to teach us how great women’s modesty ought to be: that they should not draw guests’ eyes toward themselves by a forward encounter, but perform their service while preserving modesty.

Abraham also impresses upon your ears that Sarah remains in the tent, so that you may learn what to require of a wife. Though advanced in years, Sarah still preserves a young woman’s modesty; therefore the Lord promised her a son. “Sarah had ceased to have the ways of women” (ibid., 11). This is not added idly, lest you suppose that she still retained the natural possibility of bearing a child.

43. “But Sarah laughed” (ibid., 10). I judge this to have been an indication of what was to come rather than of unbelief. For she laughed, though she did not yet know why she laughed, because she was to bear in Isaac a joy [Col. 0438B] shared by all. Therefore she denied that she had laughed because she did not know; therefore she laughed because she prophesied.

[298] ## CHAPTER VI

The destruction of Sodom is foretold to Abraham; God’s forbearance in enduring sins, examining offenses, and pardoning them is proclaimed. The angels arrive in the evening and lodge with Lot. The Sodomites’ crimes are compounded by their monstrous wickedness. Lot tries to temper their fury by offering his daughters, while the angels strike them with blindness. Lot is brought out when his sons-in-law refuse to follow; he is forbidden to look back, and the reason this also concerns us is explained. Finally, after the daughters’ incest with their father is excused, the evils of drunkenness are described.

[Col. 0438C] 44. “Then the men rose and looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah” (ibid., 16). As the Lord’s visitation is granted to those who fear him, so the punishment of sin is also reserved for the ungodly. Abraham escorted his guests, adding acts of service to the grace of hospitality. But the Sodomites increased crimes of impurity in place of the duties of piety.

45. “I will not hide from Abraham my servant what I am about to do” (Gen. 17:1). Scripture has indicated above that Abraham was of advanced age, since he had reached ninety-nine years; how then does it call him a servant-boy? But when it has portrayed him as forgetful of old age, tireless in watching, energetic in running, most patient in standing, and most eager in escorting, does not the name “boy” seem fitting to his services? [Col. 0438D] He is rightly called a boy who knew none of old age’s weariness, and who displayed the innocence and attentiveness of childhood. The grace of blessing and the inheritance of posterity are therefore given to the righteous man.

46. The offense of the sinners is then explained. “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah,” he says, “has been filled up” (ibid., 20). Great is the Lord’s patience: he does not immediately punish the sinner, but long delays while awaiting correction; [Col. 0439A] nor is he moved to vengeance unless the sinner exceeds the measure. Hence the Lord Jesus also says to the Jews in the Gospel: “Fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matt. 23:32).

47. “I will therefore go down and see whether, according to the outcry coming to me from them, their deeds are consummated; and if not, that I may know” (Gen. 18:21). The Lord did not fail to know the sins of the Sodomites; rather, he spoke such words in order to instruct you, so that you may investigate more closely the offenses of those against whom you judge punishment should be exacted. “I will go down,” he says, “to see”: that is, take care also to go down; descend with the zeal of investigation, lest there be anything that deceives or escapes one who is absent, so that you may apprehend the crime with your own eyes. Those at a distance can remain ignorant of many things.

But what “outcry” does he mean, unless perhaps that, to him from whom nothing is hidden, all things cry out, and the crimes of individuals seem to cry out? Thus Cain is told: “The blood of your brother cries to me” (Gen. 4:10)—that is, your fratricide is not hidden, but cries out. Thus God is, as it were, aroused by the outcries of our crimes, so that he may at last exact vengeance, though he willingly [Col. 0439B] forgives. [Note: In the Roman edition this passage was so disordered that, after the word “forgives,” it inserted the following verse of Genesis—“The men departed from there and went toward Sodom”—and then continued, “But what does this mean,” etc., down to “they bore the appearance of men”; afterwards it resumed, “Accordingly, to Abraham,” etc., down to “might not perish,” which concluded the chapter. We have restored everything from the manuscripts and early editions to its former integrity.]

48. Accordingly, when Abraham asked that he not destroy the righteous together with the wicked, and asked: “If there are fifty righteous persons in the city, will you destroy them?” (Gen. 18:24, 26), [299] he answered: “I will not destroy the city if there are fifty righteous persons in it, and I will preserve the whole place.” And so, in the successive exchange of questions and answers, even if he should find ten righteous persons in the city, he nevertheless promises impunity to the entire [Col. 0439C] people on account of the righteousness of the few.

From this we learn how great a wall a righteous person is for his country; how we ought not to envy holy persons or rashly disparage them. For their faith saves us, and their righteousness protects us from destruction. Sodom too, had it possessed ten righteous men, might not have perished.

49. What, then, is meant by the fact that the men who had come to Abraham with the Lord went to Sodom, except that their crime might be aggravated if the ungodly attempted with greater sacrilege to inflict violence on those whom a righteous man had honored? The reason why he called them men is clear: they bore the appearance of men.

50. They came to Sodom in the evening, but to Abraham at midday, because the presence of angels shines upon the righteous and brings darkness to the ungodly. Yet this may also be referred to the time of the Lord’s Passion: they came at evening [Col. 0439D] to the man who was to be delivered from the Sodomites’ contagions and from the destruction of the whole city. It was evening before Christ came, because the whole world lay in darkness. It was evening for all those oppressed by the dark squalor of monstrous crimes. The Lord Jesus came, [Col. 0440A] redeemed the world by his blood, and brought light.

“Now the two angels came to Sodom in the evening” (Gen. 19:1). Where grace is to be bestowed, Christ is present; where severity is to be exercised, the ministers alone are present and Jesus is absent.

51. “Lot was sitting at the gate” (ibid.). The adversities of captivity had corrected holy Lot and made him more vigilant. Thus, as he advanced in years, he learned to imitate his father. He sat at the gate, therefore, to receive arrivals. Accordingly, he rose to meet them. The more perfect man ran to meet them; this man rose, worshipped with his face to the ground, and said: “Behold, my lords, turn aside to the house of your servant” (ibid., 1–2). And he compelled them to turn aside, though they said: “We will remain in the street.”

Here the holiness of the righteous man and the grace of the angels are commended. [Col. 0440B] They did not wish their arrival to appear burdensome to their host; he, although he knew among whom he lived, nevertheless offered his house to dangers in order to withdraw the guests from them. [Note: Thus all editions with three more authoritative manuscripts. Others read: “he who knew among whom he lived offered his house as a protection”—some read “a safe house.” Which reading is preferable, let the reader judge.] Certainly, the longer they delayed in consenting, testing him for a longer time, the more fully they proved him.

52. “But the men of the city of Sodom surrounded the house, from boy to old man, the entire people together” (ibid., 5). The justice of the divine judgment is established beforehand, lest anyone perhaps say: “What had the children done, that all should be caught up in destruction?” Thus no one there was righteous, no one innocent. Hear Scripture testifying that they surrounded the house from boy to old man, the entire people together. No age was free from guilt; therefore no one was exempt from destruction. Even one who had no ability to commit the crime had the disposition for it. The old men’s strength was exhausted, [Col. 0440C] but their mind was full of lust.

Holy Lot offered the modesty of his daughters (32, q. 7, ch. *Offerebat*). For although that too was a shameful impurity, it was nevertheless less evil to have intercourse according to nature than to sin against nature. He preferred the grace of hospitality—held inviolable even among barbarian peoples—to the modesty of his household. Indeed, hospitality is unviolated even there where not even kinship is sufficiently safe.

53. “But the angels struck them with blindness, so that they could not find the door of the house which they wished to open.” Here the marvelous power of the angels is indeed shown: blindness was cast over the impure men, and they could not find the doors of the house. But this also is shown: every lust is blind and does not see what lies before it. That holy Lot was drawn back into the house by the hands of his guests shows him forgetful of danger but mindful of faith: [Col. 0440D] he did not rescue himself from danger but offered himself to it.

54. [Note: Thus six manuscripts. Others and the editions read, “The case for piety is fortified.” The Roman edition had moved these words twelve lines earlier and, with certain changes, constructed this sequence there: “The case for piety is fortified, so that hospitality too might be uninjured there,” etc. It had then patched together this passage as follows: “Holy Lot is represented as having sons-in-law, and, when the destruction of the whole region had been revealed to him, he is taught to warn them to flee.” But throughout this chapter it changed much, removed much, and added still more, inserting seven or eight passages from Genesis 19 which are found nowhere in the other editions or manuscripts.]

A point of piety is set forth in the fact that, when the destruction of the whole region had been disclosed to him through angels, holy Lot is represented as having sons-in-law and as warning them to flee. This is at once so that, by abandoning them without warning, [Col. 0441A] he might not appear less dutiful toward his daughters’ husbands; and so that their error might not be imputed to him—the error by which, deprived of a husband’s companionship, his daughters sought intercourse with their drunken father.

Scripture, therefore, does not leave the holy man without a defense, since it represents him both as having given his daughters in marriage and as having warned his sons-in-law. Yet it seemed to them that he was mocking them. And Lot still delayed, in order to persuade his sons-in-law; he almost failed to depart and escape, unless the angels pressed him and took hold of his hands, compelling him to go out.

55. Thus he did not depart but was led out; and he received the command not to look back, not to remain anywhere in that entire region, but to climb the mountain. What is said to him is said to all. If, therefore, you too wish to escape, do not look backward, but forward. Look where [Col. 0441B] Christ is, who says to you, “Go behind me,” as he says to Peter, “Go behind me” (Matt. 16:23), so that he might follow Christ and see Christ.

Behind you is Sodom, full of wickedness; behind you Gomorrah, overflowing with vices—the land of crimes. “Do not touch,” says the Apostle, “do not handle, do not taste—things which are all unto corruption” (Col. 2:21). Therefore flee Sodom; [Note: All editions read, “leave quickly, abandon the elements,” etc. Six manuscripts read, “leave your companions, abandon the elements.” More suitably, Long. and Theod. read, “leave Gomorrah quickly,” etc.] leave Gomorrah quickly; abandon the elements of this world, lest impending dangers engulf you.
