Do not halt while fleeing, nor linger in the entire region of vices. He who did not look back escaped; she who looked back could not escape.

56. The daughters of holy Lot are excused, because they believed that this destruction had occurred not merely in the neighboring district, but throughout the whole world, and that they alone, with their father, had remained survivors from all peoples. [Six manuscripts read “this conflagration had occurred”; others, including the editions, “this destruction.” Nor should one wonder that Ambrose so zealously seeks to excuse Lot’s daughters from incest, and Lot himself, who had previously offered those same daughters to the lust of the Sodomites. He did this in order to rebuke the Manichees, who loudly maintained on this occasion that the greatest crimes were approved in Scripture. Augustine admirably refutes them in Book XXII against Faustus and elsewhere. See also Haimo, Estius, and others on this passage.] Therefore, lest the human race should fail, they sought intercourse with their father, so as to raise up from their father a seed for the continuation of humankind. It was not, then, a fault of lust, but a remedy for generation; and I do not think it should be reckoned as a crime. For Eve too was taken from man—upon whose rib the woman was built—bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh; yet, for the continuity of human succession, she was joined to the man. Still, the consciousness of the righteous man is removed from this deed: for, being made drunk with wine, he did not know what he was doing. Hence it is not surprising that an opinion deceived the girls, who thought that all the peoples of the world had perished. The excuse of holy Lot would not have been the same, since he had heard from the angels that that place, not the whole world, was to perish.

57. Certainly, we learn that drunkenness must be avoided (15, q. 1, c. *Sane discimus*), since through it we cannot guard against crimes. For what we avoid while sober, we commit unknowingly through drunkenness. It is little enough that it inflames lust and kindles the desires of the body: it also undermines the very mind, takes possession of the soul, and wrests away judgment. Those who give themselves over to excessive wine do not know what they say; they lie as though buried.

Therefore, if they commit any offense through wine, before wise judges they are indeed granted pardon; yet they are marked as authors of recklessness. How great, moreover, is the deformity when one’s strength fails and one’s gait staggers?

58. Many consider themselves strong. Are they stronger than Lot? More self-controlled than Noah? Surely not. Scripture has set forth the faults of the patriarchs whom we read to have been overcome by wine, not for this purpose, but that you might learn what to avoid. The one lay naked; the other was exposed to the error of his daughters. Noah the righteous man was deceived because the power of wine was still unknown; but in his case you have been instructed, lest you be ignorant. Lot trusted himself to his daughters and, weakened by wine in his old age, unknowingly committed incest. You, then, drink in such a way that you are not overcome.

Let the patriarchs instruct you not only by teaching but also by their errors. The example of drunkenness was repeated so that the lesson of caution might be confirmed.

## CHAPTER VII

The death with which God threatened Abimelech for attempting Sarah’s chastity shows how grave a crime adultery is. Why, for the same offense, was Pharaoh punished more severely than Abimelech? How did the infertility removed from Abimelech’s household through Abraham’s prayers signify the fruitfulness granted to the Church? Isaac is born and nursed by his mother. Ishmael, at Sarah’s urging and by the divine answer, is expelled; and the moral precepts contained in these events.

59. Finally, Sarah’s chastity is again put to the test, so that chastity may be required of all. For Abimelech had taken her as his wife, and God said to him by night: “Behold, you shall die because of the woman” (Gen. 20:3). We observe that adultery is punished by death under divine judgment. Therefore He added: “But she dwells with a husband.”

Every intercourse of man and woman not celebrated within the lot of lawful marriage has its own guilt. Learn, then, you who are approaching the grace of baptism as candidates, so to speak, for faith, the sober discipline of continence. No one may know a woman except his wife. For this reason the right of marriage has been granted to you: lest you fall into a snare and sin with another woman. You are bound to a wife; do not seek release, because while your wife lives you are not permitted to take another wife. For to seek another when you have your own is the crime of adultery—more grievous because you think legal authority must be sought for your sin. It is more tolerable for fault to remain hidden than for authority to be arrogated to fault.

Nor is adultery only sinning with another’s wife, but every union that lacks the lawful authority of marriage. Yet this passage teaches that the crime is more grievous where the rights of a solemnized marriage are violated and a wife’s chastity is undone. Therefore, when Abimelech pleaded that he did not know she was another man’s wife, since the man himself had said she was his sister, the Lord answered him: “I too knew that you did this with a pure heart, and I spared you so that you should not sin against me; for this reason I did not permit you to touch her” (ibid., 6).

We recognize that God is, as it were, the overseer and guardian of marriage, who does not permit another’s marriage-bed to be defiled. If anyone does so, he sins against God, whose law he violates and whose grace he annuls. And because he sins against God, he loses fellowship in the heavenly sacrament.

60. Perhaps you are troubled as to why Pharaoh was grievously afflicted by the almighty God with examinations—that is, tortures or torments, so called because in capital cases truth is customarily sought by them—as we read above, though he too did not know that Sarah, whom he had heard was Abraham’s sister, was Abraham’s wife (Gen. 12:17); whereas Abimelech received no punishment. But you should recognize that the Egyptian king was a leader in vices: the greater license he had, the more disgraceful deeds he committed. Abimelech, however, was judged so faithful by God that he deserved to hear: “I too knew that you did this with a pure heart.” He was a king not of affliction, as the Egyptian was, but of fortification (*munitio*), as the interpretation of Gerar, over whose people he ruled, teaches. [The Roman edition, with three manuscripts, reads “but of admonition”; older editions, with others, read “but of fortification.” The latter is better, since the saint evidently wishes the Gerarites to be the same as the Gerasenes, interpreted as “enclosed” or “walled.”]

There is therefore no doubt that, by his other deeds, he had turned away the Lord’s indignation—He who is truly the judge of inward conscience and the interpreter of soul and mind. In short, he did not, like that Pharaoh who, when confronted by Moses, refused and despised God’s command, delay or spurn obedience; rather, Abimelech immediately summoned Abraham, restored his wife to him, fined himself because he had looked upon another’s wife, and paid the dowry of chastity. [The Vatican manuscript reads “refused, so as to fulfil God’s command.”]

61. From this too it may be inferred that King Abimelech deserved gentler treatment because Abraham prayed and obtained it for him. For his wife and his maidservant bore children, whom God had previously shut up because of Sarah, Abraham’s wife. This likewise pertains to the divine economy—that is, the disposition of the divine plan—that the birth of Sarah, granted by God’s promise, might be supported by this testimony also. For you observe that through God’s displeasure even fertile women become barren, and again, by the Lord’s will, barren women become fertile, according to what is written: “Have not I made the barren woman and the woman who bears?” says the Lord (Isa. 66:9).

Although this saying is understood to refer to the mystery of the Synagogue and the Church: for the Synagogue ceased to have offspring, deprived of the posterity of succession; while the assembly of the nations, barren when it did not know God, began to have eternal offspring. Hence we read: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for the children of the desolate are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1).

62. Now Isaac, Abraham’s son, was born when he was one hundred years old (Gen. 21:5). And if you are perfect, you will have the posterity of joy and the inheritance of exultation. Sarah said: “The Lord has made laughter for me; for whoever hears will rejoice with me” (ibid., 6). This certainly is not to be understood of this generation, which is liable to many misfortunes, so that at times it would have been better not to have begotten children; but of that generation by which every sinner who repents, when redeemed from death, customarily brings joy to the angels.

63. And Sarah said: “Who will announce to Abraham that Sarah is nursing an infant?” (ibid., 7). This is a moral lesson. Women are urged to remember their dignity and to nurse their own children. For this is mothers’ grace; this is the honor by which they commend their children to their own husbands. [All editions read: “This is the honor by which they commend themselves to their own husbands.” The Theodorian, Tornacensian, and Valencian manuscripts read: “This is the good by which they commend themselves,” etc.; five others read as in the text.] Indeed, mothers are accustomed to love more dearly those children whom they themselves have nursed at their breasts.

64. Abraham gave a great feast on the day when Isaac his son was weaned (ibid., 8). This was neither insignificant nor customary. Abraham did not give a great banquet because the child had been withdrawn from his nurse’s milk, but because Isaac was judged fit for the food of stronger grace and the nourishment of virtue: no longer, like the Corinthian, to drink milk, but to strengthen the sinews of his mind with the more solid feasts of heavenly commandments.

65. Envy quickly follows prosperity. Sarah had borne a child and had weaned her son. “She saw the maidservant’s son playing with her son Isaac, and said to Abraham: ‘Cast out the maidservant and her son; for the maidservant’s son shall not be heir with my son Isaac’” (ibid., 9–10). This seemed harsh to Abraham: that he should cast out his own son, though one whom he had received from a slave-woman.

Do not yourself mingle with a maidservant, lest you receive a son from her and your wife refuse to allow him to become co-heir with her son. You see that the grace of marriage is thereby dissolved. Certainly, if you have fallen into this and have a son, cast out the maidservant and her son. For it is better for the maidservant than the wife to depart, and for the maidservant’s son than the legitimate son to be cast out.

But if you hesitate, if you despise your wife’s judgment and it seems hard to you, God says to you what He said to Abraham. For what He said to him, He says to you and to all: “Let it not seem hard to you concerning the boy and the maidservant. Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice; for in Isaac shall your seed be called” (ibid., 12). Nowhere else did He say, “Listen to the voice of your wife,” except here—that is, you have injured your wife and have not soothed her feeling; you have received a son from a maidservant and have not honored your wife’s son.

Can your seed be called in the son of a maidservant? Certainly not; for true succession is in the legitimate son. But you fear, because he is your son, that perhaps when cast out he may perish or be killed. My grace will not be lacking to him. Our God nourishes all and sustains all, both righteous and unrighteous. For indeed He rains upon the righteous and the unrighteous.

As Abraham did, so do you. Cast out the maidservant, so that your wife may remain at home secure and unoffended. Cast out also the maidservant’s son, so that he may have no share in the inheritance, since he does not possess the privilege of origin.

## CHAPTER VIII

God tests Abraham in various ways, but especially by commanding him to sacrifice his son. The individual words of this command are examined, and the patriarch’s perfect obedience in his departure and the remaining preparation for the sacrifice is shown. Finally, after explaining the mystery figured in the ram offered in Isaac’s place, Abraham’s third blessing is set forth.

66. “And it came to pass after these words that God tested Abraham” (Gen. 22:1). God tests in one way, the devil in another. The devil tests in order to overthrow; God tests in order to crown. Accordingly, He tests those whom He has proved. Thus David says: “Prove me, O God, and test me” (Ps. 138:23).

God first proved holy Abraham and then tested him, lest He burden him by testing him before proving him. He proved him when He commanded him to leave Charra and found him obedient (Gen. 12, 14, 17). He proved him when, relying on the title of faith, he rescued his nephew; when he touched none of the spoil; when He promised a son to an old man and, although he was a hundred years old and considered Sarah’s generative powers dead, nevertheless believed and did not waver in faith—though he could have wavered on grounds of barrenness or old age. He proved him by the diligence of his hospitality (Gen. 18:1 ff.).

Having therefore been proved, he was considered fit, as stronger, to be tested by greater and somewhat harsher commands. By this example we are taught that a person is proved by realities, but tested by things arranged and contrived. For God did not wish a son to be sacrificed by his father, nor did He wish this service to be carried out—He who provided a sheep to be sacrificed in place of the son—but He tested the father’s affection, whether he would prefer God’s commands to his son and would not bend the force of devotion through consideration for paternal affection.

67. And He said to him: “Abraham, Abraham!” (Gen. 22:1). By repeating his name He rouses his mind, that he may be more ready. Accordingly he answered: “Here I am.” And He said: “Take your most beloved son, whom you loved, Isaac, and go into the high land; and you shall offer him to me as a whole burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I shall tell you” (ibid., 2).

He does not allow the father’s affection to remain idle. From the beginning He goads him and pricks him with the stings of affection: He adds the son’s name to the name of relationship, and the force of love. He did not consider it enough to say “son”; He adds, “most beloved, whom you loved, Isaac.”

Why does He say, “Whom you loved,” and not, “Whom you love”? We may indeed defend Scripture by divine usage, because it often employs the past for the future or the present. Thus in the Gospel you have: “This is my most beloved Son, in whom I was well pleased” (Matt. 3:17), although the Father is surely always pleased in the Son. And in the Psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand’” (Ps. 109:1), although He always sits.

Yet we may understand “most beloved” as referring to the present, and “whom you loved” as signifying that he was beloved not with some recent impulse of love, but with love long established and proven. For what increases for a time is dissolved for a time; but what has pleased for a long time, or always, cannot quickly be effaced. Nor is it absurd to think that we love those who are about to die more intensely. That is: “whom you loved before,” as though he now loved the one about to be sacrificed. [Most manuscripts and all editions read, “as though he no longer loves the one about to be sacrificed.” But Corbie, Colbert, and Mazarin manuscripts omit the negation, in the better sense, as is evident from the preceding words: “we love those who are about to die more intensely.”]

Nor did He idly add the name of holy Isaac: that is, the one whom you received from your wife as your only son; whom you received in old age; whom you received as the reward of your faith and recompense for your works; whom you received from God’s promise, not from your wife’s fertility, from which you could hope for another. “You shall offer him to me as a whole burnt offering”; but first, “Go into the high land.” A space of time is interposed, lest the affection seem suddenly precipitated, so that in that delay the grace of natural affection and the father’s longing might steal in. He added: “Upon one of the mountains which I shall tell you.” Here also for the same reason: that while the old man climbed, his impulse might be broken, his right hand wearied, his resolve fail; and while he sought to learn which mountain, he might unlearn the preparation.

68. Rising not merely on the following day but at dawn, as though the night had brought delay to the zeal of the hastening father, “he saddled his ass, took with him two servants and Isaac his son, and cut wood for the whole burnt offering” (Gen. 22:3). We are taught to bring everything prepared for sacrifice. We also learn that we ourselves should claim the preparation of sacrifice and the duty of ministry, rather than delegate them to others. Abraham was old, rich in flocks, and abundant in servants; yet he did not seek the ranks of his retinue. He himself cut the wood and did not omit offices too arduous for his strength.

69. On the third day he came to the place which God had told him of (ibid., 4). He went as the third with two others, taking his victim with him, and on the third day came to the place of sacrifice. This number is salutary and fitting for those who sacrifice. Thus Moses too later says to Pharaoh, king of Egypt: “We will go a three days’ journey and sacrifice to the Lord our God, as He has told us” (Exod. 8:27). And rightly, the sacrifice of the Trinity is celebrated on the third day.

70. “And Abraham, lifting up his eyes, saw the place from afar” (Gen. 22:4). He who hastens to fulfill the command looks about carefully. Though zeal made his aged step swift, yet, deeming this too slow, he went before with his eyes. The offices of his several limbs were vigorous, although his aged limbs could not be vigorous. The sight of old people is usually dulled, so that they do not easily discern even nearby things. But this man not only saw the place: he perceived it while still far away.

71. Nor did he hesitate when he saw it, but said to his servants: “Stay here with the ass. I and the boy will go on as far as that place; and when we have worshipped, we shall return to you” (ibid., 5). The ass is fittingly a type, because the reality is in the colt of an ass. In this animal is figured the people of the Gentiles, formerly subjected to a burden, now subject to Christ. Isaac, therefore, is a type of Christ who was to suffer. He came upon an ass, signifying the people of the nations who would believe. Therefore too, when the Lord came to undergo the Passion for us, He loosed the colt of an ass, upon which He Himself sat, gentle and meek, now offering its back to Christ in faith. [All editions read: “which He himself mounted, already gentle and meek, believing Christ upon its back.” The Theodorian and Valencian manuscripts add, with variations in place of “believing”: “yielding, he sat down”; the former reads “he made [it] offer [its back].” The Longobard manuscript agrees with the latter in this and supports our reading in the remaining particulars.]

But when he says, “I and the boy will go on,” he shows either that the father would not fail in so great a preparation, nor the son yield, or that they would pass through the severity of so great a deed by the remedy of devotion. He added: “We shall return to you.” He prophesied what he did not know. He himself intended to return alone after sacrificing his son; but the Lord spoke through his mouth what He had prepared. He spoke cautiously to the servants, lest, if the matter became known, someone should hinder him or interrupt him with groaning or tears. [“Cautiously,” as the gloss on the *Decretum* notes, means prudently, so that Ambrose may not seem to teach that Abraham spoke feignedly or falsely. Some claimed that Ambrose’s words meant only that the holy patriarch lied by speaking contrary to his thought for the purpose of dissembling, but prophesied insofar as he uttered truth unknowingly. Melchior Cano, *De locis theologicis*, II.4, endorses this. Yet this need not detract from Abraham’s piety, since the common opinion of the ancient Fathers, nearly down to Augustine’s time, was that lying for some good or duty was not sinful. Augustine thoroughly overthrew this opinion, and all later writers followed him. Nevertheless, it is quite plausible that Ambrose did not hold the former opinion: Augustine, Epistle 82, sufficiently indicates this; and Ambrose himself condemns every kind of dissimulation and falsehood in Book VII on Luke 12, Book III of *On Duties*, chapter 9, and elsewhere. Hence St Thomas, *Summa theologiae* II–II, q. 111, art. 1, teaches that Ambrose recognizes here mystery and prophecy, not falsehood or dissimulation.]

72. “He took the wood for the whole burnt offering and laid it upon Isaac his son; and he himself took fire and a sword in his hand” (Gen. 22:6). The victim is consecrated by sacred ministries and commended as the future victim of piety; beforehand it is borne in the ministry of a pious father. [The Theodorian and Valencian manuscripts read “mysteries,” and: “the future victim of piety is commended by the bearing of the pious father’s prior ministry.”] Isaac carried the wood for himself; Christ carried for Himself the gibbet of the cross. Abraham accompanied his son; the Father accompanied Christ. Neither was Isaac alone, nor Jesus alone. Thus He says: “You will leave me alone; and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32).

73. Isaac said to Abraham his father, “Father.” He answered, “What do you wish, son?” (Gen. 22:7). The father’s affection is struck by terms of affection and battered, as it were, by waves from one side and the other. The son calls him “father”; the father says, “son,” so that the father may recognize himself in the very sound of the words. How impossible it is that he could strike the one to whose wound he would wish to submit himself! Such names commonly work the grace of life, not the service of death; such words commonly incite to affection, not to death.

74. Isaac added: “Behold the wood; where is the sheep for the whole burnt offering?” (ibid.). Here too he prophesies in speech, not in knowledge. For a sheep was being prepared by the Lord for sacrifice. Abraham similarly answered: “God will provide for Himself a sheep for the whole burnt offering, my son” (ibid.). The minister, unyielding in the zeal of devotion, is not afraid frequently to call him “son,” so firmly was he grounded in steadfastness of purpose. He believed himself a better father in this, and judged that his son would remain his forever in this, if he sacrificed him to God.

He prophesied not only what immediately occurred, namely that God provided a victim in place of Isaac and restored the son to his father; but more especially that this victim was not the one of God’s disposition, but that there would be another victim which God would prepare for Himself, in order to cleanse the world. That victim would be more acceptable to all; for its sake many fathers would offer their sons and would not fear to be separated from their children in this world. Every day fathers offer their sons, that they may die in Christ and be buried with the Lord. How many fathers, when their sons had been slain in martyrdom, returned more joyful from their tomb!

75. Abraham came to the place predestined for sacrifice: “And he built an altar there and laid on the wood” (ibid., 9). How many preparations by one about to sacrifice, lest he be thought suddenly seized with the impulse to sacrifice! “And having bound the hands and feet of his son Isaac, he laid him upon the altar, over the wood” (ibid.). The father fastens bonds upon the son with his own hands, lest the son, by fleeing or by being driven by the force of fire, incur sin.

76. The angel said, “Abraham, Abraham!” (ibid., 11). The divine voice in some manner held back his hand and intercepted the blow of his brandished right hand. It did not call only once, lest he either not hear fully or suppose it an accidental sound. Thus it recalled him as it had commanded him. It repeated the voice, as though fearing that he might be anticipated by the zeal of devotion and that one utterance could not recall the impulse of the striker.

“Do not lay your hand upon the boy,” it says, “nor do anything to him; for now I know that you fear your God and have not spared your most beloved son for my sake” (ibid., 12; 2–2, q. 2, c. *Si quaelibet*, § *Non enim*). This means: “I sought your disposition; I did not demand the deed. I tested your mind, whether you would not spare even your most beloved son for my sake. I do not take away what I myself gave, nor do I begrudge the heir whom I granted to one who had none.” Nor is it idly that here again He calls him “most beloved son,” so as to show that the earlier phrase, “whom you loved,” was so spoken that you should not suppose Abraham had ceased to love him.

77. “And Abraham looked up and saw; and behold, one ram caught in a thicket” (ibid., 13). [The Roman edition reads: “And Abraham, lifting up his eyes, saw, and behold, one ram suspended by its horns in the thicket Sabec.”] Why a ram? Surely because it is preeminent over the rest of the flock. Why suspended? So that you might perceive that this victim was not earthly. Why suspended by its horns, except because it would lift its flesh from earth by a higher power? As it is written: “Whose government is upon his shoulders” (Isa. 9:6). Whom indeed does this signify but Him of whom it is written: “He has exalted the horn of his people” (Ps. 148:14)? Our horn is Christ, who surpassed all, as we read: “Beautiful in form beyond the children of men” (Ps. 44:3). He alone was lifted up and exalted from the earth, as He Himself teaches us when He says: “I am not of this world; I am from above” (John 8:23). Abraham saw Him in this sacrifice; he beheld His Passion. Therefore the Lord Himself says of him: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” (ibid., 56).

78. Hence Scripture says: “Abraham called the name of that place, ‘The Lord sees,’ so that they say today, ‘Upon the mountain the Lord appeared’” (Gen. 22:14). That is, He appeared to Abraham, revealing the future Passion of His body by which He redeemed the world, and also showing the manner of the Passion when He displayed the victim suspended. [Older editions read “he showed the ram”; the Roman edition, “the ram suspended by its horns.” Neither occurs in the manuscripts or is necessary, since the preceding discussion makes the point sufficiently clear. The Theodorian and Valencian manuscripts read: “he showed the thicket,” that is, that thicket, etc.]

That thicket is the gibbet of the cross. Upon this wood the most excellent leader of the flock, exalted, drew all things to Himself, that He might be known by all. Hence He Himself says: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he” (John 8:28). By this too Abraham merited God’s favor.

79. Finally, this is the third blessing. For he received three complete blessings: one after the victory in which he rescued his nephew, when Melchizedek met him and the Lord said to him: “Look up to heaven and count the stars, if you can; so shall your seed be.” And Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gen. 15:5–6). Another came when Abraham was commanded to be called by that name (Gen. 17:5), and received the seal of circumcision. The third came here, when he did not hesitate to offer his most beloved son to God as a whole burnt offering.

This blessing again surpassed the preceding ones. In those God promised that Abraham’s seed would be multiplied; but in this He says: “And in your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice” (Gen. 22:18). [All manuscripts and the Roman edition read “all nations of the earth”; all older editions read “all kings of the earth.”] Therefore let us also hear the voice of our God and obey His commands, if we wish to find favor with Him.

## CHAPTER IX

Sarah dies and is buried. Abraham provides a wife for his son, and for this purpose binds his chosen servant by oath. What mystery lies hidden here? In choosing a wife, her religion, upon which conduct depends, must above all be considered. How should a woman of one’s own people be sought, not a foreigner and not one unwilling? In what manner are the Church and baptism signified in Rebecca? What earrings ought Christian virgins to seek after Rebecca’s example, and what do the other gifts offered to the girl signify? What an example of modesty she gave that should be imitated; and how aptly her marriage expresses the calling of the Church and the apostolic ministry.

80. The passage which follows contains the wife’s death, the husband’s mourning, and the duty of burial, by which marital affection is proved. “And Abraham rose,” it says, “from the dead woman” (Gen. 23:3). We are taught not to cling too long to the dead, but to render as much duty as is sufficient. He hastened to pay the price for a burial-place, though it was offered freely, so that we may build the tombs of parents or relatives not in others’ places but rather in our own. [Some manuscripts read: “He hastens to pay the price for the bier,” etc.] For, when possessions are alienated, burial plots in those same places are often sold. Abraham did this because such temples of God did not yet exist, in which the remains of the faithful are laid to rest in the Lord.

81. Abraham had grown old. Therefore, as befits a good father, he ought to provide a wife for his son. But because of God’s oracle he could not return to the place from which he had been commanded to depart. He lived in the land of the Canaanites, from whose stock he avoided seeking a lawful succession for himself.

82. “And he called the eldest servant of his household” (Gen. 24:2) and told him to go to Charran and seek, from among his kinsfolk, a wife for his younger master. Learn from this that even servants of advanced age are called *boys* (*pueri*) by their masters or by anyone of higher rank. Hence a certain poet thought that this usage should be followed—whether he found it among those who consider themselves learned and wise, or transferred it from our own usage, or found it already transferred:

> “Feed the cattle as before, boys; yoke the bulls.”  
> (*Virgil, Eclogue* I)

Thus we too say *boys* when we mean servants, expressing not their age but their condition.

83. Observe now the virtues of a good householder, and consider first what charge he gives and to whom he gives it. You too should train your servants so that they show paternal affection toward your children and discharge their duties. Among the servants there was found an elder, yet one chosen to provide a wife for his younger master. He was bound by oath to place his hand under his master’s thigh.

By the thigh we understand generation; and the generation of Abraham is Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “The promises were made to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as of many, but as of one: ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16). By Christ Himself the Apostle shows that the holy sacrament and secure aid will be ours.

84. Abraham bound him not to bring a wife for his master from the seed of the Canaanites, whose ancestral founder had not honored his father and therefore transmitted to his descendants the inheritance of a curse. Thus we recognize that faith, and a certain inheritance from ancestral stock, must be sought in those whom we wish to join to ourselves. “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverted.” If this is true in other relationships, how much more in marriage, where there is one flesh and one spirit? How can love agree if faith differs?

Therefore beware, Christian, of giving your daughter to a Gentile or a Jew (28, q. 1, c. *Cave*). Beware, I say, of seeking for yourself a Gentile, a Jewess, or a foreign woman—that is, a heretical wife, or any wife foreign to your faith. The first fidelity of marriage is the grace of chastity. If she worships idols whose adulteries are proclaimed, if she denies Christ, who is the teacher and rewarder of chastity, how can she love chastity?

If she is Christian, it is not enough unless both of you have been initiated by the sacrament of baptism. You must rise together by night for prayer, and God must be entreated by your united prayers. Another distinguished mark of chastity is to believe that the marriage you have obtained was given to you by your God. Thus Solomon says: “A wife will be prepared for a man by God” (Prov. 19:14). Those unequal in faith cannot believe this: that she should think the grace of marriage bestowed upon her by Him whom she does not worship.

Reason teaches this, but examples warn more strongly. Womanly allurements have often deceived even stronger husbands and caused them to depart from religion (1 Kings 11:4). Therefore either provide for love or avoid error. Religion, then, is the first thing sought in marriage. For this reason Abraham sought a kinswoman to give to his son.

85. You too seek a kinswoman. Who is a neighbor? “The one who showed mercy,” He says. The Lord Jesus said this in the Gospel. And you, seek one near to Abraham’s seed, and a kinswoman of your neighbor (Luke 10:37). Christ is Abraham’s seed; He is the neighbor of all, who showed mercy toward all by taking away the sin of the world. Learn next what is to be sought in a wife: Abraham sought not gold, not silver, not possessions, but the grace of a good disposition.

86. Then, when asked whether, if the woman were unwilling to come, he should take his master’s son there, Abraham said: “Take heed lest you bring my son back there. The Lord, God of heaven and God of earth, took me from my father’s house and from the land in which I was born; He spoke to me and swore, saying: ‘To you I will give this land, and to your seed.’ He will send His angel before you, and you shall obtain a wife for my son from there. But if the woman is unwilling to come with you into this land, you shall be free from this oath” (Gen. 24:6 ff.).

Consider more carefully what this teaches. You are not permitted to take a foreign woman. Certainly, if she becomes a Christian, you will have praise through her. The passage instructs you, however, lest, if she refuses to become Christian, your eagerness for marriage should turn you away from the faith. Abraham advised that the woman who followed should be led away, not sought while remaining where she lived, and that his son should not go there.

He also said, as it were prophetically in his son’s case, and taught as a moral instructor, that the mercy of his Lord—who had led him away from residence in the land where he lived—would not fail, but would go before the seeker’s effort and incline the girl’s mind. Thus he taught that one seeking the increase of faith should hope that the Lord will deign to help.

87. And the servant rose and set out for Mesopotamia (ibid., 10); and, in accordance with the tenor of the vow which the servant had made on setting out, Rebekah met him, carrying a water-jar on her shoulder—a virgin exceedingly beautiful, whom no man had known. She went down to the spring, filled the jar, gave the servant drink, and watered all his camels (ibid., 15 ff.). Therefore Abraham’s servant took golden earrings, each of one drachma, and gave into her hands two bracelets, weighing ten gold pieces; and he asked her whether there was room for lodging, and whose daughter she was. The moral simplicity is indeed expressed: [Col. 0452B] there was no place for ambition even in seeking a marriage, but the Lord, the president over marriage, fulfilled the marriage suit. Yet it is possible to discern the mysteries of the Church. Where is the Church found except in Mesopotamia? There she is sought; from there she is summoned; there she is surrounded by two rivers—the washing of grace and the tears of repentance. For unless you have wept for your own sins, unless you have received the grace of baptism, the faith of the Church is not acquired for you, and a certain marital union.

> [Note: Four manuscripts: “They fortify her with a certain marital union,” etc. From these, however, Valc. prefers, “they fortify [her] with … abundance,” etc.]

The Tigris—that is, prudence—and the Euphrates—that is, justice and fruitful illumination—fortify her, separating her from barbarian nations.

88. She is a virgin exceedingly beautiful, whose beauty no age has corrupted. Exceedingly beautiful, because he also is beautiful beyond the children of men who acquired her for himself. [Col. 0452C] “Whom no man had known”: for she had union with no man,

> [Note: All editions: “the right of union.” All manuscripts: “his union.” Yet in the Corbie manuscript it is written so that either reading can almost equally be read.]

but was owed to Christ alone. She carried a water-jar upon her shoulder, with which she washes human actions. And because she consists of the gathering of the Gentiles, whom she washed, therefore you read that she went down to the spring, filled the jar, and came up again (ibid., 16). That Samaritan woman came to the spring, as is written in the Gospel (John 4:7), but she did not go down: it seemed to her to be a well, nor did she fill the jar. Finally, she says:

> [Note: The Roman edition alone: “The woman left the water-jar.” “She left [it]; therefore she did not have that by which [to wash] her actions,” etc. Yet it is evident that the holy author is not referring to those words of Scripture, “Therefore she left the water-jar,” etc., but rather to these: “Lord, you have nothing with which to draw.” He appears, however, to have read in their place, “Lord, I have nothing with which to draw.” This is found in no biblical text.]

“I have no water-jar.” She had nothing by which to wash her actions. This woman alone went down; this woman alone knew the true spring—that is, not a spring of water, but of eternal life—as David said: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10 [36:9]). Therefore she had something to give to those who thirsted, because she believed. For she who did not believe [Col. 0452D] said to this spring, which wished to give her a drink:

> [Note: The Corbie, Longpont, Colbert, Mazarin, and first-hand Tornacensis manuscripts: “which wished to give her a drink of living water. But this woman, etc.” Perhaps this is not bad, if after “living water” we mentally supply what is expressed above, namely, “I have no water-jar”; this certainly accords better with what follows.]

“Where have you [the means] to give me living water?” (John 4:11). But this woman had that with which to water not only the servant but also the camels—she who is accustomed not only to refresh the just, but also to fill the unjust. Therefore she received golden earrings and the bracelets

> [Note: *Viriae* means the same as rings or bracelets, as may be gathered from what follows.]

which Abraham sent, [Col. 0453A] as rewards for her merits.

89. Perhaps, on hearing these things, you daughters who strive after the Lord’s grace may yourselves be stirred to desire earrings and bracelets, and may say: “How can you forbid this, Bishop, that we should possess what Rebekah received as a gift, while exhorting us to be like Rebekah?” But Rebekah did not possess these earrings and bracelets, which commonly sow disputes in the Church and frequently slip off. She had other earrings—would that you possessed them—and other bracelets. Rebekah’s earrings are the marks of devout hearing, and Rebekah’s bracelets are the ornaments of deeds. She possessed earrings which did not burden the ear but delighted it; bracelets which did not weigh the hand down with material gold, but raised it by spiritual action. Therefore this adornment pleased both her brother and her parents. And [Col. 0453B] do you take the earrings which Abraham left you; take the bracelets which he transmitted. Hear the words of the Lord your God as he himself heard them; carry out the commands as he hastened

> [Note: After the word “carry out,” the Roman edition intrudes the following: “For he said, and set bread before them to eat, he who said: ‘I will not eat until I have spoken my words.’”]

to carry them out.

90. This is a most beautiful passage for instructing those to whom some duty is assigned: Abraham’s servant did not first eat the bread set before him until he had carried out the Lord’s command. When this had been obtained, he gave Rebekah gold and silver vessels and clothing. Where the Church was betrothed, she received golden and silver vessels in which the treasure of faith might be kept; for there are vessels for honour and vessels for dishonour. Hear what these vessels are: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7). The earthen vessels are our bodies; our faith is the treasure. And perhaps now even our bodies themselves, [Col. 0453C] which contain this treasure, are golden because they are full of prudence; and they are silver vessels because they seem to shine with the utterances of the heavenly command. Parents too are honoured with gifts (32, q. 2, c. *Honorantur*).

91. The maiden is not consulted about the betrothal, for in that matter she awaits her parents’ judgment: it is not consistent with virginal modesty to choose a husband. But once she has been betrothed to the man, she is consulted about the day of departure. Nor did she improperly delay; for she ought rightly to have hastened to her husband. Hence it is clear whence comes that saying of Euripides which many admire. For he says in the person of a woman who nevertheless wished to leave her husband and was being sought for another marriage:

> Νυμφευμάτων μὲν τῶν ἐμῶν πατὴρ ἐμὸς  
> Μέριμναν ἕξει, κ` οὐκ ἐμὸν κρίνειν τάδε.  
> *(Euripides, Andromache.)*

That is: “My father will take responsibility for my marriage arrangements; this is not for me to decide.” Therefore, virgins, preserve what even the philosophers themselves have admired. But also,

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions instead read: “but a woman also, who …” And after three words, where those same editions, together with the principal manuscripts, read, “fears to fall into the snare of her weakness,” three manuscripts read, “fears to cast herself into [the snare] for her weakness.”]

if any woman, having quickly lost her husband while still young, fears to fall into the snare of her weakness, then, if she wishes to marry, let her marry only in the Lord, and leave the choice of her husband to her parents; lest she be judged to be pursuing desire too boldly if she claims for herself the choice concerning her own marriage. She ought rather to appear sought by a man than to have sought a man herself. Let her show modesty before she marries, since modesty itself makes marriage more commendable. But they imitate the words; they cannot imitate the deeds.

92. It is also clear that a splendid mystery of the Church is contained in this: no one dared to call her before Christ. For the prerogative of calling the nations was reserved for Christ alone. But once called, she made no delay and therefore was more acceptable to the Lord; because the Jewish people, which had been invited to the banquet, was not worthy to come, whereas the assembly of the Gentiles, as soon as it saw itself summoned, hastened forth.

93. Finally, that you may know that it is not without mystery that, while riding a camel, she came to the bridegroom: it signifies that the people of the nations, rough with a certain beastlike ugliness of merits and possessing no beauty of their own form, were to receive the faith and consent of the Church. Nor is this without significance (30, q. 5, c. *Nec illud*): when Rebekah came, she saw Isaac walking; and when she had asked who he was and learned that he was the one to whom she was to be given as wife, she descended and began to veil her head, teaching that modesty [Col. 0454C] ought to precede marriage. Hence also marriage is called *nuptiae*, because, for modesty’s sake, maidens veil themselves. Learn, then, virgins, how you should preserve modesty and not go out before strangers with uncovered heads, when Rebekah, already betrothed, did not think that she ought to look upon her appointed husband with uncovered head.

94. Who is that servant who arranged this marriage? Surely one of the Apostles, and especially the one who says: “Men and brethren, you know that from ancient days God chose among us that the nations should hear from my mouth the word of the Gospel” (Acts 15:7). Or he who was called the teacher of the nations (1 Tim. 2:7). For when they—or John the Evangelist—are read, they gain a soul for Christ;

> [Note: The old edition reads: “when they are read, says John the Evangelist, they gain a soul for Christ.” But when the Roman editors saw that no satisfactory sense could be extracted from this, they emended the passage into this form: “When they are heard, they gain a soul for Christ … and, for those who desire to see Christ, as John the Evangelist says, [they show him] by their words,” etc. Our reading, however, is preferred by the manuscripts with great agreement.]

so that she who previously did not believe may believe; and by their words they show Christ to those who desire to see him. Thus [Col. 0454D] Abraham, after celebrating his son’s marriage, completed his days in advanced age and a good old age (Gen. 25:8).

313

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0455]

# CHAPTER ONE

After expounding the moral sense, he passes to a deeper, or allegorical, interpretation; and explains how the soul is commanded to leave its own land and its kindred, and also from what things it must withdraw in order to attain complete purification. Finally, he relates the posterity promised to Abraham.

[Col. 0455A]

1. We have pursued the moral subject with such simplicity of understanding as we could, so that those who read may draw from it instruction in conduct. But because the blade of the sword is sharp and fit for battle on either side, so also the word of God, which is sharper than every sharpest sword and pierces even to the division of soul: wherever you turn it, you will find it ready and suitable to pass through the reader’s soul [Col. 0455B] and reveal the enigmas of the prophetic Scriptures. Therefore I do not think it unfitting to raise the meaning to higher things, and through the history of different persons to unfold a certain progress in the forms of virtue—especially since in Adam we have already tasted the beginnings of a deeper understanding (*On Paradise*, ch. 2). For we said that Adam signifies the mind, Eve the sense-perception, and the serpent’s appearance the pleasure of delight. But there, from the height of blessedness and a certain natural charm of the virtues, through the entrapment of sense-perception and the allurement of pleasure,

> [Note: Roman edition: “through the entrapment of sense-perception.”]

there was a turning back into sin.

> [Note: Two manuscripts: “there was a turning aside into sin.”]

Here, however, the mind’s advance may be contemplated. For the Lawgiver wisely did this: just as he showed the fall of the mind, so that we might avoid those paths of error, so too he signified the mind’s progress and [Col. 0455C] a certain higher return, so that we might know how a mind that has been broken may restore itself. For the Lord had purified the earth by the outpouring of the flood and washed away the foulness of human frailty; but this was not enough for the advancement of virtue unless humanity were instructed how to direct and govern itself. Abraham is introduced as representing the mind. Finally,

> [Note: Ambrose seems to have derived Abraham’s name from the word *Abran*, by which “passage” is signified; or, rather, to have referred to ch. 14, no. 13, where, according to the Septuagint, Abraham is called “the passer-over.” See Nobilius on the same passage.]

Abraham is called “passage.” Therefore, so that the mind which in Adam had wholly given itself over to bodily delight and allurements might pass into the form and appearance of virtue, a wise man is set before us for imitation. Finally, according to the Hebrews Abraham is called “father,” and likewise in Latin, because the mind, with a kind of paternal [Col. 0456A] authority,

> [Note: *Censione*: that is, judgment and restraint.]

oversight, and care, governs the whole human being.

2. This mind, then, was in Haran—that is, “in caverns”—subject to various passions. Therefore it is said to it: “Go out from your land” (Gen. 12:1), that is, from your body. He went out from this land whose citizenship is in heaven. “And from your kindred,” he says. The bodily senses are kindred to our soul. For our soul is divided into two: that which is rational and that which is irrational. The senses belong to the irrational part; therefore they are kindred to the rational part, that is, to the mind. “And go out from your house,” he says. The house of the mind is its extended (*prolativum*) word.

> [Note: All editions: “the word has been brought forth.” All Gallican manuscripts: “the word is extended forth.” But *prolativum* means the same as extensive. For the word “house” is extended from its simple signification to a figurative and metaphorical one.]

For as the master of a household dwells in his own house and has authority over how he governs his [Col. 0456B] house, so the mind dwells in our words and governs our speech; its power and discipline shine forth in discourse. As a good master of a household is judged from the very entrance of his house, so our mind is assessed from our words. Finally, it also strikes and recalls by the modulations of the voice.

> [Note: The edition reads, “it strikes and recalls the modulation of the voice.” The same manuscripts read, “by the modulations of the voice,” where one should understand the passions, the body, and the bodily senses mentioned above; everyone knows by experience that these are aroused and calmed by vocal modulations.]

3. Therefore, whoever wishes to attain complete purification must separate himself from these three things: the body, bodily senses, and voice. In these lie all the body’s passions and the deceits of sense-perception by which we are deceived and mocked. For in none of these three is there any good: not in flesh, although the school of Epicurus—and many devotees of pleasure as well—burst with praises of bodily pleasure;

> [Note: Am., Er., and Gill.: “the delight of praising the body.” The Roman edition omits the word “praise.” We judged that the authority of all the manuscripts should be followed.]

not in the senses, which are often deceived; nor in the sound of the voice, which often soothes [Col. 0456C] the soul with false songs.

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts cited above, except the Corbie manuscript, in which “songs” was absent but was added by a later hand. The editions read: “soothes [the soul] with songs; this is the perfect, incorruptible good.” The reading is plainly defective.]

These things are corruptible; but what is truly good is incorruptible. The proof is plain. When a human being dies, the flesh decays, the senses perish, the voice is lost; the immortal mind remains and receives an incorporeal life. Therefore it is called into another land, full of blessedness, where it may behold the living substance of things, not false things in place of true, as in this life; for, having shaken off the murky image of body, senses, and voice, it lays aside corruptible darkness and, with unveiled face, surveys the grace of blessed life.

4. “I will bless you,” he says, “and make you into a great nation” [Col. 0457A] (Gen. 12:2). By promising a race, he promises immortality. For a species seems immortal, while the individual members are mortal—as with human beings, horses, and bees. Of these a poet says:

> “But the race remains immortal.”  
> *(Virgil, Georgics IV.)*

Yet far better is the fact that he called the great nation the Church’s everlasting posterity and that heavenly generation which is truly great,

> [Note: Thus the Corbie, Longpont, Colbert, and Mazarin manuscripts. But Valc. and the Am. and Gill. editions read, “that we may die to sin, therefore be reborn.” Er.: “that we may die to sin and be reborn to God.” Finally, the Roman edition and the Tornacensis manuscript read, “Therefore let us die to sin and be reborn to God.” Yet something appears here to have been omitted, corrupted, or perhaps transposed. Compare what he says here about the immortality of the race with the final chapter of this same book, and you will notice no small connection.]

that we may die to sin and be reborn to God.

315

# CHAPTER TWO

After Abraham’s departure, God speaks to him as to a friend. He too is proposed for our imitation, so that our mind may be reformed according to his example. Why Lot went out with him; what is signified by the seventy-fifth year; and how the wise person possesses his own soul.

[Col. 0457B]

5. Abraham went out as the Lord had spoken to him (Gen. 12:4). From this, the Gentiles derive the saying of the Seven Sages, “Follow God,” as though it were their own discovery; although not merely Abraham, but Moses—through whom the Law was given—was far earlier, saying: “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (Deut. 13:4). Abraham therefore went out: in this was manifested not so much his perfection

> [Note: The Corbie manuscript and three others, with the Er. and Gill. editions, read “progress”; Am., “advancement”; the Longpont and Mazarin manuscripts and the Roman edition, “perfection.” But we may suppose that this variation arose solely from an abbreviation of the first syllable, interpreted in different ways by different readers.]

as the devotion of his soul and the freedom of his mind. He went out from the bonds of the body and the allurements of pleasure. Thus you have it: “Abraham went out as God had spoken to him.” Above you have that God said, “Go out,” in which the explicit command of one giving orders is expressed; here you have, “as God had spoken to him.” [Col. 0457C] A certain affection of conversation is, as it were, implied; for he did everything that had been ordained. Before the deed, therefore, God speaks as to one subject to command; after the deed, he speaks as to a friend. For he is God’s friend who does what has been commanded. Hence the Lord Jesus also says in his Gospel: “You are my friends if you do what I command you. I no longer call you servants” (John 15:14–15). But, as I said, the development of the wise man is set before us for imitation, written as an example, not as perfection. For in Abraham the mind which fell in the first human being is still being re-formed. Therefore it gathers itself by steps and advances.

6. Hence he also added: “And Lot went out with him” (Gen. 12:4), that is, “turning aside.” For this is what the interpretation of the name signifies. As travellers entering upon an unfamiliar [Col. 0457D] road are often misled by certain paths and turn aside from the straight way, yet, if they are prudent, do not go astray but, though hesitant, discern the road by observing [Col. 0458A] the country itself, so Abraham too was indeed wavering,

> [Note: The Corbie, Colbert, and Mazarin manuscripts: “changing.”]

yet followed the path of truth. He was often led by a false appearance of goods, but was not altogether inclined away. It belongs to the perfect not to turn aside; to the prudent, not to turn aside completely. Yet he alone never turns aside of whom it is written: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel. He shall eat butter and honey, before he knows or utters evil, choosing the good; for before the child knows good or evil, he will not believe wickedness, so as to choose what is good” (Isa. 7:14). Abraham could not do this, so as to choose good before knowing evil. But he clung to the heavenly commandments lest he should turn aside from truth (Gen. 12:4). Therefore he is also described as having gone out from Haran at seventy-five years of age, because, when the perfect number of seventy is combined with the five that signify the senses, the sense is capable of being bent.

> [Note: The passage is obscure and perhaps corrupt. Yet some light may be shed upon it by Philo, *On the Migration of Abraham*, where he teaches that the perfection symbolized by seventy is bent and weakened by the number five, which signifies the bodily senses.]

316 For the pleasures of these senses cause our mind not always to stand upright, but at times to bend itself, hiding not in the caverns of the body but in the lurking-places of pleasure.

7. Yet, even placed among these burrows, he escaped in such a way that he took his wife, his nephew, and every soul that he had possessed in Haran. For the prudent and self-controlled are possessors of virtue and of the soul, choosing the beauty of gentle character. But lovers of the body are ensnared in its pleasures, because every excellence belonging to irrational things lies in the body’s constitution, while the excellence of rational beings lies in the virtues and disciplines of the soul. Therefore it is written (ibid., 5) that he possessed his soul,

> [Note: Since this is nowhere found in Scripture, it is probable that Saint Ambrose alluded to Genesis 12:5, where from the preceding discussion we understand that he read, “and every soul that he possessed.”]

governing it as free and subject to no slavery. This, then, is the teacher’s purpose: although situated in those byways and winding paths, whether at a younger stage of life, or before attaining fuller discipline, or dwelling in a place open to vices,

> [Note: The edition reads, “a place open to vices, he was not so bent,” etc. Better: the manuscripts read, “or [a place] open,” etc.]

he was not so bent toward sin that he could not migrate. Thus he defended and transferred his mind from that slippery possession.

# CHAPTER THREE

Abraham travels as far as Shechem, a word denoting exercise. There he sees God, whom he could not see while he was a Chaldean. He builds an altar to him but does not sacrifice; why this is so. Yet, after building an altar again, he invokes the Lord’s name.

[Col. 0458D]

8. “And Abraham travelled through,” he says, “as far as the place Shechem, to the tall oak” (Gen. 12:6). Do these details not seem superfluous, unless you seek their reason, when he did not even omit the oak’s height? But where there is reason, nothing is superfluous. For Shechem signifies either “shoulder” or “neck,” an indication of labour and exercise. Hence Jacob, a man of disciplined effort, gave it as a special possession to his son Joseph. Therefore, because exercise itself cannot confer perfection without the endowment of nature, and natural grace fails if exercise is lacking—for diligence is the aid of natural talent—the man whose imitation forms you is introduced as having exercise joined to natural grace. Thus, made more firmly grounded and more elevated, he passed as far as the tall oak. As the tree’s height, so also its strength, indicates that the soul of holy Abraham was not easily bent by the storms of this world, but [Col. 0459B] remained lofty, so as to raise itself from earthly inquiries to the height of divine knowledge.

> [Note: Thus six manuscripts. All editions: “so as to raise itself to eternal [things].”]

9. Then immediately God appeared to him (Gen. 12:7). Nowhere above do you find that God had been seen by him. Hence it is clear that this must be referred to the fact that, as long as he was a Chaldean—that is, not only in country but also in the opinion of the Chaldeans—he could not see God, because he sought him within the world. For the Chaldeans call the higher world God, and also assert that earthly things are borne and controlled by the revolutions of the stars and by the dwelling of the planets.

> [Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “by the motion of wandering stars and by the course of fixed stars.” This reading may readily be thought to have been fashioned from these words of Philo, *On Abraham*: “According to the revolutions of the sun and moon and the other wandering and fixed [stars] … they supposed that the world itself was God.” Yet, though we do not deny that Ambrose looked to that passage, we cannot depart from all the manuscripts and printed texts. Four manuscripts of the best quality read, “and by the dwelling of the planets”; others, together with the old editions, read, “… by the dwelling of the planets.” In so difficult a place it seemed necessary to adhere to these readings, especially since a common scribal error is quite likely: the holy Doctor may originally have written in Greek characters, στοιχείων δρόμῳ, “by the course of the elements,” that is, of the planets. The learned Du Cange teaches in his *Glossary of Medieval Latin*, under *elementum*, that στοιχεῖον may denote the sun and moon; nor is it perhaps absurd to use the same word for the remaining planets, so that the meaning may be as clear as *elementum*, a term which, as Du Cange shows, likewise denotes these planets. But if one wishes to retain the word “dwelling” or “by dwelling,” this too is possible without changing the sense, since “the houses of the planets” is a familiar astrological expression. Compare this passage with *Hexaemeron*, book I, chapter 4.]

Hence they called the stars gods, believing that they exercised a certain heavenly lordship, because there is a certain sympathy between the stars and earthly things. But they ought to have judged that what suffers with another cannot have sovereign right or dominion, as though it were God, over those whose suffering it shares, since it too is mortal and corruptible. The world also, being made, is certainly not itself God but his maker and creator. Therefore the mind, so long as it is bent by Chaldean errors, does not see God: it seeks him in visible things, not in invisible things.

> [Note: Thus four manuscripts of better quality. Others and the editions: “whom they suppose to be in visible things, not invisible things.”]

But visible things are temporal, while invisible things are eternal. God, however, is not temporal; therefore he is not seen. Thus the mind which follows the Chaldeans’ teaching does not see God. Hence Abraham at first did not see him. How could he see him when he believed another being above him? But when he migrated, not to another region but to the true religion prepared for humility—for this is what [Col. 0460A] Canaan signifies—then he began to see God and to know him as the God by whose invisible power he perceived that all things are ruled and governed. Scripture therefore teaches that Abraham saw God when he departed from the observation of the stars.

10. A confirming testimony is added (Gen. 12:7): in that place he built an altar to the Lord who had appeared to him. For this strong impression and manifest faith in truth were stamped upon his soul. Memory is available to the grateful person; forgetfulness steals over the ungrateful. The former cling to those by whom they are helped; from the latter all that is bestowed slips away. But he set up an altar and did not sacrifice. This might cause perplexity, unless you remembered that the sequence of Scripture preserves the progress of this mind. Therefore he waited to learn from God the manner of sacrifice. For he perceived that the sacrifice of an irrational animal, a mute beast, did not seem a victim worthy of divine worship. He had not yet recognized in Isaac the type of the coming passion; Melchizedek had not yet given him the grace of blessing, so that he might know these things.

11. “He departed from there,” he says, “to the mountain, east of Bethel” (ibid., 8). The mountain’s height signifies an increase in devotion; its ascent is an indication of fuller progress. It was eastward because he prophesied that the Sun of righteousness would come, that Wisdom would there prepare herself a house, and from there would predestine its own rising through a virgin. He therefore wished now to receive the light of mysteries to be known. For as the world is illumined by the sun, so the whole mind is illumined by the brightness of wisdom. He rightly located Bethlehem eastward.

> [Note: All editions read “Bethel”; but the manuscripts here and in what follows invariably have “Bethlehem,” a word which Ambrose appears to derive from Bethel.]

[Col. 0460C] For Bethlehem is called the house of God, in which Christ was born. Hence God says through the prophet: “And you, Bethlehem, are not least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who shall govern my people” (Mic. 5:2). He did not say “east of Bethlehem,” but called the tabernacle itself Bethlehem. For the Church of the just is a tabernacle. Who would not marvel at the mysteries there—that Bethlehem is beside the sea of Galilee in the East? For either the soul that deserves to be called God’s temple, or the Church, is struck by the waves of worldly cares but not overthrown; it is battered but not shaken, being able easily to restrain and calm the commotions of the waves and the uprisings of bodily passions. It watches others’ shipwrecks, itself free and exempt from danger, always ready for Christ to shine upon it [Col. 0461A] and, by his illumination, to gain joy for itself. For as eyes are nourished by the first light of day, so our mind too is nourished by discoveries of wisdom and seems to shine with certain of its rays. The visible rays of the sun warm the earth; invisible rays penetrate the inner recesses of our heart.

12. Again he built an altar and invoked the Lord’s name (Gen. 12:8). In the invocation of the Lord he signified the progress of faith. He added this to what had preceded.

# CHAPTER FOUR

Having stayed in the desert, which prefigures the tranquillity of the mind, Abraham went down to Egypt, which is temptation, driven by famine. Why did he there call Sarah his sister rather than his wife? When Pharaoh restores her to her husband with rebuke, this signifies the mind’s renunciation of continence.

[Col. 0461B]

13. “And Abraham went and stayed in the desert” (ibid., 9). The mind is then tested when it is in a kind of desert, where there is no wantonness of desires, no abundance of wealth, no expenditure upon luxury. Would that I might be in this desert, deprived of every incentive of desire, abandoned by every inclination to sin, stripped of boastfulness and pride. But because either God permits us to be tested or the tempter attacks, when the mind seems to itself to be tranquil in the desert, free from every appetite for earthly pleasures, it is driven into Egypt, where it may be pricked. For our flesh is the goad of the mind, and its passions are our pricks. [Col. 0461C] This is our Egypt—that is, our flesh; this is affliction. Our mind descends into it when it thinks carnal thoughts; but it ascends when it desires invisible things. Therefore Abraham too is said to have gone down into Egypt in order to be afflicted. Our mind undergoes this: at times it separates itself from the body, withdrawing in order to act alone, desiring to attend and cleave to incorporeal things. At times, because of the bond between soul and body, it inclines to carnal pleasures, by which the weak are subjected, while the strong are not held. Thus afflictions are crowns to the strong person, weaknesses to the feeble. Hence he who was not afraid of the afflictions by which he was deservedly tested says: “For even when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest; but we were afflicted in every way: conflicts without, fears within” (2 Cor. 7:5).

14. But famine compelled him to go down into Egypt (Gen. 12:10). For a fierce famine of the mind arises when the desire of this flesh overflows and the waters hoped for are hostile to salvation. We are reduced to the straits of the body when greed for possession steals in;

> [Note: Thus all manuscripts. The editions read: “all are tempted by the sweetness of luxury and the pride of the heart.”]

luxury is sweet to us and boasting to the heart. We are all tempted. Even the sober mind bends and goes down [Col. 0462A] into Egypt—that is, into bodily affliction. Yet it goes down in such a way that it appears to live there temporarily as a stranger, not to possess it as a citizen. For the just person said: “I am a stranger in this land” (Ps. 118:19 [119:19]). And elsewhere: “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:5 [120:5]).

15. When Abraham went down into Egypt (Gen. 12:11), that is, among fierce and barbarous characters who did not know how to honour virtue, he told Sarah not to call herself his wife but his sister, lest they harm him through envy. And here is a great mystery of virtue,

> [Note: The Corbie and Longpont manuscripts: “a great mystery of the sober mind.”]

which is quickly envied. Therefore, to restrain envy, it ought to make itself humbler. Let it not claim lordship over all, nor arrogate to itself alone wisdom as though it were pre-eminent. This is she whom Solomon acquired [Col. 0462B] as his wife. For a wife is especially due to one man.

> [Note: Thus all manuscripts. But Am. and Er.: “is due to a man.” This is doubtless due to a defect in the manuscripts they used; Gill. and the Roman edition corrected it by restoring, “is due to one man.”]

Therefore all desire to appear worthy of such a union, so that they grieve at anyone’s being preferred before them. Who can alone possess such great beauty? But a sister is shared with many, whether by the right of kinship or by the name itself. Therefore she preserves her true lover unharmed from injury.

16. Hence, when the Egyptians saw her (Gen. 12:15)—those who could neither discern nor recognize the form of virtue, but judged according to common opinion—they brought her to the tyrant, that is, to the proud mind which could not bear the weight of wisdom and was therefore afflicted. For when the discourse of virtue enters a wicked soul, it rebukes it for sin, covers it with shame for error, and torments it with the pain of its fall. While we are in a certain pleasure of sinning, the mind is covered with the clouds of folly, and its eyes are darkened by a kind of smoke of wickedness, [Col. 0462C] so that it may not see the ugliness of the things it desires. But when every cloud has passed away and it shines with wisdom’s brightness, severe torments are inflicted in a certain inner chamber of the guilty conscience. Thus our mind is a harsher judge through the guilt of conscience and the judgment of repentance. But if, sick through sin or weak through frailty, it cannot bear and endure the presence of virtue, it dismisses and banishes virtue from itself; it does not allow it to turn within itself and cling to its thoughts. And as weaker eyes flee the light, so the weak mind cannot endure wisdom’s brightness. Such were the Gerasenes, who begged the Lord Jesus to pass away from their territory (Matt. [Col. 0462D] 8:34).

17. Finally, this king of Egypt too says to Abraham: “What is this that you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife? Instead you said that she was your sister, and I would have taken her as my wife. And now, behold, your woman is before you: take her and return from here” (Gen. 12:18–19). Let us picture in our mind some intemperate man who, having caught sight of the grace of chastity and been captivated by a certain beauty of it, thinks that it ought to be pursued. Then, ignorant of the attendants with whom it goes accompanied and surrounded—namely sobriety, modesty and shame, restraint in food, flight from wantonness, boldness, impudence, serious caution, vigilant watchfulness—suddenly inflamed either by the heat of drunkenness, by the burning of the flesh itself, or by the encounter with a more attractive form, he does not restrain himself or resist the law of the flesh. Does he not say: “I thought it easier to follow chastity. It is above my shoulders, beyond my strength. Rare is the person in whom these things are joined. Farewell, chastity; withdraw, withdraw from the boundaries of my senses. Return quickly to the place from which you came here. I cannot endure your presence; I am tormented by severe questionings while I think that I ought to hold you, though I cannot hold you.”

[Note: All editions, with the Tornacensis manuscript: “with which it proceeds bound together.”]

[Note: The old edition reads “feminine caution.” The Roman edition, with five manuscripts, reads “a more cautious wild beast.” Of all these readings, the Corbie manuscript seems preferable, where one reads “serious caution.”]

18. Then, turning to someone who admonishes him, who has endeavoured to introduce into his mind the habit of chastity, maintaining that it will not be arduous or impossible, but is associated with many things, akin to the zealous, and suited to those who act willingly, he says: “What is this that you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife?” That is: why did you not say that she is held, not casually, but in lawful wedlock; that she carries with her the greatest dowry; that she brings in the heavy burdens of marriage and the hard interest of its union? Instead, you called her a sister, bound by no laws and a companion by nature, not proud and powerful through any legal claim of dowry-property. Thus, ignorant of her burdens, I thought that she should be joined to me and held by me; but I have understood what weight and burden she bears. “Behold your woman”—that is, behold your persuasion—is before you. Take her and return. I do not want her before me; I do not want her in my thoughts. Take yourself away from here with your counsels and your admonition; take yourself away quickly, return quickly. I cannot bear your delays; they are afflictions to me. It is enough that I was deceived before.”

And he sent out his retainers, through whom the more intemperate mind commonly wanders, turning over in its thoughts reflections of luxury, ambition, avarice, and encountering various allurements, so that they might cast out and drive chastity far away, lest it return to those territories from which it had been expelled; so that the mind, now secure and free in its more mature choice, might not fear to be reproved in its sins.

[Note: Here “the willing” means those who are drawn to something not under compulsion but spontaneously and from the heart.]

[Note: All editions read “offering allurements”; all manuscripts, “encountering allurements.”]

## CHAPTER V

Abraham departs from Egypt with his wife Sarah and all that is his—that is, with the true riches of the soul. What does his return to Bethel signify? And why is Lot not said to be rich in gold and silver?

19. Abraham therefore departed from there, having with him his wife Sarah (Gen. 13:1), that is, the principal woman, not a serving one. Hence it is also said to him: “Hear Sarah your wife” (Gen. 21:12). For she who strips herself of slavery to sins possesses rule, not servitude. Thus the stronger mind has with it the ruling virtue—that is, a virtue commanding the bodily senses, not obeying them. She brought back with her from Egypt all things; she lost there none of her disciplines. She was not stained by intemperance, arrogance, or the immodesty of shameful acts; she was not stripped of the garment of diligent sobriety, nor divested of the clothing of modesty.

20. “He was very rich” (Gen. 13:2), since nothing good was lacking to him; he did not desire what belonged to another, nor did he need anything that he might wish called his own. For this is to be rich: to have what is sufficient for one’s will. Frugality has a measure; wealth has none, for its limit lies in the choice of the seeker. He was rich in livestock, silver, and gold. What does this mean? Worldly riches do not, in my view, receive praise in a just man. Therefore, by livestock I understand the bodily senses, because they too are irrational; by silver, speech; by gold, the mind. Abraham was rightly rich because he governed the irrational senses. Indeed, he tamed them and made them gentle, so that they became rational. He possessed speech splendid in the brightness of faith, purified by the grace of spiritual discipline; he possessed a mind full of prudence. Therefore a good mind is compared to gold, because, just as gold surpasses other metals, so a good mind in a human being is superior to the other portions of human substance.

Thus the wealth of the wise person lies in three things: sense, speech, and mind. There is a certain ordered sequence, just as we read also in the Apostle: “But hope, faith, and charity remain, these three; and the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 13:13). The mind, therefore, is greater, because it is that which grinds the spiritual grain so as to produce the purification of senses and speech. Throughout, the character of the wise man is preserved.

21. Accordingly Abraham is said to have returned there (Gen. 13:3), that is, to Bethel, from which he had descended into Egypt, in order that we may recognize that even the just, set in the house of God and intent upon the word of God, are indeed tried by worldly afflictions, but are not alienated from the house of God and the keeping of heavenly commandments. To be content with one’s own bounds, not to be lifted up by an abundance of riches and by circumstances flowing with the pleasures of grace—this belongs to an excellent mind. Always to meditate upon the beginning and the end, to proceed from the one and enter into the other—this is good.

Now wisdom is good. For no one is good but God alone. From him we proceed, having been created through him; to him we return, because to be with Christ is far better. And that you may know that it is good for beginning and end to correspond, good Jesus himself says: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1:8).

[Note: All editions, with three manuscripts, read: “If you wish to be content . . . know this to belong to the mind . . . this is good.” But it is credible that someone who did not grasp the sense of the reading found in four older manuscripts arranged the passage in this way. He would easily have understood it had he noticed that the verb “we may recognize,” expressed above, must be understood here.]

22. Therefore may our mind always be with him; may it never depart from his temple or from his word. May it always be engaged in the reading of Scripture, in meditations, and in prayers, so that the Word of Him Who Is may always work within us; and so that, as we daily go forth to church or devote ourselves to prayers at home, we may begin from him and end in him. Thus every day of our whole life, and the course of each day, may take its beginning from him and end in him.

For just as, at the beginning of life, to believe and be initiated into God is salvation, so perseverance unto the end is necessary.
