It is the diligence of an excellent mind, intent upon the word of God, to do nothing irrational that may bring sorrow upon it; and, continually conscious of its good deeds, to preserve the joy of a good conscience. For that good which is without fear and without sorrow is full of security and grace. For the possession of the just person is pleasing to God; but for the foolish there is no degree of advance. Therefore Isaiah, as the good approaches, says: “Pain and sorrow and groaning shall flee away” (Isa. 35:10). John likewise says in the Apocalypse: “And God himself shall be with them, and shall wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death shall be no more, neither mourning, nor crying, nor pain any longer” (Rev. 21:3–4).

For in the resurrection of the just there will be unceasing joy and grace, when that Good begins to be with his saints, when they rest in Abraham’s bosom, placed in his tent, which is fixed between the house—or word—of God and grace. This signifies that the innocence of the faithful gives thanks to its Author, since they have nothing for which they might regret having been in this world.

[Note: That is, the Word of God; the expression is taken from Philo, *logos tou Ontos*, “the Word of Him Who Is.” He almost nowhere calls God otherwise than *ho ōn*, “He Who Is,” doubtless because God himself told Moses that he was to be called by this name, Exod. 3:14.]

[Note: The Tornacensis and Valcianus manuscripts and the editions read, “and to imitate is salvation”; the Mazarin manuscript, “and to imitate God is salvation”; the Colbertinus omits “and to be initiated.” But the Corbie and Longpont manuscripts restore the true reading.]

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Longpont, Colbertinus, and Mazarin manuscripts. Others, and all editions, read: “For the possession of the just is pleasing to God,” which, on consideration, will appear not to fit here so well or aptly.]

23. From Abraham’s simple deeds, therefore, examples of great instruction are unfolded. He was rightly rich, since he even makes rich the disputations of philosophers, who formed their own precepts from his conduct.

24. Scripture had set forth his riches; it remained to ascertain whether Lot also, his nephew, being as it were of the same succession, was rich. But Scripture declares him abundant only in livestock. For it says: “And Lot, who journeyed with Abram, had sheep and oxen and tents” (Gen. 13:5). He did not have silver, because he was not yet just. For the tongue of the just is silver refined by fire. He did not have gold, which was possessed by him who saw Christ’s back parts, of whom it is written: “His back parts are in the appearance of gold” (Ps. 67:14). Abraham saw him, as the Lord testified when he said: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” (John 8:56). And therefore he deserved both to have and to possess the appearance of gold.

[Note: The Roman edition reads “and herds.” The others, and all manuscripts, read “and tents.” Both can be defended from the Septuagint: in some of its manuscripts one reads *kai ktēnē*, “and livestock,” in others *kai skēnai*, “and tents.”]

## CHAPTER VI

In what sense it is written, “And Lot who journeyed with Abram”; likewise, “the land did not contain them.” On the shepherds and the quarrel arising between them, which Abraham attempts to settle. When he has vainly attempted to retain Lot, he lets him go with good grace. On Lot’s lack of skill and arrogance in choosing, and on the sins of the Sodomites.

25. Now I think that we must by no means pass over what seems to have troubled even the more learned: why it is written thus, “And Lot who journeyed with Abram” (Gen. 13:5), as though there were another Lot who, according to what we have received, did not journey with him. Many think that the question cannot be resolved. Therefore, to satisfy them and not depart from the rule of Scripture, we say that there is one person but two activities: in one and the same man two things are signified; he is one in number, twofold in office.

For Lot means “declension,” as the Latin translation has it. Now everyone declines either from good or from evil. Therefore, when Lot turned away from evil—that is, error, shameful conduct, crime—he was joined to his uncle; when he turned away from good—that is, from what is just, innocent, holy, and religious—he associated himself with shameful conduct. Thus Scripture rightly says: “And Lot who journeyed with Abram,” because he had not yet chosen Sodom and did not dwell with the authors of shameful acts. Afterwards he began to dwell in Sodom. Therefore, as though changed from himself, he is understood as another person, having defected not only from the just man but from himself.

26. Accordingly, because he had already begun deliberately to turn aside from his uncle, “the land did not contain them” (Gen. 13:6). No spaces can be sufficient for those at discord; for the quiet and peaceful, even narrow spaces abound; for those of discordant character, even spacious places are constricted. And because I said at the beginning that the human mind is being formed here—at first imperfect, but advancing through certain increases and stages—therefore Scripture says: “The land did not contain them”; that is, one soul did not naturally admit movements diverse and mutually opposed.

It can nevertheless happen that not all things are perfect in one and the same person; yet someone may conceal certain faults or moderate his impulses, either if there are more good things by which he conceals fewer faults, or if he turns back a sudden disturbance by more mature deliberation. But if more discordant and opposing things converge from both sides, the dwelling together of differing virtues and passions in one soul must necessarily be dissolved. Therefore, figuratively, he called the soul “earth,” following the natural philosophers. Solomon too says: “An imprudent man is like a field under cultivation” (Prov. 24). If it is fruitful with rich crops, it can hide thorns; but if thorns come together with ears of grain, there is no opportunity for harvesting.

27. Let us therefore consider who the shepherds are (Gen. 13:7), of what animals they are shepherds, and what the quarrel is between Abraham’s shepherds and Lot’s shepherds. Shepherds are masters of flocks: either diligent and sober men, who do not allow cultivated fields to be trampled underfoot or scorched by briars; or negligent and lax men, who do not call back their flock, so that it may graze on grassy but unfruitful pasture, but allow it to wander freely among the various produce of the field. The skilful guardianship of such shepherds is therefore necessary, lest what the negligence of the careless destroys be charged to the diligent.

But since the discussion is not about visible things, let us first consider of what flock they are shepherds. We may define these shepherds. “Shepherds,” it says, “of beasts of burden” (Gen. 13:7). By beasts of burden we have understood the irrational senses of the body to be signified. Who, then, are the shepherds of the senses, if not teachers and, as it were, certain leaders of the flocks—their guides—or the admonitions of a discourse, or the thoughts of our mind? If they are knowledgeable in and devoted to pastoral discipline, they do not permit the flock of the senses to wander too far or cling to useless or harmful fodder; rather, under a provident guide, they call it back, apply the reins of reason, and resist it when it struggles.

But bad teachers, or teachers of useless disputation, allow them to be carried by their own impulse, to rush into a precipice and danger, to trample cultivated ground and graze upon what is fruitful, so that they dissipate any fruits of virtue of this kind that may exist in the same soul. Hence comes the discord of our thoughts. When the flesh resists the spirit and the spirit resists the flesh, there is no slight conflict, when the Apostle himself, the Lord’s chosen vessel, says: “I see the law of my flesh resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7:23). He was unable to calm this conflict himself, and therefore fled to Christ, saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). That is, so that I may not cling to the pleasures of the flesh. Who then will loosen me from these bonds, join me in freedom to God, and turn the senses rather toward the sobriety of the soul than toward the drunkenness of the body?

But because he could find no ruler among human beings, he turned to God: “The grace,” he says, “of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:25). If one stronger than we are did not entrust it to his own powers to escape the body of death, but sought help from Christ, what ought we, who are weaker, to do? Abraham recognized that this conflict was serious, and therefore thought that it must be guarded against at the outset. For peace is the concern of the wise; quarrels are friends of the foolish.

[Note: The editions and a few manuscripts read “under a provident author.”]

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Longpont, Colbertinus, and Mazarin manuscripts. Others and the editions read “and make free, and the senses . . .”; the Tornacensis reads “and join free, and the senses . . .”]

28. “Let there not be,” he says, “a quarrel between me and you, and between my shepherds and your shepherds, because we are men, brothers” (Gen. 13:8). We read that Abraham was Lot’s uncle and Lot his nephew. How does he call him brother? But observe that the wise man employs grounds of concord. Hence he first says, “We are men.” All human beings are offspring of one nature, conceived within its womb, nourished and brought forth from one womb. Therefore, having been made by one Father and brought forth by one Mother as if from the same womb, we are rightly joined together in a kind of kinship as brothers. And because we are the offspring of rational nature, we ought to love one another with mutual, fraternal affection, not attack or persecute one another.

But this applies far more truly to one soul, whose rational part has as kindred, as we said above, the irrational senses; while its rational part has association with the virtues. Thus the vices and virtues of a human being are joined to one another by a certain fraternal bond, because the former belong to the flesh and the latter to the rational soul. Flesh and soul, moreover, are joined as if by a certain law of marriage, and from them the human being consists. A human being, therefore, ought to reconcile these as though they were his own portions, and compel them toward peace.

But because no one was so great as to conquer the flesh, therefore “our peace came, who made both one, and breaking down the middle wall of partition, the enmities in his flesh, abolishing the law of commandments in decrees, in order that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace, that he might reconcile both to God in one body through the cross, killing the enmities in himself” (Eph. 2:14 ff.). Therefore the Apostle rightly called himself an unhappy man (Rom. 7:24), since he endured within himself so great a war that he could not extinguish it.

Indeed, when Solomon spoke of one small part of the passions, namely anger, he said: “The wise person is better than the strong; and one who restrains anger is better than one who takes a city” (Prov. 16:32). Blessed, therefore, is the person who has escaped this war, not merely as a stranger and foreigner, but as a fellow citizen of the saints and a member of God’s household—one whom earthly things, though he lives on earth, do not shake.

[Note: The Corbie, Valcianus, and Tornacensis manuscripts in the first hand read: “whose irrational part has kindred . . .”; the Colbertinus and Mazarin manuscripts: “whose irrational part has the association of virtues.” But the following argument sufficiently shows that the reading of the other manuscripts and editions is genuine.]

[Note: The Amerbach and Erasmus editions and certain manuscripts read “may be able to restrain.”]

29. Abraham desired to preserve this disposition. Therefore, as a peaceful man, he says first: “Let there not be a quarrel between me and you.” Then he says: “And between my shepherds and your shepherds.” Third, he adds: “Behold, the whole land is before you”; that is, if agreement is impossible, I yield everything; take the whole, if the disagreement concerns place or possession. But if our characters are incompatible, depart from me. How much he proposed beforehand, lest he should be compelled to depart! Yet this too belongs to virtue and discipline.

For before our time a man formed by the discipline of philosophy said that these four things belong to a good man: first, he should labour to make everyone his friend; second, if he cannot make them friends, at least not enemies; third, if even this is unavailable, he should depart as he thinks fit; fourth, if someone pursues one who is withdrawing, he should defend himself as he can. But in Abraham we recognize the force of the first three not in bare words but in deeds.

30. The fourth, however, does not apply in the same way, since even toward one who withdrew he preserved a parent’s affection: he not only did not pursue him, but even rescued and freed him when he was captured. Indeed, although the Apostle teaches those first three points, he cancels by his precepts the fourth point added by philosophy. When he wished to instruct God’s people in peacefulness, he says: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. 12:18). Then, if this is impossible, there are at least to be neither disputes nor enmities. Therefore he adds: “Beloved, do not avenge yourselves” (Rom. 12:19), thereby excluding that third point, so that we should not wish at all to avenge ourselves: “But give place to wrath.” Here you have the fourth point too: depart rather and entrust vengeance to God than exact it for yourself—although he wished even this to appear as something said more according to the Law. For according to the Gospel, you have above: “Bless those who persecute you” (Matt. 5:44).

We have these precepts in the Second Epistle to Timothy: “For this reason,” he says, “I remind you to rekindle the grace of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands. For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and sobriety” (2 Tim. 1:6–7). And again: “But you, my dearest son, be strong in grace” (2 Tim. 2:1). Thus you have the precept of the first proposition: that he should bestow grace upon all. Then, if he cannot win everyone by his precepts, he must take care not to provoke some people by words—that is, not to make enemies. Therefore he says below: “Remind them of these things, charging them before God not to contend in words, which is useful for nothing except the ruin of the hearers” (2 Tim. 2:14). “And the servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all.”

A little later he adds beautifully, and supplies the reason that philosophy did not perceive: “Correcting with gentleness those who resist, lest perhaps God may grant them repentance for acknowledging the truth” (2 Tim. 2:25). For the third point too—that we should depart from those with whom we cannot agree—you have this added: he commands him to speak what befits sound doctrine, and then to avoid disputes about the Law. That is, first sow grace; then, by quarrelling with no one, turn no one away. Third, avoid a heretical person after one correction, “because one such as this has been perverted and sins, being condemned by himself” (Titus 3:10–11). How cleverly he removes one condemned by his own judgment from our vengeance, as though unworthy to be avenged upon! David, moreover, plainly removes the desire for vengeance when he says: “If I have repaid evils to those repaying me” (Ps. 7:5).

[Note: There seems to be some transposition here: what he calls third ought rather to be called fourth, and conversely. But the manuscripts offer no help in this matter.]

31. Therefore the mind of the wise man endeavours to correct and unite to itself either the falls or the irrational motions of the same soul. For it can happen that things which sometimes displease may be corrected with grace. If prodigality is cut back, it has generosity without loss. Modesty is sometimes too lax; if strengthened, it possesses both the grace of modesty and constancy of purpose. If agitation is moderated, it lays aside the horror of indignation and takes on the praise of vigour.

But if it cannot correct, it should not inflame intemperance. Let it detect the burning of desire and restrain it by marriage, lest, while continence is sought, unchastity steal in. Therefore the teacher of good things says: “I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain so, as I also do. But if they do not have self-control, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:8). Some women are bereft by the untimely death of their husbands and cannot remain continent. “I wish,” he says, “younger women to marry, bear children, manage households, and give no occasion to the adversary” (1 Tim. 5:14). But if certain pleasures delight them and they wish to live luxuriously in Christ, pursuing the glory of widowhood while not preserving sincerity, he judges them to be avoided, as you have it written: “Avoid younger widows” (1 Tim. 5:11).

[Note: All editions and the Tornacensis and Valcianus manuscripts read: “does not inflame. Intemperance reproves the burning of desire, which it restrains by marriage.” The remaining manuscripts have the text as printed, except that the Corbie manuscript in its first hand read: “let it not inflame intemperance; let it detect the burning of desire, let it restrain it by marriage.” This reading may perhaps be preferred to the other two.]

[Note: One or two manuscripts read “gravity, however”; the others and the editions better read “sincerity,” that is, truth and genuineness.]

32. Abraham therefore rightly wished, with good leave, to dismiss his nephew, whom he could not retain when he turned aside from him. So too a good mind should withdraw and separate itself from the headlong and divergent fall of irrational impulses. “If you go to the left, I to the right; or if you go to the right, I to the left” (Gen. 13:9). That is, what is on your right is on my left, and what is on your left is on my right. For to the imprudent man those things which belong to the body are on the right: he prefers them and assigns them the better place; he also puts riches and honours first. But the grace of attaining immortality he has on the left, whereas for the wise man it is on the right. “Length of days is in her right hand.” And the foolish man casts all the virtues of the soul onto the left; but the prudent man places them on his right, and bodily things on the left.

[Note: The five manuscripts read “and divergent”; the editions, “and the different fall of rational things.”]

33. “And Lot,” it says, “lifted up his eyes and looked upon the whole region of the Jordan” (Gen. 13:10). Boastfulness is a companion of those who turn away from the truth. Thus Abraham was more humble, since he offered the choice; Lot more arrogant, since he seized the choice. Virtue humbles itself; wickedness exalts itself. Lot ought to have entrusted himself to the more mature man, so that he might be safer. Indeed, he did not know how to choose. For first he lifted up his eyes and looked upon the region—that is, upon a thing that was not first in order but third, that is, last.

For first are the goods of the soul; second, those of the body, namely health, strength, beauty, and the charm of physical form; third are incidental things, namely riches, powers, homeland, friends, and glory. The region, therefore, is placed in the third rank, for it is a matter of dwelling.

34. Therefore he saw a region that was watered, before God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, “like the paradise of God and the land of Egypt, until you come to Zothopa” (Gen. 13:10). Unless you attend carefully to this, might you not say that Lot erred in choosing the parts adjoining the Jordan and those watered like the paradise of God? Certainly not according to the letter. But since Jordan is called “descent,” the person who has abandoned the fellowship of virtue descends and chooses appearance rather than truth.

Paradise is the loveliness of perfect blessedness, or the fruitful foundations of the soul, in which are plantations of wisdom, justice, and the other virtues. The land of Egypt, however, signifies bodily substance, whose plantations are the senses and passions of the body. For just as the green places of the virtues have Christ as their source and the abundance of spiritual grace by which they flourish, so intemperance is a certain source of bodily passions, by which excesses are nourished.

[Note: The Roman edition reads “until one comes to Segor.” Thus also the Vulgate, where the Septuagint reads *heōs elthein eis Zogora*, “until one comes to Zoar.” But I was unwilling to depart from the manuscripts and older editions.]

35. Scripture well says: “Lot chose for himself” (Gen. 13:11)—that is, “declension”—because God placed good and evil before us, so that each may choose what he wishes. Let us not, then, choose what appears more pleasant in outward form, but what excels in truth; lest, when the choice to follow better things has been granted us, we lift up our eyes, bent by the false beauty of pleasantness, while we obscure the truth of nature as though with eyes turned aside.

36. But the statement that the men in Sodom were cruel (Gen. 13:13) and exceedingly sinful before the Lord has no slight design, so that you may observe that the gentle God is moved by the grave bitterness of sins to take vengeance, and that Abraham could not without cause obtain pardon for the Sodomites, because they were shameful beyond measure. Many people are the more concealed the worse they are; they evade human investigation where affairs are conducted without a judge or where a just person is trapped by false testimony. Yet the just person remains before God, even if condemned by human beings, because God considers not the outcomes of judgments or proceedings entangled in the contrivances of wickedness, but the naked nature of affairs. In human examination, however, the error of false opinion commonly covers over the force of truth.

Susanna remained exceedingly chaste before God even when she was condemned for adultery, because God did not test the credibility of the deed by the assertions of false witnesses, but questioned the conscience of her inmost mind.

## CHAPTER VII

From the Lord’s words to Abraham, the philosophers drew their doctrine that all things belong to the wise man; and what possession was divinely promised to Abraham there. Five kings—that is, the senses of the body—are overcome by four, namely bodily allurements; but the same patriarch, fighting in Christ’s name, recovers the cavalry of Sodom: that is, he restrains vices and errors.

37. There follows a passage in which we are plainly taught how greatly the mind advances when the superfluous portions of its irrational part have been exhausted, and how much evil vices joined to vices bring about. For Scripture did not idly state: “And God said to Abraham, after Lot had departed from him: Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you now are, toward Africa and the North and the East and the sea; because all the land that you see I will give to you and to your seed for ever” (Gen. 13:14–15).

From this, as from a fountain, the Stoic philosophers drew the proposition of their doctrine that all things belong to the wise man (Diogenes Laertius, book 7, *Life of Zeno*). For East and West, North and South are portions of the universe. By these the whole world is encompassed. When God promised that he would give these things to Abraham, what else did he declare except that all things are at hand for the wise and faithful person, and nothing is lacking? Thus Solomon too says in Proverbs: “For the faithful person, the whole world is riches” (Prov. 17:6). How much earlier was Solomon than Zeno, master of the Stoics and founder of that school! How much earlier than Plato himself, father of philosophy, or Pythagoras, inventor of its name! But who is faithful except the wise person? For the fool changes like the moon, whereas the wise person remains immovable in faith.

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Longpont, Colbertinus, and Mazarin manuscripts. The editions, with the Tornacensis and Valcianus manuscripts, read: “when the superfluous and irrational portions have been exhausted.”]

38. But perhaps you ask: “How does the whole world belong to the wise person?” Because nature itself gives that person a share in all things, even if he possesses nothing. For wisdom, mistress and possessor of all things, regards the gifts of nature as its own, since they were given for human use; and it needs none of them, even if necessities of life are lacking. For just as a musician has instruments, a physician medicines, or a shipmaster the things necessary for a ship’s equipment, even when he does not have them at some particular time—he has them inasmuch as he is able to use them, even if their use is temporarily unavailable—how much more does the wise person judge to be his own whatever belongs to nature, since he lives according to nature!

For he does not lose his right who remembers that he was made in God’s image, and that the Lord God said to human beings: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth, rule over it, and exercise dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, all cattle, and all creeping things upon the earth” (Gen. 1:28). And he knows that wisdom is mother of all things and itself possesses the whole world. Thus Solomon, who asked for and received wisdom from the Lord our God, says: “He gave me true knowledge of the things that are, that I might know the arrangement of the world, the power of the elements, the beginning and end and middle of all things, the changes of seasons, the cycles of the year, the dispositions of the stars, the natures of animals and the rage of beasts, the force of winds, the thoughts of human beings, the varieties of plants, the virtues of roots, and whatever things are hidden and unforeseen” (Wis. 7:17 ff.). But these things are available to none but the perfect.

[Note: The Roman edition reads “hidden and manifest.”]

39. Accordingly, so long as Lot—that is, moral declension—clung to Abraham, he had not received his share in these things. But when, freed from the ambiguous winding and turning of declension, he began to tread the straight paths of virtue with the continual steps of his soul, he is sent forth as possessor into all the land, and is told: “Arise and walk through the land in its length and breadth, because I will give it to you and to your seed for ever” (Gen. 13:17).

Therefore, one who has merited wisdom and has not been the son of a slave woman, the servant of sin, or subject to the inheritance of the flesh, but has been the son of the free woman—that is, of Sarah, who is not a servant but a ruler, of good stock and good disposition—will acquire, by the title of perfect virtue, the inheritance of the universe. Therefore Abraham is told: “Arise.” This does not signify bodily rising, but spiritual rising: “Awake, you who sleep” (Eph. 5:14); arise from earthly things, arise from bodily things, leave earthly things behind, look to heaven; and “arise from the dead,” that is, from vain opinions and the disputations of the Chaldeans. Look upon the world; look also upon him who can give the whole world. “I will give you the world,” he says, “as a possession—the world which you formerly believed to be God.”

40. “Walk through the land in its length and breadth.” Certainly he could not, within a moment, have traversed that land bounded by the dominions of the Persians, from the shores of India to the Pillars of Hercules, as they say, or to the furthest borders of Britain [Col. 0473B]. And he might have seemed lacking in devotion, had he received a command to traverse this land and not obeyed the heavenly oracle. But since his devotion is proved—for he had moved his tent only as far as the oak of Mamre (ibid., 18)—we may surely understand “land” to mean perfect virtue: virtue that yields good fruits, fruitful discoveries, the firstfruits of thoughts, and a harvest of merits; that fills the inner house with grain, wine, and oil; the land of resurrection, which God promised our fathers, flowing with milk and honey (Exod. 3:17): the sweetness of life, the grace of delight, the splendor of glory. The first heir of this land was the first-born from the dead, the Son of God, Jesus Christ. And therefore he did not say “to seeds,” but “to seed” (Gal. 3:16), in order to indicate him who would be the first to acquire this inheritance for the human race.

41. We have learned of the progress of a good mind, which, rising from the slippery vice of deflection, [Note: [Col. 0473D] Thus all the manuscripts. But every edition without exception reads: “sought the first state of wisdom.”] at once sought the reward of wisdom, the inheritance of righteousness. But how greatly vices joined to fickleness do harm is taught by the sequence of the following reading. For those four kings who triumphed over five kings and carried off all the cavalry of Sodom also seized Lot, the son of Abraham’s brother, and departed. The five kings (Gen. 14:1 ff.) are the five senses of our body—sight, smell, taste, touch, hearing. The four kings are bodily and worldly allurements, since both human flesh and the world consist of four elements. They are rightly called kings, because sin has its own dominion and a great kingdom. Hence the Apostle says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6:12) [Col. 0473D]. Our senses therefore easily yield to bodily and secular pleasures and are captured by a kind of power belonging to them. Bodily pleasures and the enticements of this age are conquered only by a mind that is spiritual, clings to God, and wholly separates itself from earthly things. Every deflection is captured by these.

[Col. 0474A] Hence John says: “Woe to those who dwell on the earth” (Rev. 8:13). He certainly does not include all people then completing the course of this life—for there are those placed on earth whose citizenship is in heaven—but those conquered by attachment to earthly living and by the charm of this age. Thus we are not inhabitants but sojourners of this earth. For a sojourner entertains the hope of a temporary lodging; an inhabitant seems to place all his hope and the use of his property there where he thinks he will dwell. Therefore, whoever is a sojourner on earth is an inhabitant of heaven; but whoever is an inhabitant of earth is a possessor of death.

42. Abram numbered his three hundred and eighteen household-born servants, [Note: [Col. 0473D] The words “and struck them, and pursued them,” absent from the manuscripts and early editions, were restored by the Roman edition, not badly. We do not think they were omitted for any other reason than that a writer wishing to use abbreviation had indicated that the remainder should be supplied up to the word “Hobah” [Col. 0474D].] and struck them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, which is on the right of Damascus (Gen. 14:14–15) [Col. 0474B]. And the number is life-giving. For in it is life, if we believe in the Passion in the name of the Lord Jesus. For this is the interpretation of the name that we have called Hobah (*De Abraham*, I.2), namely, “life.” It is beautifully said to be on the right of Damascus. For the lambs are at the right, the kids at the left.

A trained mind knows whom it should enlist to bring a battle to completion, with what arms it should equip them, and beneath what standards it should lead them. It does not set before itself images of eagles or dragons; [Note: [Col. 0474D] Among the Romans the eagle was the standard of a legion, the dragon that of a cohort. Vegetius, book XI, ch. 13.] rather, it advances into battle in the cross of Christ and in the name of Jesus—strong by this sign, faithful beneath this banner. Rightly, then, is the mind trained which has received the true wisdom of a righteous man. Justice is skill in correction: by rebuke it calls sinners back and restrains the assaults of passions.

43. Therefore Scripture says that he recalled all the cavalry [Col. 0474C] of Sodom: that is, he held the reins, imposed the bit of reason, recalled fault, and laid error low. For a horse does not know how to stand still: swift to rush forward, lifting its neck, neighing toward lust. What is more like sin? At its first onset fault boils over and outruns every thought of what is right; with untimely movement it leaps forth, so that reason can scarcely call it back. It rushes headlong and throws its rider into this sea of the present age, swelling its neck and refusing the yoke of correction.

There is a particular form of lust that changes a person’s voice, corrupts the speech of one in love, [Note: [Col. 0474D] Six Gallican manuscripts, together with the Americanus, read: “and reveals itself in its own words” (Longobardus: “may reveal itself”). But everyone sees how easy it is for a pen to mistake *prodat* (“reveals”) for *probat* (“proves”) between such words.] and betrays itself in its own words. Thus the Lord God says to Judah through Jeremiah: “Now your shame shall be seen, and your adultery, and your neighing, and the estrangement of your fornication upon the hills” (Jer. 13:25–26). The righteous man recalled this cavalry [Col. 0474D]; he also turned back the habits of one who had gone astray and called them to himself, so that those who had turned aside might become his imitators, because our senses return to the discipline of the mind.

44. He also recovered the substance. This certainly does not mean an estate, but the life-giving substance of the soul, in which there is a precious treasure—not straw, not hay; in which the splendor of trustworthy speech abides; in which the treasure of our hope [Col. 0475A] is sustained. For this is our true substance, rich in the resources of wisdom; this is immortal substance. By contrast, the body and its accidents are for daily rather than lasting use. Hence some rightly think that an estate should not be called “substance.” For we do not subsist in it, since even those who lack money do not lack the substance of life.

## CHAPTER VIII

Our mind learns from Melchizedek devotion toward the worship of God; from the king of Sodom, that temptation remains to be feared even after it has been overcome; and from Abraham, that the contagion of intemperance must be avoided. Why is a reward promised to him only after victory, and why does he prefer concern for posterity? Finally, after Abraham himself has been guarded against the superstitions of divination, a manifold interpretation is added of the sacrifice offered by him.

[Col. 0475B]

45. We have spoken fully of Melchizedek in the moral treatise (*De Abraham*, I.3), in which the mystery too was neither passed over nor omitted. Here it is sufficient merely to remind us that a mind full of prudence and justice is more devoted to the worship of God, and pays him tithes from the earth’s produce in its fruits, [Note: [Col. 0475D] The Roman edition reads “of things produced by the earth.” All other editions and all manuscripts read “the earth’s products.” There is an ellipsis of words such as “namely” or “that is.” The word *gignentia* is also used passively for “things generated,” just as approved authors use *vehens* of one who is carried.] according to a higher understanding; so that it may offer God the perfection of all its senses and works, claiming nothing for itself, since it cannot govern itself unless supported by divine favor. For when it thinks it has conquered, it is tempted and assailed. This is expressed and taught by the passage: our mind must always stand, as though on guard, against the passions of the body [Col. 0475C]. For what else is meant by the saying, “The king of Sodom went out to meet Abraham and said: ‘Give me the people, but take the horses for yourself’” (Gen. 14:21), except that after these victories over luxury some force of lust can steal upon the rational mind in order to pour irrational passions into it?

46. But it belongs to a perfect mind to take nothing from earthly things, nothing from bodily allurements, and to abstain from earthly things. Therefore Abraham says: “I will take nothing from all that is yours” (ibid., 23). As though it were contagion, he avoids intemperance; as though it were a stain, he flees bodily senses; he rejects the pleasures of the world, seeking those things that are above the world—that is, stretching out his hands to the Lord. The hand is the active power of the soul. He stretches it out not to the fruit of an earthly [Col. 0475D] tree, but to the Lord: “Who made,” he says, “heaven and earth” (ibid.), that is, intelligible and visible substance. For intelligible *ousia* (οὐσία, “being/substance”) is heaven; visible or sensible substance is earth. Thus he signifies that he stretches the power of his soul upward, so that from that intelligible substance he may put on the height of the contemplative life, looking not at things seen but at things unseen: not earthly, bodily, or present things, but incorporeal, eternal, heavenly things. From this visible substance, however, he receives the grace of active and civic discipline.

47. To these matters he added the oracle of the Lord saying: “Do not fear, Abram; I will protect you; your reward shall be exceedingly great” (Gen. 15:1). I ask why this came after the outcome of the war. Now was the time for the reward to be promised. For it would have been less remarkable had he attacked the enemy in consequence of God’s promise. He would have gone forth secure of victory, invited more to triumph than ready for glory, or prepared to avenge the grief of familial devotion.

[Col. 0476B] The purpose of a devout mind does not seek a reward; rather, it counts the consciousness of a good deed and the intention of a righteous work as its reward. Narrow minds may be invited by promises and raised up by hoped-for rewards. But the good mind which undertook the contest without a written heavenly guarantee of repayment gains for itself the fruit of twofold praise: it establishes both the grace of most confident courage and that of fullest devotion. This is the fitting judgment concerning holy Abraham: [Note: [Col. 0475D] At this point the manuscripts and editions show no difference, except that, where all editions and most manuscripts have “righteous errors,” the Corbie manuscript reads “righteous griefs.” This is more appropriate, since the subject here is the grief felt by the patriarch because his brother’s son had been captured and carried away [Col. 0476D]. Yet some corruption seems to lurk in the other words; for you will not derive a fitting sense unless you change *despici se* to *despexisse*, or *divinum favorem* to *divino favore*.] he judged that, in his righteous grief, he ought not to have disdained divine favor [a conjectural emendation; the transmitted text is corrupt]; and he struck down the enemy by contempt for danger, which he thought should gloriously be faced for the sake of avenging familial devotion.

God’s justice is also proclaimed in him, for God bestows recompense upon devout minds not from the necessity of a promise, but in contemplation of his own equity, judging it fitting that those who serve without any recompense of human reward should have a reward laid up in the goodness of him to whom they have judged their souls should be devoted [Col. 0476C]. At the same time, the reward for martial honors is prepared by the outcome of victory itself or by human favor; but the reward for piety, frugality, purity, and the other, as it were, private virtues is paid by God. What is manifest to people, they themselves reward. But not all things are manifest: some are evident, others uncertain, and especially the secrets of the heart. Hence he also says: “You have made known to me the uncertainties and hidden things of the heart” (Ps. 50:8), [Note: [Col. 0476D] The biblical text consistently reads, “the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.” Yet before Ambrose, Origen cited this passage as it stands in the text. See *Philocalia*, ch. 18.] of which God is observer and searcher. Therefore he would not have promised Abraham a great reward unless he had judged his soul pure from every contagion of sins.

48. Yet the concern of a holy and prophetic mind is greater for enduring posterity. For the offspring of wisdom and faith desires an inheritance. Therefore he says: “What will you give me? Yet I depart without children” (Gen. 15:2). He desired the offspring of the Church; he sought that succession which would not be servile but free—not according to the flesh, but according to grace. And therefore there resounded such a divine [Col. 0477A] reply, [Note: [Col. 0477D] The Tornacensis and Valcellensis manuscripts and early editions read “which the chosen man heard.” The Roman edition: “which the chosen one heard.” The Corbie, Longobardus, Colbertinus, and Mazarin manuscripts: “by which, being instructed, he heard,” etc.] by which, being instructed, he heard: “Look at heaven and count the stars, if you can count them. And he said: So shall your seed be. And Abram believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6).

What did he believe? Not only the multitude of peoples who would believe in Christ, but also the splendor of heavenly grace and the resurrection to immortal life that would be bestowed on the offspring of the Church. And what is meant when it says, “He brought him outside” (ibid.)? The prophet is brought, as it were, outside, so that he may go beyond the doors of the body and the narrow confines of covering flesh, and see the infusion and, as it were, a certain descent of the Holy Spirit. We too must leave the narrow confines of this our temporary lodging, cleanse the place of our soul from every defilement, cast out the filth of malice, if we wish to receive the spirit of wisdom; for wisdom will not enter a malicious soul [Col. 0477B].

Abraham believed, not enticed by testimony of gold or silver, but because he believed with the heart unto righteousness. In that his merit was proved; in that his reward was rendered.

49. Thus the Lord immediately gave testimony to his faith, saying: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of the Chaldeans, to give you this land, that you may be its heir” (Gen. 15:7). And because Abraham had cast aside the pursuit of Chaldean practices, he now asks: “How,” he says, “shall I know that I am its heir?” (ibid., 8). That is: I have now rejected the divinations of magicians; teach me how I may know that I shall become heir of its land. One who asks how he may know does not doubt that, with God making it known, he can know; rather, he wishes to perceive the manner in which knowledge is to be acquired.

For in the Gospel too, when Mary heard from the angel that she, a virgin, would bear a son, she replied: “How will this be, since I have not known a man?” (Luke 1:34) [Col. 0477C]. And she rightly answered, that is: Since what belongs to nature is unavailable—because one who has not been joined to a man does not usually give birth—I ask how, contrary to the laws of nature, I as a virgin can bring forth a child.

50. But the Lord God said to him: “Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old goat, a three-year-old ram, a turtledove, and a dove” (Gen. 15:9). I would pass over this interpretation of the sacrifice, if I had not noticed that some people take offense from it, because a rite of divination seems to be described: after the immolation, the animals were divided, placed facing one another, and Abraham sat beside them. But if we consider the force of the preceding question and of the answer to come, we can perceive that this rite of sacrifice accords with [Col. 0478A] our hope and faith.

For the heifer is a ploughing animal, given over to earthly labor. The goat is figuratively compared with waters, because the Greek αἴξ (*aix*, “goat”) takes its name from παρὰ τὸ αἴσσειν (*para to aissein*, “from rushing forward”), from being borne along with force. For it runs as water does. We may judge this from the sound and course of rivers, or from the violent waves of the sea. The ram, however, is compared to air, because this animal is found more useful than all others to the human race, since it supplies us with clothing, just as this air supplies the life-giving substance of breath.

I think this order was adopted so that he first said, “Take for me a heifer and a goat,” and named the ram third, because the first two—the heifer and the goat—are compared with the material elements of earth and sea [Col. 0478B], and because they are said to be female. But the ram is a male animal, forceful by nature and violent with its horns. Likewise, the breath of this air is life-giving, like a male author and cause of generation, moving the generative parts of the earth and joining with them as in a certain union. Thus the kind of these three animals mystically signifies one thing in relation to earth, another to sea, and another to life-giving air.

51. This is a natural interpretation; but a moral interpretation is also present and available. For in all people there are flesh, sense, and word. Our flesh is the heifer: it labors to sow, to gather, to give birth; it is wearied by countless labors. Hence the Greeks [Note: [Col. 0477D] In several manuscripts and all editions the words “called the heifer” are absent. As for the Greek words, the Maurists imitated the manuscripts as closely as they could; but because Erasmus disliked them as corrupt, he invented another derivation: “The Greeks called the heifer δάμαλιν from τὸ δαμᾶσθαι λίαν, because it is exceedingly tamed.” Later editions retained this phrase, although incomplete. But after examining the passage more carefully in the Corbie manuscript and several others, we established our reading. Moreover, “to be tamed by injuries” here seems to mean nothing other than to be broken by labor and blows.] called the heifer δάμαν (*daman*) from τὸ δαμᾶσθαι μὲν αὐτήν (*to damasthai men autēn*, “because it is indeed tamed”), because it is tamed by hardships. It performs the labor of male oxen, the plough, and the yoke, while producing female offspring with abundant udders [Col. 0478C].

Our flesh too is subjected to the necessities of this life, is shaken by frequent pains, and grows old bent beneath a certain burden of many miseries. Who, moreover, does not know that the power of the soul is stronger, and that bodily substance clings to it as though wedded during the course of this life? Our senses, however, leap forth like goats by a kind of spring and feed on steep places, by their own impulse stirring up the movements of the soul and shaking it. They are ready at every occasion—whether at the sight of female beauty or at the smell of some fragrance. They are likewise quickly moved by hearing and touch, and by them they bend the soul’s steadfastness and estrange it, as it were, from its own nature.

Hence many think it is called ἀφορμή (*aphormē*, “without impulse”), because ὁρμή (*hormē*) means “impulse”; [Note: [Col. 0478D] Since this word was corruptly read in certain manuscripts and early editions of Ambrose’s works, Erasmus conjecturally substituted ὁρμητικήν (“impulsive”). Yet manuscripts of better quality quite clearly give ἀφορμήν, that is, “without impulse”; for in spiritual matters the word has this meaning, although in bodily matters it means the opposite. The sense, therefore, is that the soul is called free by nature from impulses and movements because the source and origin of these movements lie not in it, but in the body.] because from a certain impulse of the senses arises the cause of our bending and estrangement. Moreover, it has the appearance of the female sex, [Note: [Col. 0478D] The Maurists, with some manuscripts, read: “and also our senses, *ectasis* in Greek,” etc. Erasmus corrected this, and subsequent editions substituted the word αἰσθήσεις, which is found in the better manuscripts. Yet these contain some variation of wording: “as also our senses are called αἰσθήσεις,” where “female in gender” must certainly be understood. Again, where all editions read “like exhausted souls,” all manuscripts read more correctly “. . . living creatures.”] since even our senses are called αἰσθήσεις (*aisthēseis*) in Greek, a feminine noun [Col. 0479A]. Like exhausted living creatures, they are quickly emptied once they have discharged the offspring of their activity and pleasure; then, with desires stirred anew, they bring forth fresh impulses.

52. In the ram, however, there is a likeness of our word and speech, because it is forceful, just as our speech is effective in action, and because it serves, in a certain way, as an adornment and covering for us. By its use in clothing, the ram leads the flock in due order, just as a certain order of our life and conduct is explained by speech. Yet I think we should understand especially that Word which is the Word of God, with which this ram seems to have no slight kinship. This Word truly clothed us with the covering of its fleece and brought us into the house of eternal salvation. He offered himself to be sacrificed for us [Col. 0479B], “who was led as a sheep to the slaughter and, like a ram before its shearer, was silent and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7).

From him we have a certain order of being and of sacred redemption, because through him we were created and redeemed. Therefore the Word has a twofold natural and moral function: natural, by which he created; moral, by which he redeemed. Philosophy too establishes a twofold kind of its own in the word: natural and moral. The rational element belongs to each. It calls the natural aspect that which pertains to the creation of the world, which it attributes to the word; and the moral aspect that which pertains to justice and equality of life, whose life and reason come from the word.

53. For this reason, when forty days had been completed after the birth from the Virgin Mary, [Note: [Col. 0479D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “when eight days had been completed,” etc.] they brought our Lord Jesus to Jerusalem, to offer him to the Lord according to the law [Col. 0479C], and to offer “a sacrifice of a pair of turtledoves or two young doves” (Luke 2:22 ff.). For in the dove is spiritual grace; in the turtledove, the nature of incorrupt generation or the chastity of an undefiled body. Therefore, rightly, after the ram, the turtledove and dove are commanded to be taken for the sacrifice, so that you may understand incorrupt chastity and spiritual grace to adhere to the Word.

And in the very fact that he set birds there, we can understand the flight of heavenly merits. For there are birds of heaven which come and dwell in the branches of the tree that rose from the mustard seed, to which the kingdom of heaven is compared (Matt. 13:32). Ezekiel too says that the heavens were opened to him and that, among other things, he saw one wheel on the earth joined to the four living creatures (Ezek. 1:15). And below he says: “I heard the sound of their wings, like the sound of many waters and the voice of the Most High God; and when they went, it was like the sound of a word, like the sound of an army camp” (ibid., 24) [Col. 0479D].

[Col. 0480A] 54. Hence some have turned to the books of philosophy, because heaven itself is like a bird. Thus Plato said that heaven is a winged chariot, drawing this from what the prophet had said: “When the living creatures went, the wheels joined to them went; and when the living creatures rose from the earth, the wheels rose” (ibid., 21). But the prophet did not call heaven itself a bird [Note: [Col. 0479D] The Corbie, Longobardus, Colbertinus, and Mazarin manuscripts restore the word “bird,” which is omitted in the others and in all editions.]; he said that birds are in heaven. Thus David too says: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:1)—that is, the heavenly powers; just as, when a beautiful element is seen, its maker is praised.

The prophet, however, describes the soul, whose movements are four, like horses: λογιστικόν (*logistikon*, “the rational”); θυμητικόν (*thymētikon*, “the spirited”); ἐπιθυμητικόν (*epithymētikon*, “the appetitive”); διορατικόν (*dioratikon*, “the perceptive”). These are the four living creatures: the human being, the *logistikon*; the lion, the *thymētikon*; the calf, the *epithymētikon*; the eagle, the *dioratikon*. Reason was placed first so that the rest might follow [Col. 0480B] reason. Thus the lion is at the right with the human being: that is, with reason, spirited movement is at the right. When these living creatures rise, the wheels rise too. The wheel is life upon earth, by which we live. If the four movements of our soul are raised up, our life too is raised. Therefore he added: “For,” he says, “the spirit of life was in the wheels” (Ezek. 1:20).

Thus the soul is rather the chariot, which says in the Song of Songs: “You have made me the chariots of Amminadab” (Song 6:11), that is, of our Lord. Therefore the prophetic description does not accord with the tradition of philosophy. For the prophet says that he heard the sound of wings. These wings are the virtues which [Note: [Col. 0479D] The words enclosed in the following brackets were absent from later editions, and the passage read: “They are virtues which are required of you.” Gill first published the omitted words in the variant readings at the end of his edition, on the authority of two manuscripts in a very ancient hand, the Dionysianus and Sorbonicus. We have restored them to the text, relying on the Corbie, Longobardus, Colbertinus, and Mazarin manuscripts; the first is eight hundred years old or more. No one who carefully considers the style, affinity of subject matter, and sequence will deny that they are Ambrosian. Add that some passages are cited by Bartholomew of Urbino in the *Milleloquium Ambrosianum*, under “heaven”; hence one may infer that this fragment existed also in Italian manuscripts used by him.] with the great and twofold applause of prudence, courage, temperance, and justice, resound with the sweet beauty and melody of life. But Plato derived certain sweet sounds of the stars from the revolution of the heavenly sphere, pursuing reputation and display rather than truth [Col. 0480C].

For although our Origen too—that is, a man devoted to ecclesiastical office—asserts that there is in the movement of the planets a certain ineffable harmony producing that most sweet heavenly sound, yet very many of his writings testify that he himself also indulged the tradition of the philosophers too greatly. I have written this in order to distinguish the interpretation of this sacrifice both from the tradition of divination and from that of philosophy. Others may choose to prove their learning; I, following the Apostle, prefer to seem timid rather than learned, for he says: “See that no one despoils you through philosophy and empty deception, according to human tradition, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ” (Col. 2:8) [Col. 0480D].

55. As for the statement, “Abraham divided the bodies and sat beside them” (Gen. 15:11), lest anyone suppose it an inspection of entrails [Col. 0481A], I do not deny that these are terms of divination; for that is how I hear them. But whereas the reading establishes that the bodies of the quadrupeds were divided, it does not establish that the birds were divided. Certainly, if there had been an inspection of their entrails, the birds too would have been divided in order to permit inspection. But what if this accords with our faith? Let us therefore seek the teaching which the word gives us above divination.

We said above that in the heifer we take earth, in the goat water, and in the ram air. This is gathered from the very designation that they are commanded to be taken for sacrifice at three years old, because earth itself is divided into three kinds: it is either mainland, island, or peninsula. Water itself is divided into three, because it is either sea, rivers, or lakes. Springs and wells, however, are private matters, by no means worthy of a general and public division: wells lie hidden; springs provide an origin to other things. Air too has the divisions of the seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter. This is the worldly division [Col. 0481B].

What benefit does this bring? It enables us to know that God is the author and governor of all these things, who has given order to all things and distinguished them by this division, so that from these things you may gather that God can grant what you piously ask and fulfill what he promises.

56. Accordingly, because Abraham had answered the Lord promising an inheritance of land, “How shall I know that I shall be heir of this land?” (Gen. 15:8), he is instructed through those kinds of sacrificial victims to believe that God is above the world, since he has divided, by provident distinction, all things that belong to the world. Yet things that are divided are later dissolved; whereas those things which are not divided—for he did not divide the birds, that is, the turtledove and dove—are never dissolved [Col. 0481C]. For faith remains whole, raised on high in the manner of a dove, surveying what is above and flying around heaven with the spiritual oarage of its wings.

The mind too is compared with the turtledove: nourished in secret places according to the habit of that bird, seeking that intelligible and undivided substance of the Trinity, fleeing a certain crowd of creatures, not mixing itself with a bodily congregation, and separating itself from every stain of passions. This sacrifice is required of you. Whoever offers such victims—faith and chastity of mind, the grace of simplicity, and the disposition of charity and peace—recognizes himself as heir of that blessed land. So too the Lord declared more plainly in the Gospel, saying: [Note: [Col. 0481D] Thus the Corbie, Longobardus, Colbertinus, and Mazarin manuscripts. Other manuscripts and the early editions read: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall see God,” or, “for they shall possess the earth.” Departing from all of these, the Roman edition has the Vulgate wording: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” or, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.”] “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4).

[Col. 0481D] 57. Receive another division. Our flesh too, by God’s own ordering, has all its members divided. There are two eyes, two ears, two cheeks, divided nostrils, a double row of teeth, breasts, shoulders, hands, sides, thighs, knees, legs, and feet. Are not all things paired, so that all our functions may seem to be performed with the support of double aids? The soul too undergoes a division of its parts. For the διορατικόν (*dioratikon*, “the perceptive faculty”), that is, [Note: [Col. 0481D] Supply “of the soul.” He therefore calls the faculties of thought and reasoning, and of perception, the soul’s higher parts, because the passions or faculties of anger and desire are lower and less necessary. Under *dioratikon* he here includes what he had called *logistikon*.] [Col. 0482A] the higher faculties, like a pair of opposing eyes, is rational and irrational. The rational itself is divided into mind and speech. Its perceptive faculty is divided into hearing and sight, by which the excellence of this life is enriched. Smell and taste seem to provide services necessary for vital use. By receiving the life-giving breath through continual inhalation, the nostrils nourish the substance of the human being with a kind of uninterrupted food. Taste, however, is generated by drink and food. The fifth sense, touch, is as though mixed with the other four. Smell and taste are rather certain foods of the body, by which the service of this flesh is sustained. Sight and hearing, however, assist the mind. These are the divisions, according to our flesh and soul, made by the supreme Maker.

58. Hence we ought to infer that this world too is distributed, as it were, through paired limbs and as though into corresponding opposites (ἀντιπρόσωπα): earth into mountains and plains, as some parts of our body are higher and others flatter. The shoulders and the upper parts of feet and hands stand out; but the sides and lower parts of the neck are like [Note: [Col. 0482D] All editions read “the valleys and hollows of the earth,” contrary to the authority of all manuscripts.] worn and hollow valleys. The same may be understood of the palm of the hand. For who doubts that in the heel itself some parts rise, while the middle is hollowed? Water is salty in the sea, sweet in rivers or springs. Air is cold in winter, temperate in the months of spring, and hot in summer. Thus the Maker divided these things.

But he did not divide our mind, which, borne on the oarage of the various virtues and its own strength, now flies beyond heaven in the manner of birds; for it clings to the Trinity, which divides all things and alone is undivided [Col. 0482C]. Hence philosophers maintain that the higher substance of this world, which they call ether, is not composed from a mixture of the other elements, but is brilliant and shining with abundant light, receiving nothing of earth’s dirt, water’s moisture, air’s mist, or even fire’s redness; they assert that it consists of a certain fifth *ousia* (οὐσία, “substance”), and that the mind of this world, like a bird, is swifter and purer than its other parts. For the other parts are intermingled and congealed together.

But we consider nothing immune and separate from material composition except that sole substance of the venerable Trinity, which is truly pure and simple, of unalloyed and unmixed nature. Though some think that there is a clearer light from that fifth *ousia*, of which David said that God is “clothed with light as with a garment” (Ps. 103:2) [Col. 0482D]. And the Apostle wrote of almighty God himself that “he alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16).

59. By what reasoning he said that birds came down upon the divided bodies of the heifer, the goat, and the ram (Gen. 15:11), I do not readily discover—unless it is because all things terrestrial, maritime, and even aerial are full of snares and disturbances. For these birds seem to have come down upon the bodies for food. By nature, moreover, those more violent and stronger in power rush upon the weaker and, as it were, settle upon dead bodies, most often attacking unexpectedly. Or rather, as I think is truer: because the ruler of this world, and the birds of heaven—the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places—assail with violent agitation those who are divided by worldly anxiety and care, and tear them to pieces with a rough tooth as though they were corpses of the dead. For of these it was said: “Leave the dead to bury their own dead” (Luke 9:60), because they belong to the kingdom of the devil, who is divided against himself. But those who belong to the kingdom of God—to whom Jesus says, “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21)—are not divided, because they cling to God. For “he who clings to a prostitute is one body,” since, he says, “the two shall be in one flesh.” But “he who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:16–17). Therefore these are not dead bodies for the birds of heaven to eat; rather, they are spirits, for God “makes his angels spirits.” Thus the birds did not come down upon the dove and the turtledove, because those birds were not divided. For the righteous are not divided, who are told to be “guileless as doves” (Matt. 10:16). Therefore David says that “even the sparrow has found herself a home, and the turtledove a nest in which to place her young” (Ps. 83:4). Abraham beheld these things; he considered them with deep and spiritual sight.

60. Therefore it is written: “Abram sat beside them” (Gen. 15:12), not as an interpreter of augury but as an interpreter of heavenly revelation, investigating the signs of God’s working. For a mind directed toward Christ’s grace saw this world to be full of wickedness, which flew, as it were, from the height of heaven and oppressed the weak upon earth; but it saw chastity, faith, and sincerity subject to no passions; while greed and the cares of the age, by which those who enjoy the pleasures of riches are choked, are torn apart and divided.

> **Note:** [Col. 0483D] Am. and Era.: “Hence they are also called divided, because,” etc. Gill.: “Hence riches are also called cares, because,” etc. Rom. omits “cares.” Ambrose seems here to signify that he wished to derive the word *divitiae* (“riches”) from the verb *divido* (“I divide”), although it is by no means obscure that the holy man is alluding to the passage from the parable of the seeds which we have noted. Our reading, however, rests not only on the six manuscripts we consulted, but also, according to Gill’s report in the various readings, on the Sorbonne copy and a very ancient Dionysian copy, which are no longer found in those libraries.

Hence riches are also called the cares and thoughts of this world (Matt. 13:22), because they divide the mind, split it in different directions, draw it into parts, and do not allow it to remain uncorrupted and whole. The man of peaceful mind therefore sat and considered how he might at close hand prevent the evils brought upon human beings; for the mind of the wise and righteous man strives to heal human misfortunes and to ward off and cut away the afflictions of our souls.

## Chapter IX

Why ecstasy and fear fell upon Abraham; what the oracle delivered to him concerning the sojourning and servitude of his descendants in Egypt, his own death, and the liberation of those descendants signifies; and, finally, what the vision of the flame and furnace concerns.

61. The following words teach us with what spiritual and prophetic disposition Abraham did this. For at the setting of the sun an ecstasy fell upon him; and behold, a great and dark fear came upon him (Gen. 15:12). Ecstasy commonly comes upon prophets, as you have the Prophet saying: “I said in my ecstasy, Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:2). For the prophet’s mind passes beyond, as it were, certain limits of human prudence when it is filled with God. Beforehand it empties itself of the thoughts and disputes of this world, so that it may offer itself pure and emptied to the incoming spiritual grace. The Holy Spirit comes upon it, pouring himself in with great force, so that the human mind is suddenly disturbed.

Thus the angel came to Mary—and he came with earnestness and grace—yet Mary was troubled at his entrance. Therefore the angel said to her: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with God; and behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son” (Luke 1:30–31). We therefore recognize that when the grace of God comes upon the prophetic mind, it suddenly rushes in. Accordingly, we read that the Holy Spirit came upon and fell upon the prophets, because the mind undergoes ecstasy: it is disturbed, afraid, and covered with certain shadows of ignorance and lack of understanding. So too we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 9:4) that a light from heaven shone around Saul, and he fell; he was troubled by terror of mind and heard a voice from heaven saying: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (ibid.). For one ceases to see worldly things when one begins to hear divine things. Therefore you should not wonder at Abraham’s fear and darkness, as though they had happened to him apart from his virtue or merit, since you observe that they accord with the customary experience of prophets, when they are added in order that they may know future things.

> **Note:** [Col. 0484D] All editions, with three manuscripts, read: “when they know future things.” Five manuscripts: “when [they are] added,” etc. One must understand: fear and darkness are added, etc.

62. Immediately you have the words spoken to him: “Know certainly that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own; they shall be oppressed with servitude, harmed, and humiliated for four hundred years” (Gen. 15:13). Rightly did a great and dark terror arise, because great oracles were being conveyed when instruction was given concerning a people of the ages. How could the human mind easily grasp this, especially when it was being admonished to live as a stranger in this land? For what was being set forth was not so much what would happen as what we ought to do: “Your seed,” he says, “shall be a stranger”—either because all human beings ought to be strangers in this land, since Abraham is the father of all; or because the true seed of Abraham lives as a stranger in this world.

For that is the true seed of which it was said: “In Isaac shall your seed be called” (Gen. 21:12). Thus the one who recognized himself as Abraham’s heir says: “I am a stranger and a sojourner in this land, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 38:13). Whoever is a stranger here is a citizen in heaven; but whoever thinks that all his soul’s substance must be established in this land, and rejoices that this earth’s inheritance is to be acquired for himself, will be excluded from God’s kingdom.

> **Note:** [Col. 0485D] Roman edition: “thinks it is to be acquired for himself.” All the others, with all the manuscripts: “… rejoices.” The sense may be: he rejoices that it is to be acquired for him, etc.

Therefore the Apostle says to believing men, citizens of that Jerusalem which is in heaven and children of the Church: “You are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. 2:19). This land, then, is not ours—the land concerning which the ruler of this world can say, while displaying all the kingdoms of the earth: “I will give you this authority, if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:8). All things will belong to those who claim for themselves what is another’s and oppress the people of God with servitude, attempting to harm his servants and humiliate God’s saints.

Indeed, the Son of God himself thought that he ought to claim nothing from this world; hence he says: “The ruler of this world is coming, and in me he will find nothing” (John 14:30). Different masters desire to hold us in slavery: the devil attacks us; his angels harass us; the passions and movements of the body, like household and internal enemies, disturb us. Without are battles; within, fears. Without are battles; within, desires. For the substance of the inner body is alien to the purity of the heart; and therefore it attacks, or at least resists. Thus there is daily warfare, and a grievous battle within the same camp, until the merciful God judges the devil and his ministers, quenches the passions, subjects them to the diligent mind, and calls our souls to account against all those responsible for our offense and danger—he who says: “I will require the blood of your souls at the hands of every beast” (Gen. 9:5). And John saw and said: “Death and Hades were cast into the lake of fire” (Rev. 20:15).

> **Note:** [Col. 0485D] The Roman edition alone reads: “to the diligent mind. And the nation whom they shall serve I will judge, says the Lord. He will require,” etc. A few lines later: “into the lake of fire. After these things they shall return here with abundant possessions. Therefore,” etc.

63. Thus the righteous will depart, leaving nothing of their own in this land, lest their spoils remain with the inhabitants and possessors of this land.

> **Note:** [Col. 0485D] All editions, with three manuscripts: “Although these vessels will depart from this land,” etc.—incorrectly. On the authority of four manuscripts, we give a sounder text.

They will depart from this Egypt in such a manner that they carry away with them, and despoil the Egyptians of, the vessels which they borrowed from the Egyptians (Exod. 12:35–36), whether gold or silver vessels, to use for a time. They received these vessels by the Lord’s will and carry them away with them, because they are children of the resurrection, to whom it is said: “Not a hair of your head shall perish” (Luke 21:18). The Egyptians gave these vessels, which were taken from the land of affliction. Some are gold and some silver, because every creature of God is good, and above all the human being, the most excellent creature on earth, whom God honored by breathing into his face the spirit of life and setting him over all living creatures.

These are the vessels of which the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7). This is the garment of the Egyptians with which our soul is clothed, so that it may depart from here richer and be released from that in which it labored grievously here. For not only every creature groans and labors in childbirth, but we ourselves as well, until the redemption of our body comes. The Lord has care for his work; he has regard, in most things, for nature’s readiness for reason and goodwill.

> **Note:** [Col. 0485D] Thus all the manuscripts and old editions, except that where ours read “for reason,” the Vatican manuscript with the edition reads “for prayer.” In both cases “care” must be understood after “has.” But the Roman edition reads: “he has regard for his own nature in most things, for reason,” etc.

For we do not allow trees to be cut down and perish, whose fruitfulness first bursts forth for us in their earliest fruits, if in later age wind strips them, the sun scorches them, or their strength and substance, sufficient and able to supply moisture in drought, fails.

> **Note:** [Col. 0486D] We retain this reading, found in three manuscripts and all editions, because no better one presents itself. The Corbie, Longpont, Colbert, and Mazarin manuscripts read: “if the sun scorches; but [they are] to be examined by better ears; so that the strength sufficient and able to supply [them] in droughts fails—your substance fails, the substance of the soul fails.” The Colbert and Mazarin manuscripts read *desiccat* (“dries up”) for the first *deficiat* (“fails”). These readings are clearly faulty and differ so greatly from later manuscripts and editions that neither seems genuine. If anyone obtains the true reading, let him not begrudge it to the public good.

But we defer them for examination by better judges. Therefore the Lord our God, the rewarder of good will, considering even the earliest offspring and disposition, permits the whole inheritance of our soul to be gathered and preserved, to be tested by the temperate season of the coming age.

> **Note:** [Col. 0486D] All editions and three manuscripts read “of the first future disposition,” as also a few lines above, “our future things burst forth.” But four manuscripts of better quality restore the passage.

64. Therefore, mindful of his gift—which he willed to be immortal for the righteous, had not grave fault intervened, making it inexpedient for human beings to live long—he says to Abraham: “But you shall go to your fathers in peace, nourished in a good old age” (Gen. 15:15).

> **Note:** [Col. 0486D] Roman edition: “to live long. He permits us to depart,” omitting the intervening words.

He permits us to depart from this age, so that through the soul’s withdrawal this body may be dissolved into its own earth and sin may come to an end; then, through resurrection, it may be restored by the grace of divine generosity. Therefore he says to Abraham: “You shall go to your fathers.” Some have thought that the fathers are the elements of which our flesh consists while we live and into which we are dissolved. But we, who remember that Jerusalem above is our mother, the free woman, “the mother of us all,” as the Apostle says (Gal. 4:26), maintain that the fathers are those who preceded us in the merit and order of life. There were Abel, the devout victim; holy and devout Enoch; and Noah. Passage to them is promised to Abraham.

For one passes over when, departing from this life, one migrates to the other life in which the mind of the wise and righteous man lives—the man who is nourished in peace. For the foolish person is nourished in war and discord; the righteous person lives in a good old age. He did not say “long,” but “good” (Gen. 15:15), because the righteous person grows old well; but no unrighteous person does so, even though he lives a longer life than long-lived stags. For long life is common to wise and foolish alike; but good life is distinctive of the wise person, “whose old age is venerable, and whose mature age is an unstained life”—“not long,” he says (Wis. 4:8 ff.), “nor reckoned by number of years, nor by gray hairs upon the head, but by understanding.” Therefore that person grows old well who has understood well.

65. “But in the fourth generation they shall return” (Gen. 15:16). The historical sense appears to apply to the Jews, who went down into Egypt and came out of Egypt. For they spent four hundred and thirty years there; but not all lived a hundred years and more, as Moses or Joshua son of Nun did, so that the time of a fourth generation might correspond. Therefore let us seek rather some mystical meaning, because the tetrad is suited to all numbers and is a kind of root and foundation of the decade, as also the middle of the hebdomad.

Thus the ninety-third Psalm is inscribed “for the fourth day of the Sabbath,” because this number is the middle of those before and after it. Three precede it—the first, second, and third—and three follow it—the fifth, sixth, and seventh. Whoever sings this psalm passes through the life of this world, as it were, in well-proportioned numbers: square, stable, and perfect. The Gospel is full and perfect in four books. The mystical living creatures are four. The regions of this world are likewise four, from which the children of the Church, coming from East and West, North and South, extended Christ’s most holy kingdom. Thus the holy Church rose with four-sided breadth.

The decade also arises from this number. If you join together one through four, you make ten in this way. Count one; add two to it, making three; add three to three, making six; and add four to six, making ten. Thus the tetrad makes ten, and the decade encompasses every number. There are also four ages of the human being: childhood, adolescence, youth, and maturity. It gradually rises and is established. Thus the highest wisdom of prudence comes in the fourth order of ages. Rightly, then, even if someone was formerly under the king of Egypt, he goes forth from that ruler’s power with more mature counsel and recognizes that he must follow the law. Then the sea of this life becomes passable to him.

A similar principle applies to things generated from soil. When seed has been sown, it is dissolved in the earth; first it puts forth a root, then sprouts, the fruit is formed, and afterward ripens. Trees themselves likewise first bear fruit; then the fruit itself grows, changes color with the passage of time, and is completed in the fourth stage—that is, the final one.
