Thus, in this land of affliction, let us flee from making bricks; instead, let us call forth the Lord’s mercy with tears and groaning, that he may send us Moses and Aaron—that is, the law and the priest; but that true Priest and chief of priests, who, though he lived among human beings, was called: “Behold, the spirit before our face, Christ the Lord” (Lam. 4:20). May he free us from the land of Egypt, that we may celebrate the Lord’s Passover.

Let us bear the fruit of faith from childhood itself, increase it in adolescence, bring it to color in youth, and complete it in old age. For now the axe has been placed at the root of the tree, so that whoever acts may bear fruit. May the reaper find our harvest fully grown and ripe, that he may store mature fruits in granaries, lest winter overtake them unripe, wind shake them down, or rain spoil them.

66. Yet I think that the middle time is signified more particularly: the period between the Lord’s first coming and his second coming, which will be the day of judgment. For this reason a great fear came upon such a man at the setting of the sun: because, with the world already setting, the sacrifice by which the world would be redeemed was being declared—the sacrifice of faith, which would not be divided among Abraham’s children. For those who divide it are not Abraham’s children.

Faith is compared with the kingdom of heaven: “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed …” (Matt. 13:31). And: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant” (ibid., 45–46) who bought a field and found in it a precious pearl. The kingdom of heaven is undivided, because the kingdom of the Trinity is one. Therefore it is perpetual and eternal, because it is undivided; for every divided kingdom will easily be destroyed.

After that sacrifice, chastity too, consecrated to the Trinity, would be an offering; the heifer as well, for labors, because it is a priestly victim; the goat, because it is an offering for sins; and the ram, because it is for the whole world and for the very aerial beings or heavenly beings—not only for human beings, nor only for lambs, but also for goats, which it strips of the stench of sinful generation.

> **Note:** [Col. 0487D] The Colbert, Longpont, Corbie, and Mazarin manuscripts read “for the aerial beings,” not badly. For since above, chapter 8, §50, Ambrose wrote that air is signified by the ram, he may have designated angels by this term; hence he added “or heavenly beings.” For, as Philo—an author very familiar to him—relates in *On the Giants*, “souls are creatures flying through the air” (*ψυχαὶ δέ εἰσι κατὰ τὸν ἀέρα πετόμεναι*). He has two passages similar to these in *On the Confusion of Tongues*.

The oracle testifies that Abraham’s children are still to be in the land of affliction, so that they may prove themselves in the contest of many grave struggles; and thus, with abundant possessions and rich spoils of gold and silver vessels, souls may go forth and return, possessing precious bodies, filled with the treasure of possessions of diverse virtues and especially chastity, and may receive at Christ’s judgment vengeance upon the devil and his ministers and all others who wished to harm them. Then even the righteous will have great fear. For no one is without sin. All will have something to fear, because sins will have reached their fullness. And “where sin abounded, grace will abound still more.”

> **Note:** [Col. 0488D] The same manuscripts: “as sin abounds … grace abounds still more.”

67. Again, when the sun was already near setting, a flame appeared; and behold, a smoking furnace and lamps of fire passed through the midst of those divided pieces (Gen. 15:17). Even if there were doubt about what precedes, what follows would confirm it. For we read that a flame appeared at sunset, to illuminate the evening times of the world, shine in darkness, and reveal hidden things. Thus immediately afterward a smoking furnace was seen. By its likeness human life seems to be represented: entangled and wrapped up in the wickednesses of this age, lacking the brightness of true splendor and the radiance of sincere light.

Within, like a furnace, it burns with diverse desires and breathes with certain fires of longing; without, it is woven about, as it were, with smoke, so that it may not see the face of truth. Thus the eyes of the soul are shadowed and covered by a certain mist, so that the mind’s sight is confused by a mass, as it were, of smoky cloud and cannot behold matters in their purity—until the Lord Jesus directs the heavenly lamps, that is, the radiance of his glory. “They will not need,” he says, “the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, because the Lord himself will be light to all” (Rev. 22:5); and he himself will illuminate all things in this world whose division was recognized above and is now revealed in light. No longer through a mirror in an enigma, nor in part, but face to face, the solidity of truth and that which is perfect will be able to be seen.

## Chapter X

When it is said, “To your seed I will give this land,” true blessedness is promised to Abraham; yet the Church is more particularly prefigured, its type expressed in barren Sarah, while the Synagogue and heresies are expressed in the handmaid Hagar. What watchfulness the wise person ought to maintain; and what God promises Abraham in the words, “I will increase you exceedingly,” and so forth.

68. After these things followed the oracle of God, saying: “To your seed I will give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates” (Gen. 15:18). He who had shown future glory ought also to promise the rewards of virtue to be bestowed. For he is both helper of those who labor and rewarder of the innocent. Here Egypt is the name not of a region but of a river. For the ancients called the Nile by this name, whether because it gave its name to the region or received the region’s designation. The Greek poet also testifies that this is so, saying:

> “I stationed my ships, winding them round, in the river Egypt.”  
> (*Odyssey*, 14)

It is narrow and worthless to suppose that he promised earthly things through heavenly signs. Let us therefore consider whether perhaps he promised perfect blessedness and the completion of good merits. Perfect blessedness seems to consist of these three things: goods of body, soul, and external or incidental goods, which the Greeks called *enonta* (*ἐνόντα*, “things present”). Thus, for the body, there are chastity, endurance, and temperance; for the soul, prudence and justice.

The river Egypt, therefore, seems to signify bodily matters. Thus the same river is called Geon [Gihon] (Gen. 2:13), because the human being was formed from earth. But the Euphrates signifies the things of the soul, because justice is the fountain of the other virtues and illuminates those other virtues. Prudence without justice causes harm; courage likewise, unless justice moderates it, is intolerable arrogance, closer to madness than reason and to domination than liberty. Sobriety and temperance are private goods, of no use unless you cultivate piety with a mind of just reverence toward God and faith. Justice alone encompasses all virtues and commends them all.

> **Note:** [Col. 0489D] Here and in *On Paradise*, chapter 3, §14, Ambrose teaches that the Nile is the same as Geon [Gihon], which Scripture reports flows from the earthly Paradise. Although this opinion is more common among the Fathers, some reject it. See Petavius, *Animadversions on Epiphanius*; Scaliger, *On the Emendation of Time*; and others.

> **Note:** [Col. 0490D] Some manuscripts and certain older editions read “and of no one’s force,” which later editors emended to “and of no force.” But although the emendation is not without meaning, the better manuscripts give our reading in the same number of letters, though with the words joined in such a way that an error in reading them was easy. Hence arose the corruption in later manuscripts and editions.

Incidental goods are also commerce, trade, and agriculture—the fitting gains of labor and rural work. There are also bodily incidentals: healthfulness, the convenience of health, beauty, and strength, which occur according to time and change with age.

69. Do not think this threefold grace insignificant. For you have perfect perfection in the Gospel. When the Lord Jesus says to that teacher of the law, “You shall love the Lord your God” (Matt. 22:37), he commands the justice of the soul to be maintained. If it is just to honor parents, how much more ought honor to be rendered to the Parent of all? Again, when he says, “You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness” (Matt. 19:18), he admonishes us to preserve the virtues of the body. But when he says later:

> “There is no one who leaves house, or parents, or wife, or children for the kingdom of God and does not receive sevenfold now in this time, and in the age to come shall possess eternal life” (Luke 18:29–30),

does he not promise increases of incidental goods together with the reward of soul and body?

> **Note:** [Col. 0490D] This passage occurs somewhat differently in the Bibles, but Cyprian cites it four times in these same words. See *To Quirinus*, book 3, chapter 16.

70. What sacred Scripture expresses in simple words, Aristotle (*Ethics*, book 1, chapter 8) and the Peripatetics proclaim and exalt in lofty, tragic style. They also testify that it is a Pythagorean doctrine. But who among them equaled Abraham in time? Who equaled in authority and wisdom the Lord, by whose oracle Abraham recognizes the gift of this threefold grace?

71. Foreign nations are given to him, as it were, for training, so that the mind most observant of justice may cut off vices and correct errors. Yet the mystery of the Church is more clearly declared: through his apostles, who are Israelites, whose are the fathers and from whose fathers Christ, according to the flesh, was made under the law, the Church was to be gathered from believing peoples of the nations.

> **Note:** [Col. 0491D] Old editions: “a people of the nations about to believe.” A few verses later, the same editions: “she was barren, which pertains to the Church,” etc. The Corbie, Longpont, Colbert, and Mazarin manuscripts restored both passages for us.

He signified them not idly by the number ten, but to show that those formerly faithless, when they had fulfilled the measure of piety, would certainly obtain the crown of faith.

> **Note:** [Col. 0491D] Roman manuscript Mazarin: “would be perfected.”

72. Then follows the statement that Sarah, Abraham’s wife, was barren (Gen. 16:1); but she had an Egyptian handmaid whose name was Hagar. In the exposition that we wrote concerning moral matters, we taught by apostolic examples that this refers to the Church (*On Abraham*, book 1, chapter 4). For the Church appears barren in this age because she does not bring forth worldly or present things, but future things—that is, not things which are seen. Her handmaid is the Synagogue, or all heresies, which create slaves rather than free persons. Therefore Hagar is called “dwelling.” For she cherishes hope in what is temporal and does not possess the grace of an enduring inheritance. Therefore, lest her handmaid become insolent through bodily childbirth and claim the Church’s right for herself, it is said there: “Cast out the handmaid and her son; for the son of the handmaid shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. 21:10).

73. Yet in each individual there is Sarah, and in each there is Hagar. Sarah is true virtue and true wisdom; Hagar is cunning, as the handmaid of a more perfect virtue. For spiritual wisdom is one thing, and the wisdom of this world another. Hence she is also described as Egyptian, because philosophical learning flourished in Egypt. Thus Moses too was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, but rejected it, preferring reproach for Christ’s name to Egypt’s treasures. For if he had judged that wisdom to have any weight, he certainly would not have said: “I beseech you, Lord, I am not worthy from yesterday and the day before yesterday, nor from the time you began to speak to your servant; for I am of feeble speech and a slower tongue” (Exod. 4:10). Accordingly, as though to one untaught, the answer came that he would be taught by the Lord: “I will open your mouth and instruct you what you must say” (ibid., 12).

74. The mystery is splendid: the law was not sufficiently full to persuade peoples and summon the nations, or rather it was closed until Christ’s coming. By expounding prophetic oracles to us and bringing forth the testimonies of the Old Reading, he opened, as it were, the mouth of the law, so that the cry of faith might reach the whole world. Therefore Sarah says mystically: “The Lord has shut me up, that I may not bear; go in, then, to my handmaid, and you shall make a son from her” (Gen. 16:2). From this you may recognize that God’s Church has always existed in predestination, with fruitfulness of faith prepared when the Lord should command it to burst forth, but by the Lord’s will reserved for a definite time. Thus it is written: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and in a day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. 49:8).

We observe, therefore, that the Church’s faith was hastening, but its fruitfulness was shut up. This word demonstrates that it awaited the times of its childbirth, because what has been shut up is accustomed to be opened. The Apostle teaches you why it was shut up, saying: “For God shut up all things in unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all …” (Rom. 11:32), so that grace might belong “not to the one willing nor to the one running, but to God who has mercy” (Rom. 9:16), lest you justify yourself but attribute all things to God who called you.

Therefore let no one be sluggish or offer his own laziness as an excuse for believing later, because it is written that it belongs not to the one willing or running. For consider what was added: “but,” he says, “to God who has mercy.” Therefore present yourself in good pursuits and ready faith, that God may have mercy upon you and call you as he called the Church, saying: “I was openly found by those who did not seek me; I appeared to those who did not ask about me” (Isa. 65:1).

> **Note:** [Col. 0491D–0492D] Old editions, with the Colbert, Tornacensis, Vallicellian, and Mazarin manuscripts: “I was found by those seeking me”; later editions: “I was found by those not seeking me.” Both, with the same manuscripts, continue: “… who did not.” Better are the Corbie and Longpont manuscripts: “I was found by those not seeking me,” with which the Colbert and Mazarin manuscripts read: “who did not ask about me,” etc.

75. And rightly the inferior things were set beforehand, so that better things might follow. The handmaid bore slaves, so that the Church might make them free and call peoples from slavery to freedom, from fault to innocence, and from offense to grace. If you consider the order of individual persons as well, not all began with perfect things, nor is perfection first in time for everyone; rather, perfect virtue is older in merit. It belongs, therefore, to a prudent mind to consider, while the soul remains imperfect, what courses are available to it, so that it may exercise itself at least later in the disciplines of virtue until it gains strength by habitual practice. But when it has stripped itself of the coverings of error and untangled itself from every offense, displaying its complete purification, then let it strive in its proper order to bring forth great offspring.

76. Moreover Abraham is told: “Be without reproach” (Gen. 17:1). He was given the holy spirit of wisdom: whole, readily moved, unstained. The soul of the wise man must therefore set a watch in unceasing exercise day and night, never yielding to sleep, intent through continual wakefulness upon God, in order to comprehend the things that are and gain knowledge of their individual causes. Wisdom is also the interpreter of future things: it knows things past and judges concerning things to come. It knows the subtleties of words and the solutions of arguments. It knows signs and wonders before they happen, and the outcomes of times and ages. Therefore one who has acquired this cannot fail to be good and perfect, because he possesses every virtue and is an image of goodness. Hence the sophists of this age derived their definition: that the wise man is good and skilled in speech.

77. Let us now return to God’s gift, than which nothing is fuller. For what is better than wisdom? What worse than vanity? What more ruinous than superstition? Therefore, as though to one to whom he had promised the fullness of perfection, he says: “I will increase you exceedingly, I will make you into nations, and kings shall come from you” (Gen. 17:6). For the whole world is wealth to the faithful person, and he is increased rather than diminished, unlike the fool.

> **Note:** [Col. 0493D] Thus the Corbie, Longpont, Colbert, and Mazarin manuscripts. Others and the old editions: “because he who is his”; but the Roman edition: “because he who is of that kind.”

Abraham is made into nations—that is, his faith is transferred to the nations—and kings of the world believe and subject themselves to the Lord Jesus, of whom it is said: “Kings shall offer you gifts” (Ps. 67:30). Nor is it absurd that from Abraham’s race there will be kings not only in rank, but also those kings who do not serve sin, whom evil does not conquer, and over whom death has no dominion.

We have also recognized that the inventions of a good mind are kings and rulers. Like Abraham, it does not have the produce of an ordinary lineage, but abounds in royal things. To it the land is given as a possession: that it may rule the body and not be captive to carnal pleasures, but that the flesh, as though bound by due service, may serve the mind. In the person of Abraham, however, there is an evident mystery of the Church, which has possessed the whole world through faith’s inheritance and is rightly called the father of election, the father of faith, and the father of devout confession.

## Chapter XI

What the command of circumcision given to Abraham signifies; what destruction was threatened even to infants not circumcised on the eighth day; one letter is added to Sarah’s name; Abraham falls upon his face and laughs—whether he too doubted; the Lord assents to him as he prays for Ishmael and promises him a son by Sarah.

78. And because he is called to perfection, he receives the oracle of perfection: “You shall circumcise every male among you, and you shall circumcise your flesh” (Gen. [Col. 0493C] XVII, 10–11). Now spiritual circumcision is perfect circumcision. Indeed, the reading itself teaches this when it says: “Circumcise the hardness of your heart” (Deut. X, 16). And here most understand it in this sense: “You shall circumcise every male among you,” that is, your mind; for nothing is stronger than the mind. Then, since the male is also called holy: “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exod. XIII, 12). But what is holier than the mind, which gives the seeds of good thoughts, by which it opens the womb of the soul, shut up by barrenness from giving birth, so that it may bring forth those invisible generations from that spiritual womb of which Isaiah says: “We conceived in the womb and gave birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isa. XVI, 18)?

Therefore an intelligible circumcision of the heart and a perceptible circumcision [Col. 0493D] of the flesh are commanded. The former is in reality; the latter, in a sign. Thus circumcision is twofold, because abstinence is required both of soul and body. The Egyptians, accordingly, circumcise males in their fourteenth year; and women among them are said to be circumcised in the same year, since from that year the male passion evidently begins to burn and women’s monthly courses begin.

> [Note: The manuscripts cited above: “the passion of male impulse and women’s monthly courses (that is, passion) take their beginning”—not incorrectly.]

But the giver of the eternal Law requires the sign of carnal circumcision only in males, because for intercourse the man is more vehement than the woman; and therefore He wished to restrain his impulse by the sign of circumcision. Or because men believe that they do not go astray unlawfully if only they abstain from adultery; while they suppose that relations with prostitutes fall under the law of nature, although outside marriage it is lawful neither for a man nor for a woman to unite with another.

Yet a deeper interpretation discloses this: if the mind has been cleansed and circumcised, stripped of superfluous pleasures and thoughts, it restrains the soul to its own chastity and, suffused with pure perceptions, makes it productive of good births.

79. The Law commands that a boy be circumcised on the eighth day, certainly by a mystical precept, because this is the day of resurrection; for the Lord Jesus rose on the Lord’s Day. Therefore, if the day of resurrection finds us circumcised and stripped of the excesses of sins, washed clean of every defilement, and pure from bodily vices, then, if you depart this world clean, you shall rise clean. Circumcise yourself, then, not in the flesh, but from the vice of the flesh. And circumcise not only your home-born servant, but also the one bought with a price.

If you refer these matters severally, home-born servants are natural impulses; those bought with a price are impulses acquired by reason and instruction. But both sorts, like young shoots, need the pruning and cutting away of luxury, lest they wander like barren branches and overshadow fruitful ones while themselves useless. Like some [thing] swollen with every vice, it labours fruitlessly in many ways.

> [Note: The words here, from “labours” to “mystery,” were lacking in the editions; all the Gallican manuscripts supplied them. The gap was not obscure, and might plausibly have been filled by adding “vine” or something similar after the preceding words “labours fruitlessly.”]

Thus we must take care that our own mind too, occupied with too many things, does not merely produce good offspring but also degenerate into many useless ones; and that the vine, once pruned, does not readily run wild, quickly become unbound, and fail to be reserved for posterity. For even people of talent bring forth many things which it is useful to circumcise; and those who have acquired learning through diligence ought to discern ignorance within themselves.

But the meaning of the mystery is clear. The home-born are the Jews; those bought with a price are the Gentiles who have believed, because the Church was redeemed by the price of Christ’s blood. Therefore both Jew and Greek, and whoever has believed, ought to know that he must circumcise himself from sins, so that he may be saved. Both the household member and the foreigner, both righteous person and sinner, must be circumcised by the remission of sins, so that sin may no longer work; for no one ascends into the kingdom of heaven except through the sacrament of baptism. Nor will the righteousness of an earlier time avail one who abandons righteousness at the end of life. Therefore Paul says: “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men.” For these are opposites: slavery is contracted through sin, and by a price sin is remitted.

80. We think that this simple exposition is sufficient for understanding. Therefore we do not vainly take pains to investigate the cubes of geometry, the square number of philosophy, or the Pythagorean “confession,” as they call it, nor the numbers of the seven, whom they call ever-virgins; nor do we fashion the world by a ray, seek heaven in dust, or enclose the universe within narrow counting-boards. Rather, we disclose the true mysteries: that Christ’s resurrection is the one salvation. Let us therefore be planted together in the likeness of His death, that we may deserve fellowship in His resurrection. And let our old man be crucified with Him, so that the body of sin may be destroyed.

> [Note: Erasmus, Gillot, and the Roman edition read “quaternion”; all other editions and the manuscripts read “confession,” but in the same sense. For the word here denotes that Pythagorean oath concerning which Plutarch writes in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book I [Col. 0495C]:
>
> “Therefore the Pythagoreans would pronounce, as though the tetrad were a great oath:
>
> ‘No, by him who has bestowed upon our soul the tetractys,
> the fountain and roots possessing ever-flowing nature.’
>
> That is: “For this reason the Pythagoreans, as though the tetrad were a great oath, declared: ‘No, by him who gives our soul the tetrad, possessing the fountain and roots of eternal nature.’”
>
> An oath is called a “confession” because by it we profess and testify that divinity is everywhere present. They swore by the tetrad because, although they assigned great importance to all numbers, they considered four to have the greatest importance. Plutarch gives the reason in the same passage: they believed that our soul was composed from the tetrad. Consult him also in *On the Generation of the Soul*. Nor is the view without plausibility that some hold: that Pythagoras by his *tetractys* understood the very four-lettered name of God, the *tetragrammaton*. See Johannes Gerardus Vossius, *On the Sects of Philosophers*, Book I, chapter 6. Further, Ambrose’s statement that the seven was called ever-virgin appears to have been taken from Philo’s *On the Number Seven*, B. But it is enough to have identified the passage.]

> [Note: Thus four manuscripts of better authority. Others and the editions read: “Nor do we form the rays of the sun.”]

81. The Law fittingly commands that males, including home-born servants, be circumcised in the first cries of infancy; for just as there is sin from infancy, so there is circumcision from infancy. No time ought to be without protection, because none is without fault. Even an infant must be recalled from [Col. 0495B] sin, lest he be stained by contact with idolatry, grow accustomed to worship an idol and kiss an image, violate his parent’s nest, and injure filial devotion.

> [Note: “To violate the nest” means the marriage-bed, as in Job XXIX, 18: “I shall die in my nest,” that is, “in my bed.”]

At the same time, lest anyone be puffed up because he considers himself righteous, Abraham is commanded to be circumcised at an advanced age. Thus neither an elderly proselyte nor a home-born infant is excluded, because every age is subject to sin and therefore every age is fit for the sacrament.

> [Note: Thus the Corbie, Longpont, Tournai, and Valcian manuscripts. Erasmus, Gillot, and certain Paris editions read: “as circumcision from infancy, so also disease.” The Paris edition of 1661 reads: “disease from infancy, so also circumcision.” Since neither “disease” nor “sin” is found in the Ambrosian, Colbert, or Mazarin manuscripts, this variation seems to have arisen from that fact.]

82. “And my covenant,” He says, “shall be in your flesh” (Gen. XVII, 13). Perhaps someone may object here: How do you call circumcision spiritual when the oracle says, “The covenant of circumcision shall be in your flesh”? As though self-restraint were required only of the soul and not also of bodily passions. For a certain chastity is required of sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch, and even speech itself. An excessively forward look carries guilt; and therefore it is written: “Do not gaze upon a deceitful woman, lest you be caught by your eyes and carried away by your eyelids” (Prov. V, 2). There is guilt in hearing itself if a harlot seduces you and binds you with the abundant flattery of her speech and the snares of her lips. There is guilt in touch itself; therefore it is said to you: “Do not be excessive with another man’s woman, nor be held fast in the embraces of one who is not yours” (ibid., 20).

> [Note: The Roman edition and some Paris editions read, “nor be held fast in the embraces of one who is not yours.” This is certainly what the Septuagint reads: *mēde synechou ankalaïs tēs mē idias* (“nor be held fast in the embraces of one not your own”); nor does the Vulgate depart very far from this reading—consult it. But it would be rash to depart from all manuscripts and early editions.]

There is fault in speech as well. For one’s own lips are a very strong snare to a person, and he is led away by the lips of his own mouth. “Do not eat too much honey, lest you vomit.” Therefore there must be a keen moderation of all the senses, lest either impulse draw one into vice, excess cause harm, or delay become an occasion of stumbling.

83. Not idly or superfluously, however, many seem to be troubled by the following passage: Did the Lord really say this: “Because the uncircumcised male, who has not circumcised the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day, that soul shall perish from its people, because he has broken my covenant” (Gen. XVII, 14)? For it seems severe that a parent’s negligence should be to the disadvantage of an eight-day-old infant, so that his soul should perish, when the Law itself prescribed cities for even a homicide—provided that he had not committed the act of killing a human being deliberately—to which he might flee and thereby deserve immunity from blood-guilt (Josh. XX, 2–3). How, then, is account taken there of an accidental killing, while here no account is taken of infancy, in which there could have been no fault either of negligence or of will? Unless perhaps some think that parents are punished more severely through the death of their child. But it seems unjust that the penalty due to the guilty should be inflicted to the harm of the innocent, or that an innocent person should be punished on account of the guilty person’s penalty, or become a partner in punishment when he is unequal in deserving it.

For this reason some think that the text speaks of the parent who is to be cut off, so that his soul, not the little child’s, perishes. But this is highly ambiguous, although the assertion is supported by the words, “because he has broken my covenant.” Thus this seems to refer more to one capable of understanding than to an infant. Others think that the Lord God threatens even graver things to the parents by His silence, so that their elders may fear more, when not even the infant is spared.

84. But to me it is sufficiently clear that this was said of each person’s mind. For we have said that the mind is denoted by the name “male,” because the force of the mind is strong, draws the soul into union with itself, and is more powerful, as though superior in sex and in masculine strength. Therefore the meaning is this: every mind that has not been circumcised from bodily excesses and cleansed by the solemn gift, so as to strip itself of passions and vices, shall perish. “Not the flesh,” He says, “shall perish; not the human being; but that soul shall perish,” because it could have been saved if it had possessed cleansing. But stripped of protection and weakened by the filth of an uncircumcised heart, it could not preserve the salvation of its kind.

Every genus appears to be immortal, just as “human being” is a genus, while “someone” is a species. “Human being” is always spoken of; “someone” is not always spoken of—indeed, no “someone” fails to exist. The one who lacks faith fails; the individual person fails, but the condition or name of human beings does not fail. Thus the sinner is led from what is enduring and harmless into what is temporal and harmful—a sinner who ought to attribute to the infancy of his mind the fact that he was heedless and intemperate or did not obtain remission of sins. For “unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 5). He makes no exception at all: not an infant, not one prevented by some necessity. Yet let them have that hidden immunity from punishments; whether they have the honour of the kingdom, I do not know.

> [Note: Since above, at no. 79, he stated categorically that no one ascends into the kingdom of heaven except through the sacrament of baptism, one might reasonably suspect that these words, and several others savouring of Pelagianism, were inserted by some heretic. Even a blind person can see how little the whole latter part of this section coheres with its first part.]

> [Note: Here “genus” is used more loosely for “species,” just as “species” is used for an individual. We interpret the statement that “someone” is not always spoken of, yet no “someone” fails to exist, as follows: in the first clause *ullus*, “someone,” denotes a definite, particular human being; in the second it does not.]

85. One letter, namely R, is also added to the name Sara, so that she is called Sarra (Gen. XVII, 15). This should, as in the preceding cases, not be measured merely by the addition of a single letter. For one letter is not God’s gift; rather, it is the power of the letter that expresses the grace of the divine gift. *Sarra* means *archē emē*, “my power,” or “the beginning of my rule,” or “of a king.” Sara in Greek is *archousa*, “she who rules” in Latin.

> [Note: Erasmus and, after him, Gillot noted that someone had inserted his trifles here, prompted apparently by the obscurity of the passage. Yet anyone who compares it with Philo’s explanation of the name Sarah in *On the Change of Names* [Col. 0498D] will gain no little light for understanding it; for it was taken from that source.]

The former is mortal; the latter immortal. The former is particular; the latter universal. For prudence is in me, chastity is in me, courage is in me, justice is in me; they govern me alone, rule over me, and are mortal. For when I die, they too are dissolved and die. But that which is called prudence in general, chastity in general, courage [Col. 0497C] and the other chief virtues—in general chief, and certain immortal queens—has power in them, the immortal governing principle. Such is the queen Church, which governs not me alone but all people.

Thus we see particularity changed into universality, a part into the whole, corruptibility into incorruptibility; and all these things certainly belong to the Church. For this is not a particular principle but a universal one, and salvation belongs not to a part but to the whole. Therefore, after these preceding matters, when a person’s own prudence has led him to this governing salvation diffused through all, in which is the fountain of wisdom and justice, generation is sought: that birth of perfect delight whose name is Isaac. For no pleasure is better than the grace of an amended conscience. From this the Epicureans derived their doctrine that pleasure is the highest good, but they assessed it more by the defilement of the body than by the sobriety of the mind.

86. What is meant by the words: “And Abraham fell upon his face and laughed” (Gen. XVII, 17)? Here also reverence is signified: he feared to offend God by unrestrained laughter, although the laughter expressed the joy of the righteous man, who rejoiced in such great promises. This was not the laughter of doubt but of belief. At the same time, all things fall before God, are changed, and pass away; that one immutable substance alone stands forever. Or perhaps Abraham also prophesied the Lord Jesus in this mystery: that through the assumption of the Lord’s body and His resurrection the grace of so great an oracle would be fulfilled. Therefore he worships, not the element earth, concerning which it is said: “Worship His footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. [Col. 0498B] XCVIII, 5). For where the body is, there also are the eagles which worshipped Him moving in the body.

87. “And he said,” it says, “in his heart: Shall a son be born to one a hundred years old, and shall Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?” (Gen. XVII, 17). The Greek has *en tē dianoia*, “in his understanding,” so that we may judge that he said to his heart as though debating with himself: “Shall a son be born to a centenarian, and shall a woman of ninety give birth?” That is, the age for begetting has passed; but all things are possible to God. Therefore it is easy even to restore to the aged their years of youth, renew their strength, and give fertility to the barren.

> [Note: The Roman edition reads “arguing”; but with the other editions and all manuscripts we must retain “debating with himself,” used in nearly the same sense by Virgil, *Aeneid* IV:
>
> “As he debated these things, this judgment seemed the stronger.”]

88. Nor should this be passed over: when the generation lawfully promised to him was announced, Abraham answered God: “May Ishmael live here before you” (Gen. XVII, 18). It is the part of a righteous person to intercede even for sinners. Therefore let the Jews believe this too: that He intercedes for them, if only they believe. For this is to live before God: to conduct affairs worthy of God’s Word; for the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.

89. Therefore the Lord says: “Yes. Behold, Sarah your wife shall bear you a son . . . But concerning Ishmael I have heard you” (ibid., 19–20). When He says “yes,” He confirms the promises; for it is a confirming word. And therefore He first confirms that the generation of the Church will come to pass, so that the Prophet might know as true what God said that He had heard concerning Ishmael, foreseeing that partial blindness would happen to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles entered, and so all Israel might be saved.

Thus, just as human testaments first name an heir and afterward specify a legacy—inheritance for those of higher rank, legacies for those of lower rank—so in the Lord’s testament, from which we too have received this custom, the heir is written as naturally good, noble, born of lawful marriage; the inferior person receives a legacy.

> [Note: The Roman edition reads “write an heir.” The other editions and all manuscripts read “name an heir.” A little later the early editions read: “Thus in God in one testament, and we,” etc. The Roman edition attempted, not inelegantly, to correct this conjecturally: “Thus God uses this in a testament, and we adopt this custom: the heir,” etc. Yet the authority of all manuscripts seemed preferable to us.]

90. But the generation is promised for the following year (ibid., 21), so that you may observe what generation the Lord promises: not that of Sarah’s bodily womb, but this birth of the Church, which was to come. Thus He says below as well: “I shall return to you in the future, and Sarah shall have a son” (Gen. XVIII, 10). In this we may understand both this assembly of the Church and the resurrection of believers.

91. The reason why Ishmael is circumcised in his thirteenth year is likewise clear: one who is beginning to make use of knowledge of a woman must first cut away within himself the ardour [Col. 0499B] of lust, so that he may abstain from superfluous unions and reserve himself only for lawful [Col. 0500A] marriage.

92. The mind of the wise person ought also to be hospitable, so that it may impart its grace to others, share with others the fruit of its prudence, and thus they may feast on the good foods of doctrine, while it offers its banquet to those who desire it.

93. Further, it should know nothing except how to live according to nature, in whose constitution and order is God’s law. It should know not to associate itself with any crooked desire, but should prefer union with wisdom alone. It should not know how to prefer the glory of this world and a certain inheritance of present praise to God’s commandments. And, as it sacrifices its own advantages upon the Lord’s altars, so it should not shrink from or dread the fire of judgment, but should labour all the more to rescue others.

[ON ISAAC AND THE SOUL.]

[Col. 0499B]

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE BOOK *ON ISAAC AND THE SOUL*

[Col. 0499]

How Saint Ambrose, in the first book *On Abraham*, disclosed to catechumens by the example of this patriarch the duties of the Christian religion which they were to profess at the Easter vigil, and in the second showed the soul, fallen through Adam’s sin, how to rise again and strive toward perfection, we have explained in our Prefatory Notice to that work. The most watchful bishop continues his established discourses and instructions; and he appears to us to have ended at once the second book of the work just mentioned, where he recounted Isaac’s birth and circumcision, for no other reason than to show that from Isaac’s marriage to Rebecca the soul of the Christian, while reborn in the font of regeneration, enters into a most close covenant of spiritual marriage with the Word who is God. This he excellently accomplishes in the present book, which for that reason he wished to entitle *On Isaac and the Soul* (chapter 1).

Indeed, after briefly showing that Isaac, both by his birth and by his death, was a figure of Christ, and Rebecca a figure of the soul, he defines the nature of that same soul and maintains that the whole human being chiefly consists in it (chapter 2). He then teaches that it is imperfect because it clings to bodily things and worldly pleasures; but that it takes its first step toward perfection if it flees these things and raises itself above their mire. Taking up the proposed argument from this point, he says that Rebecca was such when she came to Isaac, since she declares that she ardently desires the divine Word in him, crying: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth” (chapter 3).

Ambrose himself admits that this passage and all the other verses of the Song of Songs may also be applied to the Church. But since he had unfolded the same mysteries elsewhere, and especially in his exposition of Psalm CXVIII, in this book he devotes himself entirely to explaining the marriage of the soul with the Word through a continuous commentary on that mystical epithalamium. Yet do not take this to mean that he omitted no verse at all. In fact, quite a few are passed over, especially those concerning the beauty of bridegroom and bride; but they do not prevent the work from having a single coherent thread.

Moreover, in order that the work begun may advance more distinctly and in better order, the holy man sets forth and explains (chapter 6) four stages by which the soul, now freed from the yoke of graver vices, ascends to that supreme perfection in which, joined to God through charity, it is thereafter never separated from Him. Whether you consider the natural and wholly unforced arrangement of the material, his concise but penetrating way of explaining Scripture, or the elegance of the transitions by which the individual parts are most fittingly joined, you may rightly say that this treatise is such that it scarcely yields to any other work of Ambrose.

It is furthermore established that the work was called by this title not only in the age of Cassiodorus (*On Divine Institutions*, chapter 5) and Augustine (*Against Julian the Pelagian*, Book I, chapter 9, and Book II, chapter 5), but also that Ambrose himself referred to it under this title in his subsequent work. Whether these were sermons first delivered to the people and later converted into this book is less clear. For since we observe that it is almost nothing else than a brief paraphrase of the Song of Songs, its subject seems scarcely suitable to the pulpit. Nevertheless, we are led to think that the procedure was no different here than in the books *On Abraham*, both by their mutual agreement and by the instructions most suitable for the formation of hearers, which anyone may observe inserted in its exposition. This is why the senator Cassiodorus, in the passage cited, writing about those who composed works on the Song of Songs, left this judgment concerning the present little work: “Hence,” he says, “Saint Ambrose, in the third book of the *Patriarchs*, where he speaks in the person of Isaac, discussed many things wholesomely and brilliantly.”

Origen had unfolded these same Songs in ten whole volumes so admirably that Jerome did not hesitate to write of them, in his Letter to Pope Damasus: “Although in his other books he surpassed all, in the Song of Songs he surpassed himself.” It is highly probable, moreover, that this outstanding work came into Ambrose’s hands, and that the holy bishop drew some assistance from the labours of so great a man, from whom almost all the other Fathers borrowed so many and such splendid things. But because the hostility of time has begrudged us that treasure, it is not permissible to set forth anything as more certain or established.

If, however, Huet is right in contending against Erasmus and many others (*Origen*, Book III, §7) that the four homilies which survive with their preface among the works of Origen and Jerome are due to no Latin Father, but are the very beginning of Origen’s ten volumes, which Rufinus—by his usual practice—interpolated when rendering them into Latin; or if you prefer to follow the oft-cited senator, who affirms that they are nothing else (*loc. cit.*) than an expansion divided into three books, which Rufinus pieced together from two homilies composed by Origen on another occasion upon the first two chapters of the Songs, and translated into Latin by Jerome—if, we say, either view must be admitted, then by comparing these fragments of Origen with Ambrose’s treatise you will perceive that the holy doctor did not unskilfully imitate the former’s method, especially where he distinguishes and expounds the three senses of Scripture: natural, moral, and mystical. In the other little works which we have examined so far, however, he interprets only two senses, mystical and moral; although the sense which he here calls natural is there combined with the latter.

Further, both the connection of this work with the books *On Abraham* and Ambrose’s own testimony found at the beginning of the book *On Joseph*, as also of the book *On the Mysteries*, which he composed immediately after this one, lead us to assign this writing to the same date as the former books, namely about the year 387. Indeed, it is not obscure that the holy bishop addresses here the same persons whom he addressed in the preceding work. Yet it may be questioned whether this occurred before the Easter festival or afterward. The subject of the work itself, treating of that spiritual marriage than which nothing in the life of the most perfect Christians is more exalted, seems to indicate that it did not concern catechumens, from whom certain mysteries were concealed and were to be revealed later, after they had been initiated through baptism. Nevertheless, if we must determine this question from the opening words of the book *On the Mysteries*, we must say that those whom Ambrose addressed still belonged to the order of catechumens. Perhaps he himself indicates this where he says: “Easter comes, the remission of sins comes,” and so forth (chapter IV, no. 35). Yet once they had already been admitted into the number of the *competentes*—to which they were admitted only at the end of Lent—the holy bishop did not hesitate, as they stood ready for baptism, to explain to them the mysteries of this sacred union and the stages by which they might attain it.

[Col. 0501C]

# ONE BOOK OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, *ON ISAAC AND THE SOUL*

> [Note: [Col. 0501B] Written about the year 387.] (C)

[Col. 0501]

## CHAPTER I

The holy Isaac is commended both for his paternal origin and grace, and as a prefiguration of the Lord’s birth and passion; and the mystery between Christ, designated by Isaac, and the soul, represented by Rebecca, is disclosed.

[Col. 0501A]

1. In his father, the origin and grace of the holy Isaac are sufficiently expressed for us; and this redounds to his whole glory: that he was born as a reward to his father Abraham, so great and so worthy of imitation a man. Nor is it surprising, since in him the figure of the Lord’s birth and passion went before. For a barren old woman bore him by God’s promise, so that we might believe that God has power to bring it about that a virgin too might give birth; and he was an only son offered for sacrifice, who neither perished to his father nor failed to fulfil the sacrifice.

> [Note: Here the manuscripts and early editions agree, except that three manuscripts have, in place of “the origin or grace of holy Isaac is sufficiently expressed,” “to holy Isaac the origin of salvation is sufficiently expressed”; and where all manuscripts have “which redounds to his whole,” etc., the editions prefer “when he was first for the whole . . . and he himself was born as a reward to so incomparable a man.” The Roman edition pieced together the whole passage thus: “In father Abraham, the origin or grace of holy Isaac is sufficiently expressed for us, since he was born as a reward to so incomparable a man . . . and it is also wonderful that in him,” etc.]

Thus he marks both the figure and grace by the very name: Isaac means “laughter” in Latin, and laughter is the mark of joy. Who does not know that He is the joy of all, who, by overcoming the terror of dreadful death and removing sorrow, became remission of sins for all? Thus the former was named, and the latter was designated; the former was expressed, and the latter announced. He is the one whom the slave-woman was already then persecuting; He is the one for whose sake it was already said: “Cast out the slave-woman, for the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. XXI, 10). He is the one for whom the Father acquired a bride, a foreign woman. He is gentle, humble, and meek—the one who, when Rebecca, that is, patience, was approaching, went out into the field to withdraw from distractions.

> [Note: Thus all manuscripts and early editions. The Roman edition alone reads, “he went out into the field to exercise himself,” following the Septuagint, which reads: *Kai exēlthen Isaak adoleschēsai* (“And Isaac went out to meditate/converse”). But Symmachus read *lalēsai*, “to speak,” and Aquila *homilēsai*, “to converse.” See Nobilius on these words. *Abalienare*, properly, means to relax the mind by drawing it away from serious and weighty thoughts. But Ambrose, transferring the point in his customary way here and below, chapter 3, no. 6, to the spiritual sense, wishes it to mean turning away from worldly cares toward the contemplation of heavenly things. See also the Commentary on Psalm CXVIII, octonary 4, verse 3, and the Letter to Chromatius, where he says that the interpreter rendered *adoleschēin* by the Latin *hallucinari* (“to wander in thought”).]

For it is the part of the wise to separate himself from pleasures of the flesh, raise the soul, and draw it away from the body; this is to recognize oneself as human. In the Chaldean tongue this person is called Enos; in Latin, “human being.” Enos is the one who undertook and hoped to call upon God, and therefore is believed to have been translated. One does not seem, therefore, to be human unless one hopes in God. But the one who hopes in God is marked by a plain interpretation of truth as not dwelling on earth, but, as though translated, cleaving to God.

> [Note: The Roman edition reads: “He hopes in God, pleases God, is changed for the better, and does not seem to dwell . . . God. Therefore Enoch is said not to have been found because God translated him”—which is an obvious interpretation, etc. The early editions and manuscripts differ here in nothing except that where the edition and some manuscripts read “of a man,” several other and better manuscripts read “of the true man.”]

2. Therefore Isaac is good and true, as one full of grace and a fountain of joy. Rebecca came to this fountain to fill her water-jar with water. For Scripture says that, descending to the fountain, she filled the water-jar and went up (Gen. XXIV, 16). Therefore either the Church or the soul descends to the fountain of wisdom, so as to fill its whole vessel [Col. 0503B] and draw the teachings of pure wisdom—teachings which the Jews refused to draw from the flowing fountain. Listen to Him who says what this fountain is: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. II, 13).

The thirsty soul of the prophets ran to this fountain, as David also says: “My soul thirsted for the living God” (Ps. XLI, 3), so that it might satisfy its thirst through the abundance of divine knowledge and wash away the blood of folly by the watering of spiritual streams. For this is the flow of blood signified by the Law (Lev. XX, 18), which is uncovered when a man lies with a woman sitting in the days of her blood. The woman is bodily pleasure and its enticements. Therefore beware lest the vigour of your mind, bent and softened by a kind of union with bodily pleasure, be wholly dissolved in its embraces and open its fountain, which ought [Col. 0503C] to be closed and sealed by earnest attention and the consideration of reason; for “a garden enclosed is a fountain sealed” (Song IV, 12).

For when the vigour of the mind is relaxed, the perceptions of bodily pleasure pour themselves forth, exceedingly harmful and rushing into an appetite full of grave danger. If the considered guard of a vigorous mind had remained, it would have restrained them.

> [Note: Thus the more numerous and better manuscripts. The Vatican, Theodoric, and early editions read: “the bodily perceptions of destructive pleasures pour themselves out . . . rushing forth”; the Theodoric manuscript has “flowing forth.” Another Vatican manuscript, the Valcian and Tournai manuscripts, and the Roman edition read “little by little the bodily,” etc., as do the early editions.]

## CHAPTER II

What the human being is, and in what part it chiefly consists; and what the soul is like both according to its own nature and according to its irrational part, through which it becomes subject to corruption.

3. Consider, therefore, O human being, what you are, and by what means you safeguard your salvation and your life. What, then, is a human being? Is it the soul, or the flesh, or the union of both? For we ourselves are one thing, and what belongs to us another: one thing is the person clothed, another the garment. We read in the Old Testament: “All the souls that went down into Egypt” (Gen. 46:26), said of human beings. And elsewhere it is said: “My spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3). Thus in either case “human being” is applied both to soul and to flesh. But this distinction obtains: where a soul is put for a human being, a Hebrew is signified, one adhering to God rather than to the body, as in: “Every simple soul is blessed” (Prov. 11:20). But where flesh is named for a human being, a sinner is denoted, as in: “But I am carnal, sold under sin; for what I do, I do not understand. For I do not do what I wish; but what I hate, that I do” (Rom. 7:14–15). This latter passage now concerns both. For one is he who wills, another [Note: Several good manuscripts: “another thing which he hates.”] he who hates, and another he who does. Accordingly he added: “If, then, I do what I hate, I agree with the law that it is good. But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (ibid. 7:16–17). More explicitly still: “I see a law of my flesh opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin” (ibid. 7:23). Yet, although he had declared the human being to be struggling in both respects—that is, inward and outward—he preferred to locate himself in the soul rather than in the body, because it was his soul that was being led captive into sin, and it was in that soul that he preferred and affirmed that he was, saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (ibid. 7:24). As though from an alien enemy, so he longs to be delivered from the flesh.

4. The soul, then, is not blood, since blood belongs to the flesh; nor is the soul harmony, since such harmony too belongs to the flesh; nor is the soul air, since the breath-like spirit is one thing and the soul another; nor is the soul fire, nor *entelecheia* [ἐντελέχεια, actuality]. But the soul is living, because “Adam was made into a living soul” (Gen. 2:7), inasmuch as the soul gives life to and governs the insensible, lifeless body. There is also a more excellent human being, of whom it is said: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:15). This person is more excellent than the rest. Thus David also says: “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, unless you visit him?” (Ps. 8:5) … “Man has been made like vanity” (Ps. 143:4). The human being according to God’s image is not the human being of vanity; rather, the one who has lost that image, fallen into sin, and slipped away into these material things—that one is the human being of vanity.

5. The soul, therefore, according to its own nature, is excellent; but often, [Note: Thus six most reliable manuscripts, with the Roman edition. But the Vatican manuscript, the Joyeus manuscript, and the old edition read: “according to its irrational part”; Longus, Theodoret, and Valcerius: “according to its motion.” Again, at the same place, where the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus read “unto impenitence,” and the Roman edition with the Vatican, Tornesian, and Theodoret manuscripts reads “and unto desire,” other manuscripts and editions have “and unto wantonness.” Thirdly, in place of “its rational [part],” as in the Roman edition, and “its visible [part],” as in all the others and our manuscripts, the Vatican manuscript prefers “its invisible [part],” which seemed preferable to follow here. Finally, there is no small room for doubt whether one should read “and becomes more unrestrained through a lack [*defectus*],” as in most manuscripts and the Amerbach, Erasmus, and Froben editions, or “and becomes more unrestrained through defect [*defectu*],” as in others. But we judge that this makes very little difference to the sense.] through its irrational element it becomes subject to corruption, so that it inclines toward bodily pleasures and wantonness, while it does not keep the proper measure of things, or is deceived by opinion; and, bent toward matter, clings to the body. Thus its invisible part is impeded and filled with wickedness; for while it attends to wickedness, it fills itself with its vices and becomes more unrestrained through a falling-short of goodness.

## CHAPTER III

The perfected soul, having renounced earthly things and subdued vices, desires to kiss the Word; and God the Word pours himself wholly into it. Delighted by him, it asks to be drawn by him. A holy man applies all this also to the Church.

6. But the perfected soul turns away from matter: it flees and rejects every immoderate, unstable, and malignant thing; it neither sees nor approaches the corruption of any earthly defilement. It attends to divine things, but flees earthly matter. Flight, however, does not mean leaving lands, but being on earth while preserving justice and sobriety, renouncing vices rather than the use of the elements. [Note: Gratian, in the cited passage, reports Ambrose’s sense rather than his words, though he indicates that he presents them as Ambrose’s own.] Holy David fled from the face of Saul (*On Penance*, distinction 2, chapter *Ut cognoverunt*, § *Fugerat*), certainly not in order to leave the earth, but to avoid the contagion of one cruel, heedless, and faithless. Yet he fled while clinging to God, as he himself says: “My soul has clung after you” (Ps. 62:9). He withdrew and raised himself above the vices of this world; he raised his soul, as Isaac did in the field, or withdrew himself, or—as others have it—walked about. For this also shows that one has a familiar partnership with the virtues: that each person may walk in the innocence of his heart, mingle with earthly vices in no practice, traverse the blameless way with an unharmed step of mind, and open no place in himself to corruption.

7. Such was Isaac when he awaited Rebecca’s arrival, preparing himself for a spiritual union. For she was now coming, endowed with heavenly mysteries; she was coming bearing with her great ornaments for ears and hands, because the beauty of the Church excels in hearing and works. To her we rightly understand the words to have been addressed: “Be thou into thousands of thousands, and let thy seed possess the cities of its adversaries.” Beautiful, therefore, is the Church, which has acquired children from hostile nations. But this can also be applied to the soul, which subdues the passions of the body and turns them to the service of virtues, making their resisting impulses obedient to itself. Therefore either the soul of the patriarch, seeing Christ’s mystery, seeing Rebecca arriving with vessels of gold and silver, as the Church with the people of the nations, amazed at the beauty of the Word and his sacraments, says: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth” (Cant. 1:1); or Rebecca, seeing the true Isaac, that true joy, that true gladness, desires to kiss him.

8. The soul’s first advance. What then is meant by: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth”? Consider either the Church, long held in expectation through many ages by the Lord’s coming promised to her through the prophets; or the soul which, lifting itself above the body, having renounced luxury, delights, and carnal pleasures, and having also stripped itself of anxious concern for worldly vanities, has long desired for itself the infusion of the divine presence and the grace of the saving Word. Since he comes late, it wastes away and is distressed; and therefore, as though wounded by love, unable to bear his delays, it turns to the Father and asks that God the Word be sent to it, declaring why it is so impatient by saying: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.” It seeks not one kiss, but many kisses, so that it may satisfy its longing. For one who loves is not content with the sparing gift of a single kiss, but demands many, claims many, and is accustomed by this means to commend herself more fully to her beloved. Thus that woman in the Gospel was approved, because, he says, “she did not cease to kiss my feet … and therefore many sins were forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7:45, 47). So too this soul desires many kisses of the Word, that it may be enlightened by the light of divine knowledge. For this is the kiss of the Word: namely, the light of sacred knowledge. God the Word kisses us when he enlightens our heart, and the ruling faculty itself of the human being, with the spirit of divine knowledge. Then the soul, granted the pledge of nuptial love, joyful and exultant, says: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118:131). For a kiss is that by which lovers mutually cleave to one another and, as it were, obtain the sweetness of inward grace. Through this kiss the soul cleaves to God the Word, by which the spirit of the kisser is transfused into it; just as those who kiss one another are not content with a tasting of lips, but seem to pour their spirits into one another.

9. Showing, therefore, that she loves not merely the Word’s outward appearance and, as it were, his countenance, but all that is within him, she adds to the grace of the kisses: “For your breasts are good above wine, and the scent of your ointments above all spices” (Cant. 1:2). She asked for a kiss; God the Word poured himself wholly into her and uncovered his breasts to her—that is, his doctrines and the teachings of inward wisdom—and made her fragrant with the sweet scent of his ointments. Captivated by these, she says that the delight of divine knowledge is richer than the pleasure of every bodily delight. For in the Word there breathes the fragrance of grace and remission of sins; diffused throughout the whole world, it has filled all things as though by an ointment poured out, because the heavy accumulation of vices has been washed away from all.

10. “Therefore,” she says, “the young maidens loved you. Draw us, that we may run after the fragrance of your ointments” (ibid. 1:2–3). Prudence is good indeed, but mercy is sweet. Few attain the former; the latter reaches everyone. “Because of this,” she says, “your forgiveness, souls renewed in spirit love you.” Thus it is also said to the soul: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102:5). For he was addressing the soul when he said: “Bless the Lord, O my soul” (ibid. 102:1). Therefore it hastens to the Word and asks to be drawn, lest perhaps it be left behind; for the Word of God runs and is not bound. Indeed, he rejoices as a giant to run his course. And because “his going forth is from the height of heaven, and his course unto its height,” seeing herself unequal to such speed, she says: “Draw us.” Good is the soul that asks not for itself alone, but for all: “Draw us,” she says. “For we have a desire to follow, inspired by the grace of your ointments; but because we cannot equal your courses, draw us, so that, supported by your help, we may be able to follow in your footsteps.” For if you draw us, we too shall run and receive the spiritual breezes of swiftness. The burden is lifted from those whom your hand supports, and your oil is poured in—the oil by which the man wounded by robbers was healed. And lest what she says, “Draw us,” appear presumptuous to you, hear him who says: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). You see that he gladly draws us, lest we remain behind while following. But whoever wishes to be drawn, let him run [Note: Some editions and a few manuscripts: “that you may attain”; the more numerous and better manuscripts: “that you may all attain.”] that he may attain; and let him run, forgetting the things behind and seeking those before him. Thus he will be able to attain Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “So run that you may all attain” (1 Cor. 9:24). This soul too wishes to arrive at the prize, because it desires to attain it. Wisely, therefore, it asks to be drawn, because not all can follow. Thus when Peter said, “Where are you going?” the Word of God replied: “You cannot follow me now, but you shall follow afterward” (John 13:36). He had entrusted to him the keys of the kingdom of heaven, yet judged him unequal to following him. This soul, however, he did not defer, because it did not presume but asked.

## CHAPTER IV

The perfected soul is introduced into the King’s chamber. When it laments that it has been darkened by contact with the body, Christ commands it to know itself, to go out, and so forth. It is compared to Solomon’s mare. What do the wells dug by Isaac signify? How, finally, does Christ, recalled by the soul, return leaping, and how does he also lovingly address it?

11. The soul’s second advance.—Accordingly, it says: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Cant. 1:3). Blessed is the soul that enters the inner sanctuary of the Word. For rising from the body, it becomes more removed from all things, seeking and examining within itself whether it may somehow attain that divine reality. When it can grasp it, having passed beyond intelligible things, it is established in him and fed by him. Such was Paul, who knew that he had been caught up into paradise, but did not know whether he had been caught up outside the body or in the body. For his soul had risen above the body; it had drawn and lifted itself away from the entrails and bonds of flesh. Made alien to himself, he held within himself the ineffable words he heard and could not make common, because he perceived that it was not permitted for a human being to utter them. A good soul, therefore, despises visible and sensible things and does not rest or linger in contemplating them; [Note: The Roman edition and the first Paris editions following it: “nor in looking upon them.” The remaining editions, with all manuscripts except one Vatican codex, read: “nor in despising them”; the Vatican codex has: “nor in seeing them.” Yet nothing should be changed in the received reading, since *despicere* does not always mean the same as *contemnere* (“to despise”), but is also used by approved authors in the sense of *dispicere*, “to discern” or “to consider.”] rather, it ascends to the eternal, invisible things full of wonders, raising itself by the pure perception of a devout mind. Indeed, striving for perfection, it attends only to that one good of the Godhead and thinks that nothing else should be sought, because it possesses what is highest. Thus a person of this kind, in whom there is beauty of soul, is sufficient to himself alone, because he himself is enough for himself. Yet one is never alone when the Lord, his leader, is present.

12. Therefore, led into that divine secret place, it says: “Let us exult and rejoice in you, and love your breasts above wine” (Cant. 1:3). For the righteous person exults not in riches, treasures of gold and silver, the fruits of possessions, offices of power, or banquets, but in God alone. [Note: A few editions and manuscripts read: “exults in God alone”; the remainder, better: “the righteous person exults in God alone.”]

13. Yet that same soul, recognizing that it has been darkened by its association with the body, says to the other souls, or to those heavenly powers assigned to sacred ministry: “Do not look upon me because I am darkened; for the sun has not looked upon me. The sons of my mother fought against me” (ibid. 1:5). That is, the body’s passions attacked me; fleshly enticements stained me. Therefore the sun of righteousness did not shine upon me. Bereft of that protection, I could not preserve my devotion and full observance; this is what “I did not keep my vineyard” means (ibid.): I brought forth thorns rather than grapes—that is, sins instead of fruits.

14. And when it speaks of the Word, turned toward him as the Word’s radiance shines upon it, it says: “Where do you feed? Where do you rest at midday?” (ibid. 1:6). It rightly says, “Where do you feed?” because the Word of God is royal; “Where do you rest?” because this is moral; “At midday?” because this is mystical. For at noon Joseph, seated at table with his brothers, revealed mysteries of times to come. David too says: “Reveal your way to the Lord, hope in him, and he shall act; he shall bring forth your righteousness as light, and your judgment as the noonday” (Ps. 36:5). Paul himself declared that a light shone around him at noon (Acts 9:3), when he was converted from persecution to grace. The soul laments, therefore, that it has been abandoned, that it has become poor after being rich. For it had abounded in gifts of grace; but it began to lack when abundance of the divine presence was denied it. Therefore it asks to be regarded, as it were, as a hired servant, though formerly it claimed for itself the grace of a more precious union.

15. The Word of God replies: “Unless you know yourself, O beautiful among women” (Cant. 1:7)—you who complain that you have been abandoned—unless you know yourself, unless you repent of your fall, unless you approve the purpose of your devotion, unless your faith and sincerity increase, complaint will profit you nothing. Or thus: Unless you know that you are beautiful, unless you preserve the beauty of your nature, and the allurements and impediments of the body do not overwhelm or hold you back, the nobility of your better creaturely nature will not assist you. [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “the nobility of a better nature,” and so forth; but the best witnesses read “of a better creature,” and so forth.]

16. Know yourself, then, and the beauty of your nature; go forth as though your foot were stripped of its bonds and your step were bared and uncovered, so that you may not feel the coverings of the flesh, and the bodily bonds may not entangle the step of your mind, so that your foot may appear beautiful. Such are those whom the Lord chooses to proclaim the kingdom of heaven, of whom it has been said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace” (Isa. 52:7). Such was Moses, to whom it is said: “Remove the sandal from your feet” (Exod. 3:5), so that, before calling the people to God’s kingdom, he might first lay aside the garments of the flesh and walk with naked spirit and the step of his mind. This, therefore, is what he says: “Go out in the footsteps of the kings, and feed your kids in the tents of the shepherds” (Cant. 1:7). For by flocks we understand a kingdom, because it belongs to authority to preside over flocks. Each person presides over himself by a certain royal power if he restrains bodily excess within himself and reduces his flesh to servitude. Hence it is said: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21). Thus he beautifully says to the soul: “Go forth”—that is, go forth from slavery, go forth from the rule and domination of the flesh; and go forth not in flesh but in spirit; go forth to the governance of authority. Therefore he added: “Feed your kids.” Rule the things that are on your left hand, for unless they are governed, they easily slip away. Restrain [Note: The Bigotian and Ebroic manuscripts: “the wanton petulance of your body and the light motions of irrational luxury; tame them,” etc.] the petulance and lasciviousness of your body, and irrational luxury; tame their light impulses; feed them not in bodily tents but in the tents of shepherds, who know how to govern the flock. For the tents of Israel are lovely, like groves shading a river. In them the soul, as if stationed in a military camp, wages good warfare, reconnoitres hostile attacks, and seeks victory through the labour of virtue, so that it may be compared with that mare belonging to Solomon—swift to run, fit for bearing young (Cant. 1:8)—because the soul’s fruitfulness is desired and sought.

17. This mare, therefore, is precious, and Pharaoh’s chariots are swift; some refer this to the Church and the people. But we have often spoken elsewhere of this mystery, especially in the one hundred eighteenth Psalm (*Sermon 2 on Psalm 118*). In this place, however, we have undertaken to speak of the soul. This soul is judged like that mare—that is, possessed of prophetic or apostolic power—because it is counted in the flock of those who, by the fruitfulness of their preaching, filled the expanses of the whole world. Though established in the body, they suffered no loss in their spiritual course. Therefore it is praised because, illuminated by a heavenly precept, it is now comely, now beautiful: in its countenance it displays the beauty of chastity, and it lifts up the necklaces of its neck, on which are the marks of patience and humility. The true Isaac loved the beauty, humility, and patience of such a soul; therefore he eagerly sought its offspring.

18. Rebecca conceived, and by her patience untied the knot of barrenness. Let us consider what the prophetic and apostolic soul gives birth to, and how it gives birth: “She went,” it says, “to inquire of the Lord” (Gen. 25:22), because the children leaped in her womb. And she received this answer: “Two nations are in your womb” (ibid. 25:23). This is because it presumes nothing of itself, but in all things seeks the supreme God as ruler of its counsels; and, full alike of peace and piety, it binds two peoples together by its faith and preaching, enclosing them, as it were, in its womb.

19. Not without reason it is called a sister rather than a wife, because the gentle and peaceful soul receives a name denoting common piety rather than a special union, and because it judges itself bound to all rather than to one.

20. Isaac dug wells—indeed very many—which his father had dug and which, after Abraham’s death, foreigners had filled in with earth. [Note: The Roman edition: “for the wells which his father Abraham had dug, they stopped up and filled with earth … his father’s [wells].” It also inserts many passages of Scripture here and there which are found nowhere else.] Yet above all he dug these wells: one in the valley of Gerar, where he found a well of living water; and the shepherds of Gerar quarrelled with Isaac’s shepherds, because they claimed the water of that well as their own, and he called its name Injustice. He dug another well, over which a dispute arose, and he gave it the name Enmities. He dug a third, over which no strife arose among the shepherds, and he called it Breadth. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “He dug another well, and when the servants reported that they had found water in it, he called it,” etc.—not even correctly. Two manuscripts read: “He dug the well of the oath; for he found water in it and called it,” etc. The remaining manuscripts and editions agree with us; indeed, so does the authority of the Septuagint translators: see Gen. 26:32 and Nobilius’s notes there.] He also dug the Well of the Oath, and did not find water in it; and he called it the Well of the Oath.

21. Who, reading this, would judge these to be earthly rather than spiritual works: that Abraham dug wells, or Isaac—such great patriarchs—or even Jacob, as we find in the Gospel (John 4:12), like certain fountains of the human race, and particularly of devotion and faith? For what is a well of living water but the deep height of doctrine? Thus Hagar saw an angel at a well; Jacob found Rachel as his wife at a well; and Moses too, beside a well, first established the merits of his future marriage.

22. Beginning from the well of vision, Isaac opened wells, and in good order, so that the water of that well might first wash and refresh the rational part of the soul and its eye, making its sight clearer. He also dug many other wells. Hence it is written: “Drink water from your own vessels and from the springs of your own wells” (Prov. 5:15). The more numerous they are, the richer is the overflowing abundance of graces. Yet he dug the well which his father Abraham had dug, concerning which the shepherds of Gerar—that is, “the wall”—quarrelled. For where there is a wall, there is division among opponents; there is injustice; and therefore he called it Injustice. He dug another also, and, when dissension arose, called it Enmities. In these wells moral doctrine seems to shine forth, because when the dividing wall is removed, the enmities in human flesh are dissolved, and the two are made one—in figure through Isaac, in truth through Christ. Rightly, therefore, pure water was afterwards found in that well, as moral doctrine useful for drawing water. What else, moreover, does the Well of Breadth signify but instruction concerning natural things? For this reason it is called Breadth: because one who has passed beyond these worldly and sensible things is now quiet and secure, without contention or dispute. Hence, when hostile and foreign thoughts have now been overcome—for what is so foreign as all worldly things, which cannot be everlasting?—the wise person can say: “The Lord has made room for us and increased us upon the earth” (Gen. 26:22), because he has transcended earthly things. Last is the Well of the Oath, in which God appeared to him and said: [Note: The Roman edition: “I am the God of Abraham your father; do not fear.”] “Do not fear, for I am with you” (ibid. 26:24). And he blessed him. This doctrine is now mystical.

23. You have these things in Solomon: his Proverbs are moral; Ecclesiastes is natural, in which he seems to despise the vanities of this world; his Song of Songs is mystical. You have them also in the prophet: “Sow for yourselves unto righteousness, reap unto the fruit of life, enlighten yourselves with the light of knowledge” (Hos. 10:12).
