For this is the light of knowledge: to possess the perfection of love. Hence it is said: “Do not fear,” for love casts fear out. And that we may know that Solomon too interpreted these wells in this way, referring them to moral, natural, and mystical doctrine, he set forth these wells in each of his books written on morals, natural things, or mysteries.

24. For in Proverbs, when he said that the appearance of worldly enticement must be avoided, he says: “Drink water from your own vessels and from the springs of your own wells, and let waters overflow for you from your own fountain” (Prov. 5:15). And below: “Let the fountain of your water be your own, and rejoice with your wife” (ibid. 5:18). [Note: The Roman edition adds: “whom you have had from your youth,” because, etc.] This is because true wisdom is our remedy against the temptations of the world. Moral doctrine also waters and washes away, with its own stream and the flow of its fountain, the image of worldly pleasure smeared with certain harlot-like cosmetics.

25. You have a saying concerning natural things also in Ecclesiastes: “I made myself pools of water to irrigate from them a forest putting forth shoots” (Eccles. 2:6). Nor should it trouble you that he put pools in place of a well, since Moses also called it the Well of Breadth, because one who transcends this world with a devout mind is released from every anxiety and narrowness. Ecclesiastes, therefore, not without reason has pools, since he saw that no abundance exists under the sun. But if anyone wishes to abound, let him abound in Christ.

26. And among mystical matters there remains for us the well which we find in the Song of Songs itself, Scripture saying: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living water, and a rush descending from Lebanon” (Cant. 4:15). For if you pursue the depth of mysteries, a well seems to you to be mystical wisdom situated, as it were, in the deep. But if you wish to draw the abundance of love—which is greater and fuller than faith and hope—then it is a fountain to you. For love overflows, so that you may draw it near at hand and water with its abundance your garden, overflowing with spiritual fruits. [Note: Thus six manuscripts of better quality. One reads: “And because beyond it there is a well,” etc. Three others and all editions: “And because it is itself a well,” etc.] And because the one who possesses love is beyond the very Well of Breadth, he therefore said that where love is, there a great rush descends from Lebanon. But lest it trouble anyone that he called the same thing both a well and a fountain, let the Gospel also instruct you, in which it is written: “Jesus came to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the estate which Jacob gave to Joseph his son. Now Jacob’s fountain was there. And Jesus, wearied, sat thus upon the well” (John 4:5–6). Thus we recognize there also that this well is to be referred to mystical doctrine, because there that Samaritan woman—that is, “the keeper,” and a keeper of heavenly precepts—drew divine mysteries from that well, knowing that God is spirit and is worshipped not in a place but in spirit (ibid. and following, 4:24); [Note: Editions: “And that the Messiah comes, who is Christ.” Manuscripts: “And that the Messiah is Christ.”] and that the Messiah is Christ. Therefore he who is still awaited by the Jews has already come. Having heard these things, that woman, who bears the figure of the Church, recognized the sacraments of the law and believed.

27. Solomon also clearly expressed this threefold wisdom in the very book of the Songs, although in Proverbs he had said (Prov. 22:20) that whoever wished to hear his wisdom should write it for himself in threefold form. Thus the bride says in the Songs concerning the bridegroom: [Note: Thus eight better manuscripts. Some others and the old edition: “Behold, the bridegroom is my cousin. And therefore the beautiful reclining-place,” etc. But the Roman edition: “Behold, you are beautiful, my cousin; behold, you are beautiful and comely; our reclining-place,” etc. The Septuagint translators: “Behold, you are fair, my kinsman, and indeed lovely; our couch is shaded.” See Nobilius’s notes on this verse.] “Behold, you are indeed my bridegroom and cousin, beautiful; our reclining-place is shaded; the beams of our houses are cedars, our ceilings cypresses” (Cant. 1:15–16). We may understand this of moral things. For where do Christ and the Church rest, except in the works of their people? Thus where there was unchastity, pride, and iniquity, the Lord Jesus says: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8:20).

28. But what do we understand concerning natural things? “I desired and sat in his shadow, and his fruit was sweet in my throat” (Cant. 2:3). For one who transcends earthly things, and to whom worldly things have died—for the world has been crucified to him and he to the world—flees and despises all things that are under the sun.

29. Concerning mystical things too, it says: “Bring me into the house of wine; establish love in me” (Cant. 2:4). For just as a vine embraces its vineyard with its branches, so the Lord Jesus, like an eternal vine, embraces his people with certain branches of love.

30. Consider each point. In moral matters he is the flower and the lily among thorns, as he himself says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (ibid. 2:1). In moral matters, therefore, he is the flower. In natural matters, he is the sun of righteousness, which illumines when rising and rising again, but casts shadow when setting. Beware lest he set for you, because it is written: “Let not the sun set upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26). In mystical matters, he is love, because Christ is the fulfilment of the law. Therefore the Church, which loves Christ, is wounded by love.

31. It therefore awakens and rouses this love until it receives his voice and summons his presence; for when sought, he not only comes, but comes leaping: “Leaping over the mountains and skipping over the hills” (Cant. 2:8). He leaps upon souls of greater grace, and skips over those of lesser grace. Or thus: how does he come leaping? He came into this world by a kind of leap. He was with the Father; he came into the Virgin, and from the Virgin he leapt into the manger. He was in the manger and shone in heaven; he descended into the Jordan, ascended upon the cross, descended into the tomb, rose from the tomb, and sits at the Father’s right hand. From there, like a young hart longing for springs of water, he descended to Paul and shone around him; and he leapt upon the holy Church, which is Bethel, that is, “the house of God.” For Paul’s calling is the Church’s strengthening.

32. Therefore he comes and is first behind the wall, in order to dissolve the enmities of soul and body, when the wall that seemed to bring an impediment to concord has been removed. Then he looks through the windows. Hear the prophet say what the windows are: “The windows have been opened from heaven” (Isa. 24:18). He means the prophets, through whom the Lord looked upon the human race before he himself descended to earth. [Note: Some Paris editions: “looked upon the human race before he himself descended and spoke.” In the old edition, *respexit* (“looked upon”) and the word *et* (“and”) are lacking. But the manuscripts read as in the text.]

33. And today, if any soul seeks him greatly, it will merit much mercy; for to the one who seeks much, very much is due. If, therefore, any soul seeks him more diligently, it hears his voice from afar; and although it seeks him through others, [Note: All editions: “although he is sought through others, before those by whom he is sought,” etc. The manuscripts, conversely: “although it seeks him through them,” etc.] it hears his voice before the very persons through whom it seeks him. It sees him coming toward it in leaps—that is, hastening and running—and skipping over those who cannot receive his power because their hearts are weak. Finally, it sees him looking through the riddles of the prophets: by reading them and holding fast to their words, it sees him looking, but as through a window, not yet as one present. It sees him standing above the nets. What is this, unless perhaps the nets are for us, not for him? They are nets because that soul is still among sensible and worldly things, which are accustomed to seize the human mind and enfold it, as it were, in their own bosom. While it is still placed among worldly things but nevertheless seeks him, he reveals himself through the nets.

34. Finally he says to such a soul: “Rise, come, my near one” (Cant. 2:10), that is, rise from the pleasures of the world, rise from earthly things, and come to me—you who still labour and are burdened, because you are anxious about worldly things. Come above the world; come to me, because I have conquered the world. Come near to me, now beautiful with the beauty of eternal life, now a dove—that is, gentle and meek—now wholly filled with spiritual grace. Rightly, therefore, it need no longer fear the nets when he who calls the soul to himself could not be caught by the temptations and nets of the world. For although we human beings walk amid snares, through desire for food we are liable alike to nets and snares. He, though placed in the body, did not fear nets but stood above the nets—that is, above the temptations of the world and the passions of the body—and indeed made others stand above them. Therefore, wishing also to establish this soul, he said: “Rise, come, my near one; do not fear the nets.”

35. “For the winter has now passed” (ibid., 11); that is, Passover has come, pardon has come, the remission of sins has come; temptation has ceased, the rain has gone, the storm and the shaking have gone. Before Christ’s coming it is winter; after his coming there are flowers. Hence he says: “Flowers have appeared on the earth” (ibid., 12). Where there were thorns before, there are now flowers. “The time,” he says, “for pruning has come.” Where there was desert before, there is now harvest. “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” The prophet aptly adds “our,” as though marveling that where there was formerly unchastity, there is now chastity.

36. “The fig tree has put forth its early figs” (ibid., 13). She who had formerly been commanded to be cut down as though unfruitful has now begun to bear fruit. But why do you doubt that he called them early figs? She shakes off the earlier fruits, in order to bring forth later and better ones. The early fig, like the fruit of the Synagogue, is cast away; that of the Church is renewed.

37. And although there is complete calm and the mysteries have matured, nevertheless he says again: “Arise, secure in the covering of the rock” (ibid., 14), that is, safe under the protection of my Passion and the defense of faith. For “they sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the firmest rock.” Clothed in this covering, the souls of the godly are no longer naked; and this is their safeguard. Therefore he says also to this soul: “And come, my dove, in the covering of the rock, beside the fortification; show me your face, and let me hear your voice.” He exhorts her to confidence, that she may not be ashamed of Christ’s cross or of its seal. He exhorts her to confession; he wishes every ambush removed, that the good fragrance of faith may breathe forth, that the day may shine, and that the shadow of an adverse night may do no harm. For one who is beside Christ says: “The night has gone before, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. XXIII, 12). There is also the shadow of worldly things, which has passed away; and Christ, the day of heavenly things, shines upon his saints. This soul receives good pledges of love.

## Chapter V

The Bridegroom, having again slipped away from the soul on her bed at night, is sought in vain; and why? Yet afterward he is found. How must he be held? Then the daughters of Jerusalem marvel at him as he ascends from the desert with the bride, accompany them to the bridal chamber, and celebrate them with a wedding song. He himself also adorns the soul, now called nearer, with various praises.

[Col. 0515B]

38. The soul’s third progress.—But because we must always be watchful, always attentive, and because the Word of God leaps like a gazelle or like a young stag, the soul must always keep watch and hold before itself the things by which it seeks him and desires to hold him. Therefore, as though he had slipped away from her, she says: “On my bed, at night, I sought him whom my soul loves.” She who seeks well should seek on her bed, should seek at night; neither feast day nor night should be idle. Let no time be free from the duty of devotion; and if she does not find him at first, let her persevere in seeking. Therefore she says: “I will arise, then, and seek in the city, in the marketplace, in the streets” (Cant. III, 2). And perhaps she has not yet found him because she sought in the marketplace, where there are disputes; in the streets, where goods for sale are traded. For Christ is purchased by no money.

[Col. 0515C]

39. We may understand it in this way as well. She seeks Christ on her bed who seeks him in calm and peace. She seeks at night because he spoke through parables. For “he made darkness his hiding-place,” and “night declares knowledge to night.” Further, the things we say in our hearts ought to pierce us upon our beds. Yet even so she does not find him; and therefore she says: “I will arise,” that is, I will raise and lift up my attention, that I may seek diligently and anxiously: “I will enter the city.” There is also a soul which says: “I am a fortified city; I am a besieged city” (Isa. XXVII, 3). There is a city fortified through Christ; it is that heavenly Jerusalem in which interpreters of the divine law and persons skilled in discipline abound. Through them the Word of God is sought.

“I will seek,” she says, “in the marketplace of that city,” in that marketplace where legal experts discuss laws, where the oil is sold that the evangelical virgins buy (Matt. XXV, 9), so that their lamps may always shine and the smoke of wickedness may not extinguish them. “I will seek,” she says, “in the streets in which waters overflow from those bursting fountains, from which Solomon says one must drink” (Prov. V, 15).

40. While she seeks Christ, therefore, she finds the watchmen who serve in ministry, and asks them about him (Cant. III, 3). But the soul that seeks God passes even beyond the watchmen. For there are mysteries which even angels desire to behold. Hence Peter says: “They were announced to you by those who preached the Gospel to you through the Holy Spirit sent from heaven—things into which angels desire to look” (I Pet. I, 12). Therefore, whoever has passed beyond the watchmen finds the Word. John passed beyond them, for he found the Word with the Father (John I, 1).

[Col. 0516A]

41. There are also many who seek Christ in leisure and do not find him, yet find him in persecutions—and find him quickly. Therefore, as though after trials, because he is present amid the dangers of his faithful ones, she says: “Scarcely had I passed beyond them when I found him; I held him and did not let him go” (Cant. III, 4). For everyone who seeks finds; and whoever has found must cling to him, lest he be able to lose him.

42. And because through the Gospel we see heavenly mysteries prefigured on earth, [Note: The Roman edition, from one Vatican manuscript, at Col. 0515D: “Let us come to Magdalene; let us come also to the other Mary.”] let us come to that Mary, and let us come also to Magdalene. Let us consider how they sought Christ on the bed of his body, in which he lay dead, at night, when the angel said to them: “You seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen. Why then do you seek the living among the dead?” (Matt. XXVIII, 5 ff.). Why seek in the tomb him who is already in heaven? Why seek within the bonds of burial him who loosens the bonds of all? The tomb is not his dwelling, but heaven is. Therefore one of them said: “I sought him and did not find him” (Cant. III, 1).

43. Yet as they went to tell the Apostles, Jesus, having compassion on those seeking him, met them and said: “Greetings.” But they came up, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him (Matt. XXVIII, 9). Jesus, therefore, is held; but he delights to be held thus, because he is held by faith. Accordingly, that woman also pleased him who touched him and was healed of the flow of blood, concerning whom he said: “Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me” (Luke VIII, 46). Touch him, therefore; hold him by faith; and faithfully clasp his feet, so that power may go out from him and heal your soul.

And if he says, “Do not touch me” (John XX, 17), [Note: The words inserted among the quotations, “you hold,” and “he said,” were absent in the editions at Col. 0515D–0516D; they have been restored on the authority of all the manuscripts.] you nevertheless hold him. He said only once: “I have not yet ascended to my Father.” He said, “Do not touch me,” when he had risen; or perhaps he said it to the woman who thought he had been taken away by theft rather than raised by his own power. For in another book you have that, when they held his feet and worshiped him, he said: “Do not be afraid” (Matt. XXVIII, 10).

You also, soul, therefore hold him, as Mary held him, and say: “I have held him and will not let him go” (Cant. III, 4), as both women said: “Let us hold you. Go to the Father, but do not leave Eve behind, lest she fall again. Take her with you—not now wandering, but holding the tree of life. Draw her along as she clings to your feet, that she may ascend with you. Do not let me go, lest the serpent again pour forth its venom, lest it again seek to bite the woman’s heel, in order to overthrow Adam.”

Let your soul, therefore, say: “I hold you, and I will bring you into the house of my mother and into the inner chamber of her who conceived me,” that I may know your mysteries and draw from your sacraments. Receive, then, [Col. 0517A] Eve—not now covered with fig leaves, but clothed in the Holy Spirit and glorious in new grace. For she no longer hides as one stripped naked; but, clothed around with the splendor of shining apparel, she comes to meet you, because grace clothes her. Nor was Adam naked at first, when innocence clothed him (*On Penance*, distinction 2, chapter *But Neither Adam*).

44. Therefore, when the daughters of Jerusalem see her clinging to Christ and still ascending with him—for he deigns often to meet those who seek and to stoop down in order to raise them—they say: “Who is this who [Note: Several manuscripts: “descends from the desert?”] ascends from the desert?” (Cant. III, 6). The desert here seems to be the uncultivated and untilled region of the earth, overgrown with the brambles and thorns of our sins. They marvel, of course, how the soul which formerly [Note: Supply: “in hell” as the place, that is, the earth, which is so called in relation to heaven, which is above.] was left in hell clings to God’s Word and has ascended like a vine shoot, raising itself upward, like smoke born from fire and seeking the heights; and further, [Note: The Roman edition, with several manuscripts: “burns with good works.”] how she burns with good works.

That fragrance of devout prayer breathes sweetness, for it is directed like incense before God. And in the Apocalypse we read: “The smoke of the incense rose from the prayers of the saints” (Apoc. VIII, 4): namely, the prayers of the saints, offered as incense through an angel upon that golden altar before God’s throne. It burns like the sweet ointment of devout supplication because it is composed from a petition for eternal and invisible things, not bodily things. Yet above all it gives forth the fragrance of myrrh and frankincense, because it is dead to sins and alive to God.

[Col. 0517B]

45. Seeing her ascend and not resist, delighted by the fragrances of her merits, and recognizing that she is the bride of that peaceful Solomon, they diligently accompany her even to Solomon’s bed, because true rest is due to her in Christ. For Christ is the bed of the saints (Cant. III, 7), in whom the hearts of all, weary from worldly battles, find rest. On this bed Isaac rested and blessed his younger son, saying: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. XXV, 23). Reclining on this bed Jacob blessed the twelve patriarchs. Reclining on this bed, the synagogue ruler’s daughter rose from death. Lying on this bed, the widow’s dead son, summoned by Christ’s voice, dissolved the bonds of death.

46. The bride, therefore, having been brought to the bridegroom’s rest, they sing a nuptial song, saying to the daughters of Jerusalem: “Go forth and see King Solomon in the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding” (Cant. III, 11). They sing an epithalamium and summon the remaining powers of heaven, or souls, to see the love which Christ has for the daughters of Jerusalem. Hence he deserved to be crowned by his mother as the Son of love, as Paul shows in saying: “God has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us [Col. 0518A] into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. I, 13).

Therefore, the Son of love is himself Love, not possessing love as an accidental quality, but always possessing it in his substance, just as he possesses the kingdom, of which he says: “For this I was born” (John XVIII, 17). Therefore they say: “Go forth,” that is, depart from the anxieties and thoughts of the age; depart from bodily constraints; depart from the vanities of the world; and see what love the peaceful king possesses on the day of his wedding; see how glorious he is, because he gave resurrection to bodies and joined souls to himself. This is the great crown of Christ’s contest, this the splendid gift of his wedding: his blood and Passion. For what more could he give—he who did not spare even himself, [Note: Several manuscripts of better quality: “and offered his death for us.”] but offered his life unto death for us?

[Col. 0518B]

47. The Lord Jesus himself, delighted by this soul’s faith, confession, and grace, and having praised her merits, calls her nearer, saying: “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon. You shall pass and pass beyond from the beginning of faith, from the summit of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards” (Cant. IV, 8). That is: Depart from the body and strip yourself wholly. For you cannot be with me unless you first become absent from the body, because those who are in the flesh are absent from God’s kingdom.

“Come,” he says, “come.” He rightly repeats it, because whether present or absent, you must be present with and pleasing to the Lord your God. Be present when present; be present when absent, even if you are still in the body. For all whose faith is with me are present to me. Present to me is the one who has departed from the world; present is the one who thinks of me, beholds me, hopes in me, for whom I am a portion. Present to me is the one who is absent from herself; present is the one who has denied herself. He is with me who is not within himself, because he who is in the flesh is not in the spirit. He is with me who goes out from himself. He is beside me who is outside himself. He is whole for me who has lost his life for my sake.

[Note: All editions read: “Come, betrothed one … and she passes beyond the others, who comes to Christ,” etc. We judge the reading of nearly all manuscripts preferable.]

Therefore, “Come, bride, come; you shall pass from the beginning of faith.” She passes and passes beyond earthly things; she passes beyond who reaches Christ. By the merit of faith and the brightness of works, she passes beyond, shining like Sanir and Hermon; that is, she passes by the lamp of the way, having conquered the temptations of the world and overcome spiritual evils, seeking the crown of lawful contest. Thus she deserved Christ’s praise as judge.

[Col. 0518D]

48. “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed. Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruit of Cyprus-apples” (Cant. IV, 12). The bride is praised because she is a garden, possessing in herself the fragrance of that full field of which Isaac says: “The smell of my son is like the smell of a full field” (Gen. XXVII, 27). Thus a good soul gives forth the fragrance of righteousness.

And perhaps the patriarch is a field; the soul of one beneath him is a garden, as though a portion of the field; and it is a garden enclosed, lest beasts rush into it; and a fountain sealed [Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read: “which, with the integrity of the seal remaining, by faith,” etc. But many more and better manuscripts read: “which has washed away her own sins by the integrity of the seal and perseverance in faith.” Again, after three words, five manuscripts read: “Does the Church receive? She has that which,” etc.; two: “Does not the Church receive what she has, so that,” etc.; others partly: “For whoever has received from the Church has that which,” etc.; partly, with the old editions, as in our text.] which has washed away her own sins by the integrity of the seal and perseverance in faith.

For she who has received from the Church has something to attribute to the grace of virginity, because, placed in the paradise of delight, she receives spiritual fruits without labor, [Note: Codex Longobardicus: “so that the souls of the patriarchs may bestow their fruits upon her by a certain rustic stream, without labor.”] so that the souls of the patriarchs may offer her their fruits by a certain rustic labor, through which she may receive perpetual sweetness. She is rightly called a sealed fountain, because the image of the invisible God is impressed upon her.

They also praise the gifts of the soul [Note: Most manuscripts: “which were sent to the bridegroom.” One or two: “which were sent to the bride.” Others, and the editions: “which were sent by the bridegroom.”] which were sent by the bridegroom, with which she came endowed. But the dowry of the devout soul consists in good fragrances: myrrh, aloes, and saffron, by which the grace of gardens breathes and the stench of sins is abolished.

[Col. 0519B]

49. Therefore, secure in so great a proclamation of praise, she asks that the north wind, a harsh wind, may rest (Cant. IV, 16), lest it scatter the flowers, and that the south wind may blow; that is, she wishes winter to pass and the mild temperature of a gentler breath to flourish in spring (Cant. V, 1). She invites the bridegroom into her garden. The bridegroom descends; delighted by the variety of its fruits, he rejoices that he has found stronger food and also sweeter food. For there is, as it were, bread of the Word and honey: [Note: The Ebner and Colbert manuscripts read “in the body,” and Bigotianus in a gloss: “one discourse more forceful, another sweeter.” But in the reading of the other manuscripts and all editions, nothing should be altered.] one discourse is more forceful, another more persuasive. There is also one faith more fervent, like wine; another clearer, like the juice of milk. Christ feasts on this food in us, drinks this cup, and by the intoxication of its draught urges us to make an ascent from lower things to better and best things.

## Chapter VI

Having briefly recalled the soul’s three preceding stages of progress, he discusses the fourth more fully. In it the soul, sleeping, is awakened by the bridegroom. But while she delays in rising, the Word passes on. She goes out, seeks him through wounds of love, scarcely finds him at last, and then holds him so that she no longer loses him.

[Col. 0519C]

50. Hearing these things, the soul drank the intoxication of heavenly mysteries; and, as though put to sleep by wine and placed as it were in ecstasy or stupor, says: “I sleep, but my heart watches” (Cant. V, 2). Then, struck by the light of the present Word, after her eyes had rested closed, she is awakened by the Word. This is the soul’s fourth stage of progress.

At first, impatient for love and unable to bear the Word’s delays, she begged that she might deserve kisses, and deserved to behold the one desired. Second, when she had been brought into the king’s chamber and exchanged mutual words with him, she rested in his shadow; and suddenly the Word departed from the midst of their conversation. Yet he was not long absent from her as she sought him, but came leaping over mountains and springing over hills. Not long afterward, while speaking to his beloved as a gazelle or a young stag, he leaped away and left her.

Third, when she had not found him though she sought him on her bed and at night, in the city, marketplace, and streets, he at last recalled her by her prayers [Note: All editions, with a few manuscripts: “he recalled her, who was seeking, by grace.” Not badly; but eight manuscripts read: “and recalled her by grace,” that is, by the grace and favor which the soul has with the bridegroom.] and grace, so that she was even called nearer by the bridegroom. Fourth, she is now awakened by him while sleeping, though her heart watched, so that she immediately heard the voice of him knocking. But because she delayed while rising, unable to comprehend the Word’s swiftness, as she opened the door the Word passed on. She herself went out in his word and, having sought him through wounds—yet wounds of love—scarcely found him at last and held him, so as not afterward to lose him.

I have briefly outlined these matters in a concise account (*above*, chapters 3, 4, and 5). Now let us examine each point.

51. Even if you sleep, provided Christ recognizes the devotion of your soul, he comes, knocks at its door, and says: “Open to me, my sister” (Cant. V, 2). “Sister” is appropriate, because the nuptials of the Word and the soul are spiritual. Souls know neither the bonds of marriage nor the practice of bodily union, but are like angels in heaven.

“Open to me,” he says, “but close to strangers. Close to the age, close to the world. Do not yourself go out to those material things; do not leave your own light to seek another’s. For material light pours in a dark mist, so that the light of true glory cannot be seen. Open to me, then; do not open to the adversary, nor give place to the devil. Open yourself to me; do not be narrowed, but be enlarged, and I will fill you. And because, having traversed the world, I have found more troubles and offense, and have not easily found where I might rest, therefore open, so that in you the Son of Man may lay down his head, for whom there is no rest [Col. 0520C] except upon one who is humble and gentle.”

52. Hearing, “Open to me … and my head is full of dew” (ibid.), that is, of worldly temptations, the soul is suddenly troubled; and, as though about to rise when she was commanded to rise, she says—while she gives off the fragrance of aloes and myrrh, signs of burial—“I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (ibid., 3). For she fears lest she rise again into temptations, return again to fault and sin, and begin to soil with earthly footprints her departures and advances in virtue.

Certainly in this way also she displays the perfection of her virtue: she has deserved such love from Christ that he comes to her, knocks at her door, comes with the Father, and dines with that same soul, and she with him, as John said in the Apocalypse (Apoc. III, 20). For when she had heard above: “Come from Lebanon, bride; come from Lebanon” (Cant. IV, 8), and understood that she could not be present to Christ in the flesh, but only if present in spirit, she conformed herself to his will, that she herself might be conformed to Christ’s image. She no longer perceives the garments of the flesh; now, as though a spirit, she strips herself of bodily union; now, as though forgetful and unable, even if she wished, to remember that union, she says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?”

For she has stripped off that tunic of skins which Adam and Eve received after their fault: the tunic of corruption, the tunic of passions. “How shall I put it on?” She does not ask how to put it on; rather, she indicates it has been cast off in such a way that it can no longer serve as a garment for her. “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” That is: I washed my footsteps when I departed and raised myself from the companionship of the body, from that union and [Note: Some manuscripts: “familiarity and embrace of the flesh.”] familiarity of the fleshly embrace. How shall I defile them, so that they return to the body’s enclosure and that dark prison of its passions?

[Col. 0521B]

53. While she says these things, the Word sent forth his operation as though through an opening—not yet face to face, but as though a hand: “And my belly,” she says, “was troubled over him. And I rose to open to my brother. My hands dripped myrrh; my fingers are full of myrrh upon the handles of the lock” (Cant. V, 4–5). Let us consider what this means.

First, as I said, God the Word is seen through his works, as though through an opening, not fully and perfectly. Then love is enlarged and what has been conceived grows; and from the seeds which the soul has received in a kind of intelligible womb, she desires to see the whole fullness of his divinity dwelling bodily in him, as we read. She arose to see that Word of God more closely. Even in this her progress is signified, in that she arose through strength and power. For the Word’s presence drew strength into the soul, just as Mary’s presence, when she was heavy with child, instructed John while he was in the womb, so that he leaped in the womb and rejoiced, recognizing the Lord’s presence.

She arose to open, and her works and deeds were put to death to the world. For such must be the soul that is to receive the Word: she must die to the world and be buried with Christ. Thus Christ is found, and such a lodging he seeks for himself. Then the very instruments of action—that is, the hands and fingers by which Christ is grasped—are put to death; we may regard these fingers as works, as it were the prominent points of our actions.

Thus, as though from her embrace, when she had already extended her intelligible hands and fingers to grasp the Word, that Word passed from her. Yet the devout soul says it has not yet wholly passed through her. This too marks a stage of progress, when the Word of God passes through and wholly passes through the soul, for it is written: “A sword will pass through your own soul also, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke II, 35). Here it is still passing through, not wholly passed through; perhaps in what follows it wholly passes through Mary, where the Lord Jesus is placed in her midst as a seal.

[Col. 0522A]

54. Finally, there is immediately another advance of the passing Word: for the soul went out in his word; that is, following his word, she went out from the body, raising herself out of its dwelling and making herself a stranger to it, that she might be present to God and be a fellow citizen of the saints. For we cannot at once be members of the household of the flesh and of God.

Therefore, as I said, in this passage the soul is said to go out when she withdraws herself from bodily pleasures. Thus it is written: “Go out from Babylon, fleeing from the Chaldeans” (Isa. XLVIII, 20). The Hebrew is certainly not instructed to flee Babylon’s territory, but its customs, by the prophetic utterance; for there may be Hebrews in Babylon who show by their conduct that they have gone out from Babylon. Those also of whom the Prophet says that they sat by the rivers of Babylon sat indeed in Babylon’s region, but were not in its vices and confusion (Ps. CXXXVI, 1). For how could those be in that confusion of vices who wept in repentance because they had fallen away from the ark of devotion, faith, and the merits of paternal virtue? The soul which goes out in the Word seeks the Word.

55. Hence, while she sought, she encountered the watchmen who go about the city: “They struck me,” she says, “and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took my cloak from me” (Cant. V, 7). She rightly came as a bride with a cloak by which to cover her head when the bridegroom met her, just as Rebecca, when she learned that Isaac was coming to meet her, dismounted from the camel and covered herself with a cloak (Gen. XXIV, 65). Thus this soul also displayed the marks of bridal dress beforehand, [Note: All editions, with a few manuscripts: “displayed the marks beforehand.”] lest perhaps she be rejected as not having a wedding garment, or that she might veil her head because of the angels.

But they struck her, that she might be proved further. For souls are trained by temptations. They took away her cloak, seeking whether she bore the true beauty of naked virtue; or because one must enter that heavenly city without a covering, bringing along no concealments of artificial adornment. There are also those who inquire lest any soul carry with her remnants of fleshly allurements and bodily desire. She is stripped of her cloak when her conscience is made manifest.

Yet there is one who is rightly stripped, who may imitate the one saying: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30). Certainly he found nothing in that one alone who committed no sin. Blessed also is she in whom he finds not grave or many things; rather, he finds in her the garment of faith and the discipline of wisdom.

[Col. 0522D]

56. Therefore she passed beyond the watchmen without loss to herself—for even if someone wishes it, he cannot take away true wisdom; even if the adversary clamors, the true integrity of a harmless way of life still shines there. Without loss, therefore, she passed beyond the watchmen; mingled with the daughters of that heavenly city, she seeks the Word. By seeking she awakens love for him within herself and recognizes where the Word is to be sought. She knows that he remains among the prayers of the saints and clings to them; and she understands that he feeds his Church, or the souls of his righteous ones, among lilies.

The Lord showed you this mystery in the Gospel (Luke VI, 1), when on the Sabbath he led his disciples through the grainfields. Moses led the Jewish people through the desert (Deut. XXIX, 5); Christ leads through grainfields, Christ leads through lilies, because through his Passion the desert blossoms like a lily. Let us follow, then, so that on the Sabbath day—that great Sabbath in which there is great rest—we may gather fruit. Nor should you fear that the Pharisees will accuse one gathering grain. Even if they accuse, Christ excuses and makes the souls who follow him like that David who, above the law, ate the loaves of presentation, already foreseeing in prophetic understanding the sacraments of new grace (I Sam. XXI, 6).

## Chapter VII

The soul is praised by the bridegroom because she has sought him so well and steadfastly; because she is faithful, powerful in word, one like a dove; finally, because she is fruitful in virtues and free from vices.

[Col. 0523B]

57. Therefore she is praised by the bridegroom because she has sought him so well and steadfastly (Cant. VI, 3). Hence she is now called not only sister but also well-pleasing, as one pleasing to him who pleased the Father; and beautiful as Jerusalem, as an ordered wonder, because she possesses all the mysteries of the eternal city and is an object of wonder to all who see her. For being full of equity and perfect, and having borrowed brightness from the light of the Word, because she always directs her attention to it, she becomes also terrible, having advanced in a certain order to the height of virtues.

Therefore he says to her as one perfected: “Turn your eyes away from me; do not gaze upon me” (ibid., 4), because through excessive devotion and faith she has gone beyond the capacity of her own nature and condition, since it is difficult to look directly upon inaccessible light. “Turn your eyes away from me,” he says, because she cannot sustain the fullness of his divinity and the brightness of the true light.

Yet we may also take it thus: “Turn your eyes away from me. Although you are perfect, there are still other souls for me to redeem, others to support. For by beholding me you raise me; but I descended in order to raise all. And though I have risen and possess the Father’s seat, yet I will not leave you orphans, deprived as it were of paternal protection, but will strengthen you by my presence.” You have this written in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the world” (Matt. XXIII, 20).

“Turn your eyes away from me, therefore, because you raise me.” For the more someone fixes attention upon the Lord, the more that person raises the Lord and is raised himself. Hence that man also says: “I will exalt you, Lord, because you have taken me up” (Ps. XXIX, 1). The holy person exalts the Lord; the sinner humbles him. Therefore he wishes her to turn away her eyes, lest, seeing that she can now follow toward higher things, he be raised and leave the other souls behind.

For this reason, in the Gospel he showed his glory not to all the disciples (Matt. XVII, 1), but to the more perfect ones. Now imagine a teacher wishing to explain an obscure matter to his hearers. Although he may himself be powerful in speech and knowledge, he nevertheless accommodates himself to the ignorance of those who do not understand and uses simpler, plainer, and more familiar speech so that he may be understood. Whoever among the hearers is quicker in understanding and can follow easily raises and draws him onward. Seeing such a person, the teacher calls him back, so that he may allow the teacher to dwell rather on humbler and plainer matters, through which the others too may be able to follow.

[Col. 0524A]

58. What Aquila renders, “Resounding as revealed,” he refers to one sounding forth in a manner worthy of admiration, as having great and resonant works; “revealed” refers to the brightness of her works, or to the fact that the works of that soul shine before the Father who is in heaven. Hence you rightly understand that her cloak was removed, so that, manifest in her merits and uncovered, she might shine.

59. She is further praised because she is faithful, powerful in word, fruitful in diverse fruits, one like a dove, possessing unity of spirit, in whom there is peace, who “made both one” (Cant. V, 2), and who is not compounded from diverse elements of divided and conflicting nature (Cant. VI, 3). For what is so different as fire and water, air and earth, of which the constitution of our body consists? But every blessed soul is simple which imitates him who says: “That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us” (John XVII, 21). For this is consummation and perfection. Hence he added: “That they may be one, as we also are one: I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one” (ibid., 23).

This, then, is the one and perfect dove-like soul: simple and spiritual, not disturbed by the passions of this body, in which there are struggles without and fears within. Finally, Scripture teaches that harmony and peace are signified by this word of unity, saying: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and there was no division among them” (Acts IV, 32).

60. Nor is the soul praised for fruitfulness without reason: not only because it is fruitful in virtues, but also because it has no evil within itself. For that in which there is no evil is beautiful and fair. What is fair is good; what is unbeautiful, however, is evil. The fruitfulness of good works is lovely; barrenness, therefore, is contrary to loveliness. For where a thing is deprived of beauty or comeliness, there is evil; and whatever is evil is barren and unfruitful. What clearer indication of this is there than nature itself? For good soil is fertile and fruitful; bad soil is lean and barren; but fertile soil is also fair. What, indeed, is more beautiful than a full field, when the corn undulates, when fruits glow ruddy, when garlands of grapes hang down, when the olive bends beneath its load of berries, or when the mountain-tops and the low places of valleys are clothed in green grass? And, to use the testimony of Scripture (Gen. 27:27), Jacob was comely, and therefore had the scent of a full field; Esau was hairy and uncomely (ibid., 11), and therefore was rustic, unable to bear any fruits. Of the Lord Himself also, after He had caused the fruitfulness of the Church to arise, it was beautifully said: “The Lord has reigned; He has clothed Himself with comeliness” (Ps. [Col. 0525A] 92:1). And elsewhere: “You have clothed Yourself with confession and beauty” (Ps. 103:2).

It is clear, then, that what is fruitful is comely, and what is unfruitful is unbeautiful. The soul’s case is like that of the soil: the soul is comely which is fruitful in merits and fruitful in counsels; unbeautiful is that which is barren.

> [Note: [Col. 0525C] Three manuscripts and the old edition read: “which is barren through weakness. But these are defects of the soul.” Two others: “… But these are harms to the soul.” The rest, and the Roman edition, read as in the text.]

For the weaknesses of the soul are barrenness and matter. Barrenness deprives it of its own fruit, brings poverty upon it, instils fear, kindles desires and vain opinions: thus the soul falls. What, then, is wickedness but a lack of good? (See St Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, I.9.) For it is deprived of what is its own and needs what belongs to another; it is emptied and filled without any measure or limit. Material vices darken the soul’s grace. Ignorance and concupiscence are diseases of the soul; but they belong more to form (*species*) than to matter.

> [Note: [Col. 0525D] A little above, *species* had been taken in the sense of beauty; it is now used of a certain accidental form which affects the soul, not the body.]

Matter is the flesh; form is ignorance and concupiscence. Why, then, is the flesh accused, when there are such great blemishes in form? Because form can do nothing without matter. Indeed, even the form of an axe does nothing without matter. For what would concupiscence be unless the flesh inflamed it? It grows cold in old people and in children as well, because their bodies are weak; it burns in the young, in whom bodily strength is fervent. Evils therefore arose from goods; for things are not evil except insofar as they are deprived of goods. (See Augustine, ibid.) Yet it came about through evils that goods should stand out more clearly. Therefore lack of good is wickedness, and wickedness is detected by the definition of good, since evil is discovered through the teaching of good.

> [Note: [Col. 0525D] Thus the manuscripts, except for a few of later date, which, with all editions, read: “Lack of good is the root of wickedness, by definition,” etc.]

But good needs nothing; it abounds in itself, gives measure, perfection, and end to all things. In it all things stand, and upon it all things depend. Such is the nature of good: it fills the mind.

61. The pure soul moves about this good, contemplates it inwardly, sees God, and abounds in every good. Therefore it says: “His mouth is sweetness, and he is altogether desirable” (Song 5:16). For God is the author of all goods, and all things that exist are certainly His.

> [Note: [Col. 0525D] The Roman edition, with three manuscripts: “and whatever is His is certainly all good, and nowhere,” etc. The other manuscripts and editions agree with our text.]

There is no evil there; and if our mind remains in Him, it knows no evil. The soul, therefore, which does not remain in God is itself the author of its evils; thus it sins. But the soul that sins, it shall die. Released from the golden chains of virtues, it is borne headlong down a profane precipice and slips to lower things.

> [Note: [Col. 0525D] Several manuscripts read: “is borne headlong down a profane precipice.”]

But blessed is the soul which no hostile conflicts of the body overcome. Such a soul, when the snare is broken, flies away like a sparrow. Bodily pleasures are the food of evils. Whoever fixes his attention upon them entangles his soul in a snare.

62. But whoever restrains himself from its foods and comes out of its darkness, his soul shines like the dawn, of which it is said: “Who is this that looks forth like the dawn, fair as the moon?” (Song 6:9). For she looks out as though from a free house. She does not say: “Darkness covers me, walls surround me, and who knows whether the Most High sees?” (Sir. 23:26). Rather, she herself seeks the light, as though in the upper rooms of her own house—that is, of her body—and, set above the world, beholds divine things and raises herself to eternal things, that she may be with God, now bearing about the circle of her own works’ light, as the moon bears her orb through the whole circuit of the world.

63. But where Aquila says, “Sounding like the sun,” there seems to be expressed that revolution of the heavenly sphere, and the courses of sun, moon, and stars, and the harmony of the spheres. This opinion also appears plausible to some of our people, who, because it does not find faith, do not think it unacceptable at least for the charm of its sweetness.

> [Note: [Col. 0525D] The old edition reads: “because it does not come to faith.” The Roman edition, with all the manuscripts: “because it does not find faith.” The latter reading better accords with what Ambrose teaches in *Hexaemeron*, II.2.6–7, and *On Abraham*, II.8.54. There, expressly treating this theory of heavenly harmony—a theory held not only by pagan philosophers but also by Christians, among whom, as he teaches in a fragment restored by us [Col. 0526C], was Origen (he might have added Philo)—he rejects and vigorously refutes it. The first reading can be better fitted to what the same saint says in the preface to his *Commentaries on the Psalms*. Although there he does not indicate that he accepts this view as true, he plainly declares that it should not be considered impossible, in these words: “Nor does this seem alien to the practice of nature, since a voice uttered resounds with more pleasing applause in woods or mountains,” etc. From all these passages, then, we judge that the following sense can be elicited: although this harmony is plainly false, yet because it has no bearing whatever on faith, it may be proposed not only as not unpleasant, but even as not altogether impossible. For it is not inconsistent that we should not deny to be possible something which we judge neither true nor probable. As for Sixtus of Siena’s statement that this opinion is numbered among the condemned doctrines of the Marcosians, he maintains that this must be understood not of the opinion itself, but of certain monstrosities which those heretics deduced from it. See him, *Bibliotheca sancta*, V, Annotation 105.]

## CHAPTER VIII

The same soul, shrinking from being praised, says that she descended into the garden of nuts, etc.; by these are signified bitterness and temptations. Amid these she does not know herself, but is known and governed by Christ, until she reaches the palm. His reclining upon her signifies three things: instruction, progress, and perfection. What follows is an exhortation to charity.

64. While she is being praised by the bridegroom, she modestly shrinks from praise; then, recalled by love for the bridegroom, she says: “I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the plants in the valley” [literally, “at the springing-up of the torrent”] (Song 6:10). For where is the Church, except where the rod and sacerdotal grace flourish? There it often happens that she is tested amid bitterness and temptations. By the nut we understand bitterness; by the torrent, temptations, yet tolerable ones, because it is written: “Our soul passed through the torrent” (Ps. 123:5).

Accordingly, she goes down into the place of bitterness, where the vine flourishes, and where there is varied and manifold fruit in the appearance of pomegranates, guarded, as it were, under one covering over the whole body by faith and charity. In that bitterness, therefore, the soul did not know herself; for the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling quickly inclines it. Yet it ought always to know itself. Peter too was tested, and Peter did not know himself; for if he had known himself, he would not have denied his Creator. But Christ knew him: indeed, He knew him who also looked upon him—for “the Lord knows those who are His”—and, as a good charioteer, recalled him as His own from his fall with the reins of His mercy. Christ, therefore, is our charioteer.

65. Accordingly the soul says: “He made me the chariots of Aminadab” (Song 6:11). The soul, then, is a chariot which bears a good charioteer. If the soul is a chariot, it has horses, either good or bad. The good horses are the soul’s virtues; the bad horses are the body’s passions. (See St Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, II.5 and III.14.) Therefore the good charioteer restrains and recalls the bad horses, and urges on the good ones. The good horses are four: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. The bad horses are anger, concupiscence, fear, and iniquity.

At times the horses themselves disagree with one another: either anger presses forward or fear does, and they hinder one another and delay the course. But the good horses fly onward, lift themselves from the earth to higher things, and raise the soul—especially when they have the easy yoke and light burden of Him who says: “Take My yoke upon you; for My yoke is easy and My burden is light” (Matt. 11:29). He Himself is the charioteer who knows how to govern His own horses so that all run at an even pace.

> [Note: [Col. 0527D] The Roman edition reads: “Prudence restrains the swifter; justice warns the more sluggish with its own whip; temperance makes the gentler, fortitude the harder; he knows,” etc. The sense is certainly clear, but we have not dared to prefer it to the reading of the old editions and all the manuscripts. Above all, the words presented from them offer a reading that should not be rejected.]

If prudence is swifter and justice slower, he urges the more sluggish with its proper whip; if temperance is gentler and fortitude more vigorous, he knows how to yoke together those that differ, lest they perhaps scatter his chariot. Thus one may behold, in an intelligible—that is, spiritual or mystical—spectacle, every soul caught up toward heaven in the greatest contest, with horses hastening to see which arrive first at Christ’s prize, that the palm may first be laid upon their necks.

> [Note: [Col. 0527D] For Ambrose here and elsewhere, “intelligible” means the same as spiritual or mystical: things which can be perceived not by bodily eyes but by the eyes of the understanding.]

These are the horses subjected to the yoke of faith, bound by the bond of charity, by the reins of justice, and by the check-straps of sobriety. Beautifully, therefore, she says: “He made me the chariots of Aminadab,” that is, “father of the people.” But he who is father of the people is likewise father Naason, that is, “of serpents.”

> [Note: [Col. 0527D] Not a few manuscripts read: “Naasson, that is, of serpentine nature.”]

Now recall who hung like a serpent upon the cross for the salvation of all, and you understand that this soul is peaceable, over which God the Father presides and Christ drives; for this title also is written among us: “My father, my father, the charioteer of Israel” (4 Kings 2:12).

66. This charioteer, then, says: “Return, Shulamite, return” (Song 6:12). Appropriately, both as charioteer and in reference to a chariot, He says: “Return, Shulamite,” that is, “peaceable one.” For the peaceable soul quickly turns and corrects itself, even if it sinned before; and Christ all the more mounts and deigns to govern it, to whom it is said: “Mount Your horses, and Your riding is salvation” (Hab. 3:8). And elsewhere: “I sent Your horses to Tharsis” (ibid., 15).

> [Note: [Col. 0527D] This is the reading of the better manuscripts and the ancient editions. Others and the Roman edition read “You sent.” Since this passage occurs nowhere in our Bibles in precisely these words, we think it drawn from Habakkuk 3 because of some correspondence. There, according to the Septuagint, we read: “And You led Your horses into the sea”; but Jerome states that by the word *Tharsis* the sea is signified. Thus that term may have been retained by some translator where others rendered εἰς θάλασσαν, “into the sea.”]

These are Christ’s horses. Therefore Christ mounts His horses; the Word of God mounts devout souls.

67. From this recognize that He mounted this soul also and led her to the place of the palm, when He says to her: “How fair and pleasant you have become, O charity, in your delights! Your stature has become like a palm tree” (Song 7:6 ff.). And she herself says: “I said, I will climb the palm.” Yet charity itself is also a palm; for it is the fullness of victory. For charity is the fulfillment of the law. Let us run, then, that we may lay hold; let us run, that we may conquer. Whoever has conquered climbs the palm and eats its fruit. Whoever has conquered no longer runs, but sits, as it is written: “To him who conquers I will grant to sit with Me on My throne, as I also conquered and sit with My Father on His throne” (Rev. 3:21).

From this the philosophers portrayed in their books those curule contests of souls; yet they could not reach the palm, because their souls did not know the summit of the Word and its height, which this soul knew, in which was the turning (*conversio*) of the Word.

68. For thus she says: “I am for my brother, and his turning is toward me” (Song 7:10). She repeated this meaning three times in different forms in the Song of Songs. At the beginning she says: “My brother is for me, and I for him, who feeds among the lilies, until day breathes and the shadows depart” (Song 2:16–17). Then she says: “I am for my brother, and my brother is for me, who feeds among the lilies” (Song 6:2). At the end she says: “I am for my brother, and his turning is toward me.”

The first expression belongs to the soul’s instruction, and therefore she put first: “My brother is for me”; for, when He manifested Himself, the soul also received the desire to cleave to God. The second belongs to progress; the third, to perfection. In the first, as though still in instruction, the soul sees shadows, not yet stirred by the revelation of the approaching Word.

> [Note: [Col. 0528D] All editions and three inferior manuscripts read: “stirred by revelation, and therefore.” The others read: “stirred by revelation,” etc.; that is, the soul has not yet been fully awakened from sleep.]

Therefore the day of the Gospel did not yet shine upon her. In the second, without the confusion of shadows, she gathers devout fragrances. In the third, now perfected, she provides rest in herself for the Word, so that He may turn toward her, recline His head, and rest; and, now holding the reward which earlier she could not find though she sought it, she invites Him to her field, saying:

> [Note: [Col. 0529D] All editions read: “and now deservedly holding what before.” The Joyeuse and Reims manuscripts read: “and having now found,” etc. Others read as in the text.]

69. “Come, my brother, let us go out into the field; let us rest in the villages” (Song 7:11). Above she invited Him into the garden; here, into the field, which has not only the charm of flowers but also wheat and barley—that is, the supports of more solid virtues—that He may look upon its fruits. “Let us rest,” she says, “in the villages,” to which Adam, when expelled from paradise, had been banished. In them he rested, but he worked the earth. The reason why she wishes Him to go out into the field is plain: that, like a good shepherd, He may feed His flock, relieve the weary, and call back the wandering.

> [Note: [Col. 0529D] Several manuscripts read: “may lift up the fallen,” or “may relieve [*ablevet*] the weary.”]

For although this soul has kept for Him both new things and old, there are still those who are as lambs and must be nourished by the juice of milk. Therefore, as one perfected, she intercedes not for herself but for others: that He may come forth from the Father’s bosom, go outside like a bridegroom proceeding from his bridal chamber, and run His course in order to win the weak; that He may not remain upon that hidden throne of the Father and in that light, where the weak cannot follow, but may be taken up and brought into the bride’s house and secret chamber.

> [Note: [Col. 0529D] All editions, with a few manuscripts: “where weak horses cannot climb; but that … into the bride’s house and secret chamber. Let Him be outside there, that He may be in our midst within.” We prefer the authority of eight manuscripts, agreeing in our reading.]

Let Him be outside for Himself, that He may be within for us. Let Him be in our midst, although He is not seen by us.

70. Therefore she says: “Who will give You to me as a brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother? Finding You outside, I shall kiss You” (Song 8:1). Good is the soul which is outside, that the Word may be within; she is outside the body, that the Word may dwell in us.

71. “I will take You,” she says, “and bring You in” (ibid., [Col. 0529C] 2). Rightly is the Word of God taken up and brought in, because He knocks upon the soul so that a door may be opened to Him. Unless He finds the door opened to Him, He does not enter. But if anyone opens the door, He enters and dines. Thus the bride takes up the Word in order to be taught by receiving Him; consequently, not undeservedly, she still ascends to higher dwelling places and continually receives progress.

> [Note: [Col. 0529D] Six good manuscripts read: “receives a progress,” which signifies the virtues called souls. Two read: “receives a progress of virtue, which signifies the souls that say.” Others and the editions agree with our text. Nevertheless, something may seem transposed here. The passage might therefore be read: “receives progress. This is signified by the Virtues or the souls which say.” Unless one prefers to take *animae* in the attributive case. In that case, by “Virtues” angels would be meant.]

72. This is signified by the Virtues—or by the souls—which say: “Who is this that comes up white, leaning upon her brother?” (ibid., 5). Above they had said: “Who is this that looks forth like the dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun?” (Song 6:9). Here something further was found to add: she ascended while leaning upon the Word of God. For those more perfect recline upon Christ, as John reclined upon Christ’s breast. Thus this soul also either leaned upon Christ or reclined herself upon Him; or rather, since we are speaking of marriage, she was now, as one handed over into Christ’s right hand, being led to the bridal chamber by her bridegroom.

73. And because she is now united in charity, the bridegroom speaks tenderly to her and says: “Under the apple tree I raised you up; there your mother travailed with you; there she travailed who bore you” (Song 8:5). Good is the soul which rests beneath a fruitful tree, especially one of sweet fragrance. For if Nathanael, a good man in whom there was no guile, was seen under the fig tree, certainly good is she who was raised up beneath the apple tree by her bridegroom.

For it is more to be raised than to be seen, and more still to be raised by the bridegroom. Although Nathanael was seen under the tree, his soul was not the bride, since he came secretly to Christ because he feared the Jews. She was not fair as the moon nor chosen as the sun who was in the shadow; for the bride is married by day and makes public confession. Therefore this woman was beneath the apple tree, that one beneath the fig tree: this one diffused farther the fragrance of her confession; the other possessed the sweetness of purity and innocence, but lacked the ardour of the Spirit.

74. “There,” He says, “your mother travailed with you; there she travailed who bore you.” For there we are born where we are reborn. They are travailed with in whom Christ’s image is being formed. Hence he says: “My little children, with whom I am in travail again until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). For one travails who receives the spirit of salvation in the womb and pours it into others.

75. Therefore, since Christ had now been formed in this soul, He says: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song 8:6). Christ is a seal on the forehead, a seal on the heart: on the forehead, that we may always confess Him; on the heart, that we may always love Him; on the arm, that we may always work. Let His image, therefore, shine in our confession, shine in love, shine in works and deeds, so that, if possible, His whole form may be expressed in us.

> [Note: [Col. 0530D] All editions read: “Let it shine in reading”; all manuscripts: “in love.”]

Let Him be our head, because Christ is the head of man; let Him be our eye, that through Him we may see the Father; let Him be our voice, through whom we may speak to the Father; let Him be our right hand, through whom we may offer our sacrifice to God the Father. He is also our seal, the emblem of perfection and charity, because the loving Father sealed the Son, as we read: “Him has God the Father sealed” (John 6:27). Thus Christ is our charity. Good is the charity which offered Himself to death for our offences; good is the charity which forgave sins.

> [Note: [Col. 0530D] Thus the Amiens edition and nearly all manuscripts. Other editions and manuscripts read: “but another work, for the beloved.”]

76. Therefore let our soul put on charity, and charity such as is strong as death; for just as death is the end of sins, so also is charity, because whoever loves the Lord ceases to sin. For charity does not think evil, nor rejoice in iniquity, but endures all things. For how will one who does not seek what is his own seek another’s goods? There is also that strong death through the laver, through which every sin is buried and guilt forgiven. Such was the charity borne by that woman in the Gospel, of whom the Lord said: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47).

There is also the strong death of holy martyrs, which abolishes former guilt; and it is therefore strong, because charity is not unequal to it—that charity which is matched to the martyrs’ suffering, so that it removes the penalty due to sins.

77. “Jealousy also [is] as hell” (Song 8:6), because whoever has zeal for God does not spare even what is his own for Christ’s sake. Thus charity has death, charity has zeal, and charity has wings of fire. Indeed, Christ, loving Moses, appeared to him as a sign. And Jeremiah, having within himself the gift of divine charity, said: “There was a burning fire in my bones; and I was dissolved on every side, and cannot endure it” (Jer. 20:9).

Good, then, is charity which has the wings of burning fire, which flits through the breasts and hearts of the saints and burns away everything material and earthly; whatever is pure, it tests; and whatever it touches, it improves by its own fire. The Lord Jesus sent this fire upon the earth: faith shone forth, devotion was kindled, charity was illuminated, justice gleamed. With this fire He kindled the hearts of His apostles, as Cleophas testifies, saying: “Was not our heart burning within us while He opened the Scriptures?” (Luke 24:32).

The flames of fire’s wings, therefore, are the divine Scriptures. For He opened the Scriptures, and fire went forth and penetrated the hearts of the hearers. And truly they are wings of fire, because “the words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire.” When Paul too was taken up by Christ, he saw a light shining around him and over those who were with him; he fell in fear and rose more approved. Indeed, he became an apostle, though he had come as a persecutor. The Holy Spirit too descended and filled the whole house in which many were sitting, and divided tongues like fire appeared.

Good are charity’s wings, true wings which flew through the mouths of the apostles, and wings of fire which spoke a purified word.

> [Note: [Col. 0531D] The manuscripts Th., Rig., Torn., Colb., and Theod. in the first hand read: “through the mouths of the peoples.”]

With these wings Enoch flew, taken up to heaven. With these wings Elijah flew in a fiery chariot and was carried above by fiery horses. With these wings the Lord God led the people of the fathers by a pillar of fire. The Seraph had these wings when he took a fiery coal from the altar, touched the prophet’s mouth, took away his iniquities, and cleansed his sins. By the fire of these wings the sons of Levi were purified, and the peoples of the nations are baptized, as John testifies, saying of the Lord Jesus: “He will baptize you in the Spirit and in fire” (Matt. 3:11).

Rightly David wished his reins and heart to be burned, because he knew that the fiery wings of charity were not to be feared. Rightly the Hebrew children in the burning furnace did not feel the flames of fire, because charity’s flame cooled them. And, that we may know more fully that perfect charity had wings, you have heard the Lord say: “How often I wished to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings!” (Matt. 23:27).

78. Let us therefore take these wings, which, like flames, direct us upward. Let each one strip his soul of its more soiled coverings [*involucris*, OCR-corrected], and, like gold tested by fire, prove it cleansed of mud. Thus the soul is purified, like finest gold. The soul’s beauty is sincere virtue, and its truer adornment is knowledge of heavenly things: that it may see that good upon which all things depend, while it itself depends on nothing.

By that good, therefore, it lives and receives understanding. For the fountain of life is that supreme Good, Christ, whose charity and desire are kindled in us; to approach and be united with Him is delight. To one who does not see Him, He is an object of desire; in one who sees Him, He is present. Therefore such a one despises everything else, is soothed and delighted by this one thing alone. This is what supplies substance to all things, while itself remains in itself; it gives to others, but receives nothing into itself from others.

> [Note: [Col. 0531D] All editions with some manuscripts read: “supplies all substance.” Other manuscripts, more numerous and of greater authority, read as in the text.]

Of Him the Prophet says: “I said to the Lord: You are my God, because You have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15:2). This alone he desired to see, as he says elsewhere: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, and see the delight of the Lord, and contemplate His temple” (Ps. 26:4).

If anyone is worthy to see that pure, incorporeal, supreme Good, what else can he desire? Indeed, Peter saw on the mountain the glory of Christ’s resurrection and did not wish to descend, saying: “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17:4). And how incomparably greater is that glory of divinity and inaccessible light! If anyone sees it, what else could he desire? Not kingdoms, wealth, honours, glory, or powers. For there is no blessedness in using those things; blessedness is in enjoying this Good, so that, despising those things, one may remain turned toward this.

Seeing, therefore, this beautiful image, let one enter within and leave outside the face of the body. For one who looks upon bodies ought not to look inward, lest, like a man sinking in a whirlpool, he be swept away and swallowed up and, plunged as it were into the depths, appear nowhere. Let us therefore flee to the truest fatherland. There is our fatherland, and there is the Father from whom we were created, where is Jerusalem, the city which is mother of all.

79. But what is this flight? Certainly not the flight of bodily feet.

> [Note: [Col. 0532D] The Reims manuscript reads: “For wherever these run,” etc.]

For wherever they run, they run upon earth and pass from ground to ground. Nor should we flee by ships, chariots, or horses, which are tied down and fall; rather, let us flee in mind and with our inner eyes or feet. Let us accustom our eyes to see things bright and clear, to behold the countenance of continence and temperance, and all virtues in which there is nothing rough, dark, or crooked. Let each person behold himself and his conscience; let him cleanse that eye, so that it may have no defilement.

> [Note: [Col. 0532D] Thus all editions and several manuscripts. But three manuscripts of no small authority read: “and let him cleanse that eye of his conscience.” Four read: “let him cleanse his conscience through that eye.” At the same place, all editions and four manuscripts read: “that it may have nothing filthy”; others, better: “that it may have no defilement,” etc.]

For what is seen ought not to disagree with the one who sees, because God willed us to be conformed to the image of His Son. This Good, therefore, has been made known to us, and it is not far from each of us: “For in Him we live and are and move. For we are also His offspring” (Acts 17:28), as the Apostle represented the Gentiles as meaning.

> [Note: [Col. 0533B] Several manuscripts read: “and he cited a pagan.” “It is the Good itself which we seek, the sole Good” (some read “the supreme Good”). Others, including those of better age and the old editions, read as in the text, except that the Amiens and Gillot editions read “to signify.” Finally the Roman edition reads: “he wished to remind the Gentiles. It is,” etc. But no room will remain for variation if one translates it thus: Paul, in his address to the Areopagites, cited—or said that pagan poets had signified—this: namely, that in God we live, are, etc.]

It is the Good which we seek, the only Good. For no one is good except God alone. This is the eye which beholds that great and true beauty. An eye that is not healthy and strong does not look upon the sun; nor can anyone see the Good except a good soul. Therefore let the one who wishes to see the Lord and that which is good become good, be like this Good, and perform works that are good according to it.

This is the Good above every operation, above every mind and understanding. It is that which always remains; all things turn toward it; in it dwells the fullness of divinity, and through it all things are reconciled into it.

> [Note: [Col. 0534B] The Long manuscript reads: “the fullness of divinity bodily, and through Him all things are turned,” etc.]

And, to define more fully what good is: LIFE is good, because it always remains, giving life and being to all things. For Christ is the fountain of every life, of whom the prophet says: “In His shadow we shall live” (Lam. 4:20). For now our life is hidden in Christ; but when Christ, our life, appears, then we too shall appear with Him in glory.

Therefore let us not fear death, for it is the body’s rest and the soul’s freedom or release. Nor let us fear one who can kill the flesh but cannot kill the soul; for we do not fear one who can take away a garment, nor do we fear one who can steal what is ours but cannot steal us ourselves. We, then, are souls—if we wish to be Hebrews, among those who are Jacob’s companions, that is, his imitators. We are souls; our limbs are garments. The garments must indeed be preserved, lest they be torn or grow old; but he who uses them must preserve and guard himself still more.

## [ON THE GOOD OF DEATH]

### ADMONITION TO THE BOOK *ON THE GOOD OF DEATH*, WHERE THE DWELLING PLACES OF SOULS AFTER DEATH AND THE FOURTH BOOK OF EZRA ARE PARTICULARLY DISCUSSED

How close a relationship the book *On the Good of Death* has with the preceding work *On Isaac and the Soul* is sufficiently declared by its opening words. If anyone wished to interpret them more strictly, he might perhaps not without reason maintain that the two books form one continuous work, as it were one body, of which one book should be called the first and the other the second. For what else does Ambrose appear to have intended when, after ending the book *On Isaac* with the thought, “Therefore let us not fear death,” etc., he begins the next with these words: “Since in the preceding book we have woven together some discourse concerning the soul, we think it easier to compose something concerning the good of death,” etc.? Thus, what had not been treated sufficiently fully at the end of the former composition is proposed for fuller and more careful discussion in this work.

Here, therefore, the holy Doctor shows that death is good, what its benefits are, and how little it ought to be feared. He pursues this purpose by a sufficiently careful method. For, after setting forth a definition of life and death and raising several objections against death’s usefulness—which he subsequently removes—he demonstrates that there are three kinds of death. He proves that the third kind, consisting in the separation of soul and body, is good and full of happiness; and that whatever may be fearful or burdensome in it must be attributed not to death, but to our own weakness.

Nothing, moreover, more clearly reveals the holy man’s piety than the fact that nearly all his arguments rest upon the authority of the sacred writings. If he adduces any argument derived from natural reason, which philosophers had already advanced in a similar matter, he never fails to confirm it with some divine testimony. Taking this occasion, he teaches Christians how little they should cling to this life, which is so full of every kind of misery, and how earnestly they should die to the world—extinguishing bodily pleasures, every desire, and the world’s allurements (chap. 3 ff.)—so that, through the benefit of a whole and holy life, they may not fear death, which sin alone can make terrible. He repeatedly proves this last point, especially throughout chapters 5, 6, and 7 of this short work.

Finally, having asserted the soul’s immortality, he explains what its condition will be when separated from companionship with the body. In conclusion, he exhorts the faithful to strive with all diligence to be joined to God and to cleave to Him with an undivided mind, so that, once the course of this life has ended, they may attain the assembly of patriarchs, the heaven of saints, and the company of the righteous, where the Lord Jesus has prepared dwelling places for His servants, that where He is, we also may be (chap. 12).

From the entire arrangement of this work one may perceive not only that nothing is more suited to moral instruction, but also that it is plainly contemporaneous with the book *On Isaac*—that is, published about the year 387. Nor does it seem unreasonable to infer from this also that it consists of sermons which Ambrose, having delivered to the same persons for whom the preceding treatises were intended, later converted into a book entitled *On the Good of Death*, under which title Augustine cites it more than once (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, IV.11). Perhaps for all these reasons it came about that one of the royal manuscripts bears the title: “Third book from the book *On the Patriarchs*, which is entitled *On the Good of Death*.”
