Yet what the holy Doctor sets forth at the end of this work concerning the condition of souls stripped of their bodies, and concerning the author from whom that doctrine proceeded, certainly throws us into two quite considerable difficulties. For first, if we interpret our Doctor’s words strictly and to the letter, we shall be compelled plainly to acknowledge that, in his judgment, souls are kept enclosed in certain dwelling-places (ch. 10) until the general resurrection; that there they await the recompense due to their works, but one not at all to be rendered before the Last Day; that meanwhile they are nevertheless affected either by certain benefits or by punishments (ibid.), according to the merits of each; and finally, that the joy of the righteous is arranged in certain orders (ch. 11).

It is indeed not surprising that Ambrose wrote in this manner about the state of souls; but it may seem almost incredible how uncertain and inconsistent the holy Fathers were in this question from the very times of the Apostles until the pontificate of Gregory XI and the Council of Florence—that is, throughout almost the whole span of fourteen centuries. For they not only disagree with one another, as commonly happens in questions of this kind not yet defined by the Church; they also do not sufficiently agree with themselves. In some passages of their writings they seem to grant that these same souls enjoy a clear sight of the divine nature, and in others to deny the very same thing.

It is not the purpose of our present undertaking to gather here those differing opinions of the ancient Fathers. Anyone wishing to learn more on this matter may consult Alphonsus a Castro (*Against Heresies*, book III), Sixtus of Siena (*Bibliotheca*, book VI, annotation 345), Bellarmine (*On the Blessed*, book I, ch. 1 ff.), Petavius (*Dogmatic Theology, On God*, chs. 13–14), and others. We merely observe here that all this diversity of language arose from various principles supplied to those holy men by their reading of the sacred pages. Hence those who embraced the error of the Millenarians denied, on the same grounds, a beatific vision before the resurrection of bodies. And although their successors vigorously attacked and overthrew that error, they still remained doubtful and divided concerning the vision of God.

For when they turn their attention to Christ’s prayer, in which he entreats the Father for the elect, “that they may be,” he says, “with me,” etc. (John 17:24); to that apostolic saying, “to be dissolved and to be with Christ is far better” (Phil. 1:23); to such expressions as “the kingdom of heaven,” “eternal life,” and others like them; and especially when they consider the distinction between those whose death preceded Christ’s resurrection and those who departed this life after those whom Christ had already freed from limbo—then they do not at all doubt that this blessed sight belongs to disembodied souls. This is particularly so when they honour either martyrs with a solemn eulogy or other outstanding persons with a funeral oration.

On the other hand, they seem by no means to admit the same thing when they consider the parables of the labourers in the vineyard, Lazarus, the Rich Man, and Abraham’s bosom; but especially when they weigh all that Scripture teaches concerning the final judgment and universal resurrection. On these two hinges turn all Christ’s exhortations and promises in his parables, those of the Apostles in the Catholic Epistles, and—in a word, as the Apostle testifies—the whole faith of Christians; indeed, also the hope of the blessed Job and Tobit, the threats of the prophets, and likewise the prayers of the saints. The scholastics themselves also acknowledge that at that time the glory of the soul will be increased not a little; so that there have not been lacking those who asserted that even the intuitive vision of God itself would be much more intense and perfect.

Certainly the great Augustine does not deny (*Sermons* 220 and 238, on the feast of martyrs; *On Psalms* 36, 43, and 116; *City of God*, book XII, ch. 9; book XX, chs. 14–16; *On Genesis*, book XII, ch. 34, and elsewhere) that he finds it very difficult to understand how those souls can attain the sight of the divine nature, since they are not borne toward it with their whole striving and impulse, being still most strongly inclined toward a created good, namely union with the body. Yet, observing on the other hand that such an inclination can be subject to God, and that after the resurrection those same souls will also be occupied with the care of governing the body, he was moved by these considerations. Having considered various solutions, he finally admits in the *Retractations* (book I, ch. 14) that his mind still remains doubtful and divided, and that he dares define nothing on this subject.

Following this Augustinian principle, Bernard (*Sermons on All Saints*, 3 and 4; *Sermon on the Dedication of a Church*, 4) went beyond its bounds so far as to seem to grant to the spirits of the righteous only the vision or knowledge of Christ’s humanity. We think no one comes closer to him in this view than the author of the *Questions to the Orthodox* (question 75), hitherto published among Justin’s works. It is for the reader to judge whence that agreement arose. Nevertheless, not a few testimonies of Bernard are advanced (*On Loving God*, book I; sermon on St Malachy and on the death of Humbert; first sermon for Pentecost, 2; *On the Ascension*, 6; sermons on the *Song of Songs*, 98 and 266, and elsewhere) which establish that he by no means denies the vision of God to the righteous dead.

Since this is so, no one ought to wonder if Ambrose also, like other Fathers, led by differing principles, sometimes granted that God is seen by the saints and sometimes denied it. Yet, since no passage in this subject is more celebrated or more difficult than the one under discussion, we seem unable to decline examining it more carefully.

First, then, it is beyond controversy that Ambrose does not here understand bodily dwellings, since both elsewhere and constantly in this book he declares the soul to be of a spiritual nature; whence it follows that it does not require a bodily place. Next, he asserts that the souls of the reprobate are tormented because they see certain dwellings of the righteous, in which they are to be received after the day of universal judgment, guarded by angels. And these are doubtless the abodes of glory, which must accordingly be bodily, because souls are again to be joined to their bodies, which will indeed fill bodily space. Finally, he signifies (chs. 10 and 12) that Christ spoke of those first dwellings: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14:2). But who does not know that these dwelling-places signify nothing other than the various degrees of glory which the souls of the blessed, who enjoy the divine vision, attain in heaven?

Therefore, we think it by no means absurd if someone affirms that when the holy Bishop explains with such earnestness of mind those abodes and the blessedness of the saints distributed into seven orders, he rather posits and holds the vision of God as certain than denies it. Does not the inference which he draws from this also point to the same conclusion? “Therefore, because the righteous,” he says (ch. 11), “have this recompense, that they may see the face of God and that light which enlightens every human being,” etc. Nor does he only once in this passage declare that the souls of the righteous will be with Christ—doubtless in that blessed contemplation of God which he expressly ascribes to Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius (*On the Death of Valentinian*; *On the Death of Theodosius*).

If we look more deeply into the matter, we shall find that Ambrose repeatedly stated and maintained this principle: the sole obstacle preventing the soul from seeing God is the bond of the corruptible body. Although this occurs frequently in his other works, it is plainly declared in this place, where he says: “Then, with unveiled face, it will be possible to behold the glory of the Lord, which souls now, wrapped in the clinging entrails of this body and in certain stains of this flesh, cannot see sincerely” (ch. 11). Therefore, when we read here that they await the recompense due to them (ch. 10), why may we not understand their reunion with their bodies, the glory of those same bodies, the sentence of the final judgment, and the consummation of all the elect, for which, as he writes elsewhere, the saints groan? “Although,” he says, “they are secure concerning their own merit, nevertheless, because the redemption of the whole body of the Church is still to come, they suffer with it. For while members of their body are still suffering, how can the other members, though higher, fail to suffer with them?” (*Letter* 39, to Orontius). How the statement that they are “secure concerning their own merit” (ch. 11) can be reconciled with another passage in book II of *Cain and Abel* (ch. 2, no. 9), you will understand from the note appended below to chapter 11.

It should not be overlooked that, among sacred writers, the author of the *Imperfect Work on Matthew* attributed to Chrysostom is the most like Ambrose in determining the blessedness of souls and in drawing testimonies from the apocryphal Ezra. Let the reader judge whether any argument may be drawn from this to confirm the opinion of those who include that author among the writers of the Latin Church (Homily 34).

We must now proceed to the second point: namely, that Ambrose borrowed from the book called Fourth Ezra all that he here teaches concerning souls freed from bodily association. The holy Bishop certainly does not hesitate to number that book among the canonical Scriptures and to ascribe it to the prophet Ezra as its parent-author. He declares that Ezra, divinely inspired, committed to writing whatever had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit. Finally, he professes, and frequently repeats, that the book possesses divine authority and is not to be regarded as inferior to any contained in our Bibles. Nor does he speak thus only here, but also in many other writings: for example, in his Commentary on Luke (book II), the second book *On the Holy Spirit* (ch. 7), the funeral oration on the death of his brother Satyrus (near the end), and finally in his letter to Orontianus (Letter 38), whom he exhorts to read it diligently, in order that he may learn that the substance of the soul is spiritual and immortal.

Almost all modern writers are troubled that the holy Doctor should have spoken thus about a book which they judge wholly apocryphal; that is, whose author, they say, is not only obscure and is not believed to have written under the dictation of the Holy Spirit, but whose authority in the Church is also obscure: first, because it was never received by any canon, either among the Jews or in the Church, but was rejected by the common consent of the Fathers; and secondly, because various errors are found in it, such as its account of the storehouses of souls and similar matters.

They indeed parade the authority of Jerome, who, disputing against Vigilantius, rejects the same book as not received by the Church, although he had not yet read it when he wrote these words. For he says: “You are awake and asleep, and asleep and writing; and you offer me an apocryphal book, which is read under Ezra’s name by you and those like you. … I have never read that book. For why should I take into my hands what the Church does not receive?” Elsewhere (*Letter to Domnion and Rogatianus*) he inveighs still more vehemently not only against the fourth book, but also against the third, although those who now follow the saint as their guide in this opinion do not show themselves so hostile to this book. Some add that the great Ezra, the scribe and doctor of the law, whom they suppose to be the author of Third Ezra, is not to be regarded as the author of Fourth Ezra, but another person bearing the same name.

Nevertheless, there have not been lacking persons who judged this work more fairly and favourably. They held that it contains not only no error, but also possesses pre-eminent authority in the Church, which has inserted some passages taken from it into its prayers (in the Mass on the Tuesday of Pentecost and on martyrs’ feasts) and has not forbidden its printing at the end of Bibles. Indeed, this very book is found listed among the canonical books in certain manuscripts of ancient date—though not in all, and not without some distinction.

For in a very ancient codex preserved in our Library, the two canonical books of Ezra having been bound together into one, the second begins with the first chapter of this Fourth Ezra, undoubtedly because this is its opening: “The second book of Ezra the prophet.” Then, from chapters intermixed from this book and the third book, four little books are formed. The most learned Faber, tutor of Louis XIII (*Letter to Cardinal Baronius*), found a manuscript of the same fourth book to differ so greatly from the printed edition that he thought its variant readings ought to be sent to Cardinal Baronius. This diversity may perhaps explain why some passages cited by Ambrose from the same book are not found in the printed text.

Finally, there has been found an author of this age who believed the last two books of Ezra to be canonical and of divine authority, and endeavoured to establish this opinion in writing (Genebrard, *Chronology*, book II, at year of the world 368). But whatever may be the case in this matter, it is established that Ambrose was not alone among the ancient Fathers in holding this view. Clement of Alexandria (*Stromata*, book III), citing the fourth book, calls Ezra a prophet; the author of the *Imperfect Work on Matthew* praises him in a similar manner (place cited above); and finally Cyprian seems to allude to him (*To Demetrianus*).

Accordingly, it does not seem at all surprising to us that Ambrose here commended and extolled the authority of a book which, as is clear from his other writings, he in good faith regarded as canonical. For, as he himself declares, he did this in order to convict of falsehood the pagans who accused Christ and his disciples of borrowing their teaching from Plato and those philosophers, by making plain that Plato himself had rather borrowed from Ezra and our other authors whatever sound teaching he gave concerning the condition of souls after death.

This accusation was not new among the heathen. Celsus had advanced it against Origen many years earlier, in precisely the same connection (*Origen, Against Celsus*, book VII). And since in Ambrose’s time the power of idolatry, which Symmachus upheld by his authority, still had considerable force, there is no doubt that the same calumny was then renewed. Accordingly, it will not seem surprising if, in order to overthrow the falsehood that was about to undermine the Christian faith at its foundation, the holy Doctor proclaimed the authority of this writer as strongly as he could. He also adds other testimonies from the sacred pages, by which he may irrefutably demonstrate to those proud pagans that Plato and their Socrates drew much from these most limpid fountains of truth—matters which they later corrupted with the diluted mud of diverse fables. It is in fact so commonly held that Plato learned very much either from the sacred books, as Ambrose teaches here, or, as others wish, from Pythagoras, who himself had heard Jewish sages, that the saying of Numenius the Pythagorean concerning him became proverbial: “For what is Plato but Moses speaking Attic Greek?” (Τί γάρ ἐστι Πλάτων ἢ Μωϋσῆς ἀττικίζων;). [Col. 0539B]

# ONE BOOK OF ST AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON THE GOOD OF DEATH

[Note: Written about the year 387.] (C)

[Col. 0539]

389 CHAPTER I

He connects this book with the preceding one, and proposes the question: How can death not be called evil, although it is contrary to life?

1. Since in the preceding book we have composed some discourse concerning the soul, we think it easier to compose something on the Good of Death. If death harms the soul, it may seem to be evil; but if it does the soul no harm, it is not even evil. Now what is not evil is also good, because what is defective is evil, whereas what is free from defect is good; and therefore goods are contrary to evils, and evils to goods. Thus innocence exists where there is no will to harm; and a person is called harmful who is not harmless; merciful, one who forgives; unmerciful, one who does not know how to forgive or be moved.

[Col. 0539B]

2. But perhaps someone may maintain: What is so contrary as life and death? If, then, life is considered good, how is death not evil? Therefore let us consider what life is, and likewise what death is. Life is the enjoyment of the faculty of breathing; death is deprivation of it. This faculty of breathing is counted among goods by most people. Therefore life is the enjoyment of goods; death, conversely, is the stripping away of goods.

And Scripture says: “Behold, I have set before your face life and death, good and evil” (Deut. 30:15), calling life good [Col. 0540A] and death evil; or else correlating the former with the former and the latter with the latter. Thus, to use the example of the divine reading: in Paradise humanity was placed in order to eat from the tree of life and from the other trees of Paradise; but from the tree in which was knowledge of good and evil it was not to eat; and on the day it ate, it would die by death (Gen. 2:16–17). It did not keep the commandment, was deprived of the fruit, and, cast out of Paradise, tasted death. Death, therefore, is evil, since it is imposed as the price of condemnation.

390 CHAPTER II

Having first distinguished three kinds of death, he shows that the third kind is intermediate; indeed, it ought rather to be judged good, because it frees us from life’s miseries and sins. Yet it must be awaited patiently.

[Col. 0540B]

3. But there are three kinds of death. One is the death of sin, of which it is written: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:4). Another is mystical death, when someone dies to sin and lives to God, of which the Apostle says: “For we were buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. 6:4). The third death is that by which we complete the course and service of this life, that is, the separation of soul and body.

We observe, therefore, that one death is evil, if we die because of sins; another [Col. 0541A] death is good, by which one who has died has been justified from sin; the third death is intermediate. For it appears good to the righteous and is to be feared by most people; though it releases all, it pleases few. Yet this is not death’s fault, but our own weakness: we are captivated by bodily pleasure and the delight of this life, and tremble to finish this course, in which there is more bitterness than pleasure. But not holy and wise men, who groaned beneath the length of this pilgrimage, considering it more beautiful “to be dissolved and to be with Christ”; indeed, they cursed the day of their birth, as someone says: “Let the day perish on which I was born” (Job 3:2).

4. For what is there to make this life delightful, full as it is of miseries and anxieties? In it are innumerable accusations, [Col. 0541B] many troubles, and many tears of those afflicted by troubles; and “there is no one,” it says, “to console them” (Lam. 1:2). Therefore Ecclesiastes praises the dead above the living. “And better,” he says, “than these two is the one not yet born, who has not seen this evil” (Eccl. 4:2–3). Elsewhere the same Ecclesiastes declares better than a man of long life (Eccl. 6:3) the one whom his mother has cast forth in miscarriage, because he has not seen these evils done in this world, has not entered into these darknesses, and has not walked in the vanity of the age. Therefore, he who did not enter this life will have more rest here than one who did. For what good is there for a human being in this life, who lives in a shadow and cannot be filled with desires? Even if one is filled with riches, one loses the fruit of peace, [Note: [Col. 0541D] Remigius: “For since it is of no use to guard what one has sought with wretched greed, one must necessarily possess it more wretchedly, since it could not benefit its possessor. For what, etc.?” Theodoret likewise, but as a correction.] because one is compelled to guard what one has sought with wretched [Col. 0541C] greed, and thus possesses it more miserably, though it cannot be of benefit. For what is more miserable than to be tormented by guarding things whose abundance is of no use?

5. Therefore, if life is full of burden, its end is certainly relief; and relief is good; but death is the end: death, therefore, is good. Simeon did not otherwise rejoice. He had received the answer that he would not see death until he had first seen the Christ of the Lord; and when his parents brought him into the temple, he took him in his arms and said: [Note: [Col. 0541D] The Roman edition reads here and below, “Now, Lord, dismiss your servant,” etc. This agrees sufficiently with the sense and sequence of words; nevertheless, all manuscripts and old editions differ from the Vulgate only in omitting “Lord.”] “Now you dismiss your servant in peace” (Luke 2:29), as though he were held in this life by some necessity, not by his will. Thus he asks to be dismissed, as though hastening from certain bonds to freedom.

For there are, as it were, certain bonds [Note: [Col. 0541D] The same Roman edition: “the thoughts of this body.” [Col. 0542D] Yet the word “thoughts” is found neither in other editions nor in any manuscripts whatsoever, nor does it seem very necessary to the sense.] of this body, and, what is more grievous, bonds [Col. 0541D] of temptations, which bind us and constrain us into the injurious captivity of a certain law of sin. Indeed, at the very moment of departure we see how the soul of a dying person gradually loosens itself from the bonds of flesh and, issuing from the mouth, flies away as though released from the prison-like hovel of this body. [Col. 0542A]

Holy David also hastened to depart from this place of pilgrimage, saying: “I am a stranger with you upon the earth, and a sojourner, like all my fathers” (Ps. 38:13). Therefore, as a sojourner he hastened to that common fatherland of all the saints, asking that his sins be forgiven because of the defilement of this temporary abode before he departed from life. For whoever has not received forgiveness of sins here will not be there. But that person will not be, who cannot attain eternal life, because eternal life is forgiveness of sins. Therefore he says: “Forgive me, that I may be refreshed before I depart and am no more” (Ps. 38:14).

6. Why, then, do we so greatly desire this life, in which the longer anyone has lived, the heavier [Col. 0542B] a burden of sins is laid upon him? The Lord himself says: “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6:34). And Jacob said: “The days of the years of my life which I have lived are one hundred and thirty, few and evil” (Gen. 47:9)—not because the days are evil, but because, with the addition of days, increases of evil are accumulated for us. For no day passes without our sin.

7. Therefore the Apostle excellently says: “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21), referring one thing to the necessity of life and the other to the advantage of death. For Christ is our life, whom we serve and to whom the service of his saints must be rendered in preaching the Gospel. Thus Simeon too, who said, “Now you dismiss your servant” (Luke 2:29), waited because of Christ. For Christ is our king; and therefore we cannot abandon or despise what the king commands.

How many persons does the emperor of this earth command to reside in foreign places, whether under the appearance of an honour or for the sake of some office? Do they depart without consulting the emperor? And how much greater it is [Note: [Col. 0542D] Several manuscripts: “to please divine powers than to live on earth. Therefore, for the saint Christ is life,” etc. Other manuscripts and the old editions read as in the text; the Roman edition substitutes “for the servant of God Christ is life” for “for the saint Christ is life.” Again, the words “Therefore the Apostle” are absent from all editions and from not a few manuscripts; some good manuscripts restore them.] to obey divine things than human! Therefore Christ is life to the saint, and death is gain. Hence the Apostle is like a servant—for he does not shrink from life’s service—and like a wise man he embraces death’s gain. For it is gain to have escaped the increase of sin, gain to have fled worse things and passed over to better things. And he added: “For to be dissolved and to be with Christ is far better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary because of you” (Phil. 1:23–24). One thing is better, another necessary: necessary because of the fruit of the work; better because of Christ’s grace and union.

## CHAPTER III

Natural death is defined and praised. Likewise, mortification, which is a certain imitation of death, is explained and commended for its manyfold benefit. Finally, a brief and elegant description of life is presented.

[Col. 0542D]

[Col. 0543A]

8. Therefore, since the Apostle has taught (Phil. 1:23–24) that one who escapes from this body, provided that one has deserved it, will be with Christ, let us consider what death is and likewise what life is. Thus, Scripture teaching us, we have learned that death is the release of soul and body, and a certain separation of the human being. For when we depart, we are loosed from this bond of soul and body. Hence David also says: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115:17). The preceding verse of this psalm teaches that the bonds of this life—that is, our union, which consists of soul and body—are signified: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (ibid., 15).

Therefore, as a prophet foreseeing that he would be among the saints and among those who, out of devotion, laid down their souls in Christ, he rejoices. For he himself faithfully offered himself for God’s people against Goliath, when he fought in single combat and alone repelled the common danger and [Note: [Col. 0543D] “Charge” (*crimen*), that is, accusation—namely, the curses and reproaches heaped by the giant Goliath upon the whole Israelite army.] reproach; or when he stood ready to expose himself to death in order to appease the Lord’s anger; or when he was prepared to offer himself to divine vengeance for the safety of the suffering people. For he knew that it was more glorious to die for Christ than to reign in this age. What indeed is more excellent than to become Christ’s sacrifice?

Thus, although we frequently read that sacrifices were offered by him to the Lord, in this passage he nevertheless added: “To you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (ibid., 17). “I do not sacrifice,” he says, “but I will sacrifice,” signifying that the sacrifice will be perfect when each person, released from the bonds of this [Col. 0543C] body, stands before the Lord and offers himself as a sacrifice of praise. For before death no praise is perfect, nor can anyone in this life be proclaimed by a final encomium, since what comes afterward remains uncertain.

Death, therefore, is the release of soul and body. Indeed, we have taught that the Apostle says: “To be dissolved and to be with Christ is far better” (Phil. 1:23). What else does this release accomplish except that the body is dissolved and rests, while the soul returns to its rest and is free—and, if devout, will be with Christ?

393 9. What else, then, do the righteous do in this life except seek to strip themselves of the contaminations of this [Note: [Col. 0543D] The Roman edition, together with manuscripts neither numerous nor ancient, reads “the contaminations of this body.” Other and more numerous, better manuscripts read “the thoughts of this body.” Not badly so: for why should thoughts of things pertaining to bodily necessity or pleasure not be called thoughts of the body?] body, which bind us like chains; endeavour to separate themselves from these troubles; renounce their pleasures [Col. 0543D] and luxury; and flee the flames of lust?

Does not everyone who can so conduct oneself while placed in this life imitate the form of death—so that all bodily pleasures die to that person, and that person also dies to every desire and the enticements of the world? So Paul was dead when he said: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). Thus, that we may know that there is a death in this life, and a good death, he exhorts [Col. 0544A] us (2 Cor. 4:10) to carry about in our body the death of Jesus. Whoever has the death of Jesus in oneself will also have the life of the Lord Jesus in one’s body. Let death, therefore, work in us, so that life too may work (see St Augustine, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book IV, ch. 11).

Good life follows death—that is, good life after victory, good life after the contest has been concluded—so that the law of the flesh may no longer know how to oppose the law of the mind; so that we may no longer have any struggle with the body of death, but that victory may be in the body of death. And I do not know whether this death may not itself be a greater virtue than life. I am certainly moved by the authority of the Apostle, who says: “Therefore death works in us, but life in you” (2 Cor. 4:12). The death of one man built up the life of how many peoples!

Therefore he teaches that this death too ought to be sought by those placed in this life, so that the death of Christ may shine forth in our body; and that blessed death by which our outer human being is corrupted, that our inner human being may be renewed, and our earthly house dissolved so that a heavenly dwelling may be opened to us. Therefore one imitates death who draws oneself away from fellowship with this flesh and loosens those bonds concerning which the Lord says to you through Isaiah: “Loose every bond of injustice, undo the obligations of violent contracts, send forth the crushed into release, and break every unjust encumbrance” (Isa. 58:6).

10. One also imitates death who strips oneself of pleasures, [Note: [Col. 0544D] So eight manuscripts of better quality. Others: “and from earthly pleasures.” All editions: “and from earthly thoughts.”] raises and lifts oneself up to eternal delights, and places oneself in that heavenly dwelling in which Paul, while still alive, had his conversation. Otherwise he would not say: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20), which may equally be referred to confidence of merit and to meditation.

For there was his meditation; there was his soul’s manner of life; there was his understanding, which certainly was not accustomed to cling within the narrow confines of this flesh. For when the wise person seeks that divine reality, one releases one’s soul from the body and sends away its companionship, when one treats of the knowledge of truth which one desires to be shown, as it were, naked and open to oneself. Therefore one seeks to strip oneself of the nets and mists of this body.

For we cannot grasp that higher truth with these hands or with eyes and ears, because “the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” Indeed, we are often deceived by sight and see very many things otherwise than they are. We are also deceived by hearing. Therefore, if we do not wish to be deceived, let us contemplate not the things that are seen but those that are not seen. [Col. 0544D]

394 When, then, is our soul not deceived? When does it reach the throne of truth, except when it separates itself from this body and is neither deceived nor mocked by it? For it is mocked by the sight of the eyes and mocked by the hearing of the ears; therefore let it leave and abandon the body. Hence [Col. 0545A] the Apostle cries: “Do not touch; do not handle; do not taste—all things which are for corruption” (Col. 2:21). For those things which belong to indulgence of the body are in corruption.

Therefore, showing that he found what is true not through bodily indulgence but through the elevation of the soul and humility of heart, he added: “But our citizenship is in heaven.” There, then, let the soul seek what is true, what both is and remains; let it gather itself into itself and concentrate all the force of its power. Let it not entrust itself to or rely upon others, but know and understand itself; and let it know that what appears true to it is what must be followed. Whatever it judges should be chosen because of fleshly delight, let it know to be false; let it flee and withdraw from it, because it is full of deceit.

[Col. 0545B]

11. Rightly, therefore, he depreciated and dishonoured this body, calling it “the body of death” (Rom. 7:24). For who has been able to see the splendour of virtue with the eyes? Who can grasp justice with the hands? Who can behold wisdom with the gaze of the eyes? Indeed, whenever we think about something, we do not want anyone to come near us or make a noise in our ears; and we concentrate our minds so intensely that we often do not see what is present. Moreover, at night we think more purely, and then meditate better in our heart upon matters that move us.

Hence the Prophet says: “What you say in your hearts, be pierced with compunction upon your beds” (Ps. 4:5). Often, too, people close their eyes if they wish to bring something forth by the deep exertion of thought, avoiding the impediments of the eyes. We often seek solitude, lest anyone’s speech whisper [Col. 0545C] in our ears and, like a path of some sort, lead away from truth the soul clinging to its thought and turn it aside from its concentration.

12. Thus the necessity of this body begets for us many occupations, and its use brings in many distractions, by which the soul’s vigor is impeded and its concentration recalled. Hence holy Job fittingly says of himself: “Remember that you fashioned me from clay” (Job 10:9). If, then, the body is clay, it surely smears us rather than washes us clean, and defiles the soul with the pollution of intemperance. “You clothed me,” he says, “with skin and flesh; you wove me together with bones and sinews” (ibid., 11). Our soul, therefore, is bound and stretched by the sinews of this body; and thus it is at times stiffened and often bent. And he adds: “You did not make me innocent of iniquity. For if I am wicked, woe is me; but if I am righteous, I shall not be able to lift up my head. For I am full of confusion. You have brought trials upon me” (ibid., 14 ff.). For what else is this life but full of snares? We walk among snares; we are occupied amid very many trials. Indeed, the same writer says above: “Is not the life of man upon earth a trial?” (Job 7:1). He rightly adds “upon earth,” because there is also a life of man in heaven. “The wage of a hired laborer,” he says, “is his life” (ibid.): that is, in toil and heat, lighter than fables, drifting and swimming in words; whose dwelling is in houses of mud, and whose very life is in mire. There is no firmness of judgment, no constancy. By day one longs for night; by night one seeks day. Before food there are groans; amid food, weeping—tears, pains, fears, anxieties. There is no rest from disturbances, no release from labors; and the stirring of anger and indignation is more dreadful.

Many desire death and do not obtain it; but if they obtain it, they rejoice, because death alone is rest for a man.

[Note: [Col. 0545D] Seven manuscripts read “time” instead of “heat.” Theodoret: “and trial.” Here, too, at the same place: “lighter than winds and beans … and life itself amid pains.” Florence, another Albinus manuscript, and another Regius manuscript read “lighter than boards,” perhaps “midges” (*tipulae*): little creatures that run about on the surface of water; whence the proverb, “lighter than a midge.” But the Regius manuscript has the final portion thus: “drifting and wavering in words, with no firmness of judgment; whose dwelling is in houses of mud, and in that very life [Col. 0546D] there is no constancy.” The Vatican codex agrees in the word “wavering.”]

## CHAPTER IV

Death is good in many respects, but especially because it is the end of sin and a passage to a better life; and because it has itself redeemed us.

[Col. 0546B]

13. But someone will say that it is written: “God did not make death” (Wisdom 1:13). There was life in Paradise, where there was the tree of life (Gen. 2:9), and life was the light of human beings. Death, therefore, is evil, since it came in and entered afterwards. But how is death evil if, according to the pagans, it lacks sensation; or if, according to the Apostle, Christ is gain, “and to be with him is far better” (Phil. 1:21)? How, then, is death an evil to us, if after death there is no sensation? For where there is no sensation, there is certainly no pain of injury, since pain is sensation.

Or, if there is sensation after death, there is also life after death; and the soul which employs sensation and enjoys life survives death. But when life and soul remain after death, the good remains: it is not lost through death, but increased. Nor is the soul delayed by any hindrance of death; rather, it acts more effectively, because it performs what belongs to it without any partnership with the body, which is a greater burden to the soul than a benefit. What evil, then, is there for a soul which has preserved its purity and maintained the discipline of the virtues? Or, if it has not maintained it, death is not evil, but life—because it was not life. For what sort of life is one overgrown with vices and sins? Why, then, do we accuse death, which either pays life’s debt or removes its pain and torment? Thus death either enjoys the good of its own repose or suffers from another’s evil.

14. Consider this further: if life is a burden, death is release; if life is punishment, death is remedy; or, if there is judgment after death, there is also life after death.

[Note: [Col. 0546D] The old edition reads: “Therefore that death is not good.” All the Gallican manuscripts: “Therefore that life,” etc. The Vatican codex more correctly: “Therefore life here,” etc. So also below, where the edition reads “but this life itself,” almost all manuscripts have “but life here.”]

Therefore life here is not good. Or if life here is good, how is death there not good, when no fear of dreadful judgment remains there? But if life here is good, by what things is it good? Certainly by virtue and good character. Therefore it is not good according to the union of soul and body, but because through virtue it repels what is its own evil and obtains what is good in death, so that it may work rather what belongs to the soul than what belongs to cohabitation and conjunction. And if that life is good which mirrors the soul as it separates itself from the body, and if the soul is good which raises and draws itself away from bodily cohabitation, then death also is good, since it releases and frees the soul from fellowship with this flesh.

15. Death, then, is good in every way: because it separates things at odds, lest they attack one another; because it is a kind of harbor for those tossed upon the great sea of this life and seeking the anchorage of trustworthy rest; and because it does not make one’s condition worse, but preserves each person for the future judgment in the state in which it finds him, cherishes him with repose itself, withdraws him from the envy of present things, and composes him in expectation of those to come.

There is this further consideration: people fear death in vain, as though it were the end of nature. For if we recall that God did not make death, but that after man fell into the disgrace of transgression and deceit, the sentence overtook him that earth should return to its own earth, we shall find that death is the end of sin (Gen. 3:19), lest, the longer life endured, the more numerous guilt might become. The Lord therefore permitted death to enter, so that guilt might cease. But lest death should once more be the end of nature, the resurrection of the dead was given: so that through death guilt might fail, but through resurrection nature might endure forever.

Therefore this death is the passage of all. You must pass through it steadfastly. It is a passage from corruption to incorruption, from mortality to immortality, from disturbance to tranquility. Let not, then, the name of death offend you; rather let the benefits of a good passage delight you. For what is death but the burial of vices and the rising of virtues? Hence that man also says: “Let my soul die among the souls of the righteous” (Num. 23:10), that is, let it be buried with them, so that it may put off its own vices and take on the grace of the righteous, who carry about in their body and soul the mortification of Christ. Now Christ’s mortification is forgiveness of sins, abolition of crimes, forgetfulness of error, and reception of graces. What more complete statement can we make about the good of death than this: death is that which redeemed the world?

## CHAPTER V

He exhorts us to contempt of death and to imitation, in this life, of its practice—that is, mortification. He then explains how the soul is raised to the likeness of God, by whom it is painted and guarded. Next he discusses the garden of the mind and the fruits on which the Word feeds.

[Col. 0547D]

16. But let us speak of the death common to all. Why should we fear that which is not accustomed to harm the soul? For it is written: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28). Through this death the soul is set free, when it is separated from bodily cohabitation and stripped of the wrappings of disturbance. Therefore, while we are in the body, imitating the practice of death, let us raise our soul from this bedchamber of the flesh, and let us rise, as it were, from this tomb. Let us withdraw ourselves from the body’s bond; let us leave behind all earthly things, so that when the adversary comes he may find nothing of his own in us.

Let us strive toward that which is eternal; let us fly toward that which is divine on the wings of love and with the oars of charity. Let us rise from here—that is, from secular and worldly things. For the Lord said: “Rise, let us go from here” (John 14:31), commanding each person to rise from earthly things, to raise the soul lying upon the ground, to lift it to things above, and to awaken his eagle—the eagle of which it is said: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102:5). This was said of the soul.

Let our soul, therefore, like an eagle seek the heights, fly above the clouds, shine with renewed plumage, and carry its flights into heaven, where it cannot fall into snares. For a bird that descends from on high, or cannot raise itself on high, is frequently caught either in snares, deceived by birdlime, or entangled by whatever traps may be laid. So, too, let our soul beware of descending to these worldly things. There is a snare in gold, birdlime in silver, a binding in landed property, and a nail in love. While we seek gold, we are choked; while we seek silver, we stick fast in its birdlime; while we seize an estate, we are bound. Why do we seek empty gain at the cost of a precious soul? The entire world is too small a price for the loss of one soul. “For what does it profit a man if he gains this world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will you give for your soul?” It is not redeemed with gold or silver; indeed, it is lost through gold. Even a woman’s beauty, when it is tested, binds one fast. Lust is a nail; sorrow is a nail; anger is a nail; all passions are nails, which, like a skewer, pierce our soul, fasten it into the body, and attach it to its inward parts.

[Note: [Col. 0547D] All editions read “while she tests”; the manuscripts, conversely, “while she is tested.” Here a woman’s beauty or form may be understood to be tested when a person, excessively confident in his own virtue, does not fear to approach it incautiously and too frequently.]

[Note: [Col. 0548D] Most manuscripts: “which, like certain worms, [pierce] the soul,” etc.]

17. Let us therefore flee these evils and raise our soul to that image and likeness of God. Flight from evils is likeness to God, and the image of God is acquired through virtues. Therefore he who painted us, as our Creator, painted us in the colors of virtues: “Behold,” he says to Jerusalem, “I have painted your walls” (Isa. 49:16). Let us not wipe away, with the brush of negligence, the mural foundations painted upon our soul. Therefore he said: “I have painted walls,” by which we may turn away the enemy.

18. The soul has its own walls, from which it rises above, and of which it says: “I am a fortified city; I am a besieged city” (Isa. 27:3). It is fortified by these walls and defended while besieged by them. And truly the soul is a wall, which spreads its tent in the camp. Hence it says itself in the Song of Songs: “I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers” (Song 8:10). Good is the wall which the Lord has painted, as he himself says: “In my hands I have painted your walls, and you are always before my eyes” (Isa. 49:16). Good is the soul which has God as its watchman and is in his hands, like the prophetic soul which, as spirit, is commended into the Lord’s hands (Ps. 30:6), and which is before God’s eyes: “For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. 33:16); as it also says: “I was in his eyes like one finding peace” (Song 8:10).

It has good towers when it has both discourse concerning intelligible realities and training concerning moral matters. Therefore this soul, possessing the grace of its breasts, enters into the gardens; and, finding there the Bridegroom seated and conversing with friends, says: “You who sit in the gardens, make your voice known to me” (ibid., 13–14). “To me,” it says, “not to the friends. Flee, my brother.” It urges the Bridegroom to flee, because it too can now follow him in fleeing earthly things. It says that he should be like a little gazelle escaping from nets. For it too wishes to flee and to fly above the world.

[Note: [Col. 0548D] All editions: “which is spread out in the camp.” All manuscripts: “which spreads [something] in the camp.” This is good if one mentally supplies “a tent” or “a canopy,” that is, “which dwells in the camp.”]

19. From this source Plato fashioned for himself that garden which he called in one place the garden of Jupiter, and elsewhere the garden of the mind. For he called Jupiter both god and the mind of the whole world. Into this garden, he said, entered the soul, which he calls Venus, so that she might fill herself with the abundance and riches of this garden, in which *poros*, who poured out nectar, lay drunk.

[Note: [Col. 0549D] The Albinus manuscript reads: “the garden of Mars … and god and Mars.” Remigius reads more suitably: “the garden of the mind … for he called Jupiter god, and mind the garden of the mind.” The other manuscripts and editions are best, as in the text. ]

[Note: [Col. 0549D] There is remarkable variety here among manuscripts and editions. In one place one reads “the drink which is nectar”; elsewhere “by the drink which is nectar”; elsewhere “pure [drink] which is nectar”; elsewhere, closer to the sense, “a vessel of pure nectar.” But the Vatican and Valcellian manuscripts are preferable to all, reading: “Poros, who [poured] nectar,” etc. For the holy man recalls what Plato writes in the *Symposium*: namely, that at the banquet celebrated because Venus had been born, Poros, god of abundance, entered Jupiter’s garden and fell asleep in a drunken stupor from nectar; Poverty, the goddess Penia, lay down beside him, became pregnant, and gave birth to Love. But since he says not that Penia, as the Roman edition substituted, but Venus, as all the other editions and all manuscripts have it, entered the garden, he seems to relate this fable only from memory. He may also have understood by the name *poros* not some god, but rather a channel or conduit from which a stream of nectar flowed; for πόρος, *poros*, is found in reputable authors in the sense of a channel or conduit.]

He fashioned this, then, from the book of the Song of Songs, because the soul cleaving to God has entered the garden of the mind, in which there is abundance of diverse virtues and flowers of discourses. Who, indeed, does not know that he considered the abundance of virtues to be transferred from that Paradise which we read in Genesis as containing the tree of life, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2:8), and the other trees, and to be planted in the garden of the mind? In the Song of Songs Solomon indicated this as the garden of the soul—or the soul itself. For thus it is written: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed; your channels are a paradise” (Song 4:12–13). And below the soul says: “Awake, north wind, and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let my perfumes flow. Let my brother come down into his garden.” How much more beautiful it is that the soul, adorned with the flowers of virtues, should be a garden, or have within itself a Paradise budding forth (ibid., 16)! Into this garden it invites the Word of God to descend, so that the soul, watered by the heavenly rain of the Word and by his abundance, may bear fruit.

The Word of God feeds on the virtues of the soul whenever he finds it obedient and rich; he plucks its fruits and delights in them. But when the Word of God descends into it, the perfumes of wholesome words flow from it, and fragrant breaths of diverse graces give forth their scent far and wide.

20. Hence the Bridegroom says—for the Bridegroom of the soul is the Word of God, to whom the soul is joined by a certain lawful covenant of marriage—“I have entered into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my perfumes; I have eaten my bread with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, my neighbors, and drink, and be intoxicated, my brothers. I sleep, and my heart watches” (Song 5:1–2).

Let us recognize what fruits and foods God feasts upon, and in what he delights. He delights if someone mortifies his sin, blots out his guilt, buries and destroys his iniquities. For myrrh belongs to the burial of the dead. But sins are dead, since they cannot possess the sweetness of life. Certain wounds of transgression are anointed with the perfumes of divine discourse and treated with the stronger food of the Word, as with bread, and with sweeter discourse, as with honey. Solomon also teaches elsewhere that discourses are food, saying: “Good words are honeycombs” (Prov. 16:24).

Therefore in that garden there are good words: one rebukes guilt; another corrects iniquity; another causes arrogance to die and, as it were, buries it when someone rebuked renounces his errors. There is also a stronger discourse that confirms the human heart with the more powerful nourishment of heavenly Scripture. There is also persuasive discourse, sweet as honey and yet pricking the sinner’s conscience amid its very sweetness. There is also a discourse of more ardent spirit, which intoxicates like wine and gladdens the human heart. There is also milky discourse, pure and white. The Bridegroom tells his neighbors to feast upon these foods of sweet and useful discourses: “Eat, my neighbors, and drink, and be intoxicated, my brothers” (Song 5:1). His neighbors are those who follow him and take part in his wedding.

Filled with this food and drink—for each person drinks water from his own vessels and from the springs of his own wells—and intoxicated, the soul slept to the world and watched for God. Therefore, as what follows teaches, God the Word asked that the door be opened to him, so that he might fill it by his entrance.

21. From this, then, came those Platonic banqueters; from this came that nectar of prophetic wine and honey; from this came that sleep; from this came that perpetual life which he said his gods enjoy at their feasts, because Christ is life. Therefore the belly of his soul was filled with the seeds of such discourses, and it went forth in the Word. But the soul which departs from this servitude and raises itself from the body follows the Word.

## CHAPTER VI

All things here are full of the snares of aerial principalities and worldly powers. How are they to be avoided, and what path must be pursued?

22. But there are aerial principalities and worldly powers which seek, as it were, to cast the soul down from its wall, to hinder those walking rightly, or to cast down those striving toward higher things and call them back to earthly matters. But let us all the more raise our mind to sublime things, following the Word of God. Those principalities spread worldly things before you, to bend your mind; then, O soul, direct your steps still more toward Christ. They cast in desire for gold, silver, and a neighboring possession, so that, in order to obtain it, you may excuse yourself from the supper of him who invites you to the wedding of the Word. But beware of making excuse: put on the wedding garment and enjoy the feast of the rich man, lest the rich man who invited you, when you have excused yourself because you are occupied with worldly things, invite others and you be shut out.

The powers of this world also implant ambition for honor, so that you may exalt yourself like Adam and, wishing to make yourself equal to God through likeness of power, despise the divine commands and begin to lose what you possessed. “For whoever does not have, even what he has shall be taken from him.”

[Note: [Col. 0551D] Some manuscripts: “to cast down the soul, as it were, from the wall.” Florence: “to cast [it] down from the mountain into the depths.” The other manuscripts and editions are better. For he alludes both to the foregoing chapter—“Truly the soul is a wall”—and to the proverb “to cast from the wall with a fork” or “with forks.” This proverb, widespread among Greeks and Romans, arose from the practice of defenders of a besieged city, who used forks to cast down and drive off enemies attempting to climb the walls.]

23. How often, during prayer, by which we most closely approach God, are things full of some shame or crime spread before us, in order to turn us away from the pursuit of prayer! How often does the enemy seek to implant something in our heart in order to divert us from the purpose of holiness and from devout vows! How often does he inflame bodily ardors! How often does he cause harlot’s eyes to meet ours, in order to test the chaste affection of the righteous person and strike one unprepared with the sudden arrow of love! How often does he implant in your mind an iniquitous word and hidden thoughts of the heart! Concerning this the Law says to you: “Take heed to yourself, lest there be a hidden iniquitous word in your heart” (Deut. 15:9); and the Lord says to you: “Why do you think evil in your heart?” Nor, when you abound in gold and silver, in rich fruits of the fields, or in honors, should you say: “My strength has given me these things,” and forget the Lord your God (Deut. 8:12 ff.).

24. By these things, therefore, the soul that desires to fly is cast down. But you, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus, resist; despise lower things, forget earthly things, and strive toward heavenly and eternal things. Lift up your soul, lest the bait of snares entice it. The pleasures of the world are certain baits—and, what is worse, baits of evils, baits of temptations. While you seek pleasure, you run into snares. “For the eye of a harlot is a snare for her lover.” Therefore a harlot’s eye is a snare. A harlot’s speech is also a snare: it sweetens your throat for a time, and afterwards makes it bitter with the bitterness of a sinful conscience. Another’s possession, full of pleasantness, is a snare. Every path of this life is full of snares. Hence the righteous person says: “In this path in which I walked, they hid snares for me” (Ps. 141:4). “In this path,” he says, “they hid them.” Therefore walk on that way which says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), so that you may say: “He restored my soul; he led me upon the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake” (Ps. 22:3).

[Note: [Col. 0552D] Most manuscripts read: “For the snare of a harlot.” Others, together with all editions: “For the eye of a harlot.” Indeed, in Book I of *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 4, and wherever this sentence is cited, it is given in the same words; Ambrose seems to indicate that the very words were drawn from Sacred Scripture. Yet they are found nowhere in it; their sense, however, can be referred to certain verses of Proverbs or Ecclesiastes.]

25. Therefore let this world die for us; let the wisdom of this flesh die for us, for it is hostile to God. Let us subject our soul to Christ alone, so that each may say: “Is not my soul subject to God?” (Ps. 61:2). “It is not subject to the age,” he says, “nor subject to the world.” The wealthy person cannot say this; the greedy person cannot say it. But the righteous and self-controlled person says it. The greedy person, however, says: “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast” (Luke 12:19), because the greedy person’s soul is subject to bodily luxury. But the soul of the righteous uses the body as an instrument or organ. Like an excellent craftsman, it directs the body’s service where it wishes, shapes from it whatever form it has chosen, and makes whatever virtues it wishes resound within it—now striking melodies of chastity, now melodies of moderation, the song of sobriety, the sweetness of integrity, the pleasantness of virginity, and the gravity of widowhood.

Yet the musician sometimes sympathizes with his instrument. Therefore play honorable melodies, so that the sympathy may be honorable. For one who sees is often affected by seeing, and one who hears by hearing. Therefore Scripture says: “Let your eyes look straight ahead” (Prov. 4:25). And elsewhere: “Do not be excessive toward another woman. Do not fix your gaze upon the eyes of a young woman. Do not fix your attention upon the words of a harlot” (Prov. 5:20 and elsewhere).

## CHAPTER VII

Snares also surround us in the body itself. The body must be ruled by the soul, though the soul sometimes sympathizes with it. Moreover, life abounds in so many troubles that it ought to be hated; death is bitter only to the wicked, for whom life ought nonetheless to be more bitter. Death, therefore, is not evil.

[Col. 0552D]

26. Why do I speak of external snares? We must beware of our own snares. Snares surround us in this very body, and we must avoid them. Let us not trust this body; let us not mingle our soul with it. “Mingle your mind with your friend,” he says, “not with your enemy” (Ecclus. 6:1). Your body is an enemy to you, resisting your mind; its works are enmities, dissensions, quarrels, and disturbances. Do not mingle your soul with it, lest you confuse both.

For if they are mingled, then the flesh, which is inferior, becomes better than the soul, which is superior; because the soul imparts life to the body, whereas the flesh communicates death to the soul. Thus the operation of each is confused, and almost the very substance of each is confused. The soul therefore receives into itself the insensibility of a dead body, while the body performs all the functions of the soul. And lest, because the soul is infused into the body, it be supposed that it is also mingled with it, let the nature of this light be our example. For light too is poured into an earthly place and yet is not confused with it. Let there not, then, be a confused operation between things whose substances are unlike; but let the soul be in the body to give life to the body, govern it, and illumine it.

27. Yet we cannot deny that it sympathizes with its body, for it is also saddened. Thus Jesus says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38), expressing in himself human feeling. And elsewhere: “My soul is greatly troubled” (Ps. 6:4). Likewise the musician sympathizes with his melodies, with the sound of pipe, lyre, or instrument, by voice, gesture, and feeling: sadder in sad sounds, happier in joyful ones, more excited in higher ones, and gentler and milder in softer ones, so that he himself may commend the sounds of the songs and, in some fashion, tune the feelings.

The soul also, in this body as though in musical strings, when it is sober, strikes the passions of this flesh with, so to speak, the very tips of its fingers, as it strikes the notes of strings, so as to render a harmonious and concordant concert of morals and virtues. In all its thoughts and deeds it preserves this: that all its counsels and acts may sound together in harmony. The soul, then, is that which uses; the body is that which is used. Accordingly, one is that which governs, the other that which serves; one is what we are, the other is what is ours. Whoever loves the beauty of the soul loves us; whoever loves the body’s beauty loves not the human being himself, but the beauty of the flesh—which nevertheless quickly withers and fades.

[Note: [Col. 0553D] The second Albinus manuscript: “That which uses the body in what is useful.”]

28. Therefore attend to him of whom the Prophet says: “Who has not received his soul in vain” (Ps. 23:4). He receives his soul in vain—now to speak of the troubles of this life—who builds worldly things and constructs bodily things. Every day we rise to eat and drink, and no one is filled so as not to hunger and thirst again shortly afterward. Every day we seek gain, and no limit is set to greed. “The eye,” he says, “will not be satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing” (Eccl. 1:8). Whoever loves silver is not satisfied with silver. There is no end to labor and no fruit of abundance.

Every day we desire to know new things; and what is knowledge itself but the addition of daily sorrow? “All things that are have already been, and there is nothing new under the sun; but all is vanity.” “I hated my whole life,” says Ecclesiastes (Eccl. 2:17). He who hated life certainly commended death. Accordingly, he praised the dead more than the living (Eccl. 4:2), and judged blessed the one who did not enter this life and did not undertake this empty labor.

“My heart went around,” he says, “that I might know the joy of the wicked, and consider and seek wisdom and number, and that I might know through experience joy, trouble, and agitation; and I found it more bitter than death” (Eccl. 6:26): not because death is bitter, but because it is bitter to the wicked—and yet life is more bitter than death. For it is more grievous to live unto sin than to die in sin, since the wicked person, so long as he lives, increases sin; if he dies, he ceases to sin.

[Note: [Col. 0553D] Thus all manuscripts and editions, except the Roman edition, which reads: “that I might consider and seek wisdom and number, and know the joy of the wicked.” This indeed comes closer to the Septuagint, from which, however, it differs, along with the other manuscripts, in the word “joy”; for the Septuagint reads: καὶ τοῦ γνῶναι ἀσεβοῦς ἀφροσύνην, “and to know the folly of the wicked.” But perhaps Ambrose read εὐφροσύνην, “joy.” For the remaining differences in this passage, see Nobilius.]

29. Many rejoice at acquittal from their crimes. If they are going to reform, rightly so; if they are going to persist in them, foolishly, since condemnation would have benefited them far more, so that they might not increase their sins. Concerning this, the Apostle’s saying is lofty: not only those who commit shameful acts, but also those who approve them are worthy of death (Rom. 1:32); and those who condemn in others such things as they themselves do are held inexcusable, condemned by their own judgment (Rom. 2:1). For when they condemn others, they condemn themselves. Nor should they flatter themselves because they appear for a time exempt from punishments and free from accusation, when they pay more grievous penalties within themselves and are guilty to themselves, though they do not appear so to others; and, while judging the sins of others, they turn against themselves the harsher sentence of conscience.

“But do not,” he says, “O man, despise the treasures of divine goodness and patience” (ibid., 4); for God’s goodness summons you to repentance and invites you to amendment. But your hardness, by which you persist obstinately in error, increases the severity of the future judgment, so that you may receive a recompense worthy of your offenses.

[Note: [Col. 0554D] Some manuscripts: “when a more grievous punishment tears them within.”]

30. Therefore death is not evil. For death is neither among the living nor among the dead: among the former it is not, because they still live; the latter have passed on. Thus it is not bitter to those who do not yet know it, precisely because they do not know it; nor is it bitter to those who now, according to the body, feel nothing and, according to the soul, have been set free.

[Note: [Col. 0554D] All editions read “it is not evil to them”; all manuscripts, “it is not bitter to them.”]

## CHAPTER VIII

Death itself has nothing fearful in it; rather, the opinion concerning death is what inspires fear, and that opinion must be referred to life. There are two reasons why death is considered terrible; when these have been refuted, death is commended by various testimonies, especially by the authority of blessed Job.

[Col. 0555A]

31. If death is considered terrible among the living, death itself is not terrible, but the opinion of death, which each person interprets according to his disposition or dreads according to his conscience. Let each, then, blame the wound of his own conscience, not the harshness of death. Death is a harbor of rest to the righteous; to the guilty it is considered a shipwreck. Certainly, for those to whom fear of death is burdensome, it is not burdensome to die, but burdensome to live under the fear of death. Death, therefore, is not burdensome, but fear of death is.

Fear belongs to opinion; opinion belongs to our weakness and is contrary to truth. For strength comes through truth, weakness through opinion. But the opinion is not, indeed, of death but of life. Therefore the burden is found to belong rather to life. It is clear, then, that the fear of death is not to be referred to death, but to life. For we have nothing to fear in death if our life has committed nothing that should be feared. For punishments for offenses are terrifying to the prudent; but offenses are not acts of the dead, but of the living. Life, therefore, pertains to us, since its actions are in our power; death does not concern us, for it is the separation of soul and body. The soul is released; the body is dissolved. What is released rejoices; what is dissolved into its own earth feels nothing; and what feels nothing is nothing to us.

[Note: [Col. 0555D] All editions and some manuscripts: “knows nothing.” But nine manuscripts of no slight authority: “is nothing to us.”]

32. Yet if death is evil, why do young people not fear becoming old, nor dread an age bordering on death? And why does one who declines under an expected death endure it more patiently than one who declines under an unexpected one? I think this is also a fitting reply to those who consider death an evil: through life there is a passage to death; through death, a return to life. For none can rise again except those who have died. The foolish dread death as though it were the greatest of evils; the wise seek it as rest after labors and the end of evils.

33. The foolish fear death for two reasons. First, because they call it destruction; but destruction of a human being cannot occur, since the soul survives the body, while the body itself remains preserved for resurrection. The second reason is that they dread punishments, frightened, of course, by the fables of poets: the barking of Cerberus, the gloomy gulf of the river Cocytus, more gloomy Charon, companies of Furies, or precipitous Tartarus, in which cruel Hydra has her abode; likewise the entrails of Tityus, fertile in punishments continually renewed, which a monstrous vulture devours without end; likewise the perpetual whirling of Ixion’s wheel beneath the horror of punishment; and then the rock poised above the heads of those reclining at feasts, threatening to fall.

These things are full of fables. Yet I would not deny that there are punishments after death. But what has that which is after death to do with death itself? If things after death are referred to death, then things after life must likewise be referred to life. Thus there will be no punishments attributable to death. For death, as we said above (chapter 4), is release and separation of soul and body; and release is not evil, because “to be dissolved and to be with Christ is far better” (Phil. 1:23).

Therefore death is not evil. “The death of sinners is most evil”: not, certainly, death in general is most evil, but, in particular, the death of sinners (Ps. 33:22). Conversely, the death of the righteous is precious. Hence it is clear that the bitterness belongs not to death but to guilt (Ps. 115:15).

34. The Greeks, moreover, aptly named death from its end; for they call death *teleutē* (τελευτή), because it is the end of this life [Col. 0556B]. But Scripture also calls death sleep, as in the passage: “Our friend Lazarus sleeps; but I am going, that I may awaken him” (John 11:11). Now sleep is good, because it is rest, as it is written: “I slept and rested and rose, because the Lord sustained me” (Ps. 3:6). Sweet, therefore, is the rest of death. Finally, the Lord awakens those who rest, because the Lord is the resurrection.

35. Excellent also is what Scripture says: “Before death, praise no one” (Ecclus. 11:30). For everyone is known in his last things, and is judged by his children—if he has instructed his children well and educated them in fitting disciplines. For the disorder of children is ascribed to the father’s negligence. Further, because everyone, as long as he lives, is liable to fall [Col. 0556C], and old age itself is not exempt from sin, therefore you read that Abraham “died in a good old age” (Gen. 25:8), because he remained steadfast in the goodness of his purpose. Death, therefore, is the testimony of life. For if a helmsman cannot be praised before he has brought his ship into port, how will you praise a person before he has reached the haven of death? He is himself his own helmsman, and he is tossed upon the deep of this life; as long as he is upon this sea, so long is he amid shipwrecks. A leader does not take the laurel before the battle is ended; nor does a soldier lay down his arms or obtain the reward of his service unless the enemy has been overcome. Death, therefore, is the completion of service, the fullness of reward, the grace of discharge.

[Note: [Col. 0556D] Thus all editions and a few manuscripts. But in others there is some variation. Some read, “it is grace”; some, “it is the grace of forgiveness”; some, “it is the grace of admission”; and finally some, “it is the grace of loss.” Yet it is clear that there is an allusion here to the discharge (*missio*) granted to soldiers who had completed their service.]

36. How much did holy Job attribute to death, when he said: “Let the blessing of him who is perishing come upon me” (Job 29:13) [Col. 0556D]? For although Isaac, when dying, blessed his sons, and Jacob blessed the patriarchs, the grace of that blessing might nevertheless be ascribed solely to the merits of those giving the blessing, or to paternal affection. But here there is no prerogative of merits, none of affection, but the privilege of death alone: since the blessing of any dying person has such power that the holy Prophet desired it for himself [Col. 0557A]. Therefore let us always ponder and keep this verse in our hearts.

37. If we see someone poor and about to die, let us help with our resources; and let each of us say: “Let the blessing of him who is dying come upon me.” If we see someone weak, let us not abandon him; if someone placed at the point of death, let us not leave him. May it also be ours to say: “Let the blessing of him who is dying come upon me.” Let everyone who dies praise you—everyone who has laid aside this life, everyone exhausted by a grievous wound, everyone consumed by disease and now near to death.

[Note: [Col. 0557D] On this expression, see Book V of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 15, no. 55.]

How many has this verse caused to be blessed! How often it has struck me with shame if I passed by one who was dying, if I did not visit one seriously ill, if I despised a needy person, if I did not ransom a captive, if I rejected an old man! Let this, therefore, always be in the heart [Col. 0557B], that it may spur the harder-hearted and remind the more ready. May the final words of one dying resound for you, and may the soul departing from the body carry with it your blessing. Rescue also the one being led to death, who would have perished unless you had helped him, so that you may say: “Let the blessing of him who is perishing come upon me.”

## CHAPTER IX

The goodness of death is concluded from the destruction of the body and the immortality of the soul; this immortality is demonstrated in many ways. An exhortation is added to flee the society of the body and pursue union with the highest good.

38. Who, then, can doubt the goodness of death, when that which is restless, shameful, hostile to us, violent, stormy, and alluring to every vice, comes to rest and lies still, and is, as it were, shut up like a wild beast in the cage of the tomb; when its frenzy is left lifeless, and the dead framework of its limbs is dissolved into the earth [Col. 0557C]; while that which is akin to virtues, friendly to disciplines, eager for glory, a follower of the good, and subject to God, flies upward to that height, remains with that pure, perpetual, good, and immortal Being, clings to Him, and is with Him from whom it derives its kinship, as one says: “For we too are His offspring” (Acts 17:28)?

For it is clear that the soul does not die with the body, because it is not of the body. Scripture teaches in many ways that it is not of the body. For Adam also received from the Lord our God the spirit of life and became “a living soul” (Gen. 2:7). And David says: “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with me” (Ps. 114:7). Hear how He has dealt bountifully: “For He has delivered,” he says, “my feet from stumbling” (ibid., 8). You see that he rejoices in the remedy of this death, because error has come to an end and fault—not nature—has failed.

39. Finally, as though stripped free and liberated, he says: “I shall be pleasing to the Lord in the land of the living” (ibid., 9) [Col. 0558A]. For that is the land of the living. Indeed, he calls that rest of souls “the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13), where sins do not enter and where the glory of virtues lives. But this region is full of the dead because it is full of offenses; and rightly it was said: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8:22).

[Note: [Col. 0557D] The Roman edition reads, “But David also says elsewhere.” The others, with all manuscripts, read, “But he also says similarly above.” It is said above with reference to Psalm 26, cited a few verses earlier. Again, shortly afterward, the Roman edition, following one Vatican manuscript, reads, “and may possess them.” The old edition and other manuscripts read, “and according to [Col. 0558D] them,” that is, near or beside them.]

But above he similarly says: “His soul shall dwell amid good things, and his seed shall inherit the land” (Ps. 24:13); that is, the soul of one who fears God will dwell amid good things, so as always to be in them and near them. This may also be understood of one who is in the body: if he fears God, he too may dwell amid good things, be in heavenly places, possess his body and rule it as reduced to servitude, and possess the inheritance of glory and heavenly promises [Col. 0558B].

40. Therefore, if we wish after the death of this body to be among good things, let us beware lest our soul be glued to this body, mingled with it, attached to it, drawn by it, and, as though drunk with its disturbances, stagger and fluctuate; let it not entrust itself to the body and its pleasures, so as to commit itself to its senses. For its eye is error and deceit, because sight is deceived; its ear is deception, because hearing too is deluded; and its taste is deception. Finally, it was not said without purpose: “Let your eyes see what is right” (Prov. 14:25), and, “Let your tongue not speak perversely” (Ps. 33:14). This would not have been said unless they frequently erred.

You saw a prostitute; you were captivated by her appearance and thought her beautiful in form: your eyes erred [Col. 0558C], saw perversely, and reported something different. For if they had truly seen, they would have seen the ugly disposition of the prostitute, appalling shamelessness, unbecoming immodesty, decaying lusts, foul pollution, wounds of the soul, scars of conscience. “Whoever looks upon a woman,” he says, “in order to lust after her” (Matt. 5:28).

[Note: [Col. 0558D] The Roman edition adds, “has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” These words are absent from the other editions and from all manuscripts, but are altogether necessary to complete the sense.]

You see that this man sought what was false, because he sought not truth but adultery. For he sought to see in order to desire, not in order to know the truth. The eye therefore errs where the affection errs. Thus affection is deception, and deception of sight. Therefore you are told: “Do not be captured by your eyes” (Prov. 6:25), that is, let not your soul be captured. For a woman captures the precious souls of men (ibid., 26). Hearing too is deception. Thus by the abundant flattery of her speech, the adulterous woman has often led astray, deceived, and mocked a young man’s heart (Prov. 7:21) [Col. 0558D].

41. Therefore let us not trust those snares and nets which deceive and mock us; for hearts are tested and thoughts hindered—hindered by sight, hearing, smell, touch, and taste. Let us not follow what is enticing and seductive; rather, let us follow that which is good, cling to it, imitate it, and let its presence and communion make us better, color our character, and form us by a certain fellowship with it [Col. 0559A]. For whoever clings to the good receives from it that which is good, because it is written: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverse, and with the innocent you will be innocent” (Ps. 17:26–27); for by constancy and imitation a certain image of likeness is formed.

Therefore he added: “For You enlighten my lamp, O Lord” (ibid., 29). Indeed, whoever approaches the light is more quickly enlightened, and the splendor of eternal light shines more abundantly upon him through nearness.
