Therefore the soul which clings to that invisible, good, and immortal God itself escapes these bodily things, leaves behind earthly and mortal things, and becomes like that which it desires, in which it lives and is nourished; and because it attends to the immortal, it is not itself mortal. For the soul that sins dies—not by any dissolution of itself, certainly, but it dies in relation to God [Col. 0559B], because it lives for sin. Therefore the soul that does not sin does not die, because it remains in its own substance, remains in virtue and glory.

42. For how can its substance perish, since the soul is what infuses life? Whatever receives a soul receives life; from whatever the soul departs, life departs. The soul, therefore, is life. How, then, can it receive death, when it is its contrary? For just as snow does not receive heat—for it is immediately dissolved—and light does not receive darkness—for it immediately dispels it (when light is introduced, the terror of darkness is removed, just as, when fire is applied, the chill of snow ceases)—so the soul, which creates life, does not receive death and does not die.

[Note: [Col. 0559D] All editions read: “does not receive death, does not die.” Several manuscripts read: “therefore does not die.” But ten manuscripts of better age read as in the text.]

But the soul does not receive death; therefore the soul does not die [Col. 0559C].

## CHAPTER X

The immortality of souls is also proved from Scripture; moreover, higher dwelling-places are assigned to them. The philosophers’ metempsychosis is refuted, and then the complaint concerning the delayed reward of the righteous is answered.

43. We have, then, a rational argument, but this is human. The divine argument is what the Lord says: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18). You see, therefore, that the soul does not die with the body, since it is both laid down and taken up again, and is commended into the hands of God the Father. But perhaps you will say:

[Note: [Col. 0559D] Thus the more numerous and better manuscripts, from which the editions differ only in having, “But lest,” etc. Other manuscripts read in part: “that what Christ is is something special”; in part: “that which belongs specially to Christ.” Again, shortly afterward [Col. 0560D], eight manuscripts and the old edition read, “yet because it is a matter of another cause.” The Roman edition reads, “because it is a matter of a higher cause.” The remaining manuscripts read, “because it is a matter of another cause,” that is, it pertains to another argument.]

that what belongs to Christ is special, and although He assumed the things that belong to humanity, nevertheless [Col. 0559D], because establishing this too belongs to another argument, lest we waste time, hear Him saying: “What do you know whether this night your soul may be demanded of you?” (Luke 12:20). Did He say: “May your soul die within you”? No; but, “May it be demanded from you.” What has been given is demanded back, or they demand it back from you. The soul is reclaimed, not destroyed. What is reclaimed remains; what is destroyed does not remain. For how can that soul be destroyed of which the Wisdom of God said [Col. 0560A] that one should not fear him who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matt. 10:28)? Of it the prophet says: “My soul is always in Your hands” (Ps. 118:109). “Always,” he says—not merely in time.

44. And you, commend your soul into the hands of the Lord—not only when it departs from the body, but also while it is in the body; it is in the hands of the Lord, because you do not see whence it comes or whither it goes. For it is in you, and it is with God. Thus the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord and is ruled and governed by Him. The heart is filled with the mind, because the mind is the ruling part and power of the soul. I do not mean the power that is in the arms, but that which is in counsel, self-control, devotion, and justice. If the human heart is in the hand of the Lord [Col. 0560B], much more is the soul. If the soul is in the hand of God, surely our soul is not enclosed in the tomb together with the body, nor held fast by the funeral pyre; rather, it enjoys holy rest. And therefore people build costly tombs in vain, as though they were receptacles for souls and not for the body alone.

45. That the dwellings of souls are above is strongly proved by the testimony of Scripture. For in the books of Ezra we read: “For when the day of judgment comes, the earth shall restore the bodies of the dead, and the dust shall restore those who rest in graves, the remains of the dead. And the storehouses,” he says, “shall restore the souls which were committed to them, and the Most High shall be revealed upon the seat of judgment” (4 Ezra 7:32) [Col. 0560C]. These are the dwelling-places of which the Lord says that there are many mansions in His Father’s house, which, as He went to the Father, He would prepare for His disciples (John 14:2).

But I have used Ezra’s writings so that the Gentiles may recognize that what they admire in the books of philosophy has been transferred from our writings. And would that they had not mixed in superfluous and useless notions: namely, that the souls of human beings and beasts are shared alike, and that the highest reward for souls of great philosophers would be to migrate into bees or nightingales—so that those who had formerly fed humankind by speech might afterward delight them with the sweetness of honey or the pleasantness of song. It would have been enough for them to say that souls liberated from bodies seek *aidēs* (αἴδην), that is, the place which is not seen; in Latin we call that place *infernum*, the lower world.

46. Finally, Scripture also calls those dwellings of souls “storehouses” (4 Ezra 7:32) [Col. 0560D]. Meeting the human complaint that the righteous who have gone before seem to be defrauded, until the day of judgment—clearly for a very long period—of the reward due to them, it wonderfully says that that day of judgment is like a crown (4 Ezra 5:42), in which:

[Note: [Col. 0560D] The manuscript of St. Theodorus alone reads: “Just as the tardiness of the last shall not be excluded, so neither shall the speed of the first be admitted beforehand.”]

just as the tardiness of the last does not exclude them, so the swiftness of the first does not admit them beforehand. For the day of the crown is awaited by all, so that on that day both the defeated may be ashamed and the victors may obtain the palm of victory [Col. 0561A].

Nor did he leave hidden the fact that those born earlier seem stronger, while those born later appear weaker. For he compared the births of this age to a woman’s womb (4 Ezra 5:53): because those born in the youth of strength are stronger, those born in the time of old age weaker. For this age has failed through the multitude of generations, like a womb that has borne children, and, like a creature growing old, it lays aside the vigor of its youth, as though the force of its strength were already withering.

47. Therefore, while the fullness of time is awaited, souls await their due recompense. One awaits punishment, another glory; yet neither are the former meanwhile without suffering nor the latter without benefit. For the former [Col. 0561B], seeing that the reward of glory is laid up for those who keep the law of God, that their dwellings are preserved by angels, and that punishments for their own negligence and stubbornness, together with shame and confusion, await them—when they behold the glory of the Most High, they are ashamed to enter His presence whose commands they have rashly violated. For as Adam’s transgression brought confusion, so too does theirs; because, just as he fell through neglect of the heavenly commandments and hid himself in shame for his fall, not daring in the shame of a guilty conscience to endure the splendor of the divine presence, so the souls of sinners will not endure the brightness of His flashing light, by whose witness they will remember that they have gone astray.

## CHAPTER XI

He expounds the seven orders in which the joy of the righteous will be arranged after this life; and he exhorts us to approach God zealously and not to dread the end of life.

48. The joy of righteous souls will be arranged in certain orders (4 Ezra 7:49 ff.) [Col. 0561C]. First, because they have conquered the flesh and have not been bent by its enticements. Then, because as the reward of their diligence and innocence they obtain security and are not entangled, like the souls of the ungodly, in certain errors and disturbances:

[Note: [Col. 0561D] One Reginensis manuscript reads, “terrors and disturbances,” which is not displeasing.]

nor tormented by the memory of their vices or agitated by certain burning anxieties. Third, because they are supported by the divine testimony of the law which they have kept, so that they do not fear an uncertain outcome in the supreme judgment concerning their deeds.

[Note: [Col. 0561D] At first sight these words seem contrary to those in Book II of *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 2, no. 9: “The soul is released from the body, and yet after the end of this life remains suspended in uncertainty concerning what is to come.” But Ambrose is readily freed from such a contradiction if we consider that these latter words, there stated only incidentally, may be explained in the sense that the soul is said to be uncertain not about its own happiness—which, according to the common opinion of the Fathers, is known and certain to it—but about the day of resurrection and judgment, and indeed about the salvation of its brethren, with whom, as Ambrose testifies [Col. 0562D], it sympathizes, as we have already said in the admonition to this book. For if the holy man had judged the righteous dead uncertain about their own salvation, how could he, in the same book, chapter 9, no. 31, have said of them: “And rightly they are counted among the living; for even if they have tasted bodily death, nevertheless they receive incorporeal life and are enlightened by the splendor of their merits, and enjoy eternal light”? And in the following chapter, no. 36, he asserts without hesitation that this is the true and blessed life which everyone of good conscience lives much more purely and happily when our soul has laid aside the covering of this flesh … flying back to that higher place from which, infused into our bodily members … it groaned.]

Fourth [Col. 0561D], because they begin to understand their rest and foresee their future glory; and, delighting themselves with this consolation, they rest in their dwelling-places with great tranquillity [Col. 0562A], surrounded by the protection of angels. The fifth order possesses the sweetness of most abundant exultation, because they have arrived from the prison of this corruptible body into light and freedom, and possess the inheritance promised them.

For there is an order of rest because there is also an order of resurrection: “For as in Adam all die, so also,” he says, “in Christ shall all be made alive. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; then those who belong to Christ, who believed in His coming; then the end” (1 Cor. 15:22 ff.). There will therefore be a differing order of brightness and glory, just as there will be an order of merits. The advance through the orders also expresses an advance in brightness (4 Ezra 7). Finally, in the sixth order it will be shown to them that their faces begin to shine like the sun and are compared to the lights of the stars [Col. 0562B]; yet their brightness can no longer experience corruption.

The seventh order will be that they exult with confidence, trust without any hesitation, and rejoice without trembling, hastening to see the face of Him to whom they rendered the offices of diligent service. Recalling Him with innocent conscience, they confidently expect the glorious reward for their small labor, and, beginning to receive it, recognize that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the greatness of the glory of eternal recompense.

“This,” he says (4 Ezra 9), “is the order of the souls which are righteous,” and in the fifth order he did not hesitate to call them immortal, because, he says, “they begin to receive space, rejoicing and immortal.” “This,” he says (ibid.), “is their rest through seven orders, and the first enjoyment of future glory, before [Col. 0562C] they enjoy the gift of tranquil assembly in their dwelling-places.” Hence the prophet says to the angel: “Will time, then, be given to souls after they have been separated from bodies, so that they may see the things as you have said?” (4 Ezra 9). And the angel said: “Their freedom will last seven days, so that in seven days they may see the things that have been foretold; and afterward they shall be gathered into their dwelling-places.”

These matters have been set out more fully concerning the orders of the righteous than concerning the sufferings of the ungodly, because it is better to know how the innocent are saved than how the criminal are tormented.

49. Therefore, since the righteous have this recompense (St. Augustine, Book IV, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 11)—to see the face of God and that light which enlightens every person—let us henceforth put on such zeal [Col. 0562D], so that our soul may draw near to God, our prayer may draw near, our desire may cling to Him, and we may not be separated from Him. And while we are here, let us be joined to God by meditation [Col. 0563A], reading, and seeking; let us know Him as far as we are able.

For here we know in part, because here all things are imperfect, but there all things are perfect; here we are children, there strong. “For now,” he says, “we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). Then it will be possible, with unveiled face, to behold the glory of the Lord; now souls, wrapped in the clinging bodily organs of this body and darkened by certain stains and pollutions of the flesh, cannot see it purely. For “Who,” he says, “shall see My face and live?” (Exod. 33:20). And rightly so. For if our eyes cannot endure the rays of the sun, and anyone who gazes too long directly at the sun is said to be blinded, then if one creature cannot look upon another creature without injury and harm to itself, how can one who is covered with the garments of this body behold without danger to himself the flashing face of the eternal Creator [Col. 0563B]? For who is justified in God’s sight, when not even an infant of one day can be free from sin and no one can boast of the integrity and purity of his own heart?

50. Therefore let us not fear being received away from human beings; let us not dread that end due to all, in which Ezra found the reward of his devotion, when the Lord said to him: “For you shall be received from among human beings, and you shall remain with My Son, and with those like you” (4 Ezra 14:9).

[Note: [Col. 0563D] The Roman edition reads, “from all men, and you shall remain.” So also the Vulgate, which instead of “My Son,” as all Ambrosian manuscripts and editions have, reads “My counsel.”]

If it was glorious and pleasant for him to be preserved with those like himself, how much more glorious and pleasant will it be for us to go to better people and dwell with those whose deeds we admire?

51. Who, then, was earlier—Ezra or Plato [Col. 0563C]? For Paul followed the sayings of Ezra, not Plato. Ezra revealed, according to the revelation given to him, that the righteous would be with Christ and with the saints. Hence Socrates too says that he hastens:

[Note: [Col. 0563D] Thus all manuscripts and editions, except the Roman edition, which reads, “to those demigods,” with an annotation in the margin referring this to the *Apology of Socrates*. Yet we do not see to what place in that *Apology* this can be referred, unless perhaps to the passage explaining how blessed is the migration to those who are said to judge justly in Hades, such as Rhadamanthus, etc., “… and all the others who are among the demigods” (καὶ ἄλλοι ὅσοι τῶν ἡμιθέων, etc.). Yet this is much more suitably [Col. 0564D] referred to another passage from the *Phaedo*, which we reproduce here in its own words: “But now be well assured that I hope to come to good men; though I would not strongly affirm this. Yet that I shall come to gods, masters who are altogether good—be assured that, if I would strongly affirm anything else of this kind, I would affirm this also.” (Νῦν δὲ εὖ ἴστε ὅτι παρ᾽ ἄνδρας τε ἐλπίζω ἀφίξεσθαι ἀγαθούς, καὶ τοῦτο μὲν οὐκ ἂν πάνυ διϊσχυρισαίμην· ὅτι μέντοι παρὰ θεοὺς δεσπότας πάνυ ἀγαθοὺς ἥξειν, εὖ ἴστε εἴπερ τι ἄλλο τῶν τοιούτων, διϊσχυρισαίμην ἂν καὶ τοῦτο.)]

to those gods of his, to those best men. Therefore what is excellent in the writings of philosophers is ours; and he put forward things for which he had no proper testimony, whereas we have the authority of divine command. Moses and Elijah appeared with Christ (Matt. 17:3); Abraham received two others together with his God in hospitality (Gen. 18:2); Jacob saw the camp of God (Gen. 32:2); Daniel, by revelation of the Holy Spirit, declared that the righteous would shine like the sun and stars in heaven (Dan. 12:3).

## CHAPTER XII

He describes eternal happiness, which he also shows to have been appointed for us. Then, continuing with its qualities, he shows that it is the land of the living, and this the land of the dead. Finally, he concludes the book with a prudent admonition.

52. Relying on these things, therefore, let us go fearlessly to our Redeemer Jesus; fearlessly, when the day comes, let us set out for the assembly of the patriarchs and for our father Abraham; fearlessly let us go to that company of saints and gathering of the righteous [Col. 0563]. For we shall go to our fathers; we shall go to those instructors of our faith, so that even if works are lacking, faith may aid us and our inheritance be defended. We shall also go where holy Abraham spreads out his bosom to receive the poor, as he received Lazarus; in that bosom those rest who endured grievous and harsh things in this world.

53. But now, Father, again and again stretch out Your hands to receive this poor man [Col. 0564B]; open Your lap, spread out Your bosom, so that You may receive more, because very many have believed in the Lord. Yet, although faith has increased, iniquity abounds and charity grows cold. We shall go to those who recline in the kingdom of God with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, because, when invited to the supper, they did not excuse themselves. We shall go where there is the paradise of delight, where Adam, who fell among robbers, no longer knows how to weep for his wounds; where even the robber himself rejoices in fellowship in the heavenly kingdom; where no clouds, thunder, lightning, storm of winds, darkness, evening, summer, or winter will bring alternations of seasons. There will be no cold, hail, rain, use of this sun, moon, or globes of stars; but the brightness of God alone will shine [Col. 0564C]. For the Lord will be the light of all, and that true light which enlightens every person will shine upon all.

We shall go where the Lord Jesus has prepared mansions for His servants, so that where He is, we too may be. For this was His will. Hear Him say what those mansions are: “In My Father’s house are many mansions” (John 14:2). And what His will is: “I come again,” He says, “and take you to Myself, so that where I am, you too may be” (ibid., 3).

54. But you will say that He spoke only to the disciples, having promised many mansions only to them. Was He then preparing them for only eleven disciples? And where is the saying that they will come from every part of the world and recline in God’s kingdom (Matt. 8:11)? Why do we doubt the fulfillment of the divine will? For Christ’s willing is His accomplishing [Col. 0564D]. Finally, He showed both the way and the place, saying: “You know where I am going, and you know the way” (John 14:4). The place is with the Father; the way is Christ, as He Himself says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” [Col. 0565A] (John 14:6).

Let us enter this way, hold fast the truth, and follow life. The way is that which leads, truth is that which establishes, life is that which is granted in itself.

[Note: [Col. 0565D] The Roman edition, from one Vatican manuscript, reads, “life which is rendered to those who persevere.” This sense is indeed true and clear; nevertheless, the reading found in all other editions and manuscripts should by no means be rejected. For in these life is said to be granted in itself because, as it is the first and fundamental good of its own order—natural life among natural goods, supernatural life among supernatural goods—other things are referred to it, not it to other things.]

And, that we may know the true will, He added later: “Father, those whom You have given Me, I will that where I am, they also may be with Me, that they may see My glory” (John 17:12).

[Note: [Col. 0565D] The same Roman edition alone reads, “My glory, righteous Father.” Doubtless the word “Father” seemed to require repetition because of what follows, “This repetition.” But these words seem to have been inserted only because the same thing appears to have been signified twice by the words, “that … they may be with Me, that they may see,” etc. [Col. 0566D].]

This repetition is confirmation, as in: “Abraham, Abraham!” (Gen. 22:1), and elsewhere: “I am, I am, who blot out your iniquities” (Isa. 43:25). It is fitting that what He promised above, He here asked for. And because He promised first and then asked, rather than asked first and then promised: He promised as the arbiter of the gift, conscious of His power; He asked the Father as the interpreter of filial devotion. He promised first so that you might recognize His power; He asked afterward so that you might understand His devotion [Col. 0565B]. He did not ask first and then promise, lest He should seem to have promised what He had obtained rather than to have bestowed what He promised. Nor should you think it superfluous that He asked, when He thereby expresses the fellowship of the Father’s will, in which there is an indication of unity, not an increase of power.

55. We follow You, Lord Jesus; but summon us, that we may follow, because without You no one ascends. For You are the way, truth, life, possibility, faith, reward.

[Note: [Col. 0566D] The Vatican manuscript and the Roman edition read, “possibility, resting-place.” The other manuscripts and editions read better: “… faith.” For just as here “possibility” refers to “You are the way,” and “reward” to “life,” so “faith” refers to “truth.” Thus Christ is called faith because His truth is, as they say, the formal object of faith.]

Receive us as the way; establish us as the truth; give us life as the life. Unveil that good of Yours which David desired to see while dwelling in the house of the Lord; and therefore he said: “Who will show us good things?” (Ps. 4:6). And elsewhere: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13). For there are good things where there is perpetual life [Col. 0565C], life without sin. Elsewhere he also says: “We shall be filled with the good things of Your house” (Ps. 64:5). He repeated this so often that you might know that the philosophers transferred from here that good which they declare to be the highest.

[Note: [Col. 0566D] The manuscripts of greater number and authority read, “which they declare to be one.”]

Unveil, therefore, that truly good thing of Yours, that divine good in which “we live and are and move” (Acts 17:28). We move as on the way; we are as in the truth; we live as in eternal life (John 14:6). Show us that good which is like itself, always indissoluble and unchangeable, in which we may be eternal in the knowledge of every good, as Paul, Your vessel of election, testified in saying: “Perhaps he therefore departed for an hour, that you might receive him forever” (Philem. 15).

Thus, writing to Philemon, he called the servant of God eternal; and he prayed that Philemon’s faith might become more manifest in the knowledge of every good that is in the saints, in Christ Jesus [Col. 0565D]. In that good are pure rest, immortal light, perpetual grace, the devout inheritance of souls, and secure tranquillity—not subject to death but rescued from death—where there are no tears and no weeping [Col. 0566A]. For whence would weeping be there where there is no falling? There Your saints are freed from errors and anxieties, folly and ignorance, fear and dread, desires, bodily pollutions, and passions—where there is the land of the living.

And, to join authority to this assertion, the Prophet says concerning this good: “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you; for He has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling. I shall be pleasing to the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:7 ff.). “I shall be pleasing,” he said, not “I am pleasing”; that is, he comforts himself concerning the future time. But future things are contrary to present things, and eternal things to temporal. Therefore, because there is the land of the living, this is surely the land of the dead.

[Col. 0566B] **56.** Is not this the region of the dead, where there is the shadow of death, where there is the gate of death, where there is the body of death? Finally, it is granted to Peter lest perhaps the gates of hell should prevail against him (Matt. 16:18). These gates of hell are earthly things. Hence he also says: “You who lift me up from the gates of death” (Ps. 9:15). For just as there are gates of righteousness in which the saints confess the Lord, so there are gates of crimes in which the impious have denied the Lord.

Hear that this region is the region of the dead. “If anyone touches a dead person, he shall be unclean” (Num. 19:11). Now every unrighteous person is unclean in the sight of the Lord. If anyone therefore touches iniquity, he will be unclean; if anyone lives in pleasures, he is dead, “for she who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:6). Those who are unbelievers descend alive into hell: although they seem to live with us, they are in hell. If anyone [14, q. 4, chap. *Si quis usuram*] accepts interest, he commits robbery; he does not live the life of the living, as you have in Ezekiel (Ezek. 33:18–19). But if a righteous person keeps the Lord’s ordinances in order to do them, “he shall surely live,” he says, “and he shall live by them.” He, then, is in the region of the living, in that region where life is not hidden but free; where there is not shadow but glory. For here even Paul himself was not living in glory. Finally, he groaned under the body of death. Hear him saying: “For our life is now hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ, our life, appears, then we too shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3–4).

**57.** Let us therefore hasten toward life. If anyone touches life, he will live. Finally, that woman touched it who touched his fringe, and was released from death; to her he said: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 8:48). For if the one who touches a dead person is unclean, undoubtedly the one who touches the living is saved.

Let us therefore seek the living one. But let us again take care lest we seek him among the dead, and it be said to us, as it was to those women: “Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen” (Luke 24:6). The Lord himself also showed where he wished to be sought, saying: “Go to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17). Let us seek him, then, where John sought him and found him. He sought him “in the beginning” (John 1:1), and found the living one with the living one, the Son with the Father.

Let us seek him at the end of time, and embrace his feet and worship him, so that he may say to us also: “Do not be afraid” (Matt. 28:5)—that is, do not fear the sins of the world; do not fear the iniquities of the world; do not fear the waves of bodily passions: I am the forgiveness of sins. Do not fear the darkness: I am the light. Do not fear death: I am life. Whoever comes to me shall never see death, because he is the fullness of divinity. To him belong glory, honor, and perpetuity from the ages, and now, and always, and for all ages of ages. Amen.

# [ON FLEEING THE WORLD]

[Col. 0567B]

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE BOOK ON FLEEING THE WORLD

[Col. 0567]

This book has occupied various positions among the works of Ambrose. For in manuscripts and in the oldest editions it stands immediately after the books *On Isaac* and *On the Good of Death*. But when Erasmus chose to distribute all the works of Ambrose into fixed classes, he forced it, together with the preceding treatise *On the Good of Death*, into the ethical order, after the books *On Duties* and *On Virgins*; Costerus and Gillotius later followed him in this. Finally, those who were in charge of the Roman edition, judging this very book to be nothing other than a mystical exposition of the passage in Genesis where Rebecca advises her son Jacob to flee to Mesopotamia (Gen. 27:43), transferred it to after the treatise *On Jacob* and *The Blessed Life*. But they relied on an unsuitable support. For although the holy Bishop mentions Jacob’s flight more than once, he never intended to work out an exposition of that passage of Scripture. Nor does he use the example of this patriarch differently from that of certain other outstanding men whom he sets before us in order to spur us more effectively to bid the world an eternal farewell. Therefore, after examining this book more carefully, we have restored it to its former place; and we have done so all the more willingly because it ought simply to be placed before the discussion of Jacob and *The Blessed Life*, which followed it in the Roman edition. No confusion can arise from this change.

Nor was the authority of the manuscripts and ancient editions alone what moved us to do this; much more decisive was the kinship of subject matter that joins it to the preceding treatises. Why should we not also consider Ambrose’s own testimony? When, at the very beginning of the book, he says, “We frequently speak of fleeing this world,” we have no doubt that he tacitly indicates the treatises *On Abraham*, *On Isaac and the Soul*, and *On the Good of Death*: in all of these, and especially in this last one, he more earnestly urges his hearers or readers to flee the world and its vanities, and especially in this last work, where three main divisions are devoted to that subject, as we observed in the preceding prefaces.

The entire structure of this little book demonstrates the same thing. We have shown above that in his sermons and treatises the holy Bishop most diligently instructed catechumens and candidates for baptism in all the precepts of Christian life; but we also showed that he impressed upon them with particular care how strongly they were bound to flee the vanities of the world. Yet his concern was not confined to these limits. He considered it especially his duty to confirm them, after they had received baptism, in the doctrine that they had already learned under his instruction.

Accordingly, from the beginning of this writing he shows (chap. 1, no. 1 and following) how easily human weakness and desire gradually relapse into worldly follies, and how difficult it is to persevere in a holy purpose; and therefore that they must strive with hands and feet, so to speak, to flee vanities with tireless speed and, having risen above them, to press continually toward perfection. Nothing else (chap. 2, 3, and the beginning of 4) does he prove to have been signified in the ancient law by those six cities of refuge that were open to those guilty of involuntary homicide; and he dwells on this matter at greater length than on any other subject treated separately.

Next he explains what this flight consists in (chap. 4, no. 17), and demonstrates how glorious, useful, and necessary it is for them by setting before them the examples of the patriarchs, the prophets, the Apostle, and even Christ the Lord himself (chap. 4, nos. 19–20); but he also teaches that it must be swift (chap. 6, no. 32). He teaches (ibid.) that its course and goal are the highest and unchangeable good, namely, God himself. Consequently, there is no other stimulus by which they ought to be more urgently aroused to escape from the world, where, by divine permission, sin and wickedness have thus far continued, and from which Christ himself did not wish to uproot them, although he condemned their author, the devil (chap. 7, no. 37 and following).

But when those new Christians could object that they were bound by certain ties which made it entirely impossible for them to flee from the world, he shows them (chap. 8, no. 45 and following) how, without abandoning the world bodily, they could escape from it in spirit, adhere to God alone, observe his commandments, and seize every opportunity for advancing further on the way of virtue.

Finally, he places a crown upon this discussion by exhorting them with the greatest force and eloquence (chap. 9, no. 51 and following) not to enter into any future association with the world to which, once for all in baptism, they had pronounced a formal divorce, bidding it keep its own affairs to itself. They were to be convinced that in them the old man ought no longer to appear, but that new life which they had received in the baptismal font, where, having died with Christ, they had also risen again with him.

Moreover, that Ambrose is addressing people newly initiated through baptism is evident from the conclusion of the work; and it is no less clear from both its beginning (chapters 1, 7, and 8) and its middle. Indeed, this very fact, like the remaining parts of the same treatise, demonstrates with midday clarity that it consists of sermons—or rather of a single sermon—which, beyond doubt, he delivered around the Easter season of the year 387, at which time we have observed that the preceding books were composed.

Whether Ambrose himself gave this same little work the title *On Fleeing the World* cannot be disputed, in view of the authority of Augustine, who praises it under that title (*Against Julian the Pelagian* II.8; and *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians* IV.11). It must nevertheless be mentioned that in several manuscripts it is found inscribed *On Esau and Fleeing the World*. But we have no idea what occasion gave rise to the addition. We must therefore retain the title now received.

Although Philo’s book *On the Fugitive* supplied the subject of the fugitive Hagar, the holy Bishop nevertheless made useful use of his assistance in several passages—for example, when he discusses the patriarchs Jacob and Joseph (chapters 4 and 8), and when he discusses the six cities of refuge (chapters 2 and following). Here you will observe two points not unworthy of notice. The first is one we have already noted: namely, that whatever Ambrose borrowed from that Jewish author, he converted to Christian uses and confirmed by various arguments and testimonies drawn from the New Testament. The second is the reason why the same Bishop so readily drew from Philo’s commentaries: namely, that several of Philo’s doctrinal points could easily be adapted to the principles of the Christian religion. The clearest example of this is supplied by what is discussed in this book (chapters 2 and 3) concerning the divine Word.

[Col. 0569B]

## ONE BOOK OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON FLEEING THE WORLD  
[Note: [Col. 0569B] Written around the year 387.] (C)

417 **CHAPTER ONE**

A person cannot flee earthly enticements and desires unless divine assistance is present. How many obstacles he suffers through his senses; and how necessary it is for him to prefer sorrowful things to joyful ones, since in these there is nothing but vanity. Finally, whoever wishes to be saved must ascend above the world.

[Col. 0569A]

**1.** We frequently speak about fleeing this world (see St. Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian* II.8, and *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 11); and would that our disposition were as cautious and watchful as our speech is easy! But what is worse, the enticement of earthly desires frequently steals in, and an obscuring of vanities [Note: [Col. 0569B] All editions read *effusio*, “an outpouring,” which occupies the mind.] takes possession of the mind, so that what you strive to avoid you think about and turn over in your mind—something difficult for a human being to put off, and impossible to cast away completely.

Finally, the Prophet testifies that it is more a matter of prayer than of achievement when he says: “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice” (Ps. 118:36). For our heart and our thoughts are not in our own power. They pour unexpectedly into the mind and spirit, confuse them, draw them elsewhere than you have purposed, recall them to worldly things, implant earthly concerns, introduce pleasures, and weave in enticements. Even at the very moment when we prepare to raise our minds, we are usually cast down to earthly things by empty thoughts inserted into us.

**2.** Who, however, is so blessed that he always ascends in his heart? But how can this happen without divine assistance? Certainly, in no way. Finally, the same Scripture says above: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you, O Lord; ascents are in his heart” (Ps. 83:6).

Truly blessed is the person whom pleasure does not turn back, whom delight does not bend downward, and who does not look toward lower things—as even Lot’s wife was unable to avoid doing. Warned by her example, the Apostle, “forgetting what was behind and reaching toward what was ahead,” hastened toward the prize and was worthy to attain it, because he saw Christ before him, by whom he was called to the crown of righteousness. But the one who denied himself reached the goal, so that he might gain Christ. Finally, it was not he himself who lived, but Christ lived in him.

**3.** For who can preserve his steps safe and undefiled amid so many passions of this body, amid so many enticements of this world? The eye looked, and turned away the mind’s perception; the ear heard, and bent away its attention; the nose breathed in a scent, and obstructed thought; the mouth tasted, and brought back guilt; the sense of touch made contact, and kindled fire.

“The death,” says the Prophet, “entered through the window” (Jer. 9:21). Your window is your eye. If you look at a woman in order to desire her, death has entered. If you hear the words of prostitutes, death has entered. If lust captivates your senses, death has penetrated.

Therefore whoever wishes to ascend should follow not the world’s joys, pleasant things, or delights, but things full of sorrow and weeping; for it is better to go into the house of mourning than into the house of joy. Finally, Adam would not have descended from paradise if he had not been deceived by pleasure.

**4.** David therefore rightly—he who had experienced even the dangerous looks of human beings [Note: [Col. 0571D] Thus nine manuscripts of the highest quality. The Vatican manuscript and the Roman edition omit *hominis*, “of human beings.” Other manuscripts, together with the ancient editions, read: “even dangerous people through their very appearance.” These words do not seem at all to be rejected.]—calls that person blessed whose every hope is in the name of God (Ps. 39:5). For such a person does not look upon vanities and false insanities if he always fixes his attention on Christ and always gazes upon Christ with the eyes within.

Hence, turning again to him, he says: “Turn my eyes away, lest they behold vanity” (Ps. 118:37). The circus is vanity, because it profits nothing; the speed of horses is vanity, because it is false with respect to salvation; the theater is vanity; every game is vanity. “All is vanity,” says Ecclesiastes, “that is in this world” (Eccles. 1:2).

Finally, whoever wishes to be saved must ascend above the world, seek the Word with God, flee this world, and leave earthly things behind. For he cannot apprehend that which truly is and always is unless he has first fled from here. Hence, wishing to draw near to God the Father, the Lord also said to the apostles: “Rise; let us go from here” (John 14:31).

## CHAPTER TWO

The law teaches that the world must be fled and God followed, through the cities of refuge. Four matters concerning them are examined: first, why they were selected from the portion of the Levites; second, why there were six in number; third, why three were beyond the Jordan and an equal number in the land of Canaan; fourth, why the homicide was commanded to await there the death of the high priest. All these matters are applied to various virtues.

[Col. 0571C]

**5.** The law also teaches you to flee the world and follow God. For what else does it teach when it says: “You shall appoint for yourselves cities of refuge, and they shall be places of refuge for you, where any homicide who has struck a person unintentionally may flee” (Num. 35:11)? And below: “There shall be six cities of refuge for you; you shall give three cities beyond the Jordan, and three cities in the land of Canaan” (ibid., 13–14).

Clearly, these refuges were appointed for those fleeing this crime of homicide [Note: [Col. 0571D] The Roman edition alone reads *apte*, “appropriately,” with the other editions: “for those fleeing on account of the crime.” But the manuscripts read as in the text. There, *confugientibus hoc crimen* means essentially “for those fleeing this accusation”; classical authors are not unfamiliar with this form of expression.].

But let us consider more deeply. Four things warn us that the hidden meaning of this reading must be examined more profoundly. First, why, from among these cities that fell by lot to the Levites as their portion, six cities were given as refuges to those burdened with the crime of homicide, and why the cities of the other tribes were not also assigned to this duty. Second, why six in number; for this number does not seem to have been prescribed without purpose, neither more nor fewer cities. Third, why three cities were established beyond the Jordan and three in the region of Canaan, to serve as refuges for those who sinned. Fourth, why a calculation and definition of time is included, within which the homicide is to live in the city of refuge: until the great priest dies, and after the death of the great priest the homicide is to return to the city of his dwelling (ibid., 25).

We must therefore speak about each matter and resolve the questions in the order we have proposed.

**6.** First, then, it must be explained appropriately why the cities of the Levites were given as refuges. It is plainly fittingly arranged, because the Levites are fugitives from this world in order to please God: they leave their homeland, parents, children, and entire kinship in order to cling to God alone.

Finally, Abraham too was told: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. 12:1). But perhaps you will say: “He was not a Levite.” Yet he had Levi in his loins, as we read written in the Letter to the Hebrews (Heb. 7:10).

And the Lord says to the Levites when he says to his disciples, that is, to the apostles: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). Although this has now been said to everyone: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for adoption” (1 Pet. 2:9).

The fullness has come; the remnants have ceased. Christ has called everyone. It is plainly open to everyone that all should follow, and the kingdom and eternal life have been set before all [Note: [Col. 0572D] Thus the most ancient manuscripts and the editions of Ambrose and Erasmus. The other manuscripts read: “perfection is open to all.” Gillotius’s edition has, not ineptly, “progress is open to all.” When that word was removed, the Roman edition reads only: “it is open to all.”].

**7.** Therefore, for the one whose portion is God [12, question 1, chapter *Cui portio*], nothing should be a concern except God, lest he be hindered by the duty of another necessity. For whatever is devoted to other duties is taken away from the worship of religion and from this office of ours.

This is the true flight of a priest: renunciation of household members and a kind of separation from those most dear, so that even the person who longs to serve God may deny his own relatives. The sanction of the eternal law therefore rightly entrusted fugitives to fugitives, so that those who have forgotten this world might receive those who, condemning their sins and works, seek oblivion of their former life and desire to erase the worldly things they have done.

The minister of the sacred altar is therefore a fugitive from his own people. Hence the Lord, as chief priest, giving the Levites their model in the Gospel, said: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” (Matt. 12:48). That is: “I do not acknowledge my mother; I do not recognize my brothers; I do not know my relatives. My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it” (ibid., 50).

The minister therefore knows only the word of God, since he knows those in whom the Word of God works. And thus he is an exile from the world, a fugitive from the body, a fugitive from passions; he renounces everything so that he may remain alone, as Elijah said: “I alone have been left” (1 Kings 19:14).

But he was not alone [Note: [Col. 0572D] The Roman edition alone adds: “with whom the Lord was.” It also reads: “Christ himself was left.” But nothing should be changed in the received reading. For here Ambrose says that Christ was with Elijah, just as in the preceding book, chapter 2, no. 8, concerning David: “For he knew,” he says, “that it was more glorious to die for Christ,” and so forth. There are many other such expressions in this Father and in others, by which they signify that the mystery of the Incarnation was known to those ancient men. In this they followed not only Paul, who says that Moses abandoned Egypt, considering “the reproach of Christ” greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, but also the Lord himself, who says in John 8:56: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad.” Ambrose uses both testimonies, but especially the latter, in several places—for example, *On Abraham* 3.21, and his *Commentary on Luke*, near the beginning, and elsewhere.] with whom Christ was. The Lord himself also was left alone; but he says: “I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32).

**8.** There is also this reason: the Levites are ministers of God. Therefore their cities are assigned by the law to homicidal fugitives, because they have the authority to carry out divine commands concerning those who have committed a mortal crime.

The Church does not publish its laws; it knows its own laws, so that the priest may obey the command of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0573D] All editions read: “The Church does not know public laws; it knows its own. So that the priest may obey the command of the Lord, hear the Levite.” Some more recent manuscripts agree, except that two of them punctuate the passage as follows: “The Church does not know public laws as its own; it knows so that … Hear the Levite.” From these readings nearly the same sense can be extracted: namely, that in administering penance the Church does not acknowledge civil laws, but has its own laws, specifically that it obey the commands of Christ. Yet Thuanus, Pratensis, Fiscianus, Ebrulphus, Albinus, Alnetus, and Bigotius prefer the reading restored by us in the text, except that Ebrulphus reads *sacerdotis*, “of the priest,” instead of *sacerdos*, “the priest.” The sense is that when the Church binds and looses, removes someone from participation in the sacred rites, and so forth, it exercises not a power assigned to it by the laws of the state, but one entrusted to it and commanded to be exercised by Christ himself. No one will deny that this fits the preceding and following context better.].

Hear the Levite saying: “I have handed such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 5:5). Therefore, struck by the Levitical sword, let the sense of the flesh in us die, so that our soul may live. For unless the sense of the flesh has been killed, there can be no fruit of eternal life.

**9.** There are six cities of refuge, so arranged that the first city is knowledge of the Word and a way of life formed according to its image. For whoever enters into that knowledge is safe from punishment, according to what the Lord also says: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15:3). And elsewhere: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

This, then, is the city like a metropolis, beside which lie the other five cities of the Levites. The second city is consideration of the divine work by which the world was created. The third city is contemplation of royal power and eternal majesty [Note: [Col. 0574D] Some manuscripts read: “contemplation of the royal city.” This is less satisfactory.]. The fourth city is contemplation of divine propitiation. The fifth city is contemplation of the divine law, which commands what must be done. The sixth city is that portion of the law which prescribes what must not be done.

What abundance of divine mercy, what riches of his compassion, that, considering the pursuits of individuals and the frailty of human condition—by which we are often led into guilt unwillingly and against our resistance, and, overcome by enticements, frequently commit offenses that we did not intend—he should set before us different refuges, namely, six cities; so that, by the same number by which the world was formed, a remedy might be provided against worldly vices and the shipwrecks of this age.

**10.** The first remedy, then, is this: if guilt should creep upon a man of good purpose, let him hasten without any postponement, if he wishes to possess perfect security, to the very citadel of all things, where the Word of God is in the paternal bosom—that is, in the secret and hidden recess of God—where the fountain of wisdom is, from which he may draw immortal drink in place of death: eternal life.

The second remedy is this: whoever cannot taste in advance a knowledge of that good, being slower either in intellect or in grasping the faith—for by quick vigor of mind and sharpness of intellect one presses toward the heights of knowledge—should at least consider the works of the Lord and, from the things that have been made, contemplate the author of so great a work. For from the good things that exist in the constitution of this creation—for “they were very good” (Gen. 1:31), as the Lord said—that highest and eternal good is grasped.

What order there is among things! What discipline! What grace! Is not even a slow intellect aroused by these things to love its creator? For if we love our parents because they gave us birth, how much more ought we to love the creator of our parents and our own author?

Therefore, although God’s operative power is not seen, it is nevertheless judged from his works; and his works reveal the worker, so that he who cannot be grasped may be understood. Hence the Lord also says: “If you do not believe me, believe the works” (John 10:38).

These things too, then, are a good city of refuge, which bears witness to the grace of its builder and arouses our affection, so that we may desire more eagerly the one who seems to have bestowed such beauty upon this structure.

The third order is contemplation of royal power, so that we may submit to the king if we do not render him honor as a parent. For fear of a ruler often makes a person obedient to authority even when he is ungrateful for salvation, so that the one who was unwilling and unable to recognize the grace of compassion may recognize the necessity of sobriety. Necessity therefore corrects the one whom compassion ought to have aroused.

**11.** These are the three cities beyond the Jordan, given as refuges for more perfect prudence: first, so that we may flee guilt by the prompting of the mind, being conformed to the image of God. For we were created in this way, as God said: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). This, then, is the law of that first city.

Next, if through the frailty of the flesh and the enticements of the world we cannot shape our mind in this way, let us lighten our sin through reverence for our paternal origin and through diligent care for our offspring. For charity covers a multitude of sins. Therefore, whoever cannot be in the image of God should at least attain the fullness of charity.

That city excludes guilt; this one releases from it. This, finally, is the law of the second city: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deut. 6:5).

But if again there are people narrow and petty in spirit, who cannot receive the abundance of charity and grace, you have a third city, so that fear of divine power may make you sober and bend you toward the good. This is its third law: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (ibid., 13).

These, then, are the principal virtues, and therefore they are placed beyond the Jordan for a few, not for the many: so that you may express the archetype as an image, love the Father as a son, and worship the King as a subject.

**12.** Those who have crossed the Jordan—Jordan is called their descent—those, therefore, who have descended from those higher virtues to these lower ones, in which integrity, charity, or humility has faltered, have refuges closer to human beings to which they may flee. Those who are liable to offenses and bent by unwilling vices may hope that the Lord can be reconciled to them if they ask forgiveness; they may hope that they can be corrected if they follow the precepts of the heavenly Testaments, by which we are either formed in innocence or recalled from guilt.

These, then, are the cities that follow within the Jordan: so that we may propitiate God, follow what he commands, and avoid what he forbids. Let there therefore be eagerness to propitiate the divinity, obedience in following his command, and caution in avoiding transgression of what is forbidden. By these things let us honor God’s propitiatory mercy and his lawgiving providence, both by obeying his ordinances and by avoiding his prohibitions.

**13.** The fourth matter remains: concerning the death of the high priest he says: “For he shall remain in the city of refuge until that time, until the great priest dies” (Josh. 20:6). In this passage the interpretation according to the letter encounters difficulties.

First, the flight itself is determined by lot rather than by a just examination. Then, in equal cases, the outcome may be unequal; for it could happen that the great priest died on the very day after that homicide had taken refuge. What judgment is this, subject to uncertainty?

Since the letter therefore presents difficulties, let us seek spiritual meanings. Who is this great priest except the Son of God, the Word of God, whose advocacy we have with the Father? He is free from all voluntary and accidental sins; in him all things that are on earth and in heaven subsist. For all things are bound together by the bond of the Word, are held by his power, and subsist in him, because all things were created in him and in him all fullness dwells.

Therefore all things remain, because what he has bound together he does not permit to be dissolved, since they subsist by his will. He restrains and governs all things by his command as long as he wills, and binds them together by natural harmony.

The Word of God therefore lives, and lives especially in the souls of the godly; nor does the fullness of divinity ever die. The eternal divinity never dies, nor does the everlasting power of God. Yet he dies to us if he is separated from our soul—not because he is corrupted by death, but because our mind is dissolved and stripped of its union with him. For the true death of the Word and the soul is their separation.

Finally, the soul immediately begins to lie open to voluntary sins [Note: [Col. 0575D] All manuscripts and editions without exception read this way, except the Roman edition, which has “to involuntary sins.” This was doubtless because Philo, in *On the Fugitive*, from which this material was taken, reads: “A descent is immediately given to involuntary errors” [Greek: *Kathodos euthys didotai tois akousiois sphalmasin*]. But both the agreement of the manuscripts and editions can show that Ambrose read *hekousiois*, “voluntary,” and the context of Philo’s discourse itself supports this. For after the first member of the preceding sentence had taught that, when the Word is present, the soul’s voluntary turning toward evil cannot occur, was it not natural that he should say that, when the same Word is absent, the soul immediately becomes open to voluntary turning toward evil—or, what is the same thing, that a return to voluntary sins is granted?].

## CHAPTER THREE

Shows, by collecting various testimonies of the Apostle, that the kinds of virtues mentioned in the preceding chapter are found in the Apostle not merely sketched but fully expressed.

[Col. 0576B]

**14.** We have these kinds of virtues not merely sketched but fully expressed in the Apostle, when he says: “Thus, as far as I am concerned, I am ready to preach the Gospel to you also who are in Rome. For I am not ashamed of the Gospel. For it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For the righteousness of God is revealed in it”—that is, in the one who believes (Rom. 1:15 and following).

Finally, he added: “From faith to faith, as it is written: The righteous person lives by faith.” In what, then, is the righteousness of God revealed, except in the one who is conformed to the image of the Son of God? Here you have the first commandment: to be made according to the image of God.

The second is that his invisible things are understood through the things that have been made—that is, his eternal power and divinity are known through his works. This is operative power.

The third concerns imperial power, because the Word of God is royal, judicial, and full of priestly righteousness, reserving the reward of good actions and the repayment of evil actions for the judgment that is to come. Concerning these the Apostle says: “We know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things” (Rom. 2:2).

Therefore, the one who has recognized the truth and righteousness of God must not do things worthy of death.

There follows the goodness of God, which is certainly propitiatory, concerning which he says: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering? Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?” (ibid., 4).

That is, it ought to lead you; it urges you because God is good, so that you may be able to hope for forgiveness of your sins [Note: [Col. 0576D] The old edition reads: “that is, it ought to lead and urge you.” The Roman edition reads: “that is, it urges you.” The manuscripts read as in the text.]. For he who is ready to forgive does not wish to exact vengeance.

He also appended legislation, that is, *nomotheticē*, so that if anyone is weakened by contemplation of divine goodness and is moved more toward negligence than toward repentance, he may follow the law. For he says: “Whoever have sinned without the law will also perish without the law; and whoever have sinned under the law will be judged by the law” (ibid., 12).

[Col. 0577A] **15.** The law, moreover, is twofold: natural and written. Natural law is in the heart; written law is on tablets. All, therefore, are under the law—under the natural law. But it is not the case that everyone is a law to himself. He is a law to himself who willingly does what belongs to the law and shows the work of the law written in his heart. You know what the good things of the law are; yet we must not merely know or hear them superficially, but also do them. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified.

You have also learned what things are evil. First, nature itself is a teacher of good conduct. You know that one must not steal, and if your servant commits theft against you, you beat him; and if someone has cast his eyes upon your wife, you think he should be prosecuted. What, then, do you yourself commit when you condemn it in others? You who preach that one must not steal—do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery—do you commit adultery? [Col. 0577B]

The law given through Moses followed as well. Through the law comes recognition of sin. You have also received instruction concerning what you should avoid, and yet you do the things you know are forbidden? What does the law accomplish, then, except that the whole world should become subject to God? For it was not enacted only for the Hebrew; it also called the foreigner and did not exclude the proselyte. But because the law could close the mouth of everyone, though it could not convert the mind, the final remedy was due to that last city, in which there would be a saving refuge: so that the death of the chief priest might free us from every fear of death and strip away our dread (see St. Augustine, *On the Book of Four [Letters] against the Pelagians*, IV, 11).

**16.** Who is he, then, except the one of whom it is written: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29) [Col. 0577C] . . . . . “whom God set forth as an expiation through faith in his blood, to demonstrate his righteousness” (Romans 3:25)?

Understand, moreover, that he himself is the great chief priest. The Father swore concerning him, saying: “You are a priest forever” (Psalm 109:4). Rightly “forever,” since all the others are temporal and subject to sin, whereas he possesses an unfailing priesthood; all are under death, whereas he lives forever. For how could he himself perish who is able to save others? “Such a one,” he says, “was fitting for us” (Hebrews 7:26–27).

The expression is correct. Indeed, among those who have taken care in the choice of words and expressions, a phrase of this kind is found, when someone says: “A higher place than was fitting for victors” (Sallust, *Histories*, book I). [Note: The Roman edition added after the word *decebat* (“was fitting”) the phrase *capit*, taken from Sallust; it is found neither in the manuscripts nor in the old edition of Ambrose. Before the word *naturalibus* (“natural”), it also inserted the negative *non* (“not”). This is wrong. Ambrose’s only point here is that the Apostle’s words, *nobis decebat* (“was fitting for us”), are not defective, as the Sallustian example proves, but are natural—that is, simple—and somewhat removed from ordinary usage and the rules of the grammarians.]

I have not passed this over so that we may know that the Apostle uses words that are natural rather than commonplace, or chosen according to formal rules. “Such a one,” he says, “was fitting for us: a chief priest, just, holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens.”

This, therefore, is the Word who, dwelling above the heavens, illumines all things. Hence he is also read as having been anointed naturally by God the Father (Acts 4:27), because he is the true light that illumines every human being coming into this world.

This is the Word [Col. 0578A] of God, in whom there is the great priesthood. Moses describes its intelligible garments in the vesture of the chief priest (Exodus 29:5 ff.); by his power he clothes the world, and, as though wrapped in him, it shines in all things. For through assuming this body and through inexpressible love he put on the kinship of the human race, pouring himself into all by the Spirit and by the fullness of his divinity. “From his fullness we have all received,” so that we might know “the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge” and be filled “unto all the fullness of God.”

For Christ is the head of all, from whom the whole body is brought forth and joined together by mutual connection, receiving its growth for the building up of love.

This, therefore, is the Word [Col. 0578B] that surpasses all things, of whom he says to Moses in the construction of the ark of the testimony: “You shall put into the ark the testimonies that I shall give you, and you shall make the cover of expiation” (Exodus 25:16–17). And further: “You shall place the cover of expiation on top of the ark, and you shall put into it the testimonies that I shall give you; and there I shall make myself known to you, and from above I shall speak with you” (ibid., 22)—that is, from there where he is above the heavens, where he is with the Father: from there I shall speak with you.

[Note: Some manuscripts have *cognitionem generis humani* (“knowledge of the human race”). Others, and the editions, more suitably have *cognationem* (“kinship”), and so forth.]

## CHAPTER IV

**What it means to flee the world, with an exhortation to flee it and its contagion. That this flight is glorious is shown both by the examples of many of the Fathers and especially by that of Saint Jacob. How successfully he benefited from fleeing in this way, and why Laban could find nothing belonging to himself with him.**

[Col. 0578C] **17.** Let us therefore approach, strengthened by the support of faith and lifted up by its oars, to that seat of grace, fleeing this world and its contagion. To flee means to abstain from sins, to assume the form of virtues according to the likeness and image of God, and to extend our strength in imitation of God according to the measure of our ability.

For the perfect man is the image and glory of God. Hence the Lord also says: “Be perfect, as your Father who is in heaven is perfect” (Matthew 5:48). To be like God, therefore, is to possess justice and wisdom, and to be perfect in virtue (*On Penance*, distinction 2, chapter “Like”). For God is without sin. Therefore whoever flees sin is in the image of God.

There is no doubt, then, that the person who abstains from sin flees. Hence the Apostle also cries out: “Flee fornication” (1 Corinthians 6:18). The enticements of sins pursue us; lust pursues us. But flee it as a raging mistress who, if she seizes you, allows you no rest by day or night: she drives you on, burns you, and sets you aflame.

Flee greed, lest it seize you inwardly. [Note: “Flee envy . . . which is accustomed to tear apart.” A little later: “But if in another . . . flee”; these words are missing from all the Gallican manuscripts.]

Flee envy, which is accustomed to tear apart not only others but still more the one whom it possesses. Flee [Col. 0579A] faithlessness, lest it entangle you in its nets. Hence the Lord also says: “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another. And when they persecute you in the other, flee into another. Truly I tell you, you will not finish the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes” (Matthew 10:23).

Although, then, he may seem to recommend flight to us on account of the weakness of the flesh, the person who flees the world’s enticement flees more successfully, so that he is not held by anxiety over his riches, by contemplation of his treasure, or by desire for this life. Rather, with the mind’s attention directed straight ahead, he hastens toward the glory of the heavenly kingdom and presses on toward the crown, nor is he recalled from suffering in his body by the sight of earthly things.

**18.** Flight, then, is either death accomplished or death represented. [Note: “Death . . . celebrated,” that is, natural death and death truly undergone; “represented death” means mortification. In this there is a likeness of the soul separating from the body, as Ambrose says in *On the Good of Death*, chapter 4, §14.]

And perhaps it signifies those cities of legitimate refuge, so that we may flee to the heights of the virtues, which he distributes elsewhere as rewards to the good lender, saying: “Because you were faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities” (Luke 19:17).

[Note: Thus the Vatican manuscript reads. But twelve of our manuscripts read: “The Law knows five cities.” We may believe that this error arose because in some manuscripts the word *vetus* (“old”) was represented by the letter *v*, which later scribes took as a numeral. This passage was missing from the earlier edition; in the Roman edition it reads: “The Law knows six cities.” But the Vatican manuscript has *vetus* (“old”) and omits *six,” although anyone can understand that this word is implied from what precedes.]

The old Law knows cities; but because he fulfilled the law who could say, “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17), he grants the more perfect number as a reward.

**19.** Let us not, then, be ashamed to flee. For this flight is glorious: to flee from the face of sin. Thus Jacob fled, at his mother’s urging. Rebecca said: “Arise and flee to Mesopotamia” (Genesis 27:43).

So Moses also fled from the face of King Pharaoh, lest the royal court contaminate him or power ensnare him. Indeed, he esteemed the reproach of Christ more precious than the riches of Egypt.

So David too fled from the face of King Saul and from the face of Absalom. Indeed, while fleeing he increased in piety: he spared his enemy and pleaded for the life of the parricide.

So the Hebrew people also fled, so that their faith and life might open a way for themselves amid the waves. That flight was a path of innocence, a road of virtue, an assumption of piety.

I dare say that Jonah too fled to Tarshish in this way—not by bodily flight but by an ascent of the mind. He rose even to the likeness of Christ, so that he might become a type of Christ. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster for three days and three nights, so, he says, “the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matthew 12:40). For if he had not fled in this way, he would never have been heard from the belly of the sea monster.

[Col. 0580A] **20.** But if you doubt, let Rebecca teach you how blessed was the flight undertaken by Jacob. Rebecca urged him: “Flee,” she said, “to Mesopotamia” (Genesis 28:2). Isaac says: “Arise and go to Mesopotamia, to the house of Bethuel.”

[Note: This is taken from Philo’s book *On the Fugitive*, where one reads: “The name of Bethuel is sung as Wisdom in the oracles” (*σοφίας δὲ ὄνομα Βαιθουὴλ ἐν χρησμοῖς ᾄδεται*). In the same book: “Whom the oracles called Isaac” (*Ὃν Ἰσαὰκ ὠνόμασαν οἱ χρησμοί*). From these passages it is clear that Ambrose, following Philo, calls the sacred Scriptures “oracles.” What he says here, “in hymns,” either means the same as “in oracles”—for *χρησμός* can sometimes signify both—or it may refer to the verb *ᾄδεται*, “is sung.” Moreover, Philo himself and the interpreters of Matthew 26:30—“and after singing a hymn they went out”—teach that the name “hymns” can also signify the psalms of David.]

In hymns or oracles, as many have written before us, Bethuel is called “wisdom”; in Latin interpretation, the name signifies “daughter of God.” Jacob is therefore sent to the house of wisdom and is instructed to take a wife from the daughters of Laban, who lived in Charris. This name signifies “caves,” in which there is an image of the senses, which are as though in the caves of the body: sight in the eyes, hearing in the ears, smell in the nostrils, and taste in the mouth.

Whoever delights in this world and rejoices in bodily pleasures is subject to the passions of the senses and dwells and moves about in them. Therefore Rebecca tells him to dwell there with him for a few days, not for a long time, lest he be colored by bodily pleasures and captured by the enticements of the world.

**21.** She persuades him to dwell there so that he may learn [Col. 0580B] more diligently the meaning of the discipline of virtue and, as it were, certain positions and regions of the flesh, so that he may know himself and understand the force of the flesh—what it was created for and for what reason—and how each sense operates.

“Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her” (Matthew 5:28). The eye sees badly in this way. Let the eye see, then, and perform its own function; let it not be directed toward a fall by the command of a slippery mind, so that it returns vice in place of duty.

A brief period, then, is granted for knowing, or rather for experiencing, the senses—perhaps the first beginnings of tender youth. Immediately afterward he is recalled, lest he stumble too long on slippery ground and the innermost traces of the soul be submerged by a certain divided flood of this body and of the world.

When he has either gained experience or stood upon unstable, uncertain, and moist soil, he is recalled by his mother, patience or perseverance, who says: “I shall send for you and bring you back from there” (Genesis 27:45). Thus, even there, you may find a safe harbor in wisdom, which will not allow you to drift about as in a shipwreck; and, when you have returned, you will know how to persevere in the worship of God and will belong to the assembly of the nations, signifying that the Church of the nations is to be gathered in his faith.

[Note: Thus the better manuscripts read; several more recent ones agree, except that they read “the sense of virtue and of discipline” . . . . The Vatican manuscript and one Colbertine manuscript have “a student of the discipline of the virtues of the senses.” This is not inept, since in the following chapter Jacob is called a lover of discipline. The old edition differs from them only in having *studiosius* (“more diligently”). Finally, the Roman edition and the first hand of the Theodulf manuscript read: “a student of the discipline of the meaning of virtue.” In the same place, the Roman edition has: “Who he is and for what reason he was created”; the old edition has: “What . . . was created.” All the manuscripts have this except Remigius and the second hand of Theodulf, which read: “What . . . he was created.”]

**22.** Instructed, therefore, in these disciplines of patience and perseverance (Genesis 29:23 ff.), Jacob set out [Col. 0581A] and acquired for himself a union [Note: The edition, with a few manuscripts of more recent date, reads: “from the house of wisdom, a companion in purpose.”] with wisdom as his companion in purpose, richly endowed with prudence, with whom he might pass through the seasons of life without any offense.

Having thus added the treasure of wisdom, he established for himself a flock of various sheep—but a rational flock, shining with the diversity of many virtues. Hence he also cut away the boastfulness of his flesh (Genesis 32:25), which signifies the paralysis of the thigh, without prejudice to the sacred interpretation of the mystery.

By these virtues, therefore, as by certain steps, his mind ascended to heaven; he came to know the secrets of God, and was strengthened and filled, so that when Laban searched his house he found nothing empty or vacant in him, no images and no likeness of vanity. For there was not an image in him but truth; not an effigy of slothfulness, but a solid form of justice and an intelligible expression of true virtue.

Laban therefore searched his spiritual house and found no images. For it was full not of figures but of deeds.

**23.** He could have found the foundations and heights of the virtues, had he not brought with him blindness of heart and the darkness of a faithless mind. Indeed, blinded by that wickedness, the Sodomites could not find the door of holy Lot. How could an impious mind see either the departure or the entrance of a holy man?

The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “The prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John 14:30). How could he find nothing in him in whom the fullness of divinity dwelt and indwelt bodily, from whom power went forth and healed all? How could he find nothing in the solidity of virtue, in the abundance of wisdom, [Note: Thus nearly all the manuscripts read; a few manuscripts and the editions have “the integrity of justice.”] understanding, and justice?

You yourself said, Lord: “I am full” (Isaiah 1:11). You yourself said: “Put your hand into my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing” (John 20:27). The one who did not believe put in his hand and found you to be Lord and God.

You, therefore, were not empty; rather, that prince of this world was blind and empty. He knows how to see only what belongs to himself; he knows how to find only what belongs to himself. He does not know how to recognize the things that belong to Christ.

**24.** Or, if the reading is as many have it, “He will find nothing in me”—that is, he will find no wickedness in me, because wickedness is nothing; he will find no dead man, because he is not dead. But how could he find a dead man in him who gives life to the dead and calls those things that are not as though they were? “He will not find sin in me,” he says, “who took away the sin of the world.”

For how can he possess nothing who possesses everything? And, what is more, he possesses everything that the Father possesses, as he himself says: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15).

## CHAPTER V

**Why we must flee from here, and how we must cross over with Moses in order to see God, removing the sandals from our feet; how also we must leave the shadow of this life and, with Saint David, if not as an eagle, at least as a sparrow, fly away—if not to heaven, at least to the mountains.**

[Col. 0582A] **25.** Let us flee, then, from here, where there is nothing, where everything thought magnificent is empty, where even the person who thinks himself to be something is nothing and altogether does not exist.

“I saw the wicked man exalted and raised up above the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Psalm 36:35). You too must pass over, as David passed over; pass over like a good servant, so that it may be said to you: “Pass over and recline” (Luke 17:7).

Pass over like Moses, so that you may see the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and see the great vision. [Note: The old edition and two manuscripts read: “that you may see the great vision.” But if . . . The Roman edition has: “the great vision, that is, the vision of mysteries.” But a large number of manuscripts read as in the text.]

This is a great vision. But if you wish to see it, remove the sandal from your feet; remove every bond of iniquity; remove the belts of the world; leave behind the sandal that is earthly.

For this reason Jesus sent out the apostles without sandals, gold, or silver, so that they would not carry earthly things with them.
