Whoever seeks the good is praised not for his sandals but for the speed and beauty of his feet, as Scripture says: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Isaiah 52:7)!

Remove, then, the sandal from your feet, so that they may be beautiful for proclaiming the Gospel. He said “Remove” (Exodus 3:5), not “bind.” Remove it, so that you may cross over and discover that the wicked man whom you admired on earth is nothing there and can do nothing.

Cross over, then—that is, flee from the lands where wickedness and greed are found. Therefore David says to you: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 33:15). To turn away is certainly to flee.

Evil is on earth, but good is in heaven. Hence he adds: “Seek peace and pursue it.” Peace is in heaven. Indeed, the one who comes from heaven says: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

Therefore, because evils must be fled and avoided, and because evils are on earth—that is, iniquities—let us flee earthly things, lest the iniquities seize us. They seized even holy David, as he himself testifies: “My iniquities have overtaken me, and I was unable to see” (Psalm 39:13), because the eye of the soul is blinded by the smoke of iniquity and cannot see what is luminous.

Thus Laban could not see Jacob’s good qualities, nor could the prince of this world see Christ’s glory.

**26.** But perhaps you will say: Why, then, was Jacob sent to Laban, if Laban was blameworthy? If we consider the name, it means “white” in Latin. Jacob is therefore commanded to go forth toward brighter things.

But because he was carnal, we understand “brighter things” better as the splendors of this life. As though not yet perfect, he first goes to him, with whom he would rejoice for a time in his light.

Laban had worse children—that is, his name was more tolerable than his deeds. Therefore, both at his mother’s counsel, through the divine oracle, and by the will of Jacob himself, the lover of discipline, he is soon abandoned and left behind.

[Note: The Greek reads, apparently corruptly: “This is, he will arrive at the splendors of life” (*Τόδ’ ἐστὶν, εἰς τὰς τοῦ βίου λαμπρότητας ἀφίξετα*). “For Laban is interpreted as white.” This is from Philo’s book *On the Fugitive*, with which it is worthwhile to compare many passages of this treatise.]

**27.** Rachel, that is, the Church or prudence, hides the sacred images, because the Church does not know empty ideas or the vain figures of images; rather, she knows the true substance of the Trinity. Indeed, she abolished the shadow and manifested the splendor of glory.

Let us therefore leave the shadow, since we seek the sun; let us abandon the smoke, since we follow the light. Smoke is iniquity, because just as smoke affects the eyes, so iniquities affect those who live by them. [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts have this reading. The old edition, however, has: “Life is a shadow for those who use it. For a shadow . . .” The Roman edition reads: “for those who use it. This life of ours on earth is also a shadow.”]

Life is a shadow; for this life of ours on earth is a shadow, as Job said (Job 8:9). What else is there here but temptations? Every moment is filled with anxiety; every life with troubles. “We walk,” he says, “in the midst of snares” (Sirach 9:20).

Another person, on the road he was traveling, was seeking snares stretched out before him but hidden, lest he be caught and fall (Psalm 141:4). He wanted to flee like a sparrow, but the snare had not yet been broken. “Flight has perished from me,” he says (Psalm 141:5).

His wings were weighed down by that dark water in the clouds of the air, and perhaps he could not fly away. Therefore he sought to receive those wings, so that he might fly away and rest, as it is written: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? I shall fly away and rest” (Psalm 54:7). For where there is flight, there is rest.

Elsewhere he says: “If you sleep among the midst of the lots, the wings of the dove are silvered” (Psalm 67:14).

**28.** But perhaps you will say: How, then, does he say here that flight has perished from him, when above he had said: “If I take my wings before the dawn” (Psalm 138:9)? Is this contradictory? Certainly not.

There are many struggles for the righteous. Does an athlete wrestle only once? How often is one who has won many crowns defeated in another contest! How often does one who had frequently conquered waver for a time and remain uncertain! It often happens that a strong opponent engages the strong, and greater contests arise where greater proofs of strength are found.

Thus, when David was seeking flight in order to escape his adversary and could not find his wings, he wavered in a perilous contest. For when he possesses his wings, the title of the psalm is “For the end” (Psalm 138), that is, for the perfection and completion of victory.

Therefore, as a victor, he says: “Lord, you have tested me and known me; you know my sitting down and my rising up” (ibid., 1). He rightly possessed the ability to fly, since he had received the wings of resurrection.

But here he is still in the cave—that is, in the flesh, in a kind of cavern of this body—struggling with King Saul, the son of hardness, and with the power of that intelligible prince, who is not seen but understood. Hence the title of the psalm is “Understanding” (Psalm 54). David, still enclosed in the flesh, brought it to completion; but he deserved to complete it by praying. Indeed, he began with the voice of prayer.

[Col. 0584A] **29.** Add also that the former psalm is said in the person of the Savior, whereas this one is in the person of David, who did not possess victory in his own power but hoped for it from Christ.

Nevertheless, after he stretched out his hands toward God like the wings of his soul, took refuge in the Lord, and asked for the guidance of the Holy Spirit, so that he might know the way by which he could ascend, he saw the heavens bend down so that Christ might descend, and he asked that Christ lift him with his hand.

Or perhaps he no longer sought his wings because, having become more perfect, he desired the hand of Christ.

**30.** Whoever, then, wishes to be lifted by the hand of Christ must first fly away himself and possess his own wings. Whoever flees the world should have wings; and if he does not have his own wings—lest perhaps he alone who has the power to fly have wings of his own—if, I say, he does not have his own, let him receive them from the one who has them.

Whoever therefore flees the world flies: “Behold,” he says, “I have fled far away and remained in the wilderness” (Psalm 54:8).

David therefore flew away like a night bird in a dwelling, like a solitary sparrow on a house. But if you refer this to Christ, he flew away in the suffering of the body, so that beneath the shadow of his wings he might protect the peoples of the nations.

He flew away in divinity, remained in the body, and dwelt in the wilderness, so that the deserted woman’s children might become more numerous than those of her who had a husband.

Let us therefore follow that body, so that we too may rise again. For where the body is, there also are the eagles.

[Note: The old edition and some Paris manuscripts read: “Let that one alone not have his own.” The other editions, together with all the manuscripts, more correctly read: “Let that one alone have his own.” The words seem to indicate that Christ alone possesses wings proper to himself, while the others need wings belonging to another—that is, divine assistance received from above.]

**31.** Whoever cannot fly like an eagle, let him fly like a sparrow. Whoever cannot fly to heaven, let him fly to the mountains; let him flee the lowlands, which quickly decay through moisture, and cross over to the mountains.

Lot’s nephew crossed over to Mount Segor and was saved. But the woman who could not ascend, bent backward by feminine affection, lost her salvation. [Note: All the editions have: “As the mountains approach . . .” All the manuscripts, at least the Gallican ones, have: “Approach the mountains . . .,” according to the Septuagint, which reads: *ἐγγίσατε ὄρεσιν αἰωνίοις* (“draw near to the everlasting mountains”). This is not found in the commonly printed edition.]

“Draw near to the everlasting mountains,” the Lord says through the prophet Micah: “Arise and depart, for you have no rest here. Because of uncleanness you have been corrupted with corruption; you have suffered persecution” (Micah 2:9–10).

And the Lord says: “Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains” (Luke 21:21), where there is Mount Zion and the city of peace, Jerusalem, built not with earthly but with living stones; and ten thousand angels; the Church of the firstborn; the spirits of the perfect; God of the righteous, who has spoken better in his blood than Abel.

Abel cried out for vengeance; Christ for forgiveness. Abel accused his brother’s sin; Christ forgave the sin of the world. Abel exposed the crime; Christ covered it, according to what is written: “Blessed are those whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31:1).

## CHAPTER VI

**For what reason one who wishes to flee must flee swiftly; where one must flee; and toward what good we ought to raise our souls.**

[Col. 0585A] **32.** But whoever flees must flee swiftly, lest he be overtaken. [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “He will be swiftly caught unless he leaves this world.”]

Let him swiftly plunder this world, as the Hebrew did Egypt. Let the woman in labor give birth, lest, with the womb of the mind burdened and weighed down by iniquities, she be unable to flee. Let him flee not like one carrying a nursing child but like one unencumbered; not carrying a little one but presenting himself perfect in Christ; not as one idle on the Sabbath but as a worker engaged in business; not as a barren person in the cold but as one rich in the harvest.

For this reason it is said: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matthew 24:2).

This flight, then, is fruitful in virtues, not produced by merits. This flight knows neither the cold of fear, nor the trembling of death, nor the contraction of anxiety, nor the idleness of dissolution, nor the holiday of wantonness, nor the sluggishness of torpor. Rather, it requires an energetic traveler toward heavenly life, an active competitor for the higher kingdom, a wealthy farmer who gathers his fruits and, by gathering them, seizes them.

**33.** For what else is sought from you, O human being, except that you fear the Lord, seek him, walk after him, and grasp his ways (Deuteronomy 10:12)?

“In what,” he says, “shall I grasp the Lord? Shall I grasp him in burnt offerings?” The Lord is not reconciled, nor are sins redeemed, by ten thousand kids, thousands of rams, or the fruits of ungodliness. Rather, the grace of the Lord is grasped in a good life.

“It has been declared to you, O human being, what is good and what the Lord requires of you.” What else, except that you do justice, love mercy, and are ready to walk with the Lord your God?

The Gospel says to you: “Arise, let us go from here” (John 14:31). The law says to you: “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 13:4).

You have learned how to flee from here. Why do you delay? The Gospel says to you again: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew 3:7). He says this to those who were coming to the baptism of repentance.

**34.** Repentance, then, is a good flight; the grace of God is a good flight, into which the fleeing person is received; the wilderness is a good flight, to which Elijah, Elisha, and John the Baptist fled.

Elijah fled from the woman Jezebel—that is, from the outpouring of vanity—and fled to Mount Horeb, which signifies drying up, so that the carnal flow of vanity might be dried up in him and he might come to know God more fully.

He was beside the torrent Chorrath, which means “knowledge,” where he might drink in the abundant stream of divine knowledge. He fled the world so completely that he did not seek food for this body except what the birds brought as ministers, although his nourishment was for the most part not earthly.

Indeed, he walked for forty days in the strength of the food he had received.

Surely such a great prophet was not fleeing a woman. Did he fear death, when he had offered himself to the one who sought him and said to the Lord, “Take my soul” (1 Kings 19:4), enduring weariness with this life rather than desire for it? No: he was fleeing the world’s enticement, the contagion of a defiled way of life, and the sacrileges of an impious and transgressing nation.

[Col. 0586A] **35.** Solomon too sets forth the corruption of this world under the figure of that woman and teaches that the arts of prostitutes must be avoided (Proverbs 7 and elsewhere). This is the strange and adulterous woman, from whom he urges you to guard yourself.

Do not incline your heart toward the ways of the world, but place it in the hand of the Lord, in whose hand is the king’s heart. For whoever rules himself—which is more valuable than ruling others—has his heart in the hand of God, and God turns it wherever he wills.

It is no wonder that he turns it toward good, since he is perfect goodness.

Let us therefore be in the hand of God, so that we may seek the good—that incorruptible and unchangeable good of which the prophet Amos says: “Seek good and not evil, so that you may live; and so the Lord God almighty will be with you” (Amos 5:14).

How, then, did you say: “We hated evil and loved good”? Where God is, there are good things—the things David desired to see and believed he would see, as he himself says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26:13).

Those are truly good things that always remain and cannot be corrupted by any change of time or age.

**36.** Whoever has sought and found God is in those good things. For where a person’s heart is, there also is his treasure. The Lord is not accustomed to deny good things to those who ask.

Since the Lord is good, and especially good to those who endure in him, let us cling to him and be with him with our whole soul, our whole heart, and our whole strength, so that we may be in his light, see his glory, and enjoy the grace of heavenly delight.

Let us therefore raise our spirits toward that good, be in it, and live in it; let us cling to it, since it is above every mind and every consideration and enjoys perpetual peace and tranquillity.

Peace is above every mind and above every sense. This is the good that penetrates all things; in it we all live, and from it we all depend. It has nothing above itself, but is divine; for no one is good except the one God.

Therefore whatever is good is divine, and whatever is divine is good. Hence it is said: “When you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness” (Psalm 103:28).

Through the goodness of God, all good things are bestowed upon us—things in which nothing evil is mixed. Scripture promises these good things to the faithful, saying: “You shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1:19).

Let us therefore be like that good one, so that we may attain the good things: the good that is without iniquity, deceit, or harshness, accompanied by grace, piety, sincerity, goodwill, love, and justice. Thus goodness embraces all the virtues as a fertile mother.

## CHAPTER VII

**That the greatest reason why we should flee from here is that this is the proper dwelling-place of wickedness; also, what it means to flee. That wickedness does not perish here, and for what reason. Concerning the condemnation of the serpent and how it differs from the sentence pronounced against humanity. To these is added an exposition of the same sentence.**

[Col. 0587A] **37.** There is therefore no insignificant reason why we should flee from here: so that we may pass from evils to good things, from uncertainties to things faithful and full of truth, and from death to life.

The Lord himself, when he said, “I have set before you good and evil, life and death” (Deuteronomy 30:15), demonstrated that the good is life—but eternal life. For if this life is subject to the world and to its wickedness, then that is truly good which is not corrupted or changed, which does not degenerate through any defect, and which is acquired through virtue.

Let us therefore flee the wickedness of this world, in which, he says, “the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:16), and let us flee energetically.

Therefore Isaiah cries out: “Strengthen the slack hands and the weak knees” (Isaiah 35:3)—that is, strengthen not the knees of the body but those of the soul, so that the footprint of the mind, directed toward the highest heavens, may be lifted up; so that its guidance may be more solid, its life more mature, its grace more abundant, and its prudence more circumspect.

[Note: Seven manuscripts have *doctus solidior* (“more solid in learning”). The editions may have restored this in order to correct it as *doctrina solidior* (“more solid in doctrine”). Six manuscripts, however, read *ductus solidior* (“more solid in guidance”), which seems to us the true reading. Three nevertheless have *actus solidior* (“more solid in action”). This is not bad.]

**38.** For this is what it means to flee: to know where you are heading, to lift yourself above the world, to lift yourself above the body. Otherwise someone may again exalt himself vainly, and, puffed up in the mind of his flesh, fail to hold fast to the head; and it may be said of such people: “They fled, and they did not see” (Job 9:25).

But this is what it means to flee from here: to die to the elements of this world, to hide one’s life in God, to avoid corruptions, not to touch desires, and not to know the things of this world—which produces various pains for us, empties us when it has filled us, and, when it has emptied us, fills us again.

All these things are empty and void, in which there is no solid fruit. The rich man died and possessed nothing, because he was not rich toward God. Therefore he was foolish, because wisdom is the worship of God, while abstaining from evils is discipline.

39. Who, then, would not flee the domain of wickedness, the workshop of evil, which does not know how to perish? Accordingly, the mark was not placed upon Cain without purpose, lest anyone kill him; this signified that wickedness would not be extinguished and removed from the earth. Cain feared that he would be killed because he did not know how to flee. For wickedness grows and accumulates through use itself, and, without restraint or end, makes its decisions through deceit and fraud; it is exposed by its deeds and by the blood of those it has slain, just as Cain too was exposed. Wickedness, therefore, is active upon the earth and wanders there; and for this reason we pray that God’s will may be done on earth as in heaven (Matt. VI, 10), so that innocence may also be found here. Since wickedness, then, no longer has a place there, it circles here, rages here, and pours itself out—neither submerged in that worldwide Flood nor consumed in the fire of Sodom. Indeed, afterward it sprouted more grievously in the seedbeds of humanity, extending murderous and sacrilegious hands even against the Author of the salvation of all. The Law condemns the act, but does not remove wickedness. The Lord Jesus himself condemned sin but postponed the punishment of its author, so that there might be one through whom the righteous could be tested. For since God did not make evil, but the devil’s wickedness introduced it, God postponed vengeance, so that the devil might be conquered by those whom he had deceived (cf. St. Augustine, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, IV.11).

[Note: Most manuscripts and the old editions read “and it was there”; because this seemed inelegant, the Roman edition removed it. The true reading, however, is supplied by the Ebrulph and Theod manuscripts. “It wanders there” has the same meaning as “it roams there and spreads itself abroad.”]

40. Those who have been deceived are therefore disciplined, both to pay the price of their heedlessness and to take up the pursuits of virtue and the diligence of caution. Hence he says: “Be wise as serpents” (Matt. X, 16). Why “as serpents”? So that the serpent may be stripped of what belongs to it, and the one who wished to strip others may lose what is his—not his poisons, but the merits of his nature. Indeed, he is cast down when you ascend. For it is written: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke X, 18). He says not “lightning,” but “like lightning,” because he lost his own light, which he possessed before he wished to take away your light. Perhaps, however, you will say that we also read of the Savior: “As lightning flashing from beneath heaven . . . so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Luke XVII, 24). Here too “like lightning” is appropriate, because he is above lightning. Lightning comes from beneath heaven; the true light, however, is above heaven. Thus Satan is “like lightning,” because he lost what he had; but you have received what you had lost.

41. The sentence was not relaxed with respect to him as it was with respect to you. For the grace of Christ, which released you, bound him. The curse pronounced upon the serpent because of your deception remains. Thus it was said to him: “Cursed are you above all the beasts of the earth” (Gen. III, 14). He is the common enemy of all, who was the enemy of the good, and he is condemned on behalf of those whom he had not yet injured; for whoever injured the human being, to whom all those things are subject, injured them all. He broke the common law by which he himself, together with the rest, is subject to humanity. Therefore his curse is weighed down by the common hatred and execration of all.

The kind of condemnation is not death, but prolonged punishment: “Upon your breast and belly you shall walk” (ibid.). The guilty conscience had to be pressed down, wickedness trampled underfoot, and the fraudulent secret banished, as it were, from the face of God. At the same time it is shown that earthly wickedness is what bends itself toward the earth. Hence he added: “And you shall eat earth all the days of your life” (ibid.).

42. These words seem indeed to describe the nature of the serpent, but they describe more fully every vessel of wickedness, every serpent of evil: one that throws itself upon its belly and shuts its poison within itself; that rolls it about inside its breast; that is slippery in its thoughts and walks upon its own deceits; that entangles itself in its own tricks; that, whenever it thinks, continually stirs and agitates its poisons; and that tramples its belly—that is, the seedbed of its heart.

Hence David beautifully says:

“ sinners were estranged from the womb;  
they went astray from the belly;  
they spoke falsehood.  
Their fury is like the fury of a serpent,  
like that of a deaf asp that stops its ears,  
which will not hear the voice of charmers,  
nor of the poisoner when he is charmed by a wise man”  
(Ps. LVII, 4 ff.).

For this reason that other saying also seems beautifully expressed, which we read in the prophetic book: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain; my belly, my belly, I am in pain” (Jer. IV, 19). For wickedness is there where innocence ought to be; and that which ought to be most tranquil within us suffers the most. It is trampled under the footprints of wickedness, goaded by claws, shaken by a certain advance and increase of evil, precisely where the generative seedbed of eternal posterity is located.

This may indeed be referred to the fact that he grieved over the destruction of those whom he had created and received as children; but much more it means that he did not possess within his belly the seed of the Word. Therefore he calls it “his belly,” as though it were something most precious. For precious is the womb of the mind, in which a fertile harvest of counsels habitually sprouts from the seed of the Word, and in which certain members of the whole life, of virtues, and of disciplines are formed.

43. But, to return to our subject: since God judged that wickedness should for the time being be restrained rather than abolished, he said to the serpent: “I will place enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and the seed of the woman. She shall watch your head, and you shall watch her heel” (Gen. III, 15). Where there is enmity, there is discord and the desire to inflict harm; where there is the desire to inflict harm, there wickedness is present. Therefore the discord between the serpent and the woman contains the wickedness of discord. Wickedness, then, has not been removed.

Indeed, the serpent was left with the ability to watch the heel of the woman and of her seed, so that it might injure it and pour in its poison. Let us therefore not walk in earthly things, and the serpent will not be able to harm us. Let us put on the Gospel footwear by which the serpent’s poison is shut out and its bite blunted, so that our feet may be shod for the Gospel. Perhaps this is why Moses was commanded to remove the footwear from his feet: so that he might take up the footwear of the Gospel; or because the preaching of the Gospel was owed not to Moses—that is, not to the prophets—but to the apostles.

This is the sentence pronounced against the serpent, which we mentioned above. Let us consider what kind of sentence was pronounced against the human being.

44. Cursed is the one who is the author of guilt; but the one deceived by another’s fraud is not himself cursed. Nevertheless, because he did not keep God’s commandment, he is condemned to the labor of his own works. The earth is indeed cursed, but in the works of the sinner (Gen. III, 17), and it is cursed until it is dissolved into earth.

Therefore Jesus assumed flesh in order to abolish the curse of sinful flesh; and he became a curse for us, so that blessing might swallow up the curse, integrity might swallow up sin, indulgence might swallow up the sentence, and life might swallow up death. He also assumed death, so that the sentence might be fulfilled and satisfaction might be made to the judgment: “The curse of sinful flesh, even unto death.” Nothing, therefore, was done contrary to God’s sentence, since the condition of the divine sentence was fulfilled. The curse lasted until death; after death came grace.

We have therefore died to the world. Why do we still contend with the world? We have died with Christ. Why do we still seek the practices of this life? We bear the death of Christ in our body, so that the life of Christ may also be manifested in us. We therefore no longer live that former life of ours, but the life of Christ: the life of innocence, the life of chastity, the life of simplicity, and the life of every virtue. We have risen with Christ; let us live in him and ascend in him, so that the serpent may find no earthly place in which to wound our heel.

[Note: All editions read: “and satisfaction might be made to the judgment through the curse of sinful flesh,” and so forth. Several manuscripts read: “and satisfaction might be made to the judgment, while bearing the curse of sinful flesh.” Others, more numerous and more ancient, have the reading found in the text. The sense of the passage, in our opinion, is this: “so that satisfaction might be made to that judgment—or sentence—namely, the curse,” and so forth. There is here an unmistakable allusion to the sentence delivered in Gen. III, 17 ff., by which human beings were condemned to perpetual labor until death, as the preceding context makes clear.]

[Note: The editions read: “who still serve the world,” and: “we have died with Christ, who still . . . require.” The manuscripts partly read: “why do we still perceive anything of the world?”—that is, why do we still strive over worldly things?—and partly: “why do we still contend with the world?”—that is, why do we still serve the world?]

## CHAPTER VIII

How, although we are retained here in the body, we can and indeed ought to flee in spirit, lest, when the figure of this world passes away, our works and we ourselves pass away with it; and, so that this may not happen, we should not pass by God’s commandments, nor the progress of any discipline, as many of the ancient saints are known to have done.

45. Let us flee from here. You can flee in spirit even if you are held back in the body. You can also be here and be present with the Lord, if your soul clings to him, if you walk after him in your thoughts, if you follow his ways by faith rather than by sight, and if you flee for refuge to him. For he is refuge and strength, to whom David says: “I have fled to you for refuge, and I have not been deceived” (Ps. LXXVI, 3).

Since God is refuge, and God is in heaven and above the heavens, we must flee from here to there—to the place where there is peace, where there is rest from works, where we may feast upon the great Sabbath, as Moses said: “The Sabbaths of the land shall be food for you” (Lev. XXV, 6). For it is a banquet, full of joy and tranquility, to rest in Christ and behold his delight. We who flee for refuge to God—shall we return to the world? We who have died to sin—shall we return to our sins? We who have renounced the world and its use—shall we again cling to its mud?

[Note: The Theod and Valc manuscripts read: “Where we may feast upon his Sabbath,” that is, Christ’s Sabbath and the Sabbath of all virtues: “the great Sabbath,” and so forth. See Philo, *On the Fugitive*.]

46. Let us flee from here, because the time is short. Hear how you should flee: “Let those who have wives live as though they had none; and those who weep as though they did not weep; and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; and those who buy as though they possessed nothing; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. VII, 29 ff.).

Let us therefore not allow our works to pass away together with the passing figure of the world, lest we too pass away; but let us remain in the truth. If we remain in Christ, we remain in the truth; we shall remain with him and shall not pass away, but shall say: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we have blessed you in the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXXVIII, 8). Those who pass away cannot say this, because they did not say, as they passed along the way, the words spoken by the Prophet: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you.”

Therefore, if we wish our works not to pass away, let us not pass by God’s commandments; let us not pass by the diligence of seeking the Lord Jesus, or of earning his grace. That woman did not pass him by who entered the Pharisee’s house, where Christ was reclining, and poured ointment over his feet.

47. Let us not pass by the progress of any discipline, just as the young Joseph did not pass it by. He was seeking his brothers and hastening to the place where they were feeding the sheep; and when he learned that they were in Dothaim, he went there. The word *Dothaim* signifies an appropriate deficiency—that is, not a moderate but a complete and perfect deficiency of vain opinions—in which the soul makes progress.

[Note: “For the wise person, when he diminishes, adds”—supply “himself,” that is, “when he is diminished.” This is taken from the same work of Philo, *On the Fugitive*: “But the wise person, even when he withdraws, advances according to Moses” (ὁ δὲ σοφὸς καὶ ἐκλείπων προστίθεται κατὰ Μωσῆν). The allusion is to Gen. XXV, 8: “and withdrawing . . . he was added,” and so forth.]

For when the wise person diminishes, he adds. Worldly opinions fail, and these are compared with weak women. Hence, to show beautifully that Sarah had come to progress so as to give birth to laughter and joy, Scripture says: “The things pertaining to women had ceased for Sarah” (Gen. XVIII, 11).

Good, therefore, is the failure of desires, the failure of vanity, because it is an addition of truth. Hence holy David also says: “My soul has failed for your salvation” (Ps. CXVIII, 81). For she was about to give birth to what God had granted and promised: she was about to give birth to joy and to that sober intoxication of delight; she was about to give birth, before the expected time, through the swiftness of her understanding, to the works of wisdom.

[Note: The old edition, together with the Gallic manuscripts, reads this way, except that some have “which he had granted and promised to her.” The Roman edition, with one Vatican manuscript, reads: “which she had conceived, as he had promised,” and so forth.]

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “before the expected birth, by the quickness of her understanding, a fetus.” Other editions have: “before the expected understanding, pregnant through the swiftness of birth.” The manuscripts, however, read “before the expected”; a few have “before she expected,” with one reading “before she understood”; “through the swiftness” (some: “through the celebration”) “of birth” (one: “by birth,” others: “a birth”) “pregnant” (others: “a fetus,” others: “made”). We think that this entire diversity arose from the fact that the phrase “before the expected” was not understood to refer, as Philo’s ὡς ἂν ἀχρόνως indicates, neither to “understanding” nor to “birth,” but to the time that must be supplied, as in Virgil, *Georgics* IV:

“Before the expected time, the camp stands in ordered array.”

Furthermore, because it was not noticed what the words “birth” and “made” governed, they substituted “birth” and “pregnant” in their place. The ellipsis should be supplied in this way: “about to give birth . . . to births, which are works,” and so forth. The same sense results if one reads “a birth and a fetus.” We do not deny that some sense can be extracted while retaining “pregnant,” but our interpretation is both more natural and supported by Philo in the work cited.]

We have also, concerning other Hebrew women, the statement that “the Hebrew women give birth before the midwives come” (Exod. I, 19). This means that the souls of the righteous do not await techniques and disciplines because of the various methods of discovery, nor do they require aids for giving birth; rather, they pour forth their offspring spontaneously and anticipate expectation.

48. Jacob was no less energetic in discovering than in carrying out what he had discovered. When his mother told him to bring food to his father (Gen. XXVII, 9 ff.), we see that he possessed the kinds of definitions necessary for the task.

[Note: To understand this otherwise rather obscure passage, one must observe that Ambrose’s intention is to show that Jacob possesses the whole progress of good discipline. He establishes this as follows: whatever is necessary for good discipline is contained and enclosed, as it were, within two boundaries, which he calls definitions—using Philo’s term, ὅροι—namely, intelligence and diligence. Intelligence is God’s gift, whereas diligence is attributed to our labor. Since holy Isaac therefore discovered in his son Jacob both limits, or definitions, of perfect discipline, it is rightly concluded that Jacob was equipped with the things necessary for good discipline. Almost this entire chapter is taken from Philo’s *On the Fugitive*.]

For he found it quickly, and he testified that God was the author of his discoveries. Thus both the prize of diligence and the abundance of intelligence are signified. The first definition concerns discovery: what is found is sought; what is sought requires time; and what requires time belongs, of course, to diligence. But what anticipates the use of time, God infuses and God gives; and what God gives belongs to nature, not to diligence.

Intelligence, therefore, is a divine gift; and whatever is a divine gift belongs to nature. Intelligence, then, belongs to nature, while discovery belongs to diligence: the former is without time, the latter requires time. Hence the former is present in time, while the latter is investigated over a period of time; the former is above us, while the latter is referred to us.

49. Isaac was seeking food from his son—the food of the Word, for “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.” Peter was hungry for such food when he saw the mysteries of the gentile people who were about to believe (Acts X, 11 ff.). Esau did not have food of spiritual and swift intelligence ready for his father. While Esau was hunting and searching and preparing to offer a harsh and rustic speech, Jacob anticipated him through his swift and gentle discovery, supplying a pleasant and almost homely answer with which to soothe and delight his father.

Therefore his father, astonished, said: “What is this, my son, that you have found so quickly?” Jacob answered: “The Lord your God brought it into my hands” (Gen. XXVII, 20). The first definition lies in the question, the second in the answer. Finding everything complete that belonged either to intelligence or to diligence, the father brought it to completion by the fulfillment of the definition, saying: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (ibid., 27).

A field possesses both the natural capacity of fertility and the temporal diligence of cultivation. It therefore rightly contains fullness, since neither of the two is lacking in it. At the same time, by adding “which the Lord has blessed,” he appears to have placed the grace of nature before the labor of cultivation. Esau confirmed this, saying: “Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me these two times, and he has taken away my birthright” (ibid., 36).

50. But perhaps you will say: What delay was there in the one who had been sent by his father to hunt? Consider, however, that the father had declared that Esau could not have ready what was being requested spiritually; and therefore, because intelligence was lacking, he demanded that diligence supply its aid. He also urges speed when he says: “Take your bow and arrows” (ibid., 3). Yet Esau did receive the fruit of diligence, since he recognized that the matter mentioned earlier was a gift of intelligence.

51. It was not without reason that Jacob brought household food, since from the household of his own seed he had acquired for himself the bond of wisdom. Good is diligence together with wisdom, and discovery together with natural intelligence.

Holy Isaac, therefore, having the bond of wisdom ready at hand, was walking in the field—or rather, he was being separated from it. Let us too first be joined to wisdom, and then go out into the field, desiring to seek and discover. For many seek badly without wisdom.

Thus Cain, because he had not received prudence from God, sought badly and went badly out into the field; Abel went well, because he completed the perfect offering of sacrifice. The sacrifice of wisdom is good, faith is a good offering, and so is every virtue.

Wisdom, accordingly, slaughtered her victims and mixed her wine in the bowl. And so, to give the drink of faith to the foolish gentiles, she summoned them to her bowl, saying: “Whoever is foolish, let him turn in to me” (Prov. IX, 4). And to those lacking sense she said: “Come, eat of my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (ibid., 5).

Plato thought that this bowl should be transferred into his books, and he summoned souls to its drink; but he did not know how to satisfy them, since he served a drink not of faith but of unbelief.

## CHAPTER IX

He urges us to flee from here, as Jacob fled from his homeland and as deer flee to the springs. Whoever longs for these springs must pour out his soul over himself, following the example of Susanna. How Paul and Lot fled; and how we too must flee to the heavenly city until the High Priest dies, with whom our old self must also die.

52. Let us therefore flee from here, as holy Jacob fled from his homeland. He knew that the true homeland was above. Let us flee as deer flee to springs of water. David thirsted for them; let our soul thirst as well. What is that spring? Hear him who says: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. XXXV, 10). To this fountain let the soul say: “When shall I come and appear before your face?” (Ps. XLI, 3).

For God is the fountain. But whoever longs for this fountain should pour out his soul over himself, leaving nothing to the suffering of the flesh, but allowing the soul to overflow everywhere.

[Note: This is the reading of the Roman edition and one Vatican manuscript. Another, together with two Gallic manuscripts, reads: “leaving nothing of possession to the flesh,” which is not displeasing. The remaining manuscripts and the older editions read: “leaving nothing to the passion of the flesh.”]

53. Susanna beautifully poured out her soul, so that the fires of the body, the fears of death, and the desires of life could not evaporate into it. Once her soul had been poured out over her, she extinguished every carnal desire and worldly ambition. She was able even to extinguish the flames of the monstrous old men and shameless presbyters, unless a flood of lust had overflowed within them.

When they brought an accusation against her, threatening her with slander if she refused to consent to adultery, Susanna groaned and said: “I am beset by anguish on every side. For if I do this, I shall perish in eternal death; but if I do not, I shall not escape your hands” (Dan. XIII, 22). Yet she judged it better to flee the crime than the danger.

Thus she wept when the crime was charged against her; she wept when they claimed for themselves the right to judge her, a chaste and virtuous woman, as an adulteress. She did not lament death, but the calumny against her chastity. She wept over the injury done to religion, and poured out over herself not her body but her soul. She would have poured out her body had she consented to carnal demands.

When she was condemned to death, she cried out as though she were the judge of the guilty and the arbiter of her accusers. By the authority of an innocent conscience she summoned divine knowledge to judge her—not driven by fear of death, but struck by the supreme power of the condemning judgment.

[Note: Some editions, both old and recent, read “could not.” This is incorrect. The expression is conditional, as the following words show: “unless in them,” and so forth. “Could” has the force of “could have,” a construction not uncommon in approved authors.]

Thus Susanna fled the world and entrusted herself to God, fleeing to that citadel of the eternal city which embraces the whole world, since all things are within God.

[Note: This is the reading of all editions and a few manuscripts. One Colbert manuscript reads: “since the whole age is within God.” Another, together with Torn., reads: “. . . all things flee”; Valc. and Theod. have “flee”; Thuan., Prat., Big., Ebrulph., and Alnet. read “. . . everything takes refuge”; and Fisc. has “. . . embraces everything while it flees.”]

54. Paul also fled, being lowered through a window in a basket so that he might escape. For he knew that a threefold cord could not be broken. But he fled so that he might preach the Lord’s Gospel throughout the whole world, and for this reason he was caught up into paradise.

Let us too flee through the window, listening to the Lord’s commandments and keeping them with sober sight and chaste eyes.

[Col. 0594C] 56. Let us flee like Lot, fearing the crimes of Sodom more than its punishments. For he is certainly more pious who flees the contagion of crimes: he shut his house against the Sodomites; though living among them, he did not know those whose abominations he did not know and whose disgrace he detested; and when fleeing, he did not look back at those whose manner of life he did not desire.

Thus he flees like Lot who renounces vices, rejects the customs of the inhabitants, does not look behind him, and enters that higher city through the entrance of his thoughts. He does not depart from it until the High Priest dies, the one who took away the sin of the world. He died once for all, but he dies for each person who is baptized into Christ’s death, so that we may be buried with him, rise with him, and walk in the newness of his life.

[Col. 0594D] 56. You flee well if your heart does not imitate the counsels and thoughts of sinners. You flee well if your eye avoids cups and bowls, lest it become lustful while lingering over wine. You flee well if your eye turns away from another woman, so that your tongue may preserve the truth. You flee well if you do not answer a fool according to his folly. You flee well if you remove the step of your feet from the mouth of the foolish. For one quickly goes astray under evil guides; but if you wish to flee well, keep your ways far from their words.

[Note: All editions read: “if your eye turns away from what belongs to another, as does your tongue”; the Roman edition has “and your tongue.” The Gallic manuscripts, almost unanimously, read: “if your eye turns away from another woman,” and so forth. Either reading can have its own meaning: the admonition may be to turn the eye either away from another’s wealth or from another’s wife. Ambrose often simply calls the latter “another,” imitating the usage of Scripture, where one reads, in Prov. V, 20: “Do not be too intimate with another woman” (Μὴ πολὺς ἴσθι πρὸς ἀλλοτρίαν). The holy bishop frequently alludes to that passage.]

57. The High Priest has died for you; he was crucified for you, so that you might cling to his nails. In that flesh he took you and your sins upon himself. The written charges of your offenses were affixed to his cross, so that you might now owe nothing to the world, to which you once renounced yourself.

And rightly you owe nothing to it, since you can say: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14). Thus you no longer fear death if you bear Christ, in whom you can say: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. XV, 55).

For when our old self was affixed to the cross, sin was destroyed, the sting was blunted, and guilt was emptied of its power, so that we might cease any longer to serve wickedness. The old self has passed away. Now it is no longer the old self in us, but a new creation, bearing within itself the likeness of Christ. Buried with him in the likeness of his death, we have assumed the image of his life and received the wings of spiritual grace.

58. Fly, then, in such a way that it may be said of you: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves with their young?” (Isa. LX, 8). Let your clouds rain justice, and let your doves give birth to simplicity.

Sail as though crossing the world, not wandering through it, like the ships of Tarshish, so that you may direct your course toward intelligible harbors and carry the riches of the sea.

Hasten in such a way that it may be said of you: “They have been made lighter than eagles” (Lam. IV, 19). You see that we must flee from the coming wrath. Those will be able to avoid it who, through repentance, have placed hope of escape within themselves and have drawn in faith in future reconciliation, through our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom is from ages past, and now, and forever, and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

# [ON JACOB]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE BOOKS ON JACOB AND THE BLESSED LIFE

From the very title of these books one can indeed learn that Ambrose treats of the history of the patriarch Jacob and of matters pertaining to the blessed life. Yet these are not the only subjects he treats, and he handles even these in a distinctive manner, which it will not be inappropriate to explain here (*Book II*, chapter 1, section 1).

Before approaching that subject, he thought it necessary to impart to the newly baptized the precepts of the virtues and to disclose by what path and with what aids they might acquire a perfection suited to the condition of life which they had publicly professed in baptism.

Accordingly, in the very first words of the first book he teaches that, in order to derive some benefit from the instructions they were receiving, they must apply a teachable mind, one that would correct the tumult of evil impulses through the treatment provided by right reason. For although virtue, however great its power, cannot uproot all those impulses, desires can nevertheless be cut away by self-restraint, which God commanded the first parent, and later commanded to be observed in the Law.

From this he concludes that all our falls must be attributed to that will which could obey the commands of the Law and the Gospel, not to the flesh, whose members that will used at its pleasure either for righteousness or for iniquity. If the devil purchases for himself a voluntary servant (*Book I*, chapter 3, section 10), Christ chooses only a voluntary soldier; and each person becomes by his own choice the servant of the one whom he had adopted as his lord.

From these considerations he splendidly sets before our eyes how much glory and benefit comes from the service of Christ. We are never anything other than his freedpersons, since he redeemed us at the immense price of his death and, in redeeming us, bestowed gifts greater than which no one could wish for anything else.

He further maintains that the ancient Law must be counted among the divine benefits, since grace was added to it and accomplished what the Law itself could not accomplish, so that we might always flee for help to that all-powerful Savior without whom it is impossible to attain the perfection of holiness.

Finally, he urges us never to allow that supreme benefit to slip from our memory: through it, our sins were forgiven in baptism, when we died and were made alive together with Christ, so that we might be joined to the life of grace in him and live. Hence he concludes that we ought not to be separated from him by either adversity or any hardship, since the whole happiness of this life is placed in these very things.

After the holy Doctor had devoted six chapters of the first book to such instructions, in the seventh, as also in the eighth, he demonstrates by general arguments that no calamity and no misery interrupts the happiness of life. For, he says, “we are tested in these things; in these things the blessed life consists, even if it is flooded with many dangers” (*ibid.*, chapter 7, section 27).

He denies, however, that this is found in anyone except the wise, just, and perfect person, who is neither diminished by losses nor broken by adversity (*ibid.*, section 31), since he places his blessedness in possession of the one supreme good, namely God himself.

Nevertheless, he does not demand from that perfect person, in losses—for example, in illnesses, the death of relatives, or captivity—the Stoic condition of apathy, but rather an evenness of mind, which he testifies that the perfect person himself teaches to others.

Having established these matters generally in the first book, he proves them in the second by the examples of illustrious men who flourished under the ancient covenant. Above all, he proposes the life of the patriarch Jacob, whose principal actions make clear how great a happiness he possessed even amid the greatest calamities.

Since he continually intersperses his discourse with explanations especially suited to shaping moral conduct, he sometimes also digresses from the subject in order to range through its mystical meaning. Finally, he does not hesitate to discuss at considerable length Jacob’s parents’ love for him, so that all parents may learn from it how they are bound to display equal love and justice toward their children.

He does touch upon a few other deeds of the same patriarch, such as those that occurred when the patriarchs were being blessed, but only very briefly—doubtless with the intention of treating those matters more fully and extensively in a work of their own.

After this, by introducing in passing examples from Joseph and certain others, he turns his style toward the priest Eleazar, the seven Maccabean brothers, and their mother. In the final three chapters of the book his entire eloquence is carried along in a powerful stream, as he demonstrates that the happiness in which those most noble martyrs, nourished under the Law and crowned through grace (*Book II*, chapter 11), rejoiced even amid the most savage punishments, was supreme.

Since he lingers so long over the example of Jacob—discussing him through almost nine chapters of the second book in order to establish that life is blessed even amid the greatest miseries—there can be no doubt that the work received the title *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*. Nor is there another reason why he writes elsewhere that he had proposed in Jacob a singular endurance of mind and hardships (*On the Patriarch Joseph*, chapter 1, section 1).

But when, in the final three chapters, he also celebrated the famous contest of the illustrious Maccabees, we think this explains why the great Cassiodorus said:

“For holy Ambrose too, when he himself speaks about the person of Joseph, mentions the Second Book of Maccabees by way of example, the greater part of which he opened up, through the sweetest flow of his eloquence, in order to demonstrate endurance” (*On the Institution of Divine Literature*, chapter 6).

The reason why this author designated these treatises by the name “Books on the Patriarchs” has now been explained. Yet someone might question whether, in the testimony just quoted, “Jacob” ought not better to have been substituted for “Joseph.” Certainly this may reasonably be inferred both because Jacob supplies Ambrose with the subject of his discourse and because it is not obscure that some corruption has entered this passage.

For where “Joseph” is now read, “Esdras” was formerly read. Nevertheless, since the holy bishop discusses those Maccabees after mentioning Joseph, whom he teaches to have found his happiness even in prison, the text of this Senator can be defended. That Ambrosian eloquence which he observed to suffuse this passage so sweetly also shines forth with no little brilliance elsewhere throughout the work.

It is beyond dispute that these books were composed from sermons which he had delivered to his people. In addition to the rhetorical modes of expression observable there, Ambrose himself explicitly indicates that he is speaking after the Gospel had been read in which it is said: “Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.” “As I heard it read,” he says, “you heard it today” (*Book II*, chapter 5, section 23).

It would be difficult to determine from how many sermons those treatises were composed. At least this may be affirmed: they were delivered to the congregation of the newly baptized during the Paschal celebrations of approximately the year 387, when he pronounced the preceding books, as can be confirmed more clearly from the book *On the Patriarch Joseph*.

Philo has a work under the title *That Every Good Person Is Free*, whose subject has considerable affinity with these labors of Ambrose. The holy Doctor borrowed nothing from it, however, except when he speaks of Esau. In that passage he seems deliberately to have compressed everything best and most excellent in Philo’s book into the narrow confines of half a page.

# Two Books of Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, On Jacob and the Blessed Life  
[Note: [Col. 0597A] Written around A.D. 387.] (C)

[Col. 0597]

## BOOK ONE

### 443. CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0597A]

A prudent discourse is necessary for the discipline of the virtues and the restraint of the passions, as is a mind attentive to reason; and although reason cannot altogether eradicate desire, it can nevertheless moderate even the gravest impulses.

1. A good discourse, full of prudence, is necessary for the discipline of everyone; and a mind attentive to reason [Col. 0598A] advances toward the virtues and restrains the passions. Virtue is teachable. Indeed, it is acquired through application and learning, and lost through neglect. Otherwise, if a good discourse were not necessary for correction, the Law would never say: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:14). But because bare speech is useful for admonition yet weak for persuasion, a consideration of right reason must therefore be added, so that what good discourse has prescribed, reason, examined more fully, may persuade.

For we are not compelled to obey by servile necessity, but by the decision of our own will, whether we incline toward virtue or turn toward sin. And therefore either our free inclination draws us into error, or our will, following reason, recalls us. [Note: [Col. 0599D] The Roman edition reads, “following reason: but the gravest cause of sin is desire, which nevertheless …” Four manuscripts have “reason.” But desire is the gravest passion of sin—Longinus has “conscience”—which nevertheless may be softened, though it cannot be uprooted, and so forth. The remaining manuscripts and editions have the reading printed in the text.]

The gravest passion leading to sin, however, is desire, which reason softens and restrains. It can soften it, but it cannot eradicate it; for the mind, which is capable of reason, is not master of its own passions but their restrainer. Nor can it happen that a person who is naturally prone to anger never becomes angry; but reason can make him control himself, restrain his indignation, and keep him from inflicting punishment, just as the Prophet teaches us when he says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). He granted what belongs to nature; he denied what belongs to sin.

[Col. 0599B] 2. [Note: [Col. 0599D] The Roman edition reads: “All temperance, therefore, derives from those things that are denied; and therefore it must be pursued. For it is either taken from natural things or from moral things; that is, it either moderates natural things or moral things.” But these words are conjectures, not Ambrose’s. We have therefore preferred not to depart from the ancient edition, since the manuscripts support it. Even among them there is some variation. Some omit the word “temperance”; others change it to “anger”; one has “sin.” Likewise, some have *secanda* where others have *secunda*. Perhaps one may reasonably suspect that, after the adjective *omnis*, a substantive noun was omitted in the older manuscripts through the scribes’ carelessness, and was later restored in various ways by different copyists. Those who restored the word “temperance” guessed more successfully, since the continuation and sequence of the discourse demanded it, as is clear from the following chapter.]

Temperance, therefore, derives its origin from other things, not from itself, and is consequently secondary. For it is either adopted from natural things or from useful things. Thus it either moderates what is natural or acts as the defender of what is useful. In the end, it does not remove desire from us, but makes us not serve desire.

Who is so powerful as to be able to take away bodily impulse, except the One who alone could say of the barren fig tree—that is, of the wickedness of the Jews—[Note: [Col. 0600D] The Roman edition has *secaverat*—“he had cut it down”—that is, the wickedness of the Jews.]

“Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and have found none. Cut it down, therefore.” The servant answered him: “Leave it this year also, until I dig around it and put a basket of manure on it; and if indeed it bears fruit—otherwise, in the future you shall cut it down” (Luke 13:7ff.). He rightly referred the matter to the Lord, because he could not claim for himself the power to cut away a temporary lapse, [Note: [Col. 0600D] Several manuscripts read “a bodily fall.”] but reserved it for the Lord.

3. Finally, whom among human beings shall we choose as better and stronger than holy David? He could not remove the desire with which he had desired water from the well at Bethlehem, which was surrounded by the enemy army, but he could moderate it. For although we do not find that water was lacking to the others—that is, to so large an army—while water from other springs could certainly have been lacking much less to the king, he suffered an irrational desire and longed for the water that was enclosed by the enemy’s surrounding forces, from where it could not easily have been brought without the greatest danger.

Therefore he said: “Who will give me a drink from the well that is in Bethlehem beside the gate?” (2 Sam. 23:15). And when three men had been found who broke through the enemy camp and brought the water he had desired with the greatest longing, he realized that the water had cost him through another’s danger and poured it out to the Lord (ibid.), lest he seem to drink the blood of those who had brought it.

This event shows that desire indeed precedes reason, but that reason resists desire. David therefore experienced what is human by desiring irrationally; but what is praiseworthy is that he defeated an irrational desire through a rational remedy prepared in advance. I praise the men who were ashamed of their king’s desire and preferred to bring its fulfillment through danger to their own lives; but I praise even more the man who was ashamed that another should be endangered by his own desire and who compared water obtained at the price of doubtful fortune to blood. Thus, as a victor over his restrained desire, he poured the water out to the Lord [Col. 0600B], to show that he extinguished his desire through the consolation of the word.

4. A sober mind can therefore restrain and suppress the impulses of even grave passions, cool every heat of burning desire, redirect its movements elsewhere, and reject the passions through the examination of right reason.

For when God established the human being and planted in him habits and senses, he then placed over his impulses the royal authority of the mind, so that all the human being’s senses and movements might be governed by its strength and power. He added to the grace of creation that he might shape the mind itself by divine commands and instruct it in the disciplines of wisdom, through which it might foresee what must be avoided and recognize what must be chosen. [Note: [Col. 0600D] All the manuscripts have this reading. The edition, however, has “and what must be avoided … and what must be read,” except for certain Paris manuscripts, where *canenda*—“what must be sung”—is read instead of *cavenda*, so that “things to be sung” might be set against “things to be read.” This is absurd, unless it is a printer’s error. Likewise, in the following line, where the edition retains “holding the discipline … instructed in the Law,” we have restored from the manuscripts “holding the discipline … is instructed in the Law.”]

The mind, therefore, holding the discipline of wisdom through right reason, so that it may know divine and human things, is instructed in the Law, through which it learns which passions it must subject to itself.

## CHAPTER II

Temperance moderates the passions both of the mind and of the body. Its effects are demonstrated by examples from the patriarchs; then, after the dignity of reason has been commended, the Saint shows that this same temperance is fortified by divine command.

5. The natural pleasures and pains are, as it were, the leaders of the passions, and the others follow them. For they embrace all the passions, both of which are passions not only of the body but also of the soul. And because we have said that other passions lie beneath these, desire precedes pleasure, while gratification follows pleasure; fear precedes pain, while sadness follows pain. Agitation of the soul is a common passion of both pleasure and pain.

I shall pass over the others—that is, pride, greed, ambition, rivalry, [Col. 0601A] envy—which are passions of the soul. I shall also pass over the insatiable lust for devouring and the outpouring of luxury and wantonness, vices that are joined to the body and operate according to it.

Temperance rightly extinguishes above all the ardor of these passions. First, through sobriety and moderation it tempers the soul and shapes the mind; then, through abstinence from pleasures, it also tightens the reins of bodily ferocity. For this reason the Law restricted license in food (Lev. 11:4ff.) and abundance at banquets, not only to cut away luxury, but also so that, through contemplation of the restraining command, it might open a path for the exercise of reason, which would cut away the provocations of the appetite and other desires [Note: [Col. 0601D] The Vatican, Victorine, Colbertine, Vallicellian, and Theodorian manuscripts in their first hand read: “bodily desires of passion.” The second hand of the Theodorian manuscript and the Remigian manuscript read: “desires of the body, passions,” and so forth.] and restrain bodily passions and impulses. Temperance is therefore the preliminary work of correction and the teacher of discipline.

6. Proceeding from this, holy Jacob received from his brother the birthright, which he did not possess (Gen. 25:33); and, having gained precedence with his consent, he taught that, in the judgment of their own conscience, the intemperate are worthless to themselves. Proceeding from this, Joseph both subdued the heat of youth and strengthened his mind, when it was tested by adulterous allurements, through the guidance of right reason.

Although he was strong and vigorous, he nevertheless preferred to support himself by reasoning, saying to his master’s wife: “Since my master does not know anything in his house except me, and he has placed everything he possesses in my hands, nor has anything been withheld from me except you, because you are his wife, how then can I do this evil thing and sin before God?” (Gen. 39:8–9).

This, then, is the exercise of right reason, which the Greeks call *λογισμός* (*logismos*, rational deliberation), through which the mind, intent upon wisdom, is strengthened. The reasoning is excellent: he ought not to be ungrateful for his master’s benefits, nor could the sin he would commit be hidden from God, whom nothing could escape.

7. Good, therefore, is the reason that often strips away a hostile disposition and removes the pain of injury. It often moderates even the victor in battle, restrains the sword poised to strike, and rescues the person pleading from death, because right reason persuades us to spare those who are subject to us.

For, in excluding or moderating the pain of injury, who is a better teacher than the patriarch Jacob? Rebuking his own sons Simeon and Levi, he said: “You have made me hateful, so that I seem savage” (Gen. 34:30). They had indeed avenged the injury done to their sister, whose modesty had been violated in defiance of the customs of their fathers; and Jacob, teacher of discipline and guardian of modesty, could not approve the committed outrage. But he preferred that the insolent be restrained by reason, knowing that reason could moderate indignation.

8. Temperance, therefore, is what cuts away desires. God commanded the first human beings to hold fast to it, saying: “But from the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise you shall not eat, nor shall you touch it, lest you die” (Gen. 2:17). And because it was not maintained, the transgressors of this outstanding virtue were made exiles from paradise and deprived of immortality. The Law teaches it and pours it into the affections of all (Exod. 20:4, and elsewhere).

### 447. CHAPTER III

The Lord teaches temperance, wisdom, and discipline; an exhortation to pursue them follows. Our guilt must be attributed solely to our own will, by which we serve either sin or righteousness; and finally, which of the two forms of servitude appears preferable to the other? [Col. 0602B]

9. [Note: [Col. 0601D] The old edition reads, “But both temperance and wisdom are taught”; the Bigotian and Tornesian manuscripts, “But it teaches both temperance and wisdom”; finally, the Roman edition reads, “But the Lord teaches both temperance and wisdom,” with which other manuscripts agree, except that they read, “it, and wisdom.” This is excellent, for the word “it” refers to temperance.]

Scripture testifies that the Lord teaches temperance, wisdom, and discipline. It speaks of temperance in the Law (Exod. 20:4, and elsewhere), and of the others in the Book of Job, where it is written: “Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and discipline?” (Job 33:16). And in the Gospel the Lord himself says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). Elsewhere he says to the disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

Why, then, were they called disciples? Or what else were they learning from Christ except to practice the commands of the virtues? Finally, David says: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 34:11). The fear of God is certainly one of the virtues, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,” through which the form of pious instruction is acquired. Of this Paul says: “But thanks be to God that, although you were slaves of sin, you obeyed from the heart the form of teaching to which you were handed over; and, having been freed from sin, you became slaves of righteousness” (Rom. 6:17–18).

Instruction, therefore, makes it possible for us to attain righteousness. Righteousness can therefore be acquired by learning. Let us apply ourselves diligently to the form of evangelical teaching. A small amount of effort is often regarded as a great deal. For everything depends upon diligence, through which obedience is supplied; and, in whichever direction it inclines, it either adds guilt or grace. This obedience drew us to death in the first Adam; it called us to life in the second Adam.

10. We must attribute our misery to nothing except our own will. No one is held guilty unless he has turned aside of his own will. Those things imposed upon unwilling people do not constitute a crime. [Note: [Col. 0602D] The editions of Erasmus and those following him read, “things imposed upon those who resist.”] Only voluntary acts are followed by the reproach of wrongdoing, which we otherwise transfer to others.

Christ chose a voluntary soldier for himself; the devil purchases a voluntary servant for himself at auction. He possesses no one bound under the yoke of servitude [Col. 0603A] unless that person has first sold himself to him for the price of sins. [Note: [Col. 0603D] This is the reading of the editions and manuscripts except the Remigian manuscript, which has: “unless the sinner has first truly sold himself to him”; and the Bigotian manuscript, where the reading is “has truly sold himself in the bonds of sins,” with a gloss, “by right.”]

Why do we accuse the flesh as though it were weak? Our members are weapons of iniquity and weapons of righteousness. You saw a poor man receiving an injury and protected him: your members are weapons of mercy, by which you rescued the poor man from injury. You saw a needy person and gave him gifts: your right hand drove death away from your breast. You saw someone being led to death and rescued him, because it is written: “Rescue the one being led to death” (Prov. 24:11): your members are weapons of righteousness, if you did not allow a person to perish unjustly.

You saw a woman, disciplined your body, put your lusts to death, turned away from the shameless eyes of the prostitute, and left her: your members are weapons of chastity. But if your eye looked upon a woman in order to desire her, you opened a wound and drove a dart into your body; [Col. 0603B] your members are weapons of sin. You saw the property of orphans and expelled them from their paternal homes; you moved the boundaries that your fathers had established: your members are weapons of iniquity.

The affection, therefore, not the flesh, is the author of guilt; the flesh is the minister of the will. Let our will, therefore, not sell us.

11. The Apostle cries out: “Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, whether of sin leading to death or of obedience leading to righteousness?” (Rom. 6:16). Therefore, if we serve either sin or righteousness, let us consider under which form of servitude the condition is more tolerable and the fruit more abundant.

But what fruit can there be in death? “The wages of sin is death”; and therefore there is no fruit in it, but only the loss of shame, since we are ashamed of the things we have done. Serving righteousness, however, is freedom. “For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman. Likewise, the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave” (1 Cor. 7:22).

Both conditions are excellent: to be under Christ, under whom servitude is precious and freedom glorious. Servitude is precious because it was purchased at the price of such great blood; freedom is glorious because no servitude to guilt, no bonds of sins, no burdens of crimes, and no transactions of wickedness bind it to a degraded condition of servitude.

12. Learn humility, O man; recognize the force of apostolic teaching. If you call yourself a slave, you are a freedman; if you boast that you are free, you are a slave. For the one who has been redeemed as a slave, as it were, possesses freedom; and the one who has been called as free, as it were, does well to recognize that he is Christ’s slave. Under him servitude is safe and freedom secure.

Who would assert that Paul was an ignorant man, even in the matter of law? He knew how to distinguish between a freedman and a free person, and therefore he said not casually but precisely: “For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman; likewise, the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave.” In truth, we are all Christ’s freedmen; no one is free. For all were born in servitude.

Why do you impose the arrogance of freedom upon a servile condition? Why do you usurp titles of nobility, you who possess a servile inheritance? Do you not know that the sin of Adam and Eve made you a slave? Do you not know that Christ redeemed you, rather than purchased you? “You were redeemed from your futile way of life inherited from your fathers, not with gold or silver, but with the precious blood of the Lamb” (1 Pet. 1:18–19), the Apostle Peter cries out.

Therefore, you have been redeemed by the Lord. You are a slave because you were created; you are a slave because you were redeemed; and you owe servitude both as to the Lord and as to the Redeemer. Do not think that the condition of a freedman under Christ is inferior to freedom. In dignity it is equal; for protection it is superior; in grace it is equal; against falling it is more cautious; against pride it is more secure.

You have received freedom in such a way that you must remember your manumitter, [Note: [Col. 0603D] A person who had been granted freedom did not thereby become so entirely his own master that he no longer owed reverence and obedience to his patron. If he was ever found to be ungrateful toward his patron, he was either reduced to a lower degree of freedom or even recalled altogether into slavery. He was subject to this punishment, among other reasons, for having undertaken military service. See volume I of the *Theodosian Code*, book II, title 22, “On Claims to Inheritances,” and the commentary of Gothofredus there; likewise book IV, title 11, “On Freedmen and Their Children,” together with Gothofredus’s commentary on it, where this passage of Ambrose is cited.] and must know that lawful obedience is owed to your patron, lest freedom be recalled from an ungrateful person. What could be more blessed for you, who reign under the Lord and serve as a soldier under your patron?

### 449. CHAPTER IV

How much God granted to the human being when he gave him the Law and added grace. Two questions are resolved here: How can the Law be good if it produces death? And how can that which produces death not be death for us?

13. What is there that the Lord has not granted you? [Col. 0604C] He gave the Law, [Note: [Col. 0604D] The Roman edition restored from the Vatican manuscript “he exposed sin,” which is absent from the old edition and the other manuscripts. In its place, the Vallicellian, Longinian, and Theodorian manuscripts have “he destroyed sin”; the Tornesian has “he gave sin.”] exposed sin, and added grace.

For the Law denounced sin, but in our unstable condition it could not restrain it completely. I came to know the sin I had not known. I came to know that desire is sin; and through this occasion of knowledge, the debt of sin accumulated, because the sin that previously seemed dead through my ignorance came alive again in me. But I died from the wound of sin, because knowledge of guilt, which seemed likely to benefit me, harmed me by making me know what I could not avoid.

The Law exposed sin, and through the goodness of its denunciation intensified the hostility of sin itself. Thus sin became exceedingly great for me, because it was multiplied by the denunciation of the commandment. Guilt increases when it is exposed but not avoided.

How, then, is the commandment good if it is death for me? Or how is that not death for me which, by the goodness of its revelation, displayed sin and brought death upon me? For it is certain that death came to me when I recognized that what I was doing was sin, just as the Lord himself says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John 15:22). [Note: [Col. 0605] The Roman edition reads, “and had not spoken.”]

14. Why are you surprised, then, if the Law is death to some, when even the saving coming of the Lord, through which we were redeemed, is death to some? For the unbeliever seeks death for himself through grace, while the grace of the commandment remains.

Just as knowledge of poisonous drinks is completed for the discipline of medicine, so the divine commandment is directed toward eternal life. But just as, for someone who uses harmful potions wrongly, knowledge of them turns into harm and danger—and the more he knows about poisons, the more he understands that he is in danger—so the form of the commandment is the cause of death for those who interpret the Law wrongly or cannot avoid the sins that have been revealed and forbidden.

Therefore, just as an antidote is good even if it is not good for the imprudent or intemperate person, so the commandment is good even if it is not good for the intemperate person. Thus the commandment is good, although it is death to someone. Accept, then, the answer to the first proposition: a commandment can be good and yet be death to me—good by the nature of its saving precept, death through the intemperance of the flesh.

15. Since we have said that the commandment can be good and yet be death to me, let us now examine how that which, through its goodness, nevertheless brought death upon me is not death for me. For the Apostle stated the matter in this way: “Therefore, did what is good become death for me? Certainly not. But sin, in order that it might appear as sin, through what is good brought death upon me” (Rom. 7:13). Let us therefore consider each point.

The commandment is certainly that of the Law. But the Law is spiritual. I see its grace, praise its beauty, proclaim its form, and marvel at its commandment. But because I am carnal, sold under sin, I am dragged unwillingly into guilt. For guilt dominates me as though I were its slave. Thus I hate the crime, yet commit it.
