The mind hates it; the flesh desires it. Yet I am present in both: in mind I consent to the Law, but in the flesh I do what I do not want.

The commandment to which I consent is therefore good, and the mind that chooses what is good is good. It is good for judging, but often weak for resisting, because bodily desire opposes it and drags it captive toward the allurements of error.

16. In this danger there is one remedy: that the grace of God set free the one whom the Law could not set free. For it is written: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid. 7:24–25).

Thus, although the sin that lay hidden—that is, my desire, which I did not think was sin—brought death upon me when it was exposed, and sin itself became exceedingly great (for it was sin even though it was unknown; but through knowledge it was heaped up and assumed, as it were, an increase of error, and the form of the commandment passed over into the nature of transgression), it is nevertheless not death for me, since I can readily flee to Christ, through whom we are released from every danger of death.

The second proposition, therefore, is also resolved: the commandment of the Law is not death for me, even though it produces death. The fact that we are troubled belongs to weakness; the fact that we escape belongs to Christ.

## CHAPTER V

Why the Law was insufficient, but grace, bestowed through the death of Christ, was necessary; and why we too must die, rise, and live with him.

17. To return, then, to the beginning of this discourse: the mind that possesses the exercise of reason and applies itself to the disciplines of wisdom is good. But it wages a difficult struggle with the body of death, and the allurements of the flesh often conquer the mind’s reason.

Therefore the Lord first gave the Law, to which the human mind submitted itself in obedience and began to serve, so that it might be subject to it. But the flesh was not subject, because the wisdom of the flesh is not subject to the Law and resisted its commands. It could not obey virtue, devoted as it was to desires and entangled in carnal enticements.

We must therefore labor to hold fast to the grace of God. The mind is good if it applies itself to reason, but it is imperfect unless it possesses the governance of Christ. For the Lord Jesus came to nail our passions to his cross and forgive sins. In his death we have been justified, so that the whole world might be cleansed by his blood. Finally, we were baptized into his death.

18. If, therefore, our sins are forgiven in his death, let the passions of our sins also die in his death and remain fastened by the nails of his cross. If we died in his death, why are we again recalled, as though alive, to the things of the world? [Col. 0606C] What have we to do with the elements of this world? What have we to do with desires? What have we to do with luxury and wantonness, with which we died together with Christ?

And if we have died in Christ, we have also risen in Christ. Let us therefore live with Christ; with Christ let us seek the things above, not the corruptible and earthly things. When Christ rose from the dead, he left the old person nailed to the cross and raised up the new. Christ died so that we too might die to sin and rise to God.

Our flesh has died; why does it come alive again to sin? Why does it obey sin again? Why does sin reign again in the dead, when death is the end of sin? We have died in the flesh and have been renewed in the spirit. Let us walk by the Spirit, since we have received the Spirit of Christ. But if the Spirit of Christ is in us, then let our flesh be dead because of sin, while the spirit lives because of righteousness.

19. Thus what was impossible for the Law is resolved if we walk in the Spirit, if we have buried the passions, if we do not loosen the cross of this body, if we do not rewrite the bond of sin that has been erased on Christ’s cross, and if we do not put on again the garment of the old person that we removed.

For it is written in the Song of Songs: “I have removed my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” (Song 5:3). Since, then, the members of our body have been put to death, why do its vices sprout again?

The Law did not prevail because it did not put the flesh to death; it passed away like a shadow because it did not give color; and it also overshadowed us from the sun of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0607D] This is the reading of the old edition and all the manuscripts. The Roman edition instead reads: “because it accumulated crimes but did not erase them.”] because it accumulated crimes. Therefore, it also harmed us.

## CHAPTER VI

The fruits of the promulgated Law are confession of sin, humility, indeed grace itself, and the pledge of love. These are followed by an exhortation to gratitude, together with an enumeration of the benefits granted to humanity.

20. [Note: [Col. 0607D] The editions read, “What benefit, then, did it provide?”] What need was there for the Law to be promulgated if it was not going to benefit us? We already had the law of nature, for each person was a law to himself, possessing the work of the law written in his heart. We did not keep that law. Why was another added, under whose works the flesh could not be justified? A bond was added, not release; recognition of sins was added, not remission.

We all sinned, although we could have pleaded ignorance as an excuse; every mouth was stopped.

21. Yet it benefited me. I began to confess what I denied; I began to recognize my offense and not conceal my injustice; I began to declare my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart.

This too benefits me: we are not justified by works of the Law. I therefore have no basis for boasting in my works; I have no basis for exalting myself. Thus I shall boast in Christ. I shall not boast because I am righteous, but because I have been redeemed. I shall boast not because I am free from sins, but because my sins have been forgiven.

I shall not boast because I have benefited anyone, nor because anyone has benefited me, but because Christ is my advocate before the Father, and because Christ’s blood was poured out for me. My guilt became the price of my redemption, through which Christ came to me. For my sake Christ tasted death. Guilt was more fruitful than innocence. Innocence had made me arrogant; guilt made me subject.

22. You see, then, how the Law benefited you. But you say that through the Law sin abounded. Yet where sin abounded, grace abounded even more. You have died to sin, O man; therefore the Law no longer harms you. You rise again through grace; therefore the Law benefited you, because it brought about grace.

You have also received the pledge of Christ’s love, because the one who died for you is your advocate, and he preserves the reward of his blood. [Note: [Col. 0607D] The old edition reads “he reserves the price”; the Roman edition, “he preserves you.” A great number of manuscripts read “he reserves the reward”; Longinus has “he preserved through the reward.” Again, in the same place, all editions and several manuscripts have “because he knows the innocent one.” But the Tornesian, Theodorian, Remigian, Longinian, Vallicellian, and Bigotian manuscripts more suitably read “who adopted the guilty one”—some have “because he adopted the guilty one.”] And the one who reconciled the sinner to the Father much more strongly commends the innocent and protects the subject, since he adopted the guilty.

23. As a debtor to such a great benefit, will you not return obedience? He made you an heir; he made you a joint heir—an heir of God and a joint heir with Christ. He poured into you the Spirit of adoption.

Count these things, and add them not so much to the burden of your debt as to the preservation of the gift you have received. You are Christ’s joint heir if you suffer with him, if you die with him, if you are buried with Christ. Take up his sufferings, so that you may deserve to be above your sufferings with him.

See how he forgave you your former sins, so that nothing you had done might harm you. See how he exhorts you not to lose what you have received. The goal of this brief labor is near, and the reward is an everlasting crown. The suffering is bearable; the reward immeasurable.

What troubles you? Is it the rejection of low birth? In the future you will possess the glorious nobility of devotion and faith. Is it a modest estate or a narrow means of living? You will possess the riches of eternal recompense, in which you can lack nothing. Is it the loss of children? You will receive as everlasting those whom you had received as temporal, and it will be said of you: “Blessed is the one who has offspring in Zion and household members in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31:9). “The sufferings of this present time,” Scripture says to you, “are not worthy of the future glory” (Rom. 8:18).

24. Add that the blessed life is not diminished by these adversities, whether worldly troubles or bodily sufferings; rather, it is tested more fully. Add that it either does not feel the losses of property or conceals the losses of loved ones with a courageous mind and absorbs the pain.

Add that the one who is always in the harbor of tranquility knows no shipwrecks. What of the fact that your labor is shared with every creature, because on your account the world itself endures the servitude of corruption, and because you share with the saints in this labor and expectation? The sun recognizes its setting, the moon its waning, the lights of the stars their wandering, while the redemption of our entire body is awaited.

25. But you fear the uncertain twists of life and the ambushes of the adversary, although you have God’s help and so great a favor from him that he did not spare his own Son for you (Rom. 8:32).

Scripture used a beautiful expression to declare the loving purpose of God the Father toward you: that he offered his Son to death. [Note: [Col. 0608D] We have restored this reading from the Thuanian, Tornesian, Vallicellian, Bigotian, Remigian, Longinian, and Theodorian manuscripts in their second hand; for the first hand, together with the Victorine, Colbertine, and one Vatican manuscript, reads: “who offered wholly to death that which, in the fullness of divinity, he himself lost nothing of, and redeemed you.” Finally, the other Vatican manuscript and the Roman edition read: “who offered himself wholly to death for you. Of what was in the Father, he kept nothing for himself: he offered everything for you, which he did not lose in the fullness of divinity, and he himself redeemed you.”] Yet the Son could not suffer the bitterness of death. Of what was in the Father, he kept nothing for himself; he offered everything for you; and, in the fullness of divinity, he lost nothing, while he himself redeemed you.

Consider the affection of the Father. In an act of devotion, as though his Son were about to die, he undertook the danger; as though he were about to be bereaved, he drank in the grief, lest the fruit of your redemption perish. Such was the Lord’s concern for your salvation that, in a sense, he nearly endangered what was his own while winning you.

He took upon himself our losses for your sake, so that he might graft you into divine things and consecrate you to heavenly things. He added this marvelous statement: “He handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:32), to show that he loves all in such a way that he handed over for each one his beloved Son.

For those, then, on whose behalf he gave what is above all things, can it be that he did not grant everything in him? For he withheld nothing who granted the author of all things.

26. There is therefore nothing that we need fear can truly be denied to us; there is nothing in which we ought to persist in distrusting the steadfastness of divine generosity, whose abundance was so prolonged and continuous that he first predestined, then called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified. Can he abandon those whom he has pursued with such great benefits all the way to their rewards? Amid so many benefits of God, are some snares of the accuser to be feared? But who would dare accuse those whom the divine judgment has declared elect? Can God the Father himself, who bestowed these gifts, revoke his own gifts and banish from the grace of paternal affection those whom he received by adoption? But there is a fear that the judge may be more severe. Consider what judge you have. Surely the Father gave all judgment to Christ. Can he then condemn you whom he redeemed from death, for whom he offered himself, whose life he knows to be the reward of his own death? Will he not say: “What profit is there in my blood” (Ps. XXIX, 10), if I condemn the one whom I myself saved? Besides, you consider the judge but do not consider the advocate. Can he deliver a harsher sentence, who does not cease to intercede that the grace of reconciliation with the Father may be bestowed upon us?

## CHAPTER VII

That such charity ought to be in us that we may not be separated from Christ by any adversities, since blessed life is not diminished by them; for blessed life is found in those in whom life has been perfected, and in what this perfection consists. Finally, that the perfect man is set above all misfortunes and hardships.

[Col. 0609C]

27. But even if some grave troubles were imminent, they ought by no means to separate us from Christ. Why should we not also endure hard and bitter things for him who endured such unworthy things for us? Therefore there ought to be such charity in us that no dangers may call us back from Christ. For it is written: “Many waters will not be able to extinguish charity, and rivers will not overwhelm it” (Song VIII, 7), because the soul of the one who loves crosses the torrent. No storm, no peril of the deep, no terror of death or punishment diminishes the power of charity. [Col. 0609D] For in these things we are tested; in these things blessed life consists, even if it is flooded by many dangers.

28. For the wise man is not broken by bodily pains, nor harassed by misfortunes; rather, he remains blessed even in hardships.

[Note: [Col. 0609D] What is set forth in these last two chapters concerning the happiness of the wise rests not only upon the doctrines of the Christian religion, but also agrees in the highest degree with the opinions of the philosophers. For they splendidly demonstrate that happiness by no means consists in bodily or external goods—things which the Stoics do not even dignify with the name of goods, but only with that of advantages—and consequently that, whether such things are present or absent, it makes no difference to happiness, which is placed solely in virtue. Quite beautifully indeed, if the teachers themselves had not corrupted their doctrine by the swelling of their spirit and arrogance, and if, by lives discordant even with their own teachings, they had not made themselves objects of ridicule to Aristophanes, Lucian, and others. If anyone wishes to know more fully this agreement of doctrine of which we are speaking, let him read the Second and Third Tusculan Disputations of Cicero, but above all the Fifth, in which he elegantly shows that virtue is sufficient for living happily. The same argument is treated more briefly by him in that Paradox whose heading is: “That virtue is self-sufficient for happiness” (Ὅτι αὐτάρκης ἡ ἀρετὴ πρὸς εὐδαιμονίαν).]

Nor do bodily adversities diminish the privilege of blessed life, nor do they take anything away from its sweetness, because blessedness of life does not consist in bodily pleasure, but in a conscience pure from every stain of sin and in the mind of one who knows that whatever is good is pleasing, even if it is harsh; whereas whatever is dishonorable, even if pleasant, does not delight. Therefore the cause of living well is not bodily pleasure but the prudence of the mind; not the flesh, which is subject to passion, but the mind, which judges that nothing delights better than the integrity of counsels and the beauty of deeds. It is therefore the interpreter of blessed life. For prudence, or reason, which rules passion, is better than passion; and that which judges is superior to that which is subject to judgment. For it cannot be that what is irrational is better than reason. [Col. 0610B] Therefore whoever follows Jesus possesses his reward within himself, and in his own affection he possesses both reward and grace: even if he endures hard things, he is nevertheless blessed in his character, blessed amid the very dangers, just as the Lord declared, saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. V, 10).

29. Blessed life is therefore found in human beings, but specifically in those in whom life has been perfected. Perfect life, however, is not this sensory life, but that rational life which proceeds according to the exercise of reason and the vitality of the mind. In this there is not a portion of the human being, but perfection, which lies not so much in the human condition as in action. For it is this that makes one blessed. What, then, is good for this man, except what he himself possesses? This good is present to him, and it will be for him the cause of future goods. [Col. 0610C] Concerning this good Solomon said: “Drink water from your own vessels and from the springs of your wells. Let your waters overflow for you from your own fountain, and let them run through your streets. Let them be established for you alone, and let no stranger share them with you. Let the fountain of your water be your own” (Prov. V, 17–18). Use, therefore, your inner good.

30. The greatest testimony to this good is that whoever possesses it seeks nothing else. For what would one seek who despises inferior things? Let him cling to what is most excellent, as it is written: “Let the deer of friendship and the young one of graces converse with you” (ibid., 19). Let friendship go before you, and let it be with you at all times. For the friendship of virtues is good, and the charity of the highest good. That perfect man seeks nothing else, therefore, except the one and splendid good. Hence he also says: [Col. 0610D] “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, and behold the delight of the Lord” (Ps. XXVI, 4). Do not despise him as narrow or destitute because he is content with the companionship, as it were, of one solitary good. Surrounded by the friendship of this good, he will be rich in all things. [Col. 0611A] For such a man abounds in blessedness and in possession of the good; and therefore he desires nothing else. For one who possesses everything expects nothing as new. There is no good that he does not possess; nor does he take pleasure in superfluities, but in necessities—and in that very necessity which is necessary not to him but to the flesh joined to him. He grants it what does not diverge from the purpose of the inner man, what makes the two one and reconciles the inner man, according to God, with the outer, so that there may be one spirit in both.

31. A man of this purpose is neither diminished by losses, nor broken by adversities, nor restrained by barriers, nor saddened by the loss of his own people. To instruct him the Apostle says: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not be sorrowful like the rest who have no hope” (I Thess. IV, 12). Comforted by faith in the resurrection and by the grace of future recompense, he does not admit into that mind of his—by which he clings to God and rejoices in the delight of divine excellence—

[Note: [Col. 0611D] All editions and a few manuscripts read “and of the divine presence,” etc. But the more numerous and better manuscripts read “and of the divine excellence,” etc.]

any grief. Whoever is saddened by these things is not saddened according to God. Whatever is not according to God is full of foolishness. The sorrow of this world, therefore, which is not according to God, and every anxiety arising from bodily hardship, are absent from the perfect man. For the condition of the body and a certain external use of nature do not belong to this formation of mind and substance, since the unconquered spirit ought to preserve an unchanging constancy against bodily pleasures and the very fragility of nature, bereavements, losses, and insults. Thus the body itself must be torn away, and the senses stripped of the flesh, if one desires to possess the palm of blessedness, whose fruit does not lie in one part alone but in the fellowship of many, and, if possible, of all the virtues.

32. The perfect man therefore does not know, or feel, the inconveniences of this body or the adversities of the world, when he possesses a spirit alien to the fear that such things may destroy him. For a more perfect life is not defined by being free from these things, but by despising them. If it were defined in such a way that blessed life were one that could be found exempt and free from such accidents, then, when these things occurred, no one could be defined as blessed. These matters have therefore been set aside, and the sole requirement in the estimation of blessed life is that its definition should be located not in other things but [Note: [Col. 0612D] Some manuscripts and all editions read “in the possession of the true good.” Other manuscripts read “in the possession of the true and good,” etc.] in the possession of what is true [Col. 0611D] and good, since whoever possesses that despises the rest and does not seek them.

## CHAPTER VIII

That the wise man may take pleasure in bodily health or in children, yet, if he loses them, does not on that account consider himself less blessed, since he desires nothing besides the highest good. Accordingly, that he does not fear his own captivity or that of his family, bodily illnesses, or other adversities, because these neither take anything away from blessedness nor do prosperous circumstances add anything to it.

33. I now ask whether the wise man takes pleasure in bodily health. We cannot deny that he takes pleasure in it according to nature, and that he more willingly accepts freedom from pain than pain itself—unless, perhaps, it is for Christ, for whom, if the cause demands it, he readily accepts bodily weakness and offers his whole body to death. Nevertheless, even apart from the cause of faith and justice, if health is absent, he is not inwardly distressed nor broken by bodily pain, since he can console himself by the perfection of the virtues.

34. I also ask whether he takes pleasure in children. Who would deny this? For the person sought is not hard and ironhearted, but perfect. Yet even if he loses his children, he is not for that reason less blessed, since he is not for that reason less perfect. For whatever is perfect is blessed. Indeed, if he endures adversities, he is ordinarily considered more perfect than if he abounds in prosperity, although neither the absence nor the presence of external advantages or bodily joys ordinarily takes anything away from virtue or adds anything to it. Yet for many people it has been as much a source of praise to have endured adversities bravely as not to have encountered them. But these things are judged by appearance, not by weight.

35. The profound truth is that the just man desires nothing except that one and splendid good; he directs himself toward it alone and counts it the sole good; he desires no other thing together with it, but always desires that good alone and takes pleasure in it. If something else that delights him is added to it, such as the sweetness of children, the former is not lost, but the latter is added. For the things that accrue do not diminish blessedness, which they cannot increase, because that blessedness remains full and inviolate, in which the soul has clothed and into which it has inserted and poured itself. Perfect virtue remains always amid adversities and pleasures; adversities take nothing from its perfection, nor do pleasures add anything to it. For what loss or advantage from transient things can one who has ascended to the highest feel?

36. Nor, again, will he consider himself wretched—a matter regarded by most people as especially grievous—if he himself or his children fall into captivity. For he will not bear intolerably what nature imposes or what seems good to the Lord. Thus the just man said: “The word that the Lord has spoken is good” (IV Kings XX, 19). And he said: “Let there be peace and faithfulness in my days” (ibid.). This just man, Hezekiah, was certainly not rejoicing that the hardship of captivity had been turned upon his children; but he could not oppose the will of the Lord, [Col. 0612D] and therefore he received his commands with equanimity, like a servant. Moreover, he could judge that even in captivity the merit of virtue might stand out. For Jeremiah was not less blessed in captivity, nor Daniel, nor Ezra, nor the blessed Ananias, Azariah, and Mishael, than they would have been had they not fallen into captivity, since they were led into captivity for the purpose of bringing the people both present consolation in captivity and hope of escaping captivity. It is characteristic of a perfect man

[Note: [Col. 0612D] That is, the perfect man ought to console people who share the same nature in common calamities and rouse them to steadfastness.]

to sustain the community of nature by strength of spirit and to lead it toward better things; not to yield to what seems terrible and fearsome to most people, but, like a strong soldier, to withstand the assaults of the gravest circumstances and enter into their struggles; and, like a prudent helmsman, to steer the ship in a storm and, by confronting the rising waves, avoid shipwreck more by plowing through the waters than by turning aside from them. Such a man is not fearful in persecution, nor softer in tortures, [Note: [Col. 0613D] Thus all editions and the better manuscripts. The Vatican, Victorine, and Colbert manuscripts read “lest he surpass the one who tortures.” Longolian and Theodorian manuscripts read “lest they surpass the torpid one.” Theodoret’s first hand has the former reading; his second hand agrees with the editions.] lest he exasperate the torturer; but, like a strong athlete, he strikes back at the one who beats him, if not with the scourge of blows, certainly with the scourge of words. He despises tortures that many fear, saying: “The arrows of infants have become their wounds” (Ps. LXIII, 8). Though he struggles with the most severe pain, he does not present himself as pitiable; rather, he shows that the virtue of his spirit shines like a lamp even amid harsh storms and the fiercest blasts, and that it cannot be extinguished. He is not soft in the injuries inflicted upon his own people, nor anxious about the tomb of his body, knowing that heaven is owed to it; nor is he more abject in the captivity of the citizen multitude. Rather, like a stern judge, he condemns the faithlessness and errors of the unbelievers, as Daniel did when he exposed the thefts of the priests and refuted their superstitions, showing that they rested upon no truth but were veiled by fraud. Finally, such is the perfect man: he wishes everyone to act well and wishes no evil to befall anyone; yet if something happens contrary to his will, he nevertheless loses nothing of his own blessedness.

37. But perhaps someone may think that sickness and bodily weakness are an impediment to fulfilling the task of perfection, because no works or deeds of the hands can be carried out. Yet the just man will not regard these things as impediments to himself. Rather, he will rebuke one who bewails them pitifully and condemn him as sluggish, because he places more value on the use of the body than on virtue of spirit; because he desires the things to which he is subject, although he possesses what could command others more effectively; because he groans in poverty, though he could rise above the riches of the world—for to the faithful the whole world is wealth; because he laments low birth, although he ought to despise royal powers and command the rich and powerful. For this is the life of the just man: he ought to regard even the resources he possesses as common; indeed, to divide them among the needy, distribute them to the poor, [Note: [Col. 0613D] An ancient edition reads “to cut away his own desires.” The manuscripts of Theodoret, Bignonius, Remigius, and others read “to withdraw from his own pleasures.”] cut away his own pleasures, reduce expenditure, practice the frugality of moderation, maintain sobriety in prosperity, patience in adversity, endurance in pain, greatness of spirit in dangers, be unfamiliar with prayers for perpetual health, not be shaken by the terror of approaching death, and not consider the one to whom, according to nature, children, relatives, health, joy, and abundance have overflowed to be superior to the one who has lacked these things. [Col. 0614A] He ought to weigh his condition not by the external things of the world, but [Note: [Col. 0614D] All editions read “to weigh it by the merit of domestic virtue.” All the manuscripts, however, strongly agree with our reading. Here the domestic goods of virtue are set against the external goods of the world.] by the merits of inward virtue.

38. Who would deny that this too is the character of the just man: that he fears and dreads nothing except losses to virtue; that he restrains the empty fears of others concerning the anxiety of dangers, the fear of death, and bodily weakness; that he teaches that it is better to be released from the body and to be with Christ; that he shows that actions are not hindered by bodily weaknesses but increased by them; and that they are commended not by nobility of birth, the support of relatives, or wealth, but by a good disposition? For Elijah was no less blessed than Moses, although the one, needing food, wearing a cheap goatskin, without children, expense, or companion, and the other, leader of a people, joyful in offspring and girded with power, established equal merit in different conditions, as was declared in the Gospel (Matt. XVII, 3), when they shone with the Lord Jesus in the glory of the resurrection. For he appears to have given them equal reward as equal witnesses of his glory. Nor was Elisha less blessed than David, although one was subject to kings and the other endowed with royal power; they attained a grace of prophetic sanctification that was by no means unequal.

39. For what is lacking to one who possesses that good and always has virtue as his companion and partner? In what condition is he not most powerful? In what poverty is he not rich? In what lowliness of birth is he not distinguished? In what leisure is he not active? In what weakness is he not vigorous? In what illness is he not strong? In what repose of sleep is he not at rest, whom his own virtue does not leave even while he rests? In what solitude is he not surrounded, whom blessed life encircles, whom grace clothes, whom the garment of glory illuminates? He is no less blessed in leisure than when he is active, and no less glorious asleep than awake, because asleep no less than awake he is sound and healthy. When can he appear at leisure whose mind is always active? When can he be alone who always has with him that good of which the Prophet says: “We shall be filled with the good things of your house” (Ps. LXIV, 5)? When can he be cast down whose conversation is in heaven? When can he be without beauty who conforms himself to the likeness of that beauty and of the one good, who, even if he is released from his limbs, nevertheless raises himself in mind? And just as a man accustomed to play the lyre, if he sees it shattered, its strings loosened and broken, and its use interrupted, will cast it aside and no longer seek its music, but soothe himself with his own voice, so this man will allow the idle lyre of his body to lie neglected, will take pleasure in his heart, soothe himself by remembering a good conscience, and lighten himself with divine oracles and prophetic writings, holding and embracing in his mind that sweetness and delight to which nothing sad can happen, since the grace of the divine presence always breathes upon him [Col. 0616A] and he himself is present to himself, steeped in the highest tranquility of spirit.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0615]

459. ## CHAPTER I

Having passed from the preceding book to this one, he shows that holy Jacob was blessed even in exile and demonstrates that the definition of blessedness applies to him most fittingly.

[Col. 0615A]

1. In the preceding book we discussed the precepts of the virtues; in the following one let us make use of the examples of illustrious men who, placed amid the greatest dangers, did not lose the blessedness of life but rather acquired it. Was Jacob not blessed even when he was leaving his homeland? Indeed, he was plainly blessed, since he undertook the hardships of exile to mitigate his brother’s anger. For if the one who avoids sin is blessed, then certainly the one who lightens another’s guilt and averts a crime cannot be denied blessedness. He therefore avoided a prepared act of fratricide by voluntary exile; by doing so he sought safety for himself and granted innocence to his brother. Rightly, therefore, divine grace accompanied him everywhere, so that even while he slept he might acquire the privilege of blessed life. For he saw the mysteries of the future and heard divine oracles (Gen. XXVIII, 5, 12 and following). A good worker in sleep and rich in poverty, he obtained both patrimony and marriage through the wages of a hired life by the same service (Gen. XXIX, 22, 29 and following). [Col. 0615C] The same man, an outstanding reconciler of brotherly affection, contended in gifts and acts of service (Gen. XXXII, 13 and following), so as to exclude all indignation and avert the pain of offense, showing that he had not been made lesser by exile, since he could give what he had not received.

2. But I am hurrying too quickly to lesser matters and passing over more useful ones, when it must first be defined what it means to be blessed. For it is written: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. I, 1). By this Scripture signifying that the man is blessed who has kept himself from the companionship of the faithless—for impiety consists in failing to acknowledge the author of life and, as it were, the parent of salvation, if one has either remained in sin or persisted in luxury and wantonness—

[Note: [Col. 0615D] Thus all the manuscripts, except that some omit the word “if.” The editions, closing the parenthesis after “acknowledge,” continue in this manner: “or if he has not remained in sin, or has not persevered …”]

the same man, meditating on the law of the Lord day and night, will be like a tree that gives its fruit in its season (ibid., 2–3). The former things are merits; this is the reward of merits.

3. What of those things that pertain to the merit of blessedness was lacking to holy Jacob? He was so far from the companionship of the ungodly that the faithful people took its name from him and were called Israel (Gen. XXXII, 28), because he beheld God with the inner eyes of the mind, abstaining from sin and sober from every intoxication of luxury, so that he absorbed the hardships of labor and disregarded the secure ease of leisure. Was it not beautifully and truly said of him that “he too will give fruit in his season,” of whom it is written: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field” (Gen. XXVII, 27)? For he was perfect in every flower of virtue and breathed forth the grace of sacred blessing and heavenly blessedness. He is the field that the Lord blessed—not this earthly field, rough with woods, broken by torrents, marshy with sluggish waters, barren of grain, useless for vines, [Note: [Col. 0616D] Some manuscripts read “or barren, rocky with stony gravel, or uncultivated,” and one reads “or barren with gravel, rocky,” etc. All, however, after “uncultivated” add “and with thorns,” which was not found in the editions.] barren and rocky with gravel, gaping and dry from drought, wet with blood, uncultivated and covered with thorns; but that field of which the Church says in the Song of Songs: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field” (Song II, 7). This is the field of which the Lord also says: “And the beauty of the field is with me” (Ps. XLIX, 11). In this field is found that vine which, when pressed, poured forth blood and washed the world. In this field is that fig tree beneath which the saints will rest, refreshed by the sweetness of spiritual grace. In this field is that fruitful olive tree, flowing with the ointment of the Lord’s peace. In this field pomegranates bloom, sheltering many fruits under the one protection of faith and, in a certain way, cherishing them in the embrace of charity.

4. Jacob therefore breathed forth these fruits, following God through dangers and believing himself safe everywhere under God’s guidance. For although the sweet and pleasant fragrance of the field is the fragrance of nature, in the holy Patriarch the grace of virtues breathed forth. How restrained was his frugality, when he did not demand the food prepared for himself but granted it without delay to his brother when he asked for it, from whom he received the primacy of blessing (Gen. XXV, 30 and following)! How dutiful toward his parents, so that by maternal affection he deserved to be preferred to his elder brother and was consecrated by the gift of his father’s blessing (Gen. XXVII, 8 and following)! How religious, in refusing to harm his brother! How modest, in fearing to deceive his father! How dutiful, in being unable to refuse his mother what she commanded!

## CHAPTER II

He excuses the parents of blessed Jacob and teaches, by their example, how other parents ought to conduct themselves toward their children. Then he explains why Jacob prevailed and what mysteries his blessing contains.

[Col. 0616D]

5. Nor should we leave the parents without an excuse because they preferred the younger son to the elder. At the same time, care must be taken lest someone, while following their example, [Col. 0617A] make an unjust judgment among his children, thinking that one should be loved and another set aside. From this arise fraternal hatreds, and a parricidal crime is contrived over the increase of insignificant wealth. Let the offspring be cherished with an equal measure of affection. Even if affection should seize something more for the gentler or more similar child, the form of justice ought to be equal toward all. More is conferred upon the beloved child when the love of his brothers is sought; but more is taken away from the one burdened by the envy of unjust preference. Esau threatened that he would kill his brother (ibid., 41), and neither brotherly kinship nor reverence for his parents restrained him from fratricidal madness. He grieved that the blessing had been snatched from him, although he ought to have shown himself worthy of it by gentleness, not by crime.

[Col. 0617B] 6. Rebecca, however, did not prefer son to son, but the just to the unjust. For in the pious mother the mystery outweighed the child. She did not so much prefer him to his brother as offer him to the Lord, knowing that the one granted to her could preserve the gift; and in this she also looked to the welfare of the other, whom she was withdrawing from divine displeasure, lest he become involved in a more serious guilt by losing the grace of the blessing he had received.

7. Yet consider the good contest between the parents. Let the mother bring affection, the father judgment. Let the mother incline toward the younger with tender devotion; let the father preserve toward the elder the honor due to nature. Let this one honor more, that one love more. While each cherishes one child, let neither conspire against the other or defraud him. [Note: [Col. 0617D] The editions and several manuscripts read, “Let there be equity”; but the manuscripts of Thuanus, Bignonius, Tornacensis, and Valcobertus read more aptly, “Let there be equality.” A few lines later the manuscripts of Remigius, Bignonius, Longolianus, and Theodoret’s second hand read, “Let equal favor be conferred upon both with equal parental love”; the others, together with the editions, have the reading found in the text.] Let there be equality amid differing contests, and let equal and comparable parental love and favor be conferred upon those whose pursuits differ; let one compensate for what the other diminishes. Thus the Patriarch Isaac and holy Rebecca contended in pious affection, so that they made neither inferior but both equal (Gen. XXV, 28).

8. Yet the one who was preferred prevailed by the oracle: diligence prevailed over sluggishness, gentleness over harshness (ibid., 23). While the other sought wild prey through harsh hunting, this one supplied the gentle foods of character, domestic grace, and the sweet dishes of tender gentleness and piety to his pious father. Whatever happens to be present in souls pleases more than whatever one has thought should be offered as a matter of affectation. Jacob went to the sheep and brought back the offspring of innocence, or the gifts of sacred prophecy (Gen. XXVII, 9 and following), because he judged that no food could be sweeter for the Patriarch than Christ, who was led like a sheep to slaughter and like a lamb to sacrifice. He judged this a useful food for the public father, or for the people whose type he bore, because it was destined to be the remission of sins.

9. Therefore he received his brother’s robe, because he surpassed him in the wisdom of old age; therefore the younger brother stripped the elder of his robe, because he shone forth in the dignity of faith. Rebecca, in the type of the Church, brought forth this robe and gave the younger son the robe of the Old Testament, the prophetic and priestly robe, that royal Davidic robe, the robe of Solomon, Hezekiah, and Josiah the kings; and she gave it to the Christian people, who would know how to use the garment they had received, since the Jewish people possessed it without use and did not know its proper adornments. This robe lay cast aside and neglected in the shadows. For it was obscured by the dark gloom of impiety and could not be unfolded more widely in the narrow heart of the Jewish people. The Christian people put it on, and it shone forth; it illuminated [Col. 0618B] it with the brightness of its faith and the light of its pious deeds. Isaac recognized the familiar fragrance of his race and recognized the robe of Scripture of old, but he did not recognize the voice of the former people, and therefore he knew that it had been changed. The same robe remains even today, but the melodious confession of the more devout people has begun to be heard. Rightly, therefore, he said: “The voice is indeed Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands. And he smelled the fragrance of his garments” (ibid., 22 and 27). Perhaps this means that we are justified not by works but by faith, because carnal weakness is an impediment to works, whereas the brightness of faith overshadows the error of deeds and earns pardon for offenses.

## CHAPTER III

Why, after the blessing of the younger brother, the elder came; and when by insistence he obtained a blessing for himself also, why he was condemned to serve his brother. Here the discussion concerns slavery and true freedom.

[Col. 0618C]

10. After the blessing had been celebrated, the elder brother later arrived (ibid., 30). This declares that the kingdom of the Church was granted first in predestination, before that of the Synagogue; but that the Synagogue entered afterward so that sin might abound, and, when sin had abounded, grace might abound also. At the same time it was made clear that the diligent soldier ought to be a candidate for the heavenly kingdom, so that he might seize the blessing and claim the privilege of his commendation. Hence the younger son was not censured by his father,

[Note: [Col. 0617D] “Censured,” that is, blamed or reproved. Horace uses the word in this sense in his Epistle to Flaccus:

“If he knew how to deal with kings,  
he who censures me would disdain vegetables.”

And in Satire 3, Book I:

“This love is foolish and wicked, and worthy of censure.”]

but praised, as Isaac says: “Your brother came with deceit and took your blessing” [Col. 0618D] (ibid., 35). [Note: [Col. 0618D] “Good deceit” is rightly so called, since among the ancients the word dolus had an intermediate meaning: at one time it was taken for lawful ingenuity, especially when employed against an enemy or robber; at another, for every kind of trickery and simulation devised to deceive, and then it was generally called not simply dolus, but dolus malus, “evil deceit.” According to Cicero, in Book III of On Duties and likewise Book III of On the Nature of the Gods, Aquilius defined the latter as occurring when one thing is pretended and another done. See also Ulpian, On Evil Deceit, first law, near the beginning.] Good deceit is such where the seizure is irreproachable; and the seizure of piety is irreproachable, because from the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it. The fathers who hurried to celebrate Passover were also hastening: they ate the lamb without delay; and holy Joseph summoned and detained his brother Benjamin by a pious stratagem of deception (Gen. XLII, 20; XLIV, 1 and following).

11. He too, nevertheless, compelled and obtained the blessing by insistence (Gen. XXVII, 38–39), but it was a blessing that agreed and harmonized with the former one: namely, that he should serve his brother. For he who could not command or rule another ought to serve, so that he might be ruled by the wiser. It was not the purpose of the holy Patriarch to consign his son to a degraded condition of slavery; rather, as a good father with two sons—one intemperate, the other prudent and sober—he set the sober son over the intemperate one, and appointed the foolish man to obey the prudent, so that he might provide for both. [Col. 0619B] For the foolish cannot willingly become a disciple of virtue or persevere in its pursuit, because the fool changes like the moon. Rightly, therefore, he denied him the freedom of his own judgment, lest he drift like a ship upon the waves without a helmsman; instead, he subjected him to his brother, according to what is written: “The imprudent serves the prudent” (Prov. XI, 29). He rightly subjected him, so that under the command of his ruler he might improve his own disposition. Therefore he says: “You shall live by your sword, and you shall serve your brother” (Gen. XXVII, 34). Piety is indeed mistress over cruelty, and gentleness prevails over harsh impulses.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] The Roman edition reads, “is superior to harsh dispositions.” It is not a bad reading, but it should not therefore be preferred to that of the other editions and all the manuscripts, since this reading too is sound. For “harsh impulses” are the same as harsh passions, as the philosophers call them.]

12. Everyone is a servant who does not possess the authority of a pure conscience: everyone is a servant who is broken by fear, ensnared by pleasure, led by desires, exasperated by indignation, or cast down by grief. For every passion is servile, since whoever commits sin is a slave of sin; and what is worse, he is the slave of many masters. Whoever is subjected to vices has handed himself over to many lords, so that he can scarcely escape their servitude. But the person who is the arbiter of his own will, the judge of his deliberation, and the interpreter of his choice; who restrains the appetite of bodily passion; who does what he does well—and whoever acts well acts rightly, while whoever acts rightly acts blamelessly and irreproachably—and who has power over his own actions: that person is certainly free. For the one who does everything prudently and lives as he wishes is alone free. It is not an accidental condition that makes someone a slave, but disgraceful folly (Prov. VII, 2).

In the end, a prudent servant rules foolish masters, and skilled servants will lend to their masters. What will they lend? Certainly not money, but wisdom, just as the Law also says: “You shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow” (Deut. XV, 6). The Jew lent the oracles of divine law to the proselyte. But because he himself was unable to see the mysteries of the Law, and did not understand the oracles he possessed—since he lent the letter to the nations—he now borrows from them the grace of spiritual instruction. And rightly is he subjected to servitude, since whoever borrows is a servant, as though bound over to the creditor’s interest. But the one who distributes the interest of pious instruction is a ruler, as the Law says: “You shall be ruler of many nations, but they shall not be rulers over you” (ibid.). For a ruler is one who governs, and he also possesses the primacy of wisdom—which the Jewish people possessed. But since it could not keep what it taught, it must learn what it did not know how to teach.

13. This, then, is what the patriarch Isaac says: “You shall serve your brother. But it shall come to pass when you cast off and break his yoke from your neck” (Gen. XXVII, 40), signifying that there would be two peoples, one the son of a slave-woman and the other of a free woman—for the letter is servile, but grace is free—and that the people devoted to the letter would remain servants for as long as they followed the interpreter of spiritual doctrine. Then also what the Apostle says will come to pass: “So that the remnant may be saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. IX, 27). You shall therefore serve your brother; but you will experience the benefit of servitude when you begin to obey your brother voluntarily rather than under compulsion.

[Note: After the word “brother,” the Roman edition adds: “Behold, your brother Esau is threatening to kill you; now therefore,” and so forth. It then continues chapter three up to these words: “he supplies everything without deficiency.”]

## CHAPTER IV

Esau threatens his brother with death; on this occasion, precepts for appeasing envy are set forth. Jacob, departing for Laban, is refreshed on the way by the appearance of angels and afterward increased in goods.

14. From this envy arose, and Esau threatened that after his father’s death he would kill his brother. [Note: Thus in five manuscripts, and in the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus. The manuscripts of Remigius and Theodulf, together with the Roman edition, read: “But lest this should happen”; Gill’s edition reads, “lest this should have happened.” Again, at this very place, where the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus read, “let us speak to Rebecca,” Gill’s and the Roman editions, together with all the manuscripts, read, “let us learn from Rebecca.”]

But if this should happen, let us learn from Rebecca how provision must be made lest envy arouse anger, and anger rush headlong into parricide. Let Rebecca come—that is, let patience be introduced, the good guardian of innocence—and let her advise us to give place to anger. Let us withdraw somewhat farther away, until indignation is softened by time and forgetfulness of the offense steals over us. Thus patience does not even fear exile, but undertakes it eagerly—not so much to avoid danger to one’s safety as to avert the stimulus to crime. The pious mother, too, endures the absence of the son most dear to her, in order to benefit more the one whom she has injured; yet she provides for both, so that one may be free from danger and the other preserved blameless from crime.

15. We have heard what intemperance, drunk with bodily desires, has said; let us consider what true virtue does. It seeks nothing except the grace of God. It follows that one and highest good, and is content with him alone from whom we have received everything; yet we contribute nothing to him, because he needs nothing, as David says: “I said to the Lord: You are my God, for you have no need of my goods” (Ps. XV, 2). For what need has he who abounds in all things, gives us everything, and supplies everything without deficiency?

16. [Note: Here the Roman edition began a new chapter with the words: “And Isaac sent Jacob away, and he departed into Mesopotamia to Laban,” and so forth. “Jacob departed, and on the way he slept.” The same edition inserted two other verses of Scripture shortly afterward, which are not irrelevant to the sense, but which are found in no other edition or manuscript.]

“And Jacob departed, and slept,” which is an indication of a peaceful mind; “and he saw the angels of God ascending and descending” (Gen. XXVIII, 11)—that is, he foresaw Christ on earth, to whom a company of angels descended and ascended, about to offer obedient service to their gracious Lord (Matt. IV, 11).

17. “And he came to the well, that he might drink from his own vessels and from the springs of his own wells, and that waters might overflow for him from his own fountain” (Gen. XXIX, 2). For the fountain of life is in the hands of the righteous.

18. “And he came to Laban, and tended his sheep.” Iniquity remains unaccompanied; wisdom does not abandon the duty of governing (Gen. XXIX, 19, and XXX, 28ff.). It does not know how to be idle even among strangers; it does not know how to be an exile in foreign lands. For how can that be an exile which everywhere preserves its own right and possesses within itself what it owns? [Note: The word *jus* (“right”) was absent from all the editions; we have restored it from all the Gallican manuscripts.]

19. The righteous man enters as a hired servant; and he is a ruler who gathered a flock shining with the splendor of many excellent virtues through the ministry of evangelical preaching [Note: Seven manuscripts of the highest quality read, “he gathered through teaching.”], so that he might set before the sheep coming to drink staffs of storax, nutwood, and plane wood at the *inventis* [reading uncertain]. [Note: The Roman edition reads “in the channels,” against all the other editions and manuscripts, in which *inventis* is read. Perhaps *in venis* or *in lenis*, ἐν ταῖς ληνοῖς; Augustine renders this “in the troughs.” But we admit none of our conjectures into the text.] Thus those desiring the mysteries prefigured by the most blessed Trinity might by no means produce discolored offspring through the conception of a devout mind. Good are the sheep that have produced offspring of good works, not degenerate from holy faith.

Storax signifies incense and the evening sacrifice offered to God the Father in the psalm. By the nutwood staff a priestly office is offered to Christ (Ps. CXL, 2). For this is Aaron’s staff, which, when laid aside, blossomed, and through which the priestly grace of sanctification shone forth (Num. XVII, 8). By the plane tree is signified the abundance of spiritual fruit, because the vine is attached to this tree, so that, rejoicing in its fruitful companionship, it may pour itself forth into abundant produce. For, through the accompanying grace of the Spirit, it customarily grants the gifts of the Lord’s Passion and the remission of all sins. [Note: Two manuscripts read, “customarily pour forth”; two others, “customarily cherish.”]

## CHAPTER V

Jacob returns to his homeland at God’s command because of the envy of Laban and his sons. If envy arises, how it is to be avoided; and by what reasoning the wise person can never be empty. After this, the mystery signified in Laban, when he searches out his son-in-law’s goods, and in Jacob and his wives, is explained.

20. Thus, as Scripture says, he became rich, nourishing a very good flock for Christ, whom he adorned with the insignia of a glorious name through the title of faith and the variety of virtues. [Note: Thus all the manuscripts and editions except the Roman, which reads: “But the Lord said to Jacob: Return to the land of your father and to your kindred, and I will be with you. Jacob had become very rich, possessing a good flock,” and so forth. Again, at the same place the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus read, “and he ennobled him with the distinctions of a variety of virtues”; Gill’s and the Roman editions read, “and he ennobled him with the distinctions of various virtues.” All the manuscripts agree with the text.]

Thus he did not even seem narrow to himself, rich in the wealth of faith; and to Laban’s sons he was regarded as exceedingly wealthy and was envied, because he had increased his own flock by adding to it another’s. And God said to him: “Return to the land of your father and to your kindred, and I will be with you” (Gen. XXXI, 3), showing that nothing is lacking to the one with whom the fullness of all things is present: that this alone is to abound perfectly, that in this all things consist, and that all things are referred to it. [Note: The Roman edition reads, “Nothing is superfluous or necessary to him.” The manuscripts of Tornacensis, Longobardus, Valcobertus, and Theodulf read, “Nothing harmful”; Theodulf, in a second hand, “Nothing new, nothing superfluous, or not necessary.” But we judge our reading, found in the other manuscripts and older editions, preferable to the others. For countless things that are new and superfluous are, through an error of judgment, regarded as necessary.] [Note: The Roman edition joins the word “fullness” to “virtues,” which the other witnesses more rightly omit. For here “fullness” signifies God himself, who is the fullness of all good things. Again, where all the editions and most manuscripts read “to abound perfectly,” several others have “to abound in the Perfect One.”]

Nothing superfluous is necessary to the one supplied with faithful peace, through which things formerly discordant might be reconciled. Nor is it surprising that he had peace, since he had set up and anointed for God a pillar, which is the Church (Gen. XXXV, 20). For it is called “the pillar and foundation of truth” (1 Tim. III, 15). He anoints it who pours out the ointment of faith toward Christ and of mercy toward the poor.

21. Now let us consider what sort of man the righteous person ought to be if envy has arisen. First, he should avoid it, for it is better to depart without strife than to remain amid quarrels. Next, he should possess such things as he can take away with him, so that he cannot be held liable in anything by his adversary, but may say: “See whether anything of yours is with me” (Gen. XXXI, 32ff.). Laban searched, and found nothing of his own with Jacob.

Great is the man, and truly blessed, who could lose nothing of his own and possess nothing belonging to another—that is, who had nothing less than he ought to have and nothing superfluous. Therefore he is perfect who lacks nothing; righteous is he who has nothing left over. For this is to keep the measure of justice. How great is the virtue whose companionship brought profit and did not inflict loss? This is perfection: to give those who cling to one great benefit and to bring them no disadvantage.

22. In the end, the man who desired to harm him could not send him away empty. For the wise person is never empty (*De poenit.* dist. 2, cap. *Sapiens*), always possessing within himself the garment of prudence, and able to say, as Job said: “I clothed myself with justice, and I covered myself with judgment” (Job XXIX, 14). These are the inward coverings of the mind, which no one else can take away unless a person strips himself through his own fault.

Thus Adam, stripped in this way, was found naked. Joseph, however, even after his outer garment had been removed, was not naked, because he still possessed the garments of virtue. The wise person, therefore, is never empty. For how could he be empty who receives from the fullness of Christ and preserves what he has received? How could he be empty whose soul is filled and guards the garments of the grace it has received?

This must be feared: that someone may lose the veil of innocence; that the wicked, pressing forward through sacrilegious persecution and overstepping the boundaries of justice, may seize the garment of the soul and mind. But this does not easily happen unless someone’s own voice of iniquity has first stripped him. Hence David also says: “If there is iniquity in my hands . . . then may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies; may the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it” (Ps. VII, 4–5).

23. No enemy, therefore, can seize your soul unless it has first become empty. Do not fear, then, those who can plunder treasures of gold and silver. They take nothing from you. They take what you did not possess; they take what you could not possess; they take what did not adorn your soul but burdened it; they take what did not enrich your heart but rather weighed it down.

“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matt. VI, 21), as you heard read today. Many shut their gold behind the bars of their doors, but they do not even trust their bolts and locks. Many employ guards, but they themselves usually fear the guards even more. Many lie upon gold buried in the ground; their gold is beneath the earth, and their heart is beneath the earth. Beware, then, lest you too bury your heart alive in the earth.

Do not fear thieves of this gold. You must beware the moneylender who searches the substance of your soul to see whether you have contracted any heavier debts of sin; who shuts your heart in the earth; who buries your soul under the sod with which you covered your gold; who bends your mind beneath the interest of one-percent loans and consigns it to a heavy tomb from which no one rises. [Note: The “one-hundredth interest” is that by which one-hundredth of the principal is paid to the moneylender each month; thus, by the hundredth month, the sum of the capital or principal equals the interest. Ambrose attacks this practice vigorously in his book *On Tobit*.]

Follow holy Jacob, who possessed nothing of another’s vices and was not empty or void of his own virtues, but was filled with the fruit of justice. But these are moral interpretations.

24. The mystical meaning is this: Laban came to him—that is, “the whitened one,” because Satan also transforms himself into an angel of light—and began to demand what belonged to him. Jacob answered him: “See whether anything of yours is with me” (Gen. XXXI, 32); that is, I possess nothing of yours. Search to see whether you recognize any of your vices and crimes. I have taken nothing of your deceits; I have left behind no companionship of fraud or guile; I have nothing of them. [Note: An older edition, with several manuscripts, reads: “I have left behind the associations of your deceits; I have none of them.” This is flat.] I have shunned all that belongs to you as contagion.

Laban searched and found nothing belonging to him. How blessed is the man in whom the enemy found nothing that he could call his own, in whom the devil found nothing offensive that he could recognize as his! This seemed impossible in a human being, but he bore the type of the one who says in the Gospel: “The prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30). For everything that belongs to the devil is nothing, since it can possess neither perpetuity nor substance.

25. He himself is the Lord Jesus, prefigured in Jacob, the man of two marriages—that is, sharing in a certain way in the Law and in grace. He first loved the virgin Rachel, and with pious affection loved her as one predestined for marriage with him. But since Leah entered in, like the Law, and, weaker in her eyes, crept in like the Synagogue, which could not see Christ because of the blindness of its mind, the grace of holy Rachel abounded (Gen. XXIXff.). She was desired above that first marriage and already signified, through the interpretation of her name, the future primacy of the Church.

Blessed Rachel, who removed reproach through her childbirth; blessed Rachel, who concealed the practices and errors of the gentiles and declared that their images were full of impurity. Let no one believe that reverence for filial piety toward the father was injured because she sat while her father was standing, since it is written: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X, 37). When the case concerned religion, faith had to occupy the seat of judgment, while unbelief had to stand as though accused.

## CHAPTER VI

Saint Jacob sees angels on the way. Meeting his brother, he worships seven times. Finally, intending to seek reconciliation from him, he sleeps in the camp. The meaning of all these things is disclosed.

26. These things were proved thus far: as holy Jacob was departing, the angels of God met him. [Note: All the manuscripts and editions except the Roman give this reading. The Roman edition begins the chapter: “And Jacob went on his way; and looking back, he saw the camps of God encamped, and the angels of God met him.”] In the end, he saw the camps of God drawing near and said: “These are the camps of God” (Gen. XXXII, 1–2). For divine defenses usually attend the perfect and faithful.

The perfect man was thinking about fraternal reconciliation, so that, with humility, he might invite him, win him over by acts of service, and consider him purchasable even by gifts. [Note: All editions and several manuscripts read, “so that he might invite him . . . and consider him fit to be won over.” Other, older and more numerous manuscripts read, “so that he might invite him . . . and consider him fit to be won over”; the manuscripts of Longobardus and Valcobertus read, “fit to be won over.” This is a syllepsis, in which the construction refers to the word “brother,” understood by implication in the preceding clause. After the word “consider,” the Roman edition adds: “For he said: I will appease his face with the gifts that go before,” which is superfluous and absent from all manuscripts and the other editions.]

Thus he met his brother with gifts, wives, and children, so that even if he were angry, he might be softened by the attentions of kinship.

27. “And he worshiped seven times upon the earth” (Gen. XXXIII, 3). What does this mean? The Law says: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. VI, 13). Yet here he worships an intemperate, angry man threatening a criminal act of parricide. Did he worship the earth—that earth congealed with human blood and filled with the poisons of serpents, or made wretched by barren gravel, or bristling with hard and jagged rocks?

What, moreover, does it mean that he worshiped seven times? The explanation would be difficult unless there came to mind what the Lord Jesus answered Peter when he asked in the Gospel: “If my brother sins against me, how often shall I forgive him—up to seven times?” He answered him: “Not only up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matt. XVIII, 21–22). [Note: The manuscripts of Longobardus and Remigius and the second hand of Theodulf add: “By this prophecy, therefore, the Patriarch signifies the Holy Spirit.”]

By this prophetic spirit, then, the holy Patriarch signifies—looking toward the one who was to come—that he would command forgiveness to be extended to his brother not only up to seven times but even up to seventy times seven. In this way Esau, seeing him, might forgive the injury he thought he had received from his brother, and, although injured, return to friendship, because the Lord Jesus was for this reason going to assume flesh and come upon earth: to grant us forgiveness for our sins in multiplied measure.

28. Finally, intending to seek reconciliation from his brother, he slept in the camp. Perfect virtue possesses the tranquility and stability of rest. Therefore the Lord reserved this gift for the more perfect, saying: “My peace I leave you; my peace I give you” (John XIV, 27).

It belongs to the perfect not to be easily moved by worldly things, not to be disturbed by fear, not to be agitated by suspicion, not to be shaken by terror, and not to be afflicted by grief, but, as though on a very safe shore against the waves rising from the storms of the world, to calm the mind in a steadfast and secure station.

Christ brought this firm foundation to Christian minds, bringing inner peace to the souls of the approved, so that our heart might not be disturbed nor our spirit agitated. The Apostle, the teacher, asserted that this peace is above every mind, saying: “And the peace of God, which surpasses every mind, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus” (Phil. IV, 7). The fruit of peace, therefore, is not to be disturbed in one’s breast.

In the end, the life of the righteous is peaceful, whereas the unjust person is full of unrest and disturbance. Thus the wicked person is more afflicted by his own suspicions than many are by the blows of others; and greater bruises from wounds are found in his soul than on the bodies of those who are beaten by others.

29. It is a great thing for someone to be tranquil within himself and to be at peace with himself. External peace is sought through the anxious providence of an emperor or by the hands of soldiers; it yields to the favorable outcome of wars or to some slaughter of barbarians, if they turn their weapons against one another in hostile agitation. In such peace there is none of our virtue, but only the outcome. Certainly the glory of that peace is attributed to the emperor; but the fruit of this peace is in us, for it exists in the minds of individuals and is held in their affections.

The fruit of this peace is greater when it repels the temptations of spiritual wickedness than when it repels hostile weapons. This peace is higher: it excludes the allurements of bodily passions and calms disturbances, whereas the other merely stills barbarian assaults. For it is more difficult to resist an enemy shut up within you than one driven far away.

## CHAPTER VII

Jacob wrestles with God and limps after the sinew of his thigh is touched. His brothers avenge the violence inflicted upon Dinah, and Jacob disapproves of them. He is commanded to dwell at Bethel, which prefigures the holy Church.

30. Jacob, therefore, who had cleansed his heart from every hostility and bore a peaceful disposition, after he had set aside all that belonged to him, remained alone and wrestled with God (Gen. XXXII, 24–25). For whoever neglects worldly things draws nearer to the image and likeness of God.

What is it to wrestle with God except to undertake a contest of virtue, to engage with one who is superior, and to become God’s better imitator than others? And because his faith and devotion were unconquerable, the Lord revealed secret mysteries to him, touching the breadth of his thigh (ibid.), because the Lord Jesus was to arise from his offspring according to the flesh, from the Virgin, and was neither inferior nor unequal to God. The breadth of his numbed thigh signified Christ’s cross, because, with the remission of sin spread throughout the whole world, it would be saving for all, and because he, through the numbness of his body and sleep, would grant resurrection to the dead.

Hence the sun rose, not without reason, upon holy Jacob, whose descendants the saving cross of the Lord illumined. Likewise, the sun of justice rises for the one who sees God, because he himself is the eternal light.

31. “Jacob limped from his thigh; therefore to this day the children of Israel do not eat the sinew” (Gen. XXXII, 32). Would that they had eaten and believed! But because they were not going to do the will of God, they did not eat. Some also understand the matter in this way: Jacob limped from one thigh because, from the two peoples flowing from his offspring, the blindness of one with respect to the grace of faith was already then being shown as future. That, then, is the people that limped through the blindness of unbelief.

32. Not long afterward, when Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, had been violated by the son of a foreigner and the modesty of her virginity had been profaned, her brothers—who did not understand the mystery—killed the foreigners who were offering fellowship in the faith through an alliance of kinship. [Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “Now Dinah, the daughter of Leah, whom Jacob bore, went out to see the daughters of the inhabitants; and Shechem, the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the land, saw her, and he took her and lay with her.” It then begins chapter VII with the words: “Finally, not long after this revelation had taken place, when . . .”]

But Jacob, who loved clemency through moral gentleness—or who, by the mystical spirit, foresaw the sacrament of the Church to be gathered from the nations—received that scene of exacted vengeance unwillingly and sorrowfully. [Note: We explained in Book II of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 8, no. 32, that a *scaena* is a place shaded by trees. But because the dramatic poems formerly performed there were later transferred to theaters, the name *scaena* came to signify such places and, by synecdoche, the bloody actions customarily exhibited in them. Therefore some manuscripts have rather ineptly substituted *caedes* (“slaughter”) for *scaenam*.]

Hence, to him who prophesied the coming of the Lord Jesus, the divine response was given: “Arise, go up to Bethel” (Gen. XXXV, 1)—that is, to the house of bread, where Christ was born, as the prophet Micah testified, saying: “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephratha, are not the least among the princes of Judah; for from you shall go forth the ruler of Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. V, 2).

Truly it is the house of bread, which is the house of Christ, who came to us as the saving bread from heaven, so that no one might now hunger, acquiring for himself the food of immortality. There the Patriarch is commanded to dwell; there he is to make an altar to God who appeared to him. There he took the foreign gods and hid them beneath the terebinth. [Note: Thus all the manuscripts and the older editions; the Roman edition, following the biblical text, has “beneath the terebinth” here and below.] There also Rachel was buried on the road to Ephratha, that is, Bethlehem. There Jacob also set up a pillar over her monument (Gen. XXXV, 1ff.).

[Note: Not only here, but also in Book I *On Abraham*, chapter 2, nos. 5–6, and Book II, chapter 5, no. 21, the better manuscripts read “Bethlehem.” Certainly that Ambrose understood Bethlehem and Bethel to be the same place is indicated both by the interpretation of the word that he always adds and by the sequence of his discourse. Nevertheless, we have retained the reading of all the editions and of not a few manuscripts, which is also supported by the authority of Scripture.]

33. What great mysteries there are, because you have the Church of God, in which God appears and speaks with his servants! There the images of the nations are seized and hidden. For the faith of the Church abolished every observance of paganism.

But why did he hide them beneath the terebinth, I ask? Certainly this kind of tree is fruitless. Therefore the gods of the nations are there, where there is no fruit. There the earrings of the gentiles are buried, which they gave to Jacob, so that they might now grow accustomed to hearing a new language, no longer know the old sound of unbelief, become deaf to their sacrilege, and be cleansed for grace.

Not without reason did holy Daniel there detect the false testimony against Susanna. For there unbelief still wished to establish its roots; but it could not remain concealed, because it was detected by the prophetic spirit. The fitting error of the presbyter, who said that chastity had been defiled there, signified the contamination of the chastity of faith where the images of the nations had been buried. [Note: The Roman edition reads, “the presbyter’s error of true confession, so that there she might learn that chastity had been contaminated.” The other editions agree with all the manuscripts, except that they have “confession.” This is less satisfactory. The sense of the passage is that the error or lie of the presbyter who asserted that Susanna had been corrupted beneath a fruitless tree signified that the chastity of faith had been contaminated there, where the images of the nations had been buried. For when it is said above that Daniel detected a false testimony there, “there” refers not to the tree at Bethel but to another tree similar to it in its barrenness.]

But the truth of the Church did not cover unbelief; rather, it concealed it and stopped the ears of paganism. [Note: The old edition reads, “did not cover unbelief, and the ears . . .”; the Roman edition reads, “did not expose unbelief, but hid it, and the ears . . .” The manuscripts read “covered,” with the old edition, but otherwise agree with the Roman. The holy Teacher seems to imply that, in the person of Daniel convicting the false witnesses, the Church does not cover—that is, does not conceal—the unbelief of paganism, but exposes it; afterward, however, among gentiles who are converted, it hides or washes it away through baptism, as what follows clearly shows.]

34. It was also fitting that holy Rachel was buried there, because all who are baptized in Christ are buried with Christ. For so we are taught when the Apostle says: “We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as he was raised from the dead through his own power, so we too may rise by his grace” (Rom. VI, 4).

Then, indeed, all the error of the gentiles is truly hidden, when someone has been washed from his vices, because our old man, nailed to the cross, no longer knows how to serve the old sin. Fittingly, too, a pillar is set up over Rachel’s monument, because the Church is the pillar and foundation of truth.

## CHAPTER VIII

On the praiseworthy old age of holy Jacob, in which he foresees future and uncertain events and the end of his life, and also arranges what must be done.

35. Jacob grew old; and he had already grown old in character. Yet in him the tireless vitality of youth and the tranquility of old age contended with one another. There is an old age flourishing with grace, and a youth gray with counsel, of which Scripture says: “For old age is honorable,” and, “The age of old age is an undefiled life” (Wis. IV, 8–9). [Note: The Roman edition reads, “Jacob therefore grew old”; the older editions, “Jacob fled from this life.” Better is the reading of all the manuscripts: “Jacob lived this life,” that is, he led the kind of life described above.]

Jacob lived this life, having anticipated by good works the time of long old age, so that he might gather its fruit before the appointed time and not fear its final period when it arrived. Blessed is the young man who lives well; but blessed also is the old man who has lived well. What the young man hopes for, the elder has attained; what the old man once was, the young man desires to become.

Certainly the young man, with a longer course still remaining before him, is tossed about by the waves of this restless sea; but the old man, like one in harbor, stands in the anchorage of old age.
