Such was Jacob, who already held, safe and secure under the key of grace, goods scarcely to be hoped for by the young. What one possesses is more excellent than what one still hopes for.

Jacob was therefore an old man to whom young people, struck by the storm of some adversity, withdrew as though into harbor. He himself, however, placed as though in a watchtower over this life, kept careful watch and foresaw remedies for uncertain circumstances far in advance. [Note: Several manuscripts read, “as though placed in a cave.”]

36. Finally, there was famine throughout the whole land (Gen. XLII, 1ff.), and the aged man, *depositus* [“set aside,” sense uncertain], knew what the vigorous young men did not. Consider, meanwhile, whether he was the first to hear of it. [Note: All the editions read, “He was the first to hear; he was the first to warn his sons.” But the manuscripts unanimously support our reading, except that several have *videbo* instead of *videto*. This agrees sufficiently with the opening of chapter 8 of *On Joseph*, where Ambrose states the matter emphatically.] He was the first to inform his sons that grain was abundant in Egypt and that they should go there to buy what was necessary for their use (Gen. XLIII, 11). He willingly accepted the advice of the young men himself, so that he might also send the younger son with them.

When they reported that his son Joseph was alive, though his body was broken, his spirit remained vigorous. He did not wait for his son to come to him, but rather went himself to his son (Gen. XLV, 28). For affection is not outweighed by the measure of age. Thus he felt none of the impediments of exhausted old age as he went on his way. Affection lightened the labor.

But after he had enjoyed the fruit of receiving his sons, when some time had passed—seventeen years, namely, which in view of the Patriarch’s longevity was only a small portion of time—he realized that the end of his life was approaching. He summoned his son Joseph and bound him by the future heir of his generation not to bury him in Egypt (Gen. XLVII, 29).

After receiving his oath, when he soon afterward fell ill and his son Joseph came to him, he sat up on his bed as though his strength had returned, blessed the twelve Patriarchs, and prophesied (Gen. XLIX, 1).

## CHAPTER IX

Jacob is shown to be blessed even when near death and weakened in sight. His many commendations are presented, especially on account of the blessings of the Patriarchs; and finally it is concluded that neither he nor any other saint ought to be considered less blessed because of hardships.

37. Let some now say that Jacob was not blessed, although, even in the days of his death, he mingled more conversations with God than with human beings; not blessed when his eyes were failing in old age and he could not see. To some, blindness seems a grievous calamity. But Jacob was blessed even then, because by the spirit he discerned what he could not discern with his eyes or see with his sight. He saw the future, although he was thought unable to see the present.

In the end, Joseph himself was mistaken. He had placed his older son at Jacob’s right and his younger son at his left—that is, at Jacob’s left—so that the order of age might preserve the order of blessing. But Jacob stretched out his right hand over the younger grandson and his left over the older grandson. When Joseph wanted to turn his father’s right hand toward Manasseh the elder, Jacob answered: “I know, my son, I know. He too shall become a people, and he too shall be exalted; but his younger brother shall be greater than he. His offspring shall become a multitude of nations” (Gen. XLVIII, 18ff.).

Although the sight of his body was impaired, he saw so much better that he taught the one who could see that he had been mistaken. For who sees better than the one who sees Christ? Or who can call a man’s eyes impaired when he saw the Church shining forth in Christ? Is it not therefore clear that physical weakness cannot impede blessedness?

He whose eyesight was impaired, whose bodily strength was exhausted, lying on his bed as though leaving his body in a tomb, rose up within himself. Withdrawing from others and gathering himself within himself, he removed himself from present circumstances and mingled with the age of future days. For it is written: “I will announce to you,” he says, “what shall meet you in the last days” (Gen. XLIX, 1).

### 38

What, then, was lacking in him, when God was with him—God who, as he was about to depart, had said to him: “I will go down with you into Egypt, and I too will lead you forth for ever” (Gen. 46:3–4)? Nor was God absent when the Holy Spirit spoke through him. Who was so powerful in his own dwelling as this man in a foreign land? Who so rich amid abundance as he amid famine? Who so strong in youth as he in old age? Who so active in business as he in leisure? Who so swift in the race as he in his bed? Who so joyful in the flower of adolescence as he at the threshold of death? Who so wealthy in a kingdom as he in a foreign place? Finally, he blessed kings (Gen. 47:7). Nor was the poor man poor without reason, for he lacked nothing. He was not poor who did not consider himself poor. And who would call poor the man whose way of life the whole world was not worthy to possess? Therefore his citizenship was in heaven.

Here, indeed, he was exceedingly rich in the wealth of simplicity and sincerity; comely with a beauty of soul greater than that of the body, a beauty that does not know decay; vigorous in age, able, whenever he wished, to depart from this bodily hovel and penetrate the heights of paradise by the strength of his mind. Rejoicing in spirit, even when he was committing himself to the final rites of the tomb, he did not presume that he was to be enclosed in an earthly grave, but received into a heavenly dwelling. Therefore, as though he were entrusting his tomb to another, while secure concerning himself he regarded that death as immortality.

He seemed entangled in the body’s impediment, yet with an alert expectation he ran ahead toward future times, saying of the persecutors of the Lord, who were to arise from the tribe of Simeon and Levi [Note: [Col. 0629D] Namely, the scribes and priests, as he himself explains in *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, chapter 3], the authors of wickedness [Note: [Col. 0629D] The Roman edition alone reads: “and let my inward parts not contend in their council . . . their fury, because it is obstinate.”], who were to arise: “Let my soul not enter their council, and let my inward parts not join their assembly” (Gen. 49:6).

Who, then, was so vigorous in virtue as this man, strong in infirmity, who said: “Cursed be their fury, because it was proud and reckless, and their anger, because it was hardened. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (ibid. 7)?

### 39

Who was, then, so melodious in song as this man in his utterances, whose voice has been heard throughout the whole world, heard among every people and through every generation? [Note: [Col. 0629D] Thus read the manuscripts Theod., Valc., Vict., and Colb. Others read: “Who has uttered his name, so sweetly (Thuan.: sweet), with the distinction of seven voices?” The old edition reads: “Who has uttered most sweetly the distinctions of seven voices?” Finally, the Roman edition reads: “Who has uttered the distinctions of seven voices in such sweet rhythms?” Ambrose may perhaps be alluding to Virgil, *Aeneid* 6: “He answers with the distinctions of seven voices in his rhythms” (*Obloquitur numeris septem discrimina vocum*).]

Who has uttered so sweet a melody, distinguishing seven voices, as this man resounded with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit? Although his limbs were dissolved, yet, lifting himself in mind and raising himself in spirit, he looked down from the height of his understanding upon the harmony of his body—as upon a lyre—now destroyed by the disjointing of its limbs. He did not seek that bodily harmony, but allowed it to lie idle upon the ground. He himself, however, soothed himself with an inward song and delighted in prophetic melody, saying:

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be upon the backs of your enemies; the sons of your father shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub; from the shoot you have risen for me; lying down, you slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub. Who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49:8ff.)

And later:

“He shall wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape. His eyes are cheerful from wine, and his teeth whiter than milk” (ibid. 11–12).

What song is sweeter, what sound more pleasing, than the forgiveness of sins and the resurrection of the dead? Holy David, that instrument of the divine voice and interpreter of the Lord’s speech, sang this song with a spiritual lyre. By these melodies he soothed that lofty soul and mind. By this song he softened the harshness of this world; by this sound he made gentle the hardness of the age; by this psalter he broke the terror of death; by this sweetness of the strings he trampled the realms below.

### 40

But let us also hear other things which holy Jacob the patriarch uttered through that marvelous instrument of his mind:

“Naphtali is a vine let loose, extending beauty in its shoot. My son Joseph is enlarged; my son is enlarged, a son pursued by jealousy; my younger son, return to me” (ibid. 21ff.).

And later:

“He prevailed over the blessings of the everlasting mountains and the desires of the eternal hills” (ibid. 26).

What is sweeter than blessing? What more welcome than eternity? The very words are a song, and in the words are great rewards of hopes, the summits of merits.

### 41

What is sweeter than holy Joseph, who delivered us from reproach through the mystery of the Lord’s cross? For just as Christ became a curse in order to dissolve the curse of the Law, and became sin in order to take away the sin of the world, so he became reproach in order to remove the reproach of paganism. Yet that reproach of Christ was esteemed more precious than the treasures of Egypt.

Therefore Moses left the royal palace of Pharaoh and chose the reproach of faith; and for him, because of that reproach, the seas were divided. Thus he himself is Naphtali, the vine spreading throughout the whole world, so that he might pour the abundance of the spiritual cup into all peoples. He is the one enlarged, possessing the name above every name. Because he offered himself to death for all, he therefore heard from the Father: “Return to me.” Jacob was speaking, and God was heard. Jacob was blessing, and God was resounding, saying to the Son: “Return to me”—that is, return after the Passion. Return to your seat; return with your trophy; return to me, so that the dead may follow you as you rise and may likewise rise by your power and example; so that you may become “the firstborn from the dead,” and sit at the right hand of the Father.

Hence the Son also said: “From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God” (Matt. 26:64).

### 42

Let anyone deny that blessed was Jacob at the very end of his death, when he poured forth divine oracles. Let anyone deny that blessed was Joseph in prison, where, by the spirit of wisdom, he interpreted the dreams he had heard and revealed the sequence of future events. Let anyone deny that blessed was Isaiah when he was being sawn in two; Jeremiah when he was being submerged; holy Daniel when he stood fearlessly among the lions and the prophet, snatched up by an angel, brought him a meal. He was not blessed because he ate another’s meal, but because by his merits he closed the lions’ mouths, which had not been fed.

Who would not call blessed the mother of the Maccabees, who added herself as an eighth to the funerals of her seven sons, for the praise of heavenly triumph?

## CHAPTER X

### How greatly the punishments steadfastly endured by the priest Eleazar were to his praise, so that he should truly be judged blessed

### 43

Nor will I pass you by, Eleazar, as a priest addressing a priest, though I must be aided by your prayers [Note: [Col. 0631D] All editions and many manuscripts read: “as being the priest of priests, but one to be aided by your prayers.” The Roman edition reads: “one whom you pray should be aided.” The best reading is found in the Torn., Theod., and Valc. manuscripts: “as being a priest among priests,” etc. Again, some manuscripts and all editions read: “who was a priest by lineage”; several others: “who belonged to the priestly race.” Thuan. and Remig. read: “who was priest of his nation.”]—a priest by birth, skilled in the Law, mature in age. When you were offered to Antiochus the persecutor, you could be captured neither by enticements, bent by rewards, nor broken by the severity of punishments (2 Macc. 6:18ff.).

Finally, he began with flatteries, because he judged that his torments could be overcome. “I blush,” he said, “for your gray hairs; I revere your old age; I admire your prudence. Why do you think you must abstain from the good foods that nature provides? Relax this obstinacy; awaken at last, while I still prefer to persuade you rather than compel you, lest, overcome by punishments, you do what you refuse when invited by reason.”

The old man replied: “We are not led, Antiochus, by intention [Note: [Col. 0632D] That is, by one’s own will and choice; unless perhaps the word means the same as firmness and obstinacy of mind], but are bound by reverence for the Law, which commands that we abstain from swine’s flesh. You judge this creature beautiful; yet you cannot deny that temperance is better than pleasure, and obedience to the Law better than transgression. But if you consider it a small matter that we eat swine’s flesh, then whoever despises the Law in small things—how will he keep it in great things? Or if such a creature is precious, you are claiming that, because it is beautiful, we are to be deprived of it. Our abstinence, however, is a discipline of chastity. For we learn to cut away luxury, conquer desires, exclude lusts, and oppose bodily pleasures. It is also an exercise of courage not to yield to punishments for the sake of the Law. It is likewise a mark of justice and prudence that what we have chosen to follow out of fear of God we should preserve even when death is set before us.

“Who would impose food upon free men? And who would offer himself to ridicule by serving in this matter?” [Note: [Col. 0632D] The old edition, with part of the manuscripts, reads: “should offer himself.” In this matter, let him serve, but he will not be ridiculed. The Roman edition reads: “should offer himself? Who would serve in this matter and not be ridiculed?” Several other manuscripts differ little from this; we have followed them.] “I am not so old that the courage of my spirit has not become young again.”

### 44

Thus, while he was suspended and severely beaten on every side, and his aged limbs could no longer endure the punishment of the blows, when the executioners and those who stretched him out had grown weary, he was bent toward the ground but retained an unbending mind.

Then someone, whether moved by pity for his long life or wishing to entrap him by a stratagem, said: “Answer only that you will eat; we shall preserve you from the food itself.”

But he cried out: “Far be it from me to become, in my old age, an incentive to youthful error, when until now I have been an example of a saving discipline. Shall I purchase a brief life by these mockeries and surrender the labors of my whole life for the short rations of old age? Old age ought to be a harbor, not the shipwreck of one’s former life. I shall not deny you, ancestral Law; I shall not renounce you, holy institutions of my forefathers; I shall not stain you, priestly fillets; I shall not openly disgrace you with the dust of faithlessness, my gray hairs!”

Why say more? By dying amid torments he became a lesson in perseverance for the others, though he had been chosen as an example of weakness. Blessed, therefore, was the man in whom torments could not conquer reason. Was he not blessed who, by the courage of his spirit, was able to conquer punishments and, by the oar of devotion, preserve his suffering intact amid such waves?

## CHAPTER XI

### On the marvelous patience and courage of the seven Maccabean brothers, to whom their mother was added as an eighth, and who acquired the merit of blessed life through their punishments

### 45

After him seven boys were brought forward with their mother (2 Macc. 7:1ff.). One may mock the tyrant, who, while cleverly thinking that he should begin with an old man, chose a teacher by whom he would make the pupils stronger—pupils whom he tempted to guilt by rewards because of their seemingly childish age and drove to fear by terror.

But they, not unworthy of so great a leader, replied: “Why do you despise or deceive us as children?” [Note: [Col. 0633D] After the word “children,” the Roman edition adds: “we are children,” a reading found nowhere else.] “Our faith, however, is gray with age; our discipline is strong. Try us indeed; subject these childish limbs to whatever punishments you please. You will not find childish hearts. Nor will the engines of torture be stronger than the sentinels of lawful observance. Youth, the rival of old age, will overcome the one whom old age conquered. We, the sons, follow our father; we, the disciples, follow our teacher. Gather the instruments of punishment that have been prepared. Let them witness the meditation of patience, not the terror of childish ignorance” [Note: [Col. 0633D] Many manuscripts, and not inferior ones, read: “they do not bring the terror of ignorance.”].

### 46

He ordered the eldest to be chosen. But he, laughing, said: “You rightly preserve the order of nature. But why do you think the Law of God may be violated? In devotion, indeed, we are all eldest; nevertheless, I rejoice that the beginning is made with me. What more do you seek, tyrant? I confess that we serve the supreme God, and you teach us what we ought to do. If you insist with such obstinacy on extorting the truth from us, why should we not think that we ought to hold to it with every strength?”

What more need be said? Various kinds of punishment were applied. But devotion conquered the fury of savagery: the soul was expelled, but not religion.

### 47

The second came forward and, not inferior to his brother, fulfilled the duty of a pious confession (ibid. 7ff.). When the skin of his head was stripped away, he replied: “You are indeed taking away the skin, but I have a spiritual helmet, which you cannot take away.” And truly no one can take away this helmet, as the Apostle later taught in the Church of the Lord: “For Christ is the head of the man” (1 Cor. 11:3), and “we are his members” (Eph. 5:30).

Rightly did the boy, by the divine Spirit, foresee this apostolic teaching. The savage beasts stripped the hide from his head and raged with leopard-like ferocity. But he, as he was dying, said: “How sweet it is to die for religion; how pleasing every bitterness of death is for devotion, because the reward for these labors remains! Yours, O king, are the heavier torments; you are tortured more violently by your own punishments, because you see yourself defeated in power.”

### 48

When he too had died, Antiochus ordered the third to be brought forward (2 Macc. 7:1, 10ff.). When he tried partly to entrap him by cunning and partly to strike him with terror, he answered him: “I shall not do your will; I shall not submit to your command. By that blessed suffering of my brothers, and by their nobility, I shall not deny our pious brotherhood. Apply whatever punishments you wish. By pressing this matter more fiercely and advancing through the harshness of your punishments, you will only obtain greater testimonies of our brotherhood.”

Therefore he ordered his tongue to be cut out. But the boy cried out: “You are defeated, Antiochus, since you order the organ of speech to be cut away. You have confessed that you cannot answer reason, and you approve greater scourges for our tongue than your own blows. We do not fear your blows, but you cannot endure the blows of our voice. These are the blows of devotion; your blows are those of faithlessness. Even when the tongue has been removed, it will scourge you more grievously with its falling murmur.

“Do you think you can escape, Antiochus, if you take away the voice? God hears those who are silent—indeed, he hears them more clearly. Behold, I have opened my mouth and loosened my tongue; cut off the tongue, but you will not cut off steadfastness; you will not take away courage; you will not erase reason; you will not remove the testimony of truth; you will not remove the cry of the heart. If the tongue is cut off, the blood will cry out, and it will be said to you: ‘The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me’ (Gen. 4:10). For he hears the voice of blood who hears inward thoughts, even though darkness covers them and walls surround them.

“Let the impious say that no witness stands beside him. God examines everything and sees everything; no crime can remain hidden from the Judge of all, who knows everything before it happens. Why do we waste words? Wounds are more eloquent. Even if wounds are covered, even if the scar is hidden, faith cannot be hidden. Yet do not rejoice that, by taking away the tongue, you have taken away the confession of praise. We have praised God sufficiently in speech; now let us praise him in suffering.”

### 49

When he too had been killed, Antiochus ordered the fourth to be bound to a wheel, so that by its turning all his limbs might be disjointed (ibid. 13). But while he was being tortured savagely, he said: “You are disjointing the limbs of my body, but you add grace to my suffering and do not take consolation away from my death. For there is a voice of thunder in the wheel, because, in the good and blameless course of this life, a heavenly oracle resounds, just as it resounded in John and James, the sons of thunder.” [Note: [Col. 0634D] Some think that Ambrose here suffered a lapse of memory, carried away by the force of his eloquence, since he attributes to that Maccabean the mention of the Apostles, who were brought forth many years later. But why should we not say that the holy Bishop ascribed prophetic spirit to this fourth brother in the same way that above we read of the second: “Rightly did the boy, by the divine Spirit, foresee this apostolic teaching”? Unless one prefers to enclose the words “as it resounded” in parentheses.]

“Therefore, what I read I now recognize more clearly: ‘For wheel within wheel runs, and is not hindered’” (Ezek. 1:16–17).

For a smooth life, without any offense, moves through every suffering, and within it this other wheel also runs. The Law runs within grace, and observance of the Law runs within the course of divine mercy; for the more it is turned, the more it is approved. It is better to endure adversity here at the hands of the impious, so that there we may be able to find consolation from the Lord. Thus, having completed his course, this man released his spirit and poured out his soul as a victor.

### 50

When the fifth was brought forward, Antiochus first had him beaten and then ordered fires to be applied and flames placed beneath him (ibid. 15ff.). Blood flowed from his wounds, and, as his sores were torn open, the blood that poured out extinguished the very balls of flame.

But amid the crackling of the fires he was heard saying: “I give you thanks, Lord, that you have granted us to say: ‘We passed through fire’” (Ps. 65:12). And, as your Prophet says elsewhere: “You tested us by fire, as silver is tested by fire” (ibid. 10). “I shall stand before you like gold purified by burning; and if there was any fault, the fire has burned it away.” Thus he too, transformed from corruption to incorruption, breathed out his life.

### 51

Torments were also brought against the sixth (2 Macc. 7:18–19). But he said: “Do not wander uselessly and attribute to your power the fact that you inflict these things upon us. This is the price of our sins, that we are punished because we sinned. And thanks be to the Lord that here our twofold sins are exacted from us, so that there consolation may be brought to us” [Note: [Col. 0635D] The twofold sins are, specifically, their own sins and those common to the whole nation.].

“And thanks also to you, because you are so harsh and pitiless that, through such punishments of ours, the Lord against whom we sinned may become merciful to our nation. We too lessen our distress while we rejoice in the sufferings of faith.”

And he too, torn apart by harsh and grievous punishments, was laid beside his brothers.

### 52

The youngest of the brothers remained, and Antiochus was already ashamed that he had been so mocked by one of such tender age (ibid. 24). Therefore, wishing to entrap him by deceit, he promised him honors, riches, his friendship, and a share in his secrets.

But his devout mother warned her son, saying to him, as to the others: “I do not know how you entered my womb, nor did I give you spirit, nor did I form your limbs. These are gifts of almighty God” (ibid. 22).

Antiochus, seeing that the mother was anxious, thought that she feared for her son’s safety. He therefore began to urge her also to recall her son from his purpose. But she said to her son in her ancestral voice:

“You alone remain, my son, the summit of my hopes. You were the last to close my labor; you are the last to complete my joys. Take pity on me, who carried you in my womb for so many months. Do not disgrace my old age in a single moment; do not tarnish the trophies of so many of your brothers; do not abandon their sacred company; do not forsake their fellowship. Those triumphs still await you.

“Look up to heaven, from which you drew your spirit, to the Father of all. Look upon the earth, which first supplied you with nourishment. Look upon your brothers, who seek a companion. Look upon your mother, who gave you milk. Repay the reward of devoted blood. Do not be torn from your brothers; do not be torn from your mother.

“The riches Antiochus promises are temporal, and temporal are the honors; but the crown bestowed by almighty God is eternal. The Lord gave me the lights of seven days; I have already closed the sixth day, and all the works were very good. You owe it to me, my son, that, after I labored through six days in them, I may rest in you on the seventh, as though now released from the works of the world.”

Then the young man sprang forward and said: “What are you waiting for?” (ibid. 30ff.). Shouting many things, since he could in no way be separated from the fellowship of his brothers—for their funerals were far more blessed than the commands of the king—he assailed the king with reproaches. Then, himself tortured by cruel forms of torment, he completed the course of this life.

### 53

Last of all, the mother was offered to death (ibid. 41). Who would deny that she was blessed—she who, as though enclosed by seven offerings [Note: [Col. 0636D] The Roman edition reads: “enclosed by mural gifts.” All the others, together with the manuscripts, read: “enclosed by gifts,” that is, by offerings and sacrifices with which she made offering to God. The Vatican manuscript has in the margin: “or, by funerals.” This reading is not inappropriate.] amid the bodies of her sons, felt no assault of death?

Who, I ask, would doubt her blessedness? She, surrounded as if by seven towers, raised her head to its place in paradise. Surrounded by seven sons, she brought into the heavenly altars a choir most sacred to God—not only with melodious voices, but also with sufferings—to sing praises to the Lord.

How good was this offspring of faith; how safe was this harbor of devotion; how splendid was this lamp of the Church, shining with sevenfold light [Note: [Col. 0636D] Thus read all the manuscripts and editions except the Roman, which has: “and from the eighth womb.” A vessel may indeed have been called a *uterus* figuratively, or perhaps the reference is to the body of the lamp itself.] and, with an eighth womb, supplying oil to all the lights!

Of these it is beautifully said: “Give a portion to seven, and indeed also to eight” (Eccles. 11:2), because in both numbers they share in grace: nourished in the Law, crowned through grace—seven as in the Sabbath, eight as in the Gospel—with the devout mother added as a supplement to their suffering. In such sons she both conceived and gave birth to the complete form of devotion.

## CHAPTER XII

### A most elegant commendation of that blessed woman, the mother of the seven martyr sons

### 54

The words of the holy woman to her sons return to our memory: “I gave birth to you; I poured into you the nourishment of milk. Do not lose your nobility.” Other mothers are accustomed to call their sons back from martyrdom, not to summon them to it. But this mother regarded it as the expression of maternal affection to urge her sons toward the life that is more enduring rather than the temporal one.

Thus the devout mother watched the struggles of her sons. Although she was shaken by the compassion of maternal entrails, nevertheless, out of devotion, she suppressed her grief. When Antiochus offered her the possibility of choosing the safety of her sons, she preferred danger; restraining the groans of nature, she wished their punishments to be increased, so that death might approach more quickly. We see a mother’s wishes turned toward her sons—not that she might leave one of them surviving, but that she might gain them all as pious co-heirs of death.

### 55

Nor were the sons inferior to such a parent. They encouraged one another, saying with one purpose and, as it were, with a united force of spirit: “Let us trample upon the assault of hostile death” [Note: [Col. 0637C] All editions read: “let us seek the assault.” All manuscripts read: “let us trample upon the assault,” except one Vatican manuscript, which has: “let us prefer the assault.”].

“For then we shall live, when we have died. Let no one abandon the order of devotion; let no one withdraw from the battle of triumph. We have devoted our souls not to a human being, but to almighty God; we serve not a human being, but the Creator of all. Such is this battle that the one who is killed more cruelly will have conquered more gloriously.”

Therefore no one was afraid, no one trembled, and among so many brothers no one was slower to meet death. Rather, as though they were going along the road to immortality, so they hastened through harsh punishments toward death. Their mother, seeing the ranks of her sons moving in harmony, offered them as a devout soul might offer the limbs of its own body in her sons; and she seemed to undergo the desired torments through her own members.

### 56

The sons, their bodies ulcerated by torments, fell; the dead were heaped upon the dead; bodies were rolled upon bodies; heads were cut off one after another. The place was filled with the corpses of her sons. The mother did not weep or lament; she did not close the eyes of any of them or shut the mouth of the dying; she did not wash their wounds, knowing that they would appear more glorious if they were seen with their entrails torn out and their bodies clotted alike with dust and blood, as victors customarily return from war, as they customarily carry trophies back from their enemies.

She judged that no coverings should be laid over them and no funeral procession conducted, except in the company of her own death as well.

What lyre could produce sweeter songs than those uttered by her dying sons amid such grievous punishments? Nature’s groaning burst forth, even against their will. You would see the corpses of the slain in succession, like the strings of a lyre; you would hear a seven-stringed psaltery resounding with triumphant groans.

The alluring songs of those Sirens, as they are said to have been, would not draw a listener in this way: they led men to shipwreck, whereas these led to the victory of sacrifice. Nor would the swans’ songs soothe the ears and spirit in this way: swans die by the lot of nature, whereas these died out of love for devotion. Nor do the hoarse murmurs of doves resound secretly in a grove as sweetly as the final words of the dying resounded.

Nor does the moon shine among the stars as the mother shone among her sons, both when she led them forth to martyrdom to illuminate them and when, having embraced them as victors, she lay among her sons.

### 57

O true mother, stronger than adamant, sweeter than honey, more fragrant than a flower! O unbreakable bond of devotion! O truly powerful love, hard as death, cruel as the underworld in its zeal for devotion and faith! [Note: [Col. 0637C] The Roman edition alone reads: “Love is strong as death, jealousy hard as the underworld.” The Septuagint supports that reading; in them this passage of Song of Songs 8:6 is written: “For love is strong as death, jealousy hard as Hades” (*ὅτι κραταιὰ ὡς θάνατος ἀγάπη, σκληρὸς ὡς ἅδης ζῆλος*).]

No floods of such great sufferings could exclude your love; no rivers of such great bitterness could overwhelm it. As the ark was carried unharmed through the spaces of the whole world during that flood of the world, so you too stood immovable in devotion against the waves of such grievous sufferings. Although you could have chosen the safety of your sons, you did not wish to do so.

### 58

With what affection shall I follow you, holy mother’s devout pledges? With what brush of my speech shall I portray the likeness of your appearance and your souls? You stood among royal armies, to which the whole world had been subjected, armies that even India, withdrawing into the remotest recesses of the sea, did not avoid. Yet you alone brought back victory over the proud king without a battle.

In you, the weapons of devotion alone conquered. The tyrant paid the penalty—both because he could not conquer you and because he was himself killed by a cruel death.

# [ON JOSEPH THE PATRIARCH]

## INTRODUCTION TO THE BOOK ON JOSEPH THE PATRIARCH

From the beginning of this work Ambrose himself professes that he was led by the order of the sacred books (chapter 1, no. 1) to meditate somewhat also upon the history of Joseph after publishing books on Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Accordingly, after expounding in Abraham the tireless devotion of faith—that is, a mind most obedient to divine commands (ibid.)—in Isaac the purity of a sincere mind—that is, a mind which, after being cleansed of all the stains and filth of the age, enters into a certain intimate covenant of spiritual marriage with the eternal Word—and finally in Jacob the singular patience of soul and of labors, by whose benefit blessedness is retained even amid the most atrocious misfortunes, he was not content merely to celebrate all these virtues in writing. He decided to set forth in Joseph something still more explicit and determinate, since Joseph’s chief praise rests upon chastity.

In our previous Introductions it has been explained how the holy Bishop, by expounding the virtues of those first patriarchs, demonstrated them through their histories. Now we must briefly inquire how he accomplished the same thing in the history of Joseph.

First he teaches that Joseph is proposed to us as a mirror of chastity (ibid., no. 2), since that virtue, together with the particular brightness of grace that accompanies chastity, shines forth most perfectly in all his character and deeds. Since the purity of the holy youth nowhere shone with greater splendor than when Potiphar’s wife, in whose household he served, attempted to undermine it by manifold seductions and most wicked efforts, Saint Ambrose therefore praises this singular ornament of the patriarch with the full force of his eloquence, although he confined that extremely difficult and perilous struggle to a single chapter (chapter 5). There he discloses every kind of enticement and every device by which corrupt women undertake to corrupt the men they love and to conquer their self-control. He magnifies the steadfastness and prudence by which Saint Joseph made her requests fruitless, sometimes by resisting, sometimes by fleeing. He inserts along the way admonitions of the greatest usefulness for the formation of character. Finally, while commending this most chaste victor, he says without the slightest hesitation: “For the sake of chastity he underwent martyrdom” (ibid., no. 26)—namely, when, for the sake of that heavenly virtue, he allowed himself to be dragged into chains, wholly unconcerned to refute his mistress’s accusations.

Besides this praise, there are many other features in Joseph’s life that deserve the closest consideration. The blessed Doctor did not wish to pass over them in silence, but treated them in a manner he had not previously employed in adorning the deeds of the ancient patriarchs. He begins (chapter 1, no. 3) with the envy that had provoked the brothers against Joseph. Taking that as his occasion, and prefacing several observations concerning the equality that parents ought to display in their love for their children, he demonstrates that Joseph was a type and figure of Christ the Lord in his dreams (chapter 2).

Then, reviewing with sufficient accuracy everything that is read in Genesis concerning the holy patriarch, he teaches that nearly all Joseph’s actions correspond mystically and figuratively to Christ, and that Joseph himself must therefore be regarded as the true Joseph of Scripture. He proves this so precisely that he shows many words of Joseph from the book of Genesis and of Christ from the Gospel, set opposite one another, to possess the closest kinship (chapters 12 and 13).

Finally, since the other sons of Jacob also have their parts in this same history, he does not leave them unmentioned. He teaches that in Benjamin was displayed the image of Paul, whom he praises with exceptional distinction; while in the other brothers was represented the faithlessness and savagery of the Jews, against whom he inveighs, although he also indicates that they themselves will eventually come to faith.

The devout Doctor intersperses throughout the whole work frequent explanations and instructions conducive to the conduct of the Christian people. Nevertheless, he labors more intensely to draw out the mystical meaning. Hence one may justly conclude in a word that this book contains nothing other than a mystical exposition of all that is recorded in Genesis concerning holy Joseph, from the account of his dreams to his undertaking the journey to meet his father, who was coming to him in Egypt.

It is by no means obscure that this work, like all the preceding ones since the books *On Abraham*, consists of sermons delivered at Milan. But since we have stated above that the date of the others can be determined chiefly from the time at which these sermons were delivered, we must now make that point clear and certain. We think there is no stronger argument for this purpose than the words spoken by the holy Bishop on the occasion of one of Pharaoh’s two eunuchs, to whom Joseph prophesied in prison the final punishment of the cross.

For another eunuch is described there (chapter 6, no. 33), who, two years earlier, swollen with the emperor’s favor, had inflicted such an insult upon the Church that our Saint was compelled to blunt it with words which he already disliked remembering. This same eunuch, like another Doeg, stirred up the king by deceit against the priest—that is, against Ambrose himself—and, like another Haman, cruelly harassing and tormenting the orthodox people, left no stone unturned in order to deprive them of their churches and to assign them to the Arians, whose impiety he followed.

At last his madness increased to such a degree that he threatened others—namely, the holy Bishop—with danger of death. But without observing what the holy man had foretold to him, he himself was soon to be handed over to the ultimate punishment (ibid., no. 34). And in fact, not long afterward, he fell from the emperor’s favor. Although that impious man fled to the servant of Christ—whose divinity he denied—that is, to Ambrose, whom he had pursued with such insolence, he was nevertheless soon beheaded by the executioner’s sword.

From this entire sequence of the discourse it can be learned that Ambrose cultivated and, as it were, clothed this history with all its circumstances so carefully that nothing seemed lacking except the name of the person whom the narrative concerned. This certainly could not have been unknown to his hearers; nor would it have been difficult for us to discover him, if we chose to compare this passage with what our Ambrose himself wrote to his sister Marcellina concerning the persecution he had suffered from the empress Justina and the other Arians. For at the end of that letter he speaks as follows:

“Finally, even in an explicit statement, Calligonus, the chamberlain, dared to order me: ‘While I live, you show contempt for Valentinian’” (Epistle 14, to Marcellina, near the end).

Clearly, this was because he refused to comply with that impious man’s orders, especially the orders by which he was instructed to hand over one of the Catholic churches to the Arians so that they might hold their assemblies there. “I shall cut off your head,” said that arrogant eunuch. Ambrose merely replied with those few words: “May God grant that you fulfill what you threaten. For I shall suffer what bishops suffer; you will do what eunuchs do,” and so forth. It is probable that these were the words whose memory the holy man now indicates that he wished to erase. If anyone wishes to know how that same eunuch suffered the punishment which he had threatened against the holy Bishop, Augustine makes this clear in the following words: “We know that Calligonus, the eunuch of the younger Valentinian, was punished by the avenging sword, having been convicted by the confession of a prostitute” (*Book VI Against Julian the Pelagian*, chapter 14).

Accordingly, to determine the time at which this book was written, what remains except to investigate the year in which Ambrose sent this letter to Marcellina? We believe that no one would act rashly who assigned the year 385 to that letter, namely the year in which Justina’s first persecution against the Catholics broke out during the Easter celebrations, and in which it flared up again during the same holy days of the following year. It must therefore be said that these sermons on the patriarch Joseph were delivered in the year 387, when Italy remained peaceful until the month of August, in which that same tyrant invaded it, while Ambrose himself had returned from his embassy to Maximus the tyrant. Certainly both the earlier books (*On Isaac and the Soul*, chapter 4, section 37, and elsewhere) and this work of which we are speaking indicate clearly enough that the blessed Doctor spoke during a period of peace. Indeed, in several passages (*On the Good of Death*, chapter 12, section 53, and elsewhere) it is suggested that at that time the Church was being enriched by the accession of those who were recovering from heresy. This could easily have happened after the end of the Arian persecution, over which Ambrose triumphed with such honor and not without a miracle.

If our reckoning of the time is correct, there can be no doubt that among the other hearers of Ambrose, and likewise among the catechumens whom he baptized in that year, 387, the great Augustine must also be counted. Moreover, since Augustine is read to have approved in a remarkable way the method by which our Saint, expounding Scripture spiritually and mystically, instructed people to adhere not to the letter that kills but to the Spirit who gives life (*Augustine, Confessions*, book VI, chapter 4, section 6), there is no reason for anyone to doubt that these treatises on the Patriarchs greatly pleased him—especially the books on Isaac and Joseph, in which the mystical and hidden meaning is unfolded and explained with such elegance.

We do not think that Ambrose should be passed over at this point, since he appears to indicate more than once (chapter 6, section 30, and chapter 7, section 38) that he had already explained this very history, perhaps in the preceding year, when, at the appointed season, that portion of Genesis was read according to custom. Those first sermons on Joseph have perished; and in this commentary the holy Bishop testifies that, at the time when he delivered them, he wished to remain silent about Calligonus. This was a mark of remarkable modesty and charity: scarcely two years having passed, he was permitted to mention an event of such exceptional importance, which he knew would be useful to the minds of his people. But that restraint shone no less brightly in the fact that he excuses Valentinian, whose ministers, under imperial authority, had raged against him with such cruelty (chapter 6, section 35).

[Col. 0641B]

**ONE BOOK OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON JOSEPH THE PATRIARCH.**  
[Note: [Col. 0641A] Written around the year 387.] (C)

[Col. 0641]

**483 CHAPTER ONE**

Why the history of Saint Joseph follows the treatises on Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Joseph is presented here as a mirror of chastity; brief discussion is also given to his parents’ love, his brothers’ envy against him, and his forgetting of injuries.

[Col. 0641A]

**1.** The life of the saints is a rule of life for others. Therefore we receive the sequence of Scripture in fuller order, so that, as by reading we come to know Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other righteous men, we may follow, as it were, a path of innocence opened for us by their virtue, advancing in their footsteps. Although I have often treated these subjects, today the history of Saint Joseph presents itself. In him there were many kinds of virtue, but chastity shone forth with particular distinction. It is therefore right that, having learned in Abraham an untiring devotion of faith, in Isaac the purity of a sincere mind, and in Jacob a singular endurance of spirit and labors, you should turn your attention from that generality of virtues to the particular forms of instruction. For although the former are more extensive, the latter are more clearly defined, and they penetrate the mind more easily because they are more circumscribed and determinate.

**2.** Let Saint Joseph, then, be set before us as a mirror of chastity. In his character and in his actions, modesty shines, and a certain radiance of grace, the companion of chastity, gleams. For this reason he was loved by his parents more than the other sons. But that circumstance gave rise to envy, and it must not be passed over in silence.

**484 3.** From this, then, the plot of the entire history proceeded, so that we may also learn that the perfect man is not moved by the injury that provokes the pain of revenge, nor does he repay evils in kind.

[Note: [Col. 0641A] All printed editions, following the reading “imitating the footsteps”; all manuscripts read “pressing forward with the footsteps,” and so forth.]

Hence David also says: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil” (Psalm 7:5). But what would there be by which Joseph deserved to be preferred to the others if he had injured those who injured him, or loved those who loved him? Most people do this. But what is marvelous is to love one’s enemy, as the Savior teaches (Matthew 5:44). Rightly, therefore, he is worthy of admiration who did this before the Gospel: though injured, he spared; though attacked, he forgave; though sold, he did not return the injury, but repaid insult with kindness. After the Gospel we have all learned this, yet we cannot practice it.

[Col. 0643A]

**4.** Let us therefore learn also about the envy of the saints, so that we may imitate their patience; and let us recognize that they were not of a nature superior to ours, but superior in discipline; they did not fail to know vices, but corrected them. If envy scorched even the saints, how much more must we beware lest it inflame sinners?

## CHAPTER II

That parents’ affection and the children’s favor ought to be equal. Blessed Jacob is nevertheless excused, since he preferred Joseph to the others because he was adorned with greater virtues—or rather, since Joseph was already endowed with the gift of prophecy, as his dreams, expounded here, make clear.

**5.** We are therefore instructed what the affection of parents and the favor shown to children ought to be. To love children is sweet, and to love them with greater devotion is exceedingly sweet; but paternal love frequently harms children unless it observes moderation—whether excessive indulgence makes the beloved child undisciplined, or the preference shown to one turns the others away from fraternal affection. More is gained for a son when he gains the love of his brothers. This is the more splendid generosity of fathers; this is the richer inheritance of children. Let equal favor unite those whom equal nature has joined. Piety knows no monetary profit where the loss is a loss of affection. Why are you surprised that quarrels arise among brothers over a field or a house, when envy flared up among the holy sons of Jacob because of a tunic?

[Note: [Col. 0643D] The edition together with most manuscripts reads “loosen the offense.” The ancient editions and the Vatican, Albi, and Valcian manuscripts read “loosen the beloved one.” This is excellent: it means “make the beloved son more lax in his way of life.”]

**6.** What, then? Is Jacob to be blamed because he preferred one to the others? But we cannot take freedom away from parents, lest they love more those whom they believe deserve more; nor ought we cut off from children the effort to please more. In the end, Jacob loved him more in whom he foresaw greater signs of virtue, so that the father seems not so much to have preferred his son as the prophet to have preferred a mystery. Accordingly, he made him a variegated tunic, signifying that he was to be preferred to his brothers, clothed in a diversity of virtues.

**7.** Finally, divine grace shone forth in the boy while he was still young. He dreamed that, when he had bound sheaves with his brothers, as it seemed to him in a vision, his sheaf rose and stood upright; but the sheaves of his brothers, having turned toward his sheaf, bowed down to it (Genesis 37:7). In this, surely, the future resurrection of the Lord Jesus was revealed: when they saw him in Jerusalem, the eleven disciples worshiped him, and all the saints, when they have risen, will worship him, bringing forward the fruits of good works, as it is written: “Coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm 125:6).

Although the brothers, because of envy, weakened the credibility of the dream, they nevertheless expressed its interpretation in their own words when they answered him: “Will you perhaps reign over us as king, or rule over us as lord?” (Genesis 37:8). That vision signified the King who was to come, before whom every human being would bend the knee in worship.

**8.** He saw another dream and recounted it to his father and his brothers: the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were worshiping him. His father therefore rebuked him, saying: “What then is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers come and worship you upon the earth?” (ibid., verse 10). Who is the one whom his parents and brothers worshiped upon the earth except Christ Jesus, when Joseph and his mother worshiped him together with the disciples, confessing the true God in that body? Of him alone it was said: “Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light” (Psalm 148:3).

But what does the father’s rebuke signify except the hardness of the people of Israel, from whom Christ was descended according to the flesh? Even today they do not believe that he is God, nor do they wish to worship him as Lord, because they recognize that he was born from them. They hear his answers, therefore, but do not understand them. They themselves read that the sun and moon praise him, yet they refuse to believe that this was spoken of Christ Jesus. Thus Jacob is mistaken through the figure belonging to another, but he is not mistaken in his own love. His paternal devotion does not err; rather, it expresses the affection of the people destined to err.

**486 CHAPTER III**

That Jacob’s rebuke of Joseph, mentioned above, was not made out of unbelief, since he knew beforehand of the future Incarnation and sent Joseph to his brothers. After Joseph wandered in the field, he came to Dothaim. His brothers saw him from a distance and planned to kill him, but, changing their plan, sold him to the Ishmaelites. These events, together with the bloodying of the tunic and the dryness of the pit, are applied as symbols to the mystery of the Passion.

[Col. 0644C]

**9.** The Patriarch, therefore, did not fail to believe such a remarkable dream, since through a twofold prophetic oracle he was proclaiming both things at once: that he might represent both the person of the righteous man and the people, and that the Son of God would come upon the earth, loved by the righteous and denied by the faithless. He was therefore contemplating the mysteries of the future Incarnation when he sent his son to his brothers (Genesis 37:14), “to see whether the sheep were well.”

[Note: [Col. 0644D] The Roman edition reads: “whether it was well with the brothers and the sheep.”]

What sheep was God already seeking at that time through the zeal of that Patriarch, except those of whom the Lord Jesus himself said in the Gospel: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24)?

[Note: [Col. 0644D] The Roman edition reads: “And he came,” it says, “to Shechem.”]

“And he sent him,” it says, “to Shechem” (Genesis 37:13), a name which by interpretation means “shoulder,” or “back”—that is, to those who would not turn toward the Lord, but, fleeing, would turn away from his face; this is characteristic of the sinner. Cain went out from the face of God. And the Prophet says: “You shall make them turn their back” (Psalm 20:13). But the righteous man does not turn away from the Lord; he runs to meet him, saying: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Psalm 24:15).

And when the Lord said through Isaiah, “Whom shall I send?” (Isaiah 6:8), Isaiah voluntarily offered himself, saying: “Here am I.” Simeon also waited to see the Christ of the Lord, and after he had seen him—because he had seen him as the forgiver of sins and the Redeemer of the whole world—he, as one lifted up from sin, asked to be released from the use of this bodily life, saying: “Now, Lord, dismiss your servant in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:30–31). Zacchaeus likewise first found the distinction of his commendation in this: he climbed a tree in order to see Christ.

Joseph, therefore, was sent by his father to his brothers by that greater Father who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all; by that Father of whom it is written: “God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8:3).

**10.** Joseph wandered because he could not find his brothers (Genesis 37:15). Not without reason did he wander, since he was seeking those who were wandering; for the Lord recognizes those who are his own. Thus Jesus, wearied from his journey, sat beside the well. He was weary because he was not finding the people of God whom he sought; for they had gone out from the face of the Lord. Whoever follows sin goes out from Christ. The sinner goes out; the righteous person enters. Thus Adam, as a sinner, hid himself, but the righteous person says: “Let my prayer enter into your presence” (Psalm 87:3).

**11.** Joseph found his brothers in Dothaim, which signifies “defection.” Where is one found, if not in defection, when he abandons God? Nor is it surprising that they were falling away, since they did not heed him who said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28).

Joseph therefore came to Dothaim. “And they saw him coming from a distance, before he approached them, and they raged against him in order to kill him” (Genesis 37:18). They were rightly far away, since they were in defection; and they raged because Christ had not drawn near to them. For if the figure of Christ had drawn near to them, they would surely have loved their brother. But those who were planning fratricide could not be near.

“Behold,” they said, “that dreamer is coming. Come now, let us kill him” (ibid., verse 19). Were these not the words of men plotting sacrilegious murder? As Solomon says of them: “Let us remove the righteous man, because he is useless to us” (Wisdom 2:12).

**12.** They added in Genesis: “And we shall see what his dreams will profit him” (Genesis 37:20). This was written about Joseph, but it was fulfilled in Christ when the Jews said during his Passion: “If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let him now deliver him, if he wants him” (Matthew 27:42).

Were those brothers also so impious that they would kill their brother? And how could the merits of so many Patriarchs have been such that the Law should designate the whole people by their names?

[Note: [Col. 0645D] Several manuscripts and the American and Gill editions read “the Law of the whole people … was designated by their names.” The Erasmian and Roman editions read “the flock of the whole people was designated by their names.” But the majority of the better manuscripts read “the Law designated the twelve tribes of the whole people ….” This is excellent, since here “Law” means the books of Moses, in which the twelve tribes are repeatedly expressed by the names of the Patriarchs.]

How do the names of piety agree with the marks of wickedness? In this way: these men too, as a type of the people, were afflicted not by a defect of character. Hence all the envy, hence the plotting of murder: envy according to the figure, piety according to their affection.

**13.** Finally, Reuben and Judah, preserving the pious rights of brotherhood, wanted to rescue him from the hands of the others. Judah is rightly preferred in the paternal blessing when it is said to him: “The sons of your father shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49:8–9). This applies uniquely to Christ, for whom it was ordained that he be worshiped by his brothers and awaited by the nations, and that he wash his robe in wine through the Passion of his own body, since he stained his flesh with no blemish of sin.

Nor did Asher believe that the words applied to him: “Asher’s bread is rich, and Asher himself is among princes.”

[Note: [Col. 0645D] The Roman edition alone reads: “and Asher himself shall give food to princes.”]

But what of Joseph himself, to whom it was said: “Joseph is a son who shall grow, Joseph is a son who shall grow; my jealous son, my younger son, return to me” (ibid., verse 22)? Against him they took counsel and cursed, yet blessing prevailed over the blessings of the everlasting mountains and over the desires of the eternal hills. Whom did they understand to be signified in him except the one who, surpassing the merits of all, would hold the summit of immeasurable power above all the desires of the saints, whom no one could equal in longing?

Thus, in the Patriarchs, envy is balanced by grace: they are both excused from guilt and consecrated by the gift of revelation.

[Note: [Col. 0645D] Above, Ambrose asserts that the Patriarchs truly fell into guilt (chapter 1, section 4); here, and in the following section, he attempts to lessen it on account of the mystery. He used the same kind of argument when discussing Abraham’s intercourse with Hagar (*On Abraham*, book I, chapter 4). But we do not think that Ambrose thereby intended to remove every consideration of guilt, although Augustine understood the matter differently.]

For it is not so culpable to have said what belongs to the people as it is blessed to have seen what belongs to Christ. They assumed the role of the sinful people in order to receive the grace of the Lord Redeemer. Certainly grace erased guilt; guilt did not diminish grace.

**14.** And so that we may recognize that all this is a mystery concerning the people and the Lord Jesus, Scripture says: “Come, let us sell Joseph to the Ishmaelites” (Genesis 37:27). What interpretation does the name Joseph have except that it signifies divine grace and the manifestation of the Most High God? Who, then, is sold except the one who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7)?

For we would not have bought him unless his own people had sold him. His own people sold him badly; foreigners bought him worse.

[Note: [Col. 0646D] All editions and the Vatican, Fulda, German, and Theodorian manuscripts read: “Unless his own people had sold him. They sold badly; they bought worse.” The Laudian, Benignian, Tornacian, Valcian, and Colbertine manuscripts read: “Unless his own people had sold him. They sold him badly,” and so forth. The Corbie manuscript reads: “Unless they had sold him. His own people sold him badly,” and so forth. Finally, the Michaelian, Albian, and Ebronian manuscripts read: “Unless they had sold him. His own people sold him badly; foreigners bought him worse.” This reading seemed to us superior to the others.]

They sold him to merchants as a good fragrance; they bought him from traitors.

[Note: [Col. 0646D] All editions and two manuscripts read “to merchants of good fragrance”; the others read “a good fragrance.”]

Judas sold him; the Ishmaelites bought him, and in the Latin interpretation they signify those who hate their God. For this reason in one place we find Joseph purchased for twenty, in another for twenty-five, and in another for thirty pieces of gold, because Christ is not valued by everyone at the same price. To some he is worth less, to others more. The faith of the buyer is the increase of the merchandise: to the more religious, God is more precious; to the sinner, the Redeemer is more precious. He is worth more to the one who possesses more grace; but he is also worth more to the one who has been forgiven much, because the one to whom more has been forgiven loves more, as the Lord himself declared in the Gospel concerning the woman who poured ointment over his feet, washed them with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and dried them with her kisses. He said to Simon: “For this reason I say to you: Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much. But the one to whom little is forgiven loves little” (Luke 7:47).

At times, differences in price express not only quantity but also number.

[Note: [Col. 0647D] The Valcian manuscripts read: “but also an expression of the mystery.”]

Thus you have the example of the ointment which the Lord remembered as having been poured out for his burial, as it is written in Judas’s words: “This could have been sold for three hundred denarii” (Mark 14:5). In that number, not quantity but the sign of the cross seems to have been expressed.

So here too the difference between twenty or thirty pieces of gold or silver contains an indication either of doubled or of tripled perfection. For twenty-five pieces of gold, the number of the Jubilee, which is the number of remission, signify the most precious portion.

Here too, so that you may recognize the figure of the Lord’s Passion, the Patriarch Judah says: “Let us sell Joseph to the Ishmaelites, but let our hands not be laid upon him” (Genesis 37:27).

[Note: [Col. 0647D] The Roman edition reads: “Earlier Reuben had said.” In fact, the words reported there are attributed in Scripture to Reuben alone. Yet the agreement of all the other editions and manuscripts leads us to believe that Ambrose also attributed them to Judah, especially since he stated above that both men were concerned to rescue Joseph.]

And earlier he had said: “Do not lay hands upon him” (ibid., verse 22). This is what the Jews said during the Lord’s Passion: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” (John 18:31), so that Jesus’ saying might be fulfilled, signifying by what death he was to die.

**15.** Even then, therefore, the emblem of the future cross was prefigured, as was also the fact that he was stripped of his tunic (Genesis 37:23): that is, he was stripped of the flesh he had assumed, adorned with the beautiful diversity of virtues. Thus his tunic—that is, his flesh—was stained with blood, not his divinity; and they were able to take away from him the garment of flesh, but not the immortality of life. The Jewish beasts stained this tunic with blood, those of whom he says: “Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves” (Luke 10:3).

[Col. 0647D]

**16.** But what wonder is it that the pit of the Jews had no water because it was dry (Genesis 37:24), since they abandoned the fountain of living water and made for themselves broken cisterns? And so that you may know that this is truly a mystery, the Lord himself says of himself: “They placed me in the lowest pit, in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Psalm 87:7).

**489**

**17.** Those, then, purchase Christ who bring good fragrances, incense with which they perfume the altars of a devout mind. Hence David also says in Greek:

> Κατευθυνθήτω ἡ προσευχή μου ὡς θυμίαμα ἐνώπιόν σου

“Let my prayer be directed like incense before you” (Psalm 140:2).

Resin, too, with which broken marble is joined together, is a spiritual resin that strengthens the fractures of your soul, joins together what has been torn apart, and binds what has come loose. This spiritual resin strengthens and restores the scattered members of the soul, so that they may be joined without offense.

Finally, Jeremiah seeks this resin in order to heal Babylon, if it can be healed, saying: “Take resin for its corruption, if perhaps it may be healed. We have healed Babylon, and it was not healed” (Jeremiah 51:8–9). The Synagogue was not healed because this resin migrated to the Church. Therefore merchants came from Gilead—that is, from the possession or dwelling-place of testimony—transferring their merchandise to the Church so that this resin might heal the sins of the nations.

Of them it is said: “Strengthen the weak hands and the feeble knees” (Isaiah 35:3). Sincere faith is resin. Peter applied it when he said to the lame man: “In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6); and rightly he rose and walked. Peter possessed it when he said to the paralytic: “Aeneas, the Lord Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed.” And he rose and made his bed (Acts 9:34). He possessed it when he said to the dead woman: “Rise in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” And the dead woman rose (ibid., verse 40). By the tempering of this resin those stones are joined together from which the Lord is able to raise up children for Abraham. By the medicine of this resin the lame man is raised, the paralytic restored, and the dead woman brought back to life.

[Col. 0648C]

**18.** The fact also that they sprinkled his tunic with a kid’s blood (Genesis 37:32) seems to signify that, attacking him with false testimonies, they brought into hatred the one who forgives the sins of all. To us he is a lamb; to them, a goat. To us the Lamb of God was slain, he who took away the sin of the world; to them he is a goat, since he heaped up their errors and accumulated their offenses. Therefore he says: “Fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matthew 23:32).

Rightly, then, Jacob, lamenting the loss suffered by his descendants, mourned the lost son as a father and grieved the destruction of the Jews as a prophet. Finally, he also tore his garments. We read that this was done during the Lord’s Passion by the high priest (Matthew 26:65), in whom there was not a private person but the office of a public function. The veil of the Temple was also torn (Matthew 27:51), so that these signs might reveal that the profaned mysteries, the people stripped of their saving garments, and the divided kingdom were destined to be destroyed, since every kingdom divided against itself will quickly be destroyed. And truly it was divided, when what belonged to Christ began also to belong to the devil. For those who separated the Son from the Father could not remain undivided.

**490 CHAPTER IV**

Joseph is taken to Egypt and bought by the chief cook, in whom there is a figure of Christ, who liberates us through his servitude. In Joseph it is shown that freedom can be retained in captivity itself, and that captivity can also be found in freedom. Finally, Joseph is proposed to all as an example.

[Col. 0649A]

**19.** Joseph was therefore sold, taken to Egypt, and bought by the chief cook.

[Note: [Col. 0649D] The Roman edition prefixed this sentence: “Joseph, however, was taken to Egypt, and he bought him,” and so forth.]

This is not an insignificant person, who cooked raw foods so that minds might feast upon the sweetness of faith. For no food is sweeter than knowledge and doctrine. In Egypt there had previously been raw unbelief, which no ardor for divine knowledge and no desire for true wisdom had softened; the fiery utterances of the Lord had not boiled it down.

Joseph was sold in Egypt because Christ was to come to those to whom it was said: “You have been sold because of your sins” (Isaiah 50:1). And so, by his own blood, he redeemed those whom their own sins had sold.

But Christ, by assuming a condition, not by assuming guilt, is not bound by the price of sin, because he himself committed no sin.

[Note: [Col. 0649D] The Erasmian, Gillian, and Roman editions read “and by the price of sin”; the American edition and all manuscripts read “by the price of sin.” Again, where all editions and six manuscripts read “is bound,” an equal number of other manuscripts read “is not bound,” doubtless because of the following words, “because he committed no sin,” and so forth. But, for our Doctor’s meaning to be understood, the passage should be explained as though it read in this order: “by assuming a condition, not guilt, because he himself committed no sin, he is not bound by the price of sin.” Further on, the old editions read: “Thus they incurred our debt by a price, not their own liability.” The Roman edition: “Thus he incurred our debt by a price, not his own liability.” The Theodorian and Valcian manuscripts: “Thus he incurred our debt by a price, not his own liability.” Finally, all the others read as in the text, where *pretio* means “by a price,” namely the price which he undertook to pay.]

Thus he took upon himself the debt that was ours, not his own; he removed the bond, dismissed the moneylender, stripped the debtor of his obligation: one man paid what was owed by all.

[Note: [Col. 0650D] Quite a few manuscripts read “he discharged the obligation.”]

It was not permitted us to leave slavery. He undertook this on our behalf, so that he might drive away the world’s slavery, restore the freedom of paradise, and bestow a new grace through the honor of fellowship with him. This concerns the mystery.

**20.** As for the moral meaning, because the Lord our God wills all to be saved, through Joseph he also gave consolation to those who are in servitude. He provided instruction, so that they might learn that even in the lowest condition character can be superior, and that no state is deprived of virtue if each person’s mind knows itself; that the flesh is subject to slavery, but not the mind; and that many servants are freer than their masters if, though placed in servitude, they believe they must abstain from servile works.

Every sin is servile; innocence is free. Hence the Lord also says: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (Romans 6:16). For how could the miser not be a slave, when for a small profit of money he auctions himself? He fears everything lest he lose what he has amassed, although he amassed it not for use; and the greater the things he has acquired, the greater the danger with which he preserves them.

[Note: [Col. 0650D] All editions read this, as do most manuscripts. Some manuscripts of good quality, however, read “for a little money.” This is not unreasonable.]

How could the man who possesses little not be a beggar? Even if he appears rich to me, he is needy in his own eyes; nor does he comfort his desires with testimony, since he does not know how to believe in what he longs for.

How, moreover, could that man not be a slave who is subject to lust? First he burns in his own fires and is consumed by the torches of his own breast.

[Note: [Col. 0650D] All editions read “and by the torches of his sin”; all manuscripts read “and by the torches of his breast,” and so forth.]

To such people the prophet rightly says: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled” (Isaiah 50:11). He takes upon himself every fear and lies in wait for everyone’s sleep; in order to possess one person through desire, he becomes the slave of all. He therefore serves this miserable slavery, the man who makes masters for himself and himself wishes to have people whom he must fear. For nothing is so characteristic of slavery as always to be afraid.

But the person who is not captured by love of the world, not held by the bonds of greed, and not shackled by fear of guilt is always free in every condition of servitude. He views the present securely, and future things do not terrify him.

Does this man not seem to you to rule in slavery, while the other serves in freedom? Joseph was a slave; Pharaoh was king. Yet Joseph’s slavery was happier than Pharaoh’s kingship. Indeed, all Egypt would have collapsed from famine unless Pharaoh had subjected his kingdom to the counsel of his servant.

**21.** Servants therefore have grounds for glorying in their origin: Joseph too served. Those who have come from freedom into servitude through some necessity have grounds for consolation. They have an example to imitate, so that they may learn that they can change their condition, but not their character; that there can be freedom among household slaves, and steadfastness in servitude.

Masters, too, have reason to hope on account of good servants. Abraham found a wife for his son through a household servant. The Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house because of Joseph, and the Lord’s blessing came upon all his property, both in the house and in the fields. “And he placed,” it says, “everything that he had into Joseph’s hands” (Genesis 39:4). We observe that the things which the masters could not govern were governed by the servant.

## CHAPTER V

Joseph is commended for his beauty, but even more for his chastity. Through no fault of his own he is loved by his mistress and solicited to commit adultery; he repels her, and, leaving his garments behind, flees more nobly adorned. But while she retains them and accuses the innocent man, she exposes her own disgrace. Joseph is nevertheless sent to prison; yet there he is not abandoned by divine protection.

22. But what shall I say about the arrangement of the private household of that servant who governed an empire? Yet greater still is the fact that he [Note: The Roman edition, after the words “before he governed himself,” closed the fourth chapter and began the fifth with these words: “And Joseph was handsome in face and exceedingly beautiful in appearance. Since Joseph was handsome in face and exceedingly beautiful in appearance,” etc. We have corrected the passage in accordance with the other editions and all the manuscripts.] governed himself first; and although he was beautiful in appearance [Col. 0650D] and exceedingly handsome in face, he did not turn the charm of his countenance toward another’s injury, but preserved it for his own grace: [Col. 0651A] he judged himself more beautiful if he proved more splendid not by sacrificing chastity but by cultivating modesty. He held that true beauty was that which did not seize the eyes of others or wound fragile minds, but won the judgment of everyone, bringing fraud to no one and praise to himself.

Now, if she looked upon him with wanton eyes, the fault belongs only to the woman who looked wrongly, not to him who did not wish to be seen wrongly; nor is there guilt in the fact that he was seen. It was not in the servant’s power not to be seen: the husband ought to have guarded his wife’s eyes. [Note: *Cavere oculos uxoris* should be understood in place of *cavere oculis uxoris*, that is, “to guard against the eyes of his wife,” or “to take care that no one approached his wife whose appearance might entice her eyes.” The expression is very uncommon, but here it is supported by the common agreement of the manuscripts and editions.] If that man feared nothing from his wife, this one considered it a testimony to her chastity, [Note: The Roman edition reads *non remissionem curae*, “not a relaxation of care.” The others, together with all the manuscripts, read *non remissionem incuriae*, “not a relaxation arising from negligence.”] not a relaxation arising from negligence.

Nevertheless, let men learn to guard even the eyes of women. For even those who do not wish to be loved are loved. Thus Joseph was loved, though he despised the woman who loved him. And Scripture rightly excuses him, saying: [Col. 0651B] “His master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph” (Gen. XXXIX, 7)—that is, he did not [492] display himself or ensnare the unwary woman; rather, she cast out her own nets and was caught in her own trap. She scattered her snares and became entangled in her own bonds.

23. But she said to him: “Sleep with me” (ibid.). The first weapons of an adulteress are her eyes, the second her words. But one who is not captured by the eyes can resist words. Defense remains possible while the affection is still free. Therefore it is written that he did not consent (ibid., 8).

First, then, he overcame her in the encounter of the mind, repelling her assault as though with a shield of courage; then he brandished his speech like a spear, so that she might withdraw. [Col. 0651C] And he said to his master’s wife (ibid.). She is rightly called “the wife of his master,” not “the mistress” herself, since she could not extort what she wished to command. For how could she be mistress, when she possessed no power of domination, did not maintain a mistress’s discipline, and offered incentives to lust to the servants? He was the master who did not receive the torches of a woman in love, who did not feel the bonds of a seductress, whom no fear of death terrified, and who preferred to die free of crime rather than choose partnership with criminal power.

He was free who considered it shameful not to return a favor with gratitude. In the end, he does not excuse himself like a frightened man, nor take precautions like one afraid of danger; rather, as a debtor to his master’s kindness and to his own innocence, he flees the crime of ingratitude and shudders, as a righteous man, at the stain of sin and the contagion of guilt.

The adulteress hurled a third dart by repeatedly addressing him; but Joseph did not listen to her. From the first words you have learned what to beware of. Lust is not only slippery [Col. 0651D] but also shameless, importunate, and wanton, and the adulteress has nothing of which she is ashamed. She who did not grieve at the first losses of modesty lies in wait in order to capture him.

24.
