Finally, by reason of the opportunity afforded by entering upon his duties and the office entrusted to him, after removing witnesses and members of the household (ibid., 11), she seized him, saying: “Sleep with me.” Joseph is excused by the testimony of Scripture, because he could not abandon the service entrusted to him by the Lord.

For it is not enough that, confident in himself, he entered the inner parts of the house [Col. 0652A] as though he could not be captured: the righteous man ought to have taken care not to give a frenzied woman the opportunity to sin, lest she perish through that sin. But when he saw that his master’s wife was setting herself against him, he ought also to have guarded against offending his master through neglect of duty. At the same time, he thought her boldness still concerned speech, not seizure.

25. He is excused for having entered; he is praised because he [Note: After the words “he escaped,” the Roman edition adds: “And leaving his garments in her hands, he fled.”] escaped, and valued the chastity of his soul more highly than the clothing of his body. He left behind, as though they were not his own, the garments that the adulteress held in her hands; and he judged alien whatever the touch of an immodest woman could seize.

Yet he was a great man: sold, he did not learn the mentality of a slave; loved, he did not return the love; asked, he did not consent; seized, he fled. When his master’s wife approached him, she could hold him by his garment, but she could not capture his spirit. [Col. 0652B] He did not even endure her words for long, judging it contagion to remain longer, lest the incentives to adulterous lust pass through the adulteress’s hands.

Thus he stripped off his garment, shook off the crime, and, leaving behind the clothing by which he had been held, fled stripped, indeed, but not naked, for he was more fully clothed in the garment [493] of modesty. No one is naked except the one whom guilt has stripped naked.

In the earlier passages we have that Adam, after abandoning God’s commands through transgression and incurring the heavy debt of sin, was naked. Hence he himself says: “I heard your voice in Paradise, and I was afraid, because I am naked, and I hid myself” (Gen. III, 10). For he understood that he was naked because he had lost the insignia of divine protection. And therefore he hid, because he did not possess the garment of faith [Col. 0652C], which he had certainly laid aside through transgression.

You see a great paradox. The man who had not lost his tunic was naked; this man was not naked, although he stripped off the garments that he left in the adulteress’s hands. The same Scripture declares the former naked and denies it of the latter. Therefore this man stripped himself rather than being stripped naked, for he preserved the uncorrupted garments of the virtues, stripping off the old man with his deeds in order to put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of the Creator.

But the other remained naked, unable to clothe himself again, stripped of the singular garment of virtue. Hence he received a tunic of skins, because a sinner could not possess a spiritual one. Joseph therefore left his garments behind and exposed the adulteress’s shamelessness, which afterward could no longer remain concealed.

[Col. 0652D] 26. Finally, she went outside and made public the very temptations of her adultery, raising her voice because the Hebrew had fled after leaving his garments behind. Thus she revealed what she ought to have concealed, in order to injure the innocent by a fabricated charge.

But the righteous man does not know how to accuse; and therefore the shameless woman did this with impunity. I should therefore truly call her stripped naked, even while she retained another’s garments, for she had lost all the coverings of chastity; and him sufficiently adorned and sufficiently defended, whose [Col. 0653A] voice was not heard but whose innocence spoke.

Thus Susanna, later, while remaining silent in judgment, spoke more effectively through the oracle; and therefore she deserved the prophet’s defense because she did not seek the aid of her own voice. I should therefore call him happier when he was sent to prison, because he entered martyrdom for the sake of chastity. Chastity is indeed a good gift, but it has less merit when it faces no danger; when it is defended even at the risk of one’s life, there it is crowned more fully. [Note: The Roman edition adds after the word “crowned”: “And it came to pass, when his master heard the words of his wife . . . Joseph took him and put him in prison.”]

27. Without a hearing of the case, without investigation into the truth, Joseph is sent to prison as though he were guilty of a crime; but the Lord did not abandon him even in prison. Let the innocent not be disturbed when they are attacked by false accusations, when, with justice suppressed, they are thrust into prison. God visits his own even in prison; and therefore there is more help where there is more danger.

But why is it surprising that Christ visits those placed in prison, when he declared that he himself was confined in prison in his own members, as you have it written: “I was in prison, and you did not come to me” (Matt. XXV, 43)? Where does divine mercy not penetrate?

Joseph found such favor that he who had been confined in prison himself rather controlled the prison’s locks; [Col. 0653B] [494] the keeper of the keys granted authority to him as a privilege, and entrusted all the prisoners to his power. Thus Joseph not only did not feel the prison, but also relieved the distress of the other prisoners.

CHAPTER VI.

After a brief attack upon the woman, he turns to the eunuchs, who were also the authors of this injury; and, showing how fragile their status was, he relates the dream of one of them and its interpretation. From this he demonstrates that the power of the world is like a dream. Then, after mystically praising the Hebrew interpreter, he attacks the eunuch who was forgetful of a kindness. Finally, while covertly striking at Calligonus, he adds a few remarks on the status and fragility of royal ministers.

[Col. 0653C]

28. [Note: Thus the old edition and all the manuscripts, except Theod. and Valc., where it reads: “The woman of the eunuch was therefore the author of this injury.” The sense is clear, for the discussion concerns the wife of Potiphar, whom Scripture calls Pharaoh’s eunuch. The Roman edition, however, which extends chapter five to the word “refused,” reads: “Yet the woman is the author of this injury, but the woman,” etc. Again, at the same place all the editions read: “But the Egyptian woman, who . . . was accustomed,” etc. Nearly all the manuscripts read: “But the Egyptian women, who . . . are accustomed,” etc. Here it is commonly asked whether, when Potiphar is called a eunuch and a *spado*, this signifies that he was actually castrated, or whether it was a title of rank. Both opinions have their supporters. If you wish to know their arguments, consult Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, book I, question 136; Jerome, *On the Traditions*; Nobilius’s notes on this passage in the Septuagint; Cornelius Jansen on Genesis; William Estius, *Notes on Difficult Passages of Scripture*; Hugo Grotius; and others.]

The woman and the eunuchs, then, are the authors of this injury; but the woman was an Egyptian, accustomed to mingle bold speech with men, provoke the modest, pursue those who fled, and press the bashful. Unable to defend her own vices, she accused the innocent, adding treachery to treachery, holding what belonged to another, condemning others herself, [Col. 0654A] and placing no limit upon her rage.

For what was the cause of her cruelty except that she saw her desires resisted and was deprived of her wishes by a forbidden refusal? Behold why the prison should be opened, to receive the innocent; why chains should be released from the guilty, to be imposed upon the faithful; why adulterers against the truth should be dismissed, while the man who refused to commit adultery against faith is confined.

29. What shall I say about these eunuchs, who ought to serve as an example to the other eunuchs: that their status was fragile and tenuous, and that all their hope lay in the royal will, so that a slight offense meant the greatest danger for them, while in prosperity their service was lowly?

One boasted that he was chief of the wine, the other that he was chief of the bakers. Both gave offense and were sent to prison [Col. 0654B], and, being commended to holy Joseph by the keeper of the prison himself, after they had spent several days there, they had a dream. When Joseph visited them, he found them sad and troubled in spirit, because they were disturbed by a dream for which they could find no interpreter.

“Is not the interpretation of a dream from God?” he said. “Tell me, then.”

And the chief of the wine related his dream. “There was a vine before me; and on the vine were three roots. It was flowering and produced mature clusters of grapes; [Note: The earlier editions read: “bearing flowers, ripe shoots, and clusters of grapes.” The Roman edition reads: “flowering, it bore shoots and mature clusters of grapes.” The manuscripts agree with the text, except that some of the better copies have “mature clusters”; one has “and mature,” etc.—excellent, provided that *erant* (“they were”) is understood.] and Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand. I took it, pressed it into Pharaoh’s cup, and gave the cup into Pharaoh’s hands.”

And Joseph said to him: “This is its interpretation: The three roots are three days. In three days Pharaoh will remember your office, restore you to your former position, and you will give the cup into Pharaoh’s hand. [Col. 0654C] But remember through yourself, when it goes well with you, [495] and show me mercy, and remember me before Pharaoh, and bring me out of this prison; for [Note: So read the majority of the more authoritative manuscripts. Others agree partly with the earlier editions, “I was secretly captured”; partly with the Roman edition, “I was stolen by theft,” that is, “I was taken away.” There is no difference in meaning among these readings. *Involare* is used from *vola*, the hollow of the hand, which thieves commonly use in stealing and concealing another’s property. The Roman edition inserted several words into the scriptural text in order to bring it more closely into agreement with the Septuagint, but these contribute little to the sense.] I was stolen from the land of the Hebrews, and here I have done nothing wrong, but they put me into this pit of a prison.”

30. I do not wish to relate the other man’s dream. You surely remember my words, that even then I shrank from interpreting it, since it concerned one whose end I shrink from and whose death I shudder to contemplate.

Let us first speak of the man who, if he seemed happy when he was chief of the wine, considered this the summit of all power because he gave the king his cup. This was his glory, this his magnificence [Col. 0655A] in this world: he grieved when deprived of it and rejoiced when restored to it.

But this is a dream, and all the power of the world is a dream, not reality. Indeed, in a dream he saw his office restored to him. Isaiah says that those who delight in prosperity in this world are like one who eats and drinks in a dream: while he sleeps, he seems to be filled with food or drink; but when he awakens, he begins to hunger more intensely. Then he understands how empty the food and drink of the dreamer had been.

So the person who sleeps in this world and does not open his eyes to divine mysteries, as long as he is weighed down by bodily sleep, thinks that worldly power is something of importance, seeing it as though in a dream; but when he awakens, he discovers how empty the pleasure of this world is (Isa. XXIX, 8).

[Col. 0655B] 31. Now consider that true Hebrew [Note: All the editions together with two manuscripts read “the true Hebrew.” Ten manuscripts read “a Hebrew man.” A little later, where the Roman edition reads “and by abundance,” the old editions and two manuscripts agree with us in reading “from freedom”; ten others have “toward freedom.”], the interpreter not of a dream but of truth and a glorious vision. From that fullness of divinity he came from the freedom of heavenly grace into this bodily prison. The enticements of this world could not change him, nor could any corruption of worldly pleasure overthrow him. Tested, he did not fall; solicited, he did not solicit. Finally, when the adulterous hand of a certain Synagogue seized him by the garment of his body, he stripped off the flesh and ascended free from death.

The harlot brought a false accusation when she could not hold him, whom prison did not terrify and the underworld did not retain. Indeed, from the place to which he had descended as though to be punished, he freed others; where the bonds of death had bound them, there he himself loosened the bonds of the dead.

[Col. 0655C] 32. Consider, therefore, this Hebrew saying to the chief of the eunuchs, who had incurred the king’s displeasure and whom he had restored to his office: “Remember through yourself, when it goes well with you, and show me mercy, and remember me.”

He repeated this twice because he knew that, once he had recovered his power, the man would not remember what injury he had escaped. He admonished him twice because he had freed him twice, so that if the memory of the earlier kindness did not hold him, at least the later one might move him; so that he would not despise the author of his salvation or violate him by treacherous transgression.

But what is worse, forgetfulness of a kindness [496] quickly steals in during prosperous circumstances. [Note: The Roman edition adds: “For it says: ‘And the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him. Having been restored,’” etc.] Restored to his office, he did not remember the interpreter but forgot him.

Yet although that man forgot, Christ did not forget. He spoke to him, and through the servant he spoke, saying: “Remember through yourself,” that is, remember, by considering your office, what you heard. [Col. 0655D] But even if you have now forgotten me, you will remember me, so that you may escape the danger, [Col. 0656A] you who have forgotten the kindness.

Yet, lifted up by power, he did not remember. And what great power was this, [Note: Thus the Gill, Roman, and five other manuscripts. Seven others read: “Where is the ministry of wine? And from where,” etc. The Ambrosian and Erasmian editions have: “. . . let the ministry overflow.”] when it was merely the ministry of wine! Behold the source of all his boasting: he was chief of the eunuchs who served wine in the royal cups.

33. [Note: The old edition reads: “And it came to pass,” he says, “after two years.” [Col. 0656D] Mention is made of our eunuch of that time for no other reason than that the interval also corresponds. The Roman edition reads: “And it came to pass after two years that Pharaoh saw a dream,” etc. “Mention is made of our eunuch of that time for no other reason”; but the manuscripts agree with the text, except that two read: “. . . of our eunuch of that time, unless the interval also corresponds.” We believe that Calligonus the eunuch is designated here by the holy Bishop not without reason. On this matter you may consult our *Admonition* to this treatise.]

“And it came to pass,” he says, “after two years” (Gen. XLI, 1). I would be speaking falsely about the time of our eunuch if the interval did not also correspond, since after two years he recovered his office, and did not remember until he was reminded. For he learned that the kingdom itself in this world was also a dream, since he had not believed his own dream; he also learned that kingdoms are dreams and that their powers are not perpetual.

But let this grief pass quickly, [Col. 0656B] lest it grow raw through the very recollection; for it is not even pleasant to remember my own words, which at that time grief either poured forth or the insult to the Church forced from me.

34. Thus reminded by the king’s dream of his own offense, he said: “I remember my sin” (ibid., 9). This confession is indeed late, but would that it were true! After the sin you confess what you ought to have guarded against before the sin. How quickly you had forgotten: “Remember me.”

You know, surely, that this was his message at that time; but your ears were stopped by the arrogance of power, and, drunk with wine, you did not hear the words of sobriety. Even now remember me, you who confess your sin late. You ask Christ’s servant—why do you deny the Lord? Be drunk now not with wine but with the Holy Spirit.

Remember what he suffered, with whom you slept your sleep and dreamed your dream. He too was a chief, and chief over the king’s banquets, [Col. 0656C] which belonged to the work of the bakers. He considered himself exalted because royal bread was in his power; he did not know how many twists and turns this power contained. He threatened others, while he himself was soon to be handed over to the final punishment; nor did he heed the man who, although the Lord’s servant, nevertheless uttered an oracle: that by the king’s command—the king in whom he greatly delighted—he would lose his head and be left as food for the birds. Even this example ought to have recalled you, so that you would not trust treachery.

35. There are also other examples of the arrogance and fragility of royal ministers, which the history of a later time records. Doeg was also an overseer, and chief of the king’s animals [Note: So read seven manuscripts of better quality. Two, together with all the editions, add, if you please, “of the mules.” Three read: “I shall add, of the mules.”], for the training of mules—that is, animals that are eunuchs. He too informed against the Lord’s priest, [Col. 0656D] and by deceit stirred up the king to endanger the priest; and he too [497] was a Syrian. Am I lying, when both his homeland and his deeds correspond?

Haman likewise was an overseer of the king’s chamber; when [Col. 0657A] he strove with wicked audacity to invade the churches of the Lord and to plunder and persecute the faithful people, he paid for his sacrileges with severe punishments.

CHAPTER VII.

Joseph is brought out of the king’s prison, and the king’s dream is presented to him; Joseph also explains it. Ambrose applies this both to the affairs of his own time and to the present and future age. He then interprets mystically, with reference to Christ, Joseph’s rewards, marriage, children, and distribution of grain; and finally exhorts us to purchase spiritual nourishment.

36. But let us return to that chief of the wine, who, as though drunk with an abundance of unmixed wine, had long forgotten the author of his kindness. At last, however, in order to provide the king with an interpreter, [Col. 0657B] he disclosed the sequence of events—not as a grateful man but as a clever one.

When the king learned of this, he ordered Joseph to be summoned and, after he had been brought out of prison, asked whether he could interpret a dream for him. Delighted by its explanation, he removed the injury and bestowed honor.

Therefore see whether these things do not also correspond to the present. Injury was inflicted before the king knew the matter; favor was returned when Joseph became known to the king. Thus the king is free from guilt, because both the injury that the holy man endured was another’s doing, and the favor that he received belonged properly to the king.

37. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “And Joseph said to Pharaoh: Pharaoh’s dream is one, and its interpretation is as follows.” We present the entire passage from the old edition and the manuscripts.]

“His dream and its interpretation are as follows: Whatever God does, he has shown to Pharaoh. [Col. 0657C] The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good ears of grain are seven years. Pharaoh’s dream is one.

And the seven lean cows that came up after them are seven years; and the seven lean ears, damaged by the wind, are seven years. There will be seven years of famine.

As for the word that I said, ‘Whatever God is about to do, he has shown to Pharaoh’: behold, seven years of great abundance are coming throughout the whole land of Egypt. But after them seven years of famine will come, and all the abundance in Egypt will be forgotten. The famine will consume the whole land, and the abundance of the land will no longer be recognized because of the famine that will follow, for it will be exceedingly severe.

As for the fact that Pharaoh’s dream was repeated twice: it is because the word from God is true, and God will hasten to accomplish it” (Gen. XLI, 25 ff.).

38. An old dream, recent events. Later things have consumed earlier ones; and where formerly there was an abundance [Col. 0657D] of all things, there has arisen a scarcity of all things. If someone had given such advice to the king as to preserve something from the earlier abundance for the later period of his reign, the remaining time too would have overflowed with a generous abundance of giving.

But the excessive dissipation of the earlier age left even later times destitute, and men who were plundering everything did not wish to employ some Joseph. [Col. 0658A] Although I was not Joseph—“for who am I?” [Note: Some manuscripts and certain Paris editions read: “Who am I? Yet they were shouting” (some have “he was shouting), etc.” More manuscripts and the old edition read: “Who is this?” Understand that he is speaking about himself, or something similar.]—I nevertheless proclaimed that those fat cows signified not only licentiousness but also neglect of reverence for God. For it is said of the treacherous: “Fat bulls have surrounded me” (Ps. XXI, 13); and of the Jewish people it is written: [498] “He grew fat and thick and swollen, and abandoned the God who made him” (Deut. XXXII, 15).

Therefore that dream of worldly abundance could not last forever; a time would come when harsh famine would succeed it.

39. Yet I do not think that this dream was shown to only one or two people, but was set before everyone, since the seven fat years of this world, rich in worldly abundance, are swallowed up by the ages [Col. 0658B] that are to come, in which there will be perpetual rest and spiritual observance of the law, which that fruitful tribe of the fathers, Ephraim, preserves for God.

A good cow is not one swollen with bodily udders, but one abounding in spiritual milk and grace. Over the beauty of whose neck God says that he sits, as it is written: “Ephraim is a trained heifer that loves to thresh; I passed over the beauty of her neck” (Hos. X, 11).

Therefore let not the oil of the sinner fatten our head, nor should false fruits delight us, lest it be said of us also: [Note: The Vulgate edition reads *Arastis impietatem* (“You have plowed impiety”); but the holy man seems to have followed the interpretation of Aquila or Symmachus. For the Septuagint has: Ἵνα τί παρεσιωπήσατε ἀσέβειαν—“Why did you keep silent about impiety?” Jerome has: “Why do you keep silent about impieties?” On the meaning of the verb “to keep silent,” see the commentary on Hosea, chapter X.] “You sowed impiety and reaped its iniquities. You ate the fruit of falsehood, because you trusted in your chariots” (ibid., 13).

Nor does the fact that the ears are lean and damaged by the wind trouble me, because David too was better [Col. 0658C] when he wasted away like a spider; a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God; and those whom the evil spirit has exercised with grievous injuries in this world emerge superior.

40. Hence I think Joseph deserved more mystical rewards, because he spoke of mystical things. For what does the ring inserted on his finger signify except that we should understand the pontificate of faith to have been entrusted to him, so that he might seal others? What does the robe, which is an adornment of wisdom, signify except that the heavenly King bestowed upon him the primacy of prudence?

The golden chain seems to express good understanding. The chariot too signifies the lofty height of merits. Who is the one who took a wife from the nations, except the one who gathered the Church from the nations for himself and received from her a son, Manasseh, through whom he forgot all the sorrows he had suffered because of the sacrileges of the Jews?

He also received another son, [Col. 0658D] Ephraim, through whose progress it became clear that the humility assumed in the flesh did not humble his divinity and increased his glory.

41. Finally, all who suffered famine were sent to Joseph. Who are these except those of whom it is said: “They will return in the evening and suffer hunger like dogs” (Ps. LVIII, 7)?

The famine was [Col. 0659A] not in one place but throughout the whole earth, because there was no one who did good. Therefore the Lord Jesus, taking pity on the world’s hunger, opened his storehouses and revealed the hidden treasures of heavenly knowledge and wisdom, so that no one would lack nourishment.

For Wisdom said: “Come, eat my bread” (Prov. IX, 5). And therefore it is said of him alone: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing” (Ps. XXII, 1), who is filled by Christ.

Christ therefore opened his storehouses and sold—not seeking money as the price, but the price of faith and the payment of devotion. He did not sell to a few in Judea, but sold to everyone, so that he might be believed by all the nations.

499 42. And all the regions came to Egypt to Joseph to buy grain (Gen. XLI, 5 and 7), for the famine had prevailed. [Col. 0659B] For all hunger whom Christ has not fed.

Let us therefore buy nourishment by which we can drive away hunger. Let no one be held back by consideration of his poverty; let no one who does not possess silver be ashamed. [Note: So read all the manuscripts except Theodoret, who, together with all the editions, prefers: “Christ is not sought with silver, but with faith.” This differs in wording more than in meaning.]

Christ does not seek silver but faith, which is more precious than silver. Thus Peter purchased it, although he had no silver. “Silver and gold I do not have,” he says; “but what I have I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk” (Acts III, 6).

And the prophet Isaiah says: “You who thirst, go to the water; and whoever has no silver, go, buy, and drink and eat. Buy wine and fat without silver and without price” (Isa. LV, 1).

For he did not seek a price from us who paid the price of his blood for us; he redeemed us not with gold and silver but with precious blood. Therefore you owe the price by which you were bought; and even if he does not always demand it, you nevertheless owe it.

Buy Christ, then, not with what few possess but with what everyone possesses. All possess it by nature; few offer it through fear. What Christ asks back from you is his own. He gave life to everyone; he offered his death for everyone. Pay on behalf of the author what you are going to pay under the law. This is no insignificant transaction.

Not everyone sees him easily. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “Not everyone buys him easily.”] Thus those virgins in the Gospel whom the bridegroom excluded when he came were left outside because they had not bought purchasable oil. [Col. 0659C] Hence it is said to them: “Go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.” And the merchant is rightly praised who sold all that he had and bought the pearl (Matt. XIII, 46).

CHAPTER VIII.

The exhortation of Jacob to his sons that they should go to Egypt to buy food: what this signifies; and likewise what is signified by the departure of the ten, leaving Benjamin at home.

[Col. 0659D]

43. And Jacob said to his sons: “Why are you idle? Behold, I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy us food” (Gen. XLII, 1 and 2).

Jacob did not say this only once. Every day he says it to all his sons [Col. 0660A] who come late to the grace of Christ: “Why are you idle? Behold, I have heard that there is grain in Egypt.”

This grain is the grain that rises. Therefore whoever endures hunger must attribute it to his own sluggishness. “Behold, I have heard,” he says, “that there is grain in Egypt.”

Younger people, being outside and going about many places, are naturally accustomed to hear something sooner than older people. But this old man hears of the commerce first—an old man in whom there is the long gray hair of faith.

The old man understands first—but the old man in whom there is venerable old age, and an age of oldness that is an unstained life.

44. Nor do all undertake this commerce, except the sons of Jacob, and they too were of more advanced age. Therefore ten proceed, while the younger one does not go. His father did not send him: “Lest,” he said, “weakness [Col. 0660B] befall him” (ibid., 3 and 4).

The younger Benjamin was still subject to weakness. The patriarch Benjamin is indeed mentioned in Scripture, but Paul, from the tribe of Benjamin, was prefigured by him. Jacob rightly doubted about his misfortune. In the end, Paul was afflicted so that he might be healed; he suffered blindness, but this weakness was for salvation. Indeed, that blindness brought light.

45. We have received the history; let us understand the mystery. Without Benjamin the patriarchs went first; without Paul, the apostles. Neither came first, but each, summoned after the first arrivals, made the reward of those who had preceded him greater through his own arrival.

“There is,” he says, “grain in Egypt”—that is, where there is greater famine, there is greater abundance. Great is the grain in Egypt. Finally, God the Father also says: “Out of Egypt I called my Son” (Hos. XI, 1). [Col. 0660C]

From this grain comes that fertility. For there could have been no harvest unless the Egyptians had first sown the grain. There is therefore grain that no one previously believed existed. In this grain the patriarchs conduct their commerce.

They indeed brought silver; but the good Joseph gave them grain and returned their silver. For Christ is not bought with money but with grace. Your price is faith. These divine mysteries are purchased by it.

That grain, formerly unclean under the law, is carried by the donkey that is now clean under grace.

CHAPTER IX.

As the famine grows severe, Jacob’s sons return to Egypt, bringing Benjamin with them and carrying gifts. Joseph addresses his brothers courteously; when invited to a feast, they suspect that an accusation is being prepared against them. They are reassured by the steward of the household. All this is interpreted concerning Paul’s calling and preaching, as well as the unbelief of the Jews.

[Col. 0660D]

46. Benjamin the younger was nevertheless held back, and still clung to his father with filial affection. [Note: Since Ambrose here teaches that Benjamin is a type of Paul, he alludes to the passage in the Epistle to the Galatians 1:14: “And I was advancing in Judaism… being more abundantly zealous for my ancestral traditions.”] The bonds of the Law and ancestral custom held him back. [Note: The Roman edition prefixes the following verse of Scripture before the word “famine”: “But the famine grew severe over the land,” etc. Thus chapter 9 begins.] The famine was growing severe because he was coming late. Two men, Reuben and Judah, intercede for him (Genesis 43:1 ff.), that is, humility and confession. He uses these two as sureties before his father; Benjamin is entrusted to them, one being primitive, the other resurrected. [Note: Several manuscripts, together with all the editions, read: “the primitive Law, the resurrected Gospel.” Benignianus, Fuldensis, Germanus, and Colbertinus read: “the primitive Law, the Gospel resurrected.” Corbeiensis and Tornacensis: “…resurrected.” Ebrulphus, Michael, and Albinus agree with these, except that they have: “the Law of the primitive,” a reading which we consider genuine. The holy man intends Reuben to represent the Law and the Jews, and Judah the Gospel and Christians. Consult the exposition of the blessings of both in the book *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, and you will find this explained more clearly. As for Reuben being called “humility” a little earlier, this is not an interpretation of the name, but an allusion to Genesis 29:32, where Leah is mentioned: “And she called his name Reuben, saying, ‘The Lord has looked upon my humiliation,’” etc.] The primitive Law, the Gospel of the resurrected one.

The younger Benjamin is led down with these men, and arrives accompanied by good fragrances, carrying resin, by which marble stones are joined together; for by his own preaching, like spiritual resin, he too joined together living stones. He also carried honey, by which the harmful matter of a wound is eaten away internally without any harshness of cutting. Such was Paul’s preaching: he wished to destroy the rottenness of their disposition and drain away the corrupted humor by the sharpness of his argument, preferring to burn the inward parts of the diseased mind rather than cut them.

The prophet David taught us that incense is a sign of prayer, and cassia and myrrh (*gutta*, “drop”) signs of burial, saying: “Myrrh and drop and cassia from your garments” (Psalm 44:9). Paul came to preach the Lord’s cross, the ever-green holm oak, and nuts whose shell is harder but whose fruit is more tender. Appropriately, therefore, Aaron’s priestly staff was made of nutwood, as was Jeremiah’s staff of the same kind. Who would doubt that the double quantity of silver signifies no idle gifts, since both the patriarch’s life and the apostle’s word always flourish in the hearts of individuals, and the speech of the saints, like silver tested by fire, shines with the radiance of salutary instruction? Nor improperly do they bring back double silver in those who foreshadowed Paul’s coming, for he bestowed double honor upon the presbyters laboring in word and teaching.

47. Joseph saw them, and Benjamin his brother, born of the same mother (Genesis 43:29). The Hebrews are now seen, and they are seen by Christ, who is the true Joseph, when they come with Paul as his type; and he speaks gently and mildly to them, so that they may eat together. Earlier, when they had come without Benjamin, he did indeed recognize them, but he turned away from them, as it is written: “And he spoke harshly to them” (Genesis 42:7), because they did not recognize the one by whom they were recognized.

Thus they made progress through Paul, whom the Lord Jesus loved more than the other brothers, as a younger brother born of the same mother. Let the Jews take heed whom they denied as Lord: although crucified, he nevertheless loves them the more, as one born from the same parent, as it were, from their synagogue, if only they would eventually recognize the author of their salvation. But conscious of their own sins, they do not believe that Christ’s mercy is so great that he can pardon sin and forgive injury. Therefore they were prefigured in the patriarchs as they would later be.

They were invited to grace and summoned to the banquet of the saving table; yet they suspected that a charge was being prepared against them and that snares were being laid.

48. “And they began to plead their case with the man who was over the house, at the entrance of the house” (Genesis 43:19). They still hesitate to enter, and prefer to be justified by their works; they wish to establish their own case rather than receive grace, and therefore they are rebuked at the gates. But whoever awaits the fruit of the virginal womb and the Lord’s inheritance, and seeks to obtain the reward of sons, will not be ashamed at the gate. Rather, at the departure from this life he repels the enemy, lest, while hastening toward higher things, a consciousness of graver guilt should obstruct him.

49. Hence the steward answered them mystically. Understand who he is when you read of Moses as faithful in all his house. The stewards are Moses, Peter, Paul, and the other saints; Christ alone is the master. It is written: “Moses was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony to the things that were to be spoken” (Hebrews 3:5); but Christ is faithful “as a son over his own house, and we are that house if we hold fast the freedom and glory of hope” (ibid., 6).

50. “Then the steward said to them: ‘May God be gracious to you; do not be afraid. Your God and the God of your fathers has given you treasures in your sacks. As for your silver, I have received it as sound’” (Genesis 43:23). They had said: “We found each man’s silver in our sacks; we have brought back our silver by weight” (ibid., 21).

O great mysteries, and clearly expressed! This is what he means: Why are you puffed up? Why do you repeatedly claim that you possess your silver in your sacks? For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it? You are already filled; you have become rich because you think you possess silver. But God, the God of your fathers, gave you the silver. He is your God, he is the God of your fathers—the one whom you denied. Yet he forgives, pardons, and receives you if you return. He is the one who does not seek your silver, but gives you his own. He himself placed the silver in your sacks.

Your sacks now contain silver, though once they contained clay; and therefore he is yours who says: “You have torn my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness” (Psalm 29:12). Christ is the gift of gladness; he is your silver, he is your price. The Lord Jesus does not demand from you the price of his grain, nor does he seek the weight of your silver. Your silver is rejected; [Note: This is how the majority and the better manuscripts read. The editions, together with several other manuscripts, read “the silver of the age.” This is less apt, since the subject is the silver which the Hebrews had brought back in their sacks. Again, in this same passage Amelote, Erasmus, and Gill, with a few manuscripts, read: “I have your silver,” that is, sound silver, which is faithful, etc. The Roman edition reads: “…I have received it as approved,” that is, as something faithful. A large number of manuscripts, as in the text, read *fida* (“faithful”); some instead have *fidei* (“of faith”), and some *fide* (“by faith”).] the silver of the sack is not good.

51. “Your silver I have received as sound” (Genesis 43:23); that is, it is not your material silver, but your spiritual silver—sound silver—which you brought with faithful devotion, like the sons of Jacob. It is given without loss and counted without any expenditure, since by such a price the injury of death is excluded and the gain of life is acquired.

## CHAPTER X

After briefly mentioning midday, the bringing in of the prepared gifts, the renewal of the banquet, and Joseph’s most gracious meeting with his brothers are related. Seeing his brother Benjamin and asking about him, Joseph blesses him; then, having withdrawn to conceal his tears, he soon returns with his face washed. A moral and mystical interpretation is added.

52. “They prepared gifts until Joseph entered at midday” (ibid., 25). Paul’s faith hastened at midday. Previously he had been blind; afterward he began to see the light of righteousness, because for the one who reveals his way to the Lord and hopes in him, the Lord will bring forth his righteousness like light and his judgment like midday. When God appeared to Abraham at the holm oak of Mamre, it was also midday, and eternal light shone upon him from the Lord’s presence. It is midday when the true Joseph enters his house to dine. For the day shines more brightly when we celebrate the mysteries.

53. “And they brought him gifts,” he says (ibid., 26 ff.). We bring gifts; he prepares the banquet. He says: “Set out the loaves,” which only the Hebrews eat; the Egyptians cannot eat them. But before the banquet, what condescension! [Note: All the manuscripts read this way. All the editions, however, read: “What is the moral teaching of this custom and attentiveness and grace?”] What moral instruction there is in this custom, attentiveness, and grace!

The brothers still suspected Joseph of the accusation they thought was being brought against them; he invited them to dinner, while their feelings wavered. His grace persists: he speaks first, asks first: “How are you?”

54. And again he said: “Is your elderly father well?” It belongs to a superior to invite an inferior to conversation, to give confidence in speaking, and to ask not only about them but also about their parents.

55. They answered him: “Your child, our father, is well.” He called him elderly in order to honor him; they called him a child in order to offer the service of humility. Old age is regarded as possessing honored dignity, whereas youth appears subject and closer to modesty than to pride.

56. “Then he lifted up his eyes and saw Benjamin his brother, born of the same mother” (ibid., 29). [Note: “Moral” here does not mean the same thing as above, namely, something contributing to the formation of character. It is as though one said: “This is how human customs operate,” or more simply: “This is customary.” Hence, shortly afterward, in the same sense, he says: “It is the custom and grace of affection that we hold our beloved,” etc.]

It is customary that we see those whom we love before others, and that our eyes rest upon those whom the attention of our mind places first. Often, being occupied with other matters, we do not see those whom we have before our eyes; thus our gaze is directed under the guidance of the mind.

Holy Joseph therefore saw his brother Benjamin, whom he held in his mind and sought with his eyes. In his absence he had scarcely seen the brothers, [Note: All the editions add: “since seeing was of no benefit”; eleven manuscripts restore this reading for us.] since seeing was of no benefit. Nor was he content merely to see him; as though he did not know, he asked: “Is this your younger brother?” It is the custom and grace of affection that we hold those dear to us not only with our eyes but also in speech. Joseph had recognized his beloved; but he asked so that the one whom his mind held might sound forth in his voice.

57. Finally, he did not wait for an answer, but immediately blessed him, and was shaken by the fulfillment of his longing. “His inward parts were moved” (ibid., 30), because he was prevented from embracing the one he had desired. Finally, “he entered into the inner chamber and wept, and washed his face, and restrained himself” (ibid., 30). [Note: This is how the ancient edition and five manuscripts read; the Roman edition does not differ, except that it alone has: “And he went out and restrained himself.” Seven other manuscripts read: “And the stings of great love quickly pierced their hearts”; among these, Valcianus, Germanus, Fuldensis, and Corbeiensis have: “Their hearts are quickly pierced.”]

The sharp stings of great love quickly pierce the heart unless the restraints of longing are loosened. Joseph was overcome by affection, but restrained by prudence; reason was contending with love. He wept so that he might temper the heat of devoted love with tears. This is the moral interpretation.

58. Mystically, however: The Lord Jesus saw Paul, for “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous,” and said: “Is this your younger brother?” (ibid., 29). He is still called younger because he had not yet reached the mature age of hoary faith, nor had he grown into a perfect man, into “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,” as he himself says (Ephesians 4:13).

Indeed, he is read of as a young man only there (Acts 7:58), where he guarded the garments of those who stoned Stephen. And for this reason Paul wished Philemon to resemble not his own youth but his old age, as he wrote: “I appeal to you, since you are such a one as Paul the old man” (Philemon 9). For this reason he teaches that younger widows should be avoided (1 Timothy 5:11), not because of their age, but because of a certain wantonness of youthful sins and immaturity in virtue. Otherwise, the praise of chastity is greater in a young man than in an old man.

I think the following is not foreign to the truth, if we understand that, when Paul was in this condition and, seized with horror, trembled because blindness had befallen him, he nevertheless began to draw near by saying: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts 9:6). [Note: All the editions and the Vatican and Theodulf manuscripts read: “When Paul was clinging to this, and was seized with horror because…” But eight manuscripts agree with our text. You will certainly not deny that they should be preferred to the others if you consider that the words “When Paul had this” refer very well to the vices of youth, the wantonness of sins, and immaturity in virtue.]

For this reason he was called younger by Christ, so that the one summoned by grace might be excused from guilt, since that condition belonged to a slippery age. Finally, Christ saw him when light shone around him. And because adolescents are recalled from vice more by fear than by reason, he applied the goad and mercifully warned him not to kick against the goad.

59. “He was troubled,” as you have in the Gospel (John 11:33), because he troubled himself in spirit when he raised Lazarus; and there he wept, so that he might first wash away the dead man’s sins with his tears. But he wept within himself and washed his face. Paul’s blindness is Christ’s weeping; he washes his face where Paul’s lost light is restored. Christ washes his face where Paul was baptized, through whom the Lord Jesus was to be seen by many.

Therefore, at the banquet his portion was made five times greater, because he was to be preferred before his elders not only in wisdom of mind, but also in bodily struggle and the grace of chastity.

## CHAPTER XI

All the brothers drink with holy Joseph, but only in Benjamin’s sack is the cup inserted. The sacks of all are inspected in order, and at last the vessel is found; their mysteries are then drawn out, especially concerning divine gifts and Paul’s calling.

60. “They drank and became drunk together with him” (Genesis 43:34). From the beginning of faith, greater privilege is assigned to Paul, concerning whom it was said to Ananias: “Go, for he is a vessel of election for me, to bear my name before the nations” (Acts 9:15). From the beginning he is intoxicated with a sober drunkenness, so that he too might say with the saints: “And your cup that intoxicates—how excellent it is!” (Psalm 22:5).

61. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “Fill the men’s sacks with food, as much as they can carry, and put each man’s silver in the mouth of his sack; and put my silver cup in the sack of the younger one.” With these words it began the chapter. It again agrees with Gill: “Paul was not deceived.” Amelote and Erasmus, with most manuscripts, read: “Paul was deceived.” Six good manuscripts have *infallebatur*, a word which, although less customary, does not differ in meaning from its simple form.] “And the silver cup was inserted only in his sack” (Genesis 44:2). Benjamin did not know this: Paul was being deceived, but he was being called. He is sent after in the morning. The night of blindness had preceded; the day of faith was approaching.

62. First the sacks of each one are inspected in order (ibid., 12 ff.). Divine Scripture teaches you morality. Earlier they had reclined in order at the banquet [Note: The Roman edition reads: “at the banquet before him.”] opposite him, the firstborn according to age (Genesis 43:33). You see that the place belongs to the elder by right of honor. Again, the sacks of each are searched in order, so that you may know that Paul was chosen by heavenly judgment. He examined the others and preferred this one. The silver cup was found in no other sack but his. What does it mean that it was inserted into the sack?

Joseph intoxicated him in order to deceive him; he sent the cup in order, by a pious deception, to recall the brother whom he loved. But the divine mysteries shine forth.

63. Christ found in us the silver which he himself had given. We possess the silver of nature, and we possess the silver of grace. Nature is the work of the Creator; grace is the gift of the Redeemer. Even if we cannot see Christ’s gifts, he nevertheless gives and works secretly, and gives to all. But to preserve them and not lose them belongs to the few.

He does not, however, give everything to everyone. Wheat is given to many; the cup to one, who is endowed with a prophetic and priestly gift. For not everyone, but the Prophet says: “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115:13).

64. In Paul’s body, therefore, the address of heavenly teaching already shone forth, since he had been instructed in the Law. But because he was not yet subject to the righteousness of God, the cup was inside the sack: doctrine was inside the Law, and the lamp inside the bushel. Nevertheless, Ananias was sent to give a blessing, lay on his hand, and loosen the sack. When the sack was loosened, the silver shone forth, and as the scales fell away, like certain bonds of the sack, he immediately saw (Acts 9:17).

His bond was unbelief; his release became faith. Therefore, as one released from the sack—that is, having laid aside the veil of the Law placed over the heart of the Jews—and turning to the Lord, free from bondage and having obtained the grace of liberty, he said: “With unveiled face, beholding the glory of God, we are transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Once the sandal of the Law had been removed, he preached the Gospel with the naked footprint of free speech. The Jews held him and wanted to hinder him; but when the silver shone in his sack, they tore their garments and turned back. For Paul’s free preaching for Christ stripped the Jewish people and cut away all their grace.

65. Therefore they went back, those who previously could not see what lay before them (Genesis 44:13). Those who lose Christ return backward. Indeed, in the Gospel (John 18:6), when they seized the Lord Jesus to put him to death, they went backward and fell to the ground. They rightly turned backward, having fallen from that heavenly grace into earthly defilement.

Morally, therefore, they did not want to return without their brother; mystically, they did not want to return without Paul. Once he was lost, they claimed that the old age of their parent people would be brought into mourning.

66. And therefore Judah wished to remain with Joseph (Genesis 44:18 ff.), so that he would not see the evils that would befall his father; that is, he already foresaw them and wanted to avert the evils that were to come upon the Jewish people. But since free preaching had not yet appeared in that type of the rulers of the Jewish people, Joseph wept—that is, Jesus wept in him.

## CHAPTER XII

Joseph’s self-revelation to his brothers, his invitation to them to approach, and his excusing of the conduct he was to employ against the Jews express the manner of action Christ would use. There follows a most elegant comparison of the words of the two; afterward, Joseph’s embrace of Benjamin is briefly explained with reference to Paul.

67. [Note: All the manuscripts and editions read this way, except the Roman edition, which prefixes this passage of Scripture: “And Joseph could not endure all those standing beside him, but said: ‘Send everyone away from me.’ Joseph ordered everyone,” etc.] “And he ordered everyone to withdraw, so that he might make himself known to his brothers.” For he had not come, as he himself says, except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel.

And, raising his voice with weeping, he said: “I am Joseph; is my father still alive?” (Genesis 45:2–3). This means that he extended his hands toward a people that did not believe and contradicted him, seeking neither a legate nor a messenger, but himself wishing to save his people: “I who was speaking—behold, I am here,” he says (Isaiah 52:6). And: “I became manifest to those who did not seek me; I appeared to those who did not ask for me” (Isaiah 65:1).

What else, then, did he cry out at that time except: “I am Jesus” (John 18:5), when, questioned by the Jewish leaders, “Are you the Son of God?” he answered: “You say that I am”; when he said to Pilate: “You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth” (ibid., 37); when the high priest said to him: “I adjure you by the living God, tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God,” and he replied: “You have said it. Truly I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Matthew 26:63–64).

This, therefore, is what he says: “I am Joseph”—I am the divine power. “Is my father still alive?” That is, I do not deny the Father; I acknowledge my brothers, if either you acknowledge the brother or the Father acknowledges the Son. “Is my people, then, still alive, from whose family I have chosen a brother for myself?”

68. “Come near to me” (Genesis 45:4), because I have drawn near to you, and have drawn so near that, by assuming flesh, I made myself a participant in your nature. Do not flee from one who shares your fellowship, even if you do not recognize the author of salvation.

69. “And they came near to him,” he says, “and he said: ‘I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt. Now therefore do not be grieved, nor let it seem hard to you that you sold me here. For God sent me before you for your life’” (ibid., 4–5).

What brotherly devotion, what sweet kinship! He even excused the parricidal deed, saying that it had been the work of divine providence, not of human impiety, since he had been offered to death not by men but sent by the Lord for life.

What else does that intercession of our Lord Jesus Christ contain, who surpassed all his brothers in devotion, when, placed upon the cross, he pleaded for the people, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34)? What else does that holy greeting contain which he spoke in the midst of the disciples: “Peace be with you; I am he; do not be afraid” (Luke 24:36)?

And when they were troubled and terrified and thought they were seeing a spirit, he said to them again: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See, my hands and my feet; for I am he himself. Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (ibid., 38–39). These mysteries, therefore, which were to occur in later times had already been revealed then.

70. Finally, these things are expressed in the very same words, so that we may understand that it was the same one who spoke earlier in Joseph and afterward in his own body, since he did not even change his words.

At that time he said: “Do not be grieved.” And below: “Go up to my father and say to him: ‘Thus says your son Joseph: God has made me lord of the whole land of Egypt.’” In the Gospel he says: “Do not be afraid. Go and announce to my brothers that they should go to Galilee, and there they will see me” (Matthew 28:10). And below he says: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (ibid., 18). This means: it was the disposition of God that I should receive power, not human bitterness. He who enumerates the reward does not charge them with their crime.

71. What is written in Genesis—“For God sent me before you for your life”—he renders in the Gospel when he says: “Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 19). For this is the reward and life of the saints: that they have also redeemed others.

72. Notice also that it was not written idly in Genesis: “And you shall be near me, you and your sons and your sons’ sons” (Genesis 45:10). This is what he said in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

73. How evident, too, is that mystery in which, as though every command had been fulfilled, Joseph embraces his brother Benjamin and falls upon his neck (Genesis 45:14), just as, when the Gospel had been fulfilled, Christ embraces Paul with certain arms of his mercy (Acts 9:4 ff.), so that he might raise him, bent inward by his former understanding, as though from the neck into heaven. Hence, raised up by Christ, he says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

## CHAPTER XIII

Pharaoh rejoices that Joseph’s brothers have been found, and his kindness toward them is explained. What do the gifts that Joseph gives to his brothers, especially to Benjamin, and sends to their father signify? What also is signified by his exhorting them, as they depart, to preserve peace? Their return to the land of Canaan follows, together with the father’s amazement when he hears that his son is alive.

74. “Pharaoh rejoiced that Joseph had recognized his brothers” (Genesis 45:16 ff.). Hence the report spread throughout Pharaoh’s house. He encouraged holy Joseph to invite his brothers to come with their father, and ordered their sacks to be filled with grain and wagons to be given to them.

Whence could such kindness come from a barbarian, unless it displayed the great mystery that the Church no longer envies when the Jews are redeemed, but the Christian people rejoice in this addition, assist them with whatever resources they can, and send those who proclaim the kingdom of God, so that they may be called more quickly? To them are given two garments (Genesis 45:22).

75. [Note: All the editions and several manuscripts read: “And he binds Paul.” Many others, and not of inferior quality, read: “And he commissions Paul.” We have preferred the latter because Benjamin, who was a figure of Paul, is not said to have been bound after this mutual recognition; and when Paul’s words are brought forward, it is less appropriate to say that he is bound than that he is commissioned, that is, sent as an ambassador.]

“And he commissions Paul,” when he brings forth his words; and Christ bestows upon him three hundred gold pieces and five garments of different colors (ibid., 23). He has three hundred gold pieces who preaches Christ’s cross. Hence he says: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2). Appropriately, he receives gold, because he preached not with persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the Spirit.

He receives five garments either because of the manifold disciplines of wisdom, or because, captured by none of the allurements of bodily senses, he held victory where others were in danger. He surpassed all bodily pleasures by singular self-restraint and virtue; neither bodily weakness nor infirmity dulled his intellect or zeal. Although he was in the body, he did not know that he had a body.

Finally, caught up into paradise, whether in the body or outside the body he did not know, he heard ineffable words which it is not permitted a human being to speak. At last he had no earthly scent while on earth, as he himself teaches, saying: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved” (2 Corinthians 2:15).

76. Paul therefore excels, and his portion overflows; yet the other preachers also have their own grace. They receive two garments. What garments are these? You should have no doubt, since you have read that it is said of Wisdom: “She made two garments for her husband” (Proverbs 31:22). [Note: By the mystical and moral garment understand the mystical and moral interpretation of the Scriptures.]

One is mystical, the other moral. But not all are apostles, not all prophets, not all pastors, not all possess powers, not all have the grace of healings, and not all speak in tongues. Where merits differ, rewards differ.

77. “And he sent gifts to his father” (Genesis 45:23). The son honors the father. Christ invites his people by promises; he invites them by gifts. Those useless and formerly laboring donkeys, now useful, carry these gifts; in the type they carry Christ’s gifts, and in the Gospel they will carry the giver of gifts.

78. “He sent his brothers away, and they departed. And Joseph said to them: ‘Do not become angry on the way’” (ibid., 24). How well he teaches that anger must be guarded against, since it can even separate brothers who love one another; and especially that discord must be avoided on the journey, where the companionship of travelers ought to possess the inviolable fellowship of grace.

What else did our Lord Jesus say when he was about to depart from this body and was dismissing his disciples, except that they should not become angry on the way, saying: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John 14:27)? Where there is peace, anger has no place; discord is driven away and dissension banished. This, then, is what he says: “I give you my peace”—that is, “Do not become angry on the way.”

And see whether, by “on the way,” he means in this course of the whole life that indignation must be avoided, since anger often (11, question 3, “Anger often”) brings even the innocent into guilt. For while we grow angry more than is right and wish to restrain another’s sin, we commit graver sins ourselves.

Therefore the Apostle says: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to anger” (Romans 12:19), that is, let us turn away from it, lest it seize us. Hence the Lord Jesus, sending his disciples to preach the Gospel, sent them without gold, without silver, without money, without a bag, and without a staff—that is, so that he might remove both the incentives to quarrel and the instruments of vengeance.

79. “And they went up from Egypt and came into the land of Canaan to Jacob their father; and they announced to him, saying: ‘Joseph your son is alive, and he is ruler of the whole land of Egypt’” (Genesis 45:25). [Col. 0670B] What is the land of Canaan? The land that was wavering. What, then, is more evident than that the times of the apostles are indicated? They entered the wavering synagogues of the Jews and preached the power of the Lord Jesus, as we have in the Acts of the Apostles, where Peter says: “God raised this Jesus, of which we are witnesses. Therefore, exalted by the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured out this gift, which you see” (Acts 2:32–33).

We clearly observe how he says both that Jesus is alive and that he is ruler of the whole land, since, opening his storehouses, he gives everyone the abundance of spiritual grace. This is what the apostles were saying (Acts 5:18), but the Jews did not believe; instead, they laid hands on them and thrust the preachers of salvation into custody.

80. Hence it is also written of Jacob: “He was stunned in mind” (Genesis 45:26), for he did not believe them. He was stunned by the emotion of the unbelieving people; but after he learned of Christ’s deeds, softened by such great benefits and works, he recovered his spirit and said: “It is a great thing for me if my son Joseph is still alive; I will go and see him before I die” (ibid., 28).

The first and greatest foundation of faith is to believe in Christ’s resurrection. For whoever believes that he has been raised seeks him eagerly, approaches him devotedly, and worships God with his inmost mind. He believes that he himself will not die if he believes in the author of the resurrection.

## CHAPTER XIV

Israel rises and comes to the well of the oath, where he also offers sacrifice. God consoles him with promises and assures him that Joseph’s hand will close his eyes. Seventy-five souls enter Egypt, and finally Israel summons his sons to himself. What mysteries are contained in all these events?

81. “And Israel, rising up, came to the well of the oath, and offered a sacrifice to the God of his father Isaac” (Genesis 46:1). Rightly does he rise who hastens toward Christ. Faith precedes devotion. First he rose, afterward he sacrificed. For the one sacrifices well who has investigated the knowledge of divinity.

82. “And God spoke to Israel in a vision at night, saying: ‘Jacob, Jacob.’ He answered: ‘What is it?’ And the Lord said: ‘I am the God of your fathers; do not be afraid. Descend into Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation. I will descend with you into Egypt, and I will lead you down forever’” (Genesis 46:2 ff.).

How is it that they do not understand what they themselves read, and deny Moses whom they praise, since they refuse to believe his writings? What is clearer than that in this passage they are invited to pass over to the holy Church of God, and that those who had previously been confined within the narrow boundaries of Judea are summoned to migrate to the people of God, who, gathered from the whole world and from all nations and peoples, have become a great nation?

Finally, “their sound has gone out into all the earth.” Thus Jacob—that is, the Jewish people—is called by his sons, Peter, Paul, and John, and is invited to grace.

83. Our God himself also encourages him by his own oracle and promises him the fruit of his office, the advancement of faith, saying to him: “Joseph will place his hand upon your eyes” (Gen. XLVI, 4). The holy Patriarch was certainly not anxious about who would close his eyes; although, even in a simple interpretation, a moral sentiment may be expressed. For if we desire frequently to embrace those whom we love, how much more, when we are about to depart from this body, are we delighted by the final touch of our beloved pledges, and comforted by this provision for the journey? Nevertheless, we may understand mystically that the Jewish people will afterward come to know God. [Col. 0671C] For this is the mystery: the true Joseph will place his hands upon its eyes, so that the people who previously did not see may now see. Come to the Gospel [Col. 0672A] (John IX, 6); read how that blind man was healed, upon whom Jesus laid his hand and removed his blindness. For Christ does not lay his hand upon those who are to die, but upon those who are to live—or, if upon those who are to die, rightly so, because we first die in order that we may live again. For we cannot live for God unless we first die to sin.

84. Thus seventy-five souls descend into Egypt, as it is written, and this also mystically signifies the number of remission, because after such great hardness and so many sins they would be held unworthy unless remission of sins were granted to them. Judah, that is, confession of error, meets him. The Jewish people that is to come sends this man ahead as its forerunner. Therefore the true Joseph also meets them—that is, the arbiter and interpreter of divinity—because confession now precedes those whom unbelief formerly possessed. [Col. 0672B] Christ is the interpreter of divinity, because “no one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.” He will receive this people of the Jews, already advanced in age and wearied, in the final times—not according to its merits, but according to the election of grace—and will place his hands upon its eyes, in order to remove its blindness. For this reason he delayed its healing: so that the one who previously had not thought it necessary to believe might be the last to believe, and might lose the privilege of the earlier election. Hence the Apostle also says: “For blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. XI, 25).

85. The deeds, therefore, of the patriarchs are mysteries of things to come. Accordingly, Jacob himself says to his sons: [Col. 0672C] “Gather yourselves together, that I may announce to you what will happen to you in the last days. Gather yourselves together and hear, O Israel, your father” (Gen. XLIX, 1–2).

# [ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE PATRIARCHS]

[Col. 0671C]

## INTRODUCTION TO THE BOOK ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE PATRIARCHS

In the preceding books we have already observed Ambrose inserting something concerning the Blessings of the Patriarchs—that is, those blessings by which Jacob, when lying at the point of death, invoked every good thing upon his sons, who by antonomasia (*μετὰ ἀντονομασίαν*) are called patriarchs. But he had touched upon these only in passing, reserving a fuller interpretation of them for another place, where he would discuss them at length. This is what the holy Doctor carries out in the present work.

Accordingly, after briefly explaining the usefulness of a father’s blessing, he teaches (chap. 1) that Joseph hastened to bring his sons Manasseh and Ephraim with him to Jacob, so that they might receive his blessing; and that their grandfather, having adopted them, assigned them a place among his own sons. Then, following the order of Scripture, he unfolds the blessings that Jacob bestowed upon his sons (chap. 2 and following). He searches out the mystical meaning in all of them, and asserts that they are not so much blessings (chap. 2, no. 7, and elsewhere) as prophecies—indeed, prophecies enriched with various graces of blessing. For this reason he discloses what is foreshadowed in each of them: for example, Jews and Christians in the blessing of Manasseh and Ephraim (chap. 1), the Antichrist in the blessing of Dan (chap. 7), and the holy Paul in the blessing of Benjamin (chap. 12). Christ, however, is signified in most of them, especially in the blessings of Judah and Joseph (chaps. 4 and 11), which for that reason he explains more fully and carefully than the others.

Moreover, in order to give greater force and authority to the interpretations he presents, he brings forward the words with which Moses, already about to depart this life, blessed the tribes descended from the seed of those same patriarchs (Deut. XXXIII, 6 and following). It should nevertheless be added that the holy Bishop did not make use everywhere of the testimonies mentioned, since he omitted three of the Mosaic blessings. One unusual feature of this little work, and one uncommon in Ambrose, is that, content to unfold mystical interpretations, he almost never inserts anything adapted to moral instruction—only once, in fact (chap. 7, no. 33).

[Col. 0673A] In this treatise the holy Doctor also cites several passages from his other works, especially his commentary (chap. 4, no. 21) on Luke. Since that work, according to the more probable opinion, was written about the year 386, it follows that the short treatise on the Blessings of the Patriarchs was not published before that year. But if the date is to be determined from the great and evident connection by which it is joined to the preceding books, it must be said that it is not much later than they and therefore should not be assigned to any time other than about the year 387. Indeed, in his book on the patriarch Joseph, Ambrose does not seem to have omitted Joseph’s blessing for any other reason than that he was reserving a separate discussion of it for the near future; otherwise, the interpretation of that blessing would have fitted admirably with the principal point of his argument, namely, his intention to demonstrate in Joseph an expressed image of Christ the Lord.

Furthermore, the close affinity of these treatises is so strongly confirmed by the headings of several ancient codices that they seem to constitute a single work. The Benignian manuscript, that is, the manuscript of Saint Benignus of Dijon, displays at the beginning of the book on the patriarch Joseph the following title: “Here begins the first book of the same author”—namely, Ambrose. At the end it reads: “Here ends the first book on Joseph”; and immediately, without another heading, it adds the book on the Patriarchs. The Utican manuscript, that is, that of Saint Ebrulphus, presents at the beginning and end of the book on Joseph almost the same words as the Benignian; but it states more explicitly that the treatise in question is entitled: “Here begins the second book on Joseph and his brothers, and on their blessings.” Finally, in certain codices the following heading is placed before the same book on the Blessings: “Here begins the second book on the Patriarchs”; and this conclusion follows: “Here ends the second book on the Patriarchs.” Jonas, bishop of Orléans, also mentions it under the title *On Joseph*, since, when he cites its opening words, he says as follows (Book II *On the Institution of the Laity*, chap. 15): “Ambrose, in the book whose title is *On Joseph*.” Finally, we have no doubt that this book should be regarded as the last of the seven books that Cassiodorus records Ambrose as having written on this subject: “Likewise,” he says (Book *On the Institutions of Divine Literature*, chap. 1), “Saint Ambrose published seven books on the Patriarchs.” Without doubt he counts these from the books *On Abraham* through this very book, inclusively, as they say.

Since all those treatises consist of sermons which, as we have shown, the holy Bishop began to deliver about the year 387, toward the end of Lent, and continued after the Easter celebrations, it remains for us to conclude that this work too was delivered during that same period, but before the month of August, in which the tyrant Maximus invaded Italy.

[Col. 0673C]

## ONE BOOK OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE PATRIARCHS

[Note: [Col. 0673B] Written about the year 387.] (C)

[Col. 0673]

## 513 CHAPTER ONE

God endowed the blessing of parents with great power, so that children might be moved to show them honor. Joseph hastened to receive his father’s blessing and also presented his sons to their father to be blessed. And what mysteries are contained in these events.

[Col. 0673A]

1. First of all, let us learn how much reverence we ought to show our parents, when we read (Gen. IX, 25 and following) that the one who was blessed by his father was blessed, and the one who was cursed was cursed! For this reason God granted this favor to parents, so that the piety of children might be stirred up. The privilege of parents, therefore, is the discipline of children. Honor your father, then, so that he may bless you. Let the dutiful honor his father because of gratitude, and the ungrateful because of fear. And even if the father is poor and does not possess an abundance of riches to leave to his sons, he nevertheless possesses the inheritance of a final blessing, by which he may bestow upon his successors the wealth of sanctification. And it is far better to become blessed than to become rich.

[Note: [Col. 0673B] Thus all manuscripts and all old editions. The Roman edition, however, has: “First of all we learn how much reverence we ought to show our parents,” and so forth.]

2. Joseph hastened to receive the blessing (Gen. XLVIII, 1 and following). Accordingly, he also presented his sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Jacob blessed; so that, since he had twelve sons and the thirteenth was to be the Apostle Paul, chosen later, a thirteenth tribe might be sanctified in the two—divided between Manasseh and Ephraim, the grandsons—so that Paul would not be found outside the number of the paternal tribes. Thus he, the distinguished preacher of the Old and New Testament, might also readily demonstrate that the inheritance of the father’s blessing had prospered for him.

3. Although these events contain splendid mysteries [514] (ibid., 13 and following), Joseph took his sons, whom he had received in Egypt, and brought Ephraim to his right and Israel his father to his left; but Manasseh to his left, so that he would be at Israel’s right, and brought them before his father. Israel stretched out his right hand and placed it upon the head of Ephraim, who was the younger and stood at the grandfather’s left; and he placed his left hand upon Manasseh, who stood at his right. Thus, with his hands crossed, he blessed them. In this Joseph preserved the order of nature, showing greater honor to the elder son, just as Isaac also wished to give the blessing to Esau, his firstborn; but he believed that the younger son, as a type of the younger people, should be preferred, just as he himself had been preferred by his mother.

4. Finally, Manasseh is designated by the interpretation of the name as “forgetfulness” (Gen. XLI, 51), because the Jewish people forgot its God, who made it. Whoever from that people believes is recalled, as it were, from forgetfulness. Ephraim, however, by the interpretation of his name, promises the fruitfulness of faith: he is the one who increased his father, as Joseph himself says: “Because God has increased me in the land of my humiliation” (ibid., 52). This is characteristic of the younger people, which is the body of Christ, increasing the Father and not abandoning its own God.

5. Finally, the elder himself declared spiritually that this was a mystery concerning the peoples. For when the son thought that he had made a mistake because of the dullness of his sight, he wished to move his hands, saying: “Not so, father, for this one is the firstborn; place your right hand upon his head.” But he refused and said: “I know, my son, I know. This one also will become a people, and he also will be exalted; but his younger brother will be greater than he, and his offspring will be a multitude of nations” (Gen. XLVIII, 18–19). Finally, he prophesied, even in the order of the blessing, that Ephraim was to be preferred to his elder brother, saying: “In you Israel shall be blessed, saying: ‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh’” (ibid., 20). And therefore, although they were grandsons, they were adopted in place of sons, so that they would not be deprived of their grandfather’s blessing.

## CHAPTER II

On the blessing of Reuben the firstborn, which is not so much a blessing as a prophecy; on the Jews’ error concerning it; and on the mysteries signified through it.

6. After this blessing had been celebrated, he also called his sons (Gen. XLIX, 1). And he who earlier had preferred the younger to the elder began with the firstborn: so that in the former case he might prefer the grace of the mystery, while in this case he might preserve the order of age. At the same time, since he had earlier blessed all their descendants and future offspring in the persons of the two, the repeated blessing of the people would not seem superfluous, nor would the earlier one be judged ineffective. And so he rightly says that he is announcing again what would happen in later times, rather than conferring a blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0675D] In the Roman edition this chapter begins as follows: “Jacob called his sons and said: ‘Gather yourselves together, that I may announce to you what will happen to you in the last days.’” After celebrating the blessing of the two grandsons, Jacob also called, and so forth.]

7. Finally, he began in this way: “Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sons, hard to bear, hard and presumptuous; you have inflicted insult upon me, like water that does not boil over. For you went up into your father’s bed; then you polluted the couch when you went up” (ibid., 3 and following). Does he not seem rather to rebuke than to bless? And therefore it is more a prophecy than a blessing. For prophecy is an announcement of future things, whereas a blessing is the votive bestowal of sanctification and graces.
