8. The Jews think that the old man says these things to his son Reuben for this reason: that he lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and polluted his father’s bed. But they are easily refuted. For this had already taken place; whereas Jacob promises that he will speak of what would happen in the last days, not of what had already happened. Therefore the Patriarch’s meaning is consistent with itself: seeing, while the Jews were persecuting him, the future passion of the Lord, he condemns the monstrous audacity of the firstborn people, which, unbelieving and not subject to God’s law, and hard because it did not know how to bear the yoke of Christ upon its neck, inflicted injury upon the author of life not only by the crime of killing him but also by sacrilegious insult.

9. “Do not boil over,” he says, lest it burst forth into greater madness, and the heat of fury and insanity prevent sinners from coming to their senses. Rather, let them repent of their offenses, because the hard people went up into the bed of its father and polluted the holy couch—that is, fastening the flesh of the Lord Jesus our Creator to the gallows of the cross, in which, as in a certain bed and paternal couch, they may rest through the holy, saving refreshment he provides. Who, then, would deny that these words were spoken about the people, when all these things fit the people? It was itself called the firstborn of Israel; it was itself called stiff-necked. Moses said of it: “But you are a stiff-necked people” (Exod. XXXIII, 3, and elsewhere). And in truth, who was so hard, presumptuous, and insulting as the Jewish people, which scourged the Lord Jesus—through whom they had seen the dead raised and the blind enlightened—and fastened him with nails, although they could not deny his divine works? The sequence of the Gospel makes clear that this was committed with the scribes and the chief priests as its instigators, and with Caiaphas, the chief of the priests, raging along with them. Therefore the holy Prophet refuses the leadership of so great a crime, lest through the succession of their race they should dare to claim fellowship with so great a Patriarch.

## CHAPTER III

The things that were to happen to the sons of Simeon and Levi, whose names designate tribes, are foretold; and the Jewish opinion concerning the mystical interpretation of this blessing is also refuted.

[Col. 0676D]

10. The righteous man protests and disowns the offspring that would not preserve the feeling of its father; and because he foresaw the crime, he recoils from participation in the plot: “Let my soul not enter into their counsel,” he says, “and let my inward parts not join their assembly; because in their anger they killed a man, and in their desire they hamstrung a bull” (Gen. XLIX, 6). What he says, he says indeed of the sons Simeon and Levi; but in their name he designates the tribes that were called by the same designation. The Jews derive a very attractive interpretation from this passage, supposing that Jacob reproved his sons because, wishing more than their other brothers to avenge the rape of their sister, these two pretended that they wished to enter into friendship with the Shechemites and therefore advised that they should be circumcised, so that, through agreement in religion, peace might be established among them and the bond of a marriage alliance secured. But after they had been circumcised, they attacked them while their wounds were still fresh and their strength weakened and broken by pain, and killed them when the third day had arrived.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] All editions read: “On the third day, when it had arrived, they killed them.” This is not a bad reading, although all Gallican manuscripts disagree with it.]

Therefore perhaps these two are called avengers above the others because they are the founders of the scribes and priests. For no one more than the learned and the priests ought to avenge chastity.

11. But in this too the Jews are mistaken. These men had indeed given their father cause for grief, claiming that, though still young, they had acted as avengers of violated piety and defenders of violated chastity. The holy man certainly could not condemn this, since they had not allowed their sister to remain unavenged as though she were a prostitute—she who had lost her virginity and had no consolation of vengeance—especially since he himself approved what had been done, inasmuch as he possessed Shechem and gave it at his death to his beloved son Joseph, saying to him: “I give you Shechem as a special portion above all your brothers, which I took from the hands of the Amorites with my sword and bow” (Gen. XLVIII, 22).

[Note: [Col. 0677D] Thus read the greater number and the better manuscripts. But all editions and a few manuscripts read: “and possessed it unto death, and gave it,” and so forth.]

This deed cannot be denied. Nevertheless, we may interpret Shechem as signifying “shoulders,” and the shoulders as works. Therefore he chose the holy Joseph as heir of good works above the others, whose works his brothers could not equal. For who could equal the deeds of Christ?

12. Moreover, the spotless and chaste one carried off spoils from this earthly dwelling and from the authors of impurity, taking possession—by heavenly words and a spiritual sword—of a place free from fornication and wickedness for the habitation of the saints. Where formerly the inhabitants were given over to lust and the leaders of debauchery, where there had been incentives to desire and fuel for wrongdoing, there holy priests now teach the principles of chastity, and many examples of virginal integrity shine forth with a kind of splendor from the light above.

13. The tribes, therefore, are designated by the names of the Patriarchs: from the tribe of Simeon came the scribes, and from the tribe of Levi the chief priests, who completed their wickedness in the Lord’s passion, filling up the full measure of their fathers’ impiety. They themselves formed a plot against the Lord Jesus in order to kill him, as Isaiah says: “Woe to their soul, because they devised an evil counsel against themselves, saying: ‘Let us bind the righteous one, because he is useless to us’” (Isa. III, 9–10). They themselves killed the prophets and the apostles who announced [Col. 0678A] the coming of the Lord and Savior and proclaimed the glory of his passion and resurrection. Later, in their desire—by which they longed for earthly crimes and rejected divine fellowship—they hamstrung the bull: namely, the one producing horns and hooves, whom the poor see and rejoice in, because by the word of God he exalted the horn of his people, with which he both drove back his enemies and earned the reward of the heavenly crown. This is the bull by which the Church is figured in the moon, becoming fuller when, as though supported by bull-like horns, it encompasses the whole expanse of the world.

14. Nevertheless, this prophecy also seems to add the grace of a blessing. For by saying to the firstborn Reuben, “Do not boil over like water,” he restrained sin, because water ordinarily cleanses offenses and draws our minds back from every heat of vices.

[Note: [Col. 0678D] “He restrained sin,” that is, he stopped sin and set up a barrier against its assaults.]

And again, by saying to Simeon and Levi, “I will divide you in Jacob and scatter you in Israel,” he shows that they would be redeemed through the gathering of the nations.

[Note: [Col. 0678D] The Roman edition reads: “to be separated by the gathering of the nations.”]

For when the shepherd was struck, that flock which had previously been gathered was scattered, so that the one who had not belonged might enter, and thus all Israel might be saved. We ought to believe this especially on account of the tribe of Levi, because the Lord Jesus appears, according to the assumption of bodily descent, to derive his lineage from that tribe. From that tribe came the priests Levi and Nathan, whom Saint Luke, in the Gospel that he wrote, counted among the ancestors of the Lord (Luke III, 29 and 31). The priest of the Father and chief of all priests, as it is written, “You are a priest forever” (Ps. CIX, 4), ought to claim the succession of priestly origin.

15. Hence Moses also blessed this tribe, saying: “Give Levi the lot of his suffrage, and his truth to the holy one” (Deut. XXXIII, 8). Moses also blessed the tribe of Reuben, as you find written: “Let Reuben live and not die, and let him be many in number” (ibid., 6). For he would not have blessed them if he had known, according to the Patriarch’s judgment, that they were unworthy of blessing. Certainly, what one passed over briefly, the other completed.

## 518 CHAPTER IV

On the blessing of Judah, which is applied to Christ, to his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and other mysteries.

[Col. 0678D]

16. And because the tribes were joined through the mingling of the lineage of Judah and Levi, Matthew describes his family from the tribe of Judah (Matt. I, 3). The Apostle also says: “For our Lord has arisen from Judah” (Heb. VII, 14). Thus from the tribe of Levi the priestly inheritance, full of holiness, might be counted; while from the tribe of Judah, from which David and Solomon and the other kings came, the splendor of royal succession might shine forth, so that the same one might be shown by the testimony of Scripture to be both king and priest.

And deservedly the holy Jacob poured himself out concerning the grace of Judah, saying: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be upon the backs of your enemies; the sons of your father shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub; from the shoot, my son, you have gone up. Reclining, you slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub; who will rouse him? A ruler shall not be lacking from Judah, nor a prince from his thighs, until he comes to whom it has been reserved; and he shall be the expectation of the nations, binding his she-ass to the vine, and the foal of his she-ass to the vine-shoot. He shall wash his robe in wine and his mantle in the blood of the grape. His eyes are cheerful with wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk” (Gen. XLIX, 8 and following).

17. The address appears to be directed to the patriarch Judah, but that later Judah, the true confessor, is expressed—the one born from that tribe, who alone is praised by his brothers, concerning whom he says: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI, 23). He is Lord by nature, brother by grace; his hands, which he stretched out toward the unbelieving people, are upon the backs of his enemies. With these same hands, and through the same passion, he sheltered his own and subdued hostile powers, making all who were excluded from faith and piety subject to himself. Concerning them the Father says to the Son: “And you shall rule in the midst of your enemies” (Ps. CIX, 2)—whom their own wickedness made enemies, not Christ’s will.

Here there is great grace from the Lord. For the spiritual wickednesses that formerly used to bend our neck beneath the yoke of captivity, so that David himself wrote that he felt, as it were, the hands of those triumphing over him, saying: “Sinners have built upon my back” [Col. 0679C] (Ps. CXXVIII, 3), now subjected to Christ’s triumph and brought under the power of certain hands of his—that is, his deeds and works—undergo the misery of perpetual captivity.

[Note: [Col. 0679D] Thus all editions and manuscripts except four, in which *qui* is absent after the word *utique*. The latest Paris edition contracted the passage in this way: “He himself, to be sure, is worshiped by us, to whom,” and so forth.]

He himself, to be sure, is worshiped by the sons of his father when he is worshiped by us, to whom he permitted us to call the Father our Father; to be his servant is a mark of virtue.

18. “Judah is a lion’s cub.” Did he not clearly express the Father and declare the Son? What could more clearly teach that the Son of God is of one nature with the Father?

[Note: [Col. 0680D] The Corbie, Laudian, Albinian, and Colbertine manuscripts read: “the Son, God.”]

That one is the lion, this one the lion’s cub. By a humble comparison, the unity of the same nature and power is understood. A king has come forth from a king, the strong from the strong. Because he foresaw those who would assert that the Son was of a younger age, he anticipated them by adding: “From the shoot, my son, you have gone up. Reclining, you slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub.” And elsewhere you find that the lion’s cub itself is “the Lion from the tribe of Judah” (Rev. V, 5).

Therefore, because he had called him a cub, he immediately and properly called him a lion, meaning: “Let your ears not be misled because you have heard ‘cub’; I expressed the Son, but I did not say that he was lesser.” He is himself a lion, as the Father is. Let them hear that he called him both lion and cub: lion, as possessing perfect and complete power; cub, as Son, lest anyone, hearing that he was equal to the Father, fail to recognize the Son. The Son is not praised in such a way that he is separated from the Father. He proves him equal who confesses him as Son.

19. He also marvelously expressed his incarnation, saying: “From the shoot, my son, you have gone up,” because, like a shrub of the earth, he germinated in the Virgin’s womb, and, like a flower of good fragrance, he rose from his mother’s womb in the splendor of a new light for the redemption of the whole world, as Isaiah says: “A branch shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI, 1). The root is the family of the Jews, the branch is Mary, and the flower is Christ. Rightly is she called a branch, since she is of royal stock, from the house and homeland of David; and her flower is Christ, who removed the stench of worldly filth and infused the fragrance of eternal life.

20. You have the incarnation; receive the passion: “Reclining,” he says, “you slept like a lion”—when he lay in the tomb, at rest as though in a kind of sleep of his body, as he himself says: “I slept, and I took rest, and I rose, because the Lord received me” (Ps. III, 6). Hence Jacob says: “Who will rouse him?” That is, whom the Lord will receive.

Who else is there to raise him except himself, who raises himself by his own power and that of his Father? I see him born by his own authority; I see him dead by his own will; I see him sleeping by his own power. He who did all things according to his own decision—whose assistance would he need in order to rise? He himself, therefore, is the author of his resurrection, just as he is the arbiter of his death; he is the one awaited by the nations.

21. And therefore, until he comes, a leader from Judah will not fail, so that the faith of the royal succession may be preserved inviolate until his birth. Afterward, as we have explained in the treatise on the Gospel (Book III, on Luke), through Herod the succession was corrupted and lost the privilege of its dignity. For because they denied the true king, they began to have false ones.

Therefore, what the Patriarch says concerning the inheritance of inviolate succession, carried on through the judges or kings of the Jews, will remain “until he comes to whom it has been reserved.”

[Note: [Col. 0680D] The Roman edition reads: “the inheritance shall remain until he comes.” All the other editions and manuscripts read: “the inheritance carried on through kings until he comes,” and so forth.]

He will gather the Church of God from the assembly of all nations and from the devotion of the Gentile peoples. That is, it remains his; it is reserved as due to him; to him the privilege of such great grace is conveyed.

22. “And he shall be the expectation of the nations.” He said more than if he had said, “the nations await him,” because the whole hope of the Church rests upon him.

For this reason Moses is told: “Remove the sandal from your feet” (Exod. III, 5), lest he be thought to be the bridegroom of the Church, since he had been chosen as leader of the people. For this reason Jesus son of Nave removed his sandal (Josh. V, 16), so that he too might reserve the grace of so great a gift for the one who was to come. For this reason John says: “After me comes a man whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen” (John I, 27). For this reason he says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy” (John III, 29).

[Col. 0680D] That is, he alone is the husband of the Church; he is the expectation of the nations. To him, bringing the bond of nuptial grace, the prophets loosened his sandal.

[Col. 0681A]

[Note: [Col. 0681D] All editions read: “the grace of the nuptial bond”; all manuscripts, as in our text.]

He is the bridegroom; I am the friend of the bridegroom. I rejoice because he has come, because I hear the nuptial voice, because we have now heard not the harsh punishments of sins and the harsh torments of the Law, but remission of offenses, a voice of joy, a sound of gladness, and the exultation of a nuptial feast.

23. He is the one who binds “his ass to the vine [Col. 0681D] and the foal of his she-ass to the vine-shoot.”

[Note: [Col. 0681D] The Roman edition reads: “his she-ass to the vine, and the foal to the vine-shoot,” and so forth. The old edition and several manuscripts read: “his she-ass and the foal’s cloak,” and so forth. Other, more numerous and better manuscripts read: “his ass and the foal to the vine-shoot,” and so forth. The Septuagint reads: “his foal, and to the vine-tendril the foal of his she-ass” (*τὸν πῶλον αὐτοῦ, καὶ τῇ ἕλικι τὸν πῶλον τῆς ὄνου αὐτοῦ*: “his foal, and to the vine-tendril the foal of his she-ass”). On this passage, see the notes of Nobilius.]

Thus the gathering of the nations, formerly sluggish and negligent but now devoted through Christ, may possess the fervor of the Holy Spirit; and we may be bound by certain unbreakable bonds of faith, like fruitful branches, to that everlasting vine—that is, the Lord Jesus, who says: “I am the vine, and my Father is the cultivator” (John XV, 1).

This is the mystery for which, in the Gospel, he ordered the foal of the she-ass to be untied, and the Lord Jesus himself sat upon it, so that, bound to the vine, it might rest in the everlasting sweetness of the saints.

24. “He shall wash,” he says, “his robe in wine.” The flesh of Christ is a good robe, which covered the sins of all, received the offenses of all, and concealed the errors of all. It is a good robe, which clothed everyone in a garment of joy. He washed this robe in wine when, as he was baptized in the Jordan, the Holy Spirit descended like a dove and remained upon him. This signifies that the fullness of the Holy Spirit was indivisibly in him and did not depart.

Hence the Evangelist also says: “The Lord Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Mark I, 10). Jesus therefore washed his robe, not to cleanse a filth of his own, which he did not have, but ours, which we did have.

[Col. 0681C] Finally he added: “And his mantle in the blood of the grape.”

[Note: [Col. 0681D] The *anaboladium*, or, as it is read in certain manuscripts, *anabolium*, perhaps *anabolaeum*, was a cloak by which the shoulders were covered. It was so called because it was raised from the lower parts to the upper, from *ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀναβάλλεσθαι* (“from being put on”).]

That is, in the passion of his body he washed the nations with his blood. For the nations are the *anaboladium* of the Word, as it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, unless I clothe them all as with a garment” (Isa. XLIX, 18). And elsewhere: “Like a garment you will change them, and they will be changed” (Ps. CI, 27).

Therefore, he cleansed not sins of his own, which did not exist, but the offenses which we committed. And he rightly spoke of the grape, because, like a grape, he hung upon the wood. He himself is the vine; he himself is the grape. He is the vine because he clung to the wood; he is the grape because the soldier’s lance opened his side and brought forth water and blood. Thus John said: “Water and blood came out from him” (John XIX, 34). Water for the washing, blood for the price. Water cleansed us; blood redeemed us.

[Col. 0681D]

25. And therefore the prophet says: “His eyes are cheerful with wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk,” signifying the prophets and the apostles.

Some, like the eyes of Christ, foresaw and announced his coming. Concerning them he himself says: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” [Col. 0682A] (John VIII, 56). And one of the prophets says: “I saw the Lord of hosts” (Isa. VI, 5); when they saw him, they were filled with spiritual joy.

Others—that is, the apostles—whom the Lord cleansed from every stain of sin, became whiter than milk, and no stain afterward darkened them. For milk is temporal, whereas the grace of the apostles remains forever. Preparing for us those spiritual and heavenly foods, they fattened the inward organs of the mind.

There are also those who think that the bright commandments of the Lord, drawn from the divine mouth, were made for us like milk; nourished by them, we have reached the food of heavenly bread. Hence Paul says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able” (I Cor. III, 2). In the beginning of faith he nourished the Corinthians with the drink of milk. And those holy men whose faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world, like children who have been weaned, are strengthened by more solid food.

## CHAPTER V

The blessing of Zebulun signifies the Church and its leaders.

26. “Zebulun shall dwell beside the sea. And he himself shall be beside the approaches of ships and shall extend as far as Sidon” (Gen. XLIX, 13). The interpretation of the name itself promises better things, since its Latin expression signifies liberation from nocturnal things. This is certainly good, and it belongs to the one who hopes in the wings of the Lord, whom his truth surrounds, so that he may not fear the terror of night or the business that walks in darkness.

### 27. “Therefore,” he says, “Zabulon shall dwell beside the sea,” so that he may see the shipwrecks of others while himself remains free from danger [Col. 0682C], and observe others struggling amid the waves in the strait of this world, being carried about by every wind of doctrine, while he himself perseveres immovable, rooted in faith, as the most holy Church is rooted and founded in faith. She watches the storms of the heretics and the shipwrecks of the Jews, because they rejected the helmsman whom they had possessed. Thus she dwells beside the waves but is not shaken by the waves, and is more prepared to offer assistance than exposed to danger, so that, if any who have been driven by severe storms should wish to flee to the harbor, the Church may be at hand as a harbor of salvation. With arms outstretched, she calls those in peril into the embrace of her tranquility, showing them a place of secure anchorage. Therefore, in this world, churches meet those who labor like maritime harbors spread along the shores, saying that a refuge has been prepared for believers [Col. 0682D], where vessels battered by the winds may be drawn ashore.

### 28. In these churches are the princes of Zabulon and the princes of Nephthalim, as Psalm LXVII teaches, whose one group are deliverers from the nocturnal storm, crying out: “Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light” (Rom. XIII, 12); while others possess apostolic breadth and can say: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart has been enlarged” (II Cor. VI, 11). These are the ones who, when they were in darkness, saw a great light, as the prophet testifies, saying: “The land of Zabulon and the land of Nephthalim, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan: the people who sat in darkness saw a great light; and for those who sat in the land and shadow of death, light has arisen” (Isa. IX, 1–2).

[Note: Some Paris editions read, “as Psalm LXX teaches”; others, “as the psalm teaches.” The older edition has, “as Psalm fifty-seventh teaches.” Some think this manner of numbering arose because the psalms were divided into three groups of fifty, and after the first group of fifty the following ones were numbered in this way: Psalm fiftieth-tenth, Psalm fiftieth-twentieth, and so on for the rest. We, however, think there is an error in the old edition, since in all the manuscripts it is designated by numerical letters as Psalm LXVII.]

### 29. Therefore our Lord God placed explorers beside the landing places of ships as heirs of this patriarch, whose watchful care extended and whose spiritual succession reaches as far as Sidon—that is, it reached even to the nations—so that the mercy of the Lord might wash away the sins of the nations. [Note: A considerable number of manuscripts read, “may lift up the sins of the nations.” A little later, where all the manuscripts and the old edition read, “son of Ham,” the Roman edition corrected the text, on the authority of the Bible, to “son of Canaan.” But Ambrose may have used a copy in which both father and son were called “Ham”; or, what is more credible, the scribe may have erred.] For Sidon is the firstborn son of Ham, that is, of the one who, because of his irreverence toward his father’s piety, was condemned by his father’s curse.

[Note: Thus all the manuscripts; the editions, however, read, “may walk/fall upon the rocky paths of this life”; the old edition has “walk,” and the Roman edition “fall upon.”]

Therefore the nocturnal deliverance, stationed as it were on guard in the spiritual stronghold, lest anyone should stumble against the rocks of this life, extends even to sinners guilty of the gravest crimes, and frees the Sidonians themselves—who formerly, because of their vehement superstition, were called hunters of crimes—and, as the interpretation teaches, releases them from the inheritance of the curse and grants them the inheritance of blessing, so that where guilt was greater, grace may now be more abundant.

## CHAPTER VI

### The blessing of Issachar, which is mystically expounded concerning Christ the Lord.

[Col. 0683C] **30.** “Issachar desired what is good, resting between the boundaries, and seeing that rest is good and that the land is fertile; he placed his shoulder under labor, and became a husbandman” (Gen. XLIX, 14 ff.).

Issachar means “reward,” and therefore is referred to Christ, who is our reward; for we purchase him, as it were, for the hope of eternal salvation—not with gold or silver, but with faith and devotion. Hence David also says of him: “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord: sons are his reward, the fruit of the womb” (Ps. CXXVI, 3). And Moses says of him: “The reward of those who inhabit beside the sea” (Deut. XXXIII, 19).

He is the one who desired what is good from the beginning and did not know how to desire what is evil. Of him Isaiah also says: “Before the child knows how to call his father or mother, he did not believe in wickedness, choosing what is good” (Isa. VIII, 4). [Col. 0683D] He rested between the lots of the Old and New Testaments, or in the midst of the prophets. Therefore he appeared between Moses and Elijah, to show us that he has rest in the words of those through whom many, renouncing their sins, believe in the living God; or because they themselves are witnesses to his resurrection and blessed repose.

**31.** Therefore, in order to call the nations to the grace of his resurrection [Col. 0684A]—for this is the fertile and fruitful land that produces eternal fruits, fruit a hundredfold and sixtyfold—he placed his shoulder under labor, submitting himself to the cross so that he might bear our sins. Hence the Prophet says: “Whose sovereignty is upon his shoulder” (Isa. IX, 6); that is, the power of divinity rests upon the suffering of the body, or the cross rises above the body.

He therefore placed his shoulder against the plow, enduring all the insults that had to be undergone, submitting himself to labor so that he might be wounded for our iniquities and weakened for our sins. And he became a husbandman, knowing how to sow his land with good grain and to plant fruit-bearing trees with deep roots.

## CHAPTER VII

### The blessing of Dan, which foretells the future Antichrist from that tribe. An exhortation to shake off the sleep of vices follows, after it has been predicted that the same tribe will come to the faith.

[Col. 0684B]

**32.** “Dan shall judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel. And Dan became for himself a serpent, sitting in the way, and biting the horse’s heel on the path; and the rider shall fall backward, awaiting salvation from the Lord” (Gen. XLIX, 16 ff.).

The literal meaning is that Dan also gave Israel a judge from the tribe. For after Joshua son of Nun, judges of the people arose from different tribes. Samson too was from the tribe of Dan, and he judged Israel for twenty years.

But the prophecy does not signify him; rather, it signifies the Antichrist, who will arise from the tribe of Dan—a savage judge and monstrous tyrant who will judge his people. Like a serpent sitting in the way and on the path, he will attempt to overthrow those who walk in the way of truth, desiring to trip up the truth.

For this is what it means to bite the horse’s heel: that, when the horse has been wounded by the infusion of poison and injured by the serpent’s bite, it may lift its heel. Thus Judas the traitor, tempted by the devil against the Lord Jesus, lifted up his heel in order to overthrow the rider—who humbled himself in order to raise everyone up.

Therefore he fell, not prostrate on his face as though sleeping, but backward, so that, extending himself from higher things toward former things, he might await salvation from the Lord. For he knew that he would be raised again, and therefore he awaited the raising up of fallen Adam.

**33.** Therefore, when we are running well along the way, let us beware lest a serpent be hiding somewhere on the path, overturn the step of the horse—that is, of our body—and suddenly cast down the sleeping rider. If we are watchful, we must take precautions to some extent and avoid the serpent’s bite.

Let the sleep of negligence, therefore, not overwhelm us; let the sleep of the world not overwhelm us; let the sleep of riches not overwhelm us, lest it also be said of us: “They have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing” (Ps. LXXV, 6).

But there are also sleeping riders, of whom it is written: “They slumbered, those who mounted horses” (ibid., 7). If avarice wounds your breast, if lust inflames you, you are a sleeping rider; and therefore you cannot restrain your body, that is, your horse.

Be watchful, then, so that even if you have been cast down—that is, if you have died—you may not fall asleep. For those who sleep their sleep find nothing. But await salvation from the Lord; look toward what is to come, so that you may find the grace of the resurrection.

Judas was sleeping; consequently, he did not hear Christ’s words. Judas was sleeping—and indeed the sleep of riches—for he was seeking payment for his betrayal. The devil saw him sleeping, overcome by the heavy sleep of avarice; he entered his heart, wounded the horse, and cast down the rider, whom he separated from Christ.

**34.** Moses also blessed this tribe, saying: “Dan is a lion’s cub, and he shall flee from Bashan” (Deut. XXXII, 22), that is, from confusion. Therefore, according to the Greek text from which the Latin translator rendered it, we should understand more precisely the statement that Dan himself became a serpent sitting in the way.

Dan means “judgment.” Consequently, this tribe underwent the grave peril of judgment; the serpent that slipped into it is the Antichrist, who would wound the one running with his poisons. Yet the tribe itself will be delivered from confusion when it confesses the risen rider, who says: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever is ashamed of me before men, I also will be ashamed of him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. X, 32–33).

## CHAPTER VIII

### The blessing of Gad foreshadows that the Jews would tempt the Lord and would in turn be tempted by him.

[Col. 0685C]

**35.** “Gad is temptation; he tempted him, and he himself tempted them beside the feet” (Gen. XLIX, 19). [Note: Some manuscripts read, “the encounter and cunning,” etc.] Temptation is the gathering and cunning of the scribes and priests who tempted the Lord Jesus concerning the tribute to Caesar and concerning John’s baptism, as Scripture teaches (Matt. XXII, 17); and the Lord Jesus, in his justice, turned the test back upon them (ibid., 21, 23).

“Beside the feet” means immediately, without any deliberation, replying in such a way that he himself might more effectively confound those who were tempting him. For when they said, “By what authority do you do these things?” he did not answer what they had asked; rather, he himself put forward a question, saying: “I also will ask you one question: if you tell me, I also will tell you by what authority I do these things” (ibid., 24).

Again, when they said, “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matt. XXII, 17), he said: “Why do you tempt me, hypocrites? Show me the coin of the census.” And when they offered it, he asked them again: “Whose image and inscription is this?” (ibid., 19). They said to him, “Caesar’s.” There he bound them by their own words and constrained them by their own obligation. Then he said to them: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (ibid., 21), so that they could not contradict their own words. Finally, they marveled and went away from him.

But it is not surprising that he answered beside the feet, since he saw ahead of his feet.

**36.** Moses clearly explained that this prophecy of holy Jacob concerns Christ [Col. 0686A]. For he says: “Blessed is the one who enlarged Gad. Like a lion he rested, breaking the arms and the princes, and he saw from the beginning that there the land of the princes gathered together with the princes of the peoples was divided. The Lord carried out justice, judgment with Israel” (Deut. XXXIII, 21).

**37.** We therefore recognize who rested like a lion, who broke the arms of the powerful, and who saw from the beginning the divisions of those who were tempting him. There, then, is the chasm of the earth that may swallow the false accusers, where the temptation of the faithless is found.

## CHAPTER IX

### The blessing of Aser expresses the riches of Christ, who was poor, and his manifold gifts to human beings.

[Col. 0686B]

**38.** “Aser’s bread is rich, and he himself will give food to princes” (Gen. XLIX, 20). In the Latin interpretation, Aser signifies “riches.” Who, then, is rich, except where there is the abundance of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God? Who is rich except the Lord Jesus, who always abounds and never fails?

He came into this world poor, and abounded for all; he filled everyone. How great are his riches, since by his poverty he made everyone rich! Yet he was poor for our sake and rich with the Father. He was poor in order to rescue us from poverty, as the Apostle teaches, saying: “Because for your sake he became poor, although he was rich, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (II Cor. VIII, 9).

His poverty enriches; his fringe heals; hunger satisfies; death gives life; burial raises up. This rich one, then, is the treasure; this is his rich bread. And rightly is it rich, for whoever eats it cannot hunger. He gave this bread to the apostles so that they might distribute it to the believing people; and even today he gives it to us, the bread that he himself, the priest, consecrates daily by his words. This bread, therefore, has become the food of the saints.

**39.** We may also understand the Lord himself, who gave us his flesh, as he himself says: “I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate manna in the desert, and they died; but this is the bread that has descended from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he may not die” (John VI, 48–49).

And lest anyone think that he is speaking of the death that comes through the separation of soul and body, and rightly raise an objection, since he knows that the holy apostles died this death, he added: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (ibid., 51–52).

That is, above I was not speaking of temporal life, nor of the death of this life, by which even if someone dies, nevertheless, if he has received my bread, he will live forever. For he receives it who proves himself. Whoever receives it will not die the death of the sinner, because this bread is the forgiveness of sins.

**40.** Moses also prophesied most beautifully in his blessings, saying: “Blessed by the sons of Aser, and he shall be acceptable to his brothers; he shall dip his foot in oil, and iron and bronze shall be his footwear. And as your days are, so shall your strength be. There is none like your God in heaven, your helper, and the great Lord of the firmament; and God, protecting you from the beginning, by the strength of powerful arms drove your enemy away from your face, saying: ‘Let him perish.’ And Israel shall dwell securely alone upon the land; Jacob shall be in grain and wine, and the heaven above you shall be with a mist of dew” (Deut. XXXIII, 24 ff.).

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “Your strength shall be,” and continues, “and the sovereignty of God shall protect you.”]

## CHAPTER X

### The blessing of Nephthalim is an image of the faithful who cling to Christ like branches to a vine and are released from the bonds of death.

[Col. 0687A] **41.** “Nephthalim is a loosened vine, extending beauty in its shoot” (Gen. XLIX, 21).

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “lest the vine luxuriate through the chance exuberance of its branches,” etc.]

One branch of a vine is cut off because it appears useless, lest the empty vine luxuriate in the exuberance of its branches; another is cut back somewhat and then allowed to grow, so that it may bear fruit, whose beauty is extended in its growth. For as it rises toward higher things, it embraces the vine; and as it climbs toward the summit, it clothes the necks of the vines with a kind of necklace of precious branches. There is also beauty in its offspring, because with full branches it pours forth many fruits.

**42.** This beauty is significant, but much more beautiful is that which signifies a branch clinging to the spiritual vine, of which we are branches and can bear fruit if we remain in the vine; otherwise, we are cut off.

**43.** The holy patriarch Nephthalim was an abundant branch. Hence Moses says: “Nephthalim is the fullness of those who receive; he shall be filled with blessing from the Lord; he shall possess the sea and the south” (Deut. XXXIII, 23).

He explains what Jacob had said: what is “a loosened vine”? It is one released from the bonds of habit through the grace of faith. This signifies the people of God, called to the freedom of faith and the abundance of grace, spread throughout the whole world. It clothes the yoke of Christ with good fruit and embraces the branches of that true vine—that is, the mysteries of the Lord’s cross. It does not fear the danger of confessing him but rather, even when placed amid persecutions, glories in the name of Christ.

**44.** Truly he is released from bonds who is bound by no chain of fear. Hence the prophet also says: “They shall go forth and leap like calves released from their bonds” (Mal. IV, 2).

Therefore he extends beauty in his shoot, because, placed in a pasture and raised beside waters of refreshment, through the sacraments of his regeneration he produces the good beauty of the word and is taken up into that most beautiful grace of Christ, who can increase the loveliness [Col. 0687D] of your beauty.

**45.** Finally, he is beautiful above all, and he gives what he possesses, because no one can give what he does not possess. Therefore it is said: “The Lord shall reign; he has clothed himself with beauty” (Ps. XCII, 1). For grace clothed the Church with beauty; in that washing she laid aside the foulness of all sins and shone with the splendor of heavenly grace.

Therefore the bridegroom says of her: “Who is this who looks forth like the dawn, chosen like the sun, beautiful like the moon, a marvel like an ornament?” (Song VI, 9).

[Note: The old edition reads, “wondrous, like an array”; the Roman edition, “wondrous like an ordering.” The manuscripts have the reading adopted in our text. The Septuagint has θάμβος, ὡς τεταγμέναι—“a terror, like battle lines drawn up,” with “armies” understood. Symmachus accordingly has ἐπίφοβος ὡς τάγματα παρεμβολῶν—“terrible as battalions of armies”; and the Vulgate, “Terrible as an army set in array.”]

## CHAPTER XI

### Jacob was more expansive in blessing Joseph because he saw in him the mysteries prefigured concerning Christ. The individual parts of the same blessing are then applied.

[Col. 0688A] **46.** Now, in order to conclude the history with something like an epilogue, just as Scripture itself concluded it, let us set forth the prophecy of holy Jacob concerning the name of holy Joseph:

“Joseph is my son who is to be increased; Joseph is my son who is to be increased; my younger son, to be envied, return to me. Against him they who were devising counsel cursed, and they directed the bow of the Lord against him; but they were crushed together with the strength of their bow, and the sinews of their arms were loosened by the hand of the mighty God of Jacob; from there Israel prevailed through the God of your father. And my God helped you and blessed you with the blessing of heaven from above and with the blessing of the earth that possesses all things.

“Because of the blessing of breasts and womb, the blessings of your father and your mother have prevailed over the blessings of enduring mountains; and the desires of the eternal hills shall be upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of those over whom he ruled, his brothers” (Gen. XLIX, 22 ff.).

[Note: In this passage the manuscripts and the old edition scarcely differ, except that where they read, “He who prevailed through the God of Israel, your father,” the Roman edition has, “your father.” Most of the manuscripts have, “From there Israel prevailed through the God of your father.”]

**47.** What is the reason that the father followed Joseph more generously than all his sons, except that he already saw in him the mysteries prefigured concerning Christ? [Note: Some manuscripts read, “the things prefiguring Christ in him.”]

Therefore, in blessing him, he referred more to the one who was awaited than to the one who was seen, saying: “Joseph is my son who is to be increased.” Who is the one who is to be increased except Christ, whose grace is always increased and whose glory has no end to its progress?

John also says of him: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John III, 30), because through that saving and perfect name grace has been heaped up and has abounded in this world.

“My son who is to be increased”; and this is because his brothers saw him increasing and began to envy him. The spiritual Joseph also incurred jealousy from those whom he favored most. Finally, he said: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV, 24). And they said: “We do not know where he is from” (John IX, 29). He cared for them, and they denied him.

**48.** “My younger son,” he says. Truly younger, since he was almost the last by birth. Indeed, Scripture says: “Jacob loved him because he was the son of his old age” (Gen. XXXVII, 3). This too is referred to Christ. For as the world was growing old and already passing away, the Son of God, dawning through the birth from the Virgin Mary, came late, as the son of old age, according to the mystery of the body he assumed—he who had always been with the Father before the ages.

[Note: The manuscripts, except the Vatican manuscript and Theodore’s text, have this wording. Those witnesses, together with the edition, read, “according to the mystery of the body assumed.” Moreover, “according to the mystery” here means “according to the mystery prefigured in Joseph.”]

[Col. 0689A] **49.** Therefore the Father says to him: “Return to me,” calling him from earth to heaven—the one whom he had sent for our salvation.

Thus, by raising his only-begotten Son, he emptied the counsel of those who cursed. Hence Isaiah also says: “The counsel of your spirit is vain” (Isa. XIX, 11). And, having convicted those who, like archers, were directing arrows at him, he dissolved everything and crushed the power of those who trusted in their own strength and not in God.

“From there,” he says, “Israel prevailed through the God of your father, and my God helped you.” Who is the one who strengthened Israel and helped the Son, except God the Father alone, who said: “Jacob is my servant; I will receive him; Israel is my chosen one; my soul has accepted him” (Isa. XLII, 1)?

**50.** “And he blessed him with the blessing of heaven above and with the blessing of the earth that possesses all things.” For he subjected all things to him: heavenly things, as the blessing of heaven, and earthly things, as the blessing of earth, so that he might rule over both human beings and angels.

**51.** Therefore, in that seemingly contemptible body, he says: “You have prevailed because of the blessing of breasts and womb, the blessings of your father and mother.”

By “breasts” he meant either the two Testaments, one of which announced him and the other revealed him. And appropriately “breasts,” since he nourished and raised us, as it were, with spiritual milk, and the Son presented us to God. [Note: All editions read, “he presented sons to God.” Against them, all the manuscripts read, “the Son.”]

Or he speaks of Mary’s breasts, which were truly blessed, with which the holy Virgin offered the Lord’s people a draught of milk. Hence that woman in the Gospel also said: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked” (Luke XI, 27)!

But if, when he says “the blessing of the womb of your father and mother,” we wish to understand only Mary’s womb, the reason why he joined both blessings together will remain unclear. For he could have spoken of the womb of the mother alone.

I think, however, that it is more beautiful to understand, according to the spiritual mystery, the Lord Jesus’ twofold generation: according to divinity and according to the flesh. For he was begotten from the Father before the ages. Hence the Father also says: “My heart has uttered the Word” (Ps. XLIV, 2), because he proceeded from that innermost and incomprehensible substance of the Father and is always in the Father.

Therefore the evangelist also says: “No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known” (John I, 18).

Just as the bosom of the Father is understood spiritually as a certain innermost secret of the Father’s love and nature, in which the Son always is, so also the womb of the Father is the spiritual secret of his interior, from which the Son proceeded as from a generative womb.

Finally, we read in different passages of the Father’s womb, of his heart from which he uttered the Word, and of his mouth from which justice proceeded and from which wisdom came forth, as he himself says: “From the mouth of the Most High it came forth” (Ecclus. XXIV, 5).

Thus, since one term is not defined and all the terms signify one thing, the spiritual mystery of the Father’s generation, rather than any bodily organ, is more clearly indicated. But just as we understand that generation from the Father, so also, for the completion of faith, let us understand Mary’s generation when the mother’s womb is blessed—that virginal womb of Mary, which gave birth to the Lord Jesus for us.

[Note: All editions, together with the Vatican manuscript, read, “Concerning this birth the Lord says”; but the manuscripts, in strong agreement, read, “Concerning this womb, the Father says.”]

Concerning this womb the Father says through the prophet Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb of your mother, I sanctified you” (Jer. I, 5).

The prophet therefore declared Christ’s twofold substance, divinity and flesh: one from the Father, the other from the Virgin. Yet when he was born from the Virgin and was in the body, he was not deprived of his own divinity.

[Col. 0690B] **52.** Hence he also grew strong above all the mountains and the desires of the eternal hills. He was exalted above all those men of lofty merit—the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles—and also beyond the sun, moon, and archangels, shining like the light of heaven, as he himself says: “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master” (Matt. X, 24).

For which of them had all things subjected to him, when it was he who granted them whatever they were? In him all his saints are blessed, because he is above the heads of all and is the head of all. “The head of the woman is the man, and the head of the man is Christ.”

And he is above the crowns of the mountains, because he is the supreme summit of all; yet he is the highest summit of the righteous. He calls them brothers, acquired through grace and sharing in a kind of regeneration.

Hence, when we speak of Joseph’s brothers, we understand especially those brothers of whom he says in the psalm: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will sing to you” (Ps. XXI, 23).

**53.** Finally, when Moses was about to complete the course of this life and blessed the tribe of Joseph, he was not blessing the already deceased Joseph, but Christ, as you find written concerning Joseph:

“Blessed by the Lord is his land, from the boundaries of heaven, from the dew, and from the depths of the springs below; according to the course of the sun at its appointed time; from the fitting months; from the crown of the mountains, from the beginning; from the crown of the eternal hills; from the fullness of the land at its appointed time; and from him who appeared in the bush. Let the blessing come upon the head of Joseph and upon his crown. Let him be honored among his brothers. The firstborn of the bull is his beauty; his horns are the horns of the unicorn. With them he shall winnow the nations together to the ends of the earth” (Deut. XXXIII, 13 ff.).

[Note: The Roman edition considerably altered this passage; since the changes concern wording more than meaning, we pass over them. We have corrected the text from the old edition and also amended it in several places from the manuscripts.]

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “from the fruits of heaven, and dew, and from the springs of the depths below, and according to the hour from the fruits of the course of the sun,” and so forth.]

“He himself has myriads of Ephraim, and he himself has thousands of Manasseh.”

[Note: The Ambrosian and Era editions, and Theodore’s manuscript, read: “The earth itself shall roar with mysteries concerning him, and he himself …” Other editions read: “They are the myriads of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh.” The manuscripts are not far from these readings, except that they all have “he himself … he himself,” apart from the Albino manuscript, which reads “they themselves … they themselves,” perhaps not incorrectly. The Colbert and German manuscripts also have “myriads … thousands.” This reading is not wholly to be rejected.]

**54.** The blessing is the same blessing that contains the fullness of all heavenly and earthly things and the particular grace of Christ: he who appeared in the bush and said to Moses: “Take off the sandals from your feet” (Exod. III, 5); he who is God above all. [Note: All editions read, “God above all gods”; nearly all the manuscripts, however, read, “God above all.”]

For he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he himself may hold primacy, because in him all fullness was pleased to dwell.

Therefore, to him alone is the prerogative of this blessing assigned, from the summit of heaven to the end of the earth. For he is before all things, and in him all things hold together. Through the blood of his cross he also made peace among all things, whether those in heaven or those on earth.

Because holy Joseph bears his type, he is fittingly blessed so that he may be honored among his brothers.

**55.** “The firstborn of the bull is his beauty, having the horns of the unicorn, with which he shall winnow the nations.” The good bull is like a sacrificial victim for sins and the sacrifice of the whole world, so that he might reconcile all things. His beauty is holy, for everything holy is called firstborn, as we have shown elsewhere (Book II, *On Abel and Cain*, ch. 2, nos. 3, 12).

Hence Levi deserved to be called firstborn, not according to the order of age, but by the prerogative of sacred succession. And truly holy is his beauty, of whom it is written after his resurrection: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV, 3), because he is the firstborn from the dead, possessing the horns of the unicorn.

But since he says “horns,” how he can then speak of the unicorn must be investigated, since, as experts say, the unicorn itself is not found among the species of wild animals. [Note: Anyone wishing to learn the various opinions of authors concerning the monoceros should consult Conrad Gesner, Book I of *Histories of Animals*, p. 781, and Ulysses Aldrovandi, *On Cloven-Footed Quadrupeds*, Book I, ch. 33, concerning the rhinoceros, pp. 878 and 888.]

Therefore we should rather understand “the unique Word,” because the substantive Word of God is one, not many words. Hence Hannah also says: “The Lord judges the ends of the earth, and he will give strength to his king, and will exalt the horn of his Christ” (I Kings II, 10).

And Isaiah says: “A vineyard was planted for the beloved on a horn, in a fertile place” (Isa. V, 1), because the Church blossoms for the only-begotten Son of God, holding the one Word of God, in whom is the fullness of power and wisdom, through whose abundance the harvest of faith has sprung up. The saints follow this Word.

**56.** “Ten thousand for Ephraim and thousands for Manasseh” (Deut. XXXIII, 17)—that is, let him rule over both Jews and nations and acquire for himself from both peoples the fullness of the Church.

Therefore holy Jacob placed his right hand upon Ephraim, because we read that the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “My brother is white and red, chosen from ten thousand” (Song V, 10).

Finally, the young women also proclaimed David, the ancestor of Mary, from whose line Christ was born through the Virgin’s childbirth, among ten thousand; Saul, however, was proclaimed among thousands, although, out of reverence for the king, they ought rather to have given greater weight to him.

Therefore whoever, by confessing Christ’s glory, exalts the horn of Christ will himself also receive horns. Hence the saints are also called unicorns in the verse of the psalm: “And the beloved is like the son of unicorns” (Ps. XXVIII, 6).

[Note: “Young women,” that is, those women who, leading choruses, went out to meet David as he returned from battle after killing Goliath, as recorded in I Kings XVIII, 6–7.]

For just as such an animal, when its horns begin to grow, signifies the progress of fuller maturity, so when horns begin to sprout from a certain head of our soul, they seem to signify the progress of more perfect virtue; and they grow for as long as they are being completed.

With this horn the Lord Jesus crushed the nations, so that he might destroy superstition and restore salvation, as he himself says: “I strike, and I heal” (Deut. XXXII, 39).

Therefore, as an imitator of this bull, the Prophet says: “In you we shall winnow our enemies with the horn” (Ps. XLIII, 6)—that is, destroying every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God.

And therefore, according to the Law, clean animals have horns (Deut. XIV, 4–5), for the Law is spiritual. Those who can repel the allurements of this world by the word of God and the observance of virtue seem to be armed with horns, as with weapons of their heads.

And rightly the marvelous power of speech is called a horn-trumpet (Ps. XCVII, 6), which rouses the good soldiers of Christ to battle so that we may carry away spoils from the enemy, the devil.

We are therefore in the battle line, and we see many of our own held captive in the adversary’s camp. They must be stripped of the most grievous yoke of servitude.

## CHAPTER XII

### The blessing of Benjamin mystically signifies Paul’s persecution of the Church, as well as his conversion and preaching.

57. The devil has very many wolves, whom he sends against Christ’s sheep; and therefore the intelligible Joseph, in order to save his sheep, seized the enemy himself, who was coming to carry off the sheep, as the wolf Paul, making a teacher out of a persecutor. Concerning him Jacob says, as it is written: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will eat still, and in the evening he will divide the spoil among princes” (Gen. XLIX, 27). He was a wolf when he scattered and devoured the sheep of the Church. But the one who had come as a wolf became a shepherd.

He was a wolf when he was Saul, when he entered houses and dragged men and women into prison. He was a wolf when, breathing threats and murder against the Lord’s disciples, he sought letters from the chief priests so that he might attack Christ’s servants. Jesus blinded him, like a wolf wandering in the darkness of night, by the outpouring of his light. Therefore, when Rachel gave birth to Benjamin, she called his name “Son of my sorrow” (Gen. XXXV, 18), prophetically indicating that from this tribe would come Paul, who would afflict the children of the Church during the time of his persecution and would torment his mother with profound grief.

Yet afterward, in a later period, he divided food among princes, evangelizing God’s word to the nations and calling many to the faith; [Note: [Col. 0692D] So the Roman edition and four manuscripts read. But the old edition and other manuscripts of better quality read: “while he was disputing, Paul the proconsul’s legate, and Publius the prince, etc.” Yet if this reading were correct, it would be necessary to suppose that the holy Doctor used an exemplar differing from all the Bibles and versions now extant. For everywhere [Col. 0693B] it is not Paul’s proconsul’s legate, but Paul himself, the proconsul, who is narrated as having been converted by the Apostle. We except, however, the Arabic version. In that version, two persons are plainly made out of Sergius Paulus; in its Latin interpretation we read as follows: “He [namely, Elymas the magician] was with Sergius the tribune, together with Paul, a prudent man.” This can indeed favor the reading of the ancient editions, if we say that Ambrose called that Sergius, whom the Arabic version calls a tribune, “Paul’s proconsul’s legate.”] while he was disputing, as we read, Paul the proconsul and Publius the prince received the Lord’s grace (Acts XIII, 12; XXVIII, 8).

58. Beautifully, too, when Moses blessed the tribe of Benjamin, he said: “The beloved of the Lord will dwell in confidence, and God will overshadow him all his days, and the one beloved by the Lord will rest between his shoulders” (Deut. XXXIII, 12)—the one who also became a chosen vessel. For he was converted only through the Lord’s mercy and love. Hence he himself, attributing nothing to his own merit but referring everything to Christ, says: “For I am the least of the apostles, and I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty” (I Cor. XV, 9–10).

He will dwell confidently in the house that he had formerly devastated; he will dwell in the tabernacles of Christ, [Col. 0694A] he who had previously wandered through the forests like a wolf. And God overshadowed him when Christ appeared to him. Although he saw nothing with open eyes, he nevertheless saw Christ. And rightly did he see the one present whom he also heard speaking. This overshadowing was not that of blindness but of grace. Indeed, it is said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I, 35).

532 59. “And he will rest between his shoulders”—that is, amid good deeds and precious works. For above you also have the statement that Issachar “put his shoulder to labor” and became a farmer. Paul imitated him and planted the young plants of faith; therefore, like a good farmer, he said: “I planted, Apollos watered” (I Cor. III, 6).

# [ON ELIJAH AND FASTING]

[Col. 0693B]

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE BOOK ON ELIJAH AND FASTING

In which certain matters concerning the Lenten fast of the Church of Milan, as well as banquets celebrated over the tombs of martyrs, are introduced.

[Col. 0693]

Anyone reading this book will easily notice three parts in it. In the first, and the principal one, fasting is discussed, especially the fast preceding the Paschal festivals. Ambrose first asserts (ch. 1) that it is a kind of battle, by whose benefit we carry away the victory of the cross and the trophy of the Lord’s resurrection. In this battle, he says, the Lord himself wished to go before us, in order to give us the art of fighting and grant us the grace of victory. He then reveals how great the power of fasting is by briefly enumerating the wonders remembered as having been performed by Elijah through its aid (chs. 2–3). Nevertheless, since he had already written many books about Elijah’s deeds, he denies that he will discuss him at length (ch. 3, no. 5), content to urge us to imitate him in the sacred forty-day fast.

Thus, as though he had prefaced his subject by speaking about fasting, he approaches his argument more directly. He shows (ch. 4) that fasting and the world are equally ancient: that the law of abstinence was given by God before all others, and that when it was violated Adam came to know his nakedness. He declares (ch. 5), by Noah’s example, that the use of wine had been unknown up to that time; that Abraham did not serve wine at his banquet to the Angels, and indeed not even to the Lord of the whole world; and that Moses finally supplied the people in the desert with water alone, by a miracle. In addition, he sets before us that same Moses, Elisha, Daniel, and other outstanding men who became famous because of fasting (chs. 6–7). From there he proceeds (chs. 8, 9, and following) to the benefits of fasting, opposing to them, after listing them in great number, the disadvantages, disturbances, and expenses of excess and luxury. Nor is this omitted (ch. 10, nos. 34 and following): through fasting we are admitted to the mystical table, that is, to communion in the Eucharist. The holy Bishop concludes by prescribing how we ought to fast (ch. 10).

In the second part Ambrose attacks the excessively intemperate banquets of his own time. First he describes (ch. 12) the drinking bouts and drunkenness of ordinary and utterly low-born people. Then he turns to the banquets of the wealthy and of the most vigorous young men (ch. 13 and following). To make their drunkenness more hateful, he places before our eyes vivid images of them, as though they were breathing and alive. He also touches upon (ch. 17, no. 64) certain modes of drinking so astonishing that, unless the gluttons of our own age gave them credibility by their madness, they would almost seem unbelievable. Finally, he rebukes (ch. 18, no. 66) the drunkenness of women as well, for when stirred by it they ran through the city streets like Bacchants and committed acts harmful not only to themselves but also to those who watched them.

In the third part, seizing the opportunity offered by the words of Isaiah that had been read in the Church on that same day, he teaches (ch. 19) that this license at the table is the seedbed and mother of every vice, including avarice itself, by which the expenses of luxury are scraped together through right and wrong alike. Yet from Isaiah’s following words he proves (ch. 20) that God is at once the most merciful and the most skilled physician, who will restore health to those who flee to his help. To urge his hearers toward this more forcefully, he recalls to their minds (ch. 21, no. 77) the final judgment, which they had heard mentioned in the prophetic reading. To this he adds (ibid., no. 79) that we are athletes who will be denied the crown on that final day unless we fight with a noble spirit. Then, turning to the catechumens, he demonstrates that they have a clearer and safer path for purifying their vices (ch. 22, no. 83), namely baptism, by which all stains are consumed as by a kind of sacred fire. But since there were certainly some who, in order to continue more freely in their sins, postponed that sacrament until the end of life, he sharply rebukes them (ch. 22, no. 84), warning them that death comes upon them while they delay. He deters them from imitating Cain rather than Abel in offering sacrifice by their postponement (ibid., no. 85).

Although, as stated above, this book consists of three parts, nevertheless, because the most important of them is the one dealing with fasting—and because the subject was undertaken on the occasion of Elijah’s fasting—it is entitled *On Elijah and Fasting*. All the manuscripts bear this title, except that some, omitting the name of Elijah, give only: “A Sermon of Saint Ambrose on Fasting.”

Anyone who compares with this Ambrosian treatise the homily of Saint Basil in which he exhorts his people to undertake the Lenten fast eagerly (*Homily on Fasting*) will easily understand that many things were transferred from it into this work. Nevertheless, here too the holy Doctor retains his customary practice: sometimes adding, sometimes cutting, sometimes transposing certain things, and, when the matter seems to require it, expanding others.

Similarly, it may be observed that in the last two parts of this work Ambrose borrowed certain things adapted to the customs of his own people from two other homilies of Basil the Great. One of these, written against the intemperance customarily committed on the very day of Holy Easter, is entitled *Against Drunkenness and Luxury*; the other is an exhortation to baptism.

In this book, therefore, one finds no little material relating to the customs of the Church of Milan. Among these, the point especially worthy of notice seems to be what is said about the Lenten fast. “During Lent,” says the holy man, “one fasts on all the days except Saturday and Sunday.” Augustine indeed teaches (*Letter* 36 to Casulanus, no. 32; and *Letter* 54 to Januarius, no. 3) that Saturdays were not ordinarily fasted at Milan, as they were fasted at Rome; but his testimony is general. Ambrose’s passage here, however, plainly reveals that even on the Saturdays of Lent fasting was not practiced there.

We except, nevertheless, Holy Saturday, or the vigil of Easter; for on that day everyone fasts in such a way that, to speak with Augustine (*Letter* 56, no. 31), even those who dine on every other Saturday throughout the year observe the fast of that Saturday with the greatest devotion. Accordingly, the Milanese fasted only thirty-one days, since they did not begin their fast until the Monday after the first Sunday in Lent. Nor should anyone be troubled by the word “Lent,” since in other Churches as well, where the fasts did not begin earlier, they fasted no more than thirty-six days—the tithes, as Gregory the Great says (*Homily* 16 on the Gospels), and many others after him, that we give to God from our year. Indeed, within living memory Saint Charles decreed in his first synod that this fast should not begin earlier at Milan and in those parts of that diocese where the divine offices are celebrated according to the institution of Saint Ambrose.

There is no controversy that this work contains nothing except sermons that Ambrose delivered to his people, composed partly of catechumens and partly of the baptized. It may, however, be questioned whether he delivered them at the beginning or at the end of Lent. For when he says, “You too have given your name for Christ’s contest; you have enrolled for the competition for the crown” (ch. 21, no. 79), this seems to indicate that he is addressing the *Competentes*, who had already given their names for baptism, for which they were enrolled only toward the end of Lent.

On the other hand, the words of the first chapter more clearly testify that these sermons were delivered before the beginning of this sacred season: “Let us sound the trumpet as we advance into battle . . . the contest is imminent . . . our contest is fasting” (no. 1). Moreover, the example of Christ proposed there, together with other material presented in the following chapters, sufficiently confirms that the holy Bishop’s intention was to prepare the faithful to undertake this fast. What is therefore said about enrolling for the competition for the crown can be explained as referring generally to all Christians, to whom he had promised victory and a trophy from the very beginning of the book. Perhaps, however, both opinions may be reconciled if we say that the work consists of three sermons, which Ambrose later fashioned into a book after the pattern of Basil’s sermons, having delivered them at different times. We shall see that he did this more than once elsewhere as well.

It is much more difficult to determine in what year those sermons should be placed. To speak frankly, scarcely anything certain that would assist in establishing this can be extracted from reading the book. Nevertheless, if we may rely upon conjectures drawn from the book itself, we learn that Ambrose had already written many books about Elijah’s deeds (ch. 3, no. 5); consequently, he must by that time have spent a considerable number of years in the episcopate. We do not see how those years can be extended more accurately from another source than by reference to the psalms and hymns whose singing he is known to have instituted in the Church of Milan during Justina’s persecution, that is, in the year 386 (ch. 15, no. 55). It would therefore have to be said that this book was not written before the return of the younger Valentinian to Milan, when he returned to the city with Theodosius after the tyrant Maximus had been destroyed, that is, in the year 389. Perhaps it is for this reason also that military men are reported to have repeatedly said during their drinking: “I wish health to the emperors” (ch. 17, no. 62).

There is one matter that might delay us: namely, the mention of banquets that Christians once celebrated over the tombs of martyrs (ibid.). For this custom seems to have been abolished through the efforts of the holy Bishop before the year we have indicated. Augustine reports (*Confessions* VI, ch. 2, no. 2) that the blessed Monica, when she came to Milan in the year 384, wished, according to her custom, to bring a sober meal to the sacred tombs, but was forbidden to do so by the doorkeeper whom Ambrose had appointed there for this very purpose. It is therefore highly probable that this custom, against whose abolition so great a bishop vigilantly labored, did not continue long afterward.

Moreover, we learn from two letters of Saint Augustine (*Letter* 22, no. 4, and *Letter* 29, no. 10), the latter of which first appeared in the most recent edition, that this practice—or rather abuse—was around the year 391 cut out and suppressed throughout almost the whole of Italy through the vigilance of good bishops, among whom Ambrose must certainly be counted as one of the foremost. Nevertheless, these considerations do little harm to our opinion. If we consider the words Ambrose uses, we shall easily perceive that he does not speak with the force he would have used in arguing against a present and active vice; nor would he have restrained himself so that, while attacking other forms of intemperance so fiercely, he would have opposed this one with so light a hand. Therefore it is not at all inconsistent with probability to say that the holy Bishop touched upon this matter only incidentally, because some private individuals were frequenting such banquets out of misguided zeal. Or perhaps he wished to indicate the Roman Church, where the same custom still held sway, as is demonstrated by the memorable example of Pammachius.

Finally, it may be added that scarcely any work of Ambrose is found in the editions to be more corrupted than this treatise; but we have carefully collated and corrected it against manuscripts of good quality, especially the Colbertine manuscript, which appears to have been written a thousand years ago.

[Col. 0697B]

# ONE BOOK OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON ELIJAH AND FASTING

[Note: [Col. 0697B] Probably written in the year 390.] (C)

[Col. 0697]

535 # CHAPTER ONE

Just as formerly the Fathers, when they went forth to war, sounded the trumpet at new moons and on days of rejoicing, so we too must sound the trumpet on days of fasting, as the Paschal feast approaches.

[Col. 0697A]

1. A divine oracle resounded to the fathers, that when they went out to war, [Note: [Col. 0697B] All the manuscripts read this way; after “incentives,” supply “are understood.” The old manuscripts and editions differ from this only in reading: “and, recognizing more fully the incentives of his mercy, on days, etc.” But the Roman editors, perhaps indulging their conjectures too freely, attempted to correct the passage as follows: “they should sound the trumpet; this would be a sign that the Lord might remember his people and grant the requested help; and also that the people might call forth the incentives of mercy: on the days of their rejoicing, at their new moons, and on feast days they should sing together, etc.”] “they should sound the trumpet” (Num. X, 9), so that by its sound the Lord might remember his people and grant the requested help, recognizing more fully the incentives of his mercy; and on the days of their rejoicing, at their new moons, they should sing to the sound of trumpets. Hence David also says: “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month” [Note: [Col. 0698B] The editions read “on the day of the frequent festival”; the manuscripts read “on the distinguished day.”] “on the day of your solemn festival” (Ps. LXXX, 4).

Therefore the day of our solemn festival will come, and it is already approaching. Let us sound the trumpet as though advancing into battle. [Col. 0697B] Let us sound the trumpet to announce the day of the solemn festival; at the same time, battle is imminent for us, and victory is promised. Our victory is the cross of Christ; our trophy is the Passover of the Lord Jesus. But he first fought in order to conquer—not because he himself needed the battle, but so that he might first prescribe for us the pattern of warfare and afterward grant the grace of triumph.

Our battle is fasting. Indeed, the Savior fasted, and thus the tempter approached him. First he directed his spear at the appetite, saying: “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread” (Luke IV, 3). He held out food as bait for a snare, so that he might entrap bodily appetite. The Lord preferred fasting in order to break the tempter’s snares and dissolve his bonds. Thus you have it written: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (ibid., 4). By that snare Adam had been strangled; by this answer to the devil’s question every human being has been set free.

# CHAPTER II

How great the power of fasting is, and how splendid and strong its warfare, is demonstrated by the example of Christ and of Saint Elijah.

2. Great is the power of fasting. Indeed, its warfare is so splendid that even Christ delighted to fast; it is so strong that it raises human beings to heaven. And, to use human rather than divine examples, a voice issued from the fasting mouth of Elijah and closed heaven against the sacrilegious people of the Jews (III Kings XVII, 1). For when King Ahab had established an altar to an idol, at the prophet’s word the dew of rain did not fall upon the earth for three years and six months. It was a punishment worthy of suitably restraining intemperance: heaven was closed against the impious, who had polluted earthly things.

It was also fitting that, for the condemnation of the sacrilegious king, the prophet should be sent to a widow at Zarephath of Sidon, who, because she preferred devotion to food, deserved to be the only one not to experience the hardship of the public drought. Thus the jar of barley meal did not fail [Note: [Col. 0698B] All the editions read “the jar of flour.” All the manuscripts read “the jar of polenta”; two manuscripts, however, have “the jar of flour and polenta.” It is likely that the word “flour” was first placed in a gloss, then received into the text, and finally displaced the genuine reading. *Polenta* is roasted barley flour.] when the streams of the torrent failed.

3. Why should I recount the rest of his deeds? Fasting, he raised the widow’s son from the underworld; fasting, he brought down rain by his word; fasting, he drew fire from heaven; fasting, he was carried to heaven in a chariot; and by a forty-day fast he attained the presence of God. In the end he merited more because he fasted more.

With his fasting mouth he halted the waters of the Jordan, and he crossed the overflowing riverbed, suddenly dried, with dusty footsteps. Divine judgment rightly deemed him worthy of heaven, so that he might be carried away together with his body, because he lived a heavenly life in the body and displayed on earth the practice of a higher way of life.

# CHAPTER III

Praise of fasting; concerning the fast of Saint John; and what kind of food we ought to seek.

4. For what is fasting [Note: [Col. 0699D] The Roman edition reads “unless it is an image of heavenly life.” The other editions, together with all the manuscripts, read as in the text.] except substance and [Col. 0699B] image of heaven? Fasting is refreshment for the soul; fasting is food for the mind, as we have said; fasting is the life of angels; the death of guilt; the destruction of sins; the remedy of salvation; the root of grace; the foundation of chastity. By this step one reaches God more quickly; by this step Elijah ascended before he did so in the chariot. As he departed for heaven, he left this inheritance of sobriety and abstinence to his disciple. In this virtue and spirit Elijah came in John.

Indeed, he too devoted himself to fasts in the desert. His food was locusts and wild honey. And because his self-restraint had surpassed the capacity of human life, he was considered not a man but an angel. We read of him: “Even more than a prophet. This is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you” [Col. 0699C] (Matt. XI, 9–10). By human strength, who could have mounted fiery horses, driven fiery chariots, and guided chariots through the air, except one who had changed the nature of the human body through the power of incorruptible fasting?

5.
