But we have already set forth many things about Elijah’s deeds in the frequent discussions of various books; and I think we must take care not to return to the same material, especially since he himself is praised in his own work. Let us therefore imitate him and seek that food by whose power we may advance day and night toward knowledge of heavenly things.

For not every food is material, nor is every nourishment bodily. There is food for the mind, as we have said, by which souls feast, concerning which the Lord says: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John IV, 34). This is the food of angels, that they may serve the divine command. They have no concern for tables, no use for banquets, no stored-up feasts, no drinking of wine or strong drink, no swelling of the body, no distress of the stomach.

# CHAPTER IV

Concerning the origin and antiquity of fasting; how the first practice of the world began with fasting; how the first law was established in paradise; and how fasting finally covers those whom gluttony stripped bare.

[Col. 0700A]

6. Therefore, lest anyone think that fasting is earthly or recent, the world’s first practice began with fasting, when the bright light shone forth (Gen. I, 3 and following). The second day was in fasting, when the firmament of heaven was made. On the third day the earth brought forth pasture; nature rendered its service, yet fasting still preserved the discipline of heaven. On the fourth day the lights of the sun and moon were made, and still there was fasting. On the fifth day the waters brought forth creeping creatures with living souls and flying birds above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven; and God saw that they were good, and blessed them, saying: “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters that are in the sea, and let the birds multiply” [Col. 0700B] “upon the earth” (ibid., 22). And still there was fasting.

Indeed, he blessed them, as it is written, and said: “Increase”—he did not say, “Eat and consume.” On the sixth day the beasts were created (Dist. 35, ch. “On the Sixth Day”), and with the beasts the power of eating and the use of food arose. Where food began, there the world’s end was made. When it began not to know its own increase, then the divine works concerning it began to cease. By this indication it was declared that through foods [Note: [Col. 0699D] Some manuscripts read “the world would have to perish.”] the world would be diminished, since through them it ceased to increase. No one knew sin, no one feared punishment, and no one knew death.

7. The Lord planted paradise for the blessed, placed the human being there to work it and guard it. And so that we may know (Dist. and chapter the same, § “And so that we may know”) that fasting is not recent, he established there the first law concerning fasting. For he knew that through food guilt would enter.

The first punishment entered through the violation of fasting, when God’s command said: “You shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for on the day you eat from it, you shall die the death” (Gen. II, 17). Up to that point (Dist. and chapter the same, § “Up to that point”) no one knew how to violate the command, so that there had not yet arisen the first [Note: [Col. 0699D] The old edition reads “which was the first violation.” “The fast was commanded, the law of abstinence, etc.” The Vall. and Mich. manuscripts read: “which first violated the commanded fast of abstinence. The law, etc.” The Roman edition and one Vatican manuscript read: “which violated the edict. The law of abstinence, etc.” The Thuan., Germ., Vict., Laud., and Colb. manuscripts agree with our text. Again, where most manuscripts and all editions read “a hiding place after the food,” four manuscripts of the highest quality read “a temptation after the food.”] violation of the commanded abstinence.

The law is from the Lord God; violation of the law is from the devil; guilt comes through food; hiding comes after food. Knowledge of weakness is in food; the strength of firmness is in fasting. Indeed, as long as they abstained from what had been forbidden, they did not know that they were naked. After they had eaten from the forbidden tree, they recognized that they had been stripped naked.

Therefore, when the woman recognized the author of her guilt, she answered when questioned: “The serpent persuaded me, and I ate” (Gen. III, 13). The serpent urges the appetite; the Lord decrees fasting (Dist. and chapter the same, § “The Serpent”). Indeed, he himself says: “Fast and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI, 41). Thus gluttony expelled the one reigning from paradise, while abstinence recalled the wanderer to paradise.

8. And God said: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us” (Gen. III, 22). God says this mockingly, not approvingly; that is: “You thought you would become like us. But because you wished to be what you were not, you ceased to be what [Note: [Col. 0701D] The old edition reads “what you were.” “And so, while you strive to be above yourself.” Good sense; nevertheless, the Roman edition from one Vatican manuscript is better. The Gallican manuscripts partly agree with this reading and partly with the others, though in them something appears to have been omitted, except in the Mich. and Vall. manuscripts, in which one reads quite suitably: “what you were. Thus, because you were striving to be above yourself,” etc.] you were. You were within yourself, and while you strove to be above yourself, you began to be beneath yourself.”

Finally, he first clothed him in a tunic of skins and then said: “Behold, Adam”—as though he were saying: “Behold your cloak; behold your worthy garment; this clothing suits you. Those who strive after divine things are considered worthy of such an adornment. Behold where your guilt has led you; behold how now, in this tunic of skins, you have opened your eyes like one of us. Look around carefully: you see yourself naked, though you thought yourself clothed.”

9. Gluttony therefore makes people naked, while fasts cover even those who have been stripped. Hence David says: “I covered my soul with fasting” [Col. 0701B] (Ps. LXVIII, 11). Good is the covering that protects the soul, so that it is not detected by the tempter and is not stripped bare by the tempter. Good is the veil that covers guilt; abstinence covers it, grace covers it. For blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered.

Grace covers when it forgives and abolishes every error; abstinence covers when it shades vice, conceals it through a sorrowful disposition, and diminishes it through repentance. Indeed, fasting and almsgiving free from sin.

Adam was formerly covered by the veil of virtues before he transgressed; but, as though stripped by his transgression, he saw that he was naked, because he had lost the garment he possessed. “In the days of your fast,” he says, “your light will arise for you like the morning” [Note: [Col. 0701D] The Roman edition, with most manuscripts, reads “your morning light,” and with some manuscripts “early.” The old edition, with other manuscripts, reads “your great light . . . early.” Certain learned men thought this passage corrupt; for where our copies have “and your healing,” Tertullian, Cyprian, and Augustine write “and your garments will arise more quickly.” It is clear that they read not ἰάματα but ἱμάτια. Perhaps Ambrose himself read it no differently.] “and your healing will rise quickly, and righteousness will go before you, [Col. 0701C] and the majesty of the Lord will surround you” (Isa. LVIII, 8).

Good is the garment of light. For it is written: “Clothed in light as with a garment” (Ps. CIII, 2). Good is the garment when the Lord surrounds and covers those who fast.

# CHAPTER V

Noah’s drunkenness is excused on the ground of ignorance; the evils arising from the use of wine, and the good resulting from abstinence from it, are demonstrated by examples set against each other.

10. Noah was naked when he became drunk; the piety of his sons covered him. But he was stripped naked through ignorance, not through intemperance, for wine was not yet known. At the beginning of the human race drunkenness was unknown (Dist. 35, ch. “On the Sixth Day,” § “At the Beginning”). He himself first planted a vineyard: he gave it its nature but did not know its power. Thus wine did not spare its own author.

What wonder is it if, when the Lord himself praised his creatures, Noah too marveled at it? When he was delighted by the grace of the gift he had discovered, the more forceful substance tested the old man’s unaccustomed limbs, and the new drink disturbed him. “Those who mounted horses slumbered,” he says (Ps. LXXV, 7). The righteous mounted the pleasures of the body and fell asleep. But his drunkenness urges sobriety upon us (Dist. and chapter the same, § “But his”).

For Noah became drunk only once. When he recognized the evil of drunkenness, he moderated his discovery for practical use; he did not pour it out into vice. Hence the Apostle also says: “Use a little wine because of your frequent infirmities” (I Tim. V, 23).

11. Before wine was discovered, freedom remained unshaken for all; no one knew how to demand the services of slavery from a fellow participant in nature. There would be no slavery today if there had been no drunkenness. Envy of fraternal superiority had indeed already crept in, but reverence for fatherly piety still remained. Piety was wounded when drunkenness was mocked.

Therefore wines harm not only those whom they tempt, but even more those before whose eyes the drunken limbs of intoxicated people are exposed. From this irreverent laughter arises; from this lust is inflamed. Thus wine disturbs with much greater drunkenness those whose eyes and minds it has intoxicated than those whose limbs it has overthrown.

12. We also read (Dist. and chapter the same, § “We read”) that the daughters made their father Lot drunk on that mountain (Gen. XIX, 33 and following) to which they had fled in fear of the fires of Sodom and where they lived in a cave. Age, sex, solitude, and place all accord with and converge upon drunkenness—a place more suited to the hiding places of wild beasts than to human dwellings. Thus drunkenness was the origin of incest, and the offspring of a most evil mother was even worse.

[Col. 0702C]

13. But Abraham did not serve wine at his banquet. Instead, he sacrificed a calf and offered butter and milk even to his angelic guests. He recognized the Lord of heaven and the creator of the world, yet he could not offer wine. But rightly was the material of sin absent where there was forgiveness of sins.

14. Finally, John announced him as one who neither ate bread nor drank wine. For whoever announces Christ ought to show himself free from every incentive to vice. Thus drunkenness overcame holy Noah, and also Lot, Abraham’s nephew—one of whom survived the flood while fasting, the other the fire.

15. We also know that Moses tempered the bitterness of the waters for the thirsty people, not with wine. The rock poured forth water for him; nor could an abundance of wine have been lacking. Indeed, God said: “You shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, and the people will drink” (Exod. XVII, 6). He did not say: “Wine will come out for the people.” For it was dangerous to serve wine to a people whom even the stronger could scarcely bear.

# CHAPTER VI

Concerning the law of fasting given by Moses and his own fasting. How abstinence from wine made the mothers of Samson and Samuel fruitful in place of their barrenness; and with what foods Elisha fed the sons of the prophets.

[Col. 0703A]

16. Finally, Moses gave a law concerning fasting; he gave none concerning wine. Even while he was fasting, neither loud voices, nor lightning and rain clouds, nor smoking Sinai terrified him. Nor would he have entered the cloud and heard the voice of God speaking from the midst of the fire without danger to his salvation, unless he had been fortified with the weapons of fasting. For he fasted forty days on the mountain while receiving the Law from the Lord our God.

Above, on the heights of the mountain, the Law was given to Moses while he fasted; below, among the eating people, sacrilegious transgression was kindled by the luxury of the banqueters. Moved by this spectacle, Moses broke the tablets, judging it unworthy that the Law should be given to a drunken people. Thus the tablets of the Law, which abstinence had received, drunkenness caused to be shattered.

17. What more should I say? Did not abstinence from wine make the mother of Samson fruitful in place of her barrenness, and cause her, though barren, to give birth? For in accordance with the Lord’s command she did not drink wine. Did not the Lord hear Hannah when she did not eat, and did fasting dissolve her infertility? From these two women were born two men, one exceedingly strong, the other exceedingly observant; they showed themselves worthy of appearing to have been long nourished in the womb of fasting and brought forth from the overflowing womb of abstinence.

Thus Samson himself, who was born through his mother’s sobriety, was avenged by the drunkenness of the foreigners who insulted him. [Note: [Col. 0703D] The Roman edition reads “he perished through the drunkenness of those who insulted him.”]

18. The prophet Elisha, who had learned frugality from his teacher, when he was feeding the sons of the prophets, loaded the tables with clusters of wild vines and fulfilled the duty of hospitality with unsuitable wild vegetables [Note: [Col. 0703D] The Era., Gill., and Roman editions read “with wild vegetables that had not been purchased.” Ambrose’s edition and all the manuscripts read “with unsuitable” wild vegetables, etc. Not incorrectly; the meaning is the same as “poorly suited for food.”]. When, offended by their bitterness, they could not eat them, he tempered all that bitterness by sprinkling in a little flour, emptying the poison of its power through the gift of prophetic abstinence.

541 # CHAPTER VII
That three boys entered the furnace with empty stomachs and brought cooling to the flames; and that even the lions were taught to fast by Daniel’s fasting.

[Col. 0703D] **19.** There is a certain property of a substance [Note: Two manuscripts read “which they call the substance of lovers”; one, “which they call adamant”; the Ambrosian and Erasmian editions read “which they call adamantium,” and likewise below. Other manuscripts and editions have “which they call amantum,” etc. The true reading is “quam amantum.” Here Ambrose intended to render Basil’s statement from Homily 1 on Fasting: “There is a certain nature of a body which they call *amianton*, indestructible by fire, etc.” Concerning this stone, much is found in Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 19; Dioscorides, Book V, chapter 93; and, on this latter passage, Matthiolus, Book V, chapter 113, where he teaches that this very stone is alum itself, which we call *alun de plume*, from which even now incombustible lamp-wicks are made. A little later, instead of “it immediately catches fire,” some manuscripts read “fire, and immediately”; others, “by the fire of the hearth,” or “by fires, and immediately,” etc.], which they call *amiantum* [Col. 0704A], not easily consumed by any fire. When placed upon hearths, it glows; but as soon as it is removed from the flame, it shines clean again, as though washed by a pouring of water. Such were the bodies of the Hebrew boys, [Note: This is the reading of the Thuaneus, German, Dionysian, Victorine, and Colbertine manuscripts. Others, following the old editions, read “which were changed by fasting … by the heat of the fire ….” The Roman edition alone has “which used fasting ….”] which, transformed by fasting into the nature of amiantum, drew from the heat of the fire not destruction but adornment. Finally, when the fires of the furnace raged, so that the flame spread more than forty cubits around, consuming many of the Chaldaeans whom it encountered—those who supplied fuel to the fires with naphtha, pitch, tow, and brushwood—when the boys entered in a state of fasting, the heat of the flames having been dispersed, they immediately began to grow moist in the spirit of the cooling dew, so that not one hair of their heads was singed, because their fasting had nourished even that hair. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “because they entered fasting … they drew in a breath of cooling dew.” The old editions, together with the manuscripts, agree with our reading, except that they prefer “they immediately began,” where the others read “immediately in the warmth,” etc.]

**20.** Daniel, the man of desires, taught even lions to fast by fasting for three weeks. Sent into the pit, with his limbs hardened by the solidity of abstinence into the firmness of adamant, he was not exposed to injury. Fasting had so constrained him that no place could be found in his body for the bites of wild beasts. [Note: The old edition reads: “The savage lions kept their mouths closed, which the abstinence of prophetic holiness … with certain bonds of merit.” The Roman edition has: “The abstinence of the holy prophet … as if by certain ….” All our manuscripts agree with the present reading.] The lions kept their mouths closed; the holiness of prophetic abstinence restrained them, so that the beasts could not open mouths bound, as it were, by certain chains of merit.

**21.** Fasting, then, extinguished the power of fire; fasting closed the mouths of lions; fasting solidified the waters of the sea; fasting released the rock into springs of water. By the power of fasting, nature was changed against itself: the waves froze, and the rock poured forth a flood.

# CHAPTER VIII

To make the benefits of fasting shine forth more clearly, Ambrose compares them with the disadvantages of gluttony and offers an exceptionally vivid description of the disturbances that gluttony commonly causes; an exhortation to sobriety is joined to it.

[Col. 0704C]

**22.** But why should I use ancient examples, when fasting abounds even in the gifts of present blessings? Who has made his household poorer by fasting? Whose resources has it diminished? To whom is luxury not suspect? To whom is abstinence not venerable? Whose bed has parsimony coveted? Whose modesty has drunkenness not wounded? Fasting is the school of self-restraint, the discipline of chastity, humility of mind, chastisement of the flesh, the form [Col. 0704D] of sobriety, the rule of virtue, purification of the soul, an expenditure [Col. 0705A] of compassion, a training in gentleness, an attraction of charity, the grace of old age, and the guardian of youth. Fasting is relief from weakness and nourishment for health. No one has contracted indigestion by fasting; no one through abstinence has suffered a stroke [Note: “A blow of blood,” that is, *apoplexy*. Aurelius Victor also used this word for the disease in his work on Marcus Antoninus.]—indeed, there is no one whom fasting has not restrained and driven away from it. It is good provision for a journey and good throughout life: good at sea, it calms shipwrecks and preserves food.

**23.** Those who say that fasting is burdensome should answer: whom has fasting caused to collapse? Many have poured out their lives at dinner; very many while vomiting up a feast. What animal, finally, has lamented that fasting was the cause of its death? One does not avoid the noose through food: the hook lies hidden in the food; food leads one into the pit and draws one into the nets; food even binds birds with birdlime; food brings flying creatures [Col. 0705B] down to death. What dangers arise on account of the belly! Dumb animals know nothing of guilt, yet for this one thing they are punished as though for a crime. Fasting is sobriety of mind; through it the senses are vigorous, and through it judgments are formed. At a banquet there are cups. Fasting guards discipline; poverty follows luxury. Luxury is the mother of hunger, according to the prophetic saying (Tob. 4). Fasting loves quiet; luxury [Note: Thus all the Gallican manuscripts, except that the Dionysian codex, beside the word “footprints,” has in the margin “or scourgers,” a reading preferred in the text by the German manuscript; in Micah it reads “our,” and in the Vallian manuscript “your.” It may be inferred that the wording here is corrupt, which caused some editors, after omitting certain words, to print the entire passage in this form: “the old restlessness. The caterer is he who, before ….” The Roman edition instead reads: “restlessness. Fasting seeks leisure; luxury pursues business. The caterer, before ….” But Basil’s passage clearly shows that what was omitted should be restored: “The knife of the cooks has ceased,” which Ambrose plainly adapted for his own use.] restlessness. Fasting sows leisure; luxury pursues business.

**24.** One day the knife of the cooks will be struck down. Let the caterer rest—the man who, before daylight, knocks at other people’s doors and, as though some war were imminent, wakes those who are sleeping. You see him agitated, you notice him panting, and you ask what is causing the disturbance. “My master,” he says, “is asking where wine is sold at its best; he is looking for where a tougher [Note: Pig’s vulva and goose liver were ancient delicacies.] vulva may be prepared, where the liver is more tender, where the pheasant is fatter, where the fish is fresher.” He runs about in every direction, and when he has found what he seeks, he hurries at full speed. He disturbs his drowsy master and bids up the prices. [Note: If the price “moves,” understand “the buyer”: that is, if the price seems too high to the buyer.] If the price of the fish is raised, he insists that none better can be found—indeed, that it is already gone. “Yesterday,” he says, “there was a storm; today, a gale. I could scarcely find this one hidden away.” Many are rushing about in the market: “If you return it, another will offer more. And what will you serve at dinner?” “That wine is from such-and-such a vintage; these oysters were taken from that lake.” Such bidding takes place over every item. [Note: That is, an auction, because the bidding for goods for sale used to be conducted in the forum with a spear set up. Shortly afterward he calls the caterer a “shepherd”—the term used for the host and provider, namely, the person who received the guests at table. In this sense, below, in chapter 13, section 49, Ambrose likewise calls him “the one who feeds”; hence in later times *pastus* came to mean the same as a banquet.] A kind of auction is conducted between the caterer and the “shepherd.” In his agitation he sells off his estate and still asks through whose hands the rights to his possessions are being diminished.

**25.** They run to the kitchen; there is enormous clamor and uproar. The entire household is thrown into agitation, and everyone curses because no rest is granted them. At last, give the cook some rest. Like a statue, the right hand of the cupbearer grows stiff in the deepest frost. One works his hands in cold water; others wash the marble. They clean floors soaked with wine and covered with fish bones—and how many are wounded while walking! At the banquet itself there is the shouting of the feasters and the groaning of those being beaten. If something happens to displease the guests, they laugh while you grow angry. Let the house at last be free of the many disturbances caused by people running back and forth; let it be free of smoke and the odor of half-roasted food. [Col. 0706B] You would think it not a kitchen but a slaughterhouse: that a battle was being fought, not a dinner prepared; everything swims in blood.

**26.** One serves the evil mistress, the belly, which is always demanding and never satisfied. For what is more insatiable than the stomach? Today it receives, and tomorrow it demands. When it has been filled, there is discussion of self-restraint; when it has digested, farewell is said to the virtues, and it seeks luxury. Philosophy is proclaimed amid cups, and wines are praised amid philosophers. [Note: Latinius conjectures that it should read: “Labor,” he says, “and bile.” One manuscript supports him; but the others, and all the editions, support our reading. The Septuagint reads: “The pain of sleeplessness, and bile, and twisting with an insatiable man” (Ecclus. 31:23).] “Sleeplessness, bile, and torment,” it says, “belong to an insatiable man” (Ecclus. 31:23). He eats and soon afterward regrets it; his intemperance has not pleased him for long.

**27.** Consider the rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day. At his gate lay that beggar Lazarus, covered with sores and longing to be filled with what fell from the rich man’s table. Shortly afterward, when he had died, he began to plead from his place in hell that the poor man might dip the tip of his finger in water and cool his tongue, which was burning in the fire. Where are those riches? Where are those drunken revelries? The man who used to get drunk thirsts; the man who used to beg has abundance. At the banquet itself, while they drink, they thirst; and when they have become drunk, they drink still more. As though wine were being poured into an open chasm, it is no longer drunk but poured in; the cup is not sipped but emptied.

# CHAPTER IX

Why the powerful are forbidden to drink wine. Judith, while fasting, beheads Holofernes; Esther, by the same means, frees her people, while the drunken Haman pays the penalty. Finally, various praises of fasting are enumerated.

[Col. 0707A]

**28.** “Thorns,” he says, “grow in the hand of a drunkard” (Prov. 26:9), because he wounds himself with his own hands and casts sores upon his own breast. With these thorns he tears the garment of faith that he received and will not be able to preserve his treasure. For every drunkard and fornicator will be poor, and he will put on the torn garments of folly. Therefore the powerful are forbidden to drink wine, lest, when they drink, they forget wisdom (Prov. 31:4).

**29.** Indeed, the powerful were drinking wine in drunkenness—those who eagerly desired to surrender themselves to Holofernes, commander-in-chief of the king of the Assyrians. But the woman Judith did not drink; she fasted throughout all the days of her widowhood, except on the solemn festivals. Armed with these weapons, she went forth and outmaneuvered the entire Assyrian army. With the vigor of a sober mind she took off Holofernes’ head, preserved her chastity, and carried away the victory. Clad in fasting, she advanced in the enemy’s camp; he lay buried in wine, unable to feel the blow of the wound. Thus the fasting of one woman laid low countless [Note: The Roman edition reads “laid low the Assyrian army.” The German codex reads “the Chaldaean army.” All other manuscripts and editions read “the army of drunkards.”] armies of drunkards.

**30.** Esther too became more beautiful through fasting, for the Lord increased the grace of her sober mind. She freed her entire race—that is, the whole Jewish people—from the bitterness of persecution. She made the king subject to her, not inflamed by the heat of lust but converted by heavenly compassion. Thus punishment was turned back upon the wicked, and honor was restored to the sacred altars. Therefore she who fasted continuously for three days and washed her body with water found greater favor and brought about vengeance. But Haman, while boasting in the royal banquet, paid the penalty of his drunkenness amid the very wines.

**31.** Fasting, therefore, is a sacrifice of reconciliation and an increase of virtue; it even made women stronger by an increase of grace. Fasting knows no moneylender; it knows nothing of the principal of a loan; the table of those who fast does not smell of interest. A continent man’s paternal hundredths do not strangle his son; the pledged rights of a deceased sober man do not harass his widow; the usury-laden hall of one who fasts does not exclude the heir.

[Col. 0708A]

**32.** Fasting even lends grace to banquets themselves. Food becomes sweeter after hunger—food that becomes wearisome through constant use and cheap through prolonged repetition. Fasting is the seasoning of food. The keener the appetite, the more pleasant the meal. Thirst commends the cup; the fasting person does not seek out aged wines. Whatever he drinks while fasting, he sends down until satisfied; he does not hold it beneath his nose for judgment. Even precious things deteriorate through use; but what is difficult to possess is pleasant to enjoy. The sun itself is more welcome after night, daylight itself brighter after darkness, sleep sweeter after wakefulness, and health more pleasing after the trials of illness. We have learned from the very Creator of the world that grace is often increased by contrasts. Hunger, therefore, also benefits the banquet, so that the table may become more pleasing through fasting.

# CHAPTER X

The mystical table is compared with fasting. What kind of hunger makes fasting acceptable, and what is meant by the words, “When you fast, anoint your head,” are examined morally and mystically.

[Col. 0708B]

**33.** [Note: All editions, together with some manuscripts, have this reading. Others, neither inferior in age nor in number, read: “That table is also compared with fasting as a mystical table.” The Tornesian manuscript alone has: “The mystical table too is compared with fasting to that table.”] The mystical table too is compared with fasting—that table of which David says: “You have prepared a table before me against those who afflict me” (Ps. 22:5). This table is acquired at the price of hunger; and that cup which intoxicates through sobriety is sought through a thirst for the heavenly sacraments. For the Lord said: “You who thirst, go to the water; and whoever has no money, go, buy, drink, and eat” (Isa. 55:1). And elsewhere he says: “Behold, those who serve me shall eat; but you shall be hungry. Behold, those who serve me shall drink; but you shall thirst” (Isa. 65:13). Whom does he mean by “you,” if not those who drank beforehand? Concerning them he said above: “You prepared a table for demons and filled a cup for Fortune” (ibid., 11). Therefore, if holy fasts lead us to that venerable table; if through this hunger we purchase the things that are eternal, why should we doubt about those things that belong to human use, since fasting also makes these things more pleasing to us?

**34.** Not every hunger, however, makes fasting acceptable, but the hunger undertaken in the fear of God. Consider: [Note: Here notice the ancient custom of the Church of Milan of not fasting on Saturday; on the same matter, consult our Admonition to this book.] During Lent one fasts on every day except Saturday and Sunday. This fasting is brought to an end by the Lord’s Pascha. Now the day of resurrection has come: the Elect are baptized [Note: “The Elect” was a stage among the catechumens. Although all candidates for baptism were commonly called catechumens, they were distinguished from one another by different grades and names. Whoever had professed to the bishop his desire to embrace the faith already bore the name Christian; after renunciations had been made, he was admitted to sacred instruction and was then properly called a catechumen. After being purified by the customary exorcisms, he was called an initiate; later, when he had requested the grace of baptism with the others, he was called a “competent”; finally, if he had been judged worthy of the same sacrament by the votes of the others, he was enrolled among the Elect. Some also list the catechumens under other names, calling them hearers, kneelers, prostrate ones, the Elect, and the competentes. If desired, see Albaspinaeus on Optatus of Milevis, Joseph Vicecomes, Book II, chapter 2, and others.] they come to the altar, receive the sacrament, and, thirsting, draw it in with all their veins. Rightly, each one, refreshed by spiritual food and spiritual drink, says: “You have prepared a table before me … and your intoxicating cup—how glorious it is!” (Ps. 22:5). Yet it is not hunger alone that is required, but the full discipline of fasting. Thus it is said to others: “On your days of fasting you find your own desires, and you goad all those subject to you. Is it for judgments and quarrels that you fast and strike with your fists? Why do you fast for me in such a way that your voice is heard in shouting? I did not choose such a fast, nor a day for a man to humble his soul; nor, if you bend your neck like a circle and spread ashes and sackcloth beneath you, will you thereby call it an acceptable fast. I did not choose such a fast, says the Lord” (Isa. 58:3ff.). We have heard what kind of fasting is rejected; now let us hear what is approved. “Undo every bond of your injustice; dissolve the obligations of violent exchanges; release the broken into freedom, and tear apart every unjust contract. Break your bread for the hungry; bring the poor who have no shelter into your house; if you see someone naked, cover him; and do not despise the members of your own race.” You see what the character and form of fasting are, [Note: Some manuscripts read “because he proves what is hidden.” The Ambrosian and Erasmian editions have “because he proves hidden minds.” Other manuscripts and editions, more correctly, have the reading in the text.] what disposition of mind is required: that you devote yourself to prayer and meditate day and night on the law of God.

**35.** The very form of the body should be full of gravity. No blush of drunkenness should suffuse the cheeks and offend the eyes of those who look upon you; rather, the face should shine with a chaste, reverent pallor; speech should be more serious, the eye more modest, the step more steady and restrained. For inner agitation is often revealed by a more disordered walk. The face should be more intent, a kind of judge of its own thoughts and a silent interpreter of the heart, so that it neither assumes a pretense of sadness [Col. 0709C] nor dissolves into uncontrolled laughter. Do not think this irrelevant to our admonition, since Wisdom says in the Gospel: “When you fast, do not become like the gloomy hypocrites” (Matt. 6:16). He called them hypocrites because by pretense they put on another person’s role, just as actors who perform tragedies stir up their own emotions according to the words of those whose characters they assume, so that they may become angry, mourn, or rejoice. These people strive to appear to fast, desiring to be approved by human beings more than by God, as the Jews did.

**36.** Therefore it is said to us: “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (ibid., 17–18). What does “Anoint your head” mean? Yet the luxurious also say: “Let us fill ourselves with wine and ointments.” Those who seek the grace of bodily fragrance anoint themselves with ointment. [Note: All editions have “those who seek bodily fragrance”; all manuscripts, by contrast, have “those who seek the grace of a bodily fragrance,” etc.] But such ointments commonly arouse the lure of lust. There is another ointment of sobriety, of which the Church says to her bridegroom: “Your name is poured-out ointment” (Song 1:2); and there is another oil by which the joints and certain members of the soul grow fat. Hence David also says: “You have made my head rich with oil” (Ps. 22:5). This is the oil of gladness with which Christ was anointed by God the Father, so that he might rise above all his companions. He commands our head to be anointed, so that every feigned sadness may be covered with the oil of gladness; so that you may not appear to sell your fasting to people or to be saddened over the salvation of your soul. No one who is sad is crowned; no one who is mournful triumphs. Anoint your head, then, where the thoughts of the wise are, for “the eyes of the wise are in his head.” [Note: Here he alludes to that extremely careful silence by which the holy fathers customarily concealed certain mysteries—and especially knowledge of the Eucharist—from catechumens.] You are called to the mysteries, yet you do not know them; you learn when you come. And remember this: “Like ointment on the head, which descended upon Aaron’s beard” (Ps. 132:2). Then you understand what “Anoint your head” means: how you may please God, so that he may disclose his sacraments to you and give you spiritual grace.

**37.** There is also another mystical head. What is it? Hear: “The head of a woman is man, but the head of man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11:3). Pour ointment upon Christ—pour it also upon his head. His head is God. The woman who represents the type of the Church, when she poured ointment upon his head, confessed his divinity; and when she poured it upon his feet, she confessed his passion. Both acts are praised. You too should do what will bring you praise and obtain forgiveness of sins (Matt. 26:10). Wash your face; cleanse your sinful soul; wash your conscience (Luke 7:44ff.). The face is often an index of the conscience and a kind of silent speech of the mind, whether we are pierced by sin or rejoice in integrity. Do not destroy this face; wash it and cleanse away all the filth of your conscience. A person destroys his face when he harbors one thing in his heart and displays another outwardly. Let us not cover ourselves with some kind of curtain [Note: The old edition, together with three manuscripts, has “Let us cover ourselves with a certain impiety.” The Roman edition and other manuscripts have “with a kind of curtain,” that is, a veil. Again, where the editions have “let him display innocence … the murderer is,” the majority of the better manuscripts have “let him purely bear innocence … it is a place of slaughter.” Two manuscripts have “it is slaughter.”] so that what is within may shine outwardly and what is outward may work inwardly. Let no one enclose guilt within his fasting; let him bear innocence openly. For fasting is the destroyer of guilt.

# CHAPTER XI

The power of fasting is illustrated by the example of bitter things; the story of Esau and Jacob shows how harmful food can be, though sweet; then follows an exhortation to avoid boasting in fasting.

[Col. 0710D]

**38.** Let no one prefer sweet things to bitter ones. Pleasure seems sweet, fasting bitter. Let the bitter remove the sweet. Bitter things often benefit the body more. For just as worms arise in the innermost bowels of children from undigested food and cannot be destroyed unless a more bitter drink is poured in or the power of harsher medicines takes effect, so that they die from its odor, in the same way the virtue of fasting, entering the depths of the soul, kills the hidden guilt.

**39.** What made Esau a slave to his brother? Was it not food sweet for an hour but bitter afterward? What made Jacob master over his brother? Was it not contempt for food, more bitter for a time but beneficial thereafter? Bodies themselves are often swollen by sweet things, and honey distends the liver; nevertheless, this too is tempered by the bitterness of food. Therefore the question is not ordinary but celebrated: “From the eater came forth food, and from the strong came forth sweetness” (Judg. 14:14). Others read: “And from the bitter came forth sweetness,” especially the Greek manuscripts. But the strong thing is also laborious; for sweetness comes forth from sadness or toil.

**40.** Do not boast, then, when you fast; do not glory, lest your fasting profit you nothing. What is done for display will not extend its fruit into the future; it consumes itself in the payment of the present. Elijah was in the desert, so that no one might see him fasting except the ravens that fed him. Elisha was in the desert, where no food could be found except bitter food. John was in the desert, where he found only locusts and wild honey. For those who fasted, food was brought by the pious ministry of angels. Daniel feasted among fasting lions. He ate another’s meal; the wild beasts did not touch their own. For those who fast, food flies; for those who feast, their feet falter. For those who fast, manna descends from heaven; for those who feast, the guilt of transgression [Col. 0711C] rises up.

# CHAPTER XII

How drunkenness drives people headlong into every crime, and how ridiculous and hateful it is, are explained in an elegant description. After this, some remarks are added about a luxurious young man converted to philosophy.

**41.** But what is this? While I am discussing fasting, I hear the clamor of banquets. Unless I am mistaken, my dinner has given off its aroma in my speech. Thus the sound of the written words invites, while examples of impatience do not frighten. For the people, unable to wait for the man who was fasting and carrying the things of the Law [Note: The things of the Law—that is, the Ten Commandments inscribed by the finger of God upon stone tablets.], “sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” We see that sacrilege was joined to drunkenness. For just as self-restraint is the mother of faith, so drunkenness is the mother of faithlessness. Into what crime does this not drive a person?

**42.** Men sit at the doors of taverns without even having a tunic or the means to meet the expenses of the following day. They pass judgment on emperors and powers; indeed, they think they are kings and command armies. Through drunkenness the poor become rich—those who in reality lack the means to pay the tavernkeeper for the price of their drink. Wine is boiling in them, and they do not know what they are saying. They are rich while they are drunk; as soon as they have digested the wine, they see that they are beggars. In one day they drink away the labor of many days.

**43.** From drunkenness men rise to arms; cups give way to weapons. Blood is poured out in place of wine, and wines themselves have poured out that blood. How strong men think themselves in wine, how wise, how eloquent, how handsome and distinguished—even though they cannot stand! The mind must stagger, the tongue stammer, a bloodless pallor overspread the face, and the stench of drunkenness become a horror. [Note: Fighting during banquets was especially customary among the Thracians. Hence the passage in Horace, Ode 1.27:

“To fight with cups made for joyful use  
Is the custom of Thracians. Remove this barbarous  
Practice,” etc.]

Barbarians rush upon the sword; the common crowd rushes into quarrels. If one of them is struck with a fist, you may see the wounded man’s face shedding tears of wine and singing pitiable closing speeches. Drunkenness has this one characteristic: it softens and loosens the hearts of drunkards. For just as fire tests hard iron, so in the burning of wine even the heart of proud men melts.

**44.** In wine, all seem equal to one another; no one is inferior. The poor man does not yield to the rich, since he does not know himself to be poor; nor the weak to the strong, since all his strength lies in drinking; nor the beggar to the wealthy; nor the lowborn to the honored. Among drinkers, the one who outdrinks the others is their king. Rightly, therefore, it is written: “Wine in drunkenness is equal to life for human beings” (Ecclus. 31:32). But if only you would hear what follows as well: “Drink it moderately, so that you may be sober” (ibid.). You have no grounds for accusation: wine was created for gladness, not for drunkenness, from the beginning. It is joy of soul and heart if you drink moderately; but excessive drinking arouses anger and produces many disasters.

**45.** But perhaps they will say that these are the drinking parties of common and worthless people. Let us therefore come to the banquets of powerful and mighty men. I will not here produce perfumed young men crowned with roses, [Note: Diogenes Laertius, Book IV, in his account of Polemo, records this about the same philosopher when he entered the school of Xenocrates.] such as they say was the man who, drenched in perfume, crowned with flowers, supported by prostitutes, drunk from drinking before dawn, and accompanied by the daylight of candles, entered the lecture room of a philosopher who was speaking. On hearing him, he is said gradually to have removed his garlands, wiped off his perfumes, and dismissed the prostitutes. Later he became so great a philosopher that he was an example of sobriety, though previously he had been the object of drunken mockery. [Note: The old edition reads: “I do not begrudge them their reformed man; let me show the type ….” The Roman edition has: “I do not begrudge them their reformed man; nevertheless, let me show the type,” etc. Beyond doubt our reading, which we present from ten Gallican manuscripts, is preferable.] I do not begrudge them one reformed man, so that I may show that this type of their luxury has not been invented by me. Certainly, although that man recovered from wine, he was always drunk with sacrilege.

# CHAPTER XIII

The banquets of military men are compared with a battle and a spectacle; their individual parts, like a prologue, rising action, and catastrophe, are described with the greatest care.

**46.** Away, then, with the wanton young men; let us come to the banquets of fighters. One must dine amid weapons. These are the military attendants who serve, girded with gold and with Babylonian belts drawn tightly around their waists. Their necks shine with golden torques; [Note: Ten manuscripts have this reading. Two others and all editions have “with golden bullae of infants.” The ancients did indeed hang golden bullae around the necks of infants, but this ornament was not so characteristic of that age that it was not also used among the more advanced in years. We therefore do not consider the word “infants” necessary here. Bullae were certain globules resembling the bubbles produced in water by falling drops of rain.] they cover their belts with golden bullae and enclose their knives in golden sheaths, with which they will fight while dividing the food. Boys stand nearby, their hair gleaming, chosen from barbarian peoples for these services, [Note: All editions have “distinguished by turns according to the intervals of their several ages. You may see the cups … golden and silver vessels displayed.” Most manuscripts agree with this, except that they omit “golden and.” Others, including the Thuaneus, written a thousand years ago, have the reading in the text. There, “according to the intervals of their several ages” means the turns of serving; or, changes of rank occur according to the age of each, so that the oldest stood in the first row, and so on.] taking turns according to the intervals of their respective ages. You may see ranks of different peoples and think that you are looking at an ordered battle line. The silver vessels are displayed; you might think it a pageant. A horn [Note: That is, a vessel made of horn, which the ancients used for storing wine, oil, and other liquids.] full of wine stands in the middle—a banqueting instrument, not a battle instrument, serving as a trumpet to rouse those reclining at table to combat.

47. With smaller cups first, as though battle were being preluded by light-armed troops. [Note: The American and Paris editions read in some copies, “as though a skirmish were being preluded”; Erasmus, “a skirmishing battle”; Gill, the Roman edition, and other Paris editions, “in a skirmishing battle.” Some manuscripts partly agree with these readings and partly with the one in the text; others, superior in age and number, have the reading given here. Moreover, *ferentarii* were lightly armed soldiers who preluded the battle before the armies engaged with all their strength.] But this is not a form of sobriety; it is a discipline of drinking. For just as actors in tragedies gradually raise their voices at first until they open a passage for a “moist” voice, [Note: The editions read “of a living voice”; some manuscripts, “of a bare voice.” Others have the better reading, “of a moist voice,” that is, a liquid and flexible voice.] so these men also exercise themselves at the beginning with preliminary cups, in order to provoke thirst—lest they perhaps quench it and, once satisfied, be unable to drink afterward. Therefore, when the matter has begun to grow hot, they call for larger cups: [Note: The early editions read “grows inflamed”; food causes thirst to boil up. Gill, in the margin, has “dry,” a word which the Roman edition transferred into the text, the rest being not greatly different. A considerable number of manuscripts agree with those readings. Yet the readings of Thuanus, Laudunensis, Victorinus, Tornacensis, and Dionysius are more elegant: “the martial heat grows inflamed; thirst boils up from the food.” The German and Colbertine manuscripts agree with them in the final part. Again, all the editions read: “And when the vessels began to diminish … they are replenished … and in the intervals the contests are often doubled … various rivalries and great struggles,” etc. Although we cannot deny that these readings produce a sufficiently suitable sense, we have nevertheless been unable not to prefer the reading of the manuscripts Thuanus, Laudunensis, Dionysius, Germanus, Victorinus, Michael, and Colbertinus.] martial heat grows inflamed, thirst boils up from the food, and whenever it seems to diminish, it is restored with purer drink. [Col. 0714A] The cups compete with the courses, and between mouthfuls they are often replenished. Then, as the drinking advances farther and more fiercely, there are various and great contests: who will excel at drinking? It is considered a serious disgrace if anyone excuses himself, if anyone thinks that the wine ought perhaps to be moderated. And this continues until the second courses are reached.

48. But when the feast has been completed, you might think that it was now time to rise. Then they renew their drinking all over again; and when they have finished that, they say that they are only then beginning. Then the small cups are brought out; then the enormous mixing-bowls, as though they were instruments of war. And lest you think this excessive, a measure is prescribed: they compete before a judge, and the contest is decided under a law. [Note: *Agonothetes* means the judge and president of a contest; here it is the same as the director of the banquet. For the ancients were accustomed, before reclining at table, to cast lots, and to entrust the rule of the wine to the person upon whom the throw of Venus—the most fortunate of all throws—had fallen, as may be learned from Horace, Book I, Ode 4, and Book II, Ode 5. The holy Doctor also suggests that there were people who offered a prize for drunkenness, something which the historians say Alexander the Great habitually did.] Their *agonothetes* is madness, their pay is debility, and the prize of victory is guilt. For a long time the outcome of the battle hangs uncertain and doubtful; that frenzy is, in fact, a kind of martial combat. The hands of the cupbearers who pour the wines give way, as do the labors of the cooks who serve hot dishes; those who carefully weigh the very measures, good ones overflowing to the brim, lest anything be spilled, give way. The drinkers do not yield.

49. Those alone are contests without excuse. In war, if someone sees that he is the weaker, he turns his weapons aside and earns pardon; here, if someone turns away the cup, he is pressed to drink. [Note: *Scamma* is a place enclosed by trenches where gladiators fought. When one of them was overcome, he acknowledged his defeat by raising his hand and asked for mercy.] In the arena, if someone raises his hand, he is indeed deprived of the palm of victory but is spared injury; at banquets, even if he withdraws his hand from the wine, it is poured into his mouth. Everyone becomes drunk; victors and vanquished alike lie there drunk, most of them unconscious. Nor is it permitted to carry them away to their tomb until the one who feeds them has seen that he has taken revenge upon them all, so that he may avenge his expenditure. [Col. 0714C] But the man who suffers no losses considers this the glory of his table, if everyone leaves it wounded and maimed, as though from the arena.

[Col. 0715A] 50. A sad spectacle for Christian eyes, and a pitiable sight. You see young men, terrifying to their enemies, carried out from the banquet, and then carried back to the banquet; filled so that they may empty themselves, and emptied so that they may drink. If someone is more modest, so that he is ashamed to rise, and can no longer contain his immoderate drinking, he breathes more heavily, sweats, groans, and reveals by signs what he is ashamed to confess. There each man recounts his battles; there they proclaim their brave deeds; wine-soaked and sleepy, they tell of their trophies and do not know in their minds what their tongues are saying. Each man snores and drinks, sleeps and fights; and whenever they have risen, the warrior men cannot stand and stagger as they go out. The little servants laugh at the disgrace of their masters, carry the soldier-warrior in their hands, and place him [Col. 0715B] on a horse. Thus they float this way and that like ships without a helmsman; and like men struck by a wound, they collapse onto the ground unless the little servants catch them. Others [Note: Those who had been wounded or killed in battle were accustomed to be carried home on a shield. Hence Ausonius, concerning a Spartan woman:

“a Spartan mother, arming her son with a shield,

said, ‘Return with this, or upon it.’”] are carried back on shields: it becomes a procession of mockery. Those whom you had seen in the morning distinguished by their weapons and threatening in appearance, you see the same men in the evening mocked with impunity even by little boys—wounded without steel, killed without battle, thrown into confusion without an enemy, trembling without old age, [Note: The early editions read, “drying up in the very flower of youth.” The Roman edition and some manuscripts have, “withering away.” Six other manuscripts of good age have, “in the beginning of youth.”] at the very beginning of their youth.

## CHAPTER XIV

Those who prepare banquets for drunkenness are reproved; and it is shown that wine’s power is greater than that of poison.

51. Who mixed such a cup of madness? Who poured so much poison into their minds? A man is in danger of becoming mud from his body; [Col. 0715C] and yet he himself is guilty of voluntary insanity and spontaneous corruption. Nevertheless, neither are you excused, you who invite them as friends and send them away as enemies. How much better you would have been to pour your wines onto the ground! But even the earth becomes drunk, and makes the wild beasts themselves more savage if the smell of wine reaches them. Indeed, at the time of the vintage, if they enter a vineyard, they are accustomed to be inflamed by drunkenness. What pleasure do you take in losses without benefit? You invite them for pleasure, you compel them to death; you invite them to a meal, [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts read, “nor do you wish to carry him to the tomb”; perhaps, “nor do you have the right to carry him,” etc.] you want to carry them to the grave; you promise food, you inflict tortures; you offer wine, you pour in poisons. For everything whatsoever that harms is poison. It destroys the senses, burns the entrails, troubles sleep, and torments the head.

[Col. 0716A] 52. Wine’s power is even greater than that of poison. Indeed, poison is excluded by wine, not wine by poison. Rightly did God, through Moses, compare wine not merely with poison but with the poison of dragons, saying: “The fury of dragons is their wine, and the venom of asps is incurable” (Deut. XXXII, 33). And beautifully he added “incurable”: for many are cured of the poison of other serpents, but no one is cured of drunkenness. Certainly poison wounds the flesh, [Note: Six manuscripts of better quality have this reading. Others, together with all the editions, read: “the flesh is wounded, the mind is unharmed; drunkenness is harmful to bodily health, and also adds … to the mind,” etc.] while the mind remains unharmed; drunkenness adds to bodily death the guilt of the mind as well. Observe also how the poison of faithlessness is expressed under the name of wine. For above he speaks of foreigners who did not know God: “For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their vine-shoot from Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is bitterness to them” (Ibid., 32).

## CHAPTER XV

He shows, by setting forth a passage from Isaiah, that he has not said everything that could have been said against drunkards; hence he attacks the wantonness of tavern revelers, and finally adds certain remarks about Babylon’s golden cup and the apostolic vessel.

[Col. 0716B]

53. Do you think that, as though drunk with wine, I have mixed this discourse too intemperately into the preaching of fasting? And even for the sake of these very strong men, how much have I passed over, how much less have I said than the Lord has spoken! You have heard what he said through Moses; hear what is written in the book of Isaiah’s discourses. [Note: All the manuscripts have this reading: “For the Lord attacks such verses, and says.” We interpret it in this sense: “He attacks such men”—namely, drunkards—“when he turns to them.” Unless someone prefers to take the words *in hujusmodi versus* as meaning “into such a judgment,” that is, “words” or “a form.” For *versus* properly signifies what we call a line. The editions, however, offered this reading: “For the Lord is found to have used such words, and he says.”] For the Lord attacks such verses, and says:

“Woe to those who rise early and pursue strong drink, who are drunk in the evening; for wine will burn them. With lyre, harp, and tambourines they drink wine, but they do not regard the works of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands. To whom is woe? he says; to whom are judgments? to whom are tumults?” (Isa. V, 11).

Different things belong to different people; to the drunkards, everything. “Woe to those who are drunk in the evening” (Prov. XXIII, 29)! What, then, of those who are soaked in wine both before evening and frequently throughout the day? Therefore, woe is owed to them. They have quarrels, they foment disputes, they rush into murder, and they come before the courts or are summoned there. Thus they have judgments as guilty men. Sometimes a more serious tumult arises, because wine perverts the drunkard’s mind: “And he does not remember the king or the magistrate,” as it is written; “he makes everything speak openly, and when they drank they did not remember friendship or brotherly relationship” (III Esdras III, 21 ff.): [Note: All the manuscripts have this reading; the editions, however, read “but not long afterward,” which is less suitable, as is clear from the sequence of the discourse.] but after the tumult they take up their swords; [Col. 0717A] and when they have been drenched in wine and have risen, they themselves do not remember what they have done. Thus they receive a fitting reward for their tumult.

54. Certainly I had passed over the lyre, harps, and tambourines, which we know are frequently brought into banquets of this kind, so that lusts may be aroused by wine and song. Many also, in the Persian fashion, order women fit for the company of drunkards to be brought in; they receive cups from them and prostrate themselves before the women as they sit. They hold this custom as a sacred observance in the service of drunkenness. Barbarians also have wine; Romans readily indulge them, so that they too may dissolve themselves in drinking and be conquered, their strength sapped by drunkenness. Nor is it wine alone that produces drunkenness, but also *sicera*. Accordingly, the Hebrews call every drink that intoxicates by the name *sicera*.

[Col. 0717B] 55. It is not without reason, then, that woe is pronounced upon those who seek the drink of drunkenness in the morning—those who ought to give praise to God, anticipate the light, and meet in prayer the Sun of justice, who visits his own and rises for us, if only we rise for Christ and not for wine and *sicera*. Hymns are being sung, and you hold a lyre? Psalms are being chanted, and you take up a harp or tambourine. Woe is rightly yours, because you abandon salvation and choose death. Scarcely has dawn appeared, and already people hurry through the taverns; wine is sought, carpets are shaken out, couches are hastened into place; silver bottles and gilded cups are displayed. “Woe,” he says, “to those who seek these things!”

56. “Babylon is a golden cup in the hand of the Lord, intoxicating the whole earth. From her wine all the nations drank; therefore they were shaken. And suddenly Babylon fell, and she was crushed” (Jer. LI, 7–8). The golden cup, therefore, was crushed, because Babylon was crushed, and Babylon is the golden cup. Yet although it boasts of its gold and value, it too is under the power of the Lord. Indeed, it is crushed by divine indignation. Why is it a golden cup? Because the one who lacks truth seeks allure; so that at least an expensive appearance may entice some to drink.

57. Place before your eyes the pomp of this world: you see an attractive lure, but an empty charm. Do not let golden and silver vessels seduce you. [553] “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV, 7). The apostolic vessel is earthen, but in it is Christ’s treasure. Woe to those who pursue *sicera* in the morning! This vessel is golden; it is a cup; and in that cup are the poison of death, [Col. 0717D] the poison of lust, and the poison of drunkenness. Whoever drinks from it is shaken and falls. He is shaken not only in body but also with a troubled heart; for to be shaken is a mark of sin.

## CHAPTER XVI

Drunkards are shown to resemble Cain and the persecutors of the Lord, and even to be more miserable than the demoniacs themselves; they are portrayed in their own colors, and the holy Doctor declares that the words of Jeremiah apply to them.

[Col. 0718A]

58. In the end, Cain, departing from the presence of God, dwelt in the land of Nod, which by interpretation signifies “shaking.” Therefore, whoever is intoxicated by the golden cup is moved by sin. Why do you place yourself under the curse of that fratricidal Cain, so that you tremble and are shaken? The persecutors of the Lord also, as they passed by, were shaking their heads. An evil spirit was driving them, the same spirit that, after filling bodies, is accustomed to move them. When that spirit is absent, the trembling ceases; but drunkenness produces perpetual trembling. The bodies of drunkards sweat wine: if you touch them lightly, you squeeze out wine.

59. Drunkenness is fuel for lust, a stimulus to madness, and the poison of folly. [Note: The Roman edition reads, “the poison of wisdom”; all the others have, “the poison of foolishness.”] It changes the senses and appearances of human beings; through it, people are transformed into neighing horses. For, inflamed by the natural vapor of a hot body and by the unnatural heat of wine, they cannot restrain themselves and are aroused to bestial lusts, so that they observe no appointed time at which it is proper to indulge in intercourse. They lose their voices, change color, their eyes blaze, they pant through their mouths, snort through their nostrils, burn with fury, and pass beyond reason. Hence dangerous delirium; hence the grievous punishment of stones; hence fatal indigestion; hence frequent vomiting, pouring out half-eaten food together with blood from the inner organs. Am I lying, unless the Lord spoke the same things through Jeremiah, saying: “Drink and become drunk, vomit, and fall, and do not rise” (Jer. XXV, 27)?

[Col. 0718C] 60. Hence also come empty images, uncertain vision, and unsteady steps; they often leap over shadows as though over pits. The ground seems to sway beneath them; suddenly it appears to rise and incline; and, as though it were turning, they fear, fall on their faces, and grasp the ground with their hands, or think that they are enclosed by mountains rushing together. There is a murmur in their ears like the roar of a surging sea and shores resounding with waves. If they see dogs, they think they are lions and flee. Some dissolve into uncontrolled laughter; others lament in inconsolable sorrow; others behold irrational terrors. Awake, they dream; asleep, they quarrel. Life is a dream to them; [Note: Where all the editions read, “sleep is death to them,” all the manuscripts restore: “their sleep is abundant.”] their sleep is abundant. They cannot be awakened by any voice; however strongly you may think they should be roused, unless they recover their senses, they cannot be awakened.

[Col. 0718D] 61. Hence Jeremiah rightly thinks that such a man, like a superfluous creature, ought to be mourned. For what is a drunkard except a superfluous creature? Thus he says: “As the mourning for Jazer, I will mourn for you, O vine, because the city of Jazer has been deserted” (Jer. XLVIII, 32). And below: “In your winepresses they did not tread wine in the morning; at midday, however, they did not perform the harvest shout” [Note: The Roman edition reads, “nor in the evening did they raise the shout.” The ancient editions and the manuscripts instead have, “but at midday they did not.” Again, the Roman edition has “Jazer, Moab, Arama, and Segor,” where the old copies had “Jaser, Mohi, Ticine, Piccot.” Those who prepared the last Paris editions have correctly noted at the end of this chapter that the true reading is the one which we have also transferred into the text on the authority of the manuscripts.] (Ibid., 33). *Jazer*, ποιήσις περισσός, “a superfluous making,” is a superfluous work. Natural moderation is a limit; whatever exceeds the measure is considered superfluous. Such is drunkenness, which is lamented with prophetic grief. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is wantonness, but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph. V, 18). There is, therefore, a drunkenness of guilt, and there is also a drunkenness of grace. The former is perhaps a drunkenness of nature, the latter a drunkenness of grace: we who have been made in the image and likeness of God ought to be filled with the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XVII

Concerning the protests, oaths, and drinking pledges of revelers; how more secret matters are often extorted through wine; and concerning a certain extraordinary manner of drinking, and how destructive it is to health.

62. Why should I speak of the protests of drinkers? Why should I recall the oaths which they consider it impious to violate? [Col. 0719B] “Let us drink,” they say. [Note: The old edition reads, “for the health of the emperors, and … let him be guilty in his devotion”; the Roman edition, “of the emperor, and … let him be guilty of irreverence.” Six very ancient manuscripts have, “I wish health to the emperors,” etc. It is therefore quite plausible that this was the formula by which they encouraged one another, in making drinking pledges, to pray for the emperors’ welfare.] “I wish health to the emperors; let whoever does not drink become guilty of irreverence.” For it seems that whoever does not drink for the emperor’s welfare does not love the emperor. O service of pious devotion! “Let us drink for the health of the armies, for the valor of the counts, for the health of our children.” And they judge that these vows reach God, like those who carry cups to the tombs of martyrs and drink there until evening, believing that they cannot otherwise be heard. O the stupidity of people who think drunkenness a sacrifice, who believe that drunkenness pleases those who learned to endure suffering through fasting! [Note: This reading is found by a strong consensus in the manuscripts. The American edition reads “that they appease them by drunkenness,” which Erasmus and later editors wished to correct to “that they are appeased by drunkenness,” etc.]

63. How many do we know to have gone from an intemperate banquet to torture? While, through drunkenness, they contended for sovereignty, promised kingdoms to themselves, and offered honors to others, these wretched men were led to punishment, not knowing what they were saying. Hence many good judges did not think that words spoken in drunkenness should be held against a person as a crime. Many also use wine as a rack; and those from whom tortures do not extract a confession of treason, they test by drinking, so that they may betray the condition of their country, the safety of their fellow citizens, and the plans of their defense. Virtue often conquers pain; drink, however, shuts out fidelity. I have known many men who, after being lacerated by [Note: We have not thought it right to pass over this passage, where the editions offer “lacerated by cords … among the cups,” etc. Almost all the manuscript codices instead give “lacerated by men of confidence … among the couches,” etc. This agreement moved us considerably, so that we suspected this to be the genuine reading. Perhaps, in an age when Latin had greatly deteriorated, men full of confidence and steadfastness—men who would reveal nothing entrusted to their faith, under any torture—were commonly called *fiduciales*. Similarly, the couches on which banqueters reclined may have been called *clindiae* or *clindia*, as though from Greek κλινίδια. Let more learned judgment decide this conjecture of ours.] cords, denied their names. Who, among the cups, concealed what he wished to remain hidden?

[555] 64. What shall I uncover—something I have heard, not a kind of cup, [Col. 0720A] but rather a kind of flow by which wines are poured into people’s mouths as through pipes or channels? Should I judge these men to be men, or rather wineskins? And yet even wineskins often burst unless the transfusion is moderate. Wine also flows through a horn into the throats of men; and if anyone draws breath, the offense is considered a breach of the agreement, the battle line broken, and his place lost. Running water dissolves the rocky cliffs of Lebanon; how can they suppose that the rushing force of flowing wine does not harm soft drunken entrails?

65. They say that elephants also draw a great deal of water with their trunks; yet they are content with moderate drinking to quench their thirst. But if they happen to have been cheated of their wages by some tavernkeeper, they become indignant and fill the hollow of their trunks—not to drink, [Col. 0720B] but to pour out—thereby watering his tavern with sudden inundations, since they think that they must exact revenge upon him. Ponds are suddenly drained for drinking and suddenly poured out again; everything swims. Who would not be astonished that such enormous bodies of beasts retain nothing superfluous?

## CHAPTER XVIII

How disgraceful and destructive women’s drunkenness is to those who witness it; after lamenting this evil, he shows by the example of the Israelites how great a good sobriety is and how great an evil intemperance is.

66. But why should we speak of men, when even women, who ought to exercise more anxious vigilance over the chastity of sobriety, drink to drunkenness? Then, rising, they dare to go out in public—women whom it is not fitting even within the privacy of the house to be heard by strangers or seen by them—with uncovered heads and shameless faces. The Apostle (I Cor. XIV, 35) orders women to be silent even in church and commands them to ask their husbands at home. Yet in the streets, in the sight of young men, they lead immodest dances even before men, tossing their hair, dragging their tunics, their garments torn, their arms bare, clapping their hands, stamping their feet in dance, making the air ring with their voices, provoking the lusts of young men by theatrical movement, a wanton eye, and disgraceful sport. A crowd of young men watches, and a pitiable theater is created. [Note: The Roman edition restored this reading from the Vatican manuscript, with which our manuscripts also agree here. The ancient editions instead read: “Amid the falls of the dancers, with an impure little eye and polluted gaze,” etc. Again, where all the editions read “is struck by obscene songs,” the manuscripts partly have “by obscene dancers,” and partly “by obscene leaps” (one has “by leapings”).] Amid the tumbles of the dancers [Col. 0721A] and the falls of the spectators, the heavens are polluted by an impure gaze, the earth is defiled by shameful dancing, and is beaten by obscene leaps.

67. How shall I speak patiently, pass over this reverently, or lament it suitably? Wine has brought us the ruin of so many souls. For if wine and women cause people to depart from God—since either drunkenness or lust are enticements to transgression—if these things do so separately and individually, what will they do when united? Hence not without reason did a certain wise man before us say: “A drunken woman is great wrath” (Ecclus. XXVI, 11).

68. And what wonder is it if women’s souls are deceived by wine, when all those tribes of the fathers, after drinking water from the rock, eating manna, and conquering the strongest nations, had no weak person among them; but when they began to desire meat and were turned toward Egypt by their desires, out of so many thousands of men only two deserved to reach the promised land? Thus one may gather from this what good sobriety is and what evil intemperance is: when they murmured, seeking the delicacies of Egypt, they were bitten by serpents; when they crossed the path through the Red Sea, they drank water. Therefore, do we not fear the example? Do we not flee delicacies, lest they deprive us of attaining future blessings? [Note: All the editions read, “Let us therefore fear the example; let us flee delicacies,” etc. This is not unsuitable, but the form of speech is more forceful when the question is joined with reproach, as we present it from seven manuscripts of better quality.]

## CHAPTER XIX

The ruin of the luxurious is announced in Isaiah’s prophecy; the sea ought not to be troubled by merchants, against whose greed he inveighs, since it was given not for navigation but for food, and not for human beings but for fish to traverse; finally, in what way the voluptuous are compared with ships.

[Col. 0721C]

69. And why should I use the sayings of others? Let us hear what those who are well fed and luxurious may expect for themselves. For the prophet Isaiah introduces them saying: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. XXII, 13). And rightly he exclaims: “Howl, ships of Carthage, which have perished and shall be no more” (Isa. XXIII, 1). This was said concerning the vision of Tyre, which we know to have been a luxurious city. Therefore it is the ninth vision, not the seventh or eighth, because it observes neither the law nor the grace of the Gospel: for the law forbids kindling the fires of lust even on the legitimate Sabbath, while in the sequence of the Gospel the eighth day of the resurrection dawns. The same day is both the first and the eighth, because the Lord’s Day returns upon itself. Luxury, therefore, [Note: Six manuscripts of better hand have this reading. Others, together with all the editions, read, “and has no end.” Either reading can be defended; nevertheless, ours seems preferable, so that “the observance of discipline” is not referred back to the earlier statements, nor “does it observe the law” to the preceding words, nor “the grace of the Gospel” to the following ones. “And not faith” would belong to the former, and “nor the grace of the Gospel” to the latter.] possesses neither faith nor observance of discipline. [Col. 0722A] Luxury is the seedbed and origin of vices. Nor should you think that I have spoken against the Apostle (I Tim. VI, 10), because he says that avarice is the root of all vices; for luxury is the mother of avarice. When someone has exhausted his own resources through luxury, he afterward seeks avaricious gains.

70. You have heard today what was read: “Merchants,” he says, “of Phoenicia crossing the sea upon many waters; the merchants’ seed is like a harvest that is carried away” (Isa. XXIII, 2–3). These cities are neighbors—Tyre, Phoenicia, and Sidon—neighbors in location and likewise in vices. [Note: The American and Erasmus editions, together with some manuscripts, read: “A dangerous crossing of the sea for trade and commerce, seeking small profits.” Gill and the Roman edition have: “seeking a small profit.” Some manuscripts partly have “merchants,” partly “to the merchants”; some have “the crossing of the sea,” others “in the crossing of the sea,” etc. Amid this variety, we preferred the readings that seemed to us to produce the more suitable sense.] Merchants seeking small profits from commerce by a dangerous crossing of the sea. [557] Their life is anxious, their intercourse restless, and always caught in a kind of whirlwind, more mobile than the very winds by which it is tossed and often thrown this way and that. In any case, you complain of frequent shipwrecks; who compels you to sail? Is it not your envy of wealth that makes even the lands unsafe and incites many to robbery? God made the sea not for sailing but for the beauty of the element. He spread the broad waters of the deep, surely so that he might enclose the lands with a strait, lest you, wandering and exiled, should stray too far. But the sea is tossed by storms. [Note: All the editions read, “Therefore we must not rashly usurp it.” All the manuscripts have, “Therefore you must fear, not usurp it,” etc.] Therefore you ought to fear it, not usurp it. The innocent element has done no wrong; human recklessness itself is its own danger. Indeed, the man who does not sail does not know the fear of shipwreck. The Lord said: “Have dominion over the fish of the sea” (Gen. I, 28); he did not say: “Sail upon the waves.” Thus the prophet Jonah, who was sent to Nineveh to preach repentance, because he wished to sail away in order to flee from the presence of God, was thrown into confusion by a storm, cast by lot, tossed into the sea, and swallowed by a whale.

71. The prophet David also, when recalling God’s grace toward humanity, says: “You have subjected all things under his feet: all sheep and oxen, moreover also the cattle of the field, the birds of the air, and the fish of the sea, which traverse the paths of the sea” (Ps. VIII, 8–9). He gave the paths of the sea to fish, not to human beings, to traverse. The sea was given to you for food, not for danger; use it for nourishment, not for commerce. Why do you create danger for yourself out of pleasure? Why do you probe the depths of a separated element? Why do you disturb the higher secrets of the world? Finally, why, impatient sailor, do you so often strive to furrow and plow the waves? Why do you frequently test harmless waters and provoke storms? O insatiable greed of merchants! [Note: The ancient edition and the manuscripts of Michael and Vallensis read: “Yield, you too, where even the sea cannot endure your restlessness. Indeed,” etc. The Roman edition reads: “The sea yields to you, and the sea cannot bear your restlessness so often,” etc. The manuscripts agree with us, except that in many the words “to bear” and “indeed” are missing.] The sea itself yields to you, and the deep cannot bear your restlessness.
