Indeed, since merchants return so often, it is written: “The sea said, ‘Be ashamed, Sidon’” (Isa. XXIII, 4). It is as though this were the voice of the exhausted element saying: “Be ashamed, Sidon”—that is, “You blame my waves, merchant, though you yourself are more restless than the waves; and be ashamed, or feel embarrassment, because you are not moved by danger.” The winds are more modest than your desires. They have their periods of rest; your eagerness to seek profit never rests. Even when the storm is idle, your ships are never idle. The wave turns beneath the rower when it is at rest from the wind.

72. “I have not labored,” it says, “nor given birth, nor nurtured young men” (Ibid.). “Why do those whom I do not know, whom I do not recognize, trouble me? Go to Carthage; howl, you who inhabit the islands” (Ibid. 6). Above he said: “Howl, ships of Carthage.” For the Tyrians founded Carthage, and therefore the Carthaginians follow the luxury of their founders, their wickedness having passed into them through a dishonorable succession; they are worse heirs of the worst vices. And rightly he called the luxurious “ships.” For just as ships are tossed by the wind, so they are tossed by food and wine. [Note: The old edition reads, “And the islands, filled with drink, inhabit,” etc. The Roman edition, with one Vatican manuscript, has, “They sail into the islands, their bodies filled with drink,” etc. The manuscripts partly read, “They inhabited islands filled with drink,” and partly, with us, “Bodies filled with drink inhabit islands,” etc. Some, finally, of inferior quality, have: “The islands which, filled with drink, invite,” etc.] Bodies filled with drink inhabit the islands; they resound with shipwrecks; drunkenness is battered by waves; they rest neither by day nor by night. Therefore, the seed of these merchants is in the water, and their harvest is in the waves. In the water they sow their labors, so that they may reap dangers. In the water their crop sprouts; in the water their harvest swells. The fruit itself is in the water, never safe or solid. Hence he rightly says (Ezek. XXVIII): “He who sowed in the earth did not enter into commerce”—rather, he who sowed in heaven. [Col. 0723C] But there is a good earth in which, whoever sows, heavenly fruits will arise for him.

## CHAPTER XX

The greater force that often lies in humble words; how the assembly of the nations sang the song of the prostitute, together with an exhortation to conversion of conduct and to redeem sins by almsgiving.

73. “Howl,” he says again, “ships of Carthage, for your fortress has perished; and it shall come to pass on that day that Tyre shall be abandoned” (Isa. XXIII, 14). And below: “And after seventy years Tyre shall be like the song of a prostitute” (Ibid. 15). Observe the words the prophet uses, and how he does not shrink from the lowliness of such expressions. We sometimes shrink from them—not because our tongue is chaster than theirs, but because our authority is lesser. For the force of the subject is greater when expressed in words of this kind, so that those who are not ashamed of sins may at least be ashamed of the names of sins. “Tyre,” he says, “shall be like the song of a prostitute.” Take care lest, when someone sees those choruses [Note: All the editions read, “when he sees them singing pious words, he says.” Two manuscripts have, “when he sees them, he says that pious words are being sung.” The latter reading, which we have followed, is better.] singing shameful words, he say: “Behold, Tyre has become like the song of a prostitute.” The oracle of the prophetic proclamation has been fulfilled.

74. And he added: “Take up the lyre, [Note: Thus all manuscripts and editions, except the Roman edition, which reads, “and go about the city, prostitute.” The Septuagint has ῥέμβευσον, πόλις πόρνη, “roam about, prostitute city.” Some copies, however, have πόλιν, “the city,” and Jerome adopted both readings. In the same place two manuscripts read, “And it shall be after one hundred and seventy years.” Others, together with the editions, read, “And it shall be after seventy years,” which agrees with the Septuagint translators and our Vulgate.] and wander about, forgotten prostitute city; play well, sing many songs, so that you may be remembered. And after seventy years Tyre shall be like the song of a prostitute, and God shall visit Tyre” (ibid. 16).

Thus we can also understand, in a good sense, the song of Rahab, that prostitute who received the spies of Jesus with faithful intent. For the Lord also says: “We sang to you, and you did not dance” (Luke 7:32). And David says: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. 95:1)—that is, the song of the prostitute, which that prostitute, the earth, formerly sang in Adam and Eve, a prostitute among the Gentile peoples. This prostitute produced many good prostitutes, [Col. 0724B] concerning whom the Lord Jesus said to that chosen and elder people of God: “Tax collectors and prostitutes are going before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. 21:31).

75. Therefore, since we have so merciful a Lord, who forgives even a grave error, let us turn away from vices; let us not depart from the law; let us diligently carry out the Lord’s commandment like obedient servants. What have we to do with impurities and indecencies? What have we to do with the works of the devil? 559 You heard today in the reading that had just been delivered what the legion said: “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of God?” [Note: All the editions and a few manuscripts read, “Son of David.” More and better manuscripts, together with the biblical text, read, “Son of God.”] (Luke 8:28). And you should say, if perhaps you see the devil’s temptations fighting against you: “What have I to do with you, Belial? I am Christ’s servant, redeemed by his blood; I have given myself wholly to him. What have I to do with you? I do not know your works; I seek nothing that is yours, possess nothing that is yours, desire nothing that is yours.” How much more ought we to separate ourselves from the devil, if he separates himself from Christ? And if we were in any way subject to him, we are so no longer: we have fled to the physician, who has healed our former wounds. And if any bitterness remains, healing will not be lacking. And if we have committed any injury, he who once forgave us will not remember it. And if we have sinned grievously, we have found a great physician and received the great medicine of his grace (On Penance, distinction 1, chapter “Medicine”). For great medicine removes great sins.

76. We also have many means by which we may redeem our sins. You have money: redeem your sin. The Lord is not for sale, but you yourself are for sale. You were sold under your sins; redeem yourself by your works, redeem yourself by your money. Money is cheap, but mercy is precious. “Almsgiving,” he says, “delivers from sin” (Tob. 12:9). And elsewhere he says: “A man’s redemption is his riches” (Prov. 13:8). And in the Gospel the Lord says: “Make friends for yourselves by means of the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16:9). An antidote is often compounded from poison—that is, poison is driven out by poison. Death is repelled by poison, and life is preserved. You too, like a good steward, make mercy a resource from the instrument of greed; draw the grace of sincerity from the lure of corruption.

## CHAPTER XXI

That for prophets the future is also present; likewise, that the world is rightly to be destroyed according to Isaiah’s prophecy, for the elucidation of which a very elegant comparison with a stadium is employed. On this occasion the holy man teaches that we are athletes and must diligently train for the crown; and finally he prays that Christ hasten his coming.

[Col. 0725B]

77. You heard what was read today: “Behold, the Lord comes to destroy the inhabited world” (Isa. 13:5). As though the holy prophet were pointing it out with his hand, as though he saw the day of judgment coming with his own eyes, he says: “Behold, the Lord comes to destroy the inhabited world.” Indeed, because through the Spirit future things are also revealed to prophets as though they were present, he wished to show us what he saw, so that he might call us back from error to conversion.

78. Yet no one should be broken in spirit when he hears that the Lord will destroy the inhabited world. Perhaps someone may say: “Granted that we have committed grave sins; what has heaven done wrong, what has the earth, what has the sea, that he should destroy them also? Why should so beautiful an adornment perish?” Such an opinion is narrow-minded. But if you look more deeply, [Col. 0725C] you will find that what you think is against us is in our favor; you will judge that what you consider to be against the world is actually for the world.

A stadium is not always filled with spectators, not always stirred by contests, not always thick with dust. But when there are contests, then the crowd is in the stands, the wrestler is in the arena, and the dust is in the stadium. When the contests have ended, the assembly is dismissed; each person departs either as a victor to receive favor or as the defeated to disgrace. A crown raises up the victor, while shame weighs upon the defeated and injury torments him.

If someone should therefore enter the stadium afterward, see it empty of its crowds, and say to the presiding judge: “Why is the stadium empty? Why are the contests silent? Why are the public games suspended?” the one in charge of the contest will reply: “The athletes must rest; the spectators must rest. For what is the fruit of labor except rest after labor?” In the same way, the inhabited world must at some time be dissolved, so that those wearied may have rest.

79. We are athletes; we contend in a certain spiritual stadium. Thus the good athlete said: “We have become a spectacle to this world” (1 Cor. 4:9). And elsewhere: “If I run, it is not aimlessly; if I fight, it is not as one beating the air; but I discipline my body” (1 Cor. 9:26). And elsewhere: “Forgetting what lies behind and reaching toward what lies ahead, I pursue the appointed prize” (Phil. 3:13).

We are therefore athletes; we must compete lawfully. There are many struggles, and the one defeated today recovers tomorrow. First one strives for the prize; afterward, for the crown. Does an athlete devote himself to idleness once he has entered his name for the contest? He trains daily; he is anointed daily. He is given athletic food; discipline is required; chastity is guarded.

You too have entered your name for Christ’s contest; you have subscribed to the competition for the crown. Meditate, train, anoint yourself with the oil of gladness, with the ointment poured out. Let your food be the food of sobriety; let it contain nothing of excess, nothing of luxury. Let your drink be sparing, lest any drunkenness creep in. Guard the chastity of your body, so that you may be fit for the crown; do not let your reputation offend the affection of the spectator, lest your supporters see you negligent and abandon you.

The Archangels, Powers, and Dominations are watching you, as are those ten thousand times ten thousand angels. Consider how disgraceful it is to blush with shame before so many spectators. Having entered the stadium, [Note: The manuscripts read, “having entered the stadium, arouse the vigor of your soul.” This is a good sense; nevertheless, the holy Doctor seems to be referring to what used to occur in contests. After wrestlers had been anointed, so that their limbs could not be grasped because they were slippery with oil, they used to sprinkle dust upon themselves, a practice they called *aphein*. Hence the readings preferred in the editions seem preferable, especially since it would have been easy for *r* to be changed into *v*, and for the word “dust” to be omitted by ignorant copyists.] arouse the firmness of your soul with dust; shake your arms.

Once you have advanced into the arena, you must receive the dust and endure the blazing heat of the summer sun. The heat is severe, but the victory is sweet; the cloud of dust is unpleasant, but endurance is splendid. No one enters the stadium covered in dust, but contests make it dusty. Dust is gathered where the palm of victory is offered. No one is crowned shining clean; victory suits the dust-covered.

80. Come, therefore, Lord Jesus. Let your crown come forth; admit the victors to rest, and the defeated to remorse. [Col. 0726C] And if you destroy the inhabited world, your invisible works are more numerous than those we have seen. The narrow-minded person does not perceive them and grieves that you destroy the inhabited world; but the one who knows how to look upon invisible things rejoices that you are coming and will set all free.

The athletes rejoice who can say: “Let your kingdom come; let your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth” (Matt. 6:10). The creation of the world will rejoice, so that it may be freed from the vanity of this world, for now it groans and is in labor; because that creation too has been subjected to vanity until the adoption of the children is increased and the redemption of the whole body is completed.

Therefore he will destroy the inhabited world for its good. For there will be a new heaven, and night will be no more. Finally, he says, “he will reveal his face,” so that with unveiled face we may behold the glory of Christ (1 Cor. 3:13). [Col. 0726D]

## CHAPTER XXII

That banquets must be avoided, lest Moses, together with the Levites, separate himself from us, and how he still comes. Likewise, whom the Apostle commands to be cut off. After this, the as-yet-unbaptized are invited to so great a grace, and finally the excuses of certain people are refuted.

81. Let us therefore consider, established in the stadium, how much joy or sorrow we will bring to those who are now our supporters, lest they begin to be ashamed on our account. For just as there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10), so there will be sorrow over the one who completes the course of this life without having obtained pardon. [Note: All the editions read, “over one sinner, if he is excluded from pardon,” and so on. This is not wrong. Nevertheless, we have preferred the wording of the manuscripts because the holy man, maintaining the allegory he has begun, clearly uses terms taken from the arena. The verb *exorare*, “to obtain pardon,” belonged to this usage, as may be seen in Horace, book 1, letter 1: “Lest the far end of the arena so often call upon the people.”]

Let us therefore discipline our body with fasts; let us flee disgraceful banquets. Let us beware lest it be said to us: “Wail over wine.” Lest Moses come and summon the Levites, and lest whoever is prepared for the Lord, bearing an armed right hand, separate himself from those who have contracted grave sins by eating and drinking. And Moses comes today when the Law is read; Moses calls when the Law commands.

82. The Apostle teaches us to separate ourselves from every brother who lives disorderly (2 Thess. 3:6). Let us strike him with the spiritual sword, which is the word of God (Eph. 6:17). Let us show no partiality toward brother or relative; rather, let us separate every unclean person from Christ’s altars, so that he may cleanse and correct his falls and thereby become worthy to return to Christ’s sacraments.

83. But if someone has not been baptized, let him turn with greater confidence, receiving the forgiveness of sins. For baptism consumes sins like a certain fire, because Christ baptizes with fire and Spirit.

Finally, you will find this type of the Law in the Books of Kings (1 Kings 18:34), where Elijah placed wood upon the altar and said that they should pour water over it from jars, and he said: “Do it again,” and they did it again; and he said: “Do it a third time,” and they did it a third time. When the water was flowing, Elijah prayed, and fire descended from heaven. [Note: All the editions and some manuscripts read, “you will find this type of the Law in the Books of Kings.” But more and better manuscripts do not contain the word “you will find” (*invenies*), which seems to have been introduced into the text only because copyists thought that *legis* was a noun, whereas it is a verb.]

You are the human being upon the altar, washed with water, whose guilt is burned away so that life may be renewed. Fire consumes wood and straw. Do not fear the fire by which you are illumined. Therefore it is said to you: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. 34:5).

Receive the yoke of Christ. Do not fear because it is a yoke; hasten, because it is light. It does not crush the neck but gives it honor. Why do you hesitate? Why do you delay? It does not bind the neck with fetters but joins the mind by grace; it does not constrain by necessity, [Note: All the editions read this way. Most manuscripts omit these words; in their place the manuscripts of Milan and the Vatican read: “but attracts by the pleasure of good work.”] but directs the will toward good work.

84. Why do you still deny that there is time? Every time is suitable for mercy. If I offer you gold, you do not say to me, “I will come tomorrow,” but demand it immediately. No one delays in receiving gold; no one makes excuses. Redemption of the soul is promised, and no one hastens.

John baptized into repentance, and all Judea gathered to him. Christ baptizes in the Spirit; Christ dispenses grace, and people approach him reluctantly. Elijah displayed a type of baptism (1 Kings 18:43 and following), and opened the heaven that had been closed for three years and six months. How much greater are the gifts of truth! He opened heaven—not with rain descending, but with grace ascending. For no one ascends into the kingdom of heaven except through water and the Spirit. Unbelief had closed heaven to human beings, but faith opened it.

85. Heaven had also been open to human beings before this. Thus Enoch was carried up to heaven. It was closed again, but Elijah opened it—he who was carried up in a fiery chariot (2 Kings 2:11). You too can ascend, if you obtain the grace of the sacrament.

How long will you pursue pleasures? How long will you pursue banquets? The day of judgment is pressing upon us. While you delay grace, death draws near. Who would say: “Now I have no time; I am occupied. Do not show me the light. I do not want you to redeem me so soon. I do not yet need the heavenly kingdom”? Does not the one who excuses himself from baptism say this?

And how great is the grace by which you are renewed, O human being! You are cleansed, and you are not burned up; you are healed, and you do not suffer; you are restored, and you are not dissolved; you do not receive the blow of death, and you rise again.

And still you dissemble; still you wait, intending to live for the world and reserve yourself for God afterward. Do you not know that Cain’s sacrifice displeased God for this reason: he did not offer the firstfruits, but, having used up the firstfruits himself, attempted to offer God a gift from what came afterward? Abel, however, was preferred because of the offering of his firstfruits and deserved to be praised in the distinguished oracle of piety. [Note: All the editions end here. The manuscripts of Thérouanne, Laon, Tournai, Dijon, Vicenza, and Corbie end with the words “he deserved to be praised in the distinguished oracle of piety”; the manuscripts of Milan and the Vatican add “the oracle.”]

# [ON NABOTH THE JEZREELITE]

[Col. 0727D]

## INTRODUCTION TO THE BOOK ON NABOTH THE JEZREELITE

[Col. 0727]

This book appears to contain nothing more than one or perhaps two sermons, which Ambrose delivered with the full ardor of his mind against the rich, by whom poorer people were most savagely despoiled. There is no doubt that the story of King Ahab and the poor man Naboth, then read in the Church, supplied him with the occasion (chapter 1, no. 1), so that in one case he might place before the eyes of his hearers the cruelty of the greedy rich man, and in the other the misery of the poor man who endured every extreme of suffering.

For this reason he first shows (ibid.) that no age lacks its Ahabs and its Naboths; and also that, even while he was speaking, there were poor people so cruelly harassed and oppressed that they were forced to flee their homeland lest they perish there from hunger and misery. He reproaches this with the utmost vehemence to the rich, to whom, from the first part of the proposed story, he also demonstrates (chapter 2, no. 4 and following) that in the midst of their wealth they are more needy than any pauper; that in their robberies (chapter 3, no. 11 and following) they seek their own advantage less than the despoiling of the poor; and finally (chapter 5, no. 9 and following) that their abstinence and their feasts alike ordinarily bring destruction upon those wretched people.

Then (chapter 6, no. 29 and following), after setting forth the Gospel passage in which a certain wealthy man is introduced as planning to build new barns after destroying the old ones, he discloses how unhappy is the condition of the wealthy. Soon returning to his subject (chapter 11, no. 46 and following), he explains how Jezebel, in order to accommodate the greed of her husband Ahab, inflicted the most terrible death upon Naboth.

On this occasion, rising against the rich of his own time, who were no more merciful to the poor than Ahab and Jezebel, he repeatedly warns them to take care lest, by imitating their crimes, they also incur the same punishments. And to persuade them of this more effectively, he teaches what the proper use of riches is (chapter 12, no. 52 and following), while at the same time proving how lacking in solidity they are (chapters 15 and 16), inserting a very brief exposition of the whole of Psalm 75, which he adapts with great skill to the subject before him. Finally (chapter 17, no. 70), by repeating the example of that same Ahab, he establishes nothing as more certain than what is declared in the last verse of the psalm just mentioned: namely, that God shows himself terrible against the kings of the earth and takes away the spirit of their princes, by whom the resources of the poor are invaded with such atrocity.

Since from what we have said above it can be understood that in this little work Ahab is mentioned much more frequently than Naboth, someone may perhaps wish to ask why it was not given the title *On King Ahab*, rather than *On Naboth the Jezreelite*, or *On Poor Naboth*, as the most ancient manuscripts present it.

A reasonable answer may be given: this should be attributed to the holy Bishop’s love for the poor, on whose behalf he discusses in that treatise no small number of matters that contribute to their consolation; and whom (chapter 4, no. 16; chapter 6, no. 29; chapter 14, no. 60; chapter 16, no. 67 and following) he not only equates with the wealthier but even places before them, as happier in their poverty and more acceptable to God himself.

Moreover, the example of this poor man who refused to yield to royal greed clearly pleased our Doctor greatly. This is indicated not only by what is read here, but also by the fact that he had already used the same example to strengthen and urge himself to resist the emperor, who, at Justina’s instigation, was ordering the Catholic churches to be handed over to the Arians:

“Naboth,” he says (*Against Auxentius on the Basilica*), “defended his vineyards even with his own blood. If he did not hand over his vineyard, shall we hand over Christ’s Church? … If he did not hand over the inheritance of his fathers, shall I hand over Christ’s inheritance? Far be it from me to hand over the inheritance of the fathers—that is, the inheritance of Dionysius,” and so forth.

It should not be concealed here that Ambrose borrowed certain things from Basil’s homilies *On Avarice* and *To the Rich*. This is demonstrated by the mere affinity between the elegant descriptions found in both authors (Basil, *Homily on Avarice*; Ambrose, chapter 5, no. 21 and following), in which the grief and distress of a certain father forced to sell one of his children in order to feed the others are expressed in both with such an impassioned style and such power to move the emotions.

If anything else found here was taken from Basil, it is almost entirely nothing more than a few statements which our saint excerpted here and there and adapted to his own subject. Anyone who considers that blessed Basil speaks only incidentally about Ahab and Naboth, while saying nothing at all about Psalm 75—although these constitute the principal part of Ambrose’s exposition—will not deny that this is beyond all controversy.

Moreover, no argument can be drawn from reading this work by which its date may be clearly established. Nevertheless, something appears to shed light on the investigation of this matter: namely, what is related there (chapter 14, no. 61, and chapter 5, no. 20 and following) about the greed of the powerful, consuls, princes, and nobles. During this period it had reached such savagery that the poor were forced to change their place of residence, abandon their wives, and take away their children lest they perish from hunger in their homeland.

For Paulinus, from whom the life of Ambrose has been transmitted to us, speaks as follows when he recounts the final actions of the blessed Bishop:

“He groaned bitterly when he saw the root of all evils, avarice, putting forth shoots—avarice which can be diminished neither by abundance nor by poverty, but grows ever more among human beings, especially among those who were established in positions of power, so that it was exceedingly difficult to intervene with them, since they put everything up for sale. This first brought every evil upon Italy, and from then on everything declined for the worse,” and so forth (Paulinus, *Life of Saint Ambrose*).

The agreement between this entire passage and what is said in the treatise under discussion is too great for it not to appear that Paulinus had it in mind. And although that same author was by no means exact in arranging the chronology when writing Ambrose’s deeds, we understand well enough that he mentioned these matters there because the greed of those nobles had never burned more fiercely than under the final years of the reign of Theodosius the Great. At that time the rapacity of Rufinus, Eutropius, and the other imperial prefects brought them into such envy and hatred that the Fathers of the Council of Carthage were compelled to ask the emperors, on account of the affliction of the poor, that defenders be appointed for them against the power of the rich, with provision made by the bishops (Third Council of Carthage, in some manuscripts Fifth, canon 9).

There is no doubt that before them Ambrose too had distinguished his charity in so holy a cause. Therefore we see nothing that prevents us from saying that, perhaps for this very reason, the book was written in the year 395 or in some adjacent year; everything fits the matter remarkably well.

[Col. 0731A]

## ONE BOOK OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON NABOTH THE JEZREELITE [Note: Probably written around the year 395.] (C)

[Col. 0731]

565 ## CHAPTER I

How, following the example of Naboth and Ahab, the poor are oppressed daily by the rich, although nature has produced everyone equal and the grave receives everyone equally; on this subject Ambrose attacks the arrogance and folly of the rich.

[Col. 0731A]

1. The story of Naboth is ancient in time but daily in application. For what rich man does not daily covet what belongs to another? What among the wealthiest does not strive to drive a poor man from his little plot and expel the needy man from the boundaries of his ancestral soil? Who is content with his own? Whom does a neighboring possession not inflame—the rich man’s mind?

Therefore, only one Ahab was not born; rather, what is worse, Ahab is born every day and never dies to this age. If one is killed, many rise up: there are more who seize than who lose. Not one poor Naboth alone has been killed; Naboth is struck down every day, the poor man is killed every day.

Terrified by this threat, the human race now yields its own lands. The poor man, burdened with his pledge, migrates with his little children; his weeping wife follows as though she were accompanying her husband to the grave. Yet she mourns less than the woman who laments the funerals of her own people; for although she has lost the protection of her husband, she still has his grave. And although she does not retain her children, she does not grieve or lament that they are exiles, nor does she suffer the hunger of tender offspring, more grievous than funerals.

2. How long will you extend your insane desires, rich men? Will you alone inhabit the earth? Why do you drive out your companion in nature and claim nature’s possession for yourselves? The earth was founded in common for all, rich and poor alike. Why do you rich men arrogate exclusive rights to yourselves?

Nature does not know the rich; she gives birth to all as poor. For we are not born with clothing, nor are we generated with gold and silver. She pours us naked into the light, lacking food, clothing, and drink; the earth receives naked those whom she brought forth, and the grave does not know how to enclose the boundaries of possessions.

A narrow patch of ground is equally sufficient for poor and rich. And the earth that did not contain the desire of the living now contains the whole rich man. Nature therefore knows no distinction when we are born, [Col. 0732A] nor does she know one when we perish. She creates all alike and closes all alike within the lap of the tomb.

Who can distinguish the appearance of the dead? Uncover the earth, and, if you can, identify the rich man. Dig up the grave a little later, and, if you can recognize the needy man, accuse me—unless perhaps the only distinction is that more things perish along with the rich man.

3. Silk garments and coverings woven with gold, by which the rich man’s body is surrounded, are the losses of the living, not aids to the dead. You receive perfume, rich man, and you stink; you destroy another’s favor and acquire none of your own. [Note: The Ambrosian and Erfurt editions read, “rich man, after you are dead, you are foul”; Gill’s edition reads, “rich man, after you have died, you are foul”; the Roman edition reads, “rich man, dead and foul you are.” All the manuscripts read, “rich man, and you are foul.” In the following sentence all the editions and some manuscripts read: “You leave heirs who will quarrel with the heirs; you leave a deposit,” and so on. The greater number of manuscripts read: “You leave heirs who will quarrel. You leave a deposit to the heirs,” and so on.]

You leave heirs who will quarrel. You leave the heirs a deposit more hereditary than voluntarily bestowed; they fear diminishing or violating what has been left. If the heirs are frugal, they preserve it; if extravagant, they drain it away. Thus you either condemn good heirs to perpetual anxiety or leave behind bad ones, so that they may condemn your deeds.

## CHAPTER II

How much poorer the rich are in disposition the more they abound in wealth. This is made clear by the contest between Ahab and Naboth. After the text of Scripture has been set forth, the baseness of that request, “Give me,” is weighed.

[Col. 0732B]

4. But what do you suppose? While you are alive, do you abound in everything? O rich man, you do not know how poor you are, how needy you appear to yourself, although you call yourself rich! The more you have, the more you demand; and whatever you acquire, you still remain in need.

Greed is inflamed by profit, not extinguished. Desire has, as it were, certain steps: the more it climbs, the more eagerly it hastens toward higher things, from which the fall of the one about to slip will be more severe.

Yet he was more bearable when he had less. In view of his means, he sought modest things; as his patrimony increased, the increase of his desire increased with it. He does not wish to be degenerate in his hopes, a pauper in his desires. Thus he joins two intolerable things together: he increases the ambitious hope of the rich man while not laying aside the disposition of a beggar.

Finally, divine Scripture teaches us how wretchedly he is in need, how abjectly he begs.

5. King Ahab was in Israel, and the poor man Naboth. The former abounded in the resources of the kingdom; [Note: Thus the Roman edition, together with all the manuscripts except one of Corbie, where one reads: “the rich man surrounded the poor man’s plot.” The old edition, however, reads: “and yet he demanded the poor man’s plot.”] the latter possessed only a small patch of land. The poor man coveted nothing from the rich man’s possessions; the king appeared needy to himself because the poor man, his neighbor, had a vineyard.

Who, then, appears poor to you: the one who is content with his own, or the one who covets what belongs to another? Certainly one appears poor in wealth, while the other is poor in disposition. A rich disposition knows no need; abundant wealth cannot fill the avaricious heart. And so the greedy rich man is an object of envy because of his possessions and a subject of complaint because of his poverty.

But now let us consider the words of Scripture.

6. “And it came to pass,” it says, “after these things, that there was a vineyard belonging to Naboth the Jezreelite in Israel, beside the house of Ahab king of Samaria. And Ahab spoke to Naboth, saying: ‘Give me your vineyard, and it shall be for me as a vegetable garden, because it is near my house; and I will give you another vineyard in its place. But if it pleases you, I will give you money for this vineyard, and it shall be for me as a vegetable garden.’ And Naboth said to Ahab: ‘Far be it from me before God that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers.’ And his spirit was troubled, and he lay down on his bed, and turned his face away, and did not eat bread” (1 Kings 21:1 and following).

7. Scripture had earlier explained (1 Kings 19:21) that Elisha, although he was poor, left his oxen, ran after Elijah, killed them, distributed them to the people, and attached himself to the prophet.

This was therefore set forth beforehand for the condemnation of the rich man who is represented in this king: although he possessed God’s benefits, like this Ahab, to whom the Lord had given both the kingdom and rain through the prayer of Elijah the prophet, he violated the divine commandments.

[Col. 0733C]

8. Let us therefore hear what he says: “Give me,” he says. What other words belong to one in need? What other words belong to one publicly begging a handout except “Give me”—that is, “Give me because I am in need; give me because I can have no other means of living; give me because I have no bread for food, no coin for drink, no expense for nourishment, no substance for clothing; give me because the Lord gave you the means by which you ought to give, but did not give them to me; give me because unless you give, I cannot have; give me because it is written: ‘Give alms’” (Luke 11:41).

How abject, how base these words are! For they do not have the disposition of humility but the fire of greed. And within that very abasement, how much shamelessness there is! “Give me,” he says, “your vineyard.” He admits that it belongs to another in order to demand what is not owed.

568 9. “And I will give you,” he says, “another vineyard in its place.” The rich man disdainfully regards as worthless what is his own; for what belongs to another he covets as supremely precious.

10. “But if it pleases you, I will give you money.” He quickly corrects his error by offering money for the vineyard. [Note: All the editions read, “For he wishes to possess nothing belonging to another.” All the manuscripts read, “For he wishes to possess nothing else.”] For he wishes to possess nothing else, since he desires to occupy everything with his own possessions.

## CHAPTER III

That the rich covet what belongs to others not so much for its usefulness as in order to exclude other people. How empty that desire is, which proves them inferior even to brute animals; how shameful it is to sell an ancestral possession for the sake of luxury; and finally, how impatiently the rich endure rejection.

[Col. 0734A]

11. “And it shall be for me,” he says, “as a vegetable garden.” So this was the whole of his madness, all his frenzy: to seek space for worthless vegetables. You do not therefore desire to possess it as something useful to yourselves; rather, you wish to exclude others. You are more concerned with despoiling the poor than with your own profits.

You consider it an injury to yourselves if a poor man possesses anything that may be judged worthy of a rich man’s possession. [Col. 0734B] You regard whatever belongs to another as your loss. What pleasure do you take in nature’s impoverishment? The world was created for everyone, yet a few rich men try to defend it for themselves. Not only the possession of land, but heaven itself, the air, and the sea are claimed for the use of a few rich men.

[Note: The editions, together with some manuscripts, read, “This field.” A much greater number of manuscripts read, “This air.” The latter is clearly the true reading from what precedes: “But heaven itself, the air, the sea,” and so on. Nor is the expression improper, for it is found in reputable authors: “human beings live by air.”]

This air, which you enclose within your widely extended possessions, how many peoples could it sustain? Do angels have divided spaces of heaven, as you distinguish the earth by boundaries you have set?

12. The Prophet cries out: “Woe to those who join house to house and field to field” (Isa. 5:8)! And he reproves them for their fruitless greed. For they avoid dwelling with other human beings and therefore exclude their neighbors; but they cannot escape them. Once they have excluded these people, they find others again; and when they have driven those away, they must necessarily come into the vicinity of still others. For they cannot inhabit the earth alone.

Birds associate with birds; indeed, the sky is often covered by the flight of a huge flock. Cattle join with cattle, fish with fish. They do not regard this as a loss but as an exchange of life: they seek abundant companionship and desire a certain protection in the comfort of more numerous fellowship.

You alone, human being, exclude your companion. You enclose wild animals; you build dwellings for beasts and destroy those of human beings. You bring the sea within your estates so that monsters may not be lacking; you extend the boundaries of the land so that you may not have a neighbor.

13. We have heard the voice of the rich man seeking what belongs to another; let us hear the voice of the poor man defending what is his own: “Far be it from me,” he says, “before God, that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers.”

He regards the rich man’s money as though it were some contagion of himself, as though he were saying: “May your money go with you to destruction” (Acts 8:20). “But I cannot sell the inheritance of my fathers.”

You have something to follow, rich man, if you are wise: do not sell your field for a prostitute’s night; 569 do not transfer your right for the expense of a banquet or the cost of luxuries; do not assign your house to gambling, lest you lose the right of hereditary piety.

14. When he heard these words, the spirit of the greedy king was troubled: “And he lay down on his bed, and turned his face away, and did not eat his bread.”

The rich grieve if they cannot seize what belongs to others. If the poor man does not yield his possessions to their wealth, they cannot conceal the force of their sorrow. They desire sleep; they cover their faces, lest they see anything in the world that belongs to another; lest they realize that anything in this world is not theirs; lest they hear that a neighbor possesses something beside them; lest they hear a poor man contradicting them.

These are the souls to whom the prophet says: “Rise up, you women of wealth” (Isa. 32:9).

## CHAPTER IV

Why it is said that Ahab did not eat his bread. An elegant comparison between the abstinence of the rich and that of the poor. How foolish it is to acquire wealth anxiously for one’s heirs; and concerning the filthiness of a certain rich man.

[Col. 0735B]

15. “And he did not eat,” it says, “his bread” (1 Kings 21:4), because he was seeking what belonged to another. Indeed, the rich eat another’s bread more than their own when they live by plunder and make their food from robbery.

Or certainly he did not eat his bread because he wished to punish himself with death, since something had been denied him.

16. Compare now the disposition of the poor man. He has nothing, and, unless voluntarily for God, he does not know how to fast; unless compelled by necessity, he does not know how to fast. You rich deprive the poor of everything, take everything away, leave nothing behind; yet, rich men, it is rather you who endure the punishment of the poor. They fast when they have nothing; you, when you have everything. Therefore you first impose upon yourselves the punishment [Col. 0735C] which you inflict upon the poor.

[Note: [Col. 0735D] Thus all the manuscripts and the old Roman edition. The Roman edition, however, reads: “before you distribute it to the poor.” This is incorrect, for Ambrose does not mean that the rich man first exacts punishment from himself before distributing it—that is, before giving alms to the poor. Rather, he means that the rich man first exacts from himself that punishment which he inflicts—that is, imposes—upon the poor, whom he drives into poverty and hunger.]

You therefore pay, by your own disposition, the penalties of miserable poverty: the poor have nothing to use, while you neither use what you possess yourselves nor allow others to use it. You extract gold from the veins of the mines, but then hide it again. How many lives do you bury in that gold!

17. For whom are those treasures being kept, when you read concerning the avaricious rich man: “He stores up treasures and does not know for whom he gathers them” (Ps. XXXVIII, 7)? An idle heir waits, a discontented heir complains that you are dying too slowly. He hates the increase of his inheritance and hastens toward loss. What, then, is more wretched, when you leave no gratitude even with the one for whom you labor? For his sake you endure hunger all day long in misery, fearing the daily losses of your table; for his sake you adorn your daily fasts.

[Note: [Col. 0735D] There is remarkable variation in this reading. The old edition has “you love daily fasts”; the Roman edition has “you heap up fasts.” Several manuscripts have “you endure long-lasting” or “daily fasts.” Some read “you undertake fasts.” Others finally have “you cling to a prolonged fast.” The true reading is found in the manuscripts of Thuaneus, the second Pontianus, and the first and second Albi, which we follow. “To adorn daily fasts” means to prepare and arrange fasts for each day; this fits very well with the following story.]

18. I knew a rich man who, when setting out for his estate, used to count the small loaves brought from the city, so that the number of loaves might determine how many days he would remain in the country. He did not want to open the sealed storeroom, lest anything be diminished from what had been stored. One loaf was allotted for each day, scarcely enough to satisfy the miser. I learned this too, on the authority of truth: whenever an egg was set before him, he complained that a chick had been killed.

[Note: [Col. 0736D] All editions, together with three manuscripts, read: “I also learned this on the testimony of a true man.” Some manuscripts have partly “on the testimony of a man,” and partly, as we do, “on the testimony of a trustworthy man.” Both readings can be explained appropriately. The first means: “I learned it from the trustworthiness and integrity of the person who told me.” The second means: “I learned it from the testimony that truth deserves and requires.”]

I write this so that you may understand that God’s justice is an avenger, and that it avenges the tears of the poor through your fasting.

CHAPTER V.

That the tables of the rich are sustained by the blood and life of many poor people; and here, concerning a certain father whose grief and anguish of spirit are most beautifully described when he is compelled by a rich man to sell his son; likewise, that the hardness of the rich is monstrous, and that women themselves increase it by their expenditure and luxury.

[Col. 0736B]

19. How devout your fasting would be if you assigned the expense of your banquet to the poor! The rich man would then be more tolerable, from whose table the poor Lazarus gathered what fell, wishing to be satisfied. Yet even his table was composed of the blood of many poor people, and his cups were moistened with the blood of many whom he had driven to the noose.

20. How many are killed so that what delights you may be prepared? Your hunger is deadly; your luxury is deadly. One man falls from the highest heights while preparing spacious storage places for your grain. Another falls from the lofty summit of a tall tree while examining the varieties of grapes he is to bring, from which wines worthy of your banquet may be poured. Another is drowned at sea while taking care that fish or oysters should not be absent from your table. Another stiffens in the winter cold while hunting hares or striving to catch birds in snares. Another, before your eyes, is beaten to death if something happens to displease you, and sprinkles the very dishes with his shed blood. Finally, the rich man was the one who ordered the head of the poor prophet to be brought to his table; and he found no other way to pay the dancing girl her reward than by ordering the poor man to be killed.

21. I saw a poor man led away because he was forced to pay what he did not have, dragged to prison because wine was lacking for the table of a powerful man, and compelled to put his children up for auction so that he might postpone his punishment for a time. When by chance he found someone to help him in that necessity, the poor man returned with his family to his lodging, seeing that everything had been taken away and that nothing had been left for his food. He groaned over his children’s hunger and grieved that he had not instead sold them to someone who could feed them. He returned to deliberate and resolved to sell them. Yet the injury of poverty and the grace of paternal affection struggled together: hunger drove him toward the price, nature toward his duty. Ready to die with his children rather than be separated from them, he often took a step forward and often drew back. Necessity nevertheless prevailed in him, not his will; and affection itself yielded to necessity.

22. Let us now consider the storms of the father’s heart boiling within him: which of his children should he surrender first? “Whom,” he says, “shall I sell first? For I know that the price of one will not be enough to feed the others.” This alone is the rich fruitfulness of his children, turned into misery. “Whom shall I offer? Whom will the grain-dealer gladly look upon? Shall I offer the firstborn? But he was the first to call me father. He is the eldest of my sons, whom I rightly honor as the older. But shall I give the younger? Yet I embrace him with a more tender love. I am ashamed for that one; I pity this one. I long for the former’s stage of life, for the latter’s age. The former already feels his misery; the latter does not know it. The former’s grief moves me; the latter’s ignorance moves me. Shall I turn to the others? One pleases me more; another is more modest. One is more like his father; another more useful. In the one I sell my own image; in the other I betray my hope. Wretched man that I am! I cannot find what to do; I have nothing to choose. Faces of calamity surround me, a chorus of misery.”

23. This is bestial madness: to choose which child you will surrender. Even wild beasts, when they sense danger threatening their offspring and themselves, are accustomed to choose which they will save, not which they will offer. How, then, shall I distinguish the feeling of nature? How shall I forget, how strip myself of, a father’s mind? How shall I arrange the sale of my child? With what words shall I bargain over the price? Into whose hands shall I deliver my son for slavery? With what eyes shall I look upon him while he serves? With what kisses shall I bid farewell to him as he departs? With what words shall I excuse what I have done? “My son, I sold you for my food.”

Thus the poor man’s table is now more deadly than the rich man’s. That man sells off others; I sell my own. He imposes necessity; I bring the will. To make the case more excusable, I shall add: “My son, you will serve for the sake of your brothers, so that food may be obtained for them.” Joseph too was sold into slavery by his brothers, and afterward fed both them and his father.

He will answer: “But his father did not sell him; rather, he wept over his loss. Yet afterward Joseph himself came under the power of a rich man and could scarcely be freed. Later his descendants served the riches of Egypt for many years.”

“Sell me at last, father, on this condition: that the rich may not buy me.”

[Col. 0737D]

24. I confess that I was perplexed; but what shall I do? Shall I sell no one? Yet while I consider one child, I shall see all the others perishing from hunger. If I surrender one, with what eyes shall I look upon the rest, who may suspect me of such impiety and fear that I will sell them also? With what shame shall I return home? How shall I enter it? With what state of feeling shall I live there, since I have denied myself a son whom neither illness consumed nor death took away?

[Note: [Col. 0737D] All editions read: “whom I sent away from myself.” The manuscripts more elegantly read: “whom I denied.”]

With what conscience shall I look upon my table, which so many sons clothed around it like young olive shoots?

[Col. 0738A]

25. The poor man laments these things in your presence, but avarice has stopped your ears, and your mind is not softened by the horror of so pitiable an act. The whole people groans, and you alone, rich man, are not moved; nor do you hear Scripture saying: “Give up your money for your brother and friend, and do not hide it beneath a stone unto death” (Eccli. XXIX, 13). And because you do not listen, Ecclesiastes cries out, saying: “There is a grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches kept to the harm of their possessor” (Eccles. V, 12).

But perhaps you will return home and consult your wife. She may urge you to redeem the one who has been sold. Rather, she will more likely urge you to part with women’s finery, by which you could free the poor man even at small expense.

[Note: [Col. 0737D] The old edition reads: “or the poor man may free the poor man.” The Roman edition reads: “or free the poor man for a short time.” The manuscripts unanimously give the better reading: “or free the poor man at little cost.” The implied meaning may be “at a small price,” “with little expense,” or something similar.]

She will impose upon you the necessity of expenditure, so that a jewel may drink, she may sleep in purple, recline upon a silver couch, load her hands with gold, and her neck with necklaces.

26. Women even take pleasure in fetters, provided that they are bound with gold. They do not think them burdens if they are precious; they do not consider them bonds if treasures glitter upon them. They even delight in wounds, so that gold may be inserted into their ears and pearls hang down. Gems too have their weight, and clothing its own coldness. They sweat in jewels and shiver in silks; nevertheless, the prices please them, and avarice commends what nature rejects.

They seek emeralds, hyacinths, beryl, agate, topaz, amethyst, jasper, and sardius with the greatest frenzy. Even if half their inheritance is demanded, they do not spare the expense while indulging their desire. I do not deny that some pleasant brilliance belongs to these stones, but they are still stones. And they themselves, polished contrary to nature, admonish us to lay aside the roughness of stones: the hardness of the mind ought to be polished more than the stones.

CHAPTER VI.

That riches have no power; and why they are called riches. That the slavery of the rich is more wretched than that of slaves; and here the Gospel passage, “What shall I do? I will tear down my barns,” and so forth, is piously and eloquently expounded.

[Col. 0738B]

27. What craftsman has been able to add a single day to a person’s life? Whom have his riches redeemed from the underworld? Whose illness has money alleviated? “His life,” it says, “does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke XII, 15). And elsewhere: “Treasures do not profit the unjust, but justice delivers from death” (Prov. X, 2). The Prophet rightly cries out: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. LXI, 11). For what do they profit me if they cannot deliver me from death? What do they profit me if they cannot remain with me after death? They are acquired here and left here. We are therefore speaking of a dream, not of an inheritance.

Accordingly, the same Prophet says well concerning the rich: “They have slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands” (Ps. LXXV, 6). That is to say: the rich who contributed nothing to the poor found nothing in their works; they helped no one’s need and could find nothing that advanced their own welfare.

28. Consider the very name. The pagans call Dis the ruler of the underworld and the arbiter of death; they call him Dis and “the rich one,” because the rich man knows how to bring nothing but death, and his kingdom is over the dead and his dwelling is the underworld. For what is a rich man except an insatiable gulf of riches, an insatiable hunger and thirst for gold? The more he drinks in, the more he burns.

Thus the Prophet warns: “He who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver” (Eccles. V, 9). And further: “This indeed is the worst sickness. For as he came, so he departed, and his abundance labors for the wind. Indeed, all his days are in darkness, mourning, great anger, sickness, and wrath” (ibid., 15 ff.), so that the condition of slaves may be more tolerable. They serve human beings; he serves sin. Thus the Apostle says: “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (Rom. VI, 16). He is always in snares, always in bonds; never free from fetters, because always involved in crimes. How wretched a slavery—to serve sins!

29. He does not know the duties of nature itself, nor the changes of sleep, nor does he enjoy the pleasure of food, whose service is free from no burden. Sweet is the slave’s sleep, whether he eats little or much; but when a man is satiated with riches, there is no one who allows him to sleep.

[Note: [Col. 0739D] This is the reading of the old edition, the Roman edition, and all the manuscripts except one, which has “when he has been satisfied”; another has “when he will be satisfied”; and a third, together with certain Paris manuscripts in the margin, has “satisfaction.” These same sources, however, have in the text “the rich man’s healing,” rather than “there is nothing that allows him to sleep.” The Septuagint renders Ecclesiastes V, 11: καὶ τῷ ἐμπληθέντι τοῦ πλουτῆσαι οὐκ ἔστιν ἀφίων αὐτὸν τοῦ ὑπνῶσαι, “and for the man filled with the desire to become rich, there is no one allowing him to sleep.” Moreover, after the words “to sleep,” most manuscripts of good antiquity add: “Finally, let us use the Gospel example to prove that the rich man cannot sleep.” Since these words seem not to belong in their present place, and are absent from many manuscripts and all editions, it has been sufficient to alert the reader to them.]

Desire rouses him, anxiety over continually seizing what belongs to others drives him on, envy torments him, delay vexes him, the barrenness of unproductive yields troubles him, and abundance harasses him.

Thus the rich man whose estate produced abundant crops thought within himself, saying: “What shall I do, because I have nowhere to gather my crops?” And he said: “This I will do: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones; there I will gather all that has been produced for me, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast.” But God answered: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XII, 17 ff.). Even God Himself does not permit him to sleep. He interrupts him while he is thinking and wakes him while he sleeps.

30. Nor does he himself allow himself to be at peace, for he is troubled by the abundance of his riches and, amid the fertility of his crops, gives voice to a needy man. “What shall I do?” he says. Is this not the voice of a poor man who lacks the means of life?

The needy man looks this way and that, searches for lodging, and finds nothing useful for food. He considers nothing more wretched than being consumed by hunger and dying from lack of food. He seeks the shortest paths to death and searches out punishments that will be easier to undergo. He seizes a sword, hangs a noose, approaches fire, investigates poison; and, uncertain which to choose among these, says: “What shall I do?”

Then, recalled by the sweetness of this life, he wishes to withdraw his decision, if he can find the means of sustaining life. He sees everything bare, everything empty, and says: “What shall I do? Where shall I find food, where clothing? I want to live, if I can find some way to sustain this life; but with what food, with what resources?”

31. “What shall I do,” he says, “because I have nowhere?” The rich man cries out that he has nowhere. This is the language of poverty: a man abundant in crops complains of want. “I have nowhere,” he says, “to gather my crops.” You might think he meant: “I have no crops from which I can live.”

Blessed is the man who is endangered by abundance; rather, he is more wretched in his riches than the poor man whose danger comes from want. The poor man has something with which to excuse his misery; he certainly has suffered wrong, but he is not guilty. This man has no one to blame except himself.

32. “And he said: I will do this; I will tear down my barns.” You might still think he meant: “I will open my barns. Let those who cannot endure hunger enter; let the needy come, let the poor go in, let them fill their bosoms. I will tear down the walls that exclude the hungry. Why should I hide what God makes abundant for me to distribute? Why should I close the grain behind barred doors, when God has filled the whole expanse of the fields with it, and it grows and abounds without a guardian?”

[Note: [Col. 0740D] Ambrose of Milan and Erasmus, ending the chapter after the word “grain,” began the following section with these words: “Let those hear to whom God has given the whole...” Several manuscripts of fairly good standing support them. But since the words are absent from many more manuscripts, it seemed best not to depart here from the editions of Gill and Rome.]

CHAPTER VII.

The Blessed Doctor continues the same passage and shows that avaricious people, when they ought to do good with their possessions, prefer to spend their money on building; and that they take more pleasure in exorbitant prices than in abundant produce. Nevertheless, he teaches them where they can safely store their crops.

[Col. 0740C]

33. The hope of the avaricious man has been defeated. The old barns are bursting under the new harvests. “I had less,” he says, “and stored it uselessly; more has been produced, and for whom am I gathering it? While I pursue increases in prices, I have lost the use of benefits. How many lives of the poor could I have preserved with the grain of the previous year? I would take greater pleasure in preserving such rewards, which are valued not in money but in gratitude.

“I will imitate the holy Joseph in proclaiming humanity. I will cry out in a loud voice: ‘Come, poor people; eat my bread; spread out your laps; receive grain.’ The rich man’s fertility and the abundance of the whole world ought to be everyone’s plenty.”

But you do not say this. Rather, you say: “I will tear down my barns.” You rightly tear them down, since no poor person returns from them laden with anything. They are storehouses of iniquity, not resources of compassion. He rightly destroys who does not know how to build wisely. The rich man destroys his own things because he does not know the eternal; he destroys his barns because he does not know how to distribute his grain, but only how to shut it up.

[Col. 0741A]

34. “And I will make them larger,” he says. Unhappy man, at least distribute to the poor what you are spending on the cost of construction. While you refuse the grace of generosity, you pay the price of construction.

35. And he added: “There I will gather all that has been produced for me, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things.”

[Note: [Col. 0741D] All editions and a few manuscripts read: “The avaricious man always confesses the abundance of his produce.” A large number of manuscripts, as in our text, read otherwise. Again, the Ambrosian and Gill editions, in the margin together with three manuscripts, read: “He is trampled by the cheapness of food.” Gill in the text and Rome have: “He maligns the cheapness of food.” Erasmus and the remaining manuscripts, superior in number and antiquity, read “he reckons it.” In some places one finds “he tramples upon and reckons its utility,” but this is a scribal or typographical error.]

The avaricious man is always worn down by the abundance of his produce while reckoning the cheapness of food. The fertility of everything benefits everyone; only for the avaricious man is barrenness profitable. He takes more pleasure in exorbitant prices than in abundant supplies, and prefers to possess what he alone can sell rather than what he can sell together with everyone else.

See him afraid that the heap of grain might overflow, lest what spills over the barns be poured out to the poor and an opportunity for some good be secured for the needy. The rich man claims the fruits of the earth for himself alone—not because he wishes to use them himself, but because he wishes to deny them to others.

36. “You have many good things,” he says. The avaricious man knows no things as “good” except those that are profitable. But I shall grant him that monetary things may be called good. Why, then, do you make bad things out of good things, when you ought to make good things out of bad things? For it is written: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke XVI, 9).

Therefore, riches are good for the person who knows how to use them; for the person who does not know how to use them, they are rightly called bad. “He distributed; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever” (Ps. CXI, 9). What could be better than this? They are good if you give them to the poor, thereby making God your debtor through a kind of pious lending. They are good if you open the storehouses of your righteousness, so that you may be the bread of the poor, the life of the needy, the eyes of the blind, and the father of orphaned children.

37. “You have the means to do it; what are you afraid of?” I confront you with your own words. You have many good things stored up for many years; you can abound both for yourself and for others. You have a fertility that belongs to the public; why do you destroy your barns? I shall show you where you can better guard your grain, where you can fence it securely, so that thieves cannot take it away from you.

Store it in the hearts of the poor, where no weevil can consume it and no age corrupt it. You have storerooms: the bosoms of the needy. You have storerooms: the homes of widows. You have storerooms: the mouths of children, so that it may be said to you: “From the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise” (Ps. VIII, 3).

These are the storerooms that endure forever; these are the barns that future fertility will not destroy. For what will you do again if more is produced for you in the following year? You will again destroy what you now plan to build, and make them larger.

God gives you fertility so that it may either overcome or condemn your avarice, leaving you no excuse. Yet what He wished to produce through you for many, you reserve for yourself alone—or rather, you deprive even yourself of it. You would preserve it for yourself more truly if you distributed it to others. For the fruits of good gifts return upon those who bestowed them, and the gratitude of generosity returns to its author.

[Note: [Col. 0742D] The editions read: “returns to the author of the good work.” The manuscripts do not recognize the words “of the good work.”]

Finally, it is written: “Sow for yourselves unto righteousness” (Hos. X, 12). Be a spiritual farmer; sow what will benefit you. Good sowing takes place in the hearts of widows. If the earth returns to you more abundant fruits than it received, how much more will the reward of mercy return multiplied what you have given!

CHAPTER VIII.

That death presses upon the thoughtless avaricious man, who is rightly called a fool in the Gospel passage mentioned; how much better money is distributed than retained; and how foolishly the rich excuse themselves from giving alms.

[Col. 0742B]

38. Furthermore, man, do you not know that the day of death overtakes the earth’s produce, while mercy shuts out the assault of death? Already those who will demand your soul are standing near, and you still postpone the fruits of your works. Do you still measure out for yourself long periods of life?

[Note: [Col. 0742D] The Roman edition reads: “you promise yourself long times of living.” The old edition, together with several manuscripts, has an uncertain reading meaning “you contemplate.” Many manuscripts have “you measure.” The oldest manuscripts have “you calculate.” The meanings differ little.]

“Fool, this night they demand your soul from you” (Luke XII, 20). He rightly says “this night,” for the soul of the avaricious man is demanded at night: it begins in darkness and persists in darkness. For the avaricious man it is always night; for the just man it is day, to whom it is said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43).

But the fool is changed like the moon (Eccli. XXVII, 12), while “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII, 43). He is rightly accused of folly who places his hope in eating and drinking. Therefore the time of death presses upon him, according to what those who serve their appetite themselves say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. XXII, 13).

He is rightly called a fool because he supplies his soul with bodily things, because he stores up what he does not know whom he is serving.

39. And therefore it is said to him: “But the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XII, 20). What do you measure, count, and seal each day? Why do you test gold on the scales and weigh silver? How much better it is to be a generous steward than an anxious guardian! How much more would it benefit you to be called the father of many orphans through your generosity than to have countless coins sealed in a purse!

Money is left here; the gratitude of good works, however, is carried with us to the Judge as the basis of our reward.

40. But perhaps you will say what you commonly say: “We ought not to give to the one whom God has cursed in such a way that He wished him to be in need.” But the poor are not cursed, since it is written: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 3).

It is not of the poor but of the rich that Scripture says: “He who hoards grain shall be cursed” (Prov. XI, 26). Moreover, do not inquire into what each person deserves. Mercy is not accustomed to judge merits, but to assist necessities; to help the poor, not to examine their righteousness.

For it is written: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Ps. XL, 1). Who is the one who understands? He who suffers with him; who recognizes that he shares the same nature; who knows that the Lord made both rich and poor; who understands that he sanctifies his own fruits if he gives some portion of them to the poor.

Therefore, when you have the means to do good, do not delay by saying: “Tomorrow I will give.” Do not lose the opportunity for generosity. Delay concerning another’s salvation is dangerous. It may happen that while you delay, he dies. Anticipate him before death, lest avarice obstruct you tomorrow as well and your promises come to nothing.

CHAPTER IX.

How Jezabel, who is avarice, promises the rich the possession they desire contrary to justice.

[Col. 0743B]

41. But what shall I say, so that you may not delay generosity? Would that you did not hasten to robbery! Would that you did not extort what you have coveted; that you did not ask for what belongs to another; that you passed over what was denied; that you patiently endured an excuse; that you did not listen to that Jezabel who is avarice, speaking through a certain torrent of vanity: “I will give you the possession you desire” (III Kings XXI, 7).

You are sad because you wish to consider the measure of justice, so as not to seize what belongs to another. “I have my rights,” she says; “I have my laws. I will bring a charge so that I may despoil him; and so that the poor man’s possession may be taken away, his life will be attacked.”

[Note: [Col. 0743D] The old edition reads: “which is a certain torrent of avarice,” and the Roman edition: “which is a certain torrent.” All the Gallican manuscripts give the better reading found in the text: “which is avarice, a certain torrent of vanity.”]

42. For what else is described in that story except the avarice of the rich, which is a vain torrent that sweeps everything away like a river and carries it off to no useful purpose? This is Jezabel—not one woman but many; not belonging to one time but to many generations. She says to everyone what that Jezabel said to her husband Achab: “Rise, eat bread, and recover your spirits; I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.”

43. “And she wrote a letter in Achab’s name and sealed it with his ring,” and sent the letter to the elders and to the free men who were dwelling with Naboth.

[Note: [Col. 0743D] The Roman edition reads: “and she wrote letters,” and then: “And it was written in the letters.”]

[Note: [Col. 0743D] Several very ancient manuscripts read: “and to his free men who were dwelling with him.” Most manuscripts, together with all editions, read: “and to the free men who were dwelling with him.” The Septuagint supports the latter reading, where it says: καὶ τοὺς ἐλευθέρους τοὺς κατοικοῦντας μετὰ Ναβουθαί, “and the free men dwelling with Naboth.” The Vulgate has: “and the leading men who were in his city.”]

And it was written in the letter: “Proclaim a fast, and set Naboth at the head of the people. Set two men, sons of iniquity, opposite him, so that they may bear false witness against him, saying: ‘He has cursed God and the king.’ Then lead him out and stone him” (ibid., 8 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0743D] Several ancient manuscripts read: “He has blessed God and the king.”]

CHAPTER X.

That when the rich cannot seize what belongs to others, they refuse food out of sorrow; and here, what makes a fast or prayers acceptable to God; then, how contrary are the commands God gives to what they themselves do.

[Col. 0744A]

44. How clearly the behavior of the rich is expressed! They are distressed if they do not seize what belongs to others; they renounce food, they fast—not to lessen sin, but to commit a crime. You see them then gathering at church, dutiful, humble, assiduous, so that they may deserve to obtain the outcome of their wickedness.

But God says to them: “This is not the fast I have chosen. Even if you bend your neck like a hoop and spread ashes and sackcloth beneath you, you will not thereby call it an acceptable fast. I have not chosen such a fast, says the Lord. But undo every bond of injustice; dissolve the obligations of violent transactions; send the broken into release; and tear apart every unjust written obligation. Break your bread for the hungry; bring the homeless poor into your house. If you see the naked, clothe him; and do not despise the members of your own household. Then your morning light will arise for you, and your healing will quickly spring up; righteousness will go before you, and the majesty of God will surround you. Then you will call, and God will answer you; while you are still speaking, He will say: ‘Behold, here I am’” (Isa. LVIII, 5 ff.).

45. Do you hear, rich man, what the Lord God says? You come to church not to give something to the poor, but to take something away; you fast not so that the expense of your banquet may benefit the needy, but so that you may obtain plunder from the needy.

What have you to do with a book and paper, a seal, a written obligation, and a bond of law?

[Note: [Col. 0744D] A “seal” is a mark impressed by a seal or signet ring. “Written obligation” is sometimes used for an inventory, but here it means the same as a contract or document drawn up between a moneylender and a debtor. Finally, the “bond of law” in this passage appears to signify nothing other than the laws concerning usury promulgated by the emperors. Strictly speaking, it refers to the coercive force of the laws, to use the terminology of the jurists; for to be held by legal bonds means precisely to be obligated to undergo the punishment prescribed by the severity of the laws. See the Theodosian Code, book IX, title 7, concerning the first Julian law, volume III, p. 55, and Gothofredus on the same law.]

Have you not heard: “Undo every bond of injustice; dissolve the obligations of violent transactions; send the broken into release; and tear apart every unjust written obligation”?

You offer me documents; I recite to you the law of God. You write with ink; I repeat to you the prophetic oracles inscribed by the Spirit of God. You compose false testimonies; I demand the testimony of your conscience, whose judgment you will not be able to escape or evade, whose testimony you will not be able to refuse on the day when the Lord reveals the secrets of human beings.

You say: “I will tear down my barns”; the Lord says: “Rather, allow whatever is inside the barn to be assigned to the poor; allow these storerooms to benefit the needy.”

You say: “I will make larger ones, and there I will gather all that has been produced for me”; the Lord says: “Break your bread for the hungry.”

You say: “I will take the poor man’s house from him”; but the Lord says that you should bring the homeless poor into your house.

How do you expect God to hear you, rich man, when you do not think that God ought to be heard? If the rich man’s decision is not accepted, a spectacle is arranged: God’s injury is considered done if the rich man’s request is rejected.

CHAPTER XI.

Naboth is accused by two false witnesses and stoned; Achab first pretends to be distressed, then seizes his possession. What sentence God pronounced against him; and especially why prostitutes are said to wash themselves in his blood; also concerning the punishment of Jezabel.

[Col. 0745A]

46. “He has blessed God and the king,” it says (III Kings XXI, 10)—persons of equal rank, so that the insult too may be equal. “He has blessed God and the king.” Since the rich man might be offended by the name of a curse and wounded by the sound of the word itself, “blessing” is used in place of “cursing.”

Two witnesses of iniquity are sought. Susanna too was attacked by two witnesses; the Synagogue found two witnesses who would utter false accusations against Christ; by two witnesses the poor man is killed.

They therefore brought Naboth outside and stoned him (ibid., 13). Would that he had at least been permitted to die among his own people! The rich man begrudges the poor man even his burial.

47. “And it happened,” it says, “when Achab heard that Naboth was dead, he tore his garments and covered himself with sackcloth. And it happened after this that Achab arose and went down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, to possess it” (ibid., 16).

The rich become angry and bring accusations in order to inflict harm if they do not obtain what they desire. But after they have injured someone through their accusations, they pretend to grieve. Nevertheless, sad and apparently mourning—not in heart but in expression—they come forward to occupy the seized possession and gain control through the injustice of their assault.

48. Divine justice is moved by this and condemns the avaricious man with fitting severity, saying: “You have killed and also taken possession of the inheritance? Therefore, in the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth, there dogs shall lick your blood; and prostitutes shall wash themselves in your blood” (ibid., 19).

How just and severe the sentence is: that the very bitterness of death which he inflicted upon another should be revealed in the horror of his own death!

[Note: [Col. 0745D] This is the reading of all editions and several manuscripts. Some others read: “he was ordered to dissolve.” But a greater number of manuscripts, and those of greater antiquity, read: “he was forbidden to dissolve,” perhaps “he was prevented.” Unless one prefers this as the meaning of the entire passage: that the punishment of King Achab was so open and manifest that it prevented the accusation of the murdered innocent man from being dissolved or evaded. For it often happens that those who escape a crime with impunity turn that very impunity into proof of their innocence. The interpretation is also supported by what follows shortly afterward: the corpse drenched in the blood of its wound revealed, in the appearance of a funeral, the cruelty of his life.]

God looks upon the poor man who lies unburied, and therefore decrees that the rich man should lie unburied. And so that, in death, he might pay the penalty of his wickedness, God condemns the man to whom it seemed that even the dead should not be spared.

Thus the corpse, drenched in the blood of its wound, revealed in the appearance of a funeral the cruelty of his life. When the poor man endured these things, the rich man was accused; when the rich man suffered them, the poor man was avenged.

49. But what does it mean that prostitutes washed themselves in his blood, unless perhaps it was intended to reveal that there had been something meretricious in the king’s treachery amid all that savagery—or a bloody luxury, since he was so luxurious that he desired a vegetable, and so bloodthirsty that he killed a man for the sake of a vegetable? A punishment worthy of the miser, worthy of avarice, consumes him. Finally, even Jezebel herself was eaten by dogs and the birds of heaven, so that it might be shown that the rich man’s burial becomes prey to spiritual wickedness. Flee, then, rich man, such an end.
