But you will flee such an end if you flee such wickedness. Do not be an Ahab, coveting your neighbor’s property. Let not that savage avarice, Jezebel, dwell with you—avarice that persuades you to bloodshed; that does not restrain your desires but drives them on; that makes you sadder even when you possess what you desired; that makes you naked when you have become rich.

## CHAPTER XII

That the miser is needy and a fugitive. How abject King Ahab was before Elijah, and how the sinner is always discovered. Finally, the rich are urged toward the proper use of wealth.

50. For everyone who has abundance judges himself poorer, because he thinks he lacks whatever is possessed by others. He who cannot contain the world’s desires is in need of the whole world; but for the faithful person the whole world is a wealth. He flees the whole world who, examining his conscience, fears being discovered. And therefore Ahab says to Elijah according to the historical account, but according to the allegory the rich man says to the poor man: “You have found me, my enemy” (ibid., 20). What a wretched conscience, which grieved that it had been exposed!

51. And Elijah said to him: “I have found you, because you have done evil in the sight of the Lord” (ibid.). He was a king, and Ahab was king of Samaria; Elijah was poor and in need of bread, and would have lacked sustenance unless the ravens had supplied him with food. So cast down was the sinner’s conscience that it was not lifted up even by the arrogance of royal power. Thus, as though he were base and degenerate, he says: “You have found me, my enemy; you have discovered in me what I thought could remain hidden; no secrets of my mind deceive you; you have found me, my wounds are open to you, captivity is at hand.” The sinner is found when his iniquity is exposed, but the righteous person says: “You have tested me by fire, and iniquity has not been found in me” (Psalm XVI, 3). Adam, while he was hiding, was found; but Moses’ burial was by no means found. Ahab was found; Elijah was not found. And the Wisdom of God said: “The wicked will seek me and will not find me” (Proverbs I, 28). Hence also in the Gospel (John VIII, 21) our Lord Jesus was sought and was not found. Guilt, therefore, exposes its author.

Thus also the Tishbite says: “I have found you, because you have done evil in the sight of the Lord”; for the Lord hands over those guilty of sin, but does not hand the innocent over to the power of their enemies. Finally, Saul sought holy David and could not find him; but holy David found King Saul, whom he was not seeking, because the Lord had handed him over to David’s power. Wealth, therefore, is captive; poverty is free.

52. You are slaves, rich men—and indeed you are slaves to a wretched slavery—since you are slaves to error, slaves to desire, slaves to avarice, which cannot be satisfied. It is a kind of insatiable whirlpool, more violent when it swallows what is cast into it; and, like a well when it overflows, it is fouled with mud and scrapes away earth that will profit it nothing. You should also be admonished by this example. For if you draw nothing from a well, it is easily corrupted through idle inactivity and ignoble neglect; but when it is worked, it becomes bright in appearance and sweet to drink. So too a heap of wealth, sandy in its accumulation, is attractive in its use but is considered useless in idleness.

Draw off, then, something from this well. Water extinguishes a burning fire, and almsgiving resists sins; but standing water quickly breeds worms. Let neither your treasure nor your fire remain stagnant: it will remain within you unless you turn it aside by works of mercy. Consider, rich man, in how many fires you are burning. Your voice is that of the one who says: “Father Abraham, tell Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue” (Luke XVI, 24).

53. Whatever you give to the needy benefits you; whatever you reduce grows for you. By the food you give to the poor, you feed yourself, because whoever has mercy on the poor is himself nourished, and the fruit is already present in these acts. Mercy is sown on earth and sprouts in heaven; it is planted in the poor and flourishes with God.

“Do not say,” God says, “I will give tomorrow” (Proverbs III, 28). If the one who does not allow you to say, “I will give tomorrow,” how can he permit you to say, “I will not give”? You do not give from what is yours to the poor; rather, you return what is his. For what was given for the common use of all, you alone usurp. The earth belongs to all, not to the rich; yet there are fewer who do not use what is theirs than those who do. You are therefore returning a debt, not bestowing an undeserved gift.

And therefore Scripture says to you: “Incline your soul to the poor, and repay your debt, and answer him peacefully in gentleness” (Sirach IV, 8).

[Note: Thus read the manuscripts, with a few exceptions, in which the final part of the sentence reads: “and it is the fruit of a person.” Mercy, and so forth. The printed editions, however, present the passage in these words: “What you distribute among the poor increases for you. It is written: ‘Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God.’ He himself is fed with the food given to the poor” (in the Roman edition: “By that which you give to the poor, you feed him”), “and the fruit is already in these acts of mercy. It is sown,” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER XIII

That the rich foolishly boast of their ancestry, although they themselves are often a disgrace to their forebears; that gold is a stumbling block. How great is the rich man’s savagery toward the poor, and what kind of commendation is fitting for a rich man.

54. Why are you proud, rich man? Why do you say to the poor man, “Do not touch me”? Were you not conceived and born from a womb just as I was, just as the poor man was born? Why do you boast of your noble lineage? You are accustomed to enumerate the origins of your dogs just as you enumerate those of the rich; you are accustomed to proclaim the nobility of your horses as though they were consuls. “This one was begotten by that father and born of that mother; this one rejoices in that grandfather; this one raises himself up by his great-grandfathers.” But none of this helps the runner: the prize is not awarded to nobility but to the race. The defeat is more shameful when the nobility of one’s lineage is also endangered.

Beware, therefore, rich man, lest the merits of your ancestors blush because of you; lest someone say even to them: “Why did you train such a person? Why did you choose such an heir?” An heir’s merit does not lie in gilded ceilings or in circles of porphyry. That praise belongs not to human beings but to the metals in which human beings are punished. Gold is sought from the needy and denied to the needy. They labor to seek it; they labor to find what they do not know how to possess.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “in which human beings are depicted.” Other editions and all the manuscripts read, “in which human beings are punished.” We believe this word refers to the words that follow: “Through the needy gold is sought,” and so forth.]

55. Yet I wonder why you rich men think you should boast of such things, and why gold should be a material of offense rather than of commendation. Gold too is a tree of stumbling, and woe to those who pursue it! Finally, the rich man is blessed who is found without blemish, who has not gone after gold and has not hoped in treasures of money (Sirach XXXI, 8). But as though such a person could not be known, he wishes him to be pointed out to him: “Who is he?” he says, “and we will praise him”; for he has done what we should regard with wonder as something new rather than recognize as customary. Therefore, whoever is found approved amid riches is truly perfect and worthy of glory. “Who could transgress,” he says, “and did not transgress, and do evil, and did not do it?” (ibid., 10). Gold, then, in which there is so great an enticement to error, is commended to you not so much for its own sake as because it brings punishment upon human beings.

56. Do your spacious halls exalt you—the halls that ought rather to pierce your conscience, since, though they can contain crowds, they exclude the poor man’s voice? Although it does no good to hear that voice, which accomplishes nothing even when heard. Moreover, does not the very hall of shame admonish you, since you wish by building to surpass your wealth, and yet you do not surpass it? You clothe your walls and strip human beings naked. A naked man cries out before your house, and you neglect him; a naked man cries out, and you are concerned with which marbles should clothe your floors. The poor man seeks money and has none; a man asks for bread, and your horse chews gold beneath its teeth. Yet you delight in expensive ornaments while others have no grain. How great a judgment you take upon yourself, rich man! The people hunger, and you close your granaries; the people lament, and you turn your jewel over and over. Wretched man, in whose power it lies to protect so many lives from death, but who has no will to do so.

[Note: The manuscript of Thuane and that of Pont read: “The gem of your ring could have preserved the life of the whole people.”]

The gem of your ring could have preserved the life of the whole people.

57. Listen carefully to the kind of praise that suits a rich man: “I delivered the poor from the hand of the powerful,” he says, “and I helped the orphan who had no helper. The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and the mouth of the widow blessed me. I clothed myself in righteousness; I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame; I was a father to the infirm” (Job XXIX, 12 and following).

And below: “The stranger did not lodge outside my doors, and my door was open to everyone who came. If I sinned unwittingly, I did not conceal my guilt, nor did I fear the multitude of the people, so as not to proclaim it before them; if I allowed the weak man to leave my door empty-handed; if I returned without delay a bond of any debtor that I possessed, having torn it up without recovering the debt” (Job XXXI, 32 and following).

For why should I repeat that he said he wept over every weak person and groaned when he saw a man in need while he himself was prosperous? But his days were rather days of evil when he saw that he himself had possessions while others were in need. If this is said by one who never caused a widow’s eye to waste away, who never ate his bread alone instead of giving it to an orphan whom he had nourished, fed, and educated with a parent’s affection from his youth; who never looked down on the naked; who clothed the dying; who warmed the shoulders of the weak with the fleeces of his sheep; who did not oppress the orphan; who never took pleasure in riches; who never rejoiced at the downfall of his enemies—if the one who did these things began to suffer the greatest poverty, if from so great a patrimony he brought back nothing except the single fruit of mercy, what will become of you, who do not know how to use your patrimony, who endure days of beggary amid the greatest riches because you give generously to no one and help no one?

[Note: Here the manuscripts differ from the editions in several places, and it seemed best to record their principal variations in a single sequence. First, the editions read, “a father of orphans”; nearly all the manuscripts read, “a father of the infirm.” The Septuagint has: πατὴρ ἀδυνάτων (“a father of the powerless”). Second, the editions read, “I did not conceal my guilt.” One manuscript of Thuane and several others of good antiquity read, “did I not conceal my guilt?” The Septuagint, however, reads: Εἰ δὲ … ἔκρυψα τὴν ἁμαρτίαν μου (“But if … I concealed my sin”). Finally, the editions read, “and also, if I had any bond of a debtor … I returned it without delay.” Seven manuscripts of better quality read: “If I have also remembered returning whatever bond I had of a debtor” (some read “to a debtor” …). Other manuscripts and the editions come closer to the Septuagint, where we read: συγγραφήν δὲ … καὶ εἰ μὴ ῥήξας αὐτὴν ἀπέδωκα, οὐθὲν λαβὼν παρὰ χρεωφειλέτου (“and if I did not tear it up and return it, receiving nothing from a debtor”).]

## CHAPTER XIV

How he urges the rich to purchase freedom and salvation with gold, proposing various arguments; he teaches what true riches are, and also makes clear through whom God is known and where his dwelling is established in peace.

58. You are therefore the guardian, not the master, of your possessions, burying gold in the earth—its servant, certainly, not its arbiter. But “where your treasure is, there also is your heart.” Therefore you have buried your heart in the earth, in that gold.

Sell gold instead and buy salvation; sell a precious stone and buy the kingdom of God; sell a field and redeem eternal life for yourself. I speak of realities, because I support my words with the word of truth: “If you wish to be perfect,” he says, “sell everything you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matthew XIX, 21). And do not be saddened when you hear this, lest what was said to that rich young man also be said to you: “How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God” (ibid., 23). Rather, when you read these words, consider that death can take these things from you, and a superior power can remove them.

Finally, because you are asked for little in exchange for great things, for things that perish in exchange for eternal things, for treasures of money in exchange for treasures of grace—these things decay, whereas those things endure.

[Note: The editions and some manuscripts read: “You will be able to sell little things for great … treasures of grace.” Several others read: “Why do you desire little things instead of great … treasures of grace?” The reading given in the text is found in more and better manuscripts.]

59. Consider that you do not possess these things alone: the moth possesses them with you, and rust possesses them, consuming your money. Avarice has given you these companions. But see what debtors grace gives you: “The lips of the righteous will bless the one generous with bread, and testimony will be borne to his goodness” (Sirach XXXI, 28).

It makes God the Father your debtor, who repays with interest for the gift by which the poor man was helped, as a good debtor to his creditor. It makes the Son of God your debtor, who says: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you gathered me in; I was naked, and you clothed me” (Matthew XXV, 35–36). For whatever has been given to any of the least, he says has been given to himself.

60. You do not know how to build wealth, human being. If you wish to be rich, be poor to the world, so that you may be rich to God. Rich in faith is rich to God; rich in mercy is rich to God; rich in simplicity is rich to God; rich in wisdom and rich in knowledge are rich to God.

There are people who abound in poverty and people who are needy amid riches. The poor abound, whose profound poverty abounded in the riches of their simplicity; but the rich “became needy and hungry.” For it was not written without purpose: “The poor will be set over the rich, and servants will lend to their masters” (Proverbs XVII, 2), because the rich and the masters sow what is superfluous and evil, from which they do not gather fruit but reap thorns.

And therefore the rich will be subjected to the poor, and servants will lend spiritual things to their masters, just as the rich man begged that the poor Lazarus lend him a drop of water. You too, rich man, can fulfill this saying: give generously to the poor, and you have lent to the Lord; for whoever gives to the poor lends to the Lord.

61. Saint David beautifully, while singing a hymn to God in Psalm LXXV, written against the Assyrian—that is, against the Assyrian of spiritual wickedness, the empty and vain prince of this world—began in this way: “God is known in Judah” (Psalm LXXV, 1–2). That is, God is known not among the rich, nor among the noble or powerful, but in the soul that confesses God.

“And in Israel,” he says, “his name is great”: not among princes and consuls, but in the one who sees God. For he is Israel in whom profound faith has been able to reach the knowledge of God.

[Note: The old edition reads: “Against spiritual wickedness, the empty and vacant prince of this world, the Assyrian, he began in this way: ‘God is known in Judah;’ that is, not among the rich, nor among the noble or powerful, but in the soul that confesses God; not among princes,” and so forth. The Roman edition reads: “Against spiritual wickedness—for the Assyrian signifies the empty and vacant prince of this world—he began in this way … not among the noble, but among penitents and in the soul,” and so forth. Our manuscripts agree with the reading we have given, with a few exceptions in which some corruption of the passage is plainly detectable.]

62. “And his place has been established in peace,” he says (ibid., 3): where a tranquil affection is shaken by no waves of differing desires, disturbed by no storms of avarice, and set ablaze by no fires of seeking riches. This is the one who contemplates eternal things and dwells in Zion, breaking all the instruments of spiritual warfare and crushing the bows with which the devil, directing flaming arrows, commonly brands grievous passions upon human hearts.

But those arrows cannot harm the righteous person for whom God is light. He is so far removed from the horror of darkness that the adversary cannot find a place in him—even though that adversary has been accustomed to pour himself into princes as well. Thus he poured himself into Judas the traitor, cutting down, as though in a forest of wood, the doors of faith, so that he might gain entry into his heart and possess the tabernacle of the eternal name, dedicated by the gift of the apostleship bestowed upon him.

[Note: Thus read a large number of manuscripts, except that several have “dedicates” in place of “dedicated”; a few others have “may be called”; and one or two have “might possess the apostleship bestowed as a gift.” Hence: “Therefore the prince of this world, as though,” and so forth. In all the editions, however, read: “might possess. Therefore the prince of this world,” and so forth.]

Thus, like a wicked usurper, he cut down the doors so that he might enter violently. But the Lord, like a gracious illuminator, enlightens his servants and, through their shining merits and the brightness of their virtues, illumines the darkness of this world.

The peaceful and gentle possess this grace with God, established in the sober tranquility of their minds. But the foolish in heart are disturbed and are themselves the authors of their own agitation, because they are tossed about in the heat of their desires and fluctuate as in a kind of sea.

## CHAPTER XV

That those who do not know how to use wealth are its slaves and sleep their own sleep. When the soul is called a chariot and the flesh a horse driven by the power of the mind; and the distinction among driver, rider, and passenger is examined.

63. Who these people are, the Prophet expressly indicated by saying: “All the men of wealth” (Psalm LXXV, 6). He said “all,” leaving no one out. And he rightly called them “men of wealth,” not “wealth of men,” to show that they are not the possessors of wealth but are possessed by their own wealth. Possession ought to belong to its possessor, not the possessor to the possession.

Whoever, therefore, does not use his patrimony as a possession, who does not know how to give to the poor and distribute his goods, is a little servant of his own wealth, not master of his possessions. He guards another’s property like a servant, rather than using it as his own like a master. In this state of mind, then, we say that he is a man of wealth, not that wealth is the possession of a man.

“Good understanding belongs to those who use it”; but whoever does not understand cannot claim for himself the favor of understanding. And therefore, overcome by the sleep of intoxication, he falls asleep. Such men sleep their own sleep—that is, they sleep their own sleep, not Christ’s. Those who do not sleep Christ’s sleep do not possess Christ’s rest and do not rise in Christ’s resurrection. He says: “I slept, and rested, and rose, because the Lord will receive me” (Psalm III, 6).

64. In this world such people drowse, deemed worthy of heavenly rebuke because they mounted horses whom they could not bridle. Elsewhere we read the Church, or the soul, saying: “The chariot of Aminadab has set me” (Song of Songs VI, 11).

If the soul is a chariot, see whether the flesh may be the horse; and the driver is the vigor of the mind, which governs the flesh and restrains its movements, like horses, with the reins of prudence. Those who mount bodily pleasures without governing them by any moderation have therefore fallen asleep. Hence he preferred to call them “passengers” rather than riders or drivers.

For a driver, with discipline and skill, drives his horses according to his own judgment: he urges those who are running, turns back the untamed, recalls the weary, and turns the gentle according to his will. Thus, when Elijah was taken up and carried toward heaven as though in a chariot, Elisha cried out to him: “Father, father, chariot of Israel and its horseman!” (2 Kings II, 12). That is: “You who governed the Lord’s people by good direction, you have received these chariots, these horses running toward divine things, as the reward of your steadfastness; because the Lord approved you as the guide of human minds, and therefore, like a good charioteer, you are crowned with the eternal reward of victory.”

In the prophet Habakkuk too it is written, spoken to the Lord himself: “You will mount upon your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Habakkuk III, 8). For he drove his apostles, whom he sent in different directions so that they might preach the Gospel throughout the whole world. “You will mount,” he says, as a ruler of horses, not merely as a passenger. A rider too mounts, but in order to govern, not merely to sit, since the slothful and lazy person cannot endure the movement of a sleepy mind.

65. Concerning the rider it is written: “The rider will fall backward, awaiting the salvation of the Lord” (Genesis XLIX, 17). Since no one is without a fall, even if a rider should fall and be bent by certain earthly vices, nevertheless, if he does not cast away the hope of rising again, trusting in divine mercy, he reaches salvation.

But concerning the passenger there is clear evidence that he is regarded as blameworthy, since Moses himself says in the song of Exodus: “He cast horse and passenger into the sea” (Exodus XV, 21). And in Zechariah the Lord says: “I will strike every horse with madness and its rider with folly” (Zechariah XII, 4). He did not mention only the horse but also its rider, just as you have in Exodus: “Horse and passenger.”

For where there is a passenger who cannot govern his own horse, the horse too is carried headlong if it is swept by untamed fury into steep and dangerous places. Why, then, do you put your trust in horses, rich men? “A horse is a false hope for salvation” (Psalm XXXII, 17). Why do you applaud yourselves in chariots? “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will glory in the name of the Lord. They are bound and have fallen, but we have risen and stand upright” (Psalm XIX, 8).

Do not love neighing horses; do not, rich men, be aroused by the roar of lust. The Lord is terrible, and no powerful or rich person can resist him; he hurls down heavenly judgment (Psalm LXXV, 9).

## CHAPTER XVI

He urges the rich to cease from wickedness and confess to the Lord. How the words “Pray and repay” are addressed to them, and what commends prayer and gifts to God. Finally, the same words are applied also to the poor, and it is shown who departs from God.

66. It is good that you now rest and, ceasing from wickedness, revere the Lord’s power. Therefore it was said to the murderer Cain: “You have sinned; be quiet” (Genesis IV, 7), so that he might put an end to his sin.

Let your thoughts confess to the Lord. Do not say, “We have not sinned.” Paul said: “Although I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Corinthians IV, 4), yet he added: “But I am not thereby justified.” Even if you are conscious of nothing, confess nevertheless to the Lord, lest there be something that escapes you. For whoever confesses the Lord and applies the remaining thoughts of his mind to confession will celebrate a feast day of the mind in secret (Psalm LXXV, 11), and will feast not on the leaven of malice and wickedness but on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

67. And so, in conclusion, the Prophet turns to you and says: “Pray and repay the Lord your God” (ibid., 12). That is: “Do not pretend, rich men. The day is at hand. Pray for your sins; repay with gifts for the benefits you possess.”

You received from him what you can offer; what you repay to him belongs to him. “My gifts,” he says (1 Chronicles XXIX, 14)—that is, “the gifts you offer me are my gifts. I gave them to you and bestowed them upon you.” Finally, the Prophet says: “I have no need of your goods” (Psalm XV, 2). Therefore I offer your own things to you, because I have nothing that you have not given.

Faith is what makes gifts acceptable; humility is what commends what is offered. By faith Abel offered God a more abundant sacrifice. Abel’s gift was pleasing above the gifts of his brother Cain because he conquered by faith. For why is the poor man’s sacrifice more pleasing than the rich man’s? Because the poor man is richer in faith and wealthier in sobriety. Although poor, he belongs among those of whom it is said: “Kings will offer you gifts” (Psalm LXVII, 30).

For the Lord Jesus is pleased not by those who offer gifts while clothed in purple, but by those who govern their own impulses, who rule bodily wantonness by the authority of the mind. Pray, then, rich men! Your works contain nothing that is pleasing. Pray for your sins and wickedness, and repay gifts to the Lord your God.

[Note: The old edition and very many manuscripts read: “Repay in the poor, pay to the needy, lend at interest to the destitute what can make God favorable” (some manuscripts read: “Lend to those destitute who can make God favorable”) “because of your wickedness; for otherwise you cannot. Therefore make him a debtor to yourselves …” The Roman edition agrees with ours up to the word “lend”; the rest agrees with the old edition. Our reading is established by eight manuscripts of better age. You may readily prefer it to the others if you observe that the relative pronoun “whom” refers to God, who is understood in each clause, as follows: “Repay in the poor”—supply, “gifts to God”; and similarly in the other clauses. Yet it is also possible to understand more simply that Christ is designated by the words “in the poor,” “in the needy,” and so forth.]

Repay in the poor, pay to the needy, lend at interest to that destitute person whom you cannot otherwise appease because of your wickedness. Make your debtor the one whose vengeance you fear. “I will not accept,” he says, “calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks, because all the beasts of the forests are mine” (Psalm XLVIII, 9–10). Whatever you offer, he says, is mine, because the whole world is mine.

“I do not demand what is mine. There is something of your own that you can offer me: devotion and faith.” I am not pleased by the ostentation of sacrifices; only, human being, “offer God a sacrifice of praise and repay your vows to the Most High” (ibid., 14).

[Note: Thus read several manuscripts of the most ancient hand. This certainly agrees better with what precedes. Yet the reading of other manuscripts and editions is not to be rejected: “I am pleased by the zeal of devotion and faith, not by the ostentation of sacrifices. Only,” and so forth.]

68. Or, if you prefer, let us understand it in this way. Since he had said that the rich slept their own sleep, he first sent the Lord’s rebukes against them, then added terror and proclaimed the power that even the rich cannot resist. Turning to everyone, he said: “Let the rich sleep; let the rich be rebuked. You pray and repay gifts to the Lord your God, all who bring gifts around him” (Psalm LXXV, 12). That is: “Give thanks, poor people, because God is not a respecter of persons.”

Let them build riches, store up money, and heap up treasures of gold and silver; you pray, since you have nothing else. You pray, because you possess this alone, and it is more precious than gold and silver. You repay gifts, you who do not depart from the Lord, you who are around him, because you who were far away have been brought near.

But those who seem to themselves to be near through wealth and power have been made far away because of avarice. No one is outside unless guilt has excluded him, as it expelled Adam from paradise and shut Eve out. No one is far away except the one whom his own wickedness has banished.

69. You, then, who have been placed near, pray and repay gifts to the one who is terrible, and to him who takes away the spirit of princes, terrible among the kings of the earth (ibid., 13). No reward from the rich can buy him off; no arrogance of the powerful can bend him. He distinguishes the penalties of guilt, and the more he has bestowed upon someone, the more he demands from him.

He gave Saul, a private man, a kingdom; but because Saul did not keep the commandment, he lost both the kingdom and the spirit.

[Note: Some manuscripts and all the editions read: “Because of their treachery he made many kings of the nations captives to the people of the fathers” (two manuscripts read “of the people”). Several other manuscripts, more numerous and more reliable, read: “He made many kings from the people of the fathers captives to the nations.” Either a transposition was made by scribes here, or there is a hyperbaton by the saint himself. The passage seems to require arrangement as follows: “He made many kings from the people of the fathers”—namely, the Israelites—“captives to the nations because of their treachery.” Indeed, the very sequence of the discourse sufficiently shows this to be Ambrose’s meaning, since it seems to demand examples not from gentile kings, all of whom equally ignored God, but rather from those kings who, although they could know God through the Scriptures, fell into treachery and paid the gravest penalties of captivity. See 2 Kings XVII, 23–25.]

He made many kings from the people of the fathers captives to the nations because of their treachery.

And, to speak now of the history under discussion (1 Kings XIX), he commanded that King Ahab, ungrateful for heavenly benefits, be killed in such a way that his wounds would be licked by dogs. Because he had coveted a poor man’s vineyard, though filled with such vast resources of royal power, he was reduced by the Lord below every condition of want. No one was found to wash his wounds; no one to cover his body. Human kindness failed him, and the harshness of dogs took its place. The miser found ministers of burial wholly worthy of him.

## CHAPTER XVII

Why Ahab, to whom God had promised pardon because of his repentance, nevertheless was defeated and killed. Two explanations of this matter; from which it is concluded that God keeps his promises even to the undeserving.

70. At this point the question arises: How do we read that the Lord said to Elijah, “Have you seen how Ahab has been moved before me? I will not bring evil in his days, but I will bring evil in the days of his son” (1 Kings XXI, 29)? Or how do we say that repentance has power with the Lord? Behold, the king was moved before the Lord’s face; he went away weeping, tore his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth, and wore the sack from the day on which he killed Naboth the Jezreelite (ibid., 27), so that he moved God to mercy and changed the sentence. Therefore either repentance had no power and did not bend the merciful Lord, or the oracle is false. For Ahab was both defeated and killed (1 Kings XXII, 35).

71. But consider that Jezebel was his wife (1 Kings XX, 25), and that he was inflamed by her will. She turned his heart and made him accursed through excessive sacrileges; and she therefore recalled him from the disposition of his repentance. The Lord, however, cannot be considered changeable; rather, he did not think that what he had promised to one who confessed should be kept for one who forgot his confession.

72. Accept another, truer explanation: the Lord preserved the tenor of his sentence even for one who was undeserving, but Ahab himself did not preserve the divine benefits bestowed upon him.

The king of Syria had brought war against him; he was defeated and spared for pardon; having also been taken captive, he was granted freedom and sent back to his kingdom. This was by the divine judgment: Ahab not only escaped but also triumphed; what was due to his own cowardice was that he armed against himself the enemy by whom he was to be defeated.

He had certainly been warned by the prophet, who said: “Know and see what you should do” (1 Kings XXI, 22). He had been warned because heavenly grace was owed to the servants of the king of Syria, since the king had said: “The God of the mountains is the God of Israel and not the god Baal; therefore,” he said, “they have prevailed against us. And therefore, if we do not completely prevail over them, appoint satraps in place of the king of Syria” (ibid., 23), so that he might take away from them the king’s strength and power.

Finally, he conquered in the first encounter, in order to put the enemy to flight; he conquered in the second, when he restored the captive to his own sovereignty. The reason for his victory was clearly confirmed by the oracle, when one of the sons of the prophets said to his neighbor: “Strike me.” But the man refused to strike him. And he said: “Because you did not obey the word of the Lord, behold, when you depart from me, a lion will kill you.” He departed from him, and a lion found him and killed him (ibid., 35 and following).

After this another prophet stood before the king of Israel and said to him: “Thus says the Lord: Because you have released from your hand a man devoted to destruction, behold, your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people.”

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “The king of Syria had brought war against him, and he was defeated by him …” and continues: “For in the first engagement Ahab conquered and put the enemy to flight; in the second he conquered and restored the captive to his authority. The fact that Ahab not only escaped but triumphed was due to the divine sentence, as the prophet said: ‘Behold, I will deliver all this multitude into your hands.’ But the fact that he was afterward defeated was due to his own guilt, as one said,” and so forth. All the old editions and manuscripts agree with us, except in a few details—for example, the editions read “against the servants of the king of Syria,” while the manuscripts read “by the servants of the king of Syria,” along with a few other minor differences. Observe in passing how differently from our Bibles and versions that codex presents this history, the codex Ambrose used.]

73. It is therefore clear from these oracles that the Lord keeps his promises even toward the undeserving. But the wicked are crushed by their own folly or condemned by another transgression, even if they have escaped the snares of their first transgression.

[Note: “They escaped the snares.” With these words the treatise ends in the old editions, the Roman edition, and certain manuscripts. What follows was added in the latest Paris editions, and is in fact found in several manuscripts. Remigius ends in this way: “By his provision, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”]

But we must act in such a way that, worthy through good works, we may deserve to receive the promises of almighty God.

## [ON TOBIT]

## ADMONITION TO THE BOOK ON TOBIT

[Col. 0755C]

[Col. 0755]

This book is first of all vindicated as the work of Saint Ambrose; his teaching on usury and on the sacred Book of Tobit is defended.

There can be no controversy that this work consists of several sermons which Ambrose delivered on different days after reading the Book of Tobit in church (chapter 1, no. 1; chapter 23, no. 87). Having compressed into a few words (chapters 1–2) what the sacred history of Tobit records about the virtues of this holy man, he examines and expands more fully the matter recorded concerning the money lent by Tobit to his kinsman Gabelus and reclaimed only when Tobit thought death was already approaching (chapter 2, no. 6). Taking this as his starting point, he attacks usury, which was extremely common at that time (chapter 2 and following). He proves that it is evil and accursed (chapter 2, nos. 14–15 and following), since it is forbidden by divine law, and is no less serious than idolatry or homicide (chapter 4). He describes and sharply rebukes (chapters 3–4) the criminal devices of moneylenders, by which they compel needy people to accept their money on condition that interest be paid. But when these people appeared to be excessively hardened in their greed, he turns his speech to debtors and, in a very forceful discourse, depicts the immense miseries into which they plunge themselves by contracting interest-bearing loans (chapters 4–5). Nevertheless, he returns to the inhumanity of moneylenders who entice new heirs and wealthy young men (chapters 6–7) to borrow money from them at interest, so that they may plunder their resources; and he presents their calamity, if they have allowed themselves to be deceived by such men, not without compassion. He pities still more deeply (chapter 8) the fate of the unhappy children whom their own parents were forced to put up for sale in order to satisfy the cruelty of moneylenders. He testifies (chapter 10) that the ferocity of the rich had advanced so far that they even prevented the bodies of their debtors from receiving burial. He then teaches that nothing at all can be found which does not yield to the treachery of moneylenders; for by their cunning they were able to strip gamblers and bring the Huns, the fiercest of all nations (chapter 11), under their control. Accordingly, he returns to their description (chapters 12–13), and to the evils that arise from so great a crime; and he demonstrates, with what are called *Achillean* arguments, that it is condemned both by the Old and by the New Testament (chapter 14). Finally, after exhorting moneylenders to another and more profitable kind of “interest,” in which spiritual interest and a spiritual pledge consist, he explains the matter at length (chapter 18 and following). Then, after rebuking those who induce sureties to give guarantees, he shows those same sureties what principle ought to guide them in giving their guarantees (chapter 23). Finally, so that his discourse may end where it began, he returns (chapter 24) to the example of Tobit that he had proposed and briefly indicates the chief virtues which we ought to learn from it.

We certainly cannot be surprised that Erasmus, and after him several others, thought fit to deprive Ambrose of this most beautiful book, by which moneylenders were so deeply affected (chapter 23, no. 87). Thus Cocus (*Censura quorumdam script.*, etc.) and Rivetus (*Critici sacri*, book III, chapter 18) maintain. It is by no means obscure that the work contains nothing at all inconsistent with the genius and character of Ambrose. For although verbal play is somewhat more frequent here than in the other treatises of the holy Bishop, this may be attributed either to the subject matter—which sometimes supplies such allusions even when they are not sought—or to some other cause. But what will Erasmus oppose to the authority of Saint Augustine (*Against Julian the Pelagian*, book I, chapter 3), who explicitly cites this book under the name of Ambrose? Will he deny that the blessed Bishop spoke against moneylenders on the occasion of Tobit, when he himself attempted, by using the example of that prophet, to urge Vigilius, bishop of Trent, to attack them (*Letter 23 to Vigilius*)? Who, moreover, would fail to recognize how great is the agreement between the more compressed statements in that letter and this entire commentary? Finally, what will he reply to those who point out so many passages transferred from Basil (*Homily 2 on Psalm XIV*) which occur throughout this treatise, as is customary with Ambrose?

In fact, we see that our Doctor borrowed a considerable portion of this book from Basil’s second homily on Psalm XIV, where the subject treated is usury alone. Indeed, we observe several passages in which the wording returns literally. Nevertheless, just as one finds in Basil much that Ambrose deliberately omitted, so in the very passages taken from Basil’s homily he altered or rearranged a good deal, so as to adapt them more conveniently to his own purpose. Finally, he drew no more from that Greek source than from his own resources—not only if one considers what is said there about Tobit, but also what is taught about usury and the spiritual pledge. At that point (chapter 20) the holy man seems to follow a certain opinion of Philo the Jew (*On Dreams*), which he treats in a thoroughly Christian manner.

We have no certain information about the time when this Ambrosian discourse was composed. We wish the judgment concerning the conjectures by which alone we can investigate the matter to remain with the reader. It is sufficiently clear that the holy Doctor preached against moneylenders before writing to Vigilius, recently installed in the see of Trent (*Letter 23 to Vigilius*). No one could reasonably believe that he labored to stir up that young bishop to attack lending at interest while himself maintaining a profound silence on the matter. Yet although assigning a precise year to that letter is not so easy, elsewhere we shall nevertheless say, not without probable grounds, that the year seems to have been 385, or some year not far removed from it. On the other hand, what Ambrose relates about the gambling of the Huns (chapter 11) cannot have been known before the end of the reign of Valens, that is, after the year 376, when historians say that this barbarous people first became known. It follows that this little work may reasonably be assigned to the intervening period, perhaps to the year 377 or to one of the immediately following years. For it is not easy to believe that Ambrose’s episcopal vigilance became so dull that, as soon as the opportunity arose, he did not labor to eradicate a vice that reigned with such cruelty and insolence.

We suppose that among Catholics no one will be found who does not willingly subscribe to Ambrose’s teaching on usury, since it is fortified not only by the authority of Basil and the other Fathers but also by that of the sacred books. But what judgment shall we form of the distinguished Salmasius (*On Usury*, *On the Manner of Usury*, and *Dissertation on Trapezite Lending*), and of certain more recent writers of the same communion, who dared to defend positions directly opposed to our Doctor? Ambrose teaches (chapter 14, no. 48, and chapter 15, no. 51) that it is unlawful for a creditor to receive anything beyond the principal; Salmasius asserts that this is lawful (*On Trapezite Lending*, preface and elsewhere). Ambrose maintains that this was always forbidden by the laws of both the Old and the New Testament (chapters 14, 15, etc.); Salmasius vehemently contends that in the old covenant it was an intolerable yoke, but that in the new Christ removed it (*On Trapezite Interest*, p. 5). Ambrose declares that usury is a crime scarcely less serious—or rather, in a certain respect worse—than homicide and idolatry (chapters 4 and 14, etc.); Salmasius swears that it was always permitted by natural law (*On Trapezite Interest*, p. 718). Ambrose rejects the empty pretexts of compensation (chapter 3, no. 10); Salmasius admits and defends them (*On Trapezite Lending*). Finally, for the one, usury is the source of innumerable evils (chapter 3, etc., and chapters 12–13, etc.), while for the other it is the origin of so many varied goods that, if it were removed, he denies that governments and commonwealths could endure (*On Usury*, chapter 21, and elsewhere). What could be more opposed than the opinions of these two men?

It is not our purpose here to confirm the teaching of the holy Bishop or to set forth its complete agreement on this subject with the views of the other Fathers. This has already been done by a learned theologian in a treatise written in French and published at Paris in 1671 under the title *The Defense of Lactantius Concerning Usury*; likewise by Monsieur du Tertre in a book entitled *Usury Explained and Condemned*; and finally, in later years, Christian duty in this matter was laid out in certain ethical treatises. We need add only one thing here: namely, that Ambrose and the other Fathers were no less acute in penetrating the meaning of Scripture than those patrons of usury who have reheated little more than the sophistries used by moneylenders in Ambrose’s time, like a stale dish of cabbage.

What else remained for those apologists of the moneychangers except, in order to diminish the number of Ambrosian arguments, to call into question the sacred authority of the Book of Tobit? They did this with great audacity. It is true that several Fathers—Athanasius (*Synopsis*), Gregory of Nazianzus (*Catalogue of Sacred Books*), Melito and Origen as cited by Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 26, and book VI, chapter 25), and the Council of Laodicea—did not list this book in the catalogue in which they placed the canonical books, evidently because it was absent from the Hebrew canon. Yet it would be difficult to find anyone who explicitly rejected the work by name. Jerome testifies somewhere (in the Galeate Prologue, the preface to the books of Solomon) that it is not admitted among the canonical Scriptures in the Jewish canon; but elsewhere he says that the Jews assigned it to the writings they call *hagiographa* (*Preface to Tobit*). According to the testimony of the same Father, it was publicly read in the Church and was also used by ecclesiastical men (*Preface to Jonah*). Hence we clearly understand that at that time the book had not yet been approved by the Church in any council, as happened later, but had been admitted by a kind of tacit consent.

Ambrose always regarded it as divine and canonical (here, chapter 1, no. 1, and *Hexaemeron*, book VI, chapter 4). Very many of the ancient Fathers—Irenaeus (book I, chapter 34), Polycarp (*Letter to the Philippians*), Cyprian (*To Quirinus*, book III, chapters 16 and 32, and elsewhere), Hilary, Chrysostom, Clement of Alexandria, Augustine, and others—supported him in this and long preceded the synods by which it was received into the catalogue of the sacred books. It may also be added that the holy Bishop appears to have attributed this same book to no other author than Tobit himself, the father. Those who have treated the question more carefully assign the first twelve chapters to the father (Serrarius, Huet), the remaining two to the son, except for the final two verses, which, they say, were added by some unknown author, perhaps one of Tobit’s grandsons. One of the more recent writers, Hay, maintains that the book was composed jointly by both father and son. But since the Church has not yet pronounced anything on this matter, everyone is free to abound in his own judgment.

[Col. 0759B]

ONE BOOK OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON TOBIT  
[Note: [Col. 0759B] Possibly written around the year 377.] (C)

[Col. 0759]

CHAPTER ONE.

He proposes to speak briefly of the virtues of Tobit commemorated historically by Scripture; first he relates how Tobit endured captivity and exile because he had provided burial even during his captivity. Then he explains how, after his return, he did not cease from the same duty; here the office of burying the dead is also praised.

[Col. 0759A]

1. Having read the prophetic book entitled *Tobias* [Note: [Col. 0759B] Manuscripts: *Tobis*. See the note on book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 4, no. 17.], although Scripture has fully made known to you the virtues of the holy prophet, I nevertheless think that I ought to use among you a concise discourse in reviewing his merits and works, so that what Scripture has arranged at greater length in historical form we may grasp more briefly, gathering together the several kinds of his virtues as though in a short compendium.

[Col. 0759B]

2. He was a just, merciful, hospitable man, and endowed with this choir of virtues. He underwent the hardship of captivity, bearing it humbly and patiently, grieving more over a common injury than a private one (Tobit 1:2 and following); he did not lament that the support of his virtues had profited him nothing, but rather judged that this insult had been inflicted upon him as a lesser price than his sins deserved (Tobit 3:1 and following).

[Col. 0760A]

3. [Note: [Col. 0759B] Latinius conjectures that one should read “He feared the edict.” But both the manuscripts and editions, as well as the meaning itself, resist this. The edict is the same thing that the following verse calls the prohibition, namely, the king’s promulgated ban.] He earned the edict [Note: [Col. 0760B] All editions read “lest anyone from among the sons of captivity”; all manuscripts read “lest anyone,” etc. From this it may be understood that Tobit alone was not included under the royal edict.], forbidding anyone among the sons of captivity to bury the dead (Tobit 1:22). But the prohibition did not restrain him any more than it incited him, lest he appear, through fear of death, to abandon the duty of piety; for the reward was mercy, and the punishment was death. Detected and convicted of such an offense, he was at last able, through a friend, to be restored to his own people—impoverished and exiled, after his property had been seized.

592

4. He was again engaged in these duties; and if he had any food, he looked for a stranger with whom he might share it. Thus, when he had returned tired from the duty of burial, he had food set before him, and, sending his son, looked for a companion at table (Tobit 2:1 and following). While the guest was being summoned, he was informed that the remains of an unburied body had been found, and he abandoned the meal. He did not think it pious to eat while a lifeless body lay exposed in public.

5. This was his daily work—and a great work indeed. For if the Law commands us to clothe the naked who are alive, how much more ought we to cover the dead? If we are accustomed to escort travelers on longer journeys, how much more should we escort those who have departed to that eternal home from which they will not return? “I,” says Job, “wept over every weak person” (Job 30:25). Who is weaker than the dead, of whom Scripture says elsewhere, “Weep over the dead” (Sirach 22:10)? Ecclesiastes, however, says: “The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of feasting” (Ecclesiastes 7:5). Nothing is more excellent than this duty: to give something to one who can no longer repay you, and to rescue from birds and beasts one who shares your nature. Wild animals are said to have shown this humanity toward the bodies of the dead, while human beings will deny it!

CHAPTER TWO.

How Tobit endured blindness, took care that no theft should be committed, and did not reclaim money lent to Gabelus until he was exhausted by old age; finally, how he abhorred evil interest-bearing lending, with a denunciation of it and praise of what is good.

6. While the Prophet, exhausted by so holy a duty, was resting in his chamber, a white substance from a sparrow’s nest fell upon him and caused blindness (Tobit 2:6, 10 and following). [Note: [Col. 0761D] The Roman edition reads: “beside the wall of the hall, when excrement and a white substance fell from a nest of sparrows,” etc. The Colbert manuscript reads: “when a nest of sparrows, consisting of excrement and a white substance, fell,” etc.; from this reading a satisfactory sense may be obtained by moving the word *de* (“from”) so that it follows *stercore* (“excrement”). Nevertheless, we have not thought it necessary to prefer this reading to that of the old edition and all the other manuscripts. In these texts, *albugo* appears to mean the birds’ excrement itself, so called from its color; hence Horace, book I, satire 8, uses *albi* as an epithet.] Yet he did not complain or groan, nor say, “This is the reward of my labors.” He was more distressed at being deprived of the service he rendered than of his eyes; he regarded blindness not as a punishment but as an impediment.

[Note: [Col. 0761D] All the manuscripts and old editions agree in the first part of this passage, whereas the Roman edition reverses and abbreviates it as follows: “And, so that nothing stolen might enter his house, he took precautions; but he supported himself by his wife’s wages. Finally”—from this last word, together with three manuscripts, it continues—“giving more thought to honor than to necessity, he had lent sustenance to his neighbor whose own resources were lacking,” etc. Other editions and the better manuscripts have the text as printed, except that the editions read “whose own resources were lacking,” and the Colbert manuscript alone prefers “some money.” After the word “sustenance,” one should apparently supply: “so that nothing stolen might enter his house, he took precautions.” Again, where the Gill and Roman editions have *commodaverat*, *commodatum*, *commodavit* (“had lent,” “lent,” “he lent”), the other editions and all the manuscripts have *commendaverat*, *commendatum*, *commendavit* (“had entrusted,” “entrusted,” “he entrusted”). Yet it should not be overlooked that just as the verb *daneizein* (δανείζειν, “to lend”) is used by the Septuagint and Aquila in both a good and a bad sense, so *fenerare* (“to lend at interest”) is used here by Ambrose and by Augustine in his commentary on Psalm 36.]

And while he supported himself by his wife’s wages, he took care that nothing stolen should enter his house. His wife had received a kid as her wages; but he, giving more heed to honor than to necessity, though his own resources were lacking, had entrusted a certain sum of money to his neighbor, which throughout his entire life, despite such great need, he did not demand back. Only when he saw himself exhausted and worn down by old age did he mention it to his son, not so much desiring to reclaim what had been entrusted as concerned that he not defraud his heir.

7. Because, then, he entrusted the money and did not lend it at interest, he fulfilled the duty of a just man. For interest-bearing lending, by which interest is sought, is evil; but that lending is not evil of which it is written: “Lend to your neighbor in his time of need” (Sirach 29:2). David also says: “The righteous shows mercy and lends” (Psalm 36:21). Another kind of lending is rightly accursed: lending money at interest, which the Law forbids (Deuteronomy 23:19). Tobit avoided this practice, warning his son not to transgress the Lord’s command: to give alms from his possessions, not to lend money at interest, and not to turn his face away from any poor person (Tobit 4:6 and following). Whoever gives this warning condemns the usurious lending from which many have made a profit and from which lending money to many became a business. Indeed, the saints forbade it.

[Col. 0762B]

8. The more serious an evil interest-bearing lending is, the more praiseworthy is the person who avoids it. Give money if you have it; let what lies idle for you benefit another. Give as though you would not receive it back, so that it may count as gain if it is returned. Whoever does not return the money returns gratitude; if you are cheated of your money, you acquire righteousness, for “the righteous shows mercy and lends.” If the money is lost, mercy is gained. For it is written: “Whoever performs an act of mercy lends to his neighbor” (Sirach 29:1).

CHAPTER THREE.

Ambrose sets before the eyes the inhumanity of moneylenders toward the poor and the methods by which they enslave them; finally, he attacks those same moneylenders.

9. Many do not lend at interest for fear of loss, since they fear fraud. This is what they customarily reply to those who ask them. To each of them it is said: “Lose your money for the sake of your brother and friend, and do not hide it beneath a stone to its destruction. Place your treasure in the commandments of the Most High, and it will profit you more than gold” (ibid., 13–14). But human ears have become deaf to such saving commandments, and the rich especially keep their ears closed with the bronze of their money. While they count their money, they do not hear the divine responses [Note: [Col. 0762D] *Responsa*, Greek χρησμοί (*chrēsmoi*), that is, the divine Scriptures. See what we noted in *On Flight from the World*, chapter 4, no. 20.]. As soon as someone, constrained by necessity or anxious for the ransom of his relatives whom a barbarian is selling as captives, begins to plead, the rich man immediately turns away his face; he does not recognize his own nature, has no pity for the humility of the suppliant, does not relieve his need, and does not consider the common frailty of human beings. He stands inflexible, arrogant; he is not bent by prayers, moved by tears, or broken by lamentations. He swears that he has nothing—or even that he himself must seek a moneylender to meet his own needs. Why do you add an oath to your hardness and greed? You will not be absolved by perjury; you will be bound by it.

10. But as soon as usury or a pledge is mentioned, the moneylender lowers his proud brow and smiles. The man whom he previously denied knowing he receives with a kiss, as though recalling a father’s friendship; he calls him a pledge of hereditary affection and forbids him to weep. “We shall search the house,” he says, “to see whether we have any money. I shall break up, for your sake, the ancestral silverware that has been crafted with great workmanship; there will be a very large loss. What interest will compensate for the value of the inlaid ornaments?” [Note: [Col. 0763D] *Emblemata* are figures and ornaments added to some vessel, which can easily be removed from it; the term is derived from Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐμβάλλειν (*apo tou emballēin*, “from inserting or putting in”).] “But for a friend I shall not fear the loss; when you repay me, I shall restore it.”

Thus, before he gives, he hastens to recover; and the man who claims that he is helping in the greatest need demands interest. “On the first day of the month,” he says, “you will pay the interest. As for the principal, if you do not have the means to repay it, I do not ask for it meanwhile.” Thus, although he gives only once, he harasses the borrower repeatedly and makes him always remain in his debt. By this art he handles the man. First he binds him with written obligations and fastens him with the bonds of his own words. The money is counted, liberty is assigned away; the wretched man is released from a smaller debt and bound by a greater one.

11. Such are your benefits, you rich men. You give less and demand more. Such is your humanity: you strip people even while you help them. For profit, the poor man is fertile ground for you. The needy man becomes a usurer because you compel him; he has what he must repay, but he does not have what he can spend. Truly merciful men: whom you release from another’s power, you assign to yourselves. He who needs food pays interest. Can anything be more grievous? He seeks medicine, and you offer poison; he begs for bread, and you hold out a sword; he pleads for freedom, and you impose slavery; he begs for release, and you tighten the knot of an ugly noose.

CHAPTER FOUR.

How moneylenders are compared with Judas and the devil; and what is signified by the names creditor, interest-bearing loan, principal, and debtor.

12. The holy David chiefly deplores this injustice, saying: “I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city; and usury and deceit did not cease from its streets” (Psalm 54:11–12). Thus, when he had placed the betrayal of Judas immediately afterward [Note: [Col. 0763D] Namely, in the following verses of the same psalm; consult them.], he set this before it—either because, beyond the odium of sacrilege, the crime of interest-bearing lending also fell upon those who conspired in the Lord’s death, or because so great a sacrilege was sufficiently and abundantly avenged by usury. Evil were the moneylenders who gave money so that they might kill the author of salvation; and evil are these men who give money so that they may kill an innocent person. The man who accepts the money also hangs himself by a noose, like the traitor Judas.

He thought Judas himself should likewise be condemned by this curse: “May the moneylender search out his substance” (Psalm 18:11), because what the proscription of tyrants or the hand of robbers usually accomplishes, the mere wickedness of the moneylender habitually inflicts. More learned interpreters, however, think that the devil himself should be compared with the moneylender [Note: [Col. 0763D] The old edition reads: “should be compared with him, who lends the resources of the soul and the patrimony of the precious mind, and, by the expenditure of usurious wickedness, captures it in this way,” etc. The Roman edition reads: “who lends the powers of the soul,” etc. Two manuscripts agree with this in the words “who lends the powers of the soul,” while three agree in the word “lends.” We have followed the better readings of the others.], for he overturns the resources of the soul and the patrimony of the precious mind through a kind of usurious wickedness; thus he captures it by his expenditure, thus entices it with gold, thus entangles it in guilt, thus demands back its head with his treasure.

13. What could be more unjust than you, who are not satisfied even with repayment under these terms? What could be more unjust than you, who give money and bind a man’s life and property? You accept gold and silver as a pledge, and yet you call him your debtor—the man who has trusted you with more than he received from you. You claim to be creditors, though you are the ones who owe more. Yes, you call yourselves creditors, although you have trusted not the man but the pledge. What you give is rightly called *fenus* (“interest-bearing loan”), since it is so base and cheap—*feneum*.

14. You call what is owed the “principal” (*sors*). Indeed, like a funerary urn, the wretched principal is cast about and must be paid through the punishment of the debtor doomed to perish. The accused stand pale, awaiting the outcome of the principal. Those whose condemnation is determined by lot do not tremble so much; those whose captivity awaits the outcome of the lot do not fear so anxiously, cast down and suspended. There one person’s captivity is assigned; here that of many. And perhaps it is called *sors* because the estates that are cast about under this arrangement are at stake [Note: [Col. 0764D] All editions read “which are cast about under this practice.” The manuscript reading, as in the text, is better.].

Great and memorable is the benefit of God. This is specially proclaimed by the prophetic voice concerning the fathers: he delivered them from usury and iniquity (Psalm 71:14). He says specifically, “He delivered them from usury,” because usury brings slavery. It is as though he said: he restored them to freedom after rescuing them from the bond of slavery.

15. The word “debts” is a grave one. Sins are called debts. Criminals too are called debtors; thus both these men and those others [Note: [Col. 0764D] A play on the word *caput* (“head”), which, when referred to criminals, means life or capital punishment, but, when referred to debtors, means the principal or capital sum; the same play occurs in the following chapter, no. 20.] make decisions concerning the *caput*. Yet faults have the names of their own, corresponding to the difference between the acts. Debts, though differing in amount, have one name, one burden, and one danger. The wretched man who asks to borrow money therefore does not know what he is asking for, nor does he understand what he is receiving.

CHAPTER FIVE.

The money of moneylenders is compared with the sea: once someone has received it, it immediately attracts a crowd of rogues; here also the principal sums of both Testaments are discussed. After that money has been consumed through excess, the moneylender drives the wretched man to sell his household goods, or grants him a postponement—but one more grievous than the postponements of war. At last, repentance for his folly follows, far too late.

[Col. 0764D]

[Col. 0765A]

16. The money of the moneylender does not know how to remain in one place for even a single day; it is accustomed to pass through many hands. It does not tolerate being kept in one purse; it longs to circulate and be counted. It seeks use so that it may acquire interest. It is a kind of wave of the sea, not fruit. Money never rests. It slips away and, as though striking a rock, beats against the debtor’s breast and immediately rolls back to where it came from. It comes with a murmur and returns with a groan. Yet the sea is often calm when the winds are still, while the wave of interest is always tossed about. It sinks the shipwrecked, spits out the naked, strips the clothed, and leaves people unburied. You ask for a coin and undertake a shipwreck.

On one side Charybdis roars around you; on the other are the Sirens, who, under the appearance of pleasure and the sweetness of melodious song, led those drawn into the shoals to destruction and, according to the stories, deceived them with the hope and desire of returning home (Homer, *Odyssey* XII).

17. Immediately sellers of perfume [Note: [Col. 0765D] By “ointment,” understand oil prepared with aromatic substances; by “spices,” fragrances and aromatics, which pleasure-seekers misuse for their delights.] and of various spices rush in, like dogs struck by the scent of wandering prey; hunters, fishermen, bird-catchers, and tavern keepers too, mixing water with unmixed wine, who loudly advertise the nobility of the wine’s ancient lineage and homeland and its vintage day. Parasites suddenly surround the man whom they had previously been accustomed to despise; they greet him, escort him, invite him to pleasure, and incite him to expenditure, saying:

“Come, and let us enjoy the good things that exist, and let us use creation as in the swift days of youth. Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and perfumes, and let no flower of the season pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; let there be no meadow that our luxury does not pass through. Everywhere let us leave signs of joy, for this is our portion, and this is our lot” (Wisdom 2:6 and following).

And truly the whole lot has become theirs; but you remain deprived of good things.

18. Scripture has not shown you such lots. David the holy one does not mean that you should sleep among such lots when he says: “If you sleep among the middle lots” (Psalm 67:14). For if you had slept in the midst of those lots—that is, of the Old and New Testaments—the desire for money would not have plunged you into the abyss of the worst usury. Spiritual grace would have given you silver through faith and, through instruction in divine wisdom, would have fashioned you into the likeness of gold. For if we have presented one testimony of divine Scripture and turned away from that luxurious banquet, this man too could have been saved if he had clung to the heavenly oracles.

19. Nevertheless, let us return to the banquet—not to taste its dishes, but to show others that they must be avoided. The table is loaded with foreign and exquisite foods. Shining servants are brought in, purchased at great cost and fed at still greater expense. Drinking continues into the night; the day ends with the banquet and gives way to drunkenness. The man rises full of wine and empty of resources. He sleeps until daylight and, while awake, thinks he is dreaming. For just as in dreams a poor man suddenly seems rich, so too the rich man becomes poor.

Meanwhile the money flows away, while interest overflows; time diminishes, and the interest increases; the treasure is emptied, and the principal accumulates. Gradually the guests withdraw, and the sureties appear. In the morning the moneylender pounds at the doors, complains that the days prescribed for repayment have passed, attacks the man awake with insults [Note: [Col. 0765D] The Era and following editions read “he attacks the waking man with quarrels.” Amerbach, together with the manuscripts, reads “with injuries,” etc.], and wakes the sleeping man from his dreams. There are no peaceful nights, no pleasant days, and no cheerful sun.

The gilded and silk garments are gradually removed and sold for half their purchase price. The wife, now more sorrowful, lays down with tears the ornaments bought dearly and to be sold cheaply. At the auction, the boys are placed before the table as attendants, and, being untrained [Note: [Col. 0765D] “Untrained,” that is, not instructed by the broker in how they should attract a buyer; or “unaccustomed,” that is, accustomed to luxuries rather than to more useful occupations.], they drive the buyer away. The money is offered to the creditor. “Hardly,” he says, “does this pay the interest; you still owe the principal.”

20. With his property exhausted, he returns liable for the principal; and when the interest has been reduced, he receives a postponement more grievous than those of war, as though he were going to fight a battle after two days. In war victory is uncertain; here poverty is certain. There one protects himself with a shield; here he meets the enemy naked. There a breastplate encloses the chest; here the whole man is enclosed in a prison. There a man loads his hands with weapons and arms himself with arrows; here he offers hands empty of money to be bound in chains. Both are commonly led away captive. The soldier has someone whom he may blame for the outcome of the war; this man has no one to blame except himself. Nothing is more intolerable than this misery, which cannot be excused. Conscience aggravates the weight of the injury.

21. Then he reckons with himself; then he remembers the Scriptures; then he says: “Was it not written for me: ‘Drink water from your own vessels and from the springs of your own wells’” (Proverbs 5:15)? What have I to do with the moneylender’s well, where even the water is enclosed (Proverbs 15:17)? Vegetables were more pleasant when eaten in security than a foreign banquet consumed with anxiety [Note: [Col. 0766D] Thus the Ambrosian, Erasmian, and Roman editions, together with three manuscripts. The Gill edition, with three others, reads “than banquets purchased with another’s money,” etc. The Thuan manuscript alone has “than banquets with another’s money,” etc. Perhaps “in the house” or “at the banquet” should be supplied.]. I should not have sought what belonged to another. Then, when I fell into debt, I should have sought a remedy from my own resources. There were smaller vessels at home; it would have been better to lack service than food. It would have been better to put clothing up for sale than to assign away my liberty. What did it profit me to be ashamed to make my poverty public? Behold, another has made it public. I did not wish to sell my servants who nurtured children [Note: [Col. 0766D] “Nurturers,” that is, slaves to whom the upbringing of children was entrusted.]; behold, another has adjudicated them for sale.

22. This reflection comes too late. You ought to have feared your own resources when you accepted what belonged to another; you ought to have come to the rescue when the first wounds began to spread. It would have been better at the beginning to reduce your expenditure and lighten your need through the narrow resources of your household than, after being enriched for an hour by another’s property, to be stripped afterward of your own.

CHAPTER SIX.

What schemes moneylenders devise in order to plunder unwary young men.

23. We accuse the debtor of having acted imprudently; yet nothing is more wicked than moneylenders, who regard the losses of others as their own profits and count as their expense whatever is possessed by others. They lie in wait for new heirs; they investigate wealthy young men through their agents; they attach themselves to them, pretending friendship inherited from father and grandfather, and wish to learn their domestic needs. If they find any occasion, they reproach their modesty and accuse them of shamefacedness, because they had not earlier hoped or presumed upon them. But if they encounter no snare of necessity, they spread out documents, say that a noble estate is for sale, a spacious house; they pile up the produce-yields and exaggerate the annual revenues, urging the young man to buy. They do the same with expensive garments and, praising costly jewels. When he says that he has no money, they offer their own, saying: “Use it as your own: you will multiply the price from the proceeds of the property purchased, and you will repay what you owe.”

24. They place other men’s estates before the young man in order to strip him of his own; they stretch their nets, and as soon as he has entered a space enclosed by their dragnet, they force him into the nets of guarantees and the snares of interest. They demand that he pledge to them his ancestral mansion and his father’s tomb. A date for repayment is fixed, while the agreement is passed over—when repayment can actually be borne. When they have made him sufficiently secure, they suddenly descend upon him and press him more urgently; they assail him when he pleads, saying: “You possess your estates; we do not possess our money. We gave gold, but we hold only a wooden tablet; the proceeds of your fruits continue to accrue, while no money increases for us. It is a pointless excuse; at least let the bond be renewed.”

[Note: Here *praetorium* does not mean the house of a praetor or of one who commanded an army, but a country house built for pleasure; it is found in this sense more than once in Livy.]

[Note: This means wooden tablets coated with wax, on which a loan security was customarily written.]

CHAPTER VII

How carefully the debtor avoids the moneylender, what sort of meeting takes place between them, how, after receiving a postponement, the debtor becomes more deeply entangled and is driven to sell his estates, and finally, deprived of everything and ready for imprisonment, falls into despair.

[Column 0767D]

25. Accordingly, while at first the young man thinks that none of his garments, or even his possessions, need be sold, he asks for a postponement in order to do these things. The interest is added to the principal, and the hundredth-part interest accumulates. Now he begins to sigh; now he recognizes his trouble. By day and night he thinks about the interest: whatever appears, he takes for the moneylender; whatever creaks, he seems to hear as the moneylender’s voice. “If you have the money, why do you not pay? If you do not have it, why do you add trouble to trouble and seek a remedy for a wound? Why do you endure the moneylender’s siege every day and fear his assault?”

There is an ancient saying: “The Lord gives sight to both when the moneylender and the debtor meet” (Prov. XXIX, 13). One, like a dog, seeks his prey; the other, like a wild beast, avoids the predator. The former, like a lion, seeks someone to devour; the latter, like a young ox, dreads the predator’s attack. The former, like a hawk, seeks to strike the swan with his talons; the latter, like a goose or coot, would rather throw himself from a precipice or plunge into the depths than endure this hawk of the human body.

Why do you flee every day? Even if the moneylender does not meet you, poverty meets you like a swift runner. Thus the Lord sees both the moneylender and the debtor; he watches both as they meet one another, a witness to the injustice of the one and the wrong suffered by the other. He condemns the avarice of the former and the folly of the latter. The one counts every step of the debtor and lies in wait for his turns; the other continually shelters his head behind pillars. For the debtor has no authority. The calculation of interest is repeatedly made on the fingers of both. The care is the same, but their feelings differ. One rejoices at the increase of the loan, the other is tormented by the accumulation of his debt. The former counts his gains; the latter his distress.

26. Why do you flee a man whom you could have faced without fear? Why do you flee, and how long will you flee? If someone knocks at night, you think it is the moneylender and immediately hide under the bed; if you suddenly sense someone entering, you leap outside. A dog barks, and your heart throbs; sweat pours out, your breath shakes your limbs, and you seek something to pretend so that you may put off the moneylender. When you obtain a postponement, you rejoice.

The moneylender pretends to be burdened by your loan, but he grants the delay willingly, like a hunter who has surrounded a wild animal and is confident of his prey. You kiss his head, embrace his knees, and, like a stag struck by a poisoned arrow, after proceeding a little way you finally collapse, overcome by the poison. Or you are like a fish into which a trident has been thrust: wherever it flees, it carries its wound with it.

Indeed, that fish devours death in its bait; it swallows the hook while seeking food. Yet it does not see the hook hidden by the prey. You see the hook and swallow it. Your hook is the creditor’s loan. You swallow the hook, but the worm continually gnaws at you. The bait itself is what deceives you. Thus, for you, the interest is neither useful as food nor the hook harmless to the wound.

Do you not know that once caught in a knot, a man tightens it more tightly himself if he tries to flee, and that when placed within nets, by fleeing he casts the nets more heavily upon himself? You flee into the streets when you cannot remain safe within your walls. The moneylender will find you whenever he wishes. Finally, when you have completed the appointed period, he rushes upon you like a wolf at night, does not allow you to sleep, and, when the expected day has come, drags you into public and compels you to sign the sale documents.

[Note: All editions read, “drags him from his bed into public.” This is not unsuitable, but it is contrary to the common agreement of the manuscripts.] In order to conceal the loss of your honor, you sign at once, intending to sell your ancestral tomb and, so that some appearance of modesty may be preserved, your paternal [estate]. The barren land is purchased; it is proclaimed that what was unproductive has been sold and that the debtor has been burdened with losses; the losses of the present are charged to the losses of the past.
