Soon even the praised possessions are sold, and instruments are brought forward—now not documents, but chains.

[Note: All printed editions read “with a frenzied face”; all manuscripts read “with a shamefaced face.”]

[Note: All printed editions read “so that something may be spared for modesty.” The manuscripts more suitably read “so that something may be put forward as a pretext,” and so forth. Accordingly, the Roman edition reads “when he has burdened the buyer with losses”; this is not bad, if even one manuscript supported it.]

27. Yet guarantors must still be sought. A respite is granted, not so that he may find the prey of freedom, but so that he may add a companion in slavery who will join himself to the sufferer. But what help can the addition of another’s calamity provide? Now even his friends flee, and his dining companions no longer recognize him. He himself avoids the sight of everyone; and as a boxer avoids the blows of his opponents, so he avoids encounters with respectable people. Anxious, whenever he has come upon someone, he leaves with a watchful gaze.

He returns prepared for chains; he returns wishing for death, thinking that, if he died, it would bring him rest. He returns miserably condemning himself because he did not avoid another man’s money and bound himself with the moneylender’s bronze.

28. O how many miserable people another man’s possessions have made! “What have you to do,” he says (Jer. II, 18), “with drinking the water of Geon?” What, I ask, have you to do with drinking the moneylender’s cup?

“Many,” he says, “borrowed for a time, attended to their needs, and repaid the money.” And how many have strangled themselves because of interest! You consider the former but do not count the latter. You remember that some escaped, but do not remember that others perished. You reckon the coins that were repaid, but do not count the nooses that were sought—nooses which many, being more sensitive to the disgrace of so shameful an agreement and more vulnerable to insult, preferred, choosing death, to humiliation and injury, fearing the reproach of life more than the punishment of death.

600 CHAPTER VIII

Children, in the height of disgrace, are put up for sale under the auctioneer’s spear because of their fathers’ debts; yet no one can remedy this evil, since the moneylender’s avarice cannot be satisfied. The relevant passage of Scripture is explained, and it is shown at the same time that moneylending is an occasion of transgression.

29. I myself have seen a pitiable spectacle: children led to auction because of their father’s debt, heirs to a calamity in which they had no share of the inheritance; and the creditor did not blush at so monstrous a crime. He presses, he insists, he assigns them. “Nourished by my money,” he says, “let them acknowledge service in return for their support; let them submit to bidding in return for the expense. Let the auctioneer’s spear be raised over the price of each.”

The spear is rightly raised when a person’s life is sought; rightly the matter reaches auction when a person’s lot is demanded. This is the inhumanity of the moneylender and the folly of the debtor: that to sons for whom he leaves no money he takes away freedom; instead of a will, he leaves a bond; instead of the profit of an inheritance, a written obligation.

What is the meaning of this paternal written curse upon the children, when there is no offense of an impious sin? Can there be any curse harsher, or any slavery more grievous?

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads “and more grievous than slavery.”]

And often, even after death, the dead man has this advantage: he does not witness his children’s misery.

30. A father often sells his children by the authority of begetting them, but not with the voice of affection. With a shamefaced expression he drags the wretched children to auction, saying: “Pay, my sons, for the expense of my appetite; pay the price of your father’s table. Vomit up what you did not devour; repay what you did not receive. This is your advantage: by your price you redeem your father; by your slavery you purchase your father’s freedom.”

[Note: All printed editions read “with a frenzied face”; all manuscripts read “with a shamefaced face.”]

31. Suppose that someone who can help approaches. Who can fill so great a Charybdis? Who can reckon the moneylender’s accounts? Who can satisfy his avarice? What prices will he not inflate when he sees redeemers? For he feeds no more on his own profit than on another’s loss.

Truly, truly it is a divine saying, since it is God’s, who, when he was angry because of the impiety of the Jewish people—because they had gone after foreign gods—said: “To whom have I sold you to a moneylender?” (Isa. L, 1).

For whoever has been bound to a moneylender is sold, and he is sold not for one price but daily; he is sold not with a fixed settlement but with continual addition. Each month brings a new auction of interest; each day brings a new sale under bidding. Whoever offers more always leads him away; he is assigned as merchandise, yet is never considered sold, as it were. Great, therefore, is the force of the heavenly judgment.

Was it not enough for the Lord to say, “To whom have I sold you?” Did he not add, “to a moneylender”? In his anger, he could find nothing more severe with which to punish the faithless. The abandoned one demands to know why they fled the author of salvation, as though the Lord had sold them to some moneylender as a fitting punishment.

[Note: The old and Roman editions differ only in that they omit the word “them,” completing the sense only after the word “leaving.” The manuscripts, however, are inconsistent in punctuation; they include “them,” as does the Roman edition. The Colbert manuscript alone presents the passage perhaps not incorrectly, as if the sense were “leaving them to a moneylender . . . . . . . . the Lord.”]

Those who abandon the Lord have, as slaves, something to fear more than the punishments and chains of prison; those who are free have something to dread for their neglect of freedom.

601 32. Observe also that moneylending has been judged an occasion of transgression, and that the person who has been able to bind himself to a moneylender easily departs from the Lord. For interest is the root of falsehood and the cause of faithlessness.

“I did not sell you,” he says; “but you were sold because of your sins” (ibid.). Therefore, whoever binds himself to a moneylender sells himself; and what is worse, he sells himself not for money but for guilt.

CHAPTER IX

The moneylender of sin is the devil, who displayed even his riches to the Savior; he resembles a moneylender; discussion is also made of the hundredth-part interest and the hundredth sheep, and of the name “creditor,” which the true exactor assumes.

33. Who is this moneylender of sin, if not the devil, from whom Eve borrowed sin, and with interest made the whole human race liable to debt? (See St. Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book I, chapter 3.) Finally, like an evil moneylender, he held the bond, which the Lord afterward erased with his own blood. For what had been written in the characters of death had to be dissolved by death.

The moneylender, then, is the devil. Finally, he displayed his riches to the Savior, saying: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. IV, 9). But the Lord, who paid another’s debt, owed him nothing, and could say: “The prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing of his own in me” (John XIV, 30).

[Note: All editions and several manuscripts read “he finds nothing of his own.” The older manuscripts, however, read “he finds nothing,” with “of his own” understood. Ambrose explains this reading in *The Flight from the World*, chapter 4, section 24.]

He owed nothing, but paid for all, as he himself testifies: “What I did not seize, then I repaid” (Ps. LXVIII, 5).

[Column 0771B] 34. What distinguishes the malice of this prince of the world? The moneylender binds the debtor’s person for the money, holds his hand—that is, the bond signed by the debtor’s own hand—and leads him away by the principal. O sorrowful name arising from sweetness! The Lord freed the hundredth sheep; that hundredth is salvation, whereas this hundredth is death; and good earth yields a hundredfold harvest.

Woe to those who say that what is bitter is sweet and what is sweet is bitter! What is more bitter than interest, and what sweeter than grace? When they call it a hundredth, should they not by that very expression recall the Redeemer, who came to save the hundredth sheep and not to destroy it?

[Note: “He holds the hand,” that is, he holds the debtor’s bond signed by the debtor’s own hand.]

35. Who is a more grievous exactor? And this too is a sorrowful name. For the Lord says: “My people, your exactors circumvent you” (Isa. III, 14). And in the Gospel you read: “When you are going with your adversary to the magistrate, make an effort to be released from him, lest perhaps he lead you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the exactor, and the exactor cast you into prison” (Luke XII, 58).

Recognize who this exactor is: he demands even the last quadrans, and calls himself a creditor, and in this name too he practices deception—like one who smears cups of poison with honey, so that death may lie hidden beneath the pleasant scent and the coated rim of the cup conceal the force of the fraud. He styles himself a creditor, as though trustworthy, though he is untrustworthy—the one to whom a trustworthy man pledges himself.

602 CHAPTER X

The story of the moneylender who prevented a debtor’s corpse from being carried out for burial.

36. How often have I seen the dead held by moneylenders as pledges, burial being denied while the interest was demanded? I willingly agreed with them, so that they might bind their debtor fast and, once he had been chosen, the guarantor might escape; for these are the moneylender’s laws.

I therefore said: “Hold your accused man; and lest he escape you, take him home and shut him in your room, harsher than executioners. For the one whom you hold, prison does not receive, but the exactor releases; prison releases the guilty after death, while you shut them in. By the severity of the laws, the dead man is released; with you he is held.

“Certainly, he is now said to have fulfilled his lot; nevertheless, I do not begrudge you—keep your pledge. There is no difference between a funeral and interest, none between death and principal. The interest on the loan sounds out, sounds out its funeral wail.

“Now truly the man whom you are suing has been reduced in status.”

[Note: “Reduced in status,” that is, deprived of the rank of nobility and reduced to the order of commoners.]

“Yet bind him with stronger chains, lest he fail to feel your bonds. The debtor is hard and rigid, one who no longer knows how to blush. There is, indeed, one thing you need not fear: he does not know how to ask for food.”

37. I therefore ordered the body to be lifted and the funeral procession to be taken to the moneylender’s house. But even there such sounds resounded from the groaning of those shut inside.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “The groans of those shut inside resounded aloud.” But the old edition and the manuscripts agree with our reading, except that through a scribal error they have “the applause of those shut inside” instead of “the groaning.” After the words “such things resounded,” something like “such as resound at funerals” seems to be understood.]

There too you would have thought there was a funeral; there too you would have thought that the dead were being mourned. Nor would you have been deceived in your judgment, except that it was clear that more people there were destined to die.

Overcome by religious custom—for it is said that even such pledges are accepted elsewhere—the moneylender asks that the remains be carried to the place of burial. Only then did I see the human moneylenders become troubled by me. Yet I was mindful of their humanity and took care that afterward they should not complain that they had been defrauded, until, bending their necks beneath the bier, they themselves led the dead man to the tombs, weeping with heavier grief over the funeral of their money.

CHAPTER XI

Interest is also exacted from gamblers, whose fortunes vary in play, but whose profit goes to the moneylender. How great is his tyranny over them, and what laws govern gamblers. Finally, the madness of certain barbarians in gambling is described.

[Column 0772C]

38. Hear of another evil no less bitter. These men watch the gatherings of gamblers and regard the misery of the loser as their own opportunity; they guarantee each player. At first chance plays out various results; victory is often transferred to different players, and their gains and misery change in turn. Everyone loses and wins; only the moneylender acquires. With the others there is merely the empty name of having won; with the moneylender alone there is profit—not annual, but momentary. They alone make a profit from everyone’s loss; they alone possess the interest of victory.

You may see the others suddenly poor, suddenly rich, then naked, changing their condition with every throw. Their life turns like a die; their wealth rolls across the board; danger becomes a game, and danger arises from the game. As many proposals, so many proscriptions. The cries of those applauding, the weeping of the despoiled, the groans of those lamenting.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “But he also condemns these.” The old edition, the Vatican manuscript, and the Victorine manuscript read “condemning.” The manuscripts of Thuan, Laon, and Dion read, “But also among these . . . condemning.” The Colbert manuscript alone has preserved the reading that allows us to recognize a scribal error: the word *sedet* in the other manuscripts has been divided into two parts.]

The creditor sits among them like a tyrant, condemning each person to a death sentence. He brandishes the spears and establishes a funeral auction from the spoils of each individual: some he consigns to proscription, others to slavery. Not so many are killed under tyrants.

I should therefore more properly call this the gamble of life than of money, since in a moment what will last forever is cast away. Drunkenness gives judgment, and no appeal is made. Gambling too has its laws, which the laws of the courts cannot dissolve. If it can be believed, the person who thinks resistance necessary is branded with disgrace; and the judgment of the disgraced inflicts reproach more severely than judicial censure. Those condemned before a judge are glorious in their eyes; those condemned before them are criminals before a judge.

Moses made the judgment of the elders noble (Exod. XVIII); yet those elders judged lesser matters. A weighty matter—that is, matters of greater importance—they customarily reserved for Moses’ judgment. Here it is said: “The council of gamblers has judged,” and their power is feared more than that of lions.

[Note: All printed editions read “than that of demons.” All manuscripts read “than that of lions.” This is excellent, since it creates a play on the words *aleonum* and *leonum*, a figure very frequent in this treatise.]

Among these beasts you live and move, moneylender. You snatch food from these beasts; you are judged more dreadful than they, and feared as more cruel than they.

39. It is reported that the peoples of the Chuni wage war against all peoples by every method, yet are subject to moneylenders; and although they live without laws, they obey the laws of gambling alone. Armed and ready for battle, they play; they carry dice as well as weapons, and more of them perish from throws of their own than from those of the enemy.

[Note: So read the manuscripts of Thuan and others; all printed editions, however, read “waging war against all nations.” This is wrong. How could those peoples be said here to wage war against all nations, when it is acknowledged that in Ambrose’s time there was very little knowledge of them? It should therefore be read as meaning “by every method.” For, as Ammianus Marcellinus and other historians testify, this people customarily fought partly by riding around their opponents, partly by making sudden attacks and opportunely withdrawing. Above all, while turning their backs, they pierced their enemies with javelins with great skill. As for this great madness of those same barbarians for gambling, no author says anything about it; Ambrose himself indicates only that he had heard it by report. Nor should we omit to mention that in all printed editions these peoples are called Huns, whereas in the manuscripts they are consistently called Chuni. Whoever wishes to know more about them should consult Ammianus Marcellinus and the notes of Valesius and Lindenbrog on him, as well as Sozomen, Jordanes, and others. See also what we have said in the Admonition to this book.]

They become captives in their own victory and suffer the spoils of their own people, things they would not know how to endure from an enemy. For this reason they never lay aside their zeal for war: when defeated in a game of dice and having lost the prize of all their booty, they seek the means of gambling through the danger of warfare. Often they are seized by such passion that, when the weapons they alone value highly have been surrendered by the defeated player, he commits his life, on a single throw of the dice, to the power of either the victor or the moneylender.

Finally, it is said that one of them, known in good faith even to the Roman emperor, paid off the price of the slavery he had brought upon himself by being defeated in such a wager through the punishment of an imposed death.

Thus the moneylender presses even upon the necks of the Chuni and drives them into iron; he oppresses the barbarians by the terror of his savage cruelty.

604 CHAPTER XII

The moneylender’s exactions and the various names they use. Their money is compared with the echidna and other serpents; the reason why the Greeks called interest *τόκοι* (*tókoi*) is explained.

40. For what is more dreadful than one who lends money today and demands it tomorrow? “And,” he says, “a man of this kind is hateful” (Eccli. XX, 16). The offer is gentle, but the exaction monstrous. Indeed, the very kindness of the offer produces the cruelty of the exaction: he brings out the money, demands mortgages, and stores them in his warehouses.

[Note: A *hypotheca* is anything pledged to the moneylender, whether a pledge handed over to him for safekeeping or immovable property bound to him by an interest-bearing instrument. The term *fiducia*, discussed below, has nearly the same meaning. See Gothofredus on book III of the Theodosian Code, title “On Rescinding Forfeitures,” p. 252ff.]

One sum of money is given by the moneylenders, yet how many things are demanded from the debtors! How many names they have devised! A coin is given and is called a loan; it is called the principal and is called the capital; it is recorded as debt. This monstrous creature of many heads produces a numerous exaction. He calls it a *syngrapha*; he names it a *chirographum*; he demands mortgages; he uses pledges; he calls them trusts; he asserts an obligation; he proclaims interest; he praises the hundredth-part interest.

41. The moneylender’s money is a kind of echidna, which gives birth to such great evils. Yet the fertile echidna, dragging along a womb pregnant with punishments, bursts open in giving birth.

[Note: The echidna—or, as the manuscripts read, *echinna*—is the female viper. On its birth, see Aristotle, *History of Animals*, book V, last chapter; Pliny, *Natural History*, book X, chapter 92; and others. This entire passage of Ambrose is taken from Basil.]

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “it bursts, and gives birth to offspring not degenerate from its mother,” for the offspring tears the mother apart with its bites. “There, therefore, where it is born,” and so forth. The old edition and certain Paris manuscripts, together with the manuscripts generally, agree with our reading, except that the words “Thus they first begin to be serpents” are absent from the old edition and from the manuscripts of Tornacum and Victor.]

Thus they begin to be serpents; they tear her apart with their bites. There, where it is born, the poison is first tested.

But the moneylender’s money conceives, gives birth to, and nourishes all its evils, and itself grows larger in its offspring, becoming more numerous through its grievous progeny. It is no less winding than a serpent, gathering itself entirely into a coil in order to preserve its head. With the rest of its body it lashes out, extending that part alone toward wounds. With enormous coils it binds whoever it has seized; with its head alone it kills. If its head is safe, even if the rest of it has been scattered, it revives.

42. Serpents also have different seasons for meeting and giving birth. Money at interest creeps upward from the day the agreement is made, its interest continually increasing; yet it does not know how to give birth, because it pours its pains into others instead. There are the pains of a woman in labor; hence the Greeks also called interest *τόκοι* (*tókoi*), because they seem to arouse the labor pains of the debtor’s soul.

The Kalends come, and the principal gives birth to the hundredth part. Each month comes, and interest is generated—the evil offspring of evil parents. This is the generation of vipers. The hundredth part grows; it is demanded but not paid; it is added to the principal. A prophetic curse is fulfilled: “Deceit upon deceit” (Ps. LIV, 12); interest is the offspring of an evil seed, still worse.

Thus it no longer begins to be merely a hundredth part, but a whole sum—that is, not the hundredth part of the loan, but the loan of the hundredth part.

605 CHAPTER XIII

Continuing the etymology of interest, he shows that it is more fertile than hares themselves and than any plants, and that nothing surpasses the moneylender’s greed; then he returns to the comparison of interest with animals and plants that he had begun.

43. I think that *usura* (“interest”) is also derived from *usus* (“use”), because, just as garments are worn away by use, so patrimonies are torn apart by interest.

[Note: The old edition, together with several manuscripts, reads: “The first letter of the rest sounds mournful; the word is the voice of pain.” The editions of Era and Gill, marking *caetera* with an asterisk, noted in the margin that it might be Greek; Gill added, “or *cerae*.” Since this did not satisfy those responsible for the Roman edition, they attempted to correct the passage on their own authority as follows: “The word *τόκος* sounds mournful in Greek; for it signifies childbirth, which is a voice of pain.” But besides the fact that the meaning of *τόκος* was already discussed at the end of the preceding chapter, all the manuscripts oppose this correction. The manuscript of Thuan, written a thousand years ago, clearly gives our reading. Several others agree, as does Gill in the margin. In some manuscripts, however, scribal ignorance introduced a defect: for example, the Laon manuscript reads *lugubrescere* as one word instead of *lugubre cerae*, which is plainly erroneous.

To remove the obscurity that caused the corruption, observe that the subject here is the word *usura*, whose first letter *u* once had the same sound as the Greek diphthong *ου*, as it is still pronounced by Italians, Germans, and other peoples. Since that sound imitates the hooting of an owl, it is called mournful or funereal. Hence the line in Ausonius’ *Technopaegnium*: “Unknown to Cecropian sounds, sounding funereally . . .” See J. Lipsius, *On the Correct Pronunciation of the Latin Language*, where this letter is discussed.

As for the word *cerae*, it has the same force here as if one wrote “of a wax-covered tablet” or “of tablets,” in which sense it is commonly found in reputable authors. The passage can therefore be made clear from its rough form if interpreted as follows: “The first letter of the tablets on whose wax the word for interest is written sounds mournful.” Perhaps in this sense it was said in chapter 10, section 35: “The interest on the loan sounds out, sounds out its funeral wail.”]

The first letter of the wax tablet sounds mournful. The word *parturit* (“gives birth”) is the voice of pain. What good can there be for you in something that begins with pain and ends with obligation?

[Note: What is said here about hares was transferred by our Ambrose, along with much else, from Basil’s Homily 2 on Psalm XIV. It applies especially to rabbits, from which arose the proverb, “They give birth more often than rabbits.”]

Hares, they say, generate and raise their young simultaneously and immediately give birth again.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “Interest is generated and generated again for these *tocoglyphs*,” and so forth. It undoubtedly had in mind Basil’s words: “For the money is at once lent to the *tokoglyphs*, is generated, and is born, and grows beneath.” But there is no reason to reject the reading of all the manuscripts and editions, since *anaglypharii* conveys the meaning perfectly. Both words derive from *γλύφειν*, that is, “to carve” or “to dig”; hence *anaglypharii* may mean those who carve the names of debtors again and again, or more frequently, into their tablets with a stylus.]

For these engravers too, interest is generated and interest is generated upon interest; it is nourished and born, and once born it gives birth again.

The roots of trees are first planted so that they may take hold. Once they have taken hold, they begin to grow green, and afterward to send out shoots. But money at interest, scarcely planted, already sends out shoots.

Seeds burst forth in their season; animals give birth in their season. “There is a time for giving birth and a time for dying; a time for planting and a time for uprooting what has been planted; a time for killing and a time for healing” (Eccl. III, 2–3). And below: “A time for acquiring and a time for repaying; a time for keeping and a time for casting away” (ibid., 6), as Ecclesiastes says.

Money at interest is sown today and bears fruit tomorrow; it always gives birth and never dies; it is always planted and scarcely uprooted. The moneylender always wants to acquire and never to lose; never to keep his money, but always to cast it out; never to heal, but always to kill.

[Note: The old editions, together with the manuscript of Tornacum, read, “always to complete his money.” The Roman edition reads, “always to pour it out.” Several other manuscripts, more suitably, read as in the text. Ambrose here had in mind Ecclesiastes’ “a time for casting away,” and wished to signify that nothing is more dear to the moneylender than to cast his money outward by placing it at interest, so that it should not remain idle at home.]

44. And since Ecclesiastes is a good teacher in all things,

[Column 0776B]

[Note: Those who have held a different opinion, attributing the book to Hezekiah, Isaiah, or Zerubbabel, may be consulted in P. Daniel Huet’s *Evangelical Demonstration*, proposition 4 on the book of Ecclesiastes, p. 192, where their arguments are refuted and this book is asserted to be Solomon’s. Its dignity is likewise defended there after the arguments of its opponents have been answered.]

let us remain with him for a little while: “The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing” (Eccl. I, 8). Neither is the moneylender satisfied with receiving, nor is his desire for the daily sound of counting money fulfilled. And again: “Whatever has been, that is what will be” (ibid., 9). Money always grows; avarice knows no leisure; interest knows no holiday.

“All the rivers flow into the sea, and the sea is not filled” (ibid., 7). This sea is the moneylender: he absorbs the patrimonies of all like waves, and he himself does not know how to be filled. Yet many use the sea for profit; no one uses the moneylender except at a loss. There, many find advantage; here, all suffer shipwreck.

606 45. There are many animals that begin to reproduce quickly but also quickly cease reproducing. The principal gives birth quickly and never ceases; indeed, once it has begun to grow, it extends its increase into infinity.

Moreover, everything that grows, once it has reached the form, measure, and size proper to its nature, ceases to increase. But the moneylenders’ money is always increased by time, and, exceeding the form of its maternal principal, observes no limit.

Many animals, once they begin to reproduce what has arisen from them, lose the power of reproduction as though their strength had been exhausted. But the principal of the loan, when it has been made equal to the growing hundredth parts, renews its age and multiplies its accustomed offspring by addition.

CHAPTER XIV

Interest is prohibited by divine law; hence the saying attributed to Cato, “To lend at interest is to kill a man.” A garment received as a pledge must be returned before night; and by the term “interest” is understood whatever is demanded beyond the principal. After this follows a reproach of the extortions familiar to the rich.

[Column 0777B]

46. This is neither a new nor a superficial evil, since it is prohibited by the prescription of the ancient and divine Law. The people who had stripped Egypt bare and crossed the sea on foot are warned to beware the shipwrecks caused by interest-bearing money. And although, concerning other sins, the Law prescribed a warning once or many times repeated [Note: Latinius thinks it should be read “only once, at most” rather than “once or many times.” But since all editions and all manuscripts agree at this point, the received reading is not so foolish that it cannot be aptly explained in this way: whether the Law prohibited the other vices only once or very many times, it nevertheless prohibited usury more frequently than those vices.] , it spoke more often about interest. You have this in Exodus: “If you lend money to a ward, an orphan, or a poor person, you shall not stifle him in your presence; you shall not impose interest upon him” (Exod. 22:25). He shows what “to stifle” means—that is, to impose interest; for the creditor’s noose strangles him and, what is worse, his soul. By this expression he conveyed both the violence of a robber and the hideous knot of death.

[Col. 0777C] “If you take your neighbor’s garment as a pledge, you shall return it to him before sunset; for this alone is his covering, this is the garment of his shame in which he will sleep. And if he cries out to me, I will hear him” (ibid., 23). You have heard, usurers, what the Law says—the Law of which the Lord said, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17). The Lord does not abolish it, yet you abolish it? “To demand interest,” he says, “is to stifle.” This too was later said by certain wise men among them: “What is it to lend at interest?” “To kill a man,” he says (Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, at the end). But surely Cato did not precede Moses, who received the Law. He came much later.

47. “If you take your neighbor’s garment as a pledge, you shall return it before sunset, lest his nakedness appear in shame” (Exod. 22:26–27). But you strip and make people naked, and you do not return the garment. Take care lest the sun set upon your greed, lest the sun of righteousness set upon you, because you do not hold to righteousness, or lest the sun of iniquity set over your crimes. The day too perishes against its will; night rushes upon Judas. When the devil had entered his heart, he rose to betray, and it became night; for the sun of righteousness had set for him and had lain down upon him. He who entered his heart made darkness for him, so that he could not see the author of light. There the wretched man perished at the very banquet at which others are saved.

Return, therefore, the garment to the debtor, so that he may sleep in it and be at rest. If you are unwilling to return it, “I will hear him,” he says, “because I am merciful” (ibid.). If you do not hear, I will hear; I will have mercy; I will not despise the prayer of the poor.

48. It is also written in Deuteronomy: “You shall not exact interest from your brother—interest on money, interest on food, or interest on anything whatever that you lend to your brother. If you lend to a foreigner, you shall exact interest from him; but from your brother you shall not exact it” (Deut. 23:19–20). You see what weight there is in these words. “Do not,” he says, “exact interest from your brother”—that is, from one with whom you ought to hold everything in common; yet from him you exact interest? Your brother is your partner in nature and fellow heir of grace. Do not exact more from one from whom it is harsh to demand back what you have given, except when he has the means to repay.

49. Since many, avoiding the commands of the Law (14, question 3, chapter *Plerique*), when they have given money to merchants do not demand interest in money but receive from their merchandise profits equivalent to interest, let them hear what the Law says: “You shall not accept interest on food, nor on anything whatever that you lend to your brother.” Such fraud and circumvention [Col. 0778C] of the Law is not observance of it. And do you think you are acting piously because you accept something from the merchant as a gift? [Note: All editions and two manuscripts read “as though you were receiving a loan.” Others, more reliable, read “as though you were receiving a gift.” From this you may understand that human greed had already devised that distinction by which they say that receiving anything beyond the principal in the form of interest is illicit, but not if it is accepted in the form of a gift.] He commits fraud in the price of the merchandise, and from that fraud he pays you the interest. You are the author and partner of that fraud; whatever he has cheated, benefits you. Food is interest, clothing is interest, and whatever is added to the principal is interest: call it by whatever name you wish—it is interest. If it is lawful, why do you avoid the word, why cover it with a veil? If it is unlawful, why do you demand an increase?

50. What is worse, this vice belongs to many, and especially to the rich, for whom storerooms are built under this pretext. If someone thinks a banquet must be prepared, he sends to a merchant [Note: *Absynthiatum*, or as it is written elsewhere, *absynthiacum*, is wine flavored with wormwood. *Picenum* and *Tyriacum* are so called from the places where they originate. Picenum is a region of Italy, whereas Tyre is a city in Asia. As for the proposed reading *hyllam* in place of *vulvam*, Latinius’s conjecture is pointless, since all editions prefer *vulvam*, which, as already stated, was sought by hunters after delicacies.] to have a cup of wormwood wine brought to him free of charge; he directs another to the tavern to obtain Picenian or Tyrian wine; another to the butcher to procure a vulva for him; another to arrange his fruit.

Thus they call “humanity” what is sustained by another’s danger. You drink, while someone else is dissolved in tears; you feast, while you choke others with your food; you take delight in music, while another wretched person laments with mournful howling; you taste fruit, while another swallows a thorn. “Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” A thorn is interest; a thorn is the hundredth-rate interest; a thistle is usury, and it burns badly. How, then, can you obtain fruit from thorns? If that fruit does not grow from thorns, an eternal one will grow from them.

You grow rich from hardships; you seek profit from tears; you feed upon another’s hunger; from the stripped possessions of despoiled people you forge silver—and you consider yourself rich, though you beg alms from a poor person? But hear what the Savior says: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation” (Luke 6:24).

## CHAPTER XV

That the foreigner from whom it is permitted to exact interest is only one whom it is permitted to kill; whereas one’s brother is a partner in the same faith or law; that every kind of interest is proscribed; and concerning the blessings of the person who abstains from it, with an exhortation to mercy and truth.

51. But perhaps you will say that it is written: “You shall lend at interest to a foreigner” (Deut. 23:20), without considering what the Gospel says, which is fuller. For the moment, however, let us set that aside and consider the words of the Law itself: “You shall not lend at interest to your brother,” it says, “but from the foreigner you shall exact it.” Who was a foreigner at that time except an Amalekite, an Amorite, or an enemy? “From him,” it says, “exact interest.” Against one whom you rightly wish to harm, against one upon whom arms are justly brought, interest is lawfully imposed. One whom you cannot easily defeat in war, you can quickly avenge yourself upon through the hundredth-rate interest. Exact interest from one whom it is not a crime to kill. He fights without a sword who demands interest; he avenges himself upon an enemy without a blade who has become a usurious exactor. Therefore, where there is the right of war, there too is the right of interest.

But every brother of yours is first a member of the faith and then of Roman law: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you” (Ps. 21:23).

52. Finally, in Leviticus also the Law prescribes that interest must not be demanded from a brother. Thus you have it: “Your brother shall live with you; you shall not give him your money at interest, and you shall not give him your food in order to receive more in return” (Lev. 25:36). This statement of God generally excludes every increase of the principal. Hence David considered blessed and worthy of heavenly habitation the one who did not give his money at interest (Ps. 14:5).

[Col. 0779D] If, then, the one who did not lend at interest is blessed, without doubt the one who lent at interest is accursed. Why, then, do you choose a curse rather than a blessing? You can be blessed if you wish; you can be righteous. For according to Ezekiel, the righteous person is one “who returns the pledge to the debtor, who does not give his money at interest, who does not receive an increase, and who turns his hand away from injustice.” “He is righteous,” he says; “he shall surely live,” says the Lord (Ezek. 18:7, 9). But the one who did not return the pledge, who set his eyes upon idols, who committed iniquity, who lent at interest and received an increase—he shall not live. He has committed all these iniquities; he shall surely die. His blood shall be upon him. See how he joined the usurer to the idolater, as though he were equating the crimes. Choose, then, what is sweet.

53. Why are you always sad, always most bitter, always anxious? Let mercy proceed from you at last; let truth proceed. Let falsehood be bound; let fraud be hated. You have taught perjury: a usurer’s oath is called the place where perjury is prepared. You have prepared it frequently when, after the money has been repaid, you arrange that the written acknowledgment not appear; afterward you swear that you did not receive the money. [Note: Erasmus, Gill, and the Roman edition read “where perjury is prepared.” “You have frequently prepared perjury.” The Victor manuscript reads “where one swears falsely: you have frequently prepared perjury.” Other manuscripts, and the Ambrosian edition with our text, imply the word “perjury” after the verb “you have prepared.”]

Do not, then, always be wretched, always greedy, always sorrowful. They are lions, yet they change their ferocity: “From the eater came forth food, and from the strong came forth sweetness” (Judg. 14:14). The Greek has “and from the sorrowful”; this is how we find it. Nevertheless, this is understood of the strong, because the lion is strong in ferocity, and what is savage is sorrowful.

And from you, who devour money and greed, let mercy come forth; for this is food for the needy. And from the sorrowful let sweetness come forth, so that you may forgive the one who has no means by which to pay. Why do you drag sins as with a long rope, and iniquity as with a long strap on a young cow? This is what you do when you prolong the interest. You hold the poor debtor, even when there is perhaps some benefit there, where there is no hope of profit. [Note: All editions and two manuscripts read “as though there were some benefit there.” Other, more reputable manuscripts read “even if there is some benefit there,” since *vel* here has the sense of “at least,” a usage not uncommon among authors.] And this I say in accordance with your greed.

## CHAPTER XVI

According to the Gospel command, one must lend to those from whom nothing is expected, and even to enemies; the most abundant interest is that of the one who lends to the Lord; nor should one distrust his poverty, which bestows true riches.

54. In the Gospel, moreover, the Lord considers that one should lend especially to those from whom repayment is not expected. Thus he says: “If you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? For sinners lend to sinners in order to receive in return. But love your enemies, do good to them, and lend, expecting nothing; and your reward will be great in heaven, and you will be sons of the Most High, because he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:34 and following).

You perceive what name the lender has received from the Lord, and what name the one who is bound to your loan also bears. “Sinners,” he says, “lend to sinners in order to receive in return”: both are sinners, the lender and the debtor. “But you,” he says, “love your enemies.” Do not examine what your enemies deserve, but what you ought to do. Lend to those from whom you do not expect to receive back what has been given. There is no loss here but gain. You give little and will receive much; you give on earth, and it will be repaid to you in heaven; you lose interest, but you will have a great reward; you cease to be lenders, and you will be sons of the Most High; you will be merciful and prove yourselves heirs of the eternal Father.

55. But you delight in the terms “lenders” and “interest.” I do not begrudge you that either. I will teach you how you can be good lenders and how you can seek good interest. Solomon says: “He who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord; according to his gift he will repay him” (Prov. 19:17). Behold, good lending has been made from what was bad; behold, an irreproachable lender; behold, interest worthy of praise.

Do not, then, think me envious of your advantages. Do you suppose that I am taking a human debtor away from you? I am providing God; I am substituting Christ; I am pointing out the one who cannot defraud you. Lend, then, your money to the Lord in the hand of the poor. He is bound and held; he records whatever the needy person has received; his Gospel is the security; he promises on behalf of all those in need; he gives his word. Why do you hesitate to give?

If some rich man of this world were offered to you, one who would pledge his own faith as guarantor for a debtor, you would immediately count out your money. The Lord of heaven and creator of this world is poor to you, and still you deliberate about what richer guarantor in faith you should seek.

56. But you object that he became poor, though he was rich. You have seen, then, that his faith is rich and his faith is reliable. He became poor when he paid on our behalf, and even that poverty does not deceive; for he made us rich whom you thought poor. The Apostle says: “He became poor though he was rich, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (2 Cor. 8:9). A good poverty, which bestows riches.

Do not, then, fear poverty, so that you may be rich. Give your idle money, and you will receive fruitful grace; you will assist the needs of the poor, and the anxiety of guarding your money will be reduced. What the poor person has received will not perish; what you have given to the needy will be kept safely for you without a guardian.

If you seek an increase of interest, there is blessing in the Law and a heavenly reward in the Gospel. What is sweeter than blessing? What is greater than heaven? If interest on food is desired, that too is available, as we read: “The one who has mercy on the poor will himself be fed” (Prov. 22:9).

## CHAPTER XVII

An objection is answered: some deny that the retention of a pledge is generally prohibited and restrict the Law to the pledges of the poor.

57. Return, then, the pledges you hold, since you have found a trustworthy guarantor. But they still murmur, saying that it is lawful to hold pledges, and they defend themselves by the Law. For they say: It is written in Deuteronomy: “If your neighbor owes you anything whatever, you shall not enter his house to take a pledge; but you shall stand outside, and the man who owes you will bring the pledge outside to you. If that man is poor, you shall not sleep in his pledge; but you shall surely return his pledge to him at sunset, and he shall sleep in his garment, and bless you, and there will be mercy for you before the Lord your God” (Deut. 24:10 and following).

And elsewhere, they say, it is written: “You shall not take as a pledge the mill or the upper millstone, for this is taking a life as a pledge” (ibid., 6). And elsewhere: “You shall not take a widow’s garment as a pledge” (ibid., 17). [Note: Thus all the Gallican manuscripts and the old editions read. The Roman edition, based on one Vatican manuscript, reads: “From this they argue that not all pledges are prohibited, but specifically those of the poor and the widow.” The reading is clear and entirely natural, but it seems rather to represent Ambrose’s paraphrase than Ambrose’s actual words.]

From this they argue that particular pledges, not all pledges, are forbidden—that is, those of the poor and the widow. They also say that it is forbidden to take the mill or the upper millstone as a pledge.

58. But since the Lord himself says through the prophet Ezekiel that the person who returns a pledge is righteous and the person who retains it is unjust (Ezek. 18:7), he plainly urges that not merely some particular pledge but every pledge in general be returned. Job says: “The written charge that I had against anyone, composed under oath, I read as though placing a crown upon it; and if I did not tear it up, I returned it, accepting nothing from the debtor” (Job 31:26 and 27).

Since the Lord commands that we expect nothing from those to whom we have lent (Luke 6:34), what we are supposed to receive back, how do they think that a pledge ought to be retained according to the Law?

## CHAPTER XVIII

To satisfy those who object that divine Law incites us to lend at interest, the question is examined of what the righteous person—for example, Peter—can lend at interest; and it is shown that the words he possesses are what he should lend.

59. But lest they renew the same objection and say that they too are incited to lend at interest by the oracle of the Law, because it is written, “You shall lend at interest to many nations, but you shall not borrow” (Deut. 28:12), it is time to discuss and teach more fully and explicitly what is to be lent and to whom the statutes of the Law apply. [Note: The Ambrosian and Erasmus editions, with two manuscripts, read: “But lest they now be ashamed to obey.” Gillot and the Roman edition read: “But lest they be ashamed in an equal manner.” Finally, one Vatican manuscript and five Gallican manuscripts have the reading printed in the text. Here *ne recrudescant* means “lest they defend themselves again,” invoking the authority of Scripture; it refers to the words above: “But they still murmur,” etc.] For the cause of the pledge is preceded by the cause of lending at interest.

“The sinner borrows and does not repay; but the righteous person has mercy and gives” (Ps. 36:21). You hear, debtor, what you ought to avoid; you hear, creditor, what you ought to imitate. And below: “I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread. All day long he has mercy and lends at interest” (ibid., 25).

From where does this righteous person have enough to lend all day? Therefore the righteous person is rich; and the richer each person is, the more righteous he is. Whoever has more with which to lend is himself more righteous. Yet it is difficult for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven.

60. What, then, does he lend at interest? Tell me, holy David. I have brought forward testimony against myself unless you help me. Peter said: “Silver and gold I do not have” (Acts 3:6). Was he not righteous? Explain to me, then, what he lent at interest. For you said: “Blessed is the man who has mercy and lends; he will order his words in judgment” (Ps. 111:5).

I have found what the righteous person lends at interest. Let Peter also teach me what he lent at interest, for he said to the poor man who was looking attentively at him and John: “Silver and gold I do not have.” Will you therefore give nothing to the poor, Apostle? Yet you give, and you give more than others. You give the poor what others cannot give; you give the poor what will prevent him from being needy again; you give the poor what even the rich long to receive; you give the poor what those who possess that silver and gold do not know how to offer, because greed obstructs them; you give the poor what makes him richer than the rich. [Note: Some manuscripts and all editions read: “You give the poor what makes him rich”; several read: “what makes him richer.” Other manuscripts read: “You give the poor that by which [the older manuscripts: whom] you make them rich,” with the relative pronoun *qui* understood in the sixth case, as though the sentence were: “You give the poor that gift by which you make him rich.”]

You have stirred my desire; I long for this gift of yours. Tell me, I ask, what you give. Do not leave me suspended for long; I want to ask, if you will quickly repay. But you repaid quickly. You did not delay the needy man; you did not despise the poor man’s prayer; you did not make him despair any longer; you did not go up to the temple empty-handed, saying, “Silver and gold I do not have.”

It is not only those who have silver and gold who go up with full hands. The poor man also goes up not empty-handed; he too goes up not empty-handed, although he does not have silver and gold. Let us hear what this poor man gives: “But what I have,” he says, “I give you. In the name of Jesus the Nazarene, rise and walk” (ibid.). O poverty to be desired! O poverty richer than wealth! The man was lame, and the rich gave to him; one poor man gave, and immediately the man who had been lame was made well.

61. The righteous person therefore has something to lend at interest; he also has silver to lend at interest: he lends his words. This is the silver of the righteous; for “the sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, proved on the earth, purified sevenfold.” This is what the one who receives the Law lends at interest, the one who meditates upon the Law, the one who practices the Law.

This is what Peter lent at interest; this is what Paul lent at interest. They were told to go to men of the nations. To Cornelius the centurion Peter was told: “Rise, go without hesitation, because I have sent them”; and he rose and went (Acts 10:20). And below he said: “Can we prevent water, so that those who have received the Holy Spirit should not be baptized?” (ibid., 47). And he ordered them to be baptized.

This is what “You shall lend at interest to the nations” means: that you forgive sins and remove debts; “but you shall not borrow.” The sinner borrows and does not repay his sins, because he is a sinner. To Paul it is said (Acts 9:15): “You shall lend at interest to the nations,” for he was sent to the nations. To John it is said: “You shall lend at interest to the nations.” To James and the others it is said: “You shall lend at interest to the nations”—to those who were told, “Go, baptize the nations” (Matt. 28:19).

62. It is said to the people of the fathers: “If you keep the commandments of God, you will be blessed, and you shall lend the word at interest to the nations” (Deut. 28:12). The following words make clear that this is not spoken of money: “You shall be ruler over many nations, but no one shall rule over you” [Note: The old edition, together with the Tornesian and Victor manuscripts, reads: “It is said to Paul: If you keep the commands of the fathers, you will be blessed, and you shall lend the word to the nations.” The Roman edition, from the Vatican manuscript and in agreement with all the Gallican manuscripts, restores the passage, except that where all the manuscripts read “the word to the nations,” it reads “to many nations.”] (ibid.). “The Lord your God will set you as head and not as tail, and you will then be above and not beneath, if you heed the voice of the Lord your God” (ibid., 13).

And it follows: “But if you do not heed, you are accursed in the city, and accursed in the field” (ibid., 16). And below: “Accursed is the offspring of your womb” (ibid., 18). Money certainly does not make one blessed, but knowledge of God and preaching of the word. We are blessed if we lend the Lord’s grace at interest, if we impart the Lord’s words to the needy, if we observe the heavenly commandments. Conversely, it is not money that would have been lent that makes one accursed; but if zeal is lacking, if observance of the heavenly statutes is lacking, you will be accursed.

## CHAPTER XIX

That the Jews first lent at interest to the nations, and later the nations believing in Christ repaid them in kind because they had lost their money; concerning the praise of that money and an exhortation to lend it at interest; and how the nations were preferred to the Israelites in this matter.

63. Finally, the mystery of the Church is clearly expressed. For he first said to the disciple of the Law: “If you heed the Law and keep it, you shall lend at interest to the nations” (Deut. 15:6). This was done by our fathers. Moses lent at interest to the nations, acquiring proselytes; Joshua son of Nun lent at interest; Gideon lent at interest; Samuel, David, Solomon, Elijah, and Elisha lent at interest. If anyone wished to know the word, he went to them. The queen of the South came to hear Solomon’s wisdom.

64. When the Jewish people began not to keep the Law, foreigners began—that is, people from the nations who believed in the Lord Jesus—to lend the interpretation of the Scriptures at interest to that ancient people. Timothy, born of a Greek father, lent the word to the Jews when he received the priesthood. Today also we priests in the Church lend the word to the Jews who have crossed over from the Synagogue to the Church.

We lend both the new and the old money. For what they once had, they no longer have: they have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear; they have money and do not have it, because they do not know how to use it, do not know its value, and have not recognized its image and form. For if they had recognized it, they would never have denied the author of the money, saying: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19:14).

When he returned after receiving the kingdom, he ordered his servants to be summoned—the servants to whom he had given the money—and he praised those who had lent the money at interest. But to the one who had kept his master’s money idle he replied: “You knew that I am a stern man; I take up what I did not deposit, and I reap what I did not sow. Why, then, did you not put my money on the table, so that when I came I might have demanded it with interest?” (ibid., 22–23).

65. You have heard what money belongs to a good lender, what money acquires good interest, what money does not disgrace the lender or oppress the debtor, what money rust cannot cover and moth cannot penetrate, what money is not from an earthly but from an eternal treasure, what money makes the recipient rich and diminishes nothing in the lender.

This money bears interest—not a hundredth part of what was given, but a hundredfold fruit. Therefore open wide the bosom of your mind, so that you may receive for yourself the counted quantity of this money. Direct the gaze of your heart, so that you may recognize the image and inscription of this money. Certainly, test this money; set a tablet upon the table of your soul, making it firm through virtues and square; store it in the treasury of your breast, from which the learned scribe brings forth things new and old.

You see what kind of money this is and how it joins together in itself the hated names of creditor and debtor. I who was attacking lenders now summon a debtor. I desire you to be lenders of this money, so that those who borrow from you may hasten willingly to you; through it you may acquire not a coin but a kingdom; through it you may seek not curses but the grace of blessing.

66. The people of the nations lend this money at interest—the people who knew how to receive what was lent, who knew how to discern it, who knew how to test it. [Note: Several manuscripts and all editions read: “You rejected the things enjoined by spiritual lending.” Dionysius’s second hand and the first hand of the Thuan manuscript read more aptly: “You rejected the things needful for spiritual lending,” which has the same sense as saying that the Synagogue, or Judea, refused the evangelical money because that people could in no way pay spiritual interest. Shortly afterward the Roman edition had “you cut this off from the Son of God,” or, as the old edition reads, “from the Son of God.” This is wrong, for Ambrose intended nothing except that David spoke in the person of Christ, a manner of expression he often uses elsewhere.]

You rejected the things needful for spiritual lending, and began to be in need. Therefore it was said of you by the Son of God: “The sinner borrows and does not repay” (Ps. 36:21). It is said to you: “The foreigner who is among you will rise above you, while you will descend to the depths” (Deut. 28:43). For he does not know the heights who does not know Christ; he is always in hell who has not ascended to Christ. But the people who receive the word are on high; they possess here the whole inheritance of faith.

Concerning them the Law says: “He will lend to you, but you will not lend to him; he will be your head, and you will be the tail” (ibid., 44)—that is, he will be first, while you will be last and rejected. I will take from Judea the head and the tail, the beginning and the end: Christ as the beginning, who, when asked who he was, replied, “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John 8:25); and Christ as the end, for “he is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). Therefore the one who does not believe unto righteousness has neither beginning nor end, but is himself the end of himself.

## CHAPTER XX

Having first distinguished between a pledge, something entrusted, and a deposit, he shows that the spiritual pledge is what the Law commands to be returned; nevertheless, bodily pledges too must be returned. The one who has heard the word of God is a debtor, and a pledge must not be taken from him. Concerning the evangelical garments and the tunic that we are all commanded to put on. The word of God is a good covering; it is the pledge of the Lord’s principal, the garment of wisdom; finally, the word must be drawn together.

67. We have learned about lawful lending at interest; let us also learn about the pledge that the Law commands to be returned before sunset. Hear the Apostle saying what this is: “God gave us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts” (2 Cor. 1:22).

A pledge, something entrusted, and a deposit are spoken of in three ways. They call a pledge what is received in exchange for borrowed money; something entrusted and a deposit are what we commit to someone for safekeeping. Hence the Apostle says: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to preserve my deposit for that day” (2 Tim. 1:12). He also taught what a deposit is when he said: “Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us” (ibid., 14).

Is the Spirit the guardian of entrusted gold and silver, or is money guarded through the Holy Spirit? Therefore a spiritual pledge is guarded by the Spirit, lest the birds of heaven come and take it away from our hearts.

68. Let us therefore ask that Christ guard within us the pledge that he himself gave, and preserve his own deposit and trust. For he received nothing from us; rather, he entrusted to us what was not ours. Therefore the person who violates another’s deposit suffers damage to his honor. If we must violate no human trust through any fraud, how much more fitting is it that we preserve a divine and spiritual deposit in good faith, lest we suffer grave losses of reputation and usefulness.

69. This, then, is the pledge that the Law prohibits us to take as a pledge and to carry away by force. For Scripture says: “If your neighbor owes you anything, you shall not enter his house to take a pledge; and the man to whom the debt belongs will bring the pledge outside to you. If that man is poor, you shall not sleep in his pledge; but you shall surely return his pledge to him at sunset, and he shall sleep in his garment and bless you, and there will be mercy for you” (Deut. 24:10 and following).

70. You will say to me: “Behold, the Law prohibited taking away a pledge, not receiving one; and it ordered that it be returned to the poor, not to everyone.” But concerning bodily pledges, holy Ezra also taught us that you, usurers, cannot oppose the profession of your fathers. For when those who had lent at interest and taken other people’s pledges were ordered to return them, they said: “We return them, and we demand nothing from them” (Neh. 5:12).

Good fathers, who decreed that the pledges of debtors should be returned; good lenders as well, who answered that they would return the pledges and would not demand the money they had given. The sentence of your fathers’ judgment binds you to this, as does the creditors’ own declaration.

71. There is also another pledge that the spiritual Law prohibits being taken away and commands to be returned before sunset—one that a debtor returns and that he himself brought forth. [Note: All editions and several manuscripts read “that a man returns the debt.” Others read more correctly “that a debtor returns”; for “he is a debtor” follows. The statement “and he himself brought it forth” means the same as “he was not deprived of it by force.” It should be referred to the words above, “he will bring the pledge outside to you,” and also to what follows below, “If through his own foolishness he has lost it.”]

Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand is a debtor. The evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart. Do not, then, enter his house to take that pledge. “Woe to the one who causes one of these little ones to stumble!” If through his own foolishness he has lost his pledge, you will not be guilty. But if he is poor, return the pledge before sunset. The pledge is a garment.

[Col. 0787B] If he seems rich to himself, he deceives himself if he has surrendered his pledge. But if he is poor, lacking the riches of the spirit, return his garment to him before sunset.

72. If the matter concerned a bodily pledge, surely it ought rather to be returned during the day, lest the shame of the naked body be exposed by daylight; darkness does not reveal the naked. And if the concern were that the poor man had nothing with which he could cover himself while sleeping, the text would surely have said that a blanket or covering should be returned. But by saying “garment,” it signifies rather the tunic with which we put on and clothe ourselves. Return, then, the poor man’s tunic to him, so that he may sleep in it at night.

73. Does he not seem to you to signify the poor man who, when commanded to go with a single tunic and not to seek another, was sent by Christ to preach the Gospel (Matt. 10:10)? For he is the poor in spirit who is able to sleep; when a person is sated with riches, there is no one who allows him to sleep. The poor man sleeps the sleep of resurrection, which the rich man cannot sleep because he is suffocated by riches and pleasures. He sleeps the rest of Christ, who says: “I slept and rested, and I rose” (Ps. 3:6).

This is that tunic woven from above with which Christ was clothed, which those soldiers whom you recognize could not tear. None of them tears Christ’s garment; rather, they divide it, as it is written: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots” (Ps. 21:19).

The evangelists divided his garments among themselves, and over his clothing—that is, over the preaching of the Gospel with which the Lord Jesus is clothed even today—they cast lots. That lot, certainly, which fell upon Matthias, so that he might be added as the twelfth apostle in number, the traitor’s name having been excluded.

It is rightly said of the evangelists that they cast lots, for a lot hangs, as it were, upon divine judgment. And because they did not speak by their own power, nor did all of them say everything in the same way, but many said different things that another had not said, we recognize that the grace of the Holy Spirit, as though by lot, bestowed upon each of them what they were to say about the works of the Lord Jesus, so that according to his will they might divide among themselves the task of recording his deeds.

74. There is also that garment of which the Apostle speaks when he says: “Put on the Lord Jesus” (Rom. 13:14). This is the garment that covers what is dishonorable in us and, in Christ, surrounds those things with a more abundant honor. In Christ we put on the heart of mercy; we put on the glory of the cross, which seemed a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks. Those are ashamed who think it ought to be an object of shame; but as for us, far be it from us to glory except in the cross of the Lord Jesus. Our dishonorable things possess a more abundant honor because, through the Lord’s passion, an eternal kingdom is prepared for us; for the more someone has sinned, the more he loves. Let us therefore be buried with the Lord Jesus, so that we may deserve to share in his resurrection. Let us strip off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, in whom there is forgiveness of sins.

75. A good covering and garment, therefore, is the word of God. With this garment the sons of Noah covered their father’s nakedness: they took the garment upon their shoulders and walked backward, so as not to see their father’s nakedness—that is, those bodily parts which possess a certain shame associated with human generation. Therefore, the one who wished to look received a fitting reward for his narrow-mindedness: he became a slave, for everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. Hence he remained among earthly things.

Let no one take this garment from the poor man; or, if he does take it, let not the sun set upon one who has been stripped. Let him restore it first, lest the poor man’s sin be charged against the moneylender, and lest he begin to labor not only under his own sin but also under another’s. Let this pledge be returned during the night of this age; let him be clothed with this garment amid the darkness of the world.

76. This pledge belongs to the lot of the Lord, not to the contrary lot. For we read of two lots in Leviticus, concerning which it is said: “You shall make one for God, and the other for the one sent away” (Lev. 16:8). The one sent away transmits his lot to moneylenders; the servants of the Lord are in Christ’s lot.

Aaron, established in this lot, excluded the misery of the contrary lot when, standing between the two divisions of the people, he did not permit death to creep from the dead into the lot of the living by the opposition of his own body. The good pledge of this lot is the garment of the Word.

Let no one take this garment from you, debtors; do not pawn this garment to anyone, if you wish never to endure disgrace—so that you may sleep among the clerical lots like Aaron, sleep between the two Testaments, sleep the sleep of resurrection, and be able to restore yourselves. This is the garment which, even if you have pawned it, holy Solomon advises you to recover in Proverbs, saying: “Take away your garment, for a transgressor is passing by” (Prov. 27:13).

77. The garment of wisdom is one of those garments that Wisdom made for herself from fine linen and purple. This means that the garment of faith consists of the preaching of heavenly things and the blood of the Lord’s passion. Fine linen signifies heavenly things; under the appearance of purple the mystery of the sacred blood is declared, through which the heavenly kingdom is bestowed.

Finally, the preceding words indicate that the garment of wisdom is being signified [Note: The Codex Dionysianus gives *pejora indicat* (“indicates worse things”); all the others give *superiora indicat* (“indicates higher things”); the editions have *... indicant* (“indicate ...”).] For he first said: “Be wise, my son, that your heart may rejoice” (Prov. 27:11). And two verses later he says: “But fools, when they arrive, pay the penalty” (ibid., 12). “Take away your garment.” Take it away, therefore, lest you suffer the penalty of folly; and lest that most wicked common moneylender, recognizing you stripped of your proper garment, attempt to expose the shame of your disgrace and persuade you to cover yourself with leaves, and, seeing that you are naked, make you fear coming into the sight of God.

78. “Repay your neighbor in due time, make the word brief, and deal faithfully with him; and at every time you will find what is necessary for you” (Sir. 29:2–3). Innocence does not like to defend itself with many words. Susanna had no need of an elaborate verbal defense: she made her word brief before the Lord and immediately deserved to obtain testimony to her own chastity. The elders were speaking at length, laboring to obscure the truth with verbal embellishment—but not the daughter of Judah. She was silent before human beings and spoke to God.

Among the people, a woman’s own defense was shameful; while modesty was being defended, shamelessness was being displayed. She made her word brief, saying to the Lord: “You know that they have spoken falsely against me” (Dan. 13:41). And the Lord stirred up the spirit of the boy Daniel to avenge her chastity.

79. Make your word brief, therefore, so that your tongue may not answer as a repayment to your creditor [Col. 0789C]. Or, mystically: “Make your word brief,” that is, bring it to completion. For “the Lord will make a consummating and abbreviated word upon the earth”; that is, may a sum abbreviated from many accounts be reckoned to you. Deduct what has been expended in diverse expenses, so that you may preserve what remains safe. Thus the Lord, from the many dispensations involving the Jews and from that great accounting of sins, finally brought matters to completion and abbreviated them, so that “the remnant might be saved according to the election of grace” and might be preserved for the seed, through whom he would revive the Synagogue’s nearly extinguished hope.

## CHAPTER XXI

Those who borrow when they are unable to repay are reproved. How degraded they are, and how, by failing to repay on the appointed day, they turn friends into enemies; hence it is concluded that no one should take a loan. What is understood by the mill and the upper millstone that must not be pledged?

80. How disgraceful it is to repay with trouble the one who helped you by a benefit! When you have defrauded the person to whom you owe a debt, you will afterward find no creditor in the time of your need. How unworthy it is that, when you cannot support your own livelihood, while still owing nothing, you should think that you can support both your livelihood and your debt!

First consider from where you will repay, and then take the loan. “I receive the produce of my fields,” you say. But if they do not produce enough for use, how will they produce enough for the increase of accumulated interest? “I am selling my property.” And from where will you obtain the proceeds by which you may meet your expenses? Interest is not paid out of the principal; it grows. By being counted, it is heaped up and increases.

81. Moreover, do you not consider the humiliation and embarrassment of the one who asks? Until you receive the money, you kiss the proud moneylender’s hands; you lower your voice, lest the louder sound of your voice offend his ears, lest more people hear you pleading. Poverty is not a crime, and there is no disgrace in need; but it is shameful to owe, and shameless not to repay [Note: All editions and several manuscripts read: “not to repay is more shameful.” This is not wrong; nevertheless, all the oldest witnesses read: “not to repay is shameless.” One has “more shameless.” This too can reasonably be explained in that sense: the person who owes is affected by a certain shame, but the one who does not repay is shameless and impudent.].

You will ask for an extension when, at the time prescribed for repayment, you begin to be summoned. Instead of money you will offer delays; you will complain about the timing; you will pile up excuses; and although you have promised everything, lest you seem to defraud him altogether, you will scarcely return half. You will turn a friend into an enemy; instead of honor you will return insult, and instead of blessing, a curse. Consider how damaging these things are to one’s reputation; recognize how far they depart from the character of a good man.

82. Therefore, while you are free from bonds, withdraw yourself from the yoke and burden of slavery. Are you rich? Do not take a loan. Are you poor? Do not take a loan. Are you rich? You suffer no necessity of asking. Are you poor? Consider the difficulty of repayment. Wealth is diminished by interest; poverty is not relieved by interest. For evil is never corrected by evil, nor is a wound healed by a wound; rather, it is aggravated into an ulcer.

83. Take care lest, while asking for money, you pledge your mill or your upper millstone. The mill is that by which fine flour is prepared—the mill by which one woman who is taken prepares fine flour, while another is left. Perhaps the woman who is taken is the one who always grinds the word of God, so that she may have fine flour and make spiritual dough, “purging out the old leaven, so that she may be a new lump” [Note: All editions read: “Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be ...,” etc. The Thuanian, Dionysian, and Colbertine manuscripts read: “Purge out ... so that it may be ...,” etc. The sequence of the exposition shows that Scripture is not being quoted here so much as adapted.]. She guards her mill, interprets the Scriptures, and keeps for herself the upper millstone. But the woman who is left is the one who pawns her mill. When she has ground something carelessly, she pawns the stone that is above the mill.

What is this stone, I ask? I read: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Ps. 117:22). Why is it above the mill? Because he is the one who helps those who grind; he is the one who says: “Search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life” (John 5:39).

84. Do not pawn this upper millstone, moneylender, lest you fall upon it. For “everyone who falls upon this stone will be shattered; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.” Nor should you accept a widow’s pledge.

It is a grave matter in either sense according to the literal meaning: that you should take away from the needy the means and instrument of living, or that you should take away a widow’s pledge. But it is graver still if you hold fast the word from the soul that is a widow in respect of the Word and impose upon it the barrenness of widowhood [Note: All editions and certain manuscripts read: “so that you may impose upon it the barrenness of widowhood”; others of better quality read: “and may indicate to it ...,” that is, command it ...].

## CHAPTER XXII

Which moneylender we ought to imitate; how God gave more to the Church, to whom the Church itself also repaid more without his demanding it; and concerning the dispensation of divine mercy and judgment.

85. And so that you may know that I recommend these things with affection, and may know that it is possible to lend well, I will show you which moneylender you ought to imitate. “There were,” he says, “two debtors to a certain moneylender: one owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both of them. Which of them, then, will love him more?” Simon the Pharisee answered: “I suppose the one to whom he forgave more” (Luke 7:41 ff.). His judgment was commended when the Lord said: “You have judged rightly.”

The Pharisee judged rightly, although he thought wrongly, supposing that the Lord knew less about the woman’s sins than he forgave. Yet his judgment is praised so that every excuse might be taken away from him.

86. More was forgiven the Church, which was gathered from the nations, because it owed more; but it too repaid more—not to one who demanded, but to one who gave. She gave water to Christ’s feet because she washed away her own sins; she kissed his feet, carrying the insignia of peace; she poured oil on his feet, herself also bestowing mercy upon the poor. These are Christ’s feet; in these Christ walks more innocently. And she wiped them with the hair of her head. For whoever possesses a disposition toward humility is humbled before Christ. And therefore, he says: “Her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much” (ibid., 47).

87. Observe that the Lord both freely grants mercy as a generous giver and dispenses judgment together with compassion. He first forgave by grace, but he knew whom he would forgive. The Jew has no excuse. He forgave me, as a sinner, more; he granted that one, as an ungrateful man, less. Yet he knew that the latter, as an ungrateful man, could not repay what he had received, and that the Church, mindful of grace, would repay more because she had received more.

## CHAPTER XXIII

When people allege the antiquity of interest, the reply is made that guilt too is ancient, and that Christ came to abolish it, while the devil introduced it. Moneylenders are likened to the devil, as are also those who bind themselves as guarantors and thereby prepare another enemy for themselves. How carefully one must avoid binding oneself for another, or at least for a sum greater than one’s resources can bear.

88. You have, therefore, someone whom you may follow as a moneylender, if you wish to be praised and do not wish to be what we condemn. For we do not attack persons but avarice.

Some people were not wrong to say, when our discourse two days earlier had pierced their feelings: “What did the Bishop intend by speaking against moneylenders, as though something new had been committed, as though those who came before us had not also done it, as though lending at interest were not ancient?”
