It is true, and I do not deny it; but guilt too is ancient. Sin began with Adam; from him came guilt, just as from him came Eve; from him came transgression, just as from him came the human condition. But Christ came for this reason: to abolish what had grown old, to establish what was new, and to renew by grace the guilt that had grown old. For this reason he offered himself to suffering, so that he might be renewed in spirit and absolve all people (cf. Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book 1, chapter 3). But the devil deceived Eve in order to overthrow the man and bind his inheritance.

89. What do moneylenders do? They deceive those from whom they collect interest and bind guarantors. But Tobit did not seek a pledge or demand a guarantor (Tob. 1:17; 4:22). You must take care, therefore, that you seek a guarantor and bind him in your own name. Look: another enemy is being prepared. For when you have nothing with which to repay the debt, he will be held liable in your place.

You are found to be a deceiver and a fraud because you have deceived your friend. He will be stripped; he will be led into bonds on your behalf. You will suffer him as an exactor more burdensome than the creditor, when he says: “Press your fellow citizen whom you guaranteed.” Thus you too will begin to be ungrateful and will pass over what is written: “Do not forget the kindness of a guarantor; for he gave his life for you” (Sir. 29:20).

The Septuagint reads: “For he gave his good soul for you. A sinner will overturn the good things of a guarantor.” [Note: The Septuagint reads: “For he gave his soul for you—good things of a guarantor he will overturn, the sinner.” One manuscript and the Complutensian edition, as Nobilius reports, read: “For he gave his soul for you—a good pledge,” etc. But Ambrose must have read: “For he gave his good soul for you. A pledge ...,” as Nobilius himself observed.]

You will necessarily say: “Who asked you to give your guarantee? If you had not given your guarantee, I would not have received the money.” “I received adulterated money; he gave me bronze mixed with gold. If only you had not offered yourself! Perhaps the creditor suborned you—or perhaps you suborned him.”

90. Therefore, beware of binding yourself to another’s debt, lest you also be accused of having sold this: lest, if a debtor gives you something owed to you by the custom of friendship as a favor, he appear to have bought you [Note: All editions read: “lest, if anything that is owed to you—as the custom of friendship has it—or if a debtor gives you a favor, he appear to have bought you.” The old edition, together with the Tornesian and Victorious manuscripts, reads in a way that suggests that he has purchased it. The Roman edition has: “so that he may appear to have bought it from you.” Other manuscripts agree with the text.

Again, where the earlier editions read: “you will blush to refuse when you are entreated by a friend,” the Roman edition and manuscripts read: “you will be moved ... and will blush.” The Thuanian, Dionysian, and Colbertine manuscripts read: “you blush to refuse.” Latinius conjectures that it should read: “for, when entreated by a true friend,” etc. But this conjecture is unnecessary, as becomes clear to anyone who examines the passage: before “you will be moved” and “you will blush,” the particle *if* is understood.

Finally, for “if the debt has not been paid,” as found in the old edition and two manuscripts, the Roman edition and two manuscripts give: “if the debtor has not been able to pay.” The oldest witnesses give: “if he is unable to pay the debt,” where the word “friend” must be understood.].

Or, if you wish to intervene, you are moved when a friend pleads with you and you blush to refuse. Intervene in such a way that, if he is unable to repay the debt, you know that it will have to be paid from your own resources.

Approach the matter prepared for this. For you have read: “Do not guarantee beyond your means; if you have guaranteed, consider it as though you were repaying” (Sir. 8:16). And further: “Receive your neighbor according to your means, and take care lest you fall” (Sir. 29:27)—that is, lest you bind yourself to a debt greater than your resources and means can bear and repay [Note: The Tornesian and Victorious manuscripts, together with the editions, read: “according to the quantity of money.” But with the Thuanian, Laudian, Dionysian, and Colbertine manuscripts, one should read: “according to the quantity of the debt.” For in this matter *nomen* means the same as “debt.” Hence the expressions “to contract debts,” “to discharge debts,” and similar phrases.].

For if you hand over what you possess, you have lost your wealth but not your good faith. You do not suffer damage to your reputation; you have redeemed your friend without fraud on your part.

Elsewhere too Solomon’s Proverbs offer you this advice, saying: “Guarantee your friend, just as one who binds himself as guarantor for his friends” (Prov. 17:18). But if you do not have the means, hear what Solomon says: “Do not become a guarantor, being ashamed of a person; for if you have nothing with which to pay, they will take away the covering from beneath your sides” (Prov. 22:26–27).

Therefore, a good moneylender will acquire favor; the wicked one, execration.

## CHAPTER XXIV

How we ought to imitate Tobit in paying wages; and what kind of lending he likewise teaches us.

91. But holy Tobit was not content with these limits of virtue alone. He also knew that a laborer must be paid his wages, and he offered him even half of them (Tob. 4:15); deservedly, in place of a laborer, he found an angel (Tob. 12:5).

And how do you know that you may not perhaps defraud some righteous person of his wages—or, worse, if he is weak? For “woe to the one who causes one of these little ones to stumble!” How do you know whether there may be an angel in him? Indeed, we should not doubt that an angel may be in a laborer, since Christ may also be in him, who is accustomed to be present even in the least.

92. Pay the laborer his wages, therefore, and do not defraud him of the compensation for his labor. For you too are a laborer of Christ; he has hired you for his vineyard, and a heavenly wage has been reserved for you. Do not therefore harm a servant who works in truth, nor a laborer who gives his life. Do not despise the needy person who supports his life by his own labor and sustains it by his wages.

For this is to kill a person: to deny him the support necessary for his life. You too are a laborer on this earth. Give the laborer his wage, so that you too may be able to say to the Lord when you pray: “Give a reward, Lord, to those who endure you” (Sir. 36:18).

93. Tobit says to you: “Luxury is the mother of hunger” (Tob. 4:15), thereby teaching self-restraint. He also says: “Pay every person who has worked for you his wages on the same day, and let a person’s wage not remain with you; and your wage will not be diminished” (ibid., 15).

He says to you: “Do not drink wine to drunkenness” (ibid., 16). He says to you: “Share your bread with the hungry” (ibid., 17). See what kind of lending he wishes you to practice: “And cover the naked with your garments; from everything that abounds for you, give alms. Bless the Lord at all times” (ibid., 18 ff.).

In these things, then, the interest is eternal and the profit perpetual.

# ON THE INTERPELLATION OF JOB AND DAVID

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOUR BOOKS ON THE INTERPELLATION OF JOB AND DAVID

It is established that this treatise consists of four books *On the Interpellation*—that is, the remonstrance or complaint—of Job and David. They did not all appear together in the editions of Ambrose’s works. Indeed, when the editors who prepared the earlier editions encountered an incomplete exemplar, they omitted the second book. Erasmus was the first to publish it, but with the following judgment prefixed to the book in the edition of Ambrose: he assigned it away from our Doctor and attributed it to the author of the book *On the Calling of the Nations*. His sole argument was a difference of style, which he judged to be very unlike Ambrose’s.

Gillotius, however, who afterward undertook considerable labor in editing Ambrose’s works, attacked this opinion with great force, arguing that it rested on a very insecure foundation (Preface to his edition of Ambrose and note to the second *Apology of David*). It was not unusual, he observed, for the holy Fathers to change their style according to the subject, the time, or the persons whom they addressed. Moreover, the manuscripts that he had sought out from various libraries unanimously attributed this entire work to Ambrose.

Gillotius is also supported by the copies that we have used. One of them, if not so ancient that one could swear it was written in the age of Saint Ambrose—as Gillotius says of one of his own copies—nevertheless predates at least a thousand years. In it these four books appear in the same order and under the same titles in which we have undertaken to publish them.

Even if manuscripts of such authority were lacking, the very words of the blessed Bishop and the whole sequence of the work would make it clear that the second book belongs to Ambrose no less than the other three. Nor do we hesitate to assert that Erasmus himself would have completely abandoned his opinion if he had compared the beginnings of these four books with one another.

For what could be clearer than the words in which Ambrose declares that he will examine, in order, the complaints uttered by the saints Job and David concerning human misery? “It is our concern,” he says, “to consider the interpellations of both” (book 1, chapter 1, section 3) ... “They must therefore be examined in their proper order.” This could have been accomplished only in the first two books, and he says as much there, when at the beginning of the third book he writes: “Our preceding discussion was about the interpellation of the saints”—namely, Job and David—“that the human condition is fragile and weak,” and so forth (chapter 1, section 1).

Finally, anyone who wishes to compare the same second book with the fourth book of the same work will undoubtedly understand for himself that the difference Erasmus proclaims is pure invention.

The Roman editors did indeed publish all these books equally under Ambrose’s name, together with his other works, but perhaps they separated them from one another rather too boldly. They inserted the first and third books, as commentaries on Job, into the first volume; but they tore the second and fourth away from the preceding books and placed them in the second volume under the title *Expositions on Psalms* 41, 42, and 72.

Since such a separation could not have been made without introducing some alteration into the author’s text, and since a distinguished work was thereby, as it were, corrupted through the dislocation and scattering of its members, this plan did not win the approval of those who rightly desire the writings of the Fathers to be presented as they were left by them.

Accordingly, Nicolas Faber, formerly superintendent of the studies of Louis XIII, a man distinguished alike for piety and learning, did not restrain himself from openly condemning this separation in one of his letters to Fronton Ducaeus. There he asserted that the editors had been compelled to interpolate something in order to institute this division, a procedure hardly credible. Yet we should not suppose that they did this with evil intent. Rather, they believed that they were serving the reader’s convenience by arranging the commentaries according to the various parts of Scripture, while failing to weigh sufficiently the disadvantages that would result from permitting such freedom with the books of the Fathers.

We have therefore restored these four books to their proper order. The fact that the book which we publish second is found in fourth place in two manuscripts of a more recent period, we believe to have occurred because those codices were copied from some mutilated exemplar in which the second book was missing. When the scribes later found the same book elsewhere, they copied it after the other three, which had already been arranged in continuous sequence.

Something similar certainly occurred in the editions as well. The oldest editions, which, as we have already said, were prepared from an incomplete codex, represent the three books they alone contain under the titles of books 1, 3, and 4. The subsequent editions of Erasmus, Coster, and Gillotius show that the aforementioned second book was printed out of its proper place.

That there was no other order in which the holy Doctor wrote these books than the one in which we arrange them here is proved not only by the manuscripts of the oldest class, but also by Gillotius, by the typographers of the latest Paris editions of Ambrose’s works, by D. Hermannus, and by others who have observed the matter. Yet the entire sequence of the work confirms it most evidently. We briefly set it before the reader’s eyes.

The first two books concern the interpellation of Job and David on account of the miserable condition and weaknesses of human life, both bodily and spiritual—that is, the diseases and calamities from which no one is exempt—as well as the unhappy necessity of committing those sins for which we must give an account before the strict judgment of the offended God.

In the first book the holy Bishop teaches this through Job’s own words, taken from the first chapters of the prophet’s book and quoted at length. He adds only a few brief observations on the more notable passages; yet he skillfully inserts a fairly extensive mystical interpretation of certain words of Job where he considered it necessary (chapter 5, section 12 ff.).

In the second book the holy man pursues the same subject by more carefully expounding Psalms 41 and 42. In them he observes a threefold complaint of the Prophet (chapter 7, section 26, and chapter 8, section 29): first, concerning the calamities that we endure through the burden of this life; second, concerning the delay of the blessings we hope for, especially the coming of the Lord, which David desired with the most ardent longing; and third, concerning the necessity of passing our life in the company of the ungodly.

In both books he also adds arguments highly suitable for confirming the divinity of the Word (book 1, chapter 9; book 2, chapters 4 and 6). We believe that he did this for no other reason than to strengthen his people against the poison of the Arians, who at that time possessed great influence at Milan.

The two later books contain the complaints that people customarily utter indignantly: that the wicked abound in prosperity while the good are afflicted by adversity. Accordingly, Ambrose demonstrates that the goods of the former are not true goods, that they were not granted to them as rewards for merit, and that possession of them brings no happiness either in the present or, still less, in the future, when the righteous will finally reign.

He establishes this truth by adducing words of Job from other chapters of the same book. Here, however, he does not describe such long periods as in the first book of this commentary. Instead, selecting the words that seem most applicable to the subject, he illustrates them with a brief exposition.

In the fourth book he establishes the same point through an elegant exposition of Psalm 72, in which David discusses the same subject very beautifully.

From the ethical precepts that Ambrose occasionally mingles into this treatise, you can readily understand that it consists of sermons composed for the instruction of the faithful. That these sermons were delivered by him on different days is shown by the opening of both the second book and, especially, the third.

As for the time when the work was written, it seems more difficult to offer anything certain. Nevertheless, it may reasonably be conjectured that it should be assigned to a date before the year 387, when the people of Antioch overthrew the statues of Flaccilla, the wife of Theodosius the Great, during a popular uprising.

When the holy Doctor speaks of the images of rulers, he says: “You see how, in cities, the images of good rulers endure, while the images of tyrants are destroyed” (book 4, chapter 8, section 24). Who would think that, after that event, a Bishop of such great prudence—and one for whom Theodosius was held in the highest esteem—would have wished to use words of this kind, which would have reopened the grievous wound of so great an emperor, and that not without insult?

Moreover, what is mentioned here concerning the psalm singers seems to provide grounds for conjecturing that Ambrose delivered these sermons before the year 385 or 386, when he instituted congregational singing in the Church (book 2, chapter 6, section 24).

Nothing, therefore, prevents us from saying that this commentary was composed around the year 383, and that our saint mentioned the statues with reference to the images of the emperor Gratian. After his death, the people—among whom that young ruler had left so justly cherished a memory—preserved them.

## THE FOUR BOOKS OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON THE INTERPELLATION OF JOB AND DAVID

[Note: Possibly written around the year 383.] (C)

## BOOK ONE: ON THE INTERPELLATION OF JOB AND ON HUMAN WEAKNESS

### CHAPTER ONE

There are many disturbances in this life and many consolations, but the latter far outweigh the former; this is proved by the examples of the saints. David and Job complained on account of our weaknesses, and hence the subject of this work.

1. Divine Scripture frequently demonstrates in many passages that we must endure many disturbances in this life, and that many consolations are available. The mind, possessing strength and conscious of what is right, ought to absorb from them whatever belongs to present troubles and look toward those things that possess everlasting joy. For consolations outweigh disturbances, since they bring relief from present troubles as well as hope for the future.

Hence the Apostle Paul also says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that is to come” (Rom. 8:18)—not worthy, certainly, when compared with consolation, though not unworthy when considered in relation to the fruit of redemption.

2. For what life on earth could be so outstanding that it could equal heavenly glory? What was more sublime than Paul, who endured so many dangers and absorbed so many sufferings and weaknesses? In the sufferings he endured daily for the name of Christ, as he himself says (1 Cor. 15:31), he was dying; yet he considered no suffering unworthy of enduring in this present time for the hope and expectation of such glory.

Elijah endured hunger, ambushes, the terrors of death, and the bitterness of labors. Yet he alone, carried from heaven to earth in fiery chariots and by fiery horses, and from earth borne back to heaven [Note: This is how the Erasmian edition reads, together with the Thuanian, Laudian, Tornesian, and Victorious manuscripts. Other editions and manuscripts read: “brought down to earth ... carried back or led back to heaven.” We think our reading is preferable, and that Ambrose was referring to Elijah’s return when he appeared in the Lord’s Transfiguration.], concealed all the merit of this service and raised the grace of his pious ascent beyond all human things.

What shall I say of Peter, who, judging even his cross unworthy of the future reward, asked to be hung with his feet upward, so that he might add something to his passion, whose harsh punishments he did not fear to impose upon himself? [Note: Jerome mentions this story in his *Catalogue*, and Hegesippus, from whom Ambrose seems to have borrowed it. We shall discuss the matter elsewhere.]

3. Therefore holy David not undeservedly testifies that he is hastening toward that glory, both throughout his other work and especially in Psalm 41, saying: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3).

In this psalm he clearly expresses both the disturbances of human frailty and the consolations that come from the Lord. In it he also addresses a complaint to God on our behalf: that God, as though he had forgotten his own work and the generosity and grace bestowed upon humanity—humanity whom he had undertaken to protect and adorn—had abandoned it and cast it away, weak and shipwrecked, to be worn down by various infirmities.

The holy Job had done the same before him, but David did so in a more morally instructive manner, while Job did so more vehemently. It is therefore our concern to consider the interpellations of both, since in them the form of human life is expressed, the case is argued, and a model is established. They must therefore be examined in their proper order.

### CHAPTER II

How blessed Job, having lost everything except his wife, did not yield to his disturbances like a good athlete, nor refuse to contend.

4. After Job had lost his children and all his possessions except his wife, who alone had been reserved for his temptation, and after he had also been covered with a severe ulcer [Note: Two editions and two manuscripts read “pierced as well”; others read “covered as well.”], when he saw that his friends had come not to console him but to intensify and aggravate his grief, he recognized that the Lord had given the adversary power to test him.

Although he felt the Lord’s arrows in his body, by which he said he was being pierced, nevertheless, like a good athlete who would not yield to pain and would not refuse the severity of the contest, he added: “Let the Lord begin by wounding me, but at the end let him not destroy me ... For what is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my allotted time, that my soul should bear it? Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh made of bronze? Or did I not trust in him himself? But help has withdrawn from me, and his visitation has disregarded me” (Job 6:9 ff.).

5. Is not the life of man upon earth a period of trial, and his life like that of a day-laborer; or like that of a servant who fears his master and shelters himself under a shadow, or like that of a laborer awaiting his wages? So I too have waited for empty months, and nights of suffering have been assigned to me. If I lie down, I say, “When will it be day?” If I rise again, “When will it be evening?” I am full of pains from evening until morning. My body ferments in the corruption of worms; I melt the clods of earth, scraping away the matter of my ulcers. But my life is lighter than a tale, and perishes in empty hope . . . . . . I will say, “He will comfort me,” my bed . . . . . . You terrify me in dreams, and strike me with visions (Job 7:1 ff.).

[Note: The Roman edition, together with the Codex Thuaneus and the Codex Laudensis, reads *levior est fabula* (“lighter than a tale”). The Septuagint has ἐλαφρότερος λαλιᾶς, “lighter than a speech.” This reading is also confirmed by what follows concerning a tale and the narration of a fool, for those passages undoubtedly refer back to this one. Nevertheless, the other editions and manuscripts consistently read *levior est favilla* (“lighter than ash”). Some Paris editions, after the words “my bed,” add: “but I will refer to myself a private speech upon my couch.” These words are omitted in the other editions and in all the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER III

On the wretched condition of man, who is daily under fear; how foolishly he thinks that he can deceive God’s knowledge concerning his sins; likewise, how wretched it is to be disturbed by anxiety in the bed given us for rest, and to rise from it empty and naked—an image of this life.

6. How wretched is the condition of man, who labors as a hired servant for others, is himself in need, and cannot sustain himself unless by another’s mercy! Every day he endures a heavy slavery under dread and fear, and, lest he be discovered by his Lord, he thinks that, as a wanderer and fugitive, he can hide beneath some shadow of this world. Consider the man of whom Syrach says in Ecclesiasticus: “Every man who transgresses in his bed, despising and saying in his soul, ‘Who sees me? Darkness surrounds me and the walls; whom should I fear?’” (Ecclesiasticus 23:25–26).

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “that this man is truly a hired servant who has squandered his own goods.”]

Does this man not truly seem to you a hired servant who has squandered his possessions, like that young man in the Gospel (Luke 15:13 ff.), who is said to have received from his father his share of the inheritance and, needy and destitute, began to pasture another’s flocks in order to earn wages with which to support himself? Yet that man was eventually converted, for he returned to his father and did not suppress his sins but confessed them. But this man, who thinks that he is not seen by the One who sees all things, and believes that what he has done can be concealed by darkness, holds out a shadow; but he believes in vain that he can remain hidden, since the eye of the Lord, brighter than the sun, detects all hidden things, illuminates what is dark, penetrates the conscience of the inmost heart, and descends into what is high and deep. Foolish, then, is the man who thinks himself safe in darkness, when he cannot avoid the light that shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. Thus, like a fugitive and wicked hired servant, he is discovered; and before he can conceal himself, he is recognized, because everything is known to the Lord before He seeks it—not only what has been done, but also what is to be done.

[Note: Thus all the manuscripts and the old edition. The Roman edition reads: “Everything that existed beforehand was known.”]

7. He therefore perishes in empty hope who thinks that he can conceal his crime: that is a tale, not the truth. Indeed, it is the idle tale of sinners, bearing no fruit but groaning. For “the narration of a fool is a burden on the road.” What else is sin but a burden that weighs down the traveler of this world, already bowed beneath the heavy load of guilt? If he did not wish to remain subject to the burden, he ought to have heard Him who says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28).

8. What could be more miserable, when the very bed given for common rest inflicts a grievous wound? For then we customarily recall what we have done, and the inner conscience is pierced by the goads of its deeds. Hence Scripture says: “Be pierced upon your beds by what you say in your hearts” (Psalm 4:5). He gave a remedy, yet at the same time wounded the conscience. But even if sleep at times steals upon the weary, we are terrified by nightmares and harassed by visions, so that rest becomes not rest but punishment. Thus the riches of this world pass away, like the dream of one who is rising. Someone has risen from the sleep of this body and possesses nothing; and what he believed he had, that too he has lost.

9. Imagine for me now that rich man who accumulated daily profits and varied gains and was harassed by his desires, suddenly coming to his senses and considering that, when he dies, he will not take everything with him, nor will the glory of his house descend with him; and that the things he possesses have some pleasure in this life, but not in the life to come.

[Note: The American edition, together with the manuscripts of Victor and Tornacensis, reads: “and that the things he possesses in this life have some pleasure, but they do not open their eyes to the future,” and so forth. The other editions and manuscripts generally agree among themselves, except in punctuation and a few words that produce no substantially different meaning.]

Opening his eyes to heavenly things, does he not seem to you like one who drank in a dream and believes he has drunk; like one who feasted in a dream and believes he has feasted; but then opened his eyes and discovered that his soul had hoped for emptiness and still hungers and thirsts? For avarice has no limit and is not satisfied by seizing; rather, the more it acquires, the more needy it becomes, driven on by what it has gained. This man too has risen, and the dream is empty.

## CHAPTER IV

How Job’s friends, coming to console him, intensified his suffering; and how magnificently he understood the divine power and indicated the mysteries of redemption.

10. But let us again hear him saying: “In truth I know that it is so; for how will a mortal be righteous?” and so forth (Job 9:1–2). His friends who had come to console him pressed upon him, as though enemies, with bitter words. For those who are placed in hardship and bitterness have one kind of consolation: to be free from guilt, so that they may not seem to endure the adversities they suffer as the price of their sin. They were eager to deprive this holy man even of that consolation, so that he might appear to be the author of his own misery, having incurred the Lord’s displeasure through grave sins and enduring those things on account of his impieties. They described the punishments of the wicked, so that those who sowed vices and reaped sorrows for themselves might perish by the command of God (Job 4:8–9), and that they might perish by the spirit of His life, by which He breathes upon those who inhabit houses of clay (ibid., 19 ff.); that He might wither them, frustrate the thoughts of the crafty, and close the mouth of the unjust (Job 5:13, 16). These statements about the Lord’s power were indeed true, but they were not appropriate to the merits of so great a man.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “and perish by the spirit of His anger.” The Septuagint supports this with the words ἀπὸ δὲ πνεύματος ὀργῆς αὐτοῦ ἀφανισθήσονται, “but by the spirit of His anger they shall be destroyed.” Nor does the Vulgate contradict it. Nevertheless, we change nothing in the reading found in all the manuscripts and the old editions. Below, where all the editions together with the more recent manuscripts read “Then he answered,” manuscripts of better quality read “To these,” and so forth.]

11. To them, therefore, he replied: “In truth I know that it is so: how can a mortal be righteous before the Lord? For if he wishes to contend with Him in judgment, He will not heed him, so that he cannot answer one of His words with a thousand arguments. For He is wise in understanding, strong and great. Who is so hard that he can stand in His sight? He makes mountains grow old, and they do not know it, and in His anger He overturns them. He shakes the earth from its foundations, and its pillars tremble. He says to the sun, and it does not rise; but against the stars He sets a seal. He alone stretches out the heavens and walks as upon a pavement over the sea. He makes the Pleiades, Hesperus, the North, and the ministry of the South. He does great and unsearchable things, glorious and immeasurable, whose number there is not. If He passes by me, I shall not see Him; and if He goes beyond me, even then I shall not know it” (ibid., 9:3 ff.).

With how much more forceful a trumpet did this man proclaim the Lord’s power! Yet in that power there is help for the righteous, not destruction. Accordingly, power seems to be expressed, but the mysteries of our redemption are revealed more fully.

## CHAPTER V

That God made the mountains grow old—that is, converted the letter of the Old Testament into a spiritual meaning; that the Jews, because they did not know this, are not excusable in view of the prodigies that accompanied Christ’s death, and especially in view of the described eclipse of the sun. Certain other works of Christ are touched upon, particularly His walking upon the sea; together with Peter’s stumbling and the shattering of the ships of Tarshish, by which our bodies are signified.

12. For who are the mountains that He makes grow old, except Moses, Aaron, Elijah, Joshua son of Nun, Gideon, the prophets, and all the books of the Old Testament? The Lord Jesus came and brought the New Testament; what had been old became new. The Christian was renewed; the Jew grew old. Grace was renewed; the letter grew old. He overturned and transformed the mountains. For He overturned and demolished the understanding according to the letter and established spiritual understanding. Thus that carnal understanding of the Law vanished and became spiritual. Hence the Apostle says: “We know that the Law is spiritual, but I am carnal” (Romans 7:14). Yet he himself, who was carnal, became spiritual, as he asserted when he said: “For I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 7:40).

Jesus therefore made these mountains old, and the Jews do not know it. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty; they would not still be following Jewish delusions. They are the ones who do not know. Hence the Lord Jesus also says in the Gospel: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

13. But they are not excused because they do not know, since they do not wish to know what they ought to have recognized. Certainly we do not envy them, if they follow the Lord’s judgment. For a judgment is accustomed to absolve what came before, not what is to come. Nor is he free from guilt who crucified the author of his salvation and afterward did not ask for pardon. Granted that previously he did not know whom he was persecuting; nevertheless, when He was upon the cross, he ought to have recognized that He was Lord of all the elements, beneath whom all the elements trembled: the heavens were darkened, the sun withdrew, the earth split open, the tombs of the dead were opened, and the dead entered into the company of the living. Hence the centurion said: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matthew 27:54). The centurion recognizes what is foreign to him; the Levite does not recognize what is his own. The Gentile reveres; the Hebrew denies. Not without reason, therefore, were the pillars of the world shaken when the chief priests did not believe. But the old pillars were shaken so that the new might be confirmed, as He Himself deigned to say: “I have established its pillars” (Psalm 74:4).

Hear which pillars He established: “Peter, James, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship” (Galatians 2:9).

14. How, then, do they excuse themselves by saying that they did not know, when some of them saw and others recognized that the sun had withdrawn before completing the course of the day, and then had emerged again before the appointed duration of the night was finished, making night into day and day into night? Surely they ought to have understood that the sun withdrew at a command and went forth at a command. For the Lord had foretold (Matthew 12:40) that He would be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights. The sun had learned this and was keeping the command.

It hesitated, therefore, saying: “What shall I do? I rise, and it is day; I set, and it is night. If I keep my course, I shall delay the world’s salvation. Let us hasten also toward our redemption. I too must hasten toward the new life, for through the benefit of the cross by which all things are renewed there will be a new sun and a new heaven. I hasten, therefore, so that I may see that Sun of righteousness who illuminates the souls of all. But what shall I do? He Himself wishes the resurrection to take place after three days. I have found what I should do, so that I may neither delay nor fail to preserve the number of days. I shall not make a complete day and a complete night. I shall shorten the hours, so that the Lord Jesus may indeed be among the dead for three days and nights, yet rise from the dead more quickly than the intervals of three days and nights ordinarily allow.

“I shall therefore shorten the hours when He ascends the cross. From the sixth hour let night immediately begin, so that I may not see the Lord’s passion but flee the spectacle of murderous persecution. I shall set, and there will be three hours of night; I shall rise, and I shall renew the day, so that it will last three hours. The first day has run its course; the second night will follow for its appointed span, and the day will likewise follow. The third night will begin; the Lord will rise during the night, and it will become day in the light of the One who rises, so that this may be fulfilled: ‘And night shall be illuminated like day’ (Psalm 139:12).

“This is that great day which Abraham saw and rejoiced in; concerning it David also says: ‘This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it’ (Psalm 118:24). I shall participate in it, not through the labor of service, but through the fruit of rejoicing.”

15. The Lord Himself therefore leads the day, and before the consummation of the world the light that illuminates every human being coming into this world will be seen. He is the Lord who marks and numbers the multitude of the stars; He is the Lord who alone stretches out the heavens and who walked as upon a pavement over the sea, when Peter saw Him walking and said: “Lord, command me to come to You upon the waters” (Matthew 14:28).

The Lord commanded him, but he stumbled; and unless the Lord had stretched out His right hand to him, he would have been overwhelmed by the waves and perished. The flesh stumbled; the right hand saved him. And He said to him: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (ibid., 31).

[Note: Four manuscripts of better quality read: “Why did you stumble?”]

Faith, then, walked in the Apostle, not the flesh. Indeed, faith stumbled, and the flesh began to experience shipwreck. This is not improperly said, because the flesh is the soul’s ship, as it is written: “Those who go down to the sea in ships” (Psalm 107:23). And elsewhere: “There are pains like those of a woman in labor; in a mighty spirit You will shatter the ships of Tarshish” (Psalm 48:8).

For when our souls give birth to the Word, they experience pains; but when one has given birth, she no longer remembers her sorrow because of the joy, since the man who redeemed the world has been born to her. The ships of Tarshish—that is, intelligible ships that carried gold and silver to Solomon—signify our bodies, which possess a treasure in earthen vessels, as the Apostle says (2 Corinthians 4:7). Or else they are also shattered in this birth, in accordance with what was said: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse infants!” (Luke 21:23).

For when the soul is shaken, the flesh is tossed about; or they will be driven by a mighty spirit poured into them when the appointed time comes for the resurrection, according to what is written: “Come, spirit, and breathe upon these dead, and they shall live” (Ezekiel 37:9). Hence Job himself later says: “For I know that He is eternal and powerful, who will release me from the earth, and raise up my skin that has borne these things” (Job 19:25–26).

Those who are raised for judgment, however, are shattered. Yet there is also a good shattering: “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm 51:19). And elsewhere: “Heal its fractures” (Psalm 60:4). It was also said to Jehoshaphat: “The ships bound for Tarshish were shattered” (2 Chronicles 20:37), because he had joined himself to a sacrilegious man.

[Note: All the editions and the manuscripts of Victor read *sacrilegio* (“by sacrilege”); other manuscripts more correctly read *sacrilego* (“with the sacrilegious one”), that is, with Ochozias, king of Israel, with whom Jehoshaphat entered into friendship.]

Thus shattering signifies both things, because both occur on the day of judgment: “All who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and they who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but they who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29). The prophet David also signifies this when he says: “There are pains like those of a woman in labor; as we have heard, so we have seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God” (Psalm 48:8–9). For he comprehends both the future sorrow and the future joy: sorrow because of judgment, and joy because of acquittal.

## CHAPTER VI

Job’s words, in which he discloses human weaknesses, are examined. It is shown how the holy man did not deny his sin; what distinction there is between sinning and acting impiously; by what words he attempts to excuse man before God; and finally, that pardon is promised to the one who confesses and that the righteous acknowledge their iniquities.

16. But let us return to the sequence of the appeal set before us. “He has made many fractures in me,” he says; “He does not permit me to breathe; He has filled me with bitterness. And because He is powerful in strength, no one can resist His judgment. If I am righteous in heart, my tongue errs . . . . He destroys the mighty and powerful in anger. The wicked are in grievous death; but the righteous are mocked. For they have been given into the hands of the wicked” (Job 9:17 ff.).

Consider each statement. To the powerful their own anger is grievous; to the wicked, their wickedness; to the righteous, the weakness of their condition. Thus nothing is free from danger. Strength and greatness are deceived by their own power; wickedness is afflicted; virtue is mocked. The one falls because he has greater power; the other is afflicted because he has none. The defect belongs to our condition, because our life is lighter than a runner. It passed by and saw nothing. Like the trace of a ship, or of an eagle flying and seeking prey (ibid., 25–26), so human life passes away. What we say, we forget, and no mark of our passing is discovered, except that it is full of mourning and groaning.

“I am shaken,” he says, “in all my limbs. Would that our mediator might be present, judging and distinguishing between the two of us” (Job 9:28, 33).

17. “I will say to the Lord: Why do You judge me thus? Is it good for You that I should be unjust, since You have rejected the works of Your hands and have attended to the counsel of the wicked? Do You see as a mortal sees, or is Your life like a man’s, or Your years like those of a human being, since You have searched out my iniquities and investigated my sins? For You know that I have not acted impiously; but who can be rescued from Your hands?” (Job 10:2 ff.).

Great is his faith, great the authority of his conscience, in calling God as witness to his mind. What belongs to his condition he does not deny; what belongs to impiety he rejects; what belongs to weakness he confesses. To have sinned belongs to our condition, because no one is free from falling. To act impiously, however, does not belong to our condition but to faithlessness and the poison of a most wicked mind.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “The righteous acknowledges his falls.” Against this stand the reading and authority of all the other editions and manuscripts. The meaning is that the righteous person acknowledges that he sins, but does not acknowledge that he acts impiously.]

The righteous man does not acknowledge this. Yet a human being’s acquittal rests in God’s mercy, not in human power.

18. “Your hands,” he says, “fashioned me; afterward You turned and struck me. Remember that You made me as clay, and You will return me to the earth. Did You not milk me like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh; You inserted me into bones and sinews. You placed life and mercy within me, and Your visitation protected my spirit” (ibid., 8 ff.).

What lamentation by the holy man for the common weakness of humanity! What force in his appeal, that God made man with His own hands! Guilt is excused on the grounds of weakness; grace is commended through the privilege of the eternal work and through the dignity of heavenly protection.

[Note: All the editions read: “and through the protection of His dignity”; all the manuscripts read: “and through the dignity of His protection.”]

David also spoke most beautifully from this passage, saying: “What is man, that You remember him, or the son of man, unless because You visit him?” (Psalm 8:5).

[Note: Thus five manuscripts of greater antiquity. The other manuscripts and all the editions read: “or the son of man, that You visit him.”]

19. “You have these things within You,” he says; “I know that You can do all things, and nothing is impossible for You. If I sin, You will guard me; but You have not made me undefiled from iniquity. If I am impious, woe to me! If I am righteous, I cannot lift myself up. For I am full of confusion; I am hunted like a lion for slaughter” (Job 10:13 ff.).

Consider three statements. “If I sin,” he says, “You will guard me.” Therefore, O man, confess your sin, so that you may obtain pardon: “Declare your iniquities,” He says, “so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:26). Why are you ashamed to confess the sins in which you were born? To deny that you were born is the crime of one who denies, not confesses. May you preserve what you have received. Why do you think you possess what you have not received? Let the sinner, therefore, confess; let the impious groan; let the righteous not raise or exalt himself, lest through arrogance he lose the fruit of righteousness.

20. Beautifully he says: “If I am righteous, I cannot lift myself up; for I am full of confusion.” The righteous person recognizes his weakness more than the unjust person does, and the wise person acknowledges it, while the foolish person does not. Indeed, the wise person is pierced by his falls; the foolish person delights in them. The righteous is his own accuser; the unjust is his own defender. The righteous wishes to forestall his accuser by confessing his sin; the unjust desires to conceal his sin. The former meets the accusation at the beginning of his speech, so as to disclose his error; the latter, through the many words of his speech, wraps up the sound of his accusation so that he will not disclose his error.

[Note: The old edition reads “the sleep of an excuse”; the Roman edition, “the sound of an excuse”; Gallican manuscripts, “the sleep of an accusation.” The Vatican manuscript reads most aptly, “the sound of an accusation.” The meaning is that, when he ought to accuse himself, he so envelops his accusation that it cannot be noticed.]

## CHAPTER VII

That adolescence is the most slippery of all the ages; that we shall be required to give an account even of those sins which we could not avoid; that our sufferings are not adequately expressed by the hardships of sea and land; that heaven and earth must be renewed, and that the resurrection will not take place before the coming of Him who will make all things new.

21. Adding again, he says: “Why have You charged evils against me and laid upon me the sins of my adolescence?” (Job 13:26).

He appropriately seized upon that period of life for his complaint which is accustomed to be more prone to vice. Childhood has innocence; old age, prudence; youth itself, near to adolescence, has regard for a good reputation and shame at wrongdoing. Adolescence alone is weak in strength, feeble in judgment, inflamed by vice, disdainful of advisers, and enticed by pleasures. In such a great, rugged, and storm-tossed whirlpool of this world, then, why are so many shipwrecks charged to an imprudent age? Hence David nobly asked the Lord’s pardon for all that period of life when he said: “Do not remember, Lord, the sin of my youth and my ignorance” (Psalm 25:7), because at that time the heat of the body burns most fiercely, and the vapor of seething blood catches fire.

22. But let us hear him again: “Mortal, born of woman, is short-lived and full of anger. He flourishes like a flower and falls; he departs like a shadow and does not endure. Is an account not also required from him? And You have made him enter into judgment under Your gaze. Who is clean from defilement? No one, even if his life upon earth is only one day” (Job 14:1 ff.).

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “He is compelled to give an account of the sin he cannot avoid, to come into the presence of the Lord, and to undergo the judgment of the Almighty.” This is a good arrangement of the words, but the ancient editions and manuscript codices do not agree with it. We have therefore restored another reading.]

Truly wretched is the condition of man: he is compelled to enter judgment, to come into the presence of the Lord Almighty, and to state the reasons for his deeds through all the many stages of his life that he has passed through, although no one can be free from sin, so that the fault of infancy may creep in from the very cradle before there is any awareness of error. And how miserable it is that his life is short, its enticement sweet, its suffering manifold, and its anger daily! Thus in a brief pleasure there is perpetual bitterness.

23. “There is hope for a tree,” he says. “For if it is cut down, it grows green again; and if its branch has died upon the rock, it will blossom at the smell of water; and it will produce a harvest like a young plant. But a man who has died has departed; and when a mortal has fallen, he is no more. Yet in time the sea fluctuates” (Job 24).

[Note: Thus the manuscripts and the old edition read, except that for *in petra* (“upon the rock”) two manuscripts and one edition have *in terra* (“upon the earth”), together with a few other insignificant variations. The Roman edition has instead: “Though cut down, it still grows green, and its branch will not fail; even if its root has died in the earth, its trunk will still bud at the smell of water,” and so forth.]

We have observed the sequence of the prophetic speech concerning the two lower elements, earth and sea, which are subject to every injury and to frequent storms. What a powerful argument it expresses for our misery! “Earthly shrubs,” he says, “and wooded trees, even when they have died, rise again for the uses of life. The sea itself also is accustomed to fluctuate with the changes of time. But our flesh is always in turmoil, and is itself a storm; nor is it ever struck by the movements of tempests and pitiable shipwrecks.”

24. “When a man has fallen asleep, he does not rise until the heavens are not sewn together” (ibid., 12).

[Note: All the editions read: “He will not rise until the heavens are sewn together . . . . . . is moved.” The American edition has *novetur* (“is renewed”). Six manuscripts read as we have in the text; the following makes it clear that this is the genuine reading.]

This seems to declare that he will not rise until heaven is renewed. For there will be a new heaven and a new earth, as it is written (Isaiah 65:17). What is sewn together is old; what is old will be changed. Hear David finally saying: “In the beginning You founded the earth, O Lord, and the heavens are the works of Your hands. They will perish, but You remain, and all things will grow old like a garment; and like a covering You will change them, and they will be changed” (Psalm 102:26–27).

We may also add this: what is old is sewn together; what is new is forced. “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it.” The Synagogue therefore sewed it together among the few, while the Church forces it among the thousands.

Or because heaven now seems to be sewn together from clouds and darkness, from the shadows of night, and from the golden-red brilliance of the rising day, often woven together in a varied and multicolored appearance. But then night will be no more, and they will not need the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, because the Lord will illuminate them, as John says (Revelation 21:23).

Or because of the words: “Woe to those who take cushions to overturn the souls of the people” (Ezekiel 13:18).

25. As the prophet lamented the misery of our frailty, which would find no rest even in this life and would lose everything through the sudden onset of death, the Holy Spirit infused the teaching that human beings would not rise until He came who would not sew old things onto new, nor attach a new garment to an old garment, but would make all things new, as He Himself said: “Behold, I will make new things.”

For He is the resurrection; He is the firstborn from the dead, in whom we have all received the privilege of the future resurrection. Yet He alone has already risen in perpetual resurrection.

## CHAPTER VIII

How blessed Job signified the resurrection and the anger of the Lord that will come at the consummation; and how he desired to escape from this life, in which faithlessness reigns.

26. Having heard what God had spoken in him, and having learned through the Holy Spirit that the Son of God would not only come upon the earth but would also descend to the underworld in order to raise the dead—a thing that was then accomplished as a testimony for the present and an example for the future—he turned to the Lord and said:

“Would that You would preserve me in the underworld, and hide me until Your anger ceases, and appoint for me a time in which You will remember me. For if a man dies, he will live when he has completed the days of his life. I will wait until I am again made; then You will call me, and I will obey You. But do not despise the works of Your hands. You have numbered my inventions, and nothing of my sins will escape You. You have sealed my iniquities in a sack and marked whether I have unknowingly passed over anything” (Job 14:13 ff.).

[Note: The Gill and Roman editions read: “which was then done as a testimony to what preceded.”]

How sweet is this passage, which confirms us concerning the resurrection! And how plainly it seems to correspond to the Lord’s voice recorded in the Gospel, where He says: “Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us’” (Luke 23:30). For there will be the Lord’s anger at the consummation of the world. Rightly, therefore, the holy man prefers to rise for judgment rather than for the time of the divine anger, which is terrifying even to the innocent.

27. He is also understood to prophesy the following when he says: “Appoint for me a time in which You will remember me,” namely, that he would be raised in the Lord’s passion, as is demonstrated at the end of this book. Yet he does not cease lamenting; and the more he understands that resurrection is set before him, the more he desires to flee this life, seeing that he has been handed over to the power of adversaries, cast into the power of the wicked, and that even his friends have been changed into enemies. Although they ought to console him, they bring ruin upon ruin.

Still mindful of his pure conscience and clean prayer, he says: “Let not the earth cover the blood of my flesh” (Job 16:19), so that his prayer may be directed like incense to the Lord and not wander upon the earth.

[Note: The old edition, together with several manuscripts, reads: “Let not the earth cover my flesh in blood”; the Roman edition, together with others, reads: “Let not the earth cover the blood of my flesh,” according to the Vatican manuscript and the Septuagint, which has ἐφ’ αἵματι τῆς σαρκός μου, “upon the blood of my flesh.”]

For the prayer of a holy person penetrates the clouds; but the earth, as God said to Cain the murderer, opening its mouth, conceals the sinner’s prayer in the blood of his flesh. “Cursed,” He says, “are you by the earth, which opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand; because you will work the earth” (Genesis 4:11).

## CHAPTER IX

Those who dare to search too inquisitively into the recesses of wisdom are rebuked. Wisdom is not to be sought in the abyss or in the sea, and for what reason; finally, its knowledge is accessible only to God and to those to whom He has revealed it.

28. Thus the holy man sorrowfully laments the times of this life: “I perish,” he says, “and am carried about in spirit. I ask for burial and do not obtain it; I plead while suffering. And what shall I do?” (Job 17:1–2).

[Note: The old edition and all the manuscripts, except the Codex Colbertinus, read: “My days have passed in honor.” The Colbertinus alone reads: “They have passed dishonorably.” But the Roman edition more correctly reads: “They have passed in horror.” For, apart from the fact that the doubled *r* could easily have coalesced into *n*, the Septuagint has Αἱ ἡμέραι μου παρῆλθον ἐν βρόμῳ, “My days have passed in tumult,” which is close in meaning.]

“My days have passed in horror; the joints of my heart have been torn apart” (ibid., 11). Yet nowhere does he detract from God’s judgment. For he knows that the depth of God’s wisdom and knowledge is profound, that His judgments are inscrutable and His ways unsearchable.

29. “The sons of those who glorify themselves have not trodden them,” he says, “nor has the lion passed along them” (Job 28:8). For who could comprehend His ways, which have penetrated hidden things concealed away? “From where,” he says, “is wisdom found, or what is the place of understanding? Mortal man does not know its way, nor is it found among human beings. The abyss said, ‘It is not in me’; and the sea said, ‘It is not with me’” (ibid., 12 ff.).

It is not permitted you, O man, to know the heights of wisdom. Therefore it is written for you: “Do not be wise in high things, but fear” (Romans 11:20). Why do you desire inquisitively to investigate what it is not useful for you to know and what you have not been granted to understand? Paul heard certain secrets of wisdom that he was forbidden to reveal to others; for this reason he was caught up into paradise, caught up to the third heaven, to hear things that, while placed on earth, he could not hear (2 Corinthians 12:3–4). If it was not permitted a man to speak what he heard, how does he investigate what he did not hear?

You are not permitted to know the counsels of this emperor on earth, and yet you wish to know divine counsels. You are not permitted to investigate too inquisitively what is being done on earth, and yet you inquire too inquisitively into what is happening above heaven. Why do you debate where Wisdom was born? Man does not know its way, nor is perfect Wisdom found among human beings. It was not in Moses, not in Aaron, not in Joshua son of Nun, nor even in David himself, who said: “You have manifested to me the uncertain and hidden things of Your wisdom” (Psalm 51:8), because later he said: “I became like a beast before You” (Psalm 73:22).

It is beyond you, O man, to know the height of Wisdom; it is enough for you to believe. For “if you do not believe,” he says, “neither will you understand” (Isaiah 7:9). You cannot know the abyss; you cannot comprehend the abyss. How, then, will you comprehend the height of Wisdom? The abyss said: “It is not in me”; and can you say that Wisdom is in you?

30. Therefore the abyss said: “It is not in me,” because the Lord himself said: “You will not abandon my soul in the underworld” (Ps. XV, 10). And the Apostle said: “Who descended into the abyss?”—that is, “to bring Christ up from the dead” (Rom. X, 7). Therefore, if the abyss is asked, “Where is Wisdom?” it answers: “It is not in me,” because she has risen again.

The sea is asked, “Where is Wisdom?” It says: “She is not with me,” because she trampled upon me, and my waves could not disturb her. You too, then, placed in the strait of this world, do not seek that perfect Wisdom of God in this world, because the world did not know her. But if you wish to find her, tread upon the waves of this world, as Peter trod upon them, and walk upon the waters of this age; and Wisdom will extend her right hand to you, as she extended it also to Peter. For no one has existed whom the wave of this world has not disturbed. It disturbed Abraham; it disturbed Moses also; it disturbed Peter. Moses passed through the sea and led an army on foot through the sea, but before that he too had been troubled. Peter trod upon the waters, but he had been submerged bodily because, with the step of weaker faith, he stumbled.

Therefore, do not seek Wisdom in the sea; for the Lord Jesus did not say that he would be with the sea, but with his apostles, so that they might know him in some measure. To them he said: “Behold, I am with you always, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20). Blessed are those with whom he is; would that he were with us also! But the sea is with us, whereas Peter is with Christ, because he too trod upon the sea.

For us, gold and silver are matters of the heart; but Wisdom is above gold, not in gold. Therefore, he who desired to possess Wisdom said: “I have neither silver nor gold; but what I have, I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk” (Acts III, 6). Because he did not have gold, he possessed, in the name of Christ, the grace of godly action.

Therefore it is said also to you: “And draw Wisdom into your inmost parts” (Job XXVIII, 18); and below it says: “She is hidden,” it says, “from every human being, and concealed from the birds of heaven” (ibid. 21). Neither did human beings know where she was, nor the angels, because they are the birds of heaven, of whom it is said: “And I saw an angel flying through the midst of heaven” (Rev. XIV, 6).

31. No one could know Wisdom, because “no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” He therefore revealed to John with whom Wisdom was; and for that reason John said—not what belonged to himself, but what Wisdom infused into him: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John I, 1).

Destruction does not know Wisdom; evil does not know her. For destruction could not hold her, since he said: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (I Cor. XV, 55). Evil does not know her, because she said: “The wicked will seek me and will not find me” (Prov. I, 28). They can say: “We have heard her glory.” God alone knows her, because it says: “God established her way well; he himself knows her place” (Job XXVIII, 23).

What the receptacle of Wisdom is, hear her disciple say: “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him” (John I, 18). The Son knew the Father, for he himself said: “As the Father knows me, so I know the Father” (John X, 15). The measure of knowledge is equal where there is unity of power.

Therefore the Father, who made all things, knows the balance of the winds and the measure of the waters (Job XXVIII, 25). He himself saw Wisdom and declared her through his prophets, because the Father declared Wisdom and investigated her; just as the Son declared the Father, whom nothing escapes. And he said: “O human being, why do you wish to know the profound things of Wisdom, which are above you? To fear God is wisdom, and to abstain from evil is discipline” (ibid. 28).

[Note: The Roman edition alone adds to the word “Wisdom,” “when he prepared her.” At this same place it had cut the words “because the Father declared Wisdom and investigated her”; nevertheless, they occur in the older edition and in all the manuscripts, except that the Laudunensis reverses the words and sense thus: “because Wisdom declared the Father,” and so forth.]

## BOOK TWO: ON DAVID’S SUPPLICATION

[Col. 0811]

### CHAPTER ONE

After Job’s more vehement supplication, David’s gentler supplication follows. He is not inappropriately compared with a stag, since Christ himself did not refuse to be represented by the same animal. This likeness applies to him especially because he assumed suffering, called the Church, defeated the devil, and sent the apostles, who themselves also were stags.

[Col. 0811B]

1. Many indeed have lamented the weakness of human frailty with greater distinction; nevertheless, among the others are the holy Job and the holy David. The former is lofty, upright, vehement, sharp, and, as though provoked by severe pains, speaks in a grander style; the latter is gentle, peaceful, and meek, with a milder feeling, so that we might truly imitate the disposition of the stag whom he set before himself as an example. Nor should it trouble you if I seem to praise so great a prophet under the likeness of a wild animal, since you have read that it was said to the apostles: “Be shrewd as serpents and wise as doves” (Matt. X, 16).

2. Yet although such comparisons are supported by godly examples, and the nature of stags is innocent and gentle, I think that the stag proposed here for the Prophet’s imitation is the one of whom Solomon, the interpreter of his father’s mind, said in Proverbs: “Let the stag of friendship and the fawn of graces converse with you” (Prov. V, 19).

For the true Son of God expressed in himself the nature that he himself had bestowed upon animals, and came into this world like a stag. In complete simplicity he joined himself to those by whom ambushes were being prepared for him. For stags are said to possess this kind of simplicity: when they see themselves being pursued, they attach themselves to the riders who have been placed there through deceit, and who, under the appearance of flight and the pretence of companionship, lead them as far as the nets.

Thus the Lord, as though unaware of danger and unsuspecting, mingled with the Jews who were plotting deceit against him, and admitted Judas the betrayer into his company. Through Judas’s deadly pretence he approached even the nooses of the cross and the nets of his Passion. Hence he turned to him and said: “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke XXII, 48). In this way he came to the nets of the Synagogue, willingly submitting himself to them; but he was not entangled or caught, he who released everyone.

[Col. 0812B]

3. Finally, he stood out above the nets. And because his own people had not received him, he called the Church and bestowed his grace upon her, just as the holy Church herself proclaims in the Song of Songs, saying: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field: do not arouse or awaken love until it wishes” (Song II, 7).

Therefore, in the fragrance of the field that holy Jacob smelled—that is, in that faith and that devotion—she asks that her bridegroom be awakened by the daughters of Jerusalem, so that he may hasten to the bride, and that her love for him may be awakened, or even that he himself may be awakened, since the bridegroom is love. For “God is love,” as John said (I John IV, 16).

But he did not suffer himself to be awakened by others, since he was hastening of his own accord. Coming forth from the bridal chamber, he rejoiced like a giant to run his course. The bride saw him and heard the voice of the one who was coming; then, suddenly turning, she said: “Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills” (Song II, 8). He leaps over the greater mountains and bounds over the lesser hills, so that he may suffer no impediment to his godly haste.

“My kinsman,” she says, “is like a gazelle or a fawn of the stags upon the mountains of Bethel” (ibid. 9). He is the good stag whose mountain is the house of God, toward which he was running with such speed that he anticipated the bride’s vows and desires.

Finally, the bride who had seen him coming from afar suddenly recognized that he was present; hence she says: “Behold, he is behind our wall, looking through the windows, showing himself through the nets.” “My kinsman answered and said to me: Arise, come, my close companion, my beautiful one, my dove; for behold, winter has passed, the rain has gone away and departed; flowers have appeared on the earth” (ibid. 10–11).

Winter is the Synagogue; the rain is the Jewish people, who could not see the sun; the flowers are the apostles. And he added: “The season of pruning has come; the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (ibid. 12). That harvest is the faith of the Church; the voice of the turtledove is chastity.

[Note: All editions read “to awaken her bride.” Against them, all the manuscripts read “I awakened her bridegroom,” which agrees better with what precedes and follows.]

4. Nor does Christ assume only the likeness of these creatures; he also assumes the likeness of a stag, because when he came upon the earth he crushed that serpent, the devil, without suffering any injury from him. He offered him his heel but felt none of his poison. Hence it was said to him: “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk” (Ps. XC, 13).

Let us therefore also be stags, so that we may be able to walk upon serpents. We shall be stags if we follow the voice of Christ, which prepares stags and teaches them not to fear the bites of serpents. And if any should happen to be wounded, it removes their pain by releasing them from sin.

Of such stags the Lord says to Job: “Have you observed the births of the stags? Have you counted their months, the months of their full-term births? Have you released their offspring, or nourished their young, so that they do not fear?” (Job XXXIX, 1 ff.).

Hear how the young of such stags do not fear. Isaiah teaches you, saying: “And a little child will put his hand into the den of asps, and they will not harm him” (Isa. XI, 8). And so that you may recognize that he seems to signify the children of the Church, he added: “You will bring forth their offspring; their young will break forth and multiply in their generation; they will go out and not turn back” (Job XXXIX, 4–5). For no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks backward is fit for the kingdom of God.

5. Rightly, therefore, the Lord became a stag, so that the voice of the Lord might prepare such stags for himself, of whom he said: “In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will take up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them” (Mark XVI, 17–18).

They took up serpents when the holy apostles, by the spirit of their mouth, dragged spiritual wickedness from the hiding places of bodies, and they felt no deadly poisons. Finally, when a viper sprang from the brushwood and bit Paul, the barbarians, seeing the viper hanging from his hand, thought that he would suddenly die. But he stood fearless, neither troubled by the wound nor penetrated by the poison. Therefore, when they saw that he had not been born according to the condition of a human being but had been brought forth by the grace of God, they thought that he was above humanity.

See the stag drawing vipers from their hiding places by the divine Spirit that was in his nostrils, as Job said (Job XXVII, 3). “Paul,” it says, “turned in spirit and, looking at her with grief, said to the python: ‘I command you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to come out of her immediately.’ And it came out at that very hour” (Acts XVI, 18).

See the stag when he comes to baptism and, washed in the cleansing waters of the sacred font, rejects all the poisons of persecution. See the stag, the Lord Jesus, when he came to John the Baptist, and when John said to him: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” he answered: “Let it be so for now” (Matt. III, 14–15). Having said this, he descended into the waters, thirsting for the salvation of all, with complete eagerness.

But enough for us at the beginning of this treatise, as at the beginning of the year, when the stag made sport in the popular fashion. Let us proceed to the remaining matters.

[Note: We would gladly subscribe to the view of the very learned Cangius, who, in his Glossary under the word *Cervula*, thinks that Ambrose is here discussing the profane games that used to be held among the pagans on the Kalends of January, unless he seemed to speak somewhat too mildly about that superstition, which was later condemned with great zeal by the holy Fathers, both in synods and from the pulpits. Nevertheless, it may be said that this most watchful bishop did not attack it more vehemently either because the pagans’ endurance and obstinacy were then harder to overcome, or because the piety of Christians, being sufficiently alien to this impiety, was greater.]

### CHAPTER II

How David desired to be freed from this life, subject to countless calamities and sins, so that he might reach the presence of God; that the earth is a place of tears, and what benefit tears have; how the Prophet, raising his soul above the weaknesses of the flesh, poured out before God the prayer by which sins are covered, so that he might enter the heavenly court; and how, in a few words, the delights of that court are touched upon, with which the Church also is compared.

[Col. 0814A]

6. David, as I said, makes his supplication to the Lord, saying: “As the stag longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI, 2–3).

[Note: The Roman edition had removed the words “David, as I said, makes his supplication,” through the words “My soul thirsted for God,” and so forth.]

The saint is burning with desire and cannot contain himself. For the magnificence of the soul is greater than the magnitude of any body; and, confident in his merit, he desires to fly from earthly things to heavenly things, as he says elsewhere also: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? I shall fly away and rest” (Ps. LIV, 7).

Here are the snares by which the just person, even if not entangled, is nevertheless hindered; here are pains and anxieties, but there is joy where grace is. Finally, here are the bonds of the body, which Paul longed to have loosed, so that, stripped of every impediment, he might stand before the Lord in freedom.

This, then, was what David’s soul thirsted for: to see God no longer through faith but face to face; and not merely to be away from the body, but to be released from the body. For “to be dissolved and to be with Christ is much better,” because for the just person to die is gain.

And indeed it is great gain to be free from sin and not to be moved by the allurements of wrongdoing. For who is clean from defilement, when not even a single day of human life on earth is free from the contamination of sin? By living, therefore, we incur losses to innocence; by death we attain an end to error. Death therefore brings gain, while through the use of life, as though we were wretched debtors to a moneylender, the interest owed for our guilt is increased.

The soul that hastens to the fountain thirsts rightly—not for this water, but for the water of eternal life, concerning which he said above: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV, 10). David rightly hastened to reach and appear before the face of God, whose countenance is light, because all whom the Lord looks upon he illuminates.

7. “My tears were my bread day and night, while they say to me daily: ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. XLI, 4). There tears are rightly bread where righteousness is hungered for. For “blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.”

There are therefore tears that are bread and strengthen the heart of a human being. To this discussion the saying in Ecclesiastes also applies: “Cast your bread upon the face of the water” (Eccl. XI, 1), because heavenly bread is found where there is the water of grace; for those to whom streams of living water flow from the belly rightly receive the substance of the Word and the nourishment of mystical understanding.

Likewise, this living bread is found where there is the water of tears and the weeping of repentance. For it is written: “They went out in weeping, and I will bring them back in consolation” (Jer. XXXI, 9). Blessed, therefore, are those whose tears are bread, who have deserved to laugh; for blessed are those who weep.

8. “Remembering these things,” he says, “I poured out my soul over myself” (Ps. XLI, 5).

[Note: The edition reads, “The saint gathers himself.” The manuscripts read more appropriately, “The saint gathers,” namely, his soul, a word expressed in the following verse.]

The saint gathers himself away from the things that are outside, and pours out his soul above himself, so that the soul, poured out above the body, may conceal the weakness of the flesh, cover the weakness of the body for repentance, and display everywhere the strength of the soul and mind.

Hence he says later: “I will pour out my prayer before him” (Ps. CXLI, 2). Where prayer is poured out, there sins are covered.

Of whom, then, does he say that he is mindful? Certainly of those things that he desired: that he might come and appear in the presence of God, that he might see that eternal court of his, in which he walked in spirit and took delight in the anticipation of entering.

[Note: All editions read “that it may cover the body”; the manuscripts, however, read “that it may cover the weakness of the body,” with “weakness” understood.]

9. “For I shall enter,” he says, “into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God, amid a voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting” (Ps. XLI, 5).

[Note: So read the manuscripts and the old edition. The Roman edition, however, reads, “the sound of one celebrating a festal rite.” Who would not lift up his spirit if he could hope that those blessed associations would be reserved for him in the heavenly tabernacle? We have restored these words to their proper place.]

He did not weep without reason, since he was living on earth while heavenly tabernacles were owed to him, and the entrance into a mighty court awaited him. Finally, he preferred that court alone to all the riches of his kingdom, as he himself testified elsewhere, saying: “One thing I have asked from the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life and see the delight of the Lord” (Ps. XXVI, 4).

The delight of the Lord is in the Church. The Church is an image of heavenly things; for after the shadow had passed away, the image succeeded. The shadow is the Synagogue: in the shadow there was the Law, in the Gospel there is truth. Therefore, in the light of the Gospel of truth, the image shines forth.

The Prophet therefore wept because the blessings full of grace and filled with joy were being delayed.

### CHAPTER III

It is not surprising if David was troubled by the evils of this life, even if they are not entirely without consolation, since Christ himself, who willingly underwent death, desired to be troubled; and in what sense this is to be understood. Also, why did the Prophet say in one place, “I will confess,” rather than “I confess”?

10. Finally, he says later: “Alas for me, that my sojourn has been prolonged!” (Ps. CXVI, 5). And therefore he made supplication to the Lord, because he was hastening toward better things.

Yet amid the afflictions of the world the hope of future things would be a great consolation for present circumstances. Who would not lift up his spirit if he could hope that those blessed associations would be reserved for him in the heavenly tabernacle?

But because future things are often burdensome to our weak condition, while present things are vexing, the soul of the holy Prophet too was troubled as the waves of the body rose against it.

11. Do not be surprised that the Prophet says that his soul was agitated, since the Lord Jesus himself said: “Now my soul is troubled” (John XII, 27). For he who assumed our weaknesses also assumed our feeling; in it he was sorrowful even unto death—not because of death.
