For voluntary death could not possess sadness, since it was to be the source of joy for all and refreshment for all.

Concerning this he also said elsewhere: “And I arose, and I saw, and sleep became sweet to me” (Jer. XXXI, 26). It is a good sleep that caused the hungry not to hunger and the thirsty not to thirst, for whom he prepared the sweetness of the sacraments.

How, then, was his soul troubled by fear, when he caused the souls of others not to fear? He was sorrowful, therefore, unto death, until grace should be completed. This is proved by his own testimony concerning his death: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!” (Luke XII, 50).

12. David, therefore, troubled by the slippery twists and turns of this world, said: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall confess to him: the salvation of my countenance and my God” (Ps. XLI, 6–7).

Therefore, whenever we are anxious and troubled, let hope strengthen us through expectation of future things. Observe each word: “Hope, for I shall confess,” he says. He does not say, “I confess,” but “I shall confess”; that is, I shall confess more perfectly then, when, with unveiled face, I behold the glory of the Lord and am transformed into that same image.

13. Suddenly, as he was comforting himself, he came back to himself and said: “My soul is troubled within me” (Ps. XLI, 7)—that is, “I who ought to strengthen others am myself troubled.”

And because I do not possess firmness from myself, let us draw upon the Author.

### CHAPTER IV

Those who are troubled are rightly advised to leave Egypt, which is signified by the Jordan; through that river Christ is also foreshadowed, since he penetrates the thoughts of hearts and divides among the saints an earthly and a heavenly possession. Yet this applies to Christ without excluding the Father. What is signified there by Shechem? Also, how Christ was a great mountain according to his divinity and a small one according to his incarnation, which he chose to assume in order to bring the Gospel when the old Law was insufficient to redeem human beings.

14. “Therefore,” he says, “I shall remember you, O Lord, from the land of the Jordan and of Hermoniim” (ibid.).

He remembers from the land of the Jordan, in which grace accumulates the memory of devotion. Naaman the Syrian descended into the Jordan and was cleansed from leprosy. Christ was baptized in the Jordan when he instituted the form of the saving washing.

The name Jordan signifies descent, by which the Lord Jesus descended, because he cleansed the neighboring contagion of sins in the river Jordan. This river comes forth from Egypt and divides the land of promise.

Therefore, whoever is troubled, if he takes good counsel, leaves Egypt.

[Note: Two manuscripts read, if he takes good counsel.]

He leaves Egypt and follows the way of light. The Canaanite woman left the regions of the nations and found Christ, to whom she said: “Have mercy on me, Son of David!” (Matt. XV, 22). Moses also left Egypt, became a prophet, and was sent back to the people so that he might free their souls from the land of affliction.

The lamp, moreover, is in Christ’s body. This lamp shows you the way. Hence holy David says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet” (Ps. CXVIII, 105). It is a lamp because it illuminated the souls of all and showed the way in darkness.

The Gospel is the way of the lamp; it shines in the shadow, that is, in the world. Hence you have elsewhere also: “They will be whitened like snow on Salmon” (Ps. LXVII, 15), that is, in the shade.

15. The Jordan is also Christ, who divides the land. Hear how he divides it: “And your own soul a sword will pierce, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke II, 35). He is the divider of our souls because he descends into the innermost secrets of the heart and detects the thoughts of minds.

This sword is the living Word of God. Finally, you read in Hebrews: “The word of God is living and powerful, and sharper than every very sharp sword; it penetrates even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow” (Heb. IV, 12).

This is the fountain of Siloam, which is said to mean “sent,” because Christ said that he had been sent by the Father (John IX, 7).

There is also that division which is inferred from the fact that the tribes of the Jews inhabited both banks of the Jordan: the Son of Man, who in the latter times descended from heaven, the true Jordan, the true divider of earthly and heavenly things, gave the fathers a divided possession—one to be possessed on earth, the other reserved for the merits of the life to come.

Both of these belong to Christ alone: either to divide heavenly things or to detect hidden things. For he divides what is inward when he detects what is hidden, which is certainly a mark of divinity.

Finally, you have it written that the Lord said: “I shall rejoice and divide Shechem” (Ps. LIX, 8). This is that magnificent portion which Jacob assigned to his son Joseph as superior to all the others. Hence he says: “I give you Shechem, a magnificent portion above your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorites with my sword and my bow” (Gen. XLVIII, 22).

This division belongs to the Lord alone, and is comprehended by the Word—that is, by that spiritual and true sword of Solomon.

What does “alone” mean? The Father without Christ, or Christ without the Father? Certainly not. When I say “the Father alone,” I do not separate the Son, because the Son is in the bosom and secret counsel of the Father. When I say “the Son alone,” I join the Father to him, just as the Son himself joined them when he said: “Behold, the hour is coming when you will leave me alone; yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John XVI, 32).

Thus the Father is called alone blessed and alone powerful, so that the Son is not separated from him, since the Son is always in the Father (I Tim. VI, 13, 16). Finally, John says splendidly: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I, 1), but he was not without the Father. God the Father was, but he was not without the Word, because “the Word was with God.”

16. This Shechem is the Church. For Solomon chose her, whose hidden affection he distinguished. This Shechem is Mary, whose soul the sword of God pierces and divides. This Shechem is the ascending one, as the interpretation has it.

Hear what the ascending one is. What is she who “comes up whitened, leaning upon her beloved” (Song VIII, 5)? She is the radiant one, called in Greek *aktinōdēs* (ἀκτινώδης), because she shines through faith and works.

[Note: So read the manuscripts of Thuaneus, Dionysianus, Tornacensis, and Victorinus. Others, as well as the editions, read “whose son says.” This is less suitable, as the context of the discourse shows. Moreover, throughout this treatise we have removed the verses of Psalm XLI that the Roman edition had inserted in order to make the commentary continuous.]

To her children he says: “Let your works shine before my Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

17. David therefore remembers God from the land of the Jordan and Hermoniim, from the small mountain.

What is this small mountain? Let us consider whether perhaps Christ’s divinity is the great mountain. Finally, the Lord says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII, 24).

Therefore, if Christ’s divinity is the great mountain, certainly his incarnation is a small mountain. Christ is both: a great mountain and a lesser one—truly great, because “the Lord is great, and great is his power”; lesser, because it is written: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. VIII, 6).

Hence Isaiah also says: “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty” (Isa. LIII, 2). Yet he was made lesser from the great and great from the lesser. Lesser from the great, because “although he was in the form of God, he emptied himself and took the form of a servant”; great from the lesser, because Daniel says: “And the stone that struck the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth” (Dan. II, 36).

If you ask who this stone is, recognize him: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Ps. CXVII, 22).

Yet even when he seemed small, he was great. Isaiah confirms this when he says: “A child is born for us, and a son is given to us; dominion is upon his shoulders, and he will be called the Angel of great counsel” (Isa. IX, 6).

Everything is Christ for your sake. He is a stone for your sake, so that you may be built; a mountain for your sake, so that you may ascend. Ascend, therefore, the mountain, you who seek heavenly things. For this reason he inclined heaven, so that you might be nearer; for this reason he rose to the summit of the mountain, so that he might raise you up.

18. Therefore it was not without reason that abyss called to abyss, so that this mountain might become small, concerning which the Prophet says: “Abyss calls to abyss in the voice of your cataracts” (Ps. XLI, 8).

The Old Testament was not sufficient for the redemption of this world; it called out and summoned the New Testament, as though for aid. The Law cried out, announcing the Gospel. For it was half-full, and therefore it was necessary that he should come who would fulfill the Law. “The end of the Law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4): he came to fulfill the Law, not to abolish it.

Hear how the Law is an abyss: “Your judgments are like a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV, 7). From this understand also that both Testaments belong to one Wisdom, since the one came, as it were, to fulfill what was its own.

By “cataracts” we understand the depths of words and the power of heavenly speech, which flowed to us like rain from heaven. Christ, therefore, and divine Scripture are the remedy for every weariness and the one refuge amid temptations.

### CHAPTER V

The Prophet, beset by miseries, implores divine mercy, which is manifested especially in adversity. God is the one who takes up and sustains human beings, both because of creation, by which he has the same right over us as a potter has over clay vessels, and because of protection, by which he preserves the life granted to human beings.

19. Finally, when David noticed that the upheavals of worldly waves were coming upon him—waves that we must undergo in great number on the salt sea of this life—he remembered the Lord’s mercies, which he had promised through countless oracles. Turning to prayer, he makes supplication to God, knowing that his mercy is commanded in the light, that is, in the Law, because “your commandments are light” (Isa. XXVI, 9); but in temptations, as in the darkness of night, mercy is manifested.

Thus, like a traveler who desires to return to his homeland and reach the place toward which he is journeying, yet is wearied by the rough road of this life, he summons a guide and begs for relief.

20. “With me,” he says, “is prayer to the God of my life; I shall say to God: You are my sustainer” (Ps. XLI, 10).

He rightly seeks aids already known to him, and appeals to the author of the promise and the giver of his accustomed gift, so that, if human merit has offended, the divine example may not be offended in coming to his aid.

Someone may say: When does God sustain him? To establish this, come with me to the beginning of sacred Scripture (Gen. II, 7), and see how the Lord fashioned the human being from clay with his own hands. Hence this same man says later: “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Ps. CXVIII, 73).

Like a potter, God worked the structure of human flesh. And Jeremiah is told: “Go down to the potter’s house, and there you will hear my words” (Jer. XVIII, 2). It often happens to a potter that, while a vessel is being fashioned, it falls from his hands; then he gathers up the clay again in order to remake the vessel.

Jeremiah says accordingly: “I went down, and I saw how the vessel that he was making fell from his hands” (ibid. 3–4). And again he says: “He made another vessel as it seemed good to him” (ibid.).

Therefore he is rightly called the sustainer, because with his own hands he himself took us up and himself formed us.

The vessels of human potters are some for honor and others for dishonor. We are all earthen vessels; whether someone is a king or an apostle, he is an earthen vessel. Hence Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV, 7).

And the Prophet says of the king: “Jeconiah has been dishonored like a vessel whose work is not needed” (Jer. XXII, 28). And he added: “Earth, hear the word of the Lord; write this man down as rejected” (Jer. XXII, 28).

As though by ancestral right, our God is accustomed to disown degenerate children; therefore he writes them on the earth, because they are children of the earth. Hence, when the Jews accused the adulterous woman, the Lord Jesus was writing with his finger on the earth.

But the just are not written on the earth; to them it is said: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20).

21. The Lord therefore sustained us when he fashioned us; he sustains us also when he commands us to be born. Hence the just man says: “He sustained me from my mother’s womb” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 13).

From what mother? “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jer. I, 5). He forms and sustains those who come forth; and before you came out of your mother’s womb, “I sanctified you.”

He is the sustainer who has taken us up with his hands, so that he is called the sustainer as the author of the human race; and he is also the sustainer who receives us through visitation, so that he may protect us.

Hence the Prophet says: “He who dwells in the help of the Most High will say to the Lord: You are my sustainer and my refuge” (Ps. XC, 1–2). The first sustaining is an act of creation; the second is an act of defense.

Finally, hear Moses saying: “Spreading out his wings, he took them up and carried them upon his shoulders” (Deut. XXXII, 11), as an eagle carries its young. The eagle is accustomed to test its offspring, so that it may hold and nourish those in whom it recognizes the character of true birth and the grace of an uncorrupted nature, but may drive away those in whom it detects, while they are still young, the weakness of a degenerate origin.

## CHAPTER VI

David asks why God appears to have forgotten him; in this he confesses both the merits of his sins and his own weakness, which cannot endure without divine assistance. In the same place he mourns that he has been rejected by God, although he had previously been sustained by him. How blessed it is to be cast upon God from the womb, and how this may be applied to Christ.

22. “Why have you forgotten me, and why have you rejected me?” (Ps. [Col. 0820C] XLI, 10). God does not forget. For it is impossible that he should forget, to whom all things that have been made and all things that will be are present. But our sins pour into him the merit of forgetfulness, so that he blots out those whom he has recognized as unworthy of his visitation. For “the Lord knows those who are his.” Yet when some practice iniquity, he says to them: “I never knew you” (Matt. VII, 23). Who, then, can say to God: “Why have you forgotten me?” Yet this is common both to the saints and to us who are weak. The saint says it as though conscious of his own merit; nevertheless, the holier he is, the humbler he is. But if the saint scarcely dares to say it, what shall I, a sinner, say, unless I refer it to this: “Why have you forgotten your work? Why have you forgotten your visitation? Finally, why have you forgotten my weakness?” For what is a human being except that you visit him? Do not, then, forget one who is weak. Remember, Lord, that you made me weak; remember that [Note: [Col. 0819D] The edition reads, “you formed me from dust”; all manuscripts read, “you formed me dust.”] you formed me from dust. How shall I be able to stand, unless you continually attend to strengthening this clay, so that my solidity may proceed from your countenance? When you turn your face away, everything will be thrown into confusion. If you attend to me, alas for me: you have nothing to see in me except the stains of sins. Yet neither is it beneficial to be abandoned nor to be seen, because while we are seen, we give offense. We may nevertheless judge that he does not reject those whom he sees, because he cleanses those upon whom he looks. Before him burns the fire that consumes guilt.

23. It is good for us, therefore, not to be rejected. For this reason David complains, because he believed that he had been rejected, although he had previously been received. Indeed, later he says: “In you I have been strengthened from the womb” (Psalm LXX, 6). But above, too, we have this written: “Upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother’s belly you are my God” (Psalm XXI, 11). It is good also to be cast forth, but into God. Accordingly, in Psalm XXI this is said in the person of Christ, who truly was cast upon the Father from the womb of the Virgin; for earthly things did not receive him when he was dying. Hence, when he had been placed upon the cross and was giving up his spirit, he said to the Father: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII, 46).

24. Therefore, let no one add “Lord,” as the psalmists do, since I have found it neither in my Latin copy nor in the Greek, nor in the Gospel, which is the clearest authority. Indeed, above he had said: “Father, forgive them this sin” [Col. 0821B] (ibid., 34). And therefore, as to the Father, he commends his spirit into the hands of him in whose bosom the Son always is. Yet even if they add that he said “Lord,” let them consider that he speaks this as a human being placed in death.

25. Therefore, he was cast from the womb upon the Father, from his mother’s belly; that is, he determined that the womb which cast him forth was his mother’s belly. But the Father said: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm CIX, 3). The Father certainly did not cast forth the Son, from whom the Son never departed, as he himself says: “I was handed over, and I did not go out” (Psalm LXXXVII, 9). He did not cast him forth, since he is joined to him by the unity of the same substance. The passage can therefore also be read as follows: “Upon you I was cast from the womb, from my mother’s belly” (Psalm XXI, 12), followed by: “You are my God; do not depart from me.” It can also be read in this way: “From my mother’s belly you are my God,” because, placed in the womb, I never departed from you; I was with you, and, like Jonah placed in the belly of the whale, I was beseeching you on behalf of the people. And truly he was with God in the belly of his mother, according to what is written: “For before the child knew good or evil, he chose what is good” (Isaiah VII, 16). And elsewhere: “Before he called his father or his mother, he plundered the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria” (Isaiah VIII, 4), so that, by calling the nations forth, he might acquire a kingdom for the Father through the devout worship of piety. [Note: [Col. 0821D] Thus all the manuscripts and the editions of Erasmus and Gill; the Roman edition, however, omits the words “Let us examine the rest,” and in the following verse has: “Why, he says, have you rejected me?” [Col. 0822D] Here it had placed the next three paragraphs, with not a few words added or altered.] Let us examine the rest.

## CHAPTER VII

While Christ’s desired coming is delayed, the devil raged so that he might crush those who would believe in Christ and imprint his own signs upon them. Here the signs that we ought to follow and those that we ought to flee are discussed: the devil places his signs in those who receive the seed of faith along the roadside; the saints, on the contrary, place the devil’s faith in an open place. Finally, provision must be made lest the devil defile God’s tabernacle; for this, perseverance is especially necessary.

26. “Why,” he says, “have you rejected me, and why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me? He crushes my bones; those who trouble me reproach me, while every day it is said to me: ‘Where is your God?’ Why are you sorrowful, my soul?” (Psalm XLI, 10). And the rest. The first appeal contained a complaint that the good things whose fruit was already desired were being deferred. The second appeal concerned the fact that Christ’s coming, awaited by the wise, was being delayed—he whom the Law had announced and the prophets had promised. The hearts of the righteous burned with all the greater impatience because they knew that he would come for the redemption of all. Of whom does “all” speak? Of those for whom he would open the way of virtue by the path of the Gospel and point out the paths of good works, as he himself said in Proverbs: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways” (Prov. VIII, 22).

Therefore it was said to him: “Where is your God?”—because Christ had not yet come, but was hoped for. The devil raged, then, so that he might crush those whom he knew would believe in the Lord’s coming, and he afflicted them with various disasters. David therefore appeals in order to rouse the one who was delaying by prophetic lament, urge him to hasten, and admonish him to come to the aid of his people. We have a likeness of this appeal also later, where the same prophet says: “Why have you rejected us, O God, forever?” (Psalm LXXIII, 1). There he openly and tearfully lamented that God had forgotten his congregation and cast away the rod of his inheritance, and that his enemies had risen up against God’s people, concerning whom he says: “Those who hate you have gloried in the midst of your festival” (ibid., 4).

This verse might perhaps seem to identify the Assyrians, who triumphed over the Jewish people, unless what follows were added: “They set up their signs as signs, and I did not know” (ibid., 5). Signs are always present in war; they customarily go before those who are about to fight and lead the military column. Each unit or legion follows its own signs. Even if they are scattered by the tumult of battle, wherever they see their signs, they return, however far away they may be. [648] Every commander establishes these signs and prescribes that they be followed. But there are also other signs, which a victorious enemy imposes and decrees must be observed as though by captives. Yet the faithful soldier follows his own signs and does not recognize alien signs.

27. Let us consider more carefully and earnestly what these alien signs are. Christ has placed his sign upon the foreheads of individuals; there, too, Antichrist will place his signs, so that he may recognize his own. But he who is a Jew inwardly, that true confessor, says: “They set up their signs as signs, and I did not know.” The devil and his ministers set them up, but I did not know them, because I did not consent to his arts and did not yield to his commands.

The Assyrian Nebuchadnezzar placed his signs upon the Hebrew boys, changed their names, and commanded them to worship his image, abandon the solemn traditions of their fathers, and follow Chaldean rites, setting aside the Law of God. The king issued this decree, but Daniel determined in his heart to avoid the pollution of the royal table (Dan. III, 18). It is therefore rightly fitting for him to say: “I did not know alien signs.” The Hebrew boys had been ordered to worship the king’s image; they answered him: “We do not worship your image.” Accordingly, each of them aptly said: “They set up their signs as signs, and I did not know” (Dan. III, 18); that is, I did not experience them, I did not receive them by any consent, I did not transfer them into myself through any association.

Hence we also read of the Son of God that “he knew no sin” (II Cor. V, 21). And elsewhere we find: “Whoever keeps the commandment does not know an evil word” (Eccles. VIII, 3). It is plainly evident that the issue is not knowledge of wickedness but criminal association. David himself also says later: “As for those who turn aside to evil, I did not acknowledge them” (Psalm C, 4).

Where, then, the adversaries wished to place these signs, he declares: “As in a forest, with axes they cut down its doors together at the top; with double axe and hatchet they cast it down” (Psalm LXXIII, 6). [Col. 0823B] What does this mean except that it shows our faith must not be as though it were by the roadside, lest the birds of heaven come and carry it away, as you read in the Gospel that the word must not be sown beside the roads and paths (Luke VIII, 5)?

28. Therefore the saints, wishing to uproot the faith of this adversary, who does not see his signs in the heart of the believer, attempted to place it as though by the roadside—that is, in an open place. But the heart is at the top, because “the eyes of the wise are in his head.” And they placed the signs as though in a forest of trees, which are quickly consumed by fire or cut down by axes. For fire comes out of the forest and consumes even the cedars of Lebanon.

They thought this should be done in order to defile the tabernacle of the divine name, which is in us. For just as we are the temple of God, so we are also God’s tabernacle, in which the Lord’s feasts are celebrated. Therefore, O human being, guard your summit, so that you may crush the heads of your enemies, “the crown of the hair of those who walk about” (Psalm LXVII, 22). For they walk about in what is superfluous, not in what is holy; in the crown of the hair, not in the crown of devotion and faith.

And if “the spirit of one who has authority rises up against you,” as you have it in Ecclesiastes, “do not abandon your place” (Eccles. X, 4). For Christ established you above, since he made you in the image of God. Hold, therefore, the higher place of faith and piety that you received from Christ, [649] so that, having been made higher, you may easily repel the evil spirit ascending from below—that is, from earthly and worldly things—and not receive his signs in your breast. Let him not occupy the vestibule of your soul or the entrance of your mind; and, as in a forest of trees, let him not ravage what is perishable and fragile with his fires, or cut down the doors of your heart with his axes.

Let there therefore be in us not a forest but a vineyard. Let the gate of our mouth and heart be carefully closed, lest the enemy enter. A door quickly fails if he finds it open. But Christ knocks; he does not cast down—he who strengthened, O Jerusalem, the bars of your gates. Christ knocks with his hand so that you may open; the adversary cuts down with axes. Therefore it is written (III Kings VI, 7) that neither axe nor hammer should enter the house of God.

Pride and deceit must be outside, not within. Outside there should be battles; within, the peace that surpasses all understanding. Let your soul not be cleft by iron. Rather, as with the soul of Joseph, let your soul pass through iron, lest your ruling faculty, like a certain tabernacle of the Word, be destroyed at the very beginning of faith and at the entrance of spiritual teaching. For once it has been founded through practice and training, it remains immovable through perseverance and gives no place to him who attempts to ascend to the summit, transforming himself as though into an angel of light. If he does not see his signs in us, he will not be able to claim authority to resist.

Therefore, lest the enemy afflict us or crush our bones, let us not fail to persevere in Christ, so that he may say of us: “They have been with me for three days, and I do not want to send them away fasting, lest they fail on the way” (Matt. XV, 32). Blessed is the one to whom he grants firmness of heart, so that, established upon the road of this life, he cannot fail. For the one who hopes in the Lord does not fail and confesses to him with inward affection. Even that horseman whose horse’s heel the serpent bit, although he fell backward, was not deceived, because he awaited salvation from the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0823D] With these words the Roman edition concludes its exposition of Psalm XLI and, under the following title, begins a new exposition with the first verse of Psalm XLII. We, however, on the authority of the manuscripts, have restored everything to its earlier form.] 

## CHAPTER VIII

David asks that his cause be distinguished from that of the wicked, but not Christ, since all judgment has been given to him by the Father. The Prophet was rightly troubled by inward and outward enemies and persisted in asking that the light of divine assistance shine upon him quickly; nevertheless, through his knowledge of the future redemption, he was restored by God.

29. The Prophet’s third appeal likewise concerns the fact that, being placed among people who practice wickedness, he wishes his cause to be separated from their contamination. Many think this should be referred to the Lord Jesus, because it belongs to him alone not to fear judgment—he who conquers when he is judged. For he receives judgment from an unrighteous man, and Christ willingly enters into it, as it is written: “My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I grieved you?” (Micah VI, 3).

But since the Father gave him all judgment—not as to one who is weak, certainly, but as to a Son—what judgment could he himself undergo? If they think that the Father’s judgment must be undergone by the Son, then the Father certainly judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, “so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” The Father honors the Son, and you sit in judgment?

We have included this so that no one might think that, through fear of the inquiry, we are substituting the person of the Prophet for that of the Lord, when holy David, foreseeing in the Spirit that the Jews would rise up against the Lord’s Passion, did not fear the judgment of his faith, but also asked that his cause be distinguished from the nation of his persecutors, lest he be entangled with the evils of the heirs of his own race and posterity, and with the lineage of the entire Jewish people.

[Note: [Col. 0824D] The older edition: “He does not fear the Lord’s judgment.” The Roman edition: “Strengthened by the judgment of his faith, let him not fear.” All the manuscripts have the reading found in the text.]

30. It is not without reason, then, that he is troubled who sees that his struggle is against flesh and blood and that within himself he faces a grievous shipwreck, a storm in his own body, which he cannot withstand unless heavenly assistance supports him. For no enemy is more burdensome to a human being than those of his own household. And what is more of one’s own household than a human being himself and the weakness of his own flesh?

Therefore the Prophet hastens and prays with all his affection that Christ may come as the strength of all, that he may take upon himself every weakness and make the two one. By removing the dividing wall that kept the inward affection from coming into harmony, he would dissolve the hostilities of mind and flesh fighting against each other.

Since, then, there was conflict within himself, since those near him—forgetful of law and justice—were preparing snares of deceit and ambushes, and since the hoped-for remedy was being delayed, he considered himself rejected, as though the one who had promised to become the remedy were refusing to come. And as though recalled from the hope of the dawning day into the depths of darkness, he prayed that light might shine forth to drive away the gloom of this age, and that eternal truth might be present to abolish the deceptive image of this world.

31. God attended to his prayers. He is accustomed both to be present unexpectedly and to reveal himself to those who do not ask him, as he himself says: “I was revealed to those who did not seek me” (Isaiah LXV, 1). Supporting the pious man’s prayers, he anticipated the succession of his petitions with a swift fulfillment. Suddenly, in the Spirit, he led the holy Prophet into the Church and his tabernacles, and placed before his eyes the sacred altar upon which the redemption of the whole world and the forgiveness of sins throughout the entire world were to be accomplished.

## CHAPTER IX

The Prophet’s words signify that God, who had been turned away from human beings because of their sins, was afterward reconciled to them through Christ’s Passion. God’s rejection of human sacrifices, and yet his ability to be reconciled, are also confirmed by the testimony of Isaiah. Likewise, it is explained in many ways how we, who had suffered shipwreck like islands battered by the waves of sins, were renewed by Christ so that we might enter the house of God.

32. Seeing in the Spirit that sweetness of the heavenly mysteries, that table which repels the assaults of those who crush us, as he himself said above: “You have prepared a table before me, against those who crush me” (Psalm XXII, 5), he says: “And I will enter the altar of my God, to God who makes my youth rejoice” (Psalm XLII, 4). [Col. 0825D] Beautifully he said, as though Adam were saying: “I will enter.” For we had been expelled from the Lord’s paradise, from which Adam, conscious of his sin, turned his face away from the Lord.

He also fittingly added: “And I will enter the altar of God,” as though he were returning into God’s presence. For God had turned away from our offerings when he did not approve the offerings of Cain, the murderer. Cain lay hidden, alienated from the Lord’s presence, his savage spirit raging because the Lord had looked upon his brother’s offerings but had not looked upon his own. In his displeasure he left his own descendants behind.

He had killed Abel—not for himself, whose blood also cried out to the Lord, but he had killed him for all of us. Almost no one’s sacrifice was now approved, because there was no one who did good, not even one; for neither faith toward God nor brotherly devotion toward his brother had been preserved. [Note: [Col. 0825D] The edition reads, “nor brotherly piety toward his brother”; the manuscripts read, “nor piety toward the brotherhood of his brother,” and so forth.]

The Lord Jesus came to raise Adam. Abel, whose offerings had pleased God, was also raised. The Lord Jesus offered himself—that is, the firstfruits of his body—through the sprinkling of blood, which spoke more powerfully than Abel’s blood had spoken upon the earth. God looked upon his offerings; from that time onward, he left the grace of divine reconciliation to good heirs.

Therefore holy David, as though speaking in the person of reconciled humanity, rightly says: “And I will enter the altar of my God, to God who makes my youth rejoice.”

33. Let us support this passage, if we can, also by the example of another prophet, showing how the Lord first rejected human sacrifices and afterward was reconciled to humanity. We have it written in the book of Isaiah, where the Lord says: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full” (Isaiah I, 11)—that is, I have an abundance of my own things; I do not seek yours. “The burnt offerings of rams, the fat of lambs, and the blood of bulls and goats I do not want, nor should you come thus into my presence.”

To be sure, Abel had offered a sacrifice from the offspring of sheep, by which he had pleased God; but the one who was awaiting the truth of the sacrifice did not seek the type. The saving Passion of the Lord was being awaited. “For who has required these things from your hands? You shall not continue to tread my court” (ibid., 12).

And below: “When you stretch out your hands toward me, I will turn my face away from you . . . .” [Col. 0826C] “But wash yourselves, be clean; remove wickedness from your souls. Judge for the orphan, and vindicate the widow, and come, let us reason together, says the Lord” (ibid., 15–16).

It is therefore clear that the Lord had first turned away from human sacrifices and was afterward reconciled, so that he might deign to look upon our sacrifices.

34. Therefore the one who enters the Lord’s mercy enters securely. Accordingly, it is said to the good servant: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV, 21). But of the wicked servant it is said: “Take him away into the outer darkness” (ibid., 30).

Thus Adam, cast down from his heavenly homeland and from that seat of paradise, was banished into the island of sin. Scripture therefore rightly says: “Be renewed, islands” (Isaiah XLI, 1). For we are surrounded by the waves of sins, like islands in the strait of this world.

These islands, then, were renewed by the Lord’s coming through the forgiveness of sins—that is, human beings, established amid the waters in the washing as islands, were battered by the masses of waves like islands, amid the loud resounding waves of sins. In them, previously, as though among reefs of deceit, the innocent frequently suffered shipwreck, because there was deceit in the heart and flattery on the lips.

But afterward, when the Lord Jesus—“in whom there is no deceit”—came into this world and, through the exposition of heavenly teaching, calmed the depths of human minds and poured tranquility back into the affections of individuals, removing the hedge of discord, then, as it were, certain harbors began to provide supports for those approaching. [Note: [Col. 0827B] The edition reads, “to become refuges for those approaching”; the manuscripts read, “to become supports.”] Thus each person may place the vessel of his own peace in the affection of his neighbor or brother and cling, as it were, to the shoreline of a devout mind in a certain retreat.

35. David therefore rightly cries out as one renewed: “And I will enter the altar of my God, to God who makes my youth rejoice.” Above, as we read in Psalm VI, he had said that he had grown old among his enemies; here he says that his youth has been renewed from the old age of humanity’s ancient falling away (Psalm VI, 8).

For we are renewed through the washing of regeneration; we are renewed through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit; and we will also be renewed through the resurrection, as he says later: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Psalm CII, 5).

Hear how we are renewed: “You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm L, 9). And in Isaiah he says: “Though your sins be like crimson, I will make them white as snow” (Isaiah I, 18).

The one who is changed from the darkness of sins into the light and grace of virtues is rightly renewed, so that the one who was previously filthy with a foul mire may shine with a radiance exceedingly whiter than snow.

## CHAPTER X

Because of the benefits described above, David promises that he will confess to God on the lyre. On this occasion, the affinity between the lyre and our body is explained, as well as what kind of sound is fitting for it.

36. “I will confess to you on the lyre, my God” (Psalm XLII, 4). Our soul has its own lyre. For Paul would not say: “I will pray with the spirit, I will pray also with the mind; I will sing psalms with the spirit, I will sing psalms also with the mind” (I Cor. XIV, 15), unless it had a lyre that resounded under the plectrum of the Holy Spirit.

Our flesh is a lyre when it dies to sin so that it may live for God; it is a lyre when it receives the sevenfold Spirit in the sacrament of baptism. For while the tortoise is alive, it is immersed in mud; once it has died, its shell is adapted for use in singing and for the grace of devout discipline, so that it may answer with the distinctions of seven notes according to measured harmonies.

Similarly, if our flesh lives in bodily allurements, it lives in a kind of mire and abyss of pleasures. If it dies to luxury and lack of self-control, then it resumes true life; then it begins to utter the sweet melody of good works.

Sweet is the sound of chastity; sweet is the sound of those who fear God. Indeed, “their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Psalm XVIII, 5). Sweet is the sound of faith that is proclaimed, as it is written (Rom. I, 8), throughout the whole world.

Let this sound go forth from us to God, just as it also went forth from the Thessalonians (I Thess. I, 8), so that even when we are not singing, we may sing, and by the harmony of our good works proclaim the Lord, to whom belong honor, glory, and eternity from ages past, and now and always, and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK THREE: ON THE APPEAL OF JOB

[Col. 0827]

## CHAPTER ONE

Many people, even wise ones, are troubled when they see the wicked abound here in prosperity while the righteous are afflicted. This is the subject of the books that follow. For the same reason, Job’s friends, ignorant of the divine plan, argued that he had been punished because of crimes he had committed.

[Col. 0827C]

1. Our preceding discussion concerned the appeal of the saints and the fact that the human condition is fragile and weak, possessing firmness nowhere except in heavenly protection. Today we must take up the matter that greatly troubles the common people and many even among the wise: they see the wicked abound in prosperity while the righteous are frequently afflicted in this age.

And truly, this is a slippery matter, in which even the saints could scarcely maintain the trace of true opinion. Thus David himself was troubled, although above he had said: “You have revealed to me the hidden things of your wisdom” (Psalm L, 8). Nevertheless, afterward he strengthened himself and investigated the way of perfect understanding.

Holy Job also struggled in speech over this opinion with those three ancient friends who had come to console him (Job IV and following). Let us therefore bring the disputations of both men into the open. They are worthy to bring us instruction for living, since, placed in adversity, they deserved to please God all the more. Let us therefore hear each in his proper order.

2. Holy Job had been vehemently rebuked by Eliphaz, king of the Temanites; Baldad, tyrant of the Sabaeans; and Sophar, king of the Minaeans, because he was enduring so much punishment on account of his sins. [Note: [Col. 0827D] The old edition, together with the Vatican, Tornesian, and Victorine manuscripts, reads: “Baldach, tyrant of the Suhites, and Sophar, king of the Naamathites.” The Roman edition and other manuscripts read: “Baldad, tyrant of the Sabaeans, and Sophar, king of the Minaeans.” The Septuagint translators: Βαλδὰδ Σαυχαίων τύραννος, Σωφὰρ Μειναίων βασιλεὺς—“Baldad, tyrant of the Sabaeans; Sophar, king of the Minaeans.”]

For, with their feeble understanding, they did not perceive that the Lord had given him over to be tested, so that, trained by the trials of Christ as an athlete, he might reach the crown with greater glory. Not seeing so great a mystery of wisdom, they feared, with narrow hearts, that they might seem to accuse God of injustice if he allowed an innocent man to be afflicted with punishments. They therefore turned the merits of punishment back upon holy Job, saying that the entire life of the wicked is anxiety (Job XV, 20), and that unjustly gathered riches will be vomited up (Job XX, 15); that everything grievous which a person suffers on earth is endured because of his sins; that even if he is prosperous, his prosperity cannot last, but quickly vanishes like a dream, and his place is not found; that the joy of the wicked is a more grievous downfall (ibid., 5).

Thus they claimed that holy Job had been changed from prosperity to adversity and had fallen from the heights to the depths as the price of his sins; that he was falling even though he asserted his innocence, since the portion of the wicked is such that, when the Lord’s indignation overtakes him, it joins pains to him and destruction envelops his house (ibid., 28–29).

## CHAPTER II

Job proved stronger than his weak but healthy friends and even than his former self. How did he rebuke his revilers? Here especially his silence, as well as that of David and the Apostle, is proposed for our imitation.

3. Holy Job heard these things and, like a strong athlete sitting upon dung, covered throughout his body with dreadful ulcers amid such livid marks and savage pains of his wound, spoke mysteries. He was not occupied with acquiring remedies for his own illness, but with sacred discourse.

Thus the words of a sick man were stronger than those of men who were not sick. For they spoke injustices, though not according to knowledge. They proclaimed divine judgments, punishments for the guilty, and rewards for the saints; but they did not know how to distinguish the guilty from the righteous. Indeed, they condemned as unjust the one whom the Lord God had pronounced righteous and accused him of iniquity.

They therefore did not know what was appropriate to each person. Holy Job, however, discerned in the Spirit how it was fitting for him to speak to each one. He was therefore stronger than those who appeared healthy and unharmed.

And why do I say that he was found stronger than the others? He was found stronger than himself. For sick Job was stronger than he had been when healthy, according to what is written: “Power is made perfect in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 9). Therefore, when Job was weakened, he was stronger. His spirit was not sick, even though his body suffered, because his soul was not in the flesh, whose sufferings it did not cling to, but in the Spirit, whose power had covered him.

4. Therefore he was not speaking the groans of the flesh or the weaknesses of the body, but the voices of the spirit—voices by which he might press forward, not yield. At first, indeed, he spoke more gently, so as to bring shame upon them, because they were unjustly pressing the righteous, saying that he was suffering punishments smaller than his sins, and yet they themselves, sinners, were not ashamed to accuse an innocent man falsely.

“Suppose,” he says (Job XIX, 4 and following), “that I have erred, and that, in me, [Note: [Col. 0829D] The Tornesian and Victorine manuscripts, together with the Ambrosian edition, read: “that that god”—or “deity”—“dwells in me who displays errors” (the Ambrosian edition: “shows”). Other manuscripts and editions read more suitably: “that that wanderer dwells in me,” and so forth. The same word means one who wanders and strays, that is, the devil, who says of himself in Job I, 7: “I have gone around the earth and traversed it.” The word πλάνος, which here for Ambrose has the same meaning as πλάνης, is rendered by others as “error” or “ignorance.” Indeed, in many copies it is replaced by ἀγνόημα, “ignorance”; and the Vulgate edition reads: “Even if I was ignorant, my ignorance will remain with me.”]

the wanderer who spreads errors over the minds of human beings dwells, so that I speak words which ought not to be spoken, as you say, and my words go astray, and my speech is not brought forth at the right time. Why do you attack me and revile me, without considering that this trial has come to me from the Lord, who has judged that I should be fenced in by a kind of rampart of troubles?

I am being tested by adversity; I am surrounded on every side by hardships and dangers. And still you insult me, wishing to crush the one whom you ought to help. Behold, I laugh at reproaches; I will not speak, nor will I answer your insults. For you are not the ones who judge me; the one who judges me is the Lord. Yet the time of his judgment has not come. Why cry out before the judgment? It is good to be silent while awaiting the one who judges. It is good not to return insult for insult, lest we too be counted among those who slander.

5. Let us therefore imitate this man, who rebuked his revilers by his silence. For he displayed the strength of his spirit, which insults did not move, and made manifest the innocence of his conscience, since he did not acknowledge the accusations but laughed at them as though they were alien to himself. [Note: [Col. 0830D] The editions of Erasmus, Gill, and Rome read: “But if something is alleged against us, while we wish to clear ourselves,” and so forth. But the Ambrosian edition and all the manuscripts agree with us. This is indeed the genuine reading, since it is contrasted with the words: “but laughed at them as though alien to himself.” The sense of the passage is therefore that Job laughed at things said against him as though they were alleged against others, whereas we take insults badly, not as though they were alleged against others, but as though they were alleged against ourselves.] But if something is alleged against us, while we wish to clear ourselves, we grow bitter; while we desire revenge, we confess. Yet Scripture says that you should turn away a shameful saying (Prov. XXVII, 11) and remove your garment (ibid., 13); for the abusive person passes by. Let us therefore be silent, so that he may pass by, lest, provoked, he burn our garment. For it is written: “Do not kindle the coals of a sinner, lest perhaps you be burned in the fire of his flame” (Ecclus. VIII, 13). Therefore the saint is silent, whether a servant is insolent or a poor person reviles him; if a sinner casts reproaches, the righteous person laughs; if one who is weak curses, the righteous person blesses.

6. David was silent when Shimei son of Gera cursed him; Job laughed; Paul blessed, as he himself says: “We are cursed, and we bless” (I Cor. IV, 2). For, through divine instruction, the progress of human virtue increased, because he had now come who made the weaker stronger, and he had heard him saying: “Bless those who curse you, and pray for those who slander you” (Luke VI, 28). What he said in word, he proved by example. Thus, when he was placed on the cross, he said of his persecutors who were reviling him: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke XXIII, 34), so that he prayed for those who slandered him, although he himself could forgive them. Job, therefore, laughed because Christ had not yet come, for whom alone the prerogative of great virtues was reserved; because he is the beginning of virtues, as he said: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways” (Prov. VIII, 22).

## CHAPTER III

Job is declared victorious in the contest of words, than which scarcely anything is more difficult. How beautiful it is to laugh and remain silent when accusations are brought against us; and how, after his gentler reply, he drove back his more importunate revilers with stronger words.

7. He laughed and remained silent. He teaches why one should be silent: “I will cry out, and there is not yet judgment” (Job XIX, 7–8). “He himself,” he says, “willed that I suffer these things.” As though enclosed by the walls of trials, I cannot flee until it pleases God to destroy the heights of my trials. For now, if I cry out, there is not yet judgment. I am still in the contest; I am still wrestling; the struggle still remains for me. The crown has not yet come forth. No one is crowned except the one who has competed lawfully.

8. A third contest was owed to him. He had lost all his possessions—that is, his estate and his children. His flesh was suffering wounds. It remained for him to conquer the trials of words. This was no insignificant contest. Adam was deceived by speech; Samson was defeated by a word. Nothing penetrates the soul so deeply as disguised speech; and nothing bites so sharply as harsh speech.

Many who had overcome tortures imposed upon them did not endure the harshness of words. Job was suffering, but he endured, and he bore the burdens of words alongside those of his wounds. His contest-judge saw him, extended a hand to the suffering man from the cloud and whirlwind, declared that those struggling against him had fallen in a grievous collapse, proclaimed him victorious, and brought him the crown.

9. What, indeed, is more beautiful than to laugh when we are cursed? For we ought to rejoice if things foreign to us are said. First, because when an enemy wishes to say something against us by which to fasten a charge upon us, he has not found what is true, but has fashioned falsehoods in place of truths. Then, because the Lord himself said in the Gospel concerning this kind of accusation, falsely brought against the innocent for the sake of righteousness: “Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. V, 12).

Therefore the one who recognizes the charge ought to keep silent, lest he aggravate the wound and tear open the scar; and the one who does not recognize it ought also to keep silent: he hears another’s charge, not his own. If he repeats it, he makes it his own; if he is silent, he throws it back and wounds the one who reviles him. The one, too, who relies upon the reward mentioned ought to keep silent. For there is no prejudice against one who has no judgment against him. And if there has been prejudice in this world, there will be none in the judgment of God.

Finally, that you may recognize that insult does not prejudice a good conscience, hear holy Job saying—certainly a richer witness than if he had possessed the rule of the Roman world: “Now I will be silent and withdraw; if there is prejudice against me now, then I shall not be hidden from your face” (Job XIII, 19–20).

10. Thus, at the beginning, he answered them rather sparingly, so that he might remind them of God’s judgment and, having recalled them from insolence and fury, make them recover their senses like a good physician. But after he noticed that they persisted in their insults, he repeated more forceful words and, as though striking them with a stronger fist, struck those who were stoning the innocent man with the rocks of their words.

“Listen,” he says, “listen to my words,

[Note: The Roman edition has, “so that this consolation may be from you to me”; the other editions and all the manuscripts have, “so that I may not seek consolation from you.” The Septuagint, however, has: ἵνα μὴ ᾖ μοι παρὰ ὑμῶν αὐτὴ ἡ παράκλησις, “so that this consolation may not be mine from you.” Nevertheless, some copies omit the negation, as Nobilius explains at this place.]

“so that I may not seek consolation from you. Bear with me, for I shall speak stronger words; the burden of my words will be heavy” (Job XXI, 1 ff.).

I too shall speak according to your opinion, since many abound in this age in the success of worldly prosperity, while others are weighed down. “They are placed in misery,

[Note: The old edition and two manuscripts have, “and it seems that this age is being abandoned deservedly because of sins”; three others have, “. . . is being handed over deservedly.” The Roman edition has, “and they seem, according to this age, to be abandoned deservedly because of sins.” The Victorius and Thuaneus manuscripts have, “and it seems that this is being handed over deservedly on account of sins.” This is suitable: in the preceding phrase two members of the sentence have been established—the first concerning those who abound in prosperous success, the second concerning those who are weighed down and are in misery. This second condition, namely being weighed down and being in misery, seems to be deservedly handed over to sins.]

“and it seems that this is deservedly handed over because of sins.” Even if I say this, do not laugh as though I had agreed with you; and if I am a sinner, I am not guilty before a human being, because the one who judges and claims power over me is himself under sin. Or, if I am judged as a human being, this is common to all; I ought not to be reproached. It is the weakness of our condition, not a particular wickedness.

## CHAPTER IV

Job rebukes his friends, who assert that evils always occur because of sins, by asking why the wicked abound in good things in this life, although these are shown not to be true goods. Also, who is truly to be regarded as blessed; then, who sows well or badly; then, what sort of posterity the unjust have; and by what distinction these are said to be free from scourges, while the just are subjected to them. Finally, it is demonstrated that the wicked possess not eternity itself, but a false likeness of it.

11. “But tell me: If I suffer this because of my sin, as you allege, why do the wicked live? And not only do they live, but they are also filled with riches and multiply their produce; they also possess children, and their houses abound.”

These things are evidently good in appearance; but in a deeper mystery you will discover that what are thought to be good are not good, and that what are thought to be evils are judged superior to them.

12. “They have grown old in riches,” he says (ibid. 7)—he used the word πεπαλαίονται, “they grow old”—so that not so much the long duration of the possession of riches as the long-established burden of possessions may be signified, just as Ecclesiastes saw “riches kept for evil by their possessor,” which perish amid the utmost constraint and anxiety (Eccles. V, 12).

For the things left here perish and cannot benefit the dead. The deceased therefore had anxiety because of them and could find no rest: he left behind what he would be ashamed of, and did not carry away with him what he could possess. He was utterly unlike the one of whom it is written: “Blessed is the man who has filled his desire from these things; he shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” (Ps. CXXVI, 5).

The Lord is his inheritance, and his reward comes from the birth of the Virgin Mary. At his departure he is proclaimed with praises of wisdom, because he had nothing of which to be ashamed: he coveted none of the things of this age. Instead, having laid aside the garments of the old man, he wounded the adversary with the weapon of self-restraint, so that the adversary could not assail him at the end of this life—lame from his wound and confounded by admiration for his virtues.

You therefore understand that the one who has grown old in the desire for money, rather than being renewed in the reception of grace, is not praiseworthy.

13. Let us consider something else: “Their seed is according to the soul” (Job XXI, 8), that is, they are not counted among the just. For the just sow in the spirit and from the spirit reap eternal life. But those who sow according to the soul cannot reap spiritual things, because “the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God”; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know the things of the Spirit. Therefore he is not filled with spiritual things, but is judged.

14. “Their children are in their sight” (ibid.), that is, they do what they do in order to be seen by human beings, not because they are concerned for the good and choose what will be approved at the future judgment.

Scripture therefore frequently indicates works by the term “children,” because our posterity is richer in good deeds than in children. Hence, when Hezekiah had been delivered from a serious illness, he said: “From this day forward I shall make children who will proclaim your righteousness, Lord, God of my salvation, and I shall not cease blessing you with the psaltery all the days of my life” (Isa. XXXVIII, 19–20).

For good is the posterity of devotion and faith, which did not know how to succumb to captivity, as the sons of Hezekiah endured.

### 15.

And he added, saying: “Because they have no fear, there is no scourge from the Lord” (Job XXI, 9). But the just man says: “For I have been scourged all day long” (Ps. LXXII, 14), and he desires to be scourged so that he may be received by the Lord; and he wishes to fear the Lord, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”

He does not consider it blessedness if his heifer does not miscarry (Job XXI, 10), as fools do. For what is signified by the ox except the labor of rural cultivation, which continually returns in a cycle and never ceases, but, when it seems to have been completed, is recalled to its beginning?

These are the ones who cultivate Sodom and Gomorrah. Therefore those who cultivate Egypt and overturn the clods of the earth with a kind of plow of a hardened mind bring labor upon themselves and reap pains. Hence their heifer does not miscarry, but gives birth, so that their labor may increase, and they bring forth everything they have conceived without fear of God.

But the just glory in something altogether different. For they do not glory in an abundance of riches or in the birth of cattle, but in the Lord, saying: “From your fear we conceived in the womb, and we gave birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isa. XXVI, 18).

Thus it is said of the just that they have generated the spirit of salvation, which they received from the fear of God, not from the wickedness of this age, concerning which we read: “Behold, he conceived injustice, was pregnant with labor, and brought forth iniquity” (Ps. VII, 15).

Miscarriage, therefore, is better than the birth of worldly things. Finally, concerning the person who came into this world and endured the vanity and darkness of this world through a long and extended old age, Ecclesiastes declared that “the miscarriage is better than he” (Eccles. VI, 3). For the miscarriage has more rest than he, because it did not experience the changing conditions of the world, in which, even if someone lives a thousand years, he cannot see what is good. To have escaped these things, therefore, is more a matter of grace than to have undergone them.

16. But perhaps what he added may cause perplexity: “Because they remain like eternal sheep; but their children play, taking up the psaltery and the lyre, and delight in the sound of the psalm. They have completed their life in good things, but in the rest of hell they have slept” (Job XXI, 11 ff.).

Distinguish these things, and because you are spiritual, discern them. The wicked are as though eternal, but are not eternal, because they cannot receive eternity from one who is not eternal. Therefore he cannot give what he does not have, nor can one who does not possess light illuminate others. But he transforms himself into an angel of light in order to deceive unbelievers.

He transforms himself, however, by the pretense of false light, not by the splendor of everlasting brightness. Hence the Savior also says: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke X, 18). He is not lightning, but is “like lightning.”

Consider some heretic intent upon abstinence from the body and upon knowledge of heavenly mysteries. He is thought to be eternal, but he does not possess the reward of eternal life, because he has a false imitation while lacking the truth of faith.

His little ones play,

[Col. 0834B]

just as she who has lived luxuriously wishes to marry. She has lived luxuriously in the psaltery and lyre—that is, in the sound of the voice, not in the depth of the mysteries—so that it might resound upon the lips but not be brought into the heart.

## CHAPTER V

The wicked end their life amid the goods of this world, but afterward lack heavenly rest; the contrary is to be desired by us, since prosperity contains the enticement of vices and the presumption of impunity. The holy man refutes this madness by declaring that punishment, both present and eternal, has been prepared. Then, after listing their crimes, he shows that they cannot be hidden from God, describes what their portion will be, and exhorts us to pursue the wisdom that they abandoned.

17. Such persons, therefore, “completed their life amid the goods of this world” (Job XXI, 13)—the life, that is, which they were living, not that whose reward they hoped for. Therefore “they slept in the rest of hell,” not in heavenly rest.

But let us pray that here we may rather undergo labor, so that in the kingdom of heaven we may deserve to attain the consolation of eternal rest. For the abundance of worldly prosperity is a great enticement to sin: it raises one into pride and pours forgetfulness of the Creator into the heart.

Consider the rich man in the Gospel (Luke XVI, 19 ff.) reclining upon purple and fine linen, while that just man, the poor Lazarus, gathered the crumbs falling from his table. Does it not seem to you that the rich man says to God: “Depart from me; I do not wish to know your ways” (Job XXI, 14)?

And truly such people do not wish to know the ways of the Lord; for if they wished to do so, they would know them. But because those ways are full of labor, they are fled and avoided by the lost. Thus, like a drunkard, he does not recognize the author of salvation (Isa. XXII, 13).

Finally, turning to his fellow banqueters, he says: “Let us eat and drink; for what does it profit if we serve him? Or what advantage is there if we observe him” (Job XXI, 15)?

[Note: The Roman edition has, “if we meet him”; the others, together with all the manuscripts, have, “if we observe him.”]

Thus, intoxicated by the abundance of worldly things, he speaks these words, because the deserts of crimes are not immediately repaid in this world. He was lying back because everything was available to him for pleasure; and, conscious of his impiety, whose punishment had been deferred, he thought that God did not see the crimes of the wicked.

18. To this opinion of his holy Job replied:

[Note: The Roman edition has, “He answered his foolishness.” Further below it has, “the overturning of circumstances usually comes.”]

Do not be secure and careless, thinking that the Lord’s scourges will not come upon you in this very age. “Nevertheless, the lamp of the wicked is extinguished” (Job XXI, 17 ff.): it shines for a time, but does not possess eternal light.

Although the age favors them—because they do the will of the one who holds dominion in this age—the overturning of circumstances and pains arising from heavenly anger and indignation usually come, so that they may be winnowed like chaff by the wind.

The unjust are winnowed like chaff; the just like wheat. Finally, hear the Lord saying to Peter: “Behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII, 31–32).

Those who are winnowed like chaff fail; the one who resembles that grain which fell and rose again, increased by the addition of abundant fruits, does not fail.

Therefore the Prophet says: “Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers straw at harvest” (Micah VII, 1)!

Thus impiety is compared with straw, which is quickly burned, and with dust. Hence, after saying, “They shall be like chaff before the wind,” he immediately added the verse:

[Col. 0835B]

“Or like dust which the wind carried away” (Job XXI, 18).

Finally, so that you may recognize that the wicked, like dust, quickly decay and vanish, you have it said in the first psalm: “Not so the wicked, not so,”

[Note: That is, “not like the just.” These words had been removed in the Roman edition.]

that is, not like the just, “but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth.”

19. And he makes a distinction between the just and the wicked. “This one,” he says, “dies in the power of his simplicity,

[Note: The Roman edition has, “in the power of his foolishness.”]

“entirely in abundance and grace; but his inward parts are full of fat, and the marrow of his bones overflows. But that one consumes the course of this life in bitterness of soul and reaches his end without having tasted anything good” (Job XXI, 23 ff.).

What worthy recompense can be rendered to him according to his deserts? He is brought into the graves and keeps vigil in his tomb. Nor is this a trivial punishment: not to possess the rest of death, to be carried not to the land of the living but to the tombs of the dead.

For the one who lives is not sought among the dead, but enjoys eternal life in Abraham’s bosom. Therefore those two men in shining garments said to the women: “Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here” (Luke XXIV, 6).

20. Then he enumerates the crimes of the wicked (Job XXIV, 2 ff.): that they crossed boundaries; that, together with the shepherd, they carried off the flock; that they took away the orphan’s beast of burden;

[Note: *Subjunctorium*, that is, a beast under the yoke. The Septuagint has: ὑποζύγιον ὀρφανῶν ἀπήγαγον, “they carried away the orphan’s beast of burden.” The Vulgate, however, has: “They took away the orphan’s ass.”]

that they pledged the widow’s ox; that they harvested a field that was not theirs; that the weak worked in their vineyards without pay or food; and that, after stripping off their garments, they made the naked sleep.

Many whose souls they had deprived of their covering were drenched by the dripping waters of the mountains; and, because they lacked a covering, they covered themselves with a rock. Orphans were torn from their mothers’ breasts; those who had fallen were crushed, though they ought rather to have been raised up. The hungry were defrauded of food, and the souls of little children groaned bitterly.

21. Could the one from whom nothing escapes have been ignorant of these things? “Hell is naked before him, and there is no covering for the wicked” (Job XXVI, 6 ff.), because they cannot remain hidden.

He stretches out the north over nothing; he suspends the earth over nothing, binding the water in his clouds, and the cloud is not torn beneath his feet. The pillars of heaven tremble and are afraid at his rebuke. By his power he restrains the sea,

[Note: Thus the old edition and all the manuscripts, except Dionysius, where it reads, “by his discipline he has laid low the sea-monster.” The Roman edition comes close to this, but omits the word “sea,” as does the Septuagint, which has: ἐπιστήμῃ δὲ ἔστρωται τὸ κῆτος, “by knowledge the sea-monster is laid low.” Symmachus has . . . . . . . . συγκλᾷ ἀλαζονείαν, “he crushes arrogance.” The Vulgate, not far from this, prefers: “and by his prudence he struck the proud.”]

and by discipline lays low the sea-monster. The bolts of heaven fear him; by his command he put to death the transgressing dragon. Who understands the power of his thunder?

In the face of such great crimes, then, what hope is there for the wicked? “Will he be saved,” if he trusts in the Lord? “I shall tell you,” he says, “what is in the hand of the Lord; and cease adding vain things to vain things” (Job XXVII, 8, 11).

22. And he describes how miserable the portion of the wicked is. Even if they have many children, they are without posterity, because they lack the succession of good merits (ibid. 14 ff.). For that is the true posterity which is not on earth but in heaven.

For such men, therefore, inheritance is poverty, and death is succession. When they have heaped up riches, they will beg;

[Note: The Roman edition has, “because when they survive, they will be in need, and they will die without finding rest,” and below, where it agrees with Gill, “deserted . . . . deprived”; Amelote, Erasmus, and the manuscripts with us have, “deserted . . . . deprived.” This can also be explained without impropriety. For why may we not say that the dead have been deserted and deprived in their widows, for whom it was considered a consolation under the Old Law if some close relative took them as wives?]

because when they are dead, they will be in need, since they cannot find rest. No one will pity their widows; they will remain deserted and deprived of every consolation of marital union.

Even if money is gathered like earth, and gold is prepared like clay, their substance will be empty like a spider’s web, and the whole patrimony of their name will be consumed as if by moths.

The rich man, sleeping, will add nothing; he opened his eyes, and he is no more (Job XXVIII, 1 ff.). He remains in pains.

All the things that are in this world are therefore nothing. Gold is in the mines, silver is in the mines: it is dug out of the mine and returns to the mine. For what else is the mind of the greedy man except a mine? Like something buried, it holds whatever it has received and hides it in the veins and recesses of the earth, because it does not know how to use it.

Every day gold is brought forth from the mines; who has been able to bring anything forth from the miser?

23. Since, therefore, the vain hunger for gold is of no benefit, because whatever one gathers slips away, those who have abandoned the righteous way and forgotten it are truly to be pitied.

That way cannot in any way be compared with precious stones; it is difficult to discover, inaccessible to the proud, closed to the boastful, but level for the humble and open to the wise.

Therefore we ought to seek wisdom, so that we may walk in the righteous way, along which that adversary, like a lion seizing and roaring, who has run through this world, could not pass.

But whoever wishes to investigate wisdom should not seek it in the abyss—as the philosophers do, who think that by their own initiative and intelligence they can comprehend its depths—nor should he seek it in the sea. For where there is storm, where there is a tempest of wind, wisdom cannot be.

Let him seek it where there is tranquility of mind and the peace that surpasses all understanding.

## BOOK FOUR: ON DAVID’S INTERPELLATION

### CHAPTER I

David frequently discusses the vanity of the world in the psalms, but especially in Psalm LXXII, where he indicates that at first he was deeply troubled by the prosperity of the wicked and the calamities of the good, yet afterward was corrected. The question is whether the author of that psalm should be called David or Asaph.

1. [Note: At the end of Book III of the *Interpellation*, which it called Book II, the Roman edition had transferred these words, “The interpellation of holy Job has been completed”; and, omitting what follows down to “David himself,” had relegated this entire book among the expositions of the psalms, under the title “Exposition of Psalm LXXII.”]

The interpellation of holy Job has been completed; let us now undertake the interpellation that we find in the psalms.

David himself did not remain silent in many places concerning the vanity of the world. He frequently asserted that the things thought good in this world are empty, especially in Psalm XXXVIII, where he says: “Nevertheless, every human being who lives is complete vanity” (Ps. XXXVIII, 6); and although a person walks in the image of God, he will nevertheless be troubled in vain, treasures up riches, and does not know for whom he gathers them.

And elsewhere: “How long, O Lord, how long will sinners boast?” (Ps. XCIII, 3)—meaning that they possess a shadowy glory here, but when they have departed from this age they cannot find the fruit of consolation.

Nevertheless, he inserted Psalm LXXII, in which, under the name of Asaph, he declares that he had begun to slip,

[Col. 0837C]

so that he had been pierced by no slight grief when he saw sinners in this world overflowing with riches and abounding in prosperity, while he, who had justified his heart, was in afflictions and hardships. Nor had he received a slight offense at the beginning; but afterward, corrected by the Lord’s scourges and illumined by the grace of divine knowledge, he learned the true sequence of the tradition.

2. Nowhere, however, do I find that holy Asaph was troubled by any adversities; but holy David endured many grievous things, full of dangers, and speaks of his own labors.

Hence Psalm LXXII is not superscribed as belonging to holy Asaph, but as belonging to “the holy Asaph,” as the title teaches. This is shown more clearly from the Greek Psalter, so that David seems to have given this psalm, which he himself had written, to Asaph to be sung, just as he gave others to him.

But since it is written in the title itself that the psalms of David had failed, how did they fail, when, after these ten psalms had been completed, a psalm of David afterward includes a title

[Note: All the editions and manuscripts have “includes the inscription,” except the Thuaneus manuscript, where one finds “the inscription may include”; perhaps the scribe erred in the word *inscriptio*, unless we say that it is an apposition or rather an ellipsis. In this place Ambrose seems to mean that after the ten succeeding psalms, whose title throughout is “of Asaph,” others again occur intermittently up to the end of the Psalter that are inscribed “a psalm of David”; unless one prefers to understand “up to the final end” as equivalent here to “to the end,” words prefixed to not a few psalms. That this difficulty is left unresolved will not surprise anyone who, with Augustine on Psalm CV, no. 1, understands how difficult it is to penetrate all the secrets of the titles. Yet that this is especially appropriate to the title of the psalm under discussion is sufficiently attested by the same Doctor, when, after its mystical interpretation, he adds: “We have passed through, as the Lord willed, the dangerous passage of the title of the present psalm.”]

up to the final end?

Setting aside, therefore, this question, let us consider the sequence of the psalm, and let us begin from the first verse of the prophetic interpellation.

## CHAPTER II

From the very beginning of the psalm David’s correction is discerned: God is always good to the just because, even when they are afflicted by adversities, they are refreshed by hope of future recompense; they consider that they suffer less than their sins deserve and cannot be deprived of wisdom by any punishments. Yet God is also good to the wicked, but they are unwilling to experience his goodness, which is prepared for all.

3. “How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart!” (Ps. LXXII, 1).

The progress of correction shines forth at the beginning. For no one can truly confess that God is good except the one who recognizes his goodness not from the success of his own advantages, but from the depth of heavenly mysteries and the height of the divine dispensation. His goodness must be weighed not by the appearance of present things but by the usefulness of future things.

God, therefore, is always good to the just. When he is tormented by bodily pains and afflicted by the bitterness of punishments, he always says: “If we receive good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” (Job II, 10).

Here he rejoices that he is crushed, so that he may be able to find consolation in the future, knowing that the one who has received good things in this life has his reward and cannot hope for future rewards if he has not struggled and been trained in the contest of various battles.

Whoever, whether justly or unjustly, is afflicted in this age rejoices either because by these sufferings he pays the price of his sins, or because he knows that there is a more abundant grace with God if, unjustly, he suffers something bitter for God’s name or for some good work, according to what is written: “For there is no glory if you are punished for sins and endure it, but if, while doing good, you endure suffering, this is grace with God. For to this you have been called, because Christ also died for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten” (1 Pet. II, 21 ff.).

Therefore the just person, even if he is on the rack, is always just, because he justifies God and says that he suffers less than his sins deserve. He is always wise; for true and perfect wisdom is not taken away by the torments of the rack. He does not lose what he is, because love’s devotion and purpose cast out fear.
