As a wise person, he knows how to say that the things we suffer in this body are unworthy of comparison with the future glory, and that all the sufferings of this present time cannot equal the coming reward.

God is therefore always good to the one who knows at what time he will reap. And so, like a good farmer, here he plows his field with the plowshare of stricter self-restraint; here he weeds it with a sickle that cuts away vices through the virtues; here he fertilizes it by humbling himself even to the ground, knowing that God raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap.

Finally, unless the Apostle Paul had reckoned them dung, he could never have acquired Christ for himself. Here he guards his fruits, so that he may store them more securely there.

God is therefore always good to him, because he always hopes for what is good from God.

4. Receive another point: “How good,” he says, “is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart!” Is God therefore not good to everyone?

Indeed, he is good to everyone, because he is the Savior of all, especially of believers. And therefore the Lord Jesus came to save what had perished: he came to take away the sin of the world and to heal our wounds.

But because not everyone seeks medicine—indeed, most flee lest the force of the ulcer be pierced by medicines—he heals those who wish it, but does not bind those who are unwilling.

Those who seek medicine therefore receive health; but those who reject the physician and do not seek him cannot experience the goodness of the physician whom they do not experience. Whoever is treated is also healed; therefore the physician is good to those whom he has healed.

God is therefore good to those to whom he has forgiven sins. But how can one who has an incurable sin in the wound of his mind consider the physician good when he flees from him?

The Apostle beautifully explained, as we have stated above, that God is good to everyone, “who desires all human beings to be saved” (1 Tim. II, 4); and that the prerogative of divine goodness is reserved especially for believers, for whom both the will of God and grace provide assistance.

But the Psalmist, by saying, “How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart!” referred it to their judgment, since they know no other way to think about God except that he is good toward all and in all things.

## CHAPTER III

The Prophet confesses that he almost fell when he envied the peace of sinners; there are two kinds of peace, but the kind that contains a stumbling block must be avoided; there is no relief in the death of sinners; scourges after death are of no benefit, as is demonstrated by the example of Lazarus and the rich man; but how much scourges benefit during life is revealed by David and Job; finally, those who have not been scourged here must be scourged forever.

5. Finally, in what follows he himself explains what he experienced, saying: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps were nearly poured out, because I envied sinners, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. LXXII, 2–3).

He does not call bodily feet “steps,” but the direction and movement of the mind, concerning which he says elsewhere: “Let not the foot of pride come upon me, and let not the hand of sinners move me” (Ps. XXXV, 12).

Therefore we must always ask that the Lord direct the footsteps of our souls, lest they slip and, poured out upon some slippery path of error, be unable to retain their stability.

The cause of his fall was that he envied the peace of sinners. But we ought to envy what is good, not what is full of disgrace, as the Apostle Paul also clearly expressed, saying: “It is good always to be zealous for what is good” (Gal. IV, 18).

6. Nor should it trouble you that he placed peace in an evil context. In the Gospel, after all, you find a peace that Christ rejects, as he himself says: “I leave you my peace; my peace I give you; not as the world gives do I give you” (John XIV, 27).

There is a peace that has no stumbling block, and one that has a stumbling block. The peace that comes from love has no stumbling block; the peace that comes from pretense does.

Therefore the Prophet also says: “Peace, peace—and where is peace?” (Ezek. XII, 10).

Let us therefore flee the peace of sinners. For they conspire against the innocent; they unite in order to oppress the just, destroy the widow, or attack her modesty.

7. And therefore “there is no reclining at their death” (Ps. LXXII).

It is not “declining,” as many Latin manuscripts have written, but “reclining.”

[Note: In truth, the Roman, Milanese, and Carthusian manuscripts, following the Greek, and Augustine with them, prefer “there is no declining at their death.” Theodoret may also be counted among them; for the word ἀνά νευσις, which is read in the Septuagint, means exactly the same as ἀπαγόρευσις, “rejection”—that is, their destruction cannot in any way be avoided. Ambrose has not rendered it badly by the word *reclinatio*, since the verb *neuo* properly signifies the action by which we bend and incline the body, while *ananeuo* signifies the contrary action by which we draw back an inclined body, that is, raise it up. For such is the force of the prefix *re-* in compound verbs: it often gives them a meaning contrary to that of the simple verbs, or even contrary to verbs compounded with *con-* and *in-*, as is evident in *signo*, *resigno*; *contego*, *retego*; *innuo*, *renuo*, and similar forms. Other differences at this place may be found in Nobilius’s notes on this verse and in the variant readings prefixed to the latest edition of Augustine’s commentaries on the psalms.]

When we labor and bend ourselves toward some work, and incline ourselves, we are accustomed to recline. But sinners burdened with grave offenses, and especially the wicked, cannot recline. Concerning them it is said: “And always bend their backs” (Ps. LXVIII, 14).

For those who have not clung to Christ do not raise themselves toward heavenly things. Therefore they do not rise again with him, and “their death is most evil,” as it is written: “The death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. XXXIII, 22).

But whoever dies with Christ and is buried with him is not merely reclined; he is also raised again.

To him the saying beautifully applies: “You have transformed his entire bed in his weakness” (Ps. XL, 4), especially if he is a martyr, whose weakness is released by suffering and whose death is released by resurrection.

### 8.

We saw that rich man who in this world reclined in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day, while the poor Lazarus gathered what fell from his table. When he was placed in torments, he could not recline in hell; scarcely did he raise himself toward Abraham—not his whole body, but only his eyes—asking that Lazarus be sent to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool his tongue (Luke XVI, 19 ff.).

There was therefore no reclining at his death, nor any firm support in his affliction (Ps. LXXII, 4). For scourges after death are of no benefit.

9. Therefore David, while he was still living in this bodily life, prepared himself for scourges, so that the Lord might receive him after he had been chastened.

Consider holy Job again. He was covered with ulcers, shaken in all his limbs, and filled with pains throughout his body; the clods of earth were dissolved by the discharge and moisture of his wounds. Since, while he was in this body, he could not recline, he found the rest of death; therefore, conscious of himself, he said: “Death is rest for a man” (Job III, 23).

He was not moved in his affliction, nor did he waver through the slipperiness of his words; for amid all those things he did not sin with his lips, as Scripture testifies (Job II, 10). Rather, he found firm support in his affliction,

[Col. 0841C]

through which he was strengthened in Christ.

Therefore both Job and David, because they were scourged here, had firm support in their affliction, because “the father scourges the son whom he receives.” But those who are not scourged here are not received there as sons.

Therefore they are not in the labors of human beings, “and they shall not be scourged with human beings” (Ps. LXXII, 5–6), so that they may be scourged forever with the devil.

## CHAPTER IV

Sinners clothe themselves with their own iniquity; this garment must be rejected by us so that we may be clothed with the garment of virtues, especially fasting. Joseph profitably clothed himself with this garment, whereas Adam stripped it off to his grave loss. Finally, the iniquity of the Jews, proceeding as though from fatness, proved to be great and deliberate.

[Col. 0841D] 10. “Therefore,” he says, “their pride has prevailed over them; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety.” Iniquity is an evil garment. If anyone wishes to keep it upon us, we must send it back, lest it begin to come into judgment with us. And if anyone tries to take away the tunic we have received, [Col. 0842A] the spiritual one, send back the cloak of iniquity; take up the covering of faith and patience, with which David covered himself in fasting, lest he lose the garments of virtue. Fasting itself is a covering. Indeed, unless holy sobriety had clothed Joseph, the shamelessness of the adulteress would have stripped him. If Adam had wished to cover himself with this fasting, he would not have been made naked. But because he tasted from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil against the heavenly prohibition, and transgressed the commanded fast through the food of self-indulgence, he recognized that he was naked. If he had fasted and preserved the garments of faith, he would not have seen himself uncovered. Let us therefore not clothe ourselves with iniquity and impiety, lest it be said of one of us: “He clothed himself with cursing” (Ps. 108:18). Adam clothed himself badly as well: while he sought coverings of leaves, he received the sentence of the curse.

11. The Jews clothed themselves with cursing; of them it is written: “Their iniquity came forth as though from fat; they passed over into the purposes of the heart” (Ps. 72:7). [Note: [Col. 0841D] Thus read the Thuaneus, Laudunensis, and Colbertinus manuscripts. Two others, however, have a lacuna in place of the word *adipsal*. The editions merely offer *adeps dicitur pingue* (“*adeps* means fat”). It is clear that this variation was introduced in order to avoid an unfamiliar word; but we reproduce the reading of the better manuscripts, especially since it may have happened that the expression *adipsal* was commonly used by the people in Ambrose’s time through corruption.] For *adipsal* is said from *adeps*, that is, “fat.” Just as the soul, nourished by good things and filled with virtues, is filled as though with fat and richness, as it is written: “My soul shall be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62:6), so the iniquity that proceeds as though from fat is not signified as thin and meager, but as full of vices. In the end, they did not fall into error through some accidental lapse; rather, by deliberation and design they passed over into sacrilege.

## CHAPTER V

Those who set their mouth against heaven are chiefly those who attribute everything to the necessity imposed by the stars; nevertheless, grace is reserved for them by God, so that they may return with Israel. The mystery of Israel’s return is explained. The same people deny that hidden things are known by God, being especially led to this opinion by the prosperity of sinners. Finally, Simon the Pharisee is shown to have thought the same thing about Christ.

[Col. 0842C]

12. “They set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue passed over the earth” (Ps. 72:9). What it means to set one’s mouth against heaven is taught us by the younger of the two brothers, who, having returned to his father, said: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke 15:18). Those set their mouth against heaven [Note: [Col. 0841D] The Era and Gill editions read: “who think that the authorities of their crimes, their births, are brought upon them”; [Col. 0842D] Gill and two manuscripts: “their vanities”; the Roman edition: “their births”; while the Vatican manuscript has: “the authority of births.” Finally, others read: “the authorities of birth,” etc. The sense of this last reading seems to be the most natural of all.] who think that the causes of their crimes are imposed upon them by some necessity of birth. They are accustomed to spare neither heaven nor earth, believing that human life is governed by a certain course of the stars. They leave nothing to providence and nothing to good morals. [Col. 0842D] Would that these people too, like that one of the two young men, had returned! The good Lord would not have denied them a remedy, [Note: [Col. 0842D] The Roman edition reads: “and yet even for them, if they wish to be healed,” etc. The Ambrosian, Era, and Gill editions, together with the Vatican and Gallican manuscripts, prefer: “and yet even for them, if they do not wish to be healed,” except for the Thuaneus, which seems preferable here both for its antiquity and for its clarity.] and yet, even if they themselves do not wish to be healed, the Lord reserves the grace of return, so that those who were cast out of Israel through the blindness of their own heart may return through the fullness of the Church; and so that they may not spend the days of this life empty, but may possess them full of good works and faith, when the Lord has filled them with spiritual grace. But hear how they will return. “Blindness,” he says, “has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26). But because the mystery had to be fulfilled, so that God might “enclose all in disobedience” (ibid., 32)—that is, rebuke and convict them (for when two contend, if one prevails, he is said to have “enclosed” the other)—therefore, through his mercy, so that the world might become subject to God, the people did indeed return in their heirs; but it was led astray by a swift error, so that it did not believe God to be aware of hidden things. Yet the Lord reserved for them the grace of future salvation, so that they might eventually be redeemed, saying: “Therefore my people shall return here” (Ps. 72:10). What does “here” mean? That is, to me; to my equity and justice; to my worship.

13. “And he will complete the days of his life” (ibid.). You should understand this as follows: the people who have believed in him will indeed be redeemed. Even if those who have not believed are not redeemed, nevertheless the privilege of God’s redeemed people is bestowed.

14. Those people, therefore, placed in error, said: “How has God known? And is there knowledge in the Most High?” (ibid., 11). They think that there is no knowledge in God because sinners abound in worldly prosperity. He further represents them as saying: “Behold, these are sinners, and, abounding in this world, they have obtained riches” (ibid., 12). [Col. 0843C] You have this expressed more plainly in the Gospel, where that Pharisee Simon, seeing that the sinful woman had come into his house and poured perfume over Christ’s feet, said within himself: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know what kind of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner” (Luke 7:39). But God’s patience does not prejudice the truth, and his foreknowledge and providence are proved all the more by this very fact: that a person living in sin flourishes in worldly prosperity. When the stronger person sees this, he laughs; the unwary person is led astray and disturbed.

## CHAPTER VI

The prophet, having at first made a rash judgment, later corrected by discipline, came to recognize that everything occurs by divine ordinance; but that wealth is not the reward of virtue, nor poverty the punishment of sin.

[Col. 0843D]

15. Finally, the Psalmist says that he had said: “Therefore I justified my heart without cause, and washed my hands among the innocent” (Ps. 72:13). That is: I see them abounding; I see every advantage attending them, while I am crushed and harassed by very many trials. In vain, therefore, did I devote myself to innocence and apply myself to the pursuit of sober conduct. And appropriately he says: “I washed my hands among the innocent” (ibid., 14), so that he might seem not to claim the highest innocence for himself, but to offer diligent effort.

16. Meanwhile, he testifies that it was not without punishment that such a statement proceeded from him. For he recalls that he was scourged all day, because he had said that he had justified his heart before the Lord without cause; but after the scourges, correction of his mistaken opinion immediately followed. “At once my avenger,” he says, “in the mornings” (ibid.), that is, in what was open and clear; for the light of truth, comprehending him, did not allow him to think what he had said. The light of truth, which had been obscured in my mind, therefore convicted and rebuked me, because I had not rightly said: “I justified my heart without cause.” I spoke those words as one situated in darkness; and when I recalled them, my heart was pierced. Once my heart was pierced, my disposition was enlightened, so that there came to be in my heart a flame-bearing fire that created in me the spiritual beginning of day. When day had dawned for me in illumination, and I was, as it were, situated amid many mornings, I understood that I had been placed outside the ordering of the generation of the sons of God. At first I had believed that the Creator of the world, caring for the human race, had made everything for our benefit, whether things that are sad or things that give little pleasure; but afterward, disturbed by wicked opinions, I lost so good a judgment.

17. I therefore conferred with my heart and said to myself: If I speak in this way, saying that I justified my heart without cause, there came before me the voice of God saying: [Note: [Col. 0843D] The Era and Gill editions read: “Behold, the generation of your sons, for whom I have ordained.” The Roman edition: “Behold, I have ordained thus for the generation of your sons.” The manuscripts read: “Behold, for the generation of your sons, for whom I have ordained.” This is a Hellenism, or attraction of government. The Septuagint: Ἰδοὺ τῇ γενεᾷ τῶν υἱῶν σου ᾗ συντέθηκα (“Behold, the generation of your sons, with whom I have made a covenant”).] “Behold, for the generation of your sons, for whom I have ordained” (ibid., 15). That is: Behold, Adam, you find in the Scriptures that I have ordained this for the generation of your sons: that riches are accidentally bestowed upon the impious, not as the result of any merit, and that the gains of treasure are not rewards of virtue; nor, conversely, is poverty the punishment of sin. Rather, these things come indiscriminately, being swept along like a river in the flood of the world.

18. “And I considered, and it seemed to me that I understood this to be true, that this accorded with and conformed to divine providence; but that I had been troubled in vain by things to which I ought not to have clung” (ibid., 16).

## CHAPTER VII

After his error was corrected, David recognizes that one labor remains for him: to enter the inner chambers of divine knowledge. As the saints advance in age, they desire to know their end—and what that end is. The first true knowledge is that by which we believe that prosperity is granted to the wicked for this one purpose: to exclude their excuses. While such men are sustained by God’s benefits, they are cast down and reduced to nothing.

[Col. 0844D]

19. Since, therefore, it seemed to me that I had grasped the true judgment and attained knowledge of the matter itself, I said to myself: “This is the labor before me, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand the end” (ibid., 17). That is: the only labor remaining for me is to enter the sanctuary of God, where the Cherubim are—that is, the depth of knowledge—[Col. 0845A] and not to labor amid uncertain and empty opinions; for “the account of a fool is like a burden on the road.” Let us therefore enter the sanctuary of sacred knowledge and the inner recesses of truth, so that labor may not remain in us; for wisdom draws us away from the experience of labor. Indeed, “there is no labor in Jacob.” The cause of labor is ignorance, because one who does not know that rewards are laid up for the just is not refreshed from his labors, but is bent and broken by the labor of his own folly. Let us therefore enter the sanctuary of God, where the Cherubim are, in whom there is remembrance of sacred knowledge and of that true and eternal light.

20. In that lampstand the image shines by which we may understand the end. For the holy person recognizes it at the end and acquires perfect wisdom through the progress of age, saying: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, that I may know what I lack” (Ps. 38:5). What is the end except that moment when the kingdom is handed over to God the Father, when the hidden things of wisdom are revealed? The Prophet was seeking this end of our contest, desiring to know what was lacking from his perfection; for the end of our discipline and studies is perfection.

21. This, then, is the first principle of true knowledge: that the things of this world happen by chance. The second is this: “Because of their evasions, you have set before them” (Ps. 72:18) flowing success in worldly advantages and an abundance of riches, lest they complain that, because of poverty or the bitterness of some pain and grief, they had been less devoted, and lest necessity should have driven them to the guilt of theft and plunder. They were not enriched with wealth or raised up by honors for the tranquility and enjoyment of life, but so that complaint might be excluded and misery heaped up.

22. Such men, therefore, are cast down while they are raised up (ibid.). It is not grace but ruin, where neither the lasting use of the gift is preserved nor an excuse for wrongdoing remains. For what burden of complaint is heavier than that divine one which you find in the book of the prophet Micah: “My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I saddened you, or in what have I troubled you? Answer me. Did I not bring you out of the land of Egypt and free you from the house of slavery?” (Mic. 6:3–4). Behold how the impious are cast down while they are lifted up: their complaint is excluded and their punishment intensified. Invited by heavenly benefits, they ought not to have abandoned the giver of security and prosperity in this life, but ought rather to have obeyed him. Yet just as God’s justice is great, so also is his vengeance severe. For how long does the impious person usually persevere? Elsewhere you read: “I saw the impious person highly exalted and lifted up above the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. 36:35–36). Incredible is the swiftness of his extinction. You see the impious person suddenly powerful in this world; while you pass by, he is already gone. What is a shadow on the earth, and how short-lived it is! Move your foot, and the shadow has passed. Or, if anything here moves you, lift the step of your mind toward the things that are to come, and you will find there that the impious person whom you thought existed here will not exist; for one who is nothing does not exist. In the end, “the Lord knows those who are his”; but those who are not his he does not recognize, because they did not recognize him who is.

## CHAPTER VIII

The impious are aptly compared in their destruction to a dream, since their souls are found empty of every good; and their dark images are erased from the light of the heavenly Jerusalem.

23. Of these people, therefore, he says here as well: “They have failed and perished because of their iniquity, like the dream of one who awakens” [Col. 0846B] (Ps. 72:19–20)—that is, the impious fail and vanish just as the dream of one awakening first vanishes, because they are in darkness and have walked in darkness. No trace of any good work remains in them; rather, they are like those who see a dream. The one who dreams, however, dreams at night; and night is in darkness. The sons of darkness are deprived of the sun of justice and the splendor of virtue; they are always asleep and never watchful. Of them it is rightly said: “They slept their sleep, and found nothing” (Ps. 75:6). For when their souls, separated from the body, find nothing—like those released from bodily sleep—they will hold nothing; and what they thought they possessed, they will lose. For when the foolish and senseless have overflowed with riches, they will leave their wealth to others, nor will the glory of their house descend with them into the underworld.

24. The following words also show how the impious person is not found, but perishes: his image is not found in that higher city of the Lord, Jerusalem. For the Lord painted us in his own image and likeness, as he himself teaches when he says: “Behold, I have painted your walls, O Jerusalem” (Isa. 49:16). [Col. 0846D] If we act well, this heavenly image remains in us; but if anyone acts badly, this image—the image, of course, of the one who descended from heaven—is erased in him, and the image of the earthly is in him. Hence the Apostle also says: “As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of this heavenly one” (1 Cor. 15:49). The images of the good, therefore, endure and shine in that city of God. [Col. 0846D] But if anyone turns to graver sins and does not repent, his image is erased or cast down, just as Adam was expelled and excluded from paradise. Whoever conducts himself piously and honorably enters the city of God and brings in his image, so that it may shine in that city of God. “Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing” (Ps. 72:20), because those who have clothed themselves in dark deeds cannot shine in the light. Let us draw an example from this world. Observe how, in the cities of good rulers, the images of the good endure, while the images of tyrants are erased.

## CHAPTER IX

The prophet is revived by knowledge of divine providence; he and all human beings are, in comparison with the heavenly citizens, scarcely unlike beasts, yet by God’s grace they are restored to human dignity.

[Col. 0847A]

25. Considering and contemplating these things, the holy Prophet was delighted, though he had previously been troubled. Hence he himself says: “Because my heart was delighted, and my reins were restored. And I was reduced to nothing and did not know; and I became like a beast before you, and I am always with you” (ibid., 21ff.). When I understood, he says, that God cares for and regards human affairs, my reins were released—that is, after the greatest weariness of my former folly, I rested through recognition of heavenly goodness and grace. There are, in fact, certain reins of the soul that are tormented in us by the labor of ignorance. These are released to rest through recognition of heavenly teaching, and, as though supported by a beautiful prop of heavenly commandments, they are comforted. “Then,” he says, “I understood that I was wearied in vain, because I did not know what is true.”

26. “And I became like a beast.” He appropriately added, “before you”; for in comparison with the heavenly beings, what is a human being except an irrational animal? Even the stars, although luminous, fade at the rising of the sun. Moses also says: “I am not capable from yesterday, from the day when you began to speak with your servant; for I am,” he says, “slow of speech and slow-tongued” (Exod. 4). Thus, in comparison not only with Christ but even with the angels, the human being appears to be a mute beast. Yet no one should despair, because God saves both human beings and beasts. And therefore, because I learned not from myself but from you, I shall always cling to you, so that I may cease to be a beast and you may say to me: “But you, stand here with me” (Deut. 5:31). Surrounded by the grace of God, the human being begins to be human, although through folly he had displayed the insensibility and ignorance of a beast. A person is proved to be human if he is capable of reason and grace. Thus he rejoices that he has been separated from mute animals and admitted into the fellowship of human beings, whom God visits and protects. For what is a human being except that the Lord remembers him, or that he is visited by the Lord?

671 ## CHAPTER X

If God is not at our right hand, that place will be occupied by the devil, as happened to our first parent. When Christ took the latter’s place, he stationed the demon at his own right hand, so that he might overthrow him all the more gloriously. Finally, the greatest benefits return to those at whose right hand Christ has stood.

[Col. 0847D]

27. Therefore, as one visited by him, he says: “You have held my right hand, and in your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me” (Ps. 72:24). Thus we have received the passage, and thus it accords with the Greek. For the Greek says: Ἐκρατῆσας τῆς χειρὸς, that is, “you held the hand,” τῆς δεξιᾶς μου, “my right hand.” He is rightly guided whose right hand God holds with his own hand. He can say: “The Lord is at my right hand, that I may not be moved” (Ps. 15:8). If Adam had wished to have the Lord at his right hand, he would not have been deceived by the serpent. But because he forgot God’s commandment and fulfilled the serpent’s will, the devil held his hand and made him extend it to the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, so that he might pluck what was forbidden. In him judgment was passed upon all, and the adversary began to stand at the right hand of everyone. Hence that form of the curse against Judas also arose: “Let the devil stand at his right hand” (Ps. 108:6). If that curse is grave, this blessing is the greatest, by which the bonds of the harsh curse are loosened. Therefore the Lord Jesus stationed the devil at his right hand, as we read in the book of Zechariah (Zech. 3:1); for he had taken up the cause and place of the human being. He therefore stood there where Adam’s inheritance had stood. Like a good athlete, Christ permitted him to stand at his right hand so that he might drive him backward, saying: “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. 4:10). Thus the adversary was cast down from his position and withdrew. But so that the devil might not stand at your right hand, Christ said to you: “Come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). Foreseeing, therefore, the coming of the Lord, who descended from heaven to free us from the power of the adversary, David said: “The Lord is at my right hand, that I may not be moved.” But the one at whose right hand the devil stood was moved. Rightly, therefore, he says here as well: “You have held my right hand”—that is, so that I may no longer be able to sin; so that I, whose foot had previously wavered amid slippery paths, may be able to stand in a secure position. How well the Apostle said this when the Lord saw him troubled, extended his right hand, did not allow him to waver, and strengthened him with an unwavering step (Matt. 14:30–31). Once Peter had been delivered, what else did he say than these prophetic verses: “You have held my right hand, and in your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me”? What is the right hand except the active virtue of the soul? If this is directed by the Lord’s will, it desires nothing else, seeks nothing, and asks for no riches or aids of this world.

## CHAPTER XI

David, content with possessing God, desires nothing besides him. Earthly things must be erased through forgetfulness so that heavenly things may take their place; one must also approach God, who rejects no one, and from whom we withdraw only through wicked actions.

28. Therefore holy David says: “For what remains for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. 72:25). That is: You are my portion; you are sufficient for me in all things. I sought nothing else except to have you as my portion. I did not subject myself to any heavenly creature, as the Gentiles do; I did not desire any riches of this age or enticements of pleasure. I lack nothing, since I have been received by you; nor does anything remain in the heavens that I might seek further. Though possessing nothing, I possess all things, because I possess Christ, whom the Most High Father did not spare but handed over for us all. “How, then, will he not also give us all things with him?” (Rom. 8:32), as the Apostle said. For all things are in Christ, through whom all things exist and in whom all things hold together. Having all things in him, therefore, I seek no other reward, because he himself is the reward of all. Hence he said to the perfect: “Take up your cross and follow me” (Mark 8:34). Whoever follows him is not led to perfection by a reward; rather, by perfection he is brought to the reward. For those who imitate Christ do so not for the hope of a benefit, but out of love for virtue. Christ is good by nature, not because of a desire for reward. He suffered because he delighted in doing good, not because he sought an increase of glory through his suffering. Therefore whoever wishes to imitate him works not for what benefits himself, but for what benefits others. Hence it is not without reason that he becomes weak in himself but grows strong in others through the increase of virtue.

29. Appropriately he says: “My heart and my flesh have failed; God is the God of my heart” (Ps. 72:26). For what is eternal cannot follow unless earthly things have failed. The flesh therefore fails when the things that are carnal are put to death. Those also fail who carry the death of Jesus Christ in their flesh; for the death of Christ works in them so that every enticement of error may die. From this it follows that the human heart also fails when the evil thoughts that proceed from the heart are put to death, so that forgetfulness may conceal all earthly things and God may become the God of the hearts of those who, being pure in heart, deserve to see God; so that they may draw near to you and not separate themselves. For God is one who draws near, not one who repels those who approach; he wishes to be the cause of salvation, not of death, for all. In the end, he repels no one except the one who thinks that he must withdraw himself from his sight.

30. “For behold,” he says, “those who distance themselves from you will perish” (ibid., 27). Each person joins himself to or separates himself from your piety through his deeds. The person who does the things whose knowledge he fears will expose him flees from God, like the one who, hidden by walls and surrounded by darkness, thinks that he is unseen by the Lord God. Yet he is seen, as it is said: “You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you” (ibid.). For just as a woman who commits fornication does not cling to her husband, is not one flesh with her husband, and is not one spirit with him, but divides and separates herself through fornication, so every soul that does not cling to God, but fornicates by serving the empty worship of idols, divides itself [Note: [Col. 0849B] All the editions read “through the obscenity of sacrilege”; all the manuscripts read “through the savagery of sacrilege.”] through the savagery of sacrilege and becomes far from the Lord, though it ought to be near. The one who is separated from the Lord perishes.

31. Therefore the Saint, who fears God’s judgment (ibid., 28), always wishes to cling to Christ and place his hope in him, so that he may praise the Lord, to whom belong honor, glory, and eternity from the ages, now and always, and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

# APOLOGY OF THE PROPHET DAVID

[Col. 0849B]

## INTRODUCTORY NOTICE TO THE APOLOGY OF THE PROPHET DAVID

Some people, when reading through the history of David and learning that so holy a prophet and king had fallen into the twofold crime of adultery and murder, had been deeply offended (Chapter I, no. 1). Therefore, when this commonly circulated rumor came to his attention, Saint Ambrose—always intent upon the welfare of his people—thought that this evil had to be addressed promptly. Accordingly, ascending the sacred pulpit, he undertook the defense of the same prophet and king. Yet he did not undertake to defend him in such a way as to assert that he was free from crime. For he admits (Chapter 1 and following) that David had been stained by two very grave sins; but he maintains that he was cleansed by his prompt confession (Chapter 2), prolonged repentance (Chapter 4), and tireless devotion to good works (Chapter 6 and following), so that sinners were in no way permitted to accuse one whom God himself had absolved (Chapter 4 and elsewhere). Moreover, it is by no means unusual that a frail human being should succumb under the force of temptation and desire (Chapter 1 and elsewhere); but it is wholly worthy of universal admiration that a most powerful king, who was not restrained by the severity of the laws, immediately upon being warned of the sin he had committed acknowledged his guilt and wiped it away through sincere and vehement grief. He adds that this fall was permitted by divine providence for the reason that David, humbled as an example for posterity, might be disciplined and tested (Chapters 2 and 3); and that in this very event there was also a figure of a mystery (Chapter 3) that diminished the atrocity of the offense. Finally, after enumerating the many remarkable and holy actions by which the Prophet covered his transgression (Chapter 6 and following), he asserts that David needs no other advocate, since in Psalm 50, in which he testified both to the repentance he had performed and to the pardon he had obtained (Chapter 8 and following), he himself left behind his own apology. This the holy man demonstrates through a brief but elegant exposition of all the verses of that Psalm, in which—as throughout the entire work—he scatters certain mystical interpretations, observations, and moral exhortations for the instruction of the people to whom he was speaking.

The very structure of this work makes it sufficiently clear that in the Roman edition it was divided rather imprudently, contrary to the authority of all the manuscripts and earlier editions, into two treatises. One retained the ancient title, *The Apology of David*; the other, given a new heading, was assigned to the expositions of the Psalms. Blessed Augustine also opposes this division; for when he cites testimony drawn from the exposition of Psalm 50, he praises it under no other title than *The Apology of David* (Book IV, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 11, and Book II, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, chapter 7). Nor do we think that anyone could approve either the alterations introduced into the author’s text by the editors of that edition, or the removal of the words by which the parts of this work—which must in fact be a single work—were joined to one another. We have therefore restored everything on the authority of the manuscript codices and ancient editions, as we have indicated in their proper places at the foot of the pages.

Ambrose pronounced the sermons composing this treatise in the Church, according to his custom, after the Gospel had been read, as is clearly indicated by the words “as was read today” (Chapter 5, no. 20), referring to the passage about a certain man who, although he was rich, went away into a distant region, etc. (Luke 19). It is no less clear that this took place not long after the murder of the Emperor Gratian, when Ambrose laments it in these words (Chapter 6, no. 27): “How grievous a devastation we still lament; by what kind of public mourning of the whole world do we pay for the murder of the king who was assailed,” etc. The holy Bishop could have spoken in this way only either of Gratian or of the younger Valentinian, since in those times no emperor other than these two young men had been killed by force. Yet it is sufficiently clear that the circumstances mentioned there fit Gratian’s violent death very well, but do not fit Valentinian’s. Moreover, this very *Apology* is cited in the commentaries on the Gospel according to Luke (on chapter 3), which were probably written around the year 385, and therefore long before Valentinian’s death. It must therefore be concluded that this treatise appeared after August of the year 383, when Gratian was murdered, and before the year 385, when the aforementioned commentaries were composed—namely, in the year 384, as seems most likely.

The Thuaneus manuscript, written a thousand years ago, as its characters indicate, and several other manuscripts of recognized authority, present this same little work under the following title: *Treatise of Saint Ambrose on the Apology of the Prophet David, addressed to Theodosius Augustus*. Someone might perhaps suspect that the final words were added by certain ignorant or presumptuous persons, since Theodosius the Great could not have been in Milan at the time when we have demonstrated that these sermons were delivered; he did not come to that city until several years later, after he had triumphed over Maximus. Nevertheless, there is nothing to prevent the holy Bishop from having given Theodosius, who had requested one of his books, this particular work—although composed many years earlier—as especially appropriate because of the royal dignity of the person discussed in it. Or perhaps Ambrose himself decided to send it spontaneously to that emperor after the massacre at Thessalonica, on account of which he imposed a public penance upon him, in order to strengthen him in his resolve to repent. Indeed, among the many admirable statements found in this treatise, there are several observations that seem to point in that direction. Ambrose could have added these to his writing before sending it to the emperor. If this is so, we may proclaim that this work has come down to us completed and revised under the Author’s final care.

[Col. 0851B]

# SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, APOLOGY [Note: [Col. 0851A] Perhaps written around the year 384.] OF THE PROPHET DAVID, ADDRESSED TO THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS. (C)

[Col. 0851]

## CHAPTER ONE

Why Ambrose undertakes to write David’s apology. The history of the event is set forth first. Then it is shown that a person whom God has justified ought not to be judged; on the contrary, he should even be praised because, despite possessing such great power, he did not commit more sins.

[Col. 0851A]

1. We have taken up the present pen to write an apology for the prophet David—not because he needs this service, since he shone with such great merits and blossomed with virtues, but because many people, after reading the sequence of his deeds without penetrating the force of the Scriptures or the hidden things of the mysteries, are amazed that so great a prophet did not avoid first the contamination of adultery and then that of murder.

2. Therefore I took pains to review the history itself, which seems to have laid bare the sin. For in the Second Book of Kings we read (II Kings 11:2 ff.) [Note: [Col. 0851A] The Roman edition alone has: “we read, as you have heard, that David, while walking on the roof of his royal house…”] that David, while walking in his royal palace, saw a woman washing herself—her name was Bathsheba—[Note: [Col. 0851A] The editions have *of pleasing form and exceptionally beautiful countenance* (*of pleasing form*, Roman edition), “by which allurements, etc.” A number of manuscripts have *pleasing in form and beautiful in countenance, and with an exceptionally handsome face, by which, etc.* Many others, both far more numerous and older, read as in the text, except that the more recent Thuaneus has “beautiful in appearance,” etc. You should not think that the words *appearance* and *face* constitute a pointless repetition (*battologia*), since *face* may signify not merely the countenance but also the composition and outward appearance of the entire body. Again, all the editions and some manuscripts read *to possess her*; many other manuscripts, and those of better age, read *to enjoy her*. The latter is preferable; thus Terence writes in the *Hecyra*: “eager to see her”—that is, his wife. See Francis Sánchez, *Minerva*, Book III, chapter 8. Finally, where the Era., Gill., and Roman editions, together with the better manuscripts, have *had conceived the desire*; Ambrosius, with the rest, has *had conceived the desire* in the subjunctive. What moved them was that they did not think the construction could otherwise stand, although, with the better reading, the verb expressed at the beginning of the sentence is mentally supplied here.] of remarkable beauty, both pleasing in form and beautiful in countenance, with an exceptionally handsome face; captivated by these attractions, he conceived the desire to possess her. The woman was married to a man whose name was Uriah, [Note: [Col. 0852B] The Thuaneus manuscript, always ancient and in every case, has *Uri*. Certainly this may be Ambrose’s reading, as is suggested by the fact that below, in chapter 3, section 14, he says that the husband’s name, Bathsheba’s husband, means the same as “my light,” which is how the name *Uri* is commonly interpreted, whereas *Uriah* is explained as “light” or “fire of the Lord.”] and a plan for his death was arranged by royal command. For although his life was not an obstacle to desire, it was thought to be a very great obstacle to the shame of adultery.

3. Therefore, to begin with what is clearer: “Do not judge the one whom God has justified.” Paul says, “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day; but I do not even judge myself” (I Corinthians 4:3). He was still situated in the body and still subject to temptation; yet he did not judge himself because the spiritual person is judged by no one except God alone. Finally, he added: “The one who judges me is the Lord. Therefore do not judge anything before the time” (ibid., 4–5). But David has already completed his time, obtained grace, and been justified by Christ; for the Lord himself was pleased to be called David’s son, and those who confessed him as such were enlightened. Why do you summon a man of God from reward to judgment? The Lord has already judged him, concerning whom he said to Solomon: “If you walk in my sight, as David your father walked, in holiness of heart and uprightness, so as to do all that I have commanded him” (I Kings 9:4). Is this man, then, worthy of judgment or of reward, who did all the heavenly commandments, walking in holiness and uprightness of heart? Where the vices and sins of others lie hidden, there David received divine testimony to his virtue and glory. Yet we idly debate his sin, on whose merit and grace the sins of others were revealed.

When Solomon offended by failing to keep the Lord’s commandments, and God resolved to divide his kingdom into many parts, he said to him: “Nevertheless, in your days I will not do this, for the sake of David your father. I will take it from the hand of your son. Yet I will not take the whole kingdom; I will give him one scepter for the sake of David my servant” (I Kings 11:12–13). Since, then, the Lord justifies him, who is there that can judge such a man? “What God has cleansed,” he says, “do not call common” (Acts 10:15).

4. Without prejudice, however, to the heavenly judgment—which should also lead you to honor the prophet so greatly—enter into his actions and character. Do you not marvel that a human being, and one whom you judge equal to the angels, having spent most of his life—or rather, from childhood—amid wealth, honors, and authority, and having been placed amid many temptations, gave error an opening only once, and gave it the same opening by which even the angels of heaven, as Scripture records, [Col. 0853D] were cast down from their virtue and grace (Genesis 6:2)? [Note: [Col. 0854D] Concerning that fall of the angels, see what we have said in our book *On Noah and the Ark*, at the end of column 231.] It is true that another error of his is also recorded: that he ordered the people to be counted. [Note: [Col. 0853D] The Roman edition has *he had slain this one*. Certainly another error of his is also recorded, namely, that he ordered the people to be counted; this is the reading we have restored from all the manuscripts and the oldest editions.]

## CHAPTER II

David is praised for the humility of his confession; three reasons are given why it is beneficial for the saints to fall into sin, and why God permits this.

5. Every one of us commits how many offenses hour by hour, and yet no ordinary person thinks that he ought to confess his sin. That king (On Penance, distinction 3, chapter “That King”)—so great and powerful—did not permit the consciousness of sin to remain with him even for the briefest moment; but by an early confession and immense grief he returned his sin to the Lord. Where could you now easily find a person honored and wealthy who, if accused of some fault, would not take it badly? Yet David, illustrious in royal power and tested by so many divine revelations, when reproved by a private person for having seriously sinned, did not angrily rage; rather, he groaned in confession under the pain of his guilt. In the end, the Lord was moved by the sorrow of his innermost feelings (ibid., § “Finally, the Lord”), so that Nathan said: “Because you have repented, the Lord has taken away your sin” (II Kings 12:13). The promptness of the pardon therefore declared how profound the king’s repentance had been: it was repentance that removed the offense of so great an error.

6. Other people, when reproved by priests, aggravate their sin by wishing to deny or defend it; and their fall is greatest precisely where correction is hoped for. But the saints of the Lord (ibid., § “Saints”) who strive to complete the contest of devotion and to run the course of salvation, if they should happen to fall as human beings—through the frailty of nature rather than through a desire to sin—rise again more eager to run, repairing greater contests through the spur of shame. Thus their fall is judged not merely to have caused no impediment, but even to have accumulated incentives to speed.

Therefore, if the course of runners is not broken when some happen to fall, the contest of those who struggle remains not defeated but unharmed. Indeed, many have conquered with greater grace after one or another fall. How much more, then, should those who have entered the contest of devotion not be judged by the offense of a single lapse, since blessed is the one who has been able to restore himself after falling; for even to rise again after death is the gift of the blessed.

7. We can also understand that sin is beneficial in other ways, and that, by the Lord’s providence, offenses have overtaken the saints. They are set before us for imitation, and therefore it was arranged that they too should sometimes stumble. For if they had passed through the slippery course of this age without any offense, they would have given us, the weaker, occasion to think that they belonged to some higher and divine nature, so that they could neither receive sin nor share in guilt. Such an opinion would have kept us away from imitation that seemed impossible, as though we had no share in their substance.

God’s grace therefore passes them by for a little while, so that their lives may become a discipline for our imitation, and so that from their deeds we may learn not only innocence but also repentance. Thus, when I read of their falls, I recognize that they share our weakness; and when I believe that they share it, I presume that they are to be imitated.

8. The apostle Paul also reminds us that our Lord God took precautions lest, either through the loftiness of revelations or through the continued success of their works, the human spirit should become exalted even in the saints, and lest they should attribute to themselves and to their own virtue what had been bestowed upon them by divine action (II Corinthians 12:7). Therefore, lest they should rush into so great a danger and fall into the pit of unbelief, the Lord allowed guilt to enter into them, so that they too might recognize their need of divine assistance and understand that they must seek the leader of their salvation.

Finally, Paul testifies that weakness benefited him, when the Lord said to him, as he pleaded that the thorn in his flesh might depart from him: “My grace is sufficient for you; for power is made perfect in weakness” (ibid., 9). And rightly he glories in his weaknesses, for he knew that, through an abundance of virtue, many saints had also fallen irreparably. How much more advantageous, then, to have given place to one or two reproaches than to have drawn upon oneself the offense of the Godhead forever?

## CHAPTER III

David was exposed to temptation because God wishes his athletes to be exercised through various contests and to serve as an example for us; furthermore, his adultery is shown to have been figurative, through various allegories.

9. What shall I add concerning those things that we can infer from the ordinary experience of the world? When we have tested most people in one office, we wish to try those same people, as capable and energetic, in another task. How many athletes, after prevailing in one kind of contest, are summoned to another kind of struggle!

What if the Lord your God, after you have given some proof of your virtue, wishes to test you in another kind of virtue? He allowed holy Job, who was running without stumbling, nevertheless to be tested by the death of his children and by ulcers covering his whole body, so that in this too he might test his virtue: whether, compelled neither by insults nor by hardships, he would diminish the devotion of his affection.

Is it not clear that he also wished to test holy David, renowned for his faith, outstanding for his gentleness, and strong in hand, to see how he would conceal a fault and correct a fall, so that he might teach us how we may cover an admitted sin?

10. Unless someone should perhaps regard it as an insignificant matter that such a great prophet erred for the sake of our correction, even though Christ, for the redemption of all, took upon himself our weaknesses and was made sin for us, although he knew no sin. It is considered unworthy and unbelievable that David should have fallen into the disgrace of a single lapse for the benefit of posterity, when the Lord himself was made a reproach for us, as he says: “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm 21:7). And elsewhere: “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me” (Psalm 68:10).

Therefore, he previously set forth in his own people the mystery of the dispensation that was to come. Servants bore the sins of their own condition, and therefore they too could not be free from sin; but the Lord took upon himself a burden that was not his own, and therefore alone was without any share in sins.

11. In sum, with the Apostle as our teacher, we have learned that many things which took place in earlier times were enacted figuratively. After saying that the fathers in the wilderness, when wounded by serpents, could be healed only if Moses had suspended a bronze serpent, and that, when they looked upon it, those deadly bites and harmful injections of poison were cured, he added: “These things happened to them figuratively” (I Corinthians 10:6), for our correction.

The bronze serpent was figuratively like one fastened to the cross, because the true one who was to be crucified was announced to the human race: he would empty the poisons of the serpent, the devil. In the figure he was accursed, but in reality he was the one who would wipe away the curses of the whole world.

Elsewhere, namely in the Epistle to the Galatians, he says: “Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman” (Galatians 4:22). And he adds: “The one who was by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, but the one by the free woman was born through promise; these things were spoken allegorically” (ibid., 23).

What “allegorically” means he clearly explains in what follows, saying that those two births—one from the slave woman and the other from the free woman—are two Testaments: one, from Mount Sinai, generating slavery, at which mountain Moses received the Law from the Lord; the other, from Jerusalem, which is free, which generated children in Isaac—that is, in the freedom of grace, not in slavery to the letter. Punishment is decreed for slaves; grace is bestowed upon the free.

Did not Jacob, as a type of the two peoples, take two wives from whom he produced different offspring? Why is the patriarch Judah said to have sought intercourse with his own daughter-in-law after the death of his son (Genesis 38:16), from which the birth of twins resulted, unless it was so that, in both cases, Jesus the Lord might be anticipated figuratively by the two Testaments? One of these was established as a type of his future death; the other, in the truth of the Gospel, so that two peoples would be generated, the later of whom, under the sign of the cross, would cut down every hedge and fortification of the earlier people.

This is the people first in hand but later in origin. Or it is because the Lord Jesus himself, born from the tribe of Judah, anticipated his works before he was born for us from the Virgin.

12. Why should I speak of Joseph, who, when attacked by his brothers, stripped of his paternal garment, thrown into a pit, and sold into slavery, clearly expressed the sign of the Lord’s Incarnation? For although he was beloved by the Father and was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself; taking the form of a servant, he came and humbled himself even to death on a cross. By his price, bought and sold by his own brothers, he redeemed the human race.

In his type, David, the younger, chosen from among his brothers and anointed to the kingship, alone faced the danger of battle and, in a single combat, delivered the entire people. He triumphed over ten thousand, so that the maidens sang with tambourines: “Saul has triumphed over thousands, and David over ten thousands” (I Kings 18:7).

What is signified by those young women except souls that sing a triumphant psalm to Christ? He begot from himself two sons, one incestuous and the other parricidal, because the incestuous and parricidal people would violate the flesh of its own author, affixed to the cross’s gibbet. Finally, in the third psalm, the title mentions Absalom, and the Lord’s Passion is prophesied.

13. Why should I speak of holy Solomon, whose later life was not free from serious error, yet whom the Jewish people generally believe to have come in the place of Christ? And how many people did the scandal of his grave error turn away? His greater fault was therefore more beneficial, lest he be believed to be above the human condition, [Note: [Col. 0857C] The Era. and Roman editions have *who had been free from human fault*; Ambrose and Gill., together with the manuscripts, have *who had not been free from human fault*. The latter is suitable, since something such as *as it were* or a similar expression seems to be understood. Again, in the following sense the Era., Gill., and Roman editions have *a persuasion toward guilt*; Ambrose and the manuscripts more suitably have *a persuasive fault*, since it persuaded or demonstrated that Solomon was not above the human condition. Here Ambrose seems clearly not to doubt Solomon’s repentance and salvation, although he does not hesitate to call him holy. Nor is he alone in this view: Cyril of Jerusalem defends it in *Catechetical Lecture* II, and Jerome in his commentary on Ezekiel 43. Jerome elsewhere also reports the Jewish opinion concerning Solomon’s repentance, according to which he wrote the books of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes for that reason. A much larger number of the Fathers believed that he died without any repentance and was therefore condemned to eternal punishment. Among these may be counted Tertullian, Book II *Against Marcion* and elsewhere; Basil, *Letter to Chilo*; Cyprian, Book I, Letter 5; and others, among whom Augustine must not be omitted. Although Augustine deliberately defends the notable men of the Old Testament, he nevertheless declares of Solomon: “Holy Scripture strongly rebukes and condemns him, and makes absolutely no mention of his repentance or of God’s forgiveness.” Finally, some thought that a middle position should be adopted, saying that although nothing concerning his sin was more certain, nothing concerning his repentance was more uncertain, nevertheless, since Scripture determines nothing about his salvation, neither should we determine anything about it.] who had not been free from human fault. Thus his wisdom was liable to envy, and his fault persuasive, since it proved him to be a human being.

14. What prevents us, then, from believing that Bathsheba too was joined to holy David in a figure, so that she might signify the gathering of the nations, which was not joined to Christ by a legitimate marriage of faith, but which, through certain transverse vestibules, would enter into his grace contrary to the prescription of the Law? [Note: [Col. 0858C] The Dion., Colb., and Maz. manuscripts, along with other manuscripts and editions, have *transverse passages*. Again, the Roman and Colbert manuscripts have *apart from the prescribed rights of the Law*; the Benignian, Albinian, and Ambrosian and Erasian editions have *apart from what the rights of the Law prescribe*; the Thuaneus and Dionysian manuscripts have *about to enter beyond the laws, according to the prescription*. Finally, other manuscripts, together with the Gill. and Roman editions, read as we have above. Ambrose himself also recognizes that a mystery existed in this adultery in his *Commentary on Luke*, chapter 3. Whether the sin should be considered removed on account of the mystery, see what we noted on chapter 3, section 13, of the book *On Joseph the Patriarch*.]

In that gathering, the naked sincerity of the mind and open simplicity, through the justifying mystery of the washing, would draw the mind of the true David and eternal King and provoke his love. Rightly he came hidden, as one who would deceive the prince of this world, like that Uriah who transforms himself into an angel of light, and whose name is interpreted as “my light.” He came, I say, into this world, and he came hidden, entering as an adulterer, in order to claim a legitimate right.

## CHAPTER IV

David’s repentance is commended at greater length; by introducing the holiest men, he openly shows that no one is found immune from falling.

15. We have distinguished [Note: [Col. 0858D] The editions have *allegories*; the manuscripts have *arguments*. There is no doubt that he means the allegorical histories of the preceding chapter, though someone might perhaps suspect that *we have distinguished* should be read as *we have touched upon briefly* or *we have sampled*. Nevertheless, *we have distinguished* can be explained as though it read: “We have related each matter in its proper order, not confusedly.”] what we believe to be strong arguments and have established that the text of this history was figurative. Now let us return to what came before and, as though stripping away its spiritual garments, examine the error.

David sinned, as kings are accustomed to do; but he repented, wept, and groaned, as kings are not accustomed to do. He confessed his guilt, begged forgiveness, lay prostrate on the ground and lamented his misery, fasted, prayed, and transmitted the testimony of his confession to all ages through the public expression of his grief. What private persons are ashamed to do, the king was not ashamed to confess.

Those who are bound by laws dare to deny their sin and disdain to ask forgiveness; yet forgiveness was sought by one who was bound by no human laws. That he sinned is a matter of his condition (On Penance, distinction 3, chapter “That King,” § “That He Sinned”); [Note: [Col. 0858D] The older edition, together with a few manuscripts, has *to erase virtue*; the Roman edition, with the rest, has *to wash away virtue*.] that he pleaded is a matter of correction. The fall is common, but the confession is exceptional. To fall into guilt, therefore, is natural; to wash it away is a matter of virtue.

“Who,” he says, “can boast that he has a pure heart?” (Proverbs 20:9). Scripture’s testimony declares that not even an infant of a single day is clean (Job 14:5).

16. Show me someone without a lapse into sin. Samson, the strongest of all, is recorded in the Book of Judges (Judges 14 ff.); he strangled even a lion with his own hands, but would that he had been able to strangle his love as well. He burned the crops of the Philistines, yet he himself burned with the fire of one woman.

Jephthah returned victorious from the enemy; but while bringing back the standards of triumph, he was defeated by his own oath, so that he thought the piety of his daughter who came out to meet him had to be repaid by parricide. First of all, why was it necessary to swear so rashly and to vow uncertain things for certain ones, when he did not know what the outcome would be? Then why did he render such a grievous vow to the Lord God, so as to fulfill his vows with bloody funeral rites?

17. Nor, I think, should we be silent about the priests, lest I seem to conceal our own sins. Aaron himself, the high priest—under whose leadership, together with Moses, the Hebrew people crossed the Red Sea on foot—was asked by the people to make gods for them to worship. He demanded gold, cast it into the fire, and the figure of a calf was formed, to which sacrifices were offered. By this event it became clear that greed for gold is the material of faithlessness, and that sacrileges commonly arise from devotion to avarice.

Again, so great a priest incurred an occasion of offense with his sister Miriam. For when both of them reproached their brother for having taken a foreign wife, Miriam immediately broke out with a contagion of diseased flesh. [Note: [Col. 0859D] That is, leprosy.]

18. Here there was an evident figure of the mystery: that priestly people would, in later times, disparage the fraternal people of the fathers, ignorant of the mystery of that Ethiopian woman. For if it had understood it, it would not have reproached him for something that agreed with the ancient mystery.

Thus, when a Jew calls the one who has believed from the Gentiles “common,” [Note: [Col. 0859D] Here interpret *common* as “impure” and “polluted,” as the word is used in Acts 10:14 and elsewhere.] and wishes to separate him from the Law, he has the leprosy, which he will not be able to escape unless recognition of the spiritual law comes to his aid for pardon.

19. Therefore David too, knowing that he had been born a human being liable to fall, asked forgiveness; yet he did not despair of the Lord’s mercy.

## CHAPTER V

The parable that Nathan proposed to David is explained and applied to Christ and to the human flesh assumed by him.

20. Nor does the parable seem to differ from the mystery. For who is the rich man except our Lord Jesus, who, as we read today, says of himself that “a certain man, when he was rich, went away into a distant country to receive a kingdom and return” (Luke 19:13)?

He was truly rich in the resources of his majesty and in the fullness of his own divinity. Angels and archangels, Virtues and Powers and Principalities, Thrones and Dominions, Cherubim and Seraphim served him with unwearied obedience.

Yet, although he was rich, he left the ninety-nine sheep on the mountains and sought the one sheep that had remained behind in weariness. The prince of this world, needy and poor in comparison with that rich man, was feeding it, as though it were his daughter, with his own provisions. It had rightly grown weak, since the substance it possessed was the food of the world. This sheep had gone astray in Adam, enticed by the serpent’s snares.

21. Yet it was not an evil sheep, since it was full of the Word, being the daughter of the rational week—that is, the spiritual and mystical week, or, as the holy Doctor often says, the intelligible week, namely, the Old Testament. [Note: [Col. 0859D] “The daughter of the rational week,” that is, of the spiritual and mystical week, or, as the holy Doctor often says, of the intelligible week, namely, the Old Testament. For the ancient covenant is signified by the week in other places as well, especially in the letter to Horontianus, where one reads: “The week is of the Old Testament; the eighth day, of the New,” etc. The sense of the entire passage is therefore this: although human nature fell in Adam, it is not evil, since it was created under the Old Testament, under which it also received the predictions and promises of the Word’s incarnation; hence it is called full of the Word.] Yet, although it was the gift of a holy creator, it was for a long time nourished not by precious resources but by the poor man’s worthless provisions.

Finally, he says: “It ate of his bread, drank from his cup, and slept in his bosom” (II Kings 12:3). The food of the Ethiopians is not good; nor is the harmful golden cup of Babylon, which intoxicates the nations. Sleep is not beneficial to those who sleep; it is better for me to keep watch. Finally, all the foolish in heart were troubled; they slept their sleep and found nothing.

Therefore, on account of the hospitality owed to a guest whom he had received in order to provide him with a banquet, he took away that poor man’s sheep. For if he had sacrificed some animal from his own flocks or herds, it could not have benefited us; unless he had sacrificed it, he would not have redeemed us.

22. Therefore, with a hospitable affection, he received the weaknesses of our frailty in his flesh. To lighten—or rather, to restore—that frailty, he offered his flesh to that saving Passion, so that he might also provide us with the food of eternal life.

And Scripture rightly called it a ewe-lamb (ibid.), because it was the offspring of a Virgin. This rich man is rightly pronounced worthy of death by prophetic judgment, because Caiaphas too prophesied when he said: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John 11:50). The Lord Jesus alone was chosen as worthy of such a death, by which he would take away the sin of the world.

He also beautifully added: “He shall restore the ewe-lamb fourfold” (II Kings 12:6), because he resurrected his own flesh and restored that flesh in its virginal integrity. Nor is it without significance that he said, “He shall restore fourfold.” The resurrection of the dead is fourfold, as the Apostle teaches: “It is sown in corruption, it rises in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it rises in glory; it is sown in weakness, it rises in power; it is sown an animal body, it rises a spiritual body” (I Corinthians 15:42 ff.).

He will plainly restore the ewe-lamb fourfold also in the manner by which a person can now say: “If I have taken anything from anyone, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19:8). He appropriately added: “Because he did not spare” (II Kings 12:6); for Christ did not spare himself, so that he might come to the aid of all.

23. Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ said to his servant David, in order to declare the mystery: “Because you did this in secret, I will do this thing before all Israel and in the sight of this sun” (II Kings 12:12).

At first, not understanding the mystery, David was stirred to indignation, but his feeling did not lead him astray. Later, when he understood the great mystery—for great is the mystery of Christ and the Church—and saw the future remission of all sins, foreseeing the radiance of grace through the washing of regeneration and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, he said, confident of pardon: “I have sinned against the Lord.” Thus he too entered the company of those to whom the remission of sins would come.

Do you see how he lamented his own sin? Who, then, should be surprised that it was forgiven him?

## CHAPTER VI

The good and the wicked differ in this: sins follow the former but precede the latter; and the works by which David covered his sin are described.

24. Now let us consider the works by which he was able to cover his sin. Since human frailty cannot exist without sin, we must beware lest there be more sins than works of virtue.

The holy Paul expressed this with great force of wisdom, saying: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment, while those of others follow after” (I Timothy 5:24). That is, no one is found free from fault: a person has good merits, but also vices and sins.

All our deeds are therefore weighed as if on a balance. If sins outweigh good deeds, they go before us to judgment; sins sink down, as it were, into the depths, whether by their weight and bitterness or by their multitude.

“But some,” he says, “they follow”—that is, those who have conducted themselves soberly but, through the frailty of their condition, have at some point given error an opening are preceded by their good deeds, while their evil deeds follow. These are more honorable, yet still human beings who have fallen through lighter vices and errors.

Thus sins follow the just; they do not go before them. They go before the unjust. Sins that sink down outweigh the rest; whatever has been done rightly follows, burdened as though by the prior prejudice of the sins that preceded it.

Good deeds likewise are manifest. They shine through works of virtue and the splendor of merits, and those that are otherwise cannot be hidden. Such sins, therefore, are not covered; the love that covers a multitude of sins does not overshadow them, nor does the grace of good works cover them, nor does the multitude of virtues conceal them. Rather, they are brought forth naked and uncovered.

For there is no one among them who says: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Psalm 16:8). The Lord’s cross wipes out and conceals all errors.

25. Who, then, covered and concealed more than holy David, who elsewhere says: “And I hoped under the shadow of your wings, until iniquity passes away” (Psalm 56:2), and who loved the Lord so greatly that through excessive love he covered and concealed every sin?

For if the holy apostle Peter wiped away his fall by confessing his love, when the Lord asked him three times, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 15:16)—so that the one who had denied him three times might confess him three times and thus conceal the fall of his threefold denial beneath a threefold veil of love—if Peter received forgiveness because he wept once, how much more did David, who washed his bed every night and watered his couch with tears; whose tears were his bread day and night; who ate ashes as bread and mixed his drink with weeping?

For if Jesus has mercy on the one who turns and groans; if he looked upon Peter, and Peter wept—how much more will he not withdraw his gaze from one who wept for a long time?

Peter denied and did not weep because Jesus had not looked upon him; he denied a second time and did not weep because the Lord had not looked upon him; he denied a third time, Jesus looked upon him, and immediately he wept—indeed, he wept most bitterly.

Therefore David, who was always weeping, said: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Psalm 25:15). He who seemed always to be seen by Christ said: “My eyes have flowed down like streams of water” (Psalm 119:136).

26. But let us now also consider his deeds. Who would not have overshadowed the reproach of a single crime with the praise of so many virtues? Chosen by divine judgment, he immediately proved himself not unworthy of so great a judgment.

He went into battle, and while the others trembled, he alone confronted the Philistine Goliath, terrifying because of his boastful words and the massive bulk of his body, and struck him down through the simultaneous action of faith and courage. The courage of one became the victory of all.

If you wish, compare a private crime with a universal triumph, the death of one with the life of so many peoples whom he freed from death.

27. Let us turn to other matters. The king was lying in wait for him and was seeking to destroy his life; but by divine arrangement the king was delivered into his power. When he lay wholly exposed to injury, David’s companions were ready to strike, but holy David intervened and turned back the deadly blow from the body of the one who was about to perish, saying: “Do not touch the Lord’s anointed” (I Kings 24:7). [Note: [Col. 0861D] This is the reading of the Gill. and Roman editions, together with the overwhelming majority of manuscripts. The Ambrosian and Erasian editions have: “holy David, separated from his companions, intervened.” A few manuscripts have: “David, separated from his companions, intervened for the holy man.”]

He even avenged the death of his enemy, lamented his demise with abundant grief, and long deferred the kingdom that he knew was owed to him by God’s authority. By this alone he taught all people not to seize a kingdom, even when it is owed to them, but to wait until it is bestowed at its proper time.

Would that his descendants had imitated this man! We would not have endured such great hardships of war. You accuse him because he killed one man, but you do not consider that he taught how peace might be preserved perpetually throughout the Roman world.

How grievous a devastation do we still suffer, as though paying for the death of a king through the public funeral of the whole world? [Note: [Col. 0862D] That is, the death of the emperor Gratian, as we said in the Preface to this book.] Alas, dreadful punishments! The barbarian enemy still insults us, while the weapons prepared against him are turned against us. Thus the strength of the state has fallen; thus Roman courage, broken by its own upheavals, has grown old and feeble, while what was undertaken in the devotion of paternal concern is seized through public parricide.

He guarded against this to such an extent that, when he discovered that his son Adonijah was usurping the kingdom and arranging assemblies, he chose not the one who was eager to seize it but the one who would wait.

28. The most powerful of kings danced before the Ark of the Lord. When his own wife reproached him for having uncovered himself before the maidens, he replied: “I will uncover myself before the Lord even more, and I will be foolish in your eyes, so that the Lord may be honored, who chose me instead of your father and appointed me king” (II Kings 6:21). He taught that the regard due to royal power has no place when obedience is being offered to religion. [Note: [Col. 0862D] The sentence *For it is honorable to act for the sake of religion*, together with what follows up to the words *Consider another example*, had been omitted from the Roman edition.] For it is honorable to act for the sake of religion, even if such conduct is incongruous with power.

29. Consider another memorable example. His parricidal son had violently invaded his father’s kingdom. At first his father yielded to his fury and avoided the place of battle, so that even in this way the impious son might recover from his rage.
