He also refused to take part in the battle and asked those who were going out to fight to spare his son. He was confident of victory, since he asked that they spare him; nor was he lacking in piety, since he did not think that even an impious son ought to perish.

He wept and lamented the death of the parricide with great mourning, saying: “My son Absalom, who will grant me death for you? My son Absalom!” (II Kings 18:33). He thought that the one who had killed him in defense of his father’s honor ought to be avenged.

30. How patient he was of insult and grief! As I said, he yielded to the fury of his son Absalom, surrounded on his right and left by strong warriors. A man named Shimei cursed him, calling him a bloodstained man and a man of blood, and declaring that he had been deservedly cast down from the kingdom by the judgment of the Lord. Yet he was not moved even by such abuse, although his companions were. Finally, one of his associates—a man named Abishai—threatened that the price of the insult would be Shimei’s head. But the king turned to Abishai and said: “What have I to do with you, son of Zeruiah? Let him curse me, because the Lord has told him to curse me” (2 Samuel 16:10).

How morally instructive he was in teaching that the times of our insults and dangers, the struggles of temptations, and the trials of testing are appointed—and that such things are therefore not ordinarily inflicted without divine judgment! A good athlete is exercised by insults, by hardships, and by dangers, so that he may be worthy to receive the crown of righteousness. Therefore, what are thought to be adversities must be endured patiently. Elsewhere, too, divine Scripture teaches you this through the words of the righteous man: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10).

31. And the holy Prophet added:

> “Behold, my son, who came forth from my womb, seeks my life. But if this Jeminite curses me, leave him to curse, because the Lord has told him to do so, that he may see my humiliation; and the Lord will repay me for this curse” (2 Samuel 16:11–12).

O depth of wisdom! O remarkable patience! O great discovery of how insult may be swallowed! “You are troubled, Abishai,” he says, “that an outsider should curse me, while my son seeks me for slaughter. The Lord has told him to curse me.” Yet the Lord is not a curser, nor does he delight in insults.

32. Observe how carefully he guards each point. He does not accuse the Lord as the author of the insult; rather, he praises him for allowing us to suffer lesser things so that we may obtain pardon for greater sins.

[Note: Seven manuscripts read, “that he allows us to suffer.” “We are unwilling to endure lesser things, so as to obtain pardon for greater things,” and so forth. The remaining manuscripts, and the better ones among them, together with all the printed editions, support our reading.]

Behold, the insult of words lightened the misery of the parricide, and acquitted the insolent man, whose curses were made more beneficial by divine recompense. Who would not balance such an insult against himself, so that God might console the one whom a human being had injured by repaying him with better things? [Col. 0863D] 686

## CHAPTER VII

David’s battles against giants and his libation of the water from the well of Bethlehem; from these and other distinguished deeds it is concluded that his sin was covered—especially since he committed it without a bloodthirsty disposition, and afterward preferred to entrust himself to God rather than to human beings; and since he himself also taught that the crime had been forgiven him.

33. Let us also consider some of his other deeds. He fought against the offspring of giants, when one of them had nearly struck the king who was engaged in battle; yet the audacious adversary paid for the king’s rescue with his death.

34. Having also won this triumph over a conquered and savage nation, he undertook another terrible war in the Valley of the Titans, contending no less against nature than against the enemy. For while he was thirsty and engaged in battle, he had nothing to drink. “Who,” he said, “will give me a drink from the well that is in Bethlehem, by the gate?” (2 Samuel 23:15).

An enemy lay between the well and holy David, with the enemy camp’s fortifications in the middle. Three men cut through the multitude of adversaries, drew water from the well that was in Bethlehem, and brought it to the king to drink. But the king refused to drink it [Col. 0864D] and poured it out to the Lord.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “and he offered it to the Lord.” So also below.]

For it was worthy of so great a gift that what had been the token of living courage should become a sacrifice of piety. And he spoke a sentence worthy of the prophetic spirit:

> “Far be it from me to do this! Is this not the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?” (ibid., 17).

Thus he conquered nature: though thirsty, he did not drink. He also gave the whole army an example by which it might learn to endure thirst. He trained his subjects in the duty of courage, so that soldiers would obey the royal command voluntarily even through danger. His refusal to drink showed that he had ordered the soldiers to be tested, rather than having been overcome by the necessity of thirst. He also took care that no king should seek the use of drinking at the cost of another’s danger. Finally, he sought to avert the wound to his pious conscience: water procured by the blood of so many men could not possess the sweetness of drinking, since it was marked by the horror of a proposed death.

35. But if you wish to look more deeply and to penetrate the mystery, David was thirsty not for water from the well that is in Bethlehem; in the spirit he foresaw Christ, born of the Virgin. He therefore wished to drink not the water of a stream but a drink of spiritual grace. That is, he was not thirsty for the element of water but for the blood of Christ. Accordingly, he did not drink the water that was offered, but poured it out to the Lord, signifying that he thirsted for Christ’s sacrifice, not for a natural stream: for that sacrifice in which there would be remission of sins; for that eternal fountain which he thirsted for—not one obtained through the dangers of others, but one that would dispel the dangers of others.

36. In view of so many deeds, so marvelous, do we not believe that the blood of one man was covered? Rightly did the voice of the blood of righteous Abel cry out to the Lord, because the impious Cain was covered by no good works, because he was a parricide, because he did not confess his crime but denied it. David, however, had indeed killed a man who was entirely innocent; but he had killed him not driven by a desire for cruelty, but in order to obscure his shame and cover the shame of his desire.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “the shame of his conscience”; other editions and manuscripts, more suitably, read, “the shame of his desire.”]

I do not dare to say that he was overcome by the force of sin—for one who knew how to raise himself from that fall of sin was not overcome—but I do say that he was bent by the force of temptation. For above he had said:

> “Test me, O Lord, and try me; burn my reins and my heart” (Psalm 25:2).

And elsewhere:

> “But I said in my prosperity, ‘I shall never be moved’” (Psalm 30:7).

And:

> “You have tested me by fire, and iniquity was not found in me” (Psalm 17:3).

The Lord willed him to be subjected to temptation, lest he arrogate something to himself beyond human capacity; for strength is perfected in weakness.

Nor did he do it with a bloodthirsty disposition. Nothing could be less compatible with the holy Prophet, who even as he was departing from life addressed his son Solomon in his final words, so that he might remove from himself the innocent blood shed by his army commander Joab. Joab had killed Abner when Abner, though commander of the opposing army, had been struck down by an ambush while negotiating an alliance. David mourned him and, after his lamentation, followed the funeral procession, laying aside the insignia of power and performing the proper rites of burial.

[Note: The Remigius manuscript reads, “and walking behind his bier.” The remaining manuscripts and all the editions read, “and after his mourning,” that is, accompanying his funeral procession. For here mourning signifies nothing other than the lamentation mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, where it is said that Stephen, the first martyr, was carried out. Again, where all editions and the great majority of manuscripts read, “he arranged the proper funeral rites,” the Benignus manuscript has “the funeral pyres”; the Albinus manuscript, “the watches”; and the Coenobitic manuscript, “he arranged the vigils.” The word “rites” (*justa*) should nevertheless be retained, since authors commonly use it for funeral offerings or funeral ceremonies.]

By doing this he also taught that a promise of fidelity must be kept even toward adversaries, and that virtue must be honored even in an enemy. Did he not, by such a gentle inheritance of piety, also wipe away the blemish of this error?

37. How remarkable, too, that when three conditions were offered to him, he chose whichever he wished after incurring guilt by numbering the people. He was offered the choice of whether there should be famine throughout the land for three years, or whether he should flee for three months from the face of his enemies pursuing him, or whether death should occur in the land for three days. He chose the third, preferring to fall into the power of the Lord rather than into the power of human beings, since the Lord would quickly have mercy and forgive.

Thus he said:

> “I am in great distress because of these three things; but let me rather fall into the hands of the Lord, for his mercies are very great, than fall into the hands of human beings” (2 Samuel 24:14).

By this humility, prudence, and gentleness he brought it about—if I may use the words of Scripture—that the Lord repented of his own commotion. For it is written:

> “Because the Lord repented of the evil” (Jeremiah 16:19).

38. How remarkable, too, was the following (On Repentance, distinction 3, chapter “Illud vero”): when the angel was striking the people, he offered himself, saying:

> “What has this flock done? Let your hand be against me and against my father’s house” (2 Samuel 24:17).

After this, he was immediately judged worthy of sacrifice, although he had been considered unworthy of absolution. Nor is it surprising that by such an offering of himself for the people he obtained forgiveness of his sin, since Moses, by offering himself to the Lord for the people’s error, also blotted out the people’s sins.

[Col. 0865D] 39. Did he therefore cover his sins, or not? Who could deny it, when the Prophet himself taught that iniquities are forgiven, sins are covered, and are not counted by the Lord? He himself taught that his sin had been forgiven, as it is written:

> “I acknowledge my sin, and I have not covered my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my iniquity to the Lord against myself,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Psalm 32:5).

If he said, “I will confess,” and obtained pardon before he confessed, how much more was every sin forgiven him when he confessed concerning himself, saying:

> “I myself acknowledge my iniquity” (Psalm 51:5)?

Indeed, the prophet Nathan specifically answered him concerning this:

> “The Lord has taken away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13).

40. Thus he both obtained remission of iniquity, covered and concealed his sins by love, and covered them by good works. His sin was not counted against him, because there was no deceit of malice in him but a fall through error. Moreover, there was not a heat of wickedness but the shadow of a mystery. Yet he confessed his offense, acknowledged his iniquity, saw the cleansing bath, and, seeing it, believed. He loved greatly, so that by excessive love he could cover any error.

## CHAPTER VIII

Why Psalm 50 was placed before certain others composed concerning earlier events; and what mysteries are contained in the number fifty. How David’s example teaches the manner in which repentance should be practiced, and how a person may be cleansed from iniquity in many ways.

41. [Note: The Roman edition, omitting the first two lines of this chapter, transferred to the class of Expositions on the Psalms everything that follows from the words “Although he had placed the history of his earlier deeds” to the end of the treatise.]

But now let him defend himself, for he composed Psalm 50 with reference to this history. Although he had placed the history of his earlier deeds before it—such as the betrayal by Doeg the Syrian, whose name appears in the title of Psalm 52, and that of the Ziphites, which seems to be included in the title of Psalm 54—he placed this later history first, even though Doeg had betrayed him earlier, as had the Ziphites, before the prophet David assumed the kingdom. At that time, while fleeing from King Saul, he was still wandering in exile through various remote and secluded places.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “through various deserts.”]

But he took Bathsheba when he was already reigning.

42. Why, then, does the order of the psalms not correspond to the order of the events? Because he wished the mystery to correspond to the events, rather than merely matching one order to another. Therefore he wished to adapt the number of remission to this history.

For the number fifty is the number of remission, as the Lord himself taught us in the Gospel:

> “There were two debtors to a certain moneylender; one owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both. Which of them, then, will love him more?” (Luke 7:41–42).

And in the Law you find (Leviticus 25:10 and following) that the jubilee is called a cycle of fifty years, a most celebrated number in which debts are cancelled, the freedom of the Hebrews is confirmed, and possessions are restored. We joyfully celebrate this number after the Lord’s Passion, when the entire debt of sin has been remitted, the bond of debt also cancelled, and we are free from every tie. We receive the grace of the Holy Spirit coming upon us on the day of Pentecost.

[Note: The Ambrosian, Gillian, and Roman editions, together with a few manuscripts, read, “with the fast vacant”; Erasmus and more manuscripts read, “with the fasts vacant.” Here one may observe the ancient custom of the Church: not fasting throughout the entire fifty days intervening between the feasts of Easter and Pentecost, but more frequently singing the Lord’s “Alleluia” during that period in the divine office. These matters are treated more fully in Book 8 of the Commentary on the Gospel of Luke, at chapter 17.]

The fasts are suspended, praise is offered to God, and “Alleluia” is sung. Finally (Decretum, part 36, question 2, chapter “Denique”), the father of the girl who had been violated by force, though betrothed to no one, shall receive fifty shekels of silver, while she shall remain in the marriage (Deuteronomy 22:29). Thus, by this number, vices too are transformed into grace.

Great, therefore, is the psalm by which we are taught how repentance should be practiced.

43. “Have mercy on me, O Lord, according to your great mercy. And according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity. Wash me greatly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I myself acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always against me. Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Psalm 51:3 and following).

Who among us, even if he confesses his sin, would not think it better to touch upon it briefly than to repeat it? Who would repeat it a second or third time? Observe how many verses the great Prophet uses to resound with his sin, and how no verse is without confession of his offense. He gathered everything together at once, proclaiming his iniquities and his injustice, joining offenses to sins; and by repeating them so often, he rightly asks for great mercy—not merely great mercy, but a multitude of mercies.

What sin, then, could such lamentation fail to wash away? What guilt could such a prayer fail to cleanse? He asks for a multitude of mercies for one sin; we scarcely believe that we should implore his mercy once for many sins.

Moreover, we read that “by his great strength and his exalted arm” he delivered his people from the land of Egypt, when he led them through the Red Sea, in which there was a figure of baptism (Psalm 136:11–12). If great strength was present in the figure of the sacraments, how much greater is the abundance of mercy in their reality? A multitude of mercies is rightly sought where there is a multitude of sinners.

44. “Wash me greatly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Psalm 51:4). He asks not so much to be washed more frequently as more thoroughly, so that he may wash away the filth with which he was conceived. According to the Law, he knew that there were many means of cleansing (Leviticus 11 and 13), but none that was complete and perfect. Therefore, with his whole attention he hastens toward that perfection in which all righteousness is fulfilled, which is the sacrament of baptism, as the Lord Jesus himself teaches.

For when he came to John, the Baptist said:

> “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matthew 3:14).

The Lord replied:

> “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (ibid., 15).

But after Christ had been baptized, and the Holy Spirit had descended upon him like a dove, and the Father had marked the Son from heaven, all righteousness was fulfilled. Therefore the Prophet says: “Wash me greatly from my iniquity.” Great filth and stain are removed not by a slight washing but by a great one.

45. But if anyone wishes to understand this differently, he may shape his interpretation as follows: the divine word cleanses; our confession cleanses—the former when it is heard, the latter when it is uttered. Good thought cleanses; honorable action cleanses; the good practice of one’s way of life also cleanses.

When each person has been cleansed by these things, he more readily draws in—and, as it were, absorbs into himself—the brightness of spiritual grace. For the precious dye does not immediately illuminate the fleece with a single infusion. First the fleece is stained with an inferior dye; then its natural appearance is repeatedly washed out by one dye after another, and it is often changed by different colors. Only afterward is the staining of a fuller bath applied, so that the truer and more perfect brilliance of purple may shine forth.

Thus, just as many sea-snails contribute to the dyeing of purple, so in the bath of regeneration there is a multitude of heavenly mercies, so that iniquity may be blotted out. Therefore, whoever is washed greatly is cleansed from injustice and from sin, and lays aside the ingrained habit of sinning formed by practices and conduct, forgetting its character. And he is rightly washed from injustice or iniquity, which is the greater; he is also cleansed from sin, which is the lesser.

## CHAPTER IX

How few acknowledge their sins with David—or rather, how many boast of them; how the wise person never lays aside the memory of his sin; how great is the power of conscience; that there is a distinction between sin and iniquity; and how both are blotted out by baptism and by repentance joined to love.

[Col. 0868C]

46. Therefore he added: “For I myself acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always against me” (Psalm 51:5). It is no small thing for each person to acknowledge his sin. Therefore he also said above: “Who understands his falls?” (Psalm 19:13)—that is, who is so great as to understand them? It is like the question: “Who will dwell in your tabernacle, or who will ascend the mountain of the Lord?” (Psalm 15:1). This does not mean no one, but few.

For whoever can acknowledge a fall can avoid it and can choose what follows. Most people boast in their falls and think that things which are crimes are grounds for praise. If someone has defiled another man’s marriage bed and overcome the affection of a chaste woman; if someone has changed a widow’s purpose by some fraud; another thinks that living by the murder of a man, by the ambushes of robbery, and by plunder is a virtue; some think that to deceive and trick others is wisdom.

None of these can say, “For I myself acknowledge my iniquity.” Only the one who can grieve over what he has done and condemn what he has committed can say it—the one whom his vices pierce with remorse. Hence the Prophet also says:

> “What you say in your hearts, and be pierced with remorse upon your beds” (Psalm 4:5).

Most horses, when they have fallen, are accustomed to throw themselves about; and those whom a fall has not injured weaken and break themselves by their struggling. Others—for this is said to be the nature of Greek horses—when they have either been thrown down in a chariot race or fallen by chance, are accustomed not to move at all, and maintain a certain discipline of quietness and endurance.

[Note: The skill of those who drove horses in a chariot race consisted in turning the chariot so expertly, amid the horses’ rushing speed, that its wheel-hub came very near the turning-post but did not touch it. For the one who struck it did not escape punishment. It often happened that the chariot was broken, the horses were dashed to the ground, and sometimes even the charioteer was miserably torn apart. Sophocles most elegantly describes the case of Pseudo-Orestes, torn to pieces in such a contest, in the *Electra*. Homer likewise, in *Iliad* 23, introduces Nestor giving careful instructions to his son, who is about to drive a chariot, on how the horses must be guided so that he may reach the prize unharmed. Among other things, he advises him as follows:

> Ἒν νύσσῃ δέ τοι ἵππος ἀριστερὸς ἐγχριμφθήτω,  
> Ὡς ἄν τοι πλήμνη γε δράσσεται ἄκρον ἰκέσθαι  
> Κύκλου ποιητοῖο, λίθου δ᾽ ἀλέασθαι ἐπαυρεῖν,  
> Μήπως ἵππους τε τρώσῃς, κατὰ δ᾽ ἅρματα ἄξῃς.

That is:

> “Let the left-hand horse press close to the turning-post, so that the hub of the well-made wheel may seem to touch its outermost edge, but avoid striking the stone; lest you wound the horses in any way and shatter the chariot by throwing it to the ground.”

Below he likewise recounts the blood-stained fall of one of the competitors. You may consult it if you wish.]

If the fall has not harmed these animals, their quietness benefits them; at any rate, the injury is not aggravated. Should we not judge those who boast of their crimes and think it a mark of virtue when there has been a fall to be worse than mute animals? Therefore it is said, as if to a mute beast:

> “You have sinned; be still” (Genesis 4:7).

47. Hence he beautifully added: “And my sin is always against me.” The foolish person delights in his errors and thinks that by overshadowing old sins with new ones he is helped; therefore he exults in his crime. But the wise person judges that his sin is against him and considers the falls of his offenses to stand against him like hostile battle lines.

Whatever has resounded, whatever has rebuked him, his own guilt always confronts him. Whatever has been said or read, he thinks has been said about him. Whatever he turns his attention to, he thinks that he himself has been marked by a sign—by a gesture, by the eyes.

Whether he feasts, thinks, prays, or pleads, his own error is always before his eyes. At every moment guilt strikes his conscience and does not allow him either to rest or to forget. Like a stern censor, it drives him on through perpetual terror.

Everything, therefore, is adverse to the one who displeases himself: he is his own accuser and his own witness, and he finds nowhere to flee, since he himself presses and goads himself. Yet this belongs to a good mind: to feel the wound of sin. Those who are without pain do not feel the bitterness of the wound, which is an incurable illness; but those who are pierced by some pain, just as they are not without a sense of pain, are not without the progress of health either.

Where there is a sense of pain, there is also a sense of life; to feel is the work and gift of vital strength. Hence the person who does not acknowledge his error is insane, raving, and foolish. But the one who acknowledges it comes to his senses, does not reject the remedies of health, restrains himself, repents of his guilt, thinks of it constantly, and condemns himself by thinking.

For the righteous person is first of all an accuser of himself. Whoever accuses himself is righteous; whoever is righteous is sober and healthy. The righteous person does not know how to favor himself and does not know how to bend the strictness of judgment even in his own case. He shudders at remembering his own fall and blushes at the error he committed. He fears, dreads, and recoils from every memory of it. He judges himself a burden to himself, avoids himself as judge, and does not dare to entrust himself to himself, because he thinks no one is more burdensome to him than the one whom he cannot conceal from, deceive, flee, or avoid—

[Note: Thus all the editions and most manuscripts read. But the Corbeiensis, Albinus, Ebrensis, and Vincentian manuscripts read: “unless he confesses himself subject to conscience.”]

—unless he denies himself to himself and takes up the Lord’s cross.

48. Great is the power of a guilty conscience; great are its punishments. Adam and Eve were afraid, and when they heard the voice of the Lord walking in paradise, they wanted to hide, although no one was seeking them. Cain likewise feared that anyone who found him might kill him. Thus he pronounced sentence upon himself, judging that he was worthy of having no one forgive him.

Hence he says well: “And my sin is always against me”—that is, without any interruption, the recollection and very image of my error attack me. Consider how it confounds us when we have committed something, how it assails our eyes, and how it continually returns to our memory. The one who is ashamed of what he has committed does not afterward know how to commit something similar, of which he would likewise be ashamed.

49. Iniquity precedes; sin follows.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “Iniquity is the root of sin.”]

Iniquity is the root, while guilt is the fruit of the root. Hence iniquity seems to refer to wickedness of mind, and sin to a bodily fall. Iniquity is more serious, as the material of sins; sin is lighter.

Finally, iniquity is forgiven through the bath, while sin is covered by good deeds and overshadowed, as it were, by other works.

[Note: The old edition reads, “by good deeds, and as if by evil things”; the Roman edition reads, “and by good works as by wings,” which is not unsuitable. Nevertheless, almost all the manuscripts support our reading.]

Hence he himself says well above:

> “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Psalm 32:1).

Love conceals error and covers a multitude of sins. Great love also forgives sins themselves, as it is written of the woman who poured perfume over the Lord:

> “Her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47).

50. There are also those who understand the first verse as referring to the bath, and the second to repentance. It was for this reason, they say, that Peter—who had already been baptized—was questioned after he had appeared to deny the Lord:

> “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He said to him, “Certainly, Lord, you know that I love you” (John 21:15 and following).

Again he was asked:

> “Simon, son of John, do you love me?”

And again he replied:

> “You know that I love you.”

A third time he was asked:

> “Simon, son of John, do you love me?”

And he was saddened because he said to him a third time, “Do you love me?” And he said to him:

> “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you.”

And it was said to him three times:

> “Feed my sheep; follow me” (ibid., 18),

as though he had covered his sin by excessive love. It was not without purpose that, after his confession of excessive love, he was ordered to govern the people: even when disturbed, he had not lost the ability to govern himself.

We have said this because of the grace of love, since love covers sin. Accordingly, some have said that the triple questioning about love took place because the denial had been threefold, so that the fall of the threefold denial might be erased by the confession of love repeated three times.

## CHAPTER X

Although David was free from human laws, he nevertheless subjected himself to God, against whom alone he had sinned; and in how many ways this last statement should be understood. The great crime of sinning in God’s presence. Whoever denies that he is a sinner accuses God himself of falsehood; God’s patience and moderation are commended. Moreover, God is justified by the one who repents of his error.

51. It follows: “Against you alone I have sinned” (Psalm 51:6). He was, of course, a king and was bound by no human laws, since kings are free from the bonds of offenses; they are not summoned to punishment by any laws, being protected by the power of their rule. Therefore he had not sinned against a human being to whom he was not subject.

But although he was protected by his authority, he was subject to God in devotion and faith. Recognizing himself as subject to God’s law, he could not deny his sin; rather, he confessed it bitterly as a defendant, knowing that he was held by greater bonds because he owed more, since more is required from the one to whom more has been entrusted.

We may also understand it in this way: Who can judge me, when everyone is under sin? Finally, concerning the adulterous woman the Lord said:

> “Let the one who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:7).

And no one threw a stone at her. Thus the Prophet says: “Against you alone I have sinned,” because you alone are without sin. But the person subject to sin cannot, as a sinner, judge another sinner.

For every person is without excuse who condemns in another what he himself does; in judging another, he condemns himself. “Against you,” he says, “I have sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Psalm 51:6).

“Against you I have sinned,” who called me to pursue virtue, who instructed me in your law. “Against you alone I have sinned,” whom alone the hidden thoughts and secrets of the mind cannot deceive.

52. “And I have done evil before you,” whom alone sanctification becomes. We avoid the testimony of human beings, yet commit what is unworthy in your sight. It is an insult to a human being to look upon crimes. We know that God is the judge of all things, yet we sin with him himself as witness.

Nevertheless, in these very things the Lord our God is more greatly justified, because our injustice commends God’s justice, and our falsehood celebrates God’s truth with praise:

> “Let God be true, and every human being a liar.”

53. “So that you may be justified in your words.” God’s words are full of truth and justice. Therefore whatever the Lord has said concerning human frailty is true: their heart is inclined toward wickedness and tends toward deceit; and he has determined that there is no person who does not sin. “All have turned aside and become worthless” (Psalm 14:3).

He prevails when he is judged because the fall of all has proved everything he judged concerning our falsehood. Therefore, if we say that we have committed iniquity, we justify God in his words; but if we say that we have not sinned, we make God a liar. Yet it is impossible for him to lie. It is therefore clear that we are all under sin.

54. How great a crime, then, is it for a person to deny that he is a sinner? For, insofar as it depends on him, he appears to accuse the Most High God of falsehood—

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “we seem to accuse the Most High God of the greatest lie.”]

—who is so moderate and patient that he prevails when he is judged.

For God comes to judgment and says:

> “My people, what have I done to you? Or in what way have I grieved you? Or in what way have I troubled you? For I brought you up from the land of Egypt, and I freed you from the house of slavery, and I sent Moses, Aaron, and Miriam before you. My people, remember what Balak intended against you” (Micah 6:3 and following).

He places each of his benefits before your eyes, so that you may judge, as it were, on the basis of the things you ought to have preserved, and so that you may become all the more guilty because you were unable to stand by the divine benefits.

“What have I done to you?” he says, as though he were placing himself on trial and making you the judge.

“Or in what way have I grieved you?” His offended countenance does not deny the charge, if you have been grieved with God as its author.

“Or in what way have I troubled you?” He acknowledges the injury of the appeal, if he has been judged troublesome. He added the benefits, whose grace did not make the ungrateful man ashamed.

In this matter also consider how the Lord offered himself to be judged by David, so that he might prevail. Nathan says:

> “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you from the hand of Saul, and I gave you all that belonged to your master, and I gave your master’s wives into your embrace, and I gave you the house of Israel; and if these things are too little, I will add more to you. Why, then, have you despised the Lord, so as to do evil in his sight?” (2 Samuel 12:7 and following).

Confronted with these recollections, and seeing himself inferior when he was judged, he said:

> “I have sinned against the Lord” (ibid., 13).

Thus he justified the Lord, since he did not dare deny his sin.

55. We may also understand it in this way: the person who confesses his sin justifies the Lord. Thus in the Gospel you find that “the tax collectors justified God, having been baptized with the baptism of John” (Luke 7:29). John the Baptist, however, administered a baptism of repentance. The one who repents does not deny his offenses.

Therefore, because David always had his sin against himself, he certainly did not deny what he also blushed at; he did not deny what he also acknowledged. By not denying it, he practiced repentance for the error he had committed. Thus, by confessing his offense, he justified the Lord, and he himself was justified by the Lord.

The Lord is justified when his righteousness is proclaimed and forgiveness is sought from him. At the same time, he justifies the one who confesses, and he is justified in his words, as it is written:

> “Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:26).

## CHAPTER XI

The words of the Prophet teach that no one is conceived without iniquity. Whether this iniquity belongs to the parents or to the offspring; and how Christ alone is shown to have been free from it.

56. For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother brought me forth (Ps. 50 [51]:7). Who undertakes repentance with such devotion? He lay prostrate on the ground, poured out in tears, tasted no food, and abstained from bathing. Why should I now mention the rest—that he abstained from royal adornment and finery (cf. Augustine, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, Book IV, chapter 11)?

[Note: All editions and by far the majority of manuscripts read *quod abstinuerit ab ornatu et comitatu regio* (“that he abstained from royal adornment and retinue”); the most highly approved [manuscripts read] “and from royal adornment and finery.” Neither reading is objectionable.]

He added a confession of his iniquity and handed it down to be sung throughout the whole world for all ages. “For behold,” he says, “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother brought me forth.”

[Note: The Roman editors had omitted the following three verses of Psalm 50.]

“Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities. Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. Deliver me from bloodshed, O God, God of my salvation.”

Before we are born, we are stained by contagion; before we make use of the light, we receive the injury of our very origin. We are conceived in iniquity: he did not specify whether it was the iniquity of our parents or our own. And his mother brings each one forth in sins; here too he did not make clear whether the mother gives birth in her own sins, or whether there are already some sins belonging to the one being born. But see whether both possibilities are to be understood.

[Note: The manuscripts and the old editions agree throughout this passage; the Roman edition, however, reverses the wording as follows: “It should be understood that the parents too are not without sin, and that conception is not free from iniquity. For if not even an infant of one day is without sin, much less are the days of its mother’s conception without sin. Indeed, marriage is good and the marital union holy, since marriage is honorable and the marriage-bed undefiled. Yet those who have wives should be as though they had none; and no one ought to defraud the other, except perhaps for a time, so that they may devote themselves to prayer, and then come together again, lest Satan tempt them because of their lack of self-control. We are therefore conceived in the sins of our parents, and born in their transgressions. But birth itself also has its contaminations, and nature itself has not merely one kind of contagion. Hence, under the Law, the days of childbirth, and many other days, were excluded from sacrifice: for a woman who has given birth cannot offer sacrifice during the days of her purification, nor enter the Sanctuary, until she has been cleansed from the child by the prescribed rite.”]

Nor is conception free from iniquity, since the parents too are not without transgression. And if not even an infant of one day is without sin, much less are the days of its mother’s conception without sin. We are therefore conceived in the sin of our parents and born in their transgressions. But birth itself also has its contaminations, and nature itself has not merely one kind of contagion.

[Col. 0873D] But marriage is indeed good, and the marital union holy; yet those who have wives should be as though they had none. The marriage-bed itself is undefiled; nevertheless, no one ought to defraud the other of it, except perhaps for a time, so that they may devote themselves to prayer. Yet, according to the Apostle, a person is not devoted to prayer during the time when he practices that bodily intercourse, and the cloth of a menstruating woman is unclean; nor can she offer sacrifice during those days of her purification. The days of childbirth for a woman who has given birth, and many other days, are likewise excluded from sacrifice, until the woman who has borne the child is cleansed by the prescribed rite.

57. Therefore, because the Lord willed that no such contaminations of origin should exist in him, the Lord says to him: “Before I formed you in your mother’s womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you, and appointed you a prophet among the nations” (Jer. 1:5). Who is so great, to whom such great things were entrusted?

[Note: Thus read the manuscripts and all the editions except the Roman, which has: “Is it perhaps Jeremiah? Certainly not. For he was appointed prophet not among the nations, but only in Judea, although now also among the nations … See therefore,” etc.]

Is it perhaps Jeremiah? Yet he was certainly not appointed a prophet among the nations, but in Judea at that time; now, however, he is also among the nations that have believed in Jesus Christ the Lord. See, however, whether this is not said of him who, before he was born from the Virgin, already existed from long ago, indeed always existed, and was also at work while he was present in Mary’s womb; and who was so holy that he sanctified his prophets. In him alone both the virginal conception and the birth were without any stain of mortal origin.

For it was fitting (cf. Augustine, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, Book IV, chapter 11) that he who was not going to have the bodily sin of falling should feel no natural contagion of generation. Rightly, therefore, David lamented in himself, with tears, the very contaminations of nature: that in the human being the stain should begin before life.

## CHAPTER XII

*That heavenly sacraments are divinely disclosed to the one who confesses sin; that when these things are called uncertain in the psalm, this signifies not that they are uncertain but that they are not yet manifest; and that above all the washing of baptism is prefigured in this passage.*

58. While he says these things and confesses the flood of particular and common sins, suddenly the splendor of truth and the radiance of spiritual grace shone upon him. Having passed beyond the shadow, he saw, by the prophetic Spirit, the very sacramental mysteries of heaven, whose type Moses prefigured in the Law (Exod. 24:7 ff.). Wounded, therefore, by the wound of love and seized by the desire to investigate the truth, he extended the gaze of his mind toward higher things; and, looking into the future, he saw the treasures of wisdom and knowledge in Christ. He foresaw the sacrament of baptism and, amazed at grace, suddenly cried out, saying: “For behold, you have loved truth; you have manifested to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Ps. 50 [51]:8).

The mysteries are not uncertain, for they are certain; nor are the secrets and hidden things of wisdom uncertain, but they are not manifest. This is what the passage signifies: that they had not yet been manifested to anyone. “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—this God has prepared for those who love him.” Seeing these things, therefore, he says: “Behold, now light shines openly, not in shadow, nor in figure, nor in type, but in truth. Behold, now I look upon the truth; I recognize the splendor of truth. Now I venerate you with greater devotion, Lord our God. For behold, you have loved truth—not through a mirror, not in an enigma, but face to face you have shown yourself to me, O Christ; in your sacraments I find you. These are the true sacraments of your wisdom, by which the hidden things of the mind are cleansed.”

59. Therefore, now joyful and secure because the fullness of wisdom had flashed its rays upon him,

[Note: “Had flashed” requires the supplement “its rays,” that is, “had shone.”]

he says to the Lord: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50 [51]:9). He rightly neither abolishes the sacraments of the Old Testament nor fails to teach that the mysteries of the Gospel are to be preferred. According to the Law, he asks to be cleansed with hyssop (Exod. 12:22); according to the Gospel, he longs to be washed; and he considers that, if he has been washed, he will be made whiter than snow.

The one who desired to be cleansed by the baptismal type was sprinkled with the blood of the lamb by means of a bundle of hyssop (Lev. 14:6). He is washed who is drenched by the irrigation of the eternal spring; and he is made whiter than snow to whom guilt is forgiven. Finally, it is said of the soul itself: “Who is this who comes up made white?” (Song 8:5). Before it was baptized, it was the one that said: “I am black and beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1:5). For it was black, dark, and disfigured by the horror of sins; but afterward, having been washed and having obtained forgiveness of transgressions through baptism, it ascended to Christ made white.

Hence also the Lord spoke through Isaiah, saying: “If your sins are like scarlet, I will make them white as snow” (Isa. 1:18)—that is, if they are bloody and foul, I will cleanse them. This is the intelligible snow of which he says that the garments of the Lord Jesus shone like snow in the Gospel (Matt. 17:2), because sin did not know the flesh.

[Note: Thus read the Gill and Roman editions, together with several manuscripts: “because his flesh did not know sin.” The American and Erasmian editions read: “because his flesh, with which he clothed himself when he came into this world, did not know sin …” Four manuscripts read: “because his flesh, with which he clothed himself … had been free from every [sin].” It is not objectionable to add the conjunction *et* (“and”), as the second hand of the Corbie manuscript has done. Vincentius’s reading is better: “because, when he clothed himself [with it], it had been clean from sin,” a reading not far removed from Albertus’s playful wording: “since, when he clothed himself [with it], it had surely been cleansed from sin.”]

For the flesh with which he clothed himself had been clean from every sin. Why are you surprised that he saw the mysteries of baptism, when above, in describing the Lord’s Passion, he had said: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of green pasture he has settled me; beside the water of refreshment he has led me” (Ps. 22 [23]:1–2)? And elsewhere: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of majesty has thundered” (Ps. 28 [29]:3). And of that sacrament itself he said more fully: “You have prepared a table before me; you have anointed my head with oil, and your cup, which makes drunk, how glorious it is!” (Ps. 22 [23]:5).

[Note: This signifies the Eucharist, which other Fathers also customarily call simply and by antonomasia “the sacrament.” Ambrose speaks this way not only here, but often elsewhere, especially in *On the Mysteries*, chapters 8 and 9, where he quotes this very passage in the following form: “Then the baptized people came and, seeing the holy altar prepared, cried out, saying: ‘You have prepared a table before me.’ David introduces it speaking in this way: ‘The Lord feeds me … You have prepared a table before me against them,’ etc.”]

## CHAPTER XIII

*David, revived solely by hearing of the future forgiveness, foretells that his humbled bones will rejoice; and what those bones are. God is to be entreated to turn his face away from our sins and to turn it instead toward us; likewise, just as sin is removed, so also is iniquity, its source, removed in the threefold manner explained here.*

[Col. 0876B]

60. Rightly, therefore, rejoicing here also, he says: “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and my humbled bones will rejoice” (Ps. 50 [51]:10). You have proved, Lord Jesus, that your words never pass away (Matt. 24:35). You have proved that Gospel saying which you uttered: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and to hear what you hear” (Matt. 13:17). Behold, David rejoices merely by hearing that the forgiveness of sins would come, and he prophesies that his humbled bones will rejoice.

Just as all the bones of the righteous will say, “Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. 34 [35]:10), so the humbled bones will rejoice—those, namely, of the righteous person who humbles his soul.

[Note: The Roman edition presents this passage in the following form: “For the righteous are said to humble their soul; therefore the bones are called virtues. For these, like certain movements of the soul, are humbled by sins and rejoice in grace,” etc. The other editions agree very closely with the manuscripts, except that elsewhere one finds “those who humble … bones of virtues,” while elsewhere the reading is “of the one who humbles … bones of virtue.” We did not think it necessary to depart from them, except in punctuation, which we have altered somewhat to make the sense clearer.]

Bones, therefore, are called virtues; bones are called, as it were, certain movements of the mind or of the soul—movements that are humbled by sins and rejoice through the gift of heavenly grace. Bones are also called the people of the Churches; hence you find it said in the psalm: “My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret” (Ps. 138 [139]:15). He called the Church his bone, and the holy gatherings of the devoted people, since we are members of Christ’s body, of his flesh and of his bones. This, then, is what he says: that the Church of the Lord will know all the divine works and will receive faith in the resurrection.

61. It follows: “Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (Ps. 50 [51]:11). It is a customary prayer that we ask those whom we have injured to forget their own offense. Morally, therefore, the Prophet asks God to turn his face away from his sins and, as it were, to assume forgetfulness of his transgressions. But because God observes everything and nothing escapes him, he cannot forget as we do, whose memory, after a short interval of time, lets slip the things we have come to know.

Therefore he rightly says that God should turn his face away—not from the sinner himself, lest he fail because he has been abandoned, but from his sins, so that his sins may have no power. For those whom the Lord looks upon he illumines, and in the face of the Lord there are mercy and forgiveness. Hence he himself says here: “From your face let my judgment come forth” (Ps. 16 [17]:2); for from the face of the Lord forgiveness proceeds, not punishment.

We must therefore ask him to look upon us, but to turn his face away from our sins, so that he may blot them out. For whatever he does not look upon, he blots out; and whatever he has blotted out will be buried in forgetfulness, as the Lord himself says: “I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them; but you, remember, and let us be judged” (Isa. 43:25–26).

62. Sin is either forgiven, blotted out, or covered: it is forgiven by grace, blotted out through the blood of the cross, and covered by love.

[Note: *De poenitentia*, distinction 3, chapter “Ille rex,” section “Peccatum aut donatur.”]

In the same way, iniquity—understood as the settled disposition of an unjust mind—is either forgiven, blotted out, or covered. Although John said in his epistle that the one who commits sin has also committed iniquity, as we read: “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity” (1 John 3:4)—sin is iniquity, because in the sin itself there is iniquity—nevertheless, as it seems to us,

[Note: All editions and several manuscripts read: “every sin is iniquity.” A larger number of more ancient manuscripts read: “sin is the work of iniquity … Therefore it is more,” etc. Gratian has: “Therefore it is prior,” etc.]

sin is the work of iniquity, while iniquity is the producer of guilt and transgression. It is therefore something greater that iniquity itself be blotted out: that the root and seedbed of sins be cut away; that the evil root be removed, lest it produce evil fruits; that every inclination toward error be abolished and every kind of iniquity be removed.

63. Therefore, just as the discipline of wisdom, entering the soul, removes imprudence, and knowledge removes ignorance, so perfect virtue removes iniquity, and the forgiveness of sins blots out every sin. Hence the Apostle says splendidly: “The Lord Jesus forgave us our sins, erasing the bond of the decree that stood against us; and he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross” (Col. 2:14). By his blood he blotted out Eve’s ink; he blotted out the bond of a condemned inheritance. Faith therefore diminishes sin. And for this reason, when the Lord forgave sins, he said: “Let it be done to you according to your faith” (Matt. 8:13).

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.”]

## CHAPTER XIV

*That a clean heart belongs only to those who have been renewed; what the “inmost parts” and the “spirit” are that the holy Prophet mentions here; that the turning away of the Lord’s face is a form of severe punishment, and how he casts someone away from his presence; who are subject to this most dreadful punishment; after which something is briefly touched upon concerning the freedom and unity of the will in the Trinity.*

64. It follows: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inmost parts” (Ps. 50 [51]:12). Above, he asks to be cleansed from hidden things (Ps. 18 [19]:13); here he asks that a clean heart be created for him, something that comes to the one who is renewed in spirit. For in the new human being the heart is clean, in whom the foulness of former sins has been wiped away and no image of iniquity has remained engraved.

It is a great gift to possess a clean heart. Hence Solomon says beautifully: “Who can boast that he has a pure heart?” (Prov. 20:9). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). The Prophet David also desired to possess a clean heart, lest he be cast away from the face of the Lord.

65. In the one whose heart is clean, the spirit within his interior parts is renewed. For the inmost parts are, as it were, the interior organs of the body; likewise there are intelligible inmost parts of the soul, such as “the inmost parts of mercy” (Col. 3:12), and those interior faculties that bless the Lord, concerning which it is said: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all my inmost parts, his holy name” (Ps. 102 [103]:1).

[Note: Thus read the old edition and the most ancient manuscripts. The Roman edition, together with more recent manuscripts, has: “The interior parts are those of the soul; for just as the inmost parts are the interior organs of the body, so …” But since the former readings produce the proper sense, it is credible that the writers of the latter indulged their pens.]

The inmost parts of the soul are the inventions of the senses, the pursuits of good thought, perseverance in the virtues, and finally those things called in Greek *εὐνομίαι*—“good orders” or “right dispositions.”

66. The right spirit is the spirit that directs well and leads along the right way; this is the spirit of truth. Or certainly it is the upright conscience of a person, bent by no sins; or the spirit that is in the human being. We have not overlooked what others think; nevertheless, it seems to us that, since the reading speaks of mysteries, the renewal of future grace is expressed and the infusion of the Holy Spirit is requested.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “the renewal of future grace.” Again, in this very passage, the Erasmian edition, together with a few manuscripts, has: “the infusion of the Holy Spirit is requested,” and some repeat the word “seems.” The American, Gill, and Roman editions, together with the greater number of manuscripts, agree with our reading. It should further be noted that the word *quoniam* (“since”) in this sentence, as often elsewhere in this Father, is used for the Greek *ἔτι*, and means the same as if it were written: “The reading seems to speak of mysteries … grace is expressed … infusion is requested.”]

67. Then it follows: “Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50 [51]:13). If one of our servant-boys offends us, we customarily turn our face away from him. Many wealthy people have also been accustomed to send their slaves away and banish them to little farms, and this punishment is considered more severe.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “They have been accustomed to correct them … and to confine them to little farms.”]

In the end, they generally prefer to offer themselves to be flogged. If this is considered serious among human beings, how much more so before the Lord our God. As though this were not the source of the murderous grief—though it should certainly have been restrained if any piety could have tempered it—that God turned his face away from Cain’s offerings, while he looked upon Abel’s offerings. Thus, by the silent expression of his face, he pronounced one innocent and the other a sinner.

Therefore, like the lowest servant, he humbles himself; and, as one caught in sin and liable for an offense, he begs to be scourged rather than cast away from the face of the Lord.

68. Hear how God casts someone away from his face: “Take him away into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22:13).

[Note: Four manuscripts of better quality read: “For the one who is cast away from his face is placed in darkness.”]

The one who is not corrected is placed in darkness, away from his face. Therefore, lest the righteous suffer darkness, he says: “I will seek your face, O Lord” (Ps. 26 [27]:8). For where the face of the Lord is, there is light, as it is written: “Make your face shine upon your servant” (Ps. 118 [119]:135). Finally, as soon as he looked upon Peter, he saw him and illumined him.

69. Great, therefore, is the punishment of being cast away from the face of God. Adam was cast away when he left paradise, and deservedly so; for he had first hidden himself from the face of God.

[Note: All editions and many manuscripts read: “Adam was cast away from paradise, and deservedly so.” Eight very ancient manuscripts read: “Adam, when he went out from paradise, was cast away, and deservedly so.” The appropriate sense requires *projectus est* (“was cast away”) to refer not to the words “from paradise,” but to the words “from the face of the Lord.”]

Cain also went out from the face of God, not only after committing the murder, but also after he thought that God could be deceived and denied the crime. The sinner, therefore, is excluded from the face of God; but the righteous says: “Here am I” (Isa. 6:8). Finally, when David saw the people perishing, he offered himself, saying: “I am the one; I have sinned, and I, the shepherd, have acted wickedly” (2 Kings 24:17). Thus the anger of the Lord was appeased, and forgiveness was granted.

70. At the same time, he shows that the holy remain, while the guilty are cast away. Therefore we must preserve spiritual grace, lest it be taken from us on account of our sins. For the one in whom the Holy Spirit is present is not cast away; rather, with the fruit of his gift uninjured, he strives always to offer himself to the Lord, like the one who, when the Lord said, “Do you also wish to depart?” replied: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we believe” (John 6:68–69).

71. We must also consider that the Spirit is taken away only by the will of the Lord,

[Note: The words “just as he is given only by the will of the Lord” were missing from the editions; we restored them on the authority of our manuscripts—Corbie, Reims, Theodore, and Dionysius.]

just as he is given only by the will of the Lord. When he is given, he does not work as though compelled, but is distributed according to his will, as the Apostle says: “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11). Since, therefore, he is taken away only by the will of the Lord, it is clear that the Trinity has one will.

## CHAPTER XV

*That only the rational nature is capable of saving joy, and that it is strengthened by the princely Spirit; and which Spirit this is.*

72. “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit” (Ps. 50 [51]:14).

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “To the one to whom saving joy is owed, it is restored; it is restored to rational nature. But joy …”]

To the one to whom it is owed, it is also restored: saving joy is restored to rational nature. Joy and gladness are a fruit of the Spirit. Our support also is the princely spirit. Finally, the one who is strengthened by the princely spirit is not subject to slavery; he does not know how to serve sin, does not know how to waver, does not know how to go astray, and does not totter uncertainly in his purpose. Rather, established upon the rock, he is stabilized by a firm footing.

73. Whom do we think is called the princely spirit? Most people refer the right spirit to the Lord Jesus, who took away the sin of the world and renewed the whole human race through the shedding of his blood. Therefore it is said: “Renew a right spirit within me.” They understand the Holy Spirit, of whom he says, “Do not take your Spirit from me,” as the Spirit of truth; but they consider God the Father to be the princely Holy Spirit.

How morally, however, he says: “Do not cast me away from your face.” With faithful fear he dreads that the grace he received should be taken from him; therefore elsewhere he says: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. 24 [25]:15). And later: “Behold, as the eyes of servants are toward the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant are toward the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us” (Ps. 122 [123]:2). Certainly this is the Spirit who teaches and rules, who governs the mind, strengthens the affections, draws them where he wills, and directs them toward the higher life.

74. There are also those who understand this as the human spirit, which is in the human being. Therefore the Apostle says: “For who knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him?” (1 Cor. 2:11). The one who can know everything, whom the hidden things of a human being do not deceive, can hold primacy within the human being.

## CHAPTER XVI

*That it belongs to an experienced teacher to teach the wicked the ways of the Lord; how this may be applied both to the person of Christ and to that of David; and what the Prophet asks when he prays to be delivered from bloodshed.*

75. It follows: “I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly will turn back to you” (Ps. 50 [51]:15). He is the outstanding helmsman who steers a ship along a rocky shore; he is the good teacher who sharpens more difficult minds for the progress of learning; he is the excellent warrior, the remarkable commander, who rouses the more timid to battle and, having examined the character of the terrain, supports them, so that he compensates for weakness of strength by the advantage of a favorable position. Likewise, he is the great zealot for the faith who teaches the wicked.

[Note: Some ancient codices read: “a preacher of the faith.”]

Hence he says beautifully: “I will teach the wicked.” He did not say, “I will teach the righteous,” for the righteous know the ways of the Lord; but, he says, “I will teach the wicked.” Finally, the author of prudence and teacher of all says: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. 9:13). And that heavenly physician says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:12).

76. Therefore, whether he speaks in the person of the one who called the nations, or in his own person, he rightly says: “I will teach the wicked your ways,” because vicious affections can be changed, a purpose can be converted by heavenly teaching, and divine action can infuse devotion into sacrilegious hearts. Thus those who lived without the law may turn to the true Lord, from whom they had formerly turned away. Likewise, by the example of royal repentance, those who practice iniquities and grievous crimes may be corrected; and, converted in faith and conduct, they may receive the remedy of saving instruction and enter the ways of the Lord, in which they encounter no winding paths of error and no byways of ruinous falling.

For just as an example of good life and a model of virtue is found in those who have passed through the years of their life without offense, so those who renounce their former crimes or errors of unbelief and amend the course of their later life are set before those who fall either in deed or in thought, so that they may imitate them.

77. It follows: “Deliver me from bloodshed, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. 50 [51]:16). This may also be referred to the death of Uriah, since David, conscious of having ordered his death, asks forgiveness for so great a crime. Although, as king, he was absolved by the laws, he was nevertheless guilty in his conscience. Desiring to be untied from these bonds, he prays for divine assistance, that he may be cleansed from every stain of the crime he committed.

And indeed, since the holy Prophet, gentle and meek of heart, had always displayed outstanding marks of his gentleness and piety, so that he frequently forgave his adversaries and thought it necessary to refrain from killing them, it is not surprising that he should grieve so deeply that the sin of shedding innocent blood had crept into his life. Therefore he asked to be delivered from bloodshed—that is, from mortal sins. He praised the Lord his God and proclaimed the Lord’s justice; for this reason he added: “My tongue shall exult in your justice.”

## CHAPTER XVII

*That David signifies by his words that his sin has been forgiven, since God shuts the sinner’s mouth; that the same words also apply to Christ, since he is the true David, by whom the future gathering of the nations and the founding of the Churches are prefigured; finally, the work is concluded with several observations concerning the sacrifice of Christ and of the martyrs.*

78. “Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise” (Ps. 50 [51]:17). The one who praises the Lord will be saved from his enemies, as it is written (Ps. 17 [18]:4). Certainly, above, in the forty-ninth psalm, he had said: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my justice?” (Ps. 49 [50]:16). Since, then, through his own mouth he had said that God had forbidden the sinner to recount his justice, by recounting God’s justice he himself clearly showed that this sin had in no way been imputed to him.

[Note: Many manuscripts read: “that it had not been imputed to him as his sin.”]

79. And he added: “You will open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise.” God closes the mouth of the sinner, so that he may not speak of God’s justice; he opens that of the righteous, so that he may speak. Therefore, whose lips he opens, that person he absolves from the guilt of sin. The Lord opens the lips of the one who receives the word in the opening of his mouth. Hence the Apostle also asks to be helped by the prayers of the people, so that a door of the word may be opened to him for speaking the mystery of Christ (Col. 4:3).

We take “tongue” to mean the speech of the one who exults in the praises of God. Hence that saying is also understood in this way: “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Ps. 44 [45]:2)—the speech infused into the Prophet.

80. But if we understand this as spoken in the person of Christ, see whether the scribe is not the Word of God writing swiftly, passing through and penetrating the inmost parts of the soul, and inscribing in it either the gifts of nature or those of grace. The tongue, meanwhile, is that holy body born of the Virgin, through which the poisons of the serpent were emptied and the works of the Gospel, destined to be celebrated throughout the whole world, were carried out.

What further removes sin is that he assumed humility; he crushed his heart, which the Lord chose as a sacrifice more than holocausts for sins, which were accustomed to be offered according to the Law. Hence above he says: “You did not desire sacrifices or offerings for sin; then I said: Behold, I come” (Ps. 39 [40]:7–8)—that is, I did not consider it robbery to be equal with God; I come, taking the form of a servant. I come in the appearance of an assumed humanity, in the reality of the cross, to prove obedience through the humility of death, so that sin might be blotted out through obedience.

81. Rightly, therefore, he also says here: “For if you had desired it, I would surely have given sacrifice; you will not be pleased with holocausts. A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50 [51]:18–19). And, as I said above, it is certain that what we see here agrees with the mystery: the Lord Jesus himself appears to speak here also in his own person, since above he uttered that statement with clear testimony concerning his own person.

For he himself is the true David, strong of hand, truly humble and meek, first and last—first in eternity, last in humility. Through his obedience the guilt of the human race was erased and righteousness was poured back upon it. Jesus himself, I say, the end of shadow and of the Law, came as the teacher of humility, teaching the proud in understanding that they must turn to meekness and simplicity, they who are puffed up by the swelling of their hearts.

How, then, can sin be imputed in the type of his mystery, when forgiveness of sins is contained in the mystery itself? Unless perhaps David confessed his iniquity and sin precisely so that he too might belong both to the forgiveness of sin and to the grace of the mystery.

82. For what does it mean that, while confessing his sin, the man sings of Zion and Jerusalem, saying: “Do good, O Lord, in your good will toward Zion, so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built” (Ps. 50 [51]:20), except that he desires the gathering of the Church to be hastened through the calling of the nations? It would spread throughout the whole world the lineage of its faith—not the lineage of the son of the slave woman, but of free Jerusalem, that Jerusalem which is in heaven—and would establish the enclosures of the spiritual walls through the proclamation of apostolic teaching.

83. The walls of Jerusalem, therefore, are the defenses of faith, the fortifications of disputation, and the summits of the virtues. The walls of Jerusalem are the gatherings of the Churches founded throughout the world. For the Church says: “I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers” (Song 8:10). And rightly, the walls of Jerusalem are the assemblies of the Churches, because whoever enters the Church in good faith and conduct becomes a citizen and inhabitant of that heavenly city which descends from heaven. A structure of living stones builds these walls.

84. Seeing, therefore, the true Jerusalem and Zion, he said:

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “when you have blessed in your good will.”]

“When you have blessed Jerusalem and Zion in your good will, then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness” (Ps. 50 [51]:21)—that is, the sacrifice of the body of Christ, who, when speaking of his own Passion, says: “Open for me the gates of righteousness, and entering through them I will confess to the Lord” (Ps. 117 [118]:19). And in the Gospel he says to John: “Allow it now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15). And later: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:10). Christ is righteousness.

He therefore asserts that Christ’s sacrifice will be acceptable to the Father. This is what he also said above: “Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness and hope in the Lord” (Ps. 4:6). This is the offering of spiritual righteousness and the holocaust of fervent devotion and the infusion of the Holy Spirit, which he says will take place when the souls of believers begin to be brought to the spiritual altar of the Lord. Renouncing pleasures and delights, they draw the plow, as it were, through their inmost parts, so that they may bear the fruits of a pious cultivation.

85. Or certainly it may be understood in this way: When you have blessed the Church acquired from the nations, and the spiritual sacrifice of righteousness has begun to be frequently offered, then the holy martyrs also, who have offered their bodies to be plowed for Christ, will be offered upon the sacred altars like calves. Thus we find written in the Apocalypse of John (Rev. 6:9), that beneath the altar were the souls of those who had offered their bodies to martyrdom for the name of the Lord Jesus, so that they might obtain for themselves the grace of Christ.

To him be honor and glory, praise and eternity, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, from ages past, and now and always, and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

*[THE SECOND APOLOGY FOR THE PROPHET DAVID.]*

[Col. 0883B]

## NOTICE ON THE SECOND APOLOGY OF DAVID

[Col. 0883]

This book has the same subject as the preceding one. For in it it is shown that there is no reason for anyone to take offense at the fact that the sacred books report David as having fallen into a double crime, namely adultery and murder. Nevertheless, whether one considers the elegance of its style, or its method and arrangement, one will find that the two works differ from each other considerably. Indeed, this work was deliberately and carefully divided by its author into three parts. In the first, he argues against the Gentiles (chap. 5, no. 31), so that the fall is attributed to human condition and the correction of it to virtue; in the second, he demonstrates against the Jews that holy David fell so that Jewish faithlessness would limp no further (ibid.); in the third, Christians are taught that this history contains many mysteries and figures which also obtain the grace promised long ago (ibid.).

In the first part the Author refutes the futile objection of the pagans (chap. 3, no. 6 ff.), who loudly complained that Christians made a vain show of pursuing innocence, when their leaders were known to have been disgraced and polluted by adulteries and murders. In the second, after proving false the Jews who asserted that David or Solomon had been the true Messiah (chap. 4, no. 21 ff.), he adds a powerful refutation (chap. 4, no. 26 ff.) of the heretics who, while denying Christ’s divinity, equated or even surpassed the faithlessness of those same Jews. Finally, after disclosing the four great mysteries hidden beneath this history of David (chap. 7, no. 37 ff.), he explains the parable of the prophet Nathan (chap. 11, no. 55 ff.), and then adds an exposition of the first verses of Psalm 50 (chap. 12, no. 61 ff.).

Although he indicates that David is there speaking on his own behalf and defending himself, it must nevertheless honestly be admitted that everything said there wanders beyond the proposed subject and is chiefly occupied with refuting the Arians and Manichaeans. For the rest, it is impossible to pronounce with certainty what the reason may be that we do not possess an explanation of the whole psalm: whether the injury of time, or the negligence of the copyist, or finally the Author himself was prevented from continuing his discourses by weakness of voice, of which he complains in this work (chap. 5, no. 28).

For it is beyond dispute that this composition consists of sermons which he mentions more than once (ibid. and chap. 11, no. 53). He delivered these in the church on different days (ibid.), after readings from the Old Testament and the Gospel (chap. 1, no. 1, and chap. 7, no. 38). Here we thought it would not be irrelevant, for the reader’s benefit, to observe that this Author, like Ambrose himself in certain of his works, always uses the words “reading” and “lection,” and not the words “chant” or similar expressions. From this it might perhaps be inferred that the readings and Gospels in the liturgies of that time were not ordinarily sung, but recited; after the recitation the people testified to their faith and spiritual obedience by something like an acclamation, as is indicated by these words of our Author: “with what devout assent,” he says, “you have followed” (chap. 7, no. 38).

Furthermore, we simply call him “our Author,” for there is no slight controversy as to whether this work can truly be attributed to Ambrose. Erasmus, by whom it was first made public, warned (in the letter prefixed to this work) that, although it was attributed to this very Father in the manuscript he had discovered, it nevertheless did not appear to be Ambrosian, but should be assigned to the same Author to whom the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* belong. To support this judgment he offers no other foundation than the difference in style. He asserts that the Author is so successful an imitator of Ambrosian diction that he even surpasses it in certain qualities: he explains things more clearly, digresses less from the subject, and so forth.

Gillotius, on the contrary, defends our Bishop (*Admonition on this work*), supported by the agreement of the manuscripts which he had gathered in no small number. In these, each of the two *Apologies of David* bears equally the title of Ambrose of Milan and is dedicated to the Emperor Theodosius. As for the stylistic discrepancy that was brought against him, Gillotius replies that it is nothing new for the holy Doctor to have altered his style according to the matter, place, time, and persons involved.

Nevertheless, most later critics have gone over to Erasmus’s opinion, each adding some new reason of his own. Bellarmine maintains (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*) that Ambrose would never have undertaken the composition of a second *Apology*; furthermore, the Author of this later *Apology* denies that David’s adultery was a true adultery and considers it to be allegorically interpreted, whereas Ambrose in the earlier *Apology* acknowledges that the sin was actually committed. Possevinus approves all Bellarmine’s arguments (*Sacred Apparatus*), with the qualification that one may nevertheless hold that the holy Doctor could both use different styles and write several *Apologies of David*, just as it is known that he wrote several books *On David’s Interpellation*.

Nicolaus Faber (*Letter to Fronton, Duke*) says, in addition to the preceding reasons, that this book is not by Ambrose but by some Origenist, who, transferring Scripture into allegories, denies that Bathsheba washed herself before the king’s palace (chap. 8, no. 39). Theophilus Raynaudus attempts to dissolve the arguments of both sides, volume XI, *On Books to Be Refuted*, part I, *Erotic Question* 10, no. 185; consult that work.

Hermanus, in his judgment concerning the Ambrosian works, observes that quite a few things said in the earlier *Apology* are also read in this later one. It therefore does not seem credible to him that Ambrose would have used such repetition. Moreover, Saint Augustine, when praising the *Apology of David*, never calls it the first; the second was entirely unknown to Sixtus of Siena; and, finally, its Author, so far as can be gathered from the heretics whom he mentions, seems to have written no later than the fifth century (*At the end of the Life of Ambrose*, Gallican edition).

In the midst of this diversity of opinion, we shall frankly state our own view, while leaving everyone free to embrace whichever position he judges preferable. In Gillotius’s favor we may affirm that the title of Ambrose is found not only in the manuscripts which he used, but also in the Italian manuscripts from which he compiled his *Milleloquium*, as well as in those to which we emended the same treatise. William of Saint-Thierry also, in his exposition of the *Song of Songs*, compiled by him from Ambrosian opinions and which we shall publish in its proper place, cites Ambrose’s “Second *Apology*.” Yet since this Author is not of very ancient times—for he scarcely died before the year 1545—we must admit that we have not encountered manuscripts much older than that period.
