Something may also be added in favor of Gillotius’s opinion: the Author whom we are discussing complains that, “because of the frailty of my voice,” as he himself puts it, “I cannot complete the entire sequence of the treatise” (chap. 5, no. 28). The same complaint is also found in the books *On the Sacraments* (Book I, chap. 16). But may this be applied to our Ambrose? Certainly we find Augustine speaking of him in these words: “Although also because of the need to preserve his voice, which was easily strained,” and so forth (*Confessions*, Book VI, chap. 3, no. 3). Yet the obvious reply is that it is not unusual for preachers to complain of the weakness of their voice. Thus Basil, in his *Homily on the First Psalm*, complains that “the ministry of the word is difficult for him because of the habitual weakness of the voice, which fails us.”

As for Faber’s opinion that the Author belonged to the sect of the Origenists because he denied that Bathsheba had washed before the king’s palace, we reply that this is certainly asserted concerning Uriah. For it is clear that in many passages (chap. 2, no. 5; chap. 3, no. 12; and elsewhere) he accepts the entire sequence of the history as true. Therefore, if he later indicates that it is to be understood not in the literal but in the allegorical sense, he has chiefly followed blessed Ambrose, who more than once, in unfolding the mystical meaning of a history, seems entirely to destroy its historical truth. Read the note appended to the words from chap. 8, no. 39, which were removed in the Roman edition.

The most learned theologian presses the point that Augustine knew only the first *Apology*. Granted—but what harm would there be if not all Ambrose’s compositions came into Augustine’s hands? Nor can anything else be inferred from Sixtus’s silence except either that this book was unknown to him or that he did not wish to pass judgment on it. Nor is there any reason for anyone to be surprised if our Doctor wrote a twofold defense of David, since he himself left it on record that he composed several books on the deeds of Elijah (*On Elijah and Fasting*, chap. 3, no. 5), and on the history of Joseph (*On Joseph the Patriarch*, chap. 6, no. 30, and chap. 7, no. 38); and since we still possess two books of his on Abraham, in which he explains the same passages of the sacred pages—though not with the same meaning—yet repeats in many places opinions that he had already committed to writing.

As for the difference of style, which we acknowledged at the beginning to be evident, let us state our view more openly and clearly. Although this Author frequently employs Ambrosian expressions, he also often uses others that have nothing of the Ambrosian character. This is especially noticeable where he addresses his hearers affectionately and wins their goodwill. Nor can it be denied that it was not Ambrose’s custom to divide his subject with such anxiety and art, or repeatedly to impress its parts upon the minds of his hearers or readers. It might also be added that in this work certain passages of Scripture are cited somewhat differently from the way they are cited in Ambrose’s accepted works, and that the Author appears in one place (the final chapter, no. 66) to have used the Vulgate version.

If these arguments are considered sufficient to attribute this work to Ambrose, it may also be inferred from what is taught in it concerning the two wills and operations of Christ (chap. 7, no. 38; chap. 12, nos. 62, 64, and elsewhere) that the Author lived after the rise of the Monothelite heresy. On this view, whoever he may have been, it is clear that he proposed to imitate Ambrose’s *Apology*. He transferred into his own work not only a great deal from it, expanded and adapted to his own style (chap. 3), but also material from other commentaries of the holy Doctor, especially from the passage in the *Commentary on the Gospel of Luke* where the reason is investigated why Christ was pleased to derive his origin from sinners.

This argument might seem sufficient by itself to vindicate that second *Apology* for Ambrose, since shortly afterward the Author refers readers to a certain writing which he himself had composed on the history of David. But that argument is weakened by the fact that the words read immediately before the cited reference are found in the first *Apology*. For these reasons, therefore, we have wished to leave judgment concerning the Author of this little book free to the reader; and since the right of possession at least remains doubtful, we have not thought it should be taken away from Ambrose, who has held it until now.

[Col. 0887A]

# THE SECOND APOLOGY OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, FOR THE PROPHET DAVID. (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0887]

## CHAPTER ONE

Some may take offense because David fell into adultery and Christ absolved the adulteress brought before him; especially because the same prophet made his sin public. But it is shown that, although David could err, Christ could not err; and therefore those who detract from God’s power or providence must be rejected.

[Col. 0887A]

### 1

Perhaps the title of the psalm that you heard read offended many people: “The prophet Nathan came to David when he had gone in to Bathsheba.” At the same time, the Gospel reading that was delivered might also have caused no slight difficulty to the inexperienced (John 8:11), in which you observed that an adulteress was brought before Christ and dismissed by him without condemnation. For if anyone receives these things with idle ears, he encounters an inducement to error when he reads of a holy man’s adultery and an adulteress’s absolution—almost an example of a fall both human and divine, since a human being supposedly thought adultery should be committed, and God judged that adultery should not be condemned. Thus the path either to falling or to pardon is slippery, as is the path of desire.

### 2

There is also this consideration, which seems to kindle the very torches of youthful wantonness: he was not ashamed of his adultery and did not conceal it, but made it public in a kind of divine song of proclamation. What, then, was holy David—so shameless, so imprudent—that he himself sang of his own disgrace, especially since in another psalm also, the one that has been read today, he said: “How long, Lord, how long will sinners boast?” (Psalm 93:3). He forbids others to boast of sin, yet he himself boasts of it in a sacred song. How, then, are we to distinguish these things?

### 3

Granted, then, that David rashly erred: did Christ also err, so that we should think he did not possess sound judgment? Therefore, as though addressing them, David prophesied today, saying: “Understand, you senseless ones, and finally become wise, you fools” (ibid., 8). For how could Christ have erred? It is not permissible for such a thought to enter our minds. Does he who planted the ear not hear, or does he who formed the eye not observe? He who reproves the nations, will he not rebuke—the one who teaches human beings knowledge (ibid., 9–10)?

Did Christ, then, not know how to question guilt and hear a just accusation? Could Christ approve wantonness? Did Christ, who reproves the nations, not consider the adulteress worthy of rebuke? Could Christ, who knows the inner things of every heart and teaches the knowledge of the Law, either be deceived by an offense or judge contrary to the order of the Law? And how did he himself say: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17)? Could Christ, who condemns hidden things, overlook things made public? [Col. 0888B] Can Christ, who made the seasons, be ignorant of the seasons? Does he who knows the vain thoughts of human beings not also know their criminal thoughts?

### 4

Let this, therefore, be a sufficient answer to those who, although unable to deny the Creator, nevertheless deny the Creator’s power; who, while acknowledging his wisdom, assert his foolishness by accusing him of ignorance concerning future things. We could speak at greater length on this matter, but another treatise seems to have been assigned to us. Although a sequence of different readings has been delivered, the title of the psalm and the Gospel reading nevertheless advance toward the same assertion. Yet although the assertion is one, the treatise should follow the order of the readings; and therefore it seems that we must first discuss the title of the psalm.

## CHAPTER II

Having stated the subject, the Author writes that judgment should not easily be passed. He then explains in what order, and before what groups of people, he will defend the cause of David in his error.

[Col. 0888C]

### 5

A history has been set before us that contains adultery and murder. For we find it written in the Book of Kings (2 Kings 11:2 ff.) that King David, while walking about in his house, saw Uriah’s wife washing herself; he immediately loved her and ordered her to be summoned. Then he ordered her innocent husband, as Scripture presents it, to be placed in the path of the fiercest combatants, so that he might be overwhelmed by the enemy’s force. These things happened, and they are not denied. How, then, are they defended?

The Gospel reading rightly warns (John 8:11) that even when sin appears to have crept in, judgment nevertheless belongs to the judge; and that each person must remember his own condition and merit. For often, even in judging, the sin of judgment is greater than the sin of the one who has been judged.

[Note: [Col. 0889D] The Gillot edition has *peccatum appareat* in the margin, and the Roman edition in the text; but the Erasmian edition and the same Gillot edition in the body of the text, together with all the manuscripts, have *peccatum appareat subreptum; tamen*, “even when it appears that sin has been secretly introduced; nevertheless,” and so forth. This can produce a sound meaning if interpreted as: “even when it appears that sin has crept upon someone; nevertheless it is not everyone’s task to pass judgment, but that of the judge, namely Christ.”]

For if it has been prescribed by certain wise men of the world that, in judging, one must take care that the punishment not be greater than the offense—and this principle is observed—how much more should it be observed that anyone who is going to judge another should first judge himself, and should not condemn lesser errors in another when he himself has committed greater ones?

[Note: [Col. 0889D] Since punishment is the vengeance for an offense, it rightly follows that proportion must be found between the two. Therefore the lawmakers, assigning different punishments to different crimes, took the greatest care that the punishments should correspond to them. On this matter a most wise general principle is laid down in volume 3 of the *Pandects*, Digest, book 48, title “On Punishments,” column 1556, as follows: “The judge must see to it that nothing is determined either more harshly or more leniently than the case requires. For one must not seek the glory either of severity or of clemency; rather, after careful judgment, the decision must be made according to what each matter demands. Clearly, in lighter cases judges should be more inclined toward leniency; in graver cases they should follow the severity of the laws with some tempering of kindness.” Horace teaches nothing contrary to this in Book I of the *Satires*, satire 3, where he says:

“Why does reason not use its own weights and measures,  
and restrain offenses with penalties  
in proportion to the nature of each matter?”

And below:

“Let there be a rule  
that imposes penalties equal to sins.”]

Who are you, then, that you judge David, a holy man? I say this to the Gentile, I say it to the Jew, I say it to the Christian; and therefore the treatise seems to me to require a threefold division: one part against the Gentiles, another against the Jews, and a third among Christians.

## CHAPTER III

He warns the Gentiles not to look merely at David in his error, but at David in his repentance, since the former is common to human beings, whereas the latter is rare among kings. He then explains how easily one is overcome by desire and confirms this with examples of holy men.

[Col. 0889C]

### 6

My first discourse, then, is against the Gentiles, who are accustomed to object: “See how Christians pursue innocence, prefer faith, venerate religion, and teach chastity, when their leaders are reported to have committed both murders and adulteries! David himself—of whose lineage, as you say, Christ chose to be born—sang of his murders and adulteries. What sort of disciples can those be whose teachers are such men?”

### 7

What, then? Do we deny that it happened, or reject the teacher? Neither. But let the one who objects to the particular fact consider the universality of nature. The particular is the form of the deed; universality is the condition of nature. There is therefore nothing surprising if a particular instance exists within the general condition.

For I acknowledge that David was a human being, and there is nothing surprising in that. I acknowledge what is common: that a human being sins. For the weakness of the human condition is not new; indeed, it seems more surprising if a human being is without sin than if he is inclined toward some sin.

[Note: [Col. 0890D] The Erasmian edition has: “than if iniquity has made sin”; the Roman edition and two manuscripts: “than if he should fall into sin.” “He therefore committed sin,” as in Gillot and the remaining manuscripts, as in the text.]

Therefore holy David sinned—I shall leave you no room for doubt about this. He committed adultery, he contrived murder, and he both contrived and carried it out. He sinned as kings commonly do; but he repented and wept, as kings commonly do not. He asked forgiveness, conscious not of his power but of his weakness. He prostrated himself on the ground, covered himself with sackcloth, forgot his sovereignty, and remembered his guilt.

### 8

Where will you find me a man of this kind, one placed in authority who does not rather cherish his sins, proclaim his guilt, and defend his crimes; one who thinks that what is unbecoming to him is therefore not permitted to him; who binds himself by his own laws; and who recognizes that what is not permitted by justice is not permitted even by power?

For power does not dissolve justice; justice dissolves power. Nor is a king released from the laws; rather, he fulfills the laws by his own example. Can it happen that one who judges others is himself free from judgment, and accepts upon himself the same standard by which he binds others?

### 9

David, then, is good—and far more admirable because he conquered power than because he conquered love. Chastity is sometimes preserved by the body, but often surrendered to error; power is subjected to God; and a person is more easily restrained in love than moderated in power. Therefore you do not forgive what is lesser in the one in whom you marvel at greater things.

Human nature is slippery and prone to sin in everyone; the license of power and the opportunity it provides are slippery even amid good morals. For the anger of a king is no different from the anger of a lion; but whoever provokes and mingles with it sins against his own soul. Let no one, therefore, provoke power, lest his soul, entangled in bodily snares, be unable to cast off its vice.

It is therefore no wonder if David also fell through the appearance and opportunity of power; but it is far more admirable that he was recalled by contemplation of faith.

### 10

You see, then, that this worldly power often accomplishes nothing useful and very often causes harm; for the outcome of guilt is frequently found in the authority of power. Therefore, whoever you are, O king, do not presume upon your power and ability, for “the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord.” Do not flatter yourself over the submission of peoples, for “a king is not saved by the multitude of his strength, nor will a giant be saved by the greatness of his strength.”

The Lord is not pleased by the lofty heights of tents or the precious summit of roofs, but by those who fear him and by those who hope in his mercy.

### 11

We therefore see that power is slippery toward vices, though I would not say that it is always bent toward them; for we read that David, exalted by royal power, increased the worship of God, and that Solomon consecrated a temple to God.

### 12

Let us now assert what we have touched upon: the ability to rule is an incentive to sin. Let us proceed according to the sequence of the history. David would not have violated the right of another man’s marriage bed and the covenant of marriage, unless he had seen a naked woman washing herself in the inner part of his house.

Therefore it is rightly written: “Do not look intently upon a woman’s beauty, and do not desire a woman” (Ecclesiasticus 25:28). Elsewhere it says: “Beware of every shameless eye” (Ecclesiasticus 26:14). Presume nothing concerning the strength of your continence. For “a woman’s fornication will be recognized by the haughtiness of her eyes and by her eyelids” (ibid., 12); therefore flee first from the cause of sin.

No one remains strong for long. And not only to the weak but to every human being it is said: “Let not desire for beauty overcome you” (Proverbs 6:25). If you do not wish to be conquered, do not engage in battle with sins, lest vices be crowned through you. Do not be captured by your eyes, nor carried away by your eyelids (ibid.).

A woman may seem of little value to you in price, but she is strong for vice, because “a woman captures the precious souls of men” (ibid.).

[Note: [Col. 0891D] Many manuscripts have *sed ad vitium est*; Erasmus and Gillot, *sed ad vitium appetibilis est*; Gillot in the margin and the Roman edition in the body, as do the Theodosian manuscripts, *sed fortis ad vitium*. The last reading seems preferable to the others.]

### 13

It is difficult, therefore, for anyone entangled in the allurements of lust to escape unharmed. Nor is this judged difficult merely by my opinion; it was judged impossible even in the Proverbs of holy Solomon. Led by his own example, he says: “Can anyone bind fire in his bosom without burning his clothes? Or can anyone walk upon fiery coals without burning his feet?” (ibid., 27–28).

Take care, then, that you do not kindle the fire of lust and love within the bosom of your mind, lest your bodily garment be consumed by that conflagration of the soul and you lose the perpetuity of the resurrection. Or at least let the footprint of your mind be burned if you suppose that you must walk through the flames of lust. For whoever is burned in his heart is consumed in his body.

### 14

In every way, therefore, the encounter with a wanton woman must be avoided.

[Note: [Col. 0891D] So read all the manuscripts and the editions of Erasmus and Gillot. The Roman edition, however, has: “Acquire prudence as a friend.” The Vulgate approaches this reading, having “Call prudence your friend,” whereas the Septuagint reads: “make prudence your intimate acquaintance.”]

Therefore, he says, acquire prudence as a disciple for yourself, so that it may guard you from a strange wife and a fornicating woman (Proverbs 7:5), lest she hold you bound by the snares of her lips and wrap you in the tresses of error. Thus the prophet taught you where you must beware of the prostitute (ibid., 6): beware her entrance through the window.

For she enters through the window of her house. Her window is her eye; therefore beware every shameless eye, lest love enter through the window and lust penetrate. A fornicating woman entices a lover by her appearance; and unless you restrain your wanton gaze, in mind and spirit, death enters through the window.

The wantonness of a prostitute is not sluggish, nor is her lust idle; it makes the hearts of young men fly away, so that they cannot maintain the steadiness of their own minds but are swept here and there by burning love. Beware, then, of such a woman (ibid., 10 ff.), who does not remain at home, wanders outside, lies in wait around corners, binds with her eyes, entices with her words, covers her bed with embroidered cloths and with tapestries spread from Egypt. She derives her adornment not from divine thought but from worldly allure; and rightly she says that her husband is absent, since no adulteress can have Christ present.

### 15

You see, then, by how many things even the hearts of holy men are captured; and therefore do not be surprised if holy David too was captured. He was indeed a great man, one who conquered by faith the monstrous Philistine, terrible in body and bristling with weapons of war. But would that he had conquered himself! Would that, just as he struck down that adversary, he had been able to overthrow and overcome his inner adversary! The battle of the one who fights within is more difficult than that of the one who fights outside.

### 16

But why do I speak only of David? Let us summon others also to an argument of this kind, lest we think David’s weakness was peculiar to one man rather than a weakness of bodily condition.

Samson was strong and powerful; he strangled a lion, but could not strangle his own love. He broke the bonds of his enemies, but did not break the chains of his own desires. He burned the harvests of others, yet, set ablaze by the spark of a single woman, he lost the harvest of his own virtue.

Solomon built a temple for God; but would that he himself had preserved the temple of his body!

But let the discourse return to the one from whom it departed. David triumphed over ten thousand, but he stumbled over twenty thousand and more. And because he stumbled, he recognized that he was human; he confessed his guilt and begged forgiveness, saying to the Lord: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chastise me in your wrath. Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” (Psalm 6:2–3).

If David was weak, are you strong? If Solomon fell, are you immovable? If Paul was the foremost of sinners, can you be foremost among the saints? Therefore, if the righteous fell, they fell as human beings; but they acknowledged their sin as righteous people.

If the righteous received a sentence of more severe punishment, how do you propose a hope of impunity for yourself, when Scripture says: “If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (1 Peter 4:18).

### 17

You perceive, then, children, how often even a good purpose is overthrown by the cause of adultery; and therefore you must first flee from and avoid the causes themselves.

Do you not wish to be captured by love? Do not gaze intently upon a woman’s beauty, because your eyes, when they see another’s, will cause your mouth to speak perversely, and you will lie as though in the heart of the sea, like a helmsman in a great storm.

For multitudes of desires create a great tempest. Like a vessel sailing through some strait of the body, the mind is disturbed from one side and the other, so that it cannot remain master of itself, ignorant day and night in the darkness of love.

[Note: [Col. 0893D] One edition and several manuscripts have: “ignorant of the darkness of love by day and night.” The Theodosian, Dionysian, Colbertine, and Mazarin manuscripts have the better reading: “day and night in darkness,” and so forth.]

### 18

Lust is therefore aroused by the eyes, but it is kindled by drunkenness. For every drunkard and fornicator will become poor. Do not flatter yourself over your power to drink.

Noah became drunk; he who had not been made drunk by the flood was made drunk by wine. But he did not know the nature of wine, for he had not drunk it before; you have learned through him what you ought to avoid.

Lot was deceived in sleep; and if you do not wish to be deceived, shake off the sleep of your mind, lest a son or daughter mock the drunk man while he sleeps. There it is not filial piety, but drunkenness, to which recourse is had; it is not the father, but the sleeping man, who is deceived.

Do you not wish to be burned? Do not approach the fire. Do you not wish to be thrown headlong? Avoid unstable things, beware precipices, shun what is ready to fall and what is slippery.

### 19

You see, then, that in those who were worthy to be righteous there was not another nature, but another discipline. After the fall of the first human being and the just sentence, when the appetite of the flesh was condemned in one person, the condition of humanity contracted vice and guilt infected nature. But faith moderated the defect of nature itself, and the intensity of devotion softened the offense.

### 20

Turn, therefore, to the Lord, you nations; know that the Lord is God. He made us, and we did not make ourselves. Know that we are flesh and dust. Let us therefore abandon what we have done and venerate him as the author of ourselves—the one who gave life and forgave sins, who alone can say: “I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will remember them no more” (Isaiah 43:25).

Great indeed and merciful is God, who grants a benefit and does not reproach the recipient with the gift of the benefit. Do you marvel that he made David a king and a conqueror of many nations? This is how he is accustomed to exalt his servants. He is not stingy with gifts, nor sparing of benefits, nor narrow and thrifty with grace; rather, rich in generosity, he increases in reward those whom he has redeemed from sin.

These things are directed against the Gentiles.

## CHAPTER IV

He rebukes the Jews, who wrongly believe that David, who was subject to sin, or Solomon, to whom the sayings concerning Christ do not apply, is the Son of God; and he refutes the perverse interpretation of certain heretics concerning the Son of God.

[Col. 0893D]

### 21

Since we promised that this treatise would have a threefold division—one part against the Gentiles, another against the Jews, and a third among the Church—it now seems necessary to treat against the Jews. Let us review what has been proposed to us.

[Note: [Col. 0893D] So read all the manuscripts and the editions of Erasmus and Gillot. The Roman edition, however, has: “The title: A psalm of David, for the end, when he came in,” and so forth. It must indeed be admitted that this title is read in the extant copies of the Psalter; but since there was once great diversity in the titles of the psalms, one should not depart from the manuscripts and ancient editions.]

“The title of the psalm,” he says, “of David, for understanding, when the prophet Nathan came to him, when he entered in to Bathsheba” (Psalm 50:1–2). This history certainly presents David as both adulterer and murderer, and you, Jews, call this man the Son of God?

But God is the God of virtues, not of crimes. And concerning him God the Father says: “His throne shall be as the days of heaven” (Psalm 88:30). Yet how can one who has committed deceit and has not conquered sin be called the Son of God?

[Note: [Col. 0894D] The Roman edition alone has: “who has not conquered sins—how is he called the Son of God, since it is written...”]

And how is it written: “No one is without sin except the one God” (Luke 18:19)? If, therefore, the one who is the Son of God cannot fail to be God, then surely the Son of God is the arbiter of justice, not one subject to guilt.

### 22

By what understanding, then, do you judge David to be the Son of God, or suppose Solomon to be so? Is it because it is written: “Give the king your judgment, O God, and your justice to the king’s son” (Psalm 71:2); and because the title of Psalm 71 says that the psalm was composed concerning Solomon?

[Note: [Col. 0894D] The same Roman edition has: “and because the title of the seventy-first psalm says that it was composed concerning Solomon.” Other editions, and all the manuscripts, read as in the text.]

But observe which Solomon it means. “Solomon” means “peaceful”; that is what the interpretation signifies. The psalm is said to concern the one whom we truly know to be the author of peace.

But how was Solomon peaceful? The blood of Joab does not show this, for he ordered him to be killed beside the temple altars. Nor does the punishment of Adonijah, whom he struck down as guilty of royal kinship, and from whose indignation he was not recalled even by his mother’s entreaty.

How, then, can you think that what is written applies to Solomon, the son of David: “He shall remain with the sun and before the moon, throughout all generations” (Psalm 71:5), when he obtained only a brief lease on life and passed the span of his living within narrow limits?

How can it be said of him: “He shall rule from sea to sea” (ibid., 8), when, established within Syria—that is, within the province of a single region—he possessed an empire with bounded borders?

Christ alone extended his empire to the ends of the whole world. For he alone is the one concerning whom the sequence of the psalm rightly prophesied: “The kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring gifts, and all the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Psalm 71:10–11).

We know that he rules over all peoples and nations, with an empire without boundaries and power without end. Solomon, therefore, is not the Son of God.

### 23.

But on what grounds did you suppose him to be the Son of God? Was it because he was wise? Yet he asked for wisdom in order to receive what he did not have: Christ himself is Wisdom, possessing naturally in its entirety what Solomon received among human beings by grace. In the end, what is received in time is possessed in time. For Solomon neither possessed wisdom at the beginning of his life nor retained it at the end. Indeed, he did not believe that he possessed what he had requested; and later, turned away from the worship of God, he fell—not as a wise man, but as a foolish one—so as to offend God. He offended to such an extent that he even lost what he had deserved. Why, then, did you believe him to be the Son of God? Was it because he built a temple for God? But from this you ought to have understood that he was not the Lord and God, because it is written: “Unless the Lord builds the house for himself, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. 126:1). He labored in vain who built that temple which the fire, once brought against it, consumed. Or was it because David his father was told: “You shall not build a house for me . . . but when you sleep, I shall raise up your offspring after you; and he shall build a house for my name” (2 Sam. 7:12–13)? Yet there too a temple that is not bodily or material is promised; for God does not dwell in things made by human hands. The temple is the holy Church, which is founded not by human but by heavenly power.

### 24.

For if we admire the works of superior, though still human, virtue, we find many of this kind whom we can compare with David and Solomon. And therefore, where there is equality of achievement, there is no superiority of power. Nor can we call several persons sons of God, since we read of one Son of God; but the Son of God must not be dishonored because of the benefits he bestowed upon our ancestors. For there were many illustrious men: yet, Scripture says, “At the word of Jesus Nave the sun stood still over Gabaon” (Josh. 10:13). You see that he went beyond the power of King David; for David ruled over earthly things, not over the stars. You also see that the sun is a servant, not a lord, since it obeyed even a human voice. It stood still, however, because in Jesus it recognized both a type of what was to come and the name itself. For Jesus Nave did not command the heavenly lights by his own power, but by the mystery of Christ; the Son of God was being signified as destined to come into this world, to delay by divine power the setting of the world’s light as it declined toward darkness, to restore the light, and to bring in brightness.

Enoch too was taken up to heaven; but he was taken up, whereas Christ returned. Enoch was taken away lest wickedness change his heart; Christ abolished the wickedness of this present age itself. Elijah ascended to heaven in a chariot and with horses; Christ, however, descended from heaven, and did not ascend as Elijah did in a chariot and with horses, since Elijah could not have done otherwise, whereas Christ returned by his own power. Elisha commanded that a leper be washed in the Jordan so that he might be cleansed from every contagion; Christ washed the whole world in the Jordan. Moses himself, to whom the people of the Jews were entrusted, divided the water; he divided the elements, indeed, but he did not divide the power of the Trinity. He separated the masses of water, but he did not separate the Father from the Son.

### 25.

You see how many men, and what sort of examples of deeds, they left behind. How, then, do you judge those whom you recognize as equal in virtue to King David or Solomon to be unequal in condition, so that you suppose Solomon, the son of David, to sit at the right hand of God? Especially since David himself clearly indicated the one about whom this had been said; for he would not have said of his own son: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 110:1). How could he call his own son “Lord”? The Law forbids it, religion resists it, and faith recoils from placing a mortal man at the right hand of almighty God.

Another is he who sits at the right hand: he who assumed a body, not he who began from a body; he who was begotten before the morning star—that is, before the splendor of all lights—for he himself created the ranks of the various lights. Solomon, however, came after the morning star. Solomon was not a priest; and therefore the almighty Lord could not say to him: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (ibid., 3). He could not say to him: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (ibid., 4), especially since, in the time when Solomon lived, the priests were according to the order of Aaron, not according to the order of Melchizedek. For at that time priests were still offering the blood of goats and bulls for the sins and errors of the people. But after Christ came, and offered himself for the salvation of the world—so that those whom the blood of bulls could not cleanse might be cleansed by the blood of Christ—the priests began to offer themselves as sacrifices.

### 26.

Thus our Lord Jesus Christ, with a single question, fenced in the mouths of all heretics and shut up their sacrileges. For by this question he refuted not only the Jews, but also the Photinians, Arians, and Sabellians. And therefore, since we now see that the Jews have failed and that their execrable unbelief has been weakened, something must now be said in the course of this discussion about the Arians, who do not differ greatly from the Jews, and about the Photinians and Sabellians.

Let Photinus be silent, who says that Christ is the son of David, not the Son of God; and let him be silent, condemned by the heavenly voice. For how does he say that Christ is the son of David, when David himself said in the Book of Psalms: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet” (Ps. 110:1)? “If David,” he says, “calls him Lord, how is he his son?” (Luke 20:13–14). Christ, therefore, is not the son of David, but the Son of God.

Let the Sabellian also be silent; and when he reads that the Lord spoke to the Lord, let him understand that the one who speaks and the one to whom he speaks are not one and the same. For the Father did not say to himself, “Sit at my right hand,” nor did he say to himself, “I will place your enemies beneath your feet.” Let all at last understand that he is the Son who sits at the right hand. Let them preserve this distinction between the Father and the Son: that there is a distinction between Father and Son, that one is the Father and the other the Son, because they possess and occupy one throne and one majesty—not by way of a distinction of dignity, nor according to an order of power, but through the bond of love. Let them understand that the Father and the Son have one power; and in this let Arius too be silent, since he follows in the contrary footsteps of Sabellius’ error.

Let him hear the Lord speaking to the Lord; let him hear the Son sitting at the right hand of the Father; and let him cease to raise questions about divinity on the basis of human speech and order. Nor should he argue that the Father says, “Sit”; for we read elsewhere that the Son sits even without the Father’s command, as it is written: “And he sits at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:20). And elsewhere: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of God” (Matt. 26:64). It is he to whom it is said, “Sit,” who is called the Son of Man: he hears as man, but sits as the Son of God. What can be said to be more exalted than this power, which placed even human flesh at the right hand of God and, after the Word became flesh, joined that weakness of human condition to eternal divinity?

### 27.

But what is this? After Photinus has fallen silent, Arius has become quiet, and Sabellius has lost his voice, I still see other mouths raising a diverse heresy against the Church. For behold, Manichaeus and Valentinian, and every offshoot of the Manichaeans, rely upon the weapon by which others were destroyed; and they attempt, by a testimony to the faith, to prejudice the faith.

[Editorial note: The Erasmus and Gill editions, with the Tornacensis, Colbertinus, and Mazarinus manuscripts, read “resists with my weapon”; the Roman edition, Gill’s marginal reading, and other manuscripts more probably read “rely upon that weapon.”]

For the detestable heresy says: “Behold, Christ denied that he was the son of David” (Luke 20:13). And therefore, it says, one must believe that he did not assume flesh. To this Scripture responds most clearly at the very beginning of the Gospel, when it says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David” (Matt. 1:1). Why, then, is he called the son of David in one place and denied to be the son of David in another, unless you understand that it is one thing for him to be Son according to divine substance, and another according to the assumption of flesh? According to divine substance he is the Son of God; according to the flesh he is the son of David.

Thus, where the Savior’s generation according to the flesh is described, he is called the son of David; but where the fullness of confession is required, when the Savior’s generation is indicated, he does not wish to be called the son of David, but to be called the Son of God. For the designation of his majesty interprets his nature.

[Editorial note: The Erasmus edition reads “for the designated … is interpreted as discourse among Christians.” Gill, with five manuscripts, agrees with Erasmus, except that these read “for the designation,” etc. The Roman editors rightly observed that the words “discourse among Christians” had intruded into the text from elsewhere; they are absent from the Dionysian, Laudunensis, Tornacensis, and Theodorianus manuscripts.]

But now that we have refuted the interpretations of the fierce, the discourse must turn to the Church.

## CHAPTER V

He confirms the arguments brought forward against the Jews and the Gentiles, and turns his discourse to the Church.

### 28.

But the fact that we have often repeated the title of the fiftieth psalm is not an example of presumption, but of weakness. In a single day, either because of the limitations of my understanding or because of the frailty of my voice, I cannot complete the whole sequence of the discourse. And therefore, since yesterday our discourse was directed against the Jews, whom the proofs of faith have compelled to such an extent that Christ has been placed upon the heavenly throne—for this certainly cannot apply to a human being—for it is not credible that anyone other than the Son of God sits at the right hand of God, and no one other than the Son of God, all ambiguity removed, is to be judged to sit at the right hand of the Father.

Again, since Scripture says: “From the fruit of your womb I will place one upon your throne” (Ps. 132:11), this same Son of God must certainly be believed to have assumed flesh from Mary, in whom there is the prophetic fruit of the womb. Thus you may truly recognize the succession of his origin, and without hesitation believe that the Son of God, later made the son of man through the assumption of flesh, sits upon the heavenly throne of the Father. For Christ did not possess any royal throne in this world, so that you might suppose that another throne resembling David’s was promised, especially since the Lord himself said: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36).

### 29.

Thus surrounded on every side, they direct the arguments of their unbelief toward this point: they assert that it is incredible that God assumed flesh. Yet they cannot explain why he could not have assumed it. For I ask whether they think that flesh could not be assumed by God because of impossibility or because of indignity. If because of impossibility, then something is impossible for God; for there is nothing he wished to do that he could not do. It remains, then, that they must show either that he wished to assume flesh or that he did not wish to do so.

What greater indication of willingness is there than the fact that he himself said: “I appeared openly to those who were not seeking me . . . I stretched out my hands to a people that did not believe and contradicted me” (Isa. 65:1–2)? If, then, he both wished and was able, are we to suppose that he refused because of indignity? And what indignity does divinity suffer? It is free from insult and is not subject to our passions; for flesh could bring neither loss nor increase to divinity.

### 30.

Yet they object that the Son of God could not assume flesh. If so, why do the Gentiles testify that their gods—since they cannot deny that they were human beings—were seen in human form?

[Editorial note: The Roman edition reads, “If [they are] Gentiles, why [do they say that] their gods were seen in human form?” Other editions and manuscripts agree with the present reading, except that they have “why [do they say] their gods.” Since that wording gives a less suitable sense, the Roman edition shortened the phrase.] Could their king, whom they place above all their gods, assume monstrous forms out of love, while Christ could not assume human flesh and take up, for the salvation of the world, that supreme work which he made in his own image? Do they really consider it more fitting that a form of flesh was assumed because of adultery with another man’s wife than because of the redemption of all human beings?

But if a Jew raises this objection, how does he read: “Behold, a virgin shall receive in her womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14), which is translated “God with us”? How does he read: “Behold, I am present, I who was speaking” (Isa. 52:6)? How, moreover, does he assert that this was read: “Behold, like a panther . . . and like a bear deprived of her cubs I shall meet them” (Hos. 13:7–8)?

Could the Son of God not assume flesh for the redemption of all, when they themselves cannot deny that, because of the punishment of our sins, God assumed a certain ferocity of wild beasts, so to speak? Though by nature he is kind and merciful, yet, moved by the atrocity of our crimes, he assumes toward us a certain savagery of beasts.

### 31.

But since I believe that yesterday and today I have sufficiently answered the Jews, I must now render an account to you, my most beloved brothers, of the meaning of the prophetic event. For when the title of this psalm was first read—that Nathan came to David when he entered in to Bathsheba—we said that many people were confused by the sequence of this history. And therefore we undertook its exposition in three parts. We thought that the division of the exposition should be made in such a way that, among the Gentiles, the fall of human condition would not be denied, but the correction of error would be established; among the Jews, however, we would teach that holy David fell for this reason: so that the unbelief of the Jews might no longer remain lame, and so that they would cease to believe him to be the Son of God when they saw that he had been subject, like everyone else, to sin.

But Christians, by contrast, might perceive the mysteries of the Church as it rises. Thus the division was made threefold: one according to nature, another according to faith, and a third according to grace. Weakness does not exclude one from pardon; faith excuses from guilt; and the sacraments promised long ago also reconcile grace.

## CHAPTER VI

He teaches the Church why David and many other ancestors of the Lord’s lineage were permitted to fall into error; and, so that it may more easily draw out the mysteries from it, he recounts the history of David’s murder and adultery.

### 32.

David sinned so that the whole world might not go astray; he sinned for himself so that he might amend us all; finally, he sinned against his own body—for “whoever commits fornication sins against his own body”—he sinned against his own body so that he might be redeemed in the body of Christ. Behold: the one whom we scarcely thought could be defended we now see must be proclaimed. For who would not wish divine gifts to be proclaimed in him rather than human works?

We believe, according to the Apostle, that “a person is justified by faith, without works of the Law” (Rom. 3:28). Let David therefore be justified by faith: through the Law he recognized sin, but through faith he believed in the forgiveness of sin. Let David be justified, because in his sin, once it had been committed, the mysteries of the Church shone forth.

[Editorial note: The Roman edition, with one Vatican and the Theodorianus manuscripts, reads: “because in his sin the mysteries of the Church were to arise.” Other editions and manuscripts have the reading given here.]

### 33.

Someone may ask how the one chosen by God as an ancestor of the Lord’s lineage committed both adultery and murder. I answer something else: such an ancestor of the Lord’s body had to be chosen. For what is embodiment except the remission of sins? And therefore he could not be free from sin, so that he might both display and proclaim divine grace by his example.

Accordingly, by that arrangement Bathsheba and Tamar are counted among the ancestors of the Lord’s lineage: one of them committed adultery, the other incest.

[Editorial note: The Erasmus and Gill editions and several manuscripts read “mothers, ancestors of the Lord’s lineage”; certain other manuscripts read “mothers of the ancestor,” while Gill’s marginal reading, some manuscripts, and the Roman edition support the present reading.] By that arrangement Ahab and Jeconiah, as the Evangelist Matthew records (Matt. 1:9, 11), are also numbered among Christ’s forefathers, so that, since he was going to redeem all human beings, he might begin the benefit with his own ancestors; and at the same time, lest anyone subject even to bodily suffering might appear to have sought the nobility of an immaculate origin.

[Editorial note: This is the reading of the Roman edition and several manuscripts. Other editions read, approximately, “and at the same time, lest anyone subject to the suffering of the body …,” a reading from which most manuscripts do not greatly depart. The Roman edition also inserts: “For this is the boastfulness of human beings: to seek not another’s glory but their own.” Although true in itself, that sentence is inappropriate here, since the subject is glory grounded in the nobility of one’s ancestors, which many eagerly seek, rather than glory acquired by one’s own good deeds.]

For this is the boastfulness of human beings: to seek the glory of another rather than their own; and yet among human beings themselves the merit of virtue is greater than that of nobility. An example also had to be given, so that everyone might understand that the disgrace of ancestors cannot be a dishonor to their descendants, since each person can abolish the stain of his lineage by the merit of his own virtue.

You see how many, and how grievously criminal, people the sequence of the Lord’s generation includes—people from whose lineage Christ did not blush to be born for your sake. If you believe these things, they are gifts of divine mercy toward you; and this too is a mark of heavenly power. For “sin abounded, so that grace might abound” (cf. Rom. 5:20). David, therefore, was not exempt from guilt, so that he might be chosen for grace.

### 34.

But now let us review the mysteries of the history itself and draw them from the very springs of Scripture. And so that we may be able to look into the entire sequence of the mysteries, let us repeat the text of the history itself.

For we remember that it is stated in the Book of Kings (2 Sam. 11:2 ff.) that, when David saw Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, bathing, he fell in love with her. Then he ordered her to come to the house, while the woman’s husband was absent. Not long afterward her husband returned—a truly religious and devoted man who, during wartime, did not think it right for him to enter his own house when he saw his comrades occupied with the war, keeping watch not in domestic dwellings but in military tents.

Afterward, by David’s command, he was recalled to battle, under instructions that he should be exposed to the enemy’s fighters, so that, after the man’s death, the king might have free opportunity to possess the woman. Here too there is some shame at sin and embarrassment over guilt: his error sought concealment, and he did not claim the authority of his royal power as a legal pretext for an unjust death, but avoided the odium. He acknowledges the fault, but a fault oppressed by shame is more tolerable than one proclaimed with arrogance.

Uriah was therefore killed, having been exposed to the fighters. But afterward those very men who had killed him were themselves killed, by David’s command, when the city had been captured. This is the sequence of the history, in which it is permitted us to behold profound mysteries.

## CHAPTER VII

Having invoked the divine Spirit, he begins to uncover the mysteries concealed beneath the adultery of David and Bathsheba, as well as beneath the birth of their child.

### 35.

And since we have undertaken not to defend David—for he does not need my help—but to excuse him, or rather to proclaim him, lest I falter in so great a depth of mysteries, it is right for me to use the words of the one whose history I am using. I shall therefore use the prophetic response, saying: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inmost parts” (Ps. 51:10).

No one without the infusion of the Holy Spirit can contemplate such great mysteries of the divine depths. For if so great a prophet asks that the gift of the Holy Spirit be infused into him, what should a weak person do? Especially since even the holy Apostle thinks that he is helped by the prayers of the people, so that a door may be opened for him to speak the mystery of the word.

O that Christ would deign to open that door to me! Yet let us knock; for he is accustomed to hear those who knock, since he himself said: “Knock, and it will be opened to you” (Luke 11:9). O that he himself would open himself to me, since Christ is the door: he himself within, he himself outside, he himself the way that leads, he himself the life to which we strive to come.

### 36.

Come, therefore, Lord Jesus, and open your springs to us, so that we may drink of the water which whoever drinks will never thirst (John 4:13). Or, if we cannot yet draw from your spring, deign at least to grant that we may draw from the well, from which you promised drink to that Samaritan woman who was still doubting.

You promise a spring to everyone, certainly, but to those who doubt, like that Samaritan woman, your spring is still a deep well. Let us too drink the water of heavenly secrets. And since we have deserved to reach your spring, let it be permitted us at least to see an image of the heavenly mysteries.

### 37.

Therefore, unless I am mistaken, through the prophet we understand the Holy Spirit; and through the adulteress we may understand the various fornications of the Synagogue. And so, long beforehand, we see it revealed by the Holy Spirit that the Lord Jesus would be born from the family of the Jews—from whose fathers Christ is descended according to the flesh (Gen. 49:10). He was indeed born, as it were, as a Jew from an adulterous family, but as the immaculate one from a Virgin.

He was under the Law; the family of the Jews was, as it were, under a husband. The observance of the Law had to be abolished so that truth and grace might take its place.

### 38.

We have one mystery; receive another as well. Yet remember that, from Bathsheba’s first conception, a little child was born who died, and that Solomon was born afterward: the little child from a secret conception, but Solomon from a marriage openly acknowledged.

It is therefore clear that by David we are to understand the prophet, and by the prophet the prophetic people. From this people and from the Synagogue the first one who was born—the Jewish people, formed through its crimes and consolidated through its vices, since it had degenerated from its ancestors—could not attain the eternity of the resurrection, nor grow into a mature man; but in the smallness of its understanding and a certain infancy of virtue it fell short.

But the one who was afterward conceived from a lawful union—the Christian people, wise and peaceful, for this is disclosed by the interpretation of the name Solomon—reached the hoary age of the long resurrection and attained that heavenly kingdom. Through the former people the Law was dissolved; through the latter grace was restored.

### 39.

Receive a third mystery as well. The Hebrews say that David means “exalted”; the Latins interpret it as “humbled.”

[Editorial note: Most manuscripts and all editions have “the Hebrews say.” The Laudunensis, Tornacensis, and certain others restore “exalted,” to which the words below—“David, exalted by nature, but humbled by mercy”—appear to refer. Yet neither interpretation has elsewhere been found; David in Hebrew signifies only “beloved.”] But who is truly humbled except the one who “did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but, taking the form of a servant, humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:6 ff.)?

This, then, is the one signified by David: exalted by nature, but humbled by mercy; sublime in divinity, but gentle in the body. Thus, where he was humbled, there he was obedient. Obedience arises from humility and reaches its end in it.

When he is said to have become obedient unto death—for death belonged not to divinity but to the body—it was not the obedience of divinity, but of the body; nor was it the humility of majesty, but of flesh.

Thus, insofar as the assumption of the body is concerned, the apostolic reading has declared in what Christ’s humility consisted. But insofar as his divine nature is concerned, it has been disclosed by the Gospel reading, which you followed with devout assent when you heard the Son of God say: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

The Father and the Son are one in divinity; but the sacrament of the body and the eternity of divinity are not one. Yet the Apostle alone did not say that the Lord was humbled; he himself also recalled that he was humble, saying: “Take my yoke, because it is easy; for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

And yet he is marked not only by interpretation but also by name, because it is written: “I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him” (Ps. 89:21). And below he says: “You are my Father” (ibid., 27); and, “I shall say to him: You are my Son.”

[Editorial note: The Roman edition alone adds: “And I will make him the firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth.” The author may perhaps have intended an allusion to that verse; but the Erasmus and Gill editions and all manuscripts support the present reading.]

Therefore, we have found the David whom we were seeking: a servant in appearance, but Lord in truth.

## CHAPTER VIII

What the royal house is in which David walks; what the exposure and washing of Bathsheba signify; and what it signifies that, when he saw her naked, he immediately loved her.

### 40.

This David, then, walked within his own house. What house is Christ’s, if not the one of which he says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2)?

In that royal dwelling he saw human condition naked, and in pity he loved it. For it was still naked of virtues, because, through the serpent’s treachery, it had been stripped of the garments of its own nature.

[Editorial note: The Roman edition omitted everything between “stripped of the garments” and “let us ask who this naked woman is,” although all other editions and the manuscripts retain it; in its place it printed only: “David therefore saw a naked woman bathing herself.” The editors evidently excised these lines lest the truth of the history be undermined. Yet the author had explicitly affirmed the historical event above (chapters 2, 3, 4, and 5); he does not deny it here, but teaches that one should attend more to the soul of the history—that is, its mystical meaning—than to its body, its literal narrative. Several passages of Ambrose must be reconciled on the same principle; see also the prefatory warning supplied for this treatise.]

For it does not seem plausible that, in front of the king’s house, a woman should be stripped naked, or that a woman should bathe in front of the king’s house (2 Sam. 11:2 ff.), as though another place suitable for bathing could not have been found.

It does not fit; it does not accord; it is not consistent with faith. It departs from truth and offends good sense. A king could have recoiled from such a woman—so wanton and so brazen—but he could not have loved her. Or, if she was not ashamed before her husband, could she not at least have feared the gaze of the king? Or, before the king saw her, could his servants not have kept her away?

### 41.

Therefore, if this cannot be reconciled with faith, let us ask who this naked woman is: namely, human condition, stripped of all the garments of nature, deprived of the covering of immortality, and robbed of the veil of innocence. For the one who is stripped naked by sin and guilt is naked.

In the beginning, that first sinner of our race—and would that he alone had been so—did not perceive himself to be naked before he sinned; after he sinned, he saw that he was naked. And therefore he thought he had to cover himself with leaves, because he recognized that he was naked. Thus he became naked to himself after he became liable to guilt.

In him all human condition was stripped naked through the succession of nature, subject not only to guilt but also to misery. He therefore perceived and saw himself naked. Hence our whole condition is such that whoever thinks himself naked both sees and feels himself naked.

Thus the one who desires riches is naked; the one who despises them is wealthy. So each person’s own perception is his misery, and each person’s own virtue is free from injury.

Therefore Christ first claimed human condition for himself in marriage through the Law, and afterward repudiated it. Hence he also says: “Where is the bill of divorce of your mother, by which I dismissed her?” (Isa. 50:1).

In this way Christ saw his family naked and loved it; for Christ loves the holy soul. Thus Jesus loved Lazarus and Mary; Christ loved his Church, though naked, though not yet clothed with any adornment of virtues.

### 42.

Finally, so that we may know that the sequence of Scripture accords with the argument proposed, let us learn that the Church was cleansed, sought, hastened, and washed herself before Christ’s house when John was baptizing in the Jordan and saying: “I indeed baptize you in water for repentance; but he who comes after me is stronger than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 3:11).

Therefore, when the people were being baptized for repentance, the Church was already seeking Christ, close to his house, so that she might reach grace. The Church was therefore seeking Christ from John, saying: “Announce to me him whom my soul loves” (Song 1:6), declaring that he himself was the cause of her desire and the cause of her washing, as you have it: “I am dark and beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon” (ibid., 4).

You have the reason why she eagerly desires to wash herself: she declares that she is dark. For, as though John were asking why the great crowd of people was eager to come and be washed, she replied: “I am dark and beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem.” Because she is dark, she desires to be washed; because she is beautiful, she is not afraid to be seen naked.

“Do not look at me,” she says, “because I am darkened, because the sun has not looked upon me.” We become dark, therefore, when we are not seen by Christ; but when we are seen, we grow white.

He therefore saw her to whom all things are naked and the hidden things of the heart cannot remain concealed, because he is the searcher of heart and kidneys: nothing is covered from him, nothing is concealed. He saw his Church naked, and he saw and loved her. He saw his beloved naked and, like a son of love, loved her.

### 43.

See how he looks; see how he calls. Here there are not the reproaches of adultery, but the mysteries of chastity. “You are wholly beautiful,” he says, “my beloved, my near one, and there is no blemish in you. Come here from Lebanon, bride; come here from Lebanon; you shall pass over and cross over from the beginning of faith” (Song 4:7–8).

And rightly, “from the beginning of faith.” Therefore, where you have faith, you need not fear adultery; faith belongs to marriage, deceit to adultery.

But so that she might be able to come from Lebanon, he first said: “Arise, come, my near one, my beautiful one, my dove, my perfect one” (Song 2:10). “Near one,” certainly, because of the desire of faith; “beautiful,” because of the adornment of virtue; “dove,” because of spiritual grace.

For the wings of the dove, silver-plated, signify that eternal power, and the dove’s flight declared the presence of the Holy Spirit. Christ therefore calls her to himself, so that she may come, since she was already coming endowed with spiritual gifts:

“For behold,” he says, “the winter has passed, the rain has gone away, it has departed; the flowers have appeared on the earth” (ibid., 11–12).

See how the holy Church is invited. “The winter,” he says, “has departed,” so that the naked woman need not fear winter—not winter as a season, but the winter of weakness, which strips the field of the soul bare of every flower.

For there is a winter that does not belong to the earthly sun: it is the winter of the mind, when cold enters the soul, when the soul’s vapor vanishes, when the vigor of perception is dissolved, when excessive moisture overflows and weighs down the mind, when the inner vision grows dark.

And therefore the Lord says: “See that your flight does not take place in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. 24:20). It is good that the day of judgment or of death should then arrive when the gentle temper of the soul is vigorous, when the heavenly mystery shines forth in clear light, when our heart burns within us.

For then Christ is present, as the two disciples testify in the Gospel, saying: “Was not our heart burning within us on the way, when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

[Editorial note: The Tornacensis manuscript reads “the two disciples”; the other manuscripts and all editions read “Ammaon and Cleophas.” Ambrose elsewhere, especially in his Commentary on Luke 24, also calls them by those names.]

The mind is vigorous when even a flower is seen upon the earth. What is this flower of good fragrance except the one who said: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1)?

Of him it is also written in Isaiah: “A shoot shall go out from the root of Jesse, and a branch shall rise from the root, and a flower shall come forth from the branch” (Isa. 11:1).

[Editorial note: The Roman edition, with several manuscripts, reads: “a branch from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root,” a reading also supported by the Septuagint and Vulgate. The Erasmus and Gill editions and most manuscripts have the wording translated above.] The root is surely the family of the Jews; the branch is Mary; the flower of Mary is Christ. When he shines forth upon our earth, and gives fragrance in the field of the soul, or blooms in his Church, we can neither fear the cold nor dread the rain, but await the day of judgment.

44. And therefore the Church hastened with every effort to behold this flower, as she herself bears witness, saying:

> In my bed, by night, I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him; I called him, and he did not answer me. I will rise, then, and enter the house, the marketplace, and the streets, and seek him whom my soul loves (Song III, 1 ff.). [Note: Thus all manuscripts, and the editions of Erasmus and Gill. The Roman edition instead has: “and I will go around the city.” Certainly the Septuagint and Vulgate support this reading, from which Ambrose also does not depart far in *On Isaac and the Soul*, book 5, chapter 5, §38, where he has: “and I will seek in the city.”]

I sought him, and did not find him . . . The watchmen who patrol the city found me; they struck me and took my cloak from me (Song V, 7). You see how she seeks the one whom she desires to find, so that she does not fear being wounded. But these wounds are not to be feared; they are to be desired, because they are wounds of love, as she herself says: “I am wounded with love” (ibid., 8). [Note: So the Roman edition and several manuscripts; Erasmus and Gill, however, with other handwritten codices, have: “as he himself says: I am wounded with love.” This is less satisfactory, since it is plainly evident that these words are attributed to the Church.]

Good are the wounds of love. Indeed, the wounds of a friend are more beneficial than the voluntary kisses of an enemy.

## CHAPTER IX

He continues the same subject and shows that the Church pleased Christ, who had rejected the veiled Synagogue, as a naked woman; then he describes her ardor in searching for him; finally, he explains how the dissolution of the Law was prefigured in the killing of Uriah.

[Col. 0905C]

45. She is rightly naked, then, because she has lost her cloak; or perhaps she is naked for this reason: that sometimes it is a mark of virtue not to have the breast covered, not to have the heart veiled. In the end, Christ rejected and despised the veiled woman—that is, the Synagogue (II Cor. III, 13 ff.), which had a veil over the reading of the Old Testament, a veil that is now removed because it is abolished in Christ. I say, Christ rejected and despised the veiled Synagogue; hence even today a veil lies over the heart of the Jews. [Note: The editions of Erasmus and Gill have: “But Christ receives and embraces the woman who turns wholly to the Lord with her mind, so that we may be able to see while contemplating the glory of God.” The Roman edition and the manuscript codices, however, have the reading given above.]

But she who turns wholly to the Lord in mind is naked [Col. 0905D] and transparent. For when someone has turned to the Lord, the veil will be removed, so that we may be able to see while contemplating the glory of God. Indeed, elsewhere too, being naked is an indication of virtue, because it is written:

> I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them? (Song V, 3).

46. What tunic she took off, and could not find how to put on again, let us disclose from the Scriptures, if we can. There is a bodily tunic, and there are woven coverings of desires; and therefore it is sometimes better to be naked in body than veiled in heart. Paul accordingly also admonishes us that it is much better to be stripped than to be clothed over, saying elsewhere:

> Having stripped off the old man with his deeds, put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created him (Col. III, 9–10).

Therefore she who has been stripped has washed feet; and because she has washed them, she does not know how they could be soiled. Through grace she forgets [Col. 0906B] what she had absorbed by nature. Great, then, is this righteous love of the woman who washes herself before David’s royal palace.

47. But she not only washed; she also called, as we learn in the same book, when the holy Church says:

> Come, my brother; let us go out into the field, let us rest in the villages, let us rise early and go into the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed (Song VII, 11–12).

She therefore not only washes, but also urges and invites Christ to come to her, saying:

> I will give you my breasts (ibid.).

She promises not only her own things, but also new and old things, as you have it:

> New and old things, my brother, I have kept for you (ibid., 13).

And, as though unable to endure her love, she seeks the assistance of someone by whom Christ may be asked to come. See her burning desire; see her longing:

> Who will give you to me, my brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother? (Song VIII, 1).

She shows in what manner she seeks him, with what grace she invites him, and how she may hold him; she shows how she awaits him while he remains outside, and implores him to enter her house, saying:

> When I find you outside, I shall kiss you; I shall take you and lead you into the house of my mother, and into the chamber of her who conceived me (ibid., 2).

You see how naked she is, since she cannot have a hidden covering—certainly the hidden place of an undefiled nature, the secret of an inner conscience not marked by any recklessness of vices. For the holy Church is a closed garden, and so is spotless virginity. It deserves this grace from Christ because it sought, desired, and found the Word of God, keeping watch before the doors of Wisdom, as she herself says:

> Blessed is the man who hears me, and the person who keeps my ways, watching daily at my doors, guarding the posts of my entrances. For my exits are the exits of life (Prov. VIII, 34).

48. Thus Christ desired the beauty of his Church and prepared to take her as his wife. But because she was under the Law—for Peter, John, and the other apostolic men were under the Law—he first considered that we should be released from the bonds of bodily observance. Although the Law is religious and the Law is just, as is represented in the person of Uriah, who was so religious and chaste that, after returning from war, he did not recognize his wife and did not go in to her, [Note: All the editions and a few manuscripts have this reading. The Tornacensis Codex, however, has: “when Uriah had been killed, David—that is, the humble man—recognized the union with the Church.” Theodoret has: “when the true David—that is, the humble man—recognized the union, the Church.” Four others have: “when Uriah was David—that is, the humble man—recognized the union with the Church,” and so forth.]

nevertheless, because Uriah recognized the union with the Church in David—that is, in the humble man—and, withdrawing from his union with the Synagogue, prepared the place for the future marriage. John therefore also received the type of the Law. Although he was descended from the Patriarchs, he announced that the ways of the Lord were to be prepared and prophesied the union with the Church. Thus he is represented as having been killed, to show the failure of legal observance. For the Law and the prophets lasted until John.

Therefore Uriah has already been killed as a type of the Law, so that the Synagogue might be released from the snares of the Law, since a woman who is under a husband is bound by the law to her husband while he is alive; but if the husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Thus, while her husband is alive, she will be called an adulteress if she joins herself to another man; but if her husband dies, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man. Therefore the human condition is not adulterous, although it was under the Law, since, with the observance of the Law in a certain sense abolished, it was reclaimed for grace. [Note: The Roman edition has: “the human condition is adulterous”; two others and all the manuscripts have: “the human condition is not adulterous.” The latter reading is not inappropriate if the word “adulterous” is understood as spoken of the Church. Again, in the same place, the edition of Erasmus and two manuscripts have: “yet she has, in a certain sense, forgotten the observance of the Law for the sake of grace”; the manuscripts read “in what manner” instead of “in a certain sense.”]

49. Christ, however, did not abolish the observance of the Law. Hence David did not kill Uriah, but allowed him to be killed by the soldiers: that is, Christ allowed the rite of observance that came from the Law to be profaned through the invasion of barbarians and the captivity of the Jews. Indeed, Uriah means “my light.” And what is the light of Christ except the Law and the Gospel? “For if you believed Moses, you would also believe me, for he wrote about me” (John V, 46).

Because Christ’s light went before in the Law, it afterward filled the whole of this world, as it were, in the *heptamyxos* Spirit, through the grace of the Gospel. [Note: Several manuscripts, and Erasmus and Gill in the margin, read: “in a seven-branched lamp, in the sevenfold Spirit.” But this is a gloss. There is no doubt that the allusion is to the candlestick of the old Law, in which were seven lamps, signifying the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.] Hence he took flesh from the Law—or the Church—and joined it to himself. The hostile people diminished the light of that Law when they violated the holy Law. Thus the light of God was diminished among the Jewish people, because a partial blindness has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved.

## CHAPTER X

With renewed attention, he probes more deeply the mystery hidden in David’s adultery—namely, the union of the divine Word with human nature.

[Col. 0907D]

50. There remains also a fourth mystery. I ask that you receive it with calm ears and weigh our mind, not our words; for the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. Adultery occurred, and murder occurred. This is what was said to the Prophet:

> Take for yourself a staff of almond wood (Jer. I, 11).

And elsewhere we read of an almond rod, through which we understand a certain authority and the fullness of prophecy, which, like an almond, is bitter on the outside in its shell, hard in the middle, but tender and fruitful within. Therefore, even if you hear bitter things in the historical account, recognize hard things in the type; nevertheless, hope for fruitful things in the mystery.

Adultery, I say, occurred as a type of salvation; for not every adultery is to be condemned. Indeed, it was said to the Prophet:

> Go, take for yourself a prostitute as your wife (Hos. I, 2).

The Lord commands that there be a marriage with one who has prostituted herself; and, as we said above (above, chapter 9 of this book), the offspring of this marriage is Christ. For the son who was born from prostitution received from the Lord the name Jezreel, which means “divine generation.” If, then, that union with the prostitute was holy, this union with the adulteress is surely likewise holy.

But that concerns the Jews. As for divine things, I do not dare to call it “holy adultery,” although the expression is pious, lest the sound of the words offend anyone, even though the meaning of reverence is evident. It can nevertheless be said more cautiously, though less explicitly, that a holy cohabitation arose from unequal unions when the Word became flesh. For the associations of divinity and flesh are not lawful in the ordinary sense; nor do divinity and flesh preserve, as it were, the law of the marriage bed in the way that, by a certain covenant, the natures of flesh and soul, and soul and flesh, come together. God assumed flesh, assumed a soul, and through an extraordinary and not legally constituted incarnation made the partnership a lawful one, so that God might be all in all.

51. Finally, to know that there is a mystery, interpret the names. You understand David as a type of Christ. Bathsheba is called “daughter of the sabbath,” or “full daughter,” or “well of the oath.” What, then, could be clearer than that the daughter of the sabbath is the flesh of Christ, because God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law? She is also “full,” because in his Passion there is the fullness of the Law, or because she is full of the grace of the Holy Spirit. For Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan.

She is also “the well of the oath,” that is, of religion and faith. And rightly a well, because “from his belly will flow rivers of living water.” Taking this flesh to himself, God the Word made the union lawful. This mystery was signified by the marriage described in the Song of Songs, in which the Church is married to Christ and flesh to spirit.

And therefore the flesh ran about and sought the Word of God everywhere, because wounded, because naked, because adulterous in all things, though undefiled in Christ, miserable flesh sought its Redeemer.

52. Christ joined this flesh to himself in order to make it undefiled; he associated it with himself in order to remove its adultery. And because it was under the Law, it had to die in order to be freed from the Law, so that through that death a kind of marriage between the Law and the flesh might be dissolved.

The flesh therefore died in Christ, so that we, having been put to death to the Law through the body of Christ, as the Apostle said (Rom. VII, 4), might belong to another, who rose from the dead; and so that the passions and desires of the flesh, and the thoughts of sins that were in our members through the Law, might die in that death. But we, freed from the law of death, might rise again as through a new union with Christ, in newness of spirit.

53. Yet all who dissolved the Law in Christ’s flesh and thought that it ought to be violated were killed by the soldiers at David’s command. By this sign it is shown that what later events taught was signified: none of those who killed Christ escaped. It is revealed most clearly that those whom Jesus had taken up before his death, like the Jews, perished as little ones and without form; but those whom he adopted into the number of sons after his death were preserved for the kingdom.

Accordingly, in keeping with this mystery, it is fitting that the first offspring among the Jews was weak, so that afterward an eternal fruit might arise among Christians.

## CHAPTER XI

The parable of Nathan is presented and transferred first to the moral sense and then to the allegorical sense.
