54. But now let us turn to the message. For in previous days our discussion concerned the notorious adultery and murder of the prophet David; and, having pursued the mysteries, we found not only nothing that should be condemned, but even something that should be praised.

Now the discussion begins to concern the message indicated by the title of the psalm, which has often been repeated. It runs as follows:

> A psalm of David, for understanding, when Nathan the prophet came to him, when he had gone in to Bathsheba (Ps. L, 1).

[Note: The Roman edition alone has: “A psalm of David unto the end.” But the considerable diversity formerly found in Psalter titles has already been observed above, at the end, p. 711.]

55. This part of the history must therefore also be unfolded. It is as follows. “A rich man,” he says (II Kings XII, 1 ff.), “and a poor man lived in one city. The rich man had many herds and many sheep; the poor man had one little ewe, which was fed from the poor man’s bread and wine and rested in his bosom.

“A traveler came to the rich man. The rich man took nothing from his own herd or flocks, but killed the poor man’s one ewe.” When David learned this, he said: “That man shall die, and he shall restore fourfold.”

Nathan answered him: “You are the man.”

Then he disclosed to him the heavenly decree, saying that the Lord had commanded that, after taking him from among the shepherds, he had bestowed many good things upon him—that is, royal riches—and had poured out his mercy upon him; and therefore, because he had provoked the Lord by sin, all his possessions were to be taken away, carried off by enemies, and his house laid waste.

Then he said: “I have sinned.” And Nathan answered: “Because you confess that you have sinned, the Lord will forgive your sin; but your son who was born from Bathsheba will die.”

While this son was sick, David wept, lay upon the ground, covered himself with sackcloth, and fasted. When he learned that the child was dead, he rose, washed, ate, and consoled others.

[Col. 0910A]

56. Consider how many matters there are here. First of all, that God is pious and merciful, and that we endure the things that befall us as the price of our error. We have therefore learned that captivity is the price of sin, for this punishment is decreed for the crime.

Next we observe that the fall of kings is the punishment of peoples. Just as we are saved by their virtue, so we are endangered by their error. Hence we ought to desire that we may have a glorious and perfect king. Do we, then, who want to have a perfect king, not want to have a perfect Lord? Or can those wish a human being to be perfect who do not want God to be perfect?

The historical narrative also briefly accomplishes this: it makes us notice how quickly the hope of forgiveness followed. Nor is it a minor matter that Nathan, the inferior prophet, announced this to him. Great indeed is the shame and embarrassment of wrongdoing when one is reproved by an inferior. You see that guilt diminishes grace. Nathan knew what David did not know; so completely was his mind darkened and obscured by a certain cloud of vices.

Moreover, this is the Nathan who had earlier prophesied to David that he was acceptable to the Lord, so that David might grieve when the same man rebuked the sin whose merit had been proclaimed through his prophecy.

57. But now let us seek the mystery. “There were two men,” he says, “in one city, one rich and the other poor” (II Kings XII, 1). Who is this rich man or poor man, unless perhaps one is the Jewish people and the other the Christian people?

The former was rich in the Law, rich in the utterances of God entrusted to him, rich in prophecies, rich in oracles; the latter, however, was poor. But do not reject this poverty, which is followed by the kingdom of heaven. For it is written:

> Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. V, 3).

Good is the poverty that does not lose what it has. Good is the poverty that, even if it has no treasures of money, nevertheless has treasures of knowledge and wisdom. Do not despise poverty, children, as though it were worthless. “This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him” (Ps. XXXIII, 7). Do not envy great riches as though they were desirable:

> The rich became poor and hungry (ibid., 11).

But if you wish to have good things, seek the Lord:

> Those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing (ibid.).

Therefore do not reject any poor person. Peter was poor, and he had not even a coin to give; but he gave salvation, more precious than all money.

That poor man was Lazarus in the Gospel (Luke XVI, 19 ff.); but the one who had previously lain rich in purple and fine linen wished, after the end of his life, to be refreshed by a drop falling from the poor man’s finger. Although that man, proud in royal purple and dressed in fine garments, had disdainfully recoiled from the poor man’s wounds, nevertheless, placed in the underworld, he wished to have been in the place where Lazarus was.

In this passage the reading does not seem to describe a rich and poor man in terms of money, but rather the poor man who, for the sake of faith and devotion, did not shrink from bodily wounds and endured hunger and fasting.

58. Although the Jewish people had abundant supplies of victims in their flocks, nevertheless they seized the one little ewe that the poor people possessed, subjecting it to a glorious Passion.

Do you wish to know what sheep this was?

> Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter (Isa. LIII, 7),

the one who was fed on the poor man’s bread, who used the poor man’s drink, and who slept in the poor man’s bosom. For he used our nourishment and rested in the embrace of our breast. Indeed, he declared that he could not rest in the bosom of the Jews, saying:

> The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Luke IX, 58).

59. “And a traveler,” he says, “came to that rich man.” Who is this traveler except pitiable sin? For guilt entered this world like a traveler, foreign and alien to our nature. Therefore he did not offer a victim from his own flocks; he took the poor man’s little ewe and killed it.

Although this creature’s Passion may have served some people for a saving sacrifice, nevertheless it seems to have been for them food for their own madness, nourishment for guilt, and an incentive to sin. Finally, Judas received bread from Christ and was then filled more completely with the devil, because he did not receive it in faith—the man who was preparing betrayal for so hospitable a Lord. [Note: The Theodoret Codex alone reads “for sacrifice” as “for the sacrarium.” With four words inserted, Erasmus and Gill have “food stolen from them”; the Tornacensis Codex has “food for their theft”; the Roman edition and the Theodoret manuscript have “an increase of their own madness.” The six Gallican codices, which we have followed, offer the better reading.]

60. “And David was angry with that man.” We have said that the Jewish people are represented through the Prophet, and therefore, under this figure, he condemns himself.

“That man deserves death who did this, and he shall restore the ewe fourfold”—that is, the Jewish people would perish, but the Christian people would enjoy more abundant blessings, because the condition granted through the resurrection is superior to the present one.

61. My purpose was, as I ask you to remember, to answer in whatever way I could those who think that the adultery and murder of holy David ought to be condemned. Thus, through the favor of your unanimity, the course of our discussion has proceeded in such a way that the man whom we thought could not be defended seemed worthy of praise in everyone’s mouth.

But since the holy man does not need our assistance, let him now speak for himself to you, and let his own words defend his deed.

## CHAPTER XII

David confesses his sin to God in the composition of Psalm L, and several of its verses are explained. In particular, he investigates what “great mercy” and “the multitude of mercies” are. He then teaches that God alone blots out our iniquities, which cannot remain hidden and must therefore be confessed by the example of David. Finally, it becomes clear that the Arians fall back into the impiety of the Manichaeans.

[Col. 0911D]

62. “Have mercy on me, Lord,” he says, “according to your great mercy” (Ps. L, 3). This expression, dearest brothers, is new, if I am not mistaken: that mercy should be called great. I do not easily remember reading it elsewhere, and therefore we shall not readily be able to say what “great mercy” is. [Note: This is the reading of Erasmus and Gill, together with almost all the manuscripts. The Roman edition and the Theodoret manuscript instead have: “We must consider what great mercy is.” Although we may not readily have read “great mercy,” etc. The words added here seem to us rather a paraphrase by some conjecturer than the author’s genuine wording.]

Yet we read of the great power of God. Therefore, by considering what great power is, we may infer what mercy he intended to designate as great. For we read in holy Jeremiah:

> Who are you, Lord? You made heaven and earth in your great power and outstretched arm (Jer. XXXII, 17).

Great power therefore made heaven. What is this great power—the Father’s or the Son’s? Certainly it is the great power of the Father, for he made heaven and earth through the Son, as you have it:

> In the beginning God made heaven and earth (Gen. I, 1).

Yet the Son too is great power. For when you read that the Son is the power of the Father (I Cor. I, 24), as you have it, “Christ the power and wisdom of God,” then, since the Son is the power of the Father, the Son is indeed great power.

How, then, can the omnipotent one be denied when we confess that he is the great power of God? This great power made heaven, because the Son also made heaven, as you have it:

> All things were made through him (John I, 3).

Therefore, if both the Father and the Son made it, the unity of the work clearly indicates unity of operation. The operation of the Father and the Son does not differ. But if there is one operation, there is certainly one power of operation, and one majesty of the works. So much concerning the Father and the Son.

63. Why, then, should we be silent about the Spirit, especially when divine Scripture does not permit us to be silent? The passage provides a most suitable testimony for proving the unity of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, so that we cannot separate his operation from the work of the Father and the Son.

We read that it is the great power of the Father that he made heaven; that the Son is also great power because he made heaven—not only made it, but also established it:

> By the word of the Lord the heavens were established (Ps. XXXII, 6).

Therefore, if making and establishing heaven belong to great power, we cannot separate the Holy Spirit from the majesty of great power, because it is written:

> And by the breath of his mouth is all their power (ibid.).

For when heaven and earth were being made, the Spirit was hovering over them. Of this the prophet David says elsewhere:

> Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created (Ps. CIII, 13).

Of this he also said elsewhere:

> For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers (Ps. VIII, 4).

God did not make heaven and earth with bodily fingers, but by the sevenfold grace of the Spirit—that finger, namely, of which you have in the Gospel:

> But if I cast out demons by the finger of God (Luke XI, 20).

Elsewhere he called this finger the Spirit, as you have it:

> But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God (Matt. XII, 28).

Therefore, if the Spirit of God is the finger, since the Son is the arm of God, the Spirit, working together with the Father and the Son through the unity of operation, made heaven and earth. He called him the finger for this reason: so that, as though of one body, he might express the unity of the divinity.

Thus, if great power founded heaven, great wisdom also founded heaven, because it is written:

> You made all things in wisdom (Ps. CIII, 24).

64. We have therefore learned what great power is. Let us now gather what great mercy is. If great power made the heavens, there must also be great mercy from heaven, and great justice must also be from heaven; for justice looked down from heaven, and mercy came from heaven.

Great, then, was the mercy that was accomplished, because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John I, 14). Thus great power made the heavens; great power also inclined the heavens, as we read:

> He inclined the heavens and came down (Ps. XVII, 10).

This shows that the Son of God was never without his divinity, not even when he lived among human beings. For although he assumed what he was not, he did not cease to be what he was.

Thus, when it is said, “He inclined the heavens and came down,” he seems not so much to have descended from heaven as to have descended together with heaven itself. For when the Father addressed the Son while he was situated on earth and angels ministered to him, the Son of God seems not so much to have changed his dwelling as to have transferred it. [Note: Erasmus, Gill, and the Roman edition have: “He seems not so much to have inclined the heavens as to have descended from heaven himself.” Five manuscripts, however, have restored the reading given above.]

We have therefore learned that mercy is great.

65. Therefore, if it is great mercy to descend from heaven, we must distinguish and understand what “the multitude of mercies” is. The verse continues:

> And according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity (Ps. L, 3).

The two verses do not signify the same thing. The first refers to the Incarnation; the second seems to refer to the injuries that the Son of God endured in the flesh: that he fasted, hungered, wept, was beaten, was crucified, died, and was buried.

These are marks of the flesh, not of divinity. It was necessary that the multitude of mercies should drive away the multitude of afflictions, to our benefit through the struggle of the Lord’s Passion.

66. He was not blotting out his own sins, since he had committed no sin; but because he was made sin, our sins had to be blotted out, as David said:

> Blot out my iniquity.

What does “blot out” mean? Let us examine this word, for it is not idle. Elsewhere he says:

> I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them (Isa. XLIII, 25).

There are certainly wounds of sins deeply impressed upon our conscience, and certain bruises of our minds and souls that are covered over by the sores of our errors. Guilt therefore has its own characters and marks by which it is exposed. We do not fabricate this by our own ingenuity; we affirm it on prophetic authority.

It has therefore been written. See where it was written:

> In the breast of your heart (Jer. XVII, 1).

That is, the record of guilt was written there where the form of virtue is also written—not on tablets of stone, but on the tablets of fleshly hearts.

Good things, however, are not written with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; wicked things are written with an iron stylus and an adamantine claw. The writing is much like the punishment of sin. The sin is written with an iron stylus; the sinner is restrained with an iron rod, as it is written:

> You shall rule them with an iron rod (Ps. II, 9).

One is the upright rod:

> The rod of your kingdom (Ps. XLIV, 7);

the former restrains the guilty with punishment, while the latter governs the innocent with authority.

The guilt, then, has been written. Let us see where. Not outside, but within, in your heart and in your breast. For just as “the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart,” so for unbelievers the image of sin and the likeness of error are impressed upon the very heart.

Guilt is therefore within, and virtue also within. Hence the Lord says:

> I perceive power going out from me (Luke VIII, 46),

to show that good things proceed from within, and, conversely, that evil things also come forth from within.

“For it is not what enters the mouth,” he says, “that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth” (Matt. XV, 11). Thoughts proceed from your heart. Therefore take care that evil thoughts do not come forth from your heart, to accuse and condemn you at a later time.

God does not need testimony or arguments to convict you. Your own guilt accuses and exposes you.

67. Moreover, David rightly says in this psalm:

> And my sin is always before me (Ps. L, 5).

Woe to me, who wish to remain hidden but cannot! How shall I hide, when I carry upon my breast the signs of my sins, written there? On that day of judgment each person’s breast will be laid bare, his conscience bearing witness against all, and thoughts accusing or even defending one another, on the day when the Lord will judge the hidden things of human beings.

What shame there will be when what we thought hidden begins to be exposed to everyone; when the image of each person’s sin begins to reveal itself, so that each person is convicted by the sequence of his own crimes!

What shame when you see that the one whom you judged contemptible in this world has been given precedence; when you recognize that your servant, the one whom, according to the clever standards of this world, you considered foolish and incapable, has been honored for the riches of his simplicity.

Therefore, while we live, let us flee to the one who can blot out sin. Nor should you fear that, because it has been written with an iron stylus and an adamantine claw, it cannot be erased. For he has broken iron and adamantine gates; do not fear confessing your guilt. [Note: The author clearly alludes to Jeremiah XVII: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with an adamantine claw,” as the Vulgate renders it. Since these words are absent from the Septuagint, the author—if he is Ambrose, or someone of his period—must have quoted them from another translator or perhaps from the common version, which was formerly read in various forms and into which many passages from other versions had been incorporated. See also Nobilius on this passage, if convenient.]

68. David confessed; he acknowledged his iniquity; he acknowledged his error. Therefore he says:

> For I acknowledge my iniquity (ibid.).

David acknowledges, and you do not acknowledge? David confesses, and you deny? Paul cries out that he is guilty (I Tim. I, 15), and you assert that you are innocent?

There is therefore no great cause for shame when fellowship in sin is shared with many—provided that we follow the desire to correct ourselves. Nor should you again be afraid that confession of guilt will be held against you for punishment. For the good and merciful God is accustomed not only to forgive those who confess their sins, but also to bestow rewards upon those who correct themselves—provided that each person asks that what he understands is not hidden from God may be pardoned.

Say, then, your iniquities, so that you may be justified (Isa. XLIII, 26). This is the voice of God, who wishes to forgive; this is the voice of God promising that he wishes to blot out your sin.

69. “Against you alone I have sinned,” David says, “and I have done evil before you.” That is: although human beings do not see, you see; although human beings cannot judge me because they share in sins, you nevertheless are the judge of each person because you are free from sins.

However deeply harmful thoughts may lie hidden in the heart, they are before you, who can say:

> Why do you think evil things in your hearts? (Matt. IX, 4).

Christ, of course, says this. Therefore the one who knows what is written in the heart can erase whatever has been written in the heart.

Our David confesses to him that he sinned not only in himself but also in the first human being, when the divine commandments were violated.

70. From this, dearest brothers, we may observe how all heresies, while attacking one another, turn back upon themselves. Thus the Arians, by separating the power of the Father and the Son, rush into an outcome of argument in which their assertion coincides with that of the Manichaeans. For the latter say that one God belongs to the Old Testament and another to the New.

The holy Church condemns this profane assertion. She recognizes one God, because there is one God the Father, from whom all things come and for whom we exist; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things come and through whom we exist (I Cor. VIII, 6).

The omnipotent power of the Father and the Son is therefore declared to be one, so that we neither separate the Father from the grace of the New Testament nor, conversely, separate the Son from the renewal of the world.

71. Finally, let us consider whether the same God is the author of both Testaments. Certainly we all sinned in the first human being, and through the succession of nature the succession of guilt was also transmitted from one person to all.

Against whom, then, did I sin—against the Father or against the Son? Certainly against the one who entrusted me with what I sinned by failing to keep. The command was given to the human being that he might taste everything that was in paradise, but that he should not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. II, 17).

Adam, therefore, is in each of us. For in him the human condition sinned, because through one person sin passed into all. I see the great sum entrusted to me; I see what records of transgression I have incurred, while tasting what was forbidden and prohibited. Hence I owe interest on the portion entrusted to me, because steadfast faith was unable to preserve the deposit of the heavenly commandments unviolated.

72. We have recognized what was entrusted; let us also recognize the one who entrusted it. For it is the creditor’s right both to demand and to release; and therefore the same person releases who has the right to demand. When, then, Christ said to me in the Gospel, “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 5:20), do I not understand him to be the master of the principal, whom I recognize as the arbiter of forgiveness? Or, if the Father entrusted the debt and the Son released it—not through unity, as we say, but, as the Arians assert, through a difference of power—did one God entrust it and another release it? Thus they fall into a position from which they do not escape the impiety of the Manichaeans. Furthermore, by declaring one God good, let them notice into what snares of their own madness they fall. If the one who entrusted it is good, how is the one who released it not good? Thus, when the Arians share a position with those whose assertion they embrace, it is no wonder that one who has once begun to deviate from the truth becomes entangled in the bonds of another’s error.

[Note: This is the reading of the editions of Erasmus and Gill, supported by the manuscripts, except that some have, “with whose assertion they agree.” Hence the Roman edition and the manuscripts of Theodore may perhaps have derived their reading, “with whose assertion they concur.” Our reading, however, seems preferable, since the author undoubtedly refers to what he had said above, namely, that all heresies return into one another.]

73. And therefore there is one doctrine that destroys the contrivances of all heretics: we must believe that the Trinity is one in power, majesty, and might; and therefore we must not separate the Father from what the Son has done, nor segregate the Son from what the Father has commanded. For thus it will come about that we do not introduce one God of the Old Testament and another of the New; rather, through the unity of power, the Son is understood in the Father and the Father in the Son; the Son makes a loan in the Father, and the Father releases in the Son. For the Father also forgives sin: we have already said that the Son forgave it.

[Note: The editions of Erasmus and Rome read, “and therefore let us not separate from the Father what the Son did,” and so forth. Gill and the manuscript of Theodore read, “let us not separate the Father.” We owe the true reading of this passage to the agreement of the other manuscripts.]

74. Hear that the Father also forgives. “Forgive us our debts,” he says, “as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12). Certainly the Son says this to the Father in our person. He does not say it as though he himself were unable to forgive; rather, he says it so that you may understand the unity of power.

75. Finally, if you seek authority in the Son: “Now you are clean,” he says, “because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15:3). He forgives by his word; he forgives by his command. But he forgives with discernment when he says, “Go, and from now on see that you do not sin” (John 5:14). You have authority, because he forgave what was past; you have judgment, because he prescribed what was to come.

# Expositions on Twelve Psalms

## Prefatory Notice concerning the Expositions on Twelve Psalms

We have already indicated more than once in the preceding books that Saint Ambrose inserted expositions of several psalms (Prefatory Notice to the book On Tobias; the book On the Intercession and the Apology of David), and we shall also observe this in the volume that follows (Oration on the Death of Theodosius). Evidently he considered it a matter of such great usefulness—indeed, of necessity—to instruct his people through expositions of this kind. No doubt for the same reason he turned his attention to explaining these twelve psalms.

He expounded them on different occasions and at different times, partly by preaching and partly by dictation, when ill health no longer allowed him to speak publicly. In the present collection, however, he did not follow the sequence of the Psalter, since he worked out the exposition of Psalm 43 last. From this it may be understood that this collection of twelve psalms, which we present according to the order of our manuscripts, cannot be Ambrose’s own. Perhaps one of his disciples arranged it, or even Paulinus himself, since he took down the last of these expositions while Ambrose dictated it. Whether, however, everything that the holy Bishop ever published on this subject is contained in this collection remains uncertain. For in the most ancient authors who wrote something about it—Jerome (Letter 89, in the new edition Letter 75) and Cassiodorus (On Divine Literature, book 1, chapter 4)—we nowhere find how many psalms he expounded.

Some have thought that it may rightly be inferred from the preface placed before the first psalm that our Doctor undertook the project of illuminating the whole Psalter with expositions. But since that preface contains merely an imitation of Basil, of whom no such undertaking is recorded, and since it is clearly a single sermon delivered to the people—in which he enlarges upon the praises of the psalms in general but does not promise to do anything further—that argument does not seem to us very compelling.

We think a somewhat stronger case may be drawn, first, from the fact that, while explaining Psalm 36, he promises an exposition of Psalm 57 (no. 32), which he did not leave behind; and, second, from the fact that he was unable to explain Psalm 43 in full, being hindered by the struggles of his final illness. To that very beautiful preface the holy man joined the exposition of the first psalm in continuous sequence, as we understand from the transition by which the two are connected. We also observed there that he delivered a sermon in his own church after the customary singing of the psalms, and that catechumens were present together with the other hearers. This perhaps gives good reason to think that it was delivered during Lent.

Although we cannot determine its year with certainty, we can nevertheless approach that determination to some extent. For it is clear not only that the sermon was later than the books On the Death of His Brother Satyrus and On Faith in the Resurrection, which it cites, but also that it was delivered after the congregational singing had been introduced into the Church of Milan. Ambrose himself sufficiently indicates that congregational singing had begun before he explained this psalm, when, after mentioning the psalmody of women, virgins, old men, children, kings, and soldiers, he adds: “When the psalm is read, it itself produces silence. Everyone speaks, and no one interrupts” (Preface, no. 9). These words plainly indicate the enthusiasm still burning around a recently established practice. Hence I do not think that this little work should be assigned later than the year 390.

The expositions of Psalm 35 and the five that follow display the same character of discourse. There is no doubt that all of them were delivered to the people; this is sufficiently shown by the frequent mention of the Scripture that had been read in the Church on the same day before Ambrose spoke (On Psalm 35, no. 20; On Psalm 36, no. 2, and elsewhere).

Since the pious shepherd looked solely to the advancement of his flock in his sermons, he therefore pursues and develops the moral sense with particular care in these works. Yet whenever a passage calling for mystical interpretation occurs, he considers that he must by no means omit it. Nevertheless, with his customary modesty, while adding his own opinion to those of others in both senses, he never fails to leave it to the judgment of his hearers which interpretation seems preferable. Hence that celebrated statement: “It is our task to seek the truth; it is yours to choose what you will follow” (On Psalm 38, no. 22).

But in these works there is not only a concern to shape conduct toward virtue; the greatest diligence is also devoted to imbuing orthodox minds with the doctrines of the faith. For this reason he attacks various heretics, such as the followers of Novatian and Apollinaris, and especially those of Arius. There too he not only explains and confirms the mysteries of the Trinity and the Incarnation with singular clarity, but also expounds Christ’s two wills and two operations in such a way (On Psalm 39, no. 16, and elsewhere) that one could scarcely expect anything more excellent after the rise of the Monothelites. This exposition of mysteries so sublime makes us think that only baptized persons were present, especially since nothing is observed there that can suitably refer to catechumens. Nevertheless, on suitable occasions he does not fail there either to blunt certain familiar accusations of idolaters.

Anyone who compares these expositions with one another, especially their beginnings, and does so with more than superficial attention, will discover such coherence and kinship among them that, once he has determined the year to which any one of them must be assigned, he will believe that the date of all the others has become entirely clear. Thus we shall readily recognize that they were not composed or delivered before 8 September of the year 393, since it is perfectly clear that Psalm 36 mentions the victory which Theodosius, with divine assistance, won over the tyrant Eugenius on that day (Exposition on Psalm 36, no. 19).

Many considerations confirm this date. First, our holy author speaks of the defection of Sarmatio and Barbatian from the monastic institution as of something by no means recent: “Long ago,” he says, “they left the monasteries” (Exposition on Psalm 36, no. 49). More exact calculation places the flight of these apostates in the year 389.

Second, when he says, “Arians arose, supported by imperial power, who thought that the temple of the Lord ought to be handed over to them, threatening the bitterness of persecutions” (Exposition on Psalm 37, nos. 19 and 43), it is by no means obscure that he is designating the persecution under Justina.

Third, does he not seem to admonish Theodosius concerning the massacre of the Thessalonians in these words: “Imitate, emperors, the divine example,” and so forth (On Psalm 40, no. 38)? Nor should anyone rightly brand us with absurdity if we say that some passages there may appropriately refer to that prince’s repentance, which can never be praised enough. It is universally acknowledged that all these events occurred before the year 389.

Finally, he cites his commentaries on Luke as though they had been composed not long before (On Psalm 38, no. 1), since he repeats the exposition of the passage mentioned, as though he despaired that it still remained present in the minds of his hearers.

Since these facts stand as they do, we think no one will insist that these expositions must more stubbornly be referred to the persecution under Justina. We are nevertheless aware that Ripamonti, in his History of Milan, decade 1, published at the command of Blessed Charles, asserts that around this same time certain battles were fought between the orthodox and the Arians, in which many miracles occurred in favor of the former, plainly similar to those described in Psalm 36.

But since this author’s account rests only on certain old images, inscriptions, or, finally, the names of particular places, his authority is not weighty enough to be preferred to the agreement of all the writers who attribute these same marvels solely to the war waged against the tyrant Eugenius. As for the fact that the holy man mentions a petition of the Arians made several years earlier, this should no more seem surprising than his failure to omit mention of the much older books On Repentance (On Psalm 40, no. 24), or even of an event that he himself had witnessed as a boy.

We now come to the explanation of Psalm 43, which is the last of our Doctor’s works. He dictated it to his deacon and secretary Paulinus a few days before his death, already full of the God whom he was soon to possess, as was foretold by the fiery shield which Paulinus saw suspended over his head. In this work he recorded certain remarkable examples of virtue (Paulinus, Life of Ambrose). For he not only reveals the greatest modesty when he professes distrust in his own ability while explaining the Scriptures, but also the highest zeal for the Catholic faith, on whose behalf he fought against heretics—especially Arians—to his final breath. Moreover, he shows extraordinary love for his flock, in whose instruction he finally died of labor.

We may also gather from the same Paulinus (ibid.) that this final writing of Ambrose should be assigned to the Easter season of the year 397, since it was at that time, according to the more probable opinion, that he ceased to live. More will be said about this elsewhere.

The final four expositions, one of which is cited by Augustine, likewise consist of sermons, as is sufficiently indicated both by their style and by the passages of Scripture cited from those read in the Church on the same days (On Psalm 45, no. 15, and elsewhere). It is also highly credible that each contains a single sermon, since the verses of the psalms are passed over rapidly, and the exposition of the final verses is much shorter than that of the earlier verses, lest the hearers be wearied by too long a delay.

Their character, moreover, is by no means different. As in the preceding works, versions of Aquila, Theodotion, or Symmachus are no longer cited, except in the last, where one is mentioned only once and almost in passing. From this one might perhaps reasonably infer that the date of the last was also the date of the others. Since it is clear that the explanation of Psalm 61 was delivered shortly after Gratian’s murder, Ambrose’s second embassy to Maximus, and Theodosius’s victory over that tyrant, it follows that all of them can scarcely be later than the year 390, to which historians assign several of Ambrose’s works of this kind.

In the preface and exposition of the first psalm, Ambrose borrowed many things from Basil, some of which we have pointed out in their proper places, following his customary practice. He also followed Origen in certain matters, as Saint Jerome observed (in the place cited above). Certainly anyone who compares the commentaries of both men on Psalms 36, 37, and 38 will find that no small number of passages from Origen have been transferred into Ambrose’s works.

But here we also find certain doctrines very close to Origen’s errors concerning judgment, resurrection (On Psalm 1, no. 54; On Psalm 36, no. 54), and even the purification of all the elect by fire. Yet, as we have noted elsewhere (Prefatory Notice to the book, and elsewhere), he did this out of respect for the honor of distinguished men: he did not hesitate to propose opinions that had not yet been clearly condemned by the Church, although, when occasion arose, he taught and approved the contrary position.

Since we know that he did this on this very subject, especially in what he teaches in the exposition of Psalm 118, sermon 20, verses 2 and 8, it is highly plausible that on these two points he himself held no view other than those later explained more clearly by Augustine, his disciple (City of God, book 20, chapter 8; book 21, chapter 26), and subsequently embraced by all theologians through common agreement.

# Expositions of Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, on Twelve Psalms of David

## Exposition of the First Psalm

[Note: The work was probably written around the year 381, and no later than 390.]

### Preface

1. Since God set the delight of future blessedness before virtue as its greatest incentive, the devil devised the delight of error as a powerful spur in the opposite direction. The first man, Adam, placed by the Lord God in the paradise of pleasure, provides evidence of both positions: he was placed there to enjoy eternal delight and to call his future offspring toward virtue.

God was not unaware that Adam would give error an opportunity, nor that the rest of humanity would need the hope of salvation set before it, by which it might strive to be restored to the place from which the human race had been deprived. And Adam, deceived by a wifely persuasion through the appearance of the serpent, which prefigured the allure of pleasure—thus, taking advantage of the occasion, the adversary worked death in me through pleasure.

Therefore what had been bestowed by divine grace for life became death to me, and the enemy found the man’s assent all the easier because he presented the appearance of nature as an excuse for the fall. For the Lord was delighted by his works; he was delighted by the first beginnings of nature, which, when he saw them, he declared to be “very good” (Genesis 1:31).

2. The angels praise the Lord; the Powers of heaven sing psalms to him; and before the beginning of the world the Cherubim and Seraphim, with the sweetness of their musical voices, say, “Holy, holy, holy” (Isaiah 6:3). Innumerable thousands of angels stand in attendance, and the elders and the great multitude sing together like the sound of many waters, “Alleluia” (Revelation 19:1 ff.).

[Note: Ambrose had already taught in book 1 of the Hexaemeron, chapter 5, no. 19, that the angels were created before the beginning of the world. Certainly this was also the opinion of many Fathers, both Greek and Latin. Hence, although the definition of the first chapter of the Lateran Council held under Innocent III may seem contrary to this, we must believe that the synod intended its censure to apply only either to those who denied altogether that spiritual substances were created, or to those who admitted that they were created but asserted that bodies were subsequently made as punishment for sins committed by them, into which bodies they were thrust as into prisons. Hence Saint Thomas, in part 1, question 61, article 3, calls the opinion of those who maintain that angels were created together with the rest of the universe not certain but merely more probable. See also his Opusculum 23, as well as Sixtus of Siena, book 5 of the Bibliotheca sancta, annotation 5.]

A more explicit account maintains that the very axis of heaven moves with a certain sweetness of perpetual harmony, so that its sound might be heard at the farthest regions of the earth, where there are certain hidden things of nature.

Nor does this seem foreign to the usage of nature, since a voice sent forth from groves or mountains returns with a more pleasing echo, and they give back with a sweeter sound what they have received. Nature has found even in cliffs and stones something that could give pleasure. Some are delighted by the reflection of sound, others by its use or charm. The wild beasts themselves and the birds are soothed by the pleasure of a more lovely place or more melodious voice. For nursing infants, severity is a terror, while gentleness is a delight. Pleasure, therefore, is natural.

[Note: This is the reading of the old edition and of the manuscripts Remigius, Longobardus, Valcellianus, Thuaneus, and Regius. The Vatican manuscript, however, reads, “the more extended discourse bears …”; the Colbertine and Victorine read, “the very heaven bears a discourse outside.” But what could “a discourse outside” mean, unless perhaps it is the same as “the discourse of outsiders,” that is, of those alien to the faith, such as Plato and his followers, concerning whom see On Abraham, chapter 8, no. 54? Finally, the Roman edition reads, “the discourse of certain persons.” As for how this passage is reconciled with other passages of our author, we explained it in On Isaac and the Soul, chapter 7, in the note appended to page 377.]

3. Hence holy David, who perceived from what condition man had fallen and by what fraud he had been cast down—for if he had retained the grace of that eternal and heavenly delight infused into him by the Lord, and had not lost it after being captivated by worldly allurements—undertook to restore and reform it. Through the ministry of psalmody he established for us an image of heavenly living.

4. For although all divine Scripture breathes the grace of God, the book of the psalms is especially sweet. Even Moses himself, who described the deeds of our ancestors in plain prose—

[Note: “In plain discourse” (plano sermone), πεζῷ λόγῳ (pezō logō), that is, “in pedestrian or prose speech,” as opposed to poetic or rhythmically constrained speech, which was called ἔποχος λόγος (epochos logos), “metrical speech.” It was the common opinion of the ancients that several parts of Scripture, especially the Psalter and nearly all the Canticles, consisted of verses, as Saint Jerome teaches in the preface to the book of Job. The later author of the Apology of David also seems to imply this in chapter 1, no. 2, where he calls Psalm 50 a divine and sacred song.

But since certain more recent writers oppose this opinion, “plain discourse,” or “pedestrian speech,” may also be understood as humble and unadorned speech, in contrast with noble and elevated speech, which, although unbound by meter, is nevertheless called poetic by reputable authors. Thus Quintilian, book 10, chapter 1, denies that Plato’s writing is pedestrian prose. Those who describe David’s psalms as songs may likewise be understood to mean that their diction is not so much bound by meter as grand, impassioned, and suited to singing.]

—yet, when he led the ancestral people across the Red Sea with memorable wonder, and saw King Pharaoh and his forces submerged, he raised his mind to greater things, because he had attained things beyond his own powers, and sang a triumphant song to the Lord (Exodus 15:1 ff.). Miriam also took a tambourine and encouraged the others, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (ibid., verse 20).

Moses himself, after he had read the law of the Lord, spoke through a song so that he might impress its memory upon the hearts of those who heard, saying: “Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak. Let my discourse be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew, like a shower upon the grass, like snow upon the hay” (Deuteronomy 32:1 ff.).

5. God, therefore, is delighted not only to be praised by song but also to be reconciled by it. Hence Moses used song especially at the time when heaven and earth were called to bear witness, so that the world might hear more eagerly its salvation resounding with the heavenly sound of grace, and so that observance of the sacred Law might be implanted forever in human minds through the sweetness of its song.

Finally, before the tablets of the Law were strengthened by song, they were broken and shattered by Moses in indignation. But once they had been consecrated by such a seal, human anger had no place, because sanctification excluded it through the sweetness of what was sacred. Thus the song of the Lord descended from heaven like softer dew and watered human faith like a shower of spiritual grace. These two songs in the books of Moses, therefore, like the two eyes of the world and the lights of heaven, illuminate the whole body of his work.

6. David, however, was chosen by the Lord above all for this ministry, so that what appears rarely to stand out in the other works might shine in this one as something constant and continuous.

We read one song in the book of Judges (Judges 5:2 ff.); the rest proceed in the manner of history, expressing the deeds of our ancestors. Isaiah wrote one song (Isaiah 12:1 ff.) to soothe the hearts of his readers; in the rest he roared with the terrifying trumpet of rebuke. Not even his enemies, who persecuted him to the point of death because of his other sayings, could bring a song against him as an accusation. Daniel wrote one (Daniel 3:52 ff.), and Habakkuk one (Habakkuk 3:2 ff.). Solomon himself, David’s son, although he is said to have sung innumerable songs, left one that the Church has received: the Song of Songs. In the others, therefore, one may observe individual features.

7. History instructs, the Law teaches, prophecy announces, rebuke chastises, morality persuades. In the book of Psalms there is the advancement of all these things, and a kind of medicine for human salvation. Whoever reads it has there a remedy by which he can heal the wounds of his own passion.

Whoever wishes to see, as though in a common gymnasium of souls and a kind of arena of virtues, various types of contests prepared for him, should choose for himself the one for which he understands himself to be best suited, so that he may reach the crown more easily.

If anyone desires to recount the deeds of his ancestors and to imitate them, he receives within a single psalm—the seventy-seventh—the whole sequence of ancestral history gathered together, so that he may acquire a treasury of memory through the brevity of his reading. What is explained more briefly also seems easier.

Consider, too, how profound it is that he distinguished adverse offenses within a brief interval and then added the favorable things of reconciliation, so that you might learn at once what harm unbelief in its offense causes and what benefit ready faith provides.

If anyone examines the force of the Law, which is wholly contained in the bond of love—for “whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the Law”—let him read in the psalms with what affection of love David alone exposed himself to grave dangers in order to repel the reproach of the entire people. In him he will recognize a glory of love equal to the triumph of virtue.

If anyone fears the severity of rebukes, let him hear the words: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chastise me in your wrath” (Psalm 6:2), and learn how to temper the judgment of an angry judge.

If anyone desires to know an example of patience, let him read in the psalms: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil” (Psalm 7:5), and observe that David anticipated the evangelical command in spirit and preceded it in virtue.

You therefore have that proverbial saying: “A gentle person is the physician of the heart” (Proverbs 14:30).

Moreover, if anyone wishes to be armed against the assaults of spiritual wickedness, what should he know more surely than that he must sing psalms? David sang when he was still a young man, and he drove away Saul’s evil spirit, which had previously gripped him.

8. What shall I say about the power of prophecy? What others announced through riddles seems to have been promised openly and clearly to this one alone: that the Lord Jesus would be born from his seed, as the Lord said to him: “From the fruit of your womb I will place one upon your throne” (Psalm 131:11).

In the psalms, therefore, Jesus is not only born for us; he also undergoes that saving suffering of the body, rests, rises again, ascends into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. What no human being had dared to say, this one prophet alone announced; afterward the Lord himself proclaimed it in the Gospel (Luke 24:44).

9. Moreover, all other writers set examples or certain sayings of their predecessors in their writings; the Psalms contain nothing except what is their own.

What, then, is sweeter than a psalm? Hence David himself beautifully says: “Praise him, for the psalm is good; let praise to our God be sweet and beautiful” (Psalm 146:1).

And truly so: the psalm is the blessing of the people, the praise of God, the praise of the assembly, the applause of all, the speech of everyone, the voice of the Church, the musical confession of faith, devotion full of authority, the joy of freedom, the cry of gladness, the echo of joy.

It softens anger, banishes anxiety, and lightens sorrow. It is a weapon by night, instruction by day; a shield in fear, a festival in holiness, an image of tranquility, a pledge of peace and concord; like a lyre, it produces one melody from diverse and unequal voices. The rising of day echoes the psalm; the setting of day resounds with the psalm.

[Note: Here Ambrose says that the Apostle forbade women to teach in the Church, but not to sing psalms. It is beyond doubt that in the age of the holy Bishop they regularly sang psalms in sacred assemblies; we shall demonstrate this in its proper place.]

The Apostle commands women to be silent in the Church; yet they too chant the psalm well. The psalm is sweet to every age and suitable to either sex.

The old sing it after laying aside the rigidity of old age. The veterans respond with it in the joy of their hearts, though they are sad. The young sing it without the envy of wantonness. Adolescents join in without the danger or temptation of the slippery age of pleasure. Young women sing it without compromising the modesty proper to matrons. Little girls, without abandoning their modesty, modulate a hymn to God with the sweetness of a restrained and serious voice.

[Note: The editions and two manuscripts read, “The tender age of childhood eagerly desires this.” Other manuscripts more correctly read, “to hold this”; for one must supply “in memory,” that is, “to know it,” in contrast with the following clause, “infancy rejoices to meditate on it,” that is, “to learn it.”]

Childhood eagerly desires to hold it; infancy rejoices to meditate upon it, while it avoids learning other things by heart. This is a kind of game that produces greater progress in learning than serious instruction when it is formally imparted.

How much effort is expended in the Church to produce silence when the readings are being proclaimed! If one person speaks, everyone interrupts.

But when the psalm is read, it itself produces silence. Everyone speaks, and no one interrupts. Kings make the psalm resound without the arrogance of power. David rejoiced to be seen in this ministry. The psalm is sung by emperors and shouted for joy by peoples. Individuals compete to cry out what benefits everyone.

The psalm is sung at home and repeated outside. It is learned without labor and retained with pleasure. The psalm joins those who disagree, unites the divided, and reconciles the offended. For who would not forgive someone with whom he had raised one voice to God? It is a great bond of unity when the entire multitude of the people comes together as one choir! The strings of a lyre are unequal, but their harmony is one. On a very few strings the fingers of a skilled musician often make mistakes; but in the people the Spirit, the true artisan, knows no error.

[Note: This is the reading of the old edition and all the manuscripts. The Roman edition, however, reads, “a solace from fear, rest from daily labor.” Basil, whom our holy author seems to have imitated, has the following in his Homily on Psalm 1: “A psalm is a weapon amid nocturnal fears, a rest from daily labors.” But there is nothing to prevent Ambrose from rendering Basil’s words and thought not slavishly but more freely, perhaps from memory. Nor did he imitate the other passage of Basil in any different way: “The psalter is the work of angels, the citizenship of heaven, the spiritual incense,” and so forth.]

The psalm is an exchange for nocturnal labor, the reward of daily rest, instruction for beginners, confirmation for the mature. It is the ministry of angels, the warfare of heaven, a spiritual sacrifice. Even the rocks respond to the psalm; the psalm is sung, and even stony hearts are softened. We see the hard-hearted weep and the merciless bend.

10. In the psalm, teaching competes together with grace. It is sung for delight and learned for instruction. Violent commands do not endure; but what you have received with sweetness, once infused into the heart, does not ordinarily slip away.

What is there that does not occur to you when you read the psalms? In them I read “a song for the beloved,” and I am inflamed with the desire for sacred love (Psalm 44:1). In them I recognize the winepresses of the divine mystery (Psalm 8:1 and elsewhere). In them I review the grace of revelations, the testimonies of the resurrection, and the promises (Psalm 50:3 ff.). In them I learn to avoid sin and unlearn shame over repentance for wrongdoing.

So great a king, so great a prophet, has roused me by his example, so that I may strive either to lessen the sin I have committed or to avoid sin not yet committed.

11. What, then, is the psalm if not an instrument of virtues? The venerable Prophet, playing it with the plectrum of the Holy Spirit, caused the sweetness of heavenly sound to resound on earth.

While he modulated distinctions of sound on strings and chords—that is, on the remains of dead things of different voices—and directed the song of divine praise toward heaven, he taught us, of course, that we must first die to sin, and only then distinguish in this body the various works of virtue by which the grace of our devotion might reach the Lord.

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “that the devotion of our grace might reach [the Lord].”]

Thus, with our attention occupied by heavenly things, no desire for earthly vices could creep in, and the soul might shine at the same time with the sweetness of heavenly grace. Therefore the Lord rightly praised the minister of so great a service, saying: “I have found David according to my heart.”

12. They also say that the more skilled players of the lyre sing “within,” as the tales about the lyre-player Aspendius relate, and that the principles of musical melodies and certain rhythmic structures are located in the upper part of the psaltery.

[Note: In his commentary on Cicero’s speech Against Verres, book 3, Asconius Paedianus explains the expression “to sing within” and teaches that it means to pluck the strings only with the left hand, so that the sound reaches only those nearby, whereas the ordinary class of lyre-players uses the right hand to strike the same strings with a plectrum. Aspendius was said to have excelled in this art. Aspendius was a city of Pamphylia, according to Stephanus. See Erasmus on the proverb “Aspendius the lyre-player.”

What Ambrose says about “the principles of melodies” appears plainly to have been taken from these words of Basil: “This psaltery receives from above the beginnings of harmonious rhythms, so that we too may practice seeking the things above and may not, through delight in melody, be brought down to the passions of the flesh.”]

David therefore taught that we must sing inwardly, psalm inwardly, as Paul also sang when he said: “I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind. I will sing psalms with the spirit; I will sing psalms also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14:15). He taught us to shape our life and actions according to the contemplation of higher things, lest the sweetness of pleasure arouse bodily passions by which our soul is not redeemed but burdened.

The holy Prophet remembered that he sang for the redemption of his soul, saying: “I will sing to you on the lyre, Holy One of Israel; my lips will rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed” (Psalm 70:22).

But now let us enter upon the beginning of the psalm set before us.

## Exposition

13. “Blessed,” he says, “is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly” (verse 1).

What an apt and timely beginning! Those who undertake to present some solemn contest commonly announce the prize and proclaim the glory of the crown, so that the contestants may assemble with greater zeal and contend with more determined effort. In the same way our Lord Jesus placed before the incentives of human virtue the glory of the heavenly kingdom, the grace of everlasting rest, and the blessedness of eternal life.

When an emperor advances to war—

[Note: Julius Lipsius observes in book 5, dialogue 16, of On Roman Military Affairs, that for more than three hundred years in the Roman Republic soldiers served at their own expense without public pay. Later, however, not only pay but various kinds of rewards were placed before them to sharpen their valor. Among these was the donative, that is, a gift from the emperor distributed individually to soldiers, just as a congiarium was distributed to citizens. There were also promotions, when someone was advanced to a higher rank on account of his valor. Hence Lucan writes of Scaeva, Caesar’s soldier:

“there, with much blood …”]

A *promotus* carries the vine-staff after a long period of service. Among the Greeks also, *promōtos* (προμῶτος) was called the man who had been enrolled into military distinction in this manner, as Lipsius likewise relates, book II, dialogue 8. But in this same book, dialogue 4, he had already shown that in the later age the numbers were frequently read both of cohorts and of legions.] He promises the soldier a donative and promotions in military ranks, so that hope of advantage may steal away labor and conceal fear of danger. Thus, like the herald of a great commander, holy David exhorts the soldiers, calls them athletes, and announces the prize, saying:

“Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly.”

He began with the prize, so as to lighten the burden of the contest to come; he set the reward before them, so that each person, leaping over in his heart the anxieties and labors of present things, might strive with eager haste to win the blessedness of things future. “Blessed,” he says, “is the man.” What greater gift could have been given to a human being than that which, by apostolic authority, could have been attributed to God in no higher terms (1 Tim. VI, 15 and 16)? For God is called “blessed,” “the only mighty one,” “King of kings,” and “Lord of lords.” He alone is mighty, he is King of kings, he is Lord of lords; yet even his power does not surpass blessedness. He granted us a common share in that title, which was judged worthy of divine honor.

14. Let us now consider why he said, “Blessed is the man,” and not rather, “Blessed are human beings,” since both sexes are called to grace. Did he exclude women from sharing in blessedness because he named only the man blessed? Far from it; for God did not exclude females from sharing in creation because he created the man first. For God said: “Let us make a human being according to our image and according to our likeness . . . . And God made the human being,” he says; “in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them” (Gen. I, 26 and 27). Both are designated in “human being”; in “man” the sex is expressed. But just as when “human being” is said, both are included, so when “man” is named, the woman whose man he is is also understood. Finally, he says: “She shall be called woman, because she was taken from her man” (Gen. II, 23). Moreover, since those whose nature is the same cannot have operations that are altogether different, and those whose work is equal must also have an equal reward, when Scripture says “man,” it did not omit the partner of the union; for when it says “human being,” it did not leave unmentioned the partner of the nature.

[Note: Several manuscripts and an old edition in the margin: “he did not leave unmentioned the partner of creation.”]

Thus, just as we read there that the human being was made, and although there is one nature we cannot deny that the principal sex was created first, so here, when we read “man,” we also recognize the corresponding sex in the principal portion. The pursuits of virtue, therefore, are equal, because the prerogative of creation is equal. Why, then, do you distinguish sex where contests are demanded of you not in the body but in the soul, which has no sex? Do not distinguish honor or divide the reward where sex is not distinguished. Yet it is not without reason if the one who was later in falling is called first to the exercise. What began badly ought to follow, not lead, so that at least after the experience it may be more modest. Eve wrongly disregarded the order of nature; she ought to have waited for the one who preceded her. The serpent cunningly began with the later one; therefore the Prophet returns to the superior, namely the one who would not have fallen had he not followed the later one.

15. Finally, he recalled us from our fall before he summoned us to the palm of victory. “Blessed,” he says, “is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly.” See where you are called blessed, human being: not in riches, not in powers and honors, not in nobility of family, or elegance and beauty, not in bodily health—in none of which is there anything naturally good. Indeed, these things not only undergo an easy change into their opposites, but also provide an instrument for guilt to the one who does not know how to use them. Who is just because of money? Who is humble because of power? Who is merciful because of nobility? Who is chaste because of beauty? These things entice more readily to sin than they bear fruit for advancement in virtue.

16. What, then, does he intend by preferring to say, “He has not gone,” and “he has not stood,” as though speaking of the past, when he could have said: “Blessed is the man who does not go in the counsel of the ungodly, who does not stand in the way of sinners, and who does not sit in the seat of pestilence”? Consider the teaching. One is not immediately blessed merely because he is not ungodly or a sinner, on account of the uncertainty of the outcome. For it was not written without reason: “Before death, praise no one” (Ecclus. XI, 30). Therefore, while anyone is in this life, he cannot be praised with a definitive commendation, since he may still remain open to error.

[Note: Two manuscripts: “whom error may still be able to claim.”]

But the one who has completed his life without offense is rightly judged worthy of the title “blessed,” because he enjoys the fellowship of the blessed.

17. But perhaps you will say: Why, then, did he say elsewhere, “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Ps. XL, 1)? He did not say “blessed is he who will have understood,” but “he who understands,” because those who do good find in the very act itself the means by which they are approved, receiving the reward of their work in the work itself. For a good deed is the fruit of a blessed conscience. But those who refrain from evil are not blessed immediately merely because they have avoided guilt once or twice; they are blessed if they have been able to escape the contagion of guilt throughout the whole course of their life.

18. Now the question arises why he preferred to call blessed not the one who has performed some duty of piety, but the one who has refrained from the counsel of the ungodly. For the one who has fulfilled the task of virtue seems more worthy of praise than the one who has escaped sin. Neither an ox, nor a horse, nor a stone is accustomed to be in sin or to sit in the seat of pestilence. But such things do not possess the fruit of blessedness, because they do not possess the understanding of virtue. For how do they reach the reward of the law when they do not possess the desire to follow the law? I see, therefore, that the sentence proposed concerns rational beings—that is, us. For us, the beginning of good things is abstinence from sins, since we read: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI, 27).

This is the order of discipline: strive from lower things toward the more perfect, so that you may not be frightened by the weight of greater things, when you ought to be summoned by beginning with lighter ones. Scripture teaches us that the ascent of piety is like a ladder (Gen. XXVIII, 12), by which holy Jacob saw the angels of the Lord ascending and descending—a man of training,

[Note: “A man of training,” that is, one exercised by hardships, such as exile, when he was compelled by fear of his brother to flee from his father’s house; and a life endured with the utmost hardship for twenty years at Laban’s, concerning which he himself says in Gen. XXXI: “By day heat consumed me, and frost by night, and sleep fled from my eyes.” Add the anguish of mind caused by Dinah’s violation, the loss of Joseph, and so forth.]

who is set before us so that through him we may learn that we must advance gradually in virtue, and that we can strive from the lowest to the highest if we proceed by small steps toward those things that seem higher than human nature.

Keep these ladders always set before you. Do not fear, human being, to climb these steps of discipline. The first step is near the earth; the next is like the first. Thus one ascends to the heights by equal steps. Do not despise, human being, that first step as though it were the most worthless. That first ascent separates you from the earth; once you have lifted your foot from the ground, you tread the air. Established in virtue, by rising you have left the earth; you leave the earth if you turn away from guilt. The beginning, then, of progress toward virtue is to abstain from sin.

19. But so that we may know that this discipline belongs to teaching, hear the Law saying: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not commit murder” (Exod. XX, 14 and 15). These commands seemed suitable for the imperfect. Finally, the Lord Jesus himself, knowing that the man who asked him by what works he might attain eternal life was imperfect, answered him: “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not commit murder, you shall not steal,” and so forth (Matt. XIX, 18). Then, when he said that he had done all these things, he added more perfect commands, saying: “Sell everything that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven” (ibid., 21).

[Note: The latest Paris edition: “so that he did not refuse them, because he judged those things easy for himself.” Other editions, together with the manuscripts: “so that he refused these things, since he judged those things,” and so forth. This is suitable. For the sense demands the following: there is so great a difference between avoiding evils and pursuing good things that the one who judged avoiding evils to be no difficulty refused to pursue good things.]

He thus taught that there is so great a distance between avoiding evils and imitating good things that the man refused the latter because he judged the former easy for himself. But because he had not even attained those things, he could not prepare himself for these higher things. For if he had loved his neighbor, he could not have refused the poor assistance from his patrimony. Therefore climb the first step of the Law, so that you may be able to reach the heavenly summit of the Gospel.

Hence I think that, as though placed under the Law and following the custom of the Law in the first psalm, the holy Prophet, speaking in his own person, declares what must rather be avoided than what must be pursued. In the fortieth psalm (Ps. XL, 1 and following), which is inscribed as spoken in the person of the Savior, there is more an exhortation to virtue than a repression of error; for it speaks of the Savior’s passion (ibid., 6 and following). And therefore the steward of the Gospel also, as we may judge, when we hear him saying, “Blessed are the merciful” (Matt. V, 7), crowned mercy both in the psalm of his own passion and in the Gospel. But let us now undertake the explanation of the psalm and examine the prophetic virtue.

20. “Blessed,” he says, “is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, who has not stood in the way of sinners, and who has not sat in the seat of pestilence.” We may say that three kinds of sin are expressed here, which we take to be those of thought, action, and persistence; and that the blessed person is signified as one who has not thought what is evil. For how can one be blessed who will be convicted on the day of judgment by his own accusing thoughts? Even if he deceived a human being, escaped a witness, and eluded an accuser, he will nevertheless be unable to escape himself as his accuser—an accuser whom he ought especially to fear, because he will have both an accuser and a confessing defendant.

Blessed, therefore, is the one who has neither thought what is evil, nor committed sin—for sometimes we sin even without deliberate thought, since “from much speaking we do not escape sin”—nor persisted in sin. Or in this way: blessed is the one who has neither thought what was erroneous, nor remained in that thought, nor, certainly, persisted in those thoughts that he recognized to be full of error. But whether these interpretations fit correctly, the reader will judge. For one who has once thought evil ought neither to remain in it nor persist in it.

[Note: The Regius manuscript: “But even if he has persisted.”]

But even if he has not persisted, he could not be blessed, because he remained in what he had wickedly thought. Even if he did not remain in it, nevertheless, merely because he thought evil, he ought to seek some merciful interpreter to determine whether he possesses the fruit of blessedness.

Finally, since no one can say that he has a pure heart, let us grant that a thought may be pardonable; but is the performance of sins pardonable? Finally, if remaining in sin is pardonable, is it also full of blessedness merely because one has not persisted in the crime? Moreover, if one has not thought what is wicked, how could he have remained in sin,

[Note: Four manuscripts: “or persisted, so as to be blessed? Whoever has rightly preserved these three things will surely be blessed. And certainly the order is divided.”]

or persisted? For the one who is to be blessed because he has rightly preserved these three things is subject to a different order. The first is that he has not persisted in sin; the second, that he has not remained in it; the third, that he has not thought what was erroneous. One who has not persisted may nevertheless have remained; one who did not remain may nevertheless have thought; but the one who did not even think is truly blessed.

21. For this reason I have also thought that another tradition should not be omitted, by which we may assert that three steps are arranged in their proper order: the one who wishes to be blessed must not go in the counsel of the ungodly—that is, he must not walk in their thoughts; next, he must not stand in the way of sinners; third, he must not sit in the seat of pestilence.

[Note: The old edition and certain Paris editions, together with nearly all the manuscripts: “You were made a Christian in the Church, or you who,” and so forth. The Roman edition and several Paris editions: “Therefore, having been made a Christian, or striving toward grace.” The Thuan manuscript is better, as we have it in the text.]

You, therefore, who have been made a Christian in the Church, or who are striving toward grace, abstain from the counsels of the ungodly, so that you may say: “Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood” (Ps. XXV, 9). Do not think what is ungodly. What are those things, except what is devised as an injury against God? For piety is first owed to God, and second to parents. Indeed, the enemy frequently inserts various things into our minds; and therefore the Prophet wisely judged that thoughts, rather than unexpected intrusions, should be held accountable for guilt.

Have you therefore abstained from the counsels of the ungodly? Good; but you are not immediately blessed. Take care also that you do not stand in the way of sinners.

22. With what precision are the words of divine Scripture set forth! Since we are all under sin, it does not demand from you what is beyond nature—that you commit no sin—for not even an infant of one day is without sin; rather, it demands that you do not remain in sin by a prolonged standing. Not all are ungodly; therefore you are recalled from all the thoughts and conspiracies of the ungodly. But all are sinners; therefore you are admonished to cease sinning.

[Note: Thus the Erasmian, Gillian, and Roman editions, together with the Vatican, Colbert, and Victor manuscripts. The Paris edition, however, with other manuscripts: “If you have fallen at an earlier age, the progress of maturity ought to,” and so forth. This is not unsuitable. Nevertheless, it seems more elegant for the statement to be understood concessively, in this sense: “Granted that it has been,” and so forth.]

Granted that there has been a fall in the earlier years, the progress of maturity ought to correct it. Therefore do not go into more serious things, and do not remain in lesser ones. You also have this said by the Lord through Isaiah: “Go out from Babylon, fleeing from the Chaldeans” (Isa. XLVIII, 20)—that is: Even if you have entered into the confusion of vices, go out. You ought not to have entered; but you entered because the law of the flesh compelled you and, by taking you captive in the law of sin. Go out; depart, even if late; strip yourself of grievous slavery.

You could not avoid entering sin because of weakness; you are permitted to leave sin through sobriety. Go out, therefore, from Babylon, fleeing from the Chaldeans. Babylon is confusion, which does not preserve the order of virtues; for we sin when our mind is confused by enticements. The Chaldeans are those who investigate the courses of the stars with the vain zeal of superstition and sow the impious errors of paganism. Flee from them, lest they seize you, lest they entangle you in the grievous snare of captivity.

Abraham was a Chaldean, but he fled from the Chaldeans—and this before the Law; you were born under the Law, flee from the ungodly.

[Note: The latest Paris edition and four manuscripts: “You, who are already condemned under the Law.” Other editions and manuscripts: “You, who were born under the Law.”]

He rejected the inheritance of his fathers in order to possess faith; you must abandon bodily succession and acquire the inheritance of devotion.

23. But if you have not stood in sin, you are still not blessed; you still have something of which you must be free. There are many enticements and many deviations from virtue: grave provocations of pleasures, a grave fuel of avarice, the desire for power, and ambition for honor. These contaminate human minds, as though with a kind of poison, and souls with a kind of pestilential decay of vices. This is the seat of pestilence upon which the scribes and Pharisees sat, who lay heavy burdens upon human beings but themselves do not wish to move them with a finger.

From the temple the Savior drove out these seats of those who boasted of their honor and sought the primacies of rank; of those who used priesthood or precedence of honor for profit; of those who indulged their appetite and did not at all provide the due guardianship of self-restraint. This is true pestilence. In fact, the sons of Eli were sons of pestilence. In this kind of seat of vices, Scripture forbids us to bend our neck and recline the strength of our whole body. Observe, therefore, the particular meanings.

24. “And he has not stood in the way of sinners, and he has not sat in the seat of pestilence.” There can be no doubt that “way” means the course of this life, since Scripture itself says: “In this way in which I was walking, they hid a snare for me” (Ps. CXLI, 4). And: “Be reconciled quickly with your adversary, while you are with him on the way” (Matt. V, 25).

Since we are running the course of this life, we have a path along which we walk each day until we reach the end. Even if we do not seem to move bodily, we advance. For just as those sleeping in ships are driven by the winds into harbors—although, while they rest, they have no awareness of sailing, the course nevertheless presses them toward the end and drives them onward unaware—so, as the span of our life flows away, each person is led by a hidden course toward his appointed end.

Hence it is said: “Rise, you who sleep” (Eph. V, 14); for you sleep, while your time walks on. See to it that, while you sleep too long, time does not pass you by. Therefore, even if you sleep, let your heart keep watch; your heart will not be struck down. If your heart is not idle, your times are not idle. You are on the way, human being; walk so that you may arrive. Let night not overtake you on the way; let the day of life not be consumed before you hasten your progress in virtue.

You are a traveler in this life; everything passes, everything is left behind you. You see everything on this road, and you pass it by. You saw the beauty of trees, the greenness of grasses, the purity of springs, and whatever else of this kind delights the eyes; it pleased you to look, it delighted you to attend for a little while; while you attended, you passed on.

Again, as you walked, you encountered a rocky and rugged road, hollowed cliffs, steep mountains, and dense forests. You were wearied for a little while, and again you passed on. Such is this life: neither its favorable circumstances remain, nor its adversities last long. Therefore, since you have been placed as though on a road, let neither prosperity lift you up nor adversity break you; let neither what wins applause delay you nor what is sorrowful hold you back. Always hasten toward the end; hasten so that you may arrive. Yet choose the road before you run.

25. There are two roads: one of the righteous, the other of sinners; one of equity, the other of iniquity, concerning which the Prophet said: “And see whether there is a way of iniquity in me” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 24). Therefore our life is not only a road, but within our life itself there is either a road of virtue or a road of iniquity.

Take care, then, lest avarice place its steps in you and you become a road of crime; lest wickedness or lust do so, and you become a road of iniquity, worn smooth for travelers by outrages. It is permitted you to choose whom you will follow, whether the righteous or the unrighteous. The road of the righteous is narrower, that of the unrighteous broader: the former is narrow with sobriety, the latter broad with drunkenness, so that it can contain those who wander.
