The latter has the enticements of this age; the former has the rewards of the future.

In the latter there is more immediate fruit; in the former, hope is slower. For pleasant things do not endure prolonged waiting but offer immediate enjoyment; what is serious, however, is sought through labor, because it is scarcely grasped by blessed thought.

[Note: The Roman edition alone: “not through prolonged waiting for completion, but they have it immediately.” Shortly afterward, where all editions and most manuscripts read, “but what is late,” the Victor and Colbert manuscripts read, “but what is serious.” This is excellent, for “serious” is here opposed to pleasant things, which are accustomed to be light.]

For “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, what God has prepared for those who love him.” We are accustomed to find it difficult to believe what we do not see; therefore the soul burns with longing and turns its thoughts this way and that, as though it had eyes. Then various forms of things meet it and spread themselves before it. If it directs itself toward eternal things, it chooses virtue; if toward present things, it prefers pleasure.

The contest against the delights of present things is difficult and unjust. Here there is freedom for desires; there, servitude under injuries—doing what you do not wish and abstaining from what you desire. Here there is a banquet; there, fasting. Here there is intemperance of joys; there, perseverance in tears. Here there is dancing; there, prayer. Here there are sweet songs; there, heavy groans.

[Note: All editions and several manuscripts: “the insult of slavery”; four manuscripts: “the slavery of insults.” Again, shortly afterward, where all editions together with three manuscripts read, “Here there is dancing, there prayer,” other manuscripts read, “there lamentation.” Although this reading does not seem at all to be despised, Basil, from whom the passage was taken, favors the former with these words: “Here dancing, and there prayer” (ἐνταῦθα ὄρχεσιν, κἀκεῖ προσευχὴν).]

It is indeed written: “The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, and the heart of fools in the house of feasting. It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise man than to hear a man listening to the song of fools” (Eccl. VII, 5 and 6). But few listen to these things, and fewer follow them. The sweetness of sin attracts human beings more—flowing in at the present moment and fattening the hearer’s affection—than the sadness of virtue, which wraps the hope of faith, as in a kind of shell, in bitter labor.

Blessed, therefore, and wondrous is the one who, placed at the point of choosing between such roads, is not bent by the enticements of pleasure, so that he may set his step upon what is shallow and crooked. It is not said to him: “Woe to you who have abandoned the straight paths by going into the ways of darkness” (Eccl. VIII, 16)!

26. We have therefore learned what the way of sinners is, in which the Prophet warns us that we must not stand. The Ecclesiastes also teaches this, saying: “Do not stand in an evil word” (ibid., 3),

[Note: Certain Paris editions: “that is, do not persist.”]

that is, do not persist in evil words, and likewise in deeds deserving condemnation. The same holy Prophet commands us to stand in good things, saying: “Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem” (Ps. CXXI, 2). One must stand in Jerusalem; one must flee from Babylon. And it is said to Moses: “But stand with me” (Deut. V, 31), who fled from Egypt and persevered while standing with the Lord. And in the Gospel (Matt. XX, 9), those who stood until the eleventh hour received equal pay with the laborers. And the virgins who stood until the bridegroom’s arrival deserved to enter together into the wedding feast; but those who went away and later returned were excluded by the authority of the Lord’s sentence (Matt. XXV, 10). We have learned, therefore, not to stand in the way of sinners, but to stand in the duty of virtue, because it is written: “But you stand by faith” (Rom. XI, 20).

[Note: Editions with three manuscripts: “But you stand by faith,” or “stand in faith.” Five manuscripts, together with all copies of the Apostle: “you stand by faith.”]

27. Let us now consider what is meant by: “And he has not sat in the seat of pestilence.” We have already stated that a simple sitting in the ordinary sense of such a seat is not being condemned. For what fault would there be in it? But since the eyes of the Lord are always upon the faithful of the earth, we ought to stand as though placed before the emperor’s gaze and set in a kind of service.

A soldier stands in battle array; he does not sit. A soldier in arms does not recline but rouses and raises himself. Therefore it is said to the soldiers of Christ: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord” (Ps. CXXXIII, 1).

In contrast, iniquity sits in a leaden talent, because, fixed in sin, it cannot separate itself from it. Those who have grown old in error and cling deliberately to crimes are said to sit because they do not wish to rise up or to hear the one who says: “Rise after you have sat” (Ps. CXXVI, 2). Finally, this same Prophet says elsewhere: “Princes sat and slandered me” (Ps. CXVIII, 23).

[Note: Some manuscripts: “They deliberated against me.”]

Are we unaware that the force of an ingrained habit of sinning is so great that it excludes nature—which, although it is curable unto salvation,

[Note: Thus one Vatican manuscript and five Gallican manuscripts. The Victor, Colbert, and old editions, however: “yet, strengthened by time, it is found incurable through its passions.” The Roman edition alone: “yet, corrupted by passions over a long period, it is incurable,” and so forth.]

is nevertheless found incurable when its passions have been strengthened by time? Let us not, therefore, remain in vices; but let each person, even if he has been in them, leap away from guilt, as it is written concerning the prostitute (Prov. V, 3). Do not direct your eyes toward her; leap away, do not delay; leap away before the years of youth overtake you.

But what is more grievous, many have not blushed at the luxury of the body even when their hair was whitening with age, and they have prolonged a stained life into old age. For the plague of guilt, conceived in the innermost parts, accumulates with the passage of time.

Take care, therefore, of the counsels of the ungodly; do not let such counsels penetrate your mind, lest it be said of you: “Can a man bind fire in his bosom and his garments not be burned?” (Prov. VI, 2). For whoever once kindles in the bosom of his mind the flame of a burning crime will quickly burn the garments of his body.

[Note: Five manuscripts: “And just as fire consumes straw, so even a small,” and so forth. The rest, together with all editions, as above.]

And just as fire leaping into straw clings to it and remains until it consumes everything it has seized, so even a tiny spark of sin, if it is stirred up by some fuel of the vices, kindles a great conflagration. Do not, therefore, stand in sin.

Finally, if you have placed your foot above the abyss of guilt, quickly remove it, lest pollution climb over the sole of your foot and, deceived by an easier fall, you settle upon the mud.

28. The first vices must therefore be avoided, lest they subsequently spread into more numerous and more serious ones. For just as those who roll about in mud become increasingly filthy the more they wallow, so one who has once splashed himself with the mud of wickedness, unless he quickly leaps away from it, covers himself each day with the heavier mire of his disgrace through a muddy way of life.

Thus, from the foul odor of that earth and of that shameful abyss, a kind of pestilence of souls is contracted; and when the breath of healthy thoughts has been corrupted, the pitiable plague of raging passions spreads. From this a deadly poison pours itself into minds; from this illness creeps into bodies and weakness into souls.

There is a wicked weakness: the weakness of error, the weakness of avarice, the weakness of insatiable desire. These are the riches, as the Ecclesiastes says: “There is a grievous weakness which I saw under the sun: riches kept to the harm of their possessor” (Eccl. V, 12). Tell me, Ecclesiastes, for what reason is this weakness grievous? He will answer: because an avaricious hope devours many. Desire is an insatiable gluttony. Whoever desires silver does not know how to be satisfied with silver (ibid., 9). Riches stretch people, but do not fill them: “And if anyone is satisfied with riches,” he says, “there is no one who permits him to sleep. Indeed, all his days are in darkness, mourning, much anger, weakness, and wrath” (ibid., 11 and 16).

For how can one sleep who keeps a watchful guard over gold, who fears losses, who thinks about profits, who calculates interest,

[Note: The Roman edition alone: “who counts mortgages.” The preceding phrase, “who calculates interest,” seems to support this. But the other editions and all the manuscripts object; nor is the sense bad if “storerooms”—that is, chests, coffers, and rooms in which riches are stored—is understood, so that the miser is said to count them.]

who counts his storerooms? The weakness, therefore, is grievous because it removes the mind’s healthy rest.

There is also the grievous weakness of luxury, lust, desire, pleasure, and worldly ambition, which quickly corrupt the health of sobriety. Finally, every corruption of this world is pestilence. Do not, therefore, touch it; do not defile yourself with it. It is a plague; it contaminates. It is a disease; it pollutes. “Do not taste the things”—all of which, through use, are directed toward corruption—as the Apostle said (Col. II, 21 and 22), who also cries elsewhere: “The root of all evils is avarice” (1 Tim. VI, 10). It arouses diseases and implants pains. Finally, those who coveted it entangled themselves in many pains (ibid.).

This is the pestilence that frequently makes people neither hot nor cold, but—which is worse than being hot or cold—lukewarm, so that those whom the Lord Jesus has rejected because of grave sins may be vomited from his mouth.

This is what arouses the illnesses not of a few but of all: “The whole head is in pain, the whole heart in sorrow” (Isa. I, 5 and 6). From the feet to the head are the ulcers of sinners. “The whole head is in pain” when those who are considered wise are tortured by the pain of avarice; for “the sense of the wise is in his head.” This may also be referred to those who preside over the Church. “The whole heart is in sorrow” when we think about carnal things and drive the edge of our heart into bodily pleasures. Hence the Lord says to such people (Ezek. XI, 19) that he will give them a heart of flesh.

29. From the feet to the head a dreadful plague of diseases creeps when people suffer from contagion, when they suffer with others if someone is deprived of the gratification of lust and cannot violate a widow’s modesty or seize a field; and all painfully pass their maladies from one to another.

[Note: The Regius manuscript: “if someone [is deprived] through the passion of lust.”]

How often do old men groan that they can no longer drink for a long time? How often do they grieve that they have ceased to consort with prostitutes, though they still possess the will to do so? How often, amid the stories of drunkards, are virtues treated as disgraceful, sins as praiseworthy, honesty as a joke, self-restraint as laughter, and mercy as vanity?

These are the diseases that transfer their evils to many. From a few, corruption reaches everyone. They sit in councils disparaging the sober while belching drunkenness; they sit in taverns competing in drunkenness. Among them is a prostitute filled with wine, smiling at one, inflaming another, and setting them all ablaze with the heat of lust.

If a modest person passes by, he blushes and is attacked by each of them; if a shameless person passes by, he is praised by everyone’s mouth, and, like a disease, passes into the souls of each one. For the person celebrated in crimes leads many into the error of imitation. Thus, while they imitate another’s sin, they make the evil their own.

Do not sit among those whom the holy Prophet fled. Imitate him as one fleeing, certainly, not sitting; for he says: “I have not sat in the council of the malicious, and I will not enter in with those who act unjustly” (Ps. XXV, 4).

For what reason did you flee from them, David? Explain it to us. Show us these groups, so that we too may be able to flee from them and not be infected by their contagion. “They were corrupted,” he says, “and became abominable; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII, 1). In general, this can be applied to all who commit crimes; then, more particularly, to those who mock the good, whom Aquila called *chleuastai* (χλευαστάς), “mockers.” These are truly diseases: by mocking the good, they produce great error in souls and corrupt minds.

[Col. 0937A]

How many things has he named from which the blessed man must abstain! And he still adds others.

30. (Verse 2.) “But his delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night”; that is, blessed is the man who does these things deliberately, rationally, and prudently. For even a little child may abstain from the things just mentioned, not through virtue but through inability and ignorance of wrongdoing. The same may be said of an irrational animal, which has no power of deliberation and no awareness of error. This, then, is the fourth point that follows, by which the definition of the blessed man is distinguished from that of an animal: the wise man is subject to the law by his will, not by necessity. There is a great difference between the two: in willing, there is the fruit of reward; in necessity, there is merely the performance of an entrusted duty. Thus the Apostle taught us when he said: “If I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship” (1 Cor. 9:17).

The proper order is to love the law first, and then to meditate upon it. Whoever loves it fulfills the commands of the law willingly; whoever fears it observes it unwillingly. We have received this discipline of instruction, and indeed God’s justice, in the Law. For it is written: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4). And: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength. And these words which I command you today shall be in your heart and in your soul; and you shall teach them to your children, and speak of them when you sit in your house, when you walk on the road, when you rest, and when you keep watch.”

[Note: The old edition and many manuscripts read: “And you shall bind them in your bosom.” The Roman edition and several manuscripts read: “And you shall bind them as a sign.” The Septuagint has: Καὶ ἁφάψεις αὐτὰ εἰς σημεῖον ἐπὶ τῆς χειρός σου, “And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand”; on this point all versions of Scripture agree. Where the Roman edition reads, “and they shall be immovable before your eyes” (apparently from the Septuagint, where one reads καὶ ἕσται ἀσάλευτον [some manuscripts: ἀσάλευτα] πρὸ ὀφθαλμῶν σου, “and it shall be immovable [or: they shall be immovable] before your eyes”), the old edition and all the manuscripts without exception read, “and they shall be necklaces,” and so forth. Moreover, since this part of the verse is rendered differently elsewhere—for example, from the Hebrew text and the Hebrew-Samaritan text the Latin translator renders it, “they shall also be frontlets,” or, as Grotius prefers, “they shall also be for spectacles,” and so forth; from the Chaldean Paraphrase, “and they shall be like a certain appendage,” and so forth—it could also have been translated by someone in a manner such as that found in our text.]

“And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be necklaces before your eyes; and you shall write them upon the doorposts of your houses and upon your gates” (Deut. 6:5–9). And later: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you, except that you love the Lord your God and walk in all his ways?” (Deut. 10:12). Wisdom also says: “Desire my words, therefore; love them, and you will possess discipline” (Wis. 6:12). Wisdom is clear and never withers; it is easily seen by those who love it and found by those who seek it.

Thus the holy Prophet rightly teaches us to have our will in the Law and our meditation according to the Law. Will in the Law consists not only in study but also in action. Will comes first, action second. Accordingly, when a man said to the Lord, “If you will, you can cleanse me,” he replied: “I will; be cleansed” (Matt. 8:2–3).

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “so that he might show that our thoughts …”]

This was to show that in our actions the will ought to come first. Indeed, the law seeks willing people, because the law of the Lord is blameless and converts the soul; but no one is converted unless he is converted willingly. A willing man, however, conceals and steals away the meaning of his labor.

31. Therefore he meditates on the Law day and night. This does not require so much the uninterrupted occupation of reading as an affection for keeping the Law. For he meditates fully who is himself a law to himself, directing his attention to the law written in his heart. Aquila, however, mentioned only the day, not the night. He did not so much differ from the others as refer the expression elsewhere: whoever meditates on the Law is always in the light and has no night. For one whose works shine cannot walk in darkness, since his righteousness gleams like light.

Let our life, then, meditate on the Law; let our conduct meditate on it, our actions meditate on it, and our understanding of heavenly mysteries meditate on it. For the Law is a model and shadow of heavenly things, a shadow of future goods, which the one who believes in the Law recognizes in the Gospel. Let him meditate on it in darkness and in day—that is, both when placed in adversity and when placed in prosperity. For the Law commands you to love your Lord. Whoever loves must preserve the affection of enduring love in every condition of life.

A father loves his son; he loves him even when he rebukes him, and even when he beats him with a rod—for “whoever spares his rod hates his son.” The Lord likewise chastises us and loves us. Therefore, even when we commit acts deserving chastisement, he still loves us, since he also receives the one who has offended him. “For the Lord chastises every son whom he receives.” And when you are chastised, love him, because you are chastised for the purpose of being received.

What great thing is it if you love the Lord your God when everything abounds for you, when you enjoy what you desire, and when you rejoice in honors, possessions, and children? We are accustomed to return thanks even to a human being from whom we have received a benefit. Thus, when Job was praised by heavenly judgment, the devil replied (Job 1:10–11): “It is hardly surprising that he should be grateful to God, since such an abundance of prosperity is available to him; but he must be tested when he loses all those things, to see whether he will still perform the duty of a devout worshiper.”

This, then, is the first virtue: that you are not broken by adversities and are not lifted up by prosperity. The Law teaches you this: in affliction, do not relax your determination, and do not fall into despair; when victorious, do not say, “My virtue and my strength have obtained this for me” (Deut. 8:17), but know that everything must be attributed to divine mercy.

[Note: Four Gallican manuscripts read: “so that you do not relax your struggle in victory, nor take on despair in temptation; do not say …”]

32. Isaiah cries out: “He who is in distress will not be put to shame until the appointed time” (Isa. 8:22). “Drink this first” (Isa. 9:1). What does “drink this first” mean? Let us set aside the mystical interpretation and pursue the moral teaching conveyed by the letter. He says that, because of the grave weight of errors, severe contritions and afflictions of the people were to come; and they had to precede the coming of mercy.

Drink tribulation first, then. For “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” Drink, so that the awareness of tribulation may be poured into the inner chambers of your heart.

[Note: Five manuscripts read: “may be poured inwardly into your breast.” “Drink the feeling of compassion, the sorrow of one who mourns.”]

Drink with the patient disposition of one who shares in another’s suffering, the grief of one who mourns. For when, having turned back, you groan, then you will reconcile to yourself the Lord whom you have offended. Drink this first, then, so that you may be in sorrow and distress.

Joy quickly introduces error. “The people grew fat and became thick, and rose up to play, and departed from the Lord.” It is beneficial for you to have a contrite heart. Drink this first, so that your sacrifice may be accepted by the Lord.

Let the Apostle teach you what this means: drink this first—that is, the cup of tribulation. For “tribulation produces endurance” (Rom. 5:3–4). There can be no endurance unless tribulation has come first. “Tribulation,” he says, “produces endurance; endurance produces testing, and testing hope; but hope does not disappoint.” Drink tribulation first, so that afterward so many cups of virtue may be served to you.

And so that you may know that tribulation is drunk, you heard the Prophet say today: “You gave us wine of compunction” (Ps. 59:5). Later he says: “And you will give us drink in tears, by measure” (Ps. 79:6). He asks for drink by measure, not beyond measure, lest he be unable to bear it. Finally, how good was the disposition with which he prayed for this is proved by his own example: he mingled his drink with weeping (Ps. 101:10), so that he might incline the Lord’s mercy toward himself.

33. Drink this first, then,

[Note: Erasmus and Gill read: “so that you may drink the second also. For now is the time to introduce the mystical interpretation.” The Roman edition has: “Now is the time,” and so forth. The manuscripts agree with us, except that some read *mystica bibis*—“you drink mystical things”—instead of *mystico bibe*. To grasp the meaning of our reading more easily, observe that the pronoun “this” refers to what immediately precedes it: “Drink this first,” and so forth. Then, after the word “mystical,” supply “interpretation,” “treatment,” or something similar.]

so that you may drink the second also—for this is the time to introduce the mystical interpretation. Drink the Old Testament first, so that you may drink the New Testament. Unless you drink the first, you cannot drink the second. Drink the first to quench your thirst; drink the second to draw in the satisfaction of drinking.

In the Old Testament there is compunction; in the New, joy.

See how the Lord met the devil’s devices on behalf of his own servants. The devil deceived one person with the food of fraud in order to ensnare everyone through that one; but Jesus redeemed everyone with the food of salvation, in order to restore through everyone even the one who had been deceived.

The devil devised Babylon’s golden cup so that the more people drank, the thirstier they would become; and because the drink itself could not please them, he lured them to drink by the price of gold. He offered wine from his own supply, for which he also sought the assistance of metal. But the Lord Jesus poured forth water from the rock, and everyone drank. Those who drank in the type were satisfied; those who drank in reality were intoxicated.

A good intoxication, which pours in joy without bringing confusion; a good intoxication, which steadies the gait of a sober mind; a good intoxication, which waters the gift of eternal life.

Drink this cup, then, of which the Prophet said: “And your cup that intoxicates—how excellent it is!” (Ps. 22:5). Do not be troubled by the fact that Babylon’s cup is golden, for you too drink the cup of wisdom, which is more precious than gold and silver.

Drink, then, both cups, of the Old and the New Testament, because in both you drink Christ. Drink Christ, because he is the vine; drink Christ, because he is the rock that poured forth water; drink Christ, because he is the fountain of life; drink Christ, because he is the river whose current makes the city of God glad; drink Christ, because he is peace; drink Christ, because rivers of living water will flow from his belly; drink Christ, so that you may drink the blood by which you were redeemed; drink Christ, so that you may drink his words.

His word is the Old Testament; his word is the New Testament. Divine Scripture is drunk, and divine Scripture is swallowed, when the sap of the eternal Word descends into the veins of the mind and the powers of the soul. For “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.” Drink this Word, but drink it in its proper order.

Drink first in the Old Testament;

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “then make haste to drink also in the New Testament.” Since he seems to be in a hurry, he says: “The region of Zebulun, and the land of Naphtali, and the other inhabitants of the seacoast, and beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations; the people who walked …”]

make haste to drink also in the New Testament. And as though he himself were hastening, he says: “Galilee of the nations and the regions of Judea: you who walk in darkness, see a great light; you who dwell in the region of death, light will shine upon you” (Isa. 9:1–2).

Drink quickly, then, so that a great light may shine upon you—not the ordinary light, nor the light of day, nor of the sun, nor of the moon, but that light which excludes the shadow of death.

[Note: Thus the edition and the Vatican manuscript read; five Gallican manuscripts agree, although in them one reads: “For if they are in the shadow …” In the Victor and Colbert manuscripts, however, the reading is: “For if they are the shadow of death …”]

For those who are in the shadow of death cannot see the light of the sun and day. And as though you were asking where such great splendor and such great grace come from, he replies: “For a child is born to us, a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6).

“Child,” because he was born of a Virgin; “Son,” because, born of God, he is the source of such great light. A child is born for us—for us who believe, not for the Jews, who did not believe; for us, not for the heretics; for us, not for the Manichaeans. He was born for us because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”; he was born for us because he assumed flesh from the Virgin, because he was born as a man from Mary.

Flesh is born for us; the Word is given. What is ours was born among us; what is above us was given to us.

34. We have ranged widely enough, as we think, but not without purpose: to teach that we must love the Lord even in tribulations and must not depart from him, since tribulation often follows joy, and joy follows tribulation. Thus the one who is not broken by tribulation and follows the law is blessed.

35. (Verse 3.) “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall yield its fruit in its season. Its leaf shall not fall, and everything that he does shall prosper.”

What is this blessedness, compared with a tree, unless we understand the tree of life, brought forth from the earth in paradise, that place of the blessed, in the midst of the other trees?

[Note: The Vatican manuscripts and five Gallican manuscripts read: “that we have read to have been brought forth from the earth in the midst.” The others, together with the editions, agree, except for the Roman edition, which has *productorum*—“of those brought forth”—instead of *productum*—“brought forth.”]

Among the many trees that were beautiful to look upon and good for food, the earth also produced this tree, and it was in the midst of paradise, so that the other trees might flourish in its verdure.

What other tree can we say this is except the tree through which salvation came to us? And rightly did the earth produce it, because the Virgin bore him who was earth according to the Creator’s pronouncement spoken of him: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Gen. 3:19).

Beautifully, too, it is read as being in the midst of the other trees, because he was in the midst of the apostles who were learning;

[Note: The word “apostles” had been removed from the Roman edition, perhaps because its editors believed that Ambrose was speaking in the manner of Tertullian, who often calls disciples simply “apostles” without qualification.]

or because he was in the midst of mind and heart, as he himself says: “There stands among you one whom you do not know” (John 1:26). And elsewhere he says: “But I am in the midst of you” (Luke 22:27).

Finally, Solomon also said of him:

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “The tree of life is in the hands of those who receive him.”]

“The tree of life is for all who receive him” (Prov. 3:18).

Therefore, the one who is blessed will be an imitator of the Lord Jesus, who is the tree of life and the tree of wisdom, planted in the Virgin’s womb by the will of the Father. It is planted by him to remain forever and yield fruit in its season. For this planting could not wither, since it contained within itself an abiding abundance of spiritual grace.

Finally, Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan. These are the streams of water of which it is said in the Gospel: “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” This he said concerning the Spirit whom those who were to believe in him were beginning to receive (John 7:38).

36. There is another tradition as well, concerning the waters from which Jeremiah forbids us to drink when he says: “What have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the water of Geon?” (Jer. 2:18).

There is also the river Tigris, flowing past the Assyrians. There is also the Euphrates, running toward Babylon. And there is the Phison, which in Latin interpretation is called “change of mouth,” surrounding the land of Evilath, where there is gold, and the gold of that land is good, as well as carbuncle and prasinus stone.

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “It is fitting that all things there are changed.”]

Fittingly, the mouth is changed there, so that the faithfulness of promises is not maintained; but there is deceit in the mouth where there is good gold. For greed breaks faith and does not preserve simplicity of speech. Precious ornaments likewise change the mind and spirit, so that one thing is in the breast and another on the tongue.

In those regions of the rivers, therefore, the Jews were captives, carried away to Egypt, to the Assyrians, and to the Babylonians. There they sat beside the rivers of Babylon and wept over the misery of their calamity; and, as this same Prophet testifies (Ps. 136:1 and following), there they hung up their instruments and laid aside all joy, where they endured heavier sufferings.

The remaining ten tribes were led away to the Assyrians; the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, crossed over into Babylon as though guilty of a more serious crime. For an adulterous priest’s daughter is punished more severely than other women, because she has stained the honor of the priestly race with disgraceful shame.

37. Just as they were subjected to the gravest temptations, so our Savior exposed himself to many temptations, so that he would pass over none of the conflicts of our temptation.

He is therefore rightly called “planted beside the streams” of these rivers, not in the streams themselves, so that you may understand him as near them, but not submerged in them.

His first conflict was with flesh and blood. Thus he says: “Father, take this cup from me; nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will” (Matt. 26:39).

There was also the temptation of riches, when the enemy offered him all the kingdoms of the earth if the Lord would fall down and worship him. You have the streams of the two rivers, Geon and Phison.

He also wrestled against the rulers of the world. During the Passion there was a contest against the tempters whom the Hebrew interpretation calls Persians,

[Note: Jerome interprets this word in the same sense in his commentaries on Ezekiel 27:10 and Isaiah 21:2. Ambrose mentions the Persians here in order to teach that, through the Tigris, which waters their borders, the tempters are signified.]

who brought false testimonies against him. These were the ones who said: “Let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Mark 15:32), which the devil was suggesting. You have the rivers Tigris and Euphrates.

38. The Apostle also comprehends that our struggle is fourfold when he says: “For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12).

These are the rivers that go forth from paradise. Hence I think that the one who longs to return to paradise must pass through these streams of water.

The same holy Prophet did not express this point without purpose,

[Note: All the editions read: “Showing that whoever has subdued all temptations may now hope that the rest of paradise is owed to him.” A few manuscripts agree, although they omit the word “hope”; the greater number have the reading found in the text.]

when he showed that those who underwent all temptations might now expect the rest of paradise as their due. Thus he says: “The streams of waters have flowed down over my eyes” (Ps. 118:136).

For just as there is a fiery sword at the entrance to paradise, so that the one who returns must return through fire, burning away his sins and testing his gold, so the one who returns returns through these streams.

And rightly the saints say: “We passed through fire and water” (Ps. 65:12). Isaiah also speaks of these streams: “If you pass through the water, the rivers will not overwhelm you” (Isa. 43:2).

What rivers? Hear David speaking of those who were hastening toward paradise:

[Note: Thus the edition reads, together with three manuscripts. Five others prefer: “David, who was hastening toward paradise.”]

“Perhaps our soul would have passed through unbearable water” (Ps. 123:5).

39. Although some also understand the following passage as referring to these four temptations: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon” (Ps. 90:13). He walked upon them in the Incarnation, trampled them in the Passion, or will trample them in the handing over of the kingdom, which he will deliver to the Father when he has emptied every principality.

Aquila beautifully rendered the expression as τὸ μεταπεφυτευμένον—that is, “transplanted”—because it was first planted in the Virgin and afterward transplanted into paradise, as he said to the thief: “Amen, amen, I say to you: today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

40. This tree, then, will yield its fruit in its season. Earthly trees are said not to give fruit but to bear it; but the tree of life and wisdom gives fruit—that is, it bestows and grants it.

Again the question arises: if it is the tree of wisdom, why will it give fruit in its season and not always? Perhaps it would be difficult for us to understand this of Christ. But when you have read that the Lord “will appoint a faithful and prudent steward over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time” (Luke 12:42)—at the proper time, certainly, not always—you ought not to be disturbed.

Wisdom can always give fruit, but because it is wisdom, it ought to give and distribute prudently,

[Note: The old edition and the Roman edition, together with the Victor and Colbert manuscripts, read: “prudently.” “Then it ought always to give, when we are able”—the Roman edition reads “deserve,” while the manuscripts read “are able”—“to receive the full measure.” As here … “it will give fruit to the good without ceasing.” The Paris edition and six other manuscripts agree with us.]

whenever we either deserve or are able to receive the full measure. Just as here it will give fruit at the end of time, so there also it will give good fruit among the nations, so that we may be able to receive and preserve a share in his resurrection.

At present we cannot do so; we cannot endure it in this hateful age.

[Note: Thus the Roman edition and the Vatican manuscripts, together with five Gallican manuscripts, read. The old edition and others have: “For here we are corruptible.”]

For here there is corruption, and it was necessary to take care lest we corrupt the good fruits that the tree of life would give. For now we are corruptible, but then incorruptible: “When the dead,” he says, “will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:52–53).

What advantage would there have been for one destined to die to receive what death was going to take away from him? Wisdom therefore knows to whom and when it ought to give, and it does not lose even a leaf of its tree. Therefore let us consider what the leaf of wisdom is, since we know what its fruit is.

41. The fruit is inward; the leaf is that by which the fruit is protected either from the scorching sun or from the cold. The fruit appears to be faith, peace, doctrine, the excellence of true knowledge, good intention, and understanding of the mysteries.

A good life guards these fruits; an evil life loses them even if it has received them. To the sinner God says: “Why do you recount my righteous acts?” (Ps. 49:16).

In mystical matters there is fruit; in moral matters, a leaf,

[Note: “By contemplation of heavenly mysteries.” These words were absent from the old edition and from the Victor and Colbert manuscripts, but they are found in the Roman edition and other codices. By these words is signified that moral virtues, or the virtues of the active life, when compared with heavenly mysteries and with faith in and contemplation of them, are like a leaf compared with fruit, as the holy Doctor explains in what follows.]

that is, contemplation of heavenly mysteries. For virtues without faith are leaves: they appear green, but they cannot be of benefit. They are shaken by the wind because they have no foundation.

How many Gentiles possess mercy and sobriety, but have no fruit because they have no faith! The leaves quickly fall when the wind blows. Some Jews also possess chastity, great diligence in reading, and carefulness; but they are without fruit and move about like leaves.

These may be the leaves that the Savior found on that fig tree, but found no fruit (Matt. 21:19).

42. Mystical realities save and free from death; moral qualities, however, are ornaments of beauty, not aids to redemption.

The Lord himself teaches in his Gospel that mystical realities surpass moral ones. Speaking of Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his word while Martha hurried about with her service and complained that her sister did not help her with the service of the table, he says: “Martha, Martha, Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:41–42).

If the woman who ministered to Christ at table was not compared with the woman who desired to hear his word, whom who is active can we compare with one who eagerly seeks eternal knowledge?

This must nevertheless be understood in such a way that faith is not absent from the action of the one, nor action, as in Mary, from the knowledge of the other; otherwise the leaves will be without fruit, or the fruit will be exposed without its natural protection and lie open to injury.

43. We may also understand the passage in this way: Adam and Eve covered themselves with leaves, seeking bodily garments, because the resurrection of the Lord’s body was being foretold. For even flesh—which had previously been accustomed to perish like leaves—was not destined to perish in Christ, nor was the flesh of all the righteous, who, according to the Gospel, were born from the Virgin in imitation of the tree of wisdom and would shape their life and actions accordingly, destined to perish.

For the Greek reads: ὃ τὸν καρπὸν αὐτοῦ δόσει, “which will give its fruit.” This may be referred to the blessed man, μακάριος καρπὸν δόσει, “the blessed man will give fruit,” in Greek; in Latin it is expressed as: “because the blessed man will give fruit,” namely in his resurrection, when he can give it perpetually.

It may also be taken as ὃ τὸν καρπὸν αὐτοῦ ὑπὲρ ξύλον, “which will give its fruit above the tree,” so that it refers to the tree, whose works will all prosper. In this there is clear testimony that the saying was spoken about the Savior. For whose works except his could all be praised and have prosperous outcomes?

Aquila, however, says, “they will be directed.” This also seems referable to any human being whom the Lord directs by heavenly favor. For “the steps of a man are directed by the Lord,” and the Prophet David asked that his prayer be directed in the sight of God (Ps. 140:2). The Lord himself also directed his works, so that they would not be bent by any winding path of error.

44. (Verse 4.) It follows: “Not so the impious, not so; but they are like the dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth.”

That is, they will not be like the blessed man, who is blessed because he did not walk in the counsel of the impious, because he did not stand in sin, because he did not sit in the council of the pestilent—those who wish to pervert either people who believe devoutly or people who live devoutly. He had his will in the Law and meditated upon it; or, as Aquila rendered it, “he will resound in the Law,” so that the life of such a man might echo the precepts of the Law and his conduct resound like that of those whose sound has gone forth into all the earth.

Perhaps the sound of human teaching goes forth here; but there, where it will be granted to see face to face, a fuller expression of the Word will appear.

Therefore, just as this blessed man who does these things will be like a planted tree whose every deed will prosper, so the impious man will not be. Thus either the writer repeated the phrase, or, as some think, someone later added it, making the statement more emphatic by repeating it: “Not so the impious, not so.” They will be like dust, for they are earthly; and just as dust is cast away from the face of the wind, so they too will be cast away and scattered by the Holy Spirit, who, like a health-giving south wind, is accustomed to breathe upon the fertile and fruitful soil of the soul.

[Note: The Scholiast in fact denies that this repetition is found in the Hexapla, as may be seen in Nobilius’s discussion of this passage.]

45. In the Song of Songs it is said to this wind: “Come, O south wind” (Song 4:16), so that the gentleness of a softer air may loosen the fields of our hearts, which, tightened by wintry frost, had refused to open their bosom to seeds waiting to be received.

It is good for us that this wind should blow, the wind that safely brings to port the ships of Tarshish bearing to the true Solomon what seems necessary for his temple. But this wind blows only when that heavy north wind has ceased to blow.

Therefore either the Church or the devout soul says: “Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind” (ibid.). That is: “Depart, O north wind, and come, O south wind; blow upon my garden,” so that you may not scatter the flowers but preserve them.

A soul full of the flowers of piety has a garden—or is itself a garden—that bears fruit. A soul open to impiety has dust, which is barren with respect to fruit. The Lord made the soul fruitful, but it gathered for itself the dust of impiety.

46. Why do you boast, O man full of impiety? Is it because you are powerful through honors and abound in riches? Do you not perceive that you are dust, and that you will be scattered and dispersed?

“I saw,” he says, “the impious man exalted above measure and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Ps. 36:35–36).

Why do you glory because many servants surround you, many friends cover your sides, and very many horses follow you, whose pedigree you recount to us as though it were the lineage of your ancestors?

You display your riches because you feed your companions at banquets. Would that you fed the poor! Would that you had not ministers of amusements, but helpers in prayers!

You boast that as soon as you appear, everyone gives way, and that people avoid you like a wild animal or a beast. Do you think these things amount to anything? Do you not hear that all of them pass away like a shadow?

What benefit are consular-bordered robes,

[Note: Some manuscripts and certain Paris editions read: “or triumphal palms shining with gold.” Other manuscripts and editions read: “palm-embroidered.” This is better; for one would not readily find palms, which were the prizes customarily carried in the hand by those who had won either at the Olympic games or in gladiatorial contests, among the ornaments of generals in triumphs. Rather, “palm-embroidered”—that is, togas embroidered with palms, or, as some wish, distinguished by broad purple stripes—were ornaments of triumphants. Likewise, the *praetextae* mentioned in this passage—that is, tunics decorated with purple borders—are known to have been garments of magistrates and noble boys. As for the reading “leaning upon gold,” found in several manuscripts instead of “shining with gold,” it may be explained as though one were reading “supported by and stiff with gold.”]

or triumphal palms shining with gold? You will go out naked; no one there will recognize the consul.

What benefit are innumerable estates? They are public, not yours. Today you hold them; tomorrow someone else will. When you leave, another enters. You have scarcely moved your foot before another has set his step there. How many possessed them before you, and how many will rule after you—and you think this is private property?

Whom have riches ever redeemed from death? Rather, whom have riches not driven to death? Whom have his possessions recalled from the underworld? Whom has power excused from punishment?

Impiety is dust, just as the power of the impious is dust. It brings darkness; it cannot give salvation. As soon as a violent wind begins to blow, it scatters and dissolves it. It troubles the air and lays the ground bare; it is cast away like dust, vanishes like smoke, and melts like wax.

47. For this reason many have raised a considerable question: does divine Scripture appear to assert that nature will perish? This is especially so because elsewhere it says: “I will crush them like dust before the face of the wind, and I will wipe them away like the mud of the streets” (Ps. 17:43); and elsewhere: “Behold, all adversaries will be confounded and put to shame; they will be like those who do not exist” (Isa. 41:11).

First, then, I ask whether they think impiety belongs to nature or is contrary to nature. If they assert that it belongs to nature,

[Note: The Victor and Colbert manuscript reads: “They assert that things which subsist naturally cannot utterly perish. They are mistaken, for …” These words, however, appear rather to be the gloss of some idle commentator than the author’s text.]

it is certain that their opinion is mistaken. Let them finally say whether sin belongs to nature or not. But it is certain that to sin is to deviate from what is according to nature.

What, then, is more absurd than to say that being impious seems less serious than being a sinner, when whatever is done against God appears to be the most bitter of all things?

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “But if acting impiously is contrary to nature, then living according to nature must neither be considered a sin nor …”]

But if acting impiously is not contrary to nature, then living impiously is according to nature and must neither be regarded as sin nor considered worthy of blame; for no one is blamed who acts according to nature. It follows, therefore, that impiety is contrary to nature.

How, then, does Scripture introduce, together with the destruction of custom, ἀπολλησομένας φύσεις—that is, “natures that will perish”—when impiety is not natural but contrary to nature? For what one does not possess, one does not lose; nor can that substance perish which did not exist.

Even dust that is stirred up is either transformed into the substance of water, or into air, or into fire—that is, it often appears to pass into another nature. It does not therefore vanish into nothing, but passes into something else.

[Col. 0946D] 48. What, then, prevents even him who is crushed like dust by the power and reason of the Word from being scattered not into nothingness but changed for the better—so that from an earthly person he becomes a spiritual human being, and so that, like the mud of the streets, it is wiped away in such a manner that whatever appears rough and dirty is removed, while whatever is smooth and clean remains? And when he says of Jerusalem’s adversaries, “They are as though they were not,” he could certainly have said, “They will not be.” But since he says, “They will be confounded and put to shame,” you understand that they will exist in substance and in the progress of their conversion, but they will not be as adversaries, as they were before. Thus, through the disappearance of their wickedness they will no longer be what they were, but they will exist transformed by faith and devotion.

Finally, elsewhere, in the person of the sinner, it is said: “And I will bear the wrath of God, because I have sinned, until he justifies my judgment” (Mic. VII, 9). For God, desiring to convert the sinner, punishes and burns him in order to cleanse him. Hence he says: “And he will bring me out into the light” (ibid.). Fire burns wax, too, and it melts so that it may be purified; and we are tested by fire; and smoke, once all the material has been consumed, is cleansed, [Note: [Col. 0947D] The older edition has *neither does it pass beyond nature*; the Roman edition and a few manuscripts have *and neither does it pass into nature*. Five others have *and nature does not pass*. Here *passes* suitably means the same as *is reduced to nothing*.] and nature does not pass away. Thus the soul, purified from every stain, perishes into what is, not into what is not. Hence Balaam says: [Note: [Col. 0947D] So five manuscripts; three others, together with the old edition, have: “May my soul die with the souls of the righteous.” The Roman edition alone has: “. . . with the souls of the righteous.” The Septuagint translators nevertheless support this reading, having: “May my soul die among the souls of the righteous . . .”] “May my soul die as the soul of the righteous” (Num. XXIII, 10)—so that its fall and a certain habit of wickedness might die, while it might pass into the way of life of the righteous. For God wills all things to be saved.

Hence Solomon also says: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wis. I, 13). He made the soul so that it might exist; he created the human being for incorruption, whom he made in his own image. But human beings, turning aside from the gift of nature, made themselves liable to death, so that, as earthly beings, they might be corrupted. Yet God compels them to repentance through tribulations, so that through repentance that incidental evil of wickedness may be burned away, consumed, and perish; and so that the place in the soul which had been occupied by the incidental possession of ungodliness may be opened for the reception of virtue and grace. It is certain that the nature of the soul is precious, since it was made in the likeness of God and admits the reception of every virtue, being one that has not been deprived of participation in heavenly knowledge.

49. We think that what remains is the question often heard from many mouths: how God—without whose will not even the most worthless sparrow falls, and with whom the hairs of the head are numbered—could have said through Isaiah: “Thus all the nations are reckoned as a drop from a jar, and as the slightest movement of a balance, and they will be reckoned as spittle” (Isa. XL, 15).

Will all the nations, then, perish like a drop from a jar, and perish like spittle, accomplishing no useful purpose? But you know that our God did not regard the nations as nothing to such an extent that he said to Abraham, “In you all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XII, 3), and spoke through David to the Son, saying, “I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II, 8), and further, “All the nations shall serve him” (Ps. LXXI, 11). You have read that God offered his Son for every nation in order to save sinners (Rom. VIII, 32). You must therefore consider here the force of the divine sentence.

For in comparison with the heavenly creatures, which are many—just as heaven is so much greater than earth that, in comparison with heaven, earth has been reckoned by many as a mere point—the nations are reckoned as a drop from a jar. [Note: [Col. 0947D] The Roman edition alone has *which are many*, namely, the angels, archangels, principalities, powers, thrones, dominions, thousands, tens of thousands, and innumerable thousands; in comparison with these, the nations are reckoned as a drop from a jar. For just as heaven is so much greater than earth that many have reckoned earth as a point in comparison with heaven, so too is its fullness. From that fullness, therefore, etc.] The angels, archangels, principalities, powers, thrones, dominions, thousands, tens of thousands, and innumerable thousands: in comparison with these, then, the nations are reckoned as a drop from a jar, whose fullness is complete. From that heavenly fullness, therefore, the nations are reckoned as a falling drop.

How could they appear great, when the earth itself on which the nations exist is the smallest portion of the world, and the nations are like a slight inclination of the balance among all that God has made? At the same time, understand through this balance that God created all things with justice, and that even among the nations there exists something naturally in which a slight measure of justice might be seen, and that spittle itself, as though belonging to the totality of the body, exists as an inward portion.

50. Here, therefore, mercy is proclaimed all the more: for he who came to seek what had perished did not despise even that drop as something worthless; he lightened that slight movement of the balance, [Note: [Col. 0948D] Several manuscripts have: “and of the spittle, when he deigned to give it the substance of a good body,” that is, to gather all the nations into one body, the Church. One manuscript has: “he gathered.”] and, giving that spittle the substance of a good body, deigned to gather all the nations into one body, the Church.

Among the nations, Israel too may by no means be counted as lacking that divine justice of his, because Moses himself said of Israel: “Behold, a wise people, and steadfast in discipline, a great nation” (Deut. IV, 6). And so that you may know that God’s goodness has overflowed beyond our merit, the Apostle, interpreting this prophetic passage, says: “God has enclosed all things in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. XI, 32 and following). And he added: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who first gave to him, and it shall be repaid to him?”

Introducing this passage, the Prophet says: “Thus all the nations are reckoned as a drop from a jar” (Isa. XL, 15), and the rest, so that you may recognize that this interpretation agrees with the Apostle’s interpretation.

[Col. 0948D] 51. (Verse 5.) But what could be clearer than the fact that he does not seem to introduce natures destined to perish, when the holy Prophet himself adds: “For the ungodly do not rise in judgment”? He did not say, “They do not rise,” but said, “They do rise, but not in judgment.” Now whoever rises certainly exists and remains; but because he did not believe in Christ, he has already been judged. Therefore he does not come into judgment, since the punishment of judgment already completed awaits him. There are, indeed, very many testimonies to the resurrection in the divine Scriptures, and we have not passed them over in our books of consolation and resurrection. But concerning what he says, “The ungodly do not rise in judgment,” the sentence is clear according to the Gospel, because not everyone will be judged.

The Apostle, however, says: “For we must all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V, 10). Many think these statements contradictory, and do not notice that the Savior was speaking of the faithless and ungodly, who did not believe in the Lord Jesus. For he says: “He who believes in me will not be judged; but he who does not believe has already been judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. And this is the judgment: that light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light, for their works were evil” (John III, 18–19).

It is therefore clear of whom this was said: namely, of those who did not believe in the Lord Jesus. The Apostle, although he said “all,” was speaking of those who believed, but who will render an account of their actions on the day of judgment. Finally, elsewhere he himself says (Rom. II, 15) that the testimony of our conscience will be revealed on the day of judgment, when our thoughts will accuse or defend one another, as it is written, and the hidden things of the heart will be brought to light.

What could be clearer than what he says elsewhere: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” (I Cor. XV, 15)? The righteous will be changed into incorruption, while the reality of the body remains. Daniel also says: “The judgment sat, and the books were opened” (Dan. VII, 10). He therefore shows that a future judgment will take place, especially since elsewhere he says the same: “Many of those who sleep in the tomb of the earth will rise, some to everlasting life, and some to eternal disgrace and confusion; and those who understand will shine like the brightness of heaven, and many of the righteous will shine like the stars” (Dan. XII, 2–3).

52. What is this judgment of the judges who sit, and what are the books that were opened, except our consciences, like books containing the sequence of our sins? Yet it is itself a paltry thing to imagine this as resembling a human judgment. The judgment of Christ is something else: there the conscience itself reveals what cannot remain hidden from the judge of secret things; there thoughts shine before him who, while they were still thinking, said: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. IX, 4).

When he said this to the Jews, he was speaking to everyone, so that no one would think that anything hidden could escape him, or that anyone could elude, behind closed walls, the witness of secret error. Therefore the Evangelist also testifies, saying: “But Jesus knew their thoughts” (Luke VI, 8).

How, then, does he say, “The books were opened”? They were certainly not written in ink, but in the traces of sins and the pollution of crimes. The book of your conscience will be opened; the book of your heart will be opened; our guilt will be read aloud. There is a book wherever there is a tablet; indeed, there are books inscribed wherever there are tablets inscribed, which apostolic teaching inscribes by the Holy Spirit, as we read Paul saying: “You are our letter . . . inscribed not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of fleshly hearts” (II Cor. III, 2–3).

The tablets of the heart are therefore inscribed by the Holy Spirit, and these will be read aloud. If you have acted well, the writing will remain. Take care not to remove the grace of the Holy Spirit; take care not to erase it and write your crimes in ink, lest the day of judgment come and the Judge say: “Let his books be read; let the tablets of his deeds be read.” And may he say to you: “I wrote your tablets—why did you erase my letters? I wrote my gifts—how did you erase my favors and write your reproaches? Have you not read that I write? Did I not say to you through the mouth of my Prophet: ‘My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe’?” (Ps. XLIV, 2). The judgment, however, belongs to the Word.

53. Many of those sleeping in the tomb of the earth will therefore rise: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment (John V, 28–29). What Daniel calls “to everlasting life,” the Savior called “to the resurrection of life.” Likewise, what Daniel calls “to disgrace and confusion,” the Savior called “to the resurrection of judgment.”

Therefore it is not advantageous for us to come to judgment, nor is it advantageous not to come—lest we appear either to have been condemned beforehand or, in this stain of our vices, undergo the burden of so great a judgment. The Prophet asks that the Lord not enter into judgment with his servant (Ps. CXLII, 2); how much more ought we to fear the Lord’s judgment?

Suppose that the merciful Lord will forgive: how much will be exposed that I thought could remain hidden? What shame and confusion will be mine when I, who professed to teach others, am myself caught in the very matter for which I reproved others?

54. And therefore, since the Savior too [Note: [Col. 0949D] Here Saint Ambrose seems not to depart greatly from the opinion of the Millenarians. I do not want you to understand this as the view which Damascene, in his *Book on Heresies*, reports the Origenists to have taught: that Christ’s reign would finally come to an end, and that the angels would likewise cease to exist; nor as the blasphemy of Gobar the tritheist, who asserted that all animals would also rise with the righteous, and so forth. Rather, it should be understood as the view according to which the righteous were said to rise first of all and reign with Christ in the greatest peace and delight for a thousand years, after which period the general resurrection and universal judgment would occur. Even if we attributed this to Ambrose, no one ought to be surprised. For it is certain that not only Origen—whose opinion our saint occasionally transferred into his writings—but also many other Fathers of great renown, both Greek and Latin, held this opinion. Out of reverence for them, Jerome, in his commentary on Jeremiah XIX, 11, and Augustine, *Book XX*, chapter 7, did not dare condemn the same view; Augustine makes clear in this very passage that what most displeased him in this doctrine was that it did not admit spiritual pleasures. That Ambrose and certain others might have admitted these can be understood from the fact that Augustine himself there confesses that, while he formerly held the view of the Millenarians, he admitted such pleasures. As for what seems to be taught here and below, in no. 56 and elsewhere—that all sinners who have believed in Christ will be saved after their crimes have been purged by fire—this was not only the view of Origen and many other Fathers of that age, but also of Jerome himself, in Book I of his work *Against the Pelagians*, chapter 9, and in several other places. From this you may infer that in those times this error had not yet been clearly rejected by the Church. But since Ambrose, in his preface to Psalm XXXVII, no. 2, says absolutely: “For if you have carried serious sins away from here, there—in the future life—you will have no rest,” and makes similar statements elsewhere, we may judge that here he spoke not so much from his own opinion as from that of the Fathers mentioned above. Whoever wishes to learn more fully about the entire doctrine of the Millenarians should consult Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca sancta*, Book V, annotation 233, and Book VI, annotation 347, as well as P. D. Huet, *Origen*, Book II, question 9.] has posited two kinds of resurrection, and John in the Apocalypse said: “Blessed is he who has a part in the first resurrection” (Rev. XX, 6). These come to grace without judgment. Those, however, who do not come to the first resurrection but are reserved for the second will be burned until they complete the period between the first and second resurrection; or, if they do not complete it, they will remain longer in punishment. Let us therefore ask that we may deserve to have a part in the first resurrection.

There are those who rose in the passion of Christ; these are truly blessed, for they received Christ’s grace and heard his voice, of which it is written: “The hour is coming when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John V, 25). And: “They entered into the holy city” (Matt. XXVII, 53). I think that this signifies the heavenly city more than that Jerusalem which he left and reproved—those who entered this earthly city on foot, but entered that heavenly one by their merits.

55. Let us also take care that, while placed here, we rise from the tomb of the earth. There are people who, while alive, are surrounded by and filled with tombs and corpses; their throat is a tomb, speaking not words of life but of death. If here we rise from the dead, we shall rise there also. If here we are not dry bones, but have received the dew of the Word and the moisture of the Holy Spirit, we shall live there as well.

May Jesus awaken us here with his great voice, as he awakened Lazarus; may he, through his disciples, release us from the bonds of death; may he bring us into Bethany, where Lazarus was—that is, into the house of obedience—and may he admit us here to his banquet. Then there we shall recline with him; there we shall feast with him forever; and there the ointment will give off its fragrance for us, the pouring out of which grieved the betrayer alone.

56. (Verse 5.) The ungodly, therefore, do not rise in judgment—that is, into the portion of those who will undergo judgment; nor do sinners rise in the counsel of the righteous. You see that the ungodly rise, but do not rise in the judgment of the righteous. For although sinners do not rise in the counsel of the righteous, they nevertheless rise in judgment.

Thus those who believed well and also carried out their faith in works appear not to be judged, but to rise in the counsel of the righteous. Sinners, however, who cannot rise among the righteous, will rise in judgment. You have two orders. A third remains: the ungodly, who, because they did not believe, have already been judged. Therefore they do not rise in judgment, but for punishment; for they loved darkness more than light (John III, 19). Their judgment is therefore punishment, and perhaps the punishment of darkness.

It could indeed be understood that those who have evil works, while nevertheless believing in Christ and wishing to live rightly, but overcome by the allurements of sins, loved darkness more than light—that is, they loved both, but darkness more. But since he first spoke of those who did not believe, I think that “they loved darkness and not light” must be understood in this way: light is Christ. Those who did not believe in the light cannot sensibly be thought to have loved the light, which they did not know. For they did not know or understand; they walk in darkness, as it is written (Ps. LXXXI, 5).

[Col. 0952B] 57. (Verse 6.) It follows: “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the path of the ungodly will perish.” Consider the meaning: “The ungodly do not rise in judgment, for the Lord knows the way of the righteous.” He certainly knows their ways whose steps he directs. For there are steps of human beings that are directed by the Lord. The ways of a man are directed by the Lord as well.

The Lord knows those ways that are straight, which lead toward the life of the one who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). This is the good way. The way of the world, however, is crooked. He does not deem himself worthy to know that way. For he recognizes those who are his own, who perform his works. But to those who practice iniquity the Lord says: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Luke XIII, 27). They are not unknown through ignorance, but are not known because they are unworthy of the knowledge of God.

[Col. 0952C] 58. Beautifully, however, he says: “And the path of the ungodly will perish.” The Latin separated the terms, using *path* and thereby distinguishing the path from the way; but the Greek used *way* in both places. The Latin nevertheless did this appropriately, because the Lord also said, “I am the way”; he did not say, “I am the path.”

He said that the path of the ungodly would perish, not the ungodly themselves. He preserves their substance; if they are converted, they will lose only the path of ungodliness, which neither existed in the beginning nor will exist. Therefore what is incidental perishes; what is substantial remains.

The ungodly perish in the manner expressed by: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII, 4)—so that they die through the sting of sin, [Note: [Col. 0952D] Some manuscripts have: “so that they die through the bond of sin.”] not through the dissolution of their entire substance.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXXV

[Note: [Col. 0951D] Written after the year 393.]

[Col. 0951]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0751D]

1. As the Prophet is about to set forth in the following psalm what the character of the righteous is, he first expressed the character of the unrighteous. For we cannot know what the form of righteousness is unless we know what the image of iniquity is; they are opposed and contrary to one another. In one there is the simple disposition of nature; in the other, the deceitful cunning of wickedness. One presents the images of virtues, [Note: [Col. 0953D] Several manuscripts have: “it displays the inventions of vices.”] while the other pretends to traffic in vices.

Reason itself also teaches that this order is appropriate. And if testimonies are to be taken from opposites, the teachers of philosophy themselves acknowledged this principle in their writings. Who, however, would doubt that David lived long before Plato’s time? Plato’s teacher, and even his teacher’s grandfathers, could not have seen David, since David lived at the beginning of the Jewish kingdom, which was extended through countless generations, whereas Plato lived after the periods of captivity, when the kingdom of his nation had already been destroyed.

Thus the very man who holds primacy over all secular wisdom, when he said that the form of justice could not be grasped unless the whole sequence of injustice were first examined, offered the example that those who wish to seek gold first smear themselves with mud. Gold, therefore, is justice; iniquity is mud. There is no doubt that this was also said earlier by our own writers, since it is written: “I will wipe them away like the mud of the streets” (Ps. XVII, 43).

And truly it is mud, because it stains those who approach it. Let us therefore flee injustice, lest we be soiled with muddy filth, and lest not our external foot but, what is more serious, our mind be plunged into its abyss.

Philosophy claims to seek gold, but it handles mud when it seeks divinity in statues; yet the potter’s vessels will be shattered by the rod. We seek the gold with which we may cleanse our bodies, carrying the death of Jesus Christ in our body, so that the life of Jesus Christ may also be manifested in our body. Good gold is the blood of Christ: rich in value, flowing forth to wash away every sin.

We have discussed the order; let us consider the title.

2. (Verse 1.) “For the end,” he says, “a psalm of David for the servant of the Lord.” In the whole body of the Psalter this is the only title that testifies that he wrote a psalm for the servant of the Lord. Let us see who this servant of the Lord is, what the sequence of the psalm signifies, and to whom this psalm is addressed.

Let us hear to whom he speaks: “Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds. Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV, 6–7). To whom is this said, except to the Son of God? These things belong not to human but to divine power.

But what does it mean that the title declares this psalm to be addressed to the servant of the Lord (Ps. LXXXIX, 1), when, in a later title, he preferred to name the prayer as that of Moses, the man of God, rather than as that of the servant of the Lord? I do not understand what the Prophet’s intention was—or rather, that of the Lord himself, who spoke through the Prophet. Truly, “his judgments are a great abyss,” since he reserved honor for the servant while ascribing to himself the condition of servitude.

I seem to understand; I seem to have drawn something from spiritual grace. As we have said, this psalm was written against injustice. Therefore the injustice of the faithless is weighed all the more heavily: they refused to receive Christ Jesus as Lord, although he assumed servitude for their sake. For what is more unjust than to have been ungrateful for such great benefits, so that those to whom he gave salvation poured out his blood?

Finally, elsewhere, when speaking of his passion, to heap reproach upon Jewish ungodliness he says: “Do not turn your face away from your servant, for I am afflicted; hear me quickly . . .” (Ps. LXVIII, 18). “I am poor and sorrowful” (ibid., 30).

3. Come, Paul, interpret for us how the Lord of heaven and earth could have called himself poor, and what this poverty is. You certainly called him rich; how, then, is he both rich and poor?

Let us hear Paul’s testimony. “You know,” he says, “the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that for your sake he became poor, although he was rich, so that you might be enriched by his poverty” (II Cor. VIII, 9).

Come also, Isaiah, and interpret for us how Christ could have said that he was in sorrow, when he was accustomed to heal the sorrows of wounds. The physician came to heal the sick; what did he himself have that could cause him pain?

Let us hear Isaiah’s testimony as well. “For our sake,” he says, “he is in sorrow, and we considered him to be in pain” (Isa. LIII, 4). He expressed the compassion of a physician who, although he himself had no wound that caused him pain, nevertheless sympathized with the wounded.

This, then, is what the Lord reproaches the Jews with in the psalm: “For your sake I was poor; for you I was in sorrow; and you laid impious hands upon me, saying: ‘Let us remove the righteous, because he is useless to us’” (Wis. II, 12). “Let us cast wood into his bread” (Jer. XI, 19). He rightly said “bread” in place of his flesh. He brought nourishment; they returned punishment in exchange for the benefit.

It is no wonder, then, that those who denied themselves the nourishment of eternal life are hungry. Beautifully they joined these two statements: “Let us cast wood into his bread.” The Jews did not know what they were saying, yet they were speaking a mystery.

The Cross of Christ restored Paradise to us. This is the wood that the Lord showed to Adam, saying that the tree of life was in the midst of Paradise and was to be eaten, but that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was not to be eaten. Adam went astray; he did not keep the commandments and tasted what was forbidden. Through wood we began to hunger, because the flesh received its nourishment through it. Therefore the Lord joined flesh and wood in Christ, so that the ancient hunger might cease and the grace of life be restored.

Blessed is the Lord’s wood, which crucified the sins of all. Blessed is the Lord’s flesh, which supplied food to everyone!

4. Concerning the Lord’s poverty and sorrow, then, we have brought forth, as I think, suitable testimonies from the saints: one saw and spoke, while the other was chosen to speak. Let us therefore again bring forth testimonies from those who were approved concerning the Lord’s servitude—or rather, let us hear what he himself spoke about himself in both passages.

Let us hear what he says: “Thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb as a servant for himself, to gather Jacob and Israel to him” (Isa. XLIX, 5). We understand, then, that he assumed the form of a servant for the sake of gathering the people.

You hear this, Jew, and return insult for grace; you turn into an occasion of unbelief what should have led you all the more to believe. He came to call you, and you revile him. He said that he was a servant from the womb.

Hear, Arian, from what womb. Go back a little above: “From the womb of my mother,” he says, “the Lord called my name” (Ps. XLIX, 1). Let us hear what his name is, by which the Father called him. “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is translated, “God with us” (Isa. VII, 14; Matt. I, 23). For what other name is Christ’s except the Son of God?

Receive another testimony. Gabriel had indeed also said to Joseph concerning Mary: “She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (ibid., 21). Receive the voice of God: “And you, Bethlehem of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall go forth a Ruler who will govern my people” (Mic. V, 2).

Consider the mystery: from the Virgin’s womb the same one came forth both servant and Lord—the servant in order to work, the Lord in order to command—so that God’s kingdom might take root in human minds. There is one on both sides, not one from the Father and another from the Virgin, but the same one who existed before the ages from the Father later assumed flesh from the Virgin.

Therefore he is called both servant and Lord: servant for our sake, but, by the unity of the divine substance, God from God, Ruler from Ruler, equal from equal. For he did not beget one who was degenerate (Matt. III, 17), in whom he declared that he himself was well pleased.

5. “It is a great thing,” he says, “for you to be called my servant, so that you may establish the tribes of Jacob.” Everywhere he preserves the terms belonging to his dignity. God is great, and the child is great. Even in the flesh he does not lose the name of his greatness, whose greatness has no end.

Therefore, confidently, although he was in the form of God, as the Apostle says, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II, 6 and following).

This, then, is the one equal as the Son of God; this is the one who assumed the form of a servant in the flesh; this is the one who tasted death, whose greatness has no end, because Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
