Let us all believe in him and worship him with our deepest affection.

Good is the servitude that made all people free. Good is the servitude that acquired the name above every name. Good is the humility that caused every knee to bow at his name—in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue to confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.

This, then, is the direction of this psalm’s purpose: that we too may be servants for righteousness, not proud in arrogance. [Col. 0956A] [Note: [Col. 0955D] All editions have: “For the wage of servitude is freedom”; all manuscripts have: “For servitude is the wage of freedom.” The Roman edition alone again has: “but the wage of arrogance is death”; the other editions and the manuscripts read as in the text. To understand this otherwise obscure passage, one should observe that it alludes to military service, in which, after a fixed number of periods of pay—that is, years—discharge was granted to soldiers. Thus we interpret it: servitude is followed by freedom, and arrogance by death, just as discharge is granted after the required terms of service have been completed; or, more briefly, servitude serves freedom, while arrogance serves death. The preceding words, “Good is the servitude,” sufficiently indicate this meaning.] For servitude is the wage of freedom; arrogance, however, is the wage of death.

But let us now approach the sequence of the psalm itself.

## EXPOSITION

6. (Verse 2.) “The unjust man spoke so as to sin against himself.” He did not specify what he said, and therefore I think it should be understood in this way: whatever the unjust man says is sin. For every injustice is sin. When the instrument is defective, how can the song not be defective? The offspring is a discolored product of degenerate material. Whatever the unjust man says, therefore, is iniquity, and it returns upon its author, like the offspring of a viper, which, as the common saying goes, first tears open its own mother in being born (see *On Tobias*, chapter 12, no. 41, and below, Psalm XXXVII, no. 8).

He therefore sins against himself. I think nothing more sublime has been said than this sentence. Among those who claimed for themselves the wisdom of the world, I have read nothing like it and learned nothing like it. Nor is this surprising, since they spoke by human ingenuity, whereas this was breathed in by the Spirit of God, the Spirit of truth: that the unjust man sins against himself, inflicts wounds upon himself, and pierces himself.

For just as thorns arise in the hand of a drunkard, as Scripture asserts (Prov. XXVI, 9), so also thorns arise from the speech of the unjust, pricking the one who speaks. The unjust man speaks, and his inward conscience is wounded, because in every word he utters he is not free from deceit. What punishment is more severe than one’s own, when one pays the penalty for every word?

The serpent pours out its poison upon others; the unjust man pours it out upon himself, for whatever he has poured forth flows back upon him. The unjust man is therefore useless to others and harmful to himself, whereas the life of the righteous is fruitful for others and sweet to himself.

For Solomon says: “My son, if you are wise, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbors; but if you become evil, you alone will bear the evil” (Prov. IX, 12).

7. We understand, then, that righteousness was born for others rather than for itself. It seeks the common benefit, not its own, and counts another’s good as its own advantage. Blessed and excellent is the righteousness whose goodness benefits everyone: from one person it frequently proceeds to many and reaches all.

Righteous was David, who spared his enemy and preferred his innocence to preserving his life, lest he should be avenged at public cost and, having taken vengeance on his ambusher, give others an example of attacking the ruler even in evil causes.

Righteous was Abel, who thought that the firstfruits of the sheep the Lord had given him ought to be offered to the Lord. For this reason he pleased God more: he did not delay, but demonstrated his devotion.

But the ungodly man could not endure this—the transgressor of righteousness, the root of iniquity. Therefore he killed his brother, because Abel’s sacrifice had been approved by God more than his own offering.

Yet Abel, once killed, spoke to God in the voice of his blood, while Cain, alive, was driven away from the face of the Lord. And while the Lord’s punishment was still delayed, the consciousness of his sins tormented him. The wretched man hid himself, trembling and afraid; and although no executioner was yet present, the life of the unjust man itself tortured him.

He had received a sign so that no one would kill him—not so that he might enjoy the sweetness of life, but so that death would not remove his misery, and so that by fearing his executioner every day he might suffer. He had indeed deserved that an executioner be restrained; but without any interruption he himself was his own executioner, himself his own killer.

### 8

What punishment is greater than fearing what you cannot avoid, and being unable to escape what you fear? Hence David, expressing most forcefully the most grievous conflict of a guilty conscience, says: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always against me” (Psalm 50:4). For the avenging image of our sin is cast before us; it does not allow the guilty person to be at peace, but imposes a wretched servitude and drags him into its chains, so that he cannot loosen himself—for he willingly sold himself to the one to whom he could have refused the price of his sins and preserved the freedom of innocence.

Thus, while we pray, sin is cast before us; when the bodily senses have relaxed in sleep, sin returns. Our error is always before us like an evil tax collector, or like a dishonest moneylender confronting his debtor. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34).

But the righteous person knows how to loosen the bonds of his sins. He does not await an accuser, but anticipates him, so that by confessing he may lighten his whole offense and leave his adversary nothing of which to accuse him. Therefore Scripture says to you: “The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Proverbs 18:17). He takes away the adversary’s voice and, as it were, restrains the teeth prepared for the prey of hostile accusation by confessing his sins.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “He breaks them by confession.”]

Judas Iscariot spoke in order to bring guilt upon himself. What did he say? “The one whom I shall kiss is he; seize him” (Matthew 26:48). He said this, and with his own mouth drove himself to death. How many torturers do we suppose were within him, so that he himself became the exactor of so grievous a punishment and strangled himself with a noose?

### 9

The unrighteous man spoke in order to bring guilt upon himself. The righteous man spoke: “Behold, I have sinned and acted wickedly; but what has this flock done?” (2 Samuel 24:17).

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “Behold, I, the shepherd, have done wickedly.”]

And every sin was forgiven. The righteous man spoke, therefore, and it benefited him.

Cain said: “Am I my brother’s keeper?” (Genesis 4:9), and he lied to himself. Ananias said that he had brought the entire price of the land he had sold, and he lied to himself, since he could have offered less without deceit. Therefore Scripture rightly says: “And iniquity has lied to itself” (Psalm 26:12). For it first lies to itself when it lies for its own destruction; the one who deprives himself of the sweetness of innocence sins against himself.

What fruit is sweeter than purity and simplicity of heart? What food is more pleasant than that upon which the mind conscious of its own goodness and the innocent soul feast? But iniquity weighs down the conscience like a lead talent, as Scripture testifies (Zechariah 5:7). Hence David rightly says: “Like a heavy burden, they have weighed upon me” (Psalm 37:5). And Solomon says: “As a sour grape to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is iniquity to all who use it” (Proverbs 10:26).

Grievous is the punishment that obstructs food and darkens the sight; and, what is more, it casts a dark mist over the eyes of the inner mind, so that the unrighteous person cannot see what is true. Therefore the one who deprives himself of what is precious sins against himself.

### 10

The unrighteous man therefore spoke in order to bring guilt upon himself. The righteous man, however, speaks so as to benefit both others and himself: the one speaks toward destruction, the other toward salvation. Of the righteous and faithful it is said: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

The tongue of the unrighteous wounds, but the tongue of the prudent heals. Thus, when David reproached King Saul because, forgetful of the benefit he had received and ungrateful for his deliverance, he pursued to the death the man by whom he had so often been saved—and sought the life of one who had exposed his own life to danger for the king’s safety—David said that the fruit of his righteousness would not perish, since he had not killed his ambusher when the Lord had delivered him into his hands (1 Samuel 24:14).

From the unrighteous iniquity proceeded; poison was poured out by serpents; poison and the weapons of iniquity perished.

### 11

Therefore it is written: “The unrighteous man spoke in order to bring guilt upon himself.” What did he say? “I shall set my throne above the clouds, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14). His words have no effect, but they do contain sin. His boastful display is empty; yet the criminal spirit of pride is not afraid, by its reproach, to violate the divine majesty.

For if any fear of God had been present in his disposition, he would not rashly have dared to conduct himself full of deceit in God’s sight—as though God, who searches the innermost parts, could not know hidden things. God sees everything; nothing escapes him, and no one can deceive him. To him all things that will be are present, and all things that are hidden are manifest.

Indeed, if this worldly sun often sends its light into the closed dwellings of houses, how much more does the supreme and eternal God search, by his knowledge, even the hidden chambers of the human mind and every counsel of the angels, and anticipate them? What else, then, does the unrighteous man do except seek iniquity and hatred for himself?

### 12

For thus it is written: “There is no fear of God before his eyes; for he acted deceitfully in his sight, so as to find his own iniquity and hatred.”

What would he find? Everyone who seeks finds. Therefore, if evil is sought, one acts so that it may be found.

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “Therefore evil too is sought, so that it may be found”; one reads: “Therefore thus evil,” and so forth.]

But just as the one who finds the good he sought is praiseworthy, so the one who labored to find the evil he had sought is blameworthy. We ought to devote our labor to good things, not to wicked deeds and crimes. What, then, is it except the height of folly and madness to seek hatred and discover iniquity by wicked methods, when no good person has sought them?

### 13

Let us therefore consider how the wicked seek their iniquity and hatred. Herodias, to be sure, was bound in lawful marriage to the tetrarch Philip and abounded in the wealth of royal power.

[Note: Thus read the manuscripts of Victorinus and Colbertinus. The Regius manuscript and the printed edition differ from them only in reading below *ille, cum quo peccata sua copulans* (“he with whom she joined her sins”), whereas they read *cum quo despecta suam copulam* (“with whom, having despised her own union”). Others prefer the passage in these words: “When Herod, proceeding as far as Rome, had been received as though he were her husband’s brother, by right of hospitality and kinship, and, discussing with him her own union, not long afterward …”]

She received Herod, who was traveling as far as Rome, as though he were her husband’s brother, by right of hospitality and kinship; and, having arranged her union with him, she soon afterward abandoned her husband and changed the rights of their relationship.

Did she not seek iniquity and hatred—the woman who abandoned her marriage in order to find adultery? And because the holy Baptist persistently rebuked the unlawful marriage, saying to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have her as your wife” (Mark 6:18)—since she had abandoned her husband contrary to the Law and had joined herself to her husband’s brother as though this were permitted by the Law—the adulteress was provoked to want to kill him.

But when she learned that she could not easily persuade Herod to put the righteous man to death, she devised a means by which she might accomplish it.

[Note: It was formerly customary among many peoples to celebrate birthdays every year with the greatest festivity; but nobles and kings in particular celebrated them with banquets and splendid feasts. Moses attests to the antiquity of this custom in Genesis, chapter 40, where he records the birthday feast held by Pharaoh. Hugo Grotius, however, prefers to understand this banquet, as also Herod’s, as celebrating the day on which the reign began rather than the beginning of life. At banquets, the customary presence of groups of dancers is too common a matter to require annotation. What is less obvious is what Ambrose records: that Herodias’s daughter was adorned so that she might dance as a royal pledge. Although, according to Lucian’s *On Dancing*, the dance may not have been “competitive” (*ἐναγώνιος ἡ ὄρχησις*), Ambrose seems here to indicate that prizes were customarily offered to girls dancing at banquets, perhaps not always fixed in advance, so that the one who deserved it might receive a greater or lesser reward according to how greatly or slightly she had pleased the audience. “To dance as a royal pledge” is the same as “to dance the dance of a royal pledge,” just as in Horace “to dance the Cyclops” means nothing other than “to dance the dance of the Cyclops.”]

It was Herod’s birthday, which he was accustomed to celebrate with excessive luxury, as is the custom of most kings. He adorned his daughter so that she might dance as a royal pledge at the king’s banquet. When she pleased Herod—though what pleased him ought to have displeased his uncle—he offered her whatever reward she wished to request in return for the disgrace of her dancing. She consulted her mother, at whose urging she asked for the Baptist’s head.

Herod, defeated because he had bound himself by an oath to give whatever his own niece requested, ordered John to be killed and his head brought to him. When it had been brought, he gave it to the girl, and she carried it to her mother.

It is true, therefore, that iniquity and hatred are sought, since that woman obtained by deceitful schemes what she could not obtain by a simple request.

### 11

What shall I say about Judas the traitor, who sought greed and found sacrilege, saying: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matthew 26:15). Not satisfied with plundering the poor, he reached the fullness of the gravest crimes by adding crime to crime, mixing the sacred mysteries of pious charity with wickedness when he said: “The one whom I shall kiss is he; seize him” (ibid., 48).

So it may truly be said of him, without any doubt: “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit.” He carried kisses upon his lips and poured poison over hearts; he was plotting bitter punishments while presenting the pledge of favor.

### 15

Prophecy rightly added concerning him: “He refused to understand how to do good.” For he did not sin by nature but by will. In the end, he was an Apostle; he heard the divine commandments every day and learned the heavenly mystery. He could have understood how to do good, if he had wished.

He saw paralytics healed, sight restored to the blind, and the dead raised. Should he not have understood that the one who could perform such deeds was God? But he refused to understand, because, being a greedy man intent upon money, he turned the vigor of his mind away from knowledge of divinity.

For everyone who has gorged himself on wicked deeds refuses to understand the things commanded by heaven, lest he be recalled from his vices. See him fleeing understanding who says: “Darkness covers me, and walls surround me; who knows whether the Lord sees?” (Ecclesiasticus 23:26). He does not wish to seek and discover that God sees and knows everything, lest fear draw him back from crime.

See King Ahab asking Naboth for his vineyard, and hear Naboth reply: “Far be it from me to give you the inheritance of my fathers” (1 Kings 21:3). Should he not have understood that Naboth was making a just reply? But he refused to understand how to do good and not seek what belonged to another.

Should he not have understood that Elijah truly served God, when he saw the heavens shut for three years and three months at Elijah’s word, and rain sent down at his prayers so that everything dry might be watered? But he refused to understand, lest he condemn his faithlessness and follow faith.

### 16

“Indeed, he meditated iniquity upon his bed,” where he ought to have sought truth. For upon our beds our sins ought to pierce us with remorse, not be committed there through further wrongdoing, as the Prophet says: “What you say in your hearts, be pierced with remorse upon your beds” (Psalm 4:5).

### 17

“He stood,” he says, “upon every way that was not good; but he did not hate evil.” For it is not without reason that he meditates injustice who stands upon the way of error and loves the evil he ought to hate.

He said more than merely “stood”: he stood as though he had already remained for a long time upon the way of wickedness. Blessed is the one who did not stand in the way of sinners (Psalm 1:1), not the one who does not cease standing there.

Therefore the first commandments of the holy prophet David are to flee impiety, not to stand in sin, and to meditate upon the Law, so that you may understand what is good and distinguish between what is just and unjust.

In everything, then, the root from which something grows must be watched, lest useless sap infect it from the beginning; for the vices of souls are much more serious than those of shrubs. Above all, care must be taken lest the practice of evil become ingrained in human nature and every later generation degenerate. For a bad tree produces bad fruits.

If we often do what we do not want, cannot avoid doing it, and do what we hate—whether compelled by some force, or through the pleasure of wickedness, or through the stealthy intrusion of sin—how can we avoid what we love? We are bound even unwillingly; how can we, when willing, not be held fast?

Paul scarcely freed himself from error by struggling daily, so that, released from the bonds of captivity, he might be preserved through the grace of Christ. And do you suppose that by standing beside your offenses you can attain the rewards of heavenly promises?

A crown is sought by struggling, not by resisting; it is gained by zeal, not by opposition. Those who are engaged in the contest must also ask for the support of divine mercy, so that the crown of righteousness may be bestowed in accordance with the merits of their labors.

### 18

Finally, let us consider what follows. “Lord,” he says, “your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds. Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; your judgments are like the great abyss.”

Did Paul not follow this passage when he said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:24–25)?

For when the human mind is troubled and the harsh and difficult struggles of our contests weary us, the Lord’s help must be sought. Therefore he turns to the Lord, calls upon him, and begs that he stand by those who labor as their helper.

Mercy, therefore, must be sought from heaven, and God’s truth gathered from the prophetic oracles, which, like clouds, cover the mysteries of divine knowledge.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “They conceal the mysteries of divine thought.”]

For God made darkness his hiding place, so that first you may receive the rain of mystical fertility, and then, soaked with heavenly dew, recognize the radiance of the light that has been disclosed, so that you may say: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16).

Who can easily comprehend the secrets of God, whose righteousness is like the mountains of God—or, as Aquila rendered it, “like strong mountains”—because his commandments are full of powerful strength?

Therefore the Apostle, seeing that what he had heard was sublime, says: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” (Romans 11:23–24).

He therefore compared the height of the riches of wisdom with the height of the mountains. Hear of what mountains he speaks. The Son of God himself is a great mountain (Isaiah 40:9). Therefore climb this mountain that proclaims good news to Zion, so that you may stand rooted and planted in Christ.

There is a mountain that is like the wisdom of God; a mountain that is like righteousness; a mountain that is like the knowledge of God; a mountain that is like sanctification; a mountain that is like redemption; a mountain that is like resurrection.

Scripture showed us these mountains when it said: “But you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

Or because the Son of God became an angel to the angels and a prophet to the prophets, his judgments are like a great abyss.

Hear something good: “Deep calls to deep at the sound of your cataracts” (Psalm 41:8)—that is, the writing of the Old Testament calls upon the sequence of the New Testament for the completion of sanctification and the fullness of grace, with a certain sound and overflowing abundance of spiritual outpouring.

### 19

“Lord, you will save humans and animals, as you have multiplied your mercy, O God. But the children of humans will hope in the protection of your wings. They will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight.”

What does “humans and animals” mean? Rational beings, certainly, and irrational beings. Judgments are given to the rational, mercy to the irrational. Some are governed; others are nourished.

Therefore he added: “But the children of humans will hope in the protection of your wings”—that is, not the generation of vipers, but the children of humans who live according to the image and likeness of God. They are placed not in pastures but at banquets: some in the place of pastures, others in the privilege of the sacraments.

For the imperfect there is the nourishment of milk; for the perfect, the table of refreshment, concerning which he said: “You have prepared a table before me” (Psalm 22:5). On it is living bread, that is, the Word of God; on it is the oil of sanctification, with which the head of the righteous is fattened and the inner sense strengthened, so that the oil of the sinner may be abolished; on it too is the intoxicating cup—how splendid, or how powerful! (ibid.).

For the Greek says *κράτιστον* (*krátiston*), meaning powerful, strong, or mighty; mighty, that is, because by it wicked deeds are washed away or erased. Good, therefore, is the intoxication produced by the cup of salvation.

But there is another intoxication arising from the overflowing abundance of the Scriptures. There is also another intoxication through the infusion of the Holy Spirit. Accordingly, those who spoke in different languages in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2:13) seemed to their hearers to be full of new wine.

The house, therefore, is the Church; the abundance of the house is the overflowing of graces; the torrent of delight is the Holy Spirit.

### 20

Nor should the name or nature of a torrent offend you, since it is sometimes more dry or more meager, so that its streams customarily cease. This torrent of spiritual outpouring also ceased at times among the Jewish people.

Why should I say that the torrent ceased, when the sea itself ceased, as today’s reading taught us, when the Lord said: “Behold, by my rebuke I shall make the sea desolate, and I shall make the rivers deserts, and their fish shall dry up” (Isaiah 50:2)—namely, the Jews, because of the dryness of their faithlessness, so that they could not swim out?

The torrent therefore ceased because of the sacrileges of the Synagogue, because that people was dry in faith, sterile in works, and captive to sins. For what would flow for those who did not drink but polluted the sacred channels, when they had killed the very fountain?

[Note: Thus read the printed edition and several manuscripts. But many others have *fontem negarint*—“they denied the fountain.” And below, where the old edition reads in the margin and the Roman edition in the body, together with a few manuscripts, “and the thirst of human desire,” a greater number read “and the thirst of human captivity.”]

It is a good torrent that ceased for them so that it might overflow for us and turn away the thirst of human desire, like a torrent in the south. Hence Scripture also says: “Rise up, north wind, and come, south wind” (Song of Songs 4:16), the wind accustomed to blow through the little trees of paradise.

### 21

We have discussed the meaning; let us also consider the expression. Why did he say, “You will give them drink from the torrent of delight,” rather than “with the torrent,” as though from a torrent? Perhaps because he wished to express the eagerness of those drinking, as though they wished to drink up the torrent itself, if they could.

This is perhaps the torrent of delight that we read about in Genesis (Genesis 2:10), the fountain that washes paradise and divides into four rivers which circle the whole earth. From this fountain the spiritual virtues flow forth: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice.

It is the good fountain of grace and splendor, of the same nature as that river of which it is said later: “The impulse of the river gladdens the city of God” (Psalm 45:5).

### 22

Therefore he most appropriately added: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light. Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to those who are upright in heart.”

After the commemoration of heavenly blessings, these words are rightly referred to their author, our Lord Jesus Christ, who, as the irrigating fountain of eternal life, descended into the earth in order to water the dryness of our hearts.

He is likewise the radiance of the glory of God the Father and the image of his substance. Therefore in his true light—which enlightens every human being coming into this world—we shall see the Father, because God is light.

It is rightly also said: “In your light we shall see light,” according to the saying: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” (John 14:9). With you, therefore, O Fountain of life, we shall see the Father present. For just as you were God the Word with the Father in the beginning, so the Father is always with you, who is in you. He is with him in whom he is.

[Note: The Thuan manuscript reads: “But the Prophet, foreseeing in the spirit the coming of the Lord Savior, to whom except him who was to come upon the earth would he say, ‘With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light’? Hence the Savior also says in the Gospel: ‘I …’”]

The coming of the Lord Savior is prophesied, the one who, coming upon the earth, would say: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)—that is, we are one light, just as we are one name.

Through the unity of light and name both are one; indeed, the Trinity is one in the unity of substance, but with the distinction of each person. “Trinity” signifies the distinction of persons; “unity” signifies power.

The words may also be referred to the Father: “For with you is the fountain of life”—that is, in you, from whom life proceeded, the Word was and always was, because he was with you. All things were made through him and in him; he is the life of all things, and he manifested you to us so that human hearts might be enlightened to know your majesty.

### 23

“Extend your mercy to those who know you.” A privilege is extended so that those may deserve mercy whose merit of knowledge supports them.

Accordingly, even among persons of lesser standing we recognize the support of the pursuit of knowledge in what follows, when the Lord says: “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me” (Psalm 86:4)—that is, I shall remember that prostitute Rahab and that Babylon among those who know me, or in the midst of them, because that prostitute acknowledged me, whom the people did not acknowledge.

[Note: The Regius, Remigius, Longobardian, Valcavian, and Thuan manuscripts read: “whom the people did not acknowledge, so that she might be chosen. Among them …”]

Among those, therefore, who knew me, Rahab will be remembered, so that she may obtain the reward worthy of faith. Hence we also observe that it was said in the Gospel: “Prostitutes and tax collectors will go before you into the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 21:31).

But because we are weak in carrying this out, although devoted in believing, extend your mercy to those who believe in you, so that our deeds also may correspond to our devotion and faith. Let the weakness of this body not abandon the purpose of our mind; rather, let us glory amid the very temptations and weaknesses in which the Apostle gloried when he said: “Therefore I will most gladly glory in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (1 Corinthians 12:9).

### 24

He therefore most beautifully added: “Let not the foot of pride come upon me, and let not the hand of sinners move me. There the workers of iniquity have fallen; they have been driven out and have not been able to stand.”

Some above understand “the torrent of your delight” as strength in temptations, such as that of the martyrs, among whom it pleased God to display the pleasure of a sweet and acceptable contest.

For if winters are understood as temptations—hence the Lord warns us to pray that our flight may not occur in winter or on the Sabbath, that is, either in temptation or in idleness (Matthew 24:20)—then in winter the torrent grows, is filled, and swells. The torrent, therefore, may be understood as a more severe temptation, such as occurs in persecutions.

Hence it is rightly called “the torrent of delight,” because where the sin of persecution abounded, the grace of confession also abounded.

### 25

Observe the power of the Prophet’s distinctions. First he described the unrighteous person who, whether in his heart or in his speech, says that he sins against himself or brings sin upon himself. The Greek manuscript has *ἐν ἑαυτῷ* (*en heautō*), that is, “in himself,” though not all manuscripts do.

Perhaps this is because “the fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 13:1). The unrighteous person might therefore say it within himself and sin within himself, although openly to deny God is the act of a madman; yet many openly profess injustice as though it were praise.

For many consider it glorious to seize, to harm even those who have not harmed them, and to deceive. First, therefore, he described the life of the unrighteous; afterward he added the mystery of divine knowledge, so that, fearing God, we might avoid iniquity and injustice.

He added a prayer, asking that God deign to free his righteous people from the company of the unrighteous, so that divine righteousness might also extend over those who are pure in heart, like a benevolent watchman, lest the assault of sins, like that of enemies, creep upon us and seize us while we sleep.

Therefore we must keep watch; the Lord’s camp must always be fortified, because the enemy and adversary comes by night, when the senses are held by sleep and the body is distended with food. We must pray that God’s righteousness may extend over us and make us stronger while we are placed in weakness, so that each of us may say: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10).

### 26

Next, he also prays specifically for himself, to teach us how we ought to pray to the Lord: “Let not the foot of pride come upon me,” he says—that is, “let me not fall into pride.” Elsewhere he likewise speaks of himself, saying: “If I have not walked in great things” (Psalm 130:1).

Here he prayed; there he fulfilled. He would not have fulfilled it unless he had prayed.

Pride must be avoided, for it overthrows even in prosperity. Thus Adam fell more grievously in paradise than he would have fallen upon the earth. To fall from the highest places is a precipice; upon level ground it is called a stumble.

Therefore the proud man’s foot goes astray because he does not keep hold of his head; for “the eyes of the wise are in his head.” It is no wonder, then, if the footstep goes astray where there is no eye. Let the eye go before, so that the foot may follow.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “How, then, would a traveler walking in darkness …”; Remigius, Longobardian, Valcavian, and Thuan read: “How, then, if a traveler were walking in darkness …” This is not bad; nevertheless the printed edition and other manuscripts read better.]

For how could a traveler walk in darkness? The foot quickly stumbles at night if the moon, as it were the eye of the world, does not show the way. You too are in the night of this age; let the Church show you the way. Let the sun of righteousness illumine you from above, so that you cannot fear falling.

### 27

Because he had mentioned the foot of pride, he added: “And let not the hand of sinners move me.” For just as the saints are members of Christ, so the wicked are members of the devil.

“Let not the hand of sinners move me”—that is, let not the deeds of those who sin move me from my position in righteousness. Often, when we see sinners abounding in prosperous successes, we waver in our feelings and are, as it were, torn away from the root of virtue by a hand of sinners.

Therefore we must beware lest the hostile hand overthrow those whom the divine hand planted in the house of God.

Yet he speaks beautifully in this way, since he is beaten by persecutors. Those who are moved from their root, to which they had already clung in Christ, fall.

### 28

Hence he added: “There have fallen those who work iniquity.”

What does “there” mean? Does it mean where pride is, where the hand of sinners is? Or does it mean where they stood, where they had previously been planted—there they fell? Or does it mean nearby, immediately, as though at that very time and in that very place? The meaning seems ambiguous.

But elsewhere we are taught what “there” means, where it says: “There were pains like those of a woman in labor” (Psalm 47:6).

[Note: The Thuan manuscript reads: “Good is the pain, and good is the way of birth”; four others have this reading, though in them the word “good” is lacking.]

Good is the pain for the one whose birth is faith, through which Christ is formed and born in the Church.

Elsewhere he says: “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me.” Indeed, “the foreigners, Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians—these were there” (Psalm 86:4)—that is, where those who know me were, where the foundations are in the holy mountains, there too were the foreigners, because they also believed that one must believe in me.

There, therefore, they fell where they ought rather to have stood. Adam fell in paradise, and Christ came for ruin and for resurrection, so that ruin might be the lot of the faithless, but resurrection the lot of the righteous and faithful.

### 29

Finally, “they were driven out,” because unrighteous men could not stand in the holy place. Hence the Apostle said: “And let the one who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). He said this, of course, to one who stood not bodily but by faith.

We can also understand “there” as referring to the future, as in: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 13:42), and: “Naked shall I go there” (Job 1:21).

[Note: The Thuan manuscript reads: “Although briefly at the end, and as though in conclusion”; four others read: “as though a conclusion.”]

How brief the ending, and how comprehensive the conclusion! “Let me not be proud,” he says, “so that I may not sin; let me not sin, so that I may not be moved; let me not be moved, so that I may not fall; let me not fall, so that I may not be driven out, as Adam was driven out of paradise,” because in that place the foot of pride could not stand at the beginning.

Pride does not know how to stand; and if it falls, it does not know how to rise again.

Therefore this same prophet spoke beautifully earlier about the proud: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we shall glory in the name of our God” (Psalm 19:8). The one is stable; the other untrustworthy.

And he added: “They were bound and fell, but we have risen and stand upright” (ibid., 9).

In the book of the prophet Micah it is also written:

[Note: The old edition reads: “Do not rejoice proudly over me”; the Roman edition: “Do not rejoice over me”; the Septuagint translator: *Μὴ ἐπίχαιρέ μοι* (“Do not rejoice over me”); the manuscripts, however, read as in the text.]

“Do not rejoice proudly over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall rise again” (Micah 7:8).

For we have fallen in this world, but in Christ we have risen. To him be honor, glory, power, and perpetuity, from the ages, and now and always, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# Exposition of Psalm 36

## Preface

### 1

All divine Scripture is either natural, mystical, or moral.

It is natural in Genesis, where it explains how heaven, the seas, and the earth were made, and how this world was established.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “In Genesis, concerning the making of creatures, in which …”; four others read: “In Genesis, concerning the formation of creation, in which …” But since this is found neither in the other manuscripts nor in the printed edition, it has the appearance of a gloss.]

It is mystical in Leviticus, in which the priestly mystery is contained.

It is moral in Deuteronomy, in which human life is formed according to the commandment of the Law.

[Note: The manuscripts of Victorinus and Colbertinus read: “In which, according to the Law, the rule of human life is formed.”]

Hence, from among many books, three books of Solomon seem to have been selected: Ecclesiastes for natural matters, the Song of Songs for mystical matters, and Proverbs for moral matters.

### 2

But because the whole body of the Psalms is one, nothing in them is divided or separated; rather, as the subject required, no discipline of this kind of teaching has been omitted.

For the Psalms most clearly contain natural teaching when they speak of angels and powers, of the sun, moon, and stars, of the light of the heaven of heavens, and of the water that is above the heavens: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. He established them forever and ever; he gave a commandment, and it shall not pass away” (Psalms 32:9 and 148:6).

They also speak of mystical matters when they write of hidden things, the oil of sacred anointing, and the completion of the Tabernacle (Psalms 88:21 and 45:5). Their grace is manifold, since the Lord spoke to the prophets in many ways and by many means.

For they foretold that the Son of God, the chief priest, would come, suffer for us, and cleanse our sins by his blood. The titles “For the winepresses” (Psalm 8 and others) declared this; and the psalm of resurrection expressed that he would rise again (Psalm 65), while another title later indicated that his land had been restored (Psalm 96), together with the future transformation of all things through the mysteries of faith.

[Note: The manuscripts mentioned immediately above add: “and also the future transformation of all things, the mysteries of faith.”]

The Psalms also wove together many moral teachings, displayed various kinds of virtues, and gave rules for living by which they healed the wounds of our errors, renewed human conduct, and changed the deepest affections.

Thus teaches the thirty-third psalm, which Saint Peter also attached to our hearts as a medicine in his letter (1 Peter 3:11), as well as this psalm that has been set before us in today’s reading.

For these psalms are found to be ethical above all others; but this one, entitled the thirty-sixth, is more expansive.

Although the other is exceedingly sweet and clear, this one is sweeter.

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “and clear; nevertheless this one is much more so, because …”]

The former taught me to restrain my tongue from evil; this one teaches me to cease from anger and to abandon indignation. The former commanded me to speak without deceit; this one teaches gentleness and shows the rewards of gentleness.

What greater remedies are there for the human heart than gentleness and simplicity? Through them every pain caused by an injury received is relieved, and every stain of guilt is excluded.

3. Let us therefore apply our hand to these medicines, so that we may cure our wounds; otherwise, if we should wish to say that we can cure others, it may be said to us: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:23). Accordingly, just as it is common not only among physicians but also among ordinary people that, although few profess medicine, many nevertheless claim to know some of its remedies—or just as the children of physicians do—we too should offer a remedy to those in need from another’s medicine. Let the rich employ a teacher; let the poor employ an attendant. Whoever grasps the heights of perfection should draw from the source itself; whoever desires easier paths should feed in the valley, like a little one. Whoever fears the river should drink from the stream; and whoever dreads the deep should swim out to the shore.

**Note:** [Col. 0967D] Five manuscripts read: “drinks; and he who thought it deep swims along the shores.”

Beautifully, then, holy David described the life of the wicked in the preceding psalm (Psalm 35), and here that of the righteous: there the wicked is exposed, here the righteous is instructed; the former sins against himself, the latter even removes the sins of others. Let us therefore consider that justice is the first medicine.

## EXPOSITION

### 4. (Verse 1)

**Note:** [Col. 0967D] The Roman edition alone reads: “Do not provoke emulation among evildoers. Let us first learn what it is to provoke emulation.” The words that follow do indeed seem to require this reading; but, on the authority of the manuscripts and the old edition, we reproduce the received wording. Whoever wishes to know the variant readings of this verse [Col. 0968D] should consult Nobilius, where he will find expositions both by other Fathers and by Ambrose himself.

“Do not provoke emulation among evildoers,” he says, “and do not emulate those who commit iniquity.”

First, let us learn what it means to emulate, although this expression has less force in Latin than in Greek. For we read of emulation both in a good sense and in a bad one. Thus the Apostle says: “It is good always to be emulated in what is good” (Galatians 4:18). Above he himself also said: “They emulate you, but not well; rather, they wish to exclude you, so that you may emulate them” (ibid., 17). Again he says: “Emulate the better gifts” (1 Corinthians 12:31). And in Romans we read: “I ask, then: Have they stumbled so as to fall? By no means; but their offense is salvation for the Gentiles, so that they may emulate them” (Romans 11:11). And below: “For I say to you Gentiles: Insofar as I am the Apostle of the Gentiles, I will glorify my ministry, if somehow I may emulate my flesh and save some of them” (ibid., 13)—that is, affect my own flesh. Indeed, the Greek has *παραζηλώσω* (*parazēlōsō*).

Here too it has: “μὴ παραζήλου ἐν πονηρευομένοις” (*mē parazēlou en ponēreuomenois*), “do not stir up the wicked to emulation”; and “μηδὲ ζήλου τοὺς ποιοῦντας τὴν ἀνομίαν” (*mēde zēlou tous poiountas tēn anomian*), “nor emulate those who commit lawlessness.” That is: do not provoke the wicked to emulation, because they contend not for what is good but for what is evil.

### 5.

What does it mean to stir someone to emulation? Let us explain by an example, if we can. There are certain unrestrained women who trouble the hearts of other women’s husbands. After subjecting these men to their own intimacy and disgrace, they are not content to keep their error secret; rather, they strive to flaunt their shame before the men’s wives, so as to provoke and inflame them to jealousy, seeking a kind of triumph from the pain of wounded minds and their agitation.

Those wives, unable to endure the insult to their own marriage bed caused by this feminine emulation, either break the bonds of the marriage they had gladly entered or contend in daily quarrels.

**Note:** [Col. 0968D] Thus read the old and Roman editions. The Victorine and Colbertine manuscripts, with the old edition in the margin, read: “or contend in everyday life.” Many others read: “or decide matters of everyday life.”

Thus from emulation comes discord, from dissension comes division, and the whole household is thrown into disorder.

From the example of the shameless woman, therefore, understand what you are reading: it is the part of the most wicked and detestable cunning to disturb another’s soul by evil emulation. Jealousy is one thing, and provoked jealousy (*parazelus*) another.

For this is the perverse emulation that enters the disposition of good people. By it the Jew also went astray: he turned aside from the true and good path of evangelical discipline through a misguided emulation of the Law, as the Apostle says of himself (Philippians 3:6), that according to emulation of the Law he persecuted the Church of Christ.

**Note:** Earlier and Roman editions, together with the Vatican, Colbertine, and Victorine manuscripts, read: “who turned aside from the true and good path of evangelical discipline through a misguided emulation of the Law.” Certain Paris manuscripts, together with the Regius, read: “. . . having strayed from the discipline, through the Law,” etc. We think the reading followed here is best supported by four other manuscripts.

### 6.

Therefore, although our God was frequently offended by the thankless feelings and complaints of the Jews, he nevertheless did not abandon the people he had once taken up and chosen for himself. But the Synagogue, like a brazen prostitute, began to provoke him to the bitterness of emulation by involving itself in sacrilegious transgressions.

Thus she said to the priest Aaron: “Make us gods whom we may worship” (Exodus 32:1), and they began to worship the head of a calf. Hence, through the great song of Moses, the Lord resounded in Moses’ mouth, saying: “They have stirred me to emulation with what is not God; they have provoked me with their idols. But I will stir them to emulation with what is not a people; with a foolish nation I will provoke them” (Deuteronomy 32:21).

See how the Lord condemned the harlot-like conduct of the Synagogue, so that he might turn their own cunning back upon them. Those who had rejected the Lord their God, from whom they had been adopted, through grave sacrileges, choosing gods for themselves to worship, would suffer through their own ingenuity. In return, he took for himself a Church from among the profane—a Church which the Jewish people would grieve to see preferred to them, without the Law and without the grace granted to the Jews. Their feeling of emulation would be aroused all the more because a more contemptible people had been chosen.

Previously that people had had no one against whom to feel such agitation, since they considered themselves alone to have been chosen by the Lord. But when it recognized that a foreign people gathered from the nations had been added, claiming for itself the Lord’s Law, the oracles of the prophets, and the Lord’s New Testament, then at last it began to be tormented by excessive feeling, after it learned that it had been rejected.

Thus, if it sees the ceremonies of the Gentiles, it is not moved; but if it hears of the Church’s progress, the miserable thing is tormented and twisted by envy. Therefore what is written concerning Judea is fulfilled: “And I will stir them to emulation with what is not a people.”

**Note:** Some manuscripts read: “it turned its attention to the knowledge of God and to a people suitable to him.”

### 7.

What adds to the misery of its more grievous torment is that sinners from the Gentiles seem to have been preferred to it—people who do not even raise up the name of a particular race or nation. Every community ordinarily claims the name of its region: Egyptians, Ethiopians, Syrians, Jews, and Arabs bear the designation of their province and lands. But we, gathered from different peoples, cannot claim for ourselves the name of a single race. Therefore, because we had no name on earth, we received one from heaven, so that we might be called the people of Christ.

The Gentile considers this foolishness; the Jew considers it a disgrace. It is true, therefore, that God avenged his own insult by seeking for himself a Church from what was not a people and by preferring it to that ancient and royal people from a foolish nation.

Hear who this foolish nation is that was preferred: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Corinthians 1:27). And again: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise” (1 Corinthians 3:18).

The Lord therefore restored, rather than introduced, a sharing in emulation, so that it would exist not as a form of imitation but as the punishment of iniquity.

### 8.

Thus the Latin translator, wishing to distinguish between emulation of virtue and emulation arising from offense, says: “Do we provoke the Lord to emulation?” (1 Corinthians 10:20). That is: Do we bring upon the Lord the offense of emulation by eating what has been sacrificed to idols, as the Jews did when they provoked him by sacrificing to idols?

If, then, among human beings the intention of provoking emulation is offensive, and the person who has been provoked is frequently found to be the superior, since what incites emulation is usually a source of harm, what folly it is to provoke the divine majesty and assail it with the offense of emulation, when there is no difficulty in its vengeance?

**Note:** The Roman edition reads: “and the person who has been provoked is found to be the instigator of emulation,” etc. Other editions read: “is found to be the inciter of emulation.” All the manuscripts read: “. . . which is the incitement,” etc. We think that *incentoria*, meaning a cause that incites something, was in use at that time; in any event, the word *quod* seems entirely necessary to the construction.

### 9.

We must not, therefore, supply the wicked with the goads of emulation against us. Even when they have not been provoked, they are stirred by the spurs of envy so as to do harm, as Cain killed his brother because Abel’s sacrifice was more acceptable than what Cain himself had thought fit to offer.

Abel did not emulate Cain; rather, the envious Cain pursued the grace of precedence through criminal fratricide. Abel did not wish to overshadow his brother’s sacrifice, but to preserve the discipline of sacrifice, so that negligence would not delay the first fruits and no misappropriation for personal use would violate them.

Saul likewise tried to ambush David, the triumphant conqueror of the Philistines, the prophet, and the preserver of his own life. Because the young women’s song placed David above him, he prepared to kill him by hurling a spear. He nearly shed the blood of his innocent son-in-law, unless David had eluded the wound by bending his body aside.

**Note:** Certain Paris editions read: “unless the wound of the emulated body”; the Regius and Thuaneus read: “unless the wound of the feigned body,” etc. Perhaps they thought that the holy Doctor was alluding to the wooden effigy which Michal is said to have placed in David’s bed in his stead. But the reading of the Gillian and other manuscripts is plainly preferable, as is shown both by the preceding and following words.

What wickedness was there in the women’s saying, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands” (1 Samuel 18:7)? How savage was the envy of King Saul, who turned an error of speech toward the destruction of an innocent man!

### 10.

“And do not emulate those who commit iniquity,” he says. He did not repeat what he had said, but changed the expression: to provoke emulation is one thing, and to emulate is another. Provocation to emulation involves cunning; emulation itself involves simplicity.

Yet even this simplicity must be cautious and prudent, so that it knows what must be avoided. For it was not said without reason: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew 10:16).

The wisdom, therefore, must be spiritual—preserving salvation and knowing no deceit. The simplicity must also be spiritual.

Scripture seems to have made the same distinction concerning provoked emulation in another passage, when it says: “The jealousy of Ephraim will be removed, and the enemies of Judah will perish. Ephraim will not be jealous of Judah, and Judah will not trouble Ephraim” (Isaiah 11:13).

Elsewhere we read: “Since you are emulators of spiritual gifts for the building up of the Church, seek that you may abound” (1 Corinthians 14:12). He uses *emulators* for those who pursue good things and imitate what is good, but *emulator* in the other sense for one who is crooked and envious.

### 11. (Verse 2)

The first point, then, is not to provoke the wicked to wicked emulation; the second is not to emulate those who commit iniquity.

For very often, when the godly see that certain people have sought wealth through fraud and cunning and have attained honors, they eagerly follow their ways through a shameful emulation, so that they may reach wealth and honors by similar means—or may deceive young women when contracting marriage.

What benefit is there in this, when wealth itself and all secular glory quickly wither like grass and perish like the herbs of the field in the very appearance of their bloom? “All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass.”

Do not therefore desire too eagerly what cannot be everlasting. Do not be envious or crooked; do not be contentious or a quarrelsome rival in jealousy.

Hence Aquila said: “Do not contend with those who act wickedly.” Symmachus: “Do not contend.”

Do not be an imitator of iniquity and fraud either. Instead, imitate apostolic teaching, prophetic grace, and the virtue of the saints, so that you may bear fruit and store up a harvest of goodness, like Joseph, who excluded the famine of prolonged barrenness by the abundance of grain; or like Habakkuk, who, bringing a meal to the harvesters, was lifted up by an angel and traversed the path through the air, then, returned to earth, provided a sweet banquet for the pious prophet amid the fierce roaring of lions.

### 12. (Verse 3)

The Prophet therefore rightly says: “Hope in the Lord, do good; inhabit the land, and you will feed on its riches.”

What land does he urge us to inhabit, if not your soul, which you ought to cultivate well, frequently plowing it with spiritual plowshares, lest it become rough through prolonged neglect?

A good farmer works his field every day with vigilant care and guards his own fields, lest the boar from the forest devastate them or a robber snatch away the ripened fruits. Plow your land, then, so that when the one who sows the word comes, he may find your soul prepared; lest the seed fall upon the uncultivated ground of your heart, and the birds of heaven come and snatch away what has been sown.

Hear, then, what the land is: “Behold, the sower went out to sow his field. And as he sowed, some fell beside the road, some upon the rock, and some upon good soil . . .” (Luke 8:5 and following). Those upon the good soil are “the ones who, hearing the word in a good heart, retain it and bear fruit through patience” (ibid., 15).

Let your heart therefore be clean; let your soul be clean, so that you may bear the fruit of goodness—that is, of spiritual grace. For goodness is a fruit of the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22).

These are the fruits whose riches feed us and whose abundance satisfies us. In this land righteous Noah planted that fruitful vine, drank from its fruit, and was released in his inmost heart, when his posterity, doubled in number, clothed him with the honorable garment of piety.

In another passage the holy Prophet also displayed to us these riches, in which he was rich in Christ and abounded in everything conducive to eternal life. And truly, who is richer than the one who is rich in the Lord, so that he can say: “I have delighted in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches” (Psalm 118:14)?

What could be lacking to a man who was enriched by heavenly oracles? Therefore, in this psalm he urges us to seek that eternal treasure for ourselves and to take delight in acquiring it.

### 13. (Verse 4)

And so he says: “Delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the requests of your heart.”

Why did he not say “your requests,” but “the requests of your heart”? For the requests of the outward and inward man are not the same, and not all are approved by Christ, because the law of the flesh frequently struggles against the law of the mind.

But the requests belonging to the inward man, who has been renewed by the Spirit, the Lord grants to the petitioner in their fulfillment. Hence he says elsewhere: “May the Lord grant you according to your heart, and fulfill all your requests” (Psalm 19:5).

He says “according to your heart,” not according to the desire of the flesh; and he says that he will fulfill those requests that proceed from the inmost heart, not those directed by the allurements and pleasures of this flesh.

**Note:** All editions, together with certain manuscripts, read: “But of your heart? The requests . . . are common.” We preferred the reading of five other manuscripts because it seemed more suitable to the sense and context and also closer to Origen’s interpretation, whom Ambrose imitates extensively in his exposition of the Psalms. See Origen, *Homily 1 on this Psalm*.

### 14. (Verses 5–6)

“Reveal your way to the Lord, hope in him, and he will act. And he will bring forth your righteousness like the light, and your judgment like midday.”

By this single verse he has declared what kind of person you ought to be. For who reveals his way except the one who confesses the secrets within his breast to God, the judge of hidden things?

He says well, “Reveal”—that is, open your conscience, lest the shadow of this age or of the flesh weigh it down. For seeds that sprout forth, if they are shaded, become thin; when exposed to the sun, they grow rich. Why do I speak of seeds? Even young trees are killed by the woodland shade before they can rise upward, and it prevents them from spreading their branching limbs.

Beautifully he said: “Reveal your way to the Lord,” because human nature, inclined toward sin, places something like a veil over our mind, lest we confess our sins to the Lord, who can heal our wounds. A person is ashamed to ask for medicine with his own mouth, lest his disgrace be exposed before human beings.

Conscience therefore presses inward within a person, although it cannot remain hidden. It delays until the wound boils over, so that it is exposed not by the healing power of faith but by the incurable severity of the ulcer.

“Reveal,” he says, “your way to the Lord”; that is, open your way, do not hide it, as Cain hid himself, wishing to remain concealed. For everyone who does evil hates the light.

David revealed his way when he said: “I have spoken of my works to the King” (Psalm 44:2). Open your understanding, so that there may be nothing you fear being reproached for.

Paul also revealed his way when he dared to say: “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Corinthians 4:4). Let your conduct and life be such that your way shines before your Father who is in heaven.

### 15.

But because every human condition is subject to frailty, and it is not in our power to direct our course according to our own will, he says to you: “Hope in the Lord, and he will act.” That is, he will open your way and will not permit you to be such that you flee the light while fearing exposure and love darkness so that you can conceal your crimes, saying: “Darkness covers me; who knows whether the Most High sees?” (Sirach 23:6).

For how can someone planning adultery fail to seek the night as suitable for his attempts? How can someone thinking up a false witness for his fraud, or seeking to corrupt a judge in order to oppress an innocent person, fail to explore the hiding place of iniquity?

**Note:** The Roman edition in the text and the old edition in the margin, together with several written manuscripts, read: “The robber lies in wait in lonely places.” The same old edition in the text and the Colbertine and Victorine manuscripts read as we have in the text: “The robber crouches in solitude.” Again, the old edition in the body and the Roman edition, together with the Thuaneus and Vatican manuscripts, read: “He is covered by the darkness of night.” The old edition in the margin and the Regius, Colbertine, and Victorine manuscripts read: “He awaits the darkness of night.”

The robber crouches in solitude; he awaits the darkness of night, so that his crime may succeed. Iniquity, then, is darkness; God is light.

And if you wish to conceal your righteousness, God will bring it forth into the light. He does not permit the judgment to remain hidden by which you chose what is good and rejected what is wicked.

He not only makes your judgment shine; he makes it shine like midday. When the sun pours itself out wholly in splendor, it is midday. It was midday when Joseph feasted with his brothers, not avenging the injury but forgetting it.

### 16. (Verse 7)

“Be subject to the Lord and entreat him.”

You are not merely warned to be subject to God; you are also told to entreat the Lord, so that you may fulfill the devotion of your subjection, just as he said above: “Reveal your way to the Lord and hope in him.”

**Note:** The Vatican and five Gallican manuscripts prefer this reading. Other manuscripts and all the editions read: “Just as above he not only says, ‘Reveal,’” etc.

It is not enough for you to reveal your way; you must also hope in the Lord. Subjection is good—not degraded or contemptible, but glorious and exalted. For the one who does the Lord’s will is subject to God.

Who does not know that the wisdom of the mind is superior to the wisdom of the flesh? The wisdom of the mind is subject to God’s law; the wisdom of the flesh is not subject. The Apostle added: “For it cannot be” (Romans 8:7).

Be subject, then—that is, be near to Christ—so that you may fulfill the Law. Christ fulfilled the Law by doing the Father’s will. Therefore he is the end of the Law and the fullness of love, because, loving the Father, he devoted all his affection to his will.

Hence the Apostle said concerning glory: “When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28).

He also says of himself: “Is not my soul subject to God? For from him comes my salvation” (Psalm 61:2).

He was subject to his parents, Joseph and Mary, out of piety, not weakness. The greatest glory of Christ is that he pours himself into the hearts of all human beings and recalls them all from the impiety of unbelief and the affection for paganism, so that he may make them subject to himself.

When he has subjected all things to himself, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and all Israel has been saved, and when throughout the whole world there has become one body in Christ, then he himself will also be subject, offering his gift to God the Father, as though he were the chief of all priests, and offering his body upon the heavenly altars, so that the faith of all may be a sacrifice.

**Note:** All editions and some manuscripts read: “composed upon the altars.” Many others read: “the body upon the altars.” This is appropriate, since nothing else is being declared here except that Christ will fulfill the role both of priest and of victim.

This subjection, then, belongs to piety: the Lord Jesus will be subject in the body, of which we are the body and members.

Be subject, then, as a human being to Christ—that is, subject to the wisdom of God, subject to the Word, subject to righteousness, subject to virtue, because Christ is all these things.

Let every human being subject himself to God. For he teaches not one person but all to subject their heart, subject their soul, and subject their flesh, so that God may be all in all.

The one who is full of grace and receives Christ’s yoke is subject, and he vigorously and without hesitation carries out the Lord’s commandments. Without subjection, however, is the one who vainly exalts himself, puffed up by the perception of his own flesh, arrogant in devotion, and avoiding the observance of pious service, which by the very law of nature we owe to the eternal Author.

Finally, the one who is without sin is subject to Christ, because he has been redeemed by the Lord. But the one who is in sin cannot be called free; he is a slave, held by the heavy chains of sin.

### 17. (Verse 7)

It follows: “Do not emulate the one who prospers in his way while committing iniquity.”

Here he clearly indicates what he meant above: that the wicked are not to be provoked to wickedness by emulation, nor those who commit iniquity to be imitated.

For it is not iniquity itself but the prosperity that comes to those who act wickedly that often troubles us, so that we think they should be imitated in order that we too may attain their success. We say: “Behold, these are sinners, yet they abound in this age and have obtained riches.” And I said: “Then in vain have I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent; and I have been scourged all day” (Psalm 72:12 and following).

If David was scourged, we must take care lest we too be scourged, and lest it be said to us that riches, honors, and powers seem to have been allotted to this generation as though they were the random and uncertain products of money and the profits of iniquity, not any rewards of virtue. Therefore they come like a dream, and with the dream they fail when you arise.

Athletes are certainly crowned after they have won, not before they win. Our struggle is with the age. Conquer the world first, so that you may seek the crown. No one is crowned before completing the contest.

Do those who run in the stadium receive the prize before they have completed the race? How many fall near the finish and are cheated of their course by the very speed of their running?

Are you more pleasing to God than Paul? He was a chosen vessel, a teacher of the Gentiles, yet he never dared to demand a crown for himself in this age. Hear him say: “I have fought the good fight; I have completed the course; I have kept the faith. What remains is the crown of righteousness laid up for me, which the Lord will render to me on that day” (2 Timothy 4:7–8).

That Paul, who was caught up into the third heaven and heard secret things that it is not lawful for a human being to speak—whether he was caught up in the body or outside the body, he does not know, as he himself testifies (2 Corinthians 12:2)—Paul says that the crown will be rendered to him on that day. Do you insist that it be rendered to you here?

Complete, then, the time of your contest. An athlete does not wrestle only once, nor does a soldier fight only once in order to complete his service. Nor is your struggle with only one passion.

### 18. (Verse 8)

If you escape the earlier passions, anger follows. Therefore Scripture says to you: “Cease from anger and abandon indignation.”

There are many vices that creep upon the foolish. Anger is a grave passion. It often inflames a person against his will and drags one who wishes to take milder vengeance into a frenzy, so that he destroys the person he thought should be punished.

In agitation, he often pierces an innocent person with a sword. Many have killed friends and brothers through indignation. Therefore the Wise Man says: “Anger destroys even the wise” (Proverbs 15:1). This is Solomon’s saying: anger destroys not only ordinary human beings but even the wise themselves.

David, the wise man, gives this warning: “Cease from anger,” lest, when you have inflamed it, it fail to cease before its flame consumes you.

“Abandon,” he says, “indignation.” That is: nature seizes you, emotion moves you, someone’s fault or injury excites you so that you become indignant; but do not go all the way to the point of losing all restraint. Abandon it; put an end to it, lest it drag you into sin.

This is what he said above: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Psalm 4:5). He does not encourage you to become angry; rather, he yields for a time to the emotion, but he supplies a medicine so that the force of the wound may not spread farther.

“Be angry,” he says, refers to your passion. A physician does not immediately apply medicine to an illness. If pain is burning, he applies soothing remedies so that the pain may subside; if fever is raging, he waits for the proper time for treatment and ordinarily withholds drink from those who thirst.

He does not say, “Do not have a fever,” when the sick person is burning with heat; rather, he says, “Wait; let the fever cease, let the agitation be digested.”

So too the Prophet could not say to a person whose flesh is stirred by various passions of agitation just as by various diseases, “Do not become angry.” Instead he says: “Cease from anger and abandon indignation, lest you sin.” For anger is a severe teacher of sin.

Another physician also says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians 4:26), lest, while you delay for a long time, the one who customarily rouses a heated body from sleep should come, prod you, implant thoughts in you, and plunge into the secret places of your heart, saying:

“Take revenge for your injury. Recognize that you are a man. It is the weakness of a woman not to take revenge. A servant should have despised you, a brother deceived you, a friend mocked you—and you still do not avenge your insult? You must proscribe him; you must rise against him with the sword; you must settle your pain by the death of your adversary. He was a man who killed his enemy; he is rightly praised, because he avenged himself in such a way that another, hearing of it, would not dare to inflict an injury upon him.”

**Note:** This is the reading of the Vatican and nearly all the Gallican manuscripts; some manuscripts and editions, however, read: “so that no other person would dare inflict an injury upon him.”

By these goads anger is kindled more intensely and becomes more agitated, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Anger destroys even the wise.”

### 19. (Verse 9)

Therefore do not listen to him, lest you emulate him and act wickedly. For “those who act wickedly will be exterminated.”

Those who have no roots are exterminated, like vegetables or grass. Let the weak person eat vegetables; but you, plant a vine in your field and establish a vineyard.

And if Ahab comes and says to you, “Give me your vineyard, so that I may plant vegetables for myself” (1 Kings 21:2), do not consent to him, lest, with your consent, he sow what is perishable and cut away what is eternal.

Therefore Naboth is counted among the saints, because he thought that the inheritance of his ancestors should not be surrendered even to a king. He preferred to be stoned rather than give his vineyard over to plunder.

The inheritance of the ancestors is the true faith. There arose Arians supported by royal power, who thought that the temple of the Lord should be handed over to them, threatening harsh punishments. But far be it from a mind devoted to the Lord that fear of punishment should outweigh the form of piety. Unbelief did not prevail, because faith resisted.

There is also a certain vineyard in the breasts of the faithful, of which Isaiah says: “A vineyard was made for the beloved on a fertile hill” (Isaiah 5:1). The Lord planted this vineyard in our hearts. Therefore we read God saying: “I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true” (Jeremiah 2:21).

Let no one, then, remove this vine from the field of our soul, for that vine is blessed. Hence it was said concerning the saints: “They have been multiplied by the fruit of grain, wine, and oil” (Psalm 4:8).

It is good, then, to have within you winepresses overflowing with wine, so that wine may flow for you into your vessel from the vine of Sorek—that splendid cup which intoxicates! For Sorek is the vine of a new beginning and a new righteousness.

**Note:** Some manuscripts, together with the editions, read: “The righteousness of a new beginning is new”; others, as in our text, read “and of a new righteousness,” except that the Thuaneus alone has the conjunction *and*. Again, the Victorine and Colbertine manuscripts, together with the same editions, read: “A new song, magnify the name,” etc. The Vatican and several Gallican manuscripts read: “A new song, its beginning; magnify the name,” etc., agreeing with the Septuagint, where one reads: “Sing to the Lord a new song; its beginning: glorify [or magnify] his name,” etc.

Hence it is also said to us: “Sing to your Lord a new song; its beginning: magnify his name from the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 42:10).

Let this vineyard therefore produce grapes, not iniquity. For this reason the vineyard of the Jews was abandoned: it produced iniquity, as it is written (Isaiah 5:7), and not justice.

Let us therefore bear fruit in Christ, so that we may deserve to be everlasting.

### 20.

“For those who await the Lord will possess the land”—that land, namely, of the living.

There is a heavenly land that bears fruit for heavenly beings, of which he says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26:13).

This earthly land supplies food to the belly through much human labor; that good land of the Lord bears fruit without any toil. In it there is the lasting possession of the righteous and the inheritance of the devout mind.

And he says well: “Those who await the Lord will possess the land as an inheritance.” For this is the land that does not pass away. Heaven and earth will pass away, but the words of the Lord will not pass away.

Therefore neither can that intelligible land of paradise pass away, in which are those who preserve the Lord’s words. Adam was placed in this land so that he might receive the fruit of eternal life. But because he did not wish to preserve the Lord’s words, he did not deserve to remain in the possession he had received.

**Note:** The old edition in the margin and seven Gallican manuscripts read: “because he was unable to preserve the Lord’s words.” If this reading is accepted, “was unable” must be taken in a broad sense, as when we commonly say that someone was unable to do something he in fact did not do, whether or not he possessed the actual possibility of doing it—as the philosophers would say.

But the one who keeps the Lord’s words confidently says: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he looked upon me” (Psalm 39:2).

Adam, however, because he did not wait for the Lord—for how could he have waited, when he fled and was afraid to present himself?—therefore the Lord did not deign to look upon him. For “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.”

Yet the Lord did not wish to look upon him so far that he sought him, saying: “Adam, where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). The one who is sought is regarded as absent.

It is faith that presents us to God; unbelief makes the wicked dwell in exile. No one, therefore, is absent from God except the one who has made himself absent.

Hence he says: “Let it be done to you according to your faith” (Matthew 9:29), for “the one who does not know will be unknown.”

Adam, therefore, as a sinner, was unable to preserve his place. Expelled from paradise, he was banished to a fortress so that he might do penance.

**Note:** This is the reading of the editions and six manuscripts, although they read *religatus*, a word that is very often found in manuscripts for *relegatus*. But the Victorine and Colbertine manuscripts and the old edition in the margin prefer: “he was confined in a prison.”

He was given a postponement, so that he might not perish immediately and completely; so that Eve might be saved through the bearing of children, together with the faith of holy Abel, the grace of the prophets, and the posterity of the Church.

### 21. (Verse 10)

But because he did not wish to be redeemed through these things and persisted in sin, the Prophet says of him: “And yet a little while, and the sinner will be no more; you will seek his place, and you will not find it.”

For how can he exist in the future, when the place of sin cannot endure for long?

This is the land that opened its mouth to receive the blood of the innocent. Therefore, in this land there is a place for sinners. But the land passes away; how can the sinner’s place be found?

I think that God ordered the firmament to exist between water and water (Genesis 1:6) for this reason: to separate sins from virtues. The upper water, which praises the Lord, would remain at rest; the lower water would be subject to sin.

Indeed, the former sees God, while the latter does not. The water that is above the heavens sees him; the water that is in the abyss does not.

Hence it was also said: “The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you, and they were afraid; the abysses were troubled, with the multitude of the sound of the waters” (Psalm 76:17).

The abysses are rightly troubled, for above them are misshapen darknesses, and therefore they cannot possess peace. Hence the legion of demons asked to be sent into the abyss and plunged itself with great tumult into the waves (Matthew 8:31), so that it might strangle the herd of pigs it had found.

Sinners, therefore, seek the abyss, where there is the gloom of darkness.

## 22. (Verse 11)

“But the meek shall possess the earth, and shall delight in an abundance of peace.” They rightly possess the earth in whom God himself rests, as the divine oracle resounded through Isaiah, saying: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet one, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).
