Who are the meek except those whom no goad of dissension agitates, whom anger does not disturb, savagery does not exasperate, and a frenzy of cruelty does not inflame? And because, while living in the body, they loved not wine, banquets, or riches, but the Lord’s peace, they shall delight in the abundance of peace in place of that enjoyment of bodily pleasures from which they thought they were being deprived in order to attain eternal grace. Our Lord Jesus bestowed this peace upon the human race in his days, just as the prophecy, which did not lie, declares: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and an abundance of peace, until the moon is lifted up” (Ps. 71:7).

What, then, is the peace by which the people of all the Churches have been multiplied, except that of which the Lord said: “My peace I leave you; my peace I give you” (John 14:27)? He gave peace who stilled the wars of the soul.

## 23. (Verses 12–13)

It continues:

> “The sinner shall watch the just man, and shall gnash his teeth against him. But the Lord shall mock him, because he sees that his day is coming.”

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “The sinner shall lie in wait for the just man,” etc. But the old edition and all the manuscripts read, “He shall watch,” etc. The Septuagint also support this reading; their words are: Παρατηρήσεται ὁ ἁμαρτωλὸς τὸν δίκαιον — “The sinner shall watch the just man.”]

It is characteristic of someone who is indignant and boiling with anger to gnash his teeth.

[Note: The old edition, together with the Victorius and Colbert manuscripts, reads: “But the wicked also have their teeth, with which,” etc. The Roman edition, with others, reads as above.]

But the heart of the wicked also has teeth, which are accustomed not to make a sound but to tear apart. Ambushes, schemes, and wickednesses are the sinner’s teeth. The sinner therefore lies in wait for the just man because he envies him. The life of the just man reproves the sinner, whom it condemns with silent and greater authority than if it spoke with a loud voice.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript and four Gallican manuscripts read: “Whom he condemns more by a silent mouth.”]

But the just man ought not to fear the sinner’s gnashing, because wickedness cannot be perpetual. Ambushes are temporary, whereas the defenses of virtue are eternal. The sinner’s death dissolves all his power and deceit.

## 24. (Verse 14)

He adds further:

> “Behold, sinners have unsheathed the sword; they have stretched their bow, to cast down the poor and needy.”

What is the sinner’s sword except the sword opposed to that of the Holy Spirit? Scripture taught me this sword; the Apostle taught it when he said that we have “the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:14 ff.). Therefore the word of God is the sword of the Holy Spirit. Conversely, the sword of the most wicked spirit is an evil word.

With this sword the Apostle Peter struck Ananias and Sapphira with his utterance, as though with a blade. With this sword Paul deprived Elymas, who opposed him, of the light of his eyes through his arguments and poured over him the night of blindness.

Now consider quarrelsome sinners, uttering bitter insults of arrogance and bringing forth reproaches and accusations. If you hear them, will you not say: “Sinners have unsheathed the sword,” when a shameful word, like a weapon drawn from its sheath, is boldly brought forth from the mouth—a word that ought to have been restrained and put back?

Just as the word of God is called a sword, so the same word can be the sinner’s sword. Likewise, the bow that sinners stretch is their mind, and the arrow they shoot is a poisoned word. For just as Christ is the arrow who is the Word of God, of whom it is said, “I have made you like a chosen arrow” (Isa. 49:2), and who is brought forth from God’s quiver, so the arrows of the faithless are launched from a certain bow of iniquity and wound the unsuspecting innocent unless their fiery darts are driven back by the shield of faith.

Therefore you must be a vigilant soldier in battle, because your struggle is not only against flesh and blood, but also against the spiritual wickednesses themselves, which are unseen. Let weapons strong in God abound for you, so that you may easily draw forth whatever missiles you wish, lest the enemy overpower you, poor and unarmed.

Be strong in God and rich in God, so that it may be said of you: “The redemption of a man is his riches” (Prov. 13:8). Abound in the treasure of wisdom; be rich in word and good works, so that you may be protected. Flee the sinner’s riches, lest he find a place where he can wound you. Be merciful, so that you may remain invulnerable—or so that, if you are wounded, you may be able to heal yourself.

There is also a poor man whom the adversaries wish to wound, one of that number concerning whom the Savior said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3).

## 25. (Verse 15)

“And therefore let the sword of the sinners enter into their own hearts, and let their bow be broken.” Thus, just as peace returns to God’s servants from those who have not received the peace of those who bless, so may the sinners’ wickedness, by which they attempt to harm the just, return upon their own destruction, so that they may be slain by their own weapons and wounds. For often arrows rebound upon those who shot them.

[Note: This passage refers to the battle waged by Theodosius the Great against the tyrant Eugenius and Arbogastes, a battle more celebrated than anything else in all antiquity. Augustine wrote about it in *The City of God*, book 5, chapter 26, and Orosius in *History*, book 7, chapter 35. The pagan poet Claudian also wrote about it in his panegyric on the third consulship of Honorius, whose two verses are reported by the two Fathers mentioned above:

> O greatly beloved of God, for whom heaven wages war,  
> And the conspiring winds come to the trumpets!

After them, ecclesiastical writers vied with one another in celebrating the same victory of Theodosius.]

This also happened in the recent war, when faithless and sacrilegious men attacked someone who trusted in the Lord and attempted to deprive him of his kingdom, threatening the Lord’s Churches with savage persecutions. Suddenly a wind arose that struck the shields from the hands of the faithless and turned all their weapons and missiles back against the sinner’s army.

[Note: “The sinner” means the devil. Ambrose uses this word elsewhere to designate him, and also in the following verse of this psalm, where he writes: “Unless perhaps, because the sinner said,” etc. In these passages the holy man probably had in mind 1 John 3:8: “For the devil sins from the beginning.”]

The enemy had not yet arrived, and already they could not withstand the battles of the winds; they were being brought down by their own darts. Worse still, the wounds to their minds were not less severe than those to their bodies: they were failing in heart when they recognized that God was fighting against them.

They had gone forth provoking others and drawing poisoned darts of faithlessness from the quiver of their hearts against the Christian people; but their impiety returned upon their own heads. In the end, they were themselves undone by their faithlessness, and the Lord dispersed the ambushes they had prepared for the faithful, so that they could not merely fail to harm the devout: they were stripped even of their own supports, and their weapons passed over to the enemy.

How much better if they had not drawn the sword from its sheath—that is, if they had never uttered their impious words! For if each person must give an account for an idle word, how much more will he expiate words of sacrilege with grievous punishments?

## 26

“ You have tested us by fire,” David says (Ps. 16:3). Therefore we shall all be tested by fire.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “And Malachi.” The words quoted here are certainly found not in Ezekiel but in Malachi. Nevertheless, the old edition and all the manuscripts read, “And Ezekiel.” It must therefore be said that the book which Origen wished to have been written by the Angel, and others by Ezra—as Jerome, in the preface to Malachi; Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca sancta*, book 5, annotation 262; and Huet, *Demonstratio evangelica*, proposition 4, “On the Book of Malachi,” numbers 2 and 3, report—was attributed by Ambrose to Ezekiel. Perhaps there was also some manuscript whose authority he followed; for it is scarcely likely that he reproduced this testimony from memory, since it is neither very brief nor so commonplace that there would have been no opportunity for error in naming its author. Yet it should by no means be omitted that our Doctor, in asserting that absolutely all people, even the holiest, will be purified by fire, follows the traces of Adimantus, as Huet correctly observed, *Origen*, book 2, question 11, numbers 2 and 8. Consult that work, as well as the admonition prefixed to these Ambrosian expositions.]

And Ezekiel says:

> “Behold, the Lord Almighty is coming; and who shall endure the day of his coming, or who shall endure when he appears to us? For he himself shall enter like a refiner’s fire and like a launderer’s vat; and he shall sit refining and purifying as gold and silver. And he shall purify the sons of Levi, and shall refine them like gold and silver, and they shall offer sacrifice to the Lord in righteousness” (Mal. 3:2–3).

[Note: The same Roman edition reads, “and like the grass of launderers,” and the Septuagint support this reading in their favor: καὶ ὡς ποιὰ πλυνόντων — “and like the grass of launderers.” But we make no change against the unanimous agreement of the old edition and all the manuscripts.]

Therefore the sons of Levi will be purified by fire, Ezekiel by fire, Daniel by fire. Yet although these will be tested by fire, they will nevertheless say: “We passed through fire and water” (Ps. 65:12).

Others will remain in the fire. For them the fire will shed dew, as it did for the Hebrew boys who were cast into the burning furnace; but the avenging fire will consume the ministers of impiety. Woe to me if my work burns and I suffer the loss of this labor! Even if the Lord saves his servants, we shall be saved through faith, yet saved as through fire. And even if we are not consumed, still we shall be burned.

How some remain in the fire while others pass through it, divine Scripture teaches us elsewhere. The Egyptian people were submerged in the Red Sea (Exod. 14:22 ff.), but the Hebrew people passed through it. Moses passed through; Pharaoh was hurled down, because heavier sins had submerged him. In the same way the sacrilegious will be cast into the lake of burning fire, those who hurled proud insults against God.

Let us therefore follow here the pillar of fire, which illuminates us while we are placed in this body and shows us the way, so that in the future the cloud may cool us at night, and we may be able to lessen the cruel fires.

## 27

But observe what Scripture says: “May the Lord break the sinners’ bow.” He placed his own bow in the cloud so that the floods might cease and tranquility be restored.

[Note: A few manuscripts read: “when the floods had ceased, so that tranquility might be restored.”]

We should therefore believe that the adversary and the evil one stretches out his bow in order to disturb peaceful minds, stir up storms, and arouse blasts of wind. Let us therefore pray that the Lord our God may dissolve the bow of wickedness; that he may be present with his poor and needy servant, who, because of the fear of God, has judged that riches must not be coveted, the estates of the lesser must not be seized, and widows must not be stripped of the inheritances left by their ancestors.

## 28. (Verse 16)

“It is better for the just man to have a little than the many riches of sinners.”

Riches, then, are not being condemned, but the riches of sinners—unless perhaps because the sinner said: “All these things have been delivered to me, and to whomever I wish I give them” (Luke 4:6).

Moreover, because riches kindle the torch of desire more intensely, each person, while desiring greater possessions, does not avoid the byways of sin. Hence the Savior also said: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16:9). For it is the wealth of iniquity that lies under the devil’s power, so that it may be bestowed upon whomever he wishes.

The passage may also be understood in this way: “It is better for the just man to have a little than the many riches of sinners,” because someone may be rich in words, as are the philosophers of this world who debate sacrileges, the movement of the stars, the star of Jupiter and Saturn, the generations of human beings, the worship of images, geometry, and dialectic.

[Note: All the editions and a few manuscripts read, “because he is indeed rich in words.” Five manuscripts read, “because he is one who is rich,” etc. In the following verse the Roman edition reads, “arguing subtle points.” But apart from the fact that all the manuscripts and the old edition read, “arguing about sacrileges,” these words seem to signify nothing other than what Origen has the pagans say: that they establish various impieties against one another through the tricks of dialectical art.]

Philosophers, then, are rich in speech but poor in faith and deprived of truth. There are also many simple priests of the Lord who are poor in speech but exalted in abstinence and virtue.

They speak much faithlessness; these affirm faith with few words. The former daily lose their own priests; this poor man gains peoples for the Church and increases the number of believers. Whoever listens to these men and observes the quality of their works says: “It is better for the just man to have a little than the many riches of sinners.”

From this Solomon derived that saying which he presented as though it were his own: “You will not escape sin through much speaking” (Prov. 10:19). Dialectic therefore flows with the riches of words, while piety preserves the fear of God. Thus the one who is sparing in words and rich in spirit wishes rather to fear than to proclaim empty words about truth. For the fear of God is the discipline of wisdom; loquacity is the shipwreck of innocence and virtue and an incentive to falling and sin.

## 29. (Verse 17)

“For the arms of sinners shall be broken,” he says, so that their deeds cannot obstruct the just, and so that “the rod of sinners may not remain over the portion of the just.”

Paul likewise says: “May God crush Satan under your feet” (Rom. 16:20). For if his arm is broken, he himself will be entirely crushed, so that his schemes may be trampled down like the poisons of a serpent.

## 30

But the Lord strengthens the just when the adversary’s arm has been broken. Therefore the just man says: “You have strengthened your hand over me” (Ps. 37:3). Job also says: “The hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job 19:21).

The Lord therefore sent his hand against his servant and broke the sinner’s hand, which had been extended against him with the power that had been granted to it, together with the sinner’s arm. Thus the devil was deceived by his own words when he said: “Put forth your hand against him, and let us see whether he will not bless you to your face” (Job 2:5). He did not dare to say, “whether he will not curse you,” but left that meaning to be understood.

God sent forth his hand, and Job was strengthened. He began to bless, although he was thought likely to curse. For when the divine hand touches the just, it heals them; it does not wound them. He sent forth his hand, and every stain of the leper disappeared; he touched the eyes of the blind, and when blindness was driven away, the light of their eyes shone forth.

Therefore always ask that you may be strengthened, since even you who stand must beware lest you fall. We must stand so that we may be strengthened by the Lord. The world is slippery; we quickly slide. Let us therefore pray that the Lord may deign to establish and strengthen us.

## 31. (Verses 18–19)

Do not think that the Lord is unaware of your way. If you are just, he knows you. Believe the prophet who says: “The Lord knows the ways of the undefiled, and their inheritance shall be undefiled.”

[Note: This is the reading of the Arabic version and the Septuagint translators, together with several Gallican psalters. But the Hebrew text, the Chaldean paraphrase, and the Syriac version, together with the Latin Vulgate, read, “the days of the undefiled.” Therefore, since Ambrose states below that he observed this latter reading in a Greek copy, we should believe that he was referring to the version of Symmachus. As for the correction made by the Roman edition, which replaces “shall be undefiled” with “shall be forever,” all the sacred manuscripts support this correction, while, conversely, all the Ambrosian editions and manuscripts oppose it.]

“They shall not be put to shame in an evil time.” Whoever knows the Lord is known by the Lord. He knows the just; he does not know the unjust. Therefore he will say to the unjust: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Matt. 7:23)—that is, because you are unworthy of divine knowledge.

“I do not know you,” because you yourselves wished not to know me. Your works do not know me; your deeds do not know me. Even if you say that you know me, your sins refute you. “Every sin is from the evil one; but whoever does not sin remains in me,” John wrote (1 John 3:6).

What shall I say about the Lord, who disdains to know the impious? Paul also disdains them, for he said: “If anyone among you is a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize what I write to you. But whoever is ignorant shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:37–38).

It is also written: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19). Let us therefore belong to the Lord, so that the Lord may know us, and let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.

## 32

The Greek text reads: “The Lord knows the days of the undefiled.” There are the days of Elijah, and there are the days of Nebuchadnezzar. Therefore the Gospel says: “In the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut” (Luke 4:25).

It was night for the faithless, but there was light for Elijah. Heaven was closed to the faithless, but it was open to Elijah. There was famine for the faithless, but abundance for Elijah. For he could not hunger when heavenly food was supplied to him.

[Note: “Heavenly” means the angel and the ravens, as you find in 2 Kings 17:6 and 19:5.]

Nor did he hunger who himself fed others. Thus the just man has day for himself in darkness, because the light also shines in darkness.

Joseph was in Egypt, and noon shone upon him, just as he says below: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous deeds?” (Ps. 49:16). Righteousness is light, for above you have: “He will bring forth your righteousness like the light” (Ps. 36:6). You therefore have something that can shine within you if you pursue righteousness.

Day shines for you; night shines for you, because for the believer night too will be illuminated like day. The Lord knows the day of the just, because he himself enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9)—that is, the one who lives according to the image and likeness of God; the one who recognizes that he is a human being, so that he may flee the lust of neighing horses, the fury of wild beasts, the fearfulness of hares, the deceit of foxes, and the rapacity of wolves; the human being who acts as though he has come into this world from elsewhere; who has been born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God.

You have come, then: do not remain here; do not cling to earthly things. To know that the days are good, hear him say: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” (John 8:56). He has a good day who knows the Son of God, the good God, and confesses him as Lord.

Again, he himself warns us that we must beware, because the days are evil (Eph. 5:16). What days are evil? Those in which the evil that comes from the evil one is recognized. Or perhaps the days of the world are evil, because the world lies in the evil one.

But we also read of an evil day after this world: “In the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. 40:2)—that is, on the day of judgment, which is evil because of the punishments of many. The unjust must indeed be tormented, while the just suffer with them. The angels also rejoice when one sinner is saved from death.

[Note: The Royal manuscript reads: “The just suffers with the unjust when he is punished.” The word “therefore” seems to have been transposed, and “suffers with” should be moved earlier. Four others read: “He is saved from death, and they suffer with him. Therefore, when the sinner is punished, the just man suffers with him, although elsewhere,” etc. All the others and all the editions read as in the text.]

Yet elsewhere we read: “The just man will rejoice when he sees the vengeance upon the impious” (Ps. 57:11). I reserve that subject for its proper place, even though you may often have heard why he rejoices. Let us not insert one discussion into another.

## 33

“The Lord knows the days of the undefiled,” because his grace and fullness, belonging to undefiled innocence, have mercy; he does not have mercy on those who wander. These people have no day, because they flee the light. Of them it is beautifully said: “Their days pass away like a shadow” (Ps. 143:4).

God’s knowledge, then, is an act of favor, not merely of vision. His eyes are light: those whom he looks upon, he illuminates. Therefore his eyes are the days of the just.

## 34

Hence their inheritance shall also be forever, because they sought eternal goods, not the advantages of a temporal inheritance. They shall have nothing of which to be ashamed in the evil time—that is, in the heavenly judgment—and in days of famine they shall be satisfied, because “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. 4:4).

But what human being? I know a human being in Christ, fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know; God knows—caught up in such a way as far as the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:2).

That human being, then, who is in Christ, who does not know himself to be in the flesh, who does not walk according to the flesh but according to the spirit; the one who is caught up not only to heaven but also to the third heaven, caught up to paradise, and hears secret words that it is not permitted for a human being to speak; the one who glories not in his own virtues but in his weaknesses—that person lives not by bread alone but by every word of God.

For the word of God is life, because the Word became flesh. Hence the Evangelist said magnificently: “What was made in him is life” (John 1:14).

## 35

[Note: All the Greeks, not only the Alexandrians and Egyptians, read this passage in the following form: Πάντα δι’ αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο, καὶ χωρὶς αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο οὐδὲ ἓν ὃ γέγονεν — “All things came to be through him, and without him not even one thing came to be that has come to be.” The Latin manuscripts offer a different punctuation, which the Latin Fathers commonly follow.]

The Alexandrians and Egyptians read: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made” (ibid., 3). With a distinction inserted, they then add: “In him is life” (ibid., 5).

Let that punctuation remain safe for the faithful. I am not afraid to read: “What was made in him is life.” And the Arian has nothing to seize upon, because I am not considering his poisons but recognizing the customary reading of sacred Scripture.

For it does not say: “The Word was made before every beginning.” It does not say: “The Word was made.” But if you wish to hear what it does say: “The Word,” it says, “was with God.” He was with God, working with him and ruling with him.

It does not say: “The Word was made,” but it says: “God was the Word.” God, however, is not a work but the maker and creator.

Open your ears and hear: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Do you learn that he is the Son, in whom the fullness of divinity exists?

Open your ears a little further and hear him say: “What was made in him is life.” “In him,” he says, “it was made”; the Word of God was not made.

Or if this gives you grounds for accusation, because he said, “it was made in him,” do you also accuse God the Father because the Son of God said: “Whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been made in God” (John 3:21)?

Or because David said: “I will confess to you, Lord, because you have heard me, and you have become my salvation” (Ps. 117:21)—that is, “you have turned into salvation for me; you have worked for my salvation”?

I could use other examples, but I do not want you to believe me, lest you think these are merely products of ingenuity rather than testimonies to the truth.

[Note: All the editions read thus; but nearly all the manuscripts read, “lest you think these arguments are exercises of ingenuity.” This is not inappropriate if the words “exercises of ingenuity” are taken to mean the tricks and quibbles of argument, or sophisms. See Du Cange’s *Glossary* under *ingenium*.]

## 36

Let the son of thunder himself, the one who reclined on Christ’s breast, the one to whom the Lord did not conceal his secrets, to whom Peter gestured that he should ask the Lord—and he asked, and the Lord revealed it—let him explain what he understood by the words: “What was made in him is life.”

Hear, then, how he interprets it, for he was already guarding against your, Arius, accusations:

> “What was from the beginning; what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have contemplated, and what our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life—and the life appeared” (1 John 1:1).

It is therefore flesh that appeared in Christ, or Christ in the flesh; he himself is our life in all things. His divinity is life; his eternity is life; his flesh is life; his passion is life.

Hence Jeremiah also says: “We shall live in his shadow” (Lam. 4:20). The shadow of wings, the shadow of the cross, the shadow of his passion.

His death is life; his wound is life; his blood is life; his burial is life; his resurrection is the life of all.

Do you wish to know that his death is life? “In his death,” he says, “we were baptized … so that we might walk with him in newness of life” (Rom. 6:3–4).

He himself also says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24–25). He was the grain that, for our sake, was dissolved in the body and died, so that he might bear much fruit in us. His death, therefore, is the fruit of life.

What was made in him, then, is life. Flesh was made in him: life. Infancy was made in him: life. Judgment was made in him: life. Death was made in him: life. The forgiveness of sins was made in him: life. A wound was made in him: life. Mockery was made in him: life. Division was made in him: life. Burial was made in him: life. Resurrection was made in him: life.

See how many things were made in him, through which the condition of our life was transformed, so that what had perished might be restored. Finally, a sale was made in him: life. Redemption was made in him: life. He was sold by Judas and bought by the Jews for death, so that we might be redeemed for life by his precious blood.

This is the life that was made; this is the life that appeared; this is the life that we heard; this is the life that was with the Father. For he who was in the beginning was afterward born of a Virgin, so that he might be life for those who were dying.

## 37

Let us question this very passage set before us: What does “a human being in Christ” mean? It means one who has been made in Christ, in whom all things were made—whether Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, or Powers. “All things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Col. 1:16–17)—that is, in his power.

A human being in Christ is one who has been made according to his image and likeness. A human being in Christ is one who is wholly in Christ. For just as, through the unity and fullness of divinity, God the Father is wholly in the Son, and the Son in the Father, so, through purpose and the affection of piety—using this as an example, not as a comparison—the whole human being is in Christ. For whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit.

A human being in Christ, then, is not the earthly human being, nor the human being of sin, but the human being of Christ.

Why, then, does it cause concern that “what was made in him is life,” if especially the inner human being was made in him, crucified in him, renewed in him, buried in him and buried with him, and raised in him?

Why does it cause concern, as I said, that it is written, “What was made in him is life,” when the human being has said: “In God we shall do valiantly” (Ps. 59:14)?

If you ask what this life is—if it troubles you that something was made in him—receive the answer: life is the Church. It was made in him, in his side; in him Eve was raised up.

Eve is life. Thus this is what was made: Eve, who had perished, was saved through the Church, that is, through the generation of her children, as it is written (1 Tim. 2:15), because a sober posterity corrected the sin of the earlier transgressor.

Hence Paul himself was also caught up to life, although previously he had been a persecutor unto death.

## 38

We have wandered at greater length so that we might speak about the human being who lives not by bread alone but by every word of God. Let us return to the psalm:

“Therefore the undefiled shall not be put to shame on the day of judgment, and in days of famine they shall be satisfied.”

## 39. (Verse 20)

“They shall fail like smoke; they shall fail.”

The Greek has ἐξέλιπον, that is, “they failed.”

You see someone suddenly come to power, adorned with the insignia of honor, and you judge him exalted. You see that he has another kind of success. Do you not say of him: “Where is that man who was honored and exalted?” He has failed.

The Greek says more for this reason: precisely where someone is thought to be honored and exalted, there he is overtaken by his own failure. Thus you may understand that river currents have passed by more swiftly than they came; while you await the waters that are coming, they have already flowed past as you continue to wait.

On the other hand, the humble and meek, while they are subjected to the rich and oppressed, are exalted through their humility and suddenly shine forth. Therefore Paul took pleasure in his weaknesses, not in his virtues.

## 40

But let us consider this, lest anyone think that he gloried in revelations; and let us repeat his words so that he himself may defend his role as a teacher of humility.

“I know,” he says, “a man in Christ fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know; God knows—caught up in such a way as far as the third heaven” (2 Cor. 12:2).

He says that this was revealed to him fourteen years earlier, and yet he kept and suppressed the revelation within himself for so long. He would not have said it unless he judged it useful for us to know it, lest we be lifted up by revelations.

For if Paul did not glory in such great grace, neither ought we to glory. Did he, while young, not glory, and should he, when old, glory? Moreover, he could not deny that he had been caught up as far as the third heaven; yet he testified that he did not know whether he had been caught up in the body or outside the body.

He therefore glories not in knowledge but in ignorance, and proclaims God’s grace toward himself. What belongs to knowledge he denies; what belongs to love he confesses. “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”

Again, he said that a human being had been caught up in this way; he recalled that it was uncertain to him whether he had been caught up in the body or outside the body. Behold the balance of wisdom. He places one person in Christ and himself as another—the one who says, “I do not know.” What is another’s, he raises up; what is his own, he humbles.

“And he heard,” he says, “unspeakable words” (2 Cor. 12:4). He did not say, “I heard,” but he did not deny that someone else had heard them. Thus, modestly, he preferred to present himself as a witness rather than a prophet, and he avoided appearing to be an arbiter of heavenly secrets.

To give testimony belongs to truth; not to refuse the glory of exaltation belongs to one who boasts.

[Note: Five manuscripts read, “the merit of election.” But we think that someone substituted *election* for *exaltation*, not noticing that the passage speaks of exaltation, not pride—the Apostle’s being caught up, by which he is said to have been carried or lifted up as far as the third heaven.]

Therefore he says: “On behalf of such a one I will glory; but on my own behalf I will not glory” (ibid., 5).

## 41

What does he mean by saying that a human being—and that human being in Christ—heard things that it is not permitted for a human being to speak? How can it be fitting that a human being was not permitted to speak what a human being was permitted to hear?

If the human being who heard was not permitted to speak, how was he entrusted with hearing what he was not permitted to speak? What is this distinction? If it was another, external human being, how could one human being know what another human being was not permitted to hear?

Hence it appears that the human being who was in Christ did not lack the grace of speech—for he did not lack it—but that those who might hear lacked the appropriate place, time, and merit.

He heard in heaven. Therefore it was judged inappropriate for him to speak on earth what he had heard in heaven. There is even on earth a distinction of this kind: what is sung in one region is not sung in another, according to what is written: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. 136:4).

Indeed, the Hebrews did not sing in the land of their captivity what they had been accustomed to sing in their homeland. This is the land of captivity; that is the land of freedom. This is the land of sin; that is the land of eternal rest. This is the earthly valley; that is the heavenly one.

Therefore Paul was then proclaiming in heaven what he could not previously proclaim on earth. For among the perfect the secrets of wisdom must be spoken.

## 42

Yet what does the recollection of this revelation accomplish except to teach that one should by no means glory in revelations, but in weaknesses? Weakness is both the remedy for revelation and the exercise of virtue.

Revelation, on the other hand, is a slippery path to exaltation. For lest Paul himself, who had been caught up into the third heaven, be lifted up by the greatness of the revelation, he received a thorn in the flesh.

Weakness therefore came to his aid, lest grace be turned into danger. Weakness is therefore more useful than grace.

That same weakness is also the workshop of virtue, as the Lord testified to the Apostle himself: “Power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

Finally, after the revelation this man asked for a remedy of health, and he did not obtain it. In weakness, however, he did not seek a remedy; rather, he completed his course and found his crown.

43. (Verse 21.) “The sinner borrows,” he says, “and does not repay; but the righteous shows mercy and gives.” This too suits Paul’s person, because the righteous shows mercy and gives. See him distributing the Lord’s sayings; see him lending out the Lord’s silver. He received one mina and returned two; he received two and returned four; he received five and returned ten. He did not tie up what he had received in a napkin, but paid it out to the moneychangers; and what he had paid out, he received back with interest. Thus he both freed the one who had received it from the greatest sin, lest the Lord’s money should perish with him, and himself earned the right to be set over ten cities. What the ten cities are, recognize in the letters that he wrote—even though the apostles are not restricted by a prescribed number, since they were told: “Go throughout the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI, 15). Thus, from Jerusalem through the East, Illyricum, and Italy, he distributed the Lord’s money. And lest anyone think that he was lending out his own money, he testified that it was the Lord’s, saying: “To those who are joined in marriage I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband” (I Cor. VII, 10). And elsewhere: “Why do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (II Cor. XIII, 3). Finally, the king himself said this, in whom there is a figure of the Lord: “You ought to have entrusted my money to the moneychangers.” “My,” he says, “not yours.” The righteous, therefore, shows mercy and gives. How he gives, hear him saying: “Throughout all the churches I teach.” But “the sinner borrows and does not repay” (I Cor. VII, 17). See the rich man lending and not returning, and the poor man receiving and immediately repaying, so that he may not remain longer in another’s debt. These are moral interpretations.

44. Now observe the mystical poor man—that is, the simple man who fears the name of God—hearing the word concerning chastity and repaying it; hearing about mercy and repaying it; hearing about gentleness and not becoming angry. Observe, on the other hand, that arrogant and proud rich man, hearing the sayings of God but casting them behind him; hearing about the condemnation of luxury, yet practicing luxury all the more. Finally, the Church repays what she received; the Synagogue does not repay. Recognize the Church’s repayment: “They were yours,” she says, “and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word” (John XVII, 6). And elsewhere: “The Father himself loves you, because you have loved me” (John XVI, 27). The Church, therefore, returned the money of love that she had received from the Lord, but the Synagogue did not return it. Hence it is said concerning the Jews: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John XV, 24), because they certainly heard and did not believe. It has therefore been proved that sinners borrowed and did not repay. The sinner, then, is always in want; but the righteous abounds and gives, for his conscience is rich. Therefore the Jews were in want amid their riches: “The rich were in want and hungry” (Ps. XXXIII, 11); but Christians did not fail amid the riches of their simplicity.

45. (Verse 22.) The righteous, then, is good; and therefore Scripture adds: “For those who bless him shall possess the land, but those who curse him shall perish.” How does the righteous possess the land, or what land, when Scripture says: “Will you alone dwell upon the land?” (Isa. V, 8). And elsewhere: “Woe to those who dwell upon the land” (Rev. VIII, 13)—a word of rebuke and curse. Of what land, then, is blessed possession promised? Not of this land, which is hidden in darkness and filled with bitterness, but of that land which flows with honey and milk—that is, which possesses the grace of sweetness and the splendor of eternal light. Receive the sweetness of good honey—or rather, what is above honey: “Pain and groaning and sorrow shall flee away” (Isa. XXXV, 10), because the sweetness of grace will exclude the bitterness of human frailty. And elsewhere: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning” (Rev. XXI, 4). Receive also the brightness of milk: “They will need neither lamp nor sunlight, for the Lord himself will shine upon them, and they will reign for ever and ever. Amen” (Rev. XXIV, 5).

46. There is also the mystical righteous one, who shows mercy and gives, who gave us every word that he received from the Father, and remitted the debts of our sins for us, and paid his blood for our debts, so that we might not remain in another’s debt, but that a good creditor might hold us in his own account. There is also that sinner who gathered what he had not begotten and borrowed what he did not possess, yet does not wish to return what he received. Hear that the devil borrowed: “I will give you power over all this,” he says, “and their glory, because it has been handed over to me, and I give it to whomever I wish, if you will fall down and worship me” (Luke IV, 6).

> [Note: All the editions, and four manuscripts, in which both the divine text and Ambrose himself—Book I of *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 5, section 17, and elsewhere—support this reading, present the passage with these same words. Four other manuscripts, however, insert after the words *power over all this* the phrase *all these kingdoms*. There is evidently no other reason for this than to provide something to which their τό (*the*) might refer. Yet there is an ellipsis, with τό τῶν πραγμάτων, in Greek χρημάτων (*of the things*, that is, *of the possessions*), understood—namely, the things that the demon was pointing out with his finger.]

Most wicked one, you received these things for temptation, not for death; that is, you received them so that God’s servants might be tested, not destroyed; you received them so that God might be worshiped, not denied. You received the things of this age—why do you take away what is eternal? You received what belongs to the world—why do you wish to remove what belongs to Christ? Give them to whomever you wish; we do not begrudge you. Why are the things we desire begrudged to us by you? You wish to be worshiped, although you are more wicked than all and yourself unworthy even of servitude.

47. (Verse 23.) “By the Lord the steps of a man shall be corrected.”

> [Note: The Roman edition reads: “By the Lord the steps of a man shall be directed, and he shall desire his way.” “The steps of a man shall be directed.” The word for “steps” in Greek is διαβήματα (*passages*), and so forth. The other editions and all the manuscripts read as we have in the text.]

The Greek says διαβήματα (*steps*), that is, “crossings” or “passages.” Therefore it is said to you: “If you pass through water, the rivers shall not overwhelm you” (Isa. XLIII, 2). Cross over, then; do not stop. Just as a good traveler, when he comes to some road-marker—

> [Note: That is, a pillar erected to indicate roads at crossroads or three-way junctions, or an ἑρμαῖον λόφος, a “Hermes-hill,” mentioned in Proverbs XXVI, 8.]

—does not stop, but passes by, so you are on the way as long as you remain engaged in this journey. If Paul had stopped, he would not have completed his course. See whether this is why he says: “And let him who stands beware lest he fall” (I Cor. X, 12). For one who has crossed over cannot fear falling. “I saw,” he says, “the wicked exalted above measure and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (below, verse 35). Thus, seeing the wicked exalted above measure, the one who did not stop did not stumble; but if he had stopped, admired him, and followed him, he would have stumbled and fallen like the wicked.

Therefore Moses, seeing the bush shining and not burning, said: “I will pass over and see this great sight” (Exod. III, 3). He who passes from this world sees a great sight; he who breaks the bonds of this connection by which we are bound to the body sees a great sight. Moses, as we read in Exodus, sees many miracles; another who is not in Exodus does not see such things. Moses himself crossed over; the people of the fathers also crossed over, because they were leaving the land of captivity. Their steps, therefore, were directed by the Lord: by night a column of fire shone for them, and by day a column of cloud, so that neither the heat of day might afflict those traveling nor the darkness of night bring hindrance to travelers.

48. And you, earn this by your deeds and ask for it in your prayers: that your steps may be directed by the Lord, lest your feet be moved, for it is written: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had very nearly slipped” (Ps. LXXII, 2). You must also beware lest you abandon the straight path and the byways of winding roads deceive you. Therefore it is said: “Prepare the way for the Lord; make his paths straight” (Isa. XL, 3). Let us therefore prepare the way for the Lord our God in our minds; let us make the paths of our souls straight, lest we slip. Let our steps not be poured out like those of Lot’s wife, who looked behind her and could not keep her steps, but they were poured out when she was suddenly turned into salt. Let them not be poured out like those of the Egyptians, whose steps the waves of the sea engulfed. The very Hebrews who were with Moses fell in the wilderness because they sinned, their footsteps failing lest they enter the land of resurrection.

> [Note: The old edition in the margin, and the Roman edition in the text, read: “lest they enter the land of promise.” But all the manuscripts consistently read: “lest they enter the land of resurrection,” the name of the figurative reality being transferred to its figure.]

49. Is it not also beautifully said of these men that their progress was poured out—that their hopes fell, their labor was poured out in vain, and their prayers were abandoned? Consider someone who for several years had pursued uprightness, guarded chastity, cultivated a more attentive way of life, undertaken a devout service, and practiced diligent observance, but who suddenly changed, departed from the monastery, said farewell to fasts, renounced continence, and indulged in pleasures and pursued luxury.

> [Note: Several manuscripts read: “to indulge in offenses … instigators of pestilence.”]

They left the monasteries some time ago, and now they are teachers of luxury, sowers of incontinence, instigators of wantonness, and detractors of modesty.

> [Note: Closely related remarks are found in the letter to the Church at Vercellae concerning the apostate monks Sarmatio and Barbatianus. When they had become impatient with stricter discipline, left the monastery at Milan, and later, after requesting to return, suffered rejection from the holy Bishop, they burned with such indignation at the disgrace that they never ceased to rage and rave against continence, fasts, and the other ornaments of monastic discipline. Hermann, in *The Life of Saint Ambrose*, Book VII, chapter 4, and one of our own writers, who recently published in the vernacular a history of the Benedictine Order, have very judiciously observed that these two are designated here. Consult the latter, Book I, chapter 3, section 5.]

Would you not aptly say of them: “Their steps have been poured out”—those who regretted having once directed them well? Thus they have performed a new kind of repentance for their virtues, but do not repent of their offenses. “They went out from us,” John says, “but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have persevered with us” (I John II, 19).

These, then, condemned their own way, and to them it is fitting to say: “O you who abandoned straight paths by going into the ways of darkness, who rejoice in evils and exult in wicked destruction, whose paths are crooked and whose courses are winding, like their author, slippery and winding—why have you begun to hate the straight way and abandoned sound counsel?” (Prov. II, 13 ff.). The Lord did not direct you. But whoever is directed by the Lord will desire his way, as it is written, and will delight in his paths.

50. Nevertheless, both interpretations can be understood; the passage is deliberately balanced. The one who is directed by the Lord will desire the Lord’s way, because under his leadership every labor is lightened, every obstacle removed, and incentives supplied. At the same time, the Lord himself does not disdain but willingly accepts the way of the man whom he has himself directed toward virtue. It is beautifully said that a man’s steps are directed by the Lord, because it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy, to preserve a footprint without stumbling. “He who plants and he who waters are nothing, but God who gives the growth” (I Cor. III, 7); to him alone the glory of virtues is rightly ascribed.

51. (Verse 24.) Finally, the righteous also sometimes falls; but if he is righteous, when he falls he will not be shaken. The fall belongs to his condition; the rising again to his righteousness. For God does not abandon the righteous, but strengthens his hand. Why did he say not “his foot” but “his hand”? Perhaps because the one who falls does not merely slip with his foot, but, being weak, is often deceived by a slippery place or stumbles against a stone. Here, however, understand the fall of the righteous—that is, of the stronger man.

Finally, among a people who wrestle, if someone fixes his knee or slips with his foot, he is considered defeated. But an athlete skilled in wrestling and striving for the crown may deliberately place his knee in order to win; if he slips, he is not disqualified; and even if he is pressed by one who is above him, he continues to contend lawfully so long as he supports himself with his hands. The prize is not taken away unless he has been thrown on his stomach or stretched out by a grip of the arms. From this arise frequent contests, because there are many kinds of falls, unknown to most people.

> [Note: The old edition and several manuscripts read: “For the Latins properly call them *casus* [falls].” But the edition opposite has *ruinam* [ruin] in the margin, a reading that the Roman edition, suppressing the word, transferred into the text. Four manuscripts agree with us.]

Their falls are properly called *ruins*, for in Greek they are called πτώματα (*falls*). Thus, when he is gripped and pressed, he often rolls over and becomes the one above who had been considered inferior; and as he rises, he knocks down the one above him. Scripture seems to signify this when it says: “You have turned his entire bed in his infirmity” (Ps. XL, 4).

Thus it is said of him: “When the good athlete has fallen, he will not be shaken.” For many who rely on their skill wish to be held down so that they may win more quickly.

> [Note: This is the reading of the edition together with part of the manuscripts. Another part reads: “But even if he is assigned … and has fled a second time.” Which reading should be preferred is uncertain. The obscurity arises because we do not know the true sense of the agonistic term *assignatus* or *assignatur*. We nevertheless suspect that those who had already been thrown to the ground and were being marked out by the spectators’ eyes and gestures as about to be defeated may have been called “assigned.”]

But even if he has been “assigned,” to use the very word, both the first and the second time, he is not disqualified. It is sometimes permitted him to renew the wrestling, and often he succeeds in winning and in making the one who prevailed in the second contest yield. Thus, even if the righteous encounters an obstacle and falls, let him nevertheless not abandon his zeal for devotion and faith; let him maintain sobriety, practice repentance, and often restore himself.

Therefore Peter asks: “If my brother sins against me, how often shall I forgive him? Up to seven times?” (Matt. XVIII, 21–22). And the Lord answered: “Not only seven times, but also seventy times seven.” But so that you may know that we are athletes, that we are thrust aside, that some fall, and that many are knocked down, hear him saying: “The Lord supports all who fall and raises up all who are cast down” (Ps. CXLIV, 14). Hence David himself—or the one who spoke in the Prophet—says concerning himself: “I was thrust down and overturned so as to fall, but the Lord received me” (Ps. CXVII, 13). For Jesus did not fall, but was thrust aside. Indeed, since he himself raises those who have been cast down, how could he himself be cast down?

Scripture testifies that the righteous, when he has fallen, can rise again. It says: “Will one who falls not rise again? Or will one who has turned away not return? Woe to those who turn away with shameless turning,” says the Lord (Jer. VIII, 4–5).

52. Would that the athlete of Christ were indeed undefeated and unconquerable, glorious in every age and in every kind of virtue, as he says: “But in all things we conquer through him who loved us” (Rom. VIII, 37). What does “in all things” mean? There are athletes who are called boys, youths, and men—that is, παῖδες (*boys*), ἔφηβοι (*youths*), and πύκται (*boxers*). Scripture too recognizes these ages among wrestlers, as David says: “Do not turn your face away from your boy” (Ps. LXVIII, 18); and: “I was young, and I have grown old” (below, verse 25).

Hence John also says: “I write to you, children, because you have known the Father; I write to you, young men, because you have conquered the evil one; I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning” (I John II, 12 ff.). Therefore, when writing to fathers, he indicates those more mature through the progress of faith and devotion. These, then, are ages of virtue, not of weakness. For the boy who has known God, the Father of virtues, is not without virtue.

These boys derive from that Boy who, before he knew how to call either father or mother, received “the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria.” He is the boy who was born for us, the Son who was given to us, whose rule is upon his shoulders. He himself taught us that boyhood is a virtue, saying: “Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them” (Luke XVIII, 16). And elsewhere: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you turn and become like this child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 3).

Even in bodily strength, boys often defeat men. Certainly, if we consider the age of boyhood, a boy cannot know every technique or endure the full force of wrestling. Yet we know that boys have frequently conquered men whom they could not carry. So great is the vigor of the spirit that it excludes the weakness of age.

53. As are the boys, so also are the youths—that is, the spiritual ones. Scripture knows Paul as a young man already near his conversion (Acts VII, 57). It knows also the young man Eutychus, who, while listening intently to Paul’s preaching, was overcome by sleep, fell from the third story, and rose again (Acts XX, 9). It knows John as a young man reclining upon Christ’s breast (John XIII, 23), who was so strong that he did not fear persecution and conquered evil.

This is the boy who left his earthly father (Matt. IV, 20), following the Father whom he recognized as eternal; the young man clothed in a linen garment who followed the Lord at the time of his passion, having abandoned everything of his own (Mark XIV, 51). When more mature, he recognized that the Word of God had always been and was in the beginning itself (John I, 1–2), and proved that he remained in himself.

54. Scripture has also taught us about spiritual men. The prophet Agabus says: “The Jews will bind this man, whose belt this is, in Jerusalem” (Acts XXI, 11). And Festus says: “A certain man has been left by Felix in custody” (Acts XXV, 14). Before his passion Paul is called a young man; in his passion he is shown as a man, one who, having completed his course, was already near the crown.

55. We have learned the ages of those who contend for faith and devotion.

> [Note: This is the reading of the Roman edition together with six manuscripts. The old edition, supported by the Victorine and Colbertine manuscripts, reads: “Let us also learn the contests of those who contend for devotion.”]

Let us also learn the kinds of contests belonging to each. The course of Scripture will teach us this as well.

In this worldly contest, then, there are some who wrestle according to a simple and lawful kind of combat, contending only with bodily grips and not knowing how to strike; they are called *palestritae*, or wrestlers. Others combine striking and the throwing of dust with the entanglements of their limbs, with every license to strike granted them.

> [Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “They combine these with the exertions of their limbs.”]

They are called *pammacharii*, because they are permitted every kind of dispute and combat against one another.

> [Note: All the editions read: “whom they call *pammacharii* … their heads are bloodied.” All the manuscripts, at least the Gallican ones, read as in the text.]

Others fight against one another with the *cestus*, or boxing gloves, and suffer as their heads are torn apart and wounded; these are called πύκται (*boxers*).

56. The Apostle Paul underwent all these contests, as he himself shows. Thus he says: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers and”—to use a concise expression—“against the spiritual forces of wickedness” (Eph. VI, 12). In most Latin copies *colluctatio* (*wrestling*) is found; in all the Greek copies πάλῃ (*wrestling*) is written. For the Greek πάλῃ is the Latin *lucta*, “wrestling.”

And truly it is wrestling, because flesh and blood and the spiritual forces of wickedness are overcome by bodily endurance and continence, and by moderation of spirit. Anger, fury, slaughter, and weapons are the devil’s arms.

Elsewhere he indicates that he was beaten with blows beyond measure, saying: “In beatings beyond measure, in deaths often” (II Cor. XI, 23). At Jerusalem he was struck in combat. When the Jews had at one point stopped beating Paul because soldiers intervened, the high priest Ananias ordered those standing nearby to strike him on the mouth. The Apostle answered him: “God is about to strike you, whitewashed wall. And you sit judging me according to the Law, while contrary to the Law you order me to be struck” (Acts XXIII, 3).

He certainly knew how to strike back, for he struck the high priest with a heavier blow in return. Paul himself was beaten bodily; to the other he returned the charge that he was being struck in the soul by Christ.

In his First Epistle to the Corinthians he also says: “I therefore run in this way, not as uncertainly; I fight in this way, not as one beating the air” (I Cor. IX, 16). What he called *enitor* in Latin, he called πυκτεύω (*I box*) in Greek. And truly, like a good boxer, he was not beating the air but the aerial powers and the heads of the Jews, because they did not have Jesus the Lord as their head.

In every contest, therefore, the Apostle was proved, and he also received the crown of his completed course. Hence he himself says: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. IV, 13).

57. Christ too has those who, in their boyhood, have conquered men mature in age. Thus Daniel, a boy with a powerful spirit, rebuked those Jewish elders and, by right of victory, cast them down to death. He also has others who wrestled in their mother’s womb before they were born. Finally, Jacob supplanted his brother Esau and conquered evil; and he came forth from his mother’s womb in such a way as to display the mark of victory, victoriously turning back the foot of the older degener­ate brother.

Jeremiah was sanctified and approved in his mother’s womb. John the Baptist, while not yet born, recognized that the Prince of the human contest and the one who rewards wrestlers had come; leaping in his mother’s womb, he earned the prize of a devout confession. He was rightly marked out for the crown even then, since before all others he had offered his name as a witness of faith and herald of virtue in Christ’s contest.

A good herald, who summoned others to the contest. And truly a good herald, who cried out with so great a voice that at its sound the heavenly mysteries echoed. What more need be said? He moved the earth and filled heaven. Therefore he received the name of “voice,” because the consecrated voice preceded the Word of God, as he himself taught us, saying: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John I, 23).

The prophet Isaiah said this; John established that it had been spoken concerning him (Isa. XL, 3). We have heard what the herald said: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (John I, 23). This is the singular and solitary voice, so sonorous that it was heard by all, so sweet that it soothed the hearts of everyone.

The Lord therefore strengthened these athletes of his so that they might conquer. For he never abandons or forsakes his own.

58. (Verse 25.) Therefore the Prophet added: “I was young, and I have grown old.” Thus read the Latin copies; some, however, following the Greek, have: “I was young, and indeed I have grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread.”

For anyone who wishes to understand it simply, the meaning is clear: during his lifetime David did not see the righteous forsaken. But this concerns only a short period and is unbelievable, since we see many righteous people in this world abandoned by human beings when some powerful person persecutes them; no one dares approach them when he sees them exposed to fear or injury.

Hence Job says: “My brothers have departed from me; they have recognized strangers more than me. My friends have become merciless, and those who knew me have forgotten my name” (Job XIX, 13). David too cries out that he was not merely abandoned but attacked by friends and relatives: “My friends and my neighbors,” he says, “have drawn near against me” (Ps. XXXVII, 12).

Therefore, if righteous people are found abandoned in this world, how could David have spoken contrary to the truth? Unless you understand that although the righteous is abandoned in this world, he is nevertheless not abandoned by the Lord. For Job, even when he was in the dung heap (Job II, 3), was not abandoned by the Lord. The Lord himself praised him in his own voice in the council of the angels; he allowed him to be tested so that he might crown him. He gave temptation against the body but denied it against the soul.

Nor was David abandoned, to whom he gave the kingdom so that he might rule over his chosen people; when David was attacked with murderous battles and driven from the borders of his kingdom, God restored him by right of victory.

Jacob too, and Elijah and Elisha, and John the Baptist, and the others who wandered about in goatskins through deserts, mountains, caves, and holes in the ground, although they may appear to have endured many insults and bitter punishments, were nevertheless not abandoned.

For when Jacob was fleeing from his brother and wandering unattended through the wilderness, he fell asleep and, rising, saw there a multitude of the heavenly army. He said: “This place is called the camp of angels” (Gen. XXXII, 2).

> [Note: Ambrose quoted this passage from memory, attributing to Jacob while he was fleeing from his brother words that are recorded as having been spoken when he was returning to his homeland. There is also some variation in the passage itself. Where the text has “the camp of angels,” the Septuagint has παρεμβολὴ Θεοῦ αὕτη (“this is the camp of God”); the sacred manuscripts in all languages agree in this reading.]

It was not enough to call it a camp; he called it camps, suited to so great a multitude. You see, then, that although he thought himself alone, camps of the heavenly army followed him.

Likewise, as Paul says (I Cor. X, 4), in the time of Moses our fathers were followed by the rock so that they might not thirst in the wilderness. For in Exodus we read that, when the people were thirsty, Moses struck the rock with his staff, water flowed, and God’s people drank (Exod. XVII, 6). Again, in Leviticus or Numbers, we read that Moses struck the rock with his staff a second time and water gushed forth for the fathers to drink (Num. XX, 11). The Apostle interpreted this splendidly, saying: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4).

The Lord therefore did not abandon those grumbling, those murmuring, those transgressing people, but followed them.

What shall I say about Elijah and Elisha, as they walked through the wilderness and horses from heaven and a fiery chariot came to meet them? How was Elijah abandoned, when he was invited by Christ (Matt. XVII, 3)? How was he abandoned on earth, when he was carried up to heaven? How was he poor, naked, and empty, when he left to his disciple the inheritance of a doubled spirit, so that, endowed with a single mantle, the heir might stop rivers, turn back the Jordan to its source, feed the armies of kings in the wilderness, and provide drink to the thirsty?

At his command cups flowed down from heaven, and on earth the dead rose again.

How was Elisha abandoned, when he was surrounded by the army of the Syrians so that he might be seized and carried off to the king? When his servant Gehazi said, “Lord, what shall we do?” he answered: “Do not fear, for there are more with us than with them.” And he said: “Lord, open his eyes, that he may see.” His eyes were opened, and he saw the mountain and all the surrounding area filled with innumerable horses and heavenly legions (IV Kings VI, 16–17).

Paul too, who said that he had been exposed to dangers at sea and dangers in the wilderness (II Cor. XI, 26), nevertheless himself testified: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rom. VIII, 31).

Therefore, if that man was abandoned and deserted by human beings, he abounds and overflows before God. Elijah too had been deserted, so that he said: “Lord, take away my life” (III Kings XIX, 4); yet he flourished before God, so that by his power he was terrifying even to kings.

59. How could this David, being young, have grasped this? A young man considers temporal things more than eternal things, because that age tends toward vices. But some are old in youth, and others young in old age. There are, I say, men whose minds are marked by the gravity of the aged, in whom the age of old age is an unblemished life, in whom hoary wisdom is vigorous.

Such was Jeremiah, who, while acknowledging the youthfulness of his age and excusing himself on account of his youth because he seemed unequal to the office of preaching, heard the Lord say to him: “Do not say, ‘I am young’; for you shall go to all those to whom I send you” (Jer. I, 7). Thus he did not consider him young whom he judged suitable for prophetic grace.

Such, then, was David in his youth: renewed and blossoming again, as he himself said, like the youth of the eagle (Ps. CII, 5). This is how it should be understood: “I was young”—but sanctified, and established as a prophet among the nations, so that I could already know the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom and contemplate the true rewards of righteousness—“but I did not see the righteous forsaken.”

> [Note: The Roman edition reads: “Afterward I also grew old,” that is, “and, strengthened by use and so forth.” This is an excellent sense. But the earlier edition and all the manuscripts oppose it; we have followed their agreement.]

“Afterward I also grew old”; and, strengthened by experience and office, I acquired increases of wisdom. I saw the same grace remain with regard to the righteous.

60. We have explained as best we could how he said, “I was young.” But let us consider how he added, “Indeed, I have grown old.” Youth is good, but old age is better; for “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.” Hence it was not casually said of the patriarch Abraham (Gen. XXV, 8) that he was nourished in a good old age.

John too began to write the Gospel, or the Epistles, as an old man. When he avoided writing “the apostle,” he wrote “the elder” (II and III Epistles); nor was he judged inferior because he possessed a certain swanlike grace of old age.

> [Note: “Swanlike … grace of old age,” that is, “a more pleasing old age,” according to the common error of the ancients, who asserted that swans sang more sweetly as death approached. No one now denies that this is mere fiction.]

The chosen vessel of the Lord, writing to Philemon, says: “Being such a one as Paul the elder, and now also a prisoner of Christ Jesus, I appeal to you for my son, whom I have begotten in my bonds, Onesimus” (Philem. 9–10). Wishing, therefore, to show himself the greatest respect, he presented himself as Paul the elder, not Paul the young man; and there he took pride in being old where he was already being held in chains.

And observe the difference: he is called a young man in another’s passion, but an old man in his own (Acts VII, 57). There he was a young man because he was guarding the garments of the Jews; here he is old, where he was stripping off the clothing of his own body.

Finally, Peter too is called old there where the contest is one of passion: “When you were younger,” he says, “you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.” He said this to signify by what death he would glorify God (John XXI, 18). Before the contest he is called younger; in the contest, old—he who would complete every contest.

This, then, is what that David says, a warrior in youth and a peacemaker in old age: “I was young”—but do not think me still young—“indeed, I have grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread.”

61. What is the seed of the righteous? The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say “to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as to one: “And to your seed,” which is Christ (Gal. III, 16). Hear of the righteous seed: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV, 19).

And now, if someone coming from the nations hears our word, and the Lord deigns to help so that Christ may be formed in his soul and bring forth the birth of faith, Christ will be his seed. In both cases the same is found.

Abraham, therefore, was both the father of generation according to the flesh and the one who first infused the word of the Lord into the breasts of the righteous. Therefore this seed of Abraham does not seek these loaves by which bodily nourishment is supplied, because it possesses the bread of righteousness that descended from heaven (John VIII, 39).

For just as those who do not perform the works of Abraham are denied to be Abraham’s children, so those who perform his work are the seed of Abraham and are received among his children.

But Elijah was the true seed of Abraham, for an angel supplied him with food, and in the strength of that food he walked for forty days. The true seed of Abraham did not seek this bodily nourishment, for loaves were brought to him from heaven. Finally, ravens supplied him with a daily meal. He was so lacking in everything that he possessed nothing of his own, and he was sent to distribute food to others.

Daniel was the true seed, for when he had been placed among the lions, dishes filled with the food of reapers were carried to him through the prophet Habakkuk. There is therefore the bread of angels, which man ate; for it is written: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII, 25).

This is the bread of which David said: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. He has settled me in a green place; he has led me beside the water of refreshment” (Ps. XXII, 2). Good David taught me the bread of angels, and he himself taught me the water of refreshment. This refreshment is spiritual; this refreshment is the repose of the inner mind.

Good is the water that washes away sin and cleanses the inward parts. Let us hear what this water is. “If anyone thirsts,” he says, “let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” He said this about the Spirit, whom those who were going to believe in him were beginning to receive (John VII, 37 ff.).

The righteous, therefore, needs neither this bread nor the water of refreshment, for the Holy Spirit is his rest and refreshment.

62. (Verse 26.) But how can one who shows mercy and lends throughout the whole day be in need? What does the righteous man lend at interest? Not bronze, iron, or lead, but silver tested by fire. He brings this to the Lord’s table and distributes it to those who ask: to one he gives one mina, to another two, to another five each day, and it never runs out.

But we have heard lending at interest censured in the Law, when Moses says: “You shall not lend at interest” (Deut. 23:19). There are two kinds of lending at interest: one involving money, the other grace. Distribute both, because it is written: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be still” (Gen. 4:7). You too, then, divide rightly, lest you sin. Let Moses himself teach you to divide rightly, since he admonished that it be divided correctly; [Note: Some handwritten codices read: “so that you may follow what Abel did, who divided rightly, and flee what Cain was—a murderer who [divided] rightly,” etc.] follow what Abel did, who divided rightly, and flee what Cain the murderer did, who did not know how to divide rightly.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, distributes divisions, since he works all things, distributing them to each one as he wills: he according to his will, you according to your ability, according to the capacity of your understanding. Distinguish when the Law speaks of money and when of grace. For it says to you: “You shall lend to the nations, whose Lord exacts interest; but you shall not borrow” (Deut. 15:6). There is money that is lent at interest, and there is grace, from which the Lord exacts interest: money lent at interest possesses bronze, whereas grace bestows faith.

Lend faith, therefore, to the nations, so that grace may abound for you; but do not borrow like one in need, [Col. 0999A] rather lend as one rich and wealthy. Peter lent, Paul lent, John the Evangelist lent—or both Johns [Note: That is, both the Evangelist and the Baptist.]—and they were not in need. That is, they lent Christ’s money; they did not lend money at interest. Lend, then, and do not cease lending.

You hear what Scripture says: “All day long he shows mercy and lends.” The righteous man lends by day; the greedy man at night. Grace belongs to the light, but greed is the interest of darkness. Therefore the seed of the lender who lends faith will be in blessing, possessing, of course, the reward of blessing.

63. (Verses 27–29.) “Turn away from evil and do good;” [Note: The Roman edition had altered this verse, and verse 29 as well, so that it placed here: “And dwell forever and ever,” while there it read: “And they will glorify God throughout the ages of ages.” It had evidently looked to the passage we read below: “But what he deserved to dwell forever and ever.” Yet we judge that this has little force against the agreement of the manuscripts and the ancient editions.] “and dwell forever and ever. For the Lord loves judgment and will not forsake his holy ones; they will be preserved forever. But the unjust will be punished, and the offspring of the ungodly will perish. The righteous will possess the earth as an inheritance; and they will dwell upon it forever and ever.”

By these little verses the Prophet shows that we belong to the Lord, and that he himself is the arbiter of our thoughts and actions, observing the merits of each person. He does nothing without judgment, but distinguishes evil and good deeds by judgment. We must therefore turn away from evil and do good. To avoid confusing good and evil, first you must be free from guilt; afterward you must bring forth the fruit of innocence, so that you may be everlasting.

Do not think that your sins escape God’s notice; for this is how many fall. He sees and condemns everything, and exterminates the offspring of the ungodly—not, of course, offspring of bodily generation, but the succession of the inner mind and of ungodliness (Job 1:1). For Scripture plainly identifies Job as descended from the offspring of Esau. [Col. 0999C] How, then, did the offspring of Esau perish in Job, when this man was so great that he foresaw the Lord who was to come upon the earth, the one who would subjugate the devil, the ruler of this world?

The question, then, concerns this: that wickedness not be transmitted to descendants. Christ accomplishes this through the sacrament of baptism, so that each person may strip off what he was born as and put on what he was reborn as: may become [Note: The editions and the manuscripts of Victor and Colbert read: “may become not the heir of the slave-girl, but of grace.” The Vatican manuscript, together with five Gallican manuscripts, reads: “may become not the heir of the household,” etc. This is better; for here heirs of family or succession are being contrasted with heirs of grace.] not an heir of the household, but of grace, so that he may acquire for himself a permanent dwelling-place of eternal habitation. But whoever has deserved to dwell forever and ever will himself also honor God throughout the ages of ages.

64. (Verses 30 and following.) After instructing the righteous person in moral disciplines—teaching you what he ought to be and what the perfect form of righteousness is—he wants his mind to rise to wisdom and to theorems [Note: “Theorems,” that is, objects of contemplation, or, as they are called, objects.] and arouses his attention, so that he may gaze with an intent heart upon heavenly things, turn divine oracles over within himself, and shape his desire toward those things that please God. Let him meditate upon the Law, and let no commandment of the Lord pass him by; [Note: The ancient edition and the manuscripts of Victor and Colbert read: “Recognize the modes of the divine sacrament.” The Roman edition reads: “Recognize the movements of the divine sacrament.” Six manuscripts read as in the text, except that the Reginensis has “sacraments.” We do not know whether the meaning may best be achieved by reading: “Let him recognize the mysteries of divine movement and action.”] let him recognize the movement of the divine sacrament.

Finally, from this point I saw the holy Prophet rise in his precepts: “The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgment. The law of his God is in his heart; and,” he says, “his steps will not be tripped. Wait for the Lord and keep his way; and he will exalt you, so that you may possess the earth as an inheritance. When sinners have perished, you will see it. I saw the ungodly exalted and raised above the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found.”

The earlier statements are moral; these are intelligible. What is the mouth of the righteous that will meditate wisdom, if not the inner man? [Col. 1000B] For there are two men in each person: one inner, the other outer. The inner man thinks about the things of the mind and speaks the things of the mind; the outer man concerns himself with the things of the body.

Yet when the Lord came, he joined both together and created the two in one man, so that they would not attack one another with divergent impulses, but would be united with one another through the unity of their wills.
