Therefore “the mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom.” For now the outer man of the righteous himself has also been infused with the discipline of the inner man and conformed to his nature; he performs his duties, so that the flesh may meditate what belongs to the inner mind.

But lest this seem incredible to you, hear the Apostle saying (Phil. 3:21) that the Lord Jesus “will transfigure the body of our lowliness, so that it may be conformed to the body of his glory.” [Note: Some manuscripts read: “he transfigured the body of our humanity.”]

Who would dare say that flesh without sin—the flesh assumed from the Virgin, flesh generated when the Spirit of God came upon Mary—which in no respect differed from the disciplines of wisdom, was without the virtues of the inner man or unable to pass into their practice, when what happened through its touch was beyond the human: the sick were healed, sight was restored to the blind, and the dead rose?

Accordingly it is fittingly written: “The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom,” because the whole person is spiritual and certainly not earthly. “As is the earthly, so are those who are earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are those who are heavenly.” Let the earthly, then, be absent; the heavenly has remained.

Therefore, referring to the times of the Redeemer, the Prophet said, “he will meditate,” although one among many may have written “he meditates.” This does not conflict with the meaning, because for the spirit of the prophets future things are present. Others think that “mouth” is used for “mind.”

Solomon beautifully explained this for us, saying: “The account of the righteous is always wisdom, but the fool changes like the moon” (Eccli. 27:12)—that is, he is often altered, does not persist in his own judgment, and seems to pour out light in darkness without being able to retain it. [Note: You may perhaps be surprised that Ecclesiasticus is here, and in the following Psalm at verse 12, attributed to Solomon. Not only do more learned writers, including Augustine—who wrote of this book, as also of the Book of Wisdom, in *The City of God*, book XVII, chapter 20—have no doubt that it is not Solomon’s; Ambrose himself, in book I of *On the Interpellation of Job*, chapter 3, no. 6, testifies that the same Ecclesiasticus was written by Sirach. Yet when he gave it the title of Solomon, he did so either because, as Augustine says in the passage cited, common usage, on account of the eloquence of its language, had found some resemblance to Solomon and therefore called it Solomon’s, or because Jesus son of Sirach had compiled it from Solomon’s sayings. As for its authority, although it was not always held in such esteem in the Eastern Church, it is clear that it was always held in the highest esteem in the Western Church, both from the passage of Augustine already cited and from the fact that Ambrose himself, in *On the Good of Death*, chapter 8, no. 35; *On Elijah and Fasting*, chapter 18, no. 67; and in *On Psalm 118*, sermon 20, verse 153, as well as elsewhere, invariably treats it as authoritative. A fuller discussion of this same book may be found in Huet, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, proposition 4 on Ecclesiasticus, nos. 1, 6, and following. See also Blessed Thomas, I, q. 89, a. 8, ad 2; likewise II-II, q. 174, a. 4, ad 4; and Father Nicolai on both passages.]

65. Let the meditation of wisdom, then, always be in your heart and on your lips, and let your tongue speak judgment; let the law of your God be in your heart. Therefore Scripture says to you: “You shall speak of them while sitting in your house, while walking on the road, while sleeping, and when you rise” (Deut. 6:7).

Let us speak of the Lord Jesus, because he is Wisdom; he is the Word and the Word of God. For this too is written: “Open your mouth to the word of God.” Whoever sounds forth his sayings and meditates on his words breathes him forth. Let us always speak of him. When we speak of wisdom, he is wisdom; when we speak of virtue, he is virtue; when we speak of righteousness, he is righteousness; when we speak of peace, he is peace; when we speak of truth, life, and redemption, he is all these.

“Open your mouth to the word of God,” it is written. You open it; he will speak. Therefore David said: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me” (Ps. 84:9). And the Son of God himself says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 81:11).

But not everyone can receive the perfection of wisdom as Solomon did, nor as Daniel did. Yet the spirit of wisdom is poured into all according to their capacity—but into all who are faithful. If you believe, you possess the spirit of wisdom. Therefore the Wise Man says: “I believed; therefore I spoke” (Ps. 115:10). When you have believed, you will receive the grace of speaking.

The one who believes is redeemed; the one who prays is redeemed—if he devoutly attends to his prayers, is constant in prayer, anticipates the day, frequents the night, and meets the sun in the morning, so that he himself may be illuminated by Christ before the earth is illuminated by the sun’s rising; [Note: Thus the edition and a few manuscripts. A larger number read: “Let him meet the sun only in the morning.” This is not inappropriate if one mentally supplies “with its rays,” “at its hours,” or something similar.] and the one who sings psalms is redeemed; the one who is pierced with repentance is redeemed.

66. Therefore always meditate and always speak of the things of God while sitting in your house. We can understand “house” as the Church; we can also understand it as the inner house within us, so that we may speak within ourselves.

Judges sit in Jerusalem; thrones sat in judgment; the council of judges also sat, and the books were opened. The prophecy says: “And do everything with counsel” (Eccli. 32:24). Judge your deeds with counsel; drink wine with counsel; speak with counsel, so that you may escape sin and not fall through excessive speech.

While sitting, speak with yourself as one who is judging. Speak on the road, so that you may never be idle. You speak on the road if you speak in Christ, because Christ is the way. Speak to yourself on the road; speak to Christ.

Hear how you should speak to him. “I desire men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger and disputation” (1 Tim. 2:8). Speak, O man, while sleeping, lest the sleep of death overtake you. Hear how you should speak while sleeping: “If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling-place for the God of Jacob” (Ps. 131:4–5).

By diligence overcome nature; drive sleep from the body. We cannot shape our nature, but we can shape our diligence. David was a man: at night he allowed himself some sleep, but he drove sleep away, washing his bed every night and watering his couch with tears. Therefore he always remembered his Lord upon his bed and meditated on him, so that he might anticipate the dawn and Christ might shine upon him in the darkness, saying: “Rise, you who sleep” (Eph. 5:14).

This grace is not found in everyone, but diligence can be found in many. Do not wait, then, for Christ to awaken you; rather awaken Christ. He awakens Christ who, while sleeping, thinks about him. If you awaken him, he too will awaken you from sleep and raise you from death, saying to you: “Rise from the dead” (ibid.).

When you rise, or rise again, speak of him, so that you may fulfill what you are commanded. Hear how Christ awakens you. Your soul says: “The voice of my brother is knocking at the door” (Song 5:2); and Christ says: “Open to me, my sister, my bride.”

Hear how you awaken Christ. The soul says: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you awaken and raise up love” (Song 3:5). Love is Christ.

Hear also how you should speak while sleeping: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2). These things are common to all; now raise your mind somewhat higher.

67. Speak while sitting in your house—in this earthly house of this dwelling, which is being dissolved, in which we are away from the Lord. For while placed in this body, and desiring rather to be clothed upon than unclothed, we are exiles from Christ and groan heavily.

While sitting in this house, then, confess your sins, because you sat and did not stand, and did not say: “Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem” (Ps. 122:2). Speak rather, and do not hide your offenses; speak while sitting, so that you may hear him say: “Rise after you have sat, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Ps. 127:2).

Speak while walking on the road—that is, while passing through the course of this life. Speak here, lest there you become mute, as the man became mute who had not previously believed the angel of Christ; afterward, however, when he believed, he received his voice again.

Speak while sleeping and rest, buried with Christ, so that you may rise with him in newness of life. Speak even when buried in the tomb, as the souls of the saints spoke when they sought vengeance from the author of death: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood?” (Rev. 6:10).

Finally, speak when you rise, as the one taught who said: “I slept, and rested, and rose again, because the Lord will receive me” (Ps. 3:6).

There also, then, “the mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom,” until he reaches the loftier secrets of the heavenly tabernacle, full of sacred delight and gladness. Scripture taught us this when David said: “I remembered these things, and I poured out my soul within me; for I shall enter into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God. Amid the voice of rejoicing and confession, the sound of one feasting” (Ps. 42:5).

Thus, whether sitting in this bodily house, or having departed from here, or walking on the road, when we are caught up—if we are worthy—to meet Christ, we shall speak even while sleeping.

68. Receive the third ἀναγωγή—that is, the third spiritual elevation—by which the soul of the righteous raises itself. For there is a certain spiritual sleep to be understood, concerning which Solomon says: “If you sit, you will sit without fear; if you sleep, you will rest sweetly, and you will not fear the terror that comes upon you, nor the attacks of the ungodly when they come upon you” (Prov. 3:24 and following).

You will rest sweetly and will fear neither terror nor the attacks of the ungodly when they come upon you, if your tongue speaks the judgment of God and you always have it before your eyes, leaving no place for sin and knowing that the price of offense will be paid by the repayment of punishment.

He interpreted this in the ninetieth Psalm, saying: “You will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow flying by day, nor the business that walks in darkness, nor the encounter and the noonday demon. A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you. Nevertheless, with your eyes you will look on, and you will see the repayment of sinners” (Ps. 91:5 and following).

For when the righteous man speaks the judgment of God—or when he himself speaks what is righteous and full of true judgment—he does not speak in anger, nor from the distress of a grieving spirit, nor from pain, nor from any passion. He speaks from truth; he speaks from equity, so that his judgment does not incline according to feeling, but what he says is weighed by a true examination. For he judges what should be said and what should not be brought forth.

A similar saying is this: “The lips of the wise are bound by understanding” (Prov. 15:7), because everything they say appears to conform to true understanding, and through the prudence of their discernment they understand what they ought to say or keep silent about. Thus they restrain what should be silenced with a kind of closure and bond of the lips; but in what ought to be said, the bonds of the lips are loosened.

Rightly, then, he first said: “The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom.” For prolonged meditation can produce a full judgment, which the righteous will speak at the proper time, when he has seen perfect things face to face. For now, concerning things we do not comprehend, we cannot speak truly.

Finally, Paul too did not presume to speak, though he was caught up into paradise and heard heavenly secrets. Rather, wishing not to err in what he said, he declared: “How inscrutable are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). But now, freed from the body, he may perhaps comprehend the kinds of unsearchable ways and his judgments, which are like a great abyss.

69. (Verse 31.) The form of righteousness is still being described and enlarged, when Scripture says: “The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps will not be tripped.” The law of God is in the heart of the righteous. What law? Not a written law, but a natural one; for the law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the unrighteous.

The law is in his heart, not superficially, as on the lips of the Jews; for one believes with the heart unto righteousness. Whoever believes also speaks, but whoever speaks does not necessarily believe. Thus the people did not believe, of whom it was said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

If, therefore, the nations do what belongs to the Law, they are a law to themselves, recognizing what they ought to follow and what they ought to avoid, how much more the faithful and righteous person, who lives according to the image and likeness of God, knows how to discern what is beautiful and honorable and to use the legitimate rudder of natural wisdom, lest his footsteps be tripped—like Esau, whom his brother tripped because of his greed for food, so that he fell and his footsteps were brought down to death.

70. (Verses 32–33.) The more righteous someone is, the more the enemy lies in wait for him. Therefore Scripture says: “The sinner watches the righteous and seeks to destroy him. But the Lord will not abandon him into his hands, nor will he condemn him when judgment is passed upon him.”

When the sinner sees that the righteous man speaks with his mouth, meditates wisdom in his heart, speaks judgment with his tongue, and keeps the Lord’s law in his heart, he tries to inflict the death of sin upon him; but the Lord protects him.

Therefore let us not fear the plots of the sinner, because God is for us. If God is for us, who is against us? Thus God will not abandon his righteous man, nor condemn him when he has passed judgment concerning him. For he is a true judge, and therefore righteousness cannot be endangered.

Hence Aquila also said: “He will not condemn him when judging him.” Symmachus: “He will not condemn him when the righteous man is judged.”

71. But because the Seventy rendered it: “When judgment is passed upon him,” [Col. 1004D] we think that he looked toward another matter, since it is written: “For the Lord himself will come into judgment” (Isa. 3:14).

But into what judgment? Hear him saying: “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 51:6). Therefore the Lord presents himself to be heard, so that he may be judged concerning himself and prevail all the more.

Hear how he presents himself: “My people, what have I done to you? Or in what have I grieved you? Or in what have I troubled you? Answer me. For I brought you out of Egypt and freed you from the house of slavery” (Mic. 6:3–4).

And elsewhere: “I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will remember them no more; but you, remember, and let us be judged” (Isa. 43:25–26).

72. [Col. 1005A] This is a grave judgment, when the Lord asks to be judged concerning himself against man. What answer will you give him who bestowed everything upon you and placed you over all things? He subjected to you the Egyptians, among whom you had come as a guest; afterward he drowned those who pursued you in the sea.

He destroyed and overthrew your enemies; he created and fashioned you; he redeemed you with his own blood—and you surrender yourself to serve his enemy! He forgave you all your sins—and you commit worse ones!

He calls you; you will come into judgment. What will you answer him, when, unless he forgives you again, you are lost?

Therefore, seeing that he was weighed down all the more by this certain accommodation of God to human custom, [Note: “By this accommodation,” that is, by God’s use of human custom and manner, in which he adapts himself to us.] holy David fled from judgment and asked for mercy, saying: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 143:2).

He confesses that he has been placed in darkness like one dead in the world. He carefully said “like one dead in the world,” not “dead”; for those who die in Christ are not dead in the world. Those are dead in the world who establish the whole life they have lived in the world in destruction and death.

Therefore, like a desperate man, he flees to a remedy, saying: “Answer me quickly, O Lord, for my spirit has failed” (ibid., 7). For, with such a judgment set before him, his spirit failed—a judgment in which truth would have to be examined rather than mercy bestowed.

73. Yet the Lord is so compassionate that, although no living person is justified in his sight—for who, however righteous, is not liable to sin? Or whose life is such that it may be judged worthy of likeness to God?—surely one who has been made in the image and likeness of God ought, just as God is without sin, likewise to be without sin.

What punishment, then, is one worthy of who has lost so great a grace of the Lord’s work and the likeness of divine beauty?

But because he is merciful, even if he submits himself to judgment, he does not judge the righteous person, but the unrighteous. He spares the righteous person, who sins as a result of the frailty of his condition; he punishes the unrighteous person, as one who detests the ungrateful.

Furthermore, even if you have many works of righteousness, do not be impatient or arrogant, imagining that you must demand the rewards of righteousness in this world, or complaining that some adversity has happened to you undeservedly. As long as you live, a contest is owed you, not a reward. [Note: Five Gallican manuscripts read: “Even if you have much righteousness in your works, do not be impatient or arrogant, demanding rewards,” etc.]

74. (Verse 34.) Wait, then, either for the Lord as helper or as rewarder: “And keep his ways”—that is, to wait for him whom you think should be awaited and to preserve his commandments.

Even if you are crushed, even if you are afflicted, even if you waste away through illness, still wait for the Lord, and hope will not put you to shame.

75. The Lord will come and exalt you, so that you may possess the earth as an inheritance. It is clear that this is the higher land, not this earthly one in the valley, but that of the eternal promise, in which whoever is established is exalted by the Lord.

76. But you will see when sinners have perished; for then the reward of the righteous will come, when judgment has been passed upon the merits of the ungodly.

But sinners do not all perish in the same way. They perish before you if you do not admire their power and riches, if you are not moved when you discover that they abound in honors, children, and friends. These things belong to the world, and the world is subject to worldly wickedness. The prince of this world favors those who serve him, according to the saying: “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9).

Why do you seek to have these things given to you, when the ungodly man himself who gives them cannot remain in them for long? He too passes away; how can the things he has bestowed not pass away?

Only maintain a steadfast mind, hold fast to righteousness, let no one move you, and you will see that the ungodly is nothing.

77. (Verse 35.) Finally, hear him saying: “I saw the ungodly exalted above measure and raised above the cedars of Lebanon. And I passed by, and behold, he was not.”

I saw him in this world; I saw him with the eyes of the body. I also saw him boasting and exalting himself in his words, thinking himself to be something when he is nothing.

How does he exalt himself? “I will set my throne above the clouds,” he says, “and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). He exalts himself, so that you see him like the cedars of Lebanon raised above measure: they too are tall, and they are on a very high mountain.

Rightly, then, they are raised above measure, and the ungodly appears exalted above measure when he establishes himself on that mountain concerning which it is written: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and cast into the sea’” (Matt. 17:19).

To what mountain? “To the demon,” he says, by whom this man had been invaded and oppressed, whom you marvel to see healed. Therefore he has more love in Christ than power in the devil.

You see a cedar raised above measure on a very high mountain; but it is broken by the wind, consumed by fire, and dissolved by age. So it is with the rich man in this world. He shines with a certain splendor of worldly grace like Lebanon; he relies upon the world’s power and exults in resources and riches.

He seems to you to be something before you say: “As I pass by, I will see” (Exod. 3:3). For just as Moses passed beyond material things in spirit and mind and saw God, so you too, if you pass beyond this place and raise the step of your mind toward God’s grace, will see that the one who seemed most powerful to himself on this earth is nothing.

Therefore God the Word says to your soul, to your mind: “Come here from Lebanon, bride; come here from Lebanon: you will pass over and pass through” (Song 4:8). If you pass beyond worldly things, you will pass through to paradise.

Hear the one passing by: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). Hear again the one passing through: “Amen, amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (ibid., 43).

78. What does “Behold, he was not” mean? “In the beginning was the Word.” Whoever sees the Word, whoever shares in the Word, himself also exists, because the Word of God always is. The speech that comes from him is not “is and is not,” but “is”; and it remains in the one who follows God.

But whoever does not know the Word does not exist, because he does not cling to the one who said: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14). [Col. 1007A] Whoever clings to him is one spirit with him. And where there is spirit, there is life.

Therefore Scripture says of God: “He gives life to the dead and calls those things that are not as though they were” (Rom. 4:17). That is, he calls the nations that did not exist as his people who did exist; for our fathers existed, those who had been chosen by God.

And elsewhere it is said: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19); he does not know those who are not. Esther also says: “Do not give the rod of your kingdom to those who are not” (Esth. 14:11).

Rightly, then, the righteous man says: “And I passed by, and behold, he was not.” That is, I saw him exalted above measure in the world before I understood that the world is nothing. But when I passed in mind above the world, I saw that the one who had previously been exalted above measure in this world was no longer there.

79. And you, if you are righteous, pass from present things to those that are future, and present things will pass away for you. “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. 24:35).

For the righteous, then, everything passes away. The ungodly passes away; he is like vanity, and his days pass like a shadow. Nor do present things merely pass away for the righteous; when he directs his attention to future things, these present things are already passing away.

See how present things passed away for the righteous man. In the time of the Prophet David there was a synagogue, and the Church from the nations did not exist. Yet he speaks of future things as though they were present: “Bless the Lord, O nations” (Ps. 66:8).

Then above he says: “God has gone up amid jubilation” (Ps. 47:6). He passed beyond the future times of unbelief—not in age, but in mind—and celebrated with devout faith the Lord’s resurrection, which was to occur many ages later, saying: “Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises” (ibid., 7).

He rejoices and exults as though he were present at the mysteries of the nuptial union of Christ and the Church. He also expressed the reason for the celebration, saying: “God reigns over all the earth” (ibid., 8).

Therefore, if we pass beyond and those future things seem to us already to have passed away, it is like passing beyond the earth while sailing: you see the earth itself passing away and, as it were, departing from you. Sailors often flee from the shore, especially during a storm; yet as they flee from it while sailing, the shore itself rather seems to flee from the sailors.

If you flee this world, it too will flee from you; if you pass beyond this earth, it too will pass beyond you. You sail upon this sea and are tossed upon the waves of this world. Flee the shore: it contains rocks and stones, as it is written: “Cast the stones out of the way” (Isa. 62:10).

If you hasten through this aerial depth toward the harbor of the divine will, you will see that all these things have passed away from you. For what difference does it make whether they have passed away, or whether you judge that they have passed away from you?

80. There is another ungodly man who appears exalted and raised above the cedars of Lebanon; if you pass beyond him, he will not exist, and you will not find his place.

Consider a Jewish scribe reciting the sequence of the ancient Scriptures but not following them. You hear him reciting them with his lips and marvel at him as learned. You ask what he thinks, and he answers according to the letter and runs through the history.

He appears to you exalted above measure and raised up if you consider the letter. Pass over to spiritual understanding, because the Law is spiritual. Then you see that he is nothing, and you say: “I saw the ungodly exalted above measure . . . and I passed by, and behold, he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found.”

I sought him where he ought to have been, where life is, but I did not find him. He was not there where life was, because he was dead, and therefore his place was not found either. For what place does a dead man have, who did not exist and never existed? The one who was in the letter did not exist, for “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.”

I sought him, therefore, in order to find him; he did not present himself to be found. That is, I wanted to convert him, but he did not wish to present himself to me for conversion. I did what belonged to one who seeks; he fled what should have belonged to one returning.

Finally, the soul that wishes to be converted seeks the Word, and when it has found him, it says: “I held him and will not let him go” (Song 3:4)—that is, the Son of God, the Word of God.

But the unrighteous man who did not wish to be healed—I sought him and did not find him. Therefore do not imitate him.

81. (Verse 37.) “Keep innocence and behold equity.” Whoever keeps innocence sees equity, because the pure see God, whose rod is upright and whose justice is straight, so that he turns away from those who have inclined toward pursuits of wickedness. Good is innocence, which sees God.

[Note: The Greek Psalter has φύλασσε ἀκακίαν, “guard innocence.” The Hebrew has “guard integrity,” that is, “integrity.” The Syriac has “simplicity.” The Arabic has “gentleness.” Many Latin witnesses have “truth.” We have seen none that has “perfection,” although that reading differs very little from the Hebrew.]

Finally, others rendered it: “Keep perfection.” For the perfect person is the one who knows no malice and no deceit. Therefore he says: “Keep perfection,” because “there are remains for the peaceful man.”

“Remains” are called what remains of a human being from a dead body, from its spoils. They are called remains because after a person’s death they appear to survive; for what is preserved for the resurrection survives.

Therefore, more truly, the remains of a human being are the hope of resurrection, the faith of conversion, and the grace of love, because the ungodly do not rise for judgment. The life of the righteous, however, is known to God and is approved by the Lord’s judgment.

That saying beautifully applies to this passage: “The remnant according to the election of grace has been saved” (Rom. 11:5).

82. (Verse 38.) “But the unjust will all perish together; the remains of the ungodly will perish.” The remains of the righteous are virtues; the remains of the ungodly are wickedness and the sin of faithlessness. These will be wiped out, so that they may no longer exist.

[Col. 1008D] **83. (Verse 39.)** “But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord,” not from the world, not from the elements. Heaven and earth will pass away. I do not entrust my salvation to heaven, because heaven itself passes away; for it is said of the many heavens: “They will perish, but you remain” (Psalm 101:27). I entrust it to God alone, who remains and who can forgive sins, so that he may be my protector in time of tribulation, help me, deliver me, rescue me from sinners at the time of his judgment, and save me, because I have hoped in him. In him alone I have hoped; for he does not wish us to serve both him and another. Whoever serves him alone is delivered, because to him belong praise, glory, and perpetuity [Col. 1010A] throughout the ages, now and always, and forever and ever.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXXVII

[Col. 1009]

**815 PREFACE**

[Col. 1009A]

**1.** I wrote two little books on repentance some time ago, and I think that I should write again. First, because it is useful to pray daily for the forgiveness of sins; and then because in those two little books the exhortation to repentance is either an advance toward it or is effective if it is practiced. Now, however, it must be explained how repentance ought to be practiced; for it is of no benefit to practice it unless it is practiced as one ought.

In this matter Saint David has set before us a model of instruction. He seems to me to have tasted sin for the purpose of teaching how sin could be abolished. For from where did medicine take its beginning, if not from a wound? While the earliest age of the human race teaches others what benefited it, and shows others how it healed its own wound, experience made an art, and illness became instruction. This is indeed the first and most effective school of medicine, formed by experience rather than conjecture. Therefore the first physicians were called from experience **ἐμπειρικοί** (*empeirikoi*, “empiricists”), and the other schools were derived from that one and drew from it a certain practical use of their own skill.

[Note: [Col. 1009D] Several manuscripts read: “and from it a certain juice,” etc.]

What, then, is more powerful for urging repentance than that the holy prophet David taught us to repent of our sins? Who would disdain to humble himself before God when a king humbled himself? Or who would hesitate to afflict his soul when so great a prophet afflicted his, paying the price of tears for the redemption of sin?

Although throughout the whole body of his writings he spread instructions concerning the practice of repentance—for which of his psalms is not a medicine for a sinful conscience, since in one place he showed how he was overwhelmed (Psalm 117:13), and in another how he was troubled (Psalm 29:8), so that he might demonstrate not only how wounds are to be healed but also how they are to be avoided, and teach us by his own example? Who, then, should believe that he stands, where even the stronger has fallen?—nevertheless, in the thirty-seventh psalm he expressed a greater force of inward grief and lamentable mourning.

[Note: [Col. 1010D] Some manuscripts read: “where he sees even the stronger man fallen.”]

**2. (Verse 1.)** Finally, at the beginning the title itself warns us that instructions of this kind are being formulated, for we read: “A psalm of David for the commemoration of the Sabbath day.” The definition of repentance is complete in the remembrance of sins, so that each person may chastise his sins, as it were, with the scourge of daily speech and condemn the crimes committed by him. Thus we are taught when the Lord says: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:26). And the Apostle says: “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

But perhaps it may cause difficulty that he did not say “the commemoration of sins,” but “of the Sabbath day,” or, as another text has it, “of Sabbaths” (Exodus 20:8 ff.). What, then, is the Sabbath except the rest of things to come and the relief of things present, by which the Law commands human works to cease and burdens to be laid down? What burdens are heavier than our sins? Let these be laid down on the days of the Sabbaths—that is, during this time of the present life.

For the whole week is completed in seven days. The world was formed in six days, and on the seventh day the Lord rested from his work. He rests in our gentleness, as he himself said: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and gentle?” (Isaiah 66:2). Therefore release yourself every Sabbath and lighten the weight of your errors, so that you may deserve to reach the rest of that future Sabbath in safety. For if you carry grievous sins from here, you will have no rest there.

Unload your mind, then; cast away everything by which your conscience is burdened and oppressed, lest your flight occur in winter or on the Sabbath. This life is labor; that one is rest. Let the end of this world find you lighter, lest, weighed down by sins, you be unable to flee. Flee beforehand, so that you may forestall it.

The person who is not held by the enticements of the world, who frees himself from all concern for it, flees the world. Flee also the wrath to come—that is, the day of judgment. The one who practices repentance flees it. Thus John the Baptist defined it when he said: “Generation of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come? Bring forth, therefore, fruits worthy of repentance” (Matthew 3:7–8).

**3.** You heard read today that John was baptizing at Aenon, near Salim (John 3:23). Aenon is interpreted as “eye of punishments”; Salim itself means “the one ascending.” This is the interpretation.

Whoever therefore chooses to be baptized foresees punishments; and for that reason he flees to the sacrament of baptism, so that he may lay down every sin and not become liable to punishments. Perhaps the person baptized with the baptism of repentance foresees punishments; but the one baptized in Christ looks toward grace.

The baptism of John, therefore, is the “eye of punishments”; the baptism of Christ is the “eye of graces.” Although John was baptizing at Aenon, he was baptizing near “the one ascending”; for this too is contained in the interpretation, since Salim is said to mean “the one ascending.” He was therefore near Christ, whose coming he announced.

For the Son of man who descended from heaven is himself also the one who ascended into heaven, in order to fulfill all things. And because “as is the heavenly one, so are the heavenly ones,” the one who lays aside earthly things and is buried with Christ also ascends into heaven, so that with Christ he may rise from the death of sin to newness of life and to participation in the inheritance, so that he may become, as it is written, “an heir of God and a joint-heir with Christ” (Romans 8:17).

[Col. 1011A]

**4.** Repentance, then, is true medicine. It was rightly proclaimed when the physician came from heaven, who would not aggravate wounds but heal them. He is a good physician, who taught us how to seek remedies in this earthly body of ours, when a flower of healing herb sprang up for us—he who condemned sin in the flesh because of sin.

The flesh therefore became an antidote, although previously it had been the poison of sin, because it was the enticement of sins. Hear how the flesh of God becomes an antidote: “The Word was made flesh” (John 1:14). He put his hand into the serpent’s cave, emptied the poison, and removed sin; that is, because of sin he condemned sin in the flesh.

[Col. 1011B]

**5.** And so that this may be considered more fully, let us review the Apostle’s passage itself. For it is written thus: “God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh because of sin, so that the justification of the Law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” (Romans 8:3–4).

The Son of God therefore came in the likeness of sinful flesh. Certainly he did not come merely in the likeness of flesh, since he assumed true flesh; but he came in the likeness of sinful flesh—that is, of flesh subject to sin. For our flesh had been made by deceit and infused with the serpent’s poison; it was flesh of sin. After it became subject to sin, it had become flesh of death, because it was bound over to death.

Christ assumed in his own flesh the likeness of this flesh, already guilty and already condemned. For although he assumed the natural substance of this flesh, he assumed none of its contagion. He was neither conceived in iniquities nor born in sins, since he was born of the Virgin not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from the Holy Spirit.

What, then, does “he condemned sin in the flesh because of sin” mean? Does it mean that he condemned sin because of the likeness of sinful flesh? Or because Christ assumed our sins not through practice but in their condition, not as a crime but through the sacrament of his mercy, and became sin for us although he himself committed no sin?

[Note: [Col. 1011D] Five manuscripts read: “He did not assume it through use and condition, nor through guilt, but through the sacrament of his mercy,” and so forth.]

Or does it mean that, even from this flesh of sin—that is, from this flesh of ours, subject to sin and already condemned—he condemned sin in the flesh, teaching how, while placed in the flesh, we should walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit?

For it is sin to walk according to the flesh. The person who lives according to the wisdom of the flesh lives for luxury, pleasures, wantonness, and the desires of the flesh; “for the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God,” and therefore those who are in the flesh cannot please God.

Thus he condemns sin because of sin: by cleansing himself from the vices of the flesh, he lives according to the Spirit, wholly devoted to God and intent upon heavenly utterances. For this reason Christ came, so that he might do not his own will—that is, the will of the flesh—but the will of God. Therefore, if anyone follows him in doing what pleases God and restraining the appetite of his flesh, he is an imitator of Christ.

[Col. 1012A]

**6.** We have expressed what we have understood. You who read, choose what you will follow. There is no error where there is a simple affection of piety and a wholly faithful understanding.

Christ condemned sin by assuming the likeness of sinful flesh, so that he might abolish the sins of our flesh. He condemned sin so that he might crucify our sins in his own flesh. He himself became sin for us, so that we might be the righteousness of God in him—we who were the captivity of death and the prey of the serpent.

This assumption of sins, therefore, belongs to piety, not to guilt. Through it the eternal God absolved us from sin, who did not spare his own Son but made him to be sin for us.

Moreover, Christ condemned sin in the flesh from the very flesh of sin—that is, through the flesh itself, which, by a certain judicial force and censorial authority, hates the vices it had been accustomed to love and shudders at the impurity it had considered pleasure. It separates itself from wantonness, rejects desires, renounces crimes and offenses, and drives away greed, which emasculates the vigor of the flesh.

Behold the imitator of Christ, himself condemning sin because of sin in the flesh. “So I run,” he says, “not as uncertainly; so I fight, not as one beating the air. But I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (2 Corinthians 9:26–27).

**817 7.** We have not, I think, wandered beyond the subject without purpose, since this too pertained to the healing of humanity. Just as God, providing for this medicine, commanded the earth to produce the wholesome juices of herbs and trees, by which wounds of the flesh might be healed, so also he filled the sequence of the divine Scriptures with saving commands, by which the weakness of the soul might be healed.

How serious it is, then, that dumb animals know how to medicate themselves, seek healing herbs for their wounds, and do not refuse to choose them, while human intelligence does not seek the remedies for which a physician has even been sent—one who would point out the seeds of saving medicine in the ancient Scriptures and himself bring new ones!

How many things, therefore, are healthful although they are casually judged harmful? Let us take examples from the earth itself.

**8.** The serpent nourishes poison, has a harmful bite, and wounds the flesh; but even in its poison you will find an antidote, if you seek it. Finally, its flesh is burned, and from its ashes theriac is prepared, by which the force of poison is accustomed to be blunted so that it cannot cause harm.

It is not the earth, therefore, that is at fault because it produces the serpent, but the person who does not know how to beware of the serpent. The serpent itself can be of benefit to you, if you understand—indeed, if you do not disregard the physician’s instructions. Learn to imitate what you think must be fled.

“Be,” he says, “wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew 10:16). Guard your head as the serpent does; and even if you have been torn throughout your whole body, you will live again. Your head is Christ, because he himself is the head of the man. If you preserve the faith, then even if you die like the serpent, you too will rise again.

Imitate the serpent, which casts off its outer covering so that its inner self may be renewed. Imitate the serpent, which vomits out its poison. Blessed are you too if you vomit out your evil thoughts and lay aside the poisons of your wickedness.

There is a well-known account, strengthened by the authority of writers, that a female serpent, by hissing, promises intercourse to a serpent approaching the waters. Concerned for her own safety, she promises to grant the intercourse she seeks on the condition that the serpent first vomit out its poison. Having been captured, it obeys her commands, lays down its weapons, and, according to the custom of their union, inserts its head into her mouth. Then, when their intercourse begins to grow heated—whether through a kind of violence of nature or through the ardor of lust—she closes her jaws around him and presses the bites of lust with kisses, and thus the serpent’s head is severed.

**9.** Will you not recognize in the nature of the serpent a mystery of faith? That ancient serpent in Paradise incited the woman to adultery against God’s command. But when its poison had been poured into this world, the offspring of that woman, through the parent’s deception and the serpent’s many frauds, stripped it of its own weapons and cut off its head.

If its poisons should prevail, and sin—whose sting is death—should creep in, follow the example of physicians, so that the serpent may die for you, even if late. Crush its poison, break up its body, and understand that, mixed with healing juices, it must be tempered, so that it may not only lose its force and venom but may even become a remedy from poison.

That intelligible serpent dies for you if you die to sin, and your sins die for you. Its poison is crushed if your deeds prick you with remorse. All its venom is abolished if you cover yourself with good works and temper the crime committed through faithful confession.

Hear how the power of the dragon itself is crushed: “May God crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). First crush your heart, in which the dragon’s lair existed, so that it may not find a place where it can dwell. Crush the dragon’s flesh; its flesh is our sins.

Therefore God says to you: “The nations feast upon him” (Job 40:25). And further he says:

[Note: [Col. 1013D] All manuscripts and the old edition read *Praecurrit mori* (“He runs ahead to die” [uncertain]); the Roman edition, however, reads *praecurrit mors ei* (“death runs ahead of him”). This is evidently from the Septuagint, where one reads **ἔμπροσθεν αὐτοῦ τρέχει ἀπώλεια** (“destruction runs before him”), or, according to Aquila, **ἐκλιμία**.]

“He runs ahead to die [uncertain]; and the flesh of his body adheres to him” (Job 41:13–14).

For just as the saints are the body and members of Christ, so sinners who do not abandon sin but cling to sin are the body and members of the dragon. Therefore we feast upon the body of Christ, while they feast upon the body of the dragon. We feast because we strive to cling to Christ, upon daily remission and forgiveness of sins; but those who connect sins to sins every day feast upon the continuation of offenses and crimes.

**10.** Crush, therefore, these fleshes, and sprinkle upon them the contrition of your heart. Then pour over all of them the water of the Jordan. For the Jordan is both descent and ascent, since whoever descends into the sacred spring also ascends, so that he may seek the things that are above.

The one who is baptized in Christ descends into Christ’s death and ascends into his resurrection. But if, having already been baptized, you have gone astray, pour out the water of tears—not false tears but true ones—so that from the depths you may cry out to the Lord your God, and it may be said of you:

“A voice was heard in Rama, mourning and great weeping; Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be comforted, because they are not” (Jeremiah 31:15).

Rachel is the Church, in whom the people of God are blessed. Let her weep for you; let her deeply lament your sins, and let her weep greatly, so that she may not readily accept consolation, as those do who suffer profound grief. For this reason she refused to be comforted, because you have ceased to be what you were.

But through this perseverance in grief and tears, let her earn the right to say: “My son was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:32).

Or perhaps Rachel refused to be comforted concerning the children of the Jews because they are not—the very ones whom she had begotten so that they might exist. For this reason she did not accept consolation when the infants had been killed by Herod, because they did not believe in the coming of Jesus, fulfilling the measure of their crime by killing the infants so that the Son of the Virgin might also be killed among them.

Therefore the Lord’s Church refused to be comforted among the Jews, because they are not; but among Christians gathered from the nations she feasts and rejoices, because those who did not exist have begun to exist.

**11.** You have therefore sent the water of the Jordan, the water of grace; drink this first. You have sent the water of tears, the water of repentance; this is the second cup, so that you may restore the first.

Drink water from your own vessels; drink water from your own tears, so that you may say: “And I mingled my drink with tears” (Psalm 101:10). Your weeping, then, is your drink, and your tears are your food. “My tears,” he says, “have been my bread” (Psalm 41:4).

If tears are bread, then from the sin of iniquity you possess the food of conversion, according to what you read in the Gospel: “To whom more is forgiven, he loves more” (Luke 7:47). Thus we often see some who were previously negligent Christians become more diligent after committing some sin and, through repentance, habitually become perfect because of it.

As conversion comes from sin, so a remedy comes from poison. Hear this remedy: “The righteous person at the beginning of his speech is his own accuser” (Proverbs 18:17). The poison is sin; the remedy is accusation of one’s own crime. The poison is iniquity; confession is the remedy for a fall. Therefore a remedy truly comes from poison if you declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified.

**820 12.** But let us now approach the psalm itself, so that it may teach us how repentance ought to be practiced. It begins in this way:

# EXPOSITION

**13. (Verse 2.)** “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury.”

The person who practices repentance must be prepared to endure reproaches and undergo insults, and must not be disturbed if someone sets the charge of his sin before him. Since he himself ought to accuse himself, how can he refuse to tolerate another who rebukes him?

If he ought not fear being rebuked by a human being, how much more ought he not fear being rebuked by the Lord his God, against whom we all sin even in those things that are hidden—especially since condemnation in the present life is absolution in the future?

Those who are not condemned in this world will not be scourged with men. Woe to me if it is said of me: “He has received his reward” (Matthew 6:2). If a good deed is condemned by this sentence, how much more is a crime aggravated? If mercy, loudly proclaimed in words, is deprived of eternal fruit, how much more is the punishment of iniquity postponed with the addition of bitter interest?

Therefore the person who practices repentance ought to offer himself to punishment, so that he may be punished by the Lord here and not be reserved for eternal punishments.

[Note: [Col. 1015D] Several manuscripts read: “and not be reserved for future punishments.”]

He should not wait for the appointed time but meet the divine indignation beforehand.

**14.** Observe how David’s deeds correspond to his prayers. He had offended the Lord because he had ordered the people to be counted. In confession he forestalled God’s messenger, acknowledging that he had sinned greatly and acted very foolishly—not as though he were reminding one who had forgotten, but as though he were urging one who delayed, so that he would not postpone the disturbance caused by the offense any longer.

“I have sinned greatly,” he said, “because I have done this thing” (1 Chronicles 21:8); “and now, Lord, take away the iniquity of your servant.”

But hear how sins are taken away, from the one who says: “His sin is forgiven, because he has received double for his sins from the hand of the Lord” (Isaiah 40:2). He does not therefore ask that his sin be completely remitted, but that it be erased by a measured payment—that is, so that its memory may be erased in the future.

Finally, as though the Lord were addressing him through the voice of an intercessor, so that punishment for the error committed might not be prolonged, he sent the prophet Nathan to him.

[Note: [Col. 1015D] The Roman edition here and below substituted *Gad* from the sacred manuscripts. Since the other editions and manuscripts agree on the name Nathan, it appears that Ambrose’s memory failed here. To correct him on one’s own authority is, however, a matter requiring caution.]

Nathan came to the king and said to him: “Choose what should be done to you: three years of famine upon the land; or three months of fleeing from the face of your enemies, while they pursue you; or three days of death in the land. And now know and see what I shall answer the one who sent me” (1 Chronicles 21:11–12).

Observe how God teaches by what moderation his indignation may be softened: not if we refuse punishment altogether, but if we ask that its severity be lightened rather than avoided. He proposed three alternatives, so that David might choose what seemed more moderate.

Observe also how he calls him to repentance, so that we may offer ourselves to injury. He commands him to choose his punishment, so that even within the punishment a certain privilege of choice might be preserved, and so that he might console the guilty man with this word.

And David said to Nathan: “I am in great distress because of these three things; but let me fall into the hands of the Lord, for his mercies are many, rather than into the hands of men” (1 Chronicles 21:13).

Did he ask that the punishment for his error be forgiven? If he had done so, he would have been marked as impudent, having shown himself ungrateful toward divine moderation. For a modest confession greatly benefits the guilty person; and punishment, which we cannot avoid by defense, we lessen through shame.

He chose not what was free from the scourge but what he judged more moderate, so that he might entrust himself more to God’s gentleness—for God knows how to forgive—than to the power of men, who frequently exceed the proper measure of vengeance. He therefore has mercy who does not know how to err; he does not have mercy who shares in error.

**15.** Saint David’s faith did not deceive him, but even in the very offense he obtained the grace of divine mercy. For although the Lord had proposed to inflict death upon the land for three days, he did not allow even one day to pass. He relented readily by the hour of the midday meal and, to use the word of Scripture, “repented of the evil” (2 Samuel 24:16).

See how Scripture urges you not to flee repentance but to follow God, whom you ought to follow. It rightly added “over the evil,” because every harsh act of vengeance appears evil. For this reason the day of judgment is also called an evil day, from which the person whom God delivers is blessed, as it is written: “The Lord will deliver him in the evil day” (Psalm 40:2).

“And the Lord,” it says, “said to the angel that he should spare there.”

Observe that whenever the Lord wishes to forgive, he gives grace and confidence for entreaty. David saw the angel striking and said: “Behold, I am the one who sinned; I, the shepherd, have acted wickedly. But what have these, this flock, done? Let your hand be against me and against my father’s house” (1 Chronicles 21:17).

If the Lord had commanded the angel to spare, how was the angel still striking, unless the Lord, even though he wishes to forgive, wishes to be asked and brings it about that he is asked?

[Note: [Col. 1016D] All editions in the text read: “and he urges that he be asked.” The old edition in the margin, together with all the manuscripts, reads: “and he brings it about that he be asked.”]

Nor would a human being have seen the angel striking unless the Lord had revealed the angel to his eyes. Hence Elisha also says: “Lord, open the eyes of this boy, that he may see.” And the eyes of his servant were opened, and he saw the mountain full of horses and chariots around the prophet (2 Kings 6:17).

Nor should you be disturbed that the status of the servant is lower than that of a prophet or king, since the appearance of horses and chariots is also lower than the holiness of angels.

**16.** Perhaps it may seem harsh to some who read carelessly that David, humble and gentle of heart, who spared his enemies, chose the death of the people rather than his own flight or famine upon the land.

He avoided famine for the people because famine is considered worse than death and every punishment, and because pestilence follows it, contaminating the sky and piling up death. He did not ask for his own flight for this reason: a prophet could intercede for the people, as happened, but the people could not intercede for the prophet.

For it is written: “If the people should err, the priest will pray for them; if the priest should err, who will pray for him?” Yet when he saw the people being killed, he offered himself to the striking angel, so that he himself might rather be struck for the people.

It is more significant that, undeterred even by the sight of the dead, he offered himself to the sword than if he had chosen the alternative stipulated in the proposal. Thus in his choice he followed reason; in his grief, piety.

**17.** Observe also the Lord’s grace: he himself departed from the condition he had proposed. Is it a crime of mercy that he threatens more and exacts less? He preserves his promises in bestowing rewards, but in exacting punishments he lessens what he had prescribed.

When he is angry with the guilty, he delays; when he has mercy, he hastens to absolve. He terrifies in order to correct; he warns in order to amend; he forestalls in order to forgive.

Hence the Prophet says elsewhere concerning the Lord: “The cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine with mixture . . . yet its dregs have not been emptied” (Psalm 74:9). The cup is full for terrifying, but it is not emptied for striking.

The cup was full when death was commanded for three days; but God’s mercy intervened and restrained the angel’s hand before he emptied that cup.

To know that the cup or sword is punishment, hear him say: “Take this cup of unmixed wine from my hand, and you shall give it to drink to all the nations to which I send you; and they shall vomit and rage because of the sword” (Jeremiah 25:15–16).

And to Jerusalem it is said: “You have drunk the cup of wrath from the hand of the Lord; you have drunk the cup of ruin and emptied it, and there was none to comfort you” (Isaiah 51:17).

[Note: [Col. 1017D] Two manuscripts and the old edition have in the margin: “for you have drunk the cup of wrath.” The Hebrew has “for you have drunk the cup of deadly poison,” or, as Grotius translates it, “a dreadful cup.” The Chaldean has “you have drunk the cup of the curse.” Shortly afterward the Roman edition alone reads: “Jerusalem drank above measure, because she sinned above measure,” and so forth. This is less suitable, since Ambrose seems clearly to have had in mind the Septuagint wording, where the passage of Isaiah reads: **τὸ ποτήριον γὰρ τῆς πτώσεως, τὸ κόνδυ τοῦ θυμοῦ ἐξέπιες** (“for you drank the cup of falling, the measure of wrath”). For **κόνδυ** is a kind of measure, which the Synagogue is here declared to have drained completely.]

Jerusalem drank the measure because she sinned beyond measure. The Church of Christians does not know how to empty the cup of wrath, but she knows the emptied ointment, for whose sake Christ emptied himself so that he might give off fragrance everywhere.

From the hand of the Lord she received this gift; but she does not know the cup of death. I read of two cups: one of death, the other of life. Christ emptied the cup of death in his blood and supplied a new cup, so that we might say: “I will take the cup of salvation” (Psalm 115:13).

The new cup is the cup of the Testament, which is poured out for the remission of sins. This cup is poured out, and its dregs are not found, because it cleanses every offense.

[Note: [Col. 1018D] The Roman edition reads: “and its dregs are not emptied.” Other editions, together with the manuscripts, read: “and its dregs are not found.” The latter is better, since the point clearly is that the cup of the New Testament is not dreg-filled but pure, as it washes away every stain of crime.]

**18.** We have explained how, in taking vengeance, the Lord bends away from his anger. Let us explain how, in rewarding, he anticipates our prayer, and let us teach by an example.

Hear one of the two criminals saying to the Lord: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). The Lord answered: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise.”

The man was still asking that the Lord remember him when he came into his kingdom; but the Lord, although he had not yet come, was already granting him the heavenly kingdom. How swift is mercy! The prayer of the one who asks is slower than the reward of the one who bestows it.

**19.** David therefore maintained moderation and did not pray for complete remission, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury.”

Fury is called **θυμός** (*thymos*) in Greek, and means the force or impulse of anger. This is what the Latin intended to express: “Do not rebuke or correct me in anger, nor in the very impulse of anger.”

Correction, however, is instruction. In Greek it is called **παίδευσις** (*paideusis*), concerning which it is said: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord” (Psalm 93:13).

God is not subject to passion, as though he became angry, since he is impassible; but because he exacts vengeance, he appears to be angry. This is how it appears to us, because we are accustomed to exact vengeance with agitation.

Yet human beings too are often found to exact vengeance without being moved, administering vengeance and inflicting punishments with complete patience. Why, then, should you be surprised in the case of God if you recognize this sometimes in a human being?

We have already said that vengeance is called anger. Customarily, for example, we say of someone who has been punished that he has incurred the anger of the laws—not because he has incurred the anger of the laws, but because he has incurred the severity of the laws.

Thus elsewhere, concerning the ten plagues of Egypt, he says: “He sent his anger through evil angels” (Psalm 77:49)—that is, vengeance. For the law does not know how to become angry, but it knows the minister of the laws.

The author of the laws therefore does not know how to become angry; he wills to terrify, not to punish. Imitate the divine example, therefore, you emperors: be more severe in establishing laws, but merciful in exacting punishments. Let the severity of laws restrain insolent boldness; let the mercy of rulers rescue the guilty from punishment.

The Prophet therefore recognizes his guilt, sees his wounds, and asks to be healed. Whoever wishes to be healed does not fear being rebuked; but he does not wish to be rebuked in fury, rather by the word of God.

The word of God is health. For thus we read: “He sent his Word and healed them” (Psalm 106:20). He does not wish to be instructed in anger but in teaching, just as if you were to ask a physician not to cut your wound but to apply medicine: he presses with the medicine, but he does not cut.

Finally, there is pain, but not pain beyond measure; it bites, but does not make bloody.

[Col. 1018C]

**20. (Verse 3.)** And he added: “For your arrows are fixed in me.”

He seems to say the same thing as Saint Job, but the circumstances are different. For Job also says: “For the arrows of the Lord are in my body, whose fury drinks my blood; when I begin to speak, they pierce me” (Job 6:4).

Job complains of the wound of his body; David here laments the wounds of his soul. Perhaps David here practices repentance for sin, while Job pleads the cause of human weakness and, as an advocate of our frailty, asks the Creator for help toward the remedy. David therefore prays; Job intercedes.

For this reason David’s pain is more intense, since wounds of the soul are more serious than wounds of the flesh. Job says that the Lord’s arrows are in his body; David laments that they are fixed in him. Job’s blood is drunk; David’s is poured out. Job is pierced; David is wounded. God’s hand touched Job; over David it was firmly placed with a heavy weight.

David laments that his soul is filled with mockeries; Job, that his body is filled with sores.

[Note: [Col. 1018D] See the first two books on the Interpellation of Saints Job and David.]

We understand the hand of God as the power of punishment. This hand scourged the king of Egypt because of the wrong done to Abraham, on account of the attempted violation of Sarah’s chastity. This hand plunged the chariots, horses, and people of Egypt into the depths of the Red Sea.

This hand weighed down the mind of King Saul, so that he hated the grace of his preserver. Abandoned by his companions because of his transgression against the heavenly kingdom, deprived also of his sons who had been killed, and defeated by his enemies—a spectacle more shameful than any other for a king—he turned his own sword against himself, lest he should live as an old captive and survive his sons and kingdom.

David experienced this hand in himself and in his children, and lamented the incest of one and the parricide of the other. What is more grievous to a pious father than the destruction of his own salvation? He lamented at once the disgrace of his offspring and the ruin of their filial devotion. One was inflamed to incest by the affection of brotherhood; the other was armed for parricide by zeal for chastity.

Observe how, in the gravest crimes, the boundaries of virtues played with them. Would that the one had not loved his sister, or the other had not avenged her! Finally, driven from his native land by his son, David fled from the enemy whom he wished to be his heir. He feared to conquer, lest he should be conquered through the loss of filial affection.

21. But perhaps someone may say: How could the hand of God have been involved in parricide or incest, when such a deed is the work of the enemy? Let us understand, then, that even where the devil wounds, the arrows of the Lord are said to wound. For thus we read: when, in the assembly of the angels, the Lord turned toward the devil and praised His holy servant Job (Job 1:8 and following)—so that the envious one, the adversary of the human race, might be burned with envy (for the praise of the man of an inferior substance [Note: [Col. 1019D] The Roman edition removed the words “of the man of an inferior substance.” Not very judiciously; for here nothing else is indicated except that the praise of Job, a man whose substance and nature were inferior to the substance and nature of the demon, is the condemnation of that same demon.] is his condemnation, since he had been cast down from a higher state)—the devil answered that Job did not revere the Lord without reason, since, by God’s command, he abounded in everything. “But stretch out your hand,” he said, “and touch everything that he has; let us see whether he will not bless you to your face” (Job 1:11).

And God gave the devil power to stretch out his hand against everything that Job possessed. When these things had been done, and holy Job remained steadfast in his strength—for Job was not shaken either by the death of his children or by the loss of his possessions—the Lord again said to the devil, mocking him because he had destroyed everything Job had possessed and killed his children, yet had been utterly unable to move Job from his station of virtue. And he answered: “Whatever a man has, he will give for his life. But stretch out your hand,” he said, “and touch his flesh and his bones” (Job 2:4–5). And he received power again [Col. 1019D] to stretch out his hand against Job’s body, though he was to preserve Job’s soul. And he covered holy Job with ulcers (Job 19:21)—and there it says, “He has gone out from the Lord.”

We therefore observe that the hand of the Lord is spoken of where there is a human temptation, while the devil is raging. Indeed, Job himself said that it was the hand of the Lord that had touched him (Job 16:12), and he recalled that the arrows of the Lord were the arrows of pirates. “And he delivered me,” he says, “into the hands of the unjust” (ibid., 14). He himself, therefore, concluded [Note: [Col. 1020D] “Concluded,” that is, he completes and proves the argument.] that when the devil wounds, the arrows belong to the Lord, who permitted the devil to have the power to wound. Finally, if you command that your servant be beaten, is he not said to have been beaten by you even if he is struck by another person standing nearby? There is also this explanation: the Lord gives the tempter power so that the disposition of human beings may be tested in temptations. Persecution therefore takes place so that faith may shine forth, virtue may excel, and the inner mind may be revealed to all.

22. Thus temptation penetrates the inner parts of a person like an arrow, and acts like the sword of God, which searches the inward parts. The sword, however, is the powerful word of God, sharper than every exceedingly sharp sword. Concerning this sword, hear Simeon saying to Mary: “And a sword will pierce your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke 2:35). For everything is revealed by the word of God, in whose sight all things are naked and open. [Col. 1020B] [Note: [Col. 1020D] Some manuscripts read, “The soul itself is divided.”]

The soul itself is seen; the innermost marrow and the thoughts are made manifest. Finally, as Scripture says, there is no creature that can hide itself from His knowledge (Heb. 4:12–13). Let us therefore sell everything in order to buy the word, and store it within our inward parts.

23. Finally, the devil himself bears witness that a person gives everything he has for his soul, yet does not acknowledge that the price of his entire inheritance is worthy of the redemption of a single soul. Why do we spare an inheritance which the devil himself judges worthless in exchange for salvation? I have said too little in calling it an exchange for salvation: he testifies that it is too little even for error. For finally he says: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9). He showed him not only the riches of the world but also honors and kingdoms. If it is worth so much that the devil is worshiped, how much ought a Christian to offer in order to be raised again with Christ?

But let us send away the devil like the scapegoat into the desert; for he is not a faithful defender of the truth, even if at times he transforms himself into an angel of light.

24. We have an abundance of testimonies from the divine Scriptures, by which we are instructed that nothing in a human being is more precious than faith, and that no inheritance is so great that it can be set against the price of our salvation and our soul. By faith Abraham left his homeland (Gen. 12:4 and following), and the land and even the relatives whom he could see; and he followed the One whom he could not see as though he were looking upon Him. Moses, too, judged the price of his soul greater than all the riches of Egypt (Heb. 11:26).

Why should I speak of men of exalted stature? Rahab the prostitute (Josh. 2:4 and following), that foreign woman from the world, nevertheless thought that her soul had to be redeemed not only by contempt for everything she possessed but also at the cost of her life. When her fellow citizens sought the spies of Jesus son of Nave, she denied that they were there; and she preferred to conceal the enemies of her country—though they were nevertheless messengers of faith—rather than betray them. Neither the threats of her fellow citizens, nor the dangers of war, nor the burning of her homeland, nor the peril of her own people frightened her.

Learn, man; learn, Christian, how you ought to follow the true Jesus: a woman despised everything she possessed and followed Jesus figuratively, because of the similarity of the name. Therefore Solomon said most aptly: “The riches of a man are the redemption of his soul” (Prov. 13:8). Redeem your soul, then. Money is worthless, but through faith it becomes precious: it is worthless when it is hoarded, precious when it is scattered. For thus it is written: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever” (Ps. 111:9).

25. If, then, you are such a person [Note: [Col. 1021D] Some manuscripts read: “so that you can despise all that is yours, but also despise your very flesh for the sake of righteousness, since no possession can be richer than this.” The Roman edition also agrees, except that it has “not only all that is yours.” But the reading of the other manuscripts and of the old editions is correct, and we reproduce it in the text.] that you can despise not only everything that is yours but even your very flesh for the sake of righteousness—for no possession can be richer than this (a precious possession is a pure human being)—even if floods higher than you should surround you, you will cross over. For although the Lord gives the tempter power to test you, He nevertheless commands the devil himself to guard your soul, according to what is written: “That you may destroy the enemy and the defender” (Ps. 8:3). He tests as an adversary; he defends as a servant.

For it is written: “And will the unicorn be willing to serve you?” (Job 39:9). A person serves when he does not carry out what he desires by his own will, but obeys unwillingly, out of necessity, the commands of the emperor. See the greatness of Christ, how He turned back upon the devil the price of his own malice. The devil compels us to do what we hate: “For I do not do what I want,” as the Apostle said, “but what I hate, that I do” (Rom. 7:15). The Lord turned this back upon him, so that he himself often does not do what he wishes, but does what he hates. For finally, the soul that he wants to conquer, he guards.

We condemn the corruption of the flesh, and yet follow it, like that widow who breaks the faith promised to her husband and afterward wishes to marry—the very thing from which she formerly fled (1 Tim. 5:20). The devil is an enemy of the saints, yet he is employed as a defender so that he may be punished more severely: he who desires to harm is not permitted to dare to harm. And how much more tolerable it is to love the virtues, even if you cannot fulfill them, than to hate the virtues, though you cannot harm them.

26. (Verse 4.) “There is no soundness in my flesh because of the face of your anger.” Isaiah explained this passage to us: “We have sinned, and you were angry with us” (Isa. 64:5). What, however, is the face of the Lord’s anger? Perhaps it is that, because “the eyes of the Lord are upon those who do evil” (Ps. 33:17). If the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, how is the Prophet weakened by the face of God’s anger? Consider also what David himself said later: “For you delivered me from all my tribulations, and my eye looked upon my enemies” (Ps. 53:9). Just as He looks upon the good deeds of the righteous, so also He detects the hidden things of sinners.

Unless perhaps you refer this to Christ, who was delivered from all those by whom He was crushed, when He withdrew from the Jewish people who crushed Him with repeated sacrileges and daily impieties; and He called His enemies to grace—those whom the eye of God had seen and loved. Since God is therefore merciful, there is absolutely no reason for despair. Although He is angry, He forgives; although He strikes, He heals; although He delivers the flesh to destruction, He saves the spirit. Do not therefore fear the weakness of the flesh, because when a holy person is weak, he is stronger.

27. What, then, does he mean by: “There is no peace in my bones because of the face of my sins”? What are these bones—of the soul or of the body? Yet there would not be such concern for bodily pain where the soul also labors, since it is characteristic of the holy person to wish the flesh to be scourged for the sake of the soul, just as Paul also scourged himself lest his proclamation should be rejected.

There are certain bones of the inner human being, just as there are other limbs: the eyes of the mind and the nostrils, as Job said: “The divine spirit that is in my nostrils” (Job 27:3). There are therefore also bones by which a certain framework of charity is formed. Thus Adam spoke of his companion in charity and fellow heir of the grace of life: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2:23). The Apostle interpreted this by saying: “This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32).

Who could doubt that the mystery of Christ and the Church is spiritual, not carnal, since every good person is held within that marriage not by the beauty of the flesh but by the beauty of virtue, and loves character in his wife, not mere physical use? Finally, hear that he is not speaking according to the flesh but according to inner virtue: “My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret” (Ps. 138:15). Virtue, therefore, is not flesh; it knows the hidden things of God the Father.

28. Thus there is no peace for the virtues of the soul when our sins run before our eyes and cast themselves over our minds. The chosen Teacher of the Gentiles also interpreted this well in the Second Letter to the Corinthians, saying: “For when we had come into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we were afflicted in every way: battles outside, fears within” (2 Cor. 7:5). The sins of the Macedonians troubled him; how much more do our own sins disturb each one of us, so that we cannot have rest?

[Note: [Col. 1022D] Some manuscripts read, “Our adversary is grievous to us,” and so forth. The same manuscripts further read, “We serve without a seller.”]

Our own guilt is a more grievous adversary to us: it troubles the idle, afflicts the healthy, saddens the joyful, disturbs the peaceful, agitates the gentle, and awakens those who sleep. We are guilty without an accuser; we are tortured without a torturer; we are bound without chains; we are sold without a seller. Therefore Scripture also says: “You were sold because of your sins” (Isa. 50:1). These, then, are the sins that are always against us, as the Prophet said: “They sold us, and they rule over us” (Isa. 3:12). A slave who is sold leaves his former service in order to pass to another master; but we neither lay down the yoke of our former masters nor bend ourselves toward new sins.

29. (Verse 5.) Therefore the Holy One groaned, saying: “For my iniquities have risen above my head; like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me.” That is: my iniquities have passed over my head and tower above me, so that they press down my understanding—for “the eyes of the wise are in his head.” Therefore Nabal was evil and hard [Note: [Col. 1023D] Five manuscripts read: “because his understanding was obstructed by malice and iniquity.”] because malice and iniquity obstructed his understanding. Thus he could not bear Abigail’s words; his heart became hardened, and, as though weakened, he collapsed.

Or see whether this is the head of which the Apostle says (Col. 2:19) that he does not hold fast to it, being puffed up with a carnal mind. This head is Christ, because “the head of every man is Christ.” This is the head that grows through the joints and bonds of the whole people for the increase of God, because Christ rises up in all of us through His individual members.

Therefore, when our sins weigh us down and we are pressed toward earthly things by a certain leaden talent of iniquity, let us break their bonds and cast their yoke away from us, so that we may lift up the eyes of our mind and hear Him saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28).
