Finally, greed burdened Egypt, money vexed it, and the commerce of the Ethiopians [Note: [Col. 1023D] Some Paris editions, together with several manuscripts, read “the market of the Ethiopians.” But “Ethiopes” can be used for “Ethiopian commerce,” since *Aethiops* is an adjective. Again, in Isaiah’s words, where all editions and some manuscripts, together with the Vulgate edition, read “The labor of Egypt, the commerce…,” several other manuscripts, along with the Septuagint, read “Egypt labored; the commerce…,” ἐκοπίασεν Αἴγυπτος, and so forth.] as it is written: “Egypt labored; the commerce of the Ethiopians, and the Sabaeans, men of stature, shall pass over to you” (Isa. 45:14). Egypt labored before it knew the truth; but now it no longer labors, after it has passed over to Christ. The Sabaean men follow willingly, though formerly they fled, because the bonds of charity hold them—bonds stronger than adamant.

The following passage from Isaiah is also beautifully applied to this place: “The whole head is in pain, and the whole heart in sorrow: from the sole of the foot even to the head there is no wound, neither scar, nor inflamed sore” (Isa. 1:5–6). [Note: [Col. 1023D] The Roman edition, together with the Vulgate, reads: “From the sole of the foot even to the head there is no soundness in it, neither wound, nor bruise, nor inflamed sore,” and so forth. But those who thus emended the text failed to notice that Ambrose customarily follows the Septuagint, in which the passage reads: ἀπὸ ποδῶν ἕως κεφαλῆς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν αὐτῷ ὁλοκηρία, οὔτε τραῦμα, οὔτε μώλωψ, οὔτε πληγὴ φλεγμαίνουσα (“from feet to head there is no soundness in him: neither wound, nor bruise, nor inflamed sore”). Basil also read this passage in the same way, as Nobilius shows.]

For iniquity burns when it rules, raising itself over our head and occupying the place, so that Christ, the teacher, may not possess it as a place of repentance. These iniquities are not insignificant if you consider that man of iniquity who will come according to the working of Satan with every power, signs, and lying wonders, and with every deceit of iniquity. The Apostle showed us that he must be avoided (2 Thess. 2:9–10), because he will receive the working of error, so that the faithful may be tested and the faithless judged.

30. Therefore, rightly placed beneath iniquities and, what is worse, beneath his own, he says that his scars have become corrupt and putrid because of the face of his folly; for the remedy that lifts the burdens of iniquities followed too slowly. Yet even holy Job, who scraped the pus from his own ulcers and was covered with sores from the soles of his feet to the top of his head, received healing; and Lazarus, the poor man who lay at the rich man’s gate, while dogs licked his sores, was lifted from the stench of his scars and placed by the angels in Abraham’s bosom. [Col. 1023D]

There is therefore hope in holy David for a remedy of healing, because his wounds do not smell sweet of perfume but of the stench of his sinful injuries, and because he is afflicted and bowed down by them, not delighted in them. Now observe some lascivious and exceptionally lustful youth, who spends his life in adulteries, lying and feasting daily in splendid fashion like that rich man, in linen and purple. His floors swim with wine; the ground is covered with flowers and with the spines of fish; the dining rooms are filled with the scents of various incense burned. See how he considers himself blessed and judges that he smells good, even though he bears grave and long-standing wounds in his soul and lets corrupted blood flow, yet perceives no stench from his scar.

His nostrils are blocked with filth, and he cannot say: “The divine spirit that is in my nostrils” (Job 27:3). Therefore the rich man could not find a remedy of salvation, while the poor man found one. Finally, the one was in punishment in the underworld, the other in rest.

31. Thus holy David, the prophet, also found the remedy of everlasting salvation. He confessed that the wounds of his soul stank to him, and said that his scars had become putrid because of the face of his folly. Yet there is also a folly which, through the foolishness of preaching, brings salvation to those who believe.

The Prophet therefore, already possessed by the Evangelical Spirit, rejects the wisdom of this world, by which God is not known—a wisdom that covers its wounds and does not reveal them to the Lord. Better, then, is the folly that has eyes to see its own sores than the wisdom that does not have them. Therefore this great king, admonished by the sight of his folly, declares that he is afflicted by miseries, so that he may find the remedy of repentance, which Judas, who acquired a field with the wages of iniquity, could not find.

32. (Verse 7.) “Afflicted and bowed down,” he says, “I have been to the end; all day long I walked in sorrow.” [Note: [Col. 1024D] The old edition reads: “To what end? To the end of repentance? So that you may understand it more fully and mystically, up to Christ.” The Roman edition has: “To what end? Namely, to the end of repentance, or, so that you may understand it more fully and mystically, to the end—that is, up to Christ.” The Regius manuscripts and four others read as in the text.]

To what end does he say that he has been bowed down? Is it the proper end, the end of repentance? Or should we understand it more fully and mystically as extending up to Christ, who is the end of the Law, who allowed Himself to be scourged and allowed His dead body to be enclosed in stone? [Note: [Col. 1024D] The Roman edition alone reads “to be wounded.” But “to be stoned” here seems plainly to signify the same thing as being enclosed in a stone tomb.]

Yet those wounds exhaled no stench of repentance, but every fragrance of grace. Finally, there did not flow from His wound the decay of death, as from the wounds of other human beings; rather, a fountain of eternal life sprang forth, as Scripture teaches us, saying: “And water shall spring forth with delight from the fountains of the Savior” (Isa. 12:3). Water therefore leapt from the wound so that we might drink salvation. All sinners of the earth will drink, so that they may lay aside their sins.

Observe each point. Christ was afflicted by miseries in order to make blessed those who were established in misery. Let no one call him miserable who is just, because he himself said: “No one will make you miserable” (Isa. 33:1). He was bowed down so that we might be raised up; he was saddened so that he might make us joyful, according to what is written: “If I make you sorrowful, who is there who will make me joyful except the one who is made sorrowful by me?” (2 Cor. 2:2). Therefore the one who is made sorrowful by the Lord Jesus Christ makes Christ joyful, and is himself made joyful by Christ.

Therefore we too recognize that we must not make satisfaction superficially. Let us be bowed down to the end—that is, offering Christ not only faith but also perseverance in our sufferings—and let us rejoice in our sufferings, just as Christ also rejoiced in His sufferings. What He accepted for the sake of His servants, let us undergo for the Lord. This, then, is the end. “That I may complete,” he says, “what is lacking of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh, for His body, which is the Church, of which I have become a minister” (Col. 1:24).

We see what we must undertake, we who have undertaken the priestly ministry: we must bravely endure bodily sufferings not only for ourselves but also for the Church of the Lord. David added the sufferings of the soul as well.

33. (Verses 8, 9, 10, 11.) Finally he himself says: “For my soul is full of mockeries, and there is no soundness in my flesh. I have been bowed down and humbled exceedingly; I roared because of the groaning of my heart. And all my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you. My heart has been troubled, and my strength has left me, and the light of my eyes is not with me.”

We therefore observe that the labor of the soul is greater than that of the flesh. Understand, then, with what mockeries the soul is filled: in temptations the devil seems to mock and insult it as though it were suffering grievously. Symmachus, however, says “loins,” in which are the sources of human generation. Therefore the Wisdom of God commands you to have your loins girded (Luke 12:35), lest your chastity be loosened.

Finally, so that you may know that the movements of lust are in the loins, and that they are often aroused by the devil when he strives to scatter the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute, Scripture says: “Behold, his strength is in his loins, and his power in his womb” (Job 40:11). The seeds of the male are in the loins, while those of the female are in the womb. The devil therefore mocks in these matters, so as to produce adultery, incest, and fornication.

Hence the one who commits fornication sins against his own body, not outside the body. First, because the flesh is weakened, flowing away in lusts and not preserving the restraints of chastity; and then because the sources that ought to serve the procreation of offspring produce the pollution of the body, not the fruit of posterity. Perhaps, therefore, they are called mockeries because in these matters the heat of the body frequently mocks a person without the act of intercourse.

Thus the Seventy translated the phrase well as “mockeries of the soul,” because the devil, mocking someone’s affections, strives in vain to pour out his strength, empty his virtue, and loosen his firmness. Therefore elsewhere he says: “And my kidneys were weakened” (Ps. 72:21).

In this regard the blessed Apostle also strengthens us: we ought not fear mockeries of the soul or weakness of the flesh, because Christ is the strength of both our soul and our body. He heals the sick like a physician; He strengthens the weak like the strength of all. Finally, “although our outward person is being corrupted, the inward person is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16).

34. Worn out by these mockeries of the soul, holy David had bowed and humbled himself exceedingly—not so as to give place, as we have said, to the iniquities that had risen above his head, or to yield to the enemy, whom he later teaches must not be yielded to, saying: “How much evil has the enemy done in your holy places, and those who hated you gloried in the midst of your festival? They set up their signs as signs, and I did not understand, as on the road above the summit. Like men in a forest, they cut down its doors with axes” (Ps. 73:3 and following).

He says: while my enemies set their signs of iniquity above the summit—for what is the summit except your head, where understanding is, where Christ, Wisdom, is—I did not understand, that is, I did not consent, I did not agree with them, and I did not add the judgment of my thought to theirs.

Therefore elsewhere you have: “I did not understand a wicked word”; and: “I did not know those who turned aside from me, the wicked” (Ps. 100:3–4). Finally, although Christ knows all things, He did not know sin; for He knows what belongs to Him—that is, what belongs to the virtues—not what belongs to crimes.

Therefore Scripture says to you: “The Lord knows those who are His” (2 Tim. 2:19). But to the wicked He says: “Depart from me, because I do not know you” (Luke 13:27). And through Jeremiah He spoke, saying: “I was led like a lamb to be sacrificed, and I did not know” (Jer. 11:19). How did He not know what He had foretold would happen? “I did not know,” He says, “their thoughts, their malice. I do not wish to know what belongs to bloodshed.” Finally: “I will not gather their assemblies from blood” (Ps. 15:4); and: “I blot out their iniquities, and I will remember them no more” (Isa. 43:25). I do not wish to know what I came to forgive.

I did not know the pieces of wood that burn, nor what is placed in a pile of wood—whether straw or hay—so that the flame may consume them more quickly with their own fuel. I want to know what will remain, so that it may receive the fruit of its reward; I want to know what has been built upon the foundation, so that it may be improved, not what is on the road, where passersby may snatch it away. I want to know what belongs to the vine, the sound wood that bears fruit, not what is gathered into bundles and prepared for burning. That is, I am not their judge and companion in what is perishable. Therefore it is not association with any thing, but criminal association, that incurs guilt.

35. Why, then, did he not acknowledge those who gloried in what was fruitless and frail? Because by evil works and the axes of their iniquity they overthrow the entrances of the faithful soul, and by cruel deeds they cut apart the vestibules of the devout mind, lest Christ be able to enter through them.

Each person ought to guard his gates and doors, so that when Christ comes and knocks, the ministering powers who go before and run ahead may say: [Note: [Col. 1027D] Some manuscripts read: “Lift up the gates of your prince.” But, apart from the fact that this fits less well with what follows, “truly princes,” it also departs from all the versions, which may be seen in the Polyglot Bibles and in Nobilius on this same verse.]

“Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates” (Ps. 23:7). Truly they are princes who have governed themselves well, so that Christ may enter their souls.

A similar passage is Solomon’s: “If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not leave your place, because care will restrain great offenses” (Eccl. 10:4). [Note: [Col. 1027D] Some manuscripts read: “because care mitigates sin. For great diligence…” Others, and the editions, more correctly read the sacred text as ὅτι ἴαμα καταπαύσει ἁμαρτίας μεγάλας, “because healing will put an end to great sins.”]

Diligence and faith therefore occupy the higher place; perfidy, the lower. Let good diligence rise up to you, then—a diligence that excludes the enemy’s ambushes and removes sin, so that the malice of the one who has power may not be able to do harm.

Ecclesiastes sees this malice in the Songs, “under the sun,” that is, in this world; hence Scripture mentioned this place as “under the sun.” [Note: [Col. 1027D] Here the book of Ecclesiastes is designated in the same way by the term “Songs,” just as Scripture as a whole is designated by the term “hymns” in *On Flight from the World*, book 4, section 20; consult that passage.]

Thus he saw it under the sun, not above the sun, where there is the peace of the angels and the holiness of the heavenly powers. Or perhaps he said “under the sun of iniquity,” for the devil presides over malice, while Christ presides over virtues.

Therefore, in order to overcome the spirit possessing power—which he had received for a time—David bowed himself in prayer, bending his neck like a circle, and humbled himself in supplication. For the prayer of one who humbles himself penetrates the clouds and transcends the heights of the elements, so that it may draw near to Christ.

36. “And he roared because of the groaning of his heart.” One roars when he expresses only groaning, not words. This, then, is that excellent prayer in which the Spirit intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings (Rom. 8:26), as the Chosen Vessel declared.

This is the groaning that God does not despise. He does not despise a younger servant deprived of his father, nor a widow, if she pours out speech in a groan. [Note: [Col. 1028D] Thus the old edition and the Roman edition, together with several manuscripts. Some Paris editions, however, together with other written copies, read: “if she pours out speech with a groan” (some manuscripts: “if they pour out speech with groanings”). Therefore, above all, let us not seize the sign that the enemy sets up—such as the sign that Antichrist will set up. But this does not follow as well from what precedes.]

37. The Apostle therefore places groaning above all else as a sign of the Holy Spirit, as we read. Let us therefore guard the doors of our soul, lest the entrance of our confession be cut apart by the axes of excessive speech. Let nothing strange or proud proceed from our mouth, lest we lift an axe or hammer, which do not enter the Church of the Lord.

Close the door when you pray, lest an evil spirit intrude and extort sin there where we wish to gain the profit of devotion. For the groaning of the one who prays in this way is not hidden from the Lord. Thus the groaning of the holy Peter was both recognized and heard when he wept most bitterly. It was not the bitter tears themselves, but the bitter affection of the one who shed them.

Even in faithless Ahab, groaning would have found grace, had he not increased his offense by retaining envy. For it is not a superficial groaning that is commended, but one that has conversion. For it is written: “If you turn and groan, you will be saved.”

38. Let us also establish every desire of ours before the Lord. What is desire? The word “desire” is used of a good thing: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke 22:15); and: “As the deer longs for the springs of water” (Ps. 41:2).

I think, however, that the person who practices repentance and afflicts himself ought to enumerate not his good deeds but the sins he has committed. Finally, I believe that we are taught this by those verses in which he says: “O God, I will declare my life to you; you have placed my tears in your sight” (Ps. 55:9). He is not announcing a life of innocence where tears are shed, for tears customarily undertake an embassy on behalf of sins.

Unless perhaps we should understand it this way: even if someone is innocent, he cannot be secure when he has daily battles against very serious enemies; and therefore, although his conscience may be joyful, the battle is nevertheless tearful.

In accordance with these verses, we can take the word more as “lust” than as “desire,” for the Greek has ἐπιθυμίαν (*epithymian*). “Lust” and “desire” are both called ἐπιθυμία (*epithymia*). Yet “lust” is spoken of both good and evil. “My soul has lusted and languished for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:3), in a good sense; but in the Law it is used otherwise: “I would not have known lust unless the Law said, ‘You shall not lust’” (Rom. 7:7), plainly in an evil sense.

The words that follow teach us this, since, taking occasion, sin works every lust in the human affections through the commandment. Yet we can also understand “I place every desire before you” in this way: “I make known to you what I desire to obtain,” so that it seems to refer to the sequence of petitions, not to the boasting of virtues. For boastfulness is offensive even in an upright person, whereas supplication is praiseworthy in a sinner.

39. The Prophet also added that, when his heart was troubled, his strength left him. There is great danger if the heart is agitated, since we believe that we approach righteousness through it. Yet just as, in serious illnesses, when pain is felt and its sensation is expressed, a remedy for healing is indicated—for it is more tolerable to feel pain than not to feel it, since one thing is a sign that life still remains, while the other is an indication of final death if there is no sensation of pain—so the heart also displays signs of salvation when it recognizes the causes of its own disturbance.

Thus David’s heart was troubled against Nabal, a pestilent man, and he found grace when Abigail came forward to calm the agitation of his indignation and receive the sanctification of blessing. But Nabal, with his hard and rigid heart, could not bear his wife’s words; he became stupefied, stiffened, and fell into death.

40. What strength, then, left the Prophet—of the flesh or of the mind? If it was the strength of the flesh, healing should certainly not be despaired of. For “power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

Concerning this, the judge and champion who understood the struggle of mind and body argued at some length [Note: [Col. 1029D] All editions, together with three manuscripts, read “judge and abridger.” Five other manuscripts read more correctly “judge and champion.” Paul is indicated, who may be called both the judge, or *agonothetes*, of the spiritual contest, since in many passages of his letters he prescribed its rules to others and set forth its prize, and also the champion, or athlete, as he himself testifies in 1 Cor. 9:26 and 2 Tim. 4:7.] and moderated the contest of each, so as to restrain the flesh if he saw it becoming stronger, lest it lead the mind captive under the law of sin. He therefore called back the flesh and joined virtue to the mind; thus he deserved to arrive at the crown.

The Prophet therefore means this: if the strength of the flesh has left me, the strength of the mind has prevailed. But if we understand him to say that the strength of the mind has left him, it is not surprising that, in the gravest temptations, with his heart troubled, a person thinks himself abandoned by the strength of his mind.

Let him himself teach you, saying: “The Lord is my strength and my praise” (Ps. 117:14). He was therefore seeking the Lord, and for that reason, lest he deserve to be abandoned, he often thought that the Lord had to be sought. Whenever he wavered, he thought that he had been abandoned.

Thus the Apostles rouse the sleeper, lest he fall asleep to himself—not because they believed that he had fallen asleep. Thus Elisha, to use examples from earlier times, said: “Where is the God of Elijah?” (2 Kings 2:14)—not because he thought Him absent, but because he sought His presence in His benefits.

Thus Jeremiah followed Him as a physician, saying: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved. I have not labored after you” (Jer. 17:14). Thus the Church sought Him in the Song of Songs and asked the daughters of Jerusalem to awaken love (Song 3:5). It sought Him in order to find Him whom it held fast by its love and never sensed to be absent.

So David, too, was not complaining that he had been abandoned by Christ; rather, in Christ’s presence, he judged that he could not be troubled.

41. Finally, so that you may know that this is to be understood more especially of Christ, he added: “And the light of my eyes is not with me.” What is the true light of all things except Christ Jesus, of whom John says: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9)? For he is the one who illuminates both the eyes of the body and the vision of the mind. Let us therefore ask that he always pour his light into us and always be with us, as he was with David; and for this reason David dared to say: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10). Certainly, as a prophet, he had seen a great light; may his lamp shine for us, lest we be able to go astray. And the Word is a lamp, just as the Word is the true light that illuminates the whole world. Finally: “Your word, Lord, is a lamp for my feet” (Ps. 118:15).

And the Prophet was also seeking that lamp—not a lantern.

[Note: [Col. 1030D] Thus the printed edition and many manuscripts, except that the latter, after the words “not a lantern,” add “but a lamp.” In Vict. and Colb., however, it reads “not a lantern.” “And the lamp, Lamp-John,” etc. Again, where the edition and some manuscripts have “The Light of the Jews, like a lamp under a bushel or a torch beneath a covering, may be seen,” etc., other codices, more numerous, read as we have in the text.]

John found and pointed out that lamp; the persecutor came with a lantern and pointed it out. For a lantern has its light enclosed, not free. The Jew, like a lamp beneath a bushel, or like torches beneath a covering, may see—but does not see. We, however, with unveiled face, behold the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, so that by the Holy Spirit we may be transformed into his image, from glory to glory.

Thus the crowd of persecutors came with lanterns; and therefore their eyes could not see the light enclosed within them. They came with torches, which contain more smoky darkness than brightness of light. Indeed, torches are customarily used to burn the corpses of the dead. The Jews were therefore already carrying fires for themselves when they persecuted the author of salvation. They came with weapons, signifying that by weapons they would perish at the hands of the Romans, even to the destruction of the whole city and temple, because they had rejected the Lord’s peace.

42. (Verses 12–15.) “My friends and my neighbors drew near against me, and stood. And my neighbors stood far away. And those who sought my life used violence. And those who sought evil for me spoke vanity, and all day long they devised deceit. But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and like a mute who does not open his mouth. And I became like a person who does not hear and who has no reproofs in his mouth.”

Let us see who those are who discuss these words with such subtlety. For my part, especially in this first verse, I think the Lord’s meaning must be retained: in temptations, even a person’s household members become his enemies. Thus holy David confesses this openly, sincerely, and sorrowfully.

For the sorrow is genuine, and it is the confession of the inner heart, when all those things are enumerated by which the secret inward parts of the mind are pierced with the bitterest emotion and embittered by domestic gall. The Prophet therefore laments that he has been attacked by friends and neighbors, by whom he ought not to have been attacked but helped.

This agrees with the complaint of holy Job (Job 16:2 ff.), for he too rebuked those three kings, who were supposed to be comforters but were comforters of evils. They brought him greater struggles when they had assembled to console him out of friendship. We must certainly beware of this. Consolation ought to be gentle, not harsh—such as rather eases grief and calms fervor than provokes agitation.

Certainly the medicine of the body itself teaches us this: for wounds that are inflamed are customarily treated with softer medications, by which pain is relieved. Therefore wounds are first fomented and only afterward cut, lest the very harshness offend and the incision aggravate the wound.

How much more, then, must we take care that, when we come to console someone, we do not speak hastily or superficially? Job was silent for seven days, and his friends were silent; they would not have spoken unless Job’s grief had burst forth into speech. For one must consider where to begin, lest your consolation give offense in the very act of speaking.

Even silence itself is medicine, and haste in speech wounds all the more. Why are you surprised if one person wounds another, when he often wounds himself, since he does not escape sin through excessive talk? For if a physician waits for the time of treatment, so that, once illnesses have subsided, the remedies of medicine may be brought forward—lest, as they say, an illness that is still bitter and immature resist the remedies of healing and be unable to experience their benefit—how much more ought we to examine the situation, so that a medicinal word may proceed from us at the proper time, appearing not to kindle grief but to soothe it?

The force of grief presses hard. The heart of the afflicted woman is crushed when she has lost her husband or children by a premature death. Why do you hurry to speak when she will not hear you unless her grief first cools? We have often seen quarrels arise over consolations. You have come to grieve, not to quarrel.

The order of speech itself must be sought, lest you incur sin before God while desiring to console a human being; lest, when you say to someone, “Hear these things, and many others that are of no benefit,” he reply, “You are comforters of evils” (Job 16:2); lest you introduce into another’s mourning a contest of chattering disputation; lest you fail to approach when you ought; or lest you approach when your speech is too harsh.

Finally, let holy Job teach you what is said of such people: “The most grievous temptations came upon me together; they surrounded me, lying in wait. My brothers departed from me; they recognized strangers more than me. My friends became merciless” (Job 19:12 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1032D] The Roman edition alone reads: “His trials alone came upon me together; they surrounded my paths, lying in wait.” In this it followed the Septuagint translators, with whom the reading is: “Together his trials came upon me; those lying in wait surrounded my paths.”]

[Note: [Col. 1031D] The Roman edition had shortened this passage as follows: “And lest it be said to you: ‘I have heard many such things—comforters of evils.’” We restored it from the older edition, from which the manuscripts Vict. and Colb. also differ only in having: “Lest, when you say to him …, he reply.” The manuscripts Vat. and five Gallican copies read: “Lest it be said to you, ‘Hear these things …,’ and he reply to you,” etc. Some Paris editions also agree with these, except that they place “and” before “lest it be said,” and omit “to you” after “he reply.” Whoever does not reject this reading should take “it be said to you” in the sense of “it be said by you.” This is not unusual in Latin ears.]

Thus the natural meaning also applies to the holy prophet David: he complains that he was attacked by his friends and abandoned by his neighbors.

43. Yet neither should the mystical interpretation be thought foreign to the feeling of piety, if he spoke of angels who are set before those who fear the Lord, in order to rescue them from temptations that they could not endure.

How, then, do they stand far away when they have been assigned to provide assistance? They do not separate themselves; rather, the person pressed by temptations thinks those whom he desires to be nearer to him are far away. He supposes that they are pretending not to notice, although they are awaiting the time for helping him at the command of their commander, who ordered his athlete to struggle longer so that he might conquer more gloriously.

This seems to fit what follows even better: when the angels relax their watch of protection, enemies lie in wait, seeking to find something harmful in his soul. For the power of a more serious temptation is permitted to them when more serious guilt is found in the soul.

Hence you have that saying in the Book of Kings, spoken by King Ahab to Elijah, when the Prophet vehemently rebuked him and announced his death: “You have found me,” he said. And Elijah answered: “I have found you, because you have done evil in the sight of the Lord” (1 Kings 21:20).

You see, then, that injury ought not rashly to be inflicted upon kings, either by the prophets of God or by priests, if there are no more serious sins for which they ought to be rebuked. But where the sins are more serious, the priest must not appear to spare them, so that they may be corrected by righteous reproofs.

44. Yet David says in this passage that they seemed to have found nothing, and therefore his enemies spoke vanity, because they found nothing that they could say truthfully. Or certainly, even if I sinned, I was cleansing my sins by the sorrow of repentance.

In this matter they spoke deceitfully with me, so that they might confound me by their rebuke and turn me back from conversion. And see whether he may not have meant rather that they sought evil against him, but, when they wished to accuse him, found themselves anticipated, because he himself had exposed his wounds, acting as his own accuser. Therefore the force of their accusation had been nullified: they had spoken vain things that could no longer harm one who had confessed his fault.

45. Therefore, excluded from the envy of accusation, they employed deceit, so that, he says, they might rise up and insult me, thereby provoking me to some agitation. But when I saw their deceit, I did not hear them, like a deaf man.

Consider the force of the wording. He did not say, “I pretended not to hear what they were saying,” but “I did not hear.” He excluded the speaker’s voice by the intention of his mind and did not open his mouth, like a mute.

Blessed is the person who can possess such virtue that, when provoked, he does not become angry, and, when agitated, does not wish to take revenge. This is what enemies seek: to provoke us to anger. They curse so that we may curse; they accuse so that we may return the accusation; they insult so that they may stir us up to answer insult with insult.

Thus Peter aptly wrote of the Lord Jesus in his epistle: “When he was reviled, he did not revile; when he suffered, he did not threaten” (1 Pet. 2:23).

Therefore, desiring to shape the practices of his life according to the likeness and image of Christ, the righteous person is silent when accused, forgives when injured, disregards provocation when challenged, and does not open his mouth, so that he may imitate him who, like a lamb led to the sacrifice, did not open his mouth. Though he could have something to say in reply, he prefers to remain silent rather than speak.

For the Lord Jesus himself, when he was accused, truly remained silent; and when struck, he did not strike back. Finally, when struck, he answered: “If I have spoken evil, bear witness to the evil; but if I have spoken well, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23).

See how, as though truly weak and as though he were unable to avenge himself, he spoke with a certain childlike feeling. So too, if you have something with which to refute the one who rebukes you, you will do better to remain silent, lest by returning the rebuke you reveal your agitation. It is better to disregard an injury than to avenge it while rebuking the offender.

Good is the mute person who does not know how to speak evil, from whose mouth no crime knows how to emerge. This is the truly blessed mute person who, while silent, speaks within himself.

“The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction, so that I may know when it is necessary for me to speak.” Zacharias was saying such things within himself when he had become mute. And truly, because speaking had not benefited him, he became mute so that he would not speak; and, so that he might speak, he was heard by Christ.

Finally, he wrote that Christ would hear him; he received back the voice that Christ granted him; and Christ added the grace that he had not previously possessed, so that he might prophesy of the one whose commands he had not previously believed.

Why do I speak of the Lord of all virtues, when the woman Susanna, though shaken neither by the weakness of her sex nor by the knowledge that she had been condemned to death, uttered a voice? She was accused, and she remained silent; she was led to death, and she covered herself with silence, lest she expose her modesty.

Yet within herself she spoke to God, who heard her more readily while she was silent. If she had wished to speak, perhaps she would not have been heard.

46. You too, therefore, who have resolved to make satisfaction for your sins to the Lord your God, cleanse yourself inwardly before him alone; look toward him who can wash away sins. He helps you when someone thinks you ought to be rebuked.

Finally, when David was being cursed and his commander Abishai wished to avenge the king’s insult, David said to him: “Leave him, so that he may curse, because the Lord told him to see my humiliation, and the Lord will repay me good for this curse” (2 Sam. 16:12).

You see, then, that you are helped by those who insult you, so that the Lord may hear you and forgive your sin. For when you ought yourself to be your own accuser, to heap up your crimes, and to offer yourself for punishment, how do you desire to deny the charges brought against you?

Repentance seeks patience, and patience mitigates great offenses. How can you be angry with others when you yourself are guilty in conscience? How can you be agitated when you ought to be pitiable? Whoever is accused—and, what is more, accused by himself—ought to tend his wounds, not wound another. No one heals himself by wounding someone else.

“Physician, heal yourself.” If this is true of a physician, how much more ought a guilty person first to heal himself! You confess your own sin and claim to be another’s physician. Even if what you throw back is true, the time is not right; for God said to the sinner: “Why do you recite my ordinances?” (Ps. 49:16).

You have presumed to rebuke someone from the Law, although you yourself have acted against the Law (Exod. 23:1). Why do you waste the time for tears? Why, by quarrelling, do you either hear or speak empty words, when it is written for you: “You shall not accept a false report,” and when you read in the Gospel that judgment must be endured for every idle word (Matt. 12:36)? Even if another speaks, remain silent; even if another insults you, close your ear.

47. (Verses 16–17.) David conquered his adversaries by remaining silent; and because he became like a mute, he received his voice again, because he turned toward the Lord and spoke, saying: “For in you, Lord, I have hoped; you will hear me, Lord my God. For I said: Let my enemies never rejoice over me.”

Observe each detail. David was silent; his enemies were speaking and provoking him so that he too might say something. They were saying: “Let us hear your voice.” Within himself, he was speaking silently: “What need is there for these people to hear things that cannot benefit them? In you, Lord, I have hoped; to you alone I speak. Hear me, you who are able to hear.”

“From you I have always asked that my enemies never rejoice over me, because even if I have sinned, you forgive the sin; and even if I have fallen, you raise me up, so that those who rejoice in the sins of others may have no reason to exult.”

We have gained more because we have sinned more, for your grace makes us happier than our innocence does. We find this same meaning in the Book of the Prophet Micah: “Do not rejoice over me, my enemy; for I have fallen, but I shall rise” (Mic. 7:8).

The fall of a weak person is not grievous if there is not also a deliberate will not to rise from it. Have the will to rise; the one who can make you rise is present.

48. David therefore said in his heart, asking to be heard by the Lord and that his enemies might not rejoice over him. He was also asking that he might remain steadfast in his purpose of conversion, lest, while the steps of his purpose—like certain feet of his soul—were being shaken, his adversaries speak arrogantly and boastfully against him, as those who desire to insult are accustomed to do.

Although he is shaken as a human being, he says that he is prepared for punishment, so that by punishment he may pay for his error. Even if the Lord’s scourges cease, he nevertheless remembers that he is scourged by his own grief, so that guilt may find nothing to condemn because a good confession has forestalled it.

This, then, is what he says: “And while my feet are shaken, they have spoken great things against me,” because they were so ready for the mockery of insult that, when my feet were shaken, they already had boastful speech prepared. Or certainly in this sense: “While my feet are shaken,” they thought I would fall, and they spoke proudly and boastfully.

49. Yet because later he says that his feet almost slipped (Ps. 72:2), so that no difficulty may arise from this, consider that here we are being taught the disposition of repentance, while there the opinion of his error is being excluded: namely, that wealth and the more prosperous success of the wicked ought not to shake us.

A similar manner of speaking is found in the divine Scriptures. Thus elsewhere too: “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted” (Ps. 125:1). Yet the holy person wishes to be tested not by the display of words but by the power of the spirit.

Therefore we must always consider the meaning itself, which frequent translation from Hebrew into Greek and from Greek into Latin has often weakened.

50. (Verse 18.) To all the foregoing, then, there is a beautiful remedy: he is prepared for scourging and offers himself to the Lord, so that he may endure whatever scourges are pleasing to God (1 Chron. 21:13).

I read that holy David chose the kind of scourge that he would endure with equanimity. But he chose because, of three possible punishments, he was commanded to select one. When no choice is commanded, the servant of God is ready for everything, whether he undergo bodily illness, flee from the face of an enemy, or endure the death of his children, whom he is not afraid to send ahead, because he can receive them again without fear.

For he knows that, if he is punished here with a temporal penalty, he may thereby lessen the punishment of eternal misery in the future. Therefore he asks that his petition be received and that he himself be chastised in order that he may be received; for the Lord chastises every son whom he receives.

51. (Verse 19.) If you see your servant confessing his own sins and voluntarily offering himself to punishment, you are moved and forgive him. Do you then distrust the Lord’s mercy?

The judge himself, who in many cases is not permitted to withhold the sword because he serves the laws, can nevertheless grant the benefit of remitting punishments. And do you still tremble about what you should ask from the Lord of the laws and the Author of mercy, for whom the law is his will and the right to grant pardon belongs to him?

Yet this applies only if you ask that your sins be forgiven and do not consider your honors or feel shame before your friends, lest you seem to have lowered your dignity.

The friend of God, the prophet of God, the king chosen by God himself and anointed for kingship, voluntarily offered himself to scourges and was not ashamed. And are you ashamed? This shame will not help you much when you come to God’s judgment. Rather, you will repent of that shame when, standing in the presence not only of human beings but also of angels and all the heavenly Powers, you begin not to deny your own sins.

How will you excuse yourself when you have committed so many things? Will you plead the weakness of your condition, because no one is without sin? You will be answered: “Then you ought to have done penance. I had given you a remedy; why did you reject it?”

Will you add that you were ashamed because you were ashamed of your honors? He will say: “If you were ashamed of me before your friends, I will also be ashamed of you before my Father who is in heaven.”

Learn that what is written is true: “There is a shame that brings sin” (Sir. 4:25).

David placed his sorrow before his own eyes, so that he might never forget it. David himself declared his iniquity. David thought about his sin, not his wealth. David was not ashamed to recount his sins, lest he be ashamed of them when he stood before my judgment. And were you ashamed?

My servant Job would not be in rest today if he had been ashamed before those three kings, his friends; nor would David himself, if he had been ashamed to confess his own offenses.

Therefore, because he was not ashamed to open his sins to me, neither will I be ashamed to disclose my secrets to him. And because neither of them was ashamed to place the price of his deeds in my power, committing himself to my judgment and will, neither will I be ashamed of such servants, whom I call friends because they have sought to do my will.

Therefore, because they were once in mourning and are now in consolation, while you were once in delights and are now in punishments, there is a great chasm between you, so that neither can their favor cross over to you nor your punishment to them.

Do you hear what David says? Hear it while you are still permitted to correct and amend yourself: if you amend yourself here, “here you shall rest.”

Do not let the sweet and pleasant things of the world—

[Note: [Col. 1035D] Some manuscripts read “of this age”; but let the bitter things delight you.]

—of this age delight you. For such pleasures are accustomed to stir up grievous gall. He was not seeking pleasures when he was placed upon the throne; rather, he preferred the death of the holy to the life of the wicked.

52. (Verses 20–21.) “My enemies,” he says, “are alive and have grown strong against me; those who hate me unjustly have multiplied. Those who repay evil for good slandered me, because I pursued justice.”

But how much more illustrious is the one who died daily in order to give life to his peoples, and who offered his body to the wounds of death, as he himself says: “In deaths often” (2 Cor. 11:23)!

For death is an honorable redemption even of a disfigured life, or a strengthening of an innocent one; and the outcome of death is in the hand of life. Therefore the Apostle preferred to die daily, so that the merit of his life might be proved.

For it is written: “Do not praise a person during his life. Those who live will die; those who die will rise again.” Therefore the person who dies in order to rise is nearer to salvation than the one who lives in order to die.

Who, then, is the one who dies daily (Eccl. 11:30), except the one who carries the death of the Lord Jesus in his body, so that all sins may die to him?

David’s enemies were strengthened and multiplied in this world, but this is not a reliable strength except that of the one who is strengthened in Christ. Finally, those who hate the righteous unjustly are strengthened in this world. Their hatred, therefore, is not just but unjust, since they hated unjustly.

53. But observe the distinction. Later he says: “Those who hate me without cause” (Ps. 68:5); here he has: “Those who hate me unjustly.” But there he speaks in the person of Christ, here in his own person. When he speaks in the person of Christ, he is hated without cause; when he speaks in his own person, he is hated unjustly.

A human being may be free from one particular wound—for example, injustice, intemperance, or impurity—but exposed to other wounds. In Christ, however, there could be no cause by which he could receive the wound of any sin, since he was free from guilt, pure from offense, and unstained by vice.

Some think that both psalms are spoken in the person of Christ, who was making satisfaction to the Father for our sins. In this passage, therefore, he said that he was attacked contrary to justice; there, contrary to grace.

54. And he rightly adds this to prove that he was attacked unjustly: “Because I pursued justice.” What force lies in the addition of a single syllable, when he says that he had pursued justice (*subsecutus*), not merely followed it (*secutus*)!

For the one who pursues closely is nearer than the one who follows; and one is called “nearly equal” (*suppar*) rather than “unequal” (*impar*), and an heir’s succession rather than an accession.

[Note: [Col. 1035D] The Roman edition alone has “and nearly equal rather than equal,” and says that the succession of an heir is called more properly succession than accession. But this is clearly an error. Who does not see that someone is signified as less distant from another if he is said to be equal to him than if he is said to be unequal to him? Yet the sequence of the discourse most clearly requires this meaning. The same method should be applied in considering the words “succession” and “accession.”]

55. (Verse 22.) And yet, although he pursues justice, he does not think this is due to his own virtue but to heavenly grace, if he is not abandoned by Christ. Therefore he prays more earnestly, saying: “Do not abandon me, Lord my God; do not depart from me.”

That is: human beings have abandoned me; my friends have attacked their beloved neighbor; they did not draw near. They fled from me as though I were dead and rejected me, because I desired to open my sins to you and confess them; because I offered myself to be wounded by your scourges; because I chose the scars of wounds rather than the banquets of kings and the boastfulness of powers.

You alone, therefore, do not abandon me. Remain attached to your servant, you who raise the needy from the earth and lift the poor from the dungheap. Trusting in your company, I shall consider myself more surrounded than by crowds of peoples.

My scars have indeed become putrid; yet I still desire the scars of your blows, which are placed over healed wounds so that afterward no ulcer may appear. Good are the scars of triumphal wounds, in which the victors of this earthly battle glory.

How much more glorious are the wounds received for the faith and the glory of your name! This is the scar that opens heaven, gains the kingdom, and finds immortality.

Therefore, brothers, this is the blessed scar, because blessed are those who have washed their robes in their own blood. Thus the flesh of death began to be a robe of glory (Rom. 7:24), in which Paul too was previously imperiled, though chosen by God, unless he had asked to be delivered from this body of death, as we read.

56. Therefore, since we are in this body of death, let us pray that the good and beloved physician of God not abandon us—the physician whom the patriarch David begged not to depart from him. Let us entrust ourselves to him, ready to be treated with whatever medicine he wishes to use.

[Note: [Col. 1037D] All editions and a few manuscripts omit “for treatment” (*ad curandum*), which is found in five Gallican manuscripts. Not improperly: “ready for treatment” has the same sense as “ready to be healed.” For the rationale of this construction, see Francisco Sánchez, *Minerva*, book III, chapter 8.]

No one tells the physician of his body how he should be healed. The physician knows which medicines are suitable for each wound and which ulcer’s putrefaction must be cut away with iron, lest destruction spread through the whole body.

If the physician prescribes the kind of medicine by which the sick person ought to be healed and the sick person finds it distasteful, the physician departs and abandons the patient.

Observe the person who wishes to be healed, submitting to every kind of medical treatment. Pay attention to the order. First he opens his wounds to the physician and says: “Heal me, but I ask that it not be in your anger, because my weaknesses cannot endure harsh medicine.”

Christ’s medicine is correction, for the Lord rebukes the one whom he wishes to convert. Therefore Paul too says to the physician: “Reprove, exhort, rebuke” (2 Tim. 4:2).

The person who asks to be rebuked does not therefore refuse to be healed; rather, he wishes the punishment to be lightened, so that he may not be rebuked in anger or chastised in a burst of wrath.

57. Observe the progression. First he asks to be rebuked; afterward, what is more serious, to be chastised. Then he not only confesses his sins but also enumerates and accuses them, for he does not wish his offenses to remain hidden.

For just as fevers, when they are deep-seated, cannot be alleviated, but when they break out they offer hope of ending, so the illness of sins grows hot while it is concealed but evaporates when exposed through confession.

Therefore, at the beginning of his speech, the righteous person is his own accuser, before the infection of the ulcer spreads inward. For the memory of sins weighs upon the conscience unless medicine is sought.

And if the physician delays, the sick person ought to offer himself so that he may be cut more quickly, just as David offered himself to the Lord’s scourges, saying: “Repay me double for my sins, provided that you punish me here; do not abandon me; do not turn your face away from me; do not disdain or shudder at the stench of my wounds.”

[Note: [Col. 1037D] All manuscripts and editions have this reading except the Roman edition, which reads: “saying, I am ready for scourges”; and elsewhere: “Let your hand be against me”—that is, “repay me,” etc.]

And your servant Job was struck with an ulcer from his feet to his head, and he found the remedy for his health—although his wound was one of virtue, while this one was the wound of error. His wounds stank, and physicians could not heal them.

You spoke, Lord, the mysteries of your sacraments; you exposed the poisons of the serpent; and the wounds of your servants were healed by the medicine of your word alone, because you did not abandon him. Therefore do not abandon me, Lord; do not depart from me.

Human beings have abandoned me because my wounds disgust them, though I thought they should be exposed to your compassion. They say: “Depart from us, for you are a sinner; go away, lest you pollute us.”

But you, Lord, heal without being polluted; you help without being contaminated, because you are the God of my salvation, Lord, and your hand is accustomed not to destroy but to heal.

58. We have completed the psalm, together with its interpretation of the verse.

[Note: [Col. 1037D] Only the Roman edition has “which some Greek manuscripts possess”; [Col. 1038D] all the Latin manuscripts possess it. You will find that verse nowhere else except in the Arabic version, where it reads as follows: “They rejected me, beloved, as a dead man to be abhorred, and they fastened my body with nails.” When Ambrose says that he has also explained this very verse, we do not doubt that he is referring to the words above: “Human beings have abandoned me because my wounds disgust them,” etc.]

Some Greek codices have the verse, but not all the Latin ones. For before the next responsory there is the verse: “And they cast me away as one dead and abominable”—that is, those who repaid me evil for good.

But you, Lord, do not abandon me; do not depart from me. For this follows: “Do not abandon me”—you who are accustomed to heal the stinking dead.

Finally, we have this in the Gospel. When Jesus came to the tomb of Lazarus and said, “Take away the stone,” Martha said: “Lord, by now he stinks, for he has been dead four days.” He answered her: “Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?” (John 11:39–40). And he called Lazarus, and he came out healthy.

Let us therefore believe also, so that from our wounds we may obtain the medicine of salvation and future glory.

59. In prayers and supplications, therefore, repentance must be undertaken with sorrow and tears, so that we may deserve to see the glory of God.

Nor should you be troubled that mourning, grief, bodily affliction, and the most severe sufferings are involved. Even if they seem very severe, such sufferings are nevertheless unworthy of comparison with the glory that is to come, as the Apostle Paul testifies to you (Rom. 8:18).

Let us therefore not be reluctant to endure lighter things here, so that there we may obtain the fullness of praise and glory, receiving eternal rewards in place of temporal ones, through the Lord Jesus, to whom belong praise, honor, glory, and eternity, from ages past, now, and always, unto all ages of ages. Amen.

# Exposition of Psalm 38

**Title: “For the end; a song for Idithum, by David himself.”**

841 1. (Verse 1.) In the preceding psalm the pattern of repentance was expressed; in this following psalm the pattern of patience is signified.

David wrote this psalm and gave it to Idithum, a man trained in Levitical and priestly disciplines, to be sung. Before the ark of the Lord, he was especially skilled at leading the sequence of psalms as they were composed.

Therefore, since Idithum did not write this psalm but the prophet David did, and David gave it to Idithum, a man skilled in singing, to be sung, the title was inscribed in this way.

Finally, even in secular writings, some were the writers, while others were accustomed to sing on the stage songs, comedies, or tragedies. Those writers and performers sought the Olympic crown.

[Note: [Col. 1039D] Those who won in the games instituted by Hercules in honor of Jupiter near the city of Olympia and celebrated every fifth year were awarded that crown. It was made from branches of olive. Moreover, *epinikia* (ἐπινίκια) are songs in which someone’s victory is celebrated, such as those that Pindar, foremost among lyric poets, has for the most part left to us.]

Hence their writings testify at the end to an *epinikion* hymn—the victory song. But David, who did not piously desire these garlands of withering crowns, but that incorruptible and undefiled inheritance of heavenly rewards, did not write a victory hymn, an *epinikion*, but wrote it for the one who granted victory to those who believe in him, who is the end of all that we ask with devout minds.

[Note: [Col. 1040D] The manuscripts Vict. and Colb. read: “Whether you seek wisdom or virtue, he himself is the power and wisdom of God; he himself is the way of truth, justice, and resurrection.”]

Whether, then, you seek wisdom, or devote yourself to virtue, or seek truth, or the way and justice, or resurrection, in all things you must follow Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God, truth, way, justice, and resurrection.

Toward whom else, then, should you strive except toward the perfection of all things and the summit of the virtues? Therefore he says to you: “Come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21)—that is, so that you may deserve to reach the consummation of the virtues.

Therefore whoever follows Christ ought, according to his ability, to imitate him, meditating continually on his commandments and on the examples of his divine deeds.

2. Therefore David meditated within himself because he retained the conviction that Christ had spoken within him. When certain people troubled him and attempted to provoke him into contention, he assumed patience and avoided the desire for quarrelling, from which empty noise and disputes frequently arise.

Accordingly, since many people who envied holy David’s virtues frequently attacked him, believing that they could draw him away from his purpose of gentleness and his disposition of humility, and since especially the spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places, against which the righteous have a grave struggle, were urging the agents of their wickedness to agitate him, the holy Prophet resolved to remain silent, lest amid the repeated conflicts of those who shouted against him and the tumult of disputes some offensive word should escape him.

O powerful shield of watchful fortification—silence! O most trustworthy foundation of steadfastness, on which, if someone can stand, he cannot fear the slipperiness of speech!

For many who were firm in heart have nevertheless often fallen through the error of heedless and wavering speech.

Seeing, then, that the Prophet was being tested by such ambushes and by the empty uproar of those who were quarrelling, he quietly withdrew into himself, imposing upon himself a law of silence. And while he remained silent, as they insulted him and provoked him to say something—as insolent disputes and speeches commonly do—they said: “Answer us, if you presume to claim equality. You see that you too have been defeated and have nothing to say in reply.”

When he saw himself being driven almost to answer their insults, he restrained himself so that he might speak in his heart.

### 3. (Verse 2)

“I said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue. I have placed a guard over my mouth, while the sinner stands against me.’” That is: I proposed, confirmed, and commanded myself; I spoke to my heart: “I will guard my ways.” If I had said this to another, my word ought to stand; how much more firmly must that stand which I myself have determined for myself! If someone deceives another, it is dishonorable; if he deceives his neighbor, it is grave; how much graver, then, if someone thinks he may defraud himself of what he has promised himself, so that he is judged unfaithful to himself and despicable in his own judgment. Who, then, can seem worthy who is contemptible to himself? Let us therefore hold firmly to the constancy of our soul, lest lips hasty to speak burst forth into offense. Job also conquered his wound through silence and surpassed his endurance by keeping silent.

One cannot safely trust the flesh. We would have overcome, if Eve had kept silent. Thus the first sin proceeded from a voice, and that most wicked and crafty serpent first tempted us through speech. Would that Adam had been deaf, or Eve had become mute: he, so that he would not hear his wife’s voice; she, so that she would not speak to her husband and, through the service of her slippery speech, transfer the serpent’s poison to the man. Cain too, although by fratricide he violated human nature [Col. 1040D] and, in his wickedness, effaced the laws of filial devotion, nevertheless added sacrilege to his crime through speech, denying to God the death of his murdered brother.

What need is there to speak of individuals? The people themselves, chosen by the Lord, to whom Moses silently opened the sea, grumbled against the heavenly benefits and thereby provoked divine displeasure. Then they rejected Moses, the leader of that pathless and unprecedented journey, and asked his brother Aaron to make gods for them to worship.

### 4.

Therefore, considering these great dangers of speech, he himself also says: [Col. 1041A] “I said, ‘I will guard my ways.’” What, then, are these “ways” of a human being, which the great Prophet warns us must be guarded with the utmost care lest they incur some graver offense? We should examine this more closely. Solomon too, his son and interpreter of his father’s mind, urges us to investigate it more perceptively. He wrote:

“Three things are impossible for me to understand, and a fourth I do not recognize: the track of an eagle in flight, the way of a serpent upon a rock, the paths of a ship sailing on the sea, and the ways of a man in his youth.”

Such is the way of an adulterous woman, who, after she has acted, washes herself and says that she has done nothing wrong (Prov. XXX, 18 ff.). Thus he said that three things were impossible for him to understand, and a fourth that he—who possessed among human beings the mark of wisdom—did not recognize: namely, the course of a man’s ways in his youth. Since their recognition is either inexplicable or difficult, how can their guardianship be easy? Hence David rightly offered no defense of the sins of his youth, but asked that they be forgotten: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Ps. XXIV, 7).

Solomon therefore rightly said that he did not recognize what his father, in whom there was a greater measure of God’s grace, had confessed himself not to know. Perhaps he referred the “sins of youth” to the fervor of the flesh, and “ignorance” to slips of speech, which are often poured forth not from deliberate intention but through a kind of impulse and rush of speaking. Recognizing this to be dangerous, the Prophet said: “I believed, because of which I spoke” (Ps. CXV, 1). Thus a voice is safe when it rests upon the foundation of virtue; without a foundation, it is slippery.

Therefore, as though with the sound of a trumpet, the chosen interpreter of divine Scripture rebuked us: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10). Faith is the principle of believers; confession is its execution.

### 5.

How, then, and for what reason, did the holy prophet David propose to guard his ways? Let us listen: “So that,” he says, “I do not sin with my tongue.” If the Prophet takes care to avoid this, will you not? If he fears it—he through whom God’s grace spoke—will you not fear it, although you do not shun words of error and delight in theatrical speech? Will you not be afraid, when it is written for you in the Gospel (Matt. XII, 36) that you will have to give an account for every idle word? If there is danger in an idle word, how much more in a criminal one! Not everything idle is criminal, but everything that is unfruitful is dangerous and subject to being uprooted; for every tree that does not produce fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.

When the mind is stirred up and agitated by adversaries who provoke, interrupt, mock, and accuse, a word of agitation slips out. Therefore silence is both safe and seemly, because it preserves caution with dignity. For what are our lips except certain bonds of ours? In the end, each person is bound by the bonds of his own lips. Hence the wise person is silent at the proper time and considers within himself at what time he ought to speak. Concerning this Solomon says admirably: “The lips of the wise are bound by understanding” (Prov. XV, 7).

When, therefore, you see a wise man remain silent while insolent people mock him, say: “This man has bound his lips with understanding”; that is, he wisely keeps silent, lest he be bound by the bonds of his own lips. He has placed a guard over his mouth; he has fenced his ears with thorns; he has applied a bar to the doors of his mouth. He guards the treasure of his heart and the silver of his eloquence, so that he may bring it forth, examined and purified, when the time is right—lest some thief or disturber first break into his heart and drag it captive to those to whom he may sell his crimes.

### 6.

Judas was meditating on selling Christ, but the Lord’s great grace and certain caresses of paternal mercy, by which his fury was softened, held him back. He would not have broken out into crime unless the adversary had plunged himself into his heart, because he thought that he could deceive Christ. Do not doubt, therefore, that when certain people trouble you as you wish to preserve righteousness, they are ministers of that most wicked sinner who is the author of all crimes.

David saw him with prophetic eyes and recognized his figure. Therefore he kept silent, lest he do the will of him who strives to disturb the affections. He suppressed his voice; he closed his gates with silence; he displayed patience in him and kept watch with the guard of silence, lest the enemy creep in, lest some wandering and heedless word escape from the enclosure of his mouth.

Therefore the patient person who restrains himself is stronger than one who captures cities. The just man is himself his own enclosure; he is himself his own ever-watchful guardian.

### 7.

Thus, while he set this protection before himself, he spoke in his heart: “I have placed a guard over my mouth, while the sinner stands against me.” The enemy is always present, because he is always lying in wait. Even if you do not see him, he is present; even if you do not feel him, he attacks. If you do not see him, believe the one who sees: “The sinner,” he says, “stands against me.” Whoever sees his own sin also sees the sinner mocking him in the things he has done. Whoever foresees the sinner can avoid sin.

David saw the sinner standing against him when Shimei cursed and pelted his king with stones and cried: “Begone, man of blood!” (2 Sam. XVI, 7). He would not have been so reckless as to be moved neither by reverence for so great a king nor by fear of his armed army, since anyone from the king’s army could have killed the man who was reviling him. But the devil had made him mad and was driving him toward death.

Therefore David fought more against the author than he pursued the minister. For what great thing would it be to take vengeance upon a feeble man whom another had driven to madness, and in whose death the sinner would have achieved the fulfillment of his will? The devil is conquered not by the sword but by the word of God. Therefore let human speech be silent; let the Word of God speak.

Indeed, Christ too remained silent when he stood before Pilate’s tribunal, giving us an example of silence, because the tongue of the body is quick to err and prone to fall. Yet there are also those who speak while remaining silent, like Moses, who stood astonished and kept silent, and to whom God said while he was silent: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. XIV, 5). So too Susanna, who was silent in her dangers, and the Lord heard her. Therefore, even if the word of God is within you, you will remain silent in the word of God and cry out silently, so that you may be heard by Christ.

### 8.

Meditate, therefore, on the things of Christ—the things that the prophet David was meditating within himself—and in whom Christ earlier spoke the things that David says he meditated within himself in this psalm. For it is written:

“But when certain people troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth; I humbled my soul with fasting, and my prayer shall return into my bosom” (Ps. XXXIV, 13).

What does “when certain people” mean? It means that this occurs especially when either an unsuitable word slips out or the emotions are stirred—when we are in some pain or sadness, when the mind grows sick with indignation, when it is obstructed by various anxieties, or when it is occupied with disputes.

Who, then, are those who trouble us? Understand first that this refers to the author of sin himself and his angels; then to those [Note: Codex Regius and four others, together with the earlier edition, have in the margin: “who prefer to be his vessels.”] who prefer to be his followers rather than Christ’s. A wife is incited, as in the case of holy Job (Job II, 10 and elsewhere); a friend, as is revealed in that same book; a son, as Absalom; a servant, a freedman, or a member of the household—for “a man’s enemies are his household,” so that each of them may agitate him.

What remedy, then, is there against such illnesses of the soul except patience and silence? And, what is more serious, the person who provokes you most is the one who has benefited from your kindness; and among them, the one who irritates you most is the one who owes you the most. This is so that you may be moved by the bitterness of an ungrateful person or by the indignity of some contemptible individual.

### 9.

Therefore the just man, even if a friend is insolent toward him, grieves for his friend, because his friend is falling precisely because he is being driven on by the tempter. If he grieves for a friend, how much more for a wife or a son! If he finds them insolent toward him; if a brother agitates him, as Esau did holy Jacob, he grieves and seeks to reconcile his brother to himself—or to flee from his presence, as Rebecca advised, lest his brother’s anger find some opportunity to cause harm.

If a neighbor or member of the household does this, he grieves; if it is a minister, freedman, or servant, he bears it patiently, and in all these cases he keeps silent, so that he may not answer the one whom he sees being driven on by another.

Does someone from the household revile him? He grieves and keeps silent. Does a freedman revile him? He keeps silent. Does a servant revile him? He keeps silent. Thus the one who stretches his snare over the soul through the bait of speech is conquered.

You too, therefore, keep silent when someone unworthy reviles you; keep silent when a servant, and especially your own servant, insults you; and say in your heart: “I am silent; but you, Lord, do not remain silent” (Ps. XXXIV, 22). And add: “Do not depart from me,” as the prophet David said—that is, “Do not abandon me alone to those who attack me.” For the one with whom God is present is not alone.

Receive the testimony: “Behold,” he says, “the hour is coming when you will be scattered, each to his own place, and you will leave me alone; yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John XVI, 32).

### 10.

The just man, therefore, keeps silent before those who are insolent toward him; the just man prays. Hear the just man praying: “Instead of loving me, they slandered me; but I prayed” (Ps. CVIII, 4). The just man blesses those who curse him, as the apostles did, as Paul asserts when he says: “We are cursed, and we bless” (1 Cor. IV, 13).

The just man loves his enemies. See how he is taught to ascend gradually, step by step, toward the increase of the virtues, when the Lord says: “Love your enemies” (Matt. V, 44). The just man prays for those who accuse him, because the Lord also commanded this, adding: “Do good to those who hate you; pray for those who accuse and persecute you” (ibid.).

The one who observes and preserves these things is just in every respect. First, because he is silent and does not answer his enemies; then because he prays—that is, he is not idle in his affection. And the one who prays prays for good things, not for things that might harm his enemy.

To pray, therefore, is more than to remain silent. The just man blesses those who curse him. This too is more than praying for oneself, for one who is secure about himself blesses the person whom he does not fear—or even the person whom he once feared. The just man loves his enemy. To love is more than to bless, because love of the mind is greater than the grace of speech. The just man does good to the person whose hatred has been directed against him. The just man prays for those who accuse him.

Charity is good, and piety is good: both are of God, and both are God, because “God is charity,” as John said in his epistle (1 John IV, 16). Therefore the two are joined together: “Love your enemies . . . and pray for those who accuse and persecute you.” Charity is the fullness of the Law; but this fullness of the Gospel also commands us to pray for those who accuse and persecute us, so that we may ask forgiveness for their sins—as holy Job was chosen by divine judgment, whose prayer would remove the offense of those kings who had accused the just man (Job XLII, 8).

### 11.

Therefore, whether you are weak or strong, pray. When you are weak, you pray for yourself; when you are strong, you pray for your enemy. Prayer is a good shield for weakness. You pray, and the Lord protects you.

Prayer is also a good shield for one who has triumphed: it enables you to defend the enemy whom you could strike, lest he be slaughtered by anyone—or, what is greater, by Christ, who said: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Rom. XII, 19).

This is the prayer that returns into the bosom of the one who prays, bearing the fruit of what he wished to obtain, so that the gifts he requested from the Lord return into his soul and mind. Thus the same prophet taught you later, saying: “So I will bless you in my life, and in your name I will lift up my hands. May my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. LXII, 5–6).

The bosom of the soul is the secret place of prayer, the innermost chambers of the will, and a kind of intimate receptacle for returning prayers. Hence the just are also read to rest in Abraham’s bosom (Luke XVI, 22): that is, they rest in his grace, in his repose, and in his peacefulness, having assumed a faith conformed to his and having made the same will evident in good works.

### 12.

But perhaps someone may wonder: since the Lord said through David’s mouth that he humbled his soul with fasting (Ps. XXXIV, 13), how could David himself later say: “If I did not think humbly, but I exalted my soul” (Ps. CXXX, 2)?

Let him consider, however, that one thing pertains to the wisdom of the mind and another to humility of heart. The wisdom of the mind is lofty; but the wisdom of the flesh must not be inflated. David therefore humbled his soul with fasting, in order to teach us that the swelling of our flesh must be chastened.

The Prophet exalted his soul through the lofty grace of God, since “whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV, 11). This should first be understood to mean not only that the proud are brought low and the humble raised up according to the worthy recompense of their merits; but because the word of God is sharp on every side, like a sword sharpened on both edges, I think it may also be understood in this way: the one who exalts himself knows how to humble himself, and the one who knows how to humble himself also knows how to exalt himself.

Paul finally demonstrates this when he says: “I have learned to be sufficient in whatever circumstances I am. I know how to be humbled, and I know how to abound” (Phil. IV, 11).

Therefore David too, “not thinking humbly,” exalted his soul concerning Christ, whom the Arians humble and cast down; and, by exalting his soul, he piously represented through the disposition of his mind the vigor of understanding, the grace of faith, and the virtue of humility.

[Note: Thus read two Vatican manuscripts and five Gallican manuscripts. Although the meaning of the words is somewhat obscure, it will receive considerable light if you look back to the preceding statement: “When the Lord said through David’s mouth,” and so forth. Understand, then, that the Prophet, in the person of Christ, exalted his soul, and everything will become clear. Since the Roman editors did not fully grasp this, they transposed the words in the following manner: “He exalted his soul concerning Christ”—whom the Arians humble and cast down—“that is, he piously represented through the vigor of understanding, the grace of faith, and the virtue of humility.” The earlier edition and the Victor and Colbert manuscripts, however, had completely excised these words, reading instead: “Concerning Christ, he exalted his soul, and through the vigor of understanding and the grace of faith, [he represented] the virtue of humility,” and so forth.]

### 13. (Verse 3)

Therefore he said: “I became mute, and I was humbled, and I was silent from good things,” because he knew when he ought to humble himself and knew when he ought to remain silent.

[Note: The Victor and Colbert manuscripts read: “He himself became mute while those who rebuked him clamored in contentious dispute.” The Thuanean manuscript has: “lest he clamor with contentious dispute against those who rebuked him.” Finally, the earlier and Roman editions, together with the Vatican and other Gallican manuscripts, read as we have in the text. A little later, where the earlier and Roman editions, together with the Vatican manuscripts and five Gallican manuscripts, have “or so that he might teach them how they ought to humble themselves,” the Victor and Colbert manuscripts read: “or so that he might teach them that they ought to humble themselves.”]

“He became mute, lest he himself raise a clamour in contentious dispute with those who rebuked him; he was humbled,” so that he might cast down the pride of the arrogant, or so that he might teach them by his own example how they ought to humble themselves; he was silent from good things,” because a good conscience has no need of a verbal defense. It rests upon its own testimony and is itself its own judge.

Therefore the just man says: “Who will contradict me, or who will resist me?” (Isa. L, 8). Paul too says: “For me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by a human tribunal” (1 Cor. IV, 3). Against those who accuse and sin, the just man is content with his own judgment; but he reserves the judgment of his merits for Christ. Therefore he added: “The one who judges me is the Lord” (ibid., 4).

He chose as judge, most beautifully, the one who cannot be deceived by any fraud, so that neither hidden things escape him nor the failures of a frail condition offend him—for he knows how to forgive weakness.

Silence, therefore, is useful for everything. If you acknowledge the sin, be silent, lest by denying it you make it worse; if you do not acknowledge it, remain silent, secure in your innocence. The words of another cannot fasten a crime upon a conscience that has not itself admitted it.

### 14.
