It follows: “And my pain was renewed.” Still placed at a lower level of virtue, he brings forth these words because his pain, he says, was renewed by the reproach of former sins—sins which forgetfulness seemed already to have covered over as though erased, or which the compensation of good works had concealed.

Finally, later, as though stronger, he says: “They saw me and shook their heads” (Ps. CVIII, 25), because they threatened him but could not harm him. And he added: “They will curse, but you will bless” (ibid., 28). Here he speaks as one more powerful, disregarding insult or shame, since the Lord’s blessing abounded for everything.

Therefore, in this thirty-eighth psalm, as in a certain meditation, though he has not yet been placed in the full perfection of virtue, he says that his pain has been renewed. The strongest person does not know what it is to feel an offense against a scar, nor can one who is stronger fear a wound.

In the very contest of fighters, it is often the stronger man’s practice to wait until he is challenged by some blow from the weaker, so that, provoked more sharply, he may rise up with greater force. He is strengthened by excessive training and patience, so that, as though insensible to pain, he cannot feel a wound: struck, he laughs; challenged, he is roused.

But if the weaker man happens to receive a blow from his attacker upon a scar covering an old wound, he feels renewed pain. So it is with the person who has former sins thrown in his face—sins which he properly mourned and lamented, so that through suitable satisfaction he might cover the wound of his sins with a scar.

If he is perfect, he remains silent when people revile him, with no pain renewed within him. For even if he sinned, he is secure because God’s gifts are without repentance; and therefore, what he has once given, he does not ordinarily revoke or renew it, since he himself said: “I am he, I am he, who blot out iniquities, and I will not remember them” (Isa. XLIII, 25).

But if he is imperfect and forgetful of the heavenly commandments, his pain is restored as though a scar had been torn open.

### 15. (Verse 4)

“My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire will burn.”

As we know, more serious wounds are healed with a caustic medicine or by applying fire. Therefore the wise man is his own physician; yet, although he is a physician, he treats his own wound.

Thus, if he has not been fully perfected into a condition of untroubled health, his heart is heated; he has a fever; he catches fire at the insults thrown at him. And even if he remains silent, he is worn down within himself. When one stone is rubbed against another, it strikes out fire. Likewise, even a good conscience is kindled with shame when the memory of its sins is renewed.

And in the very meditation the fire burns. It is not an evil fire, one that scorches but does not consume. Such was the fire of God that Moses saw in the oak tree: the oak was burning but was not consumed. There is therefore a fire that diminishes sin and consumes guilt in its own heat.

There is also a fire kindled by meditation on the heavenly Scriptures, like the one of which Jeremiah says: “There was a flaming fire in my bones” (Jer. XX, 9). Or like that fire about which Cleopas and the other disciple who was traveling with him spoke together when Christ joined them after the resurrection, saying: “Was not our heart burning within us when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV, 32).

Therefore the Lord also came to cast this fire upon the earth, so that he might illuminate the souls of all, kindle devotion, and burn away sin.

### 16. (Verse 5)

“I spoke with my tongue: Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what the number of my days is, so that I may know what is lacking to me.”

Good is the fire that caused the Prophet to speak. And consider whether this is not the very fire that appeared when, on the day of Pentecost, the disciples were gathered together in one place, and the Holy Spirit descended upon them with great force, while they spoke in various tongues. For it is written: “Tongues appeared divided among them, as though of fire” (Acts II, 3).

This, then, is the one who said to Jeremiah: “Behold, I give my words into your mouth as fire” (Jer. V, 14). David too received this tongue of fire, so that, set ablaze by the fervor of divine knowledge, he might say: “Make known to me, Lord, my end.”

He is not asking about his death—for this is not the end of the one who is to rise again—but about the end of which the Apostle spoke (1 Cor. XV, 24 ff.): the end when the Lord Jesus will hand over the kingdom to God the Father and will abolish all principalities and powers, and when death, the last of all, will be destroyed, so that evils may cease and eternal goods succeed them.

Therefore it was said: “Pain, sorrow, and lamentation will flee away” (Isa. XXXV, 10). Paul brought about this end in human beings when he said: “Who is the one who makes me glad except the person who is made sorrowful by me?” (2 Cor. II, 2). By rebuking them, he stirred up pain, sorrow, and lamentation, so that they might repent and thereby merit irrevocable forgiveness and salvation, of which God would not repent.

That, then, is the true end—not the end of one person but of all. How, then, did he call it “my end”? Consider who is speaking. It is certainly a human being, either one among human beings sharing the common substance of humanity, or because he is described as the pattern of all and instructed toward the perfection of the completed human being.

### 17.

Therefore he also added that the number of his days should be made known to him, so that he might know what was lacking to him. This refers to what is lacking for perfection, not to the life of this body, from which the prophet David desired to be released, saying: “Alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged, and I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” (Ps. CXIX, 5).

Finally, he wished to know the number of his days, but not also the number of his nights.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “For here there are days and nights.” Thus there are days of the sun alone. The Victor and Colbert manuscripts read: “Here, he would say, there are nights; there are therefore days there, and there is the sun.” The earlier edition and other manuscripts read as we have in the text.]

“For here there are days and nights; but there there are days belonging to the Sun alone, there is perpetual and enduring light.” Therefore he added: “Which is,” he says, not “which passes away.” For heaven and earth will pass away, but faith remains, and the day of Christ, because “he is the same yesterday and today and forever.”

Now receive what number he is seeking. “In my Father’s house,” he says, “there are many dwelling places” (John XIV, 2). The Lord Jesus therefore assigns each person a place—that is, a dwelling appropriate to each person’s merits. Each person is in his own order.

He went before, therefore, in order to prepare a place in himself for those who believe. Hence he also said: “If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you may also be; and you know where I am going, and you know the way” (ibid., 3–4).

There is therefore a way by which Christ, having risen, ascended. He indeed ascended above all the heavens to the seat of God; human beings, however, ascend from the first heaven to the second, then from the second to the third, and from there, by successive stages, almost to the seventh heaven.

[Note: The earlier edition and the Victor and Colbert manuscripts read: “and to the very summit of the heavens.” Four others read: “to the very axis and summit of heaven.” The Vatican and Regius manuscripts read: “and to the very highest apsis,” and so forth. Read “apsis,” or “apside,” as the Roman edition has it. An apsis is the broader part of a building, as found in the manuscript Glossary of Du Cange. Nevertheless, we would prefer the reading “higher,” since it is the highest curvature of a vault. Jerome, Book II on the Epistle to the Ephesians, has: “At the highest vault of heaven—and, to use the very word, the apsis.” The word is also found used by ecclesiastical writers to signify a part of a church separated from the rest and possessing its own vaulted chamber. See our Mabillon, volume I of the *Analecta*, and others.]

And those who are worthy ascend to the very apsis and summit of the heavens. If, therefore, there is a number of ways and a number of dwelling places, there is certainly also a number of days through which one reaches the height of heaven.

### 18. (Verse 6)

“Behold, you have made my days old.” Another has: “You have made my days *palaestas*.”

If, according to the Seventy, we understand “old days,” then we understand that they were completed according to the old man. But our old man has been fastened to the cross. Therefore the old day too has passed away, and the new has come.

The day of one human being is one thing; the day of Christ is another—the day that Abraham saw and rejoiced in, concerning which David also says: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. CXVII, 24).

The holy man therefore rejoices on the Lord’s day, in the new day in which the Lord God has shone upon us and given new light to those restored to an innocent and whole life. Hence the just man, secure in the new light and grace of God, says (Rev. XXI, 1; XXII, 5): “There will be for me a new heaven, and a new earth, and a new light.” Neither a lamp nor the light of the sun or moon will shine there; rather, the Lord will illuminate his people.

Those, then, are the things I desired and longed for; therefore I did not seek the day of man.

### 19.

But if we understand “palaestas” as days, we recognize from the name that they are full of struggle and labor, since *palaestae* are said to be wrestlers in the arena, those who wrestle for a crown.

Therefore, because our struggle is not only against flesh and blood but also against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, our days—that is, the days of this life—are filled with labor and pain.

Hence he says later: “Our years will be meditated upon like a spider’s web; the days of our years are seventy years. But if we are strong, eighty years; and most of them are labor and pain” (Ps. LXXXIX, 9–10).

Thus the apostle Paul labored more abundantly than the other apostles, so that by contending lawfully he might reach the crown he desired.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “They are in labor and pain,” that is, “in the labor of this life.” Hence, and so forth.]

### 20.

Nevertheless, because the measures of architects are also said to be called *palaestas*—measures by which they measure buildings in order to determine the number or extent of the structure and the place where the buildings are to be set—and because God spoke through Isaiah:

“Who has measured the waters in his hand, and heaven with a span, and all the earth with a closed hand? Who has placed the mountains in a balance?” (Isa. XL, 12),

let us see whether perhaps this meaning should be gathered from the present expression: namely, that God possesses knowledge of everyone’s days, since nothing is immeasurable to him, who comprehends all things according to a certain measure of his knowledge, and nothing is unassessable, unexamined, or beyond numbering for him who said: “Even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Luke XII, 7).

This, then, is what the Prophet says: “Behold, you know my days; my daily actions do not pass you by. You have placed my sins before your eyes, and therefore my substance is as nothing before you.” For what is a human being except that you are mindful of him? “Man has been made like vanity.” Man is in sin; and if he possesses some measure of probity and virtue, he is rightly set above the other earthly living creatures and excels in the sight of the animals over which he has been placed. But in the sight of God, his substance is as nothing.

Hence he says elsewhere: “For no living human being will be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII, 2). Symmachus expressed this more clearly, saying: “And my life is as nothing before you.”

### 21.

There are also those who think that the days are called “short,” because Symmachus used the word σπιθαμάς (*spithamás*). A σπιθαμή (*spithamē*) is a span; and because God is said to have measured heaven with a span (Isa. XL, 12)—for the palm or span is a portion of the hand used by the measurer to measure and encompass something—they therefore think that the days are called short.

Yet the knowledge of God may, as we said above, be understood in terms of measurement, and this heavenly knowledge may mean that all things were made according to measure. The Prophet’s days should therefore be understood not as short but as great—days that God measured with the span with which he measured heaven.

For he would not call the days of his life short when he later said: “Alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. CXIX, 5), unless perhaps God made the days of this life shorter on account of human sins. Formerly life extended to nine hundred and even seven hundred years; now it is confined within the span of a hundred years.

Thus it should be understood: “You know my days, subject to sin.” For the days of this life, which is subject to sin, are short; but the days of eternal life are without end.

### 22.

Or certainly understand it in this way—for it is our task to seek the truth through arguments, while it is yours to choose what you will follow:

“Lest sin should increase,” he says, “you shortened the days of the human life that we live upon this earth. Yet, since in this brief course of life the end of sins comes with greater maturity, through the speed of death my substance is as nothing before you. For although we were made in the image and likeness of God, a certain earthly contamination weighs us down while we are placed in this body. It would not weigh us down if we preferred to put off the old man when we put on grace, rather than put on an additional garment over him. The old man, when stripped off, would bring us less labor than when covered over.”

For what is stripped off, we cast away; what is put on over us, we assume. Therefore we groan and labor until this mortal garment of the old man, made subject to error, is swallowed up by the newness of spiritual life. If much honey is poured over poison, the poison’s venom is removed only with difficulty and very slowly. Water too, if it does not expel the poison’s gall but absorbs it, struggles with the poison for a long time.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript and several Gallican manuscripts read: “Therefore laborious repentance is followed by sweet grace.” Others agree with the edition.]

Therefore repentance is laborious, but grace is sweet: sin is stripped off where there is grace; it is swallowed up where there is repentance. There it is forgiven; here it is hidden. Hence it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. XXXI, 1).

23. (Verse 7.) And he rested for a little while, sighing over the misery of the human condition; for he had said: “Nevertheless, all is vanity; every living human being.” And after the [Note: *Diapsalma* is a certain division or change in a psalm; thus, wherever—as Hilary says in the Prologue to his *Exposition of the Psalms*—a *diapsalma* occurs, it is to be understood that either something else is to be said, or that it is to be spoken by another, or sung in another musical mode. Jerome, in Letter 138 to Marcella, differs from this opinion, maintaining that *diapsalma* signifies nothing other than the Hebrew *selah*, that is, “always,” which was placed solely as a mark of distinction. Eusebius of Caesarea, however, discusses the same word quite differently in his Greek exposition of the Fathers on the Psalms, arranged by Balthasar Corderius and published at Antwerp by Moretus in 1643. There he relates that David had chosen five singers of the Levitical order, with whom he himself stood in the midst, and that, playing their individual musical instruments, they were accustomed to sing before the Sanctuary under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. But whenever that inspiration ceased, they too ceased singing for a time, and then wrote *diapsalma*. Gregory of Nyssa, *Treatise 2 on the Psalms*, chapter 10, attributes that silence not to the cessation of divine inspiration but to some new illumination imparted by the Holy Spirit to David’s mind. One may consult him, as well as Cassiodorus, *Prologue on the Psalms*, chapter 11, and others.]

After the *diapsalma*, having recovered his breath, he says: “Although a human being walks in the image of God, yet he is troubled in vain; he stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it.” See how, before the harshness of his judgment, he softened it; afterward he completed the reasoning of his statement. He softened it by saying: “Because a human being walks in the image of God.” Blessed are you who walk by faith toward the likeness of God; blessed are you who have faith within yourself; more blessed still if you had no greed. One good belongs to the eternal mind, another is the vain burning of carnal desire. Faith serves God; greed serves the tempter. The former gathers what benefits itself, the latter what benefits others. What, then, is so vain as not to know for which heir one labors? For who knows whether his own son or grandson will outlive him? Often the heir named in the tablets of a will precedes the testator in a funeral procession to the tomb; or the survivor consumes the inheritance, or a spendthrift dissipates it, or the most foolish person fails to preserve it, or an outlaw loses it. Therefore, if you see someone zealously gathering riches, say also: “He is troubled in vain; he stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it.” For he cannot take away with him what he possesses; and when he dies, he will leave his riches to others. An enemy and an ingrate frequently succeeds him, and the successor insults his predecessor. Those whom the former loved, the latter persecutes; those whom the former nourished, the latter sells.

24. The Greek, however, does not have “in the image of God,” but simply “in the image.” In what image, then, does a human being walk? Surely in the image of whose likeness he was made—that is, in the image of God. Now Christ is the image of God, who is “the brightness of his glory and the image of his substance.” [Note: Five manuscripts read: “Therefore Christ is the image; the saints are according to the image. This image came to earth.” The other manuscripts and editions have the wording given above. Again, at this very place the same five manuscripts read: “Would that it were not in shadow.” The others, together with the editions, read: “so that it is no longer in shadow.” Finally, where the Roman edition, with some manuscripts, reads “in the image, however,” the old edition, with others, has “for in Christ,” and so forth.]

Therefore Christ, the image of God, came to earth, so that we might no longer walk in shadow but in the image. The one who follows the Gospel walks in the image, in Christ. Therefore he says to his disciple: “Go behind me” (Mark 8:33), so that you may follow me. For this reason the Jewish people went astray, because they walked in shadow. The Christian people do not go astray, because they walk in the image, having the sun of righteousness shining upon them. It is a good image—not a likeness colored with the pigment of wax painting, but one expressed through the fullness of divinity. In this image both the Father and the Son are seen together, because through both of them the unity of their operation shines forth. Although Christ has already risen, his image is still shown to us in the Gospel (John 11:44). I read that he raised Lazarus, and I believe that this was the work of both the Father and the Son. The Son called, the Father heard, and Lazarus walked. I read that demons confessed him; they confessed the Father also, because they prayed to the Son of God; and they confessed him himself, because they were cast out through him. For it is written: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Matthew 12:27). [Note: Thus the old edition and the manuscripts, from which the Roman edition does not differ except that it removed the word *fatebantur*—“they confessed”—before “and the Father.” The Regius manuscript and several others read: “the demons confessed; and they confessed the Father, because they were praying to the Son of God; and in him or through him they were cast out” (Thuanus: “and through him”).]

[Col. 1051C] 25. First, therefore, came the shadow; the image followed; the truth will come. The shadow is in the Law, the image in the Gospel, the truth in heavenly things. The shadow of the Gospel and of the gathering of the Church was in the Law; the image of the future truth is in the Gospel; the truth is in God’s judgment. Therefore, the things now celebrated in the Church had their shadow in the sayings of the prophets: a shadow in the Flood, a shadow in the Red Sea, when our fathers were baptized in the cloud and in the sea; a shadow in the rock that poured forth water and followed the people. Was not the sacrament of this most holy mystery present there in shadow? Was not the water from the rock in shadow, like blood from Christ, following the fleeing peoples so that they might drink and not thirst, be redeemed and not perish? But now the shadow of the night and darkness of the Jews has departed; the day of the Church has drawn near. We now see good things through the image, and we possess the good things of the image. We have seen the High Priest coming to us, and we have seen and heard him offering his blood for us. We follow the priests as best we can, so that we may offer a sacrifice for the people: though weak in merit, nevertheless honorable in sacrifice. For although Christ is not now seen to offer, he himself is offered on earth when Christ’s body is offered; indeed, he is shown to be the one who offers in us, whose word sanctifies the sacrifice that is offered. He himself stands as our advocate before the Father; but we do not see him now. Then we shall see him, when the image has passed away and the truth has come. Then what is perfect will be seen no longer through a mirror but face to face.

26. Ascend, then, human being, into heaven, and you will see those things whose shadow or image was here. You will see them not partially, not in an enigma, but in their completion; not under a veil, but in light. You will see the true and eternal High Priest, whose images you saw here: Peter, Paul, John, James, Matthew, and Thomas. You will see the perfect human being, no longer in image but in truth; for “as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly ones.” Surely they too are already in glory and splendor, already in the grace of resurrection—not in the body of death and the deformity of corruption.

27. Take care not to bring the image of the earthly one into the place where the light of heavenly things is. Here, if anyone possesses images of a tyrant who has already been defeated and perished, he is rightly condemned. How, then, do you bring the image of an enemy and adversary into the city of the true emperor, unless you condemn yourself? And if you wish to bring in the image of the earthly one, the prince of this world will oppose you and say: “This image is mine, and what you offer is mine.” What will you do when caught, when he says to you: “Greed is mine, ambition is mine, riches are mine; in you I recognize their image”? For he is both adversary and defender. But if you are like Jacob, you will say to Laban, who transforms himself into an angel of light: “Recognize whether you find anything belonging to you in me” (Genesis 31:32). Then he will search, and, finding nothing, will depart confuted, because you have hidden and erased all the images of vices at once. Blessed is the one who can say: “The prince of this world will come, and he will find nothing of his in me” (John 14:30). For he seeks what belongs to himself, not what belongs to Christ. If, therefore, you follow what belongs to Christ, do not desire riches that you did not have, nor increase those that you had; let the poor person feel that you are rich for him. Bring the needy into your house, break bread for the hungry, and clothe the naked, so that a treasure may be stored up for you in heaven—a treasure that will pass with you. Christ became poor, although he was rich, so that by his poverty he might make us rich. Therefore do not be troubled in vain because of riches: do not be roused from sleep, thinking how to preserve your money and increase your possessions; do not go out at night, keep watch at the judge’s door, seize another’s property, bring a lawsuit against the poor, or fear the tax collector. This disturbance is vain.

28. (Verse 8.) And therefore the Just One said: “And now, what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? And my substance is before you.” Christ is our hope and patience. He himself became our redemption; he himself is our expectation, so that each of us may say: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he looked upon me” (Psalm 39:2). Look upon us, therefore, in your judgment. May your mercy look upon us, so that although we distrust our own merit, we may be delivered by your mercy, in whose power is the substance of our souls and our life. Therefore let us not fear the death of the body, but him who can either preserve or destroy our soul; whose substance is power, which God has infused into human breasts in his own likeness.

29. (Verse 9.) Whoever, therefore, possesses this substance of his soul says: “Deliver me from all my iniquities.” The one who prays to be released from all iniquities does not confess the fall of a single crime. For he knows that unless the Lord forgives, no one can be saved—everyone who has been born under sin, whom the very inheritance of a harmful condition has bound to guilt.

30. “You have given me,” he says, “as a reproach to the foolish.” Who is foolish except the one who commits sin and chooses evils instead of goods? Therefore the one who is the author of sins is more foolish than the one who serves him. When we sin, then, we are handed over as a reproach to the adversary, so that, like an enemy, he may accuse and betray us on the day of judgment. Let us therefore accept the reproach of Christ’s cross, which Moses accepted and preferred to the royal treasures of Egypt; and for this reason he was not handed over as a reproach to the foolish. Other copies have: “Do not hand me over as a reproach to the foolish.” But David more commonly confesses his own reproaches and sins, and does not blush at his sins and reproaches, since he knows that forgiveness is found in confession and righteousness in the condemnation of one’s sin.

31. (Verse 10.) Finally, the meaning here is made clear by what follows, for he adds: “I was silent and did not open my mouth, because you made me”—that is, you gave me as a reproach to the foolish. Therefore I was silent and did not open my mouth, lest I contract greater sins. I acknowledged your will, so that for a time I might be ashamed and afterward be saved by asking forgiveness. Reproach, therefore, is sometimes beneficial. Indeed, even the destruction of the flesh is beneficial, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “I have handed him over to the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 5:5). David himself also testified that reproach is beneficial when he said to Abishai: “Let him be; let him curse me, because the Lord told him to, so that the Lord may see my humiliation and repay me with good for this curse” (2 Samuel 16:11–12). And truly the Lord saw his reproach, as he went weeping and barefoot, with his head covered, and he removed his reproach. It is therefore clear that when David, handed over to reproach, fled, humbled himself, made satisfaction to the Lord with bare feet, did not strike back at the one throwing stones, and did not permit vengeance to be taken against the one who cursed him, and afterward was restored to his kingdom intact, reproach was from the Lord and it is more beneficial to endure reproach than to refute it. Finally, victory followed afterward. Reproach, therefore, is beneficial. But what does he mean by adding: “Because you made me”? Does he not say that he was therefore silent and did not open his mouth because he recognized the Lord’s will, and that he patiently endured it so that, through reproach, he might make satisfaction to the Lord for his sin?

32. (Verse 11.) Hence he also adds: “Remove your scourges from me” (Psalm 37:18). How does this agree with what he said earlier? In the preceding psalm he offered himself to the scourges, while here he asks that the scourges be removed from him—unless it is because he has now paid the double penalty for his sins from the hand of the Lord, by being ashamed and enduring reproaches. The scourges are the compunctions of his heart and thoughts, and also the scourges of rebukes. Let us nevertheless see whether he says that the substance of his soul is before God for this reason: because the adversary would not attack it unless he had received power from the Lord; for what the Lord has done, he also protects. Finally, an angel is around the human being, standing guard so that no one may harm him. The angel does not depart unless commanded by the Lord, so that his own champion may engage in battle. Therefore, as though he were the Lord’s substance, he presumes that forgiveness of his iniquities can be granted to him by his Creator; and for this reason he asks, because he knows his Author to be merciful. Furthermore, because he has been given over to reproach, he does not resist; but he permits the sinner to stand against him, and the conscience of his substance, which is good, remains silent and can restrain the violence of the body, so that strength may take the place of guilt. Finally, because he was made by the Lord, he confidently believes that his sin can more quickly be forgiven, since he was able to endure the strength of the Lord’s hand.

33. And this is certainly characteristic of a good substance, even if he says that he has failed before the strength of the Lord’s hand. A strong hand, just as it strikes severely, so also heals quickly; strong for wounding, it is strong also for remedy. Hence he himself says: “I strike, and I heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39), so that the one who escapes healed may not remember the wound. Finally, this hand of the Lord took everything away from holy Job and restored everything—indeed, it increased everything in abundance, so that what had been lost was doubled. Nor should it disturb you that he said he had failed. There is one who fails and rises stronger; for the Lord supports all who fall and straightens all who are crushed. Whoever is corrected rises with strength. Paul failed before the strength of this hand. The persecutor fell, and the preacher of the Gospel rose. This is what he says: “I have failed before the strength of your hand.”

34. (Verse 12.) And he added: “With rebukes you instructed a human being because of iniquity, and you made his soul waste away like a spider.” The Greek says ὑπὲρ ἀνομίας (*hyper anomias*), that is, “for iniquity,” and gives the whole verse as ἐν ἐλεγμοῖς ὑπὲρ ἀνομίας ἑπαίδευσας ἄνθρωπον (*en elegmois hyper anomias epaideusas anthrōpon*), which means: “With rebukes you instructed a human being for iniquity.” Therefore the Wise One said: “Who will give me the scourges of my thoughts …” (Sirach 23:2), “and a seal upon my lips” (Sirach 22:33)? [Note: Thus the manuscripts and all editions except the Roman edition, in which one reads: “Who will impose upon me the scourges of my thoughts, and who will give me [a seal] upon my lips,” and so forth. There the passage was adapted to the words of the sacred text; consult that text.]

Thus he might scourge his own heart with his thoughts and seal his lips, so that he might lessen former sins and not renew them by speaking; so that, instructed by his own rebukes, he might put on exercises of virtue. The soul wastes away when sin is diminished; or, when the soul wastes away, guilt is laid aside. It becomes fat when sins accumulate. Hence the Lord says of sinners: “My Spirit will not remain in them forever, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6:3). And elsewhere Scripture says: “The heart of this people has become fat” (Acts 28:27). Therefore Jeremiah first saw an almond rod, then a boiling pot, so that the soul of the novice [Note: The Roman edition reads “of the foolish prophet.” Other editions and several manuscripts more correctly read “of the beginning prophet,” since these things concerning Jeremiah are reported in the very first chapter of his book. Other manuscripts, not improperly, read “of the observing prophet.” As for the rod’s being called *nuceus* or *nucinus*—“nut-like” or “almond-like”—we have found this nowhere else.] prophet might waste away; so that guilt might depart and grace might draw near. But why first a rod, and afterward a pot? Because the one who is not corrected by the rod is thrown into the pot, so that he may burn and waste away. Therefore it is said to the prophet Ezekiel: “Take a frying pan for yourself … and you shall receive the iniquities of the house of Israel … and you shall consume them, and they shall waste away in their iniquities” (Ezekiel 4:3 and following). And elsewhere in the same book the Lord says: “But I will make the fire great, and I will multiply the wood, and I will kindle the fire, so that the flesh may melt and the broth may diminish” (Ezekiel 24:9–10). By these testimonies it is signified that the souls of the faithless waste away when fire is applied, so that they may lay aside a certain fatty moisture of flesh. The souls of sinners, therefore, are thrown into the frying pan, so that a certain flesh of sin may flow away—the flesh that had covered the vigor of the soul and mind and, as though in some kind of broth, had infused the soul with the allurements of desires. Certain frying pans therefore await us. Let us crush our heart here, so that it may become refined and lay aside all hardness and a certain fatness of carnal grease. Those who have indulged themselves in this life will suffer this, and, in the manner of the Jews, have believed that the mockeries of disgrace rather than any works of virtue should be practiced. Jacob became fat and grew stout, and rose to play; that play led him from the truth of faith into the error of faithlessness. Therefore Paul rightly disciplined his body, lest he nourish the body of sin. By indulgence we make members of sin; by sobriety, members of righteousness. It is not nature, therefore, but guilt that sins.

35. Let us not again pursue vain and empty things, lest we be judged to weave a spider’s web, since sins can possess no substance of perpetuity. Therefore, when you see some people striving to enlarge their resources, accumulate powers, and pursue distinction, say to them what Isaiah said: “These people weave a spider’s web in all things of a single day” (Isaiah 59:5). [Note: Thus the Vatican manuscript and five Gallican manuscripts. Others, together with the editions, omit the words: “these people, in all things of a single day.”] It cannot last long, but is quickly torn apart, and all its work is dissolved. For it is not placed upon some solid foundation, but hangs in empty space. Nothing loose, nothing soft, befits the true soldier of Christ; for behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses. All the greedy seem clever and industrious to themselves. What is cleverer, what more diligent, than a spider, which is always intent upon its work day and night and, without any cost or expense, makes itself a garment? Yet all that it has done is vain. So is every human being who does not establish his work upon the foundation of Christ. He too is troubled in vain by night and day, while, often, like a spider, even in the very effort of his wickedness, the collapse of his work rolls him together. [Note: Five manuscripts read: “even in the pursuit of the profit of his wickedness, the ruin of his work overwhelms him.”]

36. (Verse 13.) Therefore the wise person, who knows the vanity of this age, does not pray for a long enjoyment of this life; rather, he hastens toward those eternal things and longs to be released from the labor and pain of this body, as the Prophet is known to have desired when he said: “Hear, O Lord, my prayer and my supplication; give ear to my tears. Do not be silent toward me, for I am a sojourner with you on the earth and a stranger, as all my fathers were.” One person is a resident, another a stranger, another a sojourner. A resident is one who belongs to a place and inhabits his native land; a stranger is one who comes from elsewhere; a sojourner is one who inhabits a place temporarily and changes with the succession of years. This, then, is what David says: “With you I am an alien while I am on earth; I am not now a resident of your paradise.” He himself explains this by adding: “And a stranger, as all my fathers were.” The Apostle Paul also made this clear when he asserted that, while we are in this body, we are absent from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:7), because although faith is within us, we walk by faith and not by sight—that is, not face to face, as though present. We still walk in an enigma, not in truth. Finally, he adds: “Therefore we are bold and confident, and we prefer to be absent from the body and present with the Lord” (ibid., 8). [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “a word of presumption and faith,” not “of presumption in God’s faith.” The latter reading is better in other manuscripts: “of presumption in the faith of God,” that is, of the presumption and confidence which faith in God produces in us.]

The word “we are bold” expresses confidence in God, not rashness; and we consent—that is, we willingly acquiesce and desire, not weighing the authority of fuller knowledge as though sitting in judgment by our own reasoning. We want what we desire to be true, so that we may draw near to the Lord, from whom the distance between future and present things seems to separate us. “Therefore we are bold to be present”; and for this reason he says: “We strive” (ibid., 9). You recognize the word of one who still wishes to arrive, not of one who has arrived. What is shown in this statement, therefore, is desire, not fulfillment. Finally, ask the same witness about his own words—or rather, hear him speaking, or better, hear him hesitating when he says: “Therefore we strive, whether absent or present, to please him” (ibid.): absent still through faith, present through sight. Hence this too can be understood: that, while placed here, we desire to please our Judge and also the Redeemer of our souls there. For it is necessary that we stand before him in sight, so that each person may obtain the due lot of his works through a fitting examination—whether the righteous in rest or the impious in distress.

He therefore pours out tears, because, having come to earth as a stranger, he remains here and is separated from his homeland, detained by a long exile. Consider now Adam, expelled from paradise and confined in a fortress, looking upon the place from which he had been cast down and weeping abundantly because he remembers what he lost and from what height he fell. Therefore let us give thanks to God, who has freed us from perpetual exile by opening the door through which we may return to our homeland. Hence the Apostle boldly said: “Therefore you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Ephesians 2:19).

37. (Verse 14.) Wishing to receive this before Christ came to earth, David said: “Forgive me, that I may be refreshed, before I go away and am no more”—that is, forgive me here, where I sinned. Unless you forgive me here, I shall not be able to find the rest of forgiveness there; for what has remained bound on earth will remain bound in heaven, and what has been loosed on earth will be loosed in heaven. The Prophet and herald of the Church that was to be gathered foresaw, by the spirit of the Gospel, the Lord’s acts of forgiveness, and the Lord revealed to him what was to be commanded to the apostles. Indeed, this was the ancient judgment: whoever bound himself on earth would depart from the body still bound. [Note: He seems to allude to Ecclesiastes 11:3: “If a tree falls to the south or to the north, in whatever place it falls, there it will remain.”]

Therefore the Lord gave the apostles, as something formerly belonging to his judgment, the authority to remit sins so that they might be loosed, lest sins that ought to be quickly loosed remain bound for a long time. Finally, hear him saying: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19). “I will give you,” he says, “the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” so that you may both loose and bind. Novatian did not hear this, but the Church of God heard it. Therefore he is in the state of falling, while we are in forgiveness; he is in impenitence, while we are in grace. What is said to Peter is said to the apostles. We do not usurp authority, but serve the command, lest, when the Lord comes later and finds bound those whom it was fitting to loose, he be moved against the steward who kept bound the servants whom the Lord had ordered to be loosed, saying: “The servant who knew the will of his master and did not act according to his will will be beaten with many blows; but the one who did not know and did things deserving of blows will be beaten with few” (Luke 12:47–48). [Note: All editions read “the equity of remitting sins, so that what ought quickly to be loosed …” Five Gallican manuscripts have “the equity of remitting sin, which ought to be loosed, so that it might not remain bound for long.” The Vatican, Colbert, and Victor manuscripts give the best reading, as in the text; here one should understand “which ought to be loosed” as referring to “sins” in the accusative.]

38. David therefore rightly asks that what he knew had not been granted to those priests who were according to Aaron be forgiven him; it was reserved for the Gospel. Whoever is not forgiven remains in exile and continues in the misery of pilgrimage. Forgiveness must therefore be sought here. For here it was said: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21). This is the place for seeking forgiveness. Let us therefore weep on earth, so that we may merit pardon. Unless sin is forgiven here, we shall not have rest; if there is no rest, there will be no eternal life; if there is no eternal life, we shall not exist. Therefore he asks to be forgiven before he departs, so that he may exist. For if it has not been forgiven, he says, “I shall not be” with those who are, with those who deserve to ascend into paradise. But the one who does not exist will be consumed with those who descend into the pit, abandoned in chains and prison.

39. He does not therefore say definitively, “I shall not be,” because elsewhere he says: “I will sing to you upon the harp, O Holy One of Israel. My lips will rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed” (Psalm 70:22–23). He therefore presumes upon redemption. And elsewhere hear him saying: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 114:9). There will therefore be one who presumes that he will please him.

It can also be understood in this way: he said, “I am a stranger with you on earth, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were”; and therefore, “forgive me, so that I may cease to be a sojourner; forgive me the exile to which I have been banished.” If you forgive me before I depart from here, I shall no longer be an exile and a sojourner. For when you forgive me, I shall not be a sojourner but a citizen of your saints. I shall be with my fathers, who themselves were formerly sojourners but are now citizens. I shall be a member of God’s household, so that I may not fear punishment but may merit grace: through our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom, together with the Holy Spirit, you have praise, honor, glory, and eternity, from the ages, now and forever, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXXIX

[Col. 1057]

[Col. 1057C] 1. In the preceding psalms he preached repentance; afterward he spoke of his own patience and of the human being’s distress. In the thirty-ninth psalm, however, he announces the New Testament. For the one who repents of evils waits. But it is not the mark of perfection merely to wait, but to have waited; for no one will be saved except the one who perseveres to the end. [Note: Thus the editions and the Colbert and Victor manuscripts; but the Regius manuscript, incorrectly, reads: “afterward he spoke of the disturbance of his own patience and of the human being.” The Vatican and four other Gallican manuscripts read somewhat better: “afterward he nevertheless spoke of the patience of his own distress.”]

2. (Verses 2–3.) Therefore he adds: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord.” Where, then, is this said except in the Gospel? In it the one who was awaited has now come to us. In it the shadow of the Law no longer grows dark over us, but the truth shines, because Christ has dawned, who heard the prayers of his own and brought us out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth, where we were already submerged in the abyss of our sins and our whole human being clung fast, while our mind could not extricate itself, overwhelmed by the stain of many crimes.

Thanks, therefore, to the Lord Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God and our Redeemer, who descended from heaven to forgive all our sins, so that he might rescue us from the pit and mire of this world, from a certain filthy marsh of the earth, and also from this body of death, and establish in his own flesh the inward footsteps of our soul. Thus, confirmed in the word of God and released through the sufferings of the Lord’s body on the cross, let us walk no longer in the reproach of disgrace but in the remission of sin. [Note: The word *passionibus*—“sufferings”—is absent from most manuscripts, although it does not seem superfluous to the sense.]

Established, therefore, and rooted in Christ, he recalls that the footsteps of his feet have been set upon a rock. Hence the Apostle says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). He is a rock because he follows those who thirst and confirms those who are falling, so that water may not be lacking for the thirsty and support may not be lacking for those who fall.

3. (Verse 4.) Therefore, as I waited for you, Lord Jesus, you came at last; you directed my steps in the Gospel and placed in my mouth a new song, which is the New Testament. Rejoicing, we now sing a hymn to our God, because we have learned the commandments of new virtues: to leave all that is ours, follow Christ, and love our enemies. We have also drawn in new ways of life: to offer prayer to the Lord for those who persecute us. Behold, we bless those who curse us. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “We do not know how to harm our works” (perhaps it should read “praise” them) “or despair of our sins.”] We do not know how to boast of our works or conceal our sins. We also reject marriage in the manner of angels.

4. (Verse 5.) What more need be said? From that wretched sinner a blessed person has been made, no longer looking toward the various vanities of this world. “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2): this whole world is such, as the wise Solomon said. For what is it but vanity to pursue things that cannot endure and that all pass away like a shadow? There are also the madnesses of falsehood, or those contests of wars in which so much blood is poured out for a temporary possession; the disputes of theatrical competitions; the frenzied passions displayed in the Circus; the deadly teaching of heretics; and the gestures imitated in the manner of heavenly oracles and the carefully composed words of false prophets. Thus the prophet says: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked upon vanities and false madnesses.”

5. There are therefore also true madnesses, perhaps those of the prophets who, placed in ecstasy, prophesied, filled with the Spirit of God, so that they seemed mad to some people. Forgetful of their own safety, they often ran naked and barefoot through the peoples, like the holy Isaiah, crying out not what they themselves wished but what they were commanded by the Lord. From these things, therefore, it is understood that the remedy of salvation has shone forth, because the one who was awaited is present.

6. Adam, expelled from paradise, awaited him, so that he might be freed from his long exile. He was awaited in righteous Noah, who was preserved for the seed of future generations, so that from him seeds of righteousness might sprout among human beings. Noah thought him to be the author of public salvation, since he had deserved to survive the Flood. He thought him the prince of wisdom, since he had cultivated the vine and had become drunk from its fruit. For what is the vine except wisdom? David, the heavenly interpreter of the oracle, made this clear to us when he said: “Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine within the sides of your house” (Psalm 127:3). For in him was the fullness of wisdom that was awaited in Christ, who, filled with the new mystery of wisdom—which eye has not seen and ear has not heard—hastened to bring us an unfamiliar mystery, so that he might lie naked and pour forth unheard-of cups of overflowing wisdom. Thus, forgetting what came before, we might rise into new ways of life and a new sobriety of eternal life, so that God might be recognized through the foolishness of preaching, whom this world did not know through wisdom.

Finally, in that figure of the sleeping and naked father, the one who mocked his foolishness was cursed, while those who honored him obtained the grace of blessing. Therefore those who have believed that the death of the only-begotten Son of God, the Father and Creator of all, should be brought forward as an offense or reproach against our faith are held bound by the chains of their sins for the perpetual misery of the curse; but those who accept it for the absolution of the whole human race are supported by the protection of eternal power. For the cross of Christ is an offense to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks, as the Apostle said (1 Corinthians 1:23 and following); but to us who believe in the Lord Jesus, it is the power and wisdom of God.

7. He was awaited in Moses, when he dried up and passed through the waves of the sea and opened, in the midst of the waves, a dry-road passage impossible to human strength; the rock followed and vomited forth waters, so that it might satisfy the inward organs of the thirsty fathers in the midst of the desert. [Note: The old edition and the Colbert and Victor manuscripts read: “when he held back the waves of the sea.” The Roman edition, with the same old manuscripts, has in the margin: “when he cleft the waves of the sea.” Other manuscripts read as in the text; except that the Regius manuscript has: “when he had cleft and crossed over,” and so forth.]

8. He was anticipated also in Aaron, the high priest, who stood between the living and the dead; and he stopped the plague of death as it was spreading, so that destruction would not pass from the corpses of the dead to the living. For what is so characteristic of Christ as to stand before God the Father as advocate for the peoples, to offer his own death for all, to repel destruction, and to restore life to those who were perishing?

[Note: [Col. 1060D] All editions, together with the manuscripts Vict. and Colb., read: “and through the serpent he established the plague of death.” Four other manuscripts read: “and he established the serpent; the plague of death,” and so forth. The Reg. manuscript is best of all, reading as in the text. The meaning is that Aaron caused the plague, which was spreading, to stop, as is explained below, at the end of no. 16.]

9. He was anticipated also in Joshua son of Nun, and indeed he came—he who received both his power and his name—in order both to lead the people into the promised land and truly to be called “Jesus.” He dried up the streams, turned the river back toward its source, and made the sun stand still until he completed the victory by his power. Yet that man was still a figure, not the reality. Finally, the true leader of the heavenly army shone forth to him, and Joshua son of Nun worshiped him; although the true one had not yet stood present in the body, but had still come in figure.

10. When, then, did the true one arrive? Hear him saying:

“I proclaimed and spoke: they have multiplied beyond number. You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you fashioned a body for me. Then I said, ‘Behold, I come.’ In the heading of the Book it is written concerning me, that I should do your will; my God, I willed it.”

What could be clearer than that the true Jesus came to us with the gift of his Gospel? He himself spoke, and innumerable peoples of believers were gathered, though previously scarcely any individuals believed. He himself came in the flesh, and the sacrifice of the Jews ceased. The offering for sin ceased, because the Remitter of sins had arrived. The remedy of the Law was no longer necessary where the Author of the Law stood present.

[Note: [Col. 1061D] From this point through the next number, the Roman edition altered the distribution of the verses in several places and inserted several things. These can readily be detected by comparing that edition with ours.]

11. “In the heading of the Book it is written concerning me.” Certainly it was written concerning Christ at the beginning of the Old Testament that he would come to do the will of God the Father in the redemption of humanity, when it was written that he formed Eve as a figure of the Church, for the help of man. For what can be a safeguard for us in this weakness of the body and the turmoil of this age, except the sole grace of the Church, by which we are redeemed, and our faith, by which we live?

“In the heading of the Book it is written: ‘Bone from my bones, and flesh from my flesh. For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’” (Gen. II, 23–24). Who this speaker is, or concerning whom this mystery is spoken, hear him saying: “This mystery is great; but I speak of Christ and of the Church” (Eph. V, 32). Therefore he also admonishes that a man should love his wife as Christ loved the Church (ibid., 25), because we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones.

What salvation, then, is greater than to be with Christ and to cling to him by a certain bodily unity, in whom there is neither any spot nor the distortion of sin?

[Note: [Col. 1061D] The older edition and the manuscripts Colb. and Vict. read: “nor the strength of sin”; the edition’s marginal reading has, perhaps, “deformity” or “fear.” [Col. 1062D] The Roman edition alone reads: “nor the filthiness of sin.” The Latin manuscripts read: “nor the disgrace of sin.” But five manuscripts clearly preserve our reading. The “distortion of sin” is so called because sin turns and twists away from the eternal rule.]

862 12. It is written in the heading of the Book that the sacrifice of righteous Abel pleased God, while the offering of the fratricide displeased him (Gen. IV, 4–5). Did the Lord Jesus not clearly signify that he was to be offered for us, in order to consecrate the grace of the new sacrifice in his passion and abolish the rite of the murderous people? What could be more explicit than that a son was offered by the holy Patriarch and a ram was sacrificed? Did he not clearly show that it would be the flesh of a human being, which is shared by all earthly living creatures, and not the divinity of the only-begotten Son of God, that would be subjected to the wound of the sacred passion?

[Col. 1062A] 13. It is written in the heading of the Book that a man would come who would command the heavenly Powers (Gen. XXVIII, 12). This was fulfilled when the Lord Jesus came upon earth and angels ministered to him, just as he himself deigned to say: “From now on you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of Man” (John I, 51).

14. It is written in the heading of the Book: “A lamb without blemish, clean, mature, a male one year old, shall be for you; and the whole assembly shall slaughter him” (Exod. XII, 5). Who this lamb is, you have heard him saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John I, 29). This is he who was slaughtered by the whole Jewish people, whom they still pursue with hostile hatred.

He indeed had to die for all, so that forgiveness of sins might take place through his cross, and his blood might wash away the defilements of the world. But woe to those who denied the author of their own salvation! “You have made a plan,” he says, “but not through me” (Isa. XXX, 1). How could he approve the murder who did not approve the plan? And yet what compassion! He recoiled from their plan; but if they had turned back, he would not have denied them a remedy.

[Col. 1062B] 15. It is written also—not only in the heading, but throughout the whole structure of the Law—that a man would come to preserve the human race, one who would will everything that God willed. Hence you understand that he shares the same divinity because he shares the same will. Therefore he also approached the sacrifice of the passion voluntarily, and rightly foretold: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. LIII, 8).

16. But perhaps you will say: How did he say in the Gospel, “Father, if it is possible, take this cup from me; yet not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. XXVI, 39)? There does seem to be a difference of will. Yet we understand one thing to be expressed according to the unity of divinity, when he says, “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30), and another to have been spoken according to the human affection, which he indicates ought to be cautious and not presume upon what it cannot easily accomplish, lest, while seeking a reward, it fall into sacrilege.

Therefore he says: “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matt. X, 23). Accordingly, here too, as he was about to undergo the passion of the body, he began to be sorrowful and distressed; and, taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he first declared: “My soul is sorrowful” (Matt. XXVI, 38), and afterward added: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (ibid., 41).

You see him everywhere speaking as man, praying as man, being sorrowful as man, and saying as man: “My Father, if it is possible” (Matt. X, 23). This was certainly not impossible for God; but to doubt belongs to man, while to confirm belongs to God. Therefore he took with him the more ready ones, as though they were chosen witnesses of his final judgment, who would recognize the mystery of his words. Indeed, the others were sleeping; these alone watched with faithful minds.

Therefore, through Jeremiah, before he had assumed a body, he himself says:

“I was led like a lamb, and I did not know” (Jer. XI, 19).

[Note: [Col. 1063D] The Roman edition reads: “I was led like an innocent lamb to be sacrificed,” evidently in order to render the Greek passage, where we read: Ἐγὼ ὡς ἀρνίον ἄκακον ἀγόμενον τοῦ θύεσθαι—“I was led like a harmless lamb to be sacrificed.”]

What is it that the Wisdom of God does not know, since it is always in the Father’s secret counsel? Therefore the Son of God declared everything, because he himself is the wisdom of God the Father.

How did he foresee that he would be led like a lamb, yet say that he did not know where he was being led? Or how, earlier, did he say through the mouth of David: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. XXI, 2)? How is the Son forsaken by the Father when he says: “And I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John XVI, 32)? And elsewhere: “I have been handed over, and I did not go out” (Ps. LXXXVII, 9)? And elsewhere: “I rose, and I am still with you” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 8)?

[Col. 1063B] This is so only if you observe that he expresses the human perception of those who think that they have been abandoned by their Lord when they are in danger. Finally, hear what follows: “Far from my salvation,” he says, “are the words of my sins” (Ps. XXI, 2)—that is, the words of sins are one thing, and the mysteries of eternal salvation another. Words do not prejudice power; the divine substance is supported by its own strength. He appears as man, he is heard as man, but God is recognized in his works.

And yet it was said of this man: “He is both man—and who will know him?” (Jer. XVII, 9). What does “who” mean? Not that no one will know him, but that few will, the wise—as in the saying: “Who will ascend the mountain of the Lord? Who is wise and will understand these things?” (Hos. XIV, 10). Again, elsewhere: “The foolish man does not know them, and the senseless does not understand these things” (Ps. XCI, 7).

Therefore, when you read the Gospel, understand what you read as a wise person, not as a fool. May the splendor of eternal Wisdom illuminate you. They are words, indeed; but the words themselves cleanse, illuminate, strengthen, and give life. Hence Peter says: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we will not leave you” (John VI, 69).

17. Finally, so that we might observe that he had spoken according to the human nature, shortly afterward he said: “Behold, the hour is near when the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners” (Matt. XXVI, 45).

And to Judas, who was kissing him, he said: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” That is: Do you pour poison into the kiss through which the grace of love is poured? Through the kiss that is the sign of sacred peace? Through the kiss by which faithful friendship is confirmed? Through the kiss by which holy faith is sealed? With this kiss, then, do you deliver to danger the one whom, because of the exchange of a kiss, you ought to venerate? And you, a man, betray the Son of Man who descended from heaven for the salvation of human beings?

For it is written: “The Son of Man who is in heaven is himself the one who descended from heaven” (John III, 13). You betray the Son of Man who made you an apostle from a sinner. You betray the Son of Man who came to wash away the sins of all in his blood.

I do not reject the kiss; you yourself must answer for having violated the sanctity of the kiss. Have you not read that “the wounds of a friend are better than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Prov. XXVII, 6)? And not without reason was Judas struck by the more grievous weapon of such great condescension than if he had been struck by lightning.

Finally, he could not endure the Lord’s patience, though he had betrayed his majesty, to such a degree that he could not wash away from himself the guilt of so great a crime.

[Note: [Col. 1063D] Thus the edition and the manuscripts Vict. and Colb., except that these read: “though he was guilty of so great a crime,” and so forth. The Roman edition reads: “whose majesty he betrayed, so that the guilt of so great a crime might be washed away from him; but he went away,” and so forth. The entire passage is presented as follows by five Gallic manuscripts: “By this he incurred a greater guilt, so that the guilt of so great a crime could not be washed away from himself” (four read: “from himself by God”). “And so he went away, rejected the money”; that is, he condemned his avarice, while the author of such great impiety returned to the synagogue the price of his treachery.]

Therefore he went away and returned the money; that is, he condemned his avarice, the author of such great impiety, and returned the price of his treachery to the synagogue. The betrayer is not excused because he could not find a place for repentance; rather, the sacrilege of the Jews is heaped up, since they are also convicted by the words of the betrayer.

He acknowledged his own crime, saying that he had betrayed righteous blood; they both accepted the price of the crime and pursued the Prince of righteousness with even fiercer zeal. Therefore, for the perpetual condemnation of them all, the thief crucified beside him is absolved, because he recognized in his own sufferings the Christ whom they did not recognize in his benefits. He confessed his sin to Christ, who knew how to forgive, because on his cross he perceived in his mind the Lord’s kingdom, which Judas could not see at Christ’s banquet.

Therefore the thief’s prayer was followed by this heavenly voice: “Amen, amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43).

You rejoiced, serpent, that you had torn an apostle away from Christ; you lost more than you took, since you see the thief transferred into paradise. No one can be excluded when the thief, your servant, has been received and has reached the place from which you yourself were cast down.

18. We have inserted these observations because of that verse in which he said: “That I should do your will; my God, I willed it”—that is, Father, I share one will with you according to divinity. And because there is one will, there is one substance; for the majesty and power of the Trinity are also inseparable.

But there is another voice belonging to the flesh, and yet even it consented to the will of God, saying: “Not what I will, but what you will” (Mark XIV, 37). And elsewhere: “If this cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done” (Matt. XXV, 42).

It is a common human feeling to fear death, which Christ assumed in order to crucify the flesh, just as he crucified it; for he struggled on my behalf in order to conquer for me. Although Christ’s flesh was strong and not subject to sin, he nevertheless assumed sins; he assumed infirmities, although he had nothing in himself that could cause pain.

Finally, hear him saying that he suffers for us (Isa. LIII, 4) … until he brings forth judgment in truth (Isa. XLII, 4). For he did not assume another flesh, but this one, as the Apostle teaches when he says: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (I Cor. XV, 53).

Although he was born of a Virgin and of the Holy Spirit, he is nevertheless the Son of man, because the Virgin was human. Therefore, what is born of flesh is flesh; and he who is born of a human being is called man: the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

19. Therefore the incorruptible one assumed this flesh in order to make it incorruptible, and the immortal one assumed it in order to make it immortal. If anyone follows him, he will put on immortality. If anyone does his will, he will not die forever; rather, Christ says to him: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43).

What does “today” mean? It means: You have passed through the night; you will be with me in the light. Do not fear the darkness, you whom eternal light has received.

Beautifully he also added: “You will be with me in paradise” (ibid.). That is: Do not doubt concerning the flesh—you saw me in the flesh. Do not fear that you too might fall from paradise as Adam fell; but hear that you will be with me, in whose presence you cannot fall.

The flesh fell in paradise before it was assumed by Christ. You will be received where he who assumed it is; for he did not lie when he said: “I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 24). The shepherd will not withdraw from his flocks, although you can no longer fear the wolf in paradise, to whom it was said: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke X, 18).

Therefore, before the consummation, the adversary is cast down into the fire and is also bound with everlasting chains, so that you may no longer fear any ambushes.

20. Adam was deceived by the serpent and was bent away by his wife, so that he fell. Therefore there are now no marriages in paradise, but all will be without the celebrations of marriage, like the angels in heaven.

He did not say to Adam, “You will be with me,” because he knew that Adam would fall, in order to be redeemed by Christ. Blessed is the fall that is restored to something better.

Therefore the compassionate shepherd and good merchant did not abandon his flock or his own possession. There will indeed still be a struggle with the serpent in paradise, before it is cast down; but whoever is with Christ cannot fear.

Adam was not with Christ when he was deceived. For if he had been with Christ and had remained in his command, he certainly could not have perished.

[Note: [Col. 1065D] The older edition, together with the manuscripts Vict. and Colb., reads: “he would not have been deceived.”]

He did not remain in Christ because he did not remain in Christ’s word. Finally, hear who remains in Christ: “If you remain in me and my words remain in you, whatever you wish, you will ask, and it will be done for you” (John XV, 7). And below: “If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love” (ibid., 10).

Do you wish to know that Adam was not with Christ? The Lord said to him: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. III, 9). He was seeking one who was evidently absent; he would not have said, “Where are you?” if he knew that Adam remained in him.

But let us hear what made him absent: “The two of them hid themselves,” it says, “from the face of the Lord” (ibid., 8). Christ sees everyone; but whoever hides himself is hidden, because whoever does not know is not known. For the Lord knows those who are his.

He wishes all whom he formed and created to be his. If only you, human being, would not flee and hide yourself from Christ! He even seeks those who flee and does not want those who are hidden to perish, but cries out, saying: “Adam, where are you?” That is: Human being, where are you? I placed you in the light, but you sought darkness.

21. Finally, in paradise, where the day had always been morning, evening came to be, because all sins are dark. Therefore you read that they heard “the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise toward evening” (ibid., 8).

At the same time, understand the mystery: In the morning you went astray; toward evening you will be delivered. For how can there be evening where Christ is? Although his seat is above the heaven of heavens, Christ is nevertheless in his saints.

How, then, can there be evening where God is, since God is light? Finally, light flashed upon Saul on the road when Christ met him. Therefore, when the light of God shone forth, the persecutor was blinded.

Why was he blinded, unless because he had not recognized Christ? For if he had recognized the author of light, he would not have lost the light of his eyes. Finally, when he recognized him, he received it back.

It is evidence that he had not recognized Christ that, after hearing the voice, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 4), he replied: “Who are you, Lord?” (ibid., 5). He would not have asked who he was if he had recognized him.

Therefore the Lord, as though speaking to one who did not know him, says: “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting. It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (ibid., 5). And he said: “Lord, what must I do?” (ibid., 6).

Observe the fitting instruction given on both sides. The physician threatens in order to correct; he terrifies in order to heal. At first the sick man asks about the physician’s identity, to determine whether he is one from whom he may presume he can be healed. When he heard the author of the medicine, he asked for a remedy and found salvation.

Finally, when the one who was approaching him came, he not only drove away his blindness, but also received the light that he had not possessed, so that he might see Christ, whom previously he had not seen.

[Note: [Col. 1065D] Some manuscripts read: “When he approached, he expelled the blindness.”]

22. (Verses 10–11.) But let us examine what follows, repeating the verse concerning which this treatise appears to have been composed:

“Behold, I come to do your will; my God, I willed it, and your law is within my heart. I have proclaimed your righteousness in the great Church; behold, I will not restrain my lips. Lord, you know. I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart.”

From the preceding verse, therefore, we understand: “Behold, I come” not only to do your will, but also to have your law in the midst of my heart.

[Col. 1066D] Some have: “In the midst of my belly.” For there is also a belly of the mind, which conceives the seeds of perceptions. Concerning it Isaiah said: “We conceived in the womb and gave birth; we brought forth the spirit of salvation” (Isa. XXVI, 18).

Paul also gave birth in this womb, when he said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV, 19). Christ, therefore, is formed not in a bodily belly, but in a certain belly of the soul.

The Apostle begot in this belly, as it is written: “I begot you through the Gospel” (I Cor. IV, 15). Therefore some rightly have, “In the midst of my heart,” while others have, “In the midst of my belly,” so that you may understand the belly of the inner person, which is understood to be in the midst of the heart. In it we preserve the prescriptions of the natural law, which is not only guarded but also enacted in our hearts.

Therefore it is written that not merely the hearers of the law are righteous before God, but “the doers of the law will be justified” (Rom. II, 13).

[Note: [Col. 1067C] The Roman edition reads: “but the doers of the law.”]

For there are people who naturally do what belongs to the law, like the Gentiles who do not hear the law and are a law for themselves, preserving the commandments of the law known to them.

[Note: [Col. 1067C] The Reg. manuscript reads: “and compare them with themselves, because the commandments of the law, being from one source, are known to them.” Four other manuscripts agree, except in the word “known,” for which they read “unknown.”]

Therefore, as though gathering the Gentile people, Christ assumed our person here, in order to say that he makes the law in the midst of his heart.

For the people of the nations fulfilled the law that they had not heard, so that they might recognize Christ, whom the Jewish people, which had received the law, did not accept and did not deem worthy of recognition, because it is written: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me” (Isa. I, 3).

This, then, is the belly of believers, in which the Holy Spirit has worked and which he is accustomed to fill with spiritual seed, as the Lord Jesus testifies in the Gospel when he says: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 38).

From that river these rivers come, of which we read: “The rushing of the river gladdens the city of God” (Ps. XLV, 5). Concerning those from whom such spiritual rivers flow, it is rightly said:

“The rivers have raised their voice, Lord; the rivers have raised their voice. The rivers will raise their waves” (Ps. XCII, 3–4),

at the voice of the spiritual waters that praise God above the heavens.

23. Whoever raises his voice can say: “I have proclaimed your righteousness in the great Church.” Why did he add “great,” unless because previously it had not been great? What is great except the Church gathered from all the regions of the whole world, when peoples of the nations were called from east and west, north and south?

Elsewhere too we read of the great Church: “I will give thanks to you, Lord, in the great Church; among a weighty people I will praise you” (Ps. XXXIV, 18). The great Church is therefore where there is a weighty people—that is, not restless and changeable, such as “sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”

A weighty people is one that keeps faith with its God and is not changed by any fickleness; it neither wavers nor fluctuates, but is founded in love for Christ, so that it can say: “For I am confident that neither death, nor the sword, nor tribulation can separate me from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. VIII, 35 and following).

24. Whoever preaches in the great Church does not hide God’s righteousness in his heart; rather, he raises his voice with all his strength, proclaiming Christ. He is not afraid to preach him before the people; he is not ashamed of his cross, but glories in that passion of the Lord.

He does not follow the letter of the Law, but draws out its profound mysteries, by which he reveals the glory of the Lord Jesus, whom the Law signified as one who would come to the Church that was to be gathered and would be great.

Righteousness, therefore, is faith. For “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV, 6).

“Behold, I will not restrain my lips, Lord; you have known.” So also elsewhere: “You have known my sitting down and my rising” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 2).

25. He says to the Father: “I have not hidden my righteousness in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation.”

This entire psalm is spoken in the person of Christ; therefore he says, “my righteousness.” Yet a human being too may say “his righteousness” without arrogance, if he believes in God and confesses that his faith is reckoned to him as righteousness.

Whoever proclaims the true faith and forgives sins loves truth and mercy. For Christ came in order to establish faith and grant forgiveness of sins.

26. (Verse 15.) Since we have said that this entire psalm is spoken in the person of the Savior, lest the Apollinarists perhaps say, “Behold, he said, ‘You prepared a body for me’” (Ps. verse 7), but not a soul, let them hear him say below in this psalm: “Let those who seek my soul in order to take it be confounded and put to shame together.”

[Note: [Col. 1068C] The Roman edition reads: “Behold, a body … you perfected for me.”]

27. These are the points in this psalm that we judged to be more difficult. We considered the rest clear and easy and not in need of interpretation.

[Note: [Col. 1068C] The manuscripts Vict. and Colb., together with the older edition, read: “and not worthy of interpretation.”]

If they should occur in the Treatise, we shall discuss them more appropriately in another psalm, in which they appear to be repeated, with the favor of the Lord Jesus, to whom belong praise, honor, glory, and eternity from the ages, and now and always, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# Exposition of Psalm XL

[Col. 1067]

867 1. (Verse 1.) Appropriately, in the preceding psalm he said, “Behold, I come” (Ps. XXXIX, 9); in this one he has now come and suffers. Therefore it is entitled the fortieth psalm, because the Lord Jesus fasted for forty days, so that by this number he might restore to perfection the human being who had perished.
