For just as he had lost grace through desire for the forbidden fruit, so it was necessary that his strength be restored through fasting, so that the one who had perished in Adam might be restored in Christ.

Therefore it says, “For the end,” because he himself is the end of our hope; toward him we direct our endeavors, toward him we bring our vows, because he is fullness, he is the consummation of all things, he is the sum of all virtues.

Therefore, “for David,” as for the one who alone, in his own flesh, assumed our sins; who alone, as the Lamb of God, took away the sin of the whole world; who alone, by the outpouring of his blood, erased and removed the bond of the decree and fastened it to the cross; as wisdom, knowing how to release the world’s ancient sin; as redemption, knowing how to renew the human being from guilt; as sanctification, knowing how to bring the one whom he sanctified into grace.

This, then, is the title; this is the beginning.

2. (Verse 2.) “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and poor.” Open your ears, you who are beginning to understand the mysteries of the Lord’s passion. Therefore it is said to you: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII, 8).

Therefore in the Gospel the Lord touched the ears and lips of that deaf and mute man (Mark VII, 16), so that he might know what he was hearing in the mystery, what he should also say, and when he should speak.

For it was not written without purpose: “The Lord has given me a tongue of instruction, so that I may know when it is necessary to speak” (Isa. L, 4). You must therefore know what you are hearing, know what you ought to say, and know also when you ought to speak.

868 3. Hear, then, him saying: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and poor.” Blessed indeed is the one who has compassion on the poor, who takes upon himself his needs, who knows what evil deprivation brings to the needy. But what does this opening have to do with the Lord’s passion?

It is true that he suffered on account of the poor; yet he rebuked Judas when he spoke about the ointment Mary had poured over Christ’s feet: “This could have been sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor” (Mark XIV, 5).

The other apostles had felt the same, but with a different disposition: Judas through avarice, they through mercy. Judas was looking to theft; the disciples were concerned for the nourishment of the poor.

To them all he replied: “Leave her, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me” (John XII, 7–8).

4. Therefore another blessed person is to be understood here, one who understands concerning the poor. Here he speaks of faith; elsewhere, of mercy. Faith comes first, mercy second. With faith, mercy is precious; without faith, it is naked; without faith, it is unstable. For faith is the firm foundation of all virtues.

Blessed, then, is the one who understands concerning Christ’s need and poverty—he who, though rich, became poor for us: rich in the kingdom, poor in the flesh, because he assumed this flesh of the poor.

For we became exceedingly poor when, through the serpent’s deceit, we lost the precious garments of the virtues; excluded from paradise, expelled from our homeland, and sent into exile, we were also stripped of the bodily covering which the defenses of virtue had formerly protected, but which sins afterward laid bare.

If, therefore, he was needy and poor in the flesh, then he was needy and poor in the passion of this flesh. He did not suffer in his riches, then, but in our poverty.

Therefore it was not the fullness of divinity dwelling bodily in him, as Scripture testifies (Col. II, 9), that suffered, but the flesh.

Understand this, pursue this, hold fast to it, lest it be said to you: “He did not wish to understand concerning the needy and poor.” For if you hesitate here, surely in that psalm which is spoken against Judas’s betrayal in the person of the Savior, you will not be able to hesitate concerning the verse in which he says: “And he persecuted the needy and poor man” (Ps. CVIII, 17).

Understand, then, Christ’s poverty, so that you may be rich; understand his weakness, so that you may receive health; understand his cross, so that you may not be ashamed; understand his wound, so that you may heal your wounds; understand his death, so that you may acquire eternal life; understand his burial, so that you may find resurrection.

5. But perhaps you will say: How is Christ rich in poverty? Even if my intelligence fails me, the resources of the divine writings do not fail, since the Apostle said: “The Lord Jesus became poor, though he was rich, so that you might become rich through his poverty” (II Cor. VIII, 9).

What, then, is this poverty that makes people rich? Let us consider it; let us attend to that venerable mystery itself. What could be purer and simpler than it?

No one is drenched in the blood of a bull, as the sacred rites of the Gentiles are said to possess; nor is the sinner washed in the blood of goats and rams—for no one is thereby purified, since the flesh is washed, but guilt is not dissolved.

Rather, he says: “Water will come forth with joy from the fountains of the Savior” (Isa. XII, 3); and a heavenly table is prepared in your presence, together with a cup that intoxicates—how excellent it is! (Ps. XXII, 5).

These are the riches of simplicity, in which Christ’s precious poverty consists.

There is also a good poverty in conduct; hence the Lord said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V, 3). And in the Psalms we find that “the Lord will save the humble in spirit” (Ps. XXXIII, 19).

There is also an abundant poverty in a modest contribution, if faith abounds.

[Note: [Col. 1070D] Comparison: here “contribution” means the distribution of money that has been collected.]

Hence the Apostle says: “Their profound poverty abounded in the riches of their simplicity” (II Cor. VIII, 2).

[Note: [Col. 1069D] He appears to allude to that foul sacrifice by which, among the Romans, the chief pontiff was consecrated, as can be learned from Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 10. Its ceremonies were as follows: After earth had been dug out into a deep pit, the future pontiff was lowered into it, adorned with fillets and headbands. Then the pit was covered by a wooden platform pierced with countless holes. A bull was slaughtered above it, and its blood flowed abundantly through the openings in the boards:

“Buried within, the priest receives it,

Holding his head shamefully beneath every drop,

His clothing and entire body drenched.

He turns up his face and offers his cheeks to meet it,

Presents his ears and exposes his lips and nostrils;

Nor does he spare his palate, but bathes his tongue,

Until he has wholly drunk in the dark blood.

At last the handsome pontiff, brought out from there, was worshiped from afar by the people.”

Prudentius describes all these things fully and elegantly in the cited passage.]

[Col. 1070C] 6. So that from other words of his also we may understand that he called himself poor, we have it written elsewhere: “I am poor and sorrowful” (Ps. LXVIII, 30)—that is, because he suffers for us, as we read (Isa. LIII, 4), for he had nothing in himself that could cause sorrow.

Just as, therefore, he suffers for us, as Isaiah interpreted when he saw him in the Spirit, so he was sorrowful for us, in accordance with the fact that he called his soul sorrowful even unto death, though not because of death. And he called the flesh weak, because it was subject to the weakness of death, so that he might break death’s sting, by which he would free us on the day of judgment—a death which he did not call evil merely in passing.

### 7. (Verse 2)

For thus he continues: “On the evil day the Lord will deliver him,” because that day appears bitter, since it assigns punishment to many. The way of virtue is narrow, while that of sin is broad; therefore fewer walk in virtue, whereas more are engaged in wickedness. Consequently, those who will receive the rewards of recompense are fewer than those who will bear the adverse lot of judgment on account of the penalty for their grave sins. Thus, as though grieving, he called the day of judgment evil. For if the angels rejoice at the acquittal of a single sinner, how much more will human beings be tormented at the condemnation of so many human beings! And rightly does he grieve for that sheep which he himself carried back upon his shoulders and restored to his fold after it had gone astray.

The Son of God speaks in accordance with our feelings, because the day of judgment is bitter for us, and we fear it. It seems evil to all because it is full of terror: on that day God judges not only a person’s outward deeds but also what is hidden; on that day each person is compelled to disclose what he has done or what he has thought. Therefore many are condemned, while few are crowned. Yet even those who are crowned will grieve; for the righteous will be crowned, and the righteous regard a brother’s misery as though it were their own. And who am I to pass judgment concerning that day on which a human being will be admitted into the councils of the angels? Let us hear the judgment of the Lord himself: “The hour is coming,” he says, “when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of Man, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29). Those, then, who have done evil will be judged; and therefore the Judge himself calls the day evil and harsh, so that you may know that in the Gospel he sympathizes with us, the one who sympathized with us in the prophets.

### 8.

We can also understand it in this way: “On the evil day,” that is, in an evil time; for the world is placed in evil. Therefore the days of this world are evil, and its day is full of its own wickedness. It is no small matter to be delivered here from the snares of the sinner. Whoever is free from guilt here will be free from punishment there and will not be able to undergo the severity of judgment.

### 9. (Verse 3)

Therefore vows and daily prayers are necessary, as well as the advocacy of the High Priest, concerning whom John the Evangelist says: “We have an advocate with the Father, the Lord Jesus, and he himself is the petition for our sins” (1 John 2:2).

[Note: The Roman edition alone has: “of the great High Priest … and he himself is the propitiation for sins.” Undoubtedly they thought this an allusion to Hebrews 4:14, “Therefore, having a great high priest” (Ἔχοντες οὖν ἀρχιερέα μέγαν), and to 1 John 2:2, “And he himself is the propitiation for our sins” (Καὶ αὐτὸς ἱλασμός ἐστι περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν). Nevertheless, there is no reason on that account to suppose that Ambrose’s wording should be altered.]

This advocate of ours, then, and petition for the sins of the whole world, prays for the one who understands and believes in Christ and says: “May the Lord preserve him, give him life, and make him blessed.” May he preserve him from dangers, give life to him as one established amid the shadows of death, and graciously make him blessed by the addition of good works.

### 10.

[Note: These words are found in the German and Carnotensian manuscripts of the Psalter, as well as in the Roman edition of 1583; they are absent from all the others.]

“And cleanse,” he says, “his life on earth” (ibid.). He rightly added “on earth,” because unless he is cleansed here, he will not be able to be clean there. Or certainly it may be understood in this way: “Cleanse him on earth.” For how can anyone be clean in the mud, when the earth stains him? Therefore the Lord’s hand is necessary—the hand that formed the body from the earth—so that it may deign to cleanse it.

### 11. (Verse 3)

“And do not hand him over to the hands of his enemy.” Who is the enemy except that lion who prowls around roaring, seeking someone to devour? Some Greek copies have: “And do not hand him over to the souls of his enemies.” He has put “souls” for “hands,” because the souls of enemies lie in wait for the good and try to overthrow the righteous by their thoughts. “Souls” is also used for human beings: “All the souls—seventy—which went down into Egypt” (Genesis 46:27). Therefore David preferred to entrust himself to God’s power rather than to the snares of enemies who did not know how to spare according to their own will.

### 12. (Verse 4)

It continues: “May the Lord assist him upon the bed of his pain; you have changed his entire bed in his sickness.” What is the bed of pain except the flesh of weakness? It is rightly called a bed of pain, because it is the body of death, from which the Apostle begs to be delivered (Romans 7:24), so that he may rise as though from a certain tomb in which the soul lies sick and, as it were, reclines upon a kind of bed.

Symmachus rendered it “bed of misery”; Aquila, “cot of misery”; the Seventy more explicitly judged that it should be called “bed of pain.” These verses, therefore, should be used with those who are held for a long time by bodily illness, so that they may obtain God’s medicine by which they may deserve to be healthy.

The soul’s bed, then, is the weak flesh, whose sickness our soul shares. If it has the Lord as helper, it says to him: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (Luke 5:24). Strengthened by God’s word, the sick man rises, takes up the bed on which he had lain, and returns to his former condition of health. This is what it means to return to his house: to dwell in the abode of vigorous health. Whoever dwells, governs; whoever governs has the grace of virtue assisting him.

But the Lord also changes the whole bed of the sick person to whom he deigns to be present. What is changed alters its condition, either from health to sickness or from sickness to health. Thus the one who is sick changes himself toward the remedy of health.

### 13.

Thus the Lord Jesus, although he was wounded because of our sins, did not remain in that weakness; rather, he himself changed it for the better, for the salvation of all. Accordingly, in his passion weakness was dissolved, and in his resurrection death was dissolved. Just as he himself changed his condition for the redemption of the peoples and felt neither the sting of death nor the weakness of the wound, so he changes the one who believes in him—even when gravely ill—toward life, in order to free him from death.

He therefore changed every bed—that is, the weakness of all human beings—in his own weakness. For he took upon his flesh the weaknesses of all, raised himself upon the cross, and changed all their weaknesses in the weakness of his own body. Hence Isaiah says: “By his bruise we were healed” (Isaiah 53:5).

Wrestlers have this practice: they submit themselves to those with whom they engage and wrestle, so that they may appear capable of being overpowered; then, when they are thought to have been defeated, they suddenly throw their opponent down and, by a certain technique, turn themselves so as to bring down the stronger man. The one who was being carried falls, while the one who was carrying him is found to be superior and throws down the one pressing upon him.

In this spiritual contest, therefore, the Lord Jesus, taking up our burdens, submitted himself in that struggle of his passion. And, appearing to be weak, so that the adversary might judge him a human being equal to the others and one whom he could easily overpower, he laid aside the weapons of divinity and assumed the covering of humanity. Confident of victory, the tempter drew near. He wished to wound him in the side with the soldier’s weapon, reckoning that this man too could be overthrown through the side, like Adam.

But when the Lord Jesus was wounded in the side, he brought forth life from the wound, emptied out all sin, and cast down the adversary, from whom he wrested the death of the thief. In that death, in the burial of his body, when he was thought to have been overpowered, he turned himself by his own power: the adversary fell, and the Lord rose again.

[Note: Thus the Vatican manuscript and four Gallican manuscripts. Others, including the editions, read: “when they are thought to be crushed”; the Roman edition has “crushed,” with a certain artistic adaptation, etc.]

### 14. (Verse 5)

It continues: “I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.”

This may be spoken in the person of King David, who, seeing in the spirit so great a victory and grace of Christ, asks that he too may receive mercy in that forgiveness of all sins. For although, as king, he was not subject to human laws, he nevertheless recognizes that before God he is liable on account of his sins. He therefore confesses his sin in order to receive forgiveness and obtain the gift of universal pardon.

It may also be expressed in the person of the Savior, who asks God’s mercy for us and said that he had sinned because he was made sin for us. At the same time he teaches us that, when we are engaged in any struggle against the enemies of God, we should implore God’s help and confess our sins to him. We should do so especially when we are pressed and crushed, throwing ourselves down in grief and bitterness, lest we seem to have kept silent, so that medicine may be brought more quickly to our wounds and, once healed, we may resist the adversary.

For how can a wounded person engage in combat? From this we learn that we are wounded by the stings of our sins. A wound seeks a physician, and the physician requires confession.

### 15. (Verse 6)

From this point the Savior begins more and more to disclose the mystery of his passion, which plainly agrees with the Gospel. The Jews were cursing him, seeking his death, plotting against him, and pressing him because they could not endure the glory of his works, which increased every day.

The prophecy therefore announces what was fulfilled in the Gospel: “My enemies spoke evil against me: ‘When will he die, and his name perish?’” Madmen, who believed that the author of life could die! But the Church destroyed their wishes, believing that even after death according to the condition of the body he would increase his name. Therefore she sang to him: “I will remember your name throughout every generation and generation” (Psalm 44:18). She repeated: “Your name is an ointment poured out” (Song of Songs 1:2).

“Let those who presume that you can die perish; I will not die, for I know you as the arbiter of life and the author of salvation.” For we know that during the time of the passion and resurrection the disciples prayed while gathered together—when Mary Magdalene announced to them that the Lord had risen, when the Lord, with the door closed, showed himself to them in the body of the resurrection, and when Thomas saw his wounds and believed.

The Jews therefore mocked him as though he were dead, but the Lord revealed himself alive to the apostles. When the Jews said, “Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19), and when they said that by his miraculous works he was misleading the people, what else were they saying but, “When will he die, and his name perish?” Therefore during his passion they cried out: “Take him away, take such a man from the earth; let him be crucified, let him be crucified!” (John 19:15).

What they asked was done: he was taken from the earth, he rose again, he ascended to heaven, and from us he restored his kingdom in the abodes of paradise.

[Note: The Roman edition alone has “may restore his kingdom from the new abodes of paradise.” “From us” is more suitable, since this meaning seems capable of being drawn from these words: Christ restored his kingdom in the abodes of paradise for us, a kingdom that had in some way been disfigured by the fall of the rebellious angels.]

### 16. (Verse 7)

An evident prophecy concerning Judas the betrayer is also added in the verses that follow:

“He went out to see, speaking vainly; his heart gathered iniquity for itself. He went outside and spoke.”

[Note: The same Roman edition reads, “And he entered to see,” which agrees not only with Psalters in all languages but also with Ambrose himself below: “Judas therefore entered,” etc.; nevertheless, it differs from all the manuscripts and editions of this Father. As for the addition “and he spoke” afterward, it agrees neither with the manuscripts and other editions nor sufficiently with the sequence of the discourse.]

Thus it is distinguished in the Greek copies. Judas entered, therefore, seeking to betray the Savior, in order to see what he was doing or what he might say, so that he could catch him in his speech and report him to the Jews. But he found nothing, since he understood nothing.

The Scripture rightly says (John 13) that he was not inwardly with Jesus, because he had withdrawn from his teaching and abandoned his instruction.

[Note: The Victorine and Colbertine manuscripts read, “because Jesus knew him inwardly.”]

He wanted to enter, but he could not penetrate within, because his treachery excluded him. For every impure, greedy, or unclean person—which is idolatry—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

He therefore not only tried to enter and did not enter; he also wanted to see and did not see. Indeed, Jesus spoke in parables, but Judas did not hear. He did not see the divine mysteries, for not all who seem to themselves to hear hear the word of God. For if all heard, Jesus would not say: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8).

And because he did not hear, he could not see either. He spoke vainly instead of truthfully, and he thought he could deceive Jesus by saying: “This could have been sold and given to the poor” (Matthew 26:9), whereas by his thefts he was providing not for the poor but for himself.

[Note: All editions and several manuscripts read, “calling him rabbi and teacher, from whose … teaching”; the Vatican manuscript, together with most Gallican manuscripts, more elegantly reads as in the text.]

For how could he call him teacher when he was departing from his instruction? His heart—into which the devil had plunged—was gathering and increasing iniquities for itself. He was unjust to himself, unrighteous toward himself, and sinning against himself, because he was plotting deceit within himself, though it could not remain hidden.

Jesus was not deceived by the one who was betraying him willingly; he had testified: “One of you will betray me” (John 13:21). Finally Judas confessed, saying: “Is it I, Rabbi?” And the Lord said: “You have said so” (Matthew 26:25). Even then Judas did not understand that he was known. For if he had understood, he would not have betrayed him.

### 17.

Nevertheless, “he went outside and spoke.” This verse is appropriate against those who betray someone’s secret. He rightly says: “He went outside,” for outside are the wolves, outside the robbers; inside is Moses in the cloud with Jesus, outside the Jews; inside the priest Zechariah in the temple, outside the crowd; inside the Holy Spirit cries out in our hearts to the Father, outside our adversary watches like a lion, alert for plunder; outside are the unbelievers, inside the faithful.

Therefore God will judge those who are outside, while Christ acquits those who are inside.

Judas therefore went out and spoke. He went out from the faith; he went out from the council and number of the apostles; he went out from Christ’s banquet to the devil’s robbery; he went out from the grace of sanctification to the snare of death, speaking vain things to the treacherous. He went outside because he was abandoning the mysteries of the inner life; he went out because he did not know the interior meaning of Scripture.

For if he had known, he would have understood the one who says: “Will one who sleeps not add that he may rise again?” He would also have understood: “But you, a man of one mind, my leader and my acquaintance, who always took sweet food with me, we walked in agreement in the house of the Lord” (Psalm 54:14–15).

He did not understand this psalm, nor the hundred and eighth, nor the others, nor the other testimonies of Scripture. Concerning him, the Evangelist John rightly says, also with reference to the other unbelievers: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

### 18. (Verse 8)

The betrayer therefore did not remain with the apostles; he went outside and whispered with the treacherous. Scripture uses this word to show that treachery lacks authority, since it fears that what it says will be discovered.

To the faithful, however, it is said: “Raise your voice with strength” (Isaiah 58:1). See to what depths the apostle Judas had fallen. He had been sent to preach the faith to the Gentiles with a proclamation full of authority, yet he whispered into the ear of those plotting against his Teacher what he was afraid would be heard.

Did he not condemn himself by his own judgment? He was ashamed to be heard saying what he was not afraid to do. He was ashamed because he was plotting evil against the author of his life, sanctification, and honor. He did not repay grace with benefits but returned evil for good to his good Teacher—a thing that even worldly people customarily condemn.

He was ashamed to be discovered ungrateful; he was ashamed to appear greedy, since for money he was betraying the salvation wrought by his own author; he was ashamed to appear treacherous.

Likewise the Jews, who treacherously suborned false witnesses against the teacher of the faith, so that they might say that he had preached that the temple of God, which Solomon had built, should be destroyed—although he had spoken of the temple of his body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19)—were truly outside, excluded from knowledge of the heavenly Word.

### 19. (Verse 9)

“They proposed an iniquitous word against me,” he says; that is, they proposed an unlawful speech against justice and right. They made agreements concerning human blood, which Judas most wickedly sold; and the Jews, those most foolish men, believed that it should be purchased with no lesser crime.

“As one who sleeps,” he says, “will he not add that he may rise again?” (ibid.). Let us consider what this “addition” means.

It is natural for all earthly animals, for the birds of heaven, and for the fish of the sea to be born and to die. But to the human being, whom God had made more precious than the other animals of the earth, he granted this particular grace: that, after death, he should live again.

This, then, is called an addition, for the renewal of a former life. Accordingly, when the Lord had declared to King Hezekiah that he had completed the appointed term of his life and, through Isaiah, had commanded him to set his house in order because he was going to die, and when Hezekiah had prayed to the Lord and wept with great weeping, the Lord had mercy and commanded him: “Behold, I add fifteen years to your time” (Isaiah 38:5). Elsewhere holy David says: “You will add days to the days of the king; you will add years to his years” (Psalm 60:7).

An addition has therefore been found for the human being. Nothing, however, can be added to God, because it is written: “There is no adding or taking away” in that in which all things are perfect and complete (Sirach 28:5).

Although Christ rose again, he rose in that which he had assumed; nothing could either diminish or increase the fullness of his divinity. God is incorporeal and immortal, and his supreme nature and fullness of virtues are signified without any addition of flesh.

The flesh, however, is part of the dispensation in Christ. He assumed it under the title of mercy and by the right of compassion, in order to redeem what was captive, cleanse what was defiled, and raise what was dead.

And he rightly says: “Will one who sleeps not add that he may rise again?” He did not say, “Is he not added to,” but “Will he not add that he may rise again,” because the Son of God himself raised himself, just as we said above that he told the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

The flesh received an addition, as something taken from a human being and assumed from the Virgin. But, as God, he himself effected that addition, rising by his own power so as to be the author of his own resurrection.

[Note: Thus read the Vatican manuscript and four Gallican manuscripts. The editions, however, have: “Therefore, when you read that …,” and the Reginensis manuscript supports them, except that it does not recognize the word “therefore.” The Colbertine and Victorine manuscripts read: “in which you may read that …”]

But so that you may understand that both the Father raised the Son and the Son himself raised himself, recognize that this was the work of divine power, because the Father and the Son have one power and a common operation, since the Trinity has one and the same substance.

### 20.

### 21. (Verse 10)

“But why do I accuse the others?” says the Lord Jesus. “What wonder if the people did not know me and condemned me to the cross, when my apostle demanded the price of betrayal, when my table companion sold my death? For the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, magnified his deception against me.”

Some think Judas should be excused because he returned the money he had received as the price of betrayal.

[Note: Several manuscripts have, “which he had received as the price of the purchase.”]

But behold, he is condemned even more severely than the Jews for their unbelief; for from the one to whom more has been given, more is required.

“What,” he says, “should I complain about the others? The man of my peace, to whom I had given my peace and to whom I had wished to leave my peace, handed me over to my persecutors and deceived me, though I had trusted in him.”

Did he not know that he would be betrayed by the one of whom he had foretold: “One of you will betray me” (John 13:21)? This he was saying about Judas, as it is written in the Gospel. Certainly not; but, in order to condemn him more severely, he said that he had trusted in his faithfulness.

Aquila rendered it, “I had relied on him”; Symmachus wrote, “I was trusting.” We burden the guilt of one whom we say we trusted or in whom we placed great confidence all the more heavily when he afterward disappoints our hope and expectation.

### 22.

At the same time, he shows how great is the power of divine sanctification, which excludes evil and reforms a corrupted character if the pattern of a better purpose is added.

How many people do we know to have been converted? That publican Zacchaeus was changed. He had been intent on profit with a greedy disposition, but afterward he paid back fourfold for his wrongdoing, condemned greed in himself, renounced the profits of his former life, and made compensation to the poor when no claimant was present.

The thief himself changed his wickedness for a better purpose: he recognized Christ on the cross, confessed him to be the Son of God, and with his own voice called him king. At the time when most of the righteous were wavering and the apostles themselves were certainly hiding, the executioner, the centurion, did not deny him.

Why should I speak of the time of the Gospel? Rahab was a prostitute who supported herself on the wages of treachery and licentiousness. Yet when she saw the spies whom Jesus son of Nun had sent, she put on faith and, when danger threatened, preserved righteousness. She did not betray those whom she had received but protected them with faithful kindness.

Therefore he says that he had trusted—as though he had rightly expected the apostle to lay aside what was former and follow what was better.

[Note: The earlier Roman edition reads, “to follow what was former.”]

He who had received the task of sanctifying others should himself preserve the grace of sanctity and remain devoted to the duties of sincerity.

“Rightly,” he says, “I trusted,” because he gave the human being freedom to choose what he would follow. “I have set before you,” he says, “good and evil” (Deuteronomy 30:15). If you choose evil, it is not nature that sins but the disposition of the one who chooses.

If every human being who chooses evil is condemned, what shall we say of Judas, who betrayed the one to whom he had been joined by the sweetness of the banquet?

### 23.

“He who ate my bread,” he says, “magnified his deception against me.”

Why did he add “my bread”? He could have said, “He who ate bread with me,” unless you understand it as that bread which belongs specially to Christ—that is, the nourishment of the heavenly Word. For “man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matthew 4:4).

Accordingly, elsewhere he says: “You who always took sweet food with me” (Psalm 54:15). We rightly use these verses against those who have believed that people with whom they appear to have feasted ought to be killed.

The Gentiles are said to observe this custom; enemies often do so, and even robbers, so that they may spare those with whom they remember having entered into fellowship at a banquet.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “with whom they remember having shared a dwelling.” It is otherwise acknowledged that formerly, not only among Greeks and Latins but also among barbarians, the fellowship of the table and of banquets was held in great religious observance and reverence. Nearly all peoples joined private alliances as well as public ones through the sharing of salt and bread. They regarded hospitable Jupiter as the guardian and avenger of the table; they swore by the hospitable table; and if anyone violated guests and table companions (ὁμοτραπέζους), not only was he himself considered accursed, but the house in which the crime had been committed sometimes remained deserted by its inhabitants as a place of death. See Struck, *Antiquitates Conviviales*, book 1, chapter 3.]

Even wild animals themselves are tamed by sharing food. Therefore, if we consider the words in light of this kind of affection arising from the fellowship of the table, he did not call the food “sweet” without purpose.

For how can food be sweet if it quickly decays? But consider whether he called the words of life “sweet food.” No bitterness corrupts this food, and no corruption of death contaminates it. Hence he also said “always.” No one could always eat physical food. But we can always cling to the word of God, by night and by day, if we meditate on the law of God day and night.

### 24.

What does “magnified” mean as well? The Greek says ἐμεγάλυνεν (*emegalynen*), that is, “made great.” The Lord explained both expressions for us, which might have troubled us, when he said in the Gospel: “He who eats bread with me has lifted his heel against me” (John 13:18).

Let us consider where this expression was taken from. “We were once unbelieving and wandering, slaves to desires and pleasures” (Titus 3:3). Let us confess our error so that we may be cleansed.

I myself saw a young athlete who, after throwing down his opponent, struck his forehead with his heel. This was a sign of insult, because he had mocked the defeated man.

This is what he means by: “He magnified his deception against me.” By this word he declared the boastful insolence of one who insults. Judas therefore lifted his heel against Christ when he betrayed him, but he did not lift it with impunity.

Even now Adam lifts the heel that was wounded by the serpent. Christ had washed his feet. He had heard him say: “The one who has bathed does not need to wash except his feet, but is entirely clean” (John 13:10). Yet what grace had washed, treachery had defiled.

Judas therefore lifted his heel to inflict a wound. Truly, the one who lifted his heel against Christ did not hold fast to the head. Adam lifted it against himself; Judas lifted it against Christ, and therefore the serpent wounded him more grievously than the others.

He lifted his heel—the one who offered a deceitful kiss by which he would betray the author of life. Therefore it is written in the prophet: “He magnified his deception against me.” Esau also said concerning his brother: “He has supplanted me twice already” (Genesis 27:36).

The one who supplants practices deceit by which he overthrows or wounds his adversary. Judas is therefore said to have supplanted him because with his kiss he inflicted the wound by which he showed the persecutors the signal for attacking the Savior.

He supplanted him like a serpent, because the serpent pours out poison from its mouth and wounds the heel with its tooth. Judas too wounded not Christ’s divinity but the extremity of his body, his heel.

Judas also lifted his heel like an insolent and arrogant wrestler, with which he might strike the Savior’s head. But he could not strike Christ’s head, because Christ’s head is God. His own head, however, he bound with the knot of a shameful noose, depriving himself of the remedy of salvation.

### 25.

See whether you can piously apply to this what the holy patriarch Jacob said in Genesis when prophesying about his sons: “Dan will judge his people as one tribe in Israel”; and: “Let Dan be like a serpent sitting beside the road and on the path, biting the horse’s heel; and the rider will fall backward, awaiting salvation from the Lord” (Genesis 49:16–17).

We certainly read that Samson from the tribe of Dan was a judge in Israel (Judges 13:25), but here another future figure is signified, one who will arise from that tribe and afflict the people with the punishments of sacrilegious impiety.

That Antichrist, who will sit in the temple as though he were God, truly has judgment in his interpretation; for “Dan” signifies judgment. He rightly says that he will judge his people, who will become subject to everlasting punishment. For the one who does not believe has already been judged, whereas the one who believes will not be judged, because he believes in the Son of God, the redeemer of his soul.

Therefore, as one free from judgment, he says: “It is the Lord who judges me” (1 Corinthians 4:4). He will judge the people of impiety, not the people of God. Those are judged who fall through the ruin of treachery, not those who rise through the freedom of faith.

### 26.

He will therefore sit beside the road and lie in wait on the path like a serpent, in order to wound those passing by and bite the heel of our horse. He will not be able to wound the soul of the faithful.

On what road and on what path will he sit except those from which Christ the Lord, as we read, called the people of the nations to his banquet, saying: “Go out into the roads and around the hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled” (Luke 14:23)?

And because Judas likewise is read to have magnified his deception against Christ, it seems that Judas himself is signified here: he was to bite the heel of the horse on which Christ the Lord was riding.

Hence it is said: “Your cavalry is salvation” (Habakkuk 3:8), meaning that his flesh was to take upon itself the sin of the whole world, so that salvation would take the place of destruction and eternal life the place of death.

The horse, then, was wounded: not a deceitful horse, but one alone for salvation. The horse was wounded that took upon itself the sins of the whole world and bore our burdens without becoming weary. The horse was wounded that did not know how to neigh in the frenzy of intercourse.

Perhaps for this reason the heaven was opened to John the Evangelist, and a white horse was shown, on which sat one who had diadems on his head and whose thigh bore the written name: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Revelation 19:16).

It was white because it was immaculate and had known no stain of sin. For if lust is dark, holiness rightly shines and gleams.

This horse, then, was wounded but not delayed. Indeed, with that very wound he rose from the tomb and ran to heaven above all angels and archangels. He was found swifter than all the cavalry of the heavenly host, even swifter than those fiery horses by which Elijah was carried away.

And rightly swifter, for he ascended above all the heavens and above the heaven of heavens to the seat of God Almighty and sits there, as Scripture taught us when it said: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power” (Mark 14:62).

### 27.

This horse was also previously shown in figure during the time of the Maccabees. The commander of the heavenly army sat upon it, resplendent in golden armor. He struck down and overthrew Heliodorus, that plunderer of the widow’s deposit and of the other things entrusted to sacred protection; afterward, prevailed upon by the prayers of the priest Onias, he restored Heliodorus to life.

Therefore golden arms truly shone upon him, because he alone sat upon and conquered this horse, in whom no one free from sin escaped. Not Enoch, who was carried away lest wickedness change his heart; not Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob; not Moses. All were under sin, all under death. Indeed, death reigned from Adam to Moses.

He alone is the one who committed no sin. Christ alone is the one who took away the sin of the world, who said to death: “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Corinthians 15:55).

### 28.

How, then, did Judas magnify his deception against him, and did the rider fall backward? What belongs to Judas was deceit; what belongs to Christ was voluntary suffering.

We often see a stronger man willing to be struck so that, provoked more sharply, he may rise up more fiercely and be stirred to greater force. The serpent therefore bit the horse’s heel and spat out the poison of its deceit. The rider willingly cast himself down; willingly he fell, in order to raise us up.

What, however, does Scripture mean when it says: “And the rider will fall backward” (Genesis 49:17)? Why backward, unless it was so that he might guide those following behind him?

Peter was behind, to whom he said: “Get behind me” (Mark 8:33). The apostles and the other disciples were behind. He therefore fell backward because he saves those upon whom he falls.

“For everyone who falls upon this stone,” he says, “will be shattered; but upon whomever it falls, it will cleanse him” (Luke 20:18). Others have “it will winnow him”; others, “it will crush him.”

For the one who winnows grain cleanses it of chaff. The one who crushes something reduces it to dust, so that, through the softness of the dust, it may serve without disturbance either as a healthful drink or for another medicinal use.

From this we understand that we must beware lest anyone who has once been received by Christ through baptism fall away from his body—that is, be shaken out of the Church—for this is the ruin of everlasting death.

But the one who comes intending to believe in Christ—so that his death may encounter him, his cross receive him, the nail pierce him, his blood be poured out, his burial also enfold him, and the grace of resurrection raise him from sleep and give him life from death—this one is freed from the world, cleansed from sin, healed of his wound, bent away from the hardness of impiety, softened toward the gentleness of devotion, so that, with his heart circumcised, he may draw in that uncircumscribed and incomprehensible Spirit and drink the cup of eternal salvation.

The rider therefore fell backward.

### 29.

Consider also another reason why he fell backward and not forward: everyone came after him; no one before him. He therefore fell not for himself but for everyone, so that by falling upon the hardness of our hearts he might soften it.

He fell upon Adam, whom he was seeking in order to find him. He sought him behind himself so that the good shepherd might place him upon his shoulders and carry him with himself into paradise through the redemption of that thief.

### 30

But perhaps you will say: “The persecutors also fell backward.” For so it is written (John 18:6):

[Note: The Roman edition: “because the attendants of the chief priest, whom,” etc.]

the chief priests, whom the traitor Judas had brought, and the others who had come to apprehend the Lord Jesus, “went backward and fell to the ground.” This is precisely what I also say: he wished to fall upon sinners, not upon the righteous; for the physician is needed not by the righteous but by sinners. If the shadow of the apostles healed, how much more does the flesh of Christ, which they touch, defend them from death! Indeed, he touched the leper and cleansed him without delay.

But so that you, who are reading, may know that he also wished to free his persecutors, ask Christ’s witness. When Peter inveighed against the Jews because they had killed the author of life, he showed them the remedy: they were to repent, so that they might deserve to have the sin they had committed forgiven. Why do you doubt that he fell in order to be raised, when he himself said: “I strike and I heal” (Deut. 32:19)? Observe, however, the difference between the statements. In Genesis it is written: “The horseman will fall backward, awaiting salvation from the Lord” (Gen. 49:18); that is, so that he does not turn his eyes away, nor does his action divert his own mind; rather, he claims the prerogative of his resurrection and raises himself by divine power. Here, however, it is written: “They went backward and fell to the ground” (John 18:6). Whoever is earthly falls to the earth; whoever is heavenly clings to heaven. And even if he falls in body, he does not fall in power:

[Note: The Codex Victorinus and Codex Colbertinus, together with the ancient editions, read: “he does not fall, nor does he attend to the things that are his own, but he concentrates upon the work.” Four other manuscripts read: “he does not fall, but he always attends to the things that are above.” The Regius manuscript alone reads: “he does not fall, but he always attends to the things that are his own.” This reading certainly does not seem contemptible. For if the heavenly man always attends to the things that are his own, he surely always attends to heavenly things. Nevertheless, we follow the Roman edition and the Vatican manuscript, since their reading sounds better to Christian ears.]

nor does he attend to the things that are his own, but always to the things that are above; for he always looks toward the Father, so that he may fulfill his will toward us. Would that these men also had not gone backward, but had received Christ, as Joseph received him and buried him in a new tomb!

He who is faithful does not fall to the earth; he who is unfaithful falls and descends into the lower regions of the earth, as it is written: “Let them go down alive into hell” (Ps. 54:16). Thus the persecutor falls upon the earth and into hell; Christ falls upon those who are to rise again, Christ upon the rock, Christ upon the Church.

Hear how he falls upon the Church. Peter was behind when he followed him as he was being led by the Jews to the house of Caiaphas, the ruler of the synagogue. This is the Peter to whom he said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18). Therefore, where Peter is, there is the Church; where the Church is, there is no death, but eternal life. And therefore he added: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.).

Blessed Peter, against whom the gate of hell did not prevail and to whom the gate of heaven was not closed; rather, on the contrary, he destroyed the vestibules of hell and opened the heavenly realms. Set upon the earth, therefore, he opened heaven and closed hell.

### 31

This passage may also appropriately be understood of the Samaritan, who did not pass by the man descending from Jericho, wounded by robbers; rather, he took him up, treated his wounds by pouring in oil and wine, placed him upon his own animal, and led him to the inn.

Why do you doubt the good horse, when you have read of the good animal? When you have read of that Jerusalem, and of many horsemen entering with quadrigas and chariots? Nor should what you have read disturb you: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses; but we will glory in the name of the Lord our God. They are bound and have fallen” (Ps. 19:8–9). But Elijah did not fall, for he entered in a chariot; for where the name of God is, no one is bound, but all are set free.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “In the name of the Lord our God we will call.”]

In the name of our God, both the poor and the rich are safe; the noble and the ignoble; the weak and the powerful. Wealth does not prejudice faith, provided that we know how to use wealth.

### 32

(Verse 11.) And therefore, bearing the name of God within himself, he says: “But you, O Lord, have mercy upon me, and raise me up, and I will repay them.” He does not say this as one doubting the resurrection, since he had the power to say: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19); rather, he gives mankind a model, so that it may hope for mercy from God and resurrection from God.

Next, he does not ask that he himself be raised up; he asks that Matthias be raised up in Judas’s place, so that the apostolic number may be completed. For since the son of perdition had to perish, so that Scripture might be fulfilled, the son of salvation had to be appointed in his place.

Understand a third meaning. He asks to be raised up—that is, his body; but the body of Christ is the Church. And because Judas was a figure of the unfaithful Jewish people, who either bought or sold Christ for money—for this is what those do who value money more highly than religion—he signifies that, for the destruction of the people in faith, the Church pleasing to him will rise again.

[Note: Five Gallican manuscripts have “for the destruction of the people in faith,” where perhaps “of the unfaithful people” should be read instead; although the former reading provides a meaning that should by no means be rejected. Other manuscripts and the old editions in the margin have: “it signifies that the Church pleasing to him will rise again for the destruction of the unfaithful people” (the same editions as the Roman edition have in the text: “of the Church pleasing to him”).]

Therefore she herself also says in the Song of Songs: “If you awaken and raise up love” (Song 2:7), when she was asking the young women about Christ, because Christ is love.

### 33

What he says, “And I will repay them,” we understand in this way: they will be tormented by the progress of the flourishing Church, and then they will recognize what punishment belongs to unbelief, when they perceive whose is the splendor of faith and grace.

Or the meaning may be that the Lord is good, who could say: “They repaid me evil for good” (Ps. 35:12). The middle word is one of repayment, whether for good or for evil; he says that he will repay with good, because although blindness has happened to Israel in part, nevertheless, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved through Christ’s mercy.

### 34

(Verse 12.) And he added: “By this I know that you have desired me, because my enemy will not rejoice over me.” Above, he spoke of his passion as a human being; here he already reveals his majesty: that he alone is without sin,

[Note: The Victorinus and Colbertinus manuscripts, and the old edition in the margin, read: “alone, who could not be stained by sin.” The same editions in the text, as also the Roman edition, read: “alone, whom the sinner could not insult,” and so forth. But the remaining manuscripts more appropriately suit the allegory begun above: “alone, upon whom the sinner could not ride.” Observe in passing what we noted above: Ambrose often designates the devil by the name “sinner.”]

alone upon whom the sinner could not ride, alone whom the Father loved as his only Son.

How, then, did the enemy not rejoice over him? Because although he accepted death for us, he nevertheless rose again; and he himself mocked the enemy, whose victory he destroyed and whose sting of death he broke. And we, although we are sorrowful in this world, and although the enemy rejoices in our sorrow and in the contrition of our heart and mind, nevertheless, when we rise again, we destroy his joy. Hence Micah also said: “Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall rise again” (Mic. 7:8). The resurrection, therefore, is the dissolution of all the enemy’s bonds and the abolition of every triumph.

### 35

(Verses 13–14.) It follows: “But because of my innocence you have received me, and you have established me in your presence forever. Blessed is the Lord God of Israel from age to age; let it be, let it be.”

An innocent person harms no one and sins against no one. Therefore, by the authority of divine Scripture, Christ is marked as without sin and without deceit. This is also declared here, where he says: “But because of my innocence you have received me.”

What reception is signified? For elsewhere also we read: “You received me from my mother’s womb” (Ps. 138:13). Therefore, because he was born free from every mingling of human generation—he who was born from the Spirit and the Virgin—the Father received him, because no customary mingling of bodily generation darkened his origin.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “free from every corruption of generation,” and so forth.]

He received him when he rose again, because no stain of falling touched him. Immaculate he returned to the Father, from whom he had come forth immaculate when he descended to the earth. Hence the Father says to him: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7); that is, “I recognize in you the privilege of my generation, you whom no stain of sin could defile.”

You lived among sinners; you took upon yourself the sins of all; you became sin for all; you became a curse for all. Yet no practice of sin could pass over to you. Thus you lived among sinners as though you were living among angels. You made the earth into what heaven is, so that there too you might remove sin.

“Today I have begotten you,” in whom I am well pleased. You proved yourself the Son by fulfilling the Father’s will in all things. “Today I have begotten you,” in whom I recognize the light of an immaculate offspring. Yesterday and today you are the same, and forever. There is no night in you, because you are wholly day.

He is rightly said to have been established in the Father’s presence forever, because he is always with the Father; and truly in the presence of him whose splendor he is—the glory and image of the substance. But just as the Father is well pleased in the Son, so the Son blesses the Father. For the Father glorifies the Son, and the Son glorifies the Father.

### 36

“Blessed,” he says, “is the Lord God of Israel”—that is, of the people who see God, who believe both in their Lord and in their God—“from age to age; let it be, let it be.”

In Hebrew it is written *Amen, amen*, as those who read the book written in Hebrew letters have asserted. The Greek has here **γένοιτο, γένοιτο** (*genoito, genoito*), which means “Let it be, let it be.”

This word has various meanings: sometimes it is the word of one commanding, sometimes of one praying, and sometimes of one confirming something. It belongs to one commanding when a superior determines for an inferior what must be done or followed. It belongs to one praying, as in: “Your will be done” (Matt. 6:10); for no one commands God, but pours out a prayer. It belongs to one confirming when a prophet, priest, or some holy person gives a blessing and the people respond: “Let it be, let it be.”

Here, therefore, it seems to me to be more a confirmation of the blessing than a prayer or supplication, especially because the very statement is repeated. The Hebrew expression appears to have been changed, but the same meaning has been conveyed. For just as, when a priest blesses, the people respond “Amen,” confirming for themselves the blessing that the priest asks from the Lord on behalf of the people, so in the psalm the response is “Let it be, let it be,” as though it were “Amen, amen.”

That *Amen* is plainly a word of confirmation is shown in the Gospel, where the Lord, confirming his statement, says: “Amen I say to you” (Matt. 19:23). The force is greater where the statement is repeated. We find this more frequently in the book of the Gospel according to John, because he spoke especially about heavenly and profound mysteries. Thus it is written: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). And elsewhere: “Amen, amen, I say to you: if you ask anything of the Father in my name, he will give it to you” (John 16:23). Two examples are sufficient; whoever seeks the others will find them.

### 37

“Let it be, let it be” is also an indication that the book has ended. For the Psalter appears to be divided into five books.

[Note: The division of the Psalms into five parts is famous; it is mentioned by Eusebius of Caesarea in his *Argument concerning the Psalms*; Gregory of Nyssa, *Treatise I on the Psalms*, chapters 5 and following; Jerome, Letter 134; Hilary of Poitiers, *Prologue to the Psalms*. Cassiodorus, *Prologue on the Psalms*, chapter 11, and others may be added to these. Jerome, and after him a recent commentator—otherwise a learned man—reject this division, persuaded by the authority of the Hebrews, and especially of the apostles, who always call the Psalter a book, not books. Ambrose, however, not without reason, dissolves that argument below, in section 37. But the claim of the cited author that this division is not older than Christ not only places Jerome and Hilary in conflict, although they can easily be reconciled if we agree that Jerome’s testimony does not include absolutely all Hebrews; it also clearly shows that he had not seen Eusebius’s testimony. Eusebius explicitly attributes the division in question to the Hebrews and asserts that it is found in the most accurate copies, in these words: “This, then, would be the division of the book of the Psalms, as it is found in the accurate copies, and as the Hebrew text itself contains it; for the children of the Hebrews divide the entire book of the Psalms into five parts.” See what follows in the *Exposition of the Greek Fathers on the Psalms*, already cited by us. It would not even be unreasonable to suppose that those experts in the Hebrew language whom Ambrose, as he indicates in the preceding section, questioned about the conclusion of this psalm were also asked by him about the division of the Psalter among the Hebrews.]

The first book ends with this psalm, that is, the fortieth. It is beautifully arranged that the fortieth psalm should extend as far as the Savior’s passion and end the book, because the Lord’s passion is the end of Lent. Thus the second book might begin with the mysteries of renewal; that book, as befits Lent, contains more perfect sacraments.

For it foretells the sacraments of baptism when it says: “As the deer longs for the fountains of water” (Ps. 41:2); and the rest of the saints who have reached the heavenly tabernacle; and the descent of the Holy Spirit, when spiritual grace was poured out in a kind of voice of heavenly cataracts, because the Spirit was carried along with great power, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2:2); and the entrance of the renewed human being to the altar; and the Savior’s ascension; and the sanctification of the virginal vocation.

This book ends with the seventy-first psalm, in which Christ’s peaceful kingdom spread throughout the whole world is announced in prophetic language, together with the forgiveness of sins. There, after prefacing the Lord’s blessing, he adds: “And the whole earth shall be filled with his majesty. Let it be, let it be” (Ps. 71:19).

The third book likewise ends with the eighty-eighth psalm, where it says: “Blessed is the Lord forever. Let it be, let it be” (Ps. 88:53).

The fourth book ends with the one hundred and fifth psalm, where it says: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel from age to age and forever; and all the people shall say: Let it be, let it be” (Ps. 105:48).

The fifth book continues to the end, where, in place of this expression, the Prophet says: “Let every spirit praise the Lord” (Ps. 150:6).

### 38

But perhaps you are again troubled about how I can assert that there are five books when there is one Psalter. Yet the Gospel is also one, and we cannot deny that it consists of four books. We have indicated elsewhere—if I am not mistaken, in the first book on Luke, in the preface—that there is one Gospel; and if the matter is pressed again, we can easily demonstrate it, since the Savior said: “Wherever this Gospel is preached” (Matt. 26:13).

The Apostle likewise says: “I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring yourselves to another gospel, which is not another; except that there are some who trouble you” (Gal. 1:6–7). And elsewhere: “I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel” (1 Cor. 15:1). Nowhere do you find anything else said about this body of four books except that it is designated “the Gospel.”

Finally, because the Psalms too form one body, Scripture said: “Upon the ten-stringed psaltery, with song upon the lyre” (Ps. 91:4).

[Note: The old edition, with three manuscripts, reads: “Scripture said.” But again, because there are five books, it says elsewhere: “in the vessels of the Psalms.” The Roman edition reads: “Scripture said; for it is written in the book of Psalms.” And again, because there are many psalms, as though they were books, it says elsewhere: “It is necessary that all things be fulfilled that are written about me in the Law of Moses, and the Prophets, and the Psalms.” We have restored the passage on the authority of five manuscripts.]

But again, because there are five books, it says elsewhere: “In the vessels of the Psalms” (Ps. 70:22).

### 39

It is fitting that there are five books and one Psalter, because the outer human being is enlivened through the five senses; and, again, through five spiritual senses, that hidden human being of our heart is perfected within—the one who alone is found rich before God, according to the testimony of the Apostle Peter (1 Pet. 3:4).

“He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8). You have one sense. And just as there are those who have eyes and do not see, so there are those who, though their bodily eyes do not see, are believed to see more. Hence even those who did not see with their eyes were called “seers,” namely, the prophets.

There is also that good fragrance of which the Apostle said: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2:15). Hence Job also says: “And the divine Spirit, which is in my nostrils” (Job 27:3). Therefore the fragrance of Christ and the Holy Spirit is one fragrance to God, because the Trinity has one fragrance.

There is also an inward food, of which the Lord said: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John 4:34).

There is also an inward touch, by which that woman in the Gospel touched Christ—the woman who had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years and had not received health from physicians, but received it from Christ. It is the touch of faith by which Christ is touched.

Indeed, people did not see her, but Jesus saw her and testified that he had seen her, saying: “Someone touched me; for I also knew that power had gone out from me” (Luke 8:46). Knowledge of Christ is the bestowal of health.

Therefore, since it is clear that there are ten senses in a human being, David—who sang both outwardly and inwardly, outwardly with his body and inwardly with his heart—says in the psalm: “Upon the ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you” (Ps. 143:9).

### 40

The Psalter, therefore, is the perfected human being in Christ. In him, just as the strings of instruments resound according to the art of musicians, so the harmonious works of virtues resound in concert, so that he may say: “I will sing to you, O God, upon the holy lyre of Israel; my lips shall rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed” (Ps. 70:24–25).

Paul says of himself: “Outwardly conflicts, inwardly fears” (2 Cor. 7:5). This man rejoices both inwardly and outwardly; but the other is still in the contest, while this one is in remission, because he knew that he had merited the redemption of his soul.

He who sings psalms is in joy; he who struggles is in anxiety. Yet Paul also knew how to sing psalms, but he was still reserving himself for further progress, since he was to be more fully tested before he could sing. Therefore he said: “I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind; I will sing psalms with the spirit, and I will sing psalms with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15).

### 41

And because Scripture has shown that there is a twofold task of singing psalms, it also teaches that there is a twofold voice, as the Prophet says: “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and my voice was directed to God, and he attended to me” (Ps. 76:2).

What does “my” mean? He could have said simply: “I cried to the Lord.” But what is our voice except this better voice, which does not know how to err? For through many words we incur sin and cannot avoid it.

That is the Prophet’s voice which reaches God. While Moses was silent, it cried out to the Lord. With this voice Hannah also cried in her prayers, although she did not move the lips of her mouth; and she obtained a son whom she had not previously obtained, although she had cried out earlier with her bodily voice.

Of this voice the Lord said: “But when you pray, enter your room, and after closing the door, pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. 6:6).

What does “will repay” mean? It means: what you have asked for, what you have prayed for. For just as sinners receive their sins back from the hand of the Lord twofold, so, conversely, the righteous receive their requests with favorable effect.

[Note: All the manuscripts have this reading. The edition, however, reads: “they receive their own requests with their fulfillment” (certain Parisian manuscripts: “with their own”).]

Hear how they receive them: your prayer ascends to God, and it descends to you. Hence we also read in the psalm: “And my prayer shall return into my bosom” (Ps. 35:13), so that it may bring back fruit to the one who made the request.

Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who has opened such great mysteries to us: from age to age—that is, from infinity into infinity. Let it be, let it be.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 43

[Column 1087]

### 1

(Verse 1.) The title of the psalm is: “For the end; for the sons of Korah; an instruction.” Here the holy prophet David, having traversed the mysteries of the Lord’s passion, baptism, and entrance to the most sacred altar, teaches how Christ trains his athlete, whose name is held in the contest of the saints.

For just as, without any labor on our part, not from works but from faith, he forgave us our sins by his grace and, most indulgent and kind, admitted us to seek the crown, not allowing our former crimes—by which we would have been judged unworthy of so great a contest—to stand in our way, and just as this is asked even of those who undertake this purifying contest, including discipline of life,

[Note: The ancients used to celebrate games and contests on days of purification—that is, on days when some city was purified by religious rites. This is understood from Seneca’s *Troades*, where we read: “Nor on the appointed day of purification shall the noble boy drive swift companies.” What is added concerning the discipline of life belongs to the same subject as Paul’s statement in 1 Corinthians 9:25: “Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control.” In both passages it is signified that athletes formerly followed a strict manner of life. On this subject there is the following instruction of Epictetus, *Enchiridion* 47: “You must maintain discipline, endure a constrained diet, abstain from pastries, train under compulsion at the appointed hour, in heat and cold; do not drink cold water, do not drink wine,” and so forth. There are similar remarks in Arrian, book 3; to these may be added what Horace writes on this subject in his *Art of Poetry*.]

so, conversely, lest we become lax through so great a gift of sins and return to our former crimes or to idleness, this psalm admonishes us that many and serious contests have been set before us, so that no one may be crowned except one who has competed lawfully.

We must therefore struggle against the allurements of this flesh and the heat of the blood; we must struggle against spiritual wickedness. No adversary is more formidable than the domestic one; no enemy is more harmful than the one whose heavenly substance gives power to it.

[Note: Here the substance of spiritual wickedness is called heavenly by contrast with human substance, which is earthly. It had indeed been created in heaven, from which it fell.]

When I say “no one,” remember the divine saying in which the Lord said: “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11). For the one born from the Virgin is above all.

Therefore let us fear no one, since we have Christ; for if Christ is for us, who can be against us? Let us contend to the end, so that, after everything that previously fought in our body against Jesus and the Lord’s will has been emptied out, we may devote ourselves to the true practice of virtue and serve our only God and Lord.

For this is the end, as it is written: “Christ the firstfruits … then the end, when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every principality and authority and power … so that the last enemy, death, may be destroyed” (1 Cor. 15:23ff.), and we may begin to be subject to God, preserving the heavenly kingdom within us, where the confusion of sins had previously been.

### 2

The psalm is therefore rightly entitled: “For the end; for the sons of Korah; an instruction,” so that in understanding it not ordinary hearing but spiritual understanding may operate. Indeed, Aquila rendered the title as “of discipline.”

Therefore Scripture says to you: “Give your heart to discipline, and prepare your ears for words of understanding” (Prov. 23:12). And elsewhere: “Love wisdom and discipline” (Prov. 1:3).

Wisdom is that from which understanding pours forth; discipline is a form of virtues fused into a certain disposition of nature, and a judgment confirmed by the practices of knowledge.

[Note: Five Gallican manuscripts read: “a judgment confirmed by knowledge of the disciplines.” “To understand an obscure saying through the disciplines,” and so forth. The remaining manuscripts and all the editions have the reading in the text, except that the Roman edition, following the Septuagint interpretation, has “the expressions of prudence,” whereas the others and the manuscripts have “the prudence of expressions.” Observe that *dictiones* sometimes—and perhaps in this very passage—has the same meaning as “oracles,” as the following fragment of Pacuvius teaches:

“An utterance turned, not false, is what Delphi is accustomed to declare.”]

Scripture also taught us to understand an obscure saying, the prudence of expressions, and the riddles of Proverbs (ibid.). On its authority we infer that these are the chief virtues of prudence: wisdom, like a fertile mother, is always giving birth; discipline, like a stricter teacher, restrains; understanding, like a diligent investigator, discovers and examines true justice and judgment.

### 3

Let us teach these things by the testimonies of sacred reading. Wisdom says: “Like a fountain from paradise, I said: ‘I will water my garden’ … and still I will pour forth instruction like prophecy” (Sir. 24:41–42, 46).

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “For it pours its thoughts into the human mind,” and so forth.]

For it pours its offspring—namely, good perceptions—into the human mind like a devoted mother.

Receive also the testimonies concerning discipline: “My son, do not neglect the discipline of God, nor grow weary when you are rebuked by him” (Prov. 3:11–12), for God rebukes the one whom he loves. Discipline is severe in rebuking but sweet in correcting, lest we drift and wander astray, but be received by Christ.

For unexamined discipline wanders, as it is written. Here, however, he used “discipline” in the sense of preservation. Yet just as wisdom, so also discipline—both perfect and imperfect—is called by the same name. But when either discipline or wisdom is named without qualification, it receives the definition of perfection.

Unexamined discipline therefore drifts, but examined discipline does not drift. Scripture gives the same definition concerning understanding, because “understanding is good for all who practice it” (Ps. 110:10). Since understanding contains within itself both the grace of wisdom and the order of discipline, we are plainly taught that wisdom and discipline are good for those who carry out their principles in their actions.

We have spoken about the title; let us approach the psalm.

### 4

(Verse 2.) “O God, with our ears we have heard.” Symmachus has it this way; Theodotion said: “In our ears,” as did the Seventy.

What does “with our ears” mean? If “we have heard” were not sufficient, certainly “with ears we have heard” would have been complete, if that had been his preference. Since “our” has been added, what does it mean except that you should understand those things to be ours which belong to the mind, and that they are better than those which belong to this body?

Therefore this same Prophet speaks elsewhere, as though of another: “I will not fear what flesh can do to me” (Ps. 56:5). And elsewhere: “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and my voice was directed to God, and he looked upon me” (Ps. 77:2). It is that voice of mine which is heard by Christ, not the one that echoes in public.

He does not wish what is corruptible and earthly to be his own, since he remembers that he was created in the image and likeness of God. Indeed, Scripture teaches us that the human being was first formed in the image of God (Gen. 1:27), and afterward made from clay (Gen. 2:7).

Thus the power of the soul, as though superior—for what is older is superior—and as governor and ruler of this body, says: “With our ears we have heard.” Who is this, except the one to whom it is said: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8)?

For there are those who have ears but cannot hear the mysteries. Of them Jesus says in the revelation of John: “Outside are dogs, sorcerers, and the sexually immoral” (Rev. 22:15), whose desire for shameful acts and the rust of money block the ear from hearing.

Let us therefore consider what they say they have heard, or from whom they recall having heard it.

### 5

“And our fathers,” he says, “declared it to us.”

Who are these “our fathers”? The title states that the psalm was written for the sons of Korah, so that it might be sung by those who had received the duty of singing psalms and had been appointed to this kind of service.

But Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, together with the others who had risen up against Moses and Aaron in stubborn rebellion, were swallowed up and killed when the earth opened in the desert. After their death, what other fathers could have declared the Lord’s marvelous works to their sons? For wisdom does not enter into a malicious soul.

If their own fathers did not declare these things to their sons, outsiders did so even less, since they avoided the offspring of the faithless.

Who, then, are these fathers? See whether they are the ones of whom it was said: “Ask your father, and he will tell you” (Deut. 32:7). Ask when you read Paul; or, if you do not read him and something troubles you, seek the answer in him.

For he is the good father who can teach and form the Lord Jesus in us, as he himself testified, saying: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19).

The Evangelist John shows you these fathers when he says: “I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning” (1 John 2:13). These are the fathers whose old age is an unblemished life.

Therefore, in the assembly of elders, place your finger upon your mouth, so that you may hear what benefits you and learn the mysteries of eternal life. Do not, as an insolent beginner, interrupt your teachers; and, though you still ought to be learning, do not presume to speak.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “presume to teach.”]

Let us hear, then, what these fathers declared to the sons of Korah.

### 6

“The work,” he says, “which you performed in ancient days.”

Let us investigate what days these were in which God performed great and marvelous works. Scripture teaches us that there are certain glorious days in which divine deeds shone forth, since we read that “the sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes. And everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel 2:31–32).

On that very day Christ rose for humanity, and therefore it was specifically said of it: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. 118:24).

Although God made all days, this day nevertheless received the prerogative of divine work above the others, because on it all sin was removed. The other days, however, belong to sinners.

This, then, is the day illuminated by that sun of righteousness. For righteousness itself is accustomed to have its risings and settings. Hence it is written: “In his days righteousness shall arise” (Ps. 72:7).

There are therefore days of Christ in which righteousness arose; days of Christ in which an abundance of peace arose; days of Christ in which wisdom arose.

Hear how wisdom arises: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool, so that he may be wise” (1 Cor. 3:18). Therefore Wisdom says, she who chose the foolish things of this world: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works” (Prov. 8:22).

For just as in the days of King Uzziah and in the days of Nebuchadnezzar unbelief arose and captivity held sway, so in the days of the Lord Jesus faith arose, spreading the splendor of its brightness and light throughout the whole world.

For what days are better than those in which the vision of God shone upon us, as Jacob said? For it is written: “I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved. And immediately the sun rose for him” (Gen. 32:30–31).

What sun is this except the one who caused the days of righteousness to shine, in which Christ was born on earth from the Virgin?

Jacob saw God in a figure and said that he had seen God; the Jews saw him in truth and did not believe. Therefore their days were shortened, while ours were illuminated, because day was failing for them but approaching for us.

Hence holy David, shunning Jewish blindness, says: “Do not lead me away in the middle of my days” (Ps. 102:25). For the day of the Lord is great and glorious—not because of the length of time, but because of the brightness of righteousness and grace.
