There are therefore half-days: days shortened by the darkness of impiety and the squalor of unbelief, during which the sun sets upon the prophets (Mic. 3:6), as it is written. For just as the sun of righteousness rises for the righteous, so it sets for the unbelieving.

7. But the following presents itself: the Lord says, “For the sake of the elect the days will be shortened” (Matt. XXIV, 22). This seems contradictory unless you pay close attention and recall what precedes; for the Lord says: “Then, if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘There he is,’ do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise, and they will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led astray” (ibid., 23–24). And therefore, lest the elect be deceived, the Lord warns what must be followed, so that we may not be seized by the speech of false prophets, nor deceived by any miraculous deeds of theirs; but let us believe that Christ is about to come when the days full of righteousness have begun to shine forth. For Christ will be revealed in the full light of his majesty; and just as lightning comes forth from the east and spreads its light throughout the whole world as far as the west, so also the Son of Man, coming with his angels, will illuminate this world, so that every human being may believe and all flesh may be saved. Let us not, then, believe in the Antichrist, of whom the false prophets will say, “This is the Christ”; for the days of faithlessness will be the days of the Antichrist. Let us not believe those who will say, “Christ is in the desert,” or, “Christ is in the inner chambers”; for everything is already full of Christ wherever Christ has begun to draw near. But when we see the events that Christ foretold beforehand in his Gospel, then let us believe in his coming, lest, while seeking the true light, we fall into the darkness of unbelief.

8. We must therefore beware of the signs of faithlessness, by which the days are shortened and diminished. For the sun will be darkened, and the stars will fall—that is, the righteous of God; for there are those who shine like stars in heaven. When you see these things, believe that Christ is still delaying; for where Christ is, there is brighter faith, whereas where the Antichrist is, there are half-days. The prophet David would certainly not have complained of these, if the matter seemed to refer to the brevity of time, since elsewhere he himself said: “Woe is me, because my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. CXIX, 5)! For how could he grieve either over that heavenly sojourning being delayed or over this earthly one being cut short, when earlier he had asked not to be brought into half his days, if the shortening of the days seemed to provide a means of hastening this course? Hence we may also gather the meaning of the statement: “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Exod. XX, 12). Many who honor their parents are often suddenly taken away and die at an immature age; while many who show less respect to their parents enjoy the long rewards of old age. And unless we understand that longevity as the life of eternity, Scripture is found to be deprived of the support of truth. Hence the Greek expressed it more precisely: “So that you may be many-days,” that is, πολυήμερος. For whoever diligently preserves the duties of pious worship, being estranged from the darkness of night, dwells in the light of the days. And therefore, whoever reads Deuteronomy is told: “He shall read it all the days of his life” (Deut. XVII, 19)—not, certainly, by nights but by days, because the day shines for the one who reads the mysteries of truth and the oracles of divine devotion. Let us consider what follows.

9. (Verse 3.) “Your hand destroyed the nations, and you planted them; you afflicted the peoples and drove them out.” We certainly know that the Lord uprooted and overthrew many nations, so that the Jewish people might find possession for themselves, since the Lord declared that he would give the lands of those nations to the seed of Abraham. But since this psalm announces the Lord’s Gospel and the times of his coming, it does not seem to me to recount what was formerly done by the Jews, but to indicate what was to come: namely, how the peoples of the nations would believe. It therefore confirms the faith of the Church before announcing it, and it enumerates the victories of her devotion. She did not drive out savage nations by her own arm or sword, nor put hostile troops to flight in military combat; rather, through gentleness and faith, she possessed the lands of her enemies without any bloodshed. Faith alone fought. And therefore she merited triumphs which faithlessness would not recall but increase, because the Church of the Lord is not conquered by her persecutions but tested.

Let us therefore learn what these nations are that the Church conquered. I speak of ancient names, but of new mysteries. They are the Canaanites, the Chettites, and the Amorites, the Perizzites,

[Note: The Roman edition, from the Vatican manuscript, has “and the rest”; other editions, together with all the manuscripts, have “and the Cherethites.” They are frequently mentioned in the Book of Kings, where Lyra, in his Book of Differences, says that they are the same as the Philistines.]

or the Cherethites, whose names we shall set out below. These are indeed the names of peoples, but they also signify the weaknesses of the passions and the incitements and disgraces of human sins. The first thing, therefore, is that a person in Christ subdues himself and conquers himself, so that he may live for himself. For the one who lives for God lives for himself, so that he may live the eternal life of Christ. The Church’s people therefore did not fight with military weapons and iron arms, as the Jewish people fought. That people fought in figure; we fight in the spirit. They fought against foreigners; we have war within ourselves. And therefore the passions of our own body must first be conquered by us.

10. Hear the Apostle Paul fighting against the nation of the Canaanites: “I see,” he says, “another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin” (Rom. VII, 23). Now our flesh rises up, now it casts us down. It raises itself against the mind and casts it down from its power; and when it sees itself pressed, it abandons steadfastness and is led, prepared for submission, under the law of sin, so that it may abandon faith and yield to faithlessness;

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts have “the sign of the weakness of the Chettites” (Chettaeae or Ethaeae). The Regius manuscript, together with several others, has “left under domination . . .,” which seems more suitably adapted to the allegory established.]

but, left under the domination of Chettite weakness, it yields to falsehood, serves crime, and acquiesces in error; and, like an Amorite, it speaks bitter things instead of sweet ones. For faith is sweet, while faithlessness is bitter. Hence Peter expressed excellently what faith was when he said: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we believe” (John VI, 69–70). How, then, do you command us to depart from you? Captivated by the sweetness of heavenly words, he did not wish to depart from Christ.

But the one who denies Christ separates himself

[Note: “Or is separated”; this reading was absent from all editions and two manuscripts, but is found in five others. As for what is added in all editions after the word “disputation”—namely, “of this kind”—since it is found in no manuscript, it was probably added so that the sense might somehow be completed. Even if one thinks it should be retained, the passage still does not seem to have been healed. We therefore think that the following words have fallen out there: “the apostles,” or “the faithful separates from Christ,” or something similar, which must thereafter be understood in the individual members of the sentence.]

or is separated from Christ. Nor is it the subtle disputation of the Amorites, which through philosophy leads some away from the truth; nor the shameful degradation of the Jebusites, which submits and prostrates itself beneath those running the worldly course, a course that cannot be perpetual but comes to an end at the gates of death, from which the prophet David rejoices that he has been raised (Ps. IX, 15); nor the Kenite, who is possessed through his money, like one driven by insatiable avarice; nor the Kenizzite, who thinks that possession is perpetual in riches, places vain hope in things that pass away, and boasts in an empty opinion; nor the Rephaim, who professes to bring healing to others while unable to cure his own wounds. And therefore, if anyone flees to such a physician, he must first consume all his patrimony before receiving any benefit of health, like that woman in the Gospel (Luke VIII, 43–44) who could not stop the flow of blood from bodily desires for twelve years until afterward she fled to Christ.

For she understood that no one is a perfect physician except the one who had descended from heaven, of whom she had learned it was said: “He sent his word and healed them” [Col. 1094A] (Ps. CVI, 20). And she understood that this had been said of him: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth, and I have appointed you this day over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and destroy, to ruin and build, to plant” (Jer. I, 9–10). For although God frequently spoke in the prophets, in whom did he speak more explicitly than in his own Son, who, expressing all the Father’s power, said: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John VII, 16)? It was not Jeremiah, who at the time of the captivity undertook exile, but the Lord Jesus who, by his words, uprooted the vices of the Gentiles from the depths of their hearts, destroyed the faithlessness of the nations and the evil inventions of crafty thoughts, and abolished every trace of iniquity. Then he poured in faith and the discipline of continence, lest, as in a corrupted vessel, the sacraments of the virtues should ferment amid the confusion of vices.

11. Hence the Apostle beautifully says to you: “But death reigned from Adam to Moses” (Rom. V, 1). What is Moses except the Law, since he is its interpreter? And the end of the Law is Christ Jesus. Sin therefore reigned in this world, and in sin there was a savage and intolerable death, a certain punishment of sin. Moses indeed taught us to raise our hands to the Lord, establishing the discipline of pious worship. He taught how

[Note: All editions read “Amalek’s cunning was overcome.” Several manuscripts, and old editions in the margin, read “the place of Amalek’s cunning was overcome”; read “the cunning speaker,” and so forth. For the reading found in Victor and Colbertinus, “by cunning speeches,” must be attributed to the scribes’ ignorance.]

Amalek, the crafty speaker, was to be conquered, so that we might raise our conduct and works toward Christ, and thus faithlessness might be destroyed. But if we cast down our soul, incline our affections, and turn our mind away from the pursuit of continence, so that empty persuasion overcomes us, there would be no remedy unless Jesus, as though lifting up Moses’ arms when they had already fallen, should raise the weakness of the Law and sustain it by his mercy.

Yet the help of the Law would still have been weak unless Jesus himself had come to earth, he who would take our weaknesses upon himself, the only one whom our sins could neither burden nor cause to lower his hands. He humbled himself even to death, and death on a cross; and there, stretching out his hands, he raised up the whole world that was destined to perish. He lifted up those who lay fallen and drew to himself the faith of all nations, saying to the man: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43).

This, then, is what it means “to destroy and to plant”: that vices may be uprooted and better things planted in the hearts of individuals. Concerning this Moses beautifully says in the song of Exodus: “Bringing them in, plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, in your prepared dwelling-place” (Exod. XV, 17). He asks that the Lord bring his people into those lofty plantings of virtue and wisdom, and that there they may be planted in his work and instructed in the discipline of heavenly commandments, and that he may prepare for himself in them a dwelling-place of his sanctification. This the Lord is certainly pleased to bestow, not by hereditary right or in consideration of our merits, but according to his grace. For how could we return to the place where we were unable to remain, unless supported by the privilege of eternal redemption?

12. (Verse 4.) And therefore the Prophet beautifully says: “For they did not possess the land by their own sword, and their own arm did not save them; but your right hand and your arm and the light of your face, because you were pleased with them.” What land, then, is not seized by the arm or possessed by the sword, except the land of promise, concerning which the same Prophet said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI, 13)? It is not without reason, therefore, that its possession is so glorious, for there the adversities of the world do not rule, but the eternal good things of the Lord bear fruit. And therefore it is not acquired by the sword but possessed through gentleness, as the Lord Jesus testified, saying: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V, 4).

Let no one, therefore, be contentious, arrogant, or proud, but meek and humble of heart; let him claim nothing for himself but refer everything to grace; let him not glory in his own strength but believe that he is protected by the right hand of God, saying: “The right hand of the Lord has done valiantly; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (Ps. CXVII, 16). Let him also remember that he has been preserved by the sword of God and illuminated by the face of God Almighty. In all these things Christ is the protector,

[Note: Victor, Colbertinus, and the old editions in the margin read “protector, like the right hand; defender, like the sword.”]

the right hand, the defender, and the sword. Hence Simeon also said to Mary: “And your own soul a sword shall pierce” (Luke II, 35). For the sword of God is the Word, which pierces more sharply than every sword, even to the division of the soul and the thoughts, so that no hidden things escape its knowledge.

Christ is also the splendor of the Father’s face; and therefore he says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9), as the radiance of his glory and the image of his substance. To him, therefore, all things must rightly be referred. To him Moses, to him Aaron, and to him also the Fathers consecrated everything they did, so that they might triumph over their enemies.

For Jesus son of Nave did not say in confidence in himself, “Let the sun stand still against Gibeon” (Josh. X, 12), but because he trusted in Christ, whom he recognized as the commander of the heavenly army and worshiped submissively. And therefore he deserved to uproot savage nations and lead the people of the Fathers into the land of promise, because he attributed nothing to his own works, believing that human works were unworthy of so great a reward of heavenly glory, which the Lord determined to bestow on those who believe in him more from his own mercy than in consideration of our deeds.

Hence Abraham also readily believed God, so that he might find with him the grace of justification, which he might regard as the reward of his work. For the gifts of the giver are more abundant than the reward of the laborer. Therefore the Lord answered the one who begrudged the equality of the reward: “If I am good, why is your eye evil?” (Matt. XX, 15). Our Fathers, therefore, as being close to and heirs of the patriarchs, planted in the land of promise, did not claim this on the basis of their own merits. Hence Moses did not lead them in, lest this should be thought to belong to the Law rather than to grace; for the Law examines merits, while grace regards faith.

Therefore the Apostle, beautifully following the faith of the Fathers, says: “Neither is the one who plants anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. III, 7). It was not Jesus son of Nave who led them in, nor the one who planted them, but God who gave increase to the people and holds the primacy of glory.

13. Nor should it trouble you that above he said: “Your hand destroyed the nations, and you planted them” (Ps. XLIII, 3). From this you gather that not everyone who plants or waters gives the increase, but that the one who can give the increase can himself plant, just as the Lord is said to have planted the nations. For he himself planted who gave effect to the planting; yet this was in those who by faith deserved to please the Lord Christ, to whom alone God the Father says: “You are my Son; in you I am well pleased” (Mark I, 11). Those, therefore, who are partakers of Christ obtain from him the grace of pleasing.

And he says beautifully: “You were pleased with them,” so that the distinction may rightly be preserved. For God rightly takes pleasure in the Son, because he is equal to the Father and is found dissimilar in nothing; he pleases by right of the divine nature and unity of substance. And the Father rightly takes pleasure in the Son, because the Father is honored in the Son, just as the Son is honored in the Father.

But God was pleased with us because he himself granted us the ability to please him. Scripture has also taught that this was piously granted specially to the human being, not arrogantly seized. For it is fitting that God should take pleasure in those whom he made according to his likeness and whom he willed to possess the prerogative of heavenly grace through his image. God therefore takes pleasure in his image; and in those who are according to his image, God takes pleasure. In them there is his own gift and his own donation, which will then be revealed when that perfection has come, because “when it appears what we are, we shall be like him,” as it is written (1 John III, 2).

14. (Verse 5.) Therefore the one who does not presume upon his own arm—that is, upon his own activity—but upon the grace of God, believing that it is not a person’s deeds that justify each one, but ready faith, says to the Lord: “You are yourself my King and my God, who command salvation for Jacob.” It is no casual expression to say, “You are yourself my King.” Not everyone says this, but the one in whom the kingdom of God exists. And where God reigns, sins certainly do not reign; for God’s kingdom is not shared with crime.

Who, moreover, says “my God” except the one who displays toward him a complete disposition of reverence and devotion? For it is said to the righteous: “I am your God.” Finally, when Thomas touched Christ’s side with his own hand and found clear evidence of the indisputable resurrection, he replied: “My Lord and my God” (John XX, 28). He is Lord because he redeemed his servants; God because he not only rose again but also raised himself.

He commanded salvations for Jacob because salvation is present in every oracle; salvation is also present in every dwelling-place; salvation is present in the ministries of the angels who are appointed for the protection of human beings. Therefore salvation is bestowed on a person by God’s command, not through his own activity. For God preferred that salvation should be sought for a person through faith rather than through works, lest anyone glory in his own deeds and fall into sin. But the one who glories in the Lord acquires the fruit of devotion and escapes the crime of boasting.

15. (Verse 6.) This, then, is the one who can say: “In you we shall toss our enemies with the horn.” What does “to toss with the horn” mean? The Lord gave horns to many animals so that they could defend themselves from the attacks of wild beasts. Hence an ox frequently resists a lion and tramples a bear; the stag also, although timid, protects itself with its horns; and the ram butts the wolf. Thus animals that have horns are said to toss with them.

But human beings do not have horns. How, then, do they toss with them? From where? See what Scripture says: “In you,” it says, “we shall toss our enemies with the horn.” You are our horn, Lord Jesus. And therefore, just as we do not presume upon our own arm, so we have no defense for tossing with our own horns, but in Christ. Faith has its own horns, which it borrows from Christ.

Indeed, we read not idly in the blessings of Moses: “Let him who appeared in the bush come upon the head of Joseph, and upon his crown, glorified among his brothers, the firstborn. His appearance is the beauty of a bull; his horns are the horns of a unicorn. With them he shall toss the nations together to the ends of the earth. These are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and these are the thousands of Manasseh” (Deut. XXXIII, 16–17).

Who was seen by Moses in the bush except the firstborn Son of God, who said: “I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob” (Exod. III, 6)? He therefore showed himself to human eyes because he was to come so that all might see him. The bush burned and was not consumed because he intended to burn this earth, which was producing thorns and thistles for us, through the discipline of continence, rather than consume it through the anguish of death.

Hence the Prophet says: “Burn my kidneys and my heart” (Ps. XXV, 2). He therefore revealed beforehand a certain sign of bodily splendor, by which this flesh would shine through the resurrection. For what did the harmless fire signify except the lights of those who rise again? Hence the Apostle ventured to say: “As star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. XV, 41–42).

“Let him,” therefore, “come upon the head of the tribe of Joseph,” so that he may exalt the head of his people; let him also come upon its crown, so that he may walk over the crown of its hair, cutting off the excesses of sins and sanctifying the ornaments of virtues.

16. This is the one “glorified among his brothers,” as he himself says: “I shall declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI, 23). What glory is greater than to infuse the knowledge of divinity into the hearts of the nations?

[Note: The Victor and Colbertinus manuscripts and all editions read “than to sinners of the nations.” Other manuscripts have the reading found in the text.]

Joseph saw him in a vision: his brothers’ sheaves worshiped his sheaf, and the sun and moon with the stars worshiped him. That sheaf is understood as a figure of the flesh; for all flesh is grass. He took up this grass of ours so that he might cause his own wheat to sprout and bring forth the fruit of the resurrection. Do you seek testimony? Hear him speaking of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the ground dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII, 21).

Finally, so that you may know that Moses speaks of the Son of God, he says: “Glorified among his brothers, the firstborn” (Deut. XXXIII, 17). Joseph was certainly not the firstborn among Jacob’s sons, but Reuben; Joseph was born much later. Yet he is called firstborn because he was to come in order to gather the peoples of the nations.

17. Hence Scripture beautifully says: “His beauty is that of a bull” (ibid.). For just as the bull leads the herd, so Christ led the people of the nations to the Church and brought them to pasture, so that he could say: “He has placed me in a place of pasture; he has set me beside the water of refreshment” (Ps. XXII, 2–3).

[Note: The old edition and the Roman edition, together with the Victor and Colbertinus manuscripts, read: “The herds of our weakness, seized by the perpetual beauty of this bull, followed the one going before,” and so forth. Some Paris editions have: “The herds of our weakness, according to their capacity, followed this bull’s beauty,” and so forth. The Regius manuscript and four others that come closest to it agree with us.]

The herds of our weakness followed the beauty of this bull according to their capacity, following the one who went before, so that they might obtain eternal life. This bull bellowed, and death fled. The lion roars, and who does not fear? Truly, a very great bull is the victim, so that we may take testimony from the adversaries (Virgil, Book II of the Georgics). For what victim is greater than the one whose blood cleansed the sin of the whole world?

Hear that the holy prophet Jacob also calls him this bull when he revealed the Lord’s Passion, whom the Jews afterward persecuted. “In their fury,” he says, “they hamstrung the bull” (Gen. XLIX, 6). And to make clear that he was speaking of the Jews, he added: “I shall divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (ibid., 7).

This is the man who wrestled with Jacob and touched his thigh, by which touch the Patriarch’s sinew became numb. He signified that from Jacob’s succession according to the flesh would come the one who was to be hamstrung by the Jewish people in the Passion of his body. Not understanding the mystery, they decreed that the sons of Israel should not eat the sinew. And therefore they deprived themselves of the redemption of the sacred blood and rejected the benefits of the saving Passion, lest they deserve eternal life; for it is written: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves. But whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood shall have eternal life” (John VI, 54–55).

Receive another interpretation. What is the sinew except that by which the whole body is bound together? The body of Christ is the Church, which is bound by the bond of charity. What else did the Jews do in Christ except dissolve the entire bond of charity? With good reason Peter the priest is chosen, for he bound himself threefold with the spirit of divine charity.

[Col. 1099A] 17. Receive still more, because Moses signified the same thing. He added: “The horns of a unicorn are his horns; with them he shall toss the nations” (Deut. XXXIII, 17). But do not be afraid because he tosses them, for he said: “I strike, and I heal” (Deut. XXXII, 39). Good are the horns with which he enclosed the globe of the earth; good are the horns with which he tossed that lion, our adversary; good are the horns by which he made us unable to fear the horns of the adversary. For Satan also has his horns, as Daniel testified, saying: “I saw, and behold, that horn was making war against the saints and prevailing against them, until the Ancient of Days came” (Dan. VII, 21–22). This is the Ancient of Days.

And who is the unicorn except the only-begotten Son of God and the one Word of God, which was in the beginning with the Father? By its horns that Word put the peoples of the nations to death and gave them life, so that they might become the ten thousands of Ephraim to the ends of the earth, and the thousands of Manasseh; because the people of the nations would believe in him and fill the whole world, and afterward the Jewish people also would believe, turning from forgetfulness to grace. For the one who would turn to Christ so late had forgotten its salvation. Hence Saul is associated with thousands and David with ten thousands, because he was harsh among the few and gentle among the many.

18. Yet I do not reject the view that, if someone thinks the words “the glory of his firstborn is that of a bull” were spoken of Joseph, the passage should be divided in this way, since Scripture also says that he gave horns to his saints: “He has exalted the horn of his people” (Ps. CXLVIII, 14). And Anna, the mother of the prophet Samuel,

[Col. 1099C] says: “My heart has exulted in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God” (1 Sam. II, 1). Joseph certainly also had spiritual horns in the Lord.

Let Joseph therefore be understood, provided that in him there is a figure of Christ, to whom it is said: “Joseph, my son, is enlarged; my younger son, return to me” (Gen. XLIX, 22). For Joseph does not return to Jacob; rather, Christ, raised from the dead, returns to God the Father, as it is written: “His going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his meeting-place is even to its summit” (Ps. XVIII, 7).

Still, let it be understood of Joseph as well: “Return to me,” because the people return to the land of the Canaanites, in which the patriarchs had previously dwelt. Hence Isaac says to Jacob: “You shall not take a wife from the daughters of the Canaanites” (Gen. XXVIII, 1);

[Note: Some manuscripts read “from the borders of the Canaanites.”]

and he sends him to Mesopotamia, so that he might find a wife there for himself. Did the lords of the arrows plot against him?

[Note: To show that the blessing bestowed upon the tribe of Joseph by Moses must be understood above all of Christ, certain words are here drawn from the blessing with which Jacob, dying, blessed his son Joseph; these words, however, are acknowledged to apply properly to Christ. There is therefore an allusion to Genesis XLIX, 23: “Against whom, plotting, they reviled him, and they attacked him, the masters of arrows.” And below also, verse 25: “Because of the blessing of breasts and womb,” etc. See Book 11 of *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*.]

Was he himself blessed throughout the whole world because of the blessing of his mother’s womb, and not the Lord Jesus, whom the Virgin bore? And therefore he is blessed not only above human beings but also above angels and archangels, and above every sublimity of the heavenly powers, as Scripture testifies, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is God, and he has shone upon us” [Col. 1100A] (Ps. CXVII, 26–27). For the Lord God himself is King of kings and Lord of lords among those who are in the heavens.

Because of these horns of the Lord Jesus, and because David, singing with the voice of the horn-trumpet (Ps. XCVII, 6), was heard by Christ, Moses also taught (Num. X, 10) that the rites of sacrifices were to be celebrated by the sound of the trumpet, just as it is written: “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month” (Ps. LXXX, 4). To whom was this written except to us? For the ancients were accustomed to observe the months from the beginning of the moon. The moon, however, is the Church, which is exalted by spiritual and evangelical preaching in an abundance of peace, as the Prophet said (Ps. LXXI, 7). In Christ, therefore, we shall toss our enemies with the horn.

19. “And in his name we shall despise those who rise up against us.” What is a name except that by which each person is specifically designated, something that he does not share with others? “Human being” is a common designation; unless you add the name by which someone is called, he cannot be identified. A name, therefore, is the particular property of each person, by which he can be understood.

Hence I think that Moses also, wishing to know the proper name of God and something special about him that he did not share with the heavenly powers, asked: “What is your name?” (Exod. III, 13). Finally, God, knowing his intention, did not answer with a name but with an action; that is, he expressed the reality, not the appellation, saying: “I am who I am” (ibid., 14), because nothing is so proper to God as always to be.

Since they therefore deny that Christ is co-eternal with the Father, let them see that they deny God, whose property is always to be and never at any time not to have been. By this knowledge of the divine particularity Moses wished to despise those who rose up against him—or, as Aquila and Symmachus rendered it, to trample those who resisted him like serpents and scorpions. The Lord also says in the Gospel (Luke X, 19) that these are to be crushed beneath spiritual footsteps, so that they cannot obstruct our way, which leads to the hidden places of paradise.

We therefore possess within us a desire for divine knowledge; we possess the Word of God, which is the Father’s name. This is truly God’s particular property, because he is the Father of Christ. And therefore the one who came to do the Father’s will came in the Father’s name. Hence he says: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John V, 4), signifying that the Jews would believe in the Antichrist, while they refused to believe in Christ.

Therefore the one who believes in Christ does not hope in his own bow or his own sword, but places the hope of victory in his name.

20. (Verse 7.) And therefore he says: “For I shall not hope in my bow, and my sword shall not save me.” But if one must hope in a bow, then certainly one must hope in God’s bow, which he placed in the cloud so that the human race might cease to fear the Flood. With this bow he protects us; with this bow he also shoots arrows with which to strike our enemies and adversaries.

[Col. 1101A] 21. (Verses 8–9.) Hence he also says: “For you saved us from those who afflicted us, and you put to shame those who hate us. In God we shall be praised all day long, and in your name we shall confess forever.” Hear how he saves us: the arrows that he shoots from heaven pierce the interior places of our earth, so that every earthly movement may perish and come to rest, as he says later: “From heaven you shot judgment; the earth trembled and was still” (Ps. LXXV, 9).

Thus we are saved while the hostile and adversarial powers are put to shame; or while the wisdom of this flesh, blunted by heavenly commands, is ashamed in its crimes and confounded by the disgrace of its sins: the adulterer amid the flames of his lust and the fire of insane love; the miser amid the burning of immoderate greed, who, by seizing what belongs to others, desires greater things the more he has invaded them; the drunkard in his drunkenness; the criminal in his crime. They are grievously put to shame here, but they will be put to shame much more when they see the saints of the Lord rising again and that Gospel saying fulfilled which the Lord spoke: “Many of those sleeping in the tombs of the earth will rise: some to eternal life, and others to reproach and everlasting confusion” (John V, 28–29).

22. When, therefore, they begin to rise to everlasting confusion, the saint of the Lord says: “In God we shall be praised all day long, and in your name we shall confess forever.” The wealthy man is praised in riches, the pleasure-seeker at banquets, the fornicator at night, the powerful person in this life, which has nights. But the saint will not be praised in this life; he will be praised in God, because he eagerly sought to please the Lord in all things. He can say: “The Lord is my strength and my praise” (Ps. CXVII, 14).

He will be praised all day long because he acted honorably and did not hide his works and crimes, but made them known to the eternal King, walking in the day and not in darkness and secrecy. Hence the Apostle also says: “Let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. XIII, 13)—that is, not in taverns and dens, not in bedrooms and indecencies, in which the shameless person thinks himself hidden by walls so that he can evade the knowledge of God. Yet all disgraceful deeds are uncovered before God, and human sins cannot be hidden from divine knowledge.

The saint, therefore, will be praised in the future because he did not seek the praise of present things but the grace of future ones.

23. Observe, however, the distinction. While he is here, he glories in the Lord; there he will be praised in the Lord, and for a brief time he will receive the reward of eternity. Aquila, however, rendered it: “In the Lord we shall glory all day long.” Symmachus says: “We shall sing a hymn to God throughout the whole day.” The sense of all agrees: we should not cease from the praises of God, whether by singing a hymn or by celebrating the divine glory throughout every moment.

For the one who sings a hymn sings with a pure and spiritual heart and excludes every kind of human passion, so that neither sorrow nor the bitterness of any pain may impede his duty or embitter his affection. Rather, by singing a hymn to God, he should remain steadfast and unshaken, like David himself, who says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. XXXIII, 2); and like Job, who, after losing his children, seeing all that was his destroyed and his possessions plundered, said: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away . . . blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I, 21).

[Note: The hymn from Gregory of Nyssa, *Treatise 2 on the Psalms*, chapter 3, is: “the praise offered to God for the good things that have been granted to us.” But we shall say more about this elsewhere.]

24. (Verse 10.) “But now you have rejected and confounded us, and you will not go forth, O God, with our armies.” Since holy David himself said elsewhere, “For the Lord will not reject his people” (Ps. 93:14), how does he say here, “You have rejected us”—especially since he says this of the people whose own marks of virtue he enumerates as by no means insignificant? For it is no small matter to say that storms and various trials came upon them, yet that they did not forget the Lord their God and did not act wickedly against his covenant (below, verse 19), along with the other things that follow.

Accordingly, the holy Apostle also interprets this passage (Rom. 10) and says that the Lord did not reject his people to such an extent that he made him say: “All day long I stretched out my hands to a people that did not believe and contradicted me” (Isa. 65:2). Supported by the authority of this statement, he says: “I ask, then: Has God rejected his inheritance? By no means. For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Rom. 11:1). “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.”

But it can be said here that the reason he did not reject the people was that a remnant was saved according to the election of grace. It appears that he did not reject the people in the few, although he did reject not the whole people, but very many from among them. Hence he added, setting forth God’s answer, that he had not merely preserved his people in the few, but had also left to himself seven thousand men who had not bent the knee before Baal (ibid., 4).

[Note: Five Gallic manuscripts read: “not only that he preserved the people in the few who did not bend the knee before Baal, but that this also was the case,” and so forth. Let the prudent reader decide whether this reading may perhaps be preferable to the other.]

Yet this statement was made by the Apostle according to the Gospel, because the Lord had passed over to the Gentiles; whereas the divine response should be referred to the time when the zeal of faith was still burning, when the grace of the prophets also overflowed among the Jewish people. Therefore, if in the time of Elijah the Lord denied that the people had been rejected by him, much more was this true in the time of David, or of the sons of Korah, when the faith of the chosen people still shone forth.

25. Yet, in order to ask holy David himself how the Lord had not rejected his people, let us gather the answer. Since God is one who draws near, not one who stays far away, as the Scripture of the Old Testament says (Jer. 23:23), he who draws near certainly does not reject.

[Note: [Col. 1102D] Codex Regius: “indeed, he who draws near, so that he may be the cause of death for no one,” etc. Four others: “indeed, he who draws near, thus draws near, so that for no one,” etc.]

It belongs to divine mercy that he be the cause of death for no one and consider all to be redeemed.

But see whether the one who distances himself from the Lord is rejected, as David says: “For behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish; you have destroyed all who prostitute themselves away from you” (Ps. 72:27). What does “prostitute themselves away from you” mean? It means that, in the mockery of their own shamefulness, they abandon you, withdraw from you, and go astray from your commandments.

Finally, elsewhere you find it written: “But God judges adulterers, destroying them from himself” (Heb. 13:4). Therefore, “you have rejected”—that is, by alienating them from yourself, you have destroyed them. Thus, whoever separates himself from the Lord is himself separated from the Lord; whoever does not know the Lord is not known by the Lord; and whoever is ignorant is himself ignored, just as the Lord himself said: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Matt. 7:23). For he does not deem it fitting to know the ministers of injustice and the authors of iniquity. The sinner, therefore, is not rejected, because he rejects himself. In this sense, then, he says: “But now you have rejected and confounded us.”

26. The following verse explains in what way God rejects: “For you will not go forth,” he says, “O God, with our armies.” When God does not help, he seems to reject. For everyone who does not experience the assistance of divinity being brought to his aid thinks himself rejected and abandoned.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “You will not go forth, O God”? And what does it mean when God is sometimes said to go forth, or to come out, or to rise, or to descend? God is not moved bodily, nor does he depart from one place or pass to another, since he is above all things. Nor does he truly rise, as though he were lying on some couch or sitting bodily in some seat. Rather, these expressions are used so that you may understand when and to whom he is said to go out, and to whom he is said to rise.

For we read in this very psalm: “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord?” (below, verse 25). We must consider whether he sometimes seems to sleep because of our reprehensible actions, just as we read in the Gospel that, while the apostles were still imperfect, Jesus Christ was sleeping with them (Matt. 8:24). But when they were struck by fear of shipwreck and overcome with terror, they awakened the sleeping Christ (ibid., 25). The Lord Jesus therefore sleeps for the faithless, but he is awake for the faithful.

27. Finally, the one who is faithful enters into God, while God seems to go out and depart from the negligent. Certainly, the Lord draws the imperfect and still weak to himself, as you have read the young women saying: “Draw us; we shall run after the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song 1:3).

But Moses, who was already stronger and chosen by the Lord, is read both to have ascended and to have entered in to the Lord his God, as it is written: “For Moses went up the mountain, and light surrounded the mountain, and the majesty of the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, and a cloud covered it for six days. And the Lord called Moses on the seventh day from the midst of the cloud. The appearance of the Lord’s majesty was like a burning fire upon the top of the mountain before the sons of Israel. And Moses entered into the midst of the cloud” (Exod. 24:15 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1103D] The Roman edition reads: “and a cloud surrounded the mountain.”]

Therefore, just as Moses entered the cloud here, when he was first called by the Lord to the mountain, so afterward, when he had become more perfect, as he entered his tabernacle, the pillar of cloud descended to him and stood at the entrance of the tabernacle; and while it stood there, the whole people worshiped, each one at the entrance of his own tent. “But the Lord was in the cloud, for he had made darkness his hiding place” (Exod. 33:9–10).

To make clear that the passage speaks of the Lord, it says: “And the Lord spoke to Moses” (Exod. 33:1). The statement that Moses’ tabernacle was placed outside the camp so that he might meet God does not seem contradictory. For whoever seeks God enters, as it were, into God, and enters with his whole mind into the knowledge of him.

28. The righteous, therefore, enters into the Lord, just as Moses entered the cloud; and God was in the cloud. Finally: “Behold, the Lord comes in a light cloud” (Isa. 19:1). And in the Gospel you find it written: “But when you pray, enter into your room, and when you have shut the door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. 6:6). God, then, is within, as if in your room.

Hear also elsewhere that God is within: “Behold,” it says, “the Lord will go forth from his place, and will descend and ascend upon the high places of the earth; and the mountains will be shaken beneath him, and the valleys will melt” (Mic. 1:3–4). Scripture says this, and already then signified that he would abandon the Jewish people and pass over to the Gentiles.

Finally, we find the same thing expressed in this psalm, when David says: “And he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber. He rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6).

29. In these ways, then, we find God’s going out or his entering in. The Lord Jesus himself also says that he comes to the man who fears him: “Behold,” he says, “I stand at the door and knock; and if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3:20).

We have said this, therefore, because the Prophet says: “You have rejected us, and you will not go forth, O God, with our armies.”

30. Let us also understand the passage in a simple sense: God went forth with the armies of the Jews when Joshua son of Nun worshiped the commander of the heavenly army. Therefore he conquered without iron and destroyed, without any siege, the city of Jericho, which had exceedingly strong walls. For when God went forth with the armies of his servants, victory followed.

The angel also went forth in response to Hezekiah’s prayers and struck down innumerable Assyrian forces. Yet sometimes the Lord seems for a time to abandon even those whom he wishes to crown in combat, so that they may conquer by faith and not allow their devotion to slacken because of favorable and prosperous circumstances.

Indeed, we often find that those who have fallen through the course of prosperity and the enjoyment of success are corrected by adversity. Thus we frequently find the Jews falling after victory and being corrected after servitude, because by prayers and lamentations they caused God to return to them.

31. Hence what was said according to the human condition and human feeling does not conflict with this interpretation: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21:2). This does not mean that the Lord was forsaken, since elsewhere he says: “For I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32). Rather, according to the flesh and the feeling of the human being who is placed in a difficult combat, he seems to have been abandoned by the Lord.

Finally, Scripture does not say idly that after the first temptation the devil departed from him “until a time” (Luke 4:13)—that is, until the combat. For when the great combat of the sacred Passion arrived, the adversary again returned to tempt him. But when a human being is placed, as it were, in uncertainty, he thinks that he has been abandoned by his God.

But just as we understand this according to the feeling of the flesh—that is, because the human being seemed to himself to have been abandoned, and Christ enacted this progression in his own body—so too, according to his divinity, he knew that he was never abandoned by the Father. For he himself said: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10), and he made clear that he was not alone.

[Note: In this passage Ambrose signifies that Christ assumed and displayed in his humanity every degree and mark of human feeling—namely, the blameless feelings.]

32. (Verse 11.) He also added this verse: “You have turned us back before our enemies.” It is not good for one to turn back, because “no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).

Finally, because Lot’s wife looked back, she could not reach the summit of the mountain—that is, the things above—but was changed into salt, a substance that quickly dissolves and cannot have lasting usefulness. Such are those who pursue temporal things and do not pursue eternal things: here they are made foolish by their own folly, and they cannot possess the grace of things to come.

There are, however, those who, placed behind, forget the things above and stretch themselves toward what lies ahead, so that they may be able to reach the prize. And to Peter it is said: “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark 8:33), so that he might be summoned to better things.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “And he is first in number.” Other editions and manuscripts read: “And in numbers,” and so forth. What if it were read as one word, innumeris, “innumerable”?]

He is first in the ranks who is after Christ. Therefore, “before our enemies,” because they afflict us and persecute us. You wished us to be behind them so that we might stretch ourselves toward the things above, always look before us, pursue our enemies, and desire to pass beyond their place.

33. Finally, Theodotion has the same wording as the Seventy—that is, the same sense in which this verse has been explained. Aquila has: “You have turned us back from the afflicter.” Symmachus has: “You appointed us last among all adversaries.”

What are the things opposed to us, unless they are the pleasures of this age, filled with delights and wantonness, and the incitements to luxury? Lot’s wife was deceived because behind her she had the luxury of the Sodomites and the allurements of that region. How was she deceived? Because she looked back.

Therefore, you also should not look back toward your enemies. God has placed you last in the world. Or: Whoever makes himself last through humility does not turn back, but always looks ahead.

To know who your enemies are, hear the words: “Hear, Israel . . . . What does it mean that you are in the land of your enemies . . . . You have been defiled with the dead” (Baruch 3:9–11). Yet who is so much your enemy and adversary as the prince of this world and his associates, who persecuted the Lord Jesus even to the cross, not knowing his power? “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

Therefore, even if you are last, do not follow your enemies. Follow the Lord Jesus, and follow his cross with joy; cling to his footsteps. Whoever follows Christ does not look back—that is, toward the luxuries and allurements of sinners—and therefore can say with the saints: “Our heart has not turned back” (below, verse 19).

From this it is understood that even one who is before his enemies becomes last and lowest in heart if he looks back toward them and directs the attention of his mind toward carnal rather than spiritual desires.

Someone who is last may also be first in heart if he considers the things that are in heaven and not the things that are on earth. Hear how one who is last in the world may be among the first with Christ. I think that God displayed us apostles as the last, as men sentenced to death, so that we might be a spectacle to this world, to angels, and to human beings (1 Cor. 4:9). He called himself last, yet showed that he was also first when he said: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

34. (Verse 12.) It follows: “And those who hated us seized us for themselves. You gave us as sheep for food, and you scattered us among the nations.”

Perhaps you are surprised that, although those who speak possess, as we said, the highest steadfastness of faith in what follows, they say here that they were seized by those who hated them. But do not let this frighten you. Many are seized here, yet their merits cannot be separated from Christ.

The apostles were carried away, beaten with rods, thrust into prison, and separated from one another, yet they remained with Christ. Indeed, precisely because they were seized by the faithless, their merits increased and grace in heavenly things grew.

For one who is seized by human beings is not immediately conquered as well. Look at the Apostle Paul rejoicing in his dangers; look at him glorying in being lowered in a basket through a window. Consider how holy Jeremiah, holy Ezekiel, and holy Daniel were led into captivity and seized by the Assyrians, yet suffered no captivity of their own faith. They did not sin against the covenant of the Lord; even in captivity they kept the divine precepts of the Law, and they did not think they were permitted to consume forbidden foods contrary to the tradition of their ancestors.

35. Therefore Theodotion rightly said: “And those who hated us rejoiced over us.” For the insult of enemies brings no prejudice upon good minds, nor does the seizure carried out by enemies.

Thus the saint who is certain that seizure cannot harm him says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress?” and the rest: “But in all these things we overcome and triumph through him who loved us, knowing that neither death nor life, neither angel nor Powers, neither things present nor things to come . . . can separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:35 ff.).

Therefore, whoever is such a person is not separated from Christ. Even if he is seized bodily, he is nevertheless free spiritually. He is not only not subject to seizure, but he also seeks for himself a praiseworthy seizure, as did those of whom it is written: “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven is forced, and those who force it seize it” (Matt. 11:12).

He is therefore victorious who, placed in earthly circumstances, does not know himself to be a captive of faithlessness.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “who does not know himself to be captive through faith.” This is not a bad reading, provided that “through faith” is understood to mean “by the help and protection of faith.”]

Not only is what is glorious not seized from him; rather, he himself seizes what is eternal.

36. There are also those who become “sheep for food.” Our good Lord Jesus Christ became a sheep for our feast. Do you ask how he became one? Hear him say: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7).

And consider how our ancestors, in a figure, tore apart and ate the lamb, signifying the Passion of the Lord Jesus, whose sacrament we consume daily. Through that sheep, therefore, they became flocks for food, as Aquila said; or “flocks for eating,” as Theodotion expressed it; or “the pasture of those who eat,” as Symmachus said.

But this good feast is not only not to be feared by the saints; it is also to be desired. For one cannot reach the kingdom of heaven in any other way, since the Lord himself said: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have eternal life” (John 6:54).

It has therefore been proved that our Lord is food, a feast, or nourishment for those who eat, just as he himself says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (ibid., 51).

37. And so that you may know that all these things were done for our sake, from the time when he descended, the saint says: “We are all one bread” (1 Cor. 10:17).

Therefore, let us not fear that we have become sheep for food. For just as the Lord’s flesh and his blood redeemed us, so Peter also endured many things for the Church. Holy Paul the Apostle and the other apostles likewise endured many things: they were beaten with rods, stoned, and thrust into prisons.

Through that endurance of injuries and experience of dangers, the people of the Lord were founded and the Church gained increase. The others hastened toward martyrdom when they saw that, through those sufferings, nothing had been taken away from the apostles’ virtues; rather, in exchange for this brief life, immortality had been acquired for them.

38. The following verse also demonstrates this, for they said: “And you scattered us among the nations.” Theodotion likewise said this. Aquila and Symmachus, however, have: “Among the nations,” or “between the nations,” “you winnowed us.”

The holy apostles were sent to the nations and scattered among the nations, just as the holy prophets, about whom we spoke above, were scattered, so that abundant fruit might arise from that dispersion.

For just as our Lord Jesus Christ fell into the earth like a grain and died in order to bear much fruit, so the holy apostles were scattered in order to bring good seed among the nations, so that the fruit of the nations might sprout in their likeness.

Finally, Scripture says that the Lord declared: “For this reason I sent you, so that you might go and bear much fruit, and that your fruit might remain” (John 15:16).

The Lord Jesus Christ therefore became like a seed, according to what was said to Abraham: “And to your seed” (Gen. 17:8)—which is Christ. Christ is therefore the seed of all. For this reason he allowed himself to fall and be scattered, so that he might transform the body of our lowliness into conformity with his own body.

This saving seed sprouted for all human beings, and from it, fashioned according to his image, the holy apostles were sent like seeds through various places and scattered, so that the Gentiles gathered into the field of the Church might shine throughout the whole world with diverse fruits.

[Note: Thus the Roman edition inserted: “I will multiply your seed,” which the Apostle interpreted as referring to Christ. These words are found nowhere else.]

These dispersions are called such, just as David also says later: “The Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersions of Israel” (Ps. 146:2). They were scattered in order to produce new fruits, and afterward, like new wheat, to be brought into the storehouses of the Church.

[Note: This is the reading of the edition and two manuscripts. But in five others one reads: “so that, into the field of the Church gathered from the nations, in various . . . .” [Col. 1108D] “These, therefore, are the dispersions,” and so forth. This is suitable if it is referred to the apostles, as is also the case sixteen lines later, where the edition and some manuscripts have: “he made the crops fertile, so that their fruits . . .”; the same five manuscripts prefer: “so that their fruit . . . .” This is not unreasonable, for here too there may be a syllepsis in the word “crops,” by which either the apostles or the peoples converted by them may be designated.]

39. This dispersion does not take place in lower things—that is, not on earth, but in heaven. The precepts of the Law confirm this. Through it the Lord says: “If your dispersion should be from the summit of heaven to the summit of heaven, from there I will gather you, says the Lord” (Deut. 30:4).

What is this dispersion from the summit of heaven to the summit of heaven? Who is so great that he could be scattered in this way? If it is a human being, he was born on earth; he began from below, not from above.

If these things move and trouble you, return to the earlier passages of this holy prophet and hear who is so great that he made such crops fertile on earth, so that their fruits might reach the heavenly storehouses.

He is the bridegroom who, like a giant, ran through the whole course—impassable to others, but passable to himself. Through him it began already to be passable to mortals, yet only so that they might ascend; for he alone first descended, so that afterward his saints might deserve to ascend.

Hear, then, how the sowing was from the summit of heaven to the summit of heaven: “His going forth,” he says, “is from the summit of heaven, and his course reaches to its summit” (Ps. 18:7).

To what human being could this be attributed? Moses scarcely ascended to the summit of Mount Sinai, and even this was because he was called by the Lord and encouraged by a heavenly voice. Who would descend from the summit of heaven except Christ, who, even when he descended to earth, remained in heaven?

“For no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). You see, therefore, that even when he descended and ascended, he himself was and remained in heaven. For he himself said: “I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord” (Jer. 23:24). He is the one who is in heaven.

Let this suffice concerning the dispersion.

40. As for the statement, “You winnowed us,” although the wording differs, the sense agrees. For just as those who were scattered were tested, so those who were winnowed deserved to reach the place of testing.

When wheat is winnowed and separated from the chaff, it is clean; but if it has not been winnowed, it cannot be clean, for it remains stuck together and mixed with the chaff. So too, unless a human being has been winnowed by temptations, he cannot separate from himself the fragile things, like chaff.

Hence it was also said to Peter: “Simon, behold, Satan demanded to winnow you like wheat; but I prayed for you to my Father, that your faith might not fail” (Luke 22:31–32).

See what he says and understand. Peter is winnowed so that he is compelled to deny Christ. He encounters temptations and speaks certain words as though they were full of chaff; yet he spoke by word of mouth so that he might become more firmly grounded in affection.

Finally, he wept, washed away his chaff, and through those temptations deserved that Christ intervene for him. How much greater was the protection than the trial of that disturbance! Therefore he gained more than he suffered: he gained Christ as his protector.

The adversary is compelled to tempt the saints of the Lord to his own loss. For by tempting them, he makes them better, so that the one who seemed weak to himself when tempted can also instruct others.

Finally, Peter was placed over the Church after he had been tempted by the devil. For this reason the Lord beforehand signifies what it means that he later chose him as shepherd of the Lord’s flock. He said to him: “And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (ibid., 32).

Holy Peter therefore turned back to good fruit, and he was winnowed like wheat so that, together with the saints of the Lord, he might be one bread that would be nourishment for us. For when we read Peter’s deeds and learn Peter’s commands, he becomes for us nourishment of eternal life and salvation.

41. (Verse 13.) “You sold,” he says, “your people without price.”

Buying and selling seem to be a kind of equal contract. Yet if you consider the attitude of the buyer and the seller, each person sells what is less valuable to him and buys what pleases him.

To speak of a class of people other than those who conduct business by selling slaves: scarcely anyone sells someone unless he displeases him and considers him unfit for his own use. Again, everyone desires to buy someone whom he judges suitable for his advantage or service.

Even those who spend money on the sale of slaves and pursue profits consider those whom they sell so worthless that they value them less than money. Often, however, they prefer to retain those whom they judge more useful to their business rather than sell them.

42. Thus God also sold what was less valuable and bought what was more valuable. He sold the Jewish people, not through God’s harshness, but through their own fault. They are rightly told: “Behold, you were sold because of your sins, and because of your iniquities I dismissed your mother” (Isa. 50:1).

In this way the Jewish people were sold because of sin, while the Christian people were bought with blood. Hence Peter says: “You were bought with a price—not with perishable silver or gold . . . but with precious blood” (1 Pet. 1:18–19).

What is precious blood except that of the spotless Lamb, that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ? The Jewish people, therefore, are without price, but the Christian people are precious. The former has no price because it has sin; the latter is of value because its sin has been forgiven.

Hence it is rightly said to the children of the Church: “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings” (1 Cor. 7:23). If it is said to you that you must not become a slave of human beings and lose your own freedom, much more is it said to you that you must not become a slave of sin.

And again, do not become a slave of the hostile and adversarial serpent. Serve the Lord alone, who redeemed you through his own love, because he is the redemption of his own servants.

43. The Lord therefore sells only the wicked servant; certainly not the good one. For although Joseph was sold, the Prophet did not say, “Joseph was sold by the Lord,” but rather: “Joseph was sold into slavery” (Ps. 104:17), by his own brothers. Nevertheless, the Lord, in a figure of his own Passion, redeemed him from slavery and restored him to grace.

His brothers sold him and received money; but the Lord not only restored him to freedom, he also increased his dignity. Scripture shows that he contained a figure of the Lord Jesus when it says: “My son is sought after with zeal . . . return to me” (Gen. 49:22). And elsewhere: “The firstborn of the bull is his beauty” (Deut. 33:17), because God the Father exalted the horn of his Christ.

44. Whoever is sold, therefore, is worthless and without price, as one who scarcely exists rather than truly exists. Hence Aquila said: “You handed over your people so that it might not exist.” Symmachus said: “You handed over your people without substance.”

Those who are rejected by Christ do not exist; but those whom the Lord chooses do exist, because the Lord called things that are not as though they were. The nations of the Gentiles were chosen so that the faithlessness of the Jews might be destroyed.

That people, therefore, was handed over to nothingness because it was sold through its own sin; for guilt has no substance.

45. Hence I think the statement was made: “And there was no multitude in their exchanges”—that is, you scattered us among the nations without payment.

For you do not receive anything in exchange for handing over a human soul; nothing is more pleasing to you than the conversion of a soul. But if it refuses to be converted, it hands itself over to nothingness, so that it may be enslaved to sin and crime.

Therefore, without price and without exchange, you sold the degenerate people. Hence later he says: “For there is no exchange for them” (Ps. 54:20). Why is there no exchange for them? “Because,” he says, “they did not fear God” (ibid.).

46. There is a twofold understanding of why the people of error had no exchange: first, because a human being cannot redeem his soul with silver, gold, or possessions. For what exchange will he give for his soul, since those things are temporal and perishable, while the soul remains either for reward or for punishment?

There was also no such exchange among the wicked that occurs in the resurrection, concerning which the Apostle says: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51).

It may also be understood in this way: even if a few of the redeemed deserved to be changed, such as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses, this exchange did not nevertheless reach everyone.

There is also the interpretation that there is no multitude in the exchanges of grave sins, according to what is written: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but others they follow afterward” (1 Tim. 5:24).

Those sins that are grave and manifest go before them, and without any doubt they plunge them into ruin. Those that are lighter are often lifted up by good works. “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered.” But where iniquity prevails, it is recalled by no exchange of good works.

47. Therefore, even if someone was redeemed from the Jewish people, he was not redeemed because he possessed great worth in himself, nor because he possessed a multitude in his exchange. He was redeemed freely, as the Apostle teaches when he says: “A remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. 11:5).

Where there is grace, there is certainly not the merit of works or justification through virtues, but the generosity of the giver and the choice of the redeemer. Scripture teaches you the same thing through the Apostle Paul, who says: “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (ibid., 6).

What, then, of the fact that Israel did not attain what it sought? Understand why it did not attain it: because it desired to justify itself, because it sought the boastfulness of its works, because it did not offer faith and did not recognize grace.

Therefore the election attained it—an election that heard the one calling and received the one who came.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “received the one who was hearing.” This passage contains a certain obscurity, but no alteration in the text entirely removes it. We think that the obscurity can more easily be dispelled if the reading preserved in the manuscripts and ancient editions is retained. For from the sequence of the argument it is not difficult to understand that those Israelites who were justified and those who did not attain justification are being set against one another, and that some were rejected because, full of confidence in their works, they sought justification; while others were heard and received because they invoked and approached the divine election and grace, serving humility, gratitude, and faith.]

48. (Verse 14.) Rightly, therefore, in the person of that people it is said: “You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those who are around us.”

Who these neighbors are, and how they may appear to have belonged to the vicinity of the Israelite people, is not easy to determine if spiritual proximity is being sought—one possessing a certain light of knowledge for investigating the mystery of Christ.

This is especially so since, in the very book of Solomon called Ecclesiastes, we have learned that the more wisdom is sought, the deeper it is judged to be. For it is written: “I said, ‘I will seek wisdom,’ but it was far from me, farther than it had been; and who will find its depth in the deep?” (Eccl. 7:24–25).

Hence I become hesitant to search out the mysteries of Scripture inspired by God and to examine its words—something that he could rightly do who spoke wisdom among the perfect.

I see that you are perfect, and not without reason would I call you perfect, since I see that you possess trained understanding for discerning good and evil. Yet even he who knew how to receive more solid food sought assistance, so that the word of the Lord might run through him (2 Thess. 3:1). Nor could he presume to do this without prayer, so that his praise might become pleasing to God (Ps. 146:1). For this is not the assertion of one presuming, but of one praying.

49. Nevertheless, lest we appear to have fled from the question entirely, let us consider who the neighbors of the tribes of the Jews were.

To review ancient matters: the Philistines were considered neighbors of the tribe of Judah, and on the other side they likewise approached the tribe of Reuben. The Ammonites were also in the desert. Those who were in the territories of Tyre and Sidon were joined to Galilee—that is, to the tribe of Zebulun and the tribe of Naphtali, which were in Galilee—as Isaiah said: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan” (Isa. 9:1).

From this one may gather what the particular character of each tribe was, so that they might be joined to their respective neighbors, and so that knowledge of the heavenly mysteries might gradually be poured even into the nations.

This may certainly be understood of the Canaanite woman, who went out from her own territory to meet the Lord Jesus as he passed by. Having set aside her idols, she worshiped the true author of salvation. Our Lord Jesus Christ bore witness to her that her faith was great.

The grace of the Gospel was already shining forth, and the light of its majestic presence was present.

[Note: The Codex Regius, together with certain Paris editions, reads: “the light of the author.”]

Yet because she came out of her own accord, asked for mercy, confessed the Lord with devout speech, and, although treated almost with disdain, persevered in the cry of her own petition, such a woman received no ordinary distinction: she was the first to come out from the nations of the Gentiles, and through her persevering supplication deserved to carry away so great a testimony from the Lord.

### 50

In this passage, I have learned that some have seemed to doubt what he means when he says, “I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24), as though the Lord, who came so that all might be redeemed, had sought the nobility of the chosen race in order to save souls. But he deigned to show his purpose: he by no means wished to reject those whom he had first chosen, and he often sought, with a certain paternal affection, to call back even those who had gone astray and were wandering. But when they themselves abandoned their own author, knowing that he is the God of the mountains, not of the valleys, and that the kingdom of heaven is seized not by those who disdain it [Note: Some manuscripts had “not by those who worship,” but “by those who compel it to be seized” is found in several manuscripts and old editions. The Roman edition had removed “not of the valleys,” although it is found in the other and all the manuscripts. He is alluding to 1 Kings 22:28, although he removed those words in *On Naboth*, at the very end, no. 72; consult that passage. As for restoring *compelling* in place of *worshipping*, as it is read in all the manuscripts and old editions in the text, the same editions give *compelling* in the margin, and the usage of the holy Doctor supports it. For here he plainly alludes to Matthew 11:12, “and the violent seize it,” where he invariably reads *those who compel*, in place of *the violent*.] but by those who compel it to be seized, he gradually turned toward the nations, so that both the devotion of the nations might be approved more highly and the stubbornness of the others might be condemned on its own merits.

### 51

What, then, does he mean by saying, “It is not permitted to take the children’s bread and throw it to the little dogs” (Matt. 15:26)? Clearly he called the children Israelites, that is, the Jewish people; and the little dogs, the people of the nations. What, then? Are the heavenly sacraments the possession of the rich or the nobler, and not of those who strive more earnestly to attain knowledge of the heavenly mystery with the devout fervor of their minds? If some Israelite is sluggish and negligent, or rebellious, rejecting the words of God behind him, while a Canaanite eagerly wishes to apply her mind to acquiring the mysteries, is the one who is indifferent to be preferred to the one who shows zeal? Certainly not.

And therefore we must carefully attend to what he expressed. When he had said, “It is not permitted to take the children’s bread and throw it to the little dogs,” and the Canaanite woman replied, “Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters” (ibid., 27), he praised her zeal and humility. She did not claim for herself, from the beginning, the depth of wisdom, although she had already come out from the regions of Tyre and Sidon; rather, she believed that certain crumbs of the saving word, falling from the table of their masters, ought to be gathered up. For the person who diligently and subtly searches through the words of Scripture is accustomed to reach the heights of its mysteries.

Hence he also says to her, “Great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish” (ibid., 28)—that is, so that the door of the word may be opened to you and the saving mystery of eternal life may shine forth.

### 52

Therefore, whoever is near should come out, desire to see Christ, and cry out in prayer, just as this Canaanite woman came out from her own territory, saw Christ, and cried out with unceasing voice so that she might carry away his mercy. Thus, when the Canaanites believe, the Jew should be put to shame, because he himself did not believe; he should grieve that he has been mocked and lament that he is derided by those who are round about.

### 53

And this prophecy appears to concern the nations that would believe, especially since what follows shows this, for he says: “You have made us a likeness to the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples.” For because of the fault of the Jews, salvation came to the nations; and we have learned, on the authority of the Apostle, that the things done to them in figure have benefited us for our instruction (1 Cor. 10:11).

And truly they were made a reproach among the nations, because the nations preferred the reproach of the Lord’s cross to all worldly riches. But whoever regarded that cross as a reproach and, as though it were disgraceful, fled from it, truly remained in enduring disgrace.

Yet because those who could say, “We have not acted wickedly in the covenant of the Lord” (below, v. 19), do not appear to be Israelites according to the flesh, and because their heart did not turn back from the Lord, see whether they are recalling that they were exposed to mockery and derision among those who surrounded them—of whom the Lord says, “Many bulls surrounded me” (Ps. 21:13). For persecutors surrounded him when, according to the counsel of his will, he underwent his passion. Hence elsewhere he says, “They surrounded me on every side; and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them” (Ps. 117:11).

It is therefore better to keep to the straight way, in which criminals cannot walk. They quickly fall because they do not walk in a straight course. Hence, when they wished to seize the Lord Jesus, as soon as he looked at them, they fell.

For the sake of these people, then, who are accustomed to walk around, the Lord appointed an angel to drive back the enemies who lie in ambush behind them. “The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him,” and protects and guards them. “The ungodly walk around on every side,” as it is written (Ps. 11:9).

Observe, then, the difference. The ungodly walk around on every side, but the angel encamps around those who do not walk around; and he encamps around them in order to rescue the righteous from the ambushes of their persecutors.

The righteous, therefore—those who speak these words—appear to be spiritual Israelites, because they have been subjected to the temptations of the world and have become a reproach to their neighbors, that is, to those who did not inhabit Jerusalem as their homeland. They were also exposed to mockery by spiritual wickednesses and powers, against which the righteous are accustomed to struggle.

Finally, history teaches you that when the Jews were carried away to Babylon, although they appeared to be subjected because of their sins, they were nevertheless regarded as much better than the nations around them. For those who insulted them were worse than they, even though the Jews themselves were weighed down by the burden of serious sins.

### 54

The first interpretation, then, is to be applied to the captive fathers, whom the Assyrians mocked and derided in Babylon; and over them that most wicked king, Nebuchadnezzar, also ruled.
