The second interpretation must be referred to higher matters: the most savage king is the devil. He is the Assyrian Nebuchadnezzar, who is accustomed to lie in wait for the good in order to draw them into sin through the allurements of the flesh.

Consider this king in the passage where the Apostle says, “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin” (Rom. 7:23)—that is, under the law of carnal allurements. The adversary is a lion who presses upon those subject to him and wearies the righteous.

Therefore Aquila rendered it beautifully: “You have made us contempt and spectacle to those who are around us.” For those who became a spectacle to this world, to angels, and to human beings were considered contemptible. Although they do not sin against God’s covenant and are not turned away from the Lord by the allurements of the flesh, they nevertheless seem to be carried about and despised as though in a public spectacle, since sinners are accustomed to insult the humility of the righteous and to regard the cross of the Lord Savior—and the humility of the righteous—as a reproach.

Finally, the Apostle, placed as though in a theatrical spectacle, says: “I am well pleased in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses” (2 Cor. 12:10). He is well pleased in these things who considers everything that belongs to the world a loss, so that he may gain Christ, seeking him alone through life and death: “For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain,” so that he may be found in Christ.

### 55

These Israelites continue, saying: “You have made us a parable to the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples” (v. 15). [Note: Several manuscripts and old editions read: “To which nations were we made, unless to those who would believe?” The Roman edition reads: “To which nations were they made a parable,” and so forth. The majority of manuscripts agree with our reading.]

“To which nations have you made us a parable, unless to those who would believe?” For the things that happened to the Jews were done as a likeness and figure, so that the destruction of the Jews might become a type and figure for us, and so that from that likeness, through the parable, we might seek a solution applicable to the present, in order that we might be able to avoid their examples.

Moreover, because all Jewish affairs are, as it were, parables—that is, figures requiring interpretation—the Lord spoke to the Jews in a parable, so that the inexperienced would not understand, but the wise would understand. Thus the Apostles understood, and when they were troubled by something, they questioned the Lord. The Jews, however, neither understood nor desired to learn again what they had not understood.

### 56

Understand what a parable is. Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman (Gal. 4:22). The Jew did not understand this except according to the letter. He did not know which of the two sons would receive his father’s inheritance, because he inclined toward carnal things. The parable needed interpretation.

The Teacher of the nations came, together with the faith of the nations, and understood that those two women are the two covenants: one from Mount Sinai, which generated the Jewish people into slavery, and this is Hagar (ibid., 24).

Therefore Sinai, which by interpretation signifies “their measure”—for *measure* is what belongs to the Law, whereas grace is superabundant. Sinai is also said to mean “price,” and this suits the Jewish people, who preferred to be justified by the price of works rather than by the grace of faith.

Thus the Jerusalem that was under the Law was in slavery with her children, whereas the Jerusalem above is free. Therefore Sarah, who is called the principal woman, possesses freedom, because she is mistress of herself—that is, the one who is righteous and blameless.

From the two covenants, then, there are two peoples: one of the Jews, the other of the nations, which believed in Christ. The Jewish people that did not believe is enslaved; it is the one born according to the flesh, because it interpreted divine Scripture according to the flesh and according to the letter, not according to the spirit.

But the one born of the free woman was born through the promise—that is, the one to whom the promise came from faith. He is the son of the Church, holding the freedom of grace, on whose account the Church says: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. 21:10). And the Apostle says: “Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman” (Gal. 4:31).

This, then, is the interpretation: what the Jew did not know, the faith of the nations interpreted, having been poured into the minds of the nations by Paul the teacher. Therefore the things done to them are a parable for us.

### 57

The Lord also said: “I became a parable to them; those who sat in the gate exercised themselves against me” (Ps. 68:12–13).

He became a parable because, he says, you say: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:23). He became a parable because he rebuked those sitting in the gate; for at the point of departure we ought not to be idle but active. Hence it is written: “See that your flight does not take place in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. 24:20)—that is, not in idleness but in labor.

The Jews, therefore, sat as sluggish people, because they could not stand; they did not know the courts of the true Jerusalem. If they had known that Jerusalem, they would have sought it. These people, then, sat exhausted in the gate. And he did not merely say that they sat; he also said that they hated the Lord who rebuked them in the gates.

For he was in the gate who was about to undergo the passion of his body, through which he would depart from the earth and return to heaven. He was in the gate when he said: “Walk while you have the light” (John 12:35).

What, then, does “I became a parable to them” mean (Ps. 68:12), except that Christ is the end of the Law, and that his death solved the riddles of the prophets? The things that had previously been unknown to the Jews when they were prophesied were later made manifest through the effect of the Lord’s passion.

He became a parable to them because he presented himself as something of little worth, placing himself before them without shrinking from their rebellions, and leading them to the time of his good pleasure, so that he might die for all human beings and cleanse the human race by his blood.

### 58

Likewise, it is written in a parable: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing” (Deut. 25:4). The Apostle interprets this parable, saying: “Is God concerned about oxen? Or does he certainly say this for our sake? For it was written for our sake. Who plows, unless he plows in hope?” (1 Cor. 9:9–10)—so that he may reap at the Lord’s judgment.

Therefore, like good farmers, when our land has been plowed because of hope in bodily continence [Note: *Unplowed*, that is, *plowed*. Otherwise the word is often used to mean “not plowed.” Horace, *Epodes* 16:

> “When the unplowed earth restores Ceres every year,  
> and the unpruned vine continually flourishes.”

Our earth, however, means the same as ourselves. The metaphor is straightforward.]

let us sow not carnal but spiritual things; for from carnal things corruption is gathered, but from spiritual things eternal life is acquired.

Let the deeds of our ancestors, then, be a type and figure for us. Let the Law be a figure written in our hearts, so that in it there may be for us a figure of future things, not the truth itself. Let the Law, therefore, be for us as a figure; the Gospel, as the light and seal of truth.

### 59

In a parable, then, the Lord revealed himself to the Jews. [Note: This is how all editions read, as do the manuscripts of Victor and Colbert. Five others, however, read: “but they did not understand that he was healing souls,” and so forth.]

But they did not understand the parable, because they did not receive the physician who would heal the souls of those suffering and free them from every sickness and every unevenness of affliction.

He also became a parable because he assumed flesh, which the Jews crucified, not understanding the spiritual parable. They failed to understand to such a degree that, when they crucified the author of life and saw the Lord’s saving flesh hanging on the cross, they shook their heads.

For if they had understood, they certainly would not have insulted him but would have mourned. Yet that very shaking of the head became a likeness for them, so that it signified not what they themselves intended but what the mysteries declared. For according to ordinary popular usage they shook their heads while insulting the Lord, just as those who desire to insult the righteous shake their heads if they happen to see them wearied in this world.

### 60

This shaking of the head has a twofold interpretation.

According to the authority of Scripture, those who shake their heads appear blameworthy, as Matthew also says: “Those who passed by blasphemed the Lord Jesus, shaking their heads” (Matt. 27:39). And Mark says: “Those who passed by” (Mark 15:29).

That those who pass by are considered blameworthy is taught by this same Prophet, who says of the vineyard of Sabaoth: “All who pass by the way pluck it” (Ps. 79:13). The following verse also indicates this: “The boar from the forest ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast devoured it” (ibid., 14).

And later he says: “Those who pass by the way did not say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’” (Ps. 128:8), because the one who passes by and does not stand in the courts of the Lord does not give a blessing.

Thus the Jews shook their heads at the Lord Jesus as they passed by, since they could not possess a firm and solid footing of faith. They shook their heads, though Christ ought to have been their head—Christ, whom the unbelief of the Jews should not have shaken away or cast down.

But because they did not allow themselves to be members of Christ, Christ was not their head. Nor was the Law their head, because they were being stripped even of the Law by the people of the nations. The word of God was not their head, because they had lost the prophets and did not possess the apostles.

Let this suffice concerning the blameworthy shaking of the head. Yet there is also a praiseworthy shaking of the head: blameworthy among the Jews, praiseworthy among the people of the nations.

For what is the head except that in which the senses are found? “The eyes of the wise are in his head.” Those eyes ought to be moved—that is, the perceptions of your mind—so that they do not grow sluggish through some torpor.

Move, therefore, your prudence; move your wisdom; move your thoughts through the comparison of heavenly words and the discussion of prophetic sayings, so that you do not sin against the covenant of God, but possess firm faith.

There are, however, heretics who move their perceptions in such a way as to stir up unbelief rather than faith.

### 61

But now we must speak more explicitly about the very shaking of the head that was set forth as a likeness of the people.

Who is the head of the peoples except Christ? “The head of the woman is the man, and the head of the man is Christ.” But the Law is also the head of the intelligible woman.

Thus the Jewish people is under the Law as under a husband, because the Law is called *nomos* (νόμος) in Greek. Therefore the Synagogue is joined to *nomos* (νόμῳ) as to a male, but to the bodily Law, not the spiritual Law—that is, to the Jewish rite of the Law, by whose bonds it has been bound, ignorant of the legitimate sacraments of marriage.

But if the Law dies—that is, if the bodily interpretation of the Law dies—then the people, as though their former husband had died, will legitimately marry the second husband who rose from the dead.

The Gospel is also the head of this woman. Hence some, interpreting mystically, wished her to marry the Gospel, as the brother of the deceased, once the Jewish rite had been put to death, because the Law announced the Gospel.

Therefore the first Law is the husband; afterward come the marriage rites of the second husband, that is, the mysteries of the Gospel. For there are, as it were, two marriages, namely, the two covenants.

One marriage is the Old Covenant, which was dissolved by the death of the first husband. Therefore that woman whose Law has died rightly enters upon a second marriage, that is, the New Covenant.

Thus one woman is joined to two brothers: her former sins die, and afterward better mysteries are renewed.

The Apostle clearly explained this to us, saying: “A woman who is under a husband is bound by the law to her husband while he is alive”—that is, by the law of her husband, so that she owes him chastity. “But if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband,” that is, so that she may marry whomever she wishes, provided that she marries after her husband has died. “For while her husband is alive, she will be called an adulteress if she is joined to another man; but if her husband dies, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man” (Rom. 7:2–3).

He also showed elsewhere that this mystery pertains to Christ and the Church, because “it is a great mystery” (Eph. 5:32).

Here too he did not pass it over, saying: “Therefore, my brothers, you also have died to the Law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, who rose from the dead” (Rom. 7:4).

How have you died to the Law except so that the shadow of the Law may die for you when you approach the heavenly sacraments? For you must not otherwise approach the Gospel except freed from the impediments of bodily interpretation.

Otherwise it is adultery to mix false things with true ones. Spiritual chastity consists in this: that your soul, stripped of every impediment of misguided knowledge, should approach the word of God without wrinkle.

Therefore, just as Christ is the head of the Church, so the Law is the head of the Synagogue—that is, of those who are under the Law. For their sake the Apostle made himself subject to the Law, although he was not under the Law, so that he might win those who were under the Law.

And again he became the teacher of the nations as though he himself were without the Law, so that he might acquire for Christ those who were without the Law. But he rightly says that he was not without the Law of God, and that he remained in the Law of Christ (1 Cor. 9:21).

### 62

The Law, however, was not the head of the Synagogue from the beginning, because Christ was the head of the ancient Synagogue, which Moses founded and established.

Listen, finally, to the statement that it was founded by the word of the Lord. “By faith,” he says, “Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. For he preferred to suffer affliction with the people of God rather than to enjoy the temporary pleasures of sin; and he considered and preferred the reproach of Christ to the treasures of Egypt,” because he was looking toward the reward of God’s promises (Heb. 11:24 ff.), which is the grace of the resurrection.

But when, because of the unbelief of the Jews, the Word of God died for the unbelieving and disappeared from the breasts of the Jews, the understanding of the spiritual Law set, and the Synagogue married the bodily rite and the observance of unbelief.

That was not the sobriety of a spiritual marriage but an adultery of chastity. Therefore the Synagogue could not be free: it had married wrongly and had not believed that the resurrection of Christ would come.

Hence the Church rightly married the one for whom, according to the sacred dispensation and according to the flesh, Christ died, so that that Jewish soul which had previously been bound by sin might be freed through Christ’s death from the bond of transgressions.

A woman therefore does not marry another man unless her husband has died—that is, unless she has been released from the bond of lawful love. If her husband has died, she is freed.

### 63

It was indeed prescribed by the Law that a woman should be joined to the brother of her own husband if her husband had left no seed (Deut. 25:5). This bond was tightened more by the interpretation of the letter than by spiritual grace.

For the deceased man’s brother had it in his will that, if he did not wish, he need not take his brother’s wife to raise up offspring for the dead. Hence he was ordered to remove his sandal, so that he would be stripped of the bond of that union, which he had shown to be foreign to his own favor.

For it is written that the man removed his sandal and gave it to his neighbor, saying: “This shall be a testimony in Israel.” [Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “Take it, and acquire my kinship for yourself; and this shall be a testimony in Israel.” Then: “And he removed his sandal,” and so forth.]

And the kinsman said: “Take it, acquire it for yourself.” And he removed his sandal. Those standing by also said: “May the Lord give you a wife who enters your house like Rachel and like Leah, who both built up the house of Israel and showed strength in Ephrathah” (Ruth 4:7–8, 11).

But this bound the Jew through the interpretation of the letter. In fact, it was a figure that Christ would come into the world, raise up the seed of the dead people.

He is rightly called the brother, because it is said: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21:23), and: “Their fathers are theirs, and from them is Christ according to the flesh” (Rom. 9:5).

Or it is because the Gospel would accomplish, among later generations, the restoration of the dead Law, so that the seed which the Law had not left behind might be raised up by the Gospel’s course.

### 64

It is therefore not surprising that they shook their head through a perverse interpretation, so that they themselves might drive away from themselves Wisdom, the author of their salvation. Or certainly, by shaking their head, they became the cause of a shaking of the head not for a few but for whole peoples.

This shaking of the head took place when their sound went out into all the earth, so that the whole earth might become the Lord’s and the Lord’s kingdom might be among the nations.

Hence later he says: “The Lord reigns; let the peoples rage. He sits above the cherubim; let the earth be shaken” (Ps. 98:1).

Aquila interpreted this beautifully when he used the word *alalagma* (ἀλάλαγμα), that is, “transformation,” which is a movement from one place to another—from Judea to the peoples of the nations. [Note: We can scarcely be persuaded that *alalagma* (ἀλάλαγμα) is genuine, both because the Septuagint reads *kinēsin kephalēs en tois laois* (κίνησιν κεφαλῆς ἐν τοῖς λαοῖς), “a shaking of the head among the peoples,” and because that word is very far removed from *alesa enikin* and *alesannilem*, as the manuscripts corruptly have it. We would more readily conjecture that *kephalēs kinēsin* (κεφαλῆς κίνησιν), “a shaking of the head,” or rather *alloiōsin* (ἀλλοίωσιν), “a transformation,” had been written, especially since Aquila used a word cognate with the same term in the title of this very psalm, where, according to Nobilius, it read: *hote ēlloiōse to geusma autou eis prosōpon Abimelech* (ὅτε ἠλλοίωσε τὸ γεῦμα αὐτοῦ εἰς πρόσωπον Ἀβιμέλεχ), “when he changed his taste before Abimelech,” and so forth.]

This can be clearly demonstrated from the reading found in the Gospel, which shows how the Law was moved:

“The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore, observe and do everything they tell you; but do not act according to their works, for they say things and do not do them. They bind heavy burdens and place them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves do not wish to move them even with their finger. They do all their works so that they may be seen by people” (Matt. 23:2 ff.).

### 65

What does “the scribes sat” mean except that the letter is written? Hence in Greek the scribes are called *grammateis* (γραμματεῖς), because they follow the interpretation of the letter, not the understanding of the spirit; and “the letter kills.”

Following the letter that kills, and echoing it even in their name, they are scribes. The Pharisees, however, are those who are divided from the unity of truth; for *phares* is interpreted as “division.”

The Pharisees divide the words of the Law in such a way that they may resound and meditate upon them, but they do not see the spiritual mysteries and sacraments of the Law.

For if the Law is spiritual, then certainly the commandments of the Law are spiritual, and its works are spiritual. Thus, while teaching what Moses wrote, they bind heavy burdens through the bodily elements of the Law—for what is contrary to the yoke of Christ is heavy—and through their misguided teaching they impose heavy burdens upon the ears of their hearers. Yet they themselves do not wish even to move them, so as to move from the bodily elements of the Law to the spiritual words of Scripture.

This is how we should understand the statement that they do not wish to move them with their finger: they do not transfer themselves to spiritual understanding even by the smallest point or moment.

This is also the meaning of what is written: “But if I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11:20). Scripture itself interprets what the finger is when it says elsewhere in the Gospel: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. 12:28).

The finger of God, then, is the Spirit of God. For God is Spirit, and in his substance he possesses nothing bodily; he is wholly Spirit. Therefore the one who casts out a demon by the finger of God casts it out by the Spirit of God.

Hence holy David also says: “For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8:4)—that is, the heavens are the works of your Spirit, just as it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6).

### 66

To conclude our discussion: the scribes and Pharisees refer nothing to the inner person, who, just as he was made in the image and likeness of God, ought likewise, in what he thinks and meditates upon, to think more about spiritual things than carnal things.

They strive to refer everything to the outer, earthly person. Therefore all their works are such that they may be seen by people, not that they may please the Father, who sees in secret. For they are afraid to reveal their works.

### 67

This, then, is the shaking of the head that took place among the peoples—or, as Aquila and Symmachus said, among the nations. All the nations moved their heads so that they might interpret the Law spiritually.

Let no one think that he is to be saved according to the letter of the Law, because the letter of the Law contains a curse, whereas the spirit brings a blessing. No one can be justified by works of the Law, because all who are under the letter are under a curse.

Let everyone therefore flee the curse of the Law and take refuge in the grace of blessing, so that they may have a blessing in the heavenly places, in Christ Jesus, who died for us so that faith might pass over to the nations.

Although he was previously the husband of the Synagogue and did not abandon it, he also redeemed us. He did not abandon the Synagogue so that a remnant might be saved; he redeemed us by choosing the peoples of the nations.

Therefore this election of the nations is salvation for the Jews, for the remnant was saved not through its own works but through the election of grace.

It is therefore the grace of Christ that both redeemed us and gave life to the remnant. The shaking of the head took place among the nations; but from this shaking the Jews received the grace of no small transformation, for their remnant was saved.

### 68

The text continues: “All day long my shame is against me, and the confusion of my face has covered me” (v. 16).

What does it mean that sometimes this psalm is spoken in the person of one, and sometimes in the person of many? From the beginning it began with many: “We have heard, O God, with our ears,” and the other words that follow (above, vv. 2 ff.). Then it says: “You are yourself my King and my God.” Again: “In you we shall scatter our enemies.” And afterward: “For I shall not hope in my bow”; and: “In God we shall praise all day long”; and: “All day long my shame is before me.”

What does this change mean, which is frequently repeated in the Psalms? Likewise, in Psalm 108 he says: “O God, do not be silent about my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of deceit have been opened against me” (Ps. 108:2). This is spoken of one person; what follows is spoken of many: “They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue ... and they repaid my love with hatred” (ibid., 3, 5). Then again it speaks of one: “Set a sinner over him” (ibid., 6).

This appears in Psalm 108 to refer in one part to the Jewish people and in another to Judas the betrayer: when the words are plural, to the people; when singular, to Judas.

Here too we can say that when the words are plural, they refer to the saints; when singular, to our Lord Jesus Christ. For it can be judged that the Prophet spoke both for many and for himself.

Therefore he said: “My shame is before me,” which is called *entropē* (ἐντροπή). *Entropē* is what occurs when someone wishes to bring shame upon another in order to bend his purpose, as in the words: “Let him come down now from the cross, and we shall believe him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now” (Matt. 27:42–43).

He says beautifully, “all day long,” because the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ brought light to the world. The day, therefore, is the day of the Incarnation, concerning which the Lord himself says: “Walk while you have the light” (John 12:35), and: “Abraham saw my day” (John 8:56).

This shame, then, contains confusion within itself. Hence Symmachus says: “All day long my confusion is against me.”

And what is the confusion of Christ except the cross, because he hung naked upon it? And rightly, “all day long,” because from the time he was fastened to the cross until the ninth hour darkness occurred; and after the ninth hour light shone again until evening.

[Note: Here Saint Ambrose follows the opinion of those who explained the three days of the Lord Christ’s death in such a way that they said his first night was the darkness that covered the whole world when the Lord expired, while the first day was the interval of light that came between that darkness and the following night. Nevertheless, Augustine rightly rejected this opinion in *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, book 3, chapter 24, no. 66, where, as also in *Questions on the Gospels*, book 1, question 7, he teaches that in the three days mentioned a part is to be taken for the whole; interpreters generally have followed him in this. See also Thomas Aquinas, part III, question 51, article 4, and the other scholastics, whose agreement on this matter is complete. Indeed, Ambrose himself seems to teach the same view in his letter to the bishops of Aemilia, writing: “Within that three-day period he both suffered, rested, and rose again.”]

This day is the first of the three. Yet the choir of the saints can also speak of itself in the plural and singular: for a choir possesses, as it were, a single person, although it consists of many, as in the words: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

### 68

What, then, is the confusion that covered the Lord Jesus, since sins produce confusion—for sins are what cover the sinner—while he committed no sin?

But just as there is a confusion that brings about sin, so there is a confusion that abolishes sin, such as the confusion of the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which sins are cleansed.

There is also every good confusion that you undergo for Christ’s name, and it is exceedingly glorious. For example, if during a persecution the law is that a Christian be beaten, lose his rank, be deprived of his privilege, or be led into chains:

[Note: A privilege, as Brissonius teaches in *On the Meaning of Words*, book 14, is a special right granted as a concession and favor to a particular person or cause. Christians were once so completely stripped of their privileges by the edicts of emperors that, after being declared infamous, they were deprived of the right to civil courts and military service and were even assigned to death by the sword of anyone, through a wicked proscription. See Baronius, under the years of Christ 303, 304, and 362.]

This confusion, although it has no privilege, possesses the glory of devout confession.

There is also the confusion of Christ, as he himself says: “Whoever is ashamed of me before human beings, I also shall be ashamed of him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:33).

Therefore this is a good confusion. For many, however, such confusion for Christ is bitter—that is, for those who do not believe; it is pleasant for those who believe.

### 69

Whether, then, you understand the confusion of Christ as referring to his cross, which appeared to the Jews to be a disgrace and at which they insulted him, as though Christ were ashamed of the work by which he was accomplishing public salvation; or whether you understand this confusion as that which seemed to be imposed by “the voice of one reproaching and reviling, from the face of the enemy and persecutor.”

For he was ashamed that his chosen people had fallen so far, and he was confounded because of them before the Father, whose end had arrived for them. The Father was present with the Son, from whom the Son can never be separated.

Therefore the Father heard him say to the Jews: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:38).

70. There are also those who glory in their own confusion, as the Apostle says of them: “Their glory is in their confusion” (Phil. III, 19). Their glory is contrary to the glory of Christ, who took up the cross and did not shun confusion. We too must by no means fear this, nor avoid it through dread or disgust, lest what can bring the grace of life bring sin upon us. There is indeed a glory even in confusion: if you happen to fall among many Gentiles or philosophers, and they throw the cross of Christ in your face, while you cannot answer in words or offer anyone who hears you saving words, this is confusion—but [it is] “from the voice of one reproaching and reviling, from the face of the enemy and persecutor.” Therefore, do not answer a fool according to his folly; be like a mute and silent man, as though you did not hear the words of those who insult and revile. This is not because you are unable to answer, but because you ought not to answer. For there is a proper time for everything: a time to be silent and a time to speak. One must be silent when one does not find a hearer ready; one must speak when the Lord grants a tongue of instruction, so that your speech may work upon the affections of those who hear. But how can one hear you who reviles you precisely because he does not wish to hear your salutary discourse? Or how can one yield to you who is a persecutor and wishes to claim you for himself? Or—as Aquila, or Symmachus, said—“to avenge and punish in you” the fact that Christ’s inheritance appears to have been transferred to the Gentiles? This confusion, then, is far removed from the confusion and reproach of the sinner. For the conscience of the former is illumined, since he has not forgotten his God; the latter are confused, because the memory of their offenses darkens and disturbs their understanding. 917

71. (Verses 18, 19, 20.) Therefore those who are conscious of their innocence rightly say: “All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, nor have we acted wickedly against your covenant. And our heart has not turned back; yet you have turned our paths away from your way.” The final verse seems not to agree with what precedes. For how did they turn aside, when no forgetfulness of the Godhead had stolen upon them, nor consciousness of any wickedness, nor any negligence? But if you consider that “the righteous is scarcely saved,” you will surely understand that even his steps sometimes falter, and that God appears to be the author of their turning aside, because he too permits the righteous often to be tempted, so that they may be better proved after being instructed by temptations. Who, however, is so strong that he is never shaken in temptation, unless the Lord stands beside him as his helper?

Indeed, the prophet David himself was troubled, because in his abundance he said: “I shall never be moved” (Ps. XXIX, 7). Or who is there whom the place of affliction and the corruption of the earth would not move, when the divine sentence has exempted no one from the discipline and toil of this earth, to which it was said: “Cursed is the earth in all your works … it shall bring forth thorns and thistles” (Gen. III, 17, 18)? Indeed, Paul himself, the Lord’s chosen vessel, though released from the curse of the ancient sentence through the passion of the Lord Jesus, nevertheless bitterly lamented that he was being led captive under the law of sin, and found no one but Christ by whom he might be delivered, while the law of his body and the shadow of death pressed hard upon him.

72. We have explained the meaning; but it is fitting to consider more expressly what the “place of affliction” is. Is it this world, which lies in the power of the evil one? Or is it our flesh, in which our soul is humbled when it descends into association with this flesh? Or are they the adversities by which we are disciplined while established in this body, in which we groan under our burden—not wishing to be unclothed, but to be clothed over? For grievous is the labor while we await the time when this mortal nature will be swallowed up by life, since we must be stripped of it; yet it is stripped away with less labor than it is swallowed up.

See whether there is not a distinction between stripping oneself and awaiting being swallowed up by life. Grace strips away; repentance swallows up. The sublimity of the mind strips away; diligence swallows up. How can you doubt that this is the place of affliction, when it is the body of death, in which even the shadow of death covers us? Therefore we must always direct our attention to that lamp which is the word of God, so that we may know how to direct the paths of our souls and the inward footsteps of the mind, and so that the light of our souls may dissolve bodily darkness.

73. Aquila’s interpretation has also beautifully expressed how we should understand the place of affliction, saying: “For you have humbled us in the place of sirens.” Thus it is not the flesh itself, whether in its fault or in its nature, that is at issue, but those things that made the corruptible flesh what it is. The divine Scripture mentions sirens a second (Isa. XIII, 21) and a third time (Mic. I, 8), while pagan history has handed down that they were certain maidens who, by the sweetness of their own voices, by the allurements of song, and by the eagerness to hear them, enticed sailors to bring their ships to shore; and antiquity has transmitted to posterity that, when they followed the charm of the voice, they were accustomed to suffer shipwreck in a rocky place (Hom., Od., B).

[Note: [Col. 1123D] Thus the Roman edition; the manuscripts differ little from it if one considers the sense. In the wording, however, there is this principal difference: several codices read, “they enticed them by sweetness, by singing, and by their allurements.” Victor and Colbert read, “by sweetness, by singing, which provoked their allurements.” All together: “Sailing ships toward the shore in their eagerness to hear them, they fell into shipwreck in a rocky place”—when “they follow the charm,” or, as some have it, “because of the charm,” of the voice.]

Their interpretation, then, is pleasure of the voice and a kind of flattery. Thus the pleasure of the world delights us with a certain carnal flattery in order to deceive us. Therefore, just as the shore itself was not at fault there, but the melodious sweetness that prevented the roughness of the shore from being guarded against, so the flesh is not at fault here, but the things by which this flesh is enticed and tossed about. Indeed, the sea is calm if there is no storm; if a tempest rages, it is dangerous.

74. The opinion of the Seventy also seems to agree with this, when they say that it is written: “For you have humbled us.” We must seek testimonies for this interpretation from the divine Scriptures. For in Deuteronomy he says: “If you go out to battle against your enemies, and the Lord your God delivers them into your hands, and you take their spoils, and in that plunder you see a woman beautiful in appearance, and you live with her” (Deut. XXI, 10–11). And below: “If afterward you do not want her, you shall let her go free … because you humbled her” (ibid., 14).

You see, therefore, that she is said to have been humbled not by her nature, but by the one who took away her chastity. Humbling, then, is the work by which this flesh became the body of sin and the place of affliction. Again, elsewhere: “If a virgin is betrothed to a man, and a man finds her in the city and lies with her, both shall be led out to the gate of their city and stoned, and the young woman shall die, because she did not cry out in the city, nor invoke the man who might have helped her; and the man,” he says, “because he humbled his neighbor’s wife” (Deut. XXII, 23–24). Here too the cause of the expression is the same: she is said to have been humbled by her violator.

You also have a third testimony, and more if you seek them. Nevertheless, hear from the same book: “If anyone finds a virgin who is not betrothed, and by force lies with her, and they are discovered, the man who lay with her shall give the girl’s father fifty denarii, and she shall be his wife, because he humbled her; he may not put her away all his days, because he humbled her” (ibid., 28–29). The same expression is repeated, so that you may understand that it is not the condition of the flesh that appears to humble us, but guilt.

75. Nevertheless, we cannot deny that the flesh is humbled in many ways—by the place itself, by those very allurements, and also by the frailty through which it became exposed to error. Although the flesh was deceived by no insignificant adversary—the serpent—it nevertheless possessed no small measure of its own grace before sin entered:

[Note: [Col. 1125D] Only the Roman edition has “Eve was deceived.” The word “flesh,” expressed in the preceding verse, must be understood. Apart from the fact that the relative pronoun “which,” restored from five manuscripts, demonstrates this, the sense agrees less well with the Roman reading.] Adam stood in the presence of God, flourished in paradise, shone with heavenly grace, and spoke with God. Have you ever read that he was humbled before the transgression humbled him by its own act? He transmitted the inheritance of that fault down to us, so that, established in this body, we do not wish to depart from the body and be present with God. Therefore we humble our soul, which longs to lift itself up to God; but this corruptible body weighs down the soul, and earthly dwellings outweigh it, so that the mind devoted to God is frequently bent toward the world and cannot subject itself to God, because the wisdom of the flesh, which envelops our affections, does not understand submission to itself.

76. In saying these things about ourselves, what shall we say about the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ? He certainly assumed the reality of this flesh, and therefore “humbled himself even unto death, and death on a cross” (Phil. II, 8). Attend carefully and consider each point. See that he willingly assumed this form of our body and the obligations of your servitude, being made in the likeness of human beings—not in the likeness of sinful flesh, but in the likeness of sinful human beings, for every human being is under sin. Therefore he was found in appearance as a human being, as it is written of him: “And he is a human being, and who will know him?” (Jer. XVII, 9). Human according to the flesh, but beyond humanity according to his working.

“He humbled himself as a human being,” he says (Phil. II, 8), because God came to those who had been humbled in order to set them free. He humbled himself, therefore, for our sake. His body, then, is not a body of death, since it is the body of life; nor is his flesh the shadow of death, since it is the radiance of glory; nor is there in him a place of affliction, since in that body there is consolation for all. He humbled himself so that you might learn what humility is. Hear him saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI, 29). He humbled himself so that you might be exalted; for whoever humbles himself will be exalted. But not all who are humbled will be exalted, for crime humbles many to ruin. The Lord, however, was humbled unto death so that he might be exalted from the gates of death.

77. Behold the grace of Christ; behold his benefits. After Christ came, this flesh—which was the shadow of death—began through the Lord’s grace to shine and to possess its own light. Hence it was said: “The lamp of your body is your eye” (Matt. VI, 22). But see of which eye he speaks—not the outward eye, but the inward one: “If your eye is simple,” he says, “your whole body will be luminous” (ibid.). It is certainly the inward eye that illumines the whole human body. It is also the inward eye that removes blindness from the entire body, since it is written: “But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark” (ibid., 23).

You see in one person the source from which darkness is born and the source from which light arises. You yourself, then, are darkness or light. The darkness is iniquity; the shadows are sins; the light is innocence. You yourself, therefore, are the author either of injury or of grace for yourself; the divine work does not err. The light is within you, because your infancy is innocent: the human mind is pure before the slipperiness of adolescence and the error of youth. You yourself, then, have made darkness for yourself out of what is light. Indeed, the same eye—that is, the human understanding—is dark in the sinner and radiant in the innocent.

78. Let us not pass over what Symmachus says: “You afflicted us in a deserted place.” We are afflicted, therefore, because at times we are deprived of heavenly protection, and this region is under a curse, or lies upon the slippery ground of the world. Our Lord Jesus Christ had not yet blessed his earth, and therefore they labored, nor was the gaze of their spiritual eyes directed toward the light of his piety.

Moreover, because the pleasure and delight of the world frequently creep in (Hom., Odys., M), we must not bind and fetter ourselves with the chains of that man, nor close our ears with wax, but turn our ear away whenever someone thinks that things alien to the faith and opposed or harmful to our welfare ought to be uttered against us, lest the shadow of death cover us in that discourse. And if anything of this kind is brought forward, we must nevertheless insert the word of God, which illumines the eyes of our mind with the brilliance of its exposition.

79. (Verses 21, 22.) It follows: “If we have forgotten the name of our God, and if we have spread out our hands to foreign gods. Will God not investigate these things?”

[Note: [Col. 1127D] The Roman edition, rejecting the six words “Aquila, investigated these things,” and “Symmachus, will he find these things?” into the lower margin, places the three verses “If we have forgotten,” and so forth, in continuous order, then adds: “What does he mean when he says, ‘Will God not investigate these things?’ As though …” We have scrupled to depart from the ancient edition and the manuscripts. Yet five other manuscripts differ somewhat from the editions of Victor and Colbert, preferring this final portion: “What does he mean when he says, ‘Will God investigate?’—your forgetfulness that has crept in, so that he may remove every trace of it.”]

Aquila said, “He will investigate these things.” Symmachus: “Will he find these things?” For he himself knows the secrets of the heart.

“For on your account we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter.” What does he mean by saying, “Will God investigate?” It is as though, if he did not investigate, he would be ignorant. God will investigate your forgetfulness that has crept in, so as to remove every trace of it. Hence Aquila said, “He will investigate these things.” For surely, since he knows the secrets of the heart, how does he seek what is already manifest to him, including the things that are most inward? With God, the conscience of each person reveals itself, and a person’s thought either condemns or acquits itself before him.

Accordingly, Aquila said “the visions of the heart,” because he sees our heart, and all our thought of heart lies open before God, while the image of our thoughts shines before him. Aquila rightly said: “In you we are put to death,” because to die in Christ is difficult and glorious; and the one who is crowned through sacred suffering for his name dies in him.

But why be surprised that this verse declares God to be investigating the secrets of the heart, when elsewhere you read that God is the searcher of the heart? Why be surprised if the majesty of the divine substance cannot be explained by our words (Jer. XVII, 10), when the Apostle says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will illumine the hidden things of darkness and disclose the counsels of hearts; and then each one will receive his praise from God” (I Cor. IV, 5)?

We often read of the darkness of the heart as a place of crime—indeed, almost everywhere. See, then, whether “the hidden things of darkness” are the secrets of the heart, and whether they have received the name of darkness because they are not detected by others but remain concealed. Therefore the Lord is said to illumine the hidden things of darkness on the day of judgment, because each person’s heart will be revealed, though previously hidden—known, indeed, to Christ alone, who, knowing the grace of his judgment, says: “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Matt. X, 26).

80. There are many things that we suppress out of modesty and keep silently within ourselves in order to fulfill the heavenly command, lest we appear to glory in what belongs to us and begin to lose its fruit by making it public. There are also hidden things of wisdom which the Apostle Paul, caught up into paradise, heard; and because it was not permitted to a human being to speak of them, he kept them concealed within himself—not because he begrudged others their use or grace, but because it was not permitted to a human being to speak of them; perhaps it was not beneficial even for a human being to hear them. The Lord will illumine them when the time for illuminating hidden things has arrived.

See whether you may also find some distinction in the Gospel, where he said: “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, nor covered that will not be disclosed” (ibid.). Nevertheless, that statement supports the interpretation above, so that we may believe both passages concern good things, since it is written: “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II, 19). He knows his own, therefore, and he knows those who know God; but he does not know those who do not know God, for whoever does not know will not be known.

The Lord, then, recognizes what is good: he knows what is full of divine knowledge, what is hidden in wisdom. But he turns away from what is full of iniquity and sin.

81. Finally, if you consider the person of those whom no forgetfulness of divine worship separated from God, so that they might stretch out their hands to a foreign god and refuse to open their souls, you will understand that their hidden things contained not some crimes, but things belonging to innocence, since they were put to death for the worship of God and spent the whole day in death. Paul too was in such a condition, saying: “I die every day, by your glory” (I Cor. XV, 31).

And truly Paul died every day according to the flesh, established in fastings, shipwrecks, various dangers, and hardships; but he did not die entirely. His outward man was dying, but his inward man was being renewed. Therefore he did not fail when pressed by so many dangers, because although his outward man was corrupted, his inward man was renewed day by day, since each person’s faith and the grace of his works illumine his day.

Hence the Apostle Paul knew no night, because whoever is renewed is always in the light. Does he not seem to you to be in the light who contains within himself the love of Christ?

[Note: [Col. 1128D] The Roman edition reads, “And therefore, secure in his renewal.”]

Therefore, secure in his sacrifice, he did not shun hardships; nor could any persecution, hunger, or sword separate from Christ the Lord the one whom the bonds of divine love held fast.

82. (Verse 23.) Nevertheless, even in good works the human mind is troubled and shaken by temptations. Yet this too belongs to the righteous: when they see themselves being tempted, they ask for help, as the apostles did in the Gospel (Matt. VIII, 25). While Christ slept in the boat, they feared the storm of the waves and awakened the Lord Jesus, asking him to drive away their fear.

Do not the holy apostles seem to have spoken these verses: “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord? Arise, and do not reject us forever”? Although the wording may appear different, the meaning certainly agrees.

Nor was our Lord Jesus Christ, even when established in the body, sleeping in such a way that he was ignorant of the storm at sea, or that the knowledge of the tempest which had arisen was beyond him because of the depth of his sleep. He slept in body, but he was awake in power.

It was arranged that the Son of God, the Word of God, should go up into the boat, and that his disciples should go up with him. He did not permit them to be slack and negligent, as though they were secure because of the Lord’s presence and favor; rather, he composed himself in bodily sleep. Thus, under the appearance of sleep, the Word of God showed the apostles that he was sleeping with respect to this world.

Yet his power and providence remained awake. It stirred up the storm at sea, so that the boat was almost covered by the rising waves, and so that it might become clear whether the disciples, shaken by the storm, would support themselves by prudent and salutary counsel, or whether they would go beyond the remedy,

[Note: [Col. 1129] That is, whether they would pass over, omit, or neglect it. The Roman edition reads, “would accept the remedy.”]

and so omit it. But for those for whom Jesus was not sleeping, faith was awake. Therefore they rose and awakened the Lord Jesus, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing” (Matt. VIII, 25).

83. See whether this too differs from the Gospel, where we read of Jonah (Jonah I, 5), who slept in the belly of the ship and snored. In him a figure of the sacred passion went before. For just as Jonah slept in the ship and snored securely, as though he had no fear of being discovered, so our Lord Jesus Christ, who fulfilled that figure through the mystery of his death, slept in the boat in the time of the Gospel. And just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, in the passion of his body.

When he raised himself from death and released the sleep of his body in order to rise again for the salvation of all, he visited the disciples. This, then, is the true Jonah, who offered his soul as a redemption for us. Therefore he was taken up and cast into the sea, so that he might be received and swallowed by the whale, and, placed within the whale’s belly, might empty its inward parts.

Hear to what whale this refers, when Job says: “He who has power to render the great whale captive” (Job III). Who is this? You recognize him when you read that our Lord Jesus Christ “led captivity captive”; for when the adversary and enemy had been conquered, we who were captives began through Christ to possess freedom (Eph. IV, 8).

84. Finally, Jonah’s own prayer teaches that it contains the mysteries of the Lord’s passion, when he said: “I cried,” he says, “to my Lord in my tribulation, and he heard me from the belly of hell” (Jonah II, 3). You see that he said “the belly of hell,” not “of the whale.” The Lord, however, descended not into the whale but into hell, so that those who were in hell might also be released from everlasting bonds. Indeed, many also rose again.

But what rivers surrounded Jonah, or from what abyss did Jonah speak when he said: “The abyss surrounded me utterly; my head sank into the clefts of the mountains. I descended into the earth, whose bars are everlasting” (ibid., 6–7)? This does not fit Jonah’s person—and yet it does. The Son of God descended into the clefts of the mountains when he descended into the tomb. Joseph himself, as the Gospel teaches (Matt. XXVII, 60), placed him in his new tomb, which he had hewn in the rock, and rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb. And in another book: “He placed him,” it says, “in a hewn tomb in which no one had yet been laid” (John XIX, 41).

85. Who, then, is the one who sacrificed to the Lord with a voice of praise and confession, if not the Prince of all priests, who both vowed and fulfilled vows on behalf of all? For he alone possessed power over the outcome of his work.

Just as Jonah was cast into the sea, and the sea became still from its agitation, so our Lord Jesus Christ came into this world to win the world and to reconcile all things by his blood, whether earthly or heavenly. By his coming, therefore, he redeemed all human beings and summoned them to the worship of God through his works, when he raised the dead, healed the sick, and infused the fear of God into human affections.

He is the one who sacrificed to the Lord a saving sacrifice for us and offered God worthy sacrifices of our conversion; he is the one who slept and awoke.

86. We must therefore beware lest he sleep with respect to sinners. He appears to sleep with respect to those for whom he has not risen and whom he rejects forever. But who is rejected except the one who is a stranger to the Lord, because he is not a stranger to the body? For how can those who are in the flesh please God? Therefore let us not be in the flesh but in the spirit. Let us cling to the Lord Jesus, who says in the eighty-eighth Psalm that he was rejected for our sake: “You rejected him as nothing, O Lord; you delayed your Christ; you overturned the covenant of your servant” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 39–40).

Thus he was rejected in us and became a reproach to his neighbors. He took upon himself the reproach of the cross so that he might clothe us with the glory of his resurrection. He appears rejected, as though dead, and covered with confusion, as though crucified; but blessed forever is he who removed the curse and obtained the grace of blessing.

87. (Verse 24.) It follows: “Why do you turn your face away?” We think that God turns his face away from us when we are placed in certain afflictions, so that darkness is poured over our feelings and, obstructed by it, we cannot draw in the radiance of truth with our eyes.

For if God attends to our understanding and deigns to visit our mind, we may be certain that nothing can cast darkness over us. If the face of a human being shines more brightly than the other members of the body, and whenever we look upon someone we either recognize the unknown or recognize again the known, since our gaze does not permit him to remain hidden, how much more does the face of God illumine the one upon whom it looks!

Regarding this, as with the rest of his matters, hear the glorious teaching of the holy Apostle, who is truly Christ’s interpreter and who poured Christ into our minds with more suitable meaning and speech. He says: “For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts, for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus” (II Cor. IV, 6).

We have heard, then, where Christ shines within us. He is the eternal radiance of souls, and for this reason the Father sent him into the world: so that, illumined by his face, we might be able to behold eternal and heavenly things, though previously we were held in earthly darkness.

Why should I speak of Christ, when the Apostle Peter also said to the man lame from his mother’s womb: “Look at us” (Acts III, 4)? He looked at Peter and was illumined by the grace of faith. For he would not have received the remedy of healing unless he had believed faithfully.

Therefore, when such glory was present among the apostles, Zacchaeus, hearing that the Lord Jesus was passing by, climbed a tree, because, being small and short, he could not see him in the crowd. He saw Christ and found light. He saw him, and the man who previously used to seize the property of others gave away his own.

Rightly, then, they say: “Why do you turn your face away?”

88. Or perhaps it is said for this reason: because, while they desired it, the coming of Christ was delayed. For he is the face of the Father, who is the image and glory of God.

Certainly, if we do not understand this as a mystery concerning his Incarnation, the saints rightly also take up these words, saying: “Why do you turn your face away?” That is: “Even if you turn your face away from us, O Lord, nevertheless the light of your face, O Lord, has been marked upon us.” We hold it in our hearts, and it shines in our inmost affection; for no one can subsist if you turn your face away.

All things await you, that you may give them food in due season. When you give to them, they gather; when you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness; but when you turn your face away, they will be troubled. You will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust. You will send forth your spirit, and they will be created; and you will renew the face of the earth (Ps. CIII, 27 ff.).

Do you recognize what food God supplies to human beings? It is the food on which his only-begotten Son, our Lord, feasts according to the will of the Father, as he himself says: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John IV, 34). This food is salutary for us, and all the things of God are salutary.

89. You hear of certain members of God; recognize his powers. His hands are the fullness of goodness; his face is the illumination of the mind. Therefore let us always hope in him and direct our vows and all our efforts toward him. Let us not despair, even though we cannot see him bodily.

Moses did not despair, although it was said to him: “You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see my face and live.” And he added: “Behold, there is a place with me; you shall stand upon the rock. And when my glory passes by, I shall place you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with my hand until I pass by. Then I shall take away my hand, and you shall see my back; but my face you shall not be able to see” (Exod. XXXIII, 20 ff.).

The face of God, then, is not seen by a human being. Yet there is a place in which God shows himself to a human being through faith. This place is with God. Therefore, if we stand upon the rock—that is, in the knowledge of and firm faith in this flesh, which that rock prefigured—

[Note: [Col. 1131D] That is, in the knowledge and faith of Christ’s flesh, which that rock prefigured.]

and if we cannot see his fullness, nevertheless, insofar as we are able, we shall drink in something like the remnants of his light.

For Moses did not see the whole fullness of his divinity, which dwells bodily in Christ; but he saw Christ’s back, he saw his splendor as a human being, and he saw the glory of his passion, through which he opened the heavenly kingdom to us.

90. Aquila, however, rendered it: “Why do you hide your face?” This also appears to agree with the others and with what Moses said: “Show yourself to me” (Exod. XXXIII, 13), as though he were saying: “Do not hide your face from me, but rather show it to me, since I desire to see it.”

91. And he added: “You forget,” he says, “our poverty and our tribulation.” Of what poverty does the holy Prophet say that God has forgotten it? Or what is this poverty over which he complains that it has fallen from the memory of our God and Lord?

This poverty is not meaningless, unless perhaps it is the poverty that has been accustomed to have God as its protector and rewarder. For if there is a poverty to which the kingdom of heaven lies open, these men rightly think that their poverty has fallen from the divine memory, since they lamented that their soul had been humbled in the dust and said that their belly clung to the earth. Those who cling to the earth appear to be deprived of divine protection.

Hear, then, what this poverty is: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 3). Therefore, if the poverty to which heaven lies open is blessed, let us disregard these earthly riches and avoid bodily abundance.

[Note: [Col. 1132D] Some manuscripts read, “Let us follow the deeds of the apostles.”]

Let us follow the footsteps of the apostles, before whose feet each person laid whatever money he possessed from the price of his fields, so that it might be distributed to the poor. These holy men had begun to practice this evangelical poverty long before; therefore they said: “You forget our poverty.” It is like the apostolic statement: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matt. XIX, 27). Good, therefore, is the poverty that proceeds from piety and is embraced through the practice of the virtues.

92. They lament that not only their poverty but also their tribulation has fallen into God’s forgetfulness. Tribulations too are good when they are proper to the righteous, who endure them not because of their merits but because of their piety. In them the righteous person is not crushed but enlarged, as the holy Prophet declares: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. IV, 2). The Lord Jesus himself says: “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard me in a spacious place” (Ps. CXVII, 5).

He enlarged the holy Apostle Paul when he took away the light of his eyes; for in this way he confessed Christ, whom previously he had denied. Therefore he deserved to be the chosen vessel. Finally, so that you may know that the Lord Jesus enlarged Paul, hear the Apostle himself saying: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (II Cor. VI, 11).

Open your mouth, then, and confess Christ, because he is fullness; where there is fullness, there is also breadth. And like a good teacher who desired to have disciples equal to himself, he exhorted us also to be enlarged, saying: “Be enlarged yourselves” (II Cor. VI, 13).

93. But when God enlarges someone in tribulation,

[Note: [Col. 1133A] Only the Roman edition reads, “God enlarges someone in tribulation.”]

then the breadth of the heart will become like the countless sand of the sea. Hear what this breadth is, when holy Solomon says:

[Note: [Col. 1133B] This passage of Scripture, which all the editions present, is found nowhere in our manuscripts. Immediately after the word “Solomon,” they continue: “that he might receive wisdom,” and so forth.]

“I desired, and understanding was given to me; I called, and the spirit of wisdom came to me” (Wis. VII, 7). For in order to receive wisdom from God, he asked not for riches, nobility, or power, but for wisdom; and in wisdom he found all the things he had not even asked for.

Hence Scripture says that the breadth of his heart was like the countless sand of the sea (III Kings IV, 29). And knowing from himself where one may acquire this breadth, he says: “Describe it in the breadth of your heart” (Prov. VII, 3). Therefore, whoever possesses wisdom must not keep it hidden or hold it only for a moment; but he must sing it openly, and everywhere proclaim with authority what he understands.

94. Symmachus, however, put “affliction” in place of “tribulation.” Whether it is affliction or tribulation, nevertheless, we must remain in the Lord and not depart from him, because, with the Lord presiding over us and standing beside us, we can endure every struggle bravely. But if we neglect the Lord and distance ourselves from him, we make our adversary stronger for ourselves.

## Exposition of Psalm XLV

[Col. 1133]

925 PREFACE

[Col. 1133B]

1. (Verse 1.) The title of this psalm is inscribed as follows: “For the end; for the sons of Korah; concerning hidden things; a psalm for David.” What does “concerning hidden things” mean? The holy Prophet also recalls in the fiftieth psalm that he had acquired knowledge of hidden things through the revelation of the Lord Jesus, saying: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Ps. 50:8). What those hidden things are, we are taught in the holy Gospel, where the Son of God says that the mysteries of wisdom have been hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones (Matt. 11:25). These are, unless I am mistaken, the things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart: the things which the Lord has prepared for those who love him.” Therefore let us store the hidden things of wisdom in the hidden place of our heart; let us not rashly disclose them to just anyone, except to those who share in the sacraments, whom the Lord has called to his grace—the one who wishes to be entreated in secret; for he alone knows hidden and concealed things.

2. Finally, the Lord Jesus himself wished only Moses—but not without Joshua—to ascend the mountain in order to receive the Law. In the Gospel also, from the entire number of his disciples, he revealed the glory of his resurrection only to Peter, John, and James (Matt. 17:1). Thus he wished his mystery to remain hidden, and he frequently warned them not readily to announce to anyone what they had seen, lest some weaker person stumble, unable to receive the power of the sacraments with a wavering understanding. Indeed, Peter himself did not know what he was saying when he thought that three tabernacles should be made, one for the Lord and two for his servants. Then he could not endure the radiance of the glory of the Lord who was transfiguring himself: he fell to the ground, and the sons of thunder, James and John, also fell; the cloud covered them, and they could not rise until Jesus came, touched them, ordered them to rise, and told them to put away their fear. They therefore entered into the cloud so that they might know hidden and concealed things; and there they heard the voice of God saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (ibid., 5).

What does “This is my beloved Son” mean? It means: “Do not err, Simon, by thinking that the Son of God should be compared with servants. This is my Son—not Moses the son, not Elijah the son, although one opened the sea and the other closed heaven. For by the word of the Lord each of them overcame the nature of an element; but they provided service. This is the one who made the waters solid, who closed heaven by drought, and who, whenever he wished, dissolved it into rains.”

Where the testimony of the resurrection is brought forward, the ministries of the servants lend their support; where the glory of the rising Lord is displayed, the splendor of the servants is hidden. Indeed, the rising sun eclipses the very orbs of the stars, and all their lights fade beneath the worldly sun. How, then, could the stars of the flesh be seen beneath the eternal Sun of righteousness and that divine radiance? Where, then, are those lights that shone before your eyes with a kind of miracle? Everything is darkness by comparison with eternal light.

Let others hasten to please God by their ministries; this one alone is the true and eternal light, in whom the Father is well pleased, or in whom “it has pleased me”—so that whatever he has done may be regarded as mine, and whatever I have done may rightly be believed to be the work of the Son. Hear him saying: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). He did not say, “I and Moses are one.” He did not claim for himself and Elijah any partnership in divine glory. Why are you preparing three tabernacles? This one has no tabernacle on earth, but in heaven.

The apostles heard, and fell down terrified and shaken. The Lord came, raised them up, and ordered them not to tell anyone what they had seen.

3. Therefore preserve your hidden things for him to whom David entrusted his own hidden things, saying: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults” (Ps. 18:13).

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “he cleansed his hidden things.” Other manuscripts, and the printed editions, read more suitably, “he entrusted his hidden things”—that is, he commended them in prayer.]

For the receptacles in which the hidden mysteries of piety are contained ought to be clean. Therefore it is said to you: “Drink water from your own vessels, and from the springs of your wells … and let your waters overflow in the streets, so that you may be cleansed by a watered spring” (Prov. 5:15–16). Therefore it is said to you: “Let your winepresses overflow with wine” (Prov. 3:10). Therefore it is said: “In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you; I heard you in the hidden place of the storm; I tested you at the water of contradiction” (Ps. 80:8).

There is, in tribulations, a certain fierce inward storm of the breast, when “there are battles without and fears within.” There is a water of contradiction when our thoughts, as though tossed by the swell of an exceedingly bitter sea, are agitated and cannot be calmed by any settled firmness in the depths of the mind. Then there is a hidden storm; then there is the water of contradiction, which can be stilled only by the word of Christ, by which he forgives us our sins, according to what he himself deigned to say: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15:3).

Speak, Lord Jesus: your word is medicine, your word is light, your word is the washing away of our filth, your word is a spring. You speak, and guilt is washed away.

4. And because the discourse has been drawn from the hidden storm and from the water of contradiction, the Word of God has become everything for us. He became flesh in order to preserve flesh; he became water in order by his grace to temper the water of contradiction and remove the bitterness of impiety. Therefore it is written: “Deep water is a word in the heart of a man” (Prov. 20:5). Elsewhere it is called “word,” elsewhere again “counsel”; for good counsel is found where the word of God is good.

Therefore the Law says to you: “Take heed to yourself, lest a wicked word arise in your heart” (Deut. 15:9); and Jesus says: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4). God sent his Word to heal humanity, not to destroy it. This Word is medicine, not punishment.

Let this Word be in your heart and in your mouth. Let this Word be in the hidden places where the devil lies in wait: let the Word enter, and let the devil depart. For if the devil slips in, Christ withdraws, as he withdrew from Judas after the devil had plunged himself into Judas’s heart.

You too, therefore, say: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults,” so that the devil may not lie in wait in the hidden places like a lion in his lair. If you piously and faithfully preserve the hidden things of Christ, there will be no place for the devil to lie in ambush.

Therefore, in the ninth psalm, when David writes of the Lord’s hidden mysteries—namely, the conversion of sinners, the calling of the nations, the kingdom of God, the preparation of the heart, the judgment of the poor, and the refreshment of the needy—he first says that the adversary must be driven out from the hidden and secret places of your heart, “lest he sit in ambush, desiring to kill the innocent.” Therefore it is said to you: “Enter your room, and after closing the door, pray to your Father in secret” (Matt. 6:6).

Let your prayer descend there, where the one who searches hidden things may hear it. There let him discover your patience, whether in concealing an injury or in avoiding self-display; for the wise person conceals his injury. There is the hiding-place of wisdom; for “he made darkness his hiding-place” (Ps. 17:12). “The wicked will seek me and will not find me” (Prov. 1:28).

[Col. 1136A] 5. Therefore Abraham dug a well, so that whoever sought water might find it; Isaac therefore dug a well; therefore the Lord Jesus sat beside a well—for there was Jacob’s spring. He sat beside the well so that you might seek.

[Note: Five manuscripts read, “There was a spring there. Christ is a spring for you, so that waters …” The printed editions, together with other manuscripts, have the reading given in the text.]

There is a spring wherever Christ is. It is a spring so that waters may overflow for those who seek, by which either all the defilements of the flesh may be washed away or its fires extinguished.

This, then, is the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God: that the wicked do not find it, while the good seek it and devote themselves to acquiring and contemplating it. Do you wish to know how true this is? Hear the words of Wisdom herself: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Luke 11:9).

Knock, then, at the door, because Christ is the door. Knock at the door of the Word, so that it may be opened to you for proclaiming the mystery of Christ, and so that you may be able to discover the treasures of wisdom hidden in Christ.

In him our wisdom is hidden; in him our life is hidden, as Paul declared (Col. 3:3). He was caught up even to the third heaven, to hear things that a human being is not permitted to speak. How profound is the discipline of hidden things! A person is permitted to know, but not permitted to speak. To know is life; to speak is death.

6. Since we know, therefore, that the end of hidden things—which is called in Greek σκοπός (*skopos*, “goal” or “end”)—is this, and that their supreme purpose is that the unworthy should not grasp the discipline of wisdom, while those who possess desire strive to attain knowledge of the divine mysteries, aided by the merits of life and faith and laboring and sweating through daily exercises so that they may deserve to obtain the fruit of their purpose, let us read the ninth and forty-fifth psalms more carefully, so that with faithful minds we may comprehend the wisdom hidden in the mystery.

For these two alone bear a title concerning hidden things. But now let us take up the psalm.

## EXPOSITION

7. “Our God is refuge and strength.” What does “our” mean? It means, “the refuge of those of us who believe in you.” So also elsewhere: “Lord, you have become our refuge” (Ps. 89:1). “Our,” he says—that is, of us who believe, not of unbelievers; of us who seek, not of those who flee from the truth.

Only the person who has placed the hope of his salvation in the protection of God alone can say this. Therefore you have become a refuge for us, and our refuge and strength—for we come from the peoples of the nations. The Jews denied you; the Jews did not receive you. Therefore you turned to the nations, called us, and became our refuge and our strength.

Do you wish to know that this was said of us who come from the nations? “The cross of the Lord is a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks, but to us it is the power and wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:18). And below: “You are from him in Christ Jesus, who became wisdom for us from God” (ibid., 30).

Paul was speaking neither of the Jews nor of the nations as such, but of those who, having turned to the Lord Jesus, proclaim him as the author of their salvation.

Have you therefore fled for refuge to Christ? Do not abandon the foundation; do not forsake your confirmer, so that the one who received you may himself protect you, and the pious merchant of our souls may recognize his merchandise.

8. (Verse 2.) “A helper in tribulations that have found us exceedingly.” The word “exceedingly” has rightly been understood in both ways: both that the tribulations found us exceedingly and that the helper may be understood as exceedingly great. For the greater the tribulations, the greater and more powerful are the helps we need.

Therefore it often happens that we are crowned in heavier and harsher contests, because through tears, groans, and more frequent prayers we obtain for ourselves the aid of the eternal divinity.

9. (Verse 3.) Hence it follows that we do not fear when our earth is shaken and mountains are moved, because if you are for us, who can be against us?

We cannot fear the frailties of this flesh, which is broken by fear and dread, inflamed by desires, softened by lust, weakened by pleasures, scorched by fevers, tormented by pain, and exhausted by anxieties.

Or consider those mountains being moved into the heart of the sea, of which the Savior said: “If you have faith like a mustard seed, you will not only say to the fig tree, ‘Be uprooted,’ but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and cast into the sea,’ nothing will be impossible for you” (Matt. 21:21).

[Note: The holy teacher had already taught that in this Gospel passage the hostile angel is signified by the mountain. In Psalm 36, col. 812, no. 77, he said in these words: “You will say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and cast into the sea.’” To which mountain? “To the demon,” he says, and so forth. In this interpretation some have found Ambrose lacking in gravity and moderation. But, to put it mildly, such critics are excessively fastidious. Who could deny that the proud spirit is by no means ineptly represented by the height of the mountain? As for the literal sense, it was never the intention of the holy bishop to deny that faith possesses a wonder-working power (θαυματουργικήν, *thaumatourgikēn*); he preferred, however, to pursue the mystical sense, which he judged more useful for his hearers.]

This mountain cast itself into the heart of Judas and disturbed his mind with a violent storm, driving him about on the waves of various passions. For just as the soul is compared to the fertility of the earth, fruitful in good works and in the fruits of devotion and faith—“like the fragrance of Jacob, like the fragrance of a field full of crops”—so too the soul of one who does not know how to remain at peace is represented by the turbulence of a stormy sea, raising great waves with bitter thoughts.

Finally, the Lord Jesus did not temper the bitterness of Judas the traitor even by his kiss. The traitor received the kiss, poured in poison, and inflicted death. Christ blunted its sting, but the traitor alone did not escape.
