And to make this kind of mountain clearly manifest to us, elsewhere, when he had commanded a demon to leave a man and the apostles asked why they themselves had been unable to cast it out, he said: “This kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. 17:20). He added: “If you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there’” (ibid., 19), indicating with his hand what that mountain was which perfect faith could move.

For perfect faith is compared with a mustard seed, as the Apostle says: “If I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2).

10. (Verse 4.) There are also those who punctuate the passage in this way: “And the mountains will be moved,” followed by: “They roared in the hearts of the sea, and its waters were troubled; the mountains were troubled by his strength.”

The waters that roar and are troubled and cannot provide drink are not good waters. Better are those that flow through, as it is written: “The waters will pass through the midst of the mountains, and they will give drink to all the beasts of the field; the wild asses will receive it for their thirst” (Ps. 103:10–11).

Finally, when the legion of demons asked for and received permission to enter the pigs, they rushed violently into the sea (Luke 8:32), and those waters were troubled by the plunge of the herd.

Elsewhere the same prophet David said: “The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you, and they were afraid” (Ps. 76:17)—that is, the good powers, which are tranquil through knowledge of the heavenly Word, not terrifying through noise and crashing.

But what does he say about the evil powers? “The abysses were troubled; the multitude of the sound of the waters” (ibid., 17–18). The abysses do not see God, and therefore are always subject to disturbances. He explained what the abysses were: “The multitude of the sound of the waters.”

For that beast, the Antichrist, also rises from the abyss in order to fight against Elijah, Enoch, and John, who have been restored to the earth on account of their testimony to the Lord Jesus, as we read in John’s Apocalypse. To it was given a mouth speaking great things, so that it might resound against God with insults full of fury and sacrilege (Rev. 13:5 ff.).

11. The waters therefore roared—that is, the unclean spirits—when they were troubled at the sight of God’s works and, fearing that judgment was approaching them at the saving coming of the Lord. The waters roared and were troubled also in the Lord’s Passion.

Hence it was said: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things?” (Ps. 2:1). Elsewhere Scripture says: “Their memory perished with a noise” (Ps. 9:8).

The devil seeks noise; Christ seeks silence. “As a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). And elsewhere: “He will not cry out, nor contend, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets … until he brings judgment to victory” (Isa. 42:2–3; Matt. 12:19–20).

What victory is this, if not victory over the serpent? By this strength of the Son of God the mountains were troubled when the devil and his ministers saw the dead rising.

These are the mountains that are troubled; those are the mountains that are moved into paradise, to whom it is said: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). And to another it is said: “I wish him to remain until I come; what is that to you? You follow me” (John 21:23). And Enoch was taken away, lest the wickedness of the age change him.

12. After the Lord’s Passion, what else should follow except that a river went forth from the Lord’s body, when water and blood flowed from his side, by which he gladdened the souls of all, because by that river he washed away the sin of the whole world?

There is also the river that went forth from Eden and flowed around the whole earth: the Word of God by which the intelligible paradise is watered and every soul is called to the grace of Christ. The Word of God himself says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. From the one to whom I give water, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38–39).

From that one Word of God flowed the streams of the four virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another the grace of healings in one Spirit, to another the working of powers … For one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:8 ff.).

These are the streams of the river’s surge, when by a spontaneous distribution it pours itself into the grace of ministries, operations, and power.

13. By these courses of the heavenly river, therefore, that city in which God dwells is watered; and the tabernacle of the Most High is sanctified—every soul inhabited by Christ—or that body which the Virgin brought forth, of which the angel Gabriel said: “The holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of the living God” (Luke 1:35).

It is a good tabernacle, which no sins could overshadow; a marvelous temple of God and heavenly palace, which, though dissolved, could not be corrupted, but rose again within three days, raised up by the one who had appeared to be dead.

Nor is this surprising, since God was in the midst of his city, and it was not shaken—either because the Son of God was not shaken by any fall into sin, nor did he waver through the offense of any error or falter under the impulse of bodily allurements; or because God’s grace did not abandon his soul, but remained inseparably within it, since it endured immaculate and untouched by every defilement of sin.

Therefore the Son of God said to the Father: “You will not abandon my soul in hell” (Ps. 15:10). Since, then, it was subject to him not to sin even in the flesh, he said divinely: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14:10). And elsewhere: “I was delivered up, and I did not depart” (Ps. 87:9). He did not depart from the one to whom he later said: “I rose, and I am still with you” (Ps. 138:18).

But whenever someone sins more seriously, God is shaken within him, so that he may depart from him. Thus he appeared to walk in the case of Adam when Adam sinned, and to stand in the case of Stephen: the former had fallen through transgression, while the latter was crowned in martyrdom.

And in the book of Zechariah it is written:

[Note: Most manuscripts, and all printed editions, have the reading given in the text, except that the Roman edition has “he will walk.” The Remigius manuscripts read, “He walked in the disturbance of the threat of his irritation.” The Longpont and Vallicelliana manuscripts read, “He walked in the agitation of the threat of his irritation.” In this they do not differ greatly from the Septuagint, which reads: “Καὶ πορεύσεται ἐν σάλῳ ἀπειλῆς αὐτοῦ” (“And he will go in the shaking of his threat”); the Vulgate has: “And he will go in the whirlwind of the south.”]

“The Lord walked in the agitation of the indignation of his anger” (Zech. 9:14).

A similar statement was made to the Jews in the Gospel: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:38). The Lord abandoned the Jews, and immediately the ruin of the synagogue followed. If Christ had not abandoned it, its final destruction would never have followed.

We have therefore explained the statement: “God is in the midst of her; she will not be shaken.”

14. It follows: “God will help her at dawn.” This signifies that the morning resurrection brings us the assistance of heavenly support, having driven away the night and restored the day, as Scripture says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you” (Eph. 5:14).

Consider also the mystery. Christ suffered in the evening; therefore, according to the Law, the lamb is also slaughtered in the evening (Exod. 12:6). He rose in the morning, for it is written: “On the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb at first light, while it was still dark, and she saw that the stone had been removed from the entrance” (John 20:1).

In the evening of the world he is slain, when the light was already failing, because the whole world was in darkness and would have been wrapped in even deeper gloom, unless Christ had come to us from heaven as eternal light, restoring the seasons of innocence to the human race.

The Lord Jesus therefore suffered and by his blood forgave our sins; a purer light shone upon the conscience, and the day of spiritual grace brightened. Hence the Apostle says: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13:12).

We have therefore awakened; let us no longer sleep. We have put on the garment of light; let us not return to the clothing and cast-off garments of a dark way of life. We have said farewell to banquets and pleasures, which belong to the night; we have chosen sobriety, by whose grace Jacob found the birthright that he did not possess.

15. Other manuscripts also read: “God will help her with his countenance.” Let the Prophet himself teach us what this too signifies. For later he said: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79:4). The sight of God, therefore, is our salvation, and in his countenance lies our help.

The divine Scripture declares how great is the power of this, since it did not casually add that “God looked upon Abel’s offerings, but did not look upon Cain’s offerings” (Gen. 4:4–5). Cain was therefore grieved because he learned that his sacrifice had displeased God, while his brother’s had pleased him.

Hence also the words sung today in the psalm’s responsory are of great assistance to our assertion: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he looked upon me” (Ps. 39:2).

[Note: Responsories properly mean chants placed after individual readings. They are called by this name either because they signify the assent of the hearers, or because they respond to the readings—sad things to sad things, joyful things to joyful things—or finally because they are sung with the choir responding. This is taught by Stephen, bishop of Autun, as well as by Rupert, and by the most learned Cardinal Bona in his *On the Divine Psalms*, book 1, chapter 16, §15, no. 2.

Here, however, it is clear that “responsory” is not being used in that sense, since the expression is not “the responsory of the reading” but “the responsory of the psalm.” We would therefore readily suppose that it was once customary for an individual responsory to be sung after each psalm, especially since Gennadius, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, reports that Musaeus, bishop of Massilia, wrote responsories of the psalms, and Rabanus, in book 1 of *On the Instruction of the Clergy*, chapter 51, states that responsories were in use in Italy long before antiphons.

Yet Ambrose shows that the term could also be used for the individual verses of the psalm in his exposition of Psalm 37, col. 841, no. 58: “Before the next responsory,” he says, “there is the verse: ‘And they cast me away,’ and so forth.” It is clear there that by “responsory” he means the verse: “But do not abandon me,” and so forth, as will be evident to anyone who considers the passage.

Nor should it seem surprising if the verses of the psalms, recited by alternating choirs, are called responsories, since the aforementioned cardinal also maintains that the psalms may be called antiphons for the same reason. Consult the cited work, book 1, chapter 16, §10, no. 1, as well as the most learned Du Cange, under the word “Responsory.”]

The one whom the Lord looks upon, he saves. Finally, in the Lord’s Passion, when Peter faltered in speech, though not in mind—for even Peter’s speech in his faltering was more faithful than the teaching of many—Christ looked upon him, and Peter wept, thereby washing away his particular error. Thus the one whom he had seemed to deny with his voice, he confessed with his tears.

16. “The nations were troubled, the kingdoms were bowed down; the Most High gave his voice, and the earth was moved.”

At the coming of the Lord and Savior, the hostile powers, together with their legion, were troubled. They were ordered to leave human bodies and begged to be sent into the pigs. Once the most wicked powers had been troubled, it was necessary that the worshipers of idols also be troubled and that the kingdoms of sin be bowed down.

For it was a heavy kingdom that had subjected the minds of all sinners to grievous servitude; “whoever commits sin is the slave of sin.” The kingdom of sin is the kingdom of death, which long prevailed throughout the entire world.

Hence the Apostle says: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one who was to come” (Rom. 5:14).

Truth came, and the figure ceased; life came, and the kingdom of death vanished; the forgiveness of sins came, and the bonds of sin were loosed. Previously even lighter offenses were bound by the chains of death; after the coming of the saving Lord, even graver crimes were forgiven.

The kingdoms of spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places were therefore bowed down, because the worship of idols and the allurements of sin began to diminish through the teaching of the Gospel proclamation. Unbelief was bowed down after faith began to reign in the hearts of the nations.

The kingdoms of sin are bowed down when it is read: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6:12). The Lord bowed down all the kingdoms of unbelief by his voice, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28).

17. The Most High gave this voice, and all the peoples of the nations followed him, fleeing the harsh kingdoms of sin, the cruelty of perpetual death, and the intolerable slavery of every crime. He promised rest to the weary, release to captives, and freedom to slaves; and, shaking off the iron yoke of the king of Babylon, he placed his own easy yoke upon the necks of the faithful, lest the enemy bind the empty necks of the gentiles again with the chains of his iniquity.

For Christ liberates those whom he binds, and releases those whom he shackles. Thus the one who is called a slave by the Lord is the Lord’s freedman, and the one who is called free is Christ’s slave. Therefore Paul glories in his bonds, saying: “Paul, bound for Jesus” (Eph. 3:1). What is an insult under others is glory under Christ.

The Lord gave his voice in the Passion, and all the elements trembled; the whole earth was shaken (Ps. 23:1), so that the rites of the gentiles might be dissolved and the earth might become the Lord’s, together with its fullness, as it is written; so that the omens of unbelievers might cease, and the sacrifice of impiety might be abolished by the knowledge of faith and the devotion of piety.

The Lord gives his voice every day, and it resounds in the hearts of individuals, so that everything earthly may depart from the person whose affection believes rightly, and so that all the inner senses of the soul may be moved from error, from the corruption of lust, and from dissolution toward knowledge of the heavenly mysteries and the pursuit of chastity—from wickedness toward virtue through a pious confession.

18. (Verse 8.) He therefore says that those who are on earth have been moved, either because all human beings were earth, containing earthly corruption, since they did not know how to raise and lift the eyes of their minds toward the height of heavenly grace; nor could they say, “The God of powers is with us,” since the only one with them was the instigator of their fall and the author of their error.

But after the Lord’s voice resounded in the Gospel, the Prophet dares to say: “The God of powers is with us.” He rightly says, “The God of powers is with us,” because he believes that the Virgin conceived and gave birth. We too dare to say, “The God of powers is with us,” after Emmanuel—that is, God—began to be with us. Therefore, wherever Emmanuel is, there is the God of powers with us.

19. “Our protector is the God of Jacob” (ibid.).

Let us therefore imitate the patriarch Jacob—his fragrance, his virtue, and his labor. For just as we must perform the works of Abraham so that we may rightly deserve to be called his children, so also we must undertake the exercises and contests of holy Jacob, so that the God of Jacob may be believed to be our God.

For if he does not recognize in us the works of Jacob—or, since we cannot equal him, the zeal for his works and faith—how will he deign to help us as the God of Jacob?

20. (Verse 9.) While he was saying these things, behold, through the Holy Spirit the present image of future events was infused into him. Seeing peace spread throughout the whole world after the grave disturbance of wars at the coming of the saving Lord, he cries out to all, saying: “Come and see the works of the Lord, who has placed wonders upon the earth.”

“Come” refers to gathering; “see” refers to attention and the pursuit of knowing the truth. “See,” he says, “the works of the Lord, full of miracles, in which there are signs of great powers.”

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “Finally, *prodigia* in Greek are called ‘things worthy of wonder’ in Latin.” Other manuscripts and the printed editions have the reading in the text, except that the Roman edition reads, “*prodigia* are called … in Latin.”]

Indeed, τέρατα (*terata*) in Greek means “wonders” in Latin. Therefore do not understand the works of the Lord as though they were the horror of something monstrous, but as things full of wonder. He very aptly says “upon the earth”—that is, “into the earth.”

21. (Verse 10.) “Taking away wars to the ends of the earth, he will break the bow and shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire.”

And indeed, before the Roman Empire was extended, not only did the kings of individual cities fight against one another, but the Romans themselves were frequently worn down by civil wars. Marius fought against Cinna. Roman blood was shed on both sides. Sulla rose up and, after Marius had gained victory, again stirred up civil wars.

[Note: This was M. Aemilius Lepidus, a supporter of the Marian party, who fought against Catulus, the leader of the Sullan faction, with whom he had previously held the consulship. We shall speak again of this same Lepidus shortly.]

Lepidus and Sertorius offered themselves as rebels against the Roman Empire. Caesar pursued Pompey and stirred up the fury of Gaul against Roman arms. After defeating the elder Pompey, he defeated the younger in the regions of Spain.

What shall I say of the triumvirs, who turned from enemies into friends, and from friends again into hostile upheavals? The seas too were stained with Roman blood in the Battle of Actium.

[Note: Antony, Lepidus, and Augustus, previously at odds with one another, first joined their arms and assumed triumviral power in order to avenge the death of Julius Caesar, who had been killed by Brutus and the other conspirators. But that alliance was soon dissolved. For not long afterward, Lepidus was reduced to private rank, while Antony was finally defeated by Augustus in a naval battle at Actium, a coastal city of Epirus, and turned his violent hands against his own life. Tacitus summarizes these victories of Octavian Caesar and the peace that followed in these words: “The arms of Lepidus and Antony passed over to Augustus, who, under the name of princeps, took under his command everything exhausted by civil discord.”]

Hence it happened that, out of weariness with civil wars, the Roman Empire was entrusted to Julius Augustus, and thus internal battles were quieted.

This achieved the result that the apostles could rightly be sent throughout the whole world, as the Lord Jesus said: “Go and teach all nations” (Matt. 28:19). Even kingdoms cut off by barbarian mountains were opened to them, so that India was opened to Thomas and Persia to Matthew.

Nevertheless, so that they might traverse more extensive regions of the earth, at the rise of the Church the Roman power spread throughout the whole world and, by granting peace, reconciled divided minds and separated lands. All people, living under one empire of the earth, learned through faithful proclamation to confess the rule of the one almighty God.

22. Therefore he removed wars to the ends of the earth; and there is no doubt that this happened. But see whether he removed the wars of weakness, which are in the heart of those who waver. For whoever has passed beyond earthly things no longer says, “Outside are conflicts, within are fears” (2 Cor. 7:5), but says, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Cross over the world, then, so that you may begin to be above the world; [Col. 1143C] for *περάσαι* means “to cross over,” or, to express it more precisely, “to cross by ship.”

[Note: [Col. 1143D] Thus several manuscripts, and all editions. Nevertheless, why should the word *περάσαι* occur here, unless one wishes to refer it to *περάτων*? For the verse explained here is found in the Septuagint as follows: Ἀνταναιρῶν πολέμους μέχρι τῶν περάτων τῆς γῆς—“Removing wars to the ends of the earth.” Nonetheless, it seems that our Doctor would more probably have written *περᾷν* or *περᾶσθαι* rather than *περάσαι*. For this reason, I would not be greatly swayed toward the reading of other manuscripts, where we read, “*phase* means ‘to cross over.’” Indeed, it was sufficiently customary for this holy man, by means of words in a manner concealed within Scripture, to suggest passages from which moral precepts might be drawn. The following sense could therefore be derived from it: “By crossing over from earthly things to heavenly things, imitate the Passover of the Israelites,” and so forth. For the present, however, we do not prejudice the received reading.]

Therefore the Lord removed the wars that spiritual wickedness was waging against us; and after conquering the devil, he left us his peace. He broke the bow from which the enemy’s fiery darts were scattered, and he burned the shields of faithlessness with fire, so that the shield of faith might remain inviolate.

23. (Verse 11.) “Be still,” he says, “and see that I am the Lord.” This is the Lord’s voice after the wars have been brought to peace: “Be still,” so that there may be no occupation of the soul; lest the eye of the inner mind be veiled by the confusion of worldly disturbances. “Be still,” he says, “from errors; be still from disturbances; be still from sins,” because “everyone who sins has neither seen him nor known him” (1 John 3:6), as John the Evangelist said in his Epistle. Be still, then, for the pursuit of knowing the divinity; do not occupy yourselves with earthly works.

For this reason the king of Egypt ordered the number of bricks and the other burdens of the Jews to be increased, so that they might not come to know God and devote themselves to sacred worship. He was angered by Moses and Aaron and by the voice of the holy men, who said: “Let my people go, so that we may go and serve the Lord our God” (Exod. 5:6 ff.).

24. “I will be exalted among the nations, and I will be exalted in the earth.” The Lord was exalted in the heights—that is, among the angels [Col. 1144B] and archangels, among the patriarchs and prophets, who held exalted thoughts about him and did not compare him with earthly images [Note: [Col. 1144D] Some manuscripts read “and with sculpted images.” Others, and the editions, read “with rocky images,” that is, images of stone; for *scrupus* means a stone, whence *scrupulus*. The reference to caves and caverns touches upon the superstition of the pagans, who chiefly consulted the oracles of the gods in subterranean places—for example, in the cave of Delphic Apollo, and those of the Sibyl, Trophonius, and similar figures.] and rocky statues. But he was not exalted among the peoples of the nations, who seemed to seek their god in caves and the dwelling places of caverns.

In the end, Mary Magdalene is reproved: she mourned Christ as though he were dead and sought him as though he had been buried in a tomb. Therefore Christ says to her: “Mary, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” (John 20:15). Surely, was she seeking one who could be carried away? She heard the voice, recognized him, and wanted to touch him; and the Lord said: “Do not touch me” (ibid., 17)—you who think me dead. “I am going to the Father.” Do you marvel that you did not find in the tomb the one whom heavenly things await?

Or perhaps she is reproved because Christ is touched only by perfect faith, just as the woman with the hemorrhage touched him with complete faith. Therefore the Lord says: “Someone touched me; I perceive that power has gone out from me” (Luke 8:46). At these words, she recognized in herself that she had been healed by the power that had gone out, and immediately, conscious of what she had done, confessed that she herself had touched the Lord. Therefore the Lord says: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (ibid., 48).

The Lord is exalted in the earth, moreover, according to what he himself says: “When I have been exalted, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). Or, it may mean that his will has been done both in heaven and on earth.

[Col. 1144D] 25. (Verse 12.) And he repeats it, saying: “God of powers is with us; our protector is the God of Jacob.”

[Note: [Col. 1145A] The Roman edition, after the words “God of Jacob,” adds “God of powers is with us.” He repeats what he had said above. Repetition, however, is confirmation.]

Repetition is confirmation. Or it is because God became “God with us” not only when he was born of the Virgin, but also after the resurrection, when he himself said: “Behold, I am with you … until the consummation of the world” (Matt. 28:20). To him be honor and glory, eternity from the ages, and now and always, unto all ages of ages. Amen.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM XLVII

[Col. 1145]

[Col. 1145A] 1. (Verse 1.) Its title is this:

[Note: [Col. 1145D] The psalm and the song were employed in the praises of God: the former was performed with the voice, the latter with a musical instrument. But whenever the voice led the instrument, it was called “a psalm of a song”; if the instrument led the voice, it was called “a song of a psalm.” See Cassiodorus, *Prologue on the Psalms*, chapter 5 and following; likewise Flaminio Nobili on this passage, as well as Cardinal Bona, *On the Divine Psalms*, chapter 16, § 12, no. 1, and others.]

“A psalm of a song, for the sons of Korah, on the second day of the week” (Psal. 41 and following).

Good are the sons of Korah, already approved in the preceding psalms, because, with suitable understandings and thoughts directed toward the pursuit of virtue, they composed within themselves a spiritual psalter and, intent upon the knowledge of divinity [Note: [Col. 1145D] Thus most manuscripts, although some read the words together as *speculamentis*—“with contemplative instruments.” The Colbertine and Victorine manuscripts agree, except that the former has *pervigilis* and the latter *pervigilibus*. The Reginensis and certain Paris editions have *pervigiles speculo mentis*—“watchful in the mirror of the mind.” The old editions and the Roman edition have *pervigili specula*, and so forth. A *specula* is an elevated place suitable for observing distant things. Hence the preface to Psalm 1, no. 2, says: “Some are lookouts of the cliffs, others are their uses,” and so forth. Metaphorically, the word is taken for the lofty or attentive contemplation of the mind.]—they would be worthy to draw in the secrets of heavenly mysteries.

And so, when they had received the task and duty of singing every day before the ark of the Lord, they appear to have been chosen to receive the special assignment of singing the “psalm of a song” on the second day of the week. For those to whom it seemed rightly entrusted to sing with their voice the Lord’s ascent from the underworld, after his resurrection, ought certainly to have been given the task of celebrating the very day of the resurrection through their service and ministry.

For what is “the second day of the week” except the Lord’s Day, which followed the Sabbath? The Sabbath day was later in the order of the days, but earlier in the sanctification of the Law. But when the end of the Law arrived, namely Christ Jesus—for “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4)—and when through his resurrection he sanctified the eighth day, the day that is the eighth began to be the first, and the first began to be the eighth: possessing precedence according to the order of number, and holiness from the Lord’s resurrection.

Thus in the Gospel we read of the *δευτερόπρωτον* Sabbath (Luke 6:1), which in Latin is called *secundo-primum*, “second-first.” Once the Lord’s Day began to surpass the others—the day on which the Lord rose—the Sabbath, which had been first, began to be regarded as second after the first. The first rest ceased, and the second succeeded it.

Therefore, in writing to the Hebrews, the Apostle says: “There remains, then, a rest for the people of God. Let us hasten to enter into that rest” (Heb. 4:8, 9, 11).

2. True rest, therefore, is now found not in the cessation of work but in the time of the resurrection. For this reason those who, according to the Law, observed the solemnity of the Sabbath called it “the one Sabbath,” as though there were one Sabbath and no other. We, who have put on a spiritual observance [Col. 1146A] and desire to shape our service after the likeness and rest of God, and to offer our ministry in that heavenly city, where there is not a model or shadow but the truth, call it “the first day of the week,” as it is written: “In the evening of the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning” (Matt. 28:1).

Nothing could be more beautiful or more precise. Before the resurrection he called it “the Sabbath”; after the resurrection he called it “the first day of the week.” John the Evangelist also says: “On the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene came early, while it was still dark” (John 20:1). “Darkness” refers to the time; “morning” to grace.

But these people expressed it more clearly according to the Gospel, [Note: [Col. 1146D] The Roman edition reads, “as though the veil had been cut away.”] as though the veil had been shaken aside. David, however, living under the Law, [Note: [Col. 1146D] The Roman edition reads, “and he maintained the melody.” Other editions and manuscripts read, “and he maintained moderation,” and so forth. But some, through the copyists’ error, prefer *cautionis*—“of caution”—instead of *cantionis*—“of song.”] both maintained the proper moderation of the song and did not suppress the mystery, so that he might declare the Lord’s Day as the second day of the week, while among the Jews the order of number was thought to have been preserved and the spiritual sacrament was recognized as revealed. Let us therefore hear what he says who sings to God on the second day of the week.

3. (Verse 2.) “Great,” he says, “is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, in the city of our God, in his holy place.”

Is God not great and worthy of praise everywhere? He is indeed great and powerful everywhere; but the narrow mind does not grasp the greatness of his divine power and grace. The more closely our knowledge approaches God, the more exalted his majesty appears to us.

In the end, Thomas, who had earlier said, “Unless I see the marks of the nails in his hands and put my hand into his side, I will not believe” (John 20:25), once he had placed his finger there and recognized the evidence of the resurrection, marveled within himself at God’s grace and said: “My Lord and my God” (ibid., 28). Then he confessed his divinity and lordship most fully, when he no longer doubted that he had risen from the underworld.

In the end, a hymn is fitting for God in Zion, and a vow is paid to him in Jerusalem. What wonder is it, then, if in the heavenly city, and in that high and ethereal place, his power is proclaimed with greater force?

4. (Verse 3.) He added: [Note: [Col. 1147D] The Roman edition alone, after the two complete verses of the psalm given above, appends this half-verse and then adds: “Rightly did he say above, ‘Great is the Lord.’ For truly …”]

“Spreading exultation over the whole earth.”

And truly he is called great who spread exultation throughout the whole world of this earth, where before the shoots of intolerable sins were sprouting, where there were mourning, sadness, and groaning. Thus the conscience of human beings, which previously lay grieving, submerged in the whirlpools of its own crimes, now rejoices, freed from fear through Christ’s forgiveness and the remission of all sins.

It is fitting that we understand the passage in this way, as we have said. But because in some ancient manuscripts we find *εὐρίζῳ ἀγαλλιάματι πάσης τῆς γῆς*, which in Latin means “with the well-rooted exultation of the whole earth,” we perceive that the meaning is the same. For the divine gifts of God the Father are praised in us: he has given us an exultation founded upon a good root, namely God Jesus, the true and most fruitful vine, from which the heavenly sacraments have flowed. In these there is perpetual and enduring joy, because through them every sin is washed away and the inner conscience cleansed.

We recognize also that the wording is appropriate, because we rejoice with a well-rooted exultation, since we exult in Christ. The joy of the world is temporary, but the joy of the one who rejoices in the Lord is everlasting.

5. (Verse 4.) “Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King. God will be recognized in her citadels when he receives her.”

He clearly expressed why there is exultation throughout the whole earth: because the Lord Jesus gathered the Church for himself from sinners. Thus those who previously were “the sides of the north”—that is, the companions and adherents of the devil, to whom it is said, “Awake, north wind, so that the south wind may come” (Song 4:16)—have become faithful to Christ.

They are the ones of whom it is said: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion” (Ps. 124:1). They have therefore become Mount Zion through the grace of Christ and the sacrament of baptism.

The north wind, understood spiritually, is a harsh blast. Previously it stirred up the fiercest storms and tempests in human emotions; it began to lose its own adherents, having troubled those who belonged to another. It had overturned the entire Jewish people and held all the nations bound under its dominion. They were its sides—that is, they breathed together with it.

For just as we call the sides of a ruler his bodyguards and companions, and just as a woman is called the side of a man because she is joined to him in obedient companionship, so the sides of the devil were those who carried out his will.

These, then, are now Mount Zion: those who contemplate the eternal God and devote themselves to him night and day. Consider Paul when he was persecuting the Church of the Lord: he was a side of the north. Consider him now, when he is read in the Church: he is a watchtower-like mountain through whom we know and see the glory of Christ.

And because the Greek says “mountains”—that is, *ὄρη*—see how the servants of Christ are mountains. “The mountains around him” (ibid., 2): in them is the Church of the Lord, which is the city of the great King.

Likewise, because the Lord, according to the region of the heavens, [Note: [Col. 1147D] The Victorine and Colbertine manuscripts read *Enerario passus est*—“he suffered in the Venerarium.” This is corrupt. All the others, at least the Gallican manuscripts, have *venerat, passus est ubi erat*—“he had come; he suffered where he was,” which is not much sounder. We therefore do not depart from the edition. The marginal note in the old edition, drawn from Jerome, observes that for nearly two hundred years there had been an image of Jupiter at the place of the resurrection and a marble statue of Venus on the rock of the holy cross. The authors of the persecution hoped by this device to remove from Christians their faith in the most sacred mysteries. Hence it is concluded there that Ambrose calls the place a *Venerarium*, because it had been polluted and defiled by the sacrilegious rites of Venus. But since that impious worship was not introduced until many years after the Lord’s resurrection, we fear that the holy Doctor could not suitably have said that Christ suffered in the Venerarium—especially in view of the preceding words, “according to the region of the heavens.” Let the more learned decide the matter.] suffered in the Venerarium, which was located on the side of the north, there too is Mount Zion; there is the earthly Jerusalem.

6. See whether this too has been expressly indicated: the congregation of God’s people, which had been joined to the north through guilt, became the Church of Christ through grace, so that it is now called not the Synagogue but the Church of Christ.

And because the remnant of the Jews was saved through the election of grace, God is known in them—in Peter, Paul, John, and James—men weighty and exalted, like foundations and summits of the Church.

They are weighty as foundations, whom no heavy blasts of the north wind have shaken; rather, they preserved the foundation of faith immovable, so that the whole Church would not totter. They are lofty as summits, because they raised its crown high through the towers of their virtue.

For just as the founder is recognized in his works, and the builder in his buildings, so that even if you do not hear his name you may nevertheless discern the craftsman from the quality of his works—and what wonder is this in human matters, when we understand even the invisible things of the eternal Creator, whom we do not see, through the things that have been made—so God the inhabitant is recognized in lofty and great houses, which we are, if we hold the foundation of liberty and glory firm to the end.

Thus he is recognized as “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” He is the true God who founded such men through the instruction of his commandments.

Therefore, just as he demonstrated himself to be the eternal God in those men, so, he says, when the great King receives the city, he will pour into its citadels the reception of his knowledge, so that they may become taught by God—those who have both heard his commandment and judged that it must be carried out, lest they fall away from the stability of that house built upon the rock.

7. (Verses 5–6.) “When the kings of the earth saw this,” he says, “they gathered together and passed over together. When they saw it, they were astonished.”

[Note: [Col. 1148D] The Roman edition reads: “For behold, the kings of the earth were gathered together; they passed over together. When they saw this, they were astonished, they were troubled, they were moved; trembling seized them. The kings of the earth were gathered together. Good kings …”]

They are good kings who can offer themselves as rulers of their own body, deriving their origin and formation from the patriarch Abraham, who taught that sin can be overcome. Therefore he is the true king who did not know himself to be subject to crimes, in whom the allure of guilt and error could not reign.

Hence it was said to such a man by the sons of Heth: “You are a king from God among us” (Gen. 23:6).

Such kings of the earth, then, who ruled the flesh, gathered together so that they might be of one heart and one spirit, as we read: “The multitude of believers had one soul and one heart, and there was no division among them” (Acts 4:32).

These are the ones who “passed over together”—not so much into one place as into the same disposition and purpose. For to one who has been tested it is said: “Pass over and recline” (Luke 17:7).

It is no ordinary virtue to pass from wickedness to what is honorable, from earthly things to eternal things, to change the habits of carnal life, to abolish all its practices, to assume new customs, and to transform the entire condition of one’s former way of life.

And rightly it is said to him: “If you pass through the waters, I am with you” (Isa. 43:2). God is with the one who passes over, not with the one who stops.

8. Those, then, who had previously been divided within themselves, when they came together in one mind and purpose, having received the peace that made the two one and dissolved the hostility in his flesh through the destruction of the dividing wall, were astonished—either at the one who is recognized in his citadels, or at the fact that human beings had been so transformed: those who had previously served the devil were now, in the righteousness of their piety, devoted to the service of the Lord Jesus.

And because they themselves, as kings of their bodies, had experienced no ordinary force of labor—for it is neither easy nor insignificant to conquer the mind, cut away desires, tame the wantonness of the flesh, and eradicate luxury [Note: [Col. 1149D] All editions in the text read *evacuare luxuriam*—“to empty out luxury.” All manuscripts and the old edition in the margin read *averruncare*, that is, to cut away with a *runco* or hoe; improperly, “to turn away” and “drive off,” as among the ancients *averrunci* were called those who drove away evils.] that resisted Paul also, so as to bind him captive under the law of sin—just as they marveled at the grace in those who had advanced in virtue, so too they were disturbed lest anyone should fall back into vices after being cast down from the higher summit of virtues.

For the human condition is inclined and changeable in both directions, so that wherever it turns, it inclines and bends either toward the pursuit of virtue or toward the allure of sins.

9. And therefore they were shaken by no ordinary emotion, so that trembling seized them through fear, as they considered what is written: “In the places of the wicked, the righteous groan” (Prov. 28:28).

In the end, consider Peter weeping most bitterly because error had crept over him and had bent the strength of his mind through the fall of bodily weakness. And rightly he had previously been reproved by Christ [Note: [Col. 1149D] All editions and two manuscripts read *suppresse reprehensum*—“reproved covertly.” This may allude to Luke 22:61: “And the Lord turned and looked at Peter,” for this is a kind of silent reproof. Nevertheless, the words that follow immediately seem to show that the open reproof preceding Peter’s fall is intended. For this reason we have preferred the reading of the other manuscripts.] because he had dared to claim steadfastness without considering his own vulnerable nature.

Peter corrected this error through grace; but Judas remained in guilt and persisted in lamentation. He was righteous when he was numbered among the apostles; but because he was overthrown by the devil, he now mourns and groans in the places of the wicked, having fallen from grace into punishment.

Therefore, when men of this kind fell—such as the traitor Judas, or Saul, who had been summoned by the Lord God to the kingdom—even strong men trembled.

10. (Verse 7.) Finally, as they considered by how great a struggle one reaches the end, how great are the afflictions of the righteous, how great their anxieties, what sort of adversary there is, how great the contest sustained through prolonged labor, how great the bitterness [Note: [Col. 1150D] The edition reads *propositi terroris*—“the terror of the undertaking.” Some manuscripts, however, read *praepositi terroris*—“the terror of the overseer”; others, *praepositi erroris*—“the error of the overseer.” This is not unsuitable if it is referred to the error of Judas or of those like him. But the first reading is preferable because of what follows concerning sorrows.] of the terror set before them, and what bonds of self-restraint and blows of conscience there are, they were greatly troubled, lest anyone should yield either to the hardships of a stricter life or to its pains.

For there are bitter and heavy pains there—that is, in the Church, in that city of the great King. They are like the pains of a woman in labor, until Christ is formed in us. Paul was not without pain when he saw that his progress in doctrine among the foolish Galatians was slow. Therefore he said: “My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19).

The Lord also testifies in the Gospel that the pains of a woman in labor are severe, when he says: “When a woman is in labor, she has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers her anguish, because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world” (John 16:21).

Great, therefore, is the labor by which someone acquires Christ for himself, lest, like a ship without a pilot, he drift upon the sea of this present world without a helmsman. In the end, the apostles were sad when Christ declared that he was going back to the Father, because they thought they would be left without their ruler.

Christ is joy. He is also the child whom the woman in labor brings forth, the one who has received the spirit of salvation in the womb of his mind. Whoever has given birth to him and nourished him rejoices; whoever is in labor is shaken and pierced with pain.

[Col. 1150C] 11. It is good both to give birth to him and to nourish him. “Do not cook a lamb in its mother’s milk” (Exod. 23:19), lest it be said to you: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse infants” (Matt. 24:19).

For Christ was born from Mary in such a way that you should recognize him, just as the ox recognized its owner, and know that he himself created you and himself possessed your ancestors. Do not nourish him as though he were a little child; rather, recognize that he must be worshiped as the true and perfect God from the true and perfect God.

The Magus worshiped him in such a way that he did not cook the young goat in its mother’s milk, but revered him as the eternal God. In the end, in order to find him, he looked toward heaven. He was not therefore seeking on earth the one whom the shining star revealed from heaven.

For this reason Mary did not remain in labor with him but gave birth to him, because she knew that both the Lord and the Savior was to be generated from her, as she herself testifies, saying: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior” (Luke 1:46–47).

There, then, are pains like those of a woman in labor. It is painful to give birth; it is painful to nourish the one whom at the beginning you ought to possess as perfect.

12. (Verse 8.) Therefore many are severely crushed, as the verse that follows signifies: “With a vehement spirit you will crush the ships of Tarshish.”

For while God’s servants desire to arrive at the perfection of faith, they waste away their bodies by chastising them more severely and reducing them to the service of slavery, lest those who have already been tested be rejected. They do this in a strong and vehement Holy Spirit.

For the Spirit is the spirit of counsel and strength, so that through excessive abstinence they may dissolve their bodies, emptying them of all their pleasures, so that it may be said to them: “Strengthen the weak hands and make firm the feeble knees” (Isa. 35:3).

When someone has been released from this earthly framework, then he rises again stronger for eternal life. I am wrong if Scripture does not support me; it says: “To be dissolved and to be with Christ is far better” (Phil. 1:23). Whoever is dissolved begins to be with Christ.

And elsewhere: “The time of my release is at hand” (2 Tim. 4:6). Whoever, therefore, has meditated on dissolving himself through abstinence cannot fear the day of his passion.

13. And he rightly says “a vehement spirit,” since he is about to speak of ships. He called bodies “ships,” because they are driven by the wandering waves of various passions and quickly sink unless they have a helmsman.

Therefore elsewhere also he says: “Those who go down to the sea in ships” (Ps. 106:23). They sail well who carry Christ’s cross before them in their ships as a mast and from it observe the blasts of the winds, so that they may direct their bodies toward the grace of the Holy Spirit, safe and secure upon the Lord’s wood.

They do not allow their ships to wander upon the seas in aimless waves, but strive toward the harbor of salvation and toward the completion of grace by directing their course, so that they may obtain a faithful anchorage. Once released, they will be able to recover their course in the resurrection, where they cannot fear shipwreck.

14. Let us, then, also contemplate this grace; let us be its observers and explore it, so that our bodies may become the ships of Tarshish.

The flesh is then reduced to servitude when we direct ourselves toward the grace of God, so that we follow what is bitter for a time, such as fasting, and not what is sweet and voluntary.

Tarshish, therefore, is the watchtower of grace, the intelligible city, like the higher Zion. Jonah was hastening toward it. Scripture says of it that Jehoshaphat was associated with King Ahaziah [Note: [Col. 1151D] The Roman edition alone reads: “with King Ahaziah, and it seemed good that they should make ships and go to Tarshish.”]—or, as the text here has it, with King Uzziah—and so it pleased him that ships should be made and go to him at Tarshish.

But because he joined himself to an impious man, a prophet was sent to him to say: “The Lord has destroyed your work, and your ships have been broken, and they were unable to go to Tarshish” (2 Chron. 20:35–37).

This signifies that the bodies of those who transgress God’s command cannot arrive at the completion of grace.

But ships from Tarshish came to Solomon, as to a wise and peaceful man, carrying gold, silver, and ivory tusks, without any hindrance, and he himself sent ships there. For he had with King Hiram a spiritual exchange of sacred commerce and an affection for reciprocal grace striving together.

Those, therefore, who possess royal authority within themselves for restraining bodily ferocity, seeing these ships transformed from corruptible things into incorruptible, from things stained into things shining with the highest light of grace, from things dissolved and worn out into things renewed, living from the dead and rising from the buried, celebrate them in solemn speech.

15. (Verse 9.) “As we have heard, so we have seen, in the city of the Lord of powers, in the city of our God; God founded it forever.”

“We heard” outside the city; “we saw” within the city, whose light is the eternal God, where day shines without the worldly sun and the moon is not sought. Its foundation is not temporal but eternal.

16. (Verse 10.) “We have received,” he says, “your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple.”

If this is said to the Son of God, we understand the temple according to what he himself said about his body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

Truly the body of Christ is the temple of God, in which the purification of our sins is found. Truly that flesh is the temple of God in which there could be no contagion of sin; but for the offense of the whole world it was itself the sacrifice.

Truly that flesh is the temple of God in which the image of God shone and the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily, because Christ himself is the fullness.

Therefore it is said to him: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple.” What is this except what he says: “There stands among you one whom you do not know” (John 1:26)? That is, he is in your midst and is not seen.

But if it is referred to the Father, what is meant by “in the midst of your temple” except that “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself”?

17. “In that temple,” he says, “we have received your mercy”—that is, the Word that became flesh and dwelt among us.

For just as Christ is redemption, so he is also mercy. And what mercy is greater than that he offered himself to be sacrificed for our crimes, so that by his blood he might wash the world, whose sin [Note: [Col. 1151D] Since this passage teaches that the sin of the world could be removed in no other way than by Christ’s blood, it must be understood from the standpoint of the world itself: namely, that no pure creature existed who could at least fully and perfectly make satisfaction either for the common sin or for his own, as the theologians commonly affirm. From the standpoint of God, however, St. Thomas, in part III, question 46, article 2, demonstrates on Augustine’s authority that although this was the most fitting mode of human liberation, God absolutely was not without another way by which he could have redeemed the world. We do not think Ambrose would have denied this. For the limits of divine power and wisdom should not be set so narrowly as certain people, even among Catholics, do in our own age, more boldly than prudently. Certainly, in the following Psalm, verse 8, the holy Doctor denies the ability to redeem sins only to the ordinary sinful human being.] could not have been removed in any other way?

For if the Apostle said of holy men: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (1 Cor. 3:16), how much more should I call the flesh of the Lord Jesus the temple of God, of whom it is always read that he was full of the Holy Spirit, and who himself testifies, saying: “I perceive that power has gone out from me” (Luke 8:46)—the power that healed the bitter wounds of all?

It can also be understood that he said that he and the people received the mercy of God in the midst of his temple, because he himself founded and extended his Church forever. For he truly, together with his only-begotten Son, bestowed this grace upon his people, whom he also demonstrated to be its builder, saying: “He will build my city” (Isa. 45:13).

Spread throughout the whole world, this Church caused the whole earth to be full of his praise and his name. For just as it is written, “The earth is full of his praise” (Hab. 3:3), so it is written: “He has been given the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:9 ff.).

18. (Verse 11.) Therefore the Prophet properly said: “According to your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth; your right hand is full of righteousness.”

It is no wonder if the one who is the right hand of God is full of the righteousness of God. The power of God and the righteousness of God are the same, so that you may know that, inasmuch as he is full of the righteousness of God, the fullness of righteousness that the Father possesses is in him.

And inasmuch as he is read to be the power, righteousness, and wisdom of God the Father, understand that nothing in him is different from the divine majesty. Rather, recognize that the Son has received everything from the Father and that the Son is the radiance of all the Father’s glory and the imprint of his substance. He expressed the Father so perfectly that the Father is wholly in him, just as the Son is wholly in the Father.

[Col. 1153C] 19. (Verse 12.) And because the Prophet saw in the Spirit that the praises of Christ were to be proclaimed throughout all the earth, as though making an epilogue and bringing the course of his discourse to its conclusion, he urges us toward joy and worship of his name, saying:

“Let Mount Zion rejoice”—that is, those who trust in the Lord, as he later interpreted it himself, saying: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion,” and so forth (Ps. 124:1).

The Lord Jesus himself, who is the mountain and height of his Church, which contemplates its Christ with its whole devotion, should rejoice in the faith and devotion of the Church, which has pleased God, because the faithless one has been rejected.

This too can therefore be understood piously, because he himself is the mountain above all others, to which the one who proclaims the faith is commanded to ascend, as Scripture says: “Ascend a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” [Col. 1153D] (Isa. 40:9).

20. “Let the souls,” he says, “who confess to you exult.”

[Note: [Col. 1153D] Here, as in several other places, an interpretation is given in place of the text of Scripture. Since “Judah” and “Judea,” as has already been noted, signify confession, the holy man therefore calls those whom Scripture calls the daughters of Judah, or of Judea, “confessing souls” and “daughters of confession.”]

They are the daughters of that Judea in which God is known. For that Judea which exists in the flesh or in the letter did not recognize the Lord. If it had recognized him, it would also have received him. But it did not recognize the one whom it did not receive, and it rejected his judgments—those by which he declared that they derived not from the father Abraham but from the seed of the devil, since every sin is the seed of the enemy.

The daughters of confession, however, do not commit sin but cover it. Therefore: “Blessed are those whose sins are covered.”

And rightly the daughters of confession will exult because of the Lord’s judgments, when they have come to know his judgments and his ways, which in this age are inscrutable and unsearchable to human beings. When they begin to behold the truth face to face, then they will comprehend those things that now seem inscrutable, and they will rejoice in their knowledge.

Source/review notes: The supplied source ends at Psalm 48, section 23; no section 24 text was supplied.

21. (Verse 13.) “Surround Zion,” he says, “and embrace her; tell it upon her towers.” Those who understand Zion surround her and embrace her with their minds, so that they may hold her fast and not release her, lest the discipline of watchfulness in virtue be taken away from them. Therefore she says in the Song of Songs: “I held him, and I will not let him go” (Song 3:4). She was seeking the wisdom of God and embracing the righteousness of God with the arms of charity and with the sinews, as it were, of faith and devotion—for this is the embrace of a devout mind. Let us therefore also grasp, as far as we can, the inward mysteries of truth, and write them down and fasten them in our minds, together with the power of the heavenly oracle. Moses, that man skilled in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, ascended the mountain and entered the cloud in order to learn what was covered and hidden, with Jesus as his companion; for no one without the true Jesus can grasp the uncertain and hidden things of wisdom. Therefore, in the figure of Jesus son of Nun, the coming presence of the true Savior, through whom all would become teachable by God, was signified to him—he who would open the Law and reveal the Gospel.

[Col. 1154C] 22. Those, then, who have surrounded Zion with their prudence and embraced her with their understanding, ascending her towers, tell from above him who cannot ascend her towers what must be done and what must be avoided. For the city of God is fortified with walls; therefore the Lord says elsewhere: “Behold, I, Jerusalem, have painted your walls” (Isa. 49:16). It is distinguished by towers from which an enemy may be detected if he begins to approach. He has his armies, with which he is accustomed to besiege God’s souls and bring up siege engines, so that he may be able to storm the fortified towers. “But you,” he says, “proclaim from the towers”; for there is abundance in the towers of Jerusalem. Proclaim righteousness; admonish them to keep watch. Wisdom is sung at the exit and proclaimed from the highest parts of the walls. And again, elsewhere, he says: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; by day and by night they shall never be silent” (Isa. 62:6). Tell it, therefore, without interruption and without end. The adversary keeps watch and prowls around, seeking in bestial rage whom he may find to devour. Therefore the Lord must always be sung—he who crushes the lions’ teeth and breaks their jaws—so that they may not be able to harm us.

23. (Verses 14–15.) “Set your hearts upon his strength,” he says—that is, so that you may understand his strength—“and distribute his steps, so that you may recount them to another generation. For this is God, our God forever and unto the age of ages; he himself will govern us forever.”

The Greek has *Βάρεις* (*bareis*), that is, lofty and towered houses. Hence, when the Prophet was speaking of the city of God and those who dwell in it, he says: “Distribute her steps,” that is, her high and exalted dwellings in the heavenly places. By this he teaches that the order of merits must be preserved. For “each person in his own order” (John 14:2). Hence the Lord also says that he is going away to prepare dwelling places for his disciples, so that each may obtain a habitation suited to the measure of his merits, in which he may enjoy that eternal rest.

24. There are also sublime and lofty commandments in which the hidden mysteries of piety and the doctrines of heavenly utterances are contained. “Distribute these,” he says, “and divide them according to each person’s capacity, insofar as each can comprehend them by his own understanding.” For Paul did not discuss the same matters with everyone. To some he preached nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified—not with persuasive words of wisdom, but with a demonstration of the Spirit and of power. Among the perfect, however, he spoke wisdom, because the whole people was not capable of receiving the wisdom hidden in the mystery.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “was not able.” The other editions and all the manuscripts read, “was not capable,” that is, “was not capable of receiving.” Thus here and in many other places we recognize Ambrose’s meaning in the Roman edition; nevertheless, we retain the ancient wording.]

945 25. Therefore Christ hid it, so that fools would not understand it, while the prudent would seek it more diligently and recount it to another generation, which would be more perfect through the power of the Spirit. For the earlier generation, because of the weakness of its faith, could not know the mysteries of perfect wisdom. Thus it sought a sign and rejected the truth, although it is not the truth that belongs to the sign, but the sign that belongs to the truth. Therefore the Lord answered it: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matt. 12:39).

To expose the faithlessness of the Jews, then, the example of Jonah is invoked, because the Ninevites believed the sign and thought that the preaching of Jonah, who had been in the belly of the sea-monster, ought to be followed. The Jews, however, did not believe even after the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, who rose after three days from the heart of the earth and lives and reigns throughout all ages. Amen.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 48

Its title is: “For the end; for the sons of Korah; a Psalm of David.”

[Col. 1155]

## 1. (Verses 1–2.)

945 “Hear these things, all nations; give ear, all you who inhabit the world.” At the very beginning we recognize the voice of the saving Lord calling the nations to the Church, so that they may renounce error, follow the truth, and acknowledge the offering of devout worship. But because the hearts of the human race were infected with the serpent’s poison, and because conscience, burdened with sins and despairing of pardon, could not recall itself, he promises a remedy and freely offers forgiveness through the generosity of his compassion, so that the guilty person may not fear, while the person of good conscience may rejoice that he renders the service of obedience to a good master who knows how to pardon sins and honor virtues.

Finally, in the same sequence of calling, the Lord also exhorts us in the Gospel, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:28–29). Then he declares that his yoke is easy and his burden light, because one who has despaired of a remedy cannot be healthy. Therefore gentleness is pleasing to all, since it heals the wounds of the inner souls.

[Col. 1155D] 2. Since he was coming to the sick, coming as a physician to cure our grievous sores, he offers medicines so that people may see them and hasten with faithful diligence to the remedy of salvation. Thus the woman in the Gospel who had suffered from an issue of blood for twelve years obtained healing. She heard that the physician had come and hastened to touch him, saying: “If I touch his fringe, I shall be saved” (Matt. 9:20–21). She said this within herself, and Christ heard it; she touched his fringe, and power went forth from the Savior, healing the sick woman, strengthening the infirm, stopping the flow of blood, and proving her devotion.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “he offers them, so that people may hear.”]

Likewise here he calls all nations to the fountain of wisdom and prudence. He promises redemption to all, so that no one may tremble and no one despair, since no one is excluded; rather, every soul is invited to grace, so that it may be redeemed from guilt without payment and attain the fruit of eternal life.

## 3.

This is the sense of the psalm, which we shall arrange in its proper order after we have explained the force and character of the preceding words. The nations are commanded to hear, and those who inhabit the world are commanded to give ear. It is that world of which he said above: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness; the world and those who dwell in it. He founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers” (Ps. 23:1–2). The Greeks call it *οἰκουμένη* (*oikoumenē*), because it is inhabited by Christ, just as he himself said: “For I will dwell in them.” He dwells in it in order to fill what seemed empty.

What, then, is the *οἰκουμένη* if not the holy Church, the temple of God and the dwelling-place of Christ? The Latins, not incongruously, have named it the world, although in a different expression but with the same meaning, because the life of the saints who are inhabited by the Spirit rolls around like a wheel in its orbit without any impediment to its course.

[Col. 1157A] 4. The Church, then, is founded amid tribulations, storms and tempests, anxieties and sorrow; it is prepared amid adversity and rivers. In what rivers? Hear him saying: “The rivers have lifted up their voice” (Ps. 92:3). Hear also in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive (John 7:38–39).

The Church, then, is prepared in these rivers, in which the grace of God flows forth. These are the rivers that hear the word of God with the ear and speak, so that they may pour the word into the breasts of each person. Therefore Scripture made a distinction when it said: “Hear these things, all nations; give ear, all you who inhabit the world.” All can hear, but not all can give ear, except God’s elect. Therefore the Savior says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8).

He speaks of the spiritual ears of the inner person, whose nostrils also we read of when Job says: “The divine spirit that is in my nostrils” (Job 27:3). Not all people have these ears and these nostrils. One form belongs to the body; another belongs to spiritual grace. The spiritual person hears all things and judges all things, but the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God. The one is earthly; the other heavenly.

## 5. (Verse 3.)

Therefore he added: “Both you who are earthly and you sons of men, rich and poor together in one.” He says this in order to call everyone.

What is the earthly person if not the son of man? What is the spiritual person if not the Son of God?

[Note: The Roman edition, together with an old marginal reading and two manuscripts, has: “He was formed from blood and from flesh.”]

The former is formed from blood and generated from the pleasure of flesh and man; the latter is born from God. One is rich in every word and in knowledge; another is poor, yet rich in grace, because “the poor man cried, and the Lord heard him.”

[Note: So read the editions and the Victorius and Colbertinus manuscripts; the Regius manuscript has: “Another is poor in grace. Yet because …” Four others have: “Another is poor in grace. Nevertheless, you have that the poor man also cried,” etc.]

On the other hand, someone may be rich in pride and poor in humility. All are called to the Church, so that all may be redeemed by Christ. The sick person finds a physician; the healthy person acquires wisdom; the captive finds a redeemer; the free person finds one who rewards him. Divine Scripture builds everyone up. In it each person finds either what may heal his wounds or what may confirm his merits.

The calling of rich and poor together, in one, summons us to a certain humility and equality, so that the rich may not despise the poor, nor the poor envy the rich; rather, one grace may join both to one another, because the Lord also became poor although he was rich, so that he might be both the Savior of the poor and of the rich.

## 6. (Verse 4.)

And he continued: “My mouth shall speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart shall speak prudence.” It is rightly that all are called, because the fountain of wisdom overflows for everyone and is not compared with a monetary treasure; indeed, it is declared more precious than every treasure. Therefore neither is the rich person turned away nor the poor excluded, because wisdom does not distinguish between resources but between wills. The one who is first in desire and nearest to discipline is the more suitable.

If the meditation of the heart speaks prudence, how much more does perfect teaching! We are also warned not to utter speech hastily, but to examine what is to be said by a certain exercise of meditation and by the inner balance of the mind, because it is written elsewhere:

[Note: The Roman edition alone has: “A false balance is an abomination to the Lord, and a deceitful yoke is not good before me.” It wished to restore the complete passage, of which Ambrose had offered only the final part. See the same passage below, col. 966, no. 31.]

“A false balance is not good” (Prov. 20:23).

## 7. (Verse 5.)

“I shall incline my ear to a parable; I shall open my proposition upon the psaltery.” The wise listener pays attention and inclines his ear in order to understand the figures of parables. The Savior calls himself that very ear—the one who has an ear to hear. The Lord also opens his closed proposition when he finds a suitable instrument and a vessel of election, which he calls a psaltery.

Paul, resembling it, resounded the song of sweet grace, with all his strings singing together; striking the inner and outer chord with the plectrum of the Holy Spirit, so that he prayed both with tongue and with mind. Therefore he says: “I shall pray with the spirit, and I shall pray also with the mind; I shall sing psalms with the spirit, and I shall sing psalms also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15).

Christ had promised such a man long beforehand, through whom he would make manifest hidden things and open what had been wrapped in the obscurity of prophetic speech. The psaltery is good when the life of faith agrees with it, when the flesh responds to the soul, and the will aspires to virtue. This is the sweet psaltery, in which the discipline of living is tuneful, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “The tongue of the mute shall speak clearly” (Isa. 33:6).

## 8. (Verse 6.)

It follows: “Why should I fear in the evil day? The iniquity of my heel will surround me.” That is: when my mouth speaks wisdom and the meditation of my heart speaks prudence, what can I fear on the day of judgment—unless perhaps the iniquity of my heel must be washed away?

(Compare Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book 1, chapter 3.)

One iniquity is ours; another is the iniquity of our heel, in which Adam was wounded by the serpent’s tooth and, through his wound, left a liable inheritance to the succession of the human race, so that we all limp because of that wound. Therefore the Lord washed the disciples’ feet in order to wash away the serpent’s poisons, and Peter is reproved because he refused to let the Lord wash his feet. Thus it was said to him: “Unless I wash your feet, you will have no part with me” (John 13:8).

When he heard this, he offered not only his feet but also his hands to be washed. The Lord answered him:

[Col. 1158D] “The one who has been washed does not need to wash again, except his feet; but is entirely clean” (ibid., 10).

## 9.

Therefore David says: “My iniquities have risen above my head” (Ps. 38:5), for he knew that he had been conceived in iniquity and generated in sins by his mother.

But the Lord, who had no sins of his own and knew no personal iniquities, says: “The iniquity of my heel will surround me”—that is, the iniquity of Adam, not mine.

[Note: This concerns adult believers, who are to undergo judgment not on account of original sin but on account of actual sins. The statement that the iniquity of the heel signifies more the slipperiness of sinning than some guilt belonging to our sin means, evidently, what was later decreed in the Council of Trent, session 5, final canon: that concupiscence is called sin by the Apostle not because it is truly and properly sin in the regenerate, but because it is from sin and inclines toward sin. Compare this passage with what Augustine teaches in book 2, chapter 40, *On Grace and Original Sin*. There will be another opportunity elsewhere to discuss this matter.]

But that iniquity cannot be a terror to me, for on the day of judgment the crimes that are ours in us, not another’s iniquity, are punished. Hence I judge that the iniquity of the heel signifies more the slipperiness of sinning than some guilt belonging to our sin.

Rightly, therefore, the Lord, who assumed everything on our behalf, says: “Let us wash our feet,” so that we may be able to remove the slipperiness of the heel, in order that the station of virtues may be secure, and that no one who is prepared to stand by his own resolve may slip through his ancestral error. Let the person who desires to keep the footprint of virtue not fear the slipperiness of inheritance.

The iniquity of our heel, then, is Adam’s transgression, through which he fell into contempt and disregard of the heavenly commandments.

[Col. 1159B] 10. There is also the iniquity of the heel: Judas’s betrayal, which must be spoken of hesitantly.

[Note: The word *haesitanda* suggests something that must be uttered hesitantly, only with a reluctant and almost unwilling tongue, as happens to those who suffer from stammering.]

It is called the heel because it is written: “The one who eats bread with me will lift his heel against me” (Ps. 41:9). He rightly said “his” there and “my” here: “his,” because Christ is without iniquity, while this is the iniquity of the betrayer alone; “my heel,” because Christ calls Judas the last part of his body, and we are Christ’s body and members.

The apostles are Christ’s more excellent and active members; Judas is the heel, as the extremity of the body, exposed to the serpent and open to injury. Adam, therefore, is the first heel; Judas the second heel. The former is the fall of the whole inheritance; the latter belongs to the betrayer alone, who could not entangle the inheritance, because we are no longer carnal but the Redeemer’s inheritance, as Scripture says:

[Note: The Roman edition alone has: “There is an inheritance for those who serve the Lord.”]

“There is an inheritance for those who believe in the Lord” (Isa. 54:17).

## 11.

There is also that iniquity of his heel which surrounded Christ: “They surrounded me on every side, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them” (Ps. 118:11). His heel is the Synagogue; the beauty and glory of his face is the Church, as it is written: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty” (Ps. 93:1).

## 12. (Verse 7.)

Those, then, are the heel of whom he says: “Those who trust in their strength and boast in the abundance of their riches.” “The rich have become poor and hungry” (Ps. 34:11). This was said about the Jews. But all who live luxuriously and do not hold fast to the head are also Christ’s heel. These are general statements that extend widely. More specifically, however, he was speaking about Judas the betrayer, to whom the glory of the apostleship seemed to make him strong and rich in himself.

## 13. (Verses 8–9.)

Finally, the discourse turns to the Lord’s Passion: “A brother does not redeem; a man will redeem. Nor will he give God his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul.” That is: “Why should I fear on the evil day?” For what can harm me, who not only have no need of a redeemer but am myself the redeemer of all? Shall I make others free and tremble for myself? Behold, I shall make all things new, surpassing even the affection and devotion of brotherhood.

A brother, poured forth into the light from the same maternal womb, cannot redeem, because he is held back by the weakness of a like nature. “A man will redeem”—but that man of whom it is written: “The Lord will send them a man who will save them” (Isa. 19:20), and who said of himself: “You seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you” (John 8:40).

But although he is a man, who will know him? Why will no one know him? Because, just as there is one God, so there is one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. He alone will redeem humanity, surpassing his brothers in devotion, because he poured out his blood for others, which no one can offer for his brother.

Therefore he did not spare his own body, in order to redeem us from sin, and he gave himself as redemption for all, as his true witness, the apostle Paul, asserts when he says: “I speak the truth; I do not lie” (Rom. 9:1).

But why will he alone redeem? Because no one can equal him in devotion, so as to lay down his life for his servants; no one in integrity, since all are under sin and all are subject to that fall of Adam. The Redeemer alone is chosen, who cannot be subject to the ancient sin.

Therefore by “man” let us understand the Lord Jesus, who assumed the condition of humanity, so that in his flesh he might crucify the sin of all and erase by his blood the bond written against everyone.

## 14.

But perhaps you will say: How is it denied that a brother will redeem, when he himself said: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. 22:22)?

He did not forgive us sins as our brother, but as the man Christ Jesus, in whom God was. For it is written: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). It was in that Christ Jesus alone of whom it was said: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

Therefore he dwelt among us not as a brother but as Lord, when he dwelt in flesh. Since he reconciled the world to God, he himself certainly had no need of reconciliation. For what sin of his would he propitiate God, since he knew no sins?
