Finally, when the Jews demanded the didrachma that was paid under the Law for sin, he said to Peter: “Simon, from whom do the kings of the earth collect tribute or tax—from their sons or from strangers?” Peter answered: “From strangers.” The Lord said to him: “Then the sons are free. But lest we give them offense, go, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; and when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it for me and for you” (Matt. 17:24ff.).

He showed that he did not owe a propitiation for sins, because he was not a servant of sin but the Son of God, free from every error. For the Son is free; the servant is under liability. Therefore this one, free from all things, does not give the price of redemption for his soul, since the price of his blood could have sufficed to redeem all the sins of the entire world. Rightly, then, he frees others, since he owes nothing for himself.

## 15. (Verse 10.)

I will add more. Christ owes no price of his redemption or propitiation for sin not only on his own behalf; even if the passage is understood of any faithful person, it may be taken to mean that individuals do not owe their own propitiation, because Christ is the propitiation of all and he himself is the redemption of all.

What person’s blood is now sufficient for his own redemption, since Christ poured out his blood for the redemption of all? Is anyone’s blood capable of being compared with Christ’s blood? Or who is so powerful that he could offer his own propitiation on top of the propitiation that Christ offered in himself, he alone having reconciled the world to God through his blood?

What sacrifice is greater? What offering more excellent? What advocate better than the one who became intercession for the sins of all and gave his soul as redemption for us?

The propitiation or redemption of individuals is therefore not sought, because the blood of Christ is the price of all. The Lord Jesus redeemed us by it, he alone reconciled the Father, and he labored to the end, because he himself assumed our labor, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor … and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28).

See him laboring: “I have labored crying out; my throat has become hoarse” (Ps. 69:4). And elsewhere: “Issachar desired what is good, resting among the strong.” And below: “He placed his shoulder under the labor, and became a husbandman” (Gen. 49:14–15).

Therefore a human being no longer gives his own propitiation or redemption, because he has once been washed from sin through the blood of Christ. Yet he will labor to keep the commandments of life and not depart from the heavenly commands. As long as he lives, let him remain in labor and persevere in it, so that he may live to the end and not himself die the death, since he has already been redeemed from death.

## 16. (Verse 11.)

But whoever keeps the commandments of life will not see destruction, even when he sees those who seemed to themselves the wisest and most prudent in this age dying. This applies especially to the scribes and Pharisees, who claim for themselves the chairs in the synagogues, as though they held the primacy of wisdom.

They truly labor in vain when they think that they are freed through the didrachma, after despising the spiritual price of their souls and that unique sacrifice of the Lord’s body through an empty interpretation of the Law, refusing the sacrament of baptism. No one has been redeemed by the blood of goats and bulls; one blood alone, the blood of Christ, frees everyone. Its figure, not its reality, is found in Leviticus. We are freed not through the didrachma but through the price of that one blood.

## 17.

Let us therefore be teachable by God, so that none of us may see destruction on that day when the wise men of this world and the rulers of the Jews will be condemned to everlasting death, when both the foolish and the senseless will perish together.

The two are not the same. The foolish person (*stultus*) is one who has no wisdom and understands foolish things; the unwise person (*insipiens*) is one who understands badly. “The unwise person has said: There is no God.” He is called wicked not because he does not know equity, but because he commits iniquities through the wickedness of his heart. He is also called evil because he wishes to destroy goodness by his malice, not because he is ignorant of goodness.

When the senseless and the foolish perish, therefore, they leave their riches to strangers, since they cannot find a legitimate heir of their own folly and wickedness. The legitimate heirs say: “Because we are children of God. But if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ, provided that we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified together” (Rom. 8:16–17).

The senseless, then, have no riches, because they have no inheritance.

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “They do not have riches in faith, not in possession.”]

The faithless do not have riches, not possessions; for to the faithful the whole world is a possession. They have no inheritance, because “there is an inheritance for those who believe in the Lord.”

[Note: The Roman edition has: “There is an inheritance for those who serve the Lord.”]

But they do have their own riches. Thus the miser says: “I have no place where I may gather my fruits” (Luke 12:17), for money is not true fruit but the miser’s fruit. And the Lord says to the miser: “Go, sell your possessions … and come; follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

Property is not perfect goodness; rather, these are the miser’s “goods,” which are established in some profit. “Sell,” he says, “what you think is yours,” although it is not yours, because such things pass to others like a river; “and follow me,” so that you may know immortal goodness.

The wise, therefore, are led into destruction—those from whom God hid the things he revealed to little ones. They will perish together and be in one and the same place, the senseless and the foolish, and they will leave their riches to strangers, because wickedness does not find a legitimate successor.

## 18. (Verse 12.)

“And their graves are their houses forever; their dwellings are for generation and generation; they have called their names upon their lands.”

Everywhere Scripture uses graves as a figure for the worthless, to whom degenerates and those devoted to this life are compared. “Their throat is an open grave” (Ps. 5:10).

For those who live only for the day and from day to day, graves are houses. The house of the righteous is not on earth but in heaven, as the Apostle taught, saying: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). That is our house, which is the house of Christ.

Therefore Scripture says: “Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of the things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a son over his own house” (Heb. 3:5–6). For the devout, the house is the Church; for the devout, heaven is the homeland. Therefore the righteous person says: “I am a sojourner with you on earth and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 39:12).

For the luxurious, a grave is a house. Indeed, they live as though in a grave, able to say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. 22:13), having no resurrection before their eyes. Therefore they cling to and remain fixed in their own tombs, because they did not believe that they could be raised.

Their dwelling, then, is in their own tomb, and their dwelling-place is earthly, from generation to generation.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “They are earthly, leaving the worms of their bodies as heirs,” etc.]

They leave the worms of their bodies as heirs, so that their memory may exist only here and may never pass into eternity.

## 19.

Finally, “their names are upon their lands,” because their works are corruptible and earthly. Therefore their names are written there where they preferred to live.

But to those who raised up their works it is said: “Do not rejoice because the demons are subject to you; but rejoice because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

From this, then, let us understand that the Lord did not rebuke without reason those who built graves or tombs for themselves, or the tombs of the prophets, and adorned them (Matt. 23:28). The Jews are condemned because, for the prophets whom they had killed, they offered earthly consolations, not eternal rewards.

Therefore he forbids his disciple to bury his father (Matt. 8:22), because he must remain continually intent upon the eternal Father. And in the book of Isaiah it is written: “Why,” he says, “have you built and cut out a tomb for yourself?” (Isa. 22:6).

Mary too is reproved when she sought Christ in the tomb. Leave behind the graves that were left by those who, having heard the Lord’s voice, rose from their tombs during his Passion. Do not dwell among the dead, you who live.

Hear the voice of Jesus raising the dead: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ’s light will shine upon you” (Eph. 5:14). Another light of his is the Holy Spirit, who shone upon the holy apostles in the distribution of languages like fire.

## 20. (Verses 13–14.)

It follows: “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them. This is their way, a stumbling-block to them; and afterward they will be pleased in their mouth.”

Because a human being did not understand when he was in honor—and honor consists in this, that he was made in the image of God and made capable of reason—he was compared with beasts that have no understanding. But the one who understood is compared with angels.

Therefore one is glorified by the splendor of good works; the other is regarded like a neighing horse, through the filth of a way of life that brings a stumbling-block to those who live in shame and obscenity. The foolishness of a man defiles his ways.

Such people live according to their appetite, which creates a stumbling-block, and afterward they will be pleased in their mouth, but not in their heart. They are not the good, of whom it is said: “With their mouth they blessed, but with their heart they cursed” (Ps. 62:5).

This is also the answer to those who have the following written in their books: “And afterward they will bless in their mouth.” For “the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.”

## 21. (Verse 15.)

“Like sheep they will be led down to the underworld; death will feed upon them. And the righteous will rule over them in the morning; and their help will grow old in the underworld, away from their glory.”

Those who did not want Christ to feed them will be fed upon by death. Who, then, would abandon the good shepherd, who lays down his life for his sheep, because the care of his flock belongs to him? Or who would choose a mercenary death, which is returned as the deserving reward of evil works?

Recognize at the same time, O human being, that Christ is the true shepherd, who feeds his own to life. Death entered, bringing strangers to destruction and devouring those whom it can overcome because of their crimes. Although in this life they may have devoted themselves to power and riches, so that they might rule over others, in the resurrection there will be servitude, when the morning splendor shines upon the righteous.

Their figure is that Jacob is placed as lord over his brother.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript and four Gallican manuscripts have: “He is placed before his wretched brother.” Hence the text continues: “Therefore a wretched servitude,” etc.]

A wretched servitude, then, when at the time that others are called into the glory of splendor and light, the glory of these people grows old and is consumed in the darkness of the underworld. Rightly it is said of them: “They have been expelled from their honor and their glory,” because this glory is temporal.

## 22. (Verse 16.)

“Nevertheless,” he says, “God will deliver my soul from the hand of the underworld when he receives it.”

He says this well, for he knew that his soul would not be abandoned in the underworld. He descended in order to release captives from the jaws of the underworld, not to remain captive among them.

## 23. (Verse 17.)

Since, then, the things that belong to this age cannot pass over with us, it is said to you: “Do not fear when a man becomes rich and when the glory of his house is multiplied.” For when he dies he will not take everything, nor will the glory of his house descend with him at the same time.

“Do not,” he says, “be terrified by the riches, power, and worldly glory of the rich, because these things are transitory and depart more quickly than they came.”

This treasure is a dream: you awaken, and it has withdrawn. When someone has been able to sleep off the drunkenness of this world and assume the sobriety of virtue, he despises these things and counts money as nothing.

Do not fear when you hear that the glory of the house of some powerful person has been multiplied. Examine carefully, and it is empty, having nothing in itself of the fullness of faith.

And why should I speak of a house? The whole world was empty before Christ filled it with the number of believers. Therefore it is written: “He will judge among the nations; he will fill the ruins” (Ps. 110:6).

For what else was there formerly in this world except the ruin of unbelief? What is ruin? Hear him saying: “Where there is ruin, there also are eagles” (Matt. 24:28)—that is, where there is ruin, there is also resurrection.

Ruin is emptiness of firmness; resurrection is the fullness of life. Therefore the ruin of that Adam emptied us, but the grace of Christ filled us. He emptied himself for this reason: that he might fill us and that the fullness of virtue might dwell in human flesh.

Understand what ruin is. While a human being lives, he is filled with spirit; when he has died, he is empty, certainly, of this vital spirit. The loss of spiritual grace makes one much more empty—one whom grace had been accustomed to fill—so that we may say: “From his fullness we have all received, and grace upon grace” (John 1:16).

Of another it is said: “I have labored in vain” (Isa. 49:4); but the righteous person is like the fragrance of a full field.

### 24. (Verse 18)

What, then, is not empty if it is worldly and belonging to this age, since he rightly said who despised this world with sober virtue: “Naked I was born, and naked I shall die” (Job 1:21)? Can anyone take away with him what he possesses? Here he leaves everything behind and enters the tomb alone; and empty is the grave of that rich man whom not even the earth itself could contain.

[Note: These words seem particularly applicable to Alexander of Macedon, whom Plutarch and Valerius Maximus report to have wept when he heard a certain philosopher discussing the infinity of worlds, because he scarcely possessed even one. Hence Juvenal says of him, *Satire* 10:

> One world is not enough for the youth of Pella.

> The unhappy man seethes within the narrow boundary of the world, etc.]

Hence it is said: “Will you alone dwell upon the earth? Shall the glory of his house or his riches descend into that grave?” (Isaiah 5:8). Observe the force of Scripture. The glory of this age does not descend with the sinner, but the glory of virtue ascends with the innocent. To put it more briefly: a person’s glory ascends with the one who ascends; with the one who descends, it does not descend. Whatever belongs to grace and virtue will ascend. One ascends into paradise; one descends into hell. “Let them descend,” he says, “alive into hell” (Psalm 54:16). Therefore poor Lazarus was lifted by angels into Abraham’s bosom.

The luxurious rich man, lifting his eyes in hell, asks Abraham to send the poor man and touch his tongue with his finger, so that, placed amid the fiercest heat, he might obtain some relief. Look at that poor man, abounding in every good, whom the blessed rest of the holy Patriarchs surrounded. Look at this man empty, who seemed to himself to abound in everything in this world, whose soul was blessed during his life; but now he is tormented by sluggish death (Luke 16:22 and following).

### 25. (Verse 19)

Accordingly, what follows is beautifully expressed: “For his soul shall be blessed during his life; he will praise you when you have done good to him.” “They will bless him,” he says, “with an earthly blessing.” Foolish are those who consider present things rather than future ones. His followers and parasites will bless him.

[Note: *Parasites* are those who flatter the powerful and the rich for the sake of food, from *para* and *sitos* (παρά and σῖτος).]

He himself also considers himself blessed if he has seized some estate that he desired. He gives thanks to God when favorable circumstances attend him in this world; but when adversity comes, he curses with an impious mouth. This, therefore, is what he says: the worldly person does not give thanks when placed in poverty and adversity; but the just person, in distress, blesses the Lord all the more with a grateful disposition.

Finally, the devil says to God: “Is it any wonder that Job blesses you? Everything is abundant for him. But stretch out your hand,” he says, “and touch what he possesses; let us see whether he will bless you to your face” (Job 1:11). And the Lord gave him power to take away the things of this world and to cover his flesh with the dreadful severity of sores. Yet Job blessed him, saying: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away . . . blessed be the name of the Lord” (ibid., 21).

### 26. (Verses 20–21)

“He shall enter into the generation of his fathers; forever he shall not see the light. Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with the beasts, which have no understanding, and became like them.”

Therefore, he says, this man will enter into the generation of his fathers. The Lord declared who is the father of the impious when he said: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44). There are also those fathers of whom it is said: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22). For this reason the Moabites were forbidden to enter the Church of the Lord even to the third and fourth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3), so that their children, on account of the sins of their fathers, would enter into the generation of those whose deeds and ways they imitated.

Hence it is also written: “The children of adulterers shall come to an end” (Wisdom 3:16).

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “shall be incomplete.”]

Therefore whoever does not follow that Father who is in heaven, but follows him who lives amid earthly filth, enters into the generation of an earthly father. For as is the earthly father, so also are his earthly offspring; thus his life is earthly, and after death there is no rest. “Forever he shall not see the light,” because he sought what is temporary.

But the one who followed Christ’s glory, who desired that light which enlightens every person coming into this world, will find and see eternal light, because Christ redeemed him from death.

### 27

Then he will reflect within himself that, although he was in honor, he did not understand; and therefore he will be like the beasts, though through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ he ought to have been like the angels. To him belong honor, glory, and eternity from age to age, now and always, and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 61

**Title: For the end; for Jeduthun; a psalm of David himself.**

[Col. 1165]

[Col. 1165D] 955 In the treatment of this psalm, blessed Ambrose severely rebukes the infidelity and impiety of the tyrant Maximus, who dared to destroy his lord, the emperor Gratian, by treachery and deceit. He says that this emperor dwells in the Lord’s tabernacle and rests upon his mountain.

### 1. (Verse 1)

It is the unquestionable habit of all of us to hurry toward the end and to wish to know the substance of what we have read, seen, or heard. Hence the title itself does not permit us to remain idle, nor does it allow us to pass by with inattentive ears the indication of a common desire.

For, above all—although it also shines clearly in other matters—the divine oracle particularly radiates in this kind of psalm. Let us therefore consider more carefully what “the end” is. The end is called *telos* (τέλος), the sum or completion of the matter that we wish to explain.

Christ is called the end because he himself is the end of the Law, as it is written: “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4). He is also called the end because he is both beginning and end.

Therefore those psalms that bear the title “For the end” are either about Christ or belong to Christ: about Christ when he himself is announced; belonging to Christ when he himself announces himself and promises that he will come upon the earth, and graciously reveals to us the future passion of his own body.

### 2

For this reason they are inscribed in the title “of David himself,”

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “as though to David himself by the Lord,” whereas the earlier editions and several manuscripts assign them “through the ministry of the prophetic mouth.” More manuscripts, and certain Paris editions, read: “the ministries . . . are assigned.” This is better; the entire passage must be explained in this sense: as though the singing of prophetic psalms were attributed to the Lord himself, who is the true David. Yet the sense is not without value if one retains the word “ministry.”]

as though the ministries of the prophetic mouth were assigned to David himself, that is, to the Lord, through whom the heavenly power rebuked by the service of human speech and the divine judgment resounded.

### 3

And appropriately, “for Jeduthun,” who was a prophet and sang psalms with his six sons,

[Note: You may find their names in 1 Chronicles 25:3.]

is like a kind of preface, since forgiveness was to be proclaimed for those who, established in the ministry of singing psalms, spoke divine oracles with a human voice.

And because the passion of the Lord’s body had to be undertaken for the destruction of the error of the whole world, he expressed a more commendable instruction for the people under the name of one whose devotion was approved. Therefore let us listen to him speaking.

### 4. (Verse 2)

“Will not my soul be subject to God?”

Our Lord Jesus was about to assume human flesh in order to cleanse it in himself. What, then, ought he to abolish first, if not the original contagion of the ancient sin? Since guilt had entered through disobedience, when the divine commandments were treated with contempt, he surely ought above all to restore obedience, so that he might exclude the seedbed of error.

For the root-fiber of sin had flowed from that source; therefore, like a good physician, he ought first to cut away the roots of the ulcer, so that the openings of the wound might feel the health-giving remedy of the medicines. For you will have treated the scar in vain if the interior contagion continues to spread; indeed, the wound is aggravated if it is closed externally while the poison boils within.

For what good was it to forgive sin if the inclination to sin remained? This was not to heal the scar but to close it. Therefore he wished to cleanse the wound in order to heal the inclination, so that no trace of disobedience might remain. He himself assumed obedience in order to transmit it to us.

For it was necessary that, just as through the disobedience of one human being many had been made sinners, so through the obedience of one many might again be made righteous.

### 5

The fact therefore shows that those greatly err who say that Christ assumed human flesh but deny human feeling, and who thereby oppose the intention of the Lord Jesus himself. They remove the human being from the human being, although a human being cannot exist without human feeling.

For flesh without feeling is free both from reward and from guilt. Therefore he had to assume and heal that from which guilt had flowed, so that he might close the origin of error and the gateways of erupting sin.

How, then, would I recognize the Lord Jesus as human today, whose flesh I do not see but whose feeling I read? How, I ask, would I recognize him as human unless he had been hungry, unless he had been thirsty, unless he had wept, unless he had said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38)?

Finally, it is written: “And he is man, and who shall know him?” (Jeremiah 17:9). Yet through these things he is recognized as human, while through his divine works he is judged superior to human beings.

Accordingly, although he was God, he wished to be believed to be human to such an extent that he called himself human, saying: “Why do you seek to kill me, a man who have spoken the truth to you?” (John 8:40). Nor did he call himself merely human; he also called himself the Son of Man, as he says: “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” (Matthew 16:13).

Therefore the one who recognized both the Son of God and the human being was declared to possess the fullness of faith. He himself is both at once, inseparable in number and to be recognized by the distinction of his works, not by a difference of persons.

For one is not from the Father and another from Mary; rather, he who was from the Father took flesh from the Virgin and assumed human feeling from his mother, so that he himself might take upon him our weaknesses. Hence the Prophet says: “And he suffers for us” (Isaiah 53:4). How could he suffer with my suffering if he did not bear my feeling? “A man,” he says, “in affliction and knowing how to bear weakness” (ibid., 3).

### 6

Thus he was weakened as a human being and suffered as a human being; and we considered him to be human in his sufferings. Yet, as victor over weaknesses and not conquered by them, he suffered for us, not for himself. He was weakened not on account of his own sins but on account of ours, so that he might heal us by his bruise.

What else is meant by “a man in affliction and knowing how to bear weakness” except that he had compassion for affliction? Or how did he know how to bear weakness if he had excluded the experience of weakness? What we carry, we endure as a burden.

Therefore he assumed our sins in order to bear them; he also assumed them in order to cleanse them. Finally, it is written:

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “And he himself cleansed the sins of many.”]

“And he himself cleansed their sins.” Therefore “he himself shall possess many as his inheritance, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong” (ibid., 11–12). For the greater triumph is where the inner mind is cleansed.

What he bears, therefore, pertains to forgiveness; what he cleanses pertains to correction. Accordingly, he assumed our compassion and also our subjection. For that he subjected all things to himself is his; that he was subjected is ours.

Therefore he says: “Will not my soul be subject to God?” He says “soul” subject, not divinity; “soul” subjected, not the power of God. For the power of God is not subject to authority, but makes use of its unity and fellowship.

[Note: All editions and most manuscripts read: “not subject to authority, but to unity,” and so forth. The other reading is better: “but in unity,” and so forth.]

That is subject which is often changed by the frailty of the human condition, not that which cannot be changed. The soul has compassion on the flesh, and the flesh on the soul, since they are joined together in a kind of shared dwelling.

That is subject which is sorrowful, because it is written: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38). That is subject which was assumed, not born from God the Father. Yet this subjection is not indeed in the appearance of weakness, but in the exercise of power; it is rather the witness of a temporary dispensation than enslaved to perpetual servitude.

[Note: *Arbitra* means “witness”; through this subjection of Christ’s soul, the human dispensation of redemption was manifested, since from it we understand that the divine plan of repairing the disobedience of the first Adam through the obedience of the second was fulfilled. Or perhaps *arbitra* has here something of the sense of “moderator,” because the soul of the Lord Christ accepted that dispensation not under compulsion but willingly. For “he was offered because he himself willed it,” as Isaiah 53:7 prophesies.]

Hence he also says: “Will not my soul be subject to God?”

### 7

Why did he say “will be,” if the subjection is eternal? Because the Son of God who was speaking is eternal, whereas he assumed a soul in time; therefore he speaks of the future subjection of his soul.

Through that soul, therefore, came obedience; through it, humility. Yet these were assumed not as a weakness of power but for the instruction of discipline. For the Lord Jesus, although he was in the form of God, “did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Philippians 2:6–8).

As the Apostle says, he wished to declare not an unceasing and eternal subjection but a temporary one: the kind assumed with the flesh and laid aside with the servitude of the body itself.

[Note: The Son of God assumed subjection with the body, but did not lay it aside together with the body, because what he once assumed he never abandoned. He laid it aside together with the body’s servitude when, having shaken off the yoke of mortality, the body rose again endowed with the gifts of immortality.]

The same is also written in the Letter to the Hebrews. For after setting forth the example, saying: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek,” Paul added: “Who in the days of his flesh offered prayers and supplications to him who was able to save him from death, with a loud cry and tears; and he was heard because of his reverence. Although he was a Son, he learned obedience from the things he suffered; and, having been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, being called by God a priest according to the order of Melchizedek” (Hebrews 5:6–10).

Did the Apostle not clearly proclaim that this obedience and humility belonged not to divinity but to the flesh? For what is learned is temporal. As a human being, therefore, he learned obedience from the things he suffered, so that he might be perfected in the flesh and, through the succession of obedience transmitted to us, become the cause of eternal salvation for us, for whom that first Adam had previously become the cause of death through the inheritance of disobedience.

### 8

Subjection, therefore, is the instruction of human virtue, not a diminution of divine power. For if they say that the Son is lesser than and unequal to the Father because he was subject to God the Father, was he also lesser than his mother because he was subject to his mother? For it is read of Joseph and Mary: “And he was subject to them” (Luke 2:51).

But piety is for all of us not a loss but an increase, through which the Lord Jesus infused faith and grace into us all, so that he might make us subject to God the Father by a faithful spirit.

Therefore the Apostle says, with a new and profound plan, that he himself will be subject to the Father in us when there is fullness of faith in all things and a certain unity of devotion. For now, as long as we disagree in our judgments, we in a way diminish Christ’s kingdom, because not yet are all things subject to him, whose kingdom is unity.

“But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also will be subject to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28), as it is written.

Now he is above all by power, but it is necessary that he be in all by will. He will so be when he recognizes that all things in us are filled with him and empty of sins.

Therefore Christ is not yet subject to the Father, because Christ is not yet all things and in all things. But when Christ is all things and in all things, God will be all things and in all things.

From this it follows that the kingdom of the Father and of the Son and also of the Holy Spirit is one, because whoever receives the Son receives the Father and receives the Holy Spirit, since the Trinity has one power, one grace, and one operation.

### 9

And appropriately the Lord added: “For from him comes my salvation.” It is as though he were saying: Do not be troubled because I said that my soul would be subject to God. The soul will be subject, for it is a portion of you; but my salvation is from him—that is, because I am always from the Father and in the Father.

For I came from the Father into this world. Although you see a human being, believe in the Son of God. “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from my Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from my Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:26).

The Son proceeds from the Father, and the Spirit proceeds from him. Therefore there is no ambiguity concerning the unity of divinity.

For this reason David desired that this salvation of God be given to us, because it is eternal life, if we also recognize the Father as the true God and the Son, who certainly came for our salvation. Yet he “did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.” He sets aside the assertion of his divinity and represents the office of the human dispensation.

### 10. (Verse 3)

Therefore he immediately added: “For he himself is my God, my helper, and my defender; I shall not be moved any further.”

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “My God and my Savior.” So also below, in section 18. This is evidently taken from the Septuagint, where one reads Θεός μου καὶ σωτήρ μου, “my God and my Savior,” and so forth.]

He speaks here as a human being, since we ought to place our hope in God so that we may not easily fall. Yet in what he said, “I shall not be moved any further,” he shows that he possesses the marks of divine power.

For elsewhere you have him saying: “Yet once more I will shake the earth” (Haggai 2:7). He shook it in the flood, when every creature of flesh perished except those in Noah’s ark. He shook it when Sodom and Gomorrah were consumed by sacred fire. These are signs of heavenly indignation.

But because the Lord chose rather to preserve the human race than to destroy it, he will no longer be moved to indignation, since he came for mercy. He came to redeem us with his blood, not to shed ours. He came to offer himself for us and, like a good merchant, to preserve his merchandise through the passion of his own body.

### 11. (Verse 4)

When he said this, he lifted up his eyes and saw on one side the persecutors and on the other the spiritual powers of wickedness joining together, and he said: “How long will you rush upon one man, killing everyone?”

That is: Why do you hasten to destroy the human race? Do you not know that I have come as a human being for the redemption of all? I offered myself for everyone, so that I might protect all by my offering.

We may understand “one man” as referring to the entire human multitude; or, if we take it of one individual, we understand it as said of him himself: “You rush upon him, but upon a human being,” because you cannot rush upon God, as you have elsewhere: “Why do you seek to kill me, a human being?” (John 8:40).

For divinity could not be subject to death, but only the humanity that was assumed. If, then, you rush upon me and wish to seize me, why do you wish to kill those who are with me? It is enough for you to have the one whom you seek. I do not seek a companion in suffering, since I need no helper for the salvation of all.

I do not seek an envoy; I do not send a messenger in advance. Rather, I myself, as messenger, offered myself to those who were not seeking me; I surrendered myself to those who were not apprehending me, so that I might free those who had been seized by the snares of death.

Therefore you rush upon me like a leaning wall and a tottering fence, unaware that I came not to make the wall lean or to drive down the fence, but to undo them. I came as peace, to make both one, dissolving the middle wall of the fence that divided flesh and soul, so that they could not share one understanding.

For this reason the flesh resisted the soul and could not be subject to its command, because, obstructed by the barrier of the intervening wall, it could not obey its governance.

### 12

The law of the flesh, therefore, opposed the law of the mind. The Lord Jesus removed this wall of ancient enmities like a rampart and made the gatherings of mind and flesh accessible, so that, coming together as one, they might pursue what was beneficial to both.

The wall is therefore a certain elevation of sins. Hence Paul says to the Jewish high priest: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall” (Acts 23:3), for a wall is constructed with mud and mortar.

With these materials the Egyptians built cities when the Jews were compelled to make bricks. In Egypt mud was prepared, and there the people of God were working at sin. Therefore they groaned; therefore they were heard and delivered from sin.

For this reason the Law was given and grace promised: so that the Law might cut away sin in part, while grace might forgive everything.

### 13. (Verse 5)

While he was granting these things to us and undertaking these things for us, we were rejecting his price. Therefore he says: “Yet they planned to reject my price,” when Judas the betrayer was returning the price and the Jews refused to put it into the treasury, saying: “It is not lawful for us to put it into the treasury, because it is the price of blood” (Matthew 27:6).

The betrayer is condemned by his own judgment. He returned the price he had received, weak as a witness to the sacred offering but strong as a witness against his own crime. For everyone is a more serious accuser of himself, and each person carries within himself an inescapable sentence against himself.

The rulers of the Synagogue condemn themselves by their own judgment. For they declare that the price they gave was the price of blood when they blame the one who returned it. If it was not lawful to receive it, it was not lawful to pay it either. Would that they had either not given it or, having given it, had not received it back!

They rejected what they refused to put into the treasury, and with it they bought a field for the burial of foreigners. Therefore the Gentiles, for whom the field purchased by Christ’s death became useful as a burial place, are no longer strangers and foreigners; they have become fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household, because they are buried together with the Son of God.

But the Jews, who rejected the price of his passion, wander far from Christ. In this respect the betrayer is more tolerable to them, because he confesses his error; they, however, aggravate their crime by excusing it.

Confession after sin is indeed more modest. Thus shamelessly they rejected the one who confessed their common sacrilege, saying: “What is that to us? You see to it yourself” (ibid., 4).

For what was the betrayer saying except this: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (ibid.)? If it was the crime of the one who handed him over, how could it not also be the sin of those who received him, since crime was joined to crime, so that the one whom they had wickedly purchased they might murder even more wickedly?

### 14

“I ran in thirst,” he says.

It is true that our Lord Jesus thirsted. Blessed is the Lord’s thirst, because he thirsted for us, especially in his passion. Finally, he said: “I thirst” (John 19:28).

He thirsted at the very time when from his side he poured out streams of living water to extinguish everyone’s thirst. For it is written: “Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

But in the Greek the expression is grammatically ambiguous, because ἔδραμον (*edramon*) can signify both singular and plural. Therefore, in accordance with the Greek, we may understand both “I ran” and “they ran.”

We have already explained what “I ran” expresses: namely, “I hastened to take upon myself everyone’s thirst, so that I might satisfy all with the abundance of the everlasting fountain”—“whoever drinks the water that I shall give will never thirst, neither here nor in the future” (John 4:13), as he said to the Samaritan woman.

Now let us explain what “They ran in thirst” signifies. It means that they hastened, by denying the living fountain in the heat of their unbelief, to dry their throats with eternal aridity, just as the Lord himself says: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns” (Jeremiah 2:13).

It is no wonder that they thirsted, since through the slippery fissures of their unbelief they could not hold the water of the eternal fountain. They thirsted, therefore, because they deprived themselves of the spiritual drink that they had drawn from the rock that followed them.

Hence Symmachus says: Τῷ δόλῳ αὐτῶν εὐλόγουν, that is, “it pleased them in deceit,” when they put forward false things in place of true ones. Every lie has thirst; truth has abundance, which endures forever.

### 15

How quickly he proved that they “ran in deceit”! “With their mouth,” he says, “they blessed, but with their heart they cursed.”

Wretched is the thirst of the unbelieving, who held one thing in their hearts and spoke another with their mouths. But where the abundance of faith overflows, one believes with the heart unto righteousness, and confession is made with the mouth unto salvation.

The account of the Passion shows how they blessed with their mouths and cursed with their hearts, when they said: “Let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matthew 15:32).

Fools! He rose from death, and they did not believe; how would they have believed if he had come down from the cross?

“He trusted in the Lord; let him deliver him. Let him save him now, since he delights in him” (Psalm 21:9). They spoke these words not as wishes but rather as mockery, and they asked whether he was the Son of God, speaking peacefully in their words while conceiving in their hearts an accusation of sacrilege.

### 16

But these matters are mystical; let us come to moral instruction. For just as Christ was attacked once in the body he assumed from the Virgin, so he was attacked frequently in that body which is the Church, for we are the body of Christ and members of it.

He is also attacked in each of his holy and innocent ones who have dedicated themselves to the Lord.

### 17

We recall someone who was recently attacked by everyone—Gratian the emperor—abandoned and betrayed by his own people. Not long before, he had been placed upon the throne of imperial power; suddenly he became destitute of everyone, even of those whose hereditary service had fallen to him by lot.

He began to be harried, as they rushed upon his destruction and brought death upon him, with no helper, no companion remaining at his side, and no attendant.

What better could he have said than what he had received from the one to whom he had devoted himself: “Will not my soul be subject to God?”

That is: Why do you persecute me? Why do you rage? Why do you insult me? You can kill the flesh; you cannot kill the soul. You can take away the life of the body; you cannot extinguish its merit.

For it is written: “Do not fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28).

Therefore the soul that is subject to God is not subject to human power. From him it hopes for the fruit of eternal life and the help of everlasting salvation.

He, therefore, to whom I have surrendered myself will protect me even when killed, raise me when dead, and avenge the one who was slain. The just man was snatched away, lest wickedness should change his heart. This death, therefore, is more a flight from sin than a loss for the dying man.

### 18

“For he himself is my God, my helper, and my defender; I shall not be moved any further.”

The one who slips is shaken, because he falls away from a certain standing-place of integrity and innocence. Once placed upon the rock of Christ, he ought not to have a slippery step, but to hold fast the foundation of his proper standing.

Hence the person who preserves an immovable will and carries out some purpose with the intention of a faithful mind is called immovable. We also read of the immovable will of God, as you have in Hebrews: “In which God, wishing more abundantly to show the heirs of the promise the immutability of his will, interposed an oath” (Hebrews 6:17).

Rightly, therefore, the will of God is immovable, since it is not moved by the enticements of any sin. Human beings, however, are changeable, slippery toward wrongdoing, and easily led into error.

Finally, it was said of the Jews: “Those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads” (Matthew 27:39). And the Lord himself says in the psalm: “All who saw me mocked me; they spoke with their lips and shook their heads” (Psalm 21:8).

Christ is the head of all. It is therefore better that Christ remain in us than that he be moved by any movement of ours.

Hence the Jews, shaking their heads, said: “Take such a person from the earth” (Acts 22:22). The Gerasenes asked him to depart from their borders (Luke 8:37); but the Church held on to him and did not let him go. Therefore she who held him possesses him; those who moved him cannot hold him.

The evangelist beautifully says that those passing by shook their heads (Matthew 27:39): passing by, not standing. We stand in the holy courts; we pass through the streets. The priest passed by; the Levite passed through; the one who healed the wounds inflicted stood.

Therefore those who were passing along the road did not say: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we bless you from the house of the Lord” (Psalm 128:8). The feet of those who bless stand; they do not pass by.

Finally, those passing by, not those remaining, gather the grapes from the vineyard whose protective wall has been broken. Those passing by hiss, as we read in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: “All who pass by the road have clapped their hands over you; they have hissed and shaken their heads over the daughter of Jerusalem” (Lamentations 2:15).

Therefore the priest could not be crowned, nor could the Levite, because they passed by and went past like a shadow. But Stephen was crowned through martyrdom because he saw the Lord Jesus standing, immovable and not passing by.

Thus, immovable in faith, Stephen saw the immovable Christ; he was shaken by no fear of death. Stephen did not move, nor did Christ move. The sons of the betrayer were moved, of whom it is said: “Let his children be moved away and beg” (Psalm 108:10).

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “For the one who is moved is needy and begs.” All the others, together with the manuscripts, read: “For the one who is moved needs a physician,” and so forth. The sense is good, although somewhat hidden. To understand it properly, observe that the first two words of this verse are being explained here: “let them be moved away.” Movements are disorders and illnesses of the soul; hence the Greeks call them πάθη (*pathē*). The entire verse therefore suggests that sinners are placed both in illness and in need and want. The interpretation is confirmed by what follows concerning anger, lust, and other disturbances.]

“For the one who is moved needs a physician.” The sinner is poor; the just person is rich, because the one who always seeks the Lord lacks no good thing.

### 19

Since the discussion has arisen from the phrase “I shall not be moved any further,” David himself shows that being moved is a matter of guilt when he says: “He established my soul for life and did not permit my feet to be shaken” (Psalm 65:9).

Hence the Lord our God also says to the holy man: “But stand here with me” (Deuteronomy 5:31), because whoever is near God cannot be near a fall.

Every sin is accustomed, as though by the effort of an adversary, to cast the mind from its place and move it from its proper standing; the image seems to be drawn either from an enemy or from a wrestling match.

Anger disturbs; lust sets ablaze; envy goads; avarice tortures; fear casts down; grief afflicts.

And the Lord Jesus said to Peter: “Come behind me” (Mark 8:33).

[Note: Thus read all the manuscripts and the old editions. The Roman edition, however, reads: “He did not say: Go back.” But the distinction under discussion lies in the words “behind me,” not in the verbs “go” and “come,” since Scripture uses the same verb in both places. For concerning the devil it says in Matthew 4:10, Ὕπαγε, Σατανᾶ—“Go away, Satan”; but concerning Peter, in Mark 8:33, Ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου, Σατανᾶ—“Go behind me, Satan.”]

He did not say, “Come back”—for this he said to the devil alone—but, “Come behind me”; for one who is behind Christ is not behind him.

But because Peter was in error, as the Lord himself said to him: “For you do not understand the things that are of God but those that are of human beings” (ibid.), he says, “Come behind me,” so that you may begin to think not human but divine thoughts.

Thus this just man also, destined to be snatched from the earth, says: “I shall not be moved any further.” For “to depart and to be with Christ is far better” (Philippians 1:23). The one who begins to be with Christ cannot fall, because for the just person death is not the end of nature but of guilt.

### 20

Amid these words he suddenly sees the ranks of his persecutors, and, placed among dangers, he is not concerned for himself but for those whom he desired to free. He says: “How long will you rush upon one man, killing everyone?” (above, verse 4).

If you seek me, why do you wish to kill the others? I offer myself for many, because only he who is the author of all could offer himself for everyone.

The imitator of the one whom he followed therefore says: “If you seek me, let these go, so that the word might be fulfilled which Jesus spoke: ‘I have not lost any of them except one’” (John 18:8–9). The Lord’s sentence is expressed more fully in another book. Yet that one perished more by his own will than by being punished through my severity, he says.

And while I willingly offer myself, you rush upon me and press upon me like a leaning wall and a tottering fence (Psalm, verse 4). That is: the once noble summit of the imperial throne, and the once-powerful wall of the empire spread throughout the entire Roman world, collapses like a leaning wall or a tottering fence.

21. But suppose they sought me even unto death, saying, “Let us take away the righteous man; let us take away the merciful man, for he is burdensome even to look upon.” Yet they also thought that my reputation and my chastity should be wounded by false accusations. For this is what is meant: “They plotted to reject my price”; for our price is chastity, which separates us from beasts and joins us to angels. Our price is mercy, which, when bestowed upon the needy, redeems us from death. Our price is faith, which acquired for Christ all those oppressed by pagan error and servitude. Our price is a good reputation, because each person’s record of merits is assessed. Our price is purity and simplicity, for it is written: “A pure man is a precious possession” (Prov. XII, 27); indeed, nothing is more precious than a simple man. Hence the Apostle says beautifully: “He abounded,” he says, “in the riches of his simplicity” (II Cor. VIII, 2). For what is richer than simplicity? Like a good head of a household, it has sufficient abundance in itself; content with its own purity, it neither seeks what belongs to another nor gnaws away at it, but forms others from itself. The innocent believes every word and does not repeatedly change himself into various devices, like cunning, which, in order to be cautious, fears everything and does not trust its own counsels; it constantly turns over its own judgments. Simplicity, however, knows nothing of fear. In this way, then, they attempted to reject the righteous man’s price; though the passage may also be understood in this sense: they accepted his gold with their hands but rejected it in their inmost hearts, holding on to the plunder while denying their faith.

[Note: [Col. 1175D] This was a more atrocious slander, since it is acknowledged by all historians that Gratian was distinguished by remarkable chastity. Indeed, there were even those who criticized his excessive modesty, as though it were unsuitable for the conduct of imperial affairs.]

[Note: [Col. 1175D] “Price” here signifies dignity and honor; for in what follows it is also understood as a reward. The Septuagint has: πλὴν τὴν τιμήν μου ἐβουλεύσαντο ἀπώσασθαι, “Yet they plotted to reject my honor.”]

22. Hence he also says: “I ran in thirst,” because he sought faith and could not find it, abandoned by his companions and deserted by his own people. Thus we read in the Gospel that the Lord Jesus both hungered and thirsted (Matt. IV, 2; John XIX, 28), when, hungering for our faith and thirsting for our works, he seemed to seek what belonged to another. Or, if we refer the words to bodily thirst, with what disgrace does he say, “I ran in thirst”? That is: “I was thirsty while others belched forth my wines; and from the lofty platform of supreme power and royal wealth I was brought down, with the degradation of a commoner, to the extremity of thirst.”

23. Since the Greek has ἔδραμον, which signifies both “I ran” in the singular and “they ran” in the plural, the passage may also be understood as: “They ran in thirst”—those whose throats, in their excessive eagerness to shed my blood, had dried up. For just as there is a thirst for faith, so there is also a thirst for faithlessness. The righteous man thirsts with that thirst who says: “My soul has thirsted for you, O God” (Ps. XLI, 3). The faithless thirst with this other thirst, their tongues dried up by thirst. With what thirst did that man thirst who, seated amid the dishes and cups of a banquet, plotted the death of his innocent guest, the emperor? Did it not seem to you, impious man, while you were eating and preparing slaughter, that human bones were crackling beneath your teeth? While you drank wine and contemplated parricide, did it not seem that you were pouring the blood of an innocent man into yourself through those cups?

[Note: [Col. 1176D] This detail concerning the murder of the emperor Gratian is found in no other ancient author than our present one. Orosius merely records that, while Gratian was preparing to cross into Italy, he was surrounded by the treachery of the tyrant Maximus and killed. Socrates, Sozomen, Paul the Deacon, and others report that Andragathius, whom the tyrant had sent to pursue him, spread a rumor that Gratian’s wife was coming to him. Deceived by this report, Gratian approached a litter which he thought belonged to his wife, and was killed when Andragathius sprang out of it. Sozomen, however, can readily be reconciled with Ambrose. For he writes that Gratian was not killed immediately, but not long afterward: Καὶ συλληφθεὶς, οὐκ εἰς μακρὰν ἀνηρέθῃ, “And after being captured, he was killed not long afterward.” Whatever the case, Ambrose must be believed as virtually an eyewitness.]

Thus entirely estranged not only from imitation but even from the reading of Scripture, so that the following psalm verse did not come to your mind:

> “But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food” (Ps. LIV, 14–15).

And that other verse, which the Lord Jesus himself recalls in the Gospel:

> “He who ate bread with me has lifted up his heel against me” (John XIII, 18).

24. “What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah?” (Hos. VI, 4). You have left us many heirs of your betrayal and deceit; for this passage may also be applied by apostrophe to the traitor Judas.

[Note: [Col. 1177D] Apostrophe, in Latin aversio, is a figure by which speech is turned from the subject under discussion to address someone directly.]

You betrayed life, the kingdom, and the Lord. Yet the Lord Jesus is betrayed once in his own person and frequently in his servants. “Whatever you did for one of these least of mine,” he says, “you did for me” (Matt. XXV, 40). You took charge of the purses entrusted to you and of the money of the poor; he took charge of the provinces entrusted to him. You received the honor of an apostle; he, the dignity of military service and the insignia of administration. I enumerate his honors in order to intensify the crime.

Both of you violated the fellowship of the banquet. Yet you rose from the banquet to betrayal, while he rose to murder. That is, you—though guilty, yet more restrained—denied that you had believed the Lord whom you betrayed would be put to death, and you returned the price, lest the payment for parricide appear to remain with you. He not only retained the payment he had received, but even extorted a reward for betrayal that had not been offered. He was not merely undeceived by another’s lie; he deceived others by his own lie, and deceived them in order to kill. And while the former refused the banquet because he saw that he was to be destroyed, the latter offered the sacrament, lest any part of the crime he was accumulating be lost.

Finally, the money of the earlier traitor contributed to the burial of strangers; this man denied his ruler an entire burial.

25. Nor was there lacking one who washed his hands, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matt. XXVII, 24). By this Pilate did not cleanse himself but defiled himself; he entangled himself rather than freed himself. For although another’s sentence carries no weight in the judgments of the condemned, confession creates the greater bond. The righteous are not acquitted by another’s sentence but by their own life; the wicked bind themselves all the more tightly by their own words, though they cannot bind others. Yet, lest his own confession also appear to be lacking, he swore in order to perjure himself.

[Note: [Col. 1177D] Observe in passing how ancient is the custom by which, in serious cases, we swear after touching the most holy Gospel. See the annotation of H. Valesius on Book VI, chapter 30, of Sozomen, p. 145.]

He washed his hands while touching the Gospel, so that nothing would be lacking to the example. He washed his hands with water in order to defile them more criminally with the blood of the innocent.

[Note: [Col. 1177D] Understand this of Andragothius, who, before inflicting death upon Gratian, took steps to have him led to Maximus.]

Nor was Herod absent, for the other Pilate believed that he would please him if he sent him the captured ruler. What more shall I say of the fact that he too put on a whitened garment in order to mock him, and afterward was clothed in royal dress for his death, lest he appear to have lost the honor due to him? For although he perished through crime, even in death he retained the right of the authority conferred upon him, whether by the service or by the consent of those very men who denied it to him.

26. A funeral procession was added to this enormous crime, unless the man who bitterly lamented these events, after learning what was being prepared, stirred by righteous grief, rebuked the proud victor, saying that such things were inflicted upon tyrants, not upon kings.

[Note: [Col. 1177D] Thus reads one Regius manuscript. Other manuscripts and the old edition have: “Thus, shuddering at crimes, and thus swiftly.” The Roman edition has: “Thus, the horror of the crime, thus swiftly,” and so forth. Neither reading is sufficiently satisfactory. Nevertheless, we strongly suspect that the common reading of the old edition and the manuscripts should be corrected in this manner: “Thus, roused by horror at the crime.” Moreover, it is clear that Ambrose is speaking here about himself, not only from what Paulinus relates in his Life concerning Ambrose’s second embassy to Maximus, but also from what the holy man himself wrote in his letter to Valentinian and in his Oration on the Death of Valentinian. These passages do not permit us to doubt it. Meanwhile, admire both the steadfastness of the holy man, by which he restrained the raging tyrant with such freedom, and his utmost modesty, by which he declares that he cannot be compared with the righteous Joseph.]

Thus, terrified by horror at the crime, he abandoned the preparations for that most dreadful deed. Nor was there lacking a petitioner for burial, although that Joseph who was called righteous was absent. But Maximus, far more savage, denied what Pilate himself could not take away. In this the parricide lacked humanity, yet grace was not lacking toward the innocent; and patience, assumed for a time, delayed vengeance briefly.

[Note: [Col. 1178D] The vengeance for Gratian, who had been murdered by the greatest crime, was accomplished in this way. Count Andragathius had occupied the Alpine passes with large forces. When he abandoned them after being divinely blinded, Theodosius, leading his army across even though it was much smaller, captured and killed Maximus, who had taken up residence at Aquileia as though to witness his own victory. When Andragathius learned of this, he threw himself fully armed into the sea. See Orosius, Book VII, chapter 35, and others.]

Thus vengeance was delayed for a short time.

27. (Verse 6, 7.) Therefore he says: “Nevertheless, my soul is subject to God, for my patience is from him. For he is my God and my Savior, my protector; I shall not be moved.” That is: Did the denial of burial deprive me of the dwelling of everlasting rest? I have my habitation in the Lord’s tabernacle, and I shall rest on his holy mountain. I shall not depart through human crime, because I have been received through the Lord’s favor; for neither death, nor the sword, nor tribulation will be able to separate me from the love of Christ. It is not the innocent who departs from the tabernacles of the righteous, but the sinner. The heirs of the traitor Judas depart—of whom, and of those like them, it is deservedly said: “Let his children be continually moved and beg; let them be cast out of their habitations” (Ps. CVIII, 10).

28. This is also rightly referred to the Lord Jesus Christ, who, when he had descended to earth in order to be crucified and buried, did not depart from the Father but remained in the Father. “I have been handed over, and I was not going out” (Ps. LXXXVII, 9). He did not lay aside what he was, but preserved it; he did not cease to be in the form of God, but remained so. The glory of God was not changed through the assumption of a body; rather, while remaining what it was, it gained a triumph and did not lose its power. Hence he himself says: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power” (Mark XIV, 62).

29. (Verse 9.) Therefore he exhorts the peoples of the nations, summoned and acquired for the Father by his own blood, to faith, saying: “Hope in him, all the assemblies of my people.” That is, not Israel alone, he says, but all; not merely the remnant, but also the fullness of the nations; not the nations alone, but Israel also. For when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved. Who can comprehend the divine mysteries? Their multitude is so great that Paul rightly marvels and says with justification: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. XI, 33).

The nations were rejected so that Israel might be chosen; afterward Israel was blinded because of the calling of the nations; and the blinded remnant of Israel was saved according to the election of grace after the fullness of the nations had entered. Thus Israel’s fault benefited the nations, and the faith of the nations set the people of Israel free.

30. “Pour out your hearts before him,” he says. Whoever puts on faith must first strip off faithlessness and empty his heart of every stain of wickedness, so that his heart may become capable of spiritual grace. Therefore the Apostle says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. IV, 23). When the old wickedness is poured out, new grace is taken on, by which each person is renewed.

Thus the Son of God says: “Pour out your hearts before him,” because he knew that the Father would say: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel II, 28). There is also the traditional interpretation that we are understood to pour out our heart when we disclose all our thoughts and the desires of our heart to someone. Therefore let us cast our thoughts upon God and not believe that anything can remain hidden from him. We pour out our heart before him when we empty ourselves of human disputes.

31. (Verse 10.) “Nevertheless, the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are liars, upon the scales, so that they may deceive.” If the sons of men are vain and the sons of men are liars, the sons of God can be not vain—for they are born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

For the sons of men seem to themselves to weigh equity and to examine justice with the severity of a stricter judgment: harsh toward others, lenient toward themselves; unjust in their deeds, but censors in speech.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] Thus reads the Regius manuscript already cited more than once. Other manuscripts and editions have: “Harsh toward others, lenient toward evil deeds,” and so forth.]

Hence Solomon says: “A diverse weight is an abomination to the Lord, and a deceitful balance is not good” (Prov. XX, 23). By this he signifies those who contemplate robbery with an insatiable heart while displaying sobriety on their faces. Such are the scribes of the Jews, who impose upon others the heavy burdens of a stricter observance, while they themselves do not possess the straight yoke of the soul but are bent by their inclined wickedness; they themselves flee from their own commandments.

Thus avarice is found to be, as it were, the root of all vices, the head and fuel of iniquity. A man who renounces the world, has been buried with Christ through the sacrament of baptism, and has died to the world must avoid and shun it.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] In a balance, the “yoke” is the beam from whose ends the two pans hang; hence this metaphor is derived.]

32. (Verse 11.) “Do not hope in iniquity,” he says, “and do not desire robbery; if riches flow in, do not set your heart upon them.” You see that they flow in, but you do not see that they flow past? Naked you were born; naked you will die. Why do you seek to retain what you cannot take away with you? They are streams, these things that you admire: just as they come, so they pass and depart.

Only the Jordan was turned backward, the river into which you descended.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] We all descend into the Jordan with Christ our Head, whose touch sanctified not only the water of the Jordan but all water, so that it might become a fitting instrument of our regeneration. Otherwise, many people formerly desired above all to be baptized in the Jordan, as can be read in the lives of certain saints; and Jerome relates from Eusebius the same concerning Constantine the Great. See the annotation of H. Valesius on Book IV of Eusebius’s Life of Constantine, chapter 62, where, among other matters worthy of knowledge, the following is read from the Itinerary of Antoninus, which has considerable affinity with this passage: “The priest descended into the river, and at the hour when he began to bless the water, immediately the Jordan turned back behind him with a great roar; and the upper water stood still upon itself until the baptism was completed, while the lower water fled into the sea.”]

The Jordan admonishes you to return to the very source and origin of nature, which brought you forth naked, not clothed, so that you may learn not to seek superfluous things. The fact that you are ashamed of being naked was taught by guilt, not by nature. There would be no shame concerning the sexual organs if there were no guilt. For the other animals do not wear clothing in order to be covered, nor do they wear clothing in order to be protected. Everything is sufficiently protected by the covering of its own nature; but while we seek what is superfluous, we have lost nature’s covering and forfeited the common right.

Therefore this psalm is credited with healing instruction, because either Idithun, or the psalmist himself in Idithun’s name, trained himself through spiritual exercise to undergo temptations, so that whoever is placed in distress may submit himself to God; and if he has sinned before, may cease to sin and not be shaken by a relapse into error.

[Note: [Col. 1180D] Augustine teaches essentially the same thing in Book II of On Original Sin, chapter 34; Book I of On Marriage and Concupiscence; Book V, chapter 5, Against Julian the Pelagian; and elsewhere.]

33. (Verse 12.) “God has spoken once; I have heard two things.” God has spoken once, and many things have been heard, because he did not speak through letters and syllables. He spoke through riddles, he spoke through visions, he spoke through divisions of graces, he spoke through the Spirit of individuals. We, however, speak many things and are scarcely heard.

He spoke once in the Law; he spoke the same things again in the Gospel. Or perhaps, as I think, because he spoke in many ways through the prophets, but finally spoke in his Son. He spoke once when he spoke in the Son, and even those things were heard which previously had not been heard by those to whom he had spoken through the prophets.

Thus he spoke once in the New Testament, and the Old Testament was heard, though it had not been heard; for the Lord himself said concerning the Jewish people: “They will see, and not see; they will hear, and not hear” (Mark IV, 12). They will hear with the bodily ear, but they will not hear with the hearing of the mind.

34. Therefore he spoke once to us—that is, to the Church—and two things were heard, because we both heard and understood those things which those who read did not understand; those who heard did not hear. Christ alone opened the human ear to the knowledge of the mysteries; he alone opened the seal of the book and dissolved the riddles of the prophets.

[Col. 1180D]

35. (Verse 13.) Therefore he himself will repay each person according to his works. In this he also includes the quality of works, so that he may either restore to each person the rewards corresponding to a greater number of better merits, or, conversely, so that we may be burdened both by their number and by the severity of our merits.

Here ends the first part of the fourth section of Volume Ten.

### CHAPTER SIX

That the four elements were created in heaven and earth. The nature of heaven and the position of the earth. 132

That the earth was formless, both because nothing distinct was in it and because it was covered with darkness. It is concluded from this that evil is not to be understood by darkness, since evil arises only from us. 137

On the firmament of heaven and the harmony of the spheres. 146

### CHAPTER THREE

That the firmament is not the same as heaven; it is wrongly denied that real waters remain above it. 148

How perfect is the union of the Father and the Son in their works. 154

155

That the gathering of the waters is one and continuous. Also concerning lakes and ponds. 161

Why food for cattle was created before food for human beings. Green grass is an image of the human condition. 167

### CHAPTER EIGHT

Seeds never degenerate from their own kinds. The word of God bestowed marvelous fertility upon the earth before human beings sinned. 173

[Col. 1182]

### CHAPTER ELEVEN

On the origin of trees, and on the rose, which at first was born without thorns, later bristled with them, and became a mirror of our life. 175

### CHAPTER TWELVE

## BOOK FOUR—ON THE WORK OF THE FOURTH DAY

187

### CHAPTER ONE

He prepares the reader to understand correctly the creation of the sun and to avoid idolatrous madness. Same page.

### CHAPTER TWO

The sun serves the Son of God, by whom it was created, together with the other lights, for the adornment of heaven. Fertility was given to the earth by God, not by the sun. The sun is interpreted as Christ and the moon as the Church. 189

### CHAPTER THREE

The light of day is one thing and the light of the stars another. Fire has a twofold operation—to illuminate and to burn—which will be separated in the requital of merits. God is called a consuming fire, and the reason for this. 191

### CHAPTER FOUR

The science of the mathematicians is refuted. 192

### CHAPTER FIVE

The annual seasons are determined by the nearness or remoteness of the heavenly lights; this is applied to Christ, the synagogue, and the Church. 197

### CHAPTER SIX

The size of the sun and moon is established from their appearance. An objection is resolved, and the appearance of distant objects is eloquently discussed. 200

### CHAPTER SEVEN

Many things said about the sun also apply to the moon; nevertheless, the moon has effects of its own, some of which are listed here. 202

### CHAPTER EIGHT

The moon’s change teaches the instability of things, yet this is shamefully represented in our morals. It represents the mystery of Christ and the Church; those who believe that it can be drawn down from heaven by magical songs are to be ridiculed. 203

### CHAPTER NINE

The conclusion of the fourth day; how foolish it is to fear it, and from what the offense of demons and pagans toward it derives. 205

## BOOK FIVE—ON THE WORK OF THE FIFTH DAY

Same page.

### CHAPTER ONE

After the two higher elements have been adorned, the sea is granted its own prerogative. The obedience and fertility of the waters are described. What “creeping things” are. Same page.

### CHAPTER TWO

By the power of the words “Let the waters bring forth creeping things,” far more creatures were produced in the sea than on land; and this grace was added to the waters, so that things harmful on land might be generated harmlessly in the sea. 207

### CHAPTER THREE

Fish have many methods of generation and a singular sense of affection for their offspring. Their great purity. 208

### CHAPTER FOUR

The mutual relationship of water and fish teaches what the relationship of parents and children ought to be. How water supplies the use of respiration to fish. 210

### CHAPTER FIVE

Why fish are so well toothed. How the avaricious are compared with fish. Same page.

### CHAPTER SIX

Human beings are fish; but one finds both good and bad fish. The good fish, however, ought not to fear Peter’s hook and net. 212

### CHAPTER SEVEN

The sea signifies the Gospel and the Church. Married couples are urged toward mutual charity. Same page.

### CHAPTER EIGHT

On the cunning of the octopus and the crab, by which deceitful people are represented. 215

### CHAPTER NINE

On the foreknowledge of the sea urchin. 216

### CHAPTER TEN

Human fickleness and lack of self-control are censured by the example of fish. 217

### CHAPTER ELEVEN

On the fish of the Atlantic Ocean; also on salt, coral, and certain other things. Because of these, and especially because of navigation, the sea surpasses the land. On Jonah and Peter. 220

### CHAPTER TWELVE

A discussion of the sweetness of various birds. 222

### CHAPTER THIRTEEN

On the kingfisher, and that we ought to expect help from God. On birds that foretell rain or winds, and on the faithful guardianship of geese. 224

### CHAPTER FOURTEEN

Birds are joined to fish by multiple affinities. On the various kinds and differences of birds. 225

### CHAPTER FIFTEEN

On cranes; and, on this occasion, on the condition of the ancient republic and the causes of human negligence. 227

### CHAPTER SIXTEEN

How storks migrate, are escorted and defended by crows. The hospitality of the same crows and the filial devotion of storks are praised. 228

### CHAPTER SEVENTEEN

On the swallow’s diligence, industry, devotion to its young, and poverty. 230

### CHAPTER EIGHTEEN

Human beings are taught love for their children by crows, and their impiety is condemned. Hawks and eagles are not at all to be accused of harshness; but the coot, which nourishes an abandoned eaglet, is to be commended. 232

### CHAPTER NINETEEN

The turtledove is praised for widowhood and, for this reason, is placed even above Christian women. 232

### CHAPTER TWENTY

Vultures, which are said to reproduce without union with a male, establish the possibility of virgin birth. 233

### CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE

On birds organized in a kind of republican form. Same page.

### CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO

Why flying creatures are said to fly over the earth beside the firmament of heaven; and, in the same place, on the bodily diversity observed among birds. 236

### CHAPTER TWENTY-THREE

On the Indian worm, the chameleon, the hare, and the phoenix, by which we are instructed concerning faith in the resurrection and preparation for death. On the vulture and the locust. 237

### CHAPTER TWENTY-FOUR

On nocturnal birds, especially the song of the brooding nightingale; on the owl, bat, and cock; from these certain matters are applied to our own morals. 239

### CHAPTER TWENTY-FIVE

## BOOK SIX—ON THE WORK OF THE SIXTH DAY

Same page.

# BOOK ON NOAH AND THE ARK
## BOOK ON NOAH AND THE ARK

**Chapter One.**—Noah as a model for all. We must rest from works of iniquity. 361

**Chapter II.**—What the names of Noah’s sons signify, and what is signified by the order in which they are listed. 363

**Chapter III.**—Why, with the Flood about to come, the procreation of children increased: so that good things may be attributed to divine kindness, but punishments to our iniquity. 364

**Chapter IV.**—Men devoted to the worship of the flesh are like the giants who lived in Noah’s age. Who are called “sons of God,” and in what sense God is said to become angry and be moved; why Noah nevertheless found favor with God, even though irrational creatures too were destroyed because of human sin. 365

**Chapter V.**—The earth was corrupted by human iniquity; “flesh” is taken for the whole human being, whose enticements corrupt our soul. 367
