**Chapter VII.**—Noah’s ark is compared with the Ark of the Covenant; its dimensions are shown to signify that each part of the human body has been composed for use and beauty. 370

**Chapter VIII.**—By the door placed crosswise in the ark, the less honorable part of the body is fittingly represented. 372

**Chapter IX.**—By the lower parts of the ark we are taught to regard receptacles for food as of little importance; on this occasion the structure and use of the intestines are discussed. 373

**Chapter X.**—The three reasons why mute animals were subjected to the punishment of the Flood. 375 [Col. 1185]

**Chapter XI.**—A just man is a means of salvation for himself and his own, although error may sometimes creep in when his diligence relaxes. One who is just among human beings is not always just before God. 376

**Chapter XII.**—Why the number seven is sacred and complete. There is in us something feminine corresponding to the number seven, but it is advanced toward masculine condition by an educated man. 378

**Chapter XIII.**—Why, after Noah entered the ark, the Flood occurred seven days later. Why Moses said that it lasted forty days and forty nights. 379

**Chapter XIV.**—The Flood occurred in spring so that human beings would suffer greater torment; and it occurred in Noah’s six-hundredth year so that the destruction of humankind might correspond with its creation. 383

**Chapter XV.**—By the ark shut from the outside and floating upon the waters, the human body is foreshadowed; by the fifteen cubits of water, the human senses; and finally, by the death of all flesh, the destruction of the soul corrupted by passions. 384

**Chapter XVI.**—Why it is said, “The Lord remembered Noah,” with no mention of his wife or sons. 387

**Chapter XVII.**—What the cataracts, the opening of the ark’s door, and the sending forth of the raven signify in the mystical sense. 388

**Chapter XVIII.**—As the raven expresses wickedness, so the dove expresses virtue. Noah shows that the just man is always ready to receive virtue; by keeping the dove for another seven days, he likewise teaches the patience necessary for correction. 391

**Chapter XIX.**—Why the dove is said to have returned in the evening with an olive branch in its beak; likewise, how Noah learned that the waters had subsided; finally, why the same dove, sent out for the third time after seven days, did not return. 393

**Chapter XX.**—The statement that on one day the waters diminished and on another the earth dried is explained accommodatively. On the uncovering of the ark. Why the first or second month is called by a term belonging to the spring season. 395

**Chapter XXI.**—Why Noah waited for God’s command before leaving the ark. The order in which his entrance and departure are described is explained spiritually. 397

**Chapter XXII.**—For what reason Noah built an altar to God without being commanded, and what is meant by “to God” rather than “to the Lord.” Why he offered clean animals and birds; and what the Lord means when he says, “Considering this, I will not again curse the ground,” etc. 398

**Chapter XXIII.**—The Lord’s statement, “Seedtime and harvest, cold and heat shall not cease,” is explained in a twofold sense. 399

**Chapter XXIV.**—The prerogative of power divinely granted to human beings over the other animals through the blessing bestowed on Noah and his household. 401

**Chapter XXV.**—Whether the Lord commanded that we should eat vegetables rather than meat; and how Moses fortified us against the opinions of philosophers concerning the soul, whose various teachings are recounted. 402

**Chapter XXVI.**—One who kills his brother is worse than the beasts. Each person must beware of his own thoughts and words. How the statement about the human being is to be understood: “He made him in the image of God.” 405

**Chapter XXVII.**—The promise that there will never again be a Flood of such a kind as to destroy the whole earth; this is transferred to the passions of the soul. On the heavenly rainbow. 407

**Chapter XXVIII.**—Why the generation of Ham is mentioned first: so that his sin may be magnified and the impious generation that sprang from him may be displayed. 408

**Chapter XXIX.**—How Noah became a farmer; what distinction there is between a farmer and a tiller of the soil; and how one cultivates his own land while the other works it. Why Noah first planted a vineyard—that is, something unnecessary, since springs suffice for drinking. Why it is also written of him, “And he drank of the wine”: here the twofold drunkenness and, finally, the twofold nakedness of the soul are discussed. 409

**Chapter XXX.**—Why Ham is then called “the father of Canaan,” although Canaan had not yet been born; and who are to be understood as represented by Ham, the one who mocked his father. 411

**Chapter XXXI.**—The piety of Shem and Japheth is commended. How Noah became sober. 412

**Chapter XXXII.**—Why, in the blessing of Shem, it is said, “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem”; and why it is not Ham, who sinned, but his son who is subjected to Shem’s service. 414

**Chapter XXXIII.**—The three hundred and fifty years that Noah is said to have lived after the Flood; then, the descendants of Japheth. 415

**Chapter XXXIV.**—What sort of man Ham, that wicked elder son, was; and concerning Cush’s son Nimrod, a giant and hunter. Ibid.

**FRAGMENT OF THE BOOK ON THE ARK OF NOAH.** Ibid.

Introduction to the books on Abraham. 417

# TWO BOOKS ON ABRAHAM

## BOOK ONE

417

**Chapter One.**—The benefit to be drawn from Abraham’s examples is demonstrated by divine authority and by comparison with the philosophers. 419

**Chapter II.**—How Abraham’s devotion was tested by the words of the divine command. Pharaoh’s example demonstrates how great a crime adultery is. 421

**Chapter III.**—On Abraham’s other virtues; here also on Lot’s lack of prudence, his uncle’s affection for him, and finally the promise received concerning future descendants and the Christ who was to be born. 424

**Chapter IV.**—Abraham is defended against the charge of adultery. Much is argued against adultery. Finally, the question is raised whether it was fitting that circumcision should have been instituted, since it was later to be revoked and contained in itself only the smallest degree of perfection. 428

**Chapter V.**—On Abraham’s hospitality: how he made his wife share in the merit. 435

**Chapter VI.**—The destruction of Sodom is foretold to Abraham, and divine indulgence in tolerating sinners and examining and pardoning sins is praised. After briefly touching on various circumstances of Sodom’s destruction and excusing the incest of Lot’s daughters, the evils of drunkenness are described. 438

**Chapter VII.**—The death threatened by God against Abimelech because he had attempted Sarah’s chastity demonstrates how great a crime adultery is. The mysteries represented by Abimelech, Isaac, and Ishmael. 442

**Chapter VIII.**—God tests Abraham in various ways, but especially by giving the command to sacrifice his son. Each word of the command is examined. The mystery represented by Isaac’s ram. 445

**Chapter IX.**—Sarah dies and is buried. Abraham provides a wife for his son and binds the servant chosen for this purpose by an oath. The mystery and moral discipline contained in these events. 449

## BOOK TWO

455

**Chapter One.**—He explains from what things the soul must withdraw for complete purification; then he recounts the descendants promised to Abraham. Ibid.

**Chapter II.**—After Abraham’s departure, God speaks to him as to a friend: the moral meaning. What is signified by the sixtieth year. How the wise person possesses his own soul. 457

**Chapter III.**—Abraham travels as far as Shechem. There he sees God: he builds an altar but does not sacrifice, and the reason is explained. Nevertheless, after raising an altar again, he invokes the name of the Lord. 458

**Chapter IV.**—While Abraham had been dwelling in the desert, which foreshadows tranquility of mind, he descends into Egypt, which represents temptation, driven by hunger. Why he called Sarah his sister there. 461

**Chapter V.**—Abraham leaves Egypt with the true riches of the soul. What his return to Bethel signifies. Why Lot, though rich in gold and silver, is not called wealthy. 463

**Chapter VI.**—In what sense it is written, “And Lot who walked with Abram”; likewise, “The land could not contain them.” On Abraham and Lot as shepherds, and on the quarrel between them. 465

**Chapter VII.**—From the Lord’s words to Abraham, philosophers derived their doctrine that all things belong to the wise person. A mystical explanation of Abraham’s battles. 471

**Chapter VIII.**—What Melchizedek, king of Sodom, teaches us. After defending Abraham against the superstitions of haruspices, various interpretations are added of the sacrifice he offered. 475

**Chapter IX.**—Why a trance came upon Abraham, and what the oracle returned to him signifies. 483

**Chapter X.**—When Abraham is told, “To your seed I will give this land,” true blessedness is promised to him; yet the Church is more particularly prefigured, whose type is expressed in barren Sarah, just as the synagogue and the heresies are represented in the slave-girl Hagar. 489

**Chapter XI.**—What the command of circumcision given to Abraham signifies; and what destruction was threatened even against infants who were not circumcised on the eighth day. One letter is added to Sarah’s name. Abraham falls on his face and laughs. Whether he doubted. The Lord grants his prayer for Ishmael and promises him a son from Sarah. 493

Introduction to the book on Isaac and the soul. 499

# ONE BOOK ON ISAAC AND THE SOUL

**Chapter One.**—Holy Isaac is commended both for his paternal origin and grace, and for his prefiguration of the Lord’s birth and passion. 501

**Chapter II.**—What a human being is, and in what part he chiefly consists; and what his soul is like, both according to its nature and through its irrational part, by which it becomes subject to corruption. 503

**Chapter III.**—The perfect soul, having renounced earthly things and subdued its vices, longs to kiss the Word; and God the Word pours himself wholly into it. 505

**Chapter IV.**—The righteous soul is compared with Solomon’s mare. What the wells dug by Isaac signify. 507

**Chapter V.**—The bridegroom, having again slipped away from the soul in the bed at night, is sought in vain, and the reason is given. Nevertheless, he is later found; how he must be held. He himself also adorns the soul with various praises. 515

**Chapter VI.**—The sleeping soul is awakened by the bridegroom; but while it delays in rising, the Word passes by. Going out through the wounds of love, it finally finds with difficulty the one it sought. 519

**Chapter VII.**—The soul is praised by the bridegroom for its constancy in seeking and for its other virtues. 523

**Chapter VIII.**—The same soul, shrinking from being praised publicly, says that it has gone down into the garden of nuts, etc.; these things signify bitterness and temptations. A mystical interpretation is followed by an exhortation to love. 526 [Col. 1187]

Introduction to the book on the goodness of death. 533

# ONE BOOK ON THE GOODNESS OF DEATH

**Chapter One.**—How death is not called evil, although it is contrary to life. 539

**Chapter II.**—After distinguishing three kinds of death, he shows that the third kind is good. 540

**Chapter III.**—Natural death is defined and praised. Likewise, mortification, which is a kind of imitation of death. 542

**Chapter IV.**—Death is good under many names. 546

**Chapter V.**—He urges contempt for death and the practice of mortification. Then he explains how the soul is exalted into the likeness of God. 547

**Chapter VI.**—This world is full of the snares of the rulers of the air and of the powers. 551

**Chapter VII.**—The body ought to be ruled by the soul, although the soul sometimes suffers with it. 552

**Chapter VIII.**—Death itself has nothing terrifying about it; rather, it is the opinion concerning death that is terrifying. 554

**Chapter IX.**—The goodness of death is established from the destruction of the body and the immortality of the soul. 557

**Chapter X.**—The immortality of souls is also proved from Scripture. The philosophers’ transmigration of souls is rejected; then the complaint about the delayed reward of the righteous is dispelled. 559

**Chapter XI.**—He sets forth in seven stages the joy of the righteous after this life; and he urges us to approach God zealously. 561

**Chapter XII.**—He describes eternal blessedness and demonstrates that it has also been destined for us. 563

Introduction to the book on fleeing the world. 567

# ONE BOOK ON FLEEING THE WORLD

**Chapter One.**—A human being cannot flee earthly enticements unless divine protection is present. 569

**Chapter II.**—The law concerning the cities of refuge teaches that the world must be fled; four questions concerning them are discussed. 571

**Chapter III.**—He demonstrates, by collecting various testimonies of the Apostle, that the kinds of virtue mentioned in the preceding chapter are found in him not merely foreshadowed but fully expressed. 576

**Chapter IV.**—What it means to flee the world, together with an exhortation to flee it and its contagion. 578

**Chapter V.**—Why we ought to flee from here, and how we should cross over with Moses so that we may see God. 581

**Chapter VI.**—Why one who wishes to flee must flee swiftly; where, moreover, one must flee, and toward what good we ought to raise our souls. 584

**Chapter VII.**—The greatest reason why we must flee from here is that this is the proper dwelling-place of wickedness. 586

**Chapter VIII.**—How, although we are detained here in body, we can—and indeed must—flee in spirit. 590

**Chapter IX.**—He presses us to flee from here, as Jacob fled from his homeland and as deer flee to the springs; whoever longs for those springs must pour out his soul above himself, following the example of Susanna. 593

Introduction to the books on Jacob and the blessed life. 595

# TWO BOOKS ON JACOB AND THE BLESSED LIFE

## BOOK ONE

597

**Chapter One.**—For the discipline of virtue and the restraint of passions, prudent speech and a mind intent upon reason are necessary. Ibid.

**Chapter II.**—Temperance is commended. 600

**Chapter III.**—The Lord teaches temperance, wisdom, and discipline; an exhortation to pursue them; likewise, our guilt must be attributed solely to our own will. 602

**Chapter IV.**—How much God granted to humanity when he gave the law and added grace. 604

**Chapter V.**—Why the law was insufficient, but grace, given through Christ’s death, was necessary; with Christ we too must die, rise again, and live. 606

**Chapter VI.**—The fruit of the promulgated law is confession of sin and humility, indeed grace itself and the pledge of love. 607

**Chapter VII.**—Love must be present in us so that no adversity may separate us from Christ, since such adversity does not diminish the blessed life. 609

**Chapter VIII.**—The wise person should take such pleasure in bodily health or in children that, if these are lost, he does not therefore consider himself less blessed. 611

## BOOK TWO

615

**Chapter One.**—Jacob was blessed even while in exile. Ibid.

**Chapter II.**—He excuses the parents of blessed Jacob, and teaches by their example how other parents ought to conduct themselves toward their children. 616

**Chapter III.**—Why, after the younger brother had received the blessing, the elder was condemned to serve his brother. 618

**Chapter IV.**—Esau threatens his brother with death; on this occasion instructions are given for appeasing envy. 620

**Chapter V.**—Jacob returns to his homeland because of Laban’s envy. If envy arises, how it must be avoided. 621 [Col. 1188]

**Chapter VI.**—Saint Jacob sees angels on the journey. Jacob’s meeting with Esau. The meaning of all these events is revealed. 624

**Chapter VII.**—Jacob wrestles with God and becomes lame. They avenge the outrage done to Dinah, an act for which their father Jacob reproves them. Bethel prefigures the Church. 626

**Chapter VIII.**—On the praiseworthy old age of Saint Jacob. 628

**Chapter IX.**—Jacob, near death and weakened in his eyes, is nevertheless shown to be blessed; he is further commended in many ways. 629

**Chapter X.**—How greatly Eleazar’s sufferings were to be praised, because of which he must be judged truly blessed. 632

**Chapter XI.**—On the remarkable courage of the seven Maccabees, to whom their mother was added as an eighth. 633

**Chapter XII.**—A most elegant commendation of that blessed woman, the mother of the seven martyred sons. 636

Introduction to the book on Joseph the patriarch. 637

# ONE BOOK ON JOSEPH THE PATRIARCH

**Chapter One.**—Joseph is proposed as a mirror of chastity; there is also brief discussion of his parents’ love, his brothers’ envy against him, and his own forgetfulness of injuries. 641

**Chapter II.**—The affection of parents and the gratitude of children ought to be equal. Blessed Jacob is nevertheless excused, since he preferred Joseph to the others because he was adorned with greater virtues. 643

**Chapter III.**—The fact that Joseph is said above to have been rebuked by Jacob was not due to disbelief. 644

**Chapter IV.**—Joseph is taken to Egypt and bought by the chief of the cooks, in whom there is a figure of Christ, who liberates us through his own servitude. 649

**Chapter V.**—The commendation of Joseph, who resisted Potiphar’s wife. 650

**Chapter VI.**—After a brief denunciation of the woman, he turns to the eunuchs, the authors of this injury as well; and, demonstrating how fragile their condition is, he recounts another man’s dream and its interpretation. From this he shows that the power of the world resembles a dream. 653

**Chapter VII.**—Joseph’s rewards, marriage, children, and distribution of grain are interpreted mystically of Christ. 657

**Chapter VIII.**—Jacob’s exhortation to his sons to go to Egypt to buy food—what it signifies. 659

**Chapter IX.**—The various circumstances of Jacob’s sons’ journey and their reception by Joseph are explained with reference to Paul’s calling and preaching, as well as the unbelief of the Jews. 660

**Chapter X.**—The mystical and moral interpretation of Joseph’s meeting with his brothers. 663

**Chapter XI.**—The story of the cup found in Benjamin’s sack is explained mystically. 665

**Chapter XII.**—Joseph’s revealing himself to his brothers expresses the course of action that Christ would employ against the Jews. 666

**Chapter XIII.**—Pharaoh rejoices that Joseph’s brothers have been found; his kindness toward them is explained. What the gifts Joseph bestows on his own people signify. 668

**Chapter XIV.**—Israel sacrifices at the Well of the Oath. God consoles him with promises. Seventy-five persons enter Egypt, and finally Israel calls his sons to himself: the mysteries contained in all these events. 670

Introduction to the book on the blessings of the patriarchs. 671

# ONE BOOK ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE PATRIARCHS

**Chapter One.**—Why God placed such power in these blessings. Joseph hastened to receive his father’s blessing and also brought his sons to their father to be blessed; the mysteries contained in these events. 673

**Chapter II.**—On the blessing of Reuben, the firstborn, which is not so much a blessing as a prophecy. 675

**Chapter III.**—What was to happen to the sons of Simeon and Levi is foretold; the Jewish opinion concerning the mystical interpretation of this blessing is also refuted. 676

**Chapter IV.**—On Judah’s blessing, which is applied to Christ. 678

**Chapter V.**—The blessing of Zebulun designates the Church and its leaders. 682

**Chapter VI.**—On Issachar’s blessing, which is mystically explained of Christ the Lord. 683

**Chapter VII.**—On Dan’s blessing, which foretells that the Antichrist will arise from that tribe. 684

**Chapter VIII.**—On Gad’s blessing. 685

**Chapter IX.**—On Asher’s blessing. 686

**Chapter X.**—On Naphtali’s blessing. 687

**Chapter XI.**—Jacob took longer in blessing Joseph because he saw mysteries prefigured in him. 688

**Chapter XII.**—On Benjamin’s blessing. 692

Introduction to the book on Elijah and fasting. 693

# ONE BOOK ON ELIJAH AND FASTING

**Chapter One.**—Just as the fathers blew the trumpet on new-moon days and days of rejoicing or battle, so we too must blow the trumpet on the days of fasting and at the Paschal feast. 697 [Col. 1189]

**Chapter II.**—How great a virtue fasting is. 698

**Chapter III.**—The commendation of fasting and of the fasting of Saint John; and what kind of food we should seek. 699

**Chapter IV.**—On the origin and antiquity of fasting. 700

**Chapter V.**—Noah is excused because he became drunk through ignorance; the evils that arise from the use of wine and the good things that arise from abstaining from it. 701

**Chapter VI.**—On the law of fasting given by Moses, and on Moses’ own fasting. How abstinence made the barren mothers of Samson and Samuel fruitful. 703

**Chapter VII.**—The three youths and Daniel were saved through fasting. Ibid.

**Chapter VIII.**—The benefits of fasting. 704

**Chapter IX.**—Why the powerful are forbidden to drink wine. Various praises of fasting are enumerated. 707

**Chapter X.**—The mystical table is compared with fasting. The words, “When you fast, anoint your head,” are explained morally and mystically. 708

**Chapter XI.**—The virtue of fasting is illustrated by the example of bitter herbs, and it is shown how harmful food can be even when sweet. 710

**Chapter XII.**—On drunkenness, and on a pleasure-loving young man converted to philosophy. 711

**Chapter XIII.**—The banquets of military men are compared with a kind of battle and spectacle. 713

**Chapter XIV.**—Those who prepare banquets for drunkenness are reproved. 715

**Chapter XV.**—After explaining a passage from Isaiah, he attacks the wantonness of taverns. 716

**Chapter XVI.**—Drunkards are more miserable than the demon-possessed themselves. 717

**Chapter XVII.**—On the appeals, pledges, and drinking toasts of those who carouse. On a certain astonishing method of drinking. 719

**Chapter XVIII.**—How disgraceful and harmful women’s drunkenness is to those who witness it. How great a good sobriety is, and how great an evil intemperance. 720

**Chapter XIX.**—Destruction is announced to the pleasure-loving by Isaiah’s prophecy; the sea ought not to be troubled by merchants. In what way pleasure-seekers resemble ships. 721

**Chapter XX.**—Greater effectiveness often lies in the lowliness of words. How the assembly of the nations sang the song of the prostitute. 723

**Chapter XXI.**—For the prophets, future things are present; we are athletes and must be trained for the crown. 725

**Chapter XXII.**—Carousals must be avoided. Those not yet baptized are invited to this grace. 726

Introduction to the book on Naboth the Jezreelite. 727

# ONE BOOK ON NABOTH THE JEZREELITE

**Chapter One.**—Ambrose attacks the arrogance, greed, and folly of the rich. 731

**Chapter II.**—The richer people are in wealth, the poorer they are in its true effect. The baseness of that request, “Give me,” is examined. 732

**Chapter III.**—The rich covet what belongs to others in order to exclude other human beings. How shameful it is also to sell one’s paternal inheritance for the sake of luxury. 734

**Chapter IV.**—Why it is said that Ahab did not eat his bread. An elegant comparison between the abstinence of the rich and that of the poor. 735

**Chapter V.**—The tables of the rich are sustained by the blood and life of many poor people; here also the case of a certain father is described most beautifully, whose grief and anguish were forced upon him by a rich man who compelled him to sell his son. 736

**Chapter VI.**—How little effective wealth is, and why it is called “riches.” The Gospel passage, “What shall I do? I will destroy my barns,” etc., is examined. 738

**Chapter VII.**—He shows that, when they ought to do good with their possessions, the greedy prefer to spend their money on building. 740

**Chapter VIII.**—How ineptly the rich excuse themselves from giving alms. 742

**Chapter IX.**—How Jezebel, who is greed, promises the rich the possession they desire contrary to justice. 743

**Chapter X.**—When the rich cannot seize what belongs to others, they are so distressed that they cannot take food. What makes fasting or prayers acceptable to God. 744

**Chapter XI.**—Why prostitutes are said to wash themselves in Ahab’s blood. On Jezebel’s punishment. 745

**Chapter XII.**—How humbled King Ahab was before Elijah, and how the sinner is always exposed. 746

**Chapter XIII.**—The rich foolishly boast of their lineage: gold is a wood of offense. 747

**Chapter XIV.**—He proposes various arguments by which the rich are induced to purchase freedom and salvation with gold. 749

**Chapter XV.**—Those who do not know how to use riches are slaves to them. 751

**Chapter XVI.**—He urges the rich to confess to the Lord. 753

**Chapter XVII.**—Why Ahab, although forgiveness had been promised, was defeated and killed. 754

Introduction to the book on Tobit. 755

# ONE BOOK ON TOBIT

[Col. 1190]

**Chapter One.**—Tobit’s piety toward the dead. The duty of burial is praised. 759

**Chapter II.**—How Tobit endured blindness, took care to commit no theft, and did not demand back the money lent to Gabael until he was worn out by old age. 761

**Chapter III.**—Ambrose brings before our eyes the inhumanity of moneylenders and their practices. 762

**Chapter IV.**—How moneylenders are compared with Judah and with the devil. 763

**Chapter V.**—The moneylender’s money is compared with the sea. On the lots of the two Testaments. How many evils moneylenders produce. 765

**Chapter VI.**—How much moneylenders scheme in order to plunder unsuspecting young men. 767

**Chapter VII.**—The most wretched lot of the debtor is described. Ibid.

**Chapter VIII.**—Continuation of the same subject, and how lending at interest is a source of transgression. 769

**Chapter IX.**—The devil is the moneylender of sin. On the hundredth of interest and the hundredth sheep; and on the name “creditor,” which the true exactor assumes for himself. 770

**Chapter X.**—The story of the moneylender who forbade even the debtor’s corpse to be carried out for burial. 771

**Chapter XI.**—The moneylender’s tyranny over gamblers, and the laws governing gamblers. 772

**Chapter XII.**—On the exactions of moneylenders and the various terms they use. 774

**Chapter XIII.**—It is shown that interest is more prolific than hares and any plants, and that the greed of the moneylender surpasses every other greed. 775

**Chapter XIV.**—Interest is prohibited by divine law. A garment taken as a pledge must be returned before nightfall. 777

**Chapter XV.**—The foreigner from whom it is lawful to exact interest is only the one whom it is lawful to kill. Every kind of interest is condemned. 779

**Chapter XVI.**—According to the Gospel command, we must lend to those from whom nothing is expected, indeed even to enemies. 780

**Chapter XVII.**—An objection is answered by which some deny that the retention of a pledge is generally prohibited, restricting the Law to the pledges of the poor. 781

**Chapter XVIII.**—To satisfy those who object that the divine law incites us to lend at interest, the question is examined of what a just person—for example, Peter—may lend at interest. 782

**Chapter XIX.**—The Jews first lent at interest to the nations; later, the nations who believed in Christ repaid the favor. 784

**Chapter XX.**—After distinguishing a pledge, a loan entrusted for safekeeping, and a deposit, he shows that the pledge whose return the law commands is spiritual. The good garment is the word of God. 785

**Chapter XXI.**—Those who borrow when they are unable to repay are reproved. 789

**Chapter XXII.**—Which moneylender we ought to imitate. 791

**Chapter XXIII.**—Those who invoke the antiquity of interest are refuted. How carefully one must avoid becoming surety for another. Ibid.

**Chapter XXIV.**—How we should imitate Tobit, and what kind of lending at interest he teaches us. 793

Introduction to the four books on the Intercession of Job and David. Ibid.

# FOUR BOOKS ON THE INTERCESSION OF JOB AND DAVID

## BOOK ONE—ON THE INTERCESSION OF JOB AND THE WEAKNESS OF HUMANITY

797

**Chapter One.**—There are many disturbances in this life and many consolations, but the latter far surpass the former. David and Job interceded for our weaknesses; hence the subject of this work. Ibid.

**Chapter II.**—How blessed Job, after losing everything except his wife, did not yield to his troubles like a good athlete, nor refuse to contend. 798

**Chapter III.**—On the miserable condition of humanity, and how foolishly a person thinks that his sins can deceive God’s knowledge. 799

**Chapter IV.**—How Job’s friends increased his grief; and how magnificently Job understood divine power and the mystery of redemption. 801

**Chapter V.**—God caused the mountains to grow old—that is, he converted the letter of the Old Testament into spiritual meaning. On the shattering of the ships of Tarshish, by which our bodies are signified. Ibid.

**Chapter VI.**—Job’s words, in which he reveals human weaknesses, are examined. It is shown that forgiveness is promised to the one who confesses, and that the righteous person acknowledges his iniquities. 804

**Chapter VII.**—Of all the stages of life, adolescence is the most slippery; we shall have to give an account even of sins that we were unable to avoid. 806

**Chapter VIII.**—How blessed Job signified the resurrection and the way of the Lord that will come at the consummation; and how he longed to escape from this life. 808

**Chapter IX.**—The recesses of wisdom must not be investigated with excessive curiosity. Its knowledge is open only to God and to those to whom he has revealed it. 809

## BOOK TWO—ON THE INTERCESSION OF DAVID

811

**Chapter One.**—After Job’s more vehement intercession has been completed, David’s calmer intercession follows. He is not inappropriately compared with a deer. Ibid.

**Chapter II.**—How David longed to be released from this life, and the usefulness of tears. The delights of his court are briefly touched upon, and the Church is compared with it. 813

**Chapter III.**—It is not surprising that David was troubled by the evils of this life, even though they are by no means without consolation, since Christ himself wished to be troubled. 815

**Chapter IV.**—Christ is foreshadowed by the Jordan. Christ was a great mountain through his divinity, but a small one through his incarnation. 816

**Chapter V.**—God is the sustainer and protector of humanity, both because of creation and because of preservation. 819

**Chapter VI.**—How blessed it is to be cast upon God from the womb, and how this is applied to Christ. 820

**Chapter VII.**—While Christ’s longed-for coming is delayed, the devil raged so that he might crush those who would believe in Christ and choose his own signs among them; here the signs we ought to follow and those we ought to flee are discussed. 821

**Chapter VIII.**—David asks that his cause be distinguished from that of the wicked, but this does not apply to Christ. 824

**Chapter IX.**—The prophet’s words signify that God was reconciled to humanity through Christ’s passion. Likewise, the various ways in which we were renewed by Christ so that we might enter the house of God. 825

## BOOK THREE—ON THE INTERCESSION OF JOB

Ibid.

**Chapter One.**—Most people, even the prudent, are disturbed when they see the unjust prospering here while the righteous are afflicted; this is the subject of the following books. 827

**Chapter II.**—How Job rebuked those who reviled him; here especially his silence, as well as that of David and the Apostle, is set before us for imitation. 829

**Chapter III.**—Job is declared victor in the contest of words; and after a gentler reply, how he drove back with stronger words those who persisted in their troublesome slander. 830

**Chapter IV.**—Job blunts the arguments of his friends, who maintained that evils always occur because of sins. Who is truly blessed. Finally, it is shown that the wicked possess not eternity itself but only its false likeness. 832

**Chapter V.**—The wicked end their lives amid the goods of the world, but afterward lack heavenly rest; the opposite is what we ought to desire. The madness of the wicked. 834

## BOOK FOUR—ON THE INTERCESSION OF DAVID

837

**Chapter One.**—David often discussed the vanity of the world in the Psalms, but especially in Psalm 72, where he indicates that at first he was deeply troubled by the prosperity of the wicked and the calamities of the good, yet afterward was corrected. Ibid.

**Chapter II.**—God is good to the righteous even when he permits them to be afflicted; God is also good to the wicked. 838

**Chapter III.**—The prophet confesses that he almost fell when he envied the peace of sinners. To be chastised after death is useless, but in this life it is highly useful. 840

**Chapter IV.**—Sinners are clothed in their own iniquity. The iniquity of the Jews was great and deliberate. 841

**Chapter V.**—Those who set their mouths against heaven are those who attribute everything to the necessity imposed by the stars. The mystery of Israel’s return is explained. 842

**Chapter VI.**—When the prophet had first become despondent, he later learned that everything occurs by divine ordination. 843

**Chapter VII.**—After correcting his error, David recognizes that this one labor remains for him: to enter the recesses of divine knowledge. What the end of the saints is. 844

**Chapter VIII.**—The wicked in their destruction are aptly compared with a dream. 846

**Chapter IX.**—The prophet, refreshed by knowledge of divine providence, recognizes that he himself, and with him all human beings, are scarcely unlike beasts when compared with the heavenly citizens; nevertheless, by God’s grace they are restored to human dignity. 847

**Chapter X.**—If God is not at our right hand, that place will be occupied by the devil. Christ placed the devil at his right hand so that he might overthrow him more gloriously. Ibid.

**Chapter XI.**—David, content with possessing God, desires nothing except him; earthly things must be erased through forgetfulness so that heavenly things may take their place, and we must also approach God, who rejects no one. 848

Introduction to the Apology for the Prophet David. 849

# APOLOGY FOR THE PROPHET DAVID
# APOLOGY FOR THE PROPHET DAVID

**CHAPTER ONE.** — Why Ambrose undertakes to write an apology for David. It is shown that one whom God has justified is not to be judged; indeed, on the contrary, he is also to be praised. 851

**CHAPTER II.** — David is praised for the humility of his confession; and three reasons are given why it is useful for the saints to fall into sin, and why God permits this. [Col. 1192] 853

**CHAPTER III.** — David was exposed to temptation because God wishes His athletes to be exercised through various contests, and He wishes David to be an example for us. 855

**CHAPTER IV.** — Since no one is found immune from falling, David’s repentance is commended. 857

**CHAPTER V.** — The parable that Nathan proposed to David is explained and applied to Christ. 859

**CHAPTER VI.** — How the good and the wicked differ. By what works David covered his sin. 860

**CHAPTER VII.** — Concerning David’s battles against giants and the libation from the water of the pool of Bethlehem: from these and other indications it is concluded that his sin was concealed by him. 863

**CHAPTER VIII.** — Why Psalm 50 was placed before certain others composed concerning earlier events; and what mysteries are contained in the number fifty. 866

**CHAPTER IX.** — Few acknowledge their sins, while more boast of them; a wise man never lays aside the memory of his offense; the power of conscience. 868

**CHAPTER X.** — Although David was free from human laws, he nevertheless subjected himself to God, against whom alone he had sinned; and the various ways in which this is to be understood. Whoever denies that he is a sinner accuses God Himself of falsehood; God’s patience is commended. 871

**CHAPTER XI.** — The prophet’s words teach that no one is without being conceived in iniquity. Whether this iniquity belongs to the parents or to the offspring. 873

**CHAPTER XII.** — When one confesses sin, heavenly sacraments are disclosed by God. Since the psalm calls these things uncertain, it signifies that they are not manifest; the washing of baptism is especially prefigured in this passage. 874

**CHAPTER XIII.** — Revived by hearing only of future remission, David foretells that his humbled bones will rejoice; and what those bones are is explained. 876

**CHAPTER XIV.** — What the “inmost parts” and the “spirit” are that the holy Prophet mentions in this passage. 878

**CHAPTER XV.** — Only the rational nature is capable of saving joy. What the principal spirit is. 879

**CHAPTER XVI.** — It belongs to a skilled teacher to instruct the wicked in the ways of the Lord. How this is applied both to the person of Christ and to that of David. 880

**CHAPTER XVII.** — David signifies in his own words that his sin has been forgiven when God closes the sinner’s mouth. Some matters are proposed concerning the sacrifice of Christ and of the martyrs. 881

**Notice concerning the second apology of David.** 883

# SECOND APOLOGY FOR THE PROPHET DAVID

**CHAPTER ONE.** — Some may be offended that David fell into adultery, while Christ absolved the adulterous woman brought before Him. But it is shown that, although David could err, Christ could not err. 887

**CHAPTER II.** — Ambrose explains in what order and before what sort of people he will defend the case of the erring David. 888

**CHAPTER III.** — He warns the Gentiles not to regard David merely as one who erred, but as one who repented. 889

**CHAPTER IV.** — He rebukes the Jews who wrongly believe that David, who was subject to sin, or Solomon, to whom statements concerning Christ do not apply, is the Son of God. 893

**CHAPTER V.** — He confirms the arguments brought forward against the Jews and Gentiles and turns his discourse toward the Church. 897

**CHAPTER VI.** — Why David and many other progenitors of the Lord’s lineage were permitted to fall into error. Concerning David’s murder and adultery. 899

**CHAPTER VII.** — The mysteries veiled beneath David’s adultery with Bathsheba, as well as beneath his birth. 900

**CHAPTER VIII.** — What the royal house in which David walks about signifies; what Bathsheba’s undressing and washing signify; and what is signified by the fact that, as soon as she was seen naked, she was loved. 902

**CHAPTER IX.** — He continues the same subject in a mystical manner. 905

**CHAPTER X.** — Concerning the mystery of the Incarnation signified through David’s adultery. 907

**CHAPTER XI.** — Nathan’s parable is presented and then transferred first to the moral meaning, and shortly afterward to the allegorical meaning. 909

**CHAPTER XII.** — David confesses his sin to God by composing Psalm 50; several verses of it are explained here. 911

**Notice concerning the expositions of the twelve psalms.** 915
